The research methods of biopsychology Methods chapters get skipped and then cost marks, because most exam questions about the brain are secretly questions about how somebody could possibly know. Organise the chapter by what a method lets you conclude , which sorts it into four groups: seeing structure, measuring activity, manipulating the brain, and measuring behaviour. Only the third group licenses causal claims, and that fact is the spine of the chapter. Visualising the living human brain Plain X-rays are useless for the brain because brain tissue and the fluid around it absorb X-rays almost identically. Every technique below is a way around that problem. Contrast X-ray procedures inject a substance that absorbs X-rays differently from the surrounding tissue. In cerebral angiography a radio-opaque dye is injected into an artery, making the cerebral vasculature visible; it is used to localise vascular damage and also tumours, which distort vessels. It is fast, widely available, and good for gross lesions, bleeds and skull fractures. Computed tomography (CT) uses x-rays to create a brain scan. Areas of high activity are indicated by reds and yellows. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 5.3 Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses no X-rays. Placed in a strong magnetic field, hydrogen nuclei in the tissue align; a radio pulse knocks them out of alignment and the signal they emit as they relax back is measured. Because the signal depends on the local chemical environment, MRI resolves soft tissue with much higher spatial resolution and contrast than CT, and it can produce images in any plane. Its variant diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) measures the direction in which water diffuses, which in white matter is along the fibres, and therefore maps tracts : it is the only non-invasive way to visualise the brain's wiring in a living person. A color-enhanced midsagittal MRI scan. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 5.4 MRI of a growing tumor. The tumor is colored red. Positron emission tomography (PET) injects a radioactive labelled substance, classically 2-deoxyglucose (2-DG) , and images where it accumulates. 2-DG is taken up by active neurons as though it were glucose but cannot be metabolised, so it accumulates in proportion to activity: the resulting image is a map of glucose uptake, that is, of activity, not of structure. PET can also be used with labelled ligands to map receptor distributions, which is its enduring advantage. Its costs are the injection of radioactivity and poor temporal and spatial resolution. Functional MRI (fMRI) exploits the fact that oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin have different magnetic properties, so the scanner can detect increases in oxygenated blood flowing to active regions, the BOLD signal (blood-oxygen-level-dependent). fMRI has largely displaced PET because it requires no injection, provides both structural and functional images from the same session, has better spatial resolution, and can be analysed three-dimensionally. Its limitation is temporal: the haemodynamic response is sluggish, unfolding over seconds, whereas the neural events it reflects take milliseconds. And a conceptual caution that examiners like: fMRI measures blood flow, which is a proxy for activity, and increased activity in a region during a task does not establish that the region is necessary for the task. Functional magnetic resonance image (fMRI). This image illustrates the areas of cortex that became more active when the volunteers observed strings of letters and were required to specify which strings were words—in the control condition Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 5.7 Two more methods complete the set. Magnetoencephalography (MEG) measures the tiny magnetic fields produced by neural activity at the scalp; its temporal resolution is excellent, complementing fMRI's spatial resolution. And transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) uses a magnetic coil over the scalp to turn off, or disrupt, activity in a small area of cortex for a brief period. TMS matters out of proportion to its precision because it creates a temporary, reversible virtual lesion in a healthy human volunteer: it converts a correlational question into an experimental one, which is exactly what imaging cannot do. Typical electroencephalograms and their psychological correlates. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 5.8 The electroencephalogram (EEG) records gross electrical activity from scalp electrodes. What it captures is not individual action potentials but the summed postsynaptic potentials of large populations of similarly oriented neurons, which is why EEG is a good index of global state and a poor index of local computation. Its signatures are frequency bands: alpha waves , regular 8 to 12 Hz activity, appear in relaxed wakefulness with the eyes closed, and Chapter 14 uses the rest of the bands to stage sleep. The important trick applied to EEG is signal averaging . The response to a single stimulus is buried in background noise. But if the stimulus is presented many times and the EEG segments following each presentation are averaged, the random background noise averages toward zero while the response, which is time-locked to the stimulus, survives. The result is an event-related potential (ERP) , and its early components are the sensory evoked potentials . The best-known later component is the P300 , a positive wave about 300 ms after a stimulus that the participant finds meaningful or unexpected; because its latency tracks the time taken to categorise a stimulus rather than its physical properties, it is used as an index of cognitive processing. Note also far-field potentials : because the skull conducts, activity generated in the brain stem can be recorded at the scalp, which is how brain-stem auditory function is tested in newborns. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 5.13 Invasive physiological methods Now the methods that manipulate, used in animals, and therefore the ones that establish causes. Stereotaxic surgery is the enabling technology. A stereotaxic atlas gives the three-dimensional coordinates of every structure relative to a fixed reference point on the skull, conventionally bregma , the junction of the skull sutures. A stereotaxic instrument has a head holder that fixes the skull in the standard orientation and a micromanipulator that carries an electrode or cannula to the specified coordinates. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 5.15 Lesion methods destroy tissue and then ask what behaviour is lost. Aspiration uses a fine pipette to draw off tissue on the surface. Radio-frequency lesions pass high-frequency current through an electrode to destroy tissue with heat, and their size and shape are determined by the current and the electrode tip. Knife cuts sever connections rather than removing a structure, which distinguishes a structure's function from that of its pathway. Cryogenic blockade is the important one conceptually: cooling tissue enough to stop neurons firing, but not enough to kill them, so the block is reversible and each animal can serve as its own control. A device for performing subcortical knife cuts. The device is stereotaxically positioned in the brain; then the blade swings out to make the cut. Here, the anterior commissure is being sectioned. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 5.16 Two interpretive cautions carry heavy weight. First, most brain structures are bilateral, and a unilateral lesion typically produces much milder effects than a bilateral one because the intact side compensates, so a study that lesions one side and finds nothing has not shown the structure is unimportant. Second, and this is the classic criticism of the whole method, a lesion inevitably damages fibres of passage , axons merely travelling through the region on their way elsewhere. A deficit after a lesion may therefore be caused by disconnecting two other structures rather than by removing the target's own function. This is precisely why converging operations matter. Electrical stimulation is the complement to lesioning: it typically has the opposite effect and often elicits a whole behavioural sequence, such as eating or attack, which is strong evidence that a coordinated program is being triggered rather than a muscle being twitched. Invasive recording comes in four grains. Intracellular unit recording puts the electrode inside a single neuron and gives the moment-to-moment membrane potential, the method behind Chapter 4. Extracellular unit recording places the tip beside a neuron and records the timing of its action potentials but not the graded potential; its practical problem is that a moving animal displaces the electrode, solved by implanting fine wires that move with the tissue. Multiple-unit recording uses a larger tip to pick up many neurons at once and reports the summed rate. Invasive EEG uses implanted electrodes for gross signals, either cortical or deep. The four ways of recording electrical activity, from one neuron to the whole scalp. Selective neurotoxins refine lesioning by killing only one kind of cell: 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) is taken up by catecholaminergic neurons and destroys them selectively, and kainic acid and similar excitotoxins destroy cell bodies while sparing fibres of passage, which directly addresses the interpretive problem above. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 5.18 Several techniques label chemicals in tissue. Autoradiography exposes a slice to photographic emulsion to reveal where a radioactive ligand bound, mapping receptors. The 2-DG technique is the autoradiographic version of the PET logic, giving a high-resolution activity map. Immunocytochemistry uses labelled antibodies to a specific protein to show where that protein is, and is used to locate transmitters, enzymes and receptors. In situ hybridisation uses a labelled complementary strand of nucleic acid to show where a particular mRNA is, that is, where a gene is being expressed . Cerebral dialysis is the one method that measures transmitter release in a behaving animal: a fine tube with a semipermeable section is implanted, fluid is perfused through it, and the transmitter that diffuses in is collected and assayed, so you get a chemical time-course alongside behaviour. Immunocytochemistry. This section through a rat’s pons reveals noradrenergic neurons that have attracted the antibody for dopamine-beta-hydroxylase, the enzyme that converts dopamine to norepinephrine. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 5.19 The genetic methods are the newest layer. Gene knockout animals have a target gene inactivated, so you can ask what a single protein contributes; the standing caution is that development compensates, so a knockout tells you about an animal built without the gene, not about the gene's normal moment-to-moment role. Gene knock-in inserts a gene, often a human one, to model a disorder. Antisense oligonucleotides bind a target mRNA and block its translation, giving a temporary and dose-controlled knockdown. Green fluorescent protein (GFP) , borrowed from a jellyfish, is expressed alongside a gene of interest so that the cells expressing it glow and can be traced in living tissue. Optogenetics is the transformative one: a light-sensitive ion channel such as channelrhodopsin is expressed in one genetically specified population of neurons, and a pulse of light then switches exactly that population on (or, with a different opsin, off) within milliseconds, in a behaving animal. It combines the causal power of stimulation with cell-type specificity and millisecond timing, which no earlier method had together. CRISPR gene-editing extends the same logic to precise sequence changes. Touch receptor neurons of the transparent Caenorhabditis elegans labeled by green fluorescent protein. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 5.21 Behavioural research methods The measurement of behaviour is not the soft end of the chapter; a study is only as good as its behavioural measure. A paradigm is a standard set of procedures for investigating a phenomenon, and the reason paradigms matter is comparability: results across laboratories are only combinable if the behaviour was elicited the same way. Human neuropsychological testing has passed through three approaches, and the sequence is examinable. The single-test approach looked for one test that would detect brain damage, and failed, because damage is not one thing. The standardised-test-battery approach administers a fixed battery to everyone, the Halstead-Reitan and Luria-Nebraska batteries being the standard examples; this reliably detects whether there is damage but is weak at specifying what is wrong. The customised-test-battery approach is the modern one and works in two phases: a common battery of general tests is given to everyone to identify the general area of difficulty, and then a second set of tests is selected specifically to characterise that difficulty in detail. The customised approach depends on theory, since you can only design a follow-up test if you have a model of the function. In practice the common first phase usually begins with an intelligence test such as the WAIS , used not for the IQ score but because the pattern of subtest scores flags where to look next. Individual tests worth naming: digit span for short-term verbal memory (the usual span is around seven digits), the token test for language comprehension, and the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test for frontal-lobe function, where the participant must infer a sorting rule that then changes without warning, and the diagnostic error is perseveration , continuing to use a rule that has stopped working. Memory testing must separate explicit memory (conscious recollection, which the patient can report) from implicit memory (memory expressed through improved performance without recollection), because amnesic patients characteristically lose the first and keep the second. The standard demonstration is repetition priming : shown a list of words and later given fragments to complete, amnesic patients complete the previously seen words at above-chance rates while denying having seen the list. Animal behavioural paradigms come in families. For species-typical behaviour : the open-field test measures activity and fearfulness in a large empty enclosure, with fearful animals showing thigmotaxis (staying near the walls) and more defecation; the elevated plus maze pits exploration against the aversiveness of open exposed arms and is a standard anxiety assay; and the colony-intruder paradigm elicits naturalistic aggression and defence. For learning : Pavlovian conditioning , operant conditioning in a Skinner box, conditioned taste aversion (a single pairing of a novel flavour with illness produces long-lasting avoidance, a demonstration that learning is not equipotential across stimuli), self-stimulation of reward sites, and conditioned defensive burying . For spatial memory specifically, the two workhorses are the Morris water maze , where an animal must learn the location of a hidden platform in opaque water using only distal cues, and the radial arm maze , where food is placed at the ends of arms radiating from a centre and efficient performance requires remembering which arms have already been visited. Both reappear in Chapter 11, because both are exquisitely sensitive to hippocampal damage. A radial arm maze. Ask what each method could add. The fMRI shows correlation only, and the activation might reflect a related process such as attention to landmarks. TMS over the region during navigation would test necessity in humans, though depth is a problem for the hippocampus. Human patients with selective hippocampal damage (neuropsychology) failing a comparable navigation task would strengthen it considerably. Bilateral hippocampal lesions impairing Morris water maze performance in rats would establish necessity causally, though unilateral lesions would be expected to show little, and excitotoxic lesions with kainic acid rather than aspiration would rule out fibres of passage. Optogenetic silencing of hippocampal cells only during the retrieval phase would establish the specific stage at which the structure is required. The claim is credible in proportion to how many of these agree, which is Chapter 1's converging operations turned into a research plan. 6. The visual system Vision is the model system of sensory neuroscience: it is the sense we know most about, and Pinel uses it to teach a general lesson about how brains work. The lesson is that perception is not transmission. The visual system does not deliver a picture to the cortex; it takes a spatially and temporally structured pattern of light, throws most of it away, extracts a small number of specific features, and constructs a representation that is useful. Almost every counter-intuitive fact in the chapter follows from that. Light, and the two properties that matter Light can be described as waves, and two properties of the wave correspond to two properties of experience. Wavelength relates to perceived hue (the visible range being roughly 380 to 760 nanometres) and intensity relates to perceived brightness . The word "relates" is doing real work: the correspondence is not one-to-one, because what you see also depends on the surrounding light and on your own history, which is the point of colour constancy later. The fortification illusions associated with migraine headaches. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.1 The electromagnetic spectrum and the colors that had been associated with wavelengths visible to humans. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.2 The eye's optics contribute two adjustments. The pupil sets the trade-off between sensitivity and acuity: constricted, it admits less light but gives a sharper image with greater depth of focus; dilated, it admits more light at the cost of sharpness. So in bright light the system takes the sharp option and in dim light it sacrifices sharpness for sensitivity. And accommodation is the adjustment of the lens 's shape by the ciliary muscles to focus near or far objects on the retina: for near objects the lens is allowed to become fatter and more powerful. The human eye. Light enters the eye through the pupil, whose size is regulated by the iris. The iris gives the eye its characteristic color—blue, brown, or other. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.3 The eyes also converge, and because they are set apart in the head each receives a slightly different image, a difference called binocular disparity . Disparity is greater for near objects than far ones, and the visual system uses it to construct three-dimensional depth. This is a good early example of the chapter's theme: depth is not in the image, it is computed from the relation between two images. The human eye, a product of approximately 600 million years of evolution. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.4 The retina, and its counter-intuitive design The retina has five layers of cells, and the transmission chain runs: receptors (rods and cones) to bipolar cells to retinal ganglion cells , whose axons form the optic nerve. Two further cell types run laterally rather than vertically: horizontal cells connect receptors to each other and amacrine cells connect bipolars and ganglion cells to each other. The lateral cells are the reason the retina computes rather than merely relays; they mediate the inhibition described below. The cellular structure of the retina. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.5 The design has a striking oddity: the retina is built inside-out . Light must pass through the ganglion cells and bipolar cells before reaching the receptors, which are at the back. This creates two problems, and the solutions to both are instructive. A section of the retina. The fovea is the indentation at the center of the retina; it is specialized for high-acuity vision. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.6 The first problem is that the axons must leave the eye, and they do so through a hole, the optic disc , which is therefore a blind spot with no receptors. You never notice it. The visual system fills it in by completion , using the surrounding information to construct what is presumably there. Completion is the strongest everyday evidence that what you see is a construction: the blind spot is not experienced as a gap because the brain does not represent gaps, it represents its best guess. Cones and rods. The red colored cells are cones; the blue colored cells are rods. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.7 The second problem is that overlying cells blur the image. The solution is local: at the fovea , the high-acuity centre of the retina, the overlying layers are thinned and pushed aside, forming an indentation. The system accepts blur across most of the retina and buys sharpness at the one place that is pointed at whatever you are attending to. Which is why you must move your eyes to inspect anything. The figure illustrates the number of cones and rods per square millimeter as a function of distance from the center of the fovea. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.9 The single idea that generates the whole table is convergence . When many receptors funnel into one ganglion cell, their weak individual signals sum, so very little light is needed to make that ganglion cell respond: high sensitivity. But the cell can no longer tell which of its many receptors was stimulated, so spatial detail is lost: low acuity. When one cone drives one ganglion cell, the reverse holds. Sensitivity and acuity are not two independent design goals; they are the two ends of one trade-off, and having two systems is how the retina gets both, at different times of day and in different parts of the visual field. Two consequences worth knowing. Dark adaptation follows a two-part curve, with a fast cone component and a slower, much larger rod component that continues for twenty to thirty minutes, which is simply the two systems adapting at their own rates. And the Purkinje effect : because the rod and cone systems have different spectral sensitivity curves , with rods most sensitive at shorter wavelengths than cones, a red flower and a blue flower that look equally bright in daylight will look very different at dusk, the blue appearing relatively brighter as vision shifts from cones to rods. Human photopic (cone) and scotopic (rod) spectral sensitivity curves. The peak of each curve has been arbitrarily set at 100 percent. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.11 Trap To see a very faint star, look slightly beside it. The fovea is all cones and has almost no rods, so it is the least sensitive part of the retina in dim light. This also means acuity in the dark is genuinely poor, not just subjectively vague. And note that rods are not "worse" receptors: they are the ones that let you see at all at night. From eye to cortex: the retina-geniculate-striate pathway About 90 per cent of retinal ganglion axons take this route: retina to the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus, then to primary visual cortex , also called striate cortex or V1, in the posterior occipital lobe. The pathway has three properties to hold on to. The retina-geniculate-striate pathway. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.13 It is retinotopic : neighbouring points on the retina project to neighbouring points in the LGN and in the cortex, so the cortex contains a map of the retina. The map is heavily distorted, with a disproportionate area given to the fovea, which is the cortical expression of the same acuity priority. It is contralateral by visual field, not by eye. This distinction is the most-tested point in the chapter. At the optic chiasm the fibres from the medial (nasal) half of each retina cross and those from the lateral (temporal) half do not. Because the lens inverts the image, the left half of the visual field falls on the right half of each retina. The result is that all information from the left visual field , from both eyes, ends up in the right hemisphere, and vice versa. So cutting one optic nerve blinds one eye, but a lesion behind the chiasm produces a loss of one visual field in both eyes. The perimetric maps of a man with a bullet wound in his left primary visual cortex. The scotomas (areas of blindness) are indicated in purple. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.21 It is parallel . Two channels run side by side from the start. The P (parvocellular) channel, which receives mostly from cones, is sensitive to colour, fine detail and stationary or slowly moving stimuli. The M (magnocellular) channel, receiving mostly from rods, is colour-blind and specialised for movement and rapid change. They terminate in different layers of the six-layered LGN, and this early split is the ancestor of the two cortical streams at the end of the chapter. Receptive fields: what a visual neuron is actually for The receptive field of a visual neuron is the area of the retina within which light influences its firing. The great research programme here belongs to David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel , who won the 1981 Nobel Prize for it, and their method was simple in principle: record from one cell, move a spot or bar of light around the visual field, and find out what makes the cell fire. At the level of retinal ganglion cells and LGN cells, receptive fields are small, circular and centre-surround : they have a centre and a doughnut-shaped surround that have opposite effects. An on-centre cell is excited by light in the centre and inhibited by light in the surround; an off-centre cell does the reverse. The functional consequence is the important part. Such a cell responds weakly to uniform illumination across its whole field, because centre and surround cancel, and strongly to a difference between centre and surround. In other words, these cells do not report brightness, they report contrast . The retina is throwing away information about absolute light level, which is largely irrelevant, and keeping information about edges, which is where objects are. The mechanism is lateral inhibition , implemented by the horizontal and amacrine cells: an active receptor inhibits its neighbours. Lateral inhibition also produces contrast enhancement , the perceptual exaggeration of edges, whose classic demonstration is Mach bands , the illusory bright and dark stripes seen at the boundaries between adjacent grey strips of uniform shade. The stripes are not in the stimulus; they are in the computation. Pinel's point is that this is not a flaw. Edges are what matter for identifying objects, and the visual system deliberately exaggerates them. The illusory bands visible in this figure are often called Mach bands, although Mach used a different figure to generate them in his studies (see Eagleman, 2001). Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.14 In V1, Hubel and Wiesel found two further classes, and the progression is a progression in abstraction . Simple cells have rectangular rather than circular receptive fields with excitatory and inhibitory regions side by side. They respond to a bar or edge of a particular orientation at a particular location . They are still position-specific. Complex cells respond to a bar of a particular orientation anywhere within a larger receptive field, and many respond best when it moves in one direction. They have abstracted away from position: the cell now signals "a vertical edge is present" rather than "light is at this spot". Many complex cells are also binocular , responding to input from either eye, and typically respond best to slightly different retinal positions in the two eyes, which is the cellular basis of binocular disparity and hence depth. The receptive fields of an on-center cell and an off-center cell. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.15 The responses of an on-center cell to contrast. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.16 V1 is also organised in columns running through its depth. All neurons in one column share a preferred orientation ( orientation columns ), and adjacent columns alternate in which eye drives them more strongly ( ocular dominance columns ). Combine the columnar organisation with the retinotopic map and V1 turns out to be a bank of local edge-detectors, replicated for every orientation and every eye at every point in the visual field. High-yield David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel (Nobel 1981): centre-surround fields in retina and LGN, simple cells (orientation plus location) and complex cells (orientation, position-invariant, often direction-selective and binocular) in V1, plus orientation and ocular dominance columns. Lateral inhibition gives contrast enhancement, demonstrated by Mach bands. Centre-surround cells report contrast, not brightness. Examples of receptive fields of simple striate cells. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.17 Deprivation, and the critical period David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel's second great contribution was developmental. If one eye of a kitten is deprived of patterned vision during the first months of life, the cortical territory driven by that eye shrinks dramatically and few cortical cells respond to it afterwards, while the territory driven by the open eye expands. The deprived eye is not damaged; the cortex has been rewired. Two controls make the result precise. Depriving both eyes produces far less severe cortical reorganisation than depriving one, which shows that the mechanism is competition between the two eyes' inputs rather than simple disuse. And the effect only occurs if the deprivation falls within an early critical period ; the same deprivation in an adult leaves ocular dominance largely intact. This is the origin of the clinical practice of treating childhood cataract and strabismus early, and it is the sharpest single demonstration in the book that experience physically shapes neural circuitry within a bounded developmental window. Chapter 9 generalises it. Colour vision: two theories, both correct, at different levels Two historical theories competed, and the resolution is the interesting part. Component (trichromatic) theory , from Thomas Young and developed by Hermann von Helmholtz , proposed three kinds of receptor with different spectral sensitivities, with colour coded by the ratio of activity in the three. Its strongest support is behavioural: any colour can be matched by mixing three suitably chosen wavelengths, which is exactly what a three-receptor system predicts. Opponent-process theory , from Ewald Hering , proposed instead two chromatic classes of cell each signalling opposite colours in opposite directions (red versus green, blue versus yellow) plus one achromatic black-versus-white class. Its strongest support is phenomenological: you never see a reddish green or a bluish yellow, and the complementary afterimage of staring at red is green, both of which follow if the pairs are opposed in a single channel. The absorption spectra of the three classes of cones. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.18 The resolution, and this is the examinable point, is that both are true at different levels of the system. The receptors are trichromatic, three cone types with different peak sensitivities, as Young and Helmholtz said. The cells downstream , in the retina and LGN, are opponent: they are excited by one range of wavelengths in the centre of their field and inhibited by another, as Hering said. The opponent organisation is built out of trichromatic input. A hundred-year argument dissolved because the two sides were describing different stages. Colour is then not determined by wavelength alone. Colour constancy is the fact that an object's perceived colour stays roughly the same under very different illuminations, even though the wavelengths reflected into the eye change substantially: a white shirt looks white indoors under yellow light and outdoors in blue shade. Edwin Land 's retinex theory accounts for it by proposing that the system compares the light reflected from an object with the light reflected from its surroundings across the three cone types, so what is computed is a relative reflectance, which is a property of the object rather than of the illumination. Constancy, once again, is a construction, and it is the useful thing to construct because it is the object and not the lighting that you need to recognise. The method of Land’s (1977) color-vision experiments. Participants viewed Mondrians illuminated by various proportions of three different wavelengths: a short wavelength, a middle wavelength, and a long wavelength. The flow is largely from primary to secondary to association, but with substantial feedback in the reverse direction, which is why perception is influenced by expectation. The visual areas of the human cerebral cortex. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.20 Beyond the secondary areas the pathway divides into two functional streams, and the division goes back to the P and M channels of the LGN. The completion of a migraine-induced scotoma, as described by Karl Lashley (1941). Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.22 The dorsal stream runs from V1 into the parietal lobe. It is fed heavily by the M channel and handles spatial location and the visual guidance of action. It was originally labelled the where stream and is now more often called the how stream, because its function seems to be less about knowing where things are than about controlling movements toward them. The ventral stream runs from V1 into the temporal lobe. It is fed heavily by the P channel and handles the identification of objects: the what stream. Some of the visual areas that have been identified in the human brain. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.23 The evidence that convinced people is a double dissociation between two kinds of patient. Patients with visual agnosia from ventral-stream damage cannot identify or describe an object, and cannot report the orientation of a slot, yet can reach out and post a card through that same slot with an accurately oriented, well-formed grasp. Patients with optic ataxia from dorsal-stream damage show the mirror pattern: they can describe and identify the object perfectly well but cannot guide the hand to it accurately. Conscious visual identification and visually guided action are handled by different systems, and each can be lost while the other is intact. Pinel notes the further implication that the dorsal stream's contribution is largely unconscious. Information about particular aspects of a visual display flow out of the primary visual cortex over many pathways. The pathways can be grouped into two general streams: dorsal and ventral. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.24 The “where” versus “what” and the “control of behavior” versus “conscious perception” theories make different predictions. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.25 Damage to specific ventral areas produces specific losses: prosopagnosia is a selective inability to recognise faces , with object recognition relatively spared and, tellingly, with the patient still showing physiological signs of recognising familiar faces they cannot consciously identify. Akinetopsia , from damage to the motion area, is a deficiency in seeing movement : the world is perceived as a series of static snapshots. And a lesion of V1 produces a scotoma , an area of blindness in the corresponding part of the visual field, which patients often do not notice because of completion. Some such patients show blindsight : an ability to respond to visual stimuli in the scotoma, for example by pointing at them or correctly guessing their orientation, while denying seeing anything at all. The usual explanation is that the residual ten per cent of retinal projections that bypass the geniculostriate route, going to structures such as the superior colliculi, can support responses without supporting conscious vision. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 6.26 Worked example A patient reports normal vision but keeps bumping into things on the left and does not notice food on the left of the plate; on testing, the left visual field is lost in both eyes. Where is the lesion, and why is it not in the eye? Loss confined to one eye means the damage is at or in front of the optic nerve; loss of the same visual field in both eyes means the damage is behind the chiasm, where fibres have been regrouped by field rather than by eye. Left field loss in both eyes therefore means a right-sided lesion of the optic tract, LGN, or striate cortex. Now the second half of the question: why does the patient say vision is normal? Because there is no experience of a gap. The blind region is filled by completion, the same mechanism that hides the blind spot in every healthy eye, so a scotoma is characteristically detected by testing rather than by complaint. If the patient can also point above chance to lights presented in the blind field while insisting they see nothing, you have blindsight, and the inference is that the surviving retinal projections to the superior colliculi are doing the work. 7. Mechanisms of perception: hearing, touch, smell, taste and attention Having built vision in detail, Pinel uses the remaining senses to establish that the same three organising principles hold everywhere, and then adds attention as the mechanism that decides which of all this incoming material gets processed properly. Three principles that hold in every sensory system Hierarchical organisation. Sensory systems are arranged in levels of increasing complexity and specificity: receptors, then thalamic relay, then primary sensory cortex, then secondary areas, then association cortex. Two things follow, and they are worth stating as a general rule because the exam uses them. First, damage low in a hierarchy produces a simple and total loss (destroy the cochlea and there is no hearing at all), whereas damage high in a hierarchy produces a specific and often bizarre loss with basic function preserved (the patient hears perfectly but cannot recognise what the sound is). Second, higher levels are where perception rather than sensation happens: sensation is the detection of a stimulus, perception is the higher-order process of integrating and interpreting it. Two models of sensory system organization: The former model was hierarchical, functionally homogeneous, and serial; the current model, which is more consistent with the evidence, is hierarchical, functionally segregated, and parallel. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.1 Functional segregation. Each level, and especially each cortical level, is not homogeneous. It is divided into areas with different specialised functions. This replaced the older assumption that primary, secondary and association cortex each did one thing in a more elaborate way. Parallel processing. Information flows through multiple pathways simultaneously rather than in a single series. Some of these parallel channels support conscious perception and some support unconscious response, which is exactly the dorsal-versus-ventral lesson of Chapter 6 restated. Putting the three together yields the picture Pinel calls the current model of sensory system organisation, and it creates a genuine puzzle: if the system tears the input apart into separately processed features in separately located areas, how does experience come back together as one unified object? That is the binding problem , and it is unsolved. Note that the perception feels unified even though nothing in the anatomy obviously reassembles it. Audition: from air pressure to pitch Sound is vibration of molecules, and three physical dimensions map onto three perceptual ones: frequency in hertz maps onto perceived pitch , amplitude onto loudness , and complexity onto timbre . Almost all real sounds are complex, that is, mixtures of many frequencies, and the auditory system's basic analytic operation is to break a complex sound down into the pure frequencies composing it, a decomposition mathematically equivalent to Fourier analysis . The relation between the physical and perceptual dimensions of sound. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.2 The breaking down of a sound—in this case, the sound of a clarinet—into its component sine waves by Fourier analysis. When added together, the component sine waves produce the complex sound wave. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.3 Trace the path mechanically. Sound is collected by the external ear, the pinna , and travels down the auditory canal to the tympanic membrane (eardrum), which vibrates. The vibration is transferred through the middle ear by the three smallest bones in the body, the ossicles : malleus (hammer), incus (anvil) and stapes (stirrup). The stapes presses on the oval window , a membrane on the cochlea . The ossicles exist to solve an impedance problem: they concentrate the force from the large eardrum onto the much smaller oval window, which is necessary because the cochlea is fluid-filled and fluid is far harder to move than air. Anatomy of the ear. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.4 Inside the coiled cochlea, the pressure wave travels through fluid and displaces the basilar membrane , on which sits the organ of Corti carrying the receptors, the hair cells . Above them is the tectorial membrane . When the basilar membrane is deflected, the hair cells' cilia are bent against the tectorial membrane, and that mechanical bending opens ion channels, which is the transduction step: mechanical energy becomes neural signal. The round window , an elastic membrane at the other end, exists to let the incompressible fluid move at all. How is frequency coded? By two mechanisms, divided by frequency range. Georg von Békésy (Nobel 1961) showed that the basilar membrane's stiffness varies along its length, so a travelling wave peaks at a different place for each frequency: high frequencies displace the base, near the oval window, and low frequencies displace the apex. Different hair cells are therefore maximally activated by different frequencies, which is place coding , and it accounts for high frequencies. Low frequencies, below about 500 Hz, are coded instead by rate : the whole membrane fires in synchrony with the sound wave's cycles, so the firing rate is the frequency. The two mechanisms overlap in the middle of the range. The ascending pathway is more tangled than vision's, with signals from each ear reaching both hemispheres. In outline: hair cells to the cochlear nuclei of the medulla, then to the superior olivary nuclei (the first point where input from the two ears converges, which is what makes it the site of sound localisation), then up the lateral lemniscus to the inferior colliculi of the midbrain tectum, then to the medial geniculate nuclei of the thalamus, then to primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe. Primary auditory cortex is tonotopic : it contains an orderly map of frequency, the direct analogue of vision's retinotopy. Around it are secondary areas arranged as a core , a surrounding belt and an outer parabelt , and beyond them the same two-stream logic appears again: an anterior auditory stream concerned with identifying sound and a posterior stream concerned with locating it. Some of the pathways of the auditory system that lead from one ear to the cortex. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.5 General location of the primary auditory cortex and areas of secondary auditory cortex. Most auditory cortex is hidden from view in the lateral fissure. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.6 The hypothesized anterior and posterior auditory pathways. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.7 Sound localisation uses two cues, and which one is used depends on frequency, in a way that is elegant once you see why. For low-frequency sounds the system uses the interaural time difference : the wave arrives at the nearer ear slightly earlier, and low-frequency waves are long enough that this phase difference is unambiguous. For high-frequency sounds it uses the interaural intensity difference : the head casts an acoustic shadow, so the far ear receives a quieter signal, and this works only at high frequencies because only short waves are effectively blocked by the head. Notice that a sound directly in front produces neither cue, which is why you tilt or turn your head to localise. Adjacent to the cochlea, sharing the same fluid system, is the vestibular system : three semicircular canals in three planes detecting angular acceleration of the head, plus the otolith organs detecting linear acceleration and static head position. It supplies the sense of balance and of the body's orientation in space. Clinically, hearing loss splits into two kinds with different treatments. Conductive deafness is a failure of the mechanical apparatus, typically the ossicles or eardrum, and can often be helped by amplification or surgery. Sensorineural deafness is damage to the cochlea's hair cells or to the auditory nerve; amplification does not help, because the transducer is gone, and the solution is a cochlear implant , which bypasses the hair cells entirely by converting sound into electrical stimulation delivered along the cochlea at positions chosen to exploit its tonotopic map. Superior olives = first binaural convergence, hence localisation. Medial geniculate = auditory thalamic relay. Primary auditory cortex is tonotopic. Interaural time difference for low frequencies, interaural intensity difference for high. Conductive versus sensorineural deafness, cochlear implant for the latter. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.8 The somatosensory system: touch, and the two ascending routes Somatosensation is three systems, not one: exteroceptive (stimuli applied to the skin), proprioceptive (position of the body, from receptors in muscles, tendons and joints), and interoceptive (conditions inside the body). The exteroceptive system further divides by what it senses, and the receptors differ. Mechanical stimuli are detected by encapsulated mechanoreceptors , of which four matter: Pacinian corpuscles , the largest and most deeply located, which adapt fast and therefore respond to vibration and sudden changes rather than steady pressure; Merkel's disks and Ruffini endings , which adapt slowly and therefore signal sustained pressure and skin stretch; and Meissner's corpuscles , which respond to light touch and low-frequency vibration. Pain and temperature are detected not by encapsulated receptors but by free nerve endings . The general principle to extract is adaptation : fast-adapting receptors report change, slow-adapting receptors report state, and the nervous system generally cares more about change, which is why you stop feeling your clothes. Four cutaneous receptors that occur in human skin. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.9 The body surface is divided into dermatomes , each the area of skin whose sensory input enters by one dorsal root, which is what allows a spinal lesion to be localised by the level at which sensation is lost. From the cord, two quite separate pathways ascend, and this pair is the most reliably examined fact in the chapter. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.10 The anterolateral system. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.11 The clinical pay-off is a distinctive dissociation. A lesion on one side of the spinal cord produces loss of touch and proprioception on the same side below the lesion, because those fibres have not yet crossed, but loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side , because those crossed on entry. A patient presenting with exactly that split pattern has told you where the damage is without any imaging. Cortically, the target is primary somatosensory cortex (S1) in the postcentral gyrus, with secondary somatosensory cortex (S2) largely below it. S1 is somatotopic , containing a map of the body known as the somatosensory homunculus , whose famous distortion is the point: the amount of cortex given to a body part is proportional not to its size but to its sensitivity, so lips, tongue and hands are enormous and the trunk and legs small. The locations of human primary somatosensory cortex (SI) and one area of secondary somatosensory cortex (SII) with the conventional portrayal of the somatosensory homunculus. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.12 Damage in the somatosensory hierarchy illustrates the hierarchical principle beautifully. Damage to S1 impairs detection: elevated thresholds, poor two-point discrimination. Damage higher up, in association cortex, produces the agnosias. Astereognosia is the inability to recognise objects by touch alone, with basic tactile sensation intact. Asomatognosia is the failure to recognise parts of one's own body , usually following right parietal damage and usually affecting the left side, which is the syndrome behind Oliver Sacks's account of the man who insisted that a leg in his bed was not his own. The most striking of these is contralateral neglect , a disturbance of the ability to respond to stimuli on the side contralateral to a lesion, most often in the right parietal lobe and therefore affecting the left. Neglect is not blindness or paralysis; it is a failure to attend . Patients eat from one side of the plate, shave one side of the face, read the right half of a page, and when asked to bisect a line place the mark well to the right of centre or copy a drawing with its left side missing. Two subtleties matter. First, the neglect can be egocentric (organised with respect to the patient's own midline, so it shifts when the patient turns) rather than fixed in the world, which shows the deficit is about a frame of reference rather than about a region of space. Second, neglected stimuli are nonetheless processed : patients who cannot report an object on the left will still show its influence on later behaviour and may recognise it in a forced-choice test. The information is arriving; conscious access is what is lost. One common induction method for the rubberhand illusion. The participant’s hand is hidden from view by a screen, and a rubber hand is placed next to their hidden hand but in clear sight. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.13 Pain, and the descending system that controls it Pain is the odd sense out for three reasons. It has no obvious single cortical representation , and cortical lesions rarely abolish it. It is adaptive in a way that is not obvious : people with congenital insensitivity to pain accumulate serious injuries and often die young, because pain is what enforces protection of the body. And it is strikingly modifiable by psychological factors , which is not true to the same extent of a wavelength or a frequency. Cortically, pain shows a division of labour. The somatosensory cortices handle the sensory and discriminative aspect (where it is, how intense), while the anterior cingulate cortex is associated with its emotional aspect, the unpleasantness. Hypnotic suggestion that alters how unpleasant a painful stimulus feels, without changing its intensity, changes anterior cingulate activity and not somatosensory activity, which is about as clean a dissociation of the two components as you could ask for. Location of the anterior cingulate cortex in the cingulate gyrus. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.14 The mechanism of modulation is a descending analgesia circuit , whose discovery began with the observation that electrical stimulation of the periaqueductal grey (PAG) produces analgesia. The circuit runs from cortex and hypothalamus to the PAG, from the PAG to the raphé nuclei of the brain stem, and from the raphé down the cord to the dorsal horns , where it inhibits the incoming pain signal at its point of entry. The PAG is rich in opioid receptors, and this explains the analgesic action of morphine, and the existence of the endorphins as the endogenous ligands: the brain has a built-in circuit for turning pain down, and opiates work by activating it. The thermal grid illusion. Pain is perceived when one’s hand is placed on a grid of metal rods that alternate between cool and warm. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.15 The conceptual ancestor of this is gate-control theory , proposed by Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall , which held that signals descending from the brain, and competing input from large touch fibres, act on a "gate" in the dorsal horn that can block or admit pain signals. The gate metaphor is dated in its details but the central claim was correct and radical at the time: pain is not a fixed read-out of tissue damage, it is a signal actively regulated by the brain. That single idea underwrites the placebo response, the analgesia of emergencies, and the rationale for rubbing an injury. When experienced as part of a ritual, normally excruciating conditions (e.g., walking on hot coals) often produce little pain. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.16 Trap Do not equate the descending analgesia circuit with gate-control theory . Gate-control (Melzack and Wall) is the theoretical proposal that pain transmission is gated in the dorsal horn. The PAG to raphé to dorsal horn projection is the physiological circuit later identified, and the endorphins are its transmitters. Also keep anterior cingulate = emotional component distinct from somatosensory cortex = sensory component . Basbaum and Fields’s (1978) model of the descending analgesia circuit. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.17 The chemical senses: smell and taste Smell and taste act together in the wild, since both evaluate what may be about to enter the body, and much of what people call taste is in fact flavour , a combination of the two, which is why food is bland with a blocked nose. Olfaction. Receptors sit in the olfactory mucosa in the upper nasal passages, and each receptor neuron expresses one of a few hundred different receptor protein types, with a given odour activating a particular combination across them. Receptors of the same type converge on the same glomerulus in the olfactory bulb , so the bulb contains an orderly chemical map. Then comes the anatomical fact that makes olfaction unique: the olfactory projection reaches the amygdala and piriform cortex of the medial temporal lobe without first passing through the thalamus, unlike every other sensory system. (There is a later thalamic route to orbitofrontal cortex.) This is the standard structural explanation offered for why smell is so directly and immediately tied to emotion and memory. A second unique feature: olfactory receptor neurons are continuously replaced throughout life, one of the few clear cases of ongoing neurogenesis in the mature nervous system. The human olfactory system. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.18 Gustation. Receptors are in taste buds on the tongue's papillae , and there are five primary tastes: sweet, sour, bitter, salty and umami (savoury, the taste of glutamate). The pathway runs by three cranial nerves (VII, IX and X) to the solitary nucleus of the medulla, then to the ventral posterior nucleus of the thalamus, then to primary gustatory cortex near the insula, with a second route to the amygdala and hypothalamus that presumably serves the motivational side. Taste receptors, taste buds, and papillae on the surface of the tongue, and a cross-section of a papilla that shows a taste bud and its taste receptors. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.19 Trap The "tongue map", with sweet at the tip and bitter at the back, is a myth that survives in popular science. All five tastes are detectable across the tongue; sensitivity varies only slightly by region. What is true and worth knowing is that olfaction skips the thalamus on its first cortical route while every other sense, taste included, relays through it. The corresponding deficits are anosmia , the inability to smell, and ageusia , the inability to taste. Anosmia is far commoner and its usual cause is mechanical: a blow to the head can shear the delicate olfactory nerve filaments where they pass through the perforated bone at the roof of the nose. The human gustatory system. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.20 Selective attention Attention is what the chapter has been building toward: the sensory systems deliver far more than can be fully processed, so something must select. Selective attention improves the perception of the stimuli it is focused on and interferes with the perception of the others, and Pinel's framing is that it does not simply filter input out, it improves the neural representation of what is selected. The location of the claustrum. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.21 Attention is controlled in two ways. Endogenous attention is top-down, directed by the person's own goals, and it is voluntary and relatively slow to shift. Exogenous attention is bottom-up, captured automatically by a property of the stimulus such as a sudden movement or a loud noise, and it is fast and involuntary. Endogenous control is associated with frontal and parietal mechanisms. Four phenomena establish how much selection matters. The cocktail-party phenomenon : in a room of overlapping conversations you follow one and are unaware of the content of the others, yet your own name spoken in an unattended conversation captures your attention, which means the unattended channels were being monitored at some level even though their content did not reach awareness. Dichotic listening , in which different messages are played to each ear, is the laboratory version. Change blindness : people fail to notice large changes to a scene when the change coincides with a brief interruption, because without attention drawn to the changing element no comparison is made. Inattentional blindness : an unexpected but perfectly visible object goes entirely unnoticed when attention is engaged elsewhere. Together these establish that conscious perception requires attention, and that a great deal of unattended processing goes on without producing any experience. The change blindness phenomenon. These two illustrations were continually alternated, with a brief (less than 0.1 second) interval between each presentation, and the subjects were asked to report any changes they noticed. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 7.22 Neurally, the effect of attending is measurable at the level of single cells: attending to a stimulus increases the firing rate of the neurons that represent it, and can effectively reshape a neuron's receptive field so that it is more sensitive to the attended location. Attention is therefore not a separate module that reads out the sensory areas; it is a modulation of the sensory areas themselves. Two clinical syndromes fit here. Contralateral neglect , described above, is best understood as a disorder of attention rather than of sensation. And simultanagnosia is an inability to attend to more than one object at a time, so that a patient can identify individual items but cannot see a scene as a whole. Worked example A patient after a stroke reports that the left arm lying beside them belongs to someone else, eats only the right half of the plate, and when copying a picture of a house draws only the right side. They insist nothing is wrong. Localise and explain, using the chapter's hierarchy principle. Basic sensation is not the problem: this is not a spinal or thalamic lesion, and the pattern is not a hemianopia, since the deficit is organised around the patient's body rather than the visual field and persists in drawing from memory. The failure to recognise one's own limb is asomatognosia, and the failure to respond to the left side is contralateral neglect: both point to right parietal association cortex , high in the hierarchy, which is why the loss is specific and strange rather than simple and total. The denial of illness (anosognosia) accompanies it for the same reason: the machinery that would represent the left side, and therefore represent that something is missing from it, is the machinery that is damaged. Predict two test findings: on line bisection the patient will mark well to the right of centre, and in a forced-choice test the neglected left-side information will influence responses above chance, because it is being processed without being consciously accessed. 8. The sensorimotor system The motor system is best understood backwards, from the intention down to the muscle, because that is the direction control flows and because the chapter's three principles are all about how a general intention gets translated into specific muscle contractions without any single structure having to specify everything. Three principles, and one that follows from practice The sensorimotor system is hierarchical. Signals flow down from association cortex, through secondary motor cortex, primary motor cortex, brain stem and spinal circuits, to the muscles. The higher levels specify what is to be achieved and the lower levels work out how . The immediate benefit of such an arrangement is that the higher levels are freed from detail: the instruction "pick up the cup" does not have to include a list of muscle tensions, because lower circuits already know how to produce a reach. The sensorimotor system as a hierarchy. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 8.1 Motor output is guided by sensory input. Movement is continuously corrected using feedback, which is why the system is called sensorimotor rather than motor. Some movements are too fast for feedback to correct within their own duration; these are ballistic movements, and they must be programmed in advance, which is why they are less accurate and why practice matters more for them. Learning changes the locus and nature of control. This is the principle that makes the hierarchy dynamic. When a skill is new, control sits high in the hierarchy and each component is consciously specified; as it is practised, control is shifted down to lower levels, and the individual movements are combined into single integrated units, a process called response chunking . Learning to drive is the standard illustration: what began as a conscious sequence of separate acts becomes one act performed while thinking about something else. Note the two payoffs: the movement gets faster because lower circuits are faster, and attention is freed for other things. A fourth idea, motor equivalence , sits alongside these. The same goal can be achieved by many different combinations of muscles: you can write your signature with your dominant hand, your other hand, or your foot, and it remains recognisably your signature. This tells you that what is stored is not a sequence of muscle commands but something more abstract, a representation of the movement's goal or form , which lower levels then translate into whatever muscles are available. The top of the hierarchy: association cortex Two areas of association cortex initiate voluntary movement, and each contributes something different. Posterior parietal association cortex integrates information about the original positions of the body parts with information about the location of external objects, because you cannot reach for something without knowing both where it is and where your hand currently is. It receives visual, auditory and somatosensory input and projects to dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, to the secondary motor areas and to the frontal eye field. Damage produces deficits that follow directly from that job description: apraxia , an inability to perform a movement voluntarily on command despite having the strength and coordination to perform it spontaneously (and note that apraxia from a lesion in one hemisphere is typically bilateral in its effects, usually the left hemisphere for this purpose), and contralateral neglect , discussed in Chapter 7. The major cortical input and output pathways of the posterior parietal association cortex. Shown are the lateral surface of the left hemisphere and the medial surface of the right hemisphere. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 8.2 The major cortical input and output pathways of the dorsolateral prefrontal association cortex. Shown are the lateral surface of the left hemisphere and the medial surface of the right hemisphere. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 8.3 Dorsolateral prefrontal association cortex receives from posterior parietal cortex and projects to secondary and primary motor cortex. Its neurons fire in response to a cue that a movement should be made, before the movement begins, and their activity depends on the characteristics of the intended movement rather than on the stimulus as such. The role is therefore decision : evaluating external stimuli and selecting a course of action. Secondary motor cortex, and mirror neurons Secondary motor cortex receives from association cortex and projects to primary motor cortex. It comprises the supplementary motor area (SMA) , the premotor cortex , and the cingulate motor areas . The function is programming: these areas are involved in specifying sequences and patterns of movement rather than individual contractions, and their activity precedes movement onset. A striking finding is that supplementary motor area activity increases when a person merely imagines performing a movement, without any movement occurring, which supports the idea that these areas hold the plan rather than execute it. Three sorts of secondary motor cortex—supplementary motor area, premotor cortex, and cingulate motor areas—and their output to the primary motor cortex. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 8.4 Mirror neurons , discovered by Giacomo Rizzolatti and colleagues in monkey premotor cortex, fire both when the animal performs a particular goal-directed action and when it observes another individual performing the same action. Two features make them theoretically important rather than merely curious. They code the goal of the action rather than the specific movement, since a neuron may fire for grasping performed in different ways, and some fire even when the final part of the action is hidden from view, implying the action's completion is inferred. They have been proposed as a mechanism for understanding others' intentions and, by extension, for imitation, social cognition and possibly language evolution, though those extensions remain contested and should be flagged as such rather than asserted. Responses of a mirror neuron of a monkey. Wilder Penfield and Edwin Boldrey mapped it by electrical stimulation in conscious neurosurgical patients and described the motor homunculus , a somatotopic map with the same disproportion as the sensory one: the hands, lips and tongue occupy far more cortex than the trunk, in proportion to the fineness of control rather than to size. The motor homunculus. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 8.6 The modern refinement is important and frequently examined. The classic reading of the map was that each site controls one muscle. The better-supported view is that each site is more closely associated with a movement , or with moving a limb to a target location , than with contracting a particular muscle: stimulating one site can produce contraction of different muscles depending on the limb's current position, because the goal is fixed and the required contractions vary. This is motor equivalence appearing at the cellular level, and it means primary motor cortex is not the bottom of the hierarchy but a level that still speaks in terms of movements. Damage to primary motor cortex characteristically disrupts the ability to move body parts independently , most obviously the fine independent movements of the fingers, along with reduced speed, accuracy and force. It does not abolish movement, because the lower levels of the hierarchy remain. An electron micrograph of a motor unit: a motor neuron (pink) and the muscle fibers it innervates. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 8.7 The two modulatory structures: cerebellum and basal ganglia Neither the cerebellum nor the basal ganglia are in the main descending line; both sit in loops that modulate it, receiving from cortex and projecting back to it by way of the thalamus. The cerebellum receives a large volume of information: a copy of the motor commands descending from cortex, sensory feedback about the actual consequences, and vestibular information. That combination is a strong hint about its function, which is to compare intended with actual movement and correct the discrepancy, hence its role in accuracy, timing and motor learning. Cerebellar damage does not paralyse but produces ataxia : movements lose coordination and timing, become jerky, and are inaccurate in a way that is worse the more precision is required, along with disturbed balance and impaired adaptation to novel conditions. The basal ganglia similarly participate in loops through cortex, and are involved in the initiation and modulation of movement, in habit learning and in the response to reward. Their two signature disorders point in opposite directions and are worth pairing: Parkinson's disease , from degeneration of the dopaminergic nigrostriatal input, produces poverty of movement (akinesia, bradykinesia), rigidity and resting tremor, while Huntington's disease , from degeneration of striatal neurons, produces excessive involuntary movement (chorea). Too little activity in the loop and movement is not released; too much and it is released without being asked for. Descending pathways: four tracts in two groups Signals from cortex reach the spinal cord by four tracts, which fall into two functional groups. Learn the grouping first, because the individual tract names are only useful once the grouping makes sense of them. The two dorsolateral pathways. The dorsolateral corticospinal tract descends directly from cortex, forms the visible bulges on the ventral surface of the medulla called the pyramids , decussates (crosses) there, and continues in the contralateral dorsolateral cord. The dorsolateral corticorubrospinal tract takes an indirect route by way of the red nucleus of the midbrain tegmentum, crossing there. Both terminate in the distal parts of the contralateral limbs, and are the pathways for independent movements of the extremities, especially the fingers. The two ventromedial pathways. The ventromedial corticospinal tract descends directly and ipsilaterally, and the ventromedial cortico-brainstem-spinal tract descends indirectly through several brain-stem structures (tectum, vestibular nucleus, reticular formation, motor nuclei of the cranial nerves). Both are diffuse and bilateral in their terminations, and they control the proximal muscles of the trunk and limbs: posture, whole-body movements, walking. The evidence separating the two groups is a classic experimental dissociation, from Donald Lawrence and Hans Kuypers , who transected the pathways selectively in monkeys. Cutting the dorsolateral tracts left the animals able to stand, walk, climb and use the arm in whole-limb movements, but they could no longer move the elbow, wrist and digits independently, and could not release an object once grasped. Cutting the ventromedial tracts produced the opposite profile: posture was severely disturbed, sitting and walking were impaired, and whole-body movements were lost, while the animals retained control of individual limb and digit movements when supported. The functional division is therefore not speculative; it was demonstrated by lesion. High-yield Dorsolateral group = distal, contralateral, independent movements of digits and limbs; corticospinal branch decussates at the medullary pyramids, corticorubrospinal branch relays through the red nucleus. Ventromedial group = proximal, bilateral, posture and whole-body movement. Lawrence and Kuypers established the dissociation by selective transection in monkeys. Spinal circuits, muscles and reflexes At the bottom of the hierarchy the units become concrete. A motor unit is a single motor neuron plus all the muscle fibres it innervates, and it is the smallest unit of motor activity; a motor pool is all the motor neurons innervating one muscle. Fine control requires small motor units, which is why the muscles moving the fingers and eyes have very few fibres per neuron and the large postural muscles have hundreds. Muscles that bend a joint are flexors and those that straighten it are extensors ; muscles acting together are synergistic and those acting in opposition are antagonistic . Contraction against a load that does not move is isometric and contraction that shortens the muscle is dynamic . The biceps and triceps, which are the flexor and extensor muscles, respectively, of the elbow joint. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 8.8 Two receptor types give the cord the feedback it needs, and the distinction is exactly examinable. Muscle spindles lie parallel to the muscle fibres, embedded in intrafusal muscle , and respond to muscle length and changes in length, that is, to stretch. Golgi tendon organs lie in the tendons, in series with the muscle, and respond to tension . Because they are arranged differently they answer different questions: length versus force. The spindles have their own small motor supply, which allows the system to keep them taut and therefore sensitive even while the main muscle is shortening. The muscle-spindle feedback circuit. There are many muscle spindles in each muscle; for clarity, only one much-enlarged muscle spindle is illustrated here. The stretch reflex , of which the patellar (knee-jerk) reflex is the demonstration, is the simplest circuit in the system: a tap stretches the muscle, the spindle afferent fires, it synapses directly on the motor neuron for the same muscle, and the muscle contracts to oppose the stretch. It is monosynaptic , which is why it is fast, and its function is the maintenance of limb stability and posture without any involvement of the brain. The elicitation of a stretch reflex. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 8.13 Reciprocal innervation is the arrangement by which the same afferent signal that excites a muscle's motor neurons inhibits, through an interneuron, those of its antagonist. Its purpose is smooth, efficient movement: there is no point contracting the flexor while the extensor resists. The exception proves the rule: when stability rather than movement is wanted, the nervous system does the opposite and produces co-contraction of both, which makes the joint rigid. A final circuit, recurrent collateral inhibition , has each motor neuron send a branch to a small inhibitory interneuron (a Renshaw cell ) that inhibits that same motor neuron, distributing activity across the motor pool and preventing any one unit from being driven continuously. All but the highest levels of the system contain central sensorimotor programs , stored patterns of activity that can produce an entire sequence of movement when triggered. The higher levels do not compose movements from scratch; they select and activate programs held lower down. The Ebbinghaus illusion. Notice that the central disk on the left appears larger than the one on the right. In fact, both central disks are exactly the same size. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 8.15 The evidence is startling in its simplicity. A cat whose brain stem has been transected above the level that would allow voluntary control can still be made to walk on a treadmill, with a coordinated, adaptive gait, and even a cat with the spinal cord transected can produce stepping movements of the hind limbs. The program for walking is therefore held in the spinal cord and brain stem, not in the cortex; what the cortex does is decide to walk and where. This is the anatomical vindication of the first principle: control descends by selecting among ready-made programs, and this is also what practice does when it shifts a skill downward, since practice appears to build new programs and to move existing ones to lower, faster levels. Worked example A patient has a lesion of the dorsolateral corticospinal tract on the right side, at the level of the medulla just above the pyramids. Predict the deficit precisely. The tract decussates at the pyramids, so a lesion above the crossing affects the left side of the body. It is a dorsolateral pathway, so the deficit is distal and fractionated: the patient loses independent movement of the left fingers and cannot easily release a grasped object, and fine manipulation is lost. What is preserved, and why? Posture, sitting, standing and walking, and whole-limb movements of the left arm, because those are run by the ventromedial pathways, which are intact and in any case bilateral. Strength is reduced but movement is not abolished, because primary motor cortex is not the sole source of descending drive and the spinal programs remain. If instead the lesion had been in the left dorsolateral cord below the pyramids, the deficit would be on the same side as the lesion, since the fibres have already crossed. That single question tests the whole descending anatomy. The activity recorded by PET scans during the performance of newly learned and well-practiced sequences of finger movements.
