Development of the nervous system The developmental chapter answers a question that the anatomy chapter left hanging: how does a structure as specific as the nervous system get built from a single cell, when there is nowhere near enough information in the genome to specify each connection? The answer is that development is not a blueprint being read out. It is a sequence of simple local processes, each producing conditions for the next, with experience recruited as an active participant. Nothing in the chapter makes sense if you are imagining a plan. The five phases Neural development is conventionally divided into five phases, and they occur roughly in this order though they overlap. 1. Induction of the neural plate. Early in development a patch of tissue on the dorsal surface of the embryo becomes the neural plate , and it does so because it is induced to by chemical signals from the underlying mesoderm, specifically from a region called the organizer (the dorsal lip of the blastopore), identified in the classic transplantation experiments of Hans Spemann , who received the 1935 Nobel Prize. Transplant the organizer to a different part of a host embryo and a second nervous system develops there. The lesson is that cell fate at this stage is determined by chemical signals from neighbours , not by the cell's own inherited instructions. Plate cells are initially pluripotent , capable of becoming many cell types; as development proceeds they become progressively restricted, or multipotent , and finally committed. The plate then folds: it forms a neural groove which closes into the neural tube , whose interior becomes the ventricles and central canal, and whose anterior end swells into the three primitive divisions that become the five divisions of Chapter 3. Totipotent, pluripotent, and multipotent cells are all considered to be stem cells. However, their capacity to develop into the different cells of the body differs. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 9.1 A cross section through the ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm in a developing embryo. The neural plate develops from some of the tissue in the endoderm. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 9.2 How the neural plate becomes the neural tube, across weeks three and four. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 9.3 2. Neural proliferation. Cells in the ventricular zone , lining the tube, divide at an extraordinary rate. Proliferation is not uniform; different regions divide at different times and rates, which is what produces different structures from the same tube. 3. Migration and aggregation. New cells are not born where they will live. They migrate , and they do so in two directions: radial migration outward from the ventricular zone toward the surface, and tangential migration parallel to the surface. There are also two mechanisms of travel. In somal translocation the cell extends a process, and the cell body follows it, a flexible method that permits movement in various directions. In glia-mediated migration the cell crawls along a temporary scaffolding of radial glial cells that stretch from the ventricular zone to the outer surface, which produces the orderly inside-out layering of the cortex: each new wave of neurons migrates past the earlier arrivals to form a more superficial layer. Migration and the subsequent aggregation of cells into structures both depend on cell-adhesion molecules (CAMs) on cell surfaces, which allow cells to recognise and stick to appropriate partners. Consider what this buys you: a great deal of specific structure results from cells that follow a scaffold and stick to whatever recognises them, with no address in the genome for any of it. Radial glial cells are the stem cells in the developing nervous system. Asymmetric cell division of radial glial cells leads to the production of neurons, glia, and other cells of the nervous system. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 9.6 4. Axon growth and synapse formation. Once in place, neurons grow axons and dendrites. The tip of a growing axon is the growth cone , which extends and retracts fine processes as it feels its way. How does it find the right target, sometimes at a considerable distance? Roger Sperry 's chemoaffinity hypothesis proposed that each target releases a specific chemical label and each growing axon is attracted to its own label. His evidence is one of the great experiments of the field: he cut the optic nerve in frogs and rotated the eye 180 degrees. The axons regenerated to their original targets rather than to the targets appropriate to the new eye position, so the frog's visual world was permanently inverted and it struck at prey in the wrong direction. The axons had followed chemistry, not function or feedback. Growth cones. The cytoplasmic extensions (the filopodia) of growth cones seem to search for the correct route. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 9.7 Sperry's eye-rotation experiment, the evidence for chemoaffinity. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 9.8 Chemoaffinity in its strict form cannot be the whole story, because it would require a separate label for every connection. The modern account adds three refinements. Growth cones follow gradients of attractant and repellent molecules rather than unique labels, so a small number of chemicals can specify a topographic map (the topographic gradient hypothesis ). Pioneer growth cones travel first, and later axons follow them by adhering to their surfaces, a process called fasciculation , so only the pioneers need to navigate. And the final precision comes from activity-dependent refinement, phase five. Synapse formation, incidentally, requires the presence of astrocytes , which is one of several reasons glia are no longer regarded as passive. The regeneration of the optic nerve of the frog after portions of either the retina or the optic tectum have been destroyed. These phenomena support the topographic gradient hypothesis. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 9.9 5. Neuron death and synaptic rearrangement. This phase is counter-intuitive and it is the most important one conceptually. About half of the neurons produced die during normal development. They die by apoptosis , active programmed cell death, in which the cell executes a genetic program to dismantle itself cleanly, as opposed to necrosis , passive death from injury, which spills the cell's contents and inflames surrounding tissue. Apoptosis is safer for the neighbours, and it is the normal route. Why build twice as many neurons as you need? Because it lets the system size itself by competition rather than by specification. Neurons appear to require chemical signals, neurotrophins , supplied by the targets they successfully connect to, in order to survive; the first identified was nerve growth factor , for which Rita Levi-Montalcini and Stanley Cohen received the 1986 Nobel Prize. Neurons that make appropriate connections obtain neurotrophic support and live; those that do not, die. So the number of neurons in a structure ends up matched to the amount of target tissue available, automatically, without any count being written anywhere. Alongside the death of whole cells there is extensive synaptic rearrangement : surviving neurons retract some branches and extend others, so the pattern of connections is sharpened. The general principle, which will return in Chapter 10, is that development proceeds by overproduction followed by competitive elimination . The effect of synapse rearrangement on the selectivity of synaptic transmission. The synaptic contacts of each axon become focused on a smaller number of cells. Spemann's organizer (Nobel 1935) = induction by chemical signal from neighbours. Roger Sperry's rotated-eye experiment = chemoaffinity. Radial glia guide radial migration; CAMs mediate adhesion. About half of all neurons die, by apoptosis (programmed, clean), not necrosis (injury, inflammatory). Neurotrophins, first identified as nerve growth factor (Levi-Montalcini and Cohen, Nobel 1986), are the survival signal from the target. Postnatal development of the human brain The human brain at birth is far from finished, and what changes after birth is mostly not the number of neurons. Three processes dominate: continued myelination , which proceeds for two decades and correlates with the maturation of the functions concerned; continued growth of dendrites and their branching, which is what mainly accounts for the fourfold increase in brain volume after birth; and the two-stage course of synaptogenesis , in which synapses are massively overproduced in early childhood and then pruned back, with the pruning of prefrontal cortex continuing through adolescence into the early twenties. The maturation sequence is not uniform across the brain, and this is the fact with the most practical bite: prefrontal cortex is the last region to mature . The functions it supports, working memory, planning, inhibition of inappropriate responses, risk evaluation, therefore come online late. This is the neural basis of the well-documented adolescent profile of adult-level cognitive capacity combined with immature impulse control and risk assessment, and it is why the behavioural asymmetry is developmental rather than motivational. Experience: what it does and when Experience does not merely inform a nervous system that has already been built; it participates in building it. Pinel makes several distinctions here that reward being kept straight. Critical versus sensitive periods. A critical period is a window during which a particular experience must occur for normal development, after which the opportunity is lost. A sensitive period is a window during which the relevant experience has its greatest effect, without the door closing absolutely. Most cases turn out to be sensitive rather than strictly critical periods, so use the weaker term unless the evidence supports the stronger. Permissive versus instructive experience. In the permissive role, experience simply allows an already-specified developmental program to proceed normally; in the instructive role, experience actively shapes the course of development. The ocular-dominance work of Chapter 6 illustrates both: patterned visual input is permissive for the maintenance of normal binocular cortex, while the relative amount of input from each eye instructs how the territory is divided. Three lines of evidence establish the point. Enriched environments. In the classic work associated with Mark Rosenzweig and colleagues, rats reared in large complex environments with objects and companions, compared with rats reared in bare cages, showed thicker cortex, more dendritic branching, more synapses per neuron and better learning. The manipulation is purely environmental and the outcome is anatomical: experience changes the physical brain, measurably. Competition, not just use. The David Hubel and Wiesel monocular deprivation experiments of Chapter 6 belong here too, and their crucial control is worth repeating: depriving both eyes produces much less cortical reorganisation than depriving one, which shows that what drives the reorganisation is competition between inputs rather than mere inactivity. Whichever input is more active captures more territory. A few days of early monocular deprivation: axons from the deprived eye branch far less in layer IV. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 9.11 Deprivation in humans. Children who experience severe early deprivation, and children born with cataract or uncorrected strabismus, show lasting deficits in the functions concerned unless the deficit is corrected early. This is the clinical reason paediatric cataract is operated on urgently rather than at convenience. Neuroplasticity in the adult brain The traditional view was that the adult brain produces no new neurons. That view is wrong in at least two places. Adult neurogenesis occurs in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus and in the olfactory bulb (from receptor neurons that are continuously replaced, as in Chapter 7). The new hippocampal cells integrate into circuits, most survive only if used, and their production is increased by exercise and by enriched or complex environments and decreased by stress. The extent and function of adult neurogenesis remain actively debated, and it is fair in an answer to note that the claim is well established for these two sites and contested elsewhere. Adult neurogenesis. Autism spectrum disorder is defined behaviourally by reduced capacity for social interaction and communication together with restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour and interests, with onset in early development and enormous variation in severity, which is why it is described as a spectrum. Three points to hold. It is often accompanied by intellectual disability, but a minority of individuals show savant abilities, isolated skills at an extraordinary level, which is theoretically important because it shows the condition is not a uniform reduction of ability. Its causes are heterogeneous: heritability is substantial, many different genes have been implicated, no single gene or environmental factor accounts for more than a small proportion of cases, and the widely publicised vaccine hypothesis has been thoroughly discredited. And a reasonably replicated neurodevelopmental finding is an unusual early growth trajectory, with accelerated brain growth in the first years of life. Autism is the case that teaches that a behaviourally defined syndrome need not have a single cause. Two areas of reduced cortical volume and one area of typical cortical volume observed in people with Williams syndrome. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 9.13 Williams syndrome makes the complementary point. It is caused by a specific deletion of material on chromosome 7 , and it produces a distinctive and highly recognisable profile: mild to moderate intellectual disability, a characteristic facial appearance often called elfin, connective-tissue and cardiovascular problems (the deleted region includes the gene for elastin ), and a striking cognitive dissociation. Language and sociability are relatively spared, sometimes remarkably so, with fluent talkative speech and unusual friendliness toward strangers, while spatial ability is severely impaired. Many individuals also show strong musical interest and ability. The reason the syndrome matters theoretically is that it demonstrates that cognitive abilities can be dissociated by a genetic cause: intelligence is not one quantity that a genetic defect turns down uniformly. Pair it with autism and you have the two lessons of the chapter's end: one behavioural syndrome with many causes, and one genetic cause with a highly specific behavioural pattern. Worked example A child born with a dense cataract in one eye has it removed at age nine. Vision in that eye remains poor even though the eye and retina are now normal. Explain, and say what the outcome would have been at nine months. The eye is not the problem; the cortex is. Cortical territory is allocated by competition between the two eyes' inputs during a sensitive period, and while the cataract was in place the deprived eye lost that competition, so few cortical cells now respond to it. Because the sensitive period for ocular dominance is early, restoring the input at nine does not restore the territory: the anatomy has already been settled. Surgery in infancy, before or early within the period, allows normal competition to proceed and preserves binocular cortex, which is why this is treated as an urgent operation rather than an elective one. Notice which principles the answer used: sensitive period, competition rather than disuse (from the both-eyes control), and instructive rather than merely permissive experience. 10. Brain damage and neuroplasticity This chapter has two halves that belong together. The first is a catalogue of what goes wrong with brains, and the discipline needed there is to keep the mechanism attached to each name rather than memorising the name alone. The second is the story of how the brain responds to damage, which turns out to be the most optimistic material in the book and the direct source of modern rehabilitation. Six causes of brain damage Tumours. A tumour is a mass of cells growing independently of the rest of the body. Two distinctions carry the clinical meaning. Encapsulated tumours grow within their own membrane, are therefore surgically accessible and are called benign , which is a statement about resectability rather than harmlessness, since a benign tumour can still kill by pressure. Infiltrating tumours grow diffusely into surrounding tissue, cannot be cleanly removed, and are malignant . Meningiomas , which grow from the meninges, are the standard example of encapsulated tumours. And a large proportion of brain tumours are metastatic , meaning they arose elsewhere, most often the lungs, and travelled, which is why a newly found brain tumour prompts a search of the rest of the body. A meningioma. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 10.1 Multiple metastatic brain tumors. The colored areas indicate the location of the larger metastatic brain tumors in this patient. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 10.2 Cerebrovascular disorders: strokes. A stroke is a sudden cerebrovascular event producing brain damage, and it comes in two mechanically opposite forms. In cerebral haemorrhage a vessel ruptures and blood floods into the tissue; the commonest cause is a burst aneurysm , a balloon-like weakening in a vessel wall, which may be congenital or produced by infection or hypertension. In cerebral ischaemia , which is more common, blood supply is interrupted, by a thrombosis (a plug forming in place), an embolism (a plug formed elsewhere and carried until it lodges), or arteriosclerosis (progressive thickening and hardening of vessel walls). An MRI of Professor P.’s acoustic neuroma, the very one that he took to his doctor. The arrow indicates the tumor. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 10.3 Two facts about ischaemic damage matter more than the vocabulary. First, the damage takes time to develop , so it is not simply a matter of cells starving instantly, and the area of tissue surrounding the core that is compromised but not yet dead, the penumbra , is the target of acute treatment: save the penumbra and the deficit is smaller. Second, the principal mechanism of ischaemic death is excitotoxicity . Deprived of oxygen, neurons release excessive glutamate , which overactivates NMDA receptors on neighbouring neurons, letting in large amounts of Na + and Ca 2+ , which triggers a cascade of internal damage and further glutamate release, spreading the injury outward. This is the reason damage grows for hours after the blood flow stopped, and it explains why the brain's chief excitatory transmitter is also its chief self-destruct mechanism. An angiogram that illustrates narrowing of one carotid artery (see arrow), a major pathway of blood to the brain. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 10.4 The cascade by which ischemia-induced glutamate release kills neurons. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 10.5 Closed-head injuries. Brain injury without penetration of the skull. Bruising and bleeding from the brain striking the inside of the skull produces a contusion , and a characteristic pattern is the contrecoup injury, damage on the side opposite the blow, produced when the brain slams against the far wall of the skull on the rebound. A concussion is a disturbance of consciousness with no evident structural damage, and the modern concern is cumulative: repeated concussion, as in boxing and contact sports, is associated with chronic traumatic encephalopathy , historically dementia pugilistica , a progressive dementia with characteristic pathology. Infections. An invasion of the brain by micro-organisms is a cerebral infection and the resulting inflammation is encephalitis . Bacterial infections tend to produce abscesses (pockets of pus) or meningitis (inflammation of the meninges). Two viral cases are worth knowing because they show viruses can have specific targets. Rabies is a virus with a particular affinity for the nervous system, and the fact that its bite-induced spread ends in behaviour (aggression, biting) that transmits it is a nice illustration of a pathogen selected to alter its host's behaviour. Herpes simplex has an affinity for the nervous system too, with the striking clinical consequence that herpes encephalitis characteristically attacks the medial temporal lobes and can therefore produce a profound amnesia. And general paresis , the insanity and dementia of late-stage syphilis caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum , deserves its place in history: it was the first psychiatric syndrome shown to have an identified physical cause, and it is what made a biological psychiatry plausible. Neurotoxins. Toxic chemicals reaching the brain, from outside or inside. Heavy metals are classic: mercury poisoning among hat-makers, who used it to treat felt, is the origin of the Mad Hatter, and lead exposure impairs cognitive development in children. Note also that a therapeutic drug can be a neurotoxin: the antipsychotics, given long-term, can produce tardive dyskinesia , a motor disorder of involuntary movements especially of the face and mouth, which is frequently irreversible. Some toxins are produced by the body itself, in the form of antibodies that attack neural tissue, which is the mechanism of the autoimmune diseases below. Genetic factors. Most inherited neuropsychological disorders are associated with recessive genes, since a dominant abnormal gene severe enough to disrupt the brain would usually be eliminated. The important exception to the single-gene picture is a chromosomal accident: Down syndrome results from an extra chromosome 21 ( trisomy 21 ), produced by faulty separation in meiosis, with incidence rising with maternal age, and it produces characteristic physical features, intellectual disability, and a markedly elevated risk of early Alzheimer's disease. Programmed cell death. The final cause is not an insult at all. Since apoptosis is a normal genetic program that a cell can execute, many kinds of insult (ischaemia, trauma, toxins, infection) appear to kill cells partly by triggering that program rather than by destroying them directly. That reframing matters therapeutically, because a triggered program is something one might interrupt, whereas mechanical destruction is not. A CT scan of a subdural hematoma. Diagnosis rests on the EEG, since most seizures are not convulsive. Many patients experience an aura , a psychological sensation preceding the seizure, which is diagnostically valuable in two ways: its nature indicates where the seizure begins, and it gives the patient warning. The classification worth learning has two levels. Partial (focal) seizures begin in one region and do not spread to the whole brain: a simple partial seizure involves sensory or motor symptoms without loss of consciousness, while a complex partial seizure, most often temporal lobe in origin, involves impaired consciousness and characteristic automatisms , purposeless repetitive acts such as lip-smacking or fumbling with clothes, for which the patient afterwards has no memory. Generalised seizures involve the entire brain: the tonic-clonic (grand mal) seizure has a tonic phase of rigidity followed by a clonic phase of convulsive shaking, with loss of consciousness, and a good deal of its damage comes from the hypoxia produced when breathing muscles are involved; the absence (petit mal) seizure involves a brief cessation of responsiveness with a blank stare and fluttering eyelids, has a distinctive bilaterally symmetrical 3-per-second spike-and-wave EEG signature, and is commonest in children. Its pathology is degeneration of the dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra that project to the striatum, with the surviving cells often containing clumps of protein called Lewy bodies . Symptoms appear only after a large proportion of these neurons have been lost, which is itself informative: the system compensates until it cannot. Treatment is L-DOPA , the precursor that crosses the blood-brain barrier where dopamine cannot, and it is genuinely effective but does not stop the degeneration and becomes less effective as fewer cells remain to convert it. Deep brain stimulation , through an electrode implanted in a basal ganglia target, is the standard option for advanced cases. Deep brain stimulation for Parkinson’s disease. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 10.11 Huntington's disease is the contrast case genetically. It is a progressive motor disorder of adulthood, beginning with fidgetiness and developing into chorea , rapid involuntary jerking movements, accompanied by progressive dementia, and it is invariably fatal. It is caused by a single dominant gene on chromosome 4, so a person with an affected parent has a 50 per cent chance of carrying it and, if they carry it, will develop it. Because the gene is identified, a presymptomatic genetic test exists, and because onset is typically after the reproductive years, the decision whether to take that test and whether to have children is a real dilemma rather than a textbook one, which is why Pinel raises it as an ethical case. Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks myelin in the central nervous system, producing hard scarred areas (sclerotic plaques) where myelin is lost and eventually damage to the axons themselves. Because myelin is the mechanism of saltatory conduction (Chapter 4), demyelination degrades or blocks conduction, and the symptoms are correspondingly diverse and depend on where the lesions are: visual disturbance, ataxia, numbness, weakness. The relapsing-remitting course of the common form is explained by episodes of inflammation followed by partial remyelination. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 10.12 Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia. Its clinical progression is characteristic: early anterograde amnesia for explicit episodic material, then a broadening to include other memory and cognitive functions, then confusion, personality change and, eventually, complete incapacitation. Definitive diagnosis has traditionally required autopsy , because it depends on three microscopic hallmarks: neurofibrillary tangles (twisted filaments of tau protein within neurons), amyloid plaques (extracellular clumps of beta-amyloid protein), and neuron loss. Damage is particularly pronounced in medial temporal structures, which explains the memory onset, and in the basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, notably the medial septum, which is why the disease involves a substantial loss of acetylcholine and why cholinesterase inhibitors are used, with modest effect. Whether amyloid is the cause or a marker of the disease is one of the major open arguments in neuroscience, and it is worth saying so rather than presenting the amyloid account as settled. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 10.14 Animal models, and what each one is for Three models illustrate three different modelling strategies. The kindling model of epilepsy, associated with Graham Goddard , works by delivering brief, initially subconvulsive electrical stimulations to a site such as the amygdala once a day. At first nothing happens; with repetition the convulsive response grows until each stimulation triggers a full seizure. Two properties are theoretically important: the change is permanent , so an animal left unstimulated for months is still kindled, and if stimulation continues long enough animals begin to have spontaneous seizures, which makes it a model of epileptogenesis, the process by which a brain becomes epileptic, and not merely of seizures. The MPTP model of Parkinson's disease came from a clinical accident: a group of young drug users developed severe parkinsonian symptoms after taking a synthetic opioid contaminated with MPTP , which turned out to be selectively toxic to substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons. Administering MPTP to monkeys produces the syndrome, which gave the field a model of a disease that has no natural animal form. This is the pattern where a toxin discovered by misfortune becomes a research tool. Transgenic models of Alzheimer's disease insert human genes associated with the familial early-onset form into mice, which then develop amyloid plaques and memory deficits. The strategy here is to start from a known genetic cause and let the animal build the pathology, and the standing caveat is that the model reproduces the familial genetic route, which accounts for only a small minority of human cases. How the brain responds to damage: degeneration, regeneration, reorganisation Degeneration. Cut an axon and two kinds of degeneration follow. Anterograde (or Wallerian) degeneration is the death of the segment separated from the cell body, and it is fast, because the segment has been cut off from its metabolic support. Retrograde degeneration works backward from the cut toward the cell body, and it is slower; whether the cell body dies depends largely on whether the axon manages to re-establish contact with an appropriate target. There is also transneuronal degeneration, in which the loss spreads to neurons that had synapsed with the dead one, in either direction. Neural and transneuronal degeneration following axotomy. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 10.15 Regeneration. The striking asymmetry here is one of the most useful facts in the chapter: axons regenerate well in the peripheral nervous system and essentially not at all in the central nervous system of mammals. The explanation is not in the neurons, which is what makes it interesting: it is in the glia. In the PNS, Schwann cells survive, clear debris, release growth-promoting factors and, crucially, remain in place as tubes that guide the regrowing axon back to its original target. In the CNS, oligodendrocytes do not do this, and worse, CNS myelin and the scar tissue formed after injury actively release factors that inhibit axon growth. So CNS regeneration fails because the environment forbids it, not because the neuron cannot grow, which is precisely why current experimental therapies aim at blocking the inhibitory factors or supplying a permissive bridge. Note also that even in the PNS, regeneration is accurate only if the guiding sheaths are intact and aligned: if the cut ends are separated the axons grow into the wrong sheaths and reach the wrong targets, producing a limb that is reinnervated but wrongly wired. Neurotransplantation attempts to replace lost tissue: implants of fetal substantia nigra tissue in Parkinson's disease have produced some benefit in some patients, with inconsistent results and, in some cases, troublesome side effects, and the field's hope has shifted to stem cells , which can be multiplied in culture and directed toward particular fates. Rehabilitative training is the approach with the strongest evidence, and its most instructive example is constraint-induced therapy for stroke patients with a weak arm: the intact arm is restrained so that the affected arm must be used, and function improves. The rationale is that spontaneous recovery is limited partly by learned non-use , in which the patient stops trying with the weak limb because the good one works, and the cortical territory then loses out in the competition. Forcing use restores the competitive pressure. Note how directly this therapy is derived from a principle: maps follow activity, so arrange for activity. Worked example A patient arrives two hours after sudden right-sided weakness and loss of speech. Why is the timing the most important fact in the sentence, and what is the mechanism you are racing? The presentation is a left-hemisphere ischaemic stroke. The damage is not complete at onset: there is a dead core and a surrounding penumbra of tissue that is underperfused but still viable, and it is the penumbra that will be lost over the next hours through glutamate excitotoxicity , as oxygen-starved neurons dump glutamate, overactivate NMDA receptors on their neighbours, admit destructive quantities of calcium, and release more glutamate in turn. Restoring perfusion quickly, or interrupting the cascade, saves penumbral tissue and therefore reduces the eventual deficit, which is why stroke is treated as a time-critical emergency. Then predict the medium-term course: some spontaneous recovery through cortical reorganisation and the strengthening of surviving connections, and a real risk of learned non-use of the right arm, which is the specific target of constraint-induced therapy. 11. Learning, memory and amnesia This chapter is the payoff of Chapter 1. Donald Hebb proposed that experience changes synapses; here that proposal is tested, and the route runs through a small number of patients whose losses defined what memory even is, and then down to the molecular mechanism of a single synapse. H.M., and the five things his case established In 1953, in an attempt to control intractable epilepsy, William Scoville performed a bilateral removal of the medial temporal lobes, including most of the hippocampus, amygdala and surrounding cortex, on a patient known as H.M. (Henry Molaison). His seizures improved. His memory was devastated. He was studied for more than fifty years, chiefly by Brenda Milner , and the case is the single most consequential in the history of memory research. What matters is not the story but the five distinct conclusions it forced, each of which contradicted something people believed. Medial temporal lobectomy. The portions of the medial temporal lobes removed from H.M.’s brain are illustrated in a view of the inferior surface of the brain. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 11.1 1. Memory is a distinct function. H.M.'s perception, language, reasoning and IQ were normal, indeed his IQ rose slightly after surgery. So memory is not simply a by-product of general intellectual capacity; it is separable, and there is dedicated machinery for it. 2. Short-term and long-term memory are separate systems. H.M.'s short-term memory was intact: he could repeat back a string of digits and hold a conversation. What he could not do was retain anything beyond the moment attention lapsed. The medial temporal lobes are therefore not needed to hold information briefly, but are needed to convert it into a lasting store, which is consolidation . 3. Anterograde and retrograde amnesia are dissociable. His anterograde amnesia , for events after the surgery, was profound and permanent. His retrograde amnesia , for events before it, was comparatively mild and, importantly, graded : memories from the years immediately before surgery were lost, while childhood memories were largely intact. The gradient is the crucial detail, because it implies that memories become progressively less dependent on the medial temporal lobes over time, that is, that consolidation continues for years after the event. 4. Explicit and implicit memory are separate. H.M. could learn , in ways he could not report. Milner's demonstration was mirror-drawing : over days, H.M.'s performance at tracing a shape while watching his hand in a mirror improved normally, and each day he denied ever having done the task. Comparable improvement appeared on rotary pursuit and on the incomplete-pictures test , where fragmentary drawings become easier to identify with prior exposure. So explicit memory (conscious, reportable) and implicit memory (expressed through performance, without awareness) depend on different structures, and the medial temporal lobes serve the former. The learning and retention of the mirrordrawing task by H.M. Despite his good retention of the task, H.M. had no conscious recollection of having performed it before. The medial temporal lobes are not the site of storage. Old memories survived their removal. So these structures are necessary for forming and consolidating explicit memories, not for holding them; the store is elsewhere, most likely distributed in cortex. Trap H.M. did not lose all memory, and he was not unable to learn. He had intact short-term memory, intact remote memory, intact intellectual function, and intact implicit/procedural learning. The specific loss was the formation of new explicit long-term memories. Note also that the surgery was bilateral , which is why the deficit was so severe; unilateral medial temporal removals produce far milder effects. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 11.5 Further distinctions, from further patients Endel Tulving 's division of explicit memory into episodic memory (for the experienced events of one's own life, with their context, and involving a kind of mental time travel into the past) and semantic memory (for general facts and knowledge, without any record of where they were learned) is supported by patients in whom the two come apart. The case usually cited is K.C. , who after a motorcycle accident with extensive damage retained a large body of general knowledge, including facts about his own life, while being unable to recollect a single personal experience. He knew that he had a brother who died; he could not remember any occasion involving him. Episodic memory can be destroyed with semantic memory largely spared. Korsakoff's syndrome supplies a second amnesia with a different anatomy. As established in Chapter 1 it results from thiamine deficiency , usually in the context of chronic alcoholism. Its memory deficit resembles medial temporal amnesia in being predominantly anterograde and explicit, but the damage is in the medial diencephalon , notably the mammillary bodies and the medial thalamus, and in advanced cases extends to cortex. Its characteristic additional feature is confabulation , the production of plausible but invented accounts, which patients offer without any sense of fabricating. That two different lesion sites can produce a similar amnesia is not a nuisance; it tells you that consolidation depends on a circuit, not a structure, and that circuit is essentially the one Chapter 3 described as the limbic ring. Posttraumatic amnesia , after a closed-head injury, adds the temporal picture. There is typically a period of confusion, permanent anterograde amnesia for the events immediately after the blow, and retrograde amnesia extending back before it, again graded , so that the most recent memories are the most vulnerable. During recovery, memory returns from the oldest to the most recent, and patients may show islands of memory , isolated retained events within an amnesic period. The whole pattern is what the concept of consolidation was invented to explain, originally by Müller and Pilzecker , and Donald Hebb's version proposed a dual trace : a short-lived reverberatory neural activity that is vulnerable to disruption, and a structural change that it gradually establishes. Electroconvulsive shock given shortly after a learning experience disrupts memory for it, while the same shock given later does not, which is the experimental signature of a consolidation window. Modern work adds reconsolidation : retrieving a consolidated memory returns it temporarily to a labile state in which it can again be disrupted or altered, which implies that remembering is a reconstructive act rather than a read-out. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 11.14 The hippocampus and space: place cells and grid cells The most beautiful single result in the chapter is the discovery by John O'Keefe and Jonathan Dostrovsky of place cells : hippocampal neurons that fire when, and only when, the animal is in a particular location in a familiar environment. Different cells have different place fields, and together the population specifies where the animal is. Put another way, you can read the rat's location off its hippocampus. Later, May-Britt Moser and Edvard Moser discovered grid cells in the adjacent entorhinal cortex, which fire at the vertices of a regular triangular grid tiling the environment, and which appear to supply a coordinate system, a metric, from which place fields can be constructed. O'Keefe and the Mosers shared the 2014 Nobel Prize. The theoretical claim these findings support is the cognitive map theory of hippocampal function: the hippocampus constructs an allocentric map of space, which is why its damage impairs spatial memory so severely and why the water maze is so sensitive to it. Where the memories actually are Since the medial temporal lobes are not the store, the store must be distributed, and different systems hold different content. The chapter's answer is a division of labour: The structures of the brain that have been shown to play a role in memory. Because it would have blocked the view of other structures, the striatum is not included. (See Figure 3.27 on page 93.) Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 11.16 Inferotemporal cortex stores memories of visual patterns and objects, which is unsurprising given that it is the end of the ventral "what" stream of Chapter 6. Perception and memory for a class of material tend to use the same tissue. Amygdala stores the emotional significance of experiences, and is essential for fear conditioning , the paradigm developed in detail by Joseph LeDoux . Amygdala damage does not impair memory for the facts of an event but abolishes its conditioned emotional consequences. Prefrontal cortex supports working memory , the temporal order of events, and memory for the source and context of information. Its damage produces failures of sequencing and of knowing where a memory came from rather than loss of content. Cerebellum and striatum support the implicit systems: the cerebellum for sensorimotor learning of precisely timed responses, and the striatum for habit learning , the gradual, incremental, stimulus-response learning that H.M. retained. This is the anatomical basis of the explicit/implicit distinction: patients with striatal disease show the opposite dissociation to H.M., losing habit learning while retaining explicit recall. The synaptic mechanism: long-term potentiation Finally, the mechanism, and it is where Donald Hebb is vindicated in detail. Long-term potentiation (LTP) , first reported in the hippocampus by Timothy Bliss and Terje Lømo , is a lasting increase in the strength of a synapse following brief intense high-frequency stimulation of its presynaptic input. It is the phenomenon Hebb's rule predicted: co-activity strengthens the connection. It occurs readily in the hippocampus, it can last for weeks, and it displays the properties you would want of a memory mechanism, including specificity to the stimulated pathway. Its mechanism turns on the NMDA receptor , a glutamate receptor with an unusual property: it is doubly gated . It opens only if glutamate is bound and the postsynaptic membrane is already depolarised, because at resting potential the channel is physically plugged by a magnesium ion that only leaves when the membrane depolarises. Consider what that makes the receptor: a coincidence detector . It generates a signal only when presynaptic activity (glutamate release) and postsynaptic activity (depolarisation, typically produced by other converging inputs) occur together. Hebb's rule is not merely implemented by the brain; it is built into the structure of a single protein. If researchers identified a “Harry Potter neuron” in a patient’s brain, what other stimuli might it fire in response to? Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 11.15 The cascade then runs: coincidence opens the NMDA channel, Ca 2+ enters the postsynaptic neuron, and calcium acts as the second messenger that triggers the changes. Those changes are of two kinds, and both are documented. Postsynaptically, additional AMPA receptors are inserted into the membrane, so the same amount of glutamate now produces a larger response, and over a longer term the dendritic spine itself enlarges or new spines form. Presynaptically, a retrograde messenger (nitric oxide is the classic candidate, and note that Chapter 4 flagged the soluble gases for exactly this kind of role) travels back to the terminal and increases subsequent transmitter release. So the synapse is strengthened from both sides, which is why the effect is durable. Hunger, eating and health The eating chapter is Pinel's set-piece demolition of an intuitive theory, and it is worth reading as an argument rather than as a list of structures. The intuition is that we eat because we run low on energy and stop when we are replenished. The chapter shows that this account fails on the evidence, replaces it, and then uses the replacement to explain obesity and the eating disorders. Digestion and the flow of energy Start with the physiology, because the argument depends on it. Digestion breaks food into usable form, and the body then cycles between three metabolic phases, controlled principally by two pancreatic hormones. The gastrointestinal tract and the process of digestion. Not shown in the figure is the gut microbiome, which includes the bacteria and other organisms that live inside our gastrointestinal tract and help break down, store Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 12.1 The cephalic phase begins with the sight, smell or thought of food and ends when it reaches the stomach; the body prepares, and notably releases insulin in anticipation. The absorptive phase is the period during which nutrients are being absorbed and used for immediate energy, with the surplus stored; insulin is high. The fasting phase is the period after absorption, when the body draws on its stores; insulin is low and glucagon is high. Distribution of stored energy in an average person. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 12.2 The cephalic, absorptive and fasting phases, and what insulin and glucagon do in each. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 12.3 Insulin's three jobs are worth stating together because they explain a great deal: it promotes the use of glucose as the immediate fuel, it promotes the conversion of surplus into stores , and it promotes the storage of those stores as fat. Consequently, when insulin is high, glucose is used and fat is deposited; when insulin is low and glucagon high, stored fat is converted to free fatty acids and to ketones , which most of the body then burns in place of glucose, sparing the limited glucose supply for the brain. Energy is stored in three forms: as fats (the bulk of it, because fat stores far more energy per gram and holds less water), as glycogen in the liver and muscle (a small, quickly accessible reserve), and as protein (the reserve of last resort, drawn on only in prolonged deprivation, which is why starvation wastes muscle). Set-point theories, and why they fail Set-point theories hold that eating is a negative-feedback system that defends a fixed level. The two classic versions specify what is defended: the glucostatic theory (associated with Jean Mayer ) proposes that eating is triggered by a fall in blood glucose, and the lipostatic theory (associated with Gordon Kennedy ) proposes that it defends a set level of body fat. Both are plausible and neither survives as a general account of when we eat. Pinel's objections are worth having in order, because the exam question is usually "criticise set-point theory". The energy set-point view that is the basis of many people’s thinking about hunger and eating. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 12.4 The evolutionary objection. A system that waited for a deficit before eating would be a poor design for an animal in an environment of unpredictable food supply. The adaptive strategy is to eat when food is available, before any deficit exists. The physiological objection. Blood glucose is in fact tightly regulated and does not drop appreciably before normal meals; the small pre-meal dip that does occur appears to be caused by the anticipation of eating rather than to cause it. The experimental objection. Depriving people or animals of a nutrient does not produce a specific hunger for it in most cases, and conversely, palatable food produces eating in animals that are not deprived at all. Sated animals presented with a varied, appealing selection eat substantially more, the so-called cafeteria effect. Neither observation is available to a depletion account. The everyday objection. Meal timing is governed by clocks, custom and company. People eat lunch at one o'clock and stop at the end of a plate, not at the end of a deficit. The replacement is the positive-incentive perspective : we are drawn to eat by the anticipated pleasure of eating, and the strength of that positive-incentive value at any moment is determined by the food's palatability, by what we have learned about it, by how long since we last ate, by how much is already in the gut, and by the presence of others. The reframing is from a push to a pull. Note that this does not deny that deprivation increases hunger; it denies that deprivation is the trigger. High-yield Cephalic, absorptive and fasting phases; insulin high in the first two (use glucose, store fat), glucagon high in the third (mobilise free fatty acids and ketones). Glucostatic (Mayer) and lipostatic (Kennedy) are the two set-point theories. The four objections: evolutionary implausibility, glucose does not fall before meals, deprivation does not create specific hungers while palatability creates eating without deprivation, and eating is governed by learning and context. Replacement = positive-incentive perspective. What, when and how much we eat What. Preferences and aversions are largely learned . The most compelling mechanism is conditioned taste aversion : a single pairing of a novel flavour with subsequent illness produces a lasting avoidance of that flavour, even at long delays between taste and illness, which violates the usual rules of conditioning and shows that learning is specialised for this problem. Its mirror image is conditioned preference for flavours associated with recovery or with needed nutrients. The one convincing case of an innate specific hunger is sodium : animals deprived of salt show an immediate preference for salty tastes without needing to learn it. Beyond that, humans acquire their diets culturally, and the general tendency to prefer familiar foods and be cautious of novel ones (neophobia) is itself adaptive for an omnivore. When. Meals are largely scheduled by circumstance, and the pre-meal state is instructive. Just before an expected meal the body enters the cephalic phase, releasing insulin and lowering blood glucose. So the hunger felt before lunch is not a signal that reserves have run down; it is the body's preparation for an anticipated intake, and it is produced by the expectation. That single finding inverts the naive account: the physiological state that we read as evidence of need is itself a consequence of learning when food arrives. The sham-eating preparation. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 12.5 How much. Satiety is not the correction of a deficit either. The evidence comes from several directions. Sham eating experiments, in which swallowed food is diverted out of the body through a tube so it never accumulates, show that animals still stop eating at approximately a normal meal size on familiar food, which means the signal to stop is not accumulation in the gut. The appetiser effect : a small amount of food before a meal increases subsequent intake, the opposite of what a deficit account predicts, because it raises the incentive value of eating. Social influence : people eat more in company, and animals eat more in the presence of others. And sensory-specific satiety , studied particularly by Barbara Rolls , is the finding that satiety is specific to the foods eaten: the incentive value of the food just eaten declines sharply while that of other foods declines much less, which is why there is always room for dessert. This has an obvious adaptive rationale, since it pushes an omnivore toward a varied and therefore nutritionally complete diet, and an obvious modern consequence: a varied buffet defeats satiety, which is the mechanism behind the cafeteria-diet obesity used in laboratories. Physiology: hypothalamic centres, then the honest correction The classic account, and it is still the one examined, is the dual-centre theory . Bilateral lesions of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) produce hyperphagia and gross obesity, so the VMH was designated the satiety centre. Bilateral lesions of the lateral hypothalamus (LH) produce aphagia and adipsia, a refusal to eat and drink, so the LH was designated the feeding centre. The ventromedial and lateral hypothalamus in the rat brain. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 12.6 Both interpretations are now regarded as wrong, and knowing why is more valuable than knowing the original claim. The VMH-lesioned rat's obesity is not simply a failure to feel full: such animals show greatly increased lipogenesis , converting nutrients to fat rather than burning them, so they gain weight partly because their metabolism has changed, and their overeating may be a consequence of the resulting energy shortfall rather than its cause. Moreover, VMH lesions typically damage the adjacent paraventricular nucleus and fibres passing through, which appear to be responsible for much of the effect, so this is precisely the fibres-of-passage problem from Chapter 5. As for the LH, its lesions produce a broad deficit including sensorimotor and motivational impairment: the animals are unresponsive generally, not specifically uninterested in food, and can be kept alive and will eventually eat. The general lesson is one Pinel presses repeatedly: a lesion that abolishes a behaviour does not identify a centre for that behaviour. The modern picture is a set of peripheral signals acting on a distributed hypothalamic network. Cholecystokinin (CCK) is released by the gut during a meal and acts as a short-term satiety signal, limiting meal size. Ghrelin , released by the empty stomach, increases hunger. Insulin circulates in proportion to fat stores and acts centrally as well as peripherally. And leptin is the long-term adiposity signal, with a genuinely elegant discovery history: the ob/ob mouse is grossly obese, and parabiosis experiments (surgically joining the circulations of two mice, work associated with Douglas Coleman ) established that one obese strain lacked a circulating satiety factor while another lacked the ability to respond to it. The missing factor was leptin, secreted by fat cells, and the second strain's defect was in the leptin receptor. Within the hypothalamus, leptin and insulin act on the arcuate nucleus , which contains two opposed populations: neurons releasing neuropeptide Y , which stimulate eating, and melanocortin system neurons, which suppress it. The system developed by Cannon and Washburn in 1912 for measuring stomach contractions. They found that large stomach contractions were related to pangs of hunger. But it also explains too much: it cannot accommodate the fact that average weights have risen substantially in populations over decades, that weight settles at a new level when diet changes and stays there, or that the body's defence of weight is markedly asymmetrical, resisting loss much harder than gain. The diminishing effects on body weight of a low-calorie diet and a high-calorie diet. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 12.9 Pinel's preferred alternative is the settling-point model . Weight drifts to and settles at a level where the various forces acting on it balance, in the way that the water level in a leaky bucket settles where inflow equals outflow, without anything specifying that level in advance. Change the inflow and the level moves and stabilises somewhere new. This accommodates both stability and drift, and it makes weight a consequence of the current balance rather than a defended target. The leaky-barrel model: a settling point, not a set point. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 12.10 One mechanism deserves naming because it explains why calorie arithmetic under-predicts: diet-induced thermogenesis , the increase in heat production in response to increased intake, means that some of a surplus is dissipated rather than stored, and the magnitude varies between individuals. Together with variation in spontaneous activity, this is part of why two people on the same diet gain differently. Obesity, and why it is so hard to treat The evolutionary framing is the necessary starting point. For almost all of human history the problem was insufficient and unreliable food, so selection favoured a strong positive-incentive value for calorie-dense food, efficient storage of surplus, and vigorous physiological defence against weight loss . None of these was balanced by comparable pressure against weight gain, because gain was rarely possible. Place that system in an environment of cheap, varied, palatable, energy-dense food requiring no effort to obtain and the outcome is not a malfunction; it is the system working as designed in conditions it was not designed for. Because there is substantial variation in the relevant mechanisms: in energy expenditure and diet-induced thermogenesis, in spontaneous activity, in the incentive value particular individuals place on food, in gut microbiota, and in a long list of genetic contributions each of small effect. Obesity is a normally distributed trait whose expression depends on the environment, which is Chapter 2's interaction restated. Treatment is difficult for reasons the chapter has already supplied. Dieting reduces intake, but the body responds to weight loss by reducing energy expenditure, which is the asymmetrical defence at work, so continued loss requires continued further restriction; and the positive-incentive value of food is not reduced by restriction, it is increased. Serotonergic appetite suppressants have a history of withdrawal for safety reasons. Bariatric surgery , notably gastric bypass, remains the most effective intervention, and it is worth noting that part of its effect appears to be hormonal, through altered gut signalling, rather than purely mechanical restriction. Both are far commoner in women, and both carry serious medical complications, anorexia having one of the highest mortality rates of any psychiatric disorder. Pinel's interest in anorexia is theoretical as well as clinical, because it is a hard problem for any depletion account of hunger. On a set-point theory, a severely underweight starving person should experience overwhelming hunger; the defended variable is far below its set point. Yet the anorexic patient characteristically reports diminished interest in eating. The positive-incentive perspective handles this better: what has collapsed is not the deficit but the incentive value of eating, and there is corroborating evidence from studies of voluntary starvation, notably the classic Minnesota work associated with Ancel Keys , that starvation itself changes the psychology of eating and can reduce, not merely intensify, the ordinary appetitive response. Pinel further notes the possibility that the positive-incentive value of food may be reduced by the aversive physical consequences of eating after prolonged starvation, which would make the restriction partly self-maintaining. This is an area where the honest answer includes the fact that the mechanisms are not settled. Worked example Why is a buffet the single most obesogenic way to serve food, and which two mechanisms from this chapter explain it? First, sensory-specific satiety : the decline in incentive value that normally ends a meal is specific to the food eaten, so as soon as you switch to a different dish the satiety you had accumulated does not transfer, and eating resumes. A single-dish meal ends when that dish becomes unappealing; a buffet never runs out of dishes that are still appealing. Second, the appetiser effect and the general fact that positive-incentive value, not deficit, drives intake: small early portions raise rather than lower subsequent consumption, and the visible variety keeps incentive value high throughout. Add the social facilitation of eating in company and the absence of any portion boundary and you have the laboratory cafeteria diet, which is used precisely because it reliably makes rats obese. Note what the explanation did not need: any reference to energy deficit. 13. Hormones and sex The sex chapter is the one where the intuitive model is furthest from the evidence, so it is worth naming the intuitive model before demolishing it. The intuition is that there are two sexes, that a set of male characteristics comes as a package driven by male hormones, and that a corresponding female package is driven by female ones. Pinel calls this the men-are-men-and-women-are-women assumption and shows that almost every part of it is wrong: the characteristics develop independently, the hormones are not sex-exclusive, and the developmental logic is not two parallel programs but one program with a switch. The neuroendocrine system Exocrine glands release their products through ducts onto a surface; endocrine glands release hormones directly into the bloodstream, which is why hormonal effects are slow, widespread and sustained compared with synaptic ones. The gonads are the testes and ovaries, which produce gametes (sperm and ova) and also hormones. The endocrine glands. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 13.1 Hormones come in three chemical classes and the class determines the mechanism. Peptide and protein hormones and amino-acid derivatives cannot cross the cell membrane and therefore act on receptors on the cell surface, triggering second-messenger cascades. Steroid hormones , synthesised from cholesterol, are lipid-soluble and therefore pass straight through the membrane, binding receptors inside the cell that act on DNA to influence gene expression . That mechanistic difference is why steroid effects are slower to appear and much longer-lasting, and why they can produce permanent structural change in a developing organism. The three classes of gonadal steroids are the androgens , of which the best known is testosterone , the oestrogens , of which the best known is estradiol , and the progestins , of which the best known is progesterone , whose function includes preparing the uterus and breasts for pregnancy. And here is the first correction to the intuitive model: these are not male and female hormones. The testes release some oestrogens, the ovaries release some androgens, and the adrenal cortex releases all three classes in both sexes. The difference between the sexes is a matter of relative amounts , not of kind. The pituitary, and who is actually in charge The pituitary hangs from the hypothalamus and has two lobes that are different organs in all but name. The posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) is neural tissue. It releases oxytocin and vasopressin , and the key fact is that these are not made there: they are synthesised in hypothalamic neurons whose axons run down into the posterior pituitary and release them into the bloodstream from the terminals. The posterior pituitary is a release site, not a gland in the usual sense. A midline view of the posterior and anterior pituitary and surrounding structures. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 13.2 The anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) is glandular tissue and it releases the tropic hormones , whose targets are other endocrine glands. Those relevant here are the gonadotropins : follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinising hormone (LH) , which act on the gonads. It also releases growth hormone, ACTH (acting on the adrenal cortex), TSH (thyroid) and prolactin. Since the anterior pituitary has no neural connection to the hypothalamus, how is it controlled? By releasing hormones , secreted by hypothalamic neurons into a specialised local circulatory system, the hypothalamopituitary portal system , which carries them the short distance to the anterior pituitary. The demonstration of this system is credited to Geoffrey Harris , and it is what established the hypothalamus, and therefore the brain, as the controller of the endocrine system. The relation is a loop rather than a chain: hypothalamus to anterior pituitary to gonad to circulating steroid, and the circulating steroid feeds back on both hypothalamus and pituitary to regulate further release. Note also that release is pulsatile rather than steady, which matters clinically because continuous administration of a releasing hormone can paradoxically shut a system down by desensitising it. The neural connections between the hypothalamus and the pituitary. Notice the neural input to the pituitary all goes to the posterior pituitary; the anterior pituitary has no neural connections. The anterior pituitary does synthesise its own hormones but is controlled chemically, through the portal system, not neurally. And the old idea that the pituitary is the master gland is backwards: the hypothalamus controls the pituitary. The Y chromosome carries the Sry gene , which produces Sry protein (testis-determining factor); where it is present the medulla develops into testes , and where it is absent the cortex develops into ovaries . Everything downstream follows not from the chromosomes but from which gonad developed, and therefore from which hormones it secretes. This is the switch: after it, the chromosomes have essentially done their job. The fetus initially has both sets of precursor ducts: the Wolffian system , which can become the male seminal vesicles and vas deferens, and the Müllerian system , which can become the female uterus and upper vagina. The developing testes secrete two things, and it takes both. Testosterone causes the Wolffian system to develop, and Müllerian-inhibiting substance (anti-Müllerian hormone) causes the Müllerian system to degenerate and also contributes to the descent of the testes. In the absence of testes, and therefore of both secretions, the Wolffian system degenerates on its own and the Müllerian system develops. So the female internal pattern is what happens when nothing intervenes, and the male pattern requires two separate active signals. Note that the ovaries do essentially nothing at this stage; female internal development is not driven by ovarian hormones. And crucially this holds regardless of whether ovaries are present: an individual with neither testes nor ovaries develops female external genitals. Anomalies, and what each one proves The developmental anomalies are not curiosities; each is a natural experiment that isolates one step of the sequence. Androgenic insensitivity syndrome. A genetic XY individual with functional testes has a defective androgen receptor, so androgens circulate but cannot act. Result: testes are present (Sry worked), the Müllerian system regressed (Müllerian-inhibiting substance worked), but the Wolffian system did not develop and the external genitals are female (both androgen-dependent). The individual typically develops as a girl, with a female appearance and identity, and the condition may only be discovered at puberty when menstruation does not occur. This case proves that external genital development is androgen-driven rather than chromosome-driven, and that the two testicular secretions act independently. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia. A genetic defect causes the adrenal cortex to release excessive androgens. In XX individuals the internal ducts develop as female (no Müllerian-inhibiting substance was present) but the external genitals are partly masculinised, and later behavioural differences in play and interests have been reported. This case proves that androgen exposure, from any source, is what masculinises the external genitals and influences the brain. 5-alpha reductase deficiency. Testosterone must be converted by this enzyme into dihydrotestosterone to masculinise the external genitals fully. Affected XY individuals are therefore born with ambiguous or female-appearing genitals, and then virilise at puberty when testosterone levels rise sharply. This case proves that different androgens, at different times, do different jobs. Ablatio penis and the limits of rearing. The case of David Reimer , a genetically and hormonally typical male whose penis was destroyed in infancy in a surgical accident and who was subsequently reassigned and raised as a girl on the advice of John Money , was for years presented as proof that gender identity is entirely a product of rearing. Long-term follow-up showed the opposite: the assignment did not take, the individual was persistently unhappy, and on learning the history in adolescence reverted to living as a man. The conclusion Pinel draws is deliberately measured, and it is worth reproducing carefully: the case does not show that gender identity is fixed by biology alone, but it decisively refutes the claim that rearing alone determines it, and it establishes that prenatal and perinatal hormonal history contributes. It also illustrates the ethical cost of confident theory applied to a single child. David Reimer, the twin whose penis was accidentally destroyed. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 13.10 A further distinction the chapter insists on is that gender identity (the sex one identifies as), sexual orientation (who one is attracted to), and sexual behaviour are separate and can vary independently. Bundling them is the men-are-men assumption again. Sexual orientation The evidence here should be reported with its limits. Adult hormone levels do not reliably differ by sexual orientation, so the popular idea that orientation reflects a current hormonal state has no support. In laboratory animals, perinatal hormone manipulations can change later mating preference, which makes early hormonal influence plausible in humans, though direct evidence is indirect. Twin and family studies indicate a genetic contribution, without identifying specific genes. The fraternal birth order effect , the finding that the probability of a man being homosexual increases with the number of older biological brothers, is well replicated and has been interpreted in terms of a maternal immune response, but the mechanism is not established. Simon LeVay 's report of a difference in the size of the third interstitial nucleus of the anterior hypothalamus ( INAH3 ) between homosexual and heterosexual men is frequently cited and should be cited with its caveats: the sample was small, most of the homosexual men had died of AIDS, and a structural difference does not establish direction of causation. The honest summary is that orientation is influenced by biological factors including genes and probably early hormones, and that no single determinant has been identified. Brain mechanisms of sexual behaviour Two hypothalamic structures carry most of the load, and they divide by sex-typical behaviour rather than by sex. The medial preoptic area , which contains the sexually dimorphic nucleus, is critical for male copulatory behaviour: its destruction abolishes copulation and its stimulation elicits it. The ventromedial nucleus of the hypothalamus is critical for female sexual behaviour, particularly the receptive posture called lordosis , and it mediates the effects of estradiol. Beyond the hypothalamus, the amygdala is involved in the recognition and evaluation of sexually relevant stimuli, and the ventral tegmental area and nucleus accumbens , the reward circuitry of Chapter 15, are engaged by sexual activity, which is the anatomical link between sex and the general machinery of motivation. Sleep, dreaming and circadian rhythms Sleep occupies a third of life and its function is still genuinely unsettled, which makes this the best chapter in the book for seeing how a real scientific argument is conducted. Pinel sets two theories against each other and then tests them against comparative, deprivation and physiological evidence in turn. Measuring sleep: three signals and five stages Sleep research became possible with three simultaneous recordings: the EEG (cortical activity), the EOG (eye movement) and the EMG (muscle tension, usually from the neck). Together they define the stages, and each stage is a specific combination of the three. A participant in a sleep experiment. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 14.1 Awake and alert, the EEG shows low-amplitude fast beta activity; relaxed with the eyes closed it shows regular 8 to 12 Hz alpha waves. Then: The EEG of alert wakefulness, of sleep onset, and of the three stages of sleep. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 14.2 Stage 1 (initial): low-amplitude, irregular, faster activity; a light transitional sleep. Muscle tone drops and eye movements are slow. Stage 2 : slightly higher amplitude and lower frequency, plus two distinctive waveforms, the K complex (a single large negative-then-positive wave) and the sleep spindle (a brief burst of 12 to 14 Hz activity). Stage 3 : appearance of large slow delta waves. Stage 4 : delta waves predominate. Stages 3 and 4 together are slow-wave sleep (SWS) , now often combined as N3, and this is the deepest sleep, hardest to be woken from. REM sleep : after descending to stage 4 the sleeper ascends back through the stages to what looks on the EEG like stage 1, but with two additions: rapid eye movements and a total loss of core muscle tone (atonia). This is emergent stage 1 , and it is REM sleep . The course of the EEG stages across a typical night, with REM and the loss of core-muscle tone. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 14.3 REM sleep is also called paradoxical sleep , and the paradox is worth stating because it is the single most examinable feature: the brain is highly active, with an EEG resembling wakefulness, elevated cerebral blood flow and oxygen consumption, and autonomic variability, while the body is paralysed. The paralysis is active inhibition of the motor neurons, and its function is presumably to prevent the dreamed movements from being executed. Sleep proceeds in cycles of roughly 90 minutes , and their composition shifts across the night: slow-wave sleep dominates the early cycles and progressively gives way, so that REM occupies more of the later cycles . This is why cutting sleep short by two hours removes disproportionately more REM than slow-wave sleep. Summary of the various sleep-stage terms. That gave the field an objective handle on a subjective phenomenon, and the first thing it did was overturn several common beliefs. Two areas of the brain implicated in dreaming and one implicated in visual imagery. Both lesions studies and brain imaging studies have implicated the medial prefrontal cortex and the tempero-parieto junction in dreaming. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 14.4 That external stimuli cannot affect dreams. They can, and are frequently incorporated into the ongoing dream, though usually altered. That dreams last only an instant. They do not; dreams run in something close to real time, which was established by waking sleepers after known REM durations and comparing the length of the reported dream. That some people do not dream. Everyone who is woken from REM reports dreams at high rates. People who believe they do not dream simply do not recall them, and dream recall requires waking during or shortly after the episode. That penile erections during sleep indicate sexual dreams. Erections accompany REM sleep routinely, independent of dream content, which is the physiological basis of a diagnostic test distinguishing organic from psychogenic erectile dysfunction. That sleepwalking and sleeptalking occur during dreaming. They do not, and they cannot: REM sleep is accompanied by muscular atonia, so complex movement during it is impossible in a healthy sleeper. Sleepwalking occurs in slow-wave sleep. (The exception is REM-sleep behaviour disorder , in which the atonia mechanism fails and patients do act out dreams, which is exactly the exception that confirms the rule.) On the theory of dreaming, two positions frame the debate. Sigmund Freud held that dreams are triggered by unacceptable unconscious wishes, that they express these in disguised form, and that a distinction can therefore be drawn between the remembered manifest content and the hidden latent content . Little evidence supports the mechanism, and it is not currently taken seriously as a neurobiological account, though its historical importance is real. J. Allan Hobson 's activation-synthesis theory is the physiological alternative: during REM sleep the brain stem generates essentially random activation, which reaches cortex, and the cortex does what it always does, namely construct a coherent narrative from the information available. On this account the bizarre quality of dreams is not disguise, it is the residue of trying to make a story out of noise. It is important to note that Hobson's theory explains the form of dreams well and their apparent personal meaningfulness less well, and that the question is not settled. Why do we sleep? Two theories and three bodies of evidence Recuperation theories hold that wakefulness disrupts homeostasis in some way, that sleep restores it, and that we sleep because we need to. Adaptation (circadian) theories hold that sleep is not a response to a deficit at all but an evolved behavioural strategy: an internally programmed period of inactivity that keeps the animal safe and conserves energy at times of day when activity is unprofitable. The two make different predictions and the evidence can be sorted by which prediction it favours. Comparative evidence favours adaptation. Sleep time across species varies enormously, from around two hours to twenty, and it does not track energy expenditure or body size in the way a recuperation account requires; if anything, animals that are safe when hidden sleep more, and grazing animals in exposed habitats sleep little. Some species that must remain in motion, notably certain dolphins, sleep one hemisphere at a time. And some large active animals sleep very little. If sleep repaid a debt incurred by activity, active animals should sleep most, and they do not. Deprivation evidence is more mixed than folklore suggests. The famous case of Randy Gardner , who stayed awake for eleven days, produced no lasting psychological or physical harm, and his recovery sleep was much shorter than the sleep he had lost. Controlled studies of sleep deprivation find real but relatively modest effects, concentrated on attention and executive function rather than on physical capacity, along with microsleeps , brief intrusions of sleep into waking, which account for a good deal of the measured performance loss. Two features of recovery sleep are theoretically important. It is much shorter than the deprivation, so what is recovered is not the full quantity. And it is selective : stage 4 and REM sleep are preferentially recovered , and if REM alone is selectively deprived, by waking the sleeper at each REM onset, then across successive nights the number of awakenings needed rises (increasing REM pressure) and a substantial REM rebound follows. This suggests these stages serve specific functions that the others do not. After gorging themselves on a kill, African lions often sleep almost continuously for 2 or 3 days. And where do they sleep?
