Placed in an environment without time cues, people continue to show a rhythm, which is free-running , with a period usually a little longer than 24 hours. That is the decisive observation: the rhythm is generated internally, not imposed by the day. External cues that reset it are zeitgebers , of which light is by far the most powerful, and the process of resetting is entrainment . A free-running sleep-wake cycle of 25.3 hours, with no time cues at all. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 14.8 The clock is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, sitting just above the optic chiasm as its name says. Lesion it and circadian rhythmicity is lost. Its light input does not come by the visual pathway of Chapter 6 but by a dedicated retinohypothalamic tract arising from a special class of retinal ganglion cells containing the photopigment melanopsin , which is why some blind people retain normal entrainment. Within SCN cells the rhythm is generated by a transcription-translation feedback loop : clock genes are transcribed, their protein products accumulate and then inhibit their own transcription, are degraded, and transcription resumes, a cycle that takes about a day. So the clock is a molecular oscillator inside individual cells, not a property of the circuit alone; isolated SCN cells continue to oscillate. The pineal gland secretes melatonin at night under SCN control, and melatonin is best understood as a signal of darkness that can shift the clock (a chronobiotic) rather than as a sedative. The benzodiazepines are effective in the short term and problematic in the long: they produce tolerance, withdrawal insomnia on cessation (which then motivates continued use), daytime drowsiness, and, importantly, they change the architecture of sleep, reducing slow-wave and REM sleep, so the sleep obtained is not normal sleep. Antihypnotics increase wakefulness and include the stimulants, which carry the abuse and dependence problems of Chapter 15. Melatonin has limited hypnotic action but real value in shifting the clock, so its best use is for jet lag and for blind individuals with free-running rhythms rather than for ordinary insomnia. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Table 14.3 The disorders divide into insomnias and hypersomnias, and the chapter's most useful clinical point is that many insomnias are iatrogenic , caused by the sleeping pills prescribed for them. Others are secondary to a specific physical cause and are misdiagnosed as primary insomnia: sleep apnoea , in which breathing repeatedly stops and the patient partially wakes, so the complaint is unrefreshing sleep and daytime sleepiness rather than difficulty falling asleep; and periodic limb movement disorder and restless legs syndrome . The point is that "insomnia" is a symptom, and treating it without identifying the cause is how iatrogenic cases are created. Narcolepsy is the important hypersomnia and it is best understood as an intrusion of REM sleep into waking life. Its four features are recurrent irresistible sleep attacks ; cataplexy , a sudden loss of muscle tone while awake, typically triggered by emotion such as laughter, which is REM atonia occurring out of place; sleep paralysis , the inability to move on falling asleep or waking, again atonia out of place; and hypnagogic hallucinations , dreamlike experiences at sleep onset. Narcoleptic patients also enter REM sleep immediately rather than after the usual descent through the stages. The cause in most cases is loss of the orexin neurons of the lateral hypothalamus, with evidence pointing to an autoimmune mechanism. Once you see narcolepsy as dysregulated REM, all four symptoms follow from one lesion. Finally, on long-term sleep reduction : studies of people who gradually reduce their sleep, and of natural short sleepers who function well on very few hours, suggest that reduced sleep tends to lose light sleep preferentially while preserving slow-wave sleep, and that sleep may be more efficient when compressed. Pinel is careful to note that these findings do not license general advice to sleep less, and that the long-term consequences are inadequately studied. Worked example A student sleeps four hours instead of eight before an exam. Which sleep did they actually lose, and what should the consequences be? Because slow-wave sleep is front-loaded and REM increases across the night, truncating the second half of the night removes disproportionately more REM than slow-wave sleep. Predicted consequences: attention and executive function will be measurably impaired while basic physical capacity is not, and there will be microsleeps , which are the main mechanism of lapses in a long test. On the following night expect a partial and selective recovery, with a REM rebound, rather than a full eight hours of make-up sleep. Now the second half of the question, which is the one that separates a good answer: why is it a mistake to fix this with a benzodiazepine the night before? Because it suppresses slow-wave and REM sleep, so it buys unconsciousness at the cost of the sleep stages that are selectively defended and that are implicated in memory consolidation, and it leaves residual daytime drowsiness. 15. Drug use, addiction and the brain's reward circuits The addiction chapter is built around a single question: what changes in a brain such that a person keeps taking a drug they want to stop taking? Pinel works through three successive answers, discards the first, refines the second, and lands on a distinction between wanting and liking that is the chapter's real contribution. Basic pharmacological principles Routes of administration matter more than they look. Injected, inhaled or smoked drugs reach the brain quickly and produce a sharp rise in concentration; drugs taken orally are absorbed slowly, unpredictably and are partly broken down first. The reason this matters for addiction is that rate of rise , not just amount, determines how rewarding a dose feels, which is why smoking or injecting a drug is far more addictive than swallowing the same quantity. Note the corollary: the same molecule can have quite different addictive potential depending on how it is taken, which is why coca leaf and crack cocaine belong in different risk categories. Most drugs are metabolised by liver enzymes into inactive forms and excreted. Drug tolerance is a decreased sensitivity resulting from exposure, so that a larger dose is needed for the same effect, and it comes in two mechanistically distinct kinds. Metabolic tolerance means the drug is being eliminated faster, typically because liver enzymes have been upregulated, so less reaches the site of action. Functional tolerance means the nervous system itself has become less responsive, typically through receptor downregulation. Most tolerance to psychoactive drugs is functional. Cross-tolerance is tolerance to one drug conferred by exposure to another, which occurs where they act on the same system, and it is why alcohol and benzodiazepines cross-tolerate. Tolerance as a rightward shift of the dose-response curve. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 15.1 Two refinements of tolerance are worth having because they show that tolerance is partly learned rather than purely pharmacological. Contingent drug tolerance is the finding that tolerance develops to those effects of a drug that are actually experienced while the drug is in the body: in the standard before-and-after design, animals that perform a task while intoxicated develop tolerance to the drug's effect on that task, while animals given the same doses but tested afterwards do not. Conditioned drug tolerance is situationally specific: tolerance is greatest in the environment in which the drug has usually been taken, because cues in that environment come to elicit compensatory responses in advance. The clinical implication is grim and well documented: taking a usual dose in an unfamiliar setting removes the conditioned compensation and can produce a fatal overdose at a dose that has been tolerated many times elsewhere. The relation between drug tolerance and withdrawal effects. The same adaptive neurophysiological changes that develop in response to drug exposure and produce drug tolerance manifest themselves as withdrawal effects once the drug is removed… Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 15.2 Contingent tolerance to the anticonvulsant effect of alcohol. The rats that received alcohol before each convulsive stimulation became tolerant to its anticonvulsant effect Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 15.3 Withdrawal is the appearance of adverse effects on cessation, and the withdrawal syndrome is typically opposite in direction to the drug's own effects, which is exactly what one expects if the nervous system had adapted in the opposite direction. A person who displays withdrawal is physically dependent . Sensitisation is the opposite of tolerance, an increase in sensitivity with repeated exposure, and it is important because it shows that the two directions of change can occur to different effects of the same drug at the same time. The situational specificity of tolerance to the hypothermic effects of alcohol in rats. Notice that the definition contains no reference to withdrawal, and that this is deliberate. Five drugs, and their mechanisms Tobacco. The psychoactive agent is nicotine , an agonist at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors , which also produces dopamine release in the reward circuit. Dependence is strong and relapse rates after quitting are among the highest of any drug. The harms are largely not from nicotine but from smoke: chronic respiratory disease and the constellation Pinel calls smoker's syndrome , elevated cancer risk, cardiovascular disease including Buerger's disease , and, in pregnancy, teratogenic effects with increased risk of miscarriage, low birth weight and later problems. In population terms tobacco and alcohol cause vastly more death and disability than the illegal drugs, which is a point Pinel makes deliberately because legal status tracks history rather than harm. Global prevalence of addiction to each of six commonly used psychoactive drugs. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 15.5 Alcohol. A depressant whose principal actions are as an agonist at GABA A receptors (increasing inhibition) and an antagonist at NMDA glutamate receptors (decreasing excitation), which together account for sedation, anxiolysis, disinhibition and the disruption of memory formation, since NMDA receptors are the LTP mechanism of Chapter 11. Its withdrawal syndrome is one of the few that can be fatal, progressing through tremor and agitation to delirium tremens and convulsions, and this follows directly from the pharmacology: a nervous system that has compensated for chronic inhibition and reduced excitation is left, on withdrawal, in a state of dangerous hyperexcitability. Long-term harms include cirrhosis of the liver, Korsakoff's syndrome through thiamine deficiency (Chapter 1), direct brain damage, and fetal alcohol syndrome , whose features include intellectual disability, characteristic facial anomalies and growth deficiency, and for which no safe level of exposure has been established. Cannabis. The main psychoactive constituent is THC , which acts at CB1 cannabinoid receptors , whose endogenous ligands are the endocannabinoids such as anandamide that Chapter 4 introduced as retrograde messengers. CB1 receptors are dense in the hippocampus, which is the straightforward explanation for the reliable disruption of memory formation during intoxication. Effects on motor performance and reaction time are real. The strongest long-term concern in the literature is an association with psychosis in vulnerable individuals, particularly with early and heavy use, and the direction of causation is debated, which is how it should be reported. Cocaine and the stimulants. Cocaine acts principally as a dopamine reuptake blocker , so dopamine accumulates in the synapse. Its effects are euphoria, energy and confidence; use tends to occur in sprees of repeated dosing followed by a crash, and the pattern is driven by the short duration of action. Crack , the smokable free base, is far more addictive for the reason given above, namely the steepness of the rise. High-dose chronic use can produce cocaine psychosis , closely resembling paranoid schizophrenia, which is one of the observations that supported the dopamine hypothesis of Chapter 18. Amphetamines act by the mechanism worked through in Chapter 4. Opioids. Morphine and heroin (which is more lipid-soluble and therefore enters the brain faster, hence more addictive) are agonists at opioid receptors , whose endogenous ligands are the endorphins . Their effects are analgesia, sedation and intense euphoria. Withdrawal is severe and highly aversive but, unlike alcohol withdrawal, rarely dangerous, which is a distinction worth keeping straight. Much of the harm associated with heroin in practice arises from illegality and route of administration, that is, from uncertain purity, contaminated supply, needle-borne infection and overdose, rather than from the drug's direct toxicity. Three theories of addiction Physical-dependence theories hold that people become addicted to escape or avoid withdrawal. This was the standard account and it fails on several counts, each of which is a good exam point. Detoxified addicts, whose withdrawal is long over, relapse at high rates, and if withdrawal avoidance were the motive there would be nothing left to avoid. Addicts frequently relapse after long drug-free periods. Some highly addictive drugs, notably cocaine, produce comparatively mild physical withdrawal. And many patients given opioids for pain, and therefore made physically dependent, do not become addicted. Physical dependence and addiction are separate phenomena that happen to co-occur. Two behavioral paradigms that are used extensively in the study of the neural mechanisms of addiction: the drug self-administration paradigm and the conditioned place-preference paradigm. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 15.8 Positive-incentive theories hold instead that people take drugs for the anticipated pleasure , and that the driver of relapse is craving , the anticipation of that pleasure, rather than the avoidance of discomfort. This is much better supported, and it parallels exactly the move from set-point to positive-incentive thinking in Chapter 12. Historic influences that shaped current thinking about the brain mechanisms of addiction. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 15.9 Incentive-sensitisation theory , developed by Terry Robinson and Kent Berridge , is the refinement that resolves the chapter's central puzzle. It rests on separating two things that ordinary language conflates: wanting a drug (its incentive salience, how much it is craved and pursued) and liking it (the pleasure actually obtained). The theory's claim is that repeated use sensitises the wanting system while tolerance develops to the liking. So over time the drug is craved more and enjoyed less, and the two curves move in opposite directions. That accounts for the defining clinical observation, which no earlier theory explains: addicts describe overwhelming compulsion to use a drug that they no longer particularly enjoy. It also explains cue-triggered relapse, since incentive salience attaches to drug-associated cues, and it locates the pathology in a motivational system rather than in a hedonic one. A further development the chapter notes is the shift from voluntary to habitual control: early drug use is goal-directed and sensitive to consequences, while with prolonged use control appears to migrate to the dorsal striatum and the behaviour becomes habitual and stimulus-driven, which is the same shift down the hierarchy that Chapter 8 described for motor skills. Addiction on this account is partly a motor habit that has captured the machinery of skill. The three stages in the development of an addiction. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 15.10 High-yield Contingent tolerance = tolerance only to effects experienced while drugged; conditioned tolerance = situation-specific, and its failure in a novel setting causes overdose. Withdrawal effects are opposite in direction to the drug's effects. Physical-dependence theories fail because relapse occurs long after withdrawal ends, cocaine has mild withdrawal, and medical patients made dependent often do not become addicted. Robinson and Berridge, incentive sensitisation : wanting sensitises while liking shows tolerance, so the drug is craved more and enjoyed less. The reward circuit, and what dopamine actually signals The circuit was found by accident. James Olds and Peter Milner in 1954 were stimulating the reticular formation in rats when they found that an animal would return to the place where it had been stimulated, and then that rats would press a lever to deliver stimulation to certain sites, sometimes at extraordinary rates and in preference to food. This is intracranial self-stimulation , and the effective sites lay along the medial forebrain bundle . The immediate interpretation was that they had found the brain's pleasure centres. A rat pressing a lever to obtain rewarding brain stimulation. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 15.6 The anatomy that emerged is the mesotelencephalic dopamine system : dopaminergic cell bodies in the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra of the midbrain, projecting forward, with the mesolimbic branch reaching the nucleus accumbens and other limbic sites and the mesocortical branch reaching prefrontal cortex . The nucleus accumbens is the convergence point that matters: essentially every drug with abuse potential, by whatever primary mechanism, increases dopamine there, and so do natural rewards such as food and sex. That is a genuinely unifying finding, since it explains why chemically unrelated drugs are addictive. The mesotelencephalic dopamine system: nigrostriatal pathway in green, mesocorticolimbic in red. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 15.7 But the pleasure-centre interpretation did not survive, and this is the chapter's most important conceptual correction. Blocking dopamine does not abolish the pleasure of a reward: animals with dopamine depleted continue to show the normal hedonic reactions to a sweet taste. What is lost is the pursuit : they no longer work for it. Conversely, dopamine neurons fire in response to reward- predicting cues and to rewards that are better than predicted, rather than tracking the pleasure of consumption. The conclusion is that the mesolimbic dopamine system mediates wanting , incentive salience and the learning of reward predictions, and not liking . This is what supplies the physiology for incentive-sensitisation theory: there is a wanting system that can be sensitised independently of any hedonic system. Two behavioural paradigms are used throughout this literature. In the drug self-administration paradigm the animal presses a lever for an intravenous infusion, and it maps which drugs are reinforcing and how hard an animal will work for them. In the conditioned place preference paradigm the drug is given in one distinctive compartment and, later and drug-free, the animal's preference between compartments is measured, which assesses the drug's rewarding value without any need for the animal to perform an operant response while intoxicated. The second design is the more elegant, because it removes the confound of the drug's own effects on motor performance. Relapse, and treatment Relapse is the clinical problem, and three causes are established, each with its own therapeutic implication. Stress reinstates drug seeking. Drug priming , a single dose, reinstates it, which is the pharmacological basis for the abstinence-based advice that one drink is not a neutral event. And drug-associated cues , the places, people and paraphernalia associated with use, reinstate it, which is the incentive-salience mechanism operating and the reason that changing environment is a real component of treatment rather than a platitude. Prefrontal cortex function, which supports the inhibition of prepotent responses, is impaired in chronic users, which means the control system is weakened at the same time as the drive is sensitised. Incubation of cocaine craving in rats that were previously self-administering cocaine. After cocaine withdrawal, there was a time-dependent increase in the number of lever presses the rats made in response to a drug-associated cue. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 15.11 Treatments follow the mechanisms. Agonist maintenance replaces the drug with a longer-acting, orally administered agonist at the same receptors, methadone for opioid dependence being the standard case; the rationale is precisely the route-of-administration point from the start of the chapter, since a slow oral rise occupies the receptor without producing the reinforcing surge. Antagonist treatment, such as naltrexone , blocks the receptor so that use produces no effect. Aversive treatment, such as disulfiram for alcohol, makes drinking unpleasant by blocking a step in alcohol metabolism so that a toxic intermediate accumulates. None is highly effective alone, and Pinel's honest summary is that addiction remains a disorder with high relapse rates whatever the treatment, which is what you would expect of a sensitised, cue-driven, habitual system operating against a weakened inhibitory one. Worked example A person has used heroin at the same dose in the same room for two years, then takes that exact dose in an unfamiliar place and dies of respiratory depression. Explain, and then explain why they were still using at all if they reported no longer enjoying it. The first half is conditioned drug tolerance : much of their tolerance was situationally specific, with cues in the usual room eliciting anticipatory compensatory responses that offset the drug's effect on respiration. In a novel setting those cues are absent, the compensation does not occur, and the pharmacologically identical dose now produces its full unopposed effect, which for an opioid means fatal respiratory depression. The second half is incentive sensitisation : liking shows tolerance while wanting is sensitised, so the drug's hedonic return had fallen while the craving it generated, and the incentive salience of every cue associated with it, had grown. Add the impairment of prefrontal inhibitory control and the migration of the behaviour to dorsal-striatal habit, and continued use in the absence of pleasure is exactly what the theory predicts rather than a paradox. 16. Lateralisation, language and the split brain The two cerebral hemispheres look like mirror images and are not functional duplicates. This chapter establishes that asymmetry, then uses the most extraordinary patients in neuroscience to show what each hemisphere can do alone, and then turns to the specific case of language, where it delivers a warning about a model that every textbook teaches and that is largely wrong in its details. Establishing cerebral lateralisation The observation that started it all was clinical. In 1861 Paul Broca reported a patient (Leborgne, known as Tan for the syllable he could still produce) whose speech was lost and whose autopsy showed damage to the left inferior frontal lobe, and he went on to report further cases with left-sided damage. In 1874 Carl Wernicke described a different aphasia, with fluent but meaningless speech and impaired comprehension, following damage to the left posterior temporal region. Two independent syndromes, both from the left . Adding the observation that apraxia (Chapter 8) also follows left-hemisphere damage, the nineteenth century concluded that the left hemisphere was dominant , a term that carried an unhelpful implication of the right hemisphere as a spare. The cerebral hemispheres and cerebral commissures. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 16.1 Three methods put the claim on firmer ground. The sodium amytal test , introduced by Juhn Wada , injects an anaesthetic into the carotid artery on one side, briefly anaesthetising that hemisphere; the patient is asked to speak, and speech is disrupted only when the language-dominant hemisphere is anaesthetised. It is done before neurosurgery, precisely because the answer cannot be assumed. The dichotic listening test , developed by Doreen Kimura , presents different sequences of digits to the two ears simultaneously and asks for recall. Most people report more digits from the right ear, which, because auditory projections are predominantly contralateral, indicates left-hemisphere superiority for the material. Its virtue is that it works on healthy people and is non-invasive. Functional imaging now shows the asymmetry directly, with language tasks producing predominantly left-hemisphere activation in most people. Two further facts are worth carrying. There are anatomical asymmetries that correspond to the functional ones, notably in the planum temporale and in the length and angle of the lateral (Sylvian) fissure, and these are present in newborns, which argues that the asymmetry is not simply produced by learning to talk. And the relation to handedness is looser than folklore suggests: virtually all right-handers are left-dominant for language, and so are the majority of left-handers, with a minority showing right or bilateral representation. You cannot infer language dominance from handedness, which is why the Wada test exists. The split brain The corpus callosum is the largest of the cerebral commissures, and until the middle of the twentieth century its function was unknown, since cutting it appeared to produce no deficit at all. Two lines of work solved that. Ronald Myers and Roger Sperry worked with cats, and their design is the key to everything that follows. To show that the callosum transfers learning between hemispheres, you must first arrange for the learning to reach only one hemisphere. They did this by cutting the callosum and the optic chiasm sagittally, which severs the crossing fibres and leaves each eye projecting only to the hemisphere on its own side. With one eye patched, a cat could be taught a visual discrimination, and then tested with the other eye. Intact cats performed well with either eye, since the callosum had shared the learning. Split-brain cats, taught through one eye, performed at chance through the other, and could even be taught the opposite discrimination through the second eye without conflict. Each hemisphere had learned independently and neither knew what the other knew. Restricting visual information to one hemisphere in cats. To restrict visual information to one hemisphere, Myers and Sperry (1) cut the corpus callosum, (2) cut the optic chiasm, and (3) blindfolded one eye. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 16.3 The human work followed from a surgical treatment. Commissurotomy , transection of the corpus callosum, was performed by Philip Vogel and Joseph Bogen for otherwise uncontrollable epilepsy, on the reasoning that it would confine seizures to one hemisphere. It worked, and the patients seemed remarkably normal in ordinary life, which is itself informative. Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga then designed the tests that revealed what had happened, and Sperry received the 1981 Nobel Prize for the work. Myers and Sperry (1953): the four groups, and the result that made the split brain a research programme. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 16.4 The testing method is the whole trick, and any answer on this topic should explain it. Because each hemisphere receives the contralateral visual field (Chapter 6), a stimulus flashed briefly to one side of a fixation point, too briefly for an eye movement, reaches only one hemisphere. Objects placed unseen in one hand are likewise felt by one hemisphere. Speech comes from the left. So: The testing procedure for split-brain patients: one visual field, one hemisphere, one hand. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 16.5 An object flashed to the right visual field (left hemisphere) is named readily. The same object flashed to the left visual field (right hemisphere) cannot be named; the patient may deny seeing anything. But the left hand , controlled by the right hemisphere, can pick it out from an array by touch. The information is present and usable; it simply has no access to speech. An object placed in the left hand cannot be named, but can be matched. Several further phenomena deepen the picture. Cross-cueing is the patients' habit of finding indirect routes between the hemispheres: the right hemisphere, unable to speak, produces a behaviour or a grimace that the left hemisphere can observe and interpret, so information appears to transfer when in fact it has gone out through the world and back. The experimenter must control for this, and it is a good general lesson about hidden channels in a clever preparation. The helping-hand phenomenon is the sight of one hand correcting the other's error, which makes the independence of the two systems visceral. The chimeric figures test presents a face made of two different half-faces, one to each field; asked to point to the face they saw, patients pick the left-field (right-hemisphere) half, while asked to name it they name the right-field half, and each hemisphere is satisfied with its own answer. The Z lens , a contact lens that restricts input to one hemisphere while allowing free eye movement, permitted longer and more naturalistic testing than brief flashes. When the right hemisphere is induced to produce a behaviour whose cause the left hemisphere cannot know, the left hemisphere does not report ignorance. It confabulates a plausible reason, confidently. That result has implications well beyond split-brain patients: it suggests that verbal explanation of one's own behaviour is a construction after the fact, and that the sense of knowing why one acted may often be a story rather than a report. Gazzaniga's interpreter: the left hemisphere invents reasons. What the hemispheres actually differ in The reliable differences are narrower than popular psychology claims, and Pinel is explicit about this. The left hemisphere is superior for language (speech, writing, phonology, syntax) and for controlling sequences of voluntary movement, including the ipsilateral apraxias. The right hemisphere is superior for spatial ability, for aspects of musical and emotional processing, and for the recognition of faces and of emotional tone in speech. The right hemisphere is not without language: split-brain and Wada evidence shows it can comprehend a good deal, particularly concrete nouns, while being poor at production and at syntax. Abilities that display some degree of cerebral lateralization. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Table 16.1 Three theories attempt to state the difference at a deeper level. The analytic-synthetic theory holds that the left hemisphere is specialised for analytic, sequential, piecemeal processing and the right for synthetic, holistic processing. It is the most popular and, Pinel notes, the least testable, because almost any result can be accommodated by relabelling the task. The motor theory holds that the left hemisphere is specialised not for language as such but for fine motor control, of which speech is the most demanding instance, which accounts for the co-occurrence of aphasia and apraxia. The linguistic theory holds that the left hemisphere's specialisation is specifically for language, including its written and signed forms, and its strongest support is that deaf signers with left-hemisphere damage develop aphasia for sign , which shows the specialisation is for language rather than for speech sounds or for the vocal apparatus. That last finding is worth remembering because it decides between two of the theories with a single observation. Trap "Left-brained" and "right-brained" people, and the idea that creativity lives in the right hemisphere, are not findings; they are folklore built on a real but modest asymmetry. The differences are relative, both hemispheres participate in almost everything, and the callosum normally makes them one system. In an answer, state the specific dominances with their evidence and then say the popular dichotomy is unsupported. The older idea that bilingualism impairs cognitive development has not survived. The areas in which reading-associated increases in activity were observed in the fMRI study of Bavelier and colleagues (1997). Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 16.14 On dyslexia , the essential distinction is between developmental dyslexia , present from the beginning of learning to read, and acquired dyslexia , caused by brain damage in a previously literate person. Acquired dyslexia divides usefully into surface dyslexia , in which the reader has lost the ability to recognise words as wholes and must sound them out, so that irregular words are misread as though they were regular, and deep dyslexia , in which the reader has lost the ability to sound words out and must rely on whole-word recognition, so that unfamiliar words and nonsense words cannot be read at all and errors are often semantic. The two syndromes are the clearest evidence that skilled reading uses two routes, a phonological one and a lexical one, and that each can be lost separately. Developmental dyslexia is most consistently associated with a phonological processing deficit, a difficulty in representing and manipulating the sound structure of words, and it is on that basis that phonologically explicit instruction is the intervention with the best support. Worked example A split-brain patient is shown a snow scene to the left visual field and a chicken claw to the right, and asked to choose a related picture with each hand. The left hand picks a shovel, the right hand picks a chicken. Asked why he chose the shovel, he says "to clean out the chicken shed". Explain every part of this. The chicken claw went to the left hemisphere, which chose the chicken with the right hand and can speak about it. The snow scene went to the right hemisphere, which chose the shovel with the left hand and cannot speak. When asked to explain the shovel, the left hemisphere has no access to the snow scene: it can see the shovel choice but not its cause. It does not say "I don't know". It constructs a reason that reconciles the shovel with the only premise it has, the chicken, and it reports that reason with full confidence. This is Michael Gazzaniga's interpreter , and its wider implication is that verbal accounts of one's own reasons can be post-hoc constructions rather than reports, in intact brains as well as split ones. 17. Biopsychology of emotion, stress and health The emotion chapter has a clean spine: a century-old argument about whether bodily change causes emotion or follows it, a search for the emotional brain that kept getting narrower until it settled on one structure, and then the pathological case of chronic stress, where the emotion system damages the body it is meant to protect. Darwin, and the three classical theories Charles Darwin 's The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals (1872) made the founding argument: emotional expressions evolved from behaviours that once had a direct practical function and came to serve as signals , they are broadly similar across related species and across human groups, and they are therefore products of evolution rather than of culture alone. Two implications shaped everything after: expressions should be substantially universal, and there should be a small set of basic ones. Two woodcuts from Darwin’s 1872 book, The Expression of Emotions in Man and Animals, that he used to illustrate the principle of antithesis. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 17.2 Then the argument about mechanism. Consider the sequence: you perceive a threat, your body changes (heart pounds, muscles tense), and you feel afraid. In what order? The James-Lange theory , proposed independently by William James and Carl Lange , reverses the common-sense order. The perception of the situation triggers the bodily and autonomic response first , and the experience of emotion is the perception of that response. You do not tremble because you are afraid; you are afraid because you tremble. The Cannon-Bard theory , from Walter Cannon and Philip Bard , holds instead that the emotional stimulus triggers both the bodily response and the emotional experience simultaneously and independently , both driven from the brain, so neither causes the other. Cannon's objections to James-Lange are the ones to reproduce: autonomic responses are too slow to precede the very rapid onset of emotional feeling; autonomic responses are too undifferentiated , being much the same in fear and anger, to account for the variety of distinct emotions; and animals whose visceral feedback is surgically interrupted still show emotional behaviour. Four ways of relating the perception of a stimulus, the bodily reaction, and the feeling: the commonsense, James-Lange, Cannon-Bard and modern views. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 17.3 The Schachter-Singer theory is the cognitive synthesis. Bodily arousal supplies the intensity of an emotion but is too non-specific to supply its identity, so the person attributes the arousal to a cause available in the situation, and that cognitive labelling determines which emotion is felt. Physiological arousal plus cognitive appraisal equals emotion. Its supporting evidence is the finding that arousal produced by one source can be misattributed to another and experienced as an emotion appropriate to the second. The modern position is not a winner but a partial vindication of all three, and Pinel's summary is that the three factors, perception of the situation, bodily response and cognitive interpretation, all influence each other rather than forming a line. The clearest evidence that James was not simply wrong is the facial feedback hypothesis : adopting a facial expression influences the emotion experienced, so feedback from the body does contribute to feeling, even if it is not the whole of it. High-yield James-Lange: bodily response first, emotion is the perception of it. Cannon-Bard: bodily response and emotional experience occur in parallel, both from the brain. Walter Cannon's three objections: too slow, too undifferentiated, and emotion survives interruption of visceral feedback. Schachter-Singer: undifferentiated arousal plus cognitive attribution. Facial feedback supports a role for bodily feedback. Biopsychological investigation of emotion: six early landmarks. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Table 17.1 The search for the emotional brain Walter Cannon's own work included the phenomenon of sham rage : cats whose cortex is removed display sudden, exaggerated, poorly directed aggressive displays to mild provocation. The interpretation is that the machinery for the emotional response is subcortical and the cortex normally inhibits and directs it, which is a general principle worth carrying into psychiatry. A reconstruction of the brain injury of Phineas Gage. The damage focused on the medial prefrontal lobes. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 17.1 James Papez proposed a circuit for emotion, and Paul MacLean developed it into the limbic system theory : emotion is mediated by the ring of structures around the brain stem introduced in Chapter 3, and the theory further proposed that these older structures mediate emotion while newer cortex mediates thought. The theory has not survived intact: the limbic structures turn out to have distinct rather than shared functions (the hippocampus is chiefly a memory structure), and the label "limbic system" is now more anatomical convenience than functional claim. But it narrowed the search usefully. The location of the structures that Papez proposed controlled emotional expression. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 17.4 What narrowed it decisively was Klüver-Bucy syndrome . Bilateral removal of the anterior temporal lobes in monkeys, including the amygdala, produces a striking constellation: profound tameness and loss of fear, including of previously terrifying stimuli such as snakes; a tendency to examine objects with the mouth; indiscriminate hypersexuality ; and failure to recognise objects visually. The tameness is the crucial component, because it points to the amygdala specifically, and comparable features have been reported in humans after bilateral temporal damage. Categories of aggressive and defensive behaviors in rats. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Table 17.2 Fear conditioning, and the two roads to the amygdala The paradigm that made the amygdala tractable is fear conditioning : pair a neutral tone with a mild shock, and the tone comes to elicit fear responses. The programme is chiefly associated with Joseph LeDoux , and its findings are the most detailed emotional circuit in the book. Auditory fear conditioning depends on the amygdala , and specifically on its lateral nucleus receiving auditory input and its central nucleus driving the outputs (autonomic, endocrine and behavioural). Two anatomical routes carry the sound there, and the pair is the chapter's signature idea. A short subcortical route runs from the auditory thalamus directly to the amygdala: it is fast and carries a crude, unanalysed version of the stimulus. A longer route runs from the auditory thalamus to auditory cortex and then to the amygdala: it is slower and carries a fully analysed representation. The functional logic is a speed-accuracy trade-off that favours survival, since a system that can begin to react to a possible threat before identifying it will sometimes waste a response but will never be too late. It also gives a neat account of a common experience: the startle that precedes, and is not cancelled by, the recognition that the shape on the path is a stick. The structures mediating the sympathetic and behavioural responses conditioned to a sound. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 17.9 A second distinction is that contextual fear conditioning, in which fear becomes attached to the place rather than to a discrete cue, additionally requires the hippocampus , which fits the hippocampus's role in representing spatial context (Chapter 11). In humans, amygdala damage impairs the recognition of fear in facial expressions and the acquisition of conditioned fear, while leaving the ability to identify the faces intact; the most-cited case is patient S.M. , whose amygdalae were destroyed by Urbach-Wiethe disease and who shows a striking absence of ordinary fear responses. Meanwhile medial prefrontal cortex is implicated in the regulation of amygdala-driven fear, notably in the extinction of conditioned fear, which is the theoretical basis for exposure therapy being an active learning process rather than a passive fading. Horizontal, sagittal, and coronal functional MRIs show areas of increased activity in the primary motor cortex (M1) and the premotor cortex (PMC) when volunteers watched facial expressions of emotion. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 17.10 Expression: universality, and the muscles that give it away Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen 's cross-cultural work supported Charles Darwin's prediction, identifying a small set of primary emotions whose facial expressions are recognised across widely separated cultures, conventionally happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust, with contempt sometimes added. Universality of recognition does not mean expressions are uncontrolled: cultures differ in display rules governing when expressions are shown. Ekman's six primary facial expressions. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 17.5 Three further findings deserve their place. The facial feedback hypothesis , mentioned above, that expressions influence feeling. The distinction between genuine and false expressions , of which the best example is the smile: a genuine (Duchenne) smile involves the orbicularis oculi around the eyes, which is difficult to contract voluntarily, whereas a posed smile uses mainly the mouth, which is why the eyes are the tell. And microexpressions , brief involuntary expressions that leak the suppressed emotion before voluntary control reasserts itself. The effects of facial expression on the experience of emotion. Participants reported feeling more happy and less angry when they viewed slides while making a happy face and less happy and more angry when they viewed slides while making an a… Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 17.6 A fake smile. The orbicularis oculi and the zygomaticus major are two muscles that contract during genuine (Duchenne) smiles. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 17.7 Lateralisation shows up here too: emotional expression tends to be somewhat stronger on the left side of the face, consistent with right-hemisphere dominance for emotional expression, which is a neat convergence with Chapter 16. An expression of pride. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 17.8 The applied case is polygraphy , and it should be reported sceptically because that is what the evidence supports. A polygraph measures autonomic arousal, not deception, and there is no autonomic signature of lying. The control-question technique compares responses to relevant questions with responses to control questions, and its weakness is that an innocent but anxious person may respond strongly to the relevant question. The guilty-knowledge technique is methodologically stronger: it tests for recognition of details of the crime that only a guilty person would know, so a differential response indicates knowledge rather than anxiety. Even so, accuracy is well below what legal use would require, and countermeasures are possible. The asymmetry of facial expressions. Notice that the expressions are more obvious on the left side of two well-known faces: those of Mona Lisa and Albert Einstein. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 17.11 Stress A stressor is a threat, real or perceived, and the stress response is a coordinated pattern of physiological change. Two systems produce it, and separating them is essential. The two-system view of the stress response: the anterior-pituitary-adrenal-cortex route and the sympathetic-adrenal-medulla route. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 17.12 The sympathetic-adrenal-medullary route is fast: sympathetic activation of the adrenal medulla releases epinephrine and norepinephrine, producing the immediate fight-or-flight profile described in Chapter 3. The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is slower and hormonal, and its three steps must be in order: the hypothalamus releases corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) into the portal system; the anterior pituitary releases adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) into the bloodstream; the adrenal cortex releases glucocorticoids , chiefly cortisol in humans. Cortisol mobilises energy, raising blood glucose, and suppresses inflammation and immune activity. Circulating cortisol feeds back to inhibit CRH and ACTH release, which is the brake that normally terminates the response. Hans Selye described the response as the general adaptation syndrome , with three stages: alarm , the initial mobilisation; resistance , a period of sustained coping with elevated glucocorticoids; and exhaustion , in which the resources fail and the organism becomes vulnerable to illness. Selye's central and enduring claim is that the response is non-specific : physically and psychologically very different stressors produce a largely similar physiological pattern. The standing criticism is that this understates real differences between stressors, and in particular that psychological stressors, especially those involving unpredictability and lack of control, are especially potent. The crucial reframing is the difference between acute and chronic stress. Everything in the stress response is adaptive on the timescale of minutes: mobilising glucose, raising blood pressure and postponing immune and digestive activity are exactly right for an emergency that will be over shortly. The same responses sustained for months are damaging, because the body is running an emergency program as a baseline. Nothing has malfunctioned; a short-term program is being run long-term. Stress and health Immune function. The field of psychoneuroimmunology studies the interactions among psychological factors, the nervous system and the immune system, and the core finding is that chronic stress is immunosuppressive , mediated substantially by glucocorticoids, with measurable consequences including slower wound healing, poorer vaccine response and increased susceptibility to infection. The relationship is not simple, since acute stress can transiently enhance some immune measures, and the modern emphasis is as much on chronic inflammation and cytokine signalling as on suppression. Cytokines also signal to the brain and produce the lethargy and withdrawal of illness, which is one of the routes by which inflammation is implicated in depression (Chapter 18). Phagocytosis: A phagocyte about to ingest and destroy bacteria (red blobs). Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 17.13 Gastric ulcers are the case study in getting the causal story right. Ulcers were the standard example of a psychosomatic illness caused by stress, until it was established that the bacterium Helicobacter pylori is the necessary agent. But the correction is not that stress is irrelevant: most people carrying the bacterium do not develop ulcers, and stress appears to contribute to whether they do. The honest formulation is that a pathogen is necessary and stress is a contributing factor, and Pinel uses it to warn against both the purely psychological and the purely microbial account. Social stress. Studies of dominance hierarchies show that subordination stress , chronic subordinate status with low control, is associated with elevated glucocorticoids and worse health, which is the animal analogue of the well-documented social gradient in human health. The mediating variable is not stress in the abstract; it is unpredictability and lack of control . Early experience and epigenetics. The most theoretically important body of work here concerns how early life sets the sensitivity of the stress system. Rodent pups that receive high levels of maternal licking and grooming develop, as adults, a less reactive HPA axis and better regulation, and the mechanism involves epigenetic modification, specifically differences in the methylation of the glucocorticoid receptor gene in the hippocampus, which alters how efficiently the negative-feedback brake works for life. The programme is associated with Michael Meaney and colleagues, and cross-fostering shows the effect follows the rearing rather than the genes. This closes a loop that Chapter 2 opened: here is the concrete mechanism by which early experience physically and durably regulates gene expression and thereby adult physiology. The hippocampus. Prolonged exposure to high glucocorticoids damages the hippocampus, which is rich in glucocorticoid receptors, and reduced hippocampal volume is reported in conditions involving chronic stress. The consequence is a vicious circle worth naming: the hippocampus contributes to shutting the HPA axis off, so damaging it impairs the brake, which raises cortisol further. Worked example Two employees have identical workloads. One has a predictable schedule and control over how the work is done; the other is given unpredictable assignments with deadlines set by someone else. Predict the physiological difference and the health consequence, and name the mechanism. Workload is not the variable that matters. Unpredictability and lack of control are the potent features of psychological stressors, so the second employee will show a more persistently activated HPA axis , with chronically elevated cortisol , and the sustained sympathetic activation that goes with it. Consequences follow from what cortisol does when it does not stop: immunosuppression and elevated inflammation, so more frequent infection and slower healing, elevated cardiovascular risk, and, with sufficient duration, hippocampal effects that impair the very negative feedback that would normally terminate the response. Note what this predicts about intervention: giving control back should help even if the workload is unchanged, which is the point the animal subordination work and the human social-gradient data agree on. 18. Biopsychology of psychiatric disorders The final chapter applies everything preceding to the clinic, and it has an argumentative shape worth noticing: in every case the first biological theory came from noticing what a drug did, every one of those theories turned out to be too simple, and the reason each failed is the same. So read it as four instances of one methodological lesson. Schizophrenia Schizophrenia affects roughly one per cent of the population across cultures, typically emerging in late adolescence or early adulthood, somewhat earlier in men. Its symptoms are conventionally divided. Positive symptoms are additions to normal function: delusions (including delusions of persecution, grandeur and control), hallucinations (most characteristically auditory), and disorganised or incoherent thought and speech. Negative symptoms are subtractions: flat or inappropriate affect , avolition, poverty of speech, social withdrawal, anhedonia. The division matters therapeutically because the drugs work far better on the positive symptoms, and negative symptoms account for much of the long-term disability. Two framing points. Schizophrenia is not one disease with one cause; the diagnosis identifies a syndrome, and it is likely heterogeneous. And no single symptom is present in all cases, which is why diagnosis is by pattern and duration. Genetic contribution is substantial and firmly established by the convergence of family, twin and adoption studies, with concordance markedly higher in monozygotic than dizygotic twins and risk following biological rather than adoptive parentage. But concordance in monozygotic twins is well short of 100 per cent, which is itself an important result: genes confer vulnerability rather than determine the outcome, and something else must be involved. The dopamine theory. Its origin is pharmacological and worth telling in order, because it is the standard example of a theory reverse-engineered from a treatment. Chlorpromazine and reserpine , chemically unrelated, were both found to reduce schizophrenic symptoms; what they had in common was a reduction of dopamine activity, reserpine by depleting vesicular stores and chlorpromazine by blocking receptors. The theory that schizophrenia results from excessive dopaminergic activity followed. Two further lines supported it: the clinical potency of antipsychotic drugs correlates closely with their affinity for the D 2 receptor, and drugs that increase dopamine release, notably amphetamine and cocaine, can produce a psychosis closely resembling paranoid schizophrenia and can exacerbate existing symptoms. Chlorpromazine as a receptor blocker at dopamine synapses. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 18.1 The problems with the theory are as important as the evidence for it. There is a time-lag problem : receptor blockade occurs within hours, while clinical improvement takes weeks, so blockade cannot be the therapeutic event itself and must instead initiate some slower adaptation. Many patients respond poorly or not at all. Negative symptoms respond weakly. And decisively, the atypical antipsychotics , of which clozapine is the exemplar, are effective, sometimes in patients who failed on the older drugs, while having relatively low affinity for D 2 receptors and acting on serotonin and other receptors. A drug that works without doing the thing the theory says is necessary is a serious problem for the theory. The main alternative is the glutamate hypothesis , and its evidential logic mirrors the dopamine story: phencyclidine (PCP) and ketamine , which are NMDA receptor antagonists , produce a state that resembles schizophrenia more completely than amphetamine psychosis does, in that it includes negative and cognitive symptoms as well as positive ones. That points to NMDA receptor hypofunction . Neither theory excludes the other, and dopamine dysregulation may be downstream of glutamatergic abnormality. Structural and developmental findings. The most replicated anatomical findings are enlarged cerebral ventricles , with modest reductions in cortical and hippocampal volume, and functional evidence of reduced prefrontal activation during cognitive tasks ( hypofrontality ), which fits the prominent executive and working-memory deficits. These findings support the neurodevelopmental hypothesis : that the disorder originates in disturbed brain development long before symptoms appear, with the illness manifesting when the affected systems, notably prefrontal cortex, are called on in late adolescence, precisely the period Chapter 9 identified as the last to mature. Supporting epidemiological findings include associations with obstetric complications , with maternal infection during pregnancy, and the small but repeatedly observed season-of-birth effect . Cannabis use in vulnerable individuals is a further risk factor, as Chapter 15 noted. High-yield Positive versus negative symptoms; drugs treat positive symptoms better. Dopamine theory came from chlorpromazine and reserpine, is supported by the D 2 affinity/potency correlation and amphetamine psychosis, and is undermined by the therapeutic time lag, non-responders, weak effect on negative symptoms and the efficacy of low-D 2 clozapine. Glutamate hypothesis rests on PCP and ketamine as NMDA antagonists reproducing negative as well as positive symptoms. Enlarged ventricles and hypofrontality; neurodevelopmental hypothesis. Antipsychotic potency plotted against D₂ binding: the correlation that made the dopamine theory. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 18.2 Depression and bipolar disorder Major depressive disorder involves persistent depressed mood and loss of interest or pleasure, with disturbances of sleep, appetite, energy, concentration and self-worth, and elevated suicide risk. Subtypes worth naming are seasonal affective disorder , in which episodes recur at a particular time of year and which is treated with bright-light exposure, connecting it to the circadian material of Chapter 14, and peripartum depression . The older distinction between reactive depression (following an identifiable stressor) and endogenous depression (arising without one) has largely fallen out of formal use, and knowing that it has been abandoned is more useful than knowing the categories. Bipolar disorder adds episodes of mania , characterised by elevated or irritable mood, grandiosity, reduced need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts and impulsive risk-taking. Bipolar I involves full manic episodes and bipolar II involves hypomania. Heritability is substantial for both mood disorders and higher for bipolar disorder. The monoamine theory , and its failure, follows the same pattern as the dopamine theory. Its origin was again pharmacological: the monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors , discovered when a tuberculosis drug elevated mood, and the tricyclic antidepressants both increase the availability of monoamines, the first by blocking their enzymatic breakdown and the second by blocking reuptake. Reserpine, which depletes monoamines, can produce depression. The theory that depression results from a deficiency of serotonin or norepinephrine followed, and the SSRIs and SNRIs were developed on it, with the SSRIs' advantage being tolerability and safety in overdose rather than superior efficacy. The theory fails chiefly on the same time lag . An SSRI blocks reuptake within hours and raises synaptic serotonin immediately; clinical improvement takes two to four weeks. Whatever produces the improvement is therefore a slow adaptation to raised transmitter levels, not the raised levels themselves. Adding to the problem, experimentally depleting serotonin does not make healthy people depressed, and the average superiority of antidepressants over placebo in trials is modest, larger in severe depression than in mild. How fluoxetine blocks serotonin reuptake. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 18.3 The main replacement is the neuroplasticity or neurotrophic theory : depression involves reduced neurotrophic support and impaired plasticity, with reduced BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor), reduced hippocampal volume and reduced adult hippocampal neurogenesis, and antidepressant treatments work by reversing these, which takes weeks. That timescale is the theory's principal attraction, since it explains the delay that the monoamine theory cannot. It also links depression to the chronic-stress material of Chapter 17, since sustained glucocorticoid elevation reduces BDNF and damages the hippocampus. The rapid antidepressant effect of ketamine , acting at NMDA receptors and rapidly increasing synaptic plasticity, is consistent with a plasticity account and is one of the more significant recent developments, since it breaks the assumption that antidepressant action must be slow. Implantation of bilateral anterior cingulate electrodes and a stimulator for chronic deep brain stimulation for the treatment of depression. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 18.4 Other treatments: lithium is the classic mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder, effective at reducing both manic and depressive episodes, with a narrow therapeutic window requiring blood monitoring, and a mechanism that remains unsettled. Electroconvulsive therapy is genuinely effective, particularly in severe or treatment-resistant depression, with its principal cost being retrograde amnesia around the treatment period (Chapter 11), and it too has no agreed mechanism. Total sleep deprivation produces a rapid but transient antidepressant effect in some patients, which is another link to Chapter 14. The site in the anterior cingulate gyrus at which chronic brain stimulation to subcortical white matter alleviated symptoms in treatment-resistant depressed patients. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 18.5 Anxiety disorders The anxiety disorders share persistent excessive anxiety with stress-response symptoms, and are distinguished by what triggers them: generalised anxiety disorder (pervasive and not tied to a specific object), phobic disorders (specific objects or situations), panic disorder (recurrent unexpected panic attacks, frequently with agoraphobia developing as avoidance of situations where an attack would be difficult to escape), obsessive-compulsive disorder (intrusive obsessions and the compulsive acts performed to neutralise them), and post-traumatic stress disorder (following a traumatic event, with intrusive re-experiencing, avoidance and hyperarousal). Pharmacologically, the benzodiazepines are agonists at the GABA A receptor, which is why they are anxiolytic and also sedative, anticonvulsant and muscle-relaxant, and why they carry tolerance and dependence liability. The serotonin partial agonist buspirone is anxiolytic without those liabilities. And the SSRIs are first-line for most of these disorders, which is a fact worth pausing on, because a drug developed for depression being effective for anxiety disorders indicates either shared mechanism or an effect too general to be diagnostic. The animal models used are the ones from Chapter 5, notably the elevated plus maze and defensive burying , validated by their sensitivity to clinically effective anxiolytics. Neurally, the amygdala circuits of Chapter 17 are central, with medial prefrontal regulation implicated in the failure of extinction that characterises PTSD. Tourette syndrome Tourette syndrome is a disorder of tics , involuntary repetitive movements and vocalisations, with onset in childhood. Simple tics include eye blinking, head jerking, throat clearing and grunting; complex tics can include elaborate sequences of movement, echolalia (repeating others' words) and, in a minority of cases, coprolalia (involuntary utterance of obscenities), which is much rarer than popular portrayal suggests and worth correcting. Many patients report a premonitory urge and can suppress tics briefly at the cost of mounting discomfort, which is why "involuntary" needs qualifying. The implicated circuitry is the basal ganglia , particularly the caudate, and its cortical loops, and dopamine antagonists reduce tics, which is consistent with excessive dopaminergic activity in those loops. No rebound effect above baseline was observed following periods of tic suppression by children with Tourette’s disorder. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 18.6 Clinical trials: how to read the evidence Pinel ends the book with methodology rather than content, and it is the right ending. Five problems in the evaluation of psychiatric treatments deserve to be known by name. Conflict of interest. Much of the research on a drug is funded, and often conducted, by the company that will sell it, and funding source predicts outcome across the literature. The probabilities that a drug that qualifies for testing in humans will reach each phase of testing and ultimately gain approval. Only 22 percent of the drugs that initially qualify for testing eventually gain approval. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 18.7 Publication bias. Trials with positive results are far more likely to be published than trials with negative results, so the visible literature overstates efficacy. This is not a hypothetical: comparisons of published results with complete regulatory records have repeatedly shown a substantial gap, and the antidepressant literature is the standard example. The nature of the control condition. Comparison against a placebo establishes only that a drug beats nothing; the clinically useful comparison is against the best existing treatment, and that comparison is made less often. Broken blinds. A drug with noticeable side effects tells patients and clinicians which group they are in, which undermines the double blind and inflates the apparent effect. An active placebo, which produces side effects without the therapeutic action, is the fix and is rarely used. Phases of drug development. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Table 18.1 The validity of animal models. Models are usually validated by their sensitivity to drugs that already work, which builds in a bias toward finding more drugs of the same kind and against discovering mechanistically novel ones. This is a plausible part of the explanation for why psychiatric pharmacology has produced so many variations on a few mechanisms and so few genuinely new ones. The single habit these five recommend is the one Chapter 1 taught: separate what was observed from what was concluded, and ask what method produced the observation. That is what the whole book has been for. Worked example A question asks you to evaluate the dopamine theory of schizophrenia. Structure the answer so it earns the marks. State the theory, then its three supporting lines, being specific: chlorpromazine and reserpine, chemically unrelated, both reduce dopamine activity; antipsychotic clinical potency correlates with D 2 receptor affinity; amphetamine produces a psychosis resembling paranoid schizophrenia and worsens existing symptoms. Then the four objections: receptor blockade is immediate but clinical improvement takes weeks, so blockade is not the therapeutic event; many patients do not respond; negative symptoms respond poorly; and clozapine works while having low D 2 affinity. Then offer the alternative with its own evidence: NMDA hypofunction, supported by PCP and ketamine reproducing negative and cognitive symptoms as well as positive ones. Close with the structural and neurodevelopmental findings, enlarged ventricles and hypofrontality, and the conclusion that dopamine dysregulation is probably a real component of a heterogeneous, developmentally originating disorder rather than its cause. Notice that the answer's shape, evidence then anomalies then alternative then synthesis, is the same shape you would use for the monoamine theory of depression, and for the same reason. How the eighteen chapters fit together Read straight through, the book makes one argument in eighteen instalments, and it is worth stating so that the chapters stop feeling like separate subjects. Mind is something tissue does. Chapter 1 sets it up with Donald Hebb, who showed that a local physical rule about synapses, applied repeatedly, yields something recognisably psychological. Chapter 11 cashes the cheque: the NMDA receptor is a coincidence detector, so Hebb's rule is not merely implemented in the brain, it is built into the shape of a protein. Genes and experience are not two contributions. Chapter 2 argues it, Cooper and Zubek measure it, Chapter 9 shows the developmental machinery (competition, overproduction and pruning, sensitive periods), Chapter 6 gives the cleanest single demonstration in David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel's deprivation work, and Chapter 17 supplies the molecular route in the epigenetic regulation of the stress axis by early maternal care. Perception is construction, not transmission. Chapter 6 establishes it (centre-surround cells report contrast rather than brightness, the blind spot is filled, colour is computed relative to surroundings), Chapter 7 generalises it to every sense and adds attention as the selector, and Chapter 16 extends it as far as it will go with Michael Gazzaniga's interpreter inventing reasons for actions it did not cause. Deficits are not the reverse of functions. A lesion that abolishes a behaviour does not identify a centre for it: this is the warning in Chapter 5 about fibres of passage, in Chapter 12 about the supposed hypothalamic feeding and satiety centres, and in Chapter 16 about the Wernicke-Geschwind model. Motivation is pull, not push. Chapter 12 replaces set points with positive incentives, and Chapter 15 completes the move by separating wanting from liking, which is what finally makes sense of an addict who craves a drug they no longer enjoy. Adaptive machinery becomes pathology when the timescale or the environment changes. Chapter 12's storage physiology in an environment of cheap calories, Chapter 17's emergency response run for months, Chapter 10's glutamate turning excitotoxic, Chapter 15's reward circuit captured by drugs that enter it faster than anything it evolved for. Nothing is broken in any of these; a system is being run outside its design conditions. Trust the conclusion several methods agree on. Chapter 1 names it converging operations, Chapter 5 explains why every individual method is inadequate, and Chapter 18 shows what happens when the discipline is not applied: four biological theories built on what a drug happened to do, every one of them too simple, and a clinical literature distorted by publication bias.

title: Cognitive Psychology (Eysenck & Keane), in full depth
text: Cognitive Psychology (Eysenck & Keane), in full depth Eysenck and Keane's Cognitive Psychology: A Student's Handbook , rewritten as real explanatory prose instead of bullet fragments. Every concept is built from scratch in full sentences, every mechanism is walked through step by step, the experiment or the patient behind each claim is named, the theorist is named wherever there is one, and each chapter closes with a worked example that pushes a real case through the machinery rather than restating it. Read a chapter cold and you should finish it understanding the concept, not merely recognising the words. How to read this The chapter order is Eysenck and Keane's own, so it doubles as a map of the book. Approaches to human cognition Cognitive psychology is the study of the internal processes that stand between a stimulus arriving and a response coming out: attending, perceiving, recognising, remembering, understanding language, reasoning, deciding. The word that does the work in that definition is internal . Nobody has ever observed a memory trace or a decision rule directly. What is observed is that someone was shown a word list and later recalled eleven of the twenty items, or that they named a picture 80 milliseconds faster when it had been primed. Everything cognitive psychology claims about the machinery in between is an inference from such measurements, and the whole methodological argument of this chapter is about which kinds of inference are trustworthy. That is why Eysenck and Keane open not with content but with four approaches . Each is a different way of getting evidence about an invisible process, each has a characteristic strength, and each has a characteristic blind spot. When two researchers disagree about, say, whether there are two visual systems or one, the disagreement is very often not about the data at all: it is about which approach's data should be allowed to settle the matter. Get the four straight now and the rest of the book stops looking like a list of controversies. The historical starting point: behaviourism and why it broke From roughly 1920 to 1950, North American psychology was dominated by behaviourism , whose founding claim ( John B. Watson , 1913) was that psychology should confine itself to observable stimuli and observable responses, because anything in between is unobservable and therefore unscientific. This was a genuinely reasonable position at the time. Introspection, the main alternative, had produced decades of disputes that no experiment could settle: when Wilhelm Wundt's laboratory and the Würzburg school disagreed about whether thought could be imageless, there was no way to check. Behaviourism broke on several problems at once. Edward Tolman 's rats learned the layout of a maze while being rewarded for nothing (latent learning), which meant learning had happened with no reinforced response to point to; the rats had built something like a cognitive map . Noam Chomsky 's 1959 review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior argued that language could not be a chain of reinforced responses, because speakers routinely produce and understand sentences that they have never heard and that have therefore never been reinforced. And the arrival of the digital computer supplied something behaviourism had lacked: a way of talking about internal processing that was not mystical. A computer plainly has internal states, plainly transforms input into output through a sequence of operations, and is plainly a physical machine. If that is respectable for a computer, it can be respectable for a person. High-yield The cognitive revolution is usually dated to the mid-1950s and given three landmarks: Noam Chomsky 's generative grammar and his 1959 demolition of B. F. Skinner; Allen Newell and Herbert Simon 's Logic Theorist, the first program to prove theorems in the way a human might; and Donald Broadbent 's filter theory of attention (1958), the first flow-diagram model of a mental process. Miller 's "magical number seven" paper (1956) belongs on the same list. Approach 1: experimental cognitive psychology This is the oldest of the four and still the default. Its method is to run behavioural experiments on healthy participants and infer the internal processing from the pattern of results, usually reaction times and error rates. The theoretical framework it grew up inside is the information-processing approach : the mind is treated as a series of stages, each taking an input, doing something to it, and passing the result on. Stimulus, then attention, then perception, then thought, then decision, then response. That early version carried two strong assumptions worth naming, because most of the subsequent history of the field consists of weakening them. The first is seriality : one stage at a time, each finishing before the next begins. The second is that processing is bottom-up (also called stimulus-driven), meaning it is determined by the input rather than by what the perceiver already knows. Both turned out to be too strong. Processing is now generally accepted to be substantially parallel , with stages overlapping in time, and heavily top-down : expectations, context and prior knowledge shape perception rather than merely decorating it. Read a smudged handwritten word in a sentence and you will read it correctly because the sentence told you what to expect; that is top-down processing doing visible work. The great strength of this approach is control. You can manipulate one variable, hold everything else fixed, and draw a causal conclusion. Its great weakness is that reaction times are a very indirect readout. Two quite different architectures can predict the same millisecond pattern, so behavioural data frequently underdetermine the theory. A related problem is paradigm specificity : a finding may hold for the particular laboratory task used and not generalise, which is a serious charge when the task is something like naming a letter in a briefly flashed array, an activity nobody performs outside a laboratory. Eysenck and Keane also flag lack of ecological validity and, more subtly, the fact that theories in this tradition are often stated vaguely enough that they are hard to falsify. Approach 2: cognitive neuropsychology Cognitive neuropsychology studies patients with brain damage in order to work out the structure of normal cognition. The logic is not "find out what the damaged area does"; it is subtler than that, and the difference matters. The reasoning runs: if brain damage can knock out ability A while leaving ability B intact, then A and B cannot depend on exactly the same machinery. Damage is being used as a natural experiment that cuts the system apart at joints an intact brain never reveals. Four theoretical assumptions underlie it, and they are examinable as a set. Modularity : the cognitive system consists of relatively independent modules or processors, each doing one job, so that one can be damaged without the others going down. Anatomical modularity : each module is localised in a reasonably circumscribed brain region, which is what makes brain damage selective rather than global. Uniformity of functional architecture across people : the patient's cognitive system was organised like yours before the damage, otherwise nothing generalises. Subtractivity : brain damage impairs or removes processes but does not cause the system to develop new ones, so the patient is the normal system minus a part, not a different system. Single and double dissociation A single dissociation is one patient who is impaired on task A but normal on task B. It is weak evidence on its own, because task A might simply be harder, and a general loss of resources would produce the same picture. A double dissociation is two patients showing the opposite pattern: patient 1 impaired on A but not B, patient 2 impaired on B but not A. Task difficulty can no longer explain both, so the two tasks must draw on at least partly separate mechanisms.
