A World Health Organization report in 2003 estimated that adherence to long-term therapies in developed countries averages only about 50 percent. Non-adherence may be unintentional (forgetting, a confusing regimen, cost) or intentional (side effects, a belief the medicine is unnecessary), and it is worst for symptomless conditions such as high blood pressure. Psychologists simplify regimens, use reminders, check understanding with the teach-back method (the patient explains the plan in their own words), correct beliefs and involve family. Case. Mr Ramesh, fifty-two, a shopkeeper with type 2 diabetes, takes tablets irregularly and refuses insulin. In health belief model terms, he thinks diabetes is "only sugar" (low perceived severity), fears insulin means he is dying (a barrier) and has had no symptom (no cue to action). In stages of change terms he is in contemplation. Motivational interviewing explores his ambivalence, his doctor corrects the insulin belief, and his tablets are tied to a fixed habit (opening the shop). He moves to preparation and agrees to try insulin. Chronic pain , persisting beyond normal healing (commonly more than three months), is where psychology helps most. The gate control theory of Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall (1965) proposed a "gate" in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Small pain fibres open it; large touch fibres tend to close it (which is why rubbing a bumped elbow helps); and messages descending from the brain, carrying attention, anxiety, mood and expectation, open or close it. An operant approach notices that pain behaviours such as grimacing and resting can be reinforced by sympathy and escape from work, and instead rewards activity set by planned quotas. Cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) for pain targets catastrophising , teaches pacing and relaxation, and treats depression and poor sleep. Referral to a psychologist does not mean the pain is imaginary: psychological factors act on real pain transmission. Psychoneuroimmunology studies how the mind, nervous system and immune system influence each other. Robert Ader and Nicholas Cohen (1975) gave rats saccharin water together with cyclophosphamide, an immune-suppressing drug; later, saccharin alone suppressed their immune responses, so brain and immunity must communicate. In humans, Janice Kiecolt-Glaser and Ronald Glaser showed that medical students' immune function dips at examination time and that small wounds heal more slowly in people caring for a relative with dementia. The effects are real but modest; the claim that positive thinking alone cures cancer is not supported. 9.5 Clinical neuropsychology Clinical neuropsychology applies knowledge of brain-behaviour relationships to assessing and rehabilitating people with known or suspected brain dysfunction. In 1861 Paul Broca linked the left inferior frontal lobe to speech production; in 1874 Carl Wernicke linked the left posterior temporal lobe to comprehension. Alexander Luria argued that complex functions depend on functional systems spread across the brain rather than single centres. Henry Molaison (known for decades as H.M.) had both medial temporal lobes removed in 1953 to control epilepsy and could no longer form new memories of events, yet Brenda Milner showed he could learn a mirror-drawing skill without remembering practising it: the hippocampus is needed for new memories, and there is more than one memory system. Now that brain imaging shows structure directly, the neuropsychologist's main task is describing function : what the person can do, and what that means for daily life, work and legal decisions. Domain What it covers Examples of tests Attention and speed Focusing, sustaining, dividing and switching attention Digit span, Trail Making Test Part A Memory Learning new material, delayed recall, recognition Wechsler Memory Scale, Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test Executive function Planning, flexibility, inhibition, abstract reasoning Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, Stroop test, Trail Making Test Part B Language Naming, comprehension, repetition, fluency Boston Naming Test, verbal fluency Visuospatial ability Perceiving spatial relations, copying and constructing Block design, clock drawing, Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure A full assessment also estimates premorbid (pre-injury) ability, screens mood (depression lowers scores) and uses performance validity tests to check effort. Patterns count more than single scores: someone who cannot freely recall a word list but recognises the words has a retrieval problem, typical of frontal and subcortical conditions, while someone who can neither recall nor recognise has a storage problem, typical of hippocampal damage and early Alzheimer's disease. Indian tests must suit language, schooling and literacy, which is why the NIMHANS Neuropsychology Battery and the PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction (Dwarka Pershad and S. K. Verma) were built. Three referral questions dominate. In dementia , the question is whether decline exceeds normal ageing and which type is likely: early Alzheimer's disease shows a storage memory deficit, frontotemporal dementia begins with behavioural and executive change, and depression can mimic dementia but improves when the depression is treated. In traumatic brain injury , severity is judged from the Glasgow Coma Scale (Graham Teasdale and Bryan Jennett, 1974) and the length of post-traumatic amnesia ; since the frontal and temporal lobes are vulnerable, common problems are slowed processing, poor attention and memory, executive difficulty and personality change. In epilepsy , the neuropsychologist assesses effects of seizures and medication and, before surgery, maps memory and language so that surgery does not create another Henry Molaison. Rehabilitation may be restorative (retraining a function, with limited evidence) or compensatory (diaries, phone alarms, checklists). Errorless learning helps people with amnesia: because they cannot remember which attempts were wrong, trial and error ingrains mistakes, so the correct answer is supplied from the start. Case. Kiran, twenty-four, a software engineer, had about a week of post-traumatic amnesia after a motorcycle accident. Three months later his scans look almost normal, but he forgets meetings and works slowly. Testing shows average reasoning (his premorbid level), slow processing, poor free recall with good recognition, and poor set shifting on the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (David Grant and Esta Berg, 1948), with valid effort. The report explains that his problems are real despite normal scans, and recommends a graded return to work with written task lists and phone reminders. 9.6 Forensic psychology Forensic psychology applies psychology to questions raised by the law. The client is often the court or a lawyer, not the person assessed, so the evaluator explains at the start who will read the report, considers malingering (deliberately faking symptoms for gain) and should not also be the person's therapist, because helper and neutral assessor are conflicting roles. Competence to stand trial concerns the accused person's present state. The United States standard, from Dusky versus United States (1960), requires sufficient present ability to consult a lawyer with a reasonable degree of rational understanding, and a rational as well as factual understanding of the proceedings. Indian criminal procedure (the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973, now the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023) similarly provides for inquiry into whether an accused of unsound mind is incapable of making a defence. The insanity defence concerns the mental state at the time of the offence . In 1843 Daniel M'Naghten, acting on persecutory delusions, shot and killed Edward Drummond, secretary to the Prime Minister Robert Peel, apparently believing he was shooting Peel. After his acquittal, the English judges set out the M'Naghten rules : a person is not responsible if, at the time of the act, he was labouring under such a defect of reason, from disease of the mind, as not to know the nature and quality of the act, or, if he did know it, that he did not know it was wrong. This is a purely cognitive test of knowledge, not of self-control. India follows it closely. Section 84 of the Indian Penal Code 1860 states that nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law. The Indian Penal Code has been replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 , in force from 1 July 2024, where the same provision appears as section 22 . Indian courts distinguish legal insanity from medical insanity : a diagnosis of schizophrenia does not itself establish the defence; the disorder must have made the person incapable of knowing the nature or wrongness of the act at that moment, and the burden of proving this lies on the accused. The psychologist reconstructs the mental state from records, interviews and testing; the decision belongs to the court. Trap. Competence is about the present (can the person take part in the trial now); insanity is about the past (was the person responsible at the time of the act). Someone can be insane at the time of the offence and competent now, or the reverse. Also, contrary to public belief, the insanity defence is raised rarely, succeeds rarely, and those who succeed are usually detained for treatment, not set free. Risk assessment estimates the likelihood of violence, reoffending or self-harm and how it can be managed. Unstructured clinical judgement performs poorly, largely because violence is rare and clinicians overpredict it. Actuarial methods combine fixed, mostly historical factors statistically; they are more accurate but say little about reducing risk. Structured professional judgement , now dominant, rates evidence-based items and leaves the final judgement to the clinician; the best known tool is the HCR-20, whose twenty items cover Historical, Clinical and Risk management factors. Static factors (past violence) cannot change; dynamic factors (active psychosis, substance use) can, and are the targets of intervention. As an expert witness , the psychologist may give opinions within their expertise (section 45 of the Indian Evidence Act 1872, now replaced by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023), must stay within the data and leaves the ultimate issue to the court. In child custody evaluations the governing principle is the welfare of the child , treated as paramount under the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 and the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act 1956; a sound evaluation interviews both parents and the child, observes each parent with the child and focuses on parenting capacity rather than diagnosis. 9.7 Community psychology and the logic of prevention Community psychology shifts attention from the individual to the settings people live in: families, schools, workplaces, neighbourhoods. It is often dated to a 1965 conference at Swampscott, Massachusetts. Its values are prevention, an ecological view of person and environment, strengths rather than deficits, social justice and collaboration. Julian Rappaport's writing on empowerment (1981) argued for enhancing people's control over their own lives rather than treating them as passive recipients of expert help. In parallel, the community mental health movement produced the United States Community Mental Health Act of 1963, which funded local centres as large hospitals were emptied; underfunded services left many discharged patients homeless, a warning against shrinking institutions without building community care. Gerald Caplan, in Principles of Preventive Psychiatry (1964), applied public health prevention to mental disorder. Primary prevention stops new cases, reducing incidence (emotional skills programmes for all schoolchildren). Secondary prevention detects disorder early and treats it promptly, reducing prevalence (screening mothers for depression after childbirth). Tertiary prevention reduces disability and relapse in established disorder (rehabilitation for schizophrenia). Because secondary and tertiary prevention are really treatment, Robert Gordon (1983) proposed levels defined by who is targeted , and the Institute of Medicine (United States) adopted them in 1994, reserving "prevention" for work before onset. Universal prevention targets a whole population; selective prevention targets subgroups with above-average risk, such as children of depressed parents; indicated prevention targets individuals with early signs but no full disorder. In suicide prevention, restricting highly lethal pesticides (followed in Sri Lanka by a large fall in suicides) is universal, support for those bereaved by suicide is selective, and follow-up after self-harm is indicated. Caplan (1964) Aim Institute of Medicine (1994) Target Primary Reduce incidence Universal Whole population Secondary Reduce prevalence by early detection and treatment Selective Higher-risk subgroups Tertiary Reduce disability and relapse Indicated Individuals with early signs Trap. The rows are not equivalents. Caplan's levels follow the stage of disorder, and two come after onset; the Institute of Medicine levels follow the risk status of the target group, and all three come before onset. Indicated prevention sounds like secondary prevention, but it works with people who do not yet have the disorder. 9.8 Community mental health in India and task sharing India has far too few mental health professionals for its population. The National Mental Health Survey of 2015 to 2016, carried out by the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS), found a treatment gap (the share of people with a disorder receiving no treatment) of roughly 70 to over 90 percent depending on the disorder. India launched the National Mental Health Programme in 1982, aiming to make minimum mental health care available and accessible to all, especially the most vulnerable, to apply mental health knowledge in general health care and social development, and to promote community participation, chiefly by integrating mental health into primary health care . A pilot in Bellary district, Karnataka, begun in 1985, became the model for the District Mental Health Programme , launched in 1996. Its district team (typically a psychiatrist, clinical psychologist, psychiatric social worker and psychiatric nurse) runs clinics, trains primary care staff, supplies medicines and runs outreach, though evaluations have found vacancies and underused funds in many districts. Task sharing means training people without professional mental health qualifications (community health workers, lay counsellors, nurses) to deliver specific psychological tasks under supervision, while specialists handle complex cases, training and supervision. The Indian psychiatrist Vikram Patel championed it, notably in Where There Is No Psychiatrist (2003); in Goa, the Healthy Activity Program trained lay counsellors in brief behavioural activation for depression, and a randomised trial found it effective. Similar programmes include the Thinking Healthy Programme for mothers with depression in Pakistan and the Friendship Bench in Zimbabwe, where trained older women deliver problem-solving therapy. Why it matters. Task sharing changes the psychologist's question from "How many patients can I treat?" to "How many people can my training and supervision reach?" The psychologist becomes a designer of simple protocols, a trainer and a supervisor. Without ongoing supervision, lay workers burn out and drift from the protocol, so task sharing works only inside a supporting system. 9.9 Culture and what counts as a symptom Culture is the shared beliefs, values, practices, language and ways of making meaning that a group passes on. First, it shapes what counts as a symptom : hearing a dead parent's voice during mourning, or a possession state at a festival, may be expected in some communities. The DSM defines a delusion as a belief not ordinarily accepted by the person's culture, so a clinician ignorant of the culture cannot apply the definition. Second, it shapes how distress is expressed . Many people communicate distress through the body (fatigue, aches, "gas") or through words such as "tension". These are idioms of distress . Dhat syndrome , named by N. N. Wig in 1960, is a well known Indian example: young men attribute weakness, fatigue and anxiety to loss of semen, drawing on a traditional belief that semen is concentrated vital essence. The distress is real, and dismissing the belief usually ends the relationship. Third, culture shapes help seeking and treatment , taken up in 9.11. The psychiatrist and anthropologist Arthur Kleinman gave two tools. The explanatory model is the patient's own account of what the problem is, what caused it, why now and what treatment they expect; eliciting it is the first step to a plan the patient will accept. The category fallacy (1977) is the error of taking a diagnostic category built in one culture and applying it to another where it lacks coherence. The DSM-5 (2013) responded by replacing "culture-bound syndromes" with cultural concepts of distress and adding the Cultural Formulation Interview , sixteen questions about the person's own view of the problem, its causes, their cultural identity, supports and past help seeking. The emic and etic distinction comes from the linguist Kenneth Pike (1954), from phonemics (sound distinctions meaningful within one language) versus phonetics (a universal system for all speech sounds). An emic approach studies a culture from the inside, using its own categories; an etic approach uses categories assumed to be universal so that cultures can be compared. John Berry (1969) warned against the imposed etic , applying a test built in one culture elsewhere as though it were universal, and recommended a derived etic , reached by studying each culture emically first and then identifying what is truly shared. Translating a Western depression questionnaire into Hindi and scoring villagers on it is an imposed etic; building a measure from how Tamil women themselves describe distress is emic. Tests therefore need linguistic, conceptual and metric equivalence . Trap. Emic does not mean "Indian" and etic does not mean "Western". The terms describe the researcher's stance, inside or outside the culture's own categories. An Indian researcher using an unadapted Western questionnaire in an Indian village is working in an imposed etic manner. 9.10 Cultural competence, cultural humility and working across difference in India Cultural competence is the capacity to work effectively with clients whose backgrounds differ from one's own. Derald Wing Sue and colleagues set out its best known tripartite model in the early 1980s, elaborated in 1992 with Patricia Arredondo and Roderick McDavis. Awareness is knowing one's own assumptions, values, biases and privileges. Knowledge is understanding the client's worldview, history and social situation, including discrimination and barriers to care. Skills are interventions and communication styles that fit the client. Critics note that "competence" suggests something that can be mastered, and that facts about groups harden into stereotypes ("Indian clients want advice"). Melanie Tervalon and Jann Murray-Garcia (1998) proposed cultural humility : lifelong self-critique, redressing the power imbalance between clinician and client, and partnership with communities. Key. Competence without humility slides into stereotype; humility without knowledge slides into good intentions that help no one. Hold Sue's awareness, knowledge and skills with an attitude of cultural humility. Differences in India combine; Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989) called this intersectionality , so that a poor Dalit woman experiences caste, class and gender as one position, not three. Gender. Women's distress is often shaped by marriage, dowry and domestic violence, so violence should be screened for privately; men more often present through alcohol. Caste. Discrimination in schools, colleges, work and marriage is a real and often unspoken stressor, which a client may not raise unless the therapist shows it is safe. Class. Fees, travel, lost wages and the lack of a private room shape whether therapy is possible at all. Religion. Faith is often a source of coping and should not be pathologised or overridden. Language. Therapy in a second language can lose emotional depth, and many tests are normed only in English. Sexuality and gender identity. The Supreme Court recognised transgender persons as a third gender in 2014 and decriminalised consensual same-sex relations in 2018 ( Navtej Singh Johar versus Union of India ), and affirmative practice treats these as normal variations while helping clients with family pressure and discrimination. 9.11 Stigma, help seeking and traditional healers in India Erving Goffman, in Stigma (1963), described stigma as a deeply discrediting attribute that reduces a person, in others' eyes, from a whole person to a tainted, discounted one. Patrick Corrigan later distinguished public stigma (the population's stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination) from self-stigma , in which the person internalises the stereotypes and loses hope, a "why try" effect. Structural stigma is built into law: mental disorder is a ground for divorce under the Hindu Marriage Act 1955. Label avoidance , not seeking treatment to escape the label, is one of stigma's main harms. In India stigma attaches to the whole family and to siblings' marriage prospects, so illness is kept secret, called "tension" or "weakness", and treatment is delayed. Help seeking follows explanatory models: illness may be blamed on stress, weakness, karma, the evil eye (nazar), black magic or spirit possession, often several at once. Indian pathways-to-care research repeatedly finds that many patients see faith healers or general physicians before mental health services. This is medical pluralism : families use temple, dargah and hospital side by side. Traditional healers offer an explanation that fits the family's worldview, family involvement, ritual, hope, low cost and no psychiatric label. They can also harm: chaining, beating and starvation have been documented, and delayed treatment of psychosis or epilepsy worsens outcome. In 2001 a fire at a shelter linked to the dargah at Erwadi in Tamil Nadu killed 28 chained people with mental illness; the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 now prohibits chaining. Collaboration has also been tried: in Gujarat, the Dava-Dua ("medicine and prayer") programme placed a psychiatric clinic at the dargah of Mira Datar. Case. Fatima, twenty-two, is brought to a district hospital after three months at a dargah, where her family was told she was possessed by a jinn. She is suspicious, hears voices and barely sleeps. The psychologist asks what the family believes is happening, acknowledges the hope the dargah gave them, and explains that medicine can calm the illness while they continue praying. Framing care as "both, not either" keeps them engaged; the one firm line is that Fatima must never be chained or beaten. Recap. Specialties apply the shared core of clinical psychology to particular populations, settings and problems. Child psychology rests on developmental psychopathology, treats children as more than small adults and uses parent training to break the coercive cycle. Health psychology applies the biopsychosocial model, explains stress through Selye's physiological and Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman's cognitive models, and explains health behaviour through the health belief model, the theory of planned behaviour and the stages of change. Neuropsychology maps cognitive domains to answer questions about dementia, head injury and epilepsy. Forensic psychology separates present competence from past insanity, judged in India by section 84 of the Indian Penal Code, now section 22 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. Community psychology turns from treatment to prevention, which in India means the national and district programmes and task sharing. Culture shapes symptoms and help seeking, calling for emic thinking, competence held with humility, and respectful engagement with traditional healers. Part II: Positive psychology 10 What positive psychology is, and where it came from This chapter opens the second part of the book. Part I was about clinical psychology: how psychologists understand, assess and treat distress and disorder. Positive psychology asks a different question. Instead of "what has gone wrong with this person, and how do we repair it?", it asks "what goes right in human lives, why, and how can more of it be made to happen?" This chapter teaches what the field claims to be, why it appeared in the late 1990s, which older ideas it grew from, how it organises its subject matter, how it gathers evidence and what its critics say. It matters for two reasons. The 1998 presidential address, the January 2000 special issue, the three pillars, Marie Jahoda and Corey Keyes' two continua model are standard long-answer topics. More importantly for a future clinician, positive psychology changes what "mental health" means. If health is more than the absence of illness, a psychologist who only removes symptoms has done half the job. The last section builds the bridge back to clinical practice, which chapter 16 crosses in detail. 10.1 Defining positive psychology The simplest definition, the one Martin Seligman (the American psychologist who launched the field under that name) repeats most often, is that positive psychology is the scientific study of what makes life worth living . Each word does work. "Scientific" means the field claims the same methods as the rest of psychology: measurement, hypothesis testing, experiments, longitudinal follow-up and replication. "Study" means it is first a research enterprise and only second a set of techniques. "What makes life worth living" names the subject matter: happiness and satisfaction, but also meaning, engagement, relationships, character, achievement and the social conditions that support them. Other definitions stress different aspects. Source Definition (paraphrased) What it emphasises Martin Seligman The scientific study of what makes life worth living A good life, not merely a symptom-free one Martin Seligman and Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (2000) The science of positive subjective experience, positive individual traits and positive institutions, aimed at improving quality of life and preventing pathology Three levels, from feelings to character to society Kennon Sheldon and Laura King (2001) The scientific study of ordinary human strengths and virtues Strengths are common, not the property of saints and geniuses Shelly Gable and Jonathan Haidt (2005) The study of the conditions and processes that contribute to the flourishing or optimal functioning of people, groups and institutions Processes, and groups as well as individuals Christopher Peterson The scientific study of what goes right in life A plain contrast with the study of what goes wrong Two phrases need explaining. Optimal human functioning means operating at or near one's best: not merely coping, but using one's capacities fully, relating well, learning and contributing. It is a standard above "normal" in the statistical sense, because the average person may function well below their best. Strengths and virtues are the positive side of personality. A virtue, in the older philosophical sense, is a morally valued excellence of character, such as wisdom or courage. A strength is a more specific psychological route by which a virtue shows itself: curiosity is a route to wisdom, perseverance a route to courage. Christopher Peterson and Martin Seligman organised these in 2004 as the Values in Action (VIA) classification of six virtues and 24 strengths, presented as a "manual of the sanities" to sit beside the DSM. Positive psychology is an umbrella, not a single theory. Research on subjective well-being, optimism, hope, flow and gratitude existed before 2000 in scattered corners of psychology; the new field gathered it under one name and built the journals, funding and training that made it a recognised discipline. Key. Positive psychology is the scientific study of what makes life worth living: positive experiences, positive traits and the institutions that enable them. The two words that carry the definition are "scientific" (empirical method, not inspiration) and "worth living" (the presence of a good life, not only the absence of disorder). 10.2 What positive psychology is not It is not "happiology". Critics sometimes call it a science of feeling cheerful, but feeling good is only one part of its subject. Seligman's Authentic Happiness (2002) separated pleasure, engagement and meaning, and his Flourish (2011) replaced happiness with well-being, described by the PERMA model (positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, accomplishment). A person caring for a dying parent may not feel happy, yet may be living a life the field counts as going well. It is not positive thinking. Positive thinking is a popular self-help tradition that grew from the nineteenth century American "New Thought" or "mind-cure" movement and reached a mass audience through Norman Vincent Peale's The Power of Positive Thinking (1952). It claims that cheerful thoughts, and refusing negative ones, will by themselves bring health and success. Positive psychology tests claims with data rather than testimonials, does not hold that optimism is always good (unrealistic optimism leads people to ignore real risks), and does not tell people to suppress negative feelings. It is not a denial of the negative, nor a replacement for clinical psychology. The founding complaint was that psychology had become unbalanced , not that suffering should be ignored. Seligman and Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi said plainly that treating mental illness should continue; positive psychology was a complement, useful for prevention, recovery and the many people who are not ill but not doing well. It is not humanistic psychology renamed, and it is not self-help. Humanistic psychology discussed growth and potential decades earlier, but the two differ in method (section 10.7). A large commercial market also sells coaching and books under the positive psychology label; some of it is faithful to the research and much is not. Trap. A common exam answer says positive psychology "teaches people to think positively". That is wrong twice over: it is a research field, not a doctrine, and it explicitly separates itself from Peale-style positive thinking. The key contrasts are evidence versus testimonial, realistic versus unconditional optimism, and acceptance versus suppression of negative emotion. 10.3 Why it arose: the disease model and psychology's lost missions Before the Second World War, Martin Seligman argued, psychology had three missions: to cure mental illness , to make the lives of all people more productive and fulfilling , and to identify and nurture high talent . The second and third were real programmes; Lewis Terman at Stanford University, for example, began in the 1920s a famous long-term study of gifted children. After 1945 the United States had very large numbers of returning soldiers with psychological injuries. From 1946 the Veterans Administration funded the training and employment of clinical psychologists on a large scale, and the National Institute of Mental Health, created under the National Mental Health Act of 1946, became a major research funder. Both paid for work on mental illness. Seligman's argument was economic: psychologists found they could make a living treating disorder, and researchers could win grants studying it. Over the following decades the first mission swallowed the other two. The result was the disease model (also called the medical or deficit model). Distress is understood by analogy with physical illness: it is caused by an underlying defect located inside the individual; the psychologist diagnoses it, finds its cause and applies a treatment that removes it; success is symptom reduction; the ideal endpoint is the absence of disorder. Seligman credited its achievements: diagnosis became reliable once explicit criteria arrived with the third edition of the DSM in 1980, and effective treatments were found for disorders such as depression, panic disorder and phobias. But he named three costs. Psychology came to see people as passive victims of forces acting on them, neglecting choice and strength. The missions of improving normal lives and nurturing talent were forgotten. And prevention had no science to draw on: the most effective prevention works not by fixing damage but by building competencies (courage, optimism, interpersonal skill, hope, perseverance) that buffer against disorder, and psychology knew little about them. A teaching metaphor captures the imbalance. Picture a scale from minus five (severe disorder) through zero (no disorder) to plus five (flourishing). The disease model works on the left half, moving people towards zero. Positive psychology asks what moves people from zero towards plus five, and whether the same forces prevent a slide below zero. Section 10.9 shows the metaphor's limit: illness and well-being are better seen as two scales than one line. The complaint carried weight because of who made it. In 1967, with Steven Maier, Seligman had published experiments on learned helplessness : animals exposed to inescapable shocks later failed to escape shocks they could have avoided, a passivity that became an influential model of depression. His work then turned from how helplessness is learned to how it is unlearned, leading to research on explanatory style and Learned Optimism (1990). That personal shift from helplessness to optimism is a small version of the shift he later proposed for the whole discipline. 10.4 The founding moment: the 1998 address and the January 2000 special issue Positive psychology's date of birth is usually given as 1998. Martin Seligman was President of the American Psychological Association that year, and the presidency gives its holder an annual theme and a presidential address. Seligman chose positive psychology. His address, delivered in 1998 and published in the American Psychologist in 1999, argued that psychology had become a science of damage and repair and should now build a science of human strength, with particular weight on prevention: the way to prevent depression, substance misuse or violence in the young is to build the strengths that protect against them. The second landmark is the special issue of the American Psychologist published in January 2000 , edited by Martin Seligman and Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi , on happiness, excellence and optimal human functioning. Its introduction, "Positive psychology: An introduction", is the field's most cited founding text. It set out the three levels of the field (section 10.8), told the story of the disease model and criticised humanistic psychology (section 10.7). The issue included Ed Diener on the science of subjective well-being and Richard Ryan and Edward Deci on self-determination theory. Who gave us this. Martin Seligman (born 1942), University of Pennsylvania: learned helplessness (with Steven Maier, 1967), learned optimism (1990), President of the American Psychological Association in 1998 and founder of positive psychology as a named movement. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (1934 to 2021), Hungarian-born psychologist at the University of Chicago, best known for flow , complete absorption in a challenging activity ( Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience , 1990). He recalled watching, as a child in wartime Europe, many admired adults fall apart once their supports were removed while a few kept their integrity and purpose; he wanted to know what those few drew on. Institutions followed quickly: the Journal of Happiness Studies (2000); C. R. Snyder and Shane Lopez's Handbook of Positive Psychology (2002), which in later editions became the Oxford Handbook of Positive Psychology , one of this course's references; Christopher Peterson and Seligman's classification of strengths (2004); the Journal of Positive Psychology (2006); and the International Positive Psychology Association (2007). Trap. Keep the founding events apart. The presidential address is 1998 (Seligman alone). The special issue is January 2000 (Martin Seligman and Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi). Neither coined the phrase: Abraham Maslow used "positive psychology" in 1954. 10.5 The oldest roots: philosophy and the wisdom traditions Positive psychology is young as a named field, but its questions (what is a good life, is happiness the same as pleasure, which qualities of character are worth cultivating) are among the oldest in human thought. When Christopher Peterson and Martin Seligman built their classification, they surveyed Confucian, Taoist, Buddhist, Hindu, Athenian, Jewish, Christian and Islamic texts and found six virtues recurring across them: wisdom, courage, humanity, justice, temperance and transcendence. Hedonism and eudaimonia Greek philosophy supplied the field's most important distinction. Hedonism holds that the good life is the pleasant life; Epicurus refined this into a quiet ideal in which the best pleasure is freedom from pain and mental disturbance. Aristotle, in the Nicomachean Ethics , argued instead that the highest human good is eudaimonia , usually translated "happiness" but closer to "flourishing". For Aristotle eudaimonia is not a feeling but an activity: the exercise of distinctively human capacities, above all reason, in accordance with virtue over a complete life. Just as a good knife cuts well, a good human life uses human capacities well. Virtues are dispositions built by practice, each lying at a mean between extremes; courage lies between cowardice and recklessness. Modern research turned this contrast into two traditions. The hedonic tradition studies subjective well-being: life satisfaction and the balance of pleasant over unpleasant emotion. The eudaimonic tradition studies psychological functioning: meaning, purpose, growth, autonomy and relationships, whether or not they feel pleasant at the moment. Richard Ryan and Edward Deci set out the distinction in a 2001 review, and Carol Ryff's six-dimension model of psychological well-being (1989) is the classic eudaimonic measure. Later chapters teach both. Buddhist and Indian traditions Buddhism begins with dukkha , the unsatisfactoriness of ordinary life, which it traces to craving and clinging. Its ideal of happiness ( sukha ) is a stable well-being that does not depend on getting what one wants, reached through ethical conduct, meditation and wisdom. The four "immeasurable" states it cultivates (loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy and equanimity) read like a list of positive psychology topics, and mindfulness entered Western psychology from Buddhist practice. Indian thought has its own vocabulary. The Sanskrit word for health, swastha , means being established in oneself, and the Sushruta Samhita , a classical Ayurvedic text, describes the healthy person as one whose bodily functions are in balance and whose self, senses and mind are clear and content: health as a positive state, centuries before the World Health Organization. The Bhagavad Gita describes the sthitaprajna , the person of steady wisdom who stays even-minded in pleasure and pain, and teaches nishkama karma , wholehearted action without attachment to its rewards. Why it matters. One criticism of positive psychology (section 10.11) is that it universalised a Western, individualist idea of the good life. Knowing that Indian and Buddhist thought hold older, more relational and more equanimity-centred accounts of well-being lets you answer that criticism and apply the field sensibly with Indian clients. 10.6 Psychology before the name: William James, Gordon Allport and Marie Jahoda William James (1842 to 1910), the founder of American psychology, cared about flourishing throughout his career. In The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902) he contrasted the healthy-minded temperament, which sees the world as good and passes quickly over evil, with the sick soul , acutely aware of suffering. He took both seriously and warned that healthy-mindedness could be shallow if it ignored real suffering, a warning later critics turned on positive psychology. In "The Energies of Men" (1907) he asked why most people use only a small part of their resources: a question about optimal functioning in all but name. Gordon Allport (1897 to 1967), a founder of personality psychology, insisted that psychology study healthy people and not only neurotic ones. In Pattern and Growth in Personality (1961) he described the mature personality : an extended sense of self that includes others and causes beyond oneself; warm relating to others; emotional security and self-acceptance; realistic perception; absorbing skills and tasks; insight into oneself with a sense of humour; and a unifying philosophy of life. Several of these reappear almost unchanged in later models of well-being. The most direct forerunner is Marie Jahoda (1907 to 2001), an Austrian-born social psychologist. In 1958 she wrote Current Concepts of Positive Mental Health for the Joint Commission on Mental Illness and Health in the United States. Her starting point was that the absence of illness is not a sufficient definition of mental health: many people have no disorder yet function poorly, so mental health must be defined by the presence of something positive. She proposed six criteria. Jahoda's criterion What it means Attitudes towards the self Self-acceptance, self-awareness and a stable sense of identity Growth, development and self-actualisation A continuing movement towards realising one's potential Integration A balance of inner forces, a unifying outlook and resistance to stress Autonomy Independence from social pressure; regulating behaviour from within Perception of reality Seeing the world undistorted by one's own needs, and empathy for others Environmental mastery Competence in love, work and play; adequacy in relationships; meeting demands and solving problems Jahoda admitted that each criterion carries value judgements and offered them as a starting point for research. The list was largely ignored for decades as psychiatry moved to symptom checklists, but it anticipated Carol Ryff's model, which shares self-acceptance, growth, autonomy and environmental mastery with it almost directly. 10.7 Maslow, Rogers and humanistic psychology: ancestors and rivals Abraham Maslow (1908 to 1970) actually used the phrase first. The final chapter of the first edition of Motivation and Personality (1954) was titled "Toward a Positive Psychology". In it he complained that psychology had revealed much about human shortcomings and illness and little about potential and virtue: Martin Seligman's complaint, 44 years early. Maslow's hierarchy of needs (1943) places physiological, safety, belonging and esteem needs beneath self-actualisation , the realisation of one's full potential. He described self-actualising people as realistic, self-accepting, autonomous, creative and prone to peak experiences , moments of intense joy and wonder, but his method (a small, hand-picked sample judged by Maslow himself) was weak by modern standards. Carl Rogers (1902 to 1987) developed client-centred therapy ( Client-Centered Therapy , 1951; On Becoming a Person , 1961). He held that every organism has an actualising tendency , a built-in drive towards growth that flourishes under unconditional positive regard, empathy and genuineness. Therapy aimed at helping the client become a fully functioning person : open to experience, living in the present and trusting their own judgement. Rogers was also an empirical pioneer, among the first to record therapy sessions for research. Maslow, Rogers and others formed humanistic psychology in the late 1950s and 1960s, calling it the "third force" against psychoanalysis (pessimistic and pathology-focused) and behaviourism (mechanistic). It stressed free will, subjective experience, meaning and growth: much of what positive psychology later claimed. Why, then, is positive psychology not humanistic psychology revived? In the 2000 article Seligman and Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi argued that humanistic psychology had not built a cumulative empirical base, had been wary of conventional scientific method, and had spawned self-help movements whose emphasis on the self encouraged self-centredness. The historian Eugene Taylor replied in 2001 that positive psychology was repackaging humanistic ideas without credit, that humanists had done research (Rogers' recorded sessions being the obvious case), and that a narrow science of questionnaires could not capture the lived, existential side of flourishing, where meaning often comes through confronting suffering and death. The quarrel has softened. Self-determination theory's needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness, and Ryff's personal growth dimension, are close cousins of Rogers and Maslow, and the second wave (section 10.11) accepted much of the humanist point about the value of the negative. The fair summary: humanistic psychology asked many of positive psychology's questions first; positive psychology brought stronger conventional measurement and a far larger research infrastructure. Trap. Do not write that Abraham Maslow was a positive psychologist or that Martin Seligman was a humanist. Maslow was a humanistic psychologist who used the phrase "positive psychology" in 1954; Seligman founded positive psychology as an organised field in 1998 and criticised humanistic psychology's empirical base. Related movements, not the same movement. 10.8 The three pillars: experiences, traits and institutions The 2000 article organised the field into three levels, which Seligman's Authentic Happiness (2002) called the three pillars . Positive subjective experiences are the first pillar: what a good life feels like from the inside. Martin Seligman and Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi divided it by time. About the past : well-being, contentment and satisfaction. In the present : happiness, pleasure and flow. About the future : hope and optimism. The time division lets you place almost any positive state: gratitude and forgiveness change one's relation to the past, savouring and mindfulness deepen the present, hope and optimism shape the future. Positive individual traits are the second pillar: stable qualities such as the capacity for love and vocation, courage, interpersonal skill, perseverance, forgiveness, originality, future-mindedness, spirituality, high talent and wisdom, later formalised in the VIA classification. Traits matter because they are more stable than moods and more open to the person's own influence than circumstances. Positive institutions are the third pillar: families, schools, workplaces and communities, and the civic virtues they foster, such as responsibility, nurturance, altruism, civility, tolerance and work ethic. Strengths develop and are expressed within institutions, and some make this easier than others. This has been the least developed pillar, though it has grown through positive education and research on organisational and national well-being. The pillars connect: positive institutions nurture positive traits, which make positive experiences more likely. A child in a supportive school (institution) develops curiosity and persistence (traits), which bring more frequent flow and satisfaction (experiences). Trap. Three different "threes" appear in this chapter. The three missions are psychology's pre-war goals (cure illness, improve all lives, nurture talent). The three pillars are the levels of positive psychology (experiences, traits, institutions). The three time frames sit inside the first pillar (past, present, future). PERMA, from 2011, has five elements. 10.9 Health as more than the absence of illness The constitution of the World Health Organization, in force from 1948, defines health as "a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity." It includes mental and social well-being, defines health by the presence of well-being, and denies that the absence of disease is enough. Critics note that "complete", taken literally, makes almost nobody healthy; it was an aspiration, not a criterion. In practice psychiatry and clinical psychology long worked with the opposite rule: a person is mentally healthy if they have no diagnosable disorder. What was missing was a way to measure the positive side. Corey Keyes and the mental health continuum Corey Keyes, an American sociologist and psychologist, set out in 2002 to treat mental health the way the DSM treats mental illness: as a syndrome of symptoms, a set number of which must be present for a diagnosis. His "symptoms" of mental health come from three areas. Emotional well-being (hedonic): positive feelings, interest in life and life satisfaction. Psychological well-being (eudaimonic, personal, taken from Carol Ryff): self-acceptance, personal growth, purpose in life, environmental mastery, autonomy and positive relations with others. Social well-being (Keyes' own addition): social acceptance, social actualisation (belief that society can improve), social contribution, social coherence (finding society understandable) and social integration (belonging to a community). That gives three emotional signs and eleven signs of positive functioning. The Mental Health Continuum Short Form, a 14-item questionnaire, asks how often in the past month each was felt. A person is flourishing if they report at least one of the three emotional signs "every day" or "almost every day" and at least six of the eleven functioning signs at that frequency; languishing if at least one emotional and six functioning signs occurred "never" or "once or twice"; and moderately mentally healthy otherwise. Languishing is the most useful clinical idea here: a state of emptiness and stagnation in which life feels hollow, though the person meets criteria for no disorder. Keyes' research with large United States samples found that flourishing adults were a minority, that languishing carried real impairment in daily functioning and work, and that languishing people were at higher risk of later mental illness. Trap. Languishing is not mild depression and is not a DSM or ICD diagnosis. It is defined by the absence of well-being, not the presence of depressive symptoms. A person can languish without being depressed. The two continua model Keyes' more radical claim is the two continua model . The single-line view assumes that less illness means more health. Keyes showed, through factor analysis of survey data, that mental illness and mental health behave as two separate but correlated dimensions: one axis runs from high to low symptoms of illness, the other from languishing to flourishing. People with mental illness are more likely to languish, but the correlation is only moderate, so position on one axis does not tell you position on the other. The ideal Keyes called complete mental health : flourishing and free of mental illness. Low illness symptoms High illness symptoms Flourishing Complete mental health: well and not ill Coping with a disorder while meaning, relationships and purpose stay intact Languishing Incomplete mental health: not ill, but not well Ill and not well: the most impaired group Labels for the off-diagonal cells vary between authors, so learn the logic. Three implications follow. Removing illness does not produce health : a treated patient may become symptom-free yet still languish, and still carry raised risk of relapse. People with a diagnosis can flourish , which fits the recovery movement's definition of recovery as a satisfying, hopeful life even with ongoing symptoms. Treatment and promotion are different jobs : services must reduce illness and also build well-being. Case. Ananya, 24, has bipolar I disorder; on medication she has been episode-free for two years, is finishing a master's degree she cares about and is close to her sister. She scores as flourishing. Rohit, 26, has never met criteria for any disorder, but works long hours in a job he finds pointless, has drifted from friends and describes his days as "grey". He scores as languishing. On a single illness-to-health line Rohit looks healthier. The two continua model says each is healthy on one axis only: Ananya needs continued treatment, and Rohit, who would never be referred under a disease model, is exactly who positive psychology argues services should reach before he slides into disorder. Key. The World Health Organization (1948) said health is more than the absence of disease; Marie Jahoda (1958) proposed positive criteria for mental health; Corey Keyes (from 2002) made it measurable as flourishing, moderate mental health and languishing, and showed that mental illness and mental health are two related but separate continua. 10.10 How positive psychology does its research Self-report scales. Most constructs are measured by questionnaires: the Satisfaction With Life Scale (Ed Diener and colleagues, 1985), five statements such as "In most ways my life is close to my ideal"; the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule, which rates twenty emotions; the Mental Health Continuum Short Form; and the VIA Inventory of Strengths. National surveys use single items such as the Cantril ladder (rate your life from zero, the worst possible, to ten, the best possible), which underlies the annual World Happiness Report . Self-report suits a construct that is partly subjective by definition, but it is vulnerable to social desirability, to current mood colouring global judgements and to cultural differences in scale use, so good studies cross-check with informant reports and behaviour. Experience sampling. Global questions ("how happy are you in general?") depend on memory. The experience sampling method , developed by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi and colleagues from the 1970s, signals people at random moments in daily life (once by pager, now by smartphone) to record what they are doing, with whom and how they feel. It is how flow was studied in real life, and it measures well-being as lived rather than as remembered. Longitudinal studies. To know whether positive states predict good outcomes, researchers follow people over time. In the Nun Study analysis by Deborah Danner and colleagues (2001), autobiographies written decades earlier by young Catholic nuns were coded for positive emotion, and nuns whose writing expressed more positive emotion lived longer on average. Because the nuns shared diet, housing and health care, many alternative explanations are reduced, but the design is still correlational. Intervention trials. The strongest test of cause is experimental change. Positive psychology interventions are brief deliberate activities meant to raise well-being, tested in randomised controlled trials. In a landmark 2005 study, Martin Seligman and colleagues randomly assigned several hundred online participants to one of several exercises or to a placebo (writing about early memories). Writing down three good things each day and why, and using one's signature strengths in a new way, raised happiness and lowered depressive symptoms for up to six months relative to placebo. A 2009 meta-analysis by Nancy Sin and Sonja Lyubomirsky concluded that such interventions work on average; later, more conservative meta-analyses, weighting larger and better-designed studies and correcting for the publication of small striking studies, found the effects considerably smaller. Why it matters. When asked to "critically evaluate" a positive psychology claim, look at method: is the evidence only self-report, cross-sectional or longitudinal, was there an active placebo, how large was the effect, and has it replicated outside North American university students? 10.11 Criticisms, and the second wave The tyranny of the positive attitude. The psychologist Barbara Held argued in the early 2000s that American culture imposes a "tyranny of the positive attitude", under which struggling people fail twice: once in their problem, and again in not being positive about it. Positive psychology risked lending scientific authority to this pressure. The danger is sharpest in illness: a cancer patient told that optimism aids survival may blame herself when the disease progresses, though reviews have not supported claims that positive attitudes improve cancer survival. Neglect of the value of negative emotions. Fear signals danger, anger signals injustice, sadness slows us after loss and draws support, guilt repairs relationships. Julie Norem's research on defensive pessimism showed that some anxious people perform better when they imagine what could go wrong and prepare; making them "think positive" worsened performance. Cultural bias. Much of the research was done in the United States, often with students, and critics argue its good life reflects Western individualism: the individual as the unit of well-being and happiness as excited personal achievement. Jeanne Tsai's research on "ideal affect" found that European Americans tend to value high-arousal positive states such as excitement, and East Asians low-arousal states such as calm. In many cultures happiness is relational, found in harmony and fulfilled duty, and the Indian ideals of equanimity in section 10.5 are a case in point. Measures and interventions cannot be assumed to travel. Replication problems. The clearest casualty is the positivity ratio . In 2005 Barbara Fredrickson and Marcial Losada claimed, using a model borrowed from fluid dynamics, that people flourish when positive emotions outnumber negative ones by about 2.9 to 1. In 2013 Nicholas Brown, Alan Sokal and Harris Friedman showed that the mathematics was invalid, and the journal formally withdrew the modelling; Fredrickson accepted the flaw while maintaining that more positive relative to negative emotion is broadly beneficial. The popular claim that about 40 percent of happiness is under intentional control (the "happiness pie") has also been criticised as a misreading of what variance estimates can say about an individual, and intervention effects shrink in better studies. Commercialisation. The writer Barbara Ehrenreich, in Bright-Sided: How the Relentless Promotion of Positive Thinking Has Undermined America (2009, published in Britain as Smile or Die ), described the pressure during her breast cancer treatment to see illness as a gift and stay cheerful. She traced this culture from New Thought through Peale to corporate motivational speaking and academic positive psychology, which she accused of lending respectability to a profitable industry. A related political charge is that the field places responsibility for well-being on the individual, encouraging people to adjust their attitudes to poverty or overwork rather than change the conditions. The second wave The field's main response is the second wave . Its best-known early statement is Paul Wong's 2011 proposal of "positive psychology 2.0". Wong, a Canadian psychologist and founder of meaning therapy, argued that the good life comes not from maximising positive and minimising negative but from integrating both; meaning often emerges precisely through confronting suffering. In 2016 Itai Ivtzan, Tim Lomas and colleagues published Second Wave Positive Psychology: Embracing the Dark Side of Life , studying courage (which requires fear), forgiveness (which requires an injury), post-traumatic growth (which requires trauma) and awareness of mortality. The second wave rests on what Lomas and Ivtzan call the dialectical nature of well-being: a "positive" quality can harm in the wrong context (forgiveness that keeps someone in an abusive relationship), a "negative" one can help (anger driving resistance to injustice), and the two often mingle, as in a bittersweet farewell. 10.12 Positive psychology and clinical psychology The relationship has moved from rivalry towards integration. At first positive psychology was presented as the other half of psychology: clinical psychology repairs, positive psychology builds. Alex Wood and Nicholas Tarrier, in a 2010 article in Clinical Psychology Review , called this divide artificial. Many characteristics are one dimension seen from two ends (gratitude and ingratitude, hope and hopelessness), so studying one end gives an incomplete picture. They proposed a positive clinical psychology giving equal weight to positive and negative functioning in research, assessment and treatment. Note the tension with Keyes: for some traits positive and negative form one continuum, while mental illness and overall mental health form two. Both can be true of different constructs. In practice positive psychology enters clinical work in four ways. Assessment can record strengths and well-being, not only symptoms, so the formulation shows what the client has to work with. Treatment can include structured positive interventions: positive psychotherapy, developed by Tayyab Rashid and Martin Seligman, combines exercises such as using signature strengths, gratitude and savouring with work on symptoms; well-being therapy, developed by the Italian psychiatrist Giovanni Fava on the basis of Ryff's dimensions, is used late in the treatment of depression and anxiety to build well-being and reduce relapse. Relapse prevention gains from the finding that a remitted but languishing patient has not fully recovered. Prevention and promotion programmes in schools and communities apply the founding argument that strengths buffer against disorder. In India this has particular force. Clinical psychology here, regulated through the Rehabilitation Council of India, faces a large treatment gap, and the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, chiefly a rights-based law on the care of people with mental illness, also places a duty on government to run programmes for promoting mental health and preventing mental illness. Indian clients often draw on religious, family and community resources that a strengths-based assessment notices and a deficit-based one misses, while the cultural criticisms of section 10.11 warn against importing Western interventions unadapted. This is the bridge to chapter 16. Modern practice combines both columns; they are not camps to choose between. A clinician works on two axes, reducing illness and building well-being. Clearing the first while ignoring the second leaves a client symptom-free but languishing, and at risk. Recap. Positive psychology is the scientific study of what makes life worth living: positive subjective experiences, positive individual traits and the institutions that enable them; it is not happiology, positive thinking, a denial of suffering or a replacement for clinical psychology. It arose from Martin Seligman's argument that post-war psychology, funded to treat mental illness, adopted a disease model and neglected its missions of improving all lives and nurturing talent; he made positive psychology the theme of his 1998 presidential year at the American Psychological Association, and he and Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi edited the founding special issue of the American Psychologist in January 2000. Its roots run through Abraham Maslow (who used the phrase in 1954), Carl Rogers and humanistic psychology (ancestors with whom it quarrelled over method), Marie Jahoda's six criteria of positive mental health (1958), William James and Gordon Allport, and back to Aristotle's eudaimonia and Buddhist and Indian ideas of well-being. The field is mapped by three pillars: experiences (past satisfaction, present happiness and flow, future hope and optimism), traits and institutions. The World Health Organization's 1948 definition and Corey Keyes' model of flourishing, moderate mental health and languishing establish that health is more than the absence of illness, and the two continua model shows illness and well-being are related but separate dimensions. The field works through self-report scales, experience sampling, longitudinal studies and intervention trials, and has been criticised for the tyranny of positivity, neglect of negative emotion, Western bias, replication failures such as the positivity ratio and commercialisation, to which the second wave responded by integrating the dark and the light. For clinical psychology the lesson is to work on two axes: reduce illness and build well-being. Critically evaluate positive psychology, discussing its major criticisms and the response of second wave positive psychology. 11 Happiness and well-being Clinical psychology was built to understand and reduce suffering. Positive psychology asks the other half of the question: what does it mean for a life to go well, and how would we know? This chapter starts with the two philosophical traditions that still divide the field, well-being as pleasure and well-being as living well. It then covers the four models examiners ask about most: Ed Diener's subjective well-being, Carol Ryff's psychological well-being, Corey Keyes's social well-being, and Martin Seligman's move from authentic happiness to PERMA. Finally it asks what predicts happiness and how honestly we can measure it. The positive psychology texts (Baumgardner and Crothers; the Oxford Handbook of Positive Psychology) cover this ground. It matters to a clinician because having no disorder is not the same as being healthy. A patient whose depression has remitted may still be flat, purposeless or lonely, and knowing how well-being is built tells you what is still missing. 11.1 Two old answers: hedonic and eudaimonic well-being The hedonic tradition (from the Greek hedone , pleasure) holds that a good life contains as much pleasure and as little pain as possible. Its best known ancient voice is Epicurus (341 to 270 BCE), who called pleasure the beginning and end of the blessed life. He did not mean feasting. He prized ataraxia (a mind free of disturbance and fear) and aponia (a body free of pain), reached through simple living, moderation and friendship. The modern word "epicurean", meaning a lover of rich food, distorts his teaching. The English philosopher Jeremy Bentham systematised the hedonic view in An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789). He argued that pain and pleasure govern everything humans do, and that the right action produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number (the principle of utility). His "felicific calculus" weighed a pleasure by its intensity, duration, certainty, nearness and similar properties. In modern psychology this tradition survives as the study of how pleasant people find their experiences and lives, which in practice means subjective well-being (section 11.3). The eudaimonic tradition comes from Aristotle 's Nicomachean Ethics (4th century BCE). Eudaimonia joins eu (good) and daimon (a guiding spirit, often read as one's true self). For Aristotle it was not a feeling but an activity: living, over a complete life, in accordance with virtue. His "function argument" runs like this. A good knife cuts well. The distinctive function of a human being is reason. So a good human life is one in which reason and the virtues (courage, temperance, justice, practical wisdom) are exercised well. Each virtue is a mean between two vices, as courage lies between cowardice and rashness. Aristotle thought a life of pleasure alone was fit for grazing animals. The American psychologist Alan Waterman brought eudaimonia into empirical psychology in 1993. He read the daimon as a person's true potentials and called the experience of acting in line with them personal expressiveness : the sense that "this is who I really am" and "this is what I was meant to do", with a feeling of being intensely alive. When students rated their own important activities, personal expressiveness correlated strongly with hedonic enjoyment, but the relationship was lopsided. Expressive activities were almost always enjoyable, yet many enjoyable activities were not expressive. The expressive ones involved challenge, effort and developing one's best abilities, while the merely enjoyable ones were more often about relaxing. Richard Ryan and Edward Deci 's 2001 review in the Annual Review of Psychology ("On happiness and human potentials") organised the field around these two traditions. They argued that well-being is multidimensional and placed eudaimonia inside their self-determination theory , which says people flourish when three basic psychological needs are met: autonomy (acting by one's own choice), competence (being effective) and relatedness (connection with others). Pleasant feeling then follows as a by-product. They also warned that some pleasure-bringing goals, such as chasing wealth or fame, do not bring wellness. Feature Hedonic well-being Eudaimonic well-being Philosophical roots Epicurus, Jeremy Bentham Aristotle Core question How good does my life feel? Am I living well, as the person I could be? What counts as well-being Pleasure, satisfaction, absence of pain Virtue, growth, meaning, realising potential Main psychological model Subjective well-being (Ed Diener) Psychological well-being (Carol Ryff); self-determination theory 11.2 Why the distinction matters, and where it blurs The distinction matters because pleasure and wellness can come apart. Someone who drinks every evening to feel good may report plenty of pleasant feeling while their life is shrinking. It works the other way too: raising a child, caring for a sick parent or getting through a demanding clinical internship is often stressful in the moment, yet deeply meaningful. A purely hedonic scorecard would rate these lives badly, and a eudaimonic one would not. The distinction also guides intervention. Someone lacking pleasant emotion might be taught savouring, while someone lacking direction needs work on values and purpose. In the data, though, the two blur. Corey Keyes , Dov Shmotkin and Carol Ryff (2002) found in a national American sample that subjective and psychological well-being were related but separable: most people high on one were high on the other, but a meaningful minority were not. Todd Kashdan , Robert Biswas-Diener and Laura King (2008) argued that eudaimonia has been defined in many incompatible ways, that eudaimonic theories mix the causes of well-being with the outcome itself, and that the overlap in data is so large that splitting the two may confuse more than it clarifies. Veronika Huta and Richard Ryan (2010) offered a fix: separate a person's motive for an activity (seeking pleasure versus seeking excellence and meaning) from the outcome . Hedonic motives brought more immediate positive feeling and eudaimonic motives brought more meaning, and people who pursued both tended to report the richest well-being. Trap. "Eudaimonic" does not mean "unpleasant but good for you", and "hedonic" does not mean "selfish". Epicurus recommended a quiet, moderate life full of friendship. The distinction is about what well-being consists of (feeling good versus functioning well). 11.3 Subjective well-being: Diener's model and how it is measured Warner Wilson 's 1967 review pictured the "happy person" as young, healthy, well educated, well paid, extraverted, optimistic, religious and married, a portrait later research largely qualified. Ed Diener 's 1984 review "Subjective well-being" gave the field its central definition: a person's cognitive and emotional evaluation of their own life. It has three components. Life satisfaction is the cognitive component: a considered judgement of how one's life measures up to one's own standards. Positive affect is how often a person feels pleasant emotions and moods, such as joy, interest and contentment. Negative affect is how often a person feels unpleasant emotions and moods, such as sadness, anxiety and anger. A person high in subjective well-being is satisfied with life, often feels positive emotion and seldom feels negative emotion. Diener stressed three hallmarks. The construct is subjective : the person, not an expert, judges whether their life is going well. It includes positive measures, not only the absence of distress. And it is a global assessment of life as a whole. In 1999 Diener, Eunkook Suh , Richard Lucas and Heidi Smith added a fourth element, domain satisfactions : satisfaction with work, family, health, finances, leisure and oneself. The Satisfaction With Life Scale Life satisfaction is usually measured with the Satisfaction With Life Scale by Ed Diener, Robert Emmons , Randy Larsen and Sharon Griffin (1985). It has five statements, each rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree), such as "In most ways my life is close to my ideal" and "If I could live my life over, I would change almost nothing". Scores run from 5 to 35. No item names a life domain. That is deliberate: each respondent weighs whatever matters to them, so a monk and a businessman are each judged against their own ideals. The Positive and Negative Affect Schedule The emotional components are most often measured with the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) by David Watson , Lee Anna Clark and Auke Tellegen (1988). It lists twenty emotion words. Ten measure positive affect (such as interested, enthusiastic, inspired, alert) and ten measure negative affect (such as distressed, guilty, hostile, afraid). Each is rated from 1 (very slightly or not at all) to 5 (extremely), giving two separate scores that each run from 10 to 50. The instructions can ask about "right now", "the past week" or "in general", so the same schedule can measure a passing state or a stable trait. High positive affect means energy and enthusiasm, low positive affect means lethargy, high negative affect means distress, and low negative affect means calm. The independence of positive and negative affect The most surprising finding here is that positive and negative affect are not two ends of one line. In 1969 Norman Bradburn found that his positive and negative affect items correlated only weakly and were predicted by different life circumstances. Ed Diener and Robert Emmons (1984) showed when this holds. In any single moment the two are inversely related, because it is hard to feel intense joy and intense misery at once. But when people report how often they have felt each over weeks or months, the two frequencies become largely independent. Knowing how much sadness someone has had tells you little about how much joy they have had. The clinical payoff is direct. Lee Anna Clark and David Watson's tripartite model (1991) proposed that anxiety and depression share high negative affect, while low positive affect is specific to depression. So treatment that reduces negative affect does not automatically bring positive affect back. After cognitive behaviour therapy a patient may no longer feel hopeless yet still feel very little: the negative affect has gone but the anhedonia (loss of pleasure) remains. That is the case for adding interventions that build positive emotion. Trap. Low negative affect is not the same as high positive affect. Over time they are separate dimensions, which is why the PANAS gives two scores and never one combined "mood" score. 11.4 Psychological well-being: Ryff's six dimensions Carol Ryff 's 1989 paper "Happiness is everything, or is it?" criticised subjective well-being research for lacking theory: its measures had been adopted because they were convenient, not because anyone had worked out what positive functioning is. Ryff went back to the theorists of the healthy personality: Abraham Maslow 's self-actualisation, Carl Rogers 's fully functioning person, Carl Jung 's individuation, Gordon Allport 's maturity, Erik Erikson 's psychosocial stages and Marie Jahoda 's criteria of positive mental health (1958). Where their accounts converged she found six dimensions, measured by her Scales of Psychological Well-Being . Ryff and Corey Keyes (1995) supported the six-factor structure in a national American sample.
