Distinguish religion from spirituality, and discuss religious orientation, religious coping and the religion and well-being link. 16 Positive psychology in the clinic, and Indian perspectives on well-being The earlier chapters ran on two tracks. Clinical psychology studied distress: how to assess, formulate and treat it. Positive psychology studied well-being: happiness, strengths, hope and meaning. This final chapter joins the tracks. It begins with the argument of Alex Wood and Nicholas Tarrier that well-being and distress lie on one continuum, then studies positive psychology interventions, the evidence for them (including the sobering recent reanalyses), and the therapies built from them: positive psychotherapy, well-being therapy, strengths-based cognitive behaviour therapy and hope therapy. It shows how strengths enter assessment and formulation, and looks briefly at schools and workplaces. The chapter then turns to Indian ideas of well-being, treated carefully: what the texts say, what psychologists have made of them, and where the evidence is thin. It closes with the cautions every clinician must hold and a case in which positive psychotherapy runs alongside cognitive behaviour therapy for a young woman with depression. 16.1 Positive clinical psychology: well-being and distress on one continuum When Martin Seligman launched positive psychology during his 1998 presidency of the American Psychological Association, he argued that psychology had become mainly a science of repairing damage. The new movement built its own journals and identity, and a side effect followed: positive psychology and clinical psychology came to look like two disciplines, one for the well and one for the ill. In 2010, Alex Wood and Nicholas Tarrier, both British clinical psychologists, argued in Clinical Psychology Review for a positive clinical psychology . Their claim was that the split is scientifically mistaken: clinical psychology should study well-being and distress together, with equal weight. The idea was developed in The Wiley Handbook of Positive Clinical Psychology (2016), edited by Alex Wood and Judith Johnson. Their case can be taught as four linked arguments. The continuum argument. Many characteristics positive psychology studies are one pole of a dimension whose other pole clinical psychology studies: gratitude runs to ingratitude, calm to anxiety, hope to hopelessness. A gratitude questionnaire contains items about having much to be thankful for beside reverse-scored items about seeing little to be grateful for; one scale measures both ends. Studying only one half is studying half a variable. The incremental prediction argument. Positive characteristics predict later disorder beyond what negative characteristics predict. Alex Wood and Stephen Joseph (2010) followed a community sample for about ten years and found that people low in psychological well-being on Carol Ryff's scales were considerably more likely to be depressed a decade later, even after allowing for earlier symptoms. Low well-being is itself a risk factor. The buffering argument. Strengths are protective factors that soften the impact of adversity. Ann Masten's 2001 paper "Ordinary magic" showed that most children facing adversity develop well because of ordinary resources such as a caring adult and self-regulation. Judith Johnson, with Wood, Tarrier and colleagues, argued that certain psychological resources weaken the link between risk factors such as hopelessness and suicidal thinking. A protective factor is not merely the absence of risk; it changes what the risk does. The intervention argument. If strengths predict and buffer disorder, building them is a legitimate clinical target. A therapist who reduces symptoms but leaves the client with no pleasure, purpose or close relationship has left the vulnerability in place. Trap. Do not confuse Wood and Tarrier's single continuum with Corey Keyes's dual-continua model . Keyes showed that mental illness and positive mental health (flourishing versus languishing) are correlated but separable: a person can be free of diagnosis yet languishing. Wood and Tarrier speak of specific traits sharing one scale; Keyes speaks of two related global states. Both reach the practical point examiners want: absence of illness is not presence of well-being, so the clinician must assess both. 16.2 What counts as a positive psychology intervention A positive psychology intervention is a deliberate activity or treatment whose primary aim is to build something positive (positive feelings, thoughts or behaviours, strengths, meaning, relationships) rather than primarily to remove something negative. Cognitive behaviour therapy for depression usually makes people happier, but its target is the disorder, so it is not a positive intervention; writing a gratitude letter targets no disorder, so it is. Acacia Parks and Robert Biswas-Diener later proposed stricter tests: the primary goal must be a positive variable, there must be evidence the activity changes it, and evidence that changing it leads to good outcomes. An unstudied pleasant activity is simply a pleasant activity. The optimism behind these interventions drew on the 2005 "sustainable happiness" model of Sonja Lyubomirsky, Kennon Sheldon and David Schkade, which held that happiness depends on a genetic set point, life circumstances and intentional activity, the part a person can change. Its famous pie chart (50 percent set point, 10 percent circumstances, 40 percent activity) has been heavily criticised, notably by Nicholas Brown and Julia Rohrer, because population heritability figures cannot be split into one person's happiness. The safe conclusion is that intentional activity matters, not that it matters "40 percent". Positive interventions are brief, cheap, low in stigma and scalable, which makes them attractive in India, where the National Mental Health Survey of 2015 to 2016 documented a large treatment gap. That appeal is also their danger (section 16.11). 16.3 The classic exercises and the 2005 internet trial The best-known early test is the 2005 American Psychologist study by Martin Seligman, Tracy Steen, Nansook Park and Christopher Peterson. Visitors to a website linked to Seligman's book Authentic Happiness were randomly assigned to one of five exercises or a placebo, each practised for one week, and their happiness and depressive symptoms were measured before, immediately after, and at one week, one month, three months and six months. The placebo, writing nightly about early memories, looked like an exercise but was not expected to build anything; this separated each exercise's specific effect from the general effect of expecting to feel better. Exercise What participants did for one week What happened Gratitude visit Wrote a letter to someone who had been kind but never properly thanked, then delivered and read it in person. The largest immediate gains, but gone by three months. Three good things in life Each night wrote three things that went well and why. Gains in happiness and fewer depressive symptoms, still present at six months. Using signature strengths in a new way Took the Values in Action (VIA) strengths survey, then used one top-five strength in a new way each day. Gains lasting to six months. You at your best Wrote about a time they were at their best and reviewed the strengths shown. Short-lived change, similar to placebo. Identifying signature strengths Took the survey and used top strengths more often, without the "new way" instruction. Short-lived change, similar to placebo. Two lessons followed. Exercises built on repeated daily practice with something new in it outlasted the one-off emotional event of the gratitude visit, and participants who kept practising on their own after the week showed the most lasting benefit. Positive exercises work less like a pill than like physical exercise: they help while you keep doing them. The limits matter too: participants were self-selected, educated, motivated visitors to a happiness website, and many dropped out across follow-ups. Best possible self, kindness, gratitude and savouring Laura King (2001) adapted James Pennebaker's expressive writing method, in which writing about trauma improved later health but was upsetting at the time. Her participants wrote for twenty minutes on four consecutive days about their best possible self : a future in which everything had gone as well as it could. Compared with controls, they gained in subjective well-being and made fewer health centre visits in the following months, without the distress of trauma writing. The exercise is now used mainly to build optimism, because it makes a hoped-for future concrete. In acts of kindness studies reported by Lyubomirsky, Sheldon and Schkade (2005), students performed five kind acts a week for six weeks. Those who did all five on one day gained in well-being; those who spread them across the week did not, perhaps because scattered small acts blur into ordinary life. The same work found counting blessings once a week helped more than three times a week. These small early findings introduced a vital idea: dose and timing matter. Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough (2003), in "Counting blessings versus burdens", had participants list things they were grateful for, compared with hassles or neutral events; the gratitude groups reported more positive affect and, in some conditions, better life appraisals. Savouring , set out by Fred Bryant and Joseph Veroff in Savoring: A New Model of Positive Experience (2007), means deliberately attending to, appreciating and prolonging positive experience across three time frames: anticipating, savouring the moment and reminiscing. Strategies include sharing the experience, building a memory of it, sharpening attention to sensory detail, and avoiding "kill-joy" thoughts such as "this will soon be over". Savouring suits depression, where the problem is not only fewer good events but a blunted capacity to enjoy them. 16.4 The evidence: meta-analyses, person-activity fit and who benefits A meta-analysis pools many studies into an average effect size. Three form the core of what a student needs. Nancy Sin and Sonja Lyubomirsky (2009) pooled 51 interventions with over four thousand participants and reported that positive interventions increased well-being (average correlation-type effect about 0.29) and reduced depressive symptoms (about 0.31), moderate effects. Effects were larger for depressed participants, for people who chose to take part, for older participants, for individual rather than group delivery, and for longer interventions. Linda Bolier and colleagues (2013) used stricter rules: only randomised controlled trials, with study quality rated. Across 39 studies and over six thousand participants, effects were smaller: roughly a third of a standard deviation for subjective well-being and about a fifth for psychological well-being and depression, still present at three to six months, with more rigorous studies tending to show smaller effects. Carmela White, Bob Uttl and Mark Holder (2019) reanalysed both, reporting errors in extracted effect sizes and strong small-study effects : the smallest studies showed the largest benefits, the signature of publication bias. After correction, the effect on well-being was small and the effect on depression smaller and uncertain. Their title said it plainly: the effects are much smaller than previously reported. Key. Positive psychology interventions produce real but small gains in well-being and smaller, less certain reductions in depression; early enthusiasm was inflated by small, low-quality studies. They are useful additions, not replacements for established treatment. Averages hide variation. Sonja Lyubomirsky and Kristin Layous (2013) organised it in their positive-activity model . Features of the activity matter (dose, variety, sequence, built-in social support), and so do features of the person (motivation, effort, belief that it will work, baseline mood, personality, culture). Person-activity fit is the match between them: an extravert may thrive on acts of kindness and find journalling tedious, a reflective person the reverse. People who choose activities that fit their values practise longer and gain more. Culture is part of fit. Julia Boehm, Lyubomirsky and Sheldon (2011) found Anglo American participants gained more from gratitude and optimism exercises than Asian American participants, perhaps because in interdependent cultures expressed gratitude can carry indebtedness or awkwardness. For an Indian client, reading a letter aloud to a parent may feel strange while a quiet act of service says the same thing comfortably. So who benefits most? People who are motivated and choose the activity, who practise for weeks rather than days, who have mild to moderate symptoms rather than severe illness, and for whom the activity fits their values and culture. 16.5 Positive psychotherapy (Rashid and Seligman) Positive psychotherapy assembles positive interventions into a structured, clinician-delivered treatment, originally for depression. It was introduced by Martin Seligman, Tayyab Rashid and Acacia Parks in a 2006 American Psychologist paper and set out fully in Tayyab Rashid and Martin Seligman's Positive Psychotherapy: Clinician Manual (2018). Its premise is that depression is maintained not only by symptoms but by a lack of positive emotion, engagement, meaning and good relationships, and that building these directly can relieve symptoms and guard against relapse. It does not deny distress: clients talk about their troubles and the therapist listens empathically, but equal attention goes to what is going right. The 2006 paper reported two small pilot studies. Group treatment of mildly to moderately depressed students reduced symptoms, with gains visible at one year; individual treatment of clients with major depressive disorder did better than treatment as usual and than treatment as usual with antidepressants. The results were encouraging but small-sample, and later trials have been generally positive but mixed. The manual runs about fifteen sessions in three phases, each session with a core concept, in-session practice and homework. Phase Aim Typical exercises First Build a narrative of the client as a person with strengths. The positive introduction (a one-page story of the client at their best), a nightly gratitude journal , identifying signature strengths through the VIA survey and reports from family and friends, practical wisdom in using strengths. Second Process negative memories and cultivate positive emotion. Open and closed memories (writing about bitter memories to process rather than ruminate), forgiveness (letting go of the wish for revenge, not excusing the wrong), maximising versus satisficing (Barry Schwartz's finding that always seeking the best option breeds regret), the gratitude letter and visit . Third Build relationships, meaning and purpose. Hope and optimism, post-traumatic growth, slowness and savouring, active constructive responding (Shelly Gable's finding that enthusiastic interest in another's good news strengthens relationships), altruism and the "gift of time", writing about meaning and legacy. Trap. Positive psychotherapy is not "only talking about good things". Rashid insists that strengths and weaknesses, positive and negative emotions, get equal attention, and that suppressing distress is harmful. 16.6 Well-being therapy (Giovanni Fava) Well-being therapy was developed by the Italian psychiatrist Giovanni Fava and colleagues, including Chiara Ruini, at the University of Bologna from the late 1990s. It began with an observation: many patients whose depression or anxiety had responded to treatment still carried residual symptoms and lacked psychological well-being, and these were the patients most likely to relapse. Recovery, Fava argued, requires restoring well-being, not only removing symptoms. The therapy uses Carol Ryff's (1989) six dimensions of psychological well-being as its map: environmental mastery (versus feeling overwhelmed by daily demands), personal growth (versus stagnation), purpose in life (versus directionlessness), autonomy (versus dependence on others' approval), self-acceptance (versus dissatisfaction with oneself) and positive relations with others (versus isolation). The treatment usually runs about eight sessions in three stages. In the initial sessions , the client keeps a structured diary of episodes of well-being, however brief, and rates their intensity; formerly depressed people are often surprised to find any. In the intermediate sessions , the focus is the thoughts that cut these episodes short, borrowing directly from cognitive therapy: instead of thoughts that trigger distress, the client records thoughts that interrupt well-being ("This won't last", "I don't deserve this") and learns to challenge them. In the final sessions , the therapist identifies which Ryff dimensions are impaired and works on them, for example autonomy in a client who cannot decide anything without family approval. Well-being therapy is mainly used sequentially : the acute illness is treated first with medication or cognitive behaviour therapy, then well-being therapy targets residual symptoms and relapse. Fava's group reported lower relapse rates in recurrent depression over several years of follow-up than with standard clinical management, and it has been studied in generalised anxiety disorder and cyclothymia. The trials were mostly small and mostly from one group, a limitation worth stating. Why it matters. Well-being therapy is positive clinical psychology in miniature: a positive psychology model (Ryff) plus a clinical technique (cognitive restructuring) aimed at a clinical problem (relapse). It answers "Can positive psychology help people who are already ill?": yes, especially after the acute phase. 16.7 Strengths-based CBT, hope therapy and acceptance and commitment therapy Christine Padesky and Kathleen Mooney set out strengths-based cognitive behaviour therapy in a 2012 paper subtitled "A four-step model to build resilience". Clients already show resilience somewhere, often in an area they think unimportant: a hobby, a craft, a relative they care for. The four steps follow. Search for strengths: find where the client persists despite obstacles and ask how they keep going. Construct a personal model of resilience: gather the strategies, beliefs and images they use there into their own model, in their own metaphors. Apply the model to the problem area. Practise resilience through behavioural experiments, aiming to be resilient in difficulty rather than to feel no distress. A client overwhelmed at work may be an amateur cricketer who survives a bad over by "playing one ball at a time"; that phrase becomes the core of a model he carries into meetings. The approach fits the collaborative case conceptualisation of Willem Kuyken, Christine Padesky and Robert Dudley (2009), which builds client strengths into every cognitive behavioural formulation. C. R. Snyder's hope theory defines hope as clear goals , pathways thinking (seeing routes to them) and agency thinking (the belief and motivation to use those routes). Hope therapy , described by Shane Lopez, Snyder and colleagues (2000), works through hope finding (discovering existing hope), hope bonding (a hopeful alliance), hope enhancing (clarifying goals, multiplying pathways, strengthening agency) and hope reminding (the client learning to catch hopeless thinking unaided). Jennifer Cheavens and colleagues (2006) reported, in a small group trial, gains in hope and self-esteem and reductions in depressive and anxious symptoms. It suits depression marked by "I see no way out" (low pathways) and "Why try?" (low agency). Acceptance and commitment therapy, developed by Steven Hayes and colleagues, belongs to the cognitive behavioural family, not to positive psychology. It aims at psychological flexibility : accepting painful thoughts and feelings rather than struggling with them, and acting on one's values , chosen life directions ("being a caring son") as distinct from goals that can be ticked off. Clarifying values resembles identifying strengths and meaning, and committed action resembles pursuing purpose. The difference is essential: acceptance and commitment therapy does not aim to increase positive feeling, and treats the direct chase after feeling good as one of the traps that keep people stuck. 16.8 Strengths-based assessment and the fourfront Positive clinical psychology asks that assessment gather strengths as carefully as symptoms. Strengths predict and protect (16.1); a deficit-only formulation gives the therapist nothing to build with; and a report that describes a person only as problems shapes how every later professional sees them. The key framework comes from Beatrice Wright , an American rehabilitation psychologist who worked with people with physical disabilities and noticed that reports ignored both the person's assets and the environment's part in their difficulties. With Shane Lopez she argued, in the Handbook of Positive Psychology , for widening the diagnostic focus, and Lopez and C. R. Snyder carried her approach into positive psychological assessment. It is called the fourfront because it examines four fronts at once. Within the person In the environment Weaknesses 1. Deficits and undermining characteristics (symptoms, skill deficits) 3. Lacks and destructive factors (poverty, abuse, discrimination, no services) Strengths 2. Assets (character strengths, talents, coping skills) 4. Resources and opportunities (supportive family, community, school, faith group) The fourfront guards against two biases: locating problems inside the person when the environment is much of the story (a clinical version of the fundamental attribution error (Lee Ross, 1977)), and noticing deficits while overlooking assets. In practice, the clinician fills all four cells when writing a formulation. Measures can fill the strengths cells, among them the Values in Action Inventory of Strengths (VIA), the Hope Scale, Ed Diener's Satisfaction With Life Scale and Ryff's scales, and interviews can ask "What has helped you through hard times before?" or "When is the problem less bad?" In the report, strengths should be as specific as symptoms: not "supportive family" but "her elder sister visits weekly and is the person she would call in a crisis". A strengths section is not politeness; it names the resources the treatment plan will rely on. Case. A 15-year-old boy in a Pune government school is referred for "aggression and poor studies". A deficit-only report lists fights and failing marks. The fourfront adds that he is the football team's most reliable player and protective of younger children (person, strengths), that his father has lost his job and home is full of quarrels (environment, weaknesses), and that his coach and an uncle take an interest in him (environment, resources). The plan changes: the coach becomes an ally, his protectiveness is channelled, and the family stress is addressed rather than "aggression" alone. 16.9 Positive education and positive institutions Positive education teaches the skills of well-being in schools alongside academic skills. Martin Seligman and colleagues set out its case in 2009. The Penn Resiliency Program, developed by Jane Gillham, Karen Reivich and colleagues, teaches children to spot pessimistic explanations and generate alternatives, with modest effects on depressive symptoms that vary across trials; many school programmes use Seligman's PERMA model (positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, accomplishment). In India, the Delhi government introduced a Happiness Curriculum in its schools in 2018; it attracted wide interest, but rigorous independent evaluation remains limited. Positive institutions apply the same thinking to workplaces, for example through Fred Luthans's psychological capital (hope, self-efficacy, resilience and optimism as developable resources at work). The caution mirrors the clinic: when positive programmes ask employees to feel better about unfair workloads instead of changing them, they blame individuals for institutional problems. 16.10 Indian perspectives on well-being Indian traditions contain some of the oldest systematic reflection on well-being, suffering and the mind. Indian psychologists such as Anand Paranjpe, K. Ramakrishna Rao and Ajit Dalal (editors of the Handbook of Indian Psychology , 2008), and Kiran Kumar Salagame of the University of Mysore, who has written on well-being from the Hindu perspective, argue that these traditions contain psychological theory that can be studied. Two cautions apply throughout: psychology's attempts to measure these concepts are young, so claims must be modest; and "Indian thought" is not one system but many schools (Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and others) that disagree with one another. The three gunas The gunas come from the Samkhya school and are discussed at length in the Bhagavad Gita, especially its fourteenth chapter. All of nature (prakriti), including the mind, is made of three qualities in varying balance. Sattva is clarity, calm, goodness and knowledge; rajas is activity, passion, desire and restlessness; tamas is inertia, dullness, confusion and heaviness. Everyone has all three, and the balance shifts with time and circumstance. The Gita describes sattva as binding through attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas through attachment to action, and tamas through heedlessness, and it holds up the person who goes beyond all three. The psychological reading treats the gunas as something like temperament dimensions: the sattvic person calm and content, the rajasic driven and restless, the tamasic lethargic and withdrawn. Self-report inventories exist, such as the Vedic Personality Inventory developed by David Wolf in the late 1990s, and studies have generally linked sattva with better well-being and tamas with more distress. The measures are still being refined, and the gunas are not a diagnostic system. Trap. The three gunas (sattva, rajas, tamas: qualities of mind and nature) are not the three doshas of Ayurveda (vata, pitta, kapha: bodily principles). Nishkama karma and anasakti In the Bhagavad Gita (chapter 2, verse 47), Arjuna is told that he has a right to his action but never to its fruits, and should neither be driven by the fruits nor cling to inaction. This is nishkama karma , action without attachment to results. It does not mean not caring or not working hard; it means doing one's work wholeheartedly while holding the outcome lightly, with equanimity in success and failure, like the Gita's sthitaprajna , the person of steady wisdom. Namita Pande and Ramesh Naidu made this a psychological construct in their 1992 study "Anasakti and health". Anasakti , non-attachment, involves focusing on effort rather than outcome, relative equanimity in success and failure, and not being personally shaken by results. They distinguished it from apathy or withdrawal: the non-attached person works fully but does not stake self-worth on the result. People higher in anasakti reported less strain under stress, suggesting that non-attachment buffers stress. The clinical link is direct, since much anxiety and depression involves fierce attachment to outcomes ("If I fail, I am worthless"). Western psychology reaches related ideas through process goals, mindful decentring and acceptance and commitment therapy's values; these are parallels, not identities, but they let an Indian client see a therapeutic idea as part of their own tradition. Sukha and ananda Sukha is happiness or pleasure in the ordinary sense, always paired with its opposite, dukha (suffering); it depends on circumstances and the senses, and comes and goes. Ananda is bliss, described in the Upanishads as the nature of the Self, and in the Taittiriya Upanishad as the innermost of five sheaths (koshas) of the person; it does not depend on circumstances. Salagame has used this distinction to compare Indian ideas with the Western contrast between hedonic well-being (pleasure and satisfaction) and eudaimonic well-being (meaning and growth), arguing that ananda points further, to a well-being grounded in self-realisation. The Sanskrit word for health, swastha , is often explained as "established in oneself". Yoga, meditation and the family-centred self Patanjali's Yoga Sutras define yoga as the stilling of the mind's fluctuations and set out an eightfold path from ethical restraints and observances through posture, breath regulation and withdrawal of the senses to concentration, meditation and absorption. Yoga and meditation are widely used as well-being practices, and trials, including research at the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS) in Bengaluru, have studied yoga as an add-on treatment for depression with encouraging but methodologically mixed results. Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (Zindel Segal, Mark Williams and John Teasdale), drawn from Buddhist meditation, has good evidence for preventing relapse in recurrent depression. Yoga and meditation are valuable additions, not stand-alone treatments for moderate or severe illness. Much Western research assumes an independent self whose happiness is personal. Hazel Markus and Shinobu Kitayama (1991) described the contrasting interdependent self , defined through relationships and roles, and Alan Roland, a psychoanalyst who worked with Indian patients, described an Indian "familial self". For many Indian clients, well-being means family harmony, fulfilling one's dharma (duty) to parents and children, and the family's standing. The classical four aims of life (dharma; artha, livelihood; kama, pleasure; moksha, liberation) likewise frame the good life as balance rather than maximised personal happiness. Positive interventions for Indian clients may therefore work better when they include the family, value service and duty, and use the client's own concepts. 16.11 Critiques and cautions in clinical use Toxic positivity is the insistence that people should always stay positive, so that sadness, anger and grief become failures. Barbara Held (2002) called it "the tyranny of the positive attitude". Telling a grieving client to "focus on the positives" invalidates her, damages the alliance and teaches her that real feelings are unwelcome. Research supports the worry: Joanne Wood and colleagues (2009) found people with low self-esteem felt worse after repeating "I am a lovable person", probably because it clashed with their beliefs, and Iris Mauss and colleagues (2011) found that valuing happiness very highly can make people less happy, because they keep judging themselves as falling short. In bipolar disorder, heightened positive emotion is itself part of the risk. Not a substitute for treatment. A gratitude journal does not treat severe depression, psychosis, bipolar disorder, eating disorders or suicidal crisis. These need thorough assessment including risk, evidence-based psychotherapy and psychiatric referral where indicated. In India, the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 gives every person a right to access mental healthcare, and clinical psychologists must be registered with the Rehabilitation Council of India; the clinician's first duty is to identify the disorder and ensure proper treatment, and only then to add positive work. The evidence in 16.4 places positive interventions in mild to moderate problems, as adjuncts, and in relapse prevention. Cultural fit and honesty. Exercises developed with educated Western participants, such as boasting of strengths or writing effusive letters, may clash with norms of modesty and interdependence; the remedy is adaptation with the client, not abandonment. And clinicians must not oversell: promising that "three good things will cure your depression" is untrue and, when it fails, adds a sense of personal failure. Key. Use positive interventions with distress, not instead of it: after proper assessment, alongside evidence-based treatment, fitted to the person and culture, and without promising more than the evidence supports. 16.12 Case: positive psychotherapy alongside cognitive behaviour therapy Case. Priya, 26, a primary school teacher in Mysuru living with her parents, is referred by a general physician with four months of low mood, tiredness and loss of interest since her engagement was broken off by the other family. She sleeps poorly, has stopped singing, feels she has "let her family down", and admits passive thoughts that "it would not matter if I were gone", without intent. Sessions 1 and 2. The psychologist takes a full history, explores the passive thoughts, agrees a safety plan and, with consent, involves her mother. The Patient Health Questionnaire-9 and the Beck Depression Inventory, Second Edition place her in the mild to moderate range; with no mania, psychosis or suicidal plan, psychotherapy comes first, with psychiatric review if she does not improve. The formulation uses Aaron Beck's cognitive model (core belief "I am not good enough to be chosen", withdrawal, rumination) plus a fourfront grid: kindness, love of learning and perseverance; loving but anxious parents and a close cousin; gossiping relatives. Her positive introduction describes staying late for weeks to teach a struggling pupil to read. Sessions 3 to 5. Behavioural activation begins, with activities chosen through her signature strengths: singing practice twice a week and a weekend children's reading programme. She writes three good things nightly; when it starts to feel forced, the psychologist varies it with savouring one moment in detail. Thought records tackle "Nobody will ever want to marry me" and "I have shamed my family". Sessions 6 to 8. Through open and closed memories she writes about the broken engagement until rumination gives way to a fuller account. She resists forgiveness, and the psychologist does not push: forgiveness is explained as letting go of revenge for her own sake, and she chooses to let the anger be for now. Reading a gratitude letter aloud to her mother feels "very filmy", so she writes it privately, then cooks her mother's favourite meal and tells her simply that she knows how much she has done: person-activity fit and cultural fit in practice. Sessions 9 to 12. She practises active constructive responding with her cousin and parents, and finds meaning in wanting to be remembered as a teacher who made children feel capable. For relapse prevention the psychologist borrows from well-being therapy: a diary of well-being moments and the thoughts that interrupt them ("I shouldn't enjoy myself when my life is a mess"). By session 12 her scores are minimal and she is singing again. The psychologist notes honestly that the cognitive and behavioural work was probably as important as the positive exercises, and schedules follow-ups at one and three months with a written plan of warning signs and helpful activities. Recap. Alex Wood and Nicholas Tarrier argued in 2010 that well-being and distress lie on shared continua, that low well-being predicts later disorder and that strengths buffer adversity, so clinical psychology must study and treat both; Keyes's dual-continua model reaches the same practical point. Positive psychology interventions aim primarily to build something positive; in the 2005 trial, three good things and using signature strengths in a new way gave gains lasting six months, while the gratitude visit gave a large, brief boost. Meta-analyses by Sin and Lyubomirsky and by Bolier and colleagues found moderate, then small, benefits, and White, Uttl and Holder showed that small-study bias had inflated them; benefits depend on person-activity fit. Positive psychotherapy, Fava's well-being therapy, strengths-based cognitive behaviour therapy, hope therapy and the values work of acceptance and commitment therapy turn these ideas into treatment. Beatrice Wright's fourfront puts strengths and weaknesses of person and environment into assessment. Indian thought offers the gunas, nishkama karma and anasakti, sukha and ananda, yoga and a family-centred good life, all deserving careful, modest study. Positive work must never become toxic positivity or a substitute for proper treatment. Explain Wood and Tarrier's arguments and compare them with Keyes's dual-continua model. Describe the 2005 trial by Seligman, Steen, Park and Peterson: which exercises worked, for how long, and with what limitations? Critically evaluate the evidence for positive psychology interventions using the three major meta-analyses. What is person-activity fit, and who benefits most? How would you add strengths to a formulation and report? Discuss Indian perspectives on well-being (the gunas, nishkama karma and anasakti, sukha and ananda, the family-centred self). What can Indian clinical psychology learn from them, and what cautions apply? "Positive psychology in the clinic risks becoming toxic positivity." title: Biopsychology & Neuroscience
text: Biopsychology & Neuroscience The biology of behaviour from first principles: how neurons fire and talk, how the nervous system is built and mapped, the transmitter systems and their drugs, and the circuits behind sensation, movement, memory, hunger, hormones, sleep, stress, emotion, addiction and psychiatric disorders, anchored to Pinel & Barnes and deepened with Carlson, prioritised for MET 2026 and NIMHANS clinical neuropsychology. In this book Biopsychology as a neuroscience Evolution, genetics & experience Anatomy of the nervous system The cranial nerves (I–XII) Neural conduction & the action potential Synaptic transmission & neurotransmitter systems Research methods of biopsychology The visual system Audition & the other senses The sensorimotor system Development of the nervous system Brain damage & neuroplasticity Learning, memory & amnesia Hunger, eating & health Hormones, sex & the HPA axis Sleep, dreaming & circadian rhythms Reward, drugs of abuse & addiction Lateralisation, language & the split brain Emotion, stress & health Biopsychology of psychiatric disorders Clinical neuropsychology: syndromes & batteries Genetic, chromosomal & metabolic disorders Landmark studies, walked through Extended concept bank Fast glossary (A–Z) 1. Biopsychology as a neuroscience The one idea behind the whole field. Biopsychology is the scientific study of the biology of behaviour : how the nervous system produces what we think, feel and do. It is the branch of neuroscience (the larger study of the nervous system) that keeps behaviour at the centre. The recurring lesson is that mind and brain are not two things: every thought is a physical event in tissue. The six divisions of biopsychology The field is split by what you study and how . Learn each by its defining method, because the paper tests "which division does X?". Division What it studies Typical method Physiological psychology Neural mechanisms of behaviour Direct manipulation of the brain in controlled experiments (lesions, stimulation), usually in lab animals Psychopharmacology Effects of drugs on behaviour and the brain Manipulate behaviour with drugs; develop therapeutic drugs Neuropsychology Psychological effects of brain damage in human patients Case studies + standardised tests; the most applied division (NIMHANS leans here) Psychophysiology Relation between physiology and behaviour using non-invasive body measures in healthy humans EEG, heart rate, skin conductance (GSR), pupil size Cognitive neuroscience Neural bases of cognition (thought, memory, attention) Mainly functional brain imaging (fMRI, PET) in humans Comparative psychology Behaviour across species, evolution, genetics, ethology Cross-species comparison, naturalistic + lab study Trap Psychophysiology vs physiological psychology. Both have "physiolog" in the name. Physiological psychology = invasive manipulation of the brain, usually in animals . Psychophysiology = non-invasive recording from the surface of healthy humans . And neuropsychology = the study of human brain-damaged patients. Kinds of research, kinds of inference Pure vs applied. Pure = curiosity-driven knowledge; applied = solving a practical problem. Most real work is a blend. Experiments vs non-experiments. Only a true experiment (the researcher manipulates an independent variable and randomly assigns) can support a causal claim. Quasi-experiments and case studies cannot fully rule out confounds. Converging operations. Because every single method is flawed, biopsychology trusts a conclusion only when several different methods point the same way . This is the field's signature methodological value. Morgan's Canon / law of parsimony: prefer the simplest explanation that fits; do not attribute a higher mental process when a lower one will do. High-yield Human brain-damaged patients = neuropsychology ; drugs = psychopharmacology ; non-invasive measures in healthy humans = psychophysiology ; imaging of cognition = cognitive neuroscience ; animal brain manipulation = physiological psychology ; across species = comparative . Causation needs a true experiment; trust the conclusion many methods agree on. 2. Evolution, genetics & experience The problem this fixes. The old "nature versus nurture" question is a false dichotomy. Genes and experience are not rival causes adding up to 100%; they interact continuously. A trait is a genetic program read out in an environment. You cannot say a behaviour is "60% genetic" for an individual, only how much variation in a population is associated with genetic variation (heritability). Evolution of the brain Natural selection (Charles Darwin): heritable traits that improve fitness (reproductive success) spread. Behaviour evolves too. Larger brains are not automatically "better"; what matters is brain size relative to body size and the expansion of specific regions, especially the cerebral cortex in primates. Convergent evolution = similar traits arise independently (analogous structures). Homologous structures share a common ancestor. Do not read similarity as shared ancestry. Spandrels & exaptations: not every trait is a direct adaptation; some are by-products later co-opted for new uses. Mendelian genetics & the molecular layer Gene = a stretch of DNA on a chromosome. Humans have 23 pairs; the 23rd is the sex pair (XX female, XY male). Dominant vs recessive alleles; homozygous vs heterozygous ; genotype (the genes) vs phenotype (the expressed trait). Dizygotic (fraternal) twins share ~50% of genes (like ordinary siblings); monozygotic (identical) twins share ~100%. Comparing them is the classic heritability tool. Central dogma: DNA → (transcription) → mRNA → (translation) → protein. Epigenetics: experience changes which genes are read Epigenetics is the mechanism that finally dissolves nature-versus-nurture. The DNA sequence does not change, but experience can switch genes on or off via chemical tags, especially DNA methylation (silences genes) and histone modification . These marks can persist and even be inherited, so early experience literally edits gene expression: that is how environment becomes biology. The classic demonstration is the McGowan / Meaney rat studies, where high maternal licking raised glucocorticoid-receptor expression in the hippocampus, producing calmer, less stress-reactive adults. Ontogeny vs phylogeny Term Meaning Everyday handle Ontogeny Development of the individual across its own lifespan One person growing up Phylogeny Evolutionary history of the species/lineage The family tree of life Trap Ontogeny = individual development; phylogeny = species evolution. The mnemonic "ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny" (Haeckel) is largely discredited, but examiners still test which word means which. Also: heritability is a population statistic, not a personal percentage . The Bouchard Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart gave high heritability estimates (IQ ~0.5–0.7 in adults); MZ ≈ 100% shared genes, DZ ≈ 50%. 3. Anatomy of the nervous system Before any function makes sense you need the map and the cells that build it: the cells, then the divisions, the protective wrappings, the directions, and finally the brain regions. The neuron, part by part Dendrites receive input; surface area is multiplied by spines . Soma (cell body) integrates input; holds nucleus, ribosomes, mitochondria. Axon hillock is the trigger zone; it decides whether threshold is reached. Axon conducts the action potential; may be myelinated. Axon terminals (buttons) release neurotransmitter at the synapse. Neuron types by function Sensory (afferent) — periphery → CNS. Often pseudounipolar. Motor (efferent) — CNS → muscles/glands. Multipolar. Interneurons — local processing inside the CNS; the most numerous. Glia — the six you must know Cell Location Function Oligodendrocyte CNS Myelinates many axons (one cell, many segments) Schwann cell PNS Myelinates one axon segment per cell; aids PNS regeneration Astrocyte CNS Blood-brain barrier, K⁺ buffering, NT recycling, structural support Microglia CNS Immune defence, phagocytosis Ependymal cell Ventricles Produces and circulates CSF Satellite cell PNS ganglia Supports cell bodies in the PNS Trap CNS myelination = oligodendrocyte ; PNS myelination = Schwann cell . And Schwann cells, not oligodendrocytes, support axonal regeneration . The divisions: CNS and PNS CNS = brain + spinal cord. PNS = the somatic nervous system (voluntary, skeletal muscle; afferent + efferent) and the autonomic nervous system , which splits into sympathetic ("fight/flight", thoracolumbar), parasympathetic ("rest/digest", craniosacral) and the enteric ("gut brain"). Autonomic contrasts Sympathetic Parasympathetic Origin T1–L2 (thoracolumbar) CN III, VII, IX, X + S2–S4 (craniosacral) Pre/post-ganglionic NT ACh / NE ACh / ACh Heart ↑ rate ↓ rate (vagus) Pupil Dilate Constrict GI motility ↓ ↑ Sweat glands ACh (exception) — Meninges, CSF and ventricles The CNS is protected by three membranes, the meninges , from outside in: dura mater (tough outer), arachnoid mater (web-like middle), pia mater (delicate, hugs the brain). Between arachnoid and pia is the subarachnoid space , filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) . CSF cushions the brain, removes waste, and lets it float (reducing effective weight). It is produced by the choroid plexus in the ventricles. Ventricles: two lateral → third → cerebral aqueduct → fourth → central canal / subarachnoid space. Blockage causes hydrocephalus . Directional terms (orient yourself before lesions) Term Means Anterior / rostral Toward the front (nose) Posterior / caudal Toward the back (tail) Dorsal Toward the back/top (in the brain, top) Ventral Toward the belly/bottom Medial / lateral Toward / away from the midline Ipsilateral / contralateral Same side / opposite side Planes of section: horizontal , frontal (coronal) , and sagittal . Forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain Region Structures Function Forebrain (prosencephalon) Cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, limbic system, thalamus, hypothalamus Higher cognition, emotion, motor planning, autonomic control Midbrain (mesencephalon) Tectum (superior + inferior colliculi), tegmentum, substantia nigra, red nucleus, PAG Visual/auditory reflexes, motor control, pain modulation Hindbrain (rhombencephalon) Pons, medulla, cerebellum Vital functions (breathing, heart rate), balance, fine motor coordination Mnemonic S uperior colliculus = S ight (visual reflexes/orienting); I nferior colliculus = " I hear" (auditory). The brainstem = midbrain + pons + medulla, the part keeping you alive. Cortex — the four lobes Lobe Key areas Lesion produces Frontal Motor cortex (precentral gyrus), prefrontal, Broca's (L) Paralysis, executive deficits, Broca's aphasia, personality change (Phineas Gage) Parietal Somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus), association cortex Hemispatial neglect if right, Gerstmann's syndrome if left, agnosia Temporal Primary auditory, Wernicke's (L), hippocampus, amygdala Wernicke's aphasia, anterograde amnesia, Klüver-Bucy Occipital Primary visual (V1), visual association Cortical blindness, visual agnosia, prosopagnosia (fusiform) The cortex is mostly six-layered neocortex ; the deep grey matter and limbic structures sit below it. Subcortical structures Thalamus — sensory relay for all senses except smell . LGN (vision), MGN (hearing), VPL (body touch), VPM (face). Hypothalamus — homeostasis, hormones, the "4 Fs" (feeding, fighting, fleeing, mating). VMH lesion = hyperphagia + obesity; LH lesion = aphagia; suprachiasmatic nucleus = circadian clock; supraoptic → ADH; paraventricular → oxytocin + CRH. Basal ganglia — caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra. Red nucleus is NOT basal ganglia (it is midbrain tegmentum). Function: motor initiation/selection. Lesions: Parkinson's (SN), Huntington's (caudate/putamen), hemiballismus (subthalamic). Limbic system — hippocampus (memory), amygdala (fear), cingulate (emotion/attention), fornix, mammillary bodies, septum. Cerebellum — coordination, timing, motor learning. Lesions: ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor. Hemisphere specialisation (full treatment in §18) Left: language (Broca, Wernicke), logic, sequential processing, calculation. Right: spatial, music, faces, holistic, emotional prosody. Corpus callosum — the major commissure; severance produces the split-brain (Roger Sperry, Michael Gazzaniga). High-yield CNS + PNS (somatic + autonomic). Meninges = dura-arachnoid-pia; CSF from choroid plexus through the ventricles. Thalamus relays all senses but smell; hypothalamus runs homeostasis. Glia: oligodendrocyte (CNS) vs Schwann (PNS). 4. The cranial nerves (I–XII) Twelve nerves, learned by number, name, type (sensory/motor/both), function and the deficit each produces. # Name Type Function Common deficit / MCQ hook I Olfactory Sensory Smell Only nerve that bypasses the thalamus. Anosmia is lost early in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's. Cribriform-plate trauma shears it off. II Optic Sensory Vision; decussates at the optic chiasm A CNS tract, not a true peripheral nerve (myelinated by oligodendrocytes, sheathed in meninges). Chiasm lesion = bitemporal hemianopia (pituitary adenoma). Marcus Gunn (afferent) pupil = CN II lesion. III Oculomotor Motor (+parasym) Most extraocular muscles (SR, IR, MR, IO) + levator palpebrae + parasympathetic pupil constriction (Edinger-Westphal) + accommodation Full palsy = ptosis + "down & out" eye + fixed dilated pupil. Uncal herniation compresses III early (blown pupil). IV Trochlear Motor Superior oblique only (depresses + intorts the adducted eye) Smallest CN. Only CN to decussate before exit AND the only one to exit dorsally. Vertical diplopia worse going downstairs; head tilts away from lesion (Bielschowsky). V Trigeminal Both Face sensation (V1 ophthalmic, V2 maxillary, V3 mandibular) + cornea + dura; motor to muscles of mastication Largest CN. Trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux), V2/V3 most common. Corneal-reflex afferent. Jaw deviates toward the weak side on opening. VI Abducens Motor Lateral rectus only (abduction) Longest intracranial course → first CN affected by raised ICP (false localising sign). Lesion = failure to abduct, horizontal diplopia on gaze to lesion side. VII Facial Both (+parasym) Facial expression + stapedius; taste anterior ⅔ tongue (chorda tympani); parasympathetic to lacrimal, submandibular, sublingual glands Bell's palsy (LMN) = whole half-face including forehead. UMN lesion (stroke) spares the forehead (bilateral cortical input to upper face). Hyperacusis if stapedius involved. VIII Vestibulocochlear Sensory Hearing + balance/head position Acoustic neuroma = vestibular schwannoma at the cerebellopontine angle → unilateral sensorineural hearing loss + tinnitus + vertigo, later V/VII signs. Bilateral = NF2. IX Glossopharyngeal Both (+parasym) Sensation posterior ⅓ tongue + pharynx + carotid sinus; taste posterior ⅓; motor to stylopharyngeus; parasympathetic to parotid Gag-reflex afferent limb. Glossopharyngeal neuralgia triggered by swallowing. X Vagus Both (+parasym) Motor to palate, pharynx, larynx (recurrent laryngeal); sensation of larynx, pharynx, viscera; parasympathetic to thorax/abdomen to splenic flexure; taste from epiglottis Gag-reflex efferent limb. Uvula deviates away from lesion. Recurrent laryngeal palsy → hoarseness (left loops under the aortic arch). Vagal stimulation ↓ HR. XI Spinal accessory Motor Sternocleidomastoid (turns head to opposite side) + trapezius (shrug) Lesion: weak ipsilateral shrug, weak head-turn to the contralateral side. Iatrogenic injury in posterior-triangle neck surgery. XII Hypoglossal Motor All intrinsic + extrinsic tongue muscles (except palatoglossus = X) LMN lesion: tongue deviates toward the lesion ("the lick goes to the sick"), with fasciculations + atrophy. UMN lesion: deviates away . Types, parasympathetic carriers, brainstem exit Purely sensory: I, II, VIII ("1, 2, 8" — the special senses). Purely motor: III, IV, VI, XI, XII. Mixed: V, VII, IX, X (the four "B"s). Only four CNs carry parasympathetic fibres: III (Edinger-Westphal → ciliary ganglion → pupil/lens), VII (superior salivatory → pterygopalatine + submandibular → lacrimal/salivary), IX (inferior salivatory → otic → parotid), X (dorsal motor nucleus + nucleus ambiguus → viscera to splenic flexure). Brainstem exit level: Midbrain = III, IV. Pons = V, VI, VII, VIII. Medulla = IX, X, XI, XII. (I and II are forebrain.) Sensory nuclei sit lateral, motor nuclei medial; the solitary nucleus (taste + visceral afferent) takes VII, IX, X. Mnemonic Names: "On Old Olympus' Towering Tops, A Finn And German Viewed Some Hops." Type (S/M/B): "Some Say Marry Money, But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter More" → S, S, M, M, B, M, B, S, B, B, M, M (I–XII). Trap Bypasses the thalamus = I . Exits dorsally + decussates before exit = IV . First affected by raised ICP / longest intracranial course = VI . Smallest = IV ; largest = V . Bell's palsy (LMN) hits the whole half-face; forehead-sparing = UMN = stroke. Tongue (XII) deviates toward the lesion; uvula (X) deviates away . Bulbar palsy = LMN of IX–XII (flaccid, fasciculating tongue); pseudobulbar = UMN (spastic tongue, brisk jaw jerk, emotional lability). Jugular-foramen (Vernet) syndrome = IX, X, XI together. Argyll Robertson pupil (neurosyphilis) accommodates but does not react to light. 5. Neural conduction & the action potential Definition An action potential (AP) is the basic signal a neuron uses to talk: a brief (~1–2 ms) all-or-none electrical pulse that travels down the axon and, at the terminal, triggers neurotransmitter release. Stimulus intensity is coded by the frequency of APs, never their size. The resting membrane potential (RMP) An unstimulated neuron holds its inside at about −70 mV (range −60 to −90 depending on neuron type) relative to the outside. Three forces set this up: Force What it does Effect Concentration gradient K⁺ wants to leave (high inside), Na⁺ wants to enter (high outside) Sets up the chemistry Electrical gradient Inside is negative, attracts cations Opposes K⁺ leaving Selective permeability at rest Membrane is ~50× more permeable to K⁺ than Na⁺ (leak channels) K⁺ dominates → RMP sits near K⁺'s equilibrium Ion concentrations (mEq/L) and equilibrium potentials Ion Inside Outside Equilibrium potential (E ion ) K⁺ 140 (high) 5 (low) −90 mV Na⁺ 15 (low) 145 (high) +60 mV Cl⁻ 10 (low) 110 (high) −65 mV Ca²⁺ 0.0001 (very low) 2 (high) +120 mV The Na⁺/K⁺ pump (Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase) pumps 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in , using 1 ATP. It is electrogenic (net export of +1 charge, contributing ~−4 mV) and maintains the gradients, but it does not directly set the RMP, which is the K⁺-leak phenomenon. Mnemonic "K is in, Na is out, Cl is out, Ca is way out." · "3 out, 2 in, 1 ATP" (the pump) · "K sets the rest" (RMP is a K⁺ phenomenon). The four phases, step by step Phase What opens Ion movement Voltage Threshold (~−55 mV) Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels start opening at the axon hillock Na⁺ starts in Trigger 1. Depolarisation Na⁺ channels fully open Massive Na⁺ in −55 → +30 mV Peak (+30 mV) Na⁺ channels inactivate Na⁺ stops Plateau briefly 2. Repolarisation Voltage-gated K⁺ channels open (slower) Massive K⁺ out +30 → −70 mV 3. Hyperpolarisation (undershoot) K⁺ channels still open More K⁺ out −70 → −80 mV 4. Return to RMP K⁺ channels close; pump works Pump restores Na⁺/K⁺ −80 → −70 mV High-yield All-or-none law: once threshold is reached the AP fires at constant amplitude . Intensity is coded by firing frequency , never spike size. "Na⁺ in, K⁺ out" is the whole story. Refractory periods Absolute refractory period (~1–2 ms) — Na⁺ channels are inactivated (a "ball-and-chain" inactivation gate blocks the pore, distinct from being merely closed ); no stimulus, however strong, can fire another AP. This forces one-way propagation and sets the maximum firing rate. Relative refractory period (~2–4 ms after) — K⁺ channels still open / membrane hyperpolarised; a stronger-than-usual stimulus can fire one. Caps maximum rate at ~1000 Hz. Na⁺ channels have three states: closed (resting), open (during AP), inactivated (after AP). They reset only after repolarisation. Propagation & conduction velocity Continuous (unmyelinated): AP regenerates point-by-point; slow ( 0.5–2 m/s ), e.g. C fibres (slow pain, temperature, postganglionic autonomic). Saltatory (myelinated): the AP "jumps" between Nodes of Ranvier (where voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are concentrated), which is faster and far more energy-efficient. Up to 120 m/s in large A-alpha fibres (motor, proprioception). "Saltatory" = Latin saltare , to leap. Velocity rises with myelination (biggest factor), axon diameter, and temperature. Demyelinating disease (multiple sclerosis, Guillain-Barré) destroys saltatory conduction → slowing/block → numbness, weakness, vision loss. Trap What sets RMP = K⁺ leak channels, NOT the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (the pump is the gradient-maintainer). Absolute refractory = Na⁺ inactivated (≠ closed). Intensity is coded by frequency, not amplitude. NT release is triggered by Ca²⁺ at the terminal. Fastest fibre = A-alpha; slowest = C. 6. Synaptic transmission & neurotransmitter systems The synapse, step by step AP arrives at the terminal. Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open; Ca²⁺ enters (the trigger ion — without Ca²⁺ there is no release). Ca²⁺ triggers vesicle fusion with the presynaptic membrane ( SNARE proteins ; synaptotagmin = the Ca²⁺ sensor); NT is released into the cleft. NT crosses the cleft and binds postsynaptic receptors. An EPSP (depolarising: Na⁺ in or Ca²⁺ in) or IPSP (hyperpolarising: Cl⁻ in or K⁺ out) results. Spatial summation (different synapses at once) + temporal summation (one synapse firing rapidly) at the axon hillock decide whether a new AP fires. NT is cleared by reuptake , enzymatic breakdown , or diffusion . Postsynaptic potentials are graded (vary in size, decay with distance), unlike the all-or-none AP. Receptors come in two styles: ionotropic (ligand-gated ion channels, fast, e.g. nicotinic ACh, GABA-A, AMPA/NMDA, 5-HT3) and metabotropic (G-protein-coupled, slower, longer-lasting, e.g. muscarinic ACh, most dopamine receptors). Autoreceptors on the presynaptic terminal sense the cell's own NT for feedback. Research methods of biopsychology Every claim about brain and behaviour rests on a method, and every method answers a different question: lesion, recording, imaging, stimulation, and psychophysiology. Lesion / ablation methods Ablation / lesion: remove or destroy tissue and observe the deficit (the oldest approach). Aspiration (suction), radio-frequency / electrolytic lesions, knife cuts , and chemical excitotoxic lesions (kainic acid spares fibres of passage, killing only cell bodies). Reversible lesions: cooling or local anaesthetic (lidocaine) temporarily knock out a region, then it recovers, a cleaner causal test. Stereotaxic surgery: the stereotaxic atlas + instrument reaches a deep target by 3-D coordinates from the bregma skull landmark (where coronal & sagittal sutures meet). This is how electrodes and cannulae are placed. Recording methods Method What it records Strength Single-unit recording Firing of one neuron via a microelectrode Best spatial + temporal resolution (one cell) EEG Summed cortical electrical activity from scalp electrodes Excellent temporal resolution; poor spatial. Used for sleep stages, seizures, ERPs Event-related potential (ERP) EEG time-locked and averaged to a stimulus Tracks the timing of cognitive processing (e.g. P300, N400) MEG Magnetic fields from cortical activity Superb temporal + better spatial than EEG Imaging methods Method What it shows Note CT (CAT) X-ray structural image Fast, good for bleeds/fractures; uses radiation MRI Structural image from magnetic fields Higher resolution than CT, no radiation fMRI Function: the BOLD signal (blood oxygenation) Good spatial resolution, slower temporal; the workhorse of cognitive neuroscience PET Function: metabolism/blood flow via radioactive tracer (e.g. 2-DG, or receptor ligands) Can map neurotransmitter receptors; uses radiation DTI White-matter tracts (diffusion of water) Maps connectivity Stimulation methods Electrical brain stimulation (ESB): drive a region and see the evoked behaviour (Wilder Penfield's cortical mapping; James Olds & Peter Milner's reward stimulation). Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS): a magnetic pulse non-invasively excites or transiently disrupts a cortical area, a "virtual lesion" in healthy humans, and a treatment for depression. Optogenetics (newer): light switches genetically modified neurons on/off with millisecond precision. Other tools & psychophysiological measures Histology & molecular labels: Nissl/cresyl-violet stains (cell bodies), the Golgi silver stain (whole single neurons, used by Cajal), autoradiography, immunocytochemistry, 2-deoxyglucose (2-DG) autoradiography (metabolic activity), in-situ hybridisation (mRNA), microdialysis and voltammetry (extracellular NT levels), and knockout / knock-in / transgenic animals. Psychophysiology (non-invasive, on the body): skin conductance (SCR/GSR — sympathetic arousal; lie detection, emotion), ECG/heart rate, EMG (muscle), EOG (eye movement), pupillometry. Trap CT/MRI = structure; fMRI/PET = function. EEG = great timing, poor location; fMRI = great location, poorer timing (examiners pair these opposites). BOLD is the fMRI signal. Deep target by coordinates = stereotaxic ; one neuron = single-unit ; timing of cognition = ERP/EEG ; non-invasive virtual lesion = TMS ; receptor mapping = PET . 8. The visual system Vision is the model sensory system because its wiring is best understood. The job: turn patterns of light into a neural representation of the world. The retina Light passes through the retina's layers to reach the photoreceptors at the back, so the retina is "inside out". Rods — peripheral, very light-sensitive, no colour, low acuity (night/scotopic; pigment = rhodopsin). Cones — concentrated at the fovea centralis , colour, high acuity (day/photopic). This is the duplexity theory . The Purkinje shift : in dim light sensitivity moves toward blue (reds darken first at dusk). The optic disc (where the optic nerve leaves) has no photoreceptors = the blind spot . Signal flow within the retina: photoreceptors → bipolar cells → retinal ganglion cells (whose axons form the optic nerve), with horizontal and amacrine cells doing lateral interaction. Ganglion cells have antagonistic centre-surround receptive fields (Kuffler). Lateral inhibition sharpens edges (Mach bands). The retina-geniculate-striate pathway Retina → optic nerve → optic chiasm (nasal fibres cross, so the left visual field of both eyes goes right) → optic tract → LGN of the thalamus → optic radiations → primary visual cortex (V1 / striate cortex) in the occipital lobe. The map is retinotopic . LGN layers split into magnocellular (motion/contrast/coarse) and parvocellular (colour/detail). David Hubel & Torsten Wiesel found V1 cells are feature detectors (simple, complex, hypercomplex cells tuned to edges, orientation and movement). Blindsight : cortical-blind patients respond to stimuli they deny seeing, via subcortical routes. Two cortical streams: what vs where Stream Route Job Lesion Ventral ("what") V1 → temporal lobe Object and face recognition Visual agnosia, prosopagnosia Dorsal ("where / how") V1 → parietal lobe Spatial location, visually guided action Optic ataxia, neglect Theories of colour vision (complementary, not rivals) Trichromatic (Young-Helmholtz) — three cone types (S/M/L); colour = ratio of their activity. Operates at the receptor (retinal) level . Opponent-process (Ewald Hering) — colour coded in opposing pairs: red-green, blue-yellow, black-white. Operates after the retina (ganglion cells, LGN). Explains negative afterimages and why we never see "reddish-green". Trap The two colour theories are both right at different stages : trichromatic at the cones, opponent-process downstream (afterimages = opponent-process evidence). Rods do not code colour. Dorsal = where/how (parietal); ventral = what (temporal) — "dorsal is up and points to where". 9. Audition & the other senses Audition Path: outer ear → middle-ear ossicles ( malleus, incus, stapes ) → inner-ear cochlea (via the tympanic membrane and oval window). Hair cells on the basilar membrane (the organ of Corti ) → CN VIII → cochlear nuclei → superior olive → inferior colliculus → MGN of thalamus → primary auditory cortex ( Heschl's gyrus , temporal lobe). The map is tonotopic . How is pitch coded? Three theories Theory Mechanism Best for Place theory (von Békésy) Different frequencies peak at different places on the basilar membrane: high at the base , low at the apex High frequencies Frequency (temporal) theory The whole membrane fires at the rate of the sound's frequency Low frequencies (< ~500 Hz) Volley principle Groups of neurons fire in rotating "volleys" to track frequencies above any single neuron's limit Mid-range (bridges the two) Loudness is coded by firing rate + number of hair cells, not by place. Conductive deafness = outer/middle-ear transmission failure; sensorineural = cochlea / CN VIII damage. Somatosensation: two ascending highways Dorsal column–medial lemniscus (DCML) Anterolateral / spinothalamic Carries Fine touch, vibration, proprioception Pain, temperature, crude touch Decussates In the medulla (high up) At the spinal level of entry (immediately) Speed/fibres Fast, large myelinated Slower, small fibres Cutaneous receptors: free nerve endings (pain/temp), Pacinian (deep pressure/vibration), Meissner (light touch), Merkel (sustained touch), Ruffini (stretch). Pain fibres: fast sharp "first pain" (A-delta) vs slow dull "second pain" (unmyelinated C). High-yield Because the two systems cross at different levels, a one-sided cord lesion ( Brown-Séquard ) loses fine touch/proprioception on the same side (DCML crosses up in the medulla) but pain/temperature on the opposite side (spinothalamic crossed at entry). Gate control (Melzack & Wall): non-painful input (rubbing) closes a dorsal-horn gate (substantia gelatinosa); descending signals from the PAG , via endorphins, also dampen pain. Chemical senses, vestibular, attention Taste (gustation): sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami. CN VII (anterior ⅔ tongue), IX (posterior ⅓), X (epiglottis). Insula = primary gustatory cortex. Smell (olfaction): olfactory epithelium → olfactory bulb → piriform cortex , with no thalamic relay (the exception). Direct limbic ties explain odour-evoked emotional memory. Pheromones use the accessory vomeronasal system. Vestibular system: semicircular canals (rotation) + otolith organs (utricle/saccule: linear acceleration & gravity). Attention: the cocktail-party effect (you track one voice yet your own name breaks through, so unattended channels are partly processed); posterior parietal cortex + frontal eye fields shift spatial attention; right-parietal damage → hemispatial neglect. Endogenous (top-down, goal-driven) vs exogenous (bottom-up, stimulus-driven) attention. Trap Place = high frequency (base of cochlea), frequency theory = low , volley = mid . Smell skips the thalamus. DCML (fine touch, crosses in medulla) vs spinothalamic (pain/temp, crosses at entry). 10. The sensorimotor system The organising idea: a hierarchy. Movement is planned top-down and executed bottom-up. The chain runs: association cortex (intention) → secondary motor cortex (SMA + premotor, the plan) → primary motor cortex M1 (the command) → brainstem & spinal circuits → muscle , with the basal ganglia and cerebellum tuning it from the side. Descending tracts Pyramidal (corticospinal): origin M1 (Brodmann area 4, the giant Betz cells of layer V) + premotor; path internal capsule → cerebral peduncle → pons → medullary pyramids; decussates at the pyramids of the medulla (~85–90% → lateral corticospinal tract for fine distal voluntary movement; the other 10–15% form the anterior corticospinal tract and cross at the spinal segment). Extrapyramidal: rubrospinal (red nucleus, flexor bias), vestibulospinal (postural extensors, balance), reticulospinal (locomotion, posture, gross movement), tectospinal (head/neck orienting). Parkinson's (hypokinetic, resting tremor) vs Huntington's/chorea (hyperkinetic) Cerebellum Coordination, timing, balance, error correction, motor learning; compares intended vs actual on the fly "Timing/smoothing/coordination" → cerebellum. Lesion = ataxia, intention tremor, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia Basal-ganglia loops & mirror neurons (the mechanism layer) Direct vs indirect pathway. The direct pathway (cortex → striatum → GPi/SNr → thalamus → cortex) facilitates movement; the indirect pathway (striatum → GPe → STN → GPi) inhibits it. D1 receptors sit on direct-pathway ("go") neurons, D2 on indirect-pathway ("no-go") neurons. Dopamine from substantia nigra excites direct and inhibits indirect, biasing toward "go" — lose it and you get Parkinson's bradykinesia; L-DOPA restores both. Mirror neurons (di Pellegrino, Giacomo Rizzolatti; area F5 of macaque premotor cortex) fire both when an action is executed and when it is observed; hypothesised roles in imitation, action understanding and theory of mind, with human homologues in inferior frontal gyrus + inferior parietal lobule. Alpha motor neurons drive the main (extrafusal) fibres; gamma set spindle sensitivity (intrafusal). Reciprocal innervation relaxes the antagonist; central pattern generators produce rhythmic walking without cortical command; a motor unit = one motor neuron + its fibres. SMA = internal, premotor = external. Pyramidal crosses at the medullary pyramids. Development of the nervous system How a single fertilised cell becomes a brain with ~86 billion neurons wired into the right circuits: five phases, then two sculpting processes. Neural tube formation (neurulation): ectoderm folds into the neural tube (~week 3–4); its hollow centre becomes the ventricles, the anterior end the brain. Failure = spina bifida / anencephaly (folic acid protects). The neural crest cells migrate off the tube edges to form the PNS, adrenal medulla and other tissues. Proliferation: cells in the ventricular zone divide to produce neurons and glia. Migration: new neurons travel to their destinations, many climbing radial glia ; the cortex is built inside-out (deep layers first). Differentiation & axon growth: neurons take on their type; the growth cone navigates by chemical cues (chemoaffinity, Roger Sperry). Synaptogenesis: synapses form, in huge excess at first. Then refinement: Neural death (apoptosis) & synaptic pruning: ~50% of neurons die and unused synapses are eliminated. Neurotrophins (NGF, BDNF) are target-derived survival factors that keep useful connections alive: "use it or lose it". Myelination: continues for years; the prefrontal cortex finishes myelinating in the early–mid 20s (why mature judgement comes late). High-yield Critical / sensitive periods. Some circuits must get the right experience within a time window or they wire abnormally for life. David Hubel & Torsten Wiesel's monocular-deprivation kittens lost cortical responses to the closed eye ( amblyopia ) — but the same deprivation in an adult did not. Language and binocular vision have sensitive periods. Experience is part of construction, not a finishing touch. Trap Sequence: proliferation → migration → differentiation → synaptogenesis → cell death/pruning → myelination . The cortex develops inside-out . Pruning reduces synapses. Do not confuse apoptosis (programmed, tidy death) with necrosis (messy injury death with inflammation). 12. Brain damage & neuroplasticity Causes of brain damage Cause Key facts Tumours (neoplasms) Encapsulated/benign (meningioma) vs infiltrating/malignant (glioma); metastatic from elsewhere Cerebrovascular (stroke) Ischaemic (clot: thrombosis/embolism) vs haemorrhagic (bleed). Penumbra = salvageable tissue. Excitotoxic glutamate cascade kills neurons Traumatic brain injury (TBI) Closed-head: contusions, contrecoup injury, concussion. Repeated TBI → chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) Infections Encephalitis, meningitis, abscess; neurosyphilis Neurotoxins Heavy metals (lead, mercury), MPTP (causes Parkinsonism), alcohol Genetic / programmed See §22 (genetic disorders) and the dementias below Degeneration & regeneration Anterograde degeneration = the cut axon segment away from the cell body dies. Retrograde = the segment toward the cell body (and sometimes the cell) degenerates. Regeneration is much better in the PNS than the CNS, because Schwann cells guide and support regrowth, whereas CNS oligodendrocytes / glial scarring inhibit it. Plasticity & recovery of function "Plasticity" = the brain changes its structure and connections with experience and after injury. Recovery mechanisms: cortical reorganisation , collateral sprouting , redundant circuits, and behaviourally driven relearning (e.g. constraint-induced therapy , forcing use of the affected limb). Diaschisis is dysfunction of an intact area that lost its input from a lesion elsewhere, recovering over time. Adult neurogenesis occurs mainly in the hippocampal dentate gyrus (subgranular zone) and the subventricular zone → olfactory bulb, but is limited. Related plasticity phenomena: LTD (long-term depression, the weakening partner to LTP), kindling (repeated subthreshold stimulation lowers seizure threshold), and excitotoxicity (glutamate/Ca²⁺ overload kills neurons after stroke).
