No mnemonic meaning, it is simply the letter assigned to the mental-disorders chapter (Chapter V) in ICD-10's alphanumeric scheme. If asked "F-codes refer to," the answer is mental and behavioural disorders . 4.4 ICD-10 F-codes — the F00–F99 blocks (memorise the ranges) Range Block Examples F00–F09 Organic, incl. symptomatic, mental disorders Dementia (Alzheimer's, vascular), delirium F10–F19 Mental/behavioural due to psychoactive substance use Alcohol, opioids, cannabis dependence F20–F29 Schizophrenia , schizotypal & delusional disorders Schizophrenia (F20), delusional disorder F30–F39 Mood (affective) disorders Mania, bipolar, depression, recurrent depressive F40–F48 Neurotic, stress-related & somatoform Phobias, panic, GAD, OCD, PTSD, dissociative, somatoform F50–F59 Behavioural syndromes + physiological/physical factors Eating disorders, sleep disorders, sexual dysfunction F60–F69 Disorders of adult personality & behaviour Personality disorders, gender identity, habit/impulse F70–F79 Mental retardation (ICD-10 term; "intellectual disability" in ICD-11) Mild → profound F80–F89 Disorders of psychological development Speech/language, scholastic, autism (F84) F90–F98 Behavioural/emotional onset usually in childhood/adolescence ADHD/hyperkinetic (F90), conduct, tic disorders F99 Unspecified mental disorder Mnemonic Fast recall by last digit: 0 organic · 1 substances · 2 schizophrenia · 3 mood · 4 neurotic/anxiety · 5 physiological (eat/sleep/sex) · 6 personality · 7 retardation · 8 development · 9 childhood-onset. Trap In ICD-10, OCD and PTSD sit inside F40–F48 (neurotic/stress-related), not as standalone chapters. That is the opposite of DSM-5, which pulled OCD and trauma out into their own chapters. Always know which manual the question is about. 4.5 ICD-11 — what actually changed Coding format changed. Mental disorders moved from F-codes to alphanumeric 6-codes (Chapter 06). E.g. schizophrenia = 6A20 , bipolar type I = 6A60. Complex PTSD added. ICD-11 has PTSD AND Complex PTSD (PTSD core + the three "disturbances in self-organization" / DSO: affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, relationship disturbance). DSM-5 does not have Complex PTSD. High-yield difference. Gaming disorder added as a formal diagnosis. "Mental retardation" → "Disorders of intellectual development." Gender incongruence moved out of the mental-disorders chapter into a new sexual-health chapter (depathologised). Schizophrenia subtypes removed (paranoid, catatonic, etc. dropped), matching DSM-5; rated by symptom dimensions instead. Bereavement → Prolonged grief disorder recognised. Neurodevelopmental added to the chapter title; autism + ADHD grouped here. Dimensional personality model: ICD-11 scrapped categorical PD types and uses severity + five trait domains (negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, anankastia) with one retained pattern qualifier, borderline . High-yield NIMHANS angle: India officially codes on ICD . Expect "which body publishes ICD" (WHO), "ICD chapter for mental disorders" (Chapter V / F-codes in ICD-10), and an ICD-vs-DSM difference (Complex PTSD, free-vs-paid, global-vs-US, guidelines-vs-criteria). 5. DSM vs ICD & the DSM-5 structure 5.1 DSM-5 vs ICD-11, side by side DSM-5 (2013) / DSM-5-TR (2022) ICD-11 (2019, in force 2022) Publisher / body APA , US-centric WHO , global (~194 countries) Scope Mental disorders only All diseases; mental = 1 chapter Cost Sold / copyrighted Free Style Explicit operational criteria (count symptoms, thresholds) Clinical guidelines (flexible, prototype-based) Use Clinical + research Clinical + epidemiology + billing Sections 3 sections, 22 chapters ; no axes (dropped from DSM-IV) Chapter 6 = mental, behavioural, neurodevelopmental Multiaxial? DSM-IV had 5 axes; DSM-5 dropped axes Never multiaxial OCD Own chapter (separated from anxiety) Own chapter PTSD Own chapter (Trauma- & stressor-related) Own chapter; also adds Complex PTSD Schizophrenia subtypes Removed Removed "Mental Retardation" Renamed Intellectual Developmental Disorder Disorders of Intellectual Development Asperger's Folded into ASD Folded into ASD Bereavement exclusion (MDD) Removed (can dx MDD within 2 mo of loss) More cautious; ICD-11 adds Prolonged grief disorder Hoarding, Excoriation New in DSM-5 Also recognised Gender dysphoria / incongruence Renamed from "Gender Identity Disorder" Moved out of mental-disorders chapter to "Conditions related to sexual health" Complex PTSD No Yes Trap The multi-axial system was DSM-IV . DSM-5 dropped axes and nothing replaced them. If a question references "Axis I disorder" it is testing pre-DSM-5 vocabulary. ICD was never multiaxial. Swapping WHO ↔ APA is the #1 setup. 5.2 The 22 DSM-5 chapters (the order MET likes to test) # Chapter One-line anchor 1 Neurodevelopmental IDD, ASD, ADHD, SLD, tics. ADHD onset before 12. 2 Schizophrenia spectrum ≥ 2 of 5 sx, ≥ 6 mo total. Subtypes removed. 3 Bipolar & related Bipolar I = mania. Bipolar II = hypomania + MDE, never mania. 4 Depressive MDD = SIG-E-CAPS, ≥ 5 of 9, ≥ 2 wks. Bereavement exclusion REMOVED. 5 Anxiety GAD / panic / phobia / social / agoraphobia. Mostly ≥ 6 mo. 6 OCD & related OCD, BDD, Hoarding (NEW), Trichotillomania, Excoriation (NEW). 7 Trauma- & stressor-related PTSD > 1 mo. ASD 3 days–1 mo. RAD, DSED. 8 Dissociative DID, dissociative amnesia, depersonalization/derealization. 9 Somatic symptom & related SSD, IAD, Conversion, Factitious. Malingering NOT a disorder. 10 Feeding & eating AN, BN, BED, ARFID, Pica, Rumination. 11 Elimination Enuresis, encopresis. 12 Sleep-wake Insomnia, narcolepsy (cataplexy), parasomnias, OSA. 13 Sexual dysfunctions Lifelong vs acquired, generalized vs situational. 14 Gender dysphoria Renamed from Gender Identity Disorder. ICD-11 moved out of mental ch. 15 Disruptive, impulse-control, conduct ODD, Conduct Disorder, IED, Pyromania, Kleptomania. 16 Substance-related & addictive SUD = ≥ 2 of 11. Gambling = the one behavioral addiction in DSM-5. 17 Neurocognitive Delirium, Major NCD (dementia), Mild NCD. 18 Personality disorders Cluster A odd, B dramatic, C anxious. 10 disorders total. 19 Paraphilic disorders Atypical sexual interests + distress/impairment or non-consenting other. 20 Other mental disorders Catch-all. 21 Medication-induced movement Tardive dyskinesia, NMS, akathisia. 22 Other conditions, focus of clinical attention V-codes / Z-codes. Malingering lives here. High-yield Two questions MET keeps asking from the DSM-5 structure: "Which was REMOVED in DSM-5?" → multi-axial system, schizophrenia subtypes, bereavement exclusion, Asperger's as a separate diagnosis. "Which is NEW in DSM-5?" → Hoarding, Excoriation, DMDD, Binge Eating Disorder (moved from appendix to full dx), PMDD (moved from appendix), Mild NCD. 6. Mental status examination (MSE) Order matters — ABS-MTPCIJ : A ppearance, B ehavior, S peech, M ood/affect, T hought (form + content), P erception, C ognition, I nsight, J udgment. Mood = subjective ("how do you feel?"). Affect = observed (range, congruence, intensity). Thought form = how thoughts flow (loose associations, tangential, flight of ideas, circumstantial, blocking, perseveration). Thought content = what is thought (delusions, suicidal/homicidal ideation, obsessions, phobias). Perception = hallucinations (auditory, visual, etc.), illusions, depersonalization. Cognition = orientation, attention, memory, abstract thinking. Insight = awareness of being ill. Judgment = decision-making in real situations. 7. Neurodevelopmental disorders IDD (Intellectual Developmental Disorder) — onset in the developmental period; deficits in intellectual + adaptive functioning. Severity rated by adaptive function , not just IQ. (Formerly "Mental Retardation"; ICD-11: Disorders of Intellectual Development.) Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) — social-communication deficits + restricted/repetitive behaviors. DSM-5 merged Asperger's, PDD-NOS, and autistic disorder into one spectrum. ADHD — inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity ≥ 6 months; onset before 12 ; present in ≥ 2 settings. Specific Learning Disorder — dyslexia (reading), dysgraphia (writing), dyscalculia (math). Tic Disorders — Tourette's = motor + vocal tics ≥ 1 year, onset before 18. Communication Disorders — language disorder, speech sound disorder, childhood-onset fluency disorder (stuttering), social (pragmatic) communication disorder. Trap ADHD onset cutoff is before 12 (DSM-5), changed from "before 7" (DSM-IV). Asperger's is no longer a separate diagnosis (folded into ASD). 8. Schizophrenia & other psychotic disorders 8.1 Conceptual history Emil Kraepelin — coined dementia praecox , emphasised early onset + deteriorating course. Eugen Bleuler — renamed it schizophrenia , emphasised cognitive fragmentation. 4 As : Associations (loose), Affect (flat), Ambivalence, Autism (withdrawal — here "autism" = social withdrawal, NOT autism spectrum). Schneider — First-Rank Symptoms (FRS) : thought insertion/withdrawal/broadcasting, audible thoughts, voices commenting/arguing, made impulses/actions, somatic passivity, delusional perception. Suggestive but not diagnostic alone in DSM-5. 8.2 Symptom domains Positive (added) — hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior. Negative (taken away) — flat affect, alogia (poverty of speech), avolition (low motivation), anhedonia, asociality. Cognitive — attention, working memory, executive function deficits. 8.3 DSM-5 criteria for schizophrenia ≥ 2 of (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, negative symptoms), with at least one from the first three. Active phase ≥ 1 month; total disturbance ≥ 6 months (including prodrome / residual). Significant social or occupational dysfunction. Not better explained by mood disorder, substance, or medical condition. 8.4 Duration distinguishes the chapter Disorder Duration / defining feature Brief Psychotic Disorder 1 day to < 1 month Schizophreniform 1 month to < 6 months Schizophrenia ≥ 6 months Schizoaffective Mood episode + psychosis, but ≥ 2 wks of psychosis without mood symptoms (key differentiator from a mood disorder with psychotic features) Delusional Disorder ≥ 1 month, delusions only, no other psychotic symptoms Shared Psychotic Disorder (folie à deux) Removed as standalone in DSM-5; now under "Other Specified" Trap Schizophrenia ≠ DID. Schizophrenia = "split mind" (fragmented thought). DID = multiple identities. Different chapters, different mechanisms. Trap DSM-5 removed schizophrenia subtypes (paranoid, catatonic, etc.). They belong to DSM-IV. If subtypes appear in the answer choices, the question is testing DSM-IV vocabulary. 9. Mood disorders (bipolar & depressive) 9.1 Depressive disorders Disorder Episode Duration Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) ≥ 5 of 9 SIG-E-CAPS, must include depressed mood OR anhedonia ≥ 2 weeks Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia) Chronic low-grade depression ≥ 2 yrs (≥ 1 yr in kids) PMDD Severe mood symptoms premenstrually Most cycles in the last year Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (DMDD) Severe recurrent temper outbursts in kids Onset before 10, dx between 6–18 Mnemonic SIG-E-CAPS for MDD: S leep, I nterest (anhedonia), G uilt, E nergy, C oncentration, A ppetite, P sychomotor (agitation/retardation), S uicidal ideation. Plus depressed mood = 9 total. 9.2 Bipolar & related Disorder Required Duration Bipolar I ≥ 1 manic episode (depression / MDE not required for dx) Mania ≥ 1 week (or any duration if hospitalised) Bipolar II Hypomania + at least one MDE; never full mania Hypomania ≥ 4 days Cyclothymia Hypomanic + depressive symptoms, never a full episode of either ≥ 2 yrs Mnemonic DIG-FAST for mania: D istractibility, I ndiscretion (risky behavior), G randiosity, F light of ideas, A ctivity increase, S leep decrease, T alkativeness. Trap Bipolar I needs mania ≥ 1 week . Bipolar II = hypomania + MDE, never full mania. One full manic episode anywhere in the person's entire history → Bipolar I, even if all current episodes are hypomanic. 10. Anxiety disorders Disorder Core feature Duration Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) Excessive worry, multiple domains, hard to control ≥ 6 months Panic Disorder Recurrent unexpected panic attacks + worry about more / behavior change Attack peaks ≤ 10 min Specific Phobia Marked fear of a single object/situation ≥ 6 months Social Anxiety Disorder Fear of scrutiny / judgment in social situations ≥ 6 months Agoraphobia Fear of places where escape/help is hard (≥ 2 of 5 situations) ≥ 6 months Separation Anxiety Disorder Excessive fear of separation from attachment figure ≥ 4 wk (kids), ≥ 6 mo (adults) Selective Mutism Failure to speak in specific social situations despite ability ≥ 1 month (not first month of school) Trap OCD is NOT in the anxiety chapter in DSM-5 (its own chapter, §11). Same for PTSD (Trauma- and stressor-related chapter, §12). In ICD-10, by contrast, both live inside F40–F48 neurotic/stress-related. 11. OCD & related disorders OCD — obsessions (intrusive thoughts) + compulsions (repetitive acts to neutralize). Ego-dystonic. Time-consuming (≥ 1 hr/day) or distressing. Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) — preoccupation with a perceived flaw in appearance. Hoarding Disorder — persistent difficulty discarding possessions. New in DSM-5 . Trichotillomania — recurrent hair-pulling. Excoriation — recurrent skin-picking. New in DSM-5 . Trap OCPD ≠ OCD. OCPD = perfectionist, rigid personality style , ego-syntonic, in the personality-disorders chapter. OCD = ego-dystonic obsessions/compulsions, in the OCD-related chapter. First-line therapy for OCD is ERP , not CBT alone (see §20). 12. Trauma- & stressor-related disorders PTSD — exposure to actual/threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence + intrusion symptoms (flashbacks, nightmares) + avoidance + negative alterations in cognition/mood + arousal/reactivity. Duration > 1 month . Acute Stress Disorder — same symptom clusters but duration 3 days to 1 month . Adjustment Disorders — emotional/behavioral symptoms within 3 months of a stressor; does not meet criteria for another disorder. Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD) — withdrawn, emotionally inhibited toward caregivers; from severe early neglect. Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder (DSED) — overly familiar with strangers; from severe early neglect. ICD-11 adds Complex PTSD — PTSD core + disturbances in self-organization (DSO): emotion dysregulation, negative self-concept, relational disturbance. DSM-5 does not have Complex PTSD. 13. Dissociative disorders Dissociative Amnesia — gaps in autobiographical memory, often after trauma. Specifier: with dissociative fugue (sudden travel + identity confusion). Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID) — ≥ 2 distinct personality states, recurrent gaps in recall. Strongly linked to severe early trauma. Renamed from Multiple Personality Disorder. Depersonalization / Derealization Disorder — feeling unreal/detached from self or surroundings, reality testing intact (key differentiator from psychosis). 14. Somatic symptom & related disorders DSM-5 renamed this chapter from "somatoform disorders." Key entries: Somatic Symptom Disorder (SSD) — distressing somatic symptoms + excessive thoughts/behaviors about them. Symptoms may have a medical basis (the focus is on the response, not whether a cause exists). Illness Anxiety Disorder (IAD) — preoccupation with having an illness, with few/no somatic symptoms. Replaces hypochondriasis. Conversion Disorder (Functional Neurological Symptom) — neurological symptoms (paralysis, blindness, seizures) without medical explanation. La belle indifférence (oddly calm despite the symptom) is a soft sign. Factitious Disorder — intentional faking for sick-role gain (no external incentive). Munchausen = on self; Munchausen by proxy = on another (often a child). Malingering — conscious faking for external gain (money, avoiding work/court, drugs). NOT a mental disorder; coded as a V-code / Z-code. Trap The three are constantly confused. Conversion = unconscious, no gain (symptoms are real to the person). Factitious = conscious symptom production, internal sick-role gain. Malingering = conscious, external gain (money, court). La belle indifférence is a conversion soft sign. 15. Feeding & eating disorders Disorder Hallmark BMI / weight Anorexia Nervosa Restriction, intense fear of weight gain, body image disturbance Significantly low weight required Bulimia Nervosa Binge + compensatory behaviors (vomiting, laxatives, exercise) Typically normal or above weight Binge Eating Disorder (BED) Binges without regular compensation Often overweight ARFID Avoidant/restrictive food intake, no body image disturbance Various Pica Eating non-food substances (any age, dx ≥ 2 yrs) Rumination Disorder Repeated regurgitation (any) Trap Anorexia requires low weight ; bulimia does not . The defining difference between bulimia and BED is the compensatory behavior (present in bulimia, absent in BED). 16. Sleep-wake disorders Insomnia Disorder — difficulty falling/staying asleep, ≥ 3 nights/wk, ≥ 3 months. Hypersomnolence — excessive sleepiness despite ≥ 7 hr sleep. Narcolepsy — recurrent sleep attacks; cataplexy (sudden muscle-tone loss) often present; low CSF hypocretin/orexin. Sleep apnea — obstructive (most common) vs central. Parasomnias — sleepwalking, sleep terrors (NREM); nightmare disorder, REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (REM, often pre-Parkinson's). Circadian rhythm disorders — delayed/advanced sleep phase, shift-work type. 17. Substance-related & addictive disorders DSM-5 collapsed "abuse" + "dependence" into a single Substance Use Disorder (SUD) spectrum (no more "abuse vs dependence"). Criteria: ≥ 2 of 11 in a 12-month period. Severity: 2–3 mild; 4–5 moderate; ≥ 6 severe. The 11 criteria cluster into 4 groups: impaired control, social impairment, risky use, pharmacological (tolerance, withdrawal). Tolerance + withdrawal are pharmacological criteria but are not required for diagnosis. Gambling Disorder is the one behavioral (non-substance) addiction formally in DSM-5. Trap Tolerance/withdrawal due to prescribed medications taken as directed do NOT count toward SUD criteria. 18. Personality disorders Cluster Theme Disorders A Odd / eccentric Paranoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal B Dramatic / emotional / erratic Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic C Anxious / fearful Avoidant, Dependent, Obsessive-Compulsive PD 18.1 One-line distinguishers (Cluster B is the most exam-tested) Antisocial — disregard for others' rights; age ≥ 18 + Conduct Disorder before 15. Higher in males. Borderline — instability of relationships, self-image, and affect; impulsivity; fear of abandonment; chronic emptiness; self-harm common. Higher in females. First-line: DBT (Marsha Linehan) . Histrionic — attention-seeking, theatrical, sexually provocative. Narcissistic — grandiosity, need for admiration, lack of empathy. Trap Schizoid vs Schizotypal. Schizoid = detached, indifferent to relationships, no eccentric beliefs. Schizotypal = detached + odd beliefs, magical thinking, perceptual oddities. Schizotypal lies on the schizophrenia spectrum; schizoid does not (in DSM-5). Trap OCPD ≠ OCD. OCPD = ego-syntonic perfectionism (personality chapter). OCD = ego-dystonic obsessions/compulsions (OCD-related chapter). High-yield ICD-11 abandoned these categorical clusters entirely, replacing them with a dimensional model (severity + five trait domains, plus a retained borderline pattern qualifier — see §4.5). DSM-5 keeps the 10 categorical disorders in 3 clusters. 19. Suicide risk assessment SAD PERSONS: S ex (male), A ge (< 19 or > 45), D epression, P revious attempt, E thanol/drugs, R ational thinking loss, S ocial supports lacking, O rganized plan, N o spouse, S ickness. Trap Strongest single predictor of completed suicide = previous attempt . Most common method globally = hanging . Highest-risk diagnosis = MDD with comorbid substance use. 20. Treatments & therapy quick-map Disorder First-line psychotherapy Common pharmacology MDD CBT, IPT, behavioral activation SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline) GAD CBT, applied relaxation SSRIs / SNRIs; buspirone Panic Disorder CBT (interoceptive exposure) SSRIs; benzo for acute OCD ERP (Exposure + Response Prevention) SSRIs (high dose), clomipramine PTSD Trauma-focused CBT, EMDR, Prolonged Exposure SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine FDA-approved) Specific Phobia Exposure (in vivo, gradual) (rarely) Schizophrenia CBTp, family psychoeducation, social skills Atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, etc.) Bipolar Psychoeducation, IPSRT, CBT Lithium, valproate, lamotrigine, atypicals BPD DBT (Marsha Linehan), MBT, schema therapy (symptom-targeted, no specific drug) Anorexia Family-Based Therapy (Maudsley) for adolescents; CBT-E (meds limited, weight restoration first) Bulimia / BED CBT-E, IPT Fluoxetine (only SSRI FDA-approved for bulimia) ADHD Behavioral parent training, CBT Stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamine), atomoxetine 21. Master MCQ trap list OCD is NOT in the anxiety chapter (DSM-5); it has its own chapter. In ICD-10 it sits in F40–F48. OCPD ≠ OCD (ego-syntonic personality style vs ego-dystonic obsessions/compulsions). Schizophrenia (Eugen Bleuler) ≠ Dementia praecox (Emil Kraepelin). Schizophrenia ≠ DID (split mind ≠ split personality). DSM-5 dropped axes; the multi-axial system was DSM-IV. ICD was never multiaxial. DSM-5 (and ICD-11) removed schizophrenia subtypes. Schizophreniform = 1–6 mo; Brief Psychotic = < 1 mo; Schizophrenia = ≥ 6 mo. Bipolar I needs mania ≥ 1 wk; Bipolar II = hypomania + MDE, never full mania. MDD needs ≥ 5 of 9 SIG-E-CAPS, must include depressed mood OR anhedonia. Strongest predictor of completed suicide = previous attempt; most common method globally = hanging. Conversion (unconscious) ≠ Factitious (conscious, sick role) ≠ Malingering (conscious, external gain). La belle indifférence is a conversion soft sign. Munchausen = factitious on self; Munchausen by proxy = factitious on another. Hoarding and Excoriation are NEW disorders in DSM-5. Bereavement exclusion was REMOVED in DSM-5 (can dx MDD within 2 mo of loss). Asperger's no longer a separate dx (folded into ASD). Schizoid (detached, no odd beliefs) ≠ Schizotypal (detached + odd beliefs). OCD first-line therapy = ERP (Exposure + Response Prevention), not CBT alone. BPD first-line = DBT (Marsha Linehan). Schneider's First-Rank Symptoms are suggestive , not diagnostic alone in DSM-5. Bleuler's 4 As: Associations, Affect, Ambivalence, Autism (withdrawal) — NOT anhedonia. ADHD onset cutoff is "before 12" (DSM-5), not "before 7" (DSM-IV). ICD-11 adds Complex PTSD; DSM-5 does not. Anorexia requires low weight; bulimia does not. Tolerance/withdrawal from prescribed meds taken as directed do NOT count toward SUD. ICD = WHO; DSM = APA. Swapping these is the most common setup. "F-codes" → mental & behavioural disorders (ICD-10 Chapter V); don't overthink the letter. First mental-disorders edition of ICD = ICD-6 (1949). ICD-11 added gaming disorder and depathologised gender incongruence (moved to sexual-health chapter). India / NIMHANS officially codes on ICD. 22. 30-second recall script High-yield Abnormal core: 4 Ds (deviance, distress, dysfunction, danger). Classification: ICD (WHO, global, free, all disease, mental = Chapter V/F-codes in ICD-10 and Chapter 06/6-codes in ICD-11; ICD-6 1949 first mental section; adds Complex PTSD + gaming disorder, depathologises gender incongruence) vs DSM-5 (2013, APA, US, mental-only, 22 chapters, axes dropped, criteria-based). MSE = ABS-MTPCIJ. Anxiety chapter = GAD/Panic/Phobia/Social/Agoraphobia (≥ 6 mo); OCD + PTSD are own chapters in DSM-5 but inside F40–F48 in ICD-10. Mood: MDD (SIG-E-CAPS, ≥ 5/9, ≥ 2 wks), Bipolar I (mania ≥ 1 wk), Bipolar II (hypomania + MDE, never mania). Schizophrenia: Bleuler's 4 As, ≥ 2 of 5 symptoms, ≥ 6 mo total; Schizophreniform 1–6 mo; Brief Psychotic < 1 mo; subtypes removed. Personality clusters: A odd, B dramatic (Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic), C anxious; ICD-11 went dimensional. SUD = ≥ 2 of 11. Conversion vs factitious vs malingering by consciousness + gain. ERP for OCD, DBT for BPD.

title: Abnormal Psychology — the integrative approach, disorder by disorder (Barlow & Durand + DSM-5-TR + ICD-11)
text: Abnormal Psychology — the integrative approach, disorder by disorder (Barlow & Durand + DSM-5-TR + ICD-11) The Abnormal section built the way Barlow & Durand, Abnormal Psychology: An Integrative Approach teaches it: every disorder opens with a clinical case , then runs the book's four-beat frame — (1) clinical description · (2) statistics (prevalence, onset, sex ratio, course) · (3) causes , read through the multidimensional integrative model (biological × psychological × emotional × social × developmental) · (4) treatment . On top of the book, every disorder's classification is cross-checked against the current criteria so nothing is outdated: DSM-5-TR (APA, 2022) and ICD-11 (WHO, in force Jan 2022), shown side by side where they differ (the ICD-11 reclassifications are exactly what MET/NIMHANS/RCI fish for). Look-alike distinctions MCQs live on are in red trap boxes; where NIMHANS pushes past the book it's in purple . This is the companion to the Ahuja full-book page — same disorders, the integrative/case lens instead of the Indian-psychiatry lens. Built 2026-06-07. Abnormal (Barlow & Durand) Abnormal (Ahuja, full book) Abnormal cheatsheet ICD breakdown High-yield sheet Counselling (Sharf) Lookalikes What is "Barlow & Durand" and why a second abnormal page. The Ahuja page reads the field as Indian psychiatry: definitions, criteria, drugs, fast and exam-tight. Barlow & Durand reads it as integrative science : it refuses any single cause and forces every disorder through a multidimensional model , and it teaches from cases . That's the angle this page adds. Same syllabus, deeper "why does it happen" answers (causes), plus the triple vulnerability theory (Barlow's own) for the anxiety block and the equifinality / multifinality developmental ideas — both pure B&D, both testable. Use Ahuja for the cut-offs and drugs, use this for the model questions ("which approach / what causes it / which dimension"). Two ideas hold the whole book together. (1) The multidimensional integrative model. No disorder has one cause; each is the product of biological (genes, brain circuits, neurotransmitters), psychological (learning, cognition, conditioning), emotional , social/cultural and developmental dimensions interacting. (2) Diathesis-stress run forward in time. A vulnerability (diathesis) only becomes a disorder when life delivers the stress; genes and environment are not separate but reciprocal (your genes shape the environments you pick), and experience switches genes on and off ( epigenetics ). Hold these two and you can reconstruct almost every "what causes X / which model" answer. Jump to: 1. Defining a disorder (the 3 components) 2. The integrative model 3. Assessment & diagnosis 4. Anxiety disorders + triple vulnerability 5. Panic disorder & agoraphobia 6. Specific & social phobia 7. Trauma- & stressor-related (PTSD) 8. OCD & related 9. Somatic symptom disorders 10. Dissociative disorders 11. Mood disorders 12. Suicide 13. Eating disorders 14. Sleep–wake disorders 15. Physical disorders & health psychology 16. Sexual, gender & paraphilic 17. Substance-related & addictive 18. Personality disorders 19. Schizophrenia spectrum 20. Neurodevelopmental 21. Neurocognitive 22. Legal & ethical issues DSM vs ICD at a glance All the MCQ traps Names & studies roster Fast glossary (A–Z) Self-test (active recall) Part One · Foundations & the integrative model Ch 1. What makes behaviour a disorder, and the three traditions Barlow & Durand do not use a "4 Ds" list. Their working definition of a psychological disorder has three components , and all three usually travel together: (1) psychological dysfunction — a breakdown in cognitive, emotional or behavioural functioning; (2) distress or impairment — it hurts the person or wrecks their day-to-day functioning; (3) an atypical or culturally unexpected response — it deviates from what the culture expects (and is not merely a deviant act society dislikes). They lean on Wakefield's "harmful dysfunction" : a disorder is a failure of an internal mechanism to do what it evolved to do ( dysfunction ) and that failure is harmful to the person by their culture's standards. B&D's 3 vs Ahuja's 4 Ds. If a question cites " dysfunction + distress/impairment + atypical/culturally unexpected ," that's the Barlow & Durand definition (3 components). The "Deviance, Distress, Dysfunction, Danger" 4-D list is the more common Indian-text framing. Danger is NOT one of B&D's three. Both agree dysfunction/impairment is the indispensable core and distress alone is neither necessary nor sufficient (a person in mania feels great). Tradition Core claim · key names Treatment it implies Supernatural Possession, sin, the moon, witchcraft; Malleus Maleficarum (1487); the "mass hysteria"/St Vitus dances Exorcism, prayer, shunning Biological Hippocrates' four humours (imbalance = illness); Galen ; Emil Kraepelin (classification, dementia praecox ); the discovery that general paresis = late-stage syphilis cemented "mental illness can be physical" Rest, drugs, ECT, psychosurgery Psychological Moral therapy (Pinel at Bicêtre, Tuke's York Retreat — humane treatment); Sigmund Freud & psychoanalysis (unconscious, defences); Watson/Pavlov/Skinner behaviourism (learning); humanism (Carl Rogers) Talk therapy, conditioning, person-centred B&D frame the modern clinician as a scientist-practitioner : a consumer and producer of research who treats each case as testable. The whole book is then an argument that the three traditions are not rivals but dimensions of one integrative explanation. Recap Ch 1. B&D disorder = psychological dysfunction + distress/impairment + atypical/culturally unexpected (3 components, NOT 4 Ds; "harmful dysfunction," Wakefield). Three historical traditions — supernatural, biological (humours → Kraepelin → general paresis), psychological (moral therapy → Freud → behaviourism) — converge in the integrative model. The clinician is a scientist-practitioner. Ch 2. The integrative (multidimensional) model — the signature of the book This is the chapter the rest of the book runs on, and the one most worth knowing cold. No disorder has one cause; B&D insist on a multidimensional integrative reading where several dimensions interact over time. Dimension What it contributes · the B&D concepts Genetic Genes rarely cause a disorder alone; they set vulnerability . Key B&D ideas: diathesis-stress (a gene/vulnerability lies dormant until stress triggers it), the reciprocal gene-environment model (your genetic make-up makes you seek environments that then express the gene), and epigenetics (experience switches gene expression on/off without changing DNA). Polygenic, not one "gene for" anything. Neuroscience Brain structure (limbic system, amygdala = fear; hippocampus; prefrontal cortex; basal ganglia; HPA axis) and neurotransmitters as currents, not switches: serotonin (regulation/restraint of behaviour), GABA (the brake — reduces anxiety; benzodiazepines act here), glutamate (the accelerator), norepinephrine (alarm/arousal), dopamine (reward, "switch" for other systems; implicated in schizophrenia & addiction). The HPA axis → cortisol is the body's stress engine. Behavioural & cognitive Classical & operant conditioning (B. F. Skinner) of maladaptive responses; learned helplessness (Martin Seligman — uncontrollable aversive events → giving up → a model of depression); prepared learning (Seligman — we are evolutionarily primed to fear snakes/heights, not electrical outlets); cognitive appraisal and attributional style. Learning is not just behaviour : even one bad experience plus information transmission plants a fear. Emotional Emotions (basic-emotion theory) are action tendencies that, dysregulated, drive disorders; emotion contributes to behaviour (panic = the fight-flight emotion fired with no danger). Suppressing/avoiding emotion maintains anxiety. Social & cultural Social relationships buffer or worsen risk (loneliness predicts illness and death); culture shapes the form a disorder takes (e.g. somatic expression of depression, culture-bound syndromes). Gender roles channel which disorders appear. Developmental / life-span The principle of equifinality — many different paths can lead to the same disorder — and its partner multifinality — the same risk factor can lead to different outcomes. Timing matters: the same insult has different effects at different ages. NIMHANS/MET love these named B&D concepts: the diathesis-stress model, the reciprocal gene-environment model, epigenetics , equifinality (many roads → one disorder) vs multifinality , learned helplessness (Seligman → depression), prepared learning (why phobias cluster on evolutionary threats), and the neurotransmitter "currents" reading (GABA = brake, glutamate = accelerator, serotonin = regulator). The integrative model itself is the answer to any "which approach best explains psychopathology today" item. Equifinality vs multifinality. Equifinality = different starting points reach the same endpoint (abuse, genes, or loss can all end in depression). Multifinality = one starting point reaches different endpoints (one abused child becomes depressed, another resilient). Same prefix logic as "equi = equal end." Recap Ch 2. Every disorder = biological × psychological × emotional × social × developmental, interacting. Genetic dimension: diathesis-stress, reciprocal gene-environment, epigenetics. Neuroscience: GABA brake / glutamate accelerator / serotonin regulator / dopamine reward / HPA-cortisol stress. Behavioural-cognitive: learned helplessness, prepared learning. Developmental: equifinality & multifinality. Ch 3. Clinical assessment & diagnosis Good assessment is reliable (consistent — same result across raters/time), valid (measures what it claims), and standardised (fixed procedure + norms). B&D's tools: the clinical interview + mental status exam (appearance/behaviour, thought process & content, mood & affect, intellectual functioning, sensorium); behavioural assessment (ABCs — antecedent, behaviour, consequence); psychological tests — projective (Rorschach, TAT — unstructured, weak psychometrics), objective/personality (MMPI), intelligence (WAIS/WISC), and neuropsychological (Halstead-Reitan, Luria-Nebraska); plus neuroimaging (CT/MRI structure; fMRI/PET function) and psychophysiology (EEG, heart rate, EDA). DSM-5-TR (APA, 2022) Mostly categorical (you have it or you don't) with criteria sets + thresholds. Multiaxial system abandoned in DSM-5 (the old Axes I–V are gone). Organised so related disorders sit together (anxiety / OCD / trauma split into 3 chapters). Adds dimensional severity ratings and cross-cutting measures alongside categories. ICD-11 (WHO, in force 2022) Global standard; mental disorders = Chapter 06 . India follows ICD officially. More prototype/description-based — leans on clinician judgement, fewer rigid counts. Built-in dimensionality (clearest in personality disorders). Never used DSM-style axes. Reliability ≠ validity. A test can be reliable (consistent) yet invalid (consistently wrong). Validity requires reliability but not the reverse. Projective tests (Rorschach/TAT) = high clinical richness, weak reliability/validity; objective tests (MMPI) = empirically keyed, strong psychometrics. Recap Ch 3. Assessment must be reliable + valid + standardised. Tools: interview + MSE, behavioural ABC, projective vs objective tests, IQ, neuropsych, imaging, psychophysiology. DSM-5-TR = categorical, no axes; ICD-11 = more dimensional, prototype-based, Chapter 06. Part Two · Anxiety, trauma & OCD (B&D Ch 5) Ch 4. Anxiety disorders, and Barlow's triple vulnerability B&D draw a sharp line between three states. Anxiety = a future-oriented mood state, apprehension about possible threat (cognitive/somatic tension). Fear = an immediate alarm reaction to present danger — the fight-flight response firing now. Panic attack = fear occurring when there is nothing to be afraid of — a false alarm. Cued (situational) vs uncued/unexpected panic attacks; only unexpected ones define panic disorder. The triple vulnerability theory (Barlow) — pure B&D, very testable. Anxiety disorders grow from three vulnerabilities stacking : (1) generalised biological vulnerability (a heritable tendency to be tense/neurotic); (2) generalised psychological vulnerability (a sense, from early experience, that the world is dangerous and uncontrollable); (3) specific psychological vulnerability (learning, from family/experience, what to focus the anxiety on — e.g. "physical symptoms are dangerous" → panic; "social evaluation is dangerous" → social anxiety). General vulnerabilities alone aren't enough; the specific one points the anxiety at its target. Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD) Clinical snapshot A woman describes herself as a lifelong worrier: she frets about her kids, money, her health, being late, things that "might" go wrong, can't switch it off, feels keyed-up and tired, sleeps badly, neck always tense. There's no single feared object, just a roving, uncontrollable worry that has been there for years. Clinical description: excessive, uncontrollable worry about multiple everyday domains, with physical tension. The cognition (worry) is the engine; B&D note GAD patients show autonomic restriction (chronically tense, not spiking) — worry may be an avoidance of worse imagery. Statistics: ~3% (1-yr), insidious onset, often early; ~2:1 female. Causes: generalised biological + psychological vulnerability; worry as cognitive avoidance. Treatment: CBT (especially targeting the worry process), SSRIs/SNRIs, short-term benzodiazepines for acute relief only. DSM-5-TR — GAD Excessive anxiety/worry, more days than not, for ≥6 months , about several events. Worry is hard to control . ≥3 of 6 : restlessness, easily fatigued, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance. Distress/impairment; not substance/medical. ICD-11 — GAD Marked general apprehension or worry about multiple events, ≥ several months (most days). Plus additional symptoms: muscle tension, restlessness, autonomic overactivity, difficulty concentrating, irritability, sleep disturbance. Less wedded to the exact "≥3 of 6 / 6-month" count — clinician judgement of persistence. GAD vs normal worry vs OCD. GAD = free-floating worry about real-life domains, ego-syntonic ("I'm a worrier"). OCD = intrusive, unwanted, often senseless thoughts (contamination, harm) that the person resists. The GAD cut-off is the 6-month rule in DSM. Recap Ch 4. Anxiety (future) vs fear (present alarm = fight-flight) vs panic (false alarm). Triple vulnerability = generalised biological + generalised psychological + specific psychological. GAD = uncontrollable free-floating worry ≥6 months (DSM) + ≥3 symptoms; CBT + SSRIs. Ch 5. Panic disorder & agoraphobia Clinical snapshot A young man's heart suddenly races in a supermarket, he can't breathe, his hands tingle, he's sure he's having a heart attack and is going to die. ER tests are normal. Now he scans his body constantly and avoids supermarkets, then buses, then leaving home alone, in case "it" happens again where he can't get help. Clinical description: recurrent unexpected panic attacks (abrupt surge of fear peaking within minutes — palpitations, sweating, choking, chest pain, derealisation, fear of dying/going crazy) followed by persistent worry about more attacks or a maladaptive change in behaviour. Agoraphobia = fear/avoidance of situations where escape is hard or help unavailable if panic strikes (transport, open/enclosed spaces, crowds, queues, being out alone). Statistics: panic ~2–3%, onset adolescence–mid-30s, ~2:1 female; agoraphobia often follows panic. Causes (B&D's model): an initial false alarm (a panic attack out of the blue) becomes a learned alarm through interoceptive conditioning — the body's own sensations (racing heart) become conditioned cues for panic — layered on anxiety sensitivity (the belief that bodily sensations are dangerous). Treatment: CBT with interoceptive exposure (deliberately bring on the sensations and disconfirm catastrophe) + in-vivo exposure for agoraphobia; SSRIs/SNRIs; benzodiazepines only short-term. DSM-5-TR — Panic disorder Recurrent unexpected panic attacks. ≥1 month of persistent worry about further attacks or a maladaptive behaviour change. Agoraphobia is a separate, standalone diagnosis (can be coded with or without panic). "Panic attack" can be a specifier on any disorder. ICD-11 — Panic disorder Recurrent unexpected panic attacks + persistent concern/avoidance. Agoraphobia also a standalone category (marked fear in multiple situations where escape is difficult). Panic attacks can be added as a qualifier to other anxiety/fear disorders. The attack is not the disorder. A panic attack can occur in many conditions; panic disorder requires the attacks be unexpected + ≥1 month of anticipatory worry/behaviour change. Interoceptive conditioning (fearing your own heartbeat) is the B&D mechanism — a classic MCQ term. Recap Ch 5. Panic disorder = unexpected attacks + ≥1 month worry; false alarm → learned alarm via interoceptive conditioning + anxiety sensitivity. Agoraphobia is now standalone in both DSM-5 and ICD-11. Treat with interoceptive + in-vivo exposure CBT and SSRIs. Ch 6. Specific phobia & social anxiety disorder Clinical snapshot (B&D's classic "Judy" case) A bright teenager faints whenever she sees blood, even a drop, even on TV in biology class — her blood pressure spikes then crashes (the vasovagal drop), she goes pale and passes out. She has reorganised her whole life to avoid the sight of blood or injury. Specific phobia = marked, persistent, unreasonable fear of a specific object/situation, ≥6 months, with avoidance. B&D's four subtypes: blood-injection-injury (BII) , situational (planes, lifts), natural environment (heights, water, storms), animal (+ "other"). BII is unique : a biphasic, diphasic vasovagal response — BP and HR briefly rise then sharply drop , causing fainting — and it runs strongly in families (the only phobia where you faint). Social anxiety disorder (social phobia) = marked fear of scrutiny/negative evaluation in social or performance situations. Causes: direct conditioning, vicarious learning (watching someone else's fear), information transmission, all on a base of prepared learning (Martin Seligman) + the triple vulnerability. Treatment: exposure is first-line (graded exposure, systematic desensitisation, participant modelling); for BII add applied tension (tense muscles to keep BP up and prevent the faint); social anxiety adds cognitive restructuring + SSRIs. BII phobia is the one that makes you faint. Every other phobia drives BP/HR up (sympathetic) and you want to flee; BII is biphasic — up then a parasympathetic crash → vasovagal fainting . Treatment quirk: applied muscle tension , not relaxation. High-yield distractor. Social anxiety vs avoidant PD vs agoraphobia. Social anxiety = fear of judgement/embarrassment ; agoraphobia = fear that escape/help is unavailable; avoidant personality disorder = a pervasive, lifelong pattern of feeling inadequate & hypersensitive to rejection (the trait-level version of social anxiety). Recap Ch 6. Specific phobia (4 types: BII, situational, natural-environment, animal), ≥6 months; BII = biphasic vasovagal faint, treated with applied tension. Social anxiety = fear of evaluation. Learned by conditioning/vicarious/information on a prepared-learning base; exposure is first-line. Ch 7. Trauma- & stressor-related disorders (PTSD) Clinical snapshot Months after a motorway pile-up, a driver still jolts awake from nightmares of the crash, can't drive past the spot, feels numb and detached from his family, can't remember part of the crash, and snaps at any sudden noise. It hasn't faded; it's running his life. PTSD follows exposure to actual/threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence (directly, witnessed, or learned-of for close others). DSM-5 moved PTSD out of the anxiety chapter into "Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders." Four symptom clusters: intrusion (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance , negative alterations in cognition/mood , arousal/reactivity (hypervigilance, exaggerated startle), lasting >1 month . Acute Stress Disorder = the same picture lasting 3 days–1 month right after the trauma. Causes: the trauma is necessary but not sufficient — pre-trauma vulnerability (biological reactivity, prior trauma), peri-trauma severity, and post-trauma factors (lack of social support) decide who develops it; a conditioned-fear + failure-of-extinction model. Treatment: trauma-focused CBT, prolonged exposure , cognitive processing therapy, EMDR; SSRIs. DSM-5-TR — Trauma disorders One PTSD diagnosis, 4 clusters (intrusion, avoidance, negative cognition/mood, arousal), >1 month. Acute Stress Disorder for the 3-day–1-month window. A dissociative subtype of PTSD (depersonalisation/derealisation). No Complex PTSD category. ICD-11 — Trauma disorders Simplified PTSD : re-experiencing in the here-and-now + avoidance + sense of current threat. Adds a separate Complex PTSD (CPTSD) : PTSD + disturbances in self-organisation (affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, relationship difficulties) after prolonged/repeated trauma. Adds Prolonged Grief Disorder and Adjustment disorder in this grouping. The reclassification MET likes: ICD-11 has Complex PTSD, DSM-5-TR does not. CPTSD = PTSD core + the three "self-organisation" disturbances, after chronic trauma (childhood abuse, captivity). Also know: both manuals now have Prolonged Grief Disorder (DSM-5-TR added it in 2022). Recap Ch 7. PTSD = post-trauma, 4 clusters (intrusion/avoidance/negative mood/arousal), >1 month; ASD = 3 days–1 month. ICD-11 adds Complex PTSD (+ disturbances in self-organisation); DSM doesn't. Trauma necessary, not sufficient — vulnerability + support decide. Prolonged exposure / TF-CBT / EMDR (Francine Shapiro) + SSRIs. Ch 8. Obsessive-Compulsive & Related Disorders Clinical snapshot A student washes his hands until they bleed because an intrusive image of "germs spreading death to my family" floods him with dread; the washing relieves it for minutes, then it returns. He knows it's irrational, hates it, and it now eats four hours a day. DSM-5 carved OCD out of anxiety into its own grouping (ICD-11 too). OCD = obsessions (recurrent, intrusive, unwanted thoughts/images/urges that cause anxiety — contamination, doubt, symmetry, taboo/aggressive) and/or compulsions (repetitive behaviours/mental acts done to neutralise the anxiety — washing, checking, counting, ordering, praying), time-consuming (>1 hr/day). Insight is usually retained ( ego-dystonic ). Related: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (preoccupation with an imagined/slight defect + mirror-checking), Hoarding disorder (new), Trichotillomania (hair-pulling), Excoriation (skin-picking). Causes: cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop overactivity, serotonin; cognitively, thought-action fusion (treating a thought as morally equal to the act) and inflated responsibility maintain it; the compulsion is negatively reinforced by anxiety relief. Treatment: Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) is the treatment of choice (expose to the trigger, block the compulsion, let anxiety habituate) + SSRIs (often high-dose); clomipramine. OCD vs OCPD. OCD = ego-dystonic intrusive obsessions + compulsions, the person is distressed by them (a clinical disorder). OCPD = ego-syntonic personality style — perfectionism, orderliness, control, rigidity, no true obsessions/compulsions — the person thinks they're right. Distressed by the thoughts → OCD; thinks the rigidity is correct → OCPD. Obsession vs compulsion vs delusion. Obsession = intrusive thought ; compulsion = the act that relieves it; both retain insight. A delusion = a fixed false belief held with conviction (no insight) — that's psychosis, not OCD. Recap Ch 8. OCD = obsessions (thoughts) + compulsions (acts), ego-dystonic, >1hr/day, own DSM-5/ICD-11 chapter. Relatives: BDD, hoarding, trichotillomania, excoriation. Maintained by negative reinforcement + thought-action fusion. ERP is first-line + SSRIs/clomipramine. Don't confuse with OCPD. Part Three · Somatic symptom & dissociative disorders (B&D Ch 6) Ch 9. Somatic symptom & related disorders Clinical snapshot A man is convinced his stomach aches mean cancer. Test after test is clear, doctor after doctor reassures him, but within days the fear is back; he reads symptom websites for hours, books more scans, and his life narrows to monitoring his body. The body is the stage; the distress is psychological. DSM-5 collapsed the old "somatoform" list into fewer, clearer categories and dropped the requirement that symptoms be medically unexplained — what matters now is the excessive response to symptoms. Disorder Core Somatic Symptom Disorder One+ distressing somatic symptoms + excessive thoughts/feelings/behaviours about them (≥6 months). Symptom may even be medically real — it's the disproportionate response that's the disorder. Illness Anxiety Disorder Preoccupation with having/getting a serious illness with few or no somatic symptoms; high health anxiety, checking or avoidance. (The reworked "hypochondriasis.") Conversion Disorder (Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder) Neurological symptoms (paralysis, blindness, non-epileptic seizures, aphonia) incompatible with any medical disease; classic sign la belle indifférence (oddly calm about a dramatic deficit). Sigmund Freud's original "hysteria." Factitious Disorder Deliberately faking/inducing symptoms to assume the sick role (no external reward). Imposed on another = factitious disorder imposed on another (old Munchausen by proxy). Conversion vs factitious vs malingering — the classic 3-way. All three present with symptoms that don't fit disease. Conversion = symptom is unconscious/genuine (not faked), no external gain. Factitious = consciously faked for the internal reward of being a patient (the sick role). Malingering = consciously faked for an external reward (money, drugs, avoiding work/jail) — and malingering is not a mental disorder . Split on: conscious? and external gain? Recap Ch 9. DSM-5 dropped "medically unexplained" — it's the excessive response that defines somatic symptom disorder. Illness anxiety = fear of disease, few symptoms. Conversion = genuine, unconscious neuro symptom (la belle indifférence). Factitious (sick role, no reward) vs malingering (external reward, not a disorder). Ch 10. Dissociative disorders A disruption of the normally integrated functions of consciousness, memory, identity and perception — usually trauma-linked. Disorder Core Dissociative Amnesia Inability to recall important (usually traumatic) autobiographical information, beyond ordinary forgetting. Dissociative fugue = amnesia + sudden purposeful travel /wandering, now a specifier of amnesia. Depersonalisation / Derealisation Disorder Persistent detachment from one's self (depersonalisation — "I'm watching myself," unreal body) or surroundings (derealisation — the world looks dreamlike/foggy), with intact reality testing . Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID) Two+ distinct personality states + recurrent gaps in memory. Strongly linked to severe, early, chronic trauma (the post-traumatic model). Formerly "multiple personality disorder." DID ≠ schizophrenia. "Split mind" (Eugen Bleuler's term for schizophrenia) = split among thought/emotion/behaviour, not split into multiple people. DID = multiple identity states. A common deliberate distractor. Also: depersonalisation keeps reality testing intact (you know it's not real), unlike psychosis. Recap Ch 10. Dissociation = breakdown of integrated consciousness/memory/identity. Amnesia (± fugue travel), depersonalisation/derealisation (detachment, reality intact), DID (≥2 identity states + amnesia, trauma-driven). DID is not schizophrenia. Part Four · Mood disorders & suicide (B&D Ch 7) Ch 11. Mood (depressive & bipolar) disorders Clinical snapshot For two months a woman has felt flat and hopeless, dropped the things she used to love, sleeps badly and wakes at 4am, can't concentrate at work, feels worthless and "a burden," and has started thinking everyone would be better off without her. B&D build the chapter from mood episodes (the building blocks) up to the disorders (defined by which episodes occur). Episode Definition Major depressive episode ≥5/9 over the same 2 weeks (≥1 = depressed mood or anhedonia): mood, anhedonia, weight/appetite, sleep, psychomotor change, fatigue, worthlessness/guilt, poor concentration, suicidality ( SIG E CAPS ). Manic episode Abnormally elevated/expansive/ irritable mood + increased energy, ≥1 week , ≥3 symptoms ( DIG FAST : distractibility, indiscretion, grandiosity, flight of ideas, activity↑, sleep need↓, talkativeness); marked impairment / may be psychotic. Hypomanic episode Same symptoms, ≥4 days , no marked impairment, no psychosis, no hospitalisation. Disorder Defining requirement Major Depressive Disorder ≥1 major depressive episode, no mania/hypomania ever. Persistent Depressive Disorder (dysthymia) Depressed mood most days ≥2 years (1 yr in youth); chronic but milder. "Double depression" = MDD on top of PDD. Bipolar I ≥1 full manic episode (depression not required). Bipolar II ≥1 hypomanic + ≥1 major depressive ; never a full manic episode. Cyclothymia ≥2 years of fluctuating subthreshold hypomanic + depressive symptoms. Statistics: MDD lifetime ~16%, ~2:1 female , mean onset late 20s; bipolar ~1–2%, equal sexes, the most heritable mood disorder (MZ concordance ~60–70%). Causes (integrative): heritability ~40% (depression) up to ~80% (bipolar); monoamine (serotonin/NE/dopamine) dysregulation; HPA-axis/cortisol overactivity; psychologically, Aaron Beck's negative cognitive triad (negative view of self, world, future) + depressogenic schemas, and Martin Seligman's learned helplessness → hopelessness theory (attributing bad events to internal-stable-global causes). Stressful life events + low social support trigger episodes in the vulnerable. Treatment: depression — SSRIs first-line, SNRIs/TCAs/MAOIs, ECT for severe/psychotic/refractory; psychotherapy CBT & IPT have the best evidence. Bipolar — lithium (mood stabiliser, anti-suicidal, narrow therapeutic index), valproate/lamotrigine, atypical antipsychotics; antidepressant monotherapy avoided (can flip to mania). DSM-5-TR — Mood Depressive and bipolar disorders are two separate chapters . Bereavement exclusion removed — MDD can be diagnosed soon after a loss. Added DMDD (child irritability) and PMDD as depressive disorders; Prolonged Grief Disorder (2022). Specifiers: melancholic, atypical, peripartum, seasonal, with mixed features, with anxious distress. ICD-11 — Mood Single "Mood disorders" grouping, then depressive vs bipolar. Depression graded by severity (mild/moderate/severe ± psychotic) and single vs recurrent. Has Bipolar I and II and cyclothymia; no DMDD (irritability handled differently). Prolonged Grief Disorder sits under trauma/stress, not mood. BP-I vs BP-II vs cyclothymia. One full mania ever = BP-I (forever). Hypomania + depression, no mania = BP-II. Chronic subthreshold ups-and-downs ≥2 yrs = cyclothymia. MDD vs grief: grief comes in waves, centres on the loss, self-esteem preserved; MDD is pervasive with worthlessness/anhedonia (and DSM-5 dropped the bereavement exclusion). The psychodynamic names: Sidney Blatt's two depressions and René Spitz's infant depression B&D's psychological dimension of mood disorders is mostly Beck and Seligman, but the NIMHANS paper asked about two psychodynamic names, and both use the same word. Anaclitic means "leaning on" (Greek anaklinein , to lean upon): a depression organised around dependency and the loss of the person you lean on. Sidney Blatt (1974), adults Anaclitic (dependent) Introjective (self-critical) Line of development that goes wrong Relatedness (closeness, trust) Self-definition (identity, self-worth) Core theme Loss of the other, fear of abandonment ; helpless, lonely, empty, longing to be cared for Failure and worth; guilt , worthlessness, a harsh superego , perfectionism Aaron Beck's parallel Sociotropy Autonomy Improves mainly through The therapeutic relationship Insight and interpretation Suicide risk Lower Higher : self-critical perfectionism (Sidney Blatt, 1995, "The Destructiveness of Perfectionism") Blatt's view: personality grows along these two lines in a dialectic, and depression comes from one line over-developed at the cost of the other. His types are measured by the Depressive Experiences Questionnaire (DEQ) (Sidney Blatt and colleagues, 1976), which gives Dependency , Self-Criticism and Efficacy scores. René Spitz, infants Anaclitic depression (1946) Hospitalism (1945) Who Infants in the second half of the first year who had a good bond with the mother Infants reared in an institution (a foundling home) with no individual mothering What happened Separated from the mother for about 3 months with no adequate substitute Total, prolonged emotional deprivation , even with good food and hygiene Picture Crying and clinging, then withdrawal, weepiness, weight loss, poor sleep, slowed development Severe developmental delay, marasmus (wasting), infections, a very high death rate Outcome Reversible if the mother returns within about 3 to 5 months Often irreversible Spitz's babies in a prison nursery, cared for by their own mothers, thrived; the foundling-home babies declined. That contrast fed straight into John Bowlby's protest → despair → detachment sequence and the maternal-deprivation work of Harry Harlow and Mary Ainsworth . Same word, two theorists. Infant + separation from the mother → René Spitz . Adult + dependency vs self-criticism → Sidney Blatt . Inside Blatt, the introjective (self-critical) type carries the higher suicide risk. Inside Spitz, hospitalism is the total, often irreversible one; anaclitic depression is partial and reversible. Full one-pager: Blatt & Spitz (also in the Library under Requested Topics). Recap Ch 11. Episodes (MDE ≥5/9 / 2wk; mania ≥1wk; hypomania ≥4 days) build the disorders (MDD, PDD ≥2yr, BP-I one mania, BP-II hypomania+depression, cyclothymia ≥2yr). Monoamine + HPA + Beck's triad + learned helplessness. SSRIs/ECT + CBT/IPT for depression; lithium for bipolar, no antidepressant alone. Psychodynamic names: Sidney Blatt's anaclitic (dependent) vs introjective (self-critical, higher suicide risk) adult depression; René Spitz's infant anaclitic depression (reversible) vs hospitalism (often irreversible). Ch 12. Suicide B&D treat suicide in the mood chapter. Durkheim's sociological types: egoistic (low social integration, isolation), altruistic (over-integration, dying for the group), anomic (sudden disruption of norms — a crash, a job loss), fatalistic (over-regulation, no escape). Risk factors: prior attempt (the strongest predictor), a clear plan/means, hopelessness, male sex (men complete more; women attempt more), older age, substance use, recent loss, family history, access to lethal means. Terms: ideation → plan → attempt → completion ; parasuicide /non-suicidal self-injury (self-harm without intent to die). Prevention: means restriction, crisis lines, treating the underlying disorder; lithium specifically lowers suicide in bipolar. Men vs women. Women attempt suicide more often; men complete (die by) suicide more often, largely because of more lethal means. The single best predictor of a future attempt is a past attempt . Recap Ch 12. Durkheim: egoistic / altruistic / anomic / fatalistic. Strongest predictor = prior attempt; hopelessness + plan + means raise risk. Women attempt more, men complete more. Restrict means, treat the disorder. Part Five · Eating & sleep–wake disorders (B&D Ch 8) Ch 13. Eating disorders Clinical snapshot A 17-year-old at 78% of expected weight insists she is "fat," skips meals, runs daily, weighs herself five times a day, and has stopped menstruating; her family is frightened but she cannot see a problem. Disorder Core Anorexia Nervosa Restriction → significantly low weight , intense fear of weight gain, distorted body image / denial of seriousness. Subtypes: restricting vs binge-eating/purging . (DSM-5 dropped the amenorrhoea requirement .) Highest mortality of any mental disorder. Bulimia Nervosa Recurrent binge + compensatory behaviour (vomiting, laxatives, fasting, over-exercise), self-evaluation over-tied to shape/weight; weight usually normal . Signs: Russell's sign (knuckle calluses), parotid swelling, eroded enamel. Binge-Eating Disorder Recurrent binges with no compensatory behaviour; distress; new full DSM-5 category . Most common eating disorder; linked to obesity. Statistics: ~90% female, onset adolescence, Western/industrialised & weight-focused subcultures over-represented. Causes (integrative): sociocultural thin-ideal internalisation + dieting + perfectionism + low self-esteem, on a genetic/temperamental base; serotonin involvement. Treatment: CBT is first-line for bulimia and binge-eating ; anorexia — weight restoration first, then family-based treatment (Maudsley) for adolescents; SSRIs help bulimia. DSM-5-TR — Eating Anorexia, bulimia, binge-eating, ARFID, pica, rumination. Anorexia: no amenorrhoea requirement; severity by BMI . Binge-Eating Disorder = a full standalone diagnosis. ICD-11 — Eating Same core set; adds ARFID and recognises Binge-Eating Disorder . Anorexia defined by significantly low body weight for age/height + dread of weight gain (no amenorrhoea either). Allows an "anorexia with dangerously low weight" severity flag. Anorexia vs bulimia. The split is weight : anorexia = significantly underweight (the binge/purge subtype of anorexia still exists, but they're underweight); bulimia = normal/near-normal weight with binge-purge cycles. If markedly underweight → anorexia regardless of purging. Recap Ch 13. Anorexia (low weight, fear of gain, distorted image; no amenorrhoea criterion; highest mortality), bulimia (binge + compensation, normal weight), binge-eating (no compensation, new category). Thin-ideal + perfectionism on a genetic base. CBT first-line for bulimia/BED; FBT (Maudsley) for adolescent anorexia. Ch 14. Sleep–wake disorders Group Key disorders Dyssomnias (amount/quality/timing) Insomnia disorder (trouble falling/staying asleep); Hypersomnolence ; Narcolepsy (sleep attacks + cataplexy + sleep-onset REM, low hypocretin/orexin); breathing-related ( sleep apnoea ); circadian-rhythm disorders. Parasomnias (abnormal events) NREM : sleepwalking & sleep terrors (deep slow-wave sleep, no dream recall, hard to wake). REM : nightmare disorder (vivid dreams, easily recalled) & REM sleep behaviour disorder. Sleep terror vs nightmare. Sleep terror = NREM (slow-wave), early night, child screams/agitated but unwakeable and amnesic for it. Nightmare = REM, later night, person wakes fully and remembers the dream. Narcolepsy's giveaway = cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone with emotion). Treatment: insomnia — CBT-I (stimulus control, sleep restriction, sleep hygiene) is first-line over hypnotics; narcolepsy — stimulants/modafinil + scheduled naps; apnoea — CPAP. Recap Ch 14. Dyssomnias (insomnia, narcolepsy+cataplexy, apnoea, circadian) vs parasomnias (NREM sleep terrors/sleepwalking — amnesic; REM nightmares — recalled). CBT-I first-line for insomnia. Part Six · Physical disorders & health psychology (B&D Ch 9) Ch 15. Physical disorders and health psychology Clinical snapshot Arjun, 48, a branch manager, is always racing the clock, finishes other people's sentences and loses his temper in traffic. He has had high blood pressure for six years, smokes "only at work" and sleeps five hours. After a shouting match with a client he gets crushing chest pain. In the cardiac unit the doctor tells him the medicine is only half the plan: how he handles stress, anger, cigarettes and sleep will decide whether there is a second attack. This chapter flips the rest of the book. Instead of a mental disorder, the person has a physical disease (heart disease, cancer, HIV, chronic pain), and the question is how psychological and social factors change who gets it, how fast it progresses and how well treatment works. Barlow & Durand say those factors act through two routes : (1) directly on biology (stress hormones, immune function, blood pressure) and (2) through long-standing behaviour (smoking, diet, inactivity, alcohol, unsafe sex, not taking medicine). The second route is huge: J. Michael McGinnis and William Foege (1993) traced about half of all US deaths to behaviour, with tobacco, diet and inactivity, and alcohol leading the list. Term What it means Behavioural medicine The interdisciplinary field (psychology, medicine, nursing, public health) that applies behavioural science to the prevention, diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation of physical disease. The wider umbrella. Health psychology The branch of psychology inside that umbrella: the study of psychological factors in promoting health , preventing illness and the way people respond to being ill. Psychosomatic / psychophysiological disorders The old labels for physical diseases with a psychological contribution. Dropped because they implied the illness was "all in the mind". DSM-5-TR uses Psychological Factors Affecting Other Medical Conditions instead. Stress: the biology Idea Who / when Core Fight-or-flight Walter Cannon (1915) Threat triggers the sympathetic nervous system and adrenaline from the adrenal medulla: heart rate, blood pressure and glucose rise, digestion shuts down. Built for short emergencies. General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) Hans Selye (1936) The body's response to any long stressor runs in three stages : alarm (mobilise) → resistance (cope, hormones stay high) → exhaustion (reserves run out, illness and even death follow). Selye borrowed the word "stress" from physics. HPA axis (physiology) Hypothalamus releases CRH → pituitary releases ACTH → adrenal cortex releases cortisol . Cortisol mobilises energy and damps inflammation; kept high for months it suppresses immunity and can damage the hippocampus . Status and control Robert Sapolsky (1990) In wild baboon troops, the low-ranking males, who had little control and little predictability, ran chronically higher cortisol . In humans the Whitehall studies of British civil servants ( Michael Marmot ) found the lowest grades, with the least control over their work, had the highest heart-disease death rates. Stress: the psychology Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman (1984) gave the transactional model : stress is not the event but the appraisal . In primary appraisal you ask "is this a threat, a loss or a challenge?"; in secondary appraisal you ask "do I have what it takes to cope?". Stress is high when the threat looks big and the resources look small. Coping then goes two ways: problem-focused (change the situation: make a study plan, talk to the boss) or emotion-focused (change how you feel about it: reappraise, seek comfort, distract, deny). Thomas Holmes and Richard Rahe (1967) built the Social Readjustment Rating Scale (SRRS) : 43 life events scored in life change units , with death of a spouse = 100 and marriage = 50 ; about 300+ units in a year went with a higher risk of illness. The point examiners love: positive events (marriage, a new job) count as stress too, because any change demands readjustment. Later work by Allen Kanner, Richard Lazarus and colleagues (1981) found that small daily hassles predict symptoms better than the big life events. What protects: hardiness ( Suzanne Kobasa, 1979 ), the "3 Cs" of commitment, control and challenge , found in executives who stayed healthy under heavy stress; social support ( Lisa Berkman and S. Leonard Syme, 1979 , Alameda County: the most socially isolated adults had about two to three times the death rate over nine years); a sense of control and self-efficacy ( Albert Bandura, 1977 ); and optimism . Stress and the immune system (psychoneuroimmunology) The immune system finds and destroys antigens (viruses, bacteria, tumour cells). Its white blood cells split into the humoral arm ( B cells make antibodies ) and the cellular arm ( T cells : helper T cells boost the response, suppressor T cells shut it down, killer T cells destroy infected cells), plus natural killer (NK) cells . When it attacks the body's own tissue the result is an autoimmune disease (rheumatoid arthritis). Psychoneuroimmunology (PNI) , a term coined by Robert Ader , studies how the mind and nervous system talk to this system. Study What it showed Robert Ader and Nicholas Cohen (1975) Rats drank saccharin water paired with cyclophosphamide , a drug that suppresses immunity. Later the saccharin alone suppressed immune response (and some rats died). The immune system can be classically conditioned : the founding PNI study. Janice Kiecolt-Glaser and Ronald Glaser Medical students had lower NK-cell activity during exams (1984). Family caregivers of people with Alzheimer's disease took about 24% longer to heal a standard small wound (1995). Sheldon Cohen, David Tyrrell and Andrew Smith (1991) Volunteers given nasal drops of a cold virus: the more stressed they were beforehand, the more likely they were to catch the cold , in a dose-response pattern. The diseases B&D cover Condition The psychological angle HIV / AIDS HIV attacks the CD4 helper T cells . Stress and depression are linked with faster progression in some studies; cognitive-behavioural stress management ( Michael Antoni and colleagues) improves mood and coping. With antiretroviral drugs HIV became a chronic illness, so adherence and prevention (condoms, needle exchange, testing) are the main behavioural targets. Cancer Psycho-oncology. David Spiegel (1989) reported that women with metastatic breast cancer in weekly support groups lived about twice as long (roughly 37 vs 19 months). His own larger trial ( 2007 ) found no survival gain , but the groups still cut distress and pain. Children facing painful procedures do better with distraction, relaxation and coaching. Hypertension About 90% of cases are essential hypertension (no single physical cause). Often symptomless, a "silent" killer. Linked to stress reactivity, suppressed anger, salt, weight, alcohol and inactivity; relaxation, exercise, weight loss and less salt all lower it. Coronary heart disease (CHD) Blocked coronary arteries (atherosclerosis) → angina, heart attack. Type A behaviour pattern ( Meyer Friedman and Ray Rosenman, 1959 ): competitive, time-urgent , impatient, hostile . In the Western Collaborative Group Study Type A men had about twice the CHD rate; later studies were mixed and the toxic core turned out to be hostility / anger ( Redford Williams ), not hurry. Type D ( Johan Denollet, 1996 ) = negative affectivity + social inhibition , linked with worse outcomes after a heart attack. Depression after a heart attack raises later death rates several-fold ( Nancy Frasure-Smith, 1993 ). Chronic pain Acute pain follows an injury and fades as it heals; chronic pain persists beyond normal healing (ICD-11: pain that persists or recurs for longer than 3 months ). Pain has a sensory part and an emotional, meaning-laden part. Gate control theory ( Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall, 1965 ): a "gate" in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord lets pain signals through or blocks them. Small pain fibres open it; large touch fibres close it (why rubbing helps); messages down from the brain (attention, mood, beliefs) open or close it too (why anxiety worsens pain and distraction eases it). The brain's own endogenous opioids (endorphins, enkephalins) damp pain, and placebo pain relief is partly opioid-driven ( naloxone blocks it). Operant view ( Wilbert Fordyce, 1976 ): pain behaviours (limping, grimacing, staying home) are kept going by reinforcement such as attention or escape from work; a very solicitous spouse can increase them. Catastrophising ("this will never end") predicts more pain and disability. Chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) Disabling fatigue for 6 months or more , not relieved by rest, worse after exertion, cause unknown. B&D discuss CBT and graded exercise; note that the UK's NICE (2021) guideline stopped recommending graded exercise therapy , and CBT is now offered for coping, not as a cure. ICD-11 places it under diseases of the nervous system , not mental disorders. Psychosocial treatment of physical disorders Method Core Biofeedback A body signal (muscle tension by EMG , skin temperature, heart rate) is shown back to the person so they learn to control it. EMG biofeedback for tension headache ; thermal (hand-warming) biofeedback for migraine . Rests on Neal Miller's work (1960s) on learning to control autonomic responses. Relaxation and meditation Progressive muscle relaxation ( Edmund Jacobson, 1929 ): tense and release muscle groups. The relaxation response ( Herbert Benson, 1975 ): a quiet place, a repeated word, a passive attitude. Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction ( Jon Kabat-Zinn, 1979 ) for chronic pain and illness. Comprehensive stress and pain programmes Packages of education, relaxation, cognitive restructuring and coping skills. Dean Ornish's Lifestyle Heart Trial (1990) : a low-fat diet, exercise, stress management and group support reversed some coronary artery narrowing within a year. Multidisciplinary pain clinics combine CBT, graded activity and reinforcing "well" behaviour. Denial as coping Useful short term (calmer patients in the cardiac unit) but harmful long term (skipped medicine, missed check-ups). Changing health behaviour Injury prevention (helmets, seat belts), HIV prevention, quitting smoking. The Stanford Three Community Study ( John Farquhar, 1977 ) cut heart-disease risk factors with a mass-media campaign. Models: the Health Belief Model ( Irwin Rosenstock, 1966 : perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers, cues to action) and the stages of change ( James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente, 1983 ; the familiar five-stage form, precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance, dates from 1991 to 1992, when preparation was added). DSM-5-TR: Psychological Factors Affecting Other Medical Conditions Sits in the Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders chapter (code F54 ). A medical symptom or condition (not a mental disorder) is present. Psychological or behavioural factors adversely affect it: they change its course, interfere with treatment, add a health risk, or worsen the underlying physiology. Severity: mild, moderate, severe, extreme. The factors must not be better explained by another mental disorder. ICD-11: 6E40 "Psychological or behavioural factors affecting disorders or diseases classified elsewhere" , in Chapter 06. Lets you name the factor: a mental disorder, psychological symptoms, personality traits or coping style, maladaptive health behaviours, or a stress-related physiological response. Chronic pain has its own codes ( MG30 , including chronic primary pain ), outside the mental disorders chapter. The pairs they swap. Behavioural medicine = the interdisciplinary umbrella; health psychology = psychology's branch inside it. GAS order = alarm → resistance → exhaustion (Hans Selye), not "resistance first". Primary appraisal = is it a threat? Secondary = can I cope? Ader and Cohen's immune conditioning is classical , not operant. The harmful part of Type A is hostility , not time urgency; Type D = negative affectivity + social inhibition. The pain "gate" is in the spinal cord (dorsal horn), not the thalamus. On the SRRS, happy events score as stress too. Where the entrances push past the book. Expect the SRRS anchors (spouse's death 100, marriage 50, 300+ risk), Lazarus and Folkman's two appraisals and two coping styles, Kobasa's 3 Cs, Ader and Cohen's saccharin study, and the matching items: EMG biofeedback → tension headache, thermal biofeedback → migraine, Jacobson → progressive muscle relaxation, Benson → relaxation response, Kabat-Zinn → MBSR. Recap Ch 15. Psychological factors hit the body two ways: through biology (HPA axis, cortisol, immunity, blood pressure) and through behaviour (about half of deaths). Cannon fight-or-flight; Selye GAS alarm → resistance → exhaustion; Lazarus and Folkman appraisal; Holmes and Rahe SRRS; hardiness, support and control protect. PNI: Ader and Cohen conditioned immunosuppression, Kiecolt-Glaser exams and wounds, Cohen colds. Type A's toxic core is hostility; Type D; gate control in the spinal cord. Treat with biofeedback, relaxation, stress management and behaviour change. Part Seven · Sexual / gender, substance & impulse (B&D Ch 10–11) Ch 16. Sexual dysfunctions, gender dysphoria & paraphilic disorders B&D split this into three very different things — don't blur them. Group Core Sexual dysfunctions Problems in the sexual response cycle: desire (low desire), arousal (erectile, female arousal), orgasm (premature/delayed/female orgasmic), pain (genito-pelvic pain/penetration). Persistent + distressing. Gender dysphoria Distress from a marked incongruence between experienced and assigned gender. The diagnosis is the distress, not the identity. Paraphilic disorders Intense atypical sexual interest (e.g. voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic, sexual sadism/masochism, pedophilic, fetishistic) that causes distress/impairment or harms others . A paraphilia is only a disorder when it harms or distresses. DSM-5-TR Keeps "Gender Dysphoria" as a diagnosis (distress-based) within mental disorders. Paraphilia vs paraphilic disorder distinction (interest vs harmful/distressing). ICD-11 Moved gender out of mental disorders : renamed "Gender incongruence," placed in a new chapter on sexual health — explicitly de-pathologised . Paraphilic = "Paraphilic disorders," focused on risk/non-consent. The MET/RCI favourite: ICD-11 removed gender incongruence from the mental-disorders chapter (it's now under sexual health), while DSM-5-TR still lists Gender Dysphoria. Also: a paraphilia (the interest) is not itself a disorder — it becomes a paraphilic disorder only with distress, impairment, or harm to others/non-consent. Recap Ch 16. Three separate things: sexual dysfunctions (response-cycle problems), gender dysphoria/incongruence (distress, NOT the identity — ICD-11 moved it out of mental disorders), paraphilic disorders (atypical interest only a disorder if harmful/distressing). Ch 17. Substance-related, addictive & impulse-control disorders DSM-5 merged abuse + dependence into a single Substance Use Disorder on a severity spectrum (mild/moderate/severe by symptom count across 4 groups: impaired control, social impairment, risky use, pharmacological = tolerance + withdrawal). Key terms: tolerance (need more for the same effect), withdrawal (a substance-specific syndrome on stopping), intoxication . Substance classes: depressants (alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids — though opioids are often listed apart), stimulants (cocaine, amphetamines, nicotine, caffeine), opioids , hallucinogens , cannabis . Behavioural addiction: DSM-5 added Gambling Disorder (the first non-substance addiction, reflecting a shared reward-circuit/dopamine basis); ICD-11 added Gaming disorder too. Causes: dopamine reward pathway (nucleus accumbens, VTA), positive then negative reinforcement (use to feel good → use to stop feeling bad), genetic vulnerability, social learning, conditioning of cues.
