Treatment: motivational interviewing (William Miller and Stephen Rollnick), CBT/relapse-prevention, contingency management, 12-step; agonist/antagonist meds (methadone/buprenorphine, naltrexone, disulfiram, nicotine replacement). Reclassifications to know: DSM-5 collapsed abuse + dependence into one Substance Use Disorder (severity-graded), and added Gambling Disorder as a behavioural addiction; ICD-11 added Gaming disorder . These "behavioural addictions" sitting beside substances is exactly the kind of update MET tests. Recap Ch 17. One Substance Use Disorder, severity-graded (impaired control / social / risky / pharmacological). Tolerance vs withdrawal vs intoxication. Gambling Disorder (DSM-5) & Gaming disorder (ICD-11) = behavioural addictions on the dopamine reward circuit. MI + CBT + agonist/antagonist meds. Part Eight · Personality disorders (B&D Ch 12) Ch 18. Personality disorders An enduring, pervasive, inflexible pattern of inner experience and behaviour deviating markedly from cultural expectation, stable from adolescence/early adulthood, causing distress/impairment — across cognition, affect, interpersonal functioning, impulse control. DSM-5 keeps 10 categorical types in three clusters . Cluster Theme Disorders (the one-line tell) A — "odd / eccentric" Withdrawn, mistrustful Paranoid (pervasive distrust); Schizoid (detached loner, no desire for relationships); Schizotypal (eccentric, magical thinking, odd perceptions — on the schizophrenia spectrum) B — "dramatic / erratic" Emotional, impulsive Antisocial (disregard for/violation of others' rights, deceit, no remorse; ≥18, conduct disorder before 15); Borderline (instability of relationships, self-image, affect + impulsivity, fear of abandonment, self-harm); Histrionic (attention-seeking, shallow dramatic emotion); Narcissistic (grandiosity, need for admiration, lack of empathy) C — "anxious / fearful" Tense, inhibited Avoidant (social inhibition, feels inadequate, hypersensitive to rejection); Dependent (clinging, can't decide alone, needs to be taken care of); Obsessive-Compulsive PD (perfectionism, orderliness, control — ego-syntonic) DSM-5-TR — PDs Kept the 10 categorical types in 3 clusters (Section II). An Alternative DSM-5 Model (dimensional: impairment + 5 trait domains) sits in Section III for study. ICD-11 — PDs Abolished the categorical types entirely. A single "Personality disorder" diagnosis graded by severity (mild/moderate/severe). Then optional trait domain qualifiers : negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, anankastia. Plus a borderline pattern qualifier (kept for treatment relevance). The single biggest PD reclassification: ICD-11 went fully dimensional — it scrapped the named types and grades severity + trait domains, keeping only a "borderline pattern" specifier. DSM-5 kept the 10 categories (dimensional model only in Section III). This DSM-categorical vs ICD-dimensional split is a stock MET/NIMHANS item. BPD vs NPD. The BPD feature NOT in NPD = pervasive instability of relationships, self-image and affect + frantic efforts to avoid abandonment + self-harm. NPD = stable grandiosity + need for admiration + lack of empathy. Schizoid vs avoidant: schizoid doesn't want relationships; avoidant wants them but fears rejection. Schizotypal = the odd-beliefs/eccentric one, on the schizophrenia spectrum. Recap Ch 18. Enduring, pervasive, inflexible pattern from early adulthood. Cluster A odd (paranoid/schizoid/schizotypal), B dramatic (antisocial/borderline/histrionic/narcissistic), C anxious (avoidant/dependent/OCPD). DSM keeps 10 categories; ICD-11 is fully dimensional (severity + traits + borderline pattern). BPD = instability; schizoid doesn't want vs avoidant fears. Part Nine · Schizophrenia spectrum (B&D Ch 13) Ch 19. Schizophrenia & other psychotic disorders Clinical snapshot A 21-year-old, withdrawn over the past year, now believes the TV is sending him coded messages, hears two voices commenting on everything he does, speaks in derailed half-sentences, and has stopped washing or going to class. Clinical description: a disturbance of thought, perception, affect and behaviour. Positive symptoms (excess of normal function): delusions (fixed false beliefs — persecutory, grandiose, referential, of control), hallucinations (usually auditory ), disorganised speech (derailment, tangentiality, word salad), grossly disorganised/catatonic behaviour. Negative symptoms (loss): avolition (apathy), alogia (poverty of speech), anhedonia , asociality , flat affect . Disorganised symptoms (speech + behaviour + inappropriate affect). Statistics: lifetime ~ 1% , equal sexes, earlier onset in men (late teens–20s) than women. Causes (integrative): strongest is genetic (MZ concordance ~48%, ~10% in a first-degree relative); the dopamine hypothesis (mesolimbic D2 overactivity → positive symptoms; all antipsychotics block D2) refined to include glutamate/NMDA; neurodevelopmental markers (enlarged ventricles, reduced grey matter, obstetric complications, winter birth, maternal infection); and the psychosocial expressed emotion (EE; George Brown and colleagues) finding — high family criticism/over-involvement predicts relapse . Treatment: antipsychotics — typical/first-gen (haloperidol, chlorpromazine; strong D2 block → extrapyramidal effects, tardive dyskinesia) and atypical/second-gen (risperidone, olanzapine; clozapine for treatment-resistant, needs WBC monitoring for agranulocytosis) + psychosocial (CBT for psychosis, family therapy to lower EE, social-skills training). DSM-5-TR — Schizophrenia ≥2 of [delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised/catatonic, negative], ≥1 of the first three. Continuous signs ≥6 months (≥1 month active) + functional decline. Subtypes abolished. ICD-11 — Schizophrenia ≥2 core symptoms (≥1 of delusions, hallucinations, disorganised thinking, experiences of influence/passivity) for ≥1 month . No 6-month / functional-decline requirement. Subtypes dropped; replaced by symptom specifiers (positive, negative, depressive, manic, psychomotor, cognitive). Spectrum neighbour Tell Brief psychotic disorder (DSM) / acute & transient (ICD) Psychosis <1 month , full recovery Schizophreniform (DSM) Full picture 1–6 months Schizoaffective Schizophrenia + mood episode, PLUS ≥2 weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms Delusional disorder ≥1 month of delusion(s), function otherwise intact Shared psychotic (folie à deux) Delusion transferred to a close, dependent partner The duration delta: schizophrenia = 6 months in DSM, 1 month in ICD . By duration: brief psychotic <1mo → schizophreniform 1–6mo → schizophrenia ≥6mo. Emil Kraepelin named it dementia praecox ; Eugen Bleuler renamed it schizophrenia ("splitting of psychic functions" — NOT split personality / DID). Subtypes (paranoid, catatonic, hebephrenic) are abolished in both manuals. Recap Ch 19. Positive (delusions/hallucinations/disorganised) + negative (avolition/alogia/anhedonia/asociality/flat affect). ~1%, genes strongest, dopamine D2 + neurodevelopment + high EE → relapse. DSM 6mo / ICD 1mo; subtypes gone. Antipsychotics (clozapine if resistant) + family therapy. Bleuler ≠ split personality. Part Ten · Neurodevelopmental & neurocognitive disorders (B&D Ch 14–15) Ch 20. Neurodevelopmental disorders Onset in the developmental period (childhood), with deficits that impair personal/social/academic functioning. Disorder Core Intellectual Disability Deficits in intellectual (reasoning, IQ ~<70) and adaptive functioning, onset in development. Severity now graded by adaptive functioning , not IQ score alone. Autism Spectrum Disorder Two domains: (1) persistent deficits in social communication/interaction; (2) restricted, repetitive behaviours/interests + sensory sensitivities. DSM-5 merged autistic disorder, Asperger's and PDD-NOS into one spectrum with severity levels. ADHD Inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity , ≥6 symptoms, several before age 12 , in ≥2 settings. Presentations: inattentive, hyperactive-impulsive, combined. Treated with stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamines) + behavioural therapy. Specific Learning Disorder Difficulty in reading (dyslexia), writing or maths (dyscalculia) well below age, despite adequate instruction/IQ. Tic disorders Tourette's = multiple motor + ≥1 vocal tic, >1 year. ASD reclassification. DSM-5 abolished Asperger's as a separate diagnosis — it's folded into Autism Spectrum Disorder with severity levels. ADHD onset moved from "before 7" (DSM-IV) to "before age 12 " (DSM-5). High-yield change items. Recap Ch 20. ID (intellectual + adaptive, graded by adaptive function), ASD (social-communication + repetitive; Asperger's merged in), ADHD (inattention/hyperactivity, <12, ≥2 settings, stimulants), specific learning disorder, Tourette's. Ch 21. Neurocognitive disorders Disorder Core · the delirium vs dementia split Delirium Acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention & awareness + cognition, over hours–days, from a medical cause (infection, drugs, metabolic). Reversible , clouded consciousness. A medical emergency. Major Neurocognitive Disorder (dementia) Gradual, progressive decline in ≥1 cognitive domain (memory, executive, language, etc.) that impairs independence, with clear consciousness . Subtypes: Alzheimer's (commonest — amyloid plaques + tau tangles, insidious memory-first), vascular, frontotemporal, Lewy body, Parkinson's, HIV. Mild NCD = decline without loss of independence. Delirium vs dementia — the exam's favourite pair. Delirium = acute onset, fluctuating , attention impaired, consciousness clouded , usually reversible . Dementia = gradual , progressive , memory -led, consciousness clear , usually irreversible. (DSM-5 renamed dementia " major neurocognitive disorder .") Recap Ch 21. Delirium = acute, fluctuating, attention/consciousness, reversible. Major NCD (dementia) = gradual, progressive, memory, clear consciousness; Alzheimer's = plaques + tangles, commonest. Don't swap the two. Part Eleven · Mental health services: legal & ethical issues (B&D Ch 16) Ch 22. Mental health law, the insanity defence and ethics Clinical snapshot Ravi, 30, has schizophrenia. He has stopped his medicine, believes the neighbours are poisoning the tap water and has barely eaten for a week. His family wants him admitted; Ravi says he is fine and refuses. Can a hospital keep him against his will? On what grounds, for how long, and who decides? If he had hit a neighbour while psychotic, would he be responsible for it? Those are the questions of this chapter. Mental health law balances two things that pull against each other: the person's liberty and rights , and the duty to protect the person and the public. The state acts through two powers: police power (protecting society from a dangerous person) and parens patriae , Latin for "parent of the country" (protecting people who cannot protect themselves ). B&D also stress that the legal word "mental illness" is not a diagnosis: it is defined by each law, and it is narrower or wider than any DSM category. Civil commitment (no crime involved) The typical grounds are: (1) the person has a mental illness and needs treatment, (2) is dangerous to self or others , or (3) is gravely disabled , unable to provide food, clothing or shelter. Emergency commitment is short (often 72 hours ) on a professional's word; longer stays need a hearing. Two side stories B&D tell: deinstitutionalisation (from the 1950s, helped by chlorpromazine, people were moved out of the big hospitals) turned partly into transinstitutionalisation (many ended up in nursing homes, prisons or homeless). And dangerousness is misjudged: most people with a mental illness are not violent ; risk rises mainly with substance use , past violence and some active psychotic symptoms (the MacArthur Violence Risk Assessment Study , Henry Steadman, John Monahan and colleagues, 1998 : discharged patients without substance abuse were no more violent than their neighbours). Clinicians predict violence better in the short term than the long term, and actuarial tools beat unaided judgement. Case Year What it settled Wyatt v. Stickney 1972 Right to treatment : people committed to a state hospital (Alabama) must get adequate treatment, a humane setting and enough staff, not just custody. O'Connor v. Donaldson 1975 Kenneth Donaldson was held about 15 years with no real treatment. The US Supreme Court ruled a state cannot confine a non-dangerous person who can live safely in freedom alone or with willing family or friends. Mental illness alone is not enough. Addington v. Texas 1979 Commitment needs "clear and convincing evidence" : stricter than "preponderance" (civil cases), looser than "beyond reasonable doubt" (criminal cases). Youngberg v. Romeo 1982 Residents have a right to safe conditions and freedom from undue restraint; courts defer to professional judgement on how. Sell v. United States 2003 When the only purpose is to restore competence to stand trial, forced medication is allowed only if serious charges and important state interests are at stake, the drugs are likely to restore competence without harming a fair trial, nothing less intrusive will do, and the treatment is medically appropriate. Medicating because a person is dangerous is a separate route ( Washington v. Harper, 1990 ). The right to refuse treatment is real but limited. Criminal commitment: the insanity defence Not guilty by reason of insanity (NGRI) asks about the mental state at the time of the offence . It is a legal decision, not a diagnosis, and it is far rarer than the public thinks: in an eight-state US study ( Lisa Callahan and colleagues, 1991 ) it was raised in under 1% of felony cases and succeeded in about a quarter of those. People found NGRI are usually committed to a hospital, often for as long as or longer than a prison term. Test Year / origin The question it asks M'Naghten rule 1843 , England Daniel M'Naghten shot Edward Drummond, thinking he was Prime Minister Robert Peel, and was acquitted. Rule: because of a " disease of the mind ", did he not know the nature and quality of the act, or not know it was wrong ? A cognitive ("right-wrong") test. Irresistible impulse test 19th-century US states Added a volitional prong: he knew it was wrong but could not control himself. Durham rule 1954 , Judge David Bazelon (Washington, DC) Not responsible if the act was the "product of mental disease or defect" . Too vague; it handed the verdict to the experts and was dropped in 1972. ALI standard (American Law Institute, Model Penal Code) 1962 Lacked "substantial capacity" either to appreciate the wrongfulness of the act (cognitive) or to conform conduct to the law (volitional). Excludes a pattern of repeated criminal or antisocial conduct. Insanity Defense Reform Act 1984 , US federal Passed after John Hinckley , who shot President Ronald Reagan in 1981, was found NGRI in 1982 under the ALI test. Back to a cognitive-only test (severe mental disease, unable to appreciate the nature or wrongfulness of the act), the defence now carries the burden of proof , and experts may not state the final verdict. Guilty but mentally ill (GBMI) Michigan, 1975 Found guilty and sentenced, but treated while confined; once well, the rest of the sentence is served in prison. Diminished capacity (US states) Mental disorder reduced the ability to form intent (mens rea), so the charge is reduced (murder → manslaughter). The 1979 Dan White trial (mocked as the "Twinkie defence") led California to abolish it. Competence, the duty to warn and expert witnesses Idea Core Competence to stand trial Dusky v. United States (1960) : the defendant needs "sufficient present ability to consult with his lawyer with a reasonable degree of rational understanding" and a rational as well as factual understanding of the proceedings. Jackson v. Indiana (1972) : a defendant found incompetent cannot be held indefinitely ; if competence cannot be restored in a reasonable time, the state must commit civilly or release. Far more defendants are assessed for competence than ever plead insanity. Duty to warn / protect Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California ( 1974 , duty to warn; 1976 , broadened to a duty to protect). Prosenjit Poddar told a university psychologist he would kill Tatiana Tarasoff; the campus police held him briefly and let him go; nobody warned her, and in 1969 he killed her. The court: "The protective privilege ends where the public peril begins." When a client poses a serious threat of violence to an identifiable person, the therapist must take reasonable steps to protect that person. Mental health professionals as expert witnesses Courts use them on competence, insanity, malingering and risk. They are reasonably good at short-term risk and at spotting some malingering, poor at long-term violence prediction. Therapeutic jurisprudence ( David Wexler and Bruce Winick ) asks how the law itself helps or harms well-being, and underpins problem-solving courts such as mental health courts . Patients' rights, research ethics and practice guidelines Informed consent needs four things: the person is competent , takes part voluntarily , is given full information (risks, benefits, alternatives) and understands it. Treatment should be in the least restrictive setting that works. Research ethics grew out of abuses such as the Tuskegee syphilis study (1932 to 1972) ; the Belmont Report (1979) set three principles: respect for persons, beneficence and justice , which ethics committees (IRBs, required under US federal rules) apply when they review research. The APA Ethics Code (2002, amended 2010 and 2016) has five general principles: Beneficence and Nonmaleficence; Fidelity and Responsibility; Integrity; Justice; Respect for People's Rights and Dignity . Confidentiality is the clinician's ethical duty not to disclose; privileged communication is the client's legal right to stop the clinician testifying in court, and it belongs to the client. Both have limits (danger to others, child abuse, a court order). Clinical practice guidelines. B&D describe judging a treatment on two axes : clinical efficacy (does it work in controlled research? internal validity) and clinical utility (does it work in real practice: feasibility, generalisability, cost? external validity). A treatment can score high on one and low on the other. The pairs they swap. Insanity = mental state at the time of the crime ; competence = mental state now, at trial . M'Naghten = cognitive only (knew it was wrong?); irresistible impulse = volitional; Durham = "product of" mental disease; ALI = cognitive or volitional with "substantial capacity"; IDRA 1984 = back to cognitive only. NGRI = not guilty, hospital; GBMI = guilty, treatment then prison. Police power protects society; parens patriae protects the person. Tarasoff = duty to warn / protect; Dusky = competence; O'Connor v. Donaldson = no confinement for the non-dangerous; Addington = clear and convincing evidence; Wyatt = right to treatment. Confidentiality is an ethical duty; privilege is a legal right that belongs to the client. The Indian law the entrances actually ask. Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (in force 29 May 2018, replaced the Mental Health Act 1987): rights-based. A right to access mental healthcare (Section 18); advance directives (Section 5) and a nominated representative (Section 14); admission is independent or supported (supported admission up to 30 days under Section 89, longer under Section 90), reviewed by Mental Health Review Boards . Section 115 : a person who attempts suicide shall be presumed, unless proved otherwise, to have severe stress , and shall not be tried and punished (under IPC Section 309). Section 95 bans ECT without anaesthesia and muscle relaxants , ECT for minors (except with guardian consent and Board permission), sterilisation as treatment, and chaining . The Indian insanity defence is Section 84 IPC , a M'Naghten-type test ("incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law"); since 1 July 2024 it is Section 22 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita , same wording. To practise, a clinical psychologist must be registered with the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI Act 1992). The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 lists mental illness among its 21 disabilities. Recap Ch 22. Civil commitment = mental illness + danger to self/others or grave disability; police power vs parens patriae; clear and convincing evidence (Addington); no confinement of the non-dangerous (O'Connor); right to treatment (Wyatt). Insanity tests: M'Naghten 1843 (cognitive) → irresistible impulse (volitional) → Durham 1954 (product) → ALI 1962 (substantial capacity) → IDRA 1984 after Hinckley (cognitive, burden on defence); GBMI; diminished capacity. Competence (Dusky) is about now; insanity about then. Tarasoff = duty to warn / protect. Informed consent, Belmont, APA's five principles, confidentiality vs privilege, efficacy vs utility. India: MHCA 2017 (Sections 5, 14, 18, 89, 95, 115), IPC 84 → BNS 22, RCI registration. buffers stress (Suzanne Kobasa) Interoceptive conditioning Bodily sensations become conditioned cues for panic La belle indifférence Odd calm about a dramatic deficit (conversion) Learned helplessness Giving up after uncontrollable aversive events (Martin Seligman) Malingering Faking symptoms for external reward (not a disorder) Parens patriae The state as "parent", protecting people who cannot protect themselves Prepared learning Evolutionary readiness to fear certain stimuli Psychoneuroimmunology (PNI) How the mind and nervous system affect immune function (Robert Ader) Reciprocal gene-environment Genes shape which environments you select, which then express the genes Russell's sign Knuckle calluses from self-induced vomiting (bulimia) Tarasoff duty Duty to warn or protect an identifiable person a client threatens Tardive dyskinesia Late involuntary movements from long-term D2-blocking antipsychotics Thought-action fusion Treating a thought as morally equal to the act (OCD) Triple vulnerability Generalised biological + generalised psychological + specific psychological (Barlow) Self-test (cover the answers, active recall) What are Barlow & Durand's three components of a psychological disorder, and which "D" is missing vs the 4-D list? — dysfunction + distress/impairment + atypical/culturally unexpected; Danger is missing. Name the three vulnerabilities in Barlow's triple vulnerability theory. — generalised biological, generalised psychological, specific psychological. Equifinality vs multifinality? — many roads to one disorder vs one cause to many outcomes. Which neurotransmitter is the "brake" and which the "accelerator"? — GABA (brake), glutamate (accelerator). Panic disorder needs how long of anticipatory worry after the attacks? — ≥1 month. What is the B&D mechanism that turns a first panic attack into panic disorder? — interoceptive conditioning + anxiety sensitivity (false alarm → learned alarm). Which phobia makes you faint, and how is it treated? — blood-injection-injury (biphasic vasovagal); applied tension. Which manual has Complex PTSD? — ICD-11 (not DSM-5-TR). Conversion vs factitious vs malingering — split them. — unconscious / sick-role (internal) / external reward (and malingering isn't a disorder). DID vs schizophrenia — what does "split" actually mean in schizophrenia? — split among thought/emotion/behaviour (Eugen Bleuler), not multiple people. Schizophrenia duration: DSM vs ICD? — 6 months vs 1 month. BP-I vs BP-II? — one full mania (BP-I) vs hypomania + depression and never mania (BP-II). First-line therapy for OCD? — Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP). What did ICD-11 do with gender incongruence and personality disorders? — moved gender out of mental disorders; made PDs fully dimensional. Delirium vs dementia in four words each. — acute/fluctuating/attention/reversible vs gradual/progressive/memory/clear. Sleep terror vs nightmare — sleep stage and recall? — NREM, amnesic vs REM, recalled. Anorexia vs bulimia — the deciding feature? — weight (underweight vs normal). Durkheim's four suicide types? — egoistic, altruistic, anomic, fatalistic. Which two behavioural addictions did the manuals add (and to which)? — Gambling Disorder (DSM-5), Gaming disorder (ICD-11). Best single predictor of a future suicide attempt? — a prior attempt. Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome: the three stages, in order? → alarm, resistance, exhaustion. Primary vs secondary appraisal (Lazarus and Folkman)? → "is it a threat?" vs "can I cope?". Who first showed the immune system can be classically conditioned, and how? → Robert Ader and Nicholas Cohen (1975): saccharin water paired with the immunosuppressant cyclophosphamide. Which part of the Type A pattern actually predicts heart disease? → hostility / anger, not time urgency. Where is the "gate" in gate control theory? → the dorsal horn of the spinal cord (Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall, 1965). EMG vs thermal biofeedback: which for which? → EMG for tension headache, thermal (hand-warming) for migraine. Insanity vs competence to stand trial: which moment does each judge? → insanity: the time of the offence; competence: now, at trial (Dusky, 1960). M'Naghten vs the ALI test? → did not know the nature or wrongfulness of the act (cognitive only) vs lacked substantial capacity to appreciate wrongfulness or to conform conduct. What did Tarasoff establish? → a duty to warn or protect an identifiable person a client threatens. What does Section 115 of India's Mental Healthcare Act 2017 say? → a person who attempts suicide is presumed, unless proved otherwise, to have severe stress and shall not be tried and punished. Sidney Blatt's two types of depression, and which carries the higher suicide risk? → anaclitic (dependent) and introjective (self-critical); introjective. René Spitz: anaclitic depression vs hospitalism? → partial loss of a mother the infant had, reversible within about 3 to 5 months vs total institutional deprivation, often irreversible. title: Personality — the full book, chapter by chapter
text: Personality — the full book, chapter by chapter Not a summary. This is your Schultz & Schultz, Theories of Personality walked through in the book's own order, one chapter per theorist, with the book's signature recurring frame kept intact for each: the life (how the theorist's own biography shaped the theory), the theory unpacked in full, the book's Questions About Human Nature scorecard, Assessment , Research , and Reflections (the criticisms). After the book's chapters come the four domains the book underweights but NIMHANS tests hard, flagged in purple: object relations & self · existential · type theories · Indian / Triguna · assessment in depth . Built 2026-05-22 · Rewritten as a teaching chapter 2026-05-24 · Poured out to full-book, chapter-by-chapter depth 2026-05-24 . Expanded to full depth 2026-05-24 (added the key studies walked through, an extended concept bank, an A–Z glossary, and a by-chapter self-test). How to read this page. Read it like the textbook, top to bottom, once; then revise off the coloured boxes. Each chapter follows the book: amber = the intuition / why it matters, amber "Human nature" = where the theorist lands on the book's six recurring issues. Green = the line to lock. Red = the MCQ trap. Purple = NIMHANS-specific (clinical / Indian / rival-theory swaps). Grey recap = the chapter in one breath. The one-line testable list lives in Rapid Recall ; the personality tests in depth (MMPI (Starke Hathaway and J. Charnley McKinley, 1943)/16PF (Raymond Cattell)/NEO/projectives, scoring) are on the tests deep-dive . Jump to: 1. What personality theory is 2. Freud 3. Jung 4. Adler 5. Horney 6. Erikson 7. Allport 8. Maslow 9. Rogers 10. Kelly 11. Skinner 12. Bandura 13. The trait approach & Five-Factor Model 14. Facets of personality 15. Personality in perspective S1. Object relations & self S2. The other neo-Freudians S3. Existential S4. Type theories S5. Indian psychology / Triguna S6. Assessment in depth At-a-glance compare All the MCQ traps Key studies, walked through Extended concept bank Fast glossary (A–Z) Self-test (active recall) The one frame that organises the whole book. The book ends every chapter by scoring the theorist on six recurring Questions About Human Nature . Hold these six and you can predict any theorist's "view of the person" answer: (1) free will vs determinism · (2) nature vs nurture (heredity vs environment) · (3) past vs present (does childhood fix us, or does the here-and-now/future drive us) · (4) uniqueness vs universality · (5) equilibrium vs growth (is the basic motive to reduce tension and stay balanced, or to grow ) · (6) optimism vs pessimism . Sigmund Freud is the dark end of all six; the humanists are the bright end. Everyone else sits between. Part One · The study of personality Ch 1. Personality: what it is, and how the book studies it Personality is the relatively enduring, distinctive pattern of thoughts, feelings and behaviours that characterises a person and how they adapt to the world. The word comes from the Latin persona , the mask the Roman actor wore, which already hides the book's central tension: is personality the mask we show, or the real face behind it? Every theory in the book is one answer to four questions: what is personality made of , where does it come from , why do people differ , and can it change . The book groups the theorists into approaches , and that grouping is the spine of the table of contents: the psychoanalytic (Sigmund Freud); the neopsychoanalytic (Carl Jung, Alfred Adler, Karen Horney); the life-span (Erik Erikson); the genetics/trait pioneer (Gordon Allport); the humanistic (Abraham Maslow, Carl Rogers); the cognitive (Kelly); the behavioural (B. F. Skinner); the social-learning (Albert Bandura); the trait approach (Raymond Cattell, Hans Eysenck, the Five-Factor Model); and the facet / limited-domain theories (Julian Rotter, Zuckerman, Martin Seligman). How the book assesses and researches personality The book insists every theory must answer two practical questions, and the recurring "Assessment" and "Research" sections grade each theorist on them: Assessment = how do you measure this theory's constructs? The methods recur: self-report inventories (objective, scored against norms, e.g. MMPI, 16PF, NEO), projective techniques (ambiguous stimuli, e.g. Rorschach, TAT), clinical interviews , behavioural assessment , and idiographic personal documents (diaries, letters). A good test must clear three bars: reliability (consistency), validity (measures what it claims), and standardised norms . Research = how was the theory tested ? Three designs recur: the clinical method (case studies, the dominant psychoanalytic tool, rich but unreliable and unrepresentative), the experimental method (manipulate a variable, the only route to cause and effect), and the correlational method (relate two measured variables, covariation only, never causation). TRAP — method by camp. Case study / clinical method = the psychoanalysts (Sigmund Freud, Carl Jung, Alfred Adler). Correlational + factor analysis = the trait theorists (Raymond Cattell, Hans Eysenck, FFM). Controlled experiment = the behaviourists and social-learning theorists (B. F. Skinner, Albert Bandura) and Carl Rogers, who pioneered experimental psychotherapy research. The method usually tells you the camp. Recap Ch 1. Personality = the enduring, distinctive pattern of how a person thinks, feels and behaves. The book is organised by approach and grades every theorist on six human-nature issues plus Assessment and Research. Nomothetic (general laws, trait research) vs idiographic (the unique individual, case studies) is the master methodological split. Part Two · The psychoanalytic approach Ch 2. Sigmund Freud — psychoanalysis The life (1856–1939). Born in Moravia, raised in Vienna, the adored eldest son of a young mother (the book notes this shaped his Oedipal theory). Trained as a neurologist; studied hysteria under Charcot in Paris and worked with Josef Breuer , whose patient Anna O. coined the "talking cure". A flirtation with cocaine, a long self-analysis after his father's death (the engine of The Interpretation of Dreams , 1900), decades of jaw cancer, and finally flight from the Nazis to London in 1938, where he died. The theory is, in part, Freud analysing Freud. The problem he was solving. Patients had real symptoms (paralysis, blindness, fits) with no physical cause. Freud concluded the cause was mental and hidden : a painful idea pushed out of awareness, leaking out as a symptom. The whole edifice grows from that one move, that an unconscious drives behaviour we cannot explain. Instincts: the engine Behaviour is powered by instincts (drives), psychological representations of bodily needs. Two classes: Eros , the life instinct, whose energy is libido ; and Thanatos , the death instinct, source of aggression. An instinct has a source, aim, object and impetus; cathexis is libido invested in an object. The two maps of the mind Topographic model (the iceberg): conscious (current awareness, the tip), preconscious (retrievable, just below), unconscious (repressed, inaccessible, the vast mass below the waterline that steers slips, symptoms and dreams). Structural model (three agencies in constant negotiation): Id — present at birth, wholly unconscious, runs on the pleasure principle (gratification now), thinks in illogical primary process . The screaming toddler. Ego — runs on the reality principle , finds realistic ways to satisfy the id, delays gratification, uses rational secondary process thinking, and deploys the defences. The negotiator. Superego — the internalised moral code, formed ~age 5 when the Oedipus complex (Sigmund Freud) resolves. Conscience (punishes with guilt) + ego-ideal (rewards with pride). The strict parent's voice. Rider on a horse. Id = the horse's raw power; superego = the rulebook of where it may go; ego = the rider trying to get somewhere real without being thrown or paralysed. Anxiety is the ego's alarm that it is losing the negotiation; defences buy relief. Anxiety and the defence mechanisms Freud named three anxieties: reality anxiety (a real external threat), neurotic anxiety (fear the id will break loose), and moral anxiety (fear of the superego, i.e. guilt/shame). When anxiety threatens the ego, it distorts reality unconsciously: the defence mechanisms , catalogued by Anna Freud . Defence What it does Everyday example Repression The master defence: shove threatening material out of awareness. No memory of a childhood trauma. Denial Refuse to accept an external reality. "The biopsy was wrong, I'm fine." Projection Attribute your own unacceptable impulse to someone else. Attracted to a colleague, so you accuse them of flirting. Displacement Redirect the impulse onto a safer substitute target . Boss yells at you → you snap at the dog. Reaction formation Behave as the opposite of the true impulse. Hating someone but being sickly-sweet to them. Rationalisation Invent a logical-sounding excuse for the real reason. "I didn't want that job anyway." Sublimation Channel the impulse into a socially valued outlet (the healthiest). Aggression → becoming a surgeon or boxer. Regression Retreat to an earlier developmental stage under stress. A stressed adult sulking or throwing a tantrum. Intellectualisation Strip out the emotion, deal only with abstract facts. Discussing your own cancer purely in statistics. Identification Take on the qualities of an admired or feared other. Bullied kid starts bullying (identification with the aggressor). Undoing A ritual act to magically "cancel" a bad thought/deed. Compulsive hand-washing after an aggressive thought. Isolation of affect Keep the memory, sever the feeling. Recounting an assault flatly, with no emotion. Splitting See self/others as all-good or all-bad. "My doctor is perfect / a monster" within a week (borderline). TRAP — the three "redirect" defences they swap: Displacement = redirect to a substitute target (yell at the dog). Sublimation = redirect into a socially acceptable activity (aggression → surgery). Projection = put your impulse onto another person . Read the stem for "target" vs "activity" vs "another person". NIMHANS — George Vaillant's hierarchy of defences. George Vaillant ranked defences by maturity: psychotic (denial of external reality, delusional projection, distortion) → immature (projection, acting out, passive aggression, fantasy, splitting, somatisation) → neurotic (repression, displacement, reaction formation, intellectualisation, rationalisation, undoing) → mature (sublimation, humour, altruism, suppression , anticipation). Trap: repression is unconscious + neurotic; suppression is the deliberate, conscious set-aside, and is mature, the only conscious defence. Psychosexual stages Libido settles on a different body zone at each age; how the conflict resolves shapes the adult, and getting stuck (over- or under-gratified) is fixation . Stage Age Focus / conflict Fixation in an adult Oral 0–1 Mouth; weaning Smoking, overeating, dependency, sarcasm ("biting" remarks) Anal 1–3 Bowel control; toilet training Anal- retentive (orderly, stingy, stubborn) vs anal- expulsive (messy, reckless) Phallic 3–6 Oedipus/Electra ; castration anxiety / penis envy; superego forms Vanity, recklessness, problems with authority & sexual identity Latency 6–puberty Sexuality dormant; school, skills, same-sex friends (Consolidation phase, no fixation) Genital puberty+ Mature adult sexuality and intimacy Healthy love and work if earlier stages resolved The Oedipus complex is the centrepiece: the boy desires his mother, sees his father as rival, fears castration anxiety , and resolves it by identifying with the father, thereby absorbing his morality (the superego). The female parallel, the Electra complex (Carl Jung, 1913) with penis envy , is the most criticised piece and was rejected outright by Karen Horney. Stage order mnemonic: O ld (oral) A ge P ensioners (phallic) L ove (latency) G uinness (genital). And: the superego forms in the phallic stage, not at birth. Assessment in Freud's theory Three windows onto the unconscious: free association (say whatever comes, censorship off; blocks reveal resistance), dream analysis ("the royal road to the unconscious", separating the remembered manifest content from the disguised latent content , undoing the dream-work of condensation, displacement and symbolism), and Freudian slips / parapraxes (the tongue betraying the wish). Projective tests later operationalised the same logic. Research on the theory Built almost entirely on case studies (Anna O., Little Hans, Dora, the Rat Man, the Wolf Man), the clinical method at its richest and least controllable. Later controlled research gives a split verdict: the existence of unconscious processing and of some defences (especially displacement and projection ) finds support; the psychosexual stages , the Oedipus complex and dream symbolism do not. Questions about human nature (Freud's answers) Strong determinism (we are run by instincts and childhood); nature and nurture, but biological instincts lead; the past rules (the first five years fix us); universality (the same stages and structures in everyone); equilibrium (the goal is to discharge tension, the pleasure principle); and deeply pessimistic about human nature. The dark end of all six issues. Reflections (the criticisms) Unscientific and largely unfalsifiable ; built on a small, biased sample (neurotic, wealthy Viennese women); reliant on patients' fallible retrospective memory; overweighted on sex; and rigidly deterministic. Yet it is the foundation the entire book is reacting to: every later theorist defines themselves partly against Freud. Recap Ch 2. Unconscious conflict → id/ego/superego → three anxieties → defences (Anna Freud) → five psychosexual stages → assessed by free association, dreams, slips → tested by case study → human nature: determinist, past-bound, pessimistic. Part Three · The neopsychoanalytic approach Ch 3. Carl Jung — analytical psychology The life (1875–1961). Swiss pastor's son, solitary, drawn to dreams, myth and the occult. Sigmund Freud's anointed "crown prince" after their famous 13-hour first conversation (1907); president of the psychoanalytic association; then the bitter break in 1913 over Freud's insistence that libido is sexual. The split triggered Jung's own years-long "confrontation with the unconscious" (the Red Book ), which became the raw material of his theory. Jung kept the unconscious but enlarged it and de-sexualised libido into general psychic energy. His map of the psyche: Ego — the conscious mind. Personal unconscious — your own repressed/forgotten material, organised into emotionally charged complexes (a "mother complex"). Collective unconscious — a deeper, inherited layer shared by all humanity, his single most testable idea, containing the archetypes : universal images. The key ones: persona (the social mask), shadow (the dark, denied side), anima/animus (the inner feminine/masculine), and the self (the unifying centre, symbolised by the mandala). Attitudes & functions. Jung coined introversion vs extraversion (energy turned inward vs outward). He added four functions : the rational pair thinking and feeling , and the irrational pair sensing and intuiting . Two attitudes × four functions = his eight psychological types (later the seed of the MBTI). Individuation is the lifelong integration of all parts into the self, and Jung uniquely stressed midlife as its turning point. Assessment & research The word-association test (delays and odd responses expose complexes), symptom analysis , dream analysis (read in series, with amplification rather than free association), and comparative study of myth and symbol across cultures. The MBTI descends from his types but has weak psychometrics. Questions about human nature A balance of free will and determinism; past, present and future (uniquely teleological , we are pulled by aspirations and the self-to-be); nature and nurture; both unique and universal (archetypes are shared); strongly growth -oriented (individuation); cautiously optimistic. Reflections Criticised for mysticism, obscurity and untestable occult elements, but introversion/extraversion and the idea of complexes are permanent contributions. Recap Ch 3. Jung: collective unconscious + archetypes (persona, shadow, anima/animus, self), introversion/extraversion + 4 functions → 8 types, individuation, midlife. De-sexualised libido. Teleological, growth-oriented. Ch 4. Alfred Adler — individual psychology The life (1870–1937). A sickly Viennese child (rickets, near-fatal pneumonia, run over twice in the street) who lived in the shadow of a healthy older brother, the autobiography behind inferiority and birth order . An ophthalmologist turned GP turned psychiatrist; an early member of Sigmund Freud's circle who broke in 1911 , rejecting the sexual emphasis for a social one. Coined "inferiority complex"; a huge influence on humanistic and cognitive therapy. Adler said the one dynamic force in life is not pleasure but striving for superiority (really, striving for completion, competence and perfection). Every child begins small, weak and dependent and so feels inferiority ; healthy growth means compensating for it. When it derails you get an inferiority complex (paralysing self-doubt, from organ inferiority, pampering, or neglect) or an over-compensating superiority complex . Other core ideas: Style of life — the unique pattern each person builds by ~age 5 to pursue their goals. Creative power of the self — we are not passive products of heredity and environment; we actively shape our own personality. (This is why Adler is a forerunner of humanism.) Fictional finalism — we are pulled by future fictional goals (ideals like "honesty pays") and live " as if " they were true. Social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefühl) — an innate, developable feeling of kinship with humanity; its presence is the mark of mental health. Birth order — first-born (dethroned, conservative), second/middle (competitive, ambitious), youngest (pampered), only child (precocious, rivalrous with adults). Assessment & research Early recollections (your earliest memory reveals your style of life), dream analysis (about future problem-solving, not the past), and birth-order position. Research on social interest and early recollections is modest; birth-order findings are mixed. Questions about human nature Strong free will (the creative self); present and future over past (fictional goals pull us); nature and nurture but what you do with them matters most; uniqueness ; growth ; and firmly optimistic , the brightest of the psychoanalysts. Reflections Enormously influential (humanistic and cognitive therapy owe him a great deal) but the theory is loose, sometimes commonsensical, and hard to test. Lock the trio: Freud → will to pleasure (sex); Adler → will to power (overcome inferiority); Carl Jung → will to meaning /the collective unconscious. (Viktor Frankl later literally named the "will to meaning", see S3.) The single most-tested cluster in personality. Ch 5. Karen Horney — neurotic needs and trends The life (1885–1952). German; an unhappy childhood (felt unloved by a harsh father, clung to her mother) fed bouts of depression and her lifelong interest in how parenting breeds anxiety. Trained in psychoanalysis, emigrated to the US in 1932, and broke with orthodoxy to found her own institute, the first major theorist to challenge Sigmund Freud's account of women from the inside. Horney's foundation is basic anxiety : the feeling of being isolated and helpless in a potentially hostile world , rooted in a childhood lacking warmth and security. To cope, the child develops one of three neurotic trends (overuse of an otherwise-normal strategy), distilled from a longer list of 10 neurotic needs : Trend The move The neurotic version Moving toward people Compliance, seeking affection & approval The "self-effacing" type, needs a partner to run their life Moving against people Aggression, seeking power, control, prestige The "expansive" type, must dominate and win Moving away from people Detachment, seeking self-sufficiency & privacy The "resigned" type, withdraws to avoid needing anyone She also described the idealised self-image and the "tyranny of the should" (we tyrannise ourselves trying to match an impossible ideal self), and contrasted the real self with the idealised self . On gender she rejected penis envy , countering that men may feel "womb envy" (envy of women's capacity to bear life) and that apparent penis envy is really envy of men's social power . Questions about human nature Free will; the present (current character, though rooted in childhood); heavily nurture and culture over biology; growth/self-realisation; and optimistic (neurosis is learned, so it can be unlearned). Reflections Anticipated feminist psychology and the cultural turn; criticised because her data are clinical observations from a now-dated era. Recap Chs 3–5. Carl Jung = collective unconscious + archetypes. Alfred Adler = inferiority/superiority, birth order, social interest, creative self. Horney = basic anxiety → three trends (toward/against/away), womb envy. All three traded Freud's sex drive for, respectively, meaning, power, and social safety. Part Four · The life-span approach Ch 6. Erik Erikson — identity theory The life (1902–1994). The theorist of identity who never knew his biological father and never took a degree, a Dane raised in Germany who felt an outsider everywhere (Jewish at school, Nordic-looking at temple). An artist who drifted into teaching at a Montessori-style school, was analysed by Anna Freud , emigrated to the US, and ended up a Harvard professor. His own "identity crisis" is the theory. Erikson extended Freud in two decisive ways: development is lifelong (eight stages, birth to death, not five) and psychosocial rather than psychosexual (each stage is a social crisis). Growth follows the epigenetic principle (an inborn plan unfolding in fixed order). Each stage poses a tension between a healthy pole and an unhealthy one; resolving it yields a basic strength / virtue . Stage (age) Crisis Virtue Infancy (0–1) Trust vs mistrust Hope Early childhood (1–3) Autonomy vs shame/doubt Will Play age (3–5) Initiative vs guilt Purpose School age (6–11) Industry vs inferiority Competence Adolescence (12–18) Identity vs role confusion Fidelity Young adult Intimacy vs isolation Love Adulthood Generativity vs stagnation Care Old age Ego integrity vs despair Wisdom Erikson coined the term "identity crisis" and studied identity in culture (the Sioux and Yurok) and in history (his psychobiographies of Luther and Gandhi ). Assessment & research Play therapy and play constructions , psychohistory, and dream analysis. The big research spin-off is James Marcia's identity statuses , which cross "crisis explored?" with "commitment made?": diffusion (neither), foreclosure (commitment without exploration), moratorium (exploring, not yet committed), achievement (committed after exploring). Questions about human nature A genuine balance of free will and determinism; past, present and future; nature and nurture (biology + society); universal stages but unique resolutions; growth ; and optimistic (each crisis can be re-worked later). TRAP — Sigmund Freud vs Erikson stage pairing. Erik Erikson's first four stages map onto Freud's (trust↔oral, autonomy↔anal, initiative↔phallic, industry↔latency), but Erikson's are psychosocial and run to eight across the whole lifespan; Freud's are psychosexual and stop at five by puberty. "Identity vs role confusion" and "intimacy vs isolation" are pure Erikson. Part Five · The trait pioneer Ch 7. Gordon Allport — motivation and personality The life (1897–1967). A dutiful, orderly American academic whose most famous story is his one meeting with Sigmund Freud : the 22-year-old Allport, to break the ice, described a boy on his train with a dirt phobia; Freud studied him and asked, "And was that little boy you?" Allport left convinced psychoanalysis digs for hidden meaning where none exists, and built a theory of the conscious, present, normal adult instead. Allport defined traits as real neuropsychic structures that make many stimuli functionally equivalent and guide consistent behaviour. He organised them at three levels: Cardinal traits — so dominant they define a whole life (rare; a "Scrooge", a "Machiavellian"). Central traits — the 5–10 core descriptors you'd put in a reference letter (honest, anxious, sociable). Secondary traits / dispositions — situational preferences shown only sometimes. His distinctive concepts: the proprium (his word for the self, developing through seven aspects from bodily self to propriate striving); functional autonomy (a motive can become independent of its origin, you ran to lose weight, now you run because you love it, so adult motives are not chained to childhood); and the lexical hypothesis (with Odbert he counted ~18,000 trait words: if a trait matters, language coins a word for it). Allport championed the idiographic (he called it morphogenic ) study of the unique individual and, crucially, did not use factor analysis. Assessment & research Personal documents — most famously the case study Letters from Jenny (300+ letters analysed for her central traits) — plus the Study of Values (Allport-Vernon-Lindzey: theoretical, economic, aesthetic, social, political, religious) and expressive behaviour. He largely rejected the lab. Questions about human nature Strong free will ; the present , not the past (functional autonomy frees us); the great champion of uniqueness (idiographic); nature and nurture; growth; and optimistic . There is even a discontinuity between the child (driven, Freudian) and the adult (autonomous, future-oriented). Reflections Made personality a respectable field and bridged academic and applied work, but functional autonomy's mechanism is left vague, and idiographic methods are hard to generalise from, so the theory generated little research. TRAP — the "3" and the factor-analysis swap. Gordon Allport = 3 trait levels (cardinal/central/secondary), idiographic, NO factor analysis. Hans Eysenck = 3 dimensions (PEN). Raymond Cattell = 16 factors and IS the factor-analysis man. Don't pin factor analysis on Allport. Part Six · The humanistic approach (the "third force" (Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers)) Humanism arose in the 1950s–60s as a revolt against the two ruling forces, psychoanalysis (which made us slaves of the unconscious) and behaviourism (which made us puppets of conditioning). Its creed: people have free will , are basically good , and are pulled forward by an innate drive toward growth and self-actualisation . Ch 8. Abraham Maslow — needs-hierarchy theory The life (1908–1970). A lonely, unhappy child of immigrant Jewish parents in Brooklyn (he openly loathed his mother). Began studying dominance and sexuality in monkeys with Harry Harlow ; after WWII and the birth of his children he turned to the healthy end of human nature and became the acknowledged "father of humanistic psychology" and the third force. Maslow proposed that human needs stack in a hierarchy : lower needs must be reasonably satisfied before higher ones can motivate us. Bottom to top: physiological → safety → belongingness/love → esteem → self-actualisation . The lower four are deficiency needs (D-needs) , felt as a lack you scramble to fill; the top is a being need (B-need) or growth need, felt as a pull. Late in life he added self-transcendence above self-actualisation. He studied unusually healthy, accomplished people (Lincoln, Einstein, Eleanor Roosevelt) and described the self-actualiser : realistic, accepting, spontaneous, problem-centred, autonomous, with deep but few relationships, a fresh appreciation of life, and peak experiences (moments of ecstasy and wholeness). The Jonah complex is the fear of one's own greatness that keeps people from self-actualising. Assessment & research Biographical analysis of his self-actualisers (the sample is the chief criticism, hand-picked and small) and the Personal Orientation Inventory (POI, Shostrom) , which operationalised self-actualisation as a measurable trait. Questions about human nature Free will ; present and future; needs are innate ("instinctoid", so nature) but expressed through nurture; uniqueness blooms at the top of the hierarchy; pure growth ; and strongly optimistic . Ch 9. Carl Rogers — person-centred theory The life (1902–1987). Raised on a strict religious Illinois farm; left agriculture and then the ministry for psychology after a trip to China loosened his faith. Years of clinical work with troubled children convinced him that the client, not the expert, holds the key, hence client-centred therapy . The most research-minded of the humanists. Rogers built everything on one motive, the actualising tendency (an innate push of every organism to maintain and enhance itself), and on the self / self-concept (your picture of who you are). He contrasted the real self with the ideal self : a rough match is congruence and well-being; a large gap is incongruence and distress. Why does incongruence develop? Because others love us conditionally, imposing conditions of worth ("I'll value you if you become a doctor"), which makes us betray our own organismic valuing process (the gut sense of what is right for us). The cure is unconditional positive regard (UPR) . The goal of growth is the fully functioning person (open to experience, living existentially in the present, trusting the organism, free, creative). In therapy this distils to three core conditions : empathy, congruence/genuineness, and unconditional positive regard . Assessment & research Rogers pioneered psychotherapy research : he was the first to tape-record and transcribe sessions for analysis, and he used the Q-sort technique (sort cards describing the self, then the ideal self; the correlation between the two sorts is an objective measure of self-ideal congruence that should rise over successful therapy). Questions about human nature Free will ; present and future; the actualising tendency is innate (nature) but conditions of worth are learned (nurture); uniqueness; growth ; and optimistic . TRAP — the two humanists they pair. Carl Rogers = self-concept, real vs ideal self, congruence, conditions of worth, UPR, Q-sort, the three core conditions. Abraham Maslow = the hierarchy of needs, D- vs B-needs, self-actualisers, peak experiences, the POI. Both believe in growth; only Rogers gives you the therapy triad and the Q-sort. Recap Chs 8–9. Abraham Maslow: needs hierarchy, self-actualisation, peak experiences, POI. Rogers: actualising tendency, self vs ideal self, conditions of worth → UPR, fully functioning person, Q-sort + recorded sessions. Third force = free will + innate goodness + growth. Part Seven · The cognitive approach Ch 10. George Kelly — personal construct theory The life (1905–1967). A Kansas farm boy with an engineering and education background who ran travelling psychology clinics across Depression-era rural Kansas. The practical, no-dogma setting (no Freudian couch to be had) led him to a theory in which there is no fixed human nature to uncover, only the way each person construes the world. Kelly's image is man-the-scientist : every person constantly forms hypotheses ( personal constructs ) about the world, tests them against events, and revises them. A construct is bipolar (kind–cruel, safe–dangerous). The philosophy behind it is constructive alternativism : there is always more than one way to construe any situation, so we are never prisoners of our biography, we can always re-construe. The theory is one fundamental postulate ("a person's processes are psychologically channelised by the ways in which they anticipate events") plus 11 corollaries (construction, individuality, organisation, dichotomy, choice, range, experience, modulation, fragmentation, commonality, sociality). Kelly even re-defined emotions cognitively: anxiety = events lie outside your constructs; threat = awareness of imminent comprehensive change to your constructs; guilt = acting against your core role construct; hostility = forcing reality to fit a failed construct. Assessment & research The Role Construct Repertory Test (Rep Test) and its grid form (the rep grid ) elicit a person's own constructs; the self-characterisation sketch (write about yourself in the third person) feeds fixed-role therapy , where the client rehearses being a deliberately different character. Questions about human nature Free will (we choose our constructs); present and future (we are run by anticipation , so Kelly needs no separate "motivation", anticipation is the motive); both unique and common (the commonality corollary); growth-leaning; and optimistic . The environment matters only as we construe it. Reflections The pioneering cognitive theory of personality, decades ahead of its time, but criticised as cold and over-rational (it slights emotion, the unconscious, and development) and it spawned relatively little research outside the rep grid. Part Eight · The behavioural approach Ch 11. B. F. Skinner — reinforcement theory The life (1904–1990). An American who wanted to be a novelist, failed ("the dark year"), and turned to psychology. The most influential, and most provocative, behaviourist: in Walden Two (a utopia engineered by reinforcement) and Beyond Freedom and Dignity he argued that "autonomous inner man" is an illusion we should discard. Skinner's radical move: there is no inner "personality" to study at all . What we call personality is just a learned bundle of operant response patterns maintained by a history of reinforcement, so look at the environment, not inside the "black box". His machinery: Operant conditioning — behaviour is shaped by its consequences . Reinforcement (positive = add something pleasant; negative = remove something aversive) increases a behaviour; punishment decreases it (and Skinner argued punishment is unreliable, it suppresses without teaching). Schedules of reinforcement — fixed/variable × ratio/interval . Variable-ratio (the slot machine) produces the highest, most extinction-resistant responding. Shaping — reinforcing successive approximations to build a complex behaviour. Extinction — stop reinforcing and the behaviour fades; the superstition experiment showed accidental reinforcement can create "superstitious" behaviour in pigeons. Assessment & research Functional analysis (the A-B-C : Antecedent → Behaviour → Consequence) and direct observation, never a personality "test" of inner traits. The empirical base is strong: rat and pigeon labs, plus applied successes in behaviour modification and token economies (Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin, 1968). Questions about human nature Extreme determinism (the environment controls us absolutely); the present (current contingencies plus reinforcement history); pure nurture ; universality (the laws of learning are the same for all species); neither equilibrium nor growth (behaviour is shaped from outside); pessimistic about free will but optimistic that we can engineer better behaviour. Reflections Rigorous, testable and hugely applicable, but criticised for extrapolating from animals to humans and for ignoring genetics, cognition and the inner life that Albert Bandura would put back. Part Nine · The social-learning approach Ch 12. Albert Bandura — modeling / social-cognitive theory The life (1925–2021). Canadian, from a tiny prairie town with a two-teacher school that taught him self-directed learning, a lived rehearsal of his later theme of human agency . Spent his career at Stanford; the most-cited living psychologist for years; renamed his approach "social-cognitive" to stress thought. Bandura's correction to B. F. Skinner: we learn far more by watching than by being reinforced, and thought sits in the middle. His pillars: Observational learning / modeling — we learn by watching models, no personal reinforcement needed (the Bobo doll studies: children who watched an adult hit the doll imitated the aggression). It runs through four processes: attention → retention → production (reproduction) → motivation . Vicarious reinforcement (seeing the model rewarded) raises imitation. Reciprocal determinism — behaviour, personal/cognitive factors , and the environment all influence one another in a three-way loop; you are neither a free agent nor a passive product. Self-efficacy — your belief in your ability to succeed at a specific task , which predicts whether you'll even try, persist, and recover. Its four sources: mastery experiences (the strongest), vicarious experience (seeing similar others succeed), verbal persuasion , and physiological/emotional state . Self-regulation and the self-system (we set internal standards and judge ourselves against them); later, moral disengagement and collective efficacy . Assessment & research Direct behavioural observation and microanalytic self-efficacy scales . Strong experimental base: the Bobo doll (Albert Bandura, 1961) series, and the demonstration that modeling (guided mastery) treats phobias better than insight. Questions about human nature Human agency within reciprocal limits (a middle position on free will); the present; nurture-leaning, but cognition is central; uniqueness possible; growth via agency; and optimistic (efficacy can be built). TRAP — self-efficacy vs locus of control. Self-efficacy = Albert Bandura = "can I do this task ?" (task-specific competence belief). Locus of control = Rotter = "do I or outside forces control outcomes ?" (source of control). Both sound like "belief about control"; the split is task-ability vs outcome-source. Recap Chs 11–12. Skinner: no inner self, behaviour = operant patterns shaped by reinforcement schedules; functional analysis (A-B-C); determinist. Bandura: observational learning (Bobo doll, 4 processes), reciprocal determinism, self-efficacy (4 sources); agency + cognition put back in. Part Ten · Advances in personality theory Ch 13. The trait approach & the Five-Factor Model Trait theorists got impatient with unprovable unconscious forces and asked a measurable question: what stable dispositions do people have, and how many basic ones are there? Their engine is factor analysis , a statistic that scans thousands of trait ratings and finds the few underlying dimensions ("factors") that explain the correlations. Raymond Cattell (1905–1998) The factor-analysis champion. He split surface traits (visible clusters of behaviour) from source traits (the deeper factors that cause them) and reduced personality to 16 source traits , which became the 16PF questionnaire. He drew on three data sources, L-data (life records), Q-data (questionnaires) and T-data (objective tests), and added dynamic traits (ergs = innate drives, sentiments = learned, attitudes), plus the famous distinction of fluid vs crystallised intelligence . Hans Eysenck (1916–1997) Argued for a few biologically based super-dimensions, the PEN model: P sychoticism, E xtraversion, N euroticism (he began with E and N on the EPI, then added P on the EPQ). His biological theory is elegant and testable: extraverts have chronically low cortical arousal (an under-active reticular activating system), so they seek stimulation to top up; neuroticism reflects an over-reactive limbic/autonomic system. Eysenck stressed strong heritability . McCrae & Costa — the Five-Factor Model (OCEAN) When researchers re-ran the trait data across languages and decades, five factors kept reappearing, the convergence that made the Five-Factor Model (championed by Paul Costa & Robert McCrae , measured by the NEO-PI-R ) today's dominant model. (The lexical lineage: Francis Galton → Gordon Allport & Henry Odbert → Goldberg , who coined "Big Five".) Factor High scorer Low scorer O penness Curious, imaginative, novelty-seeking Conventional, practical, routine-preferring C onscientiousness Organised, disciplined, dependable Careless, spontaneous, disorganised E xtraversion Sociable, assertive, energetic Reserved, quiet, solitary A greeableness Trusting, cooperative, warm Competitive, sceptical, antagonistic N euroticism Anxious, moody, emotionally reactive Calm, secure (= "emotional stability") McCrae & Costa later built the FFM into a full Five-Factor Theory : genetically based basic tendencies (the five traits) express as characteristic adaptations (habits, roles, goals) shaped by culture; the five traits are strongly heritable, cross-culturally universal, and largely stable after about age 30 . Mnemonic: OCEAN (or CANOE). Neuroticism's healthy pole = emotional stability , same axis flipped. NIMHANS — HEXACO & Gray. HEXACO (Ashton & Lee) = 6 factors, adding H = Honesty-Humility (sincerity, fairness, modesty); the "dark triad" (Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams, 2002) (narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy) maps onto low Honesty-Humility. And Gray's Reinforcement Sensitivity Theory reframes Eysenck biologically into the BIS (punishment-sensitive → anxiety, stop-and-check) and BAS (reward-sensitive → impulsivity, approach). Reward/punishment sensitivity in a stem = Gray, not Eysenck. Questions about human nature (the trait camp) More deterministic and biological than the humanists (especially Eysenck and McCrae-Costa, who stress genes); nature -heavy; the present (stable dispositions); universality (the same factors everywhere); neither growth nor equilibrium is the focus, traits simply are ; relatively neutral on optimism. TRAP — the trait numbers & theory-vs-description. Raymond Cattell = 16 (16PF, factor analysis). Hans Eysenck = 3 (PEN, biological). FFM = 5 (OCEAN, NEO-PI-R). HEXACO = 6 (adds H). And: the Big Five is descriptive/atheoretical (says what traits exist); Eysenck's PEN is causal/biological (says why ). Both contain Extraversion and Neuroticism, which is exactly why they get paired to trip you. Ch 14. Facets of personality (the limited-domain theories) The book's penultimate chapter collects theorists who illuminate one slice of personality rather than the whole person. Each is a high-yield "who studied X" item. Julian Rotter — locus of control From his social-learning theory, behaviour potential = expectancy × reinforcement value (how likely you think a reward is, times how much you want it). His famous slice is locus of control (measured by the I-E Scale ): do you believe outcomes flow from your own actions ( internal ) or from luck, fate and powerful others ( external )? Internals generally cope and achieve better. Marvin Zuckerman — sensation seeking A biologically based trait, the need for "varied, novel, complex and intense sensations and experiences", measured by the Sensation Seeking Scale (SSS) with four facets: thrill & adventure seeking, experience seeking, disinhibition, boredom susceptibility . Linked to dopamine and to risk-taking. Martin Seligman — helplessness, optimism, positive psychology The clearest example of a theorist who turned one finding into a whole programme. Learned helplessness (dogs that couldn't escape shock stopped trying even when escape became possible) became a model of depression; reformulated as explanatory / attributional style along three axes, internal–external, stable–unstable, global–specific (the pessimist explains bad events as internal-stable-global). That flipped into learned optimism , and Seligman went on to found positive psychology (the study of well-being: the PERMA model, signature character strengths). Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi — flow Flow : the absorbed, timeless state of total engagement when a task's challenge exactly matches your skill, a cornerstone of positive psychology alongside Seligman. TRAP — the facet owners. Locus of control = Julian Rotter . Sensation seeking = Zuckerman . Learned helplessness / learned optimism / positive psychology = Martin Seligman . Flow = Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi . Self-efficacy is Albert Bandura , not a facet theorist. Part Eleven · Personality in perspective Ch 15. Personality in perspective The book's closing chapter steps back and asks what, after all the theories, we actually know. Its main threads, all examinable: The person–situation debate, resolved by interactionism. Walter Mischel (see Albert Bandura's neighbours) showed behaviour is less cross-situationally consistent than pure trait theory assumed. The settled view is interactionism : stable traits and situations jointly produce behaviour, and people also select and shape the situations they enter. Biological foundations. Twin and adoption studies put the heritability of major traits around 40–60%. Temperament appears early: Buss & Plomin (emotionality, activity, sociability, the EAS model) and Jerome Kagan (the inhibited vs uninhibited infant, a precursor of introversion). Alexander Thomas & Stella Chess's easy/difficult/slow-to-warm-up temperaments belong here too. Gender and culture. Personality expression and even which traits matter differ across individualist vs collectivist cultures; the FFM replicates broadly but not perfectly, and "indigenous" dimensions (e.g. the Indian Triguna, see S5) capture variance Western models miss. The image of human nature. The book's parting note: the theories disagree most on the six human-nature questions, and which theory you find convincing says as much about your own assumptions as about the evidence. Recap Chs 13–15. Trait approach (Cattell 16 / Eysenck 3 PEN / FFM 5 OCEAN / HEXACO 6) + facets (Rotter locus of control, Zuckerman sensation seeking, Seligman helplessness→optimism→positive psych, Csikszentmihalyi flow). Perspective: interactionism settles person vs situation; heritability ~40–60%; temperament (Buss-Plomin, Kagan); culture & gender matter. NIMHANS supplements · what Schultz & Schultz underweights but the exam tests Why these are here. Schultz & Schultz is an American survey that gives little or no chapter space to object relations, existential therapy as a personality school, the old type theories, or Indian psychology. NIMHANS (clinical, Indian, research-heavy) asks all four by name constantly. Treat S1–S5 as required, not optional. S1. Object relations & self psychology The shift in one sentence: Sigmund Freud thought the baby seeks pleasure ; the object-relations school says the baby seeks relationship . An "object" is the internal mental image of a person (the mother first). Personality is built from the internalised templates of our earliest relationships , which we re-enact for life. This is also where borderline personality is explained, so clinical exams love it. Theorist Own it by Melanie Klein Founder; part-objects (good/bad breast); two positions (not stages): paranoid-schizoid (split into all-good/all-bad, uses projective identification ) → depressive (realises good & bad mother are one, feels guilt, makes reparation). Child play therapy. Donald Winnicott The "good-enough mother" ; the transitional object (blanket/teddy) in the transitional space ; true self vs false self (a compliant shell over the spontaneous self). W. R. D. Fairbairn The cleanest break: libido is object-seeking, not pleasure-seeking . Margaret Mahler Separation-individuation : normal autism → symbiosis → differentiation → practising → rapprochement → object constancy (stable inner image of mother when absent). Otto Kernberg Borderline personality organisation (splitting persists into adulthood); developed Transference-Focused Psychotherapy (TFP) . Heinz Kohut Self psychology : narcissism , the cohesive self , selfobjects , empathic mirroring ; failed mirroring → pathological narcissism. John Bowlby Attachment : innate need for a secure base ; the internal working model ("are others reliable, am I worthy?"); maternal deprivation. Mary Ainsworth operationalised it with the Strange Situation (secure / anxious-ambivalent / avoidant; Main added disorganised). TRAP — the pairings: good-enough mother / transitional object = Donald Winnicott · separation-individuation / rapprochement = Margaret Mahler · self / narcissism / mirroring = Heinz Kohut · borderline organisation / TFP = Otto Kernberg · paranoid-schizoid & depressive positions = Melanie Klein (positions, not stages) · object-seeking libido = Fairbairn · internal working model / secure base = John Bowlby . S2. The other neo-Freudians (no chapter in the book) Beyond Jung, Alfred Adler and Karen Horney (who get full chapters above), the exam tests three more neo-Freudians by their single signature phrase: Theorist Own it by Erich Fromm "Escape from freedom" (modern freedom is so isolating that people flee it into conformity, submission or destructiveness, his account of fascism); character orientations (receptive, exploitative, hoarding, marketing, and the healthy productive ). Harry Stack Sullivan Interpersonal theory : personality exists only in relationships ; the self-system built from anxiety-reducing interactions, organised into good-me / bad-me / not-me . Anna Freud & Heinz Hartmann Anna Freud = founded child psychoanalysis, catalogued the defences. Hartmann = "father of ego psychology", the conflict-free ego sphere and adaptation . TRAP: escape from freedom = Erich Fromm · interpersonal / self-system / good-me-bad-me = Harry Stack Sullivan · conflict-free ego sphere = Hartmann · catalogued the defences = Anna Freud . S3. Existential theories Existentialism overlaps with humanism (both prize freedom and meaning) but its mood is darker: it asks how we face the unavoidable "givens" of existence, death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness. Theorist Own it by Viktor Frankl Logotherapy ("logos" = meaning); the primary motive is the "will to meaning" ; its frustration = existential vacuum ; book Man's Search for Meaning ; techniques paradoxical intention & dereflection . Rollo May Brought existential thought to US psychology; The Meaning of Anxiety ; the daimonic ; freedom vs destiny . Irvin Yalom Existential psychotherapy ; the four ultimate concerns : death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness . Ludwig Binswanger Daseinsanalysis ("being-in-the-world"); applied Heidegger to psychiatry. Lock the three "wills": will to pleasure = Sigmund Freud · will to power = Alfred Adler · will to meaning = Frankl. S4. Type theories (the older, body-based ones) Before traits, people sorted personality into discrete types , often tied to the body. Largely discredited, still examined because of who proposed them. Theorist Typology Hippocrates / Galen Four bodily humours → temperaments: sanguine (blood, cheerful), choleric (yellow bile, irritable), melancholic (black bile, sad), phlegmatic (phlegm, calm). William Sheldon Somatotypes : endomorph (round → viscerotonic: sociable), mesomorph (muscular → somatotonic: assertive), ectomorph (thin → cerebrotonic: restrained, introverted). Ernst Kretschmer Body build → psychiatric tendency: pyknic (round → manic-depressive), asthenic/leptosomic (thin → schizophrenic), athletic, dysplastic. Friedman & Rosenman Type A (competitive, hostile, time-urgent → heart disease) vs Type B (relaxed). Later Type C (cancer-prone, emotion-suppressing) and Type D (distressed: negative affect + social inhibition). TRAP — type vs trait, and the two body theorists. Type = discrete category (you ARE an endomorph); trait = continuous dimension (you score 7/10 on extraversion). Sheldon = somatotypes (endo/meso/ecto); Ernst Kretschmer = body build linked to psychosis type. S5. Indian psychology — Triguna & allied concepts Indian thought locates personality in the balance of three fundamental qualities ( gunas ) of nature ( prakriti ). Everyone has all three; the dominant one defines temperament, and the balance can shift. Concept What it is Triguna (Samkhya / Bhagavad Gita) Sattva (purity, clarity, balance, wisdom), Rajas (activity, passion, restlessness, ambition), Tamas (inertia, dullness, lethargy). Measured by the Vedic Personality Inventory (VPI) . Ayurvedic Tridosha Mind-body constitution: Vata (air/movement), Pitta (fire/metabolism), Kapha (earth-water/structure). A body-typology parallel to William Sheldon. Panchakosha Five "sheaths" of the self (Taittiriya Upanishad): annamaya (body) → pranamaya (vital energy) → manomaya (mind) → vijnanamaya (intellect) → anandamaya (bliss). Lock this line: Sattva = goodness/balance · Rajas = activity/passion · Tamas = inertia/darkness. Three "gunas" in a stem = Triguna, measured by the VPI. S6. How personality is measured (assessment in depth) Two philosophies of testing with a built-in trade-off. Projective tests show an ambiguous stimulus and assume you'll unconsciously project hidden material onto it: rich, hard to fake, but low reliability/validity. Objective (self-report) tests use fixed items scored against norms: far more reliable, but vulnerable to faking and social desirability. Type Tests Logic & trade-off Projective Rorschach (inkblots, Exner scoring), TAT (Murray), CAT (children), Sentence Completion (RISB), Draw-A-Person, Rosenzweig P-F, Word Association (Carl Jung) Ambiguous stimulus → person projects unconscious content. Rich, hard to fake, low reliability/validity. Objective / self-report MMPI-2 (clinical; validity scales L, F, K), 16PF (Raymond Cattell), NEO-PI-R (Big Five), EPQ (Hans Eysenck), CPI, MCMI (Millon) Standardised, norm-referenced, objectively scored. High reliability, but fakeable / socially-desirable responding.
