NIMHANS — Henry Murray. Murray ( personology ) built a system of needs and press (internal needs like achievement/affiliation/power meeting environmental press ) and, with Christiana Morgan , created the TAT . Need for achievement was then run hard by David McClelland . Constructs + Rep Grid = Kelly ; approach-avoidance conflict + drive-cue-response-reinforcement (Freud recast as learning) = John Dollard & Neal Miller . Person-situation debate settled by interactionism . The key studies & research, walked through Schultz & Schultz grades each theory on a "Research" section, and NIMHANS/MET stems routinely describe a study and ask you to name it, its author, or its conclusion. Here each landmark is walked through in the same shape: the question , what they did , what they found , why it matters , and the trap . The psychoanalysts ran case studies (rich, unreliable); the trait theorists ran factor analyses on questionnaires; the behaviourists and social-learning theorists ran controlled experiments. Learn the method along with the finding, because the design is often the giveaway in the stem. Freud's case studies — the clinical method at its richest Sigmund Freud built psychoanalysis almost entirely on a handful of intensively studied cases, the clinical / case-study method : deep, qualitative, theory-generating, but unrepeatable, unrepresentative and unfalsifiable. Each case is tied to a specific concept, and the exam pairs the case to what it "illustrates". Case Whose / what What it illustrated Anna O. Josef Breuer's patient (Bertha Pappenheim), reported with Freud in Studies on Hysteria , 1895 The "talking cure" / catharsis : hysterical symptoms eased when the buried memory and its trapped affect were spoken out. The seed of the whole method (and of transference ). Not Freud's own patient — Breuer's. Little Hans A 5-year-old boy with a horse phobia, treated largely through the father's letters The Oedipus complex and castration anxiety in childhood: the fear of horses read as displaced fear of the father. Freud's main "evidence" for the phallic stage. Dora Ida Bauer, an 18-year-old with hysteria; an incomplete analysis Freud published Dream analysis, transference and resistance (and Freud's failure to handle the transference, which he later flagged as why she broke off). Often cited in the feminist critique of Freud. Rat Man Ernst Lanzer, a lawyer with obsessional fears The classic study of obsessional neurosis : ambivalence (love–hate), undoing , isolation of affect and magical thinking. Wolf Man Sergei Pankejeff, who dreamed of white wolves in a tree The primal scene and infantile sexuality reconstructed from a childhood dream; one of Freud's most detailed analyses of a single neurosis. TRAP — Anna O. is Breuer's, not Freud's. Anna O. (talking cure, catharsis) belongs to Josef Breuer ; Sigmund Freud reported it with him. Little Hans = phobia → Oedipus/castration; Dora = hysteria, transference, the feminist critique; Rat Man = obsessional neurosis (undoing); Wolf Man = primal scene. "Talking cure" coined by the patient herself. NIMHANS angle. Verdict from later controlled research: the existence of unconscious processing and of defences (especially displacement and projection) finds support; the psychosexual stages , the Oedipus complex and fixed dream symbolism do not. Know the case-study method's weaknesses by name: not replicable, biased sample, reliant on fallible retrospective report, examiner suggestion. Bandura's Bobo doll experiments (1961–63) — observational learning Question: can aggression be learned simply by watching, with no reinforcement to the learner? What: nursery-school children watched an adult model either attack or ignore an inflatable Bobo doll (hitting it with a mallet, kicking it, shouting novel phrases); the children were then mildly frustrated and left alone with the doll. A later variant had the children see the model rewarded , punished , or face no consequence. Found: children who saw aggression imitated it, including novel acts and verbal aggression they had not seen before. Seeing the model rewarded raised imitation ( vicarious reinforcement ); seeing the model punished lowered performance but not learning — when later offered an incentive, the "punished" children reproduced the acts just as well. Matters: founded social-learning / social-cognitive theory and the crucial learning-vs-performance distinction ; learning happens through observation alone, consequences only govern whether it is shown. Trap: the children learned the aggression regardless of the model's fate; consequences only changed whether they performed it. (Contrast Skinner, for whom learning requires the learner's own reinforcement.) Bandura's self-efficacy & snake-phobia mastery studies Question: what most powerfully raises a person's belief that they can do something, and does that belief drive behaviour? What: Albert Bandura treated people with severe snake phobia by guided mastery / participant modeling (the therapist models touching the snake, then the client does it in graded steps), comparing it with watching a model only, and with symbolic/imaginal methods. Found: mastery experiences (actually performing the feared act successfully) produced the strongest, most generalised rise in self-efficacy and the biggest behaviour change, outperforming insight or vicarious methods alone. Matters: established the four sources of self-efficacy in rank order — mastery experiences (strongest) → vicarious experience → verbal persuasion → physiological/emotional state — and showed efficacy beliefs predict effort, persistence and recovery. The clinical lineage of exposure-based therapy. Trap: the strongest source of self-efficacy is mastery (performance accomplishment) , not encouragement (verbal persuasion). Self-efficacy = Bandura , task-specific; do not confuse with Julian Rotter's locus of control (outcome-source). Rogers' Q-sort & self/ideal-self congruence research Question: can the humanistic idea of "congruence" be measured objectively, and does therapy raise it? What: Rogers (with the Q-sort technique, devised by William Stephenson ) had clients sort a deck of self-descriptive cards twice — once for the real / actual self ("how I am") and once for the ideal self ("how I'd like to be"). The correlation between the two sorts is an objective index of self-ideal congruence . He also tape-recorded and transcribed therapy sessions, a field first. Found: in successful client-centred therapy the real-self and ideal-self sorts moved closer together (congruence rose), and largely because the ideal became more realistic, not only because the real self "improved". Matters: Rogers turned a humanistic construct into a measurable, research-friendly variable and pioneered psychotherapy process research . Trap: a large real–ideal gap = incongruence (distress); a close match = congruence (adjustment). Q-sort = Carl Rogers (Stephenson devised the tool). Marcia's identity-status interview — operationalising Erikson Question: can Erikson's "identity vs role confusion" be made measurable? What: James Marcia built a semi-structured Identity Status Interview that scores an adolescent on two axes: has the person undergone a crisis (active exploration of alternatives) and have they made a commitment ? Found: crossing the two yields four identity statuses : diffusion (no exploration, no commitment), foreclosure (commitment without exploration — borrowed wholesale from parents), moratorium (in active crisis, exploring, not yet committed), achievement (committed after exploring). Matters: the single most-cited research operationalisation of an Eriksonian stage; achievement and moratorium are the more mature statuses. Trap: the trickiest pair is foreclosure (commitment, no exploration) vs moratorium (exploration, no commitment yet). Marcia ≠ Erik Erikson: Erikson gave the stage, Marcia gave the four statuses. Mischel — the person–situation debate & the marshmallow studies Question (1968): how cross-situationally consistent is behaviour, really? What: Walter Mischel's book Personality and Assessment reviewed the evidence and argued trait scores predict behaviour only modestly across situations (the famous " personality coefficient " of about r ≈ 0.30), igniting the person–situation debate . Found / resolution: behaviour is more situation-dependent than pure trait theory assumed, but the settled answer is interactionism — stable dispositions and situations jointly produce behaviour, and Mischel's own CAPS model (cognitive-affective personality system) reframes consistency as stable "if–then" behavioural signatures (this person is aggressive when teased by peers but not when criticised by adults). The marshmallow / delay-of-gratification studies: preschoolers could eat one marshmallow now or wait alone for two; the seconds they could wait predicted later (correlational) outcomes — adolescent self-control and academic measures. Later large replications found the link is weaker and largely explained by background factors (affluence, home environment), a cautionary tale on over-claiming. Trap: Mischel = the person-situation critique and delay of gratification ; the resolution of the debate is interactionism , not "situations win". Don't confuse delay of gratification (a cognitive self-regulation skill) with Sigmund Freud's reality principle. Friedman & Rosenman — Type A behaviour & coronary heart disease Question: does a behaviour pattern predict heart disease? What: two cardiologists , Meyer Friedman & Ray Rosenman , classified men as Type A (competitive, hostile, impatient, time-urgent, achievement-driven) or Type B (relaxed, easygoing) and followed them prospectively (the Western Collaborative Group Study). Found: Type A men developed roughly twice the rate of coronary heart disease (CHD) . Later analysis narrowed the toxic ingredient to hostility / anger rather than the whole pattern. Matters: a landmark in health/personality psychology; spawned Type C (cancer-prone, emotion-suppressing) and Type D ("distressed": negative affect + social inhibition, a cardiac risk marker — Denollet ). Trap: Type A → heart disease ; the most cardiotoxic component is hostility . Type = discrete category (the older, body-/pattern-based tradition), unlike a continuous trait. Seligman — learned helplessness → learned optimism Question: what does uncontrollable aversive experience do to motivation? What: Martin Seligman & Steven Maier gave dogs inescapable shock; later, in a box where escape was easy (just jump the barrier), these dogs failed to even try , unlike dogs that had earlier been able to escape. Found: learned helplessness — having learned that responses don't matter, the organism stops responding and shows deficits resembling depression . Reformulation (with Abramson): whether helplessness follows depends on the person's explanatory / attributional style along three axes — internal–external, stable–unstable, global–specific . The depressive/pessimist explains bad events as internal, stable, global ("it's me, it always happens, it ruins everything"). Matters: a leading cognitive model of depression; flipped into learned optimism and launched positive psychology (PERMA, signature strengths). Trap: the pessimistic style for bad events = internal + stable + global. Learned helplessness / optimism / positive psychology all = Seligman . Rotter — locus of control & the I-E Scale Question: do people differ in whether they believe they control their own outcomes? What: from his social-learning theory (behaviour potential = expectancy × reinforcement value ), Julian Rotter built the Internal-External (I-E) Scale , a forced-choice self-report. Found: people array along a dimension from internal locus (outcomes flow from my own actions/ability) to external locus (outcomes flow from luck, fate, powerful others). Internals generally show better coping, achievement, health behaviour and stress resistance. Matters: one of the most-used constructs in clinical and health psychology. Trap: locus of control = Rotter , about the source of outcomes ("who controls what happens"); contrast Albert Bandura's self-efficacy ("can I perform this task"). Both sound like "belief about control". The Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart (Bouchard) — heritability Question: how much of personality is genetic? What: Thomas Bouchard's Minnesota study assessed identical ( MZ ) and fraternal ( DZ ) twins, crucially including pairs reared apart , on personality inventories and other measures. Found: MZ twins reared apart were strikingly similar on the major personality traits — heritability estimates of roughly 40–60% for the big trait dimensions — and shared environment contributed surprisingly little (the non-shared environment matters more than the shared family environment). Matters: the empirical backbone for the biological/trait camp (Hans Eysenck, Robert McCrae & Paul Costa) and the "Part Eleven" perspective chapter's heritability figure. Trap: lock ~40–60% heritability ; and note the counter-intuitive finding that the shared family environment explains little — siblings differ largely because of non-shared experiences. Eysenck's factor-analytic & arousal studies Question: are there a few biologically based super-dimensions, and what causes them? What: Hans Eysenck factor-analysed large samples to extract the PEN dimensions (Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism), then tested their biological basis with arousal measures (lemon-juice salivation tests, EEG, conditioning studies). Found: introverts show higher baseline cortical arousal (a more active reticular activating system (Giuseppe Moruzzi and Horace Magoun, 1949)) and so avoid extra stimulation, while extraverts are chronically under-aroused and seek stimulation; neuroticism reflects an over-reactive limbic/autonomic system. Traits showed high heritability . Matters: the model of a causal, biological trait theory (says why , not just what ). Trap: Eysenck = 3 dimensions (PEN), biological, arousal-based ; introverts are over -aroused (hence stimulation-shy). Contrast Cattell's 16 and the descriptive Big Five. Reward/punishment sensitivity in a stem = Gray (BIS/BAS) , not Eysenck. Cattell's lexical/factor work — the 16PF Question: how many basic source traits underlie personality? What: Raymond Cattell started from the lexical pool, reduced thousands of trait words to clusters, and applied factor analysis to three data sources — L-data (life records), Q-data (questionnaires) and T-data (objective tests). Found: he distilled personality to 16 source traits (the deep causal factors) beneath the visible surface traits , operationalised as the 16PF questionnaire. He also separated fluid from crystallised intelligence. Matters: the prototypical factor-analytic trait programme and a direct ancestor of the Big Five (re-analyses of his variables kept yielding five higher-order factors). Trap: Cattell = 16 source traits, 16PF, factor analysis ; surface trait (visible cluster) vs source trait (underlying cause). McCrae & Costa — cross-cultural stability of the Five-Factor Model Question: are the Big Five universal and stable? What: Paul Costa & Robert McCrae administered the NEO-PI-R across many languages and cultures and re-tested adults longitudinally. Found: the same five factors ( OCEAN ) replicated broadly across cultures, and individual trait levels are largely stable after about age 30 (with small normative shifts — neuroticism and openness tend to decline, agreeableness and conscientiousness to rise, with age, the "maturity principle"). Matters: evidence that the FFM taps something cross-culturally real and trait-like, feeding the Five-Factor Theory (heritable basic tendencies → culturally shaped characteristic adaptations ). Trap: FFM = 5 (OCEAN), NEO-PI-R, descriptive, stable after ~30, cross-cultural . The Big Five describes what traits exist; Eysenck's PEN explains why . Murray's TAT & McClelland's need for achievement Question: can hidden motives ("needs") be read from imaginative fantasy? What: Henry Murray (with Christiana Morgan ) built the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) — ambiguous picture cards the person tells stories about — as a window onto his system of needs (achievement, affiliation, power, etc.) meeting environmental press (his theory: personology ). David McClelland then scored TAT stories for need for achievement (nAch) and linked high nAch to entrepreneurial striving and even economic growth, plus need for power and affiliation. Found: projective fantasy reliably elicits implicit motives that self-report misses. Matters: the projective-test lineage and the motive-measurement tradition. Trap: TAT = Murray (& Morgan) ; need for achievement run hard by McClelland . TAT is projective (apperception of pictures); don't confuse with the Rorschach (inkblots). Allport & Odbert (1936) — the lexical study Question: how many trait words does the language hold? What: Gordon Allport & Henry Odbert combed an unabridged English dictionary and extracted about 18,000 person-describing words, sorting them into stable traits, temporary states, evaluative terms, etc. Found: the sheer size of the lexicon, taken as support for the lexical hypothesis — if an individual difference matters to human life, language will have coined a word for it. Matters: the starting point for the whole trait/lexical tradition that Raymond Cattell and then the Big Five mined. Trap: the ~18,000 figure and the lexical hypothesis = Allport & Henry Odbert ; but note Allport himself was idiographic and did not use factor analysis (Cattell did the reduction). Harlow's monkeys — contact comfort & the roots of attachment Question: do infants bond for food or for comfort? What: Harry Harlow raised infant rhesus monkeys with two surrogate "mothers": a bare wire mother that dispensed milk and a soft cloth mother that gave none. Found: the monkeys clung to the cloth mother for comfort and ran to her when frightened, going to the wire mother only to feed, decisively contradicting the drive-reduction (Clark Hull, 1943)/"cupboard-love" view that attachment is learned through feeding. Total isolation produced lasting social and emotional damage. Matters: "contact comfort" showed love/attachment is a primary need, not a by-product of feeding, undercutting both behaviourist and orthodox Freudian (oral-stage) accounts and supporting object-relations/attachment theory. Trap: the monkeys preferred the cloth (comfort) mother over the wire (feeding) mother — comfort, not food, drives bonding. (Maslow began his career studying monkeys with Harlow.) Bowlby & Ainsworth — attachment and the Strange Situation Question: what is the bond between infant and caregiver, and how is it measured? What: John Bowlby proposed attachment as an innate, evolved system: the infant seeks a secure base , builds an internal working model ("are others reliable? am I worthy?"), and is harmed by maternal deprivation . Mary Ainsworth operationalised it with the Strange Situation , a structured lab sequence of separations and reunions. Found: infants sort into secure (uses mother as a base, distressed at separation, comforted at reunion), insecure-avoidant (indifferent, avoids reunion), and insecure-resistant/ambivalent (clingy yet angry, hard to soothe); Main & Solomon later added disorganised . Matters: the bridge from object relations to empirical developmental psychology; attachment styles predict later relationships (the adult four-category model). Trap: Bowlby = the theory (secure base, internal working model, maternal deprivation); Ainsworth = the Strange Situation and the three styles; Main = disorganised. Don't credit the Strange Situation to Bowlby. Recap — studies. Sigmund Freud's cases (Anna O. = Breuer's, talking cure; Little Hans = Oedipus/phobia; Dora = transference; Rat Man = obsessional) · Bandura Bobo (observational learning; learning ≠ performance) + snake-phobia (mastery is the strongest efficacy source) · Rogers Q-sort (real–ideal congruence rises in therapy) · James Marcia (four identity statuses operationalise Erik Erikson) · Walter Mischel (person-situation debate → interactionism; marshmallow delay of gratification) · Friedman & Rosenman (Type A → CHD; hostility is the toxic bit) · Martin Seligman (learned helplessness → attributional style → learned optimism) · Julian Rotter (locus of control, I-E Scale) · Bouchard Minnesota twins (heritability ~40–60%) · Hans Eysenck (PEN, introverts over-aroused) · Cattell (16 source traits via factor analysis) · Robert McCrae & Paul Costa (FFM cross-culturally stable after 30) · Murray TAT & McClelland nAch · Gordon Allport & Henry Odbert (~18,000 trait words, lexical hypothesis) · Harry Harlow (contact comfort > food) · Bowlby/Ainsworth (attachment, Strange Situation). Extended concept bank (the rest of the book, chapter by chapter) The chapters above are the spine. This bank picks up the remaining named terms theorist by theorist — the full defence-mechanism list, every Jungian archetype, Alfred Adler's safeguarding tendencies, Karen Horney's ten neurotic needs, Erik Erikson's virtues, Maslow's B-values, George Kelly's eleven corollaries, and so on — so each has a home you can slot it into. Every entry is the kind of one-line fact an MCQ distractor is built from. Freud — the full defence-mechanism list (catalogued by Anna Freud) Defence One line Repression The master defence: unconscious blocking of threatening material. (Conscious version = suppression , the only mature/conscious one.) Denial Refuse to accept an external reality. Projection Attribute your own unacceptable impulse to someone else. Displacement Redirect an impulse onto a safer substitute target . Sublimation Channel the impulse into a socially valued activity (the healthiest classical defence). Reaction formation Act as the opposite of the true impulse. Rationalisation Invent a logical-sounding excuse for the real reason. Regression Retreat to an earlier developmental stage under stress. Intellectualisation Strip the emotion out, deal only with abstract facts. Identification Take on the qualities of an admired/feared other (incl. identification with the aggressor). Introjection Absorb another's values/qualities wholesale into the self. Undoing A ritual act to magically "cancel" a bad thought/deed. Isolation of affect Keep the memory, sever the feeling. Splitting See self/others as all-good or all-bad (borderline; Klein/Kernberg). Projective identification Project a part of the self into another and induce them to act it out (Melanie Klein). Compensation Make up for a weakness by excelling elsewhere (more Adlerian). Fantasy / daydreaming Gratify frustrated wishes imaginatively (immature). Acting out / somatisation Discharge conflict through action / bodily symptoms (immature). Mature set (George Vaillant) Sublimation, humour , altruism , suppression , anticipation . NIMHANS — Vaillant's maturity hierarchy. Psychotic (denial of external reality, delusional projection, distortion) → immature (projection, acting out, passive aggression, fantasy, splitting, somatisation) → neurotic (repression, displacement, reaction formation, intellectualisation, rationalisation, undoing) → mature (sublimation, humour, altruism, suppression, anticipation). Repression = unconscious/neurotic; suppression = conscious/mature. Jung — the full archetype list Archetype What it is Persona The public mask, the role we present to society. Shadow The dark, animal, denied side; the source of creativity as well as vice. Anima The feminine side within a man. Animus The masculine side within a woman. Self The unifying, central archetype of wholeness; goal of individuation, symbolised by the mandala . Great Mother Archetype of nurturance and fertility (and devouring). Wise Old Man Archetype of meaning, wisdom, the spirit/sage. Hero The figure who conquers evil; champion of the ego against the unconscious. Trickster / others Plus rebirth, child, maiden, etc. — Jung held archetypes are innumerable. Other Jung terms to own: complexes (emotionally charged clusters in the personal unconscious, e.g. a mother complex), the two attitudes (introversion / extraversion), the four functions (thinking, feeling = rational; sensing, intuiting = irrational), individuation (lifelong integration into the self), and the transcendent function (uniting opposites). Adler — birth order & safeguarding tendencies Position Typical Adlerian portrait First-born "Dethroned" by the next child; often conservative, responsible, power-oriented, may feel insecure. Second / middle Competitive, ambitious (runs to catch the pacemaker ahead); often the best-adjusted. Youngest Pampered baby of the family; can be highly motivated to outdo all, or dependent and avoidant. Only child Never dethroned; precocious, may be pampered, rivalrous with adults rather than peers. Safeguarding tendencies (Alfred Adler's neurotic protections of self-esteem, a forerunner of defence mechanisms): excuses ("yes, but…" / "if only…"), aggression (depreciation, accusation, self-accusation), and distancing / withdrawal (moving backward, standing still, hesitating, constructing obstacles). Plus the core terms: inferiority feelings → compensation → (if it fails) inferiority complex or over-compensating superiority complex ; style of life ; creative power of the self ; fictional finalism ; social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefühl) ; the three life tasks (work, friendship/society, love). Horney — the ten neurotic needs & three trends The three trends (toward / against / away) are distilled from ten neurotic needs : (1) affection & approval, (2) a dominant partner to run one's life, (3) narrow limits to life (undemanding), (4) power, (5) exploitation of others, (6) prestige/social recognition, (7) personal admiration, (8) personal achievement/ambition, (9) self-sufficiency & independence, (10) perfection & unassailability. Trend Needs it groups Type Moving toward people (compliance) Affection, a dominant partner, narrow limits (1–3) Self-effacing / compliant Moving against people (aggression) Power, exploitation, prestige, admiration, achievement (4–8) Expansive / aggressive Moving away from people (detachment) Self-sufficiency, perfection (9–10) Resigned / detached Plus: basic anxiety (isolated and helpless in a hostile world) vs basic hostility ; the idealised (self-)image and the "tyranny of the should" ; real self vs idealised self; rejection of penis envy in favour of cultural power-envy and men's "womb envy" . Erikson — the eight stages with virtues (and Marcia's statuses) Stage (age) Crisis Basic virtue / strength Maladaptation Infancy (0–1) Trust vs mistrust Hope Withdrawal Early childhood (1–3) Autonomy vs shame/doubt Will Compulsion Play age (3–5) Initiative vs guilt Purpose Inhibition School age (6–11) Industry vs inferiority Competence Inertia Adolescence (12–18) Identity vs role confusion Fidelity Repudiation Young adulthood Intimacy vs isolation Love Exclusivity Middle adulthood Generativity vs stagnation Care Rejectivity Old age Ego integrity vs despair Wisdom Disdain James Marcia's four identity statuses (crisis/exploration × commitment): diffusion (neither), foreclosure (commitment, no exploration), moratorium (exploring, no commitment yet), achievement (commitment after exploration). Erik Erikson coined "identity crisis" ; key term epigenetic principle . Allport — the trait taxonomy & the proprium Level / term What it is Cardinal trait So dominant it pervades a whole life (rare; a "Scrooge"). Central traits The 5–10 core descriptors of a person (the reference-letter words). Secondary dispositions Situation-specific preferences, shown only sometimes. Common vs individual traits Shared/comparable across people vs unique to the person (he favoured the latter, personal dispositions ). Proprium Gordon Allport's word for the self/ego, developing through ~7 aspects (bodily self → self-identity → self-esteem → self-extension → self-image → rational coping → propriate striving ). Functional autonomy A motive becomes independent of its origin (perseverative vs propriate functional autonomy). Idiographic / morphogenic Study of the unique individual (Allport's preferred approach; he rejected factor analysis). Maslow — the full hierarchy, B-values & the self-actualiser Hierarchy (bottom → top): physiological → safety → belongingness/love → esteem → self-actualisation ; later additions split the upper region into cognitive (know/understand) and aesthetic needs below self-actualisation, and self-transcendence above it. Lower four = deficiency (D-)needs ; the top = being (B-)needs / growth needs . Characteristics of self-actualisers: accurate perception of reality; acceptance of self/others/nature; spontaneity & naturalness; problem-centred (not self-centred); need for privacy & autonomy; freshness of appreciation; peak experiences ; Gemeinschaftsgefühl (social interest); deep but few interpersonal relationships; democratic character; ethical discrimination of means/ends; philosophical humour; creativeness; resistance to enculturation. B-values (the "meta-needs" pursued at the top): truth, goodness, beauty, unity/wholeness, aliveness, uniqueness, perfection, justice, order, simplicity, richness, effortlessness, playfulness, self-sufficiency, meaningfulness. The Jonah complex = fear of one's own greatness; metapathology = the malaise from frustrated B-values; measured by the POI (Shostrom) . Rogers — the fully functioning person Core machinery: the actualising tendency (and the organism's organismic valuing process ); the self / self-concept ; real self vs ideal self → congruence vs incongruence ; conditions of worth imposed by conditional positive regard; the cure = unconditional positive regard (UPR) ; the therapist's three core conditions = empathy, congruence/genuineness, UPR. The fully functioning person (Carl Rogers' ideal of growth) shows: (1) openness to experience (no defensiveness), (2) existential living (fully in the present moment), (3) organismic trusting (trusting one's own judgement), (4) experiential freedom (sense of free choice and responsibility), and (5) creativity . Kelly — the fundamental postulate & eleven corollaries Fundamental postulate: "a person's processes are psychologically channelised by the ways in which they anticipate events." The eleven corollaries : Corollary One line Construction We anticipate events by construing their replications (we read recurring themes). Individuality People differ in how they construe the same event. Organisation Each person organises constructs into a hierarchy (some superordinate to others). Dichotomy Constructs are bipolar (kind–cruel). Choice We pick the pole of a construct that promises the most extension/definition of our system. Range Each construct applies only to a limited range of events (its range of convenience). Experience We revise constructs as we successively construe events. Modulation How much a system can change is limited by the permeability of its constructs. Fragmentation We can hold sub-systems that are mutually inconsistent. Commonality People who construe experience similarly are psychologically similar. Sociality To relate to someone you must construe their construction processes (role-taking). Plus Kelly's cognitive re-definitions of emotion: anxiety (events lie outside one's constructs), threat (awareness of imminent comprehensive change), fear (imminent incidental change), guilt (acting against one's core role construct), hostility (forcing reality to validate a failed construct). Assessment: Rep Test / rep grid , self-characterisation sketch , fixed-role therapy ; philosophy = constructive alternativism . Skinner & Bandura — the learning machinery Term Whose / what Operant vs respondent B. F. Skinner: operant (emitted, shaped by consequences) vs respondent/classical (elicited reflex). Positive/negative reinforcement Add pleasant / remove aversive — both increase behaviour. Positive/negative punishment Add aversive / remove pleasant — both decrease behaviour (Skinner thought punishment unreliable). Schedules Fixed/variable × ratio/interval; variable-ratio = highest, most extinction-resistant responding (the slot machine). Shaping Reinforcing successive approximations. Extinction / superstition Stop reinforcing → behaviour fades; accidental reinforcement → "superstitious" pigeon behaviour. Functional analysis (A-B-C) Antecedent → Behaviour → Consequence (Skinner's "assessment"). Observational learning Albert Bandura: attention → retention → production → motivation; vicarious reinforcement . Reciprocal determinism Behaviour ↔ personal/cognitive factors ↔ environment, a three-way loop. Self-efficacy (4 sources) Mastery (strongest) → vicarious → verbal persuasion → physiological/emotional state. Self-regulation / self-system Internal standards + self-judgement; later moral disengagement , collective efficacy . Trait, facet & temperament terms Term Whose / what Surface vs source trait Cattell: visible cluster vs underlying causal factor (16 source traits → 16PF). Erg / sentiment / attitude Cattell's dynamic traits: ergs (innate drives), sentiments (learned), attitudes. Fluid vs crystallised intelligence Cattell: raw reasoning vs accumulated knowledge. PEN Hans Eysenck: Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism (EPI → EPQ); biological, arousal-based. Big Five / OCEAN Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism (Goldberg coined "Big Five"; NEO-PI-R (Paul Costa and Robert McCrae)). HEXACO Ashton & Lee: 6 factors, adds Honesty-Humility (low H = the dark triad). BIS / BAS Gray's Reinforcement Sensitivity: BIS (punishment → anxiety), BAS (reward → impulsivity). Locus of control / I-E Scale Julian Rotter (internal vs external; from expectancy × reinforcement value). Sensation seeking / SSS Zuckerman: thrill-and-adventure, experience, disinhibition, boredom susceptibility. Learned helplessness / optimism Martin Seligman; explanatory style = internal–external × stable–unstable × global–specific. Flow Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi: challenge matches skill → absorbed engagement. EAS temperament Buss & Plomin: Emotionality, Activity, Sociability. Inhibited / uninhibited Jerome Kagan's infant temperament (precursor of introversion). Easy / difficult / slow-to-warm-up Alexander Thomas & Stella Chess's temperament types; goodness of fit . Recap — bank. Defences (full list, Anna Freud; George Vaillant's maturity ladder) · Carl Jung's archetypes (persona, shadow, anima/animus, self + Great Mother, Wise Old Man, Hero) · Alfred Adler's birth order + safeguarding tendencies + three life tasks · Karen Horney's ten neurotic needs → three trends · Erik Erikson's eight virtues (hope→wisdom) + James Marcia's four statuses · Gordon Allport's trait levels + proprium + functional autonomy · Abraham Maslow's full hierarchy + B-values + self-actualiser traits + Jonah complex · Carl Rogers' fully functioning person (5 features) + core conditions · George Kelly's postulate + 11 corollaries + cognitive emotions · Skinner/Bandura learning machinery · trait/facet/temperament terms. Fast glossary (one line each, A–Z) Last-mile recall: every nameable personality term/theorist on this page reduced to a single line and its author, alphabetical so you can self-test by covering the right column. If a name fires but the definition doesn't, that is the gap to drill. Term One-line definition (and who) Actualising tendency Innate drive of every organism to maintain and enhance itself (Carl Rogers). Anal stage 1–3 yrs, toilet training; fixation → retentive (orderly/stingy) or expulsive (messy) (Freud). Anima / animus The inner feminine in a man / masculine in a woman (Carl Jung). Archetype Universal inherited image in the collective unconscious (Jung). Attachment / Strange Situation Innate secure-base bond (John Bowlby); measured by the Strange Situation (Mary Ainsworth). Basic anxiety Feeling isolated and helpless in a hostile world (Karen Horney). Birth order First-born dethroned, middle competitive, youngest pampered, only precocious (Alfred Adler). Bobo doll Children imitate observed aggression; learning ≠ performance (Albert Bandura). Cardinal / central / secondary Gordon Allport's three trait levels (dominant / core / situational). Castration anxiety / penis envy Phallic-stage fears of boy / girl in the Oedipus/Electra complex (Freud). Collective unconscious Inherited layer shared by all humanity, holds archetypes (Jung, NOT Freud). Compensation Overcoming felt inferiority by developing strengths (Adler). Conditions of worth "I'll value you only if…"; the root of incongruence (Rogers). Congruence Close match of real self and ideal self (well-being) (Rogers). Constructive alternativism There is always another way to construe any event (Kelly). Creative power of the self We actively shape our own personality, not passive products (Adler). Defence mechanisms Unconscious ego distortions reducing anxiety; catalogued by Anna Freud. Displacement Redirect an impulse onto a safer target (Freud). Epigenetic principle An inborn plan unfolds the stages in fixed order (Erik Erikson). Eros / Thanatos Life instinct (libido) / death instinct (aggression) (Freud). Expectancy × reinforcement value Behaviour potential in social-learning theory (Julian Rotter). Factor analysis Statistic that finds the few dimensions behind many trait ratings (Raymond Cattell; Hans Eysenck). Fictional finalism We live "as if" toward future fictional goals (Adler). Fixation Libido stuck at a psychosexual stage from over/under-gratification (Freud). Five-Factor Model (OCEAN) Five universal trait dimensions; NEO-PI-R (Paul Costa & Robert McCrae; Goldberg "Big Five"). Flow Absorbed state when challenge matches skill (Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi). Free association Say whatever comes, censorship off, to reach the unconscious (Freud). Fully functioning person Open, present-living, organism-trusting, free, creative (Rogers). Functional analysis (A-B-C) Antecedent → Behaviour → Consequence (B. F. Skinner). Functional autonomy A motive becomes independent of its origin (Allport). Good-enough mother / transitional object Adequate (not perfect) mothering; the security blanket (Donald Winnicott). Humours / temperaments Sanguine, choleric, melancholic, phlegmatic (Hippocrates/Galen). Id / ego / superego Pleasure principle / reality principle / internalised morality (Freud). Idealised self / tyranny of the should The impossible self-image we tyrannise ourselves toward (Horney). Identity statuses Diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, achievement (James Marcia, operationalising Erikson). Identity vs role confusion The adolescent crisis; virtue = fidelity (Erikson). Idiographic / morphogenic Study of the unique individual (Allport) vs nomothetic general laws. Individual psychology Adler's school: striving for superiority, social interest. Individuation Lifelong integration of all parts into the self (Jung). Inferiority / superiority complex Paralysing self-doubt / over-compensation for it (Adler). Internal working model "Are others reliable, am I worthy?" template from early care (Bowlby). Introversion / extraversion Energy turned inward vs outward (coined by Jung). Jonah complex Fear of one's own greatness that blocks self-actualisation (Abraham Maslow). Latent vs manifest content The hidden wish vs the remembered dream (Freud). Learned helplessness → optimism Uncontrollable shock kills effort; flips via explanatory style (Martin Seligman). Lexical hypothesis If a trait matters, language coins a word; ~18,000 words (Allport & Henry Odbert). Libido Sexual life-energy (Freud); de-sexualised general psychic energy (Jung). Locus of control / I-E Scale Outcomes from self (internal) vs fate/others (external) (Rotter). Logotherapy / will to meaning Meaning is the primary motive; existential vacuum if frustrated (Viktor Frankl). Man-the-scientist Each person forms, tests and revises personal constructs (Kelly). Mandala Symbol of the self / wholeness (Jung). Mature defences Sublimation, humour, altruism, suppression, anticipation (George Vaillant). Minnesota twins / heritability Traits ~40–60% heritable; shared environment adds little (Bouchard). Need for achievement (nAch) Motive scored from TAT stories (David McClelland; Murray's needs). Needs & press / personology / TAT Inner needs meet environmental press (Murray & Morgan). Neurotic trends Moving toward / against / away from people (Horney). Oedipus / Electra complex Phallic-stage desire for opposite-sex parent, rivalry with same-sex (Freud). Operant conditioning Behaviour shaped by its consequences (Skinner). Organismic valuing process The gut sense of what is right for the organism (Rogers). Peak experience Moment of ecstasy and wholeness in self-actualisers (Maslow). PEN Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism; biological (Eysenck). Persona / shadow / self Mask / dark denied side / unifying centre — archetypes (Jung). Personal constructs / Rep Grid Bipolar templates; elicited by the Role Construct Repertory Test (Kelly). Personal vs collective unconscious Your own repressed material vs the inherited human layer (Jung). Positions (paranoid-schizoid / depressive) Early modes of relating to objects, not stages (Melanie Klein). Possible / proprium Proprium = Allport's self, developing through ~7 aspects to propriate striving. Projection Attribute your own impulse to another (Freud). Projective identification Project a part of self into another and induce them to enact it (Klein). Psychosexual stages Oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital (Freud). Q-sort Sort cards for real vs ideal self; correlation = congruence (Rogers; Stephenson's tool). Reaction formation Behave as the opposite of the true impulse (Freud). Reciprocal determinism Behaviour, person and environment shape each other (Bandura). Reinforcement schedules Variable-ratio gives the most extinction-resistant responding (Skinner). Repression vs suppression Unconscious blocking (neurotic) vs deliberate set-aside (mature, conscious) (Freud; Vaillant). Safeguarding tendencies Excuses, aggression, distancing that protect self-esteem (Adler). Self-actualisation Top need; realising one's full potential (Maslow). Self-efficacy Belief one can perform a specific task; strongest source = mastery (Bandura). Self psychology / mirroring Cohesive self, selfobjects, narcissism from failed mirroring (Heinz Kohut). Sensation seeking / SSS Need for varied, novel, intense experience (Zuckerman). Separation-individuation Symbiosis → rapprochement → object constancy (Margaret Mahler). Shaping Reinforcing successive approximations to a target behaviour (Skinner). Social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefühl) Innate feeling of kinship with humanity; mark of health (Adler). Somatotypes Endomorph / mesomorph / ectomorph body-temperament types (Sheldon). Source vs surface trait Deep causal factor vs visible cluster; 16 source traits (Cattell). Splitting All-good / all-bad views of self and others (Klein; Otto Kernberg, borderline). Striving for superiority The one dynamic force: striving toward completion/perfection (Adler). Style of life The unique goal-pursuing pattern formed by ~age 5 (Adler). Sublimation Channel an impulse into a socially valued activity; healthiest classical defence (Freud). Topographic model Conscious / preconscious / unconscious (the iceberg) (Freud). Triguna Sattva (balance), Rajas (activity), Tamas (inertia); VPI (Indian / Samkhya). Tridosha Vata / Pitta / Kapha mind-body constitution (Ayurveda). Type A / B / C / D Hostile-urgent → CHD / relaxed / cancer-prone / distressed (Friedman & Rosenman; Denollet). Ultimate concerns Death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness (Irvin Yalom). Unconditional positive regard Acceptance with no conditions of worth; the cure (Rogers). Womb envy Men's envy of women's capacity to bear life (Horney, vs penis envy). Word-association test Delays/odd responses expose complexes (Jung). Recap — glossary. Cover the right column and recover the definition + author for every row; that named-concept layer is exactly what NIMHANS/MET test hardest. Drill the rows that don't fire instantly, then re-run the trap boxes. Self-test (active recall, by chapter) Recall beats re-reading. Cover the answers, ask each question aloud, then check. If you miss one, jump back to its chapter. The answer follows in green . Freud Name the three structures and their governing principles. Id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle), superego (morality, formed in the phallic stage). Which defence is the only conscious /mature one, and how does it differ from its twin? Suppression (deliberate set-aside, mature) vs repression (unconscious, neurotic). Whose patient was Anna O., and what did she illustrate? Breuer's; the "talking cure"/catharsis (Sigmund Freud reported it with him). Order the psychosexual stages. Oral → anal → phallic → latency → genital. Jung, Adler, Horney Collective unconscious belongs to whom, and what does it contain? Carl Jung; archetypes (persona, shadow, anima/animus, self). Match the three "wills": pleasure, power, meaning. Sigmund Freud (pleasure), Alfred Adler (power), Viktor Frankl (meaning). What is Adler's mark of mental health, and his term for actively shaping one's own personality? Social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefühl); the creative power of the self. Karen Horney's three neurotic trends? Moving toward / against / away from people. Inferiority complex vs basic anxiety, whose is each? Inferiority complex = Adler; basic anxiety = Horney. Erikson How do Erik Erikson's stages differ from Sigmund Freud's in number and type? Eight (lifelong) and psychosocial, vs Freud's five (to puberty) and psychosexual. Give the adolescent crisis and its virtue. Identity vs role confusion → fidelity. James Marcia's four identity statuses, and the tricky pair? Diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, achievement; foreclosure (commit, no exploration) vs moratorium (explore, no commitment yet). Allport & the trait approach Gordon Allport's three trait levels, and did he use factor analysis? Cardinal / central / secondary; no, he was idiographic. Match the trait numbers: Raymond Cattell, Hans Eysenck, FFM, HEXACO. 16 (16PF), 3 (PEN), 5 (OCEAN), 6 (adds Honesty-Humility). Are introverts over- or under-aroused in Eysenck's theory? Over-aroused (high baseline cortical arousal), so they avoid extra stimulation. What does functional autonomy mean? A motive becomes independent of its childhood origin (Allport). Maslow & Rogers D-needs vs B-needs? Deficiency needs (lower four, felt as lack) vs being/growth needs (self-actualisation, felt as pull). Carl Rogers' three therapeutic core conditions? Empathy, congruence/genuineness, unconditional positive regard. What does the Q-sort measure and how? Self-ideal congruence, via the correlation between real-self and ideal-self card sorts (Rogers; Stephenson's tool). Which test operationalised self-actualisation? The Personal Orientation Inventory, POI (Shostrom). Kelly, Skinner, Bandura George Kelly's image of the person and his philosophy? Man-the-scientist; constructive alternativism. Which reinforcement schedule is most extinction-resistant? Variable-ratio (the slot machine). In the Bobo doll studies, what did the model's punishment affect? Performance, not learning (children still learned the acts). The four sources of self-efficacy in order of strength? Mastery (strongest) → vicarious → verbal persuasion → physiological/emotional state. Self-efficacy vs locus of control? Self-efficacy = Albert Bandura ("can I do this task?"); locus of control = Julian Rotter ("who controls outcomes?"). Facets & perspective Match the facet owners: locus of control, sensation seeking, learned helplessness, flow. Julian Rotter, Zuckerman, Martin Seligman, Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi. Seligman's pessimistic explanatory style for bad events? Internal, stable, global. What settles the person–situation debate, and roughly how heritable are traits? Interactionism; ~40–60% (Bouchard's Minnesota twins). Supplements (object relations, existential, type, Indian) Match: good-enough mother, separation-individuation, mirroring/self, borderline organisation/TFP, positions. Donald Winnicott, Margaret Mahler, Heinz Kohut, Otto Kernberg, Melanie Klein. John Bowlby vs Mary Ainsworth, who gave the theory and who the Strange Situation? Bowlby = theory (secure base, internal working model); Ainsworth = Strange Situation + the three styles (Main added disorganised). What did Harry Harlow's monkeys prefer, and what does it prove? The cloth (comfort) over the wire (feeding) mother; attachment is about contact comfort, not food. Viktor Frankl, May, Irvin Yalom, own each by a phrase. Logotherapy/will to meaning; the daimonic/meaning of anxiety; four ultimate concerns (death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness). Triguna's three gunas and the test that measures them? Sattva (balance), Rajas (activity), Tamas (inertia); the Vedic Personality Inventory (VPI). Sheldon vs Ernst Kretschmer? Sheldon = somatotypes (endo/meso/ecto); Kretschmer = body build linked to psychosis type. Recap — self-test. If you can answer these cold, you own the spine, the named layer and the rival-theory discriminations. Re-test the misses, then run "All the MCQ traps" and the A–Z glossary once more the night before. That sequence (recall → trap discrimination → glossary sweep) is the highest-yield last-mile routine for this domain. Companion pages: the compact version is in the general-psych notes (§10) ; the one-line testable list is in the textbook's Rapid Recall ; the personality tests in depth (MMPI/16PF/NEO/projectives, scoring) are on the tests deep-dive . title: Social & General Psychology
text: Social & General Psychology One consolidated revision chapter for the whole domain: the foundational ("general") psychology of perception, attention, memory, learning, emotion, motivation, intelligence, cognition, personality, development, consciousness and stress, and the full social-psychology arc from research methods through social cognition, attribution, the self, attitudes, prejudice, attraction, influence, prosocial behaviour, aggression and groups, closing with the landmark experiments walked through and a fast A–Z glossary. Anchored to Baron & Branscombe's Social Psychology and standard general-psychology texts; every named effect, theorist, date, table, mnemonic and MCQ trap from both source sets is preserved. The dominant question type NIMHANS and MET test is which name goes with which effect , so the lookalike pairs are flagged throughout in trap boxes. Read it like a textbook, then drill the traps and glossary. In this book Psychology as a science: methods & perspectives Sensation & perception Attention Memory Learning Cognition: thinking, language & social cognition Emotion Motivation Intelligence Personality Developmental psychology Consciousness & sleep Stress, coping & health Social perception & attribution The self Attitudes & persuasion Stereotyping, prejudice & discrimination Attraction, relationships & love Social influence: conformity, compliance, obedience Prosocial behaviour (helping) Aggression Groups & individuals Landmark studies, walked through Schools & history of psychology The MCQ traps, collected Fast glossary (A–Z) 1. Psychology as a science: methods & perspectives What the field claims. Social psychology is the scientific study of how the thoughts, feelings and behaviour of individuals are influenced by the actual, imagined or implied presence of others (Gordon Allport's classic definition). The key word is scientific : it settles questions by study, not intuition. The governing insight, repeated throughout, is the power of the situation : ordinary people help, conform, obey and aggress far more because of where they are and who is around than because of fixed traits. That theme, situation over disposition, returns in obedience (Stanley Milgram), bystander apathy (Bibb Latané & John Darley) and attribution (the fundamental attribution error is precisely our failure to see it). The role of theory. A theory is an integrated set of principles that explains and predicts observed events. Good science runs a loop: a theory generates a falsifiable hypothesis ; a study tests it; results refine or refute it. A theory is never "proven", only supported or disconfirmed. The core research methods Method What you do Strength / limit Experimental Manipulate one factor (the independent variable, IV ), hold all else constant, measure the effect on the dependent variable, DV . Use random assignment to conditions. The only method that establishes cause and effect . Limit: artificiality, low external validity if over-controlled. Correlational Measure two or more variables as they naturally occur and see if they covary (correlation coefficient, −1 to +1). Good for real-world variables you cannot ethically manipulate. Limit: correlation ≠ causation (direction problem + third-variable problem). Survey Ask a representative sample questions to describe a population's attitudes/behaviour. Cheap, broad. Limit: sampling bias, wording effects, social-desirability responding. Systematic / naturalistic observation Watch and record behaviour as it occurs without intervening (e.g. counting jaywalkers). High realism. Limit: no control, observer effects, no causal claim. High-yield The IV is the cause you dial (the knob), the DV the effect you read off (the dial). Random assignment is what lets you claim the knob, not pre-existing differences between people, moved the dial; correlational work has no knob, so it cannot tell you which dial drives. A mediator is the mechanism between cause and effect, explaining why (frustration → anger → aggression: anger mediates). A moderator changes the strength or direction of a relationship, telling you when / for whom it holds (heat raises aggression more for provoked people). A meta-analysis statistically combines many studies to estimate the true effect size. Ethics, deception and replication Because the true purpose can change behaviour, social psychology often uses deception (a cover story), permitted only under strict safeguards: informed consent , the right to withdraw, minimising harm, and a thorough debriefing that reveals the true purpose and removes any after-effects. An Institutional Review Board / ethics committee must approve the study first. The field also takes its replication crisis seriously: a finding is trusted only when independent labs replicate it, which is why classics (Stanley Milgram, marshmallow studies) are now discussed alongside their replications and failures. The four perspectives Baron uses Perspective Core claim Cognitive To explain social behaviour, study how people think : notice, store, recall, interpret. The dominant modern lens (schemas, heuristics, attribution live here). Evolutionary Some tendencies (mate choice, helping kin, fear of strangers) were shaped by natural selection for survival/reproduction. Social neuroscience Links social behaviour to brain and biology (fMRI, hormones): amygdala in out-group fear, oxytocin in trust. Cultural / multicultural Many findings hold differently across cultures; must test whether an effect is universal or culture-bound (individualist vs collectivist). High-yield The researcher is also a thinker prone to the very biases the field studies, so methods (random assignment, double-blind procedures, pre-registration, replication) exist partly to fence out the researcher's expectancy bias / experimenter effects. NIMHANS asks methods crisply: name the only method that proves causation (experimental), say why correlation cannot (third-variable + directionality), and distinguish mediator (the why ) from moderator (the when/for whom ); also the purpose of debriefing after deception and what an ethics board protects. Lock: Gordon Allport's definition = "actual, imagined or implied presence of others"; IV = manipulated, DV = measured; a theory is supported or disconfirmed, never proven; four perspectives = cognitive · evolutionary · social neuroscience · cultural. 2. Sensation & perception Sensation is detecting raw stimulus energy at the receptors; perception is the brain organising and interpreting it. Transduction converts stimulus energy into neural signals. Psychophysics (thresholds) Concept Meaning Absolute threshold Smallest intensity detectable 50% of the time Difference threshold (JND) Smallest detectable change between two stimuli (50% of the time) Weber's law The JND is a constant proportion of the stimulus, not a fixed amount Fechner's law Sensation grows with the logarithm of stimulus intensity Stevens' power law Sensation is a power function of intensity (often fits better than Fechner) Subliminal / priming Stimuli below the absolute threshold can still prime responses Signal detection theory Detection is a decision under uncertainty, not a fixed threshold. Four outcomes: hit , miss , false alarm , correct rejection . d-prime (d′) measures true sensitivity; beta is the response criterion (willingness to say "yes"). Motivation and expectation shift beta, not sensitivity. Theories of perception High-yield The two camps: Gibson's direct / bottom-up theory (the stimulus itself carries enough information; perception is data-driven) versus Gregory's constructivist / top-down theory (perception is an active hypothesis built from prior knowledge and inference). Most modern views combine both. Gestalt organisation, depth & constancy "The whole is greater than the sum of its parts." Gestalt laws: proximity, similarity, closure, continuity (good continuation), common fate, figure-ground, prägnanz (simplicity). Founders: Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Köhler . Binocular depth cues: retinal disparity, convergence. Monocular cues: relative size, interposition, linear perspective, texture gradient, motion parallax, aerial perspective. Perceptual constancies: size, shape, colour, brightness, the object looks stable despite a changing retinal image. Feature integration theory (Anne Treisman): a preattentive stage detects individual features in parallel, then focused attention binds them into a whole object; failed binding produces illusory conjunctions . Pattern recognition & perceptual set Template, prototype and feature-detection theories of recognition; Irving Biederman's recognition-by-components (geons) builds objects from basic 3D primitives. Perceptual set / expectancy: context, motivation, culture and prior knowledge bias what we perceive (top-down). Illusions: Müller-Lyer, Ponzo, Ames room, moon illusion, Kanizsa triangle (illusory contours), the McGurk effect (vision alters what we hear). Illusions reveal the brain's interpretive shortcuts. 3. Attention Attention is the selective allocation of limited processing capacity. The big debate: where in the stream does selection happen (early vs late), and how much capacity is there (bottleneck vs flexible resources)? Bottleneck / filter models (where does selection happen?) Model Claim Donald Broadbent (1958, early selection) A single filter blocks unattended input early , by physical features (pitch, location), before meaning. Based on Colin Cherry's dichotic-listening / shadowing work. Anne Treisman (1964, attenuation) The filter attenuates (turns down) rather than fully blocks; high-priority words with low thresholds (your name, "fire") still break through. Deutsch & Deutsch / Norman (late selection) All input is fully processed for meaning; selection happens late , at the response/awareness stage. Johnston & Heinz (multimode) Selection is flexible, early or late depending on task demands, but later selection costs more capacity. Capacity / resource models (how much is there?) Model Claim Daniel Kahneman (1973, single capacity) One limited pool of effort allocated across tasks; arousal changes the pool size; an allocation policy decides where it goes. Wickens (multiple resources) Several separate pools (visual vs auditory, verbal vs spatial); two tasks interfere most when they draw on the same pool (why you can drive and listen but not read and listen). Norman & Bobrow Data-limited (poor stimulus quality) vs resource-limited (available attention) performance. Lavie (perceptual load theory) High load → early selection (no spare capacity, distractors filtered); low load → spare capacity spills onto distractors (late). Reconciles the early/late debate. Spatial / visual attention & control Spotlight model (Michael Posner): attention is a movable spotlight enhancing processing wherever it points. Zoom-lens (Eriksen): it widens or narrows, trading area for resolution. Posner cueing paradigm: a valid cue speeds detection, an invalid one slows it. Endogenous (voluntary, goal-driven, central cue) vs exogenous (reflexive, stimulus-driven, peripheral cue) orienting; phases: disengage → move → engage. Feature integration theory (Anne Treisman): preattentive parallel feature registration, then focused attention binds features; feature search ("pop-out") is parallel and fast, conjunction search is serial; failed binding = illusory conjunctions. Guided search (Wolfe) refines FIT: top-down knowledge guides attention to likely targets. Automatic vs controlled (Schneider & Richard Shiffrin): automatic is fast, parallel, effortless, hard to suppress (Stroop happens because reading is automatic); controlled is slow, serial, effortful, flexible; practice automatises a skill. Supervisory Attentional System (Norman & Shallice): routine action runs on automatic schemas via contention scheduling; the SAS (frontal) intervenes only for novel/risky situations; failures → action slips / capture errors. Types: selective (one source), divided (across tasks), sustained (vigilance), alternating/switching (toggle, with a switch cost). Key phenomena Cocktail-party effect (Cherry): follow one voice yet still detect your own name in an ignored stream. Stroop effect: naming the ink colour of a colour-word is slowed because reading is automatic. Inattentional blindness (Simons & Chabris invisible-gorilla) and change blindness : without attention, even large changes go unnoticed. Attentional blink: in rapid serial visual presentation a second target is missed ~200–500 ms after the first. Vigilance decrement (Mackworth's clock test): sustained-attention performance declines over time, faster when signals are rare. Psychological refractory period: a second response is delayed when two stimuli arrive close together (evidence for a central bottleneck). Spatial neglect: right-parietal damage leaves patients ignoring the left side of space (a clinical breakdown of spatial attention). Trap The cocktail-party effect (hearing your name in an unattended conversation) supports late /attenuation selection, NOT Broadbent's early filter, the most common attention MCQ. Broadbent = early/physical; Anne Treisman = attenuation; Deutsch-Norman = late/meaning; Lavie = depends on load. Feature search pops out (parallel); conjunction search is serial. 4. Memory Multi-store model (Atkinson-Shiffrin) Sensory memory → short-term/working memory → long-term memory, with attention and rehearsal as the gates. Store Capacity / duration Sensory: iconic (visual) Large; ~0.25–1 s (George Sperling's partial-report) Sensory: echoic (auditory) ~2–4 s Short-term memory 7 ± 2 items (Miller), ~15–30 s; chunking expands it Long-term memory Effectively unlimited, durable Working memory (Baddeley & Hitch) Four parts: central executive (control), phonological loop (verbal/acoustic), visuospatial sketchpad (visual/spatial), and the episodic buffer (added 2000, integrates information across systems). Types of long-term memory Explicit / declarative (conscious): episodic (events) and semantic (facts, meanings). Implicit / non-declarative (unconscious): procedural (skills), priming, classical conditioning. Processes, forgetting & distortion Encoding → storage → retrieval. Levels of processing (Fergus Craik & Robert Lockhart): deep semantic encoding beats shallow. Forgetting: decay; interference (proactive = old disrupts new; retroactive = new disrupts old); cue-dependent / retrieval failure; encoding failure. Ebbinghaus forgetting curve: rapid early loss then levelling; spacing and overlearning slow it. Serial position effect: primacy (LTM) + recency (STM); a delay wipes recency, not primacy. Reconstructive memory: Frederic Bartlett (schemas distort recall, "War of the Ghosts"); Elizabeth Loftus (misinformation effect, leading questions reshape memory). Amnesia: anterograde (cannot form new memories, e.g. H.M.) vs retrograde (cannot recall old). Korsakoff = thiamine deficiency + confabulation. Retrieval, cues & enhancement Encoding specificity (Endel Tulving): retrieval is best when recall cues match encoding cues. Context-dependent (same place) and state-dependent (same mood/physiological state) memory; mood-congruent recall. Recall vs recognition vs relearning (savings) as measures of retention; recognition is usually easier than recall. Flashbulb memories: vivid, confident memories of shocking events, felt accurate but still prone to distortion. Tip-of-the-tongue = retrieval failure with partial access. Spacing and testing effects: spaced practice and active retrieval beat massed re-reading. Consolidation: the hippocampus binds new memories; sleep aids consolidation; reconsolidation makes reactivated memories briefly editable. 5. Learning Classical conditioning (Pavlov) A neutral stimulus paired with an unconditioned stimulus (UCS) becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS) eliciting a conditioned response (CR). Phases: acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation, discrimination, higher-order conditioning. Watson's Little Albert = conditioned fear. Garcia effect = taste aversion learned in one trial over a long delay (biological preparedness). Operant conditioning (Thorndike, Skinner) Thorndike's law of effect : responses followed by satisfaction are stamped in. B. F. Skinner formalised it. Add (positive) Remove (negative) Increase behaviour (reinforcement) Positive reinforcement (give a reward) Negative reinforcement (remove an aversive) Decrease behaviour (punishment) Positive punishment (add an aversive) Negative punishment (remove a reward) High-yield Schedules of reinforcement: Fixed Ratio, Variable Ratio, Fixed Interval, Variable Interval. Variable Ratio gives the highest, steadiest rate and the most resistance to extinction (gambling). Ratio beats interval; variable beats fixed. Shaping = reinforcing successive approximations. Premack principle = a high-frequency behaviour reinforces a low-frequency one ("eat your vegetables, then dessert"). Cognitive & observational learning Edward Tolman: latent learning + cognitive maps (rats learned the maze without reinforcement). Wolfgang Köhler: insight learning (chimps solved problems suddenly, the "aha"). Albert Bandura: observational learning / modelling (Bobo doll); steps = attention, retention, reproduction, motivation. Martin Seligman: learned helplessness; biological constraints (preparedness) limit what can be conditioned. High-yield Rescorla-Wagner model: conditioning depends on surprise / prediction error , not mere pairing; the CS must reliably predict the UCS. Explains blocking (a new cue learns nothing if an existing cue already predicts the UCS) and the contingency (not just contiguity) requirement, Robert Rescorla showed the CS must signal information. More terms: stimulus generalisation vs discrimination ; spontaneous recovery of an extinguished CR; overshadowing (a salient cue overshadows a weak one); latent inhibition (a pre-exposed stimulus is harder to condition). Operant: escape vs avoidance learning, discriminative stimulus (signals when a response pays off), extinction burst , and the partial-reinforcement extinction effect (intermittently reinforced behaviour resists extinction). 6. Cognition: thinking, language & social cognition Thinking, problem-solving & decision making Concepts & categories: classical (defining features) vs prototype vs exemplar theories; we categorise by comparison to a best example (prototype); basic-level categories (Eleanor Rosch). Problem solving: algorithms (guaranteed, slow) vs heuristics (fast rules of thumb); strategies = means-end analysis, working backward, analogy; insight vs incremental search; incubation. Barriers: fixation, mental set, functional fixedness. Decision making: System 1 (fast, intuitive) vs System 2 (slow, deliberate). Reasoning: deductive (general → specific, logically certain) vs inductive (specific → general, probabilistic); confirmation bias and belief bias distort it. Mental imagery: Shepard & Metzler's mental rotation, imagery is analog and spatial. Metacognition: thinking about and monitoring one's own thinking. Language Structure: phonemes → morphemes → syntax → semantics → pragmatics. Stages: cooing, babbling, one-word (~12 mo), telegraphic (~24 mo). Noam Chomsky: language acquisition device + universal grammar (nativist). B. F. Skinner: language learned by reinforcement (behaviourist), demolished by Chomsky's review. Benjamin Lee Whorf: linguistic relativity (language shapes thought). Critical/sensitive period (Eric Lenneberg); the case of Genie. Social cognition: how we think about the social world The problem. The social world throws more information at us than we can fully process, so the mind takes shortcuts. We are "cognitive misers" , spending mental effort sparingly, defaulting to fast, cheap strategies that are usually good enough but sometimes badly wrong. Underlying everything is the dual-process view (System 1 vs System 2): automatic processing is fast, effortless, unconscious, emotional; controlled processing is slow, effortful, deliberate, logical. This same automatic/controlled split reappears in persuasion (peripheral vs central route) and prejudice (implicit vs explicit attitudes). Heuristics and the schemas they run on Term Who What it is Heuristics (availability, representativeness, anchoring & adjustment) Tversky & Daniel Kahneman Mental shortcuts: judge by ease of recall (availability) / resemblance to a prototype (representativeness) / clinging to a first value then adjusting too little (anchoring). Schema Frederic Bartlett (social use: Fiske & Taylor) Mental framework guiding what we notice, encode and recall about people/situations. Priming — A recently activated schema shapes the next interpretation, even unconsciously. High-yield Availability: you fear plane crashes more than car crashes because crashes make the news and spring to mind easily. Representativeness: told someone is quiet and loves poetry you guess "librarian" over "salesperson" because they fit the prototype, ignoring that salespeople vastly outnumber librarians (base-rate neglect). Anchoring: the first value you hear drags your estimate toward it. A schema is the bigger structure these run on; priming switches a schema on so it colours what comes next. Schemas bias three things, attention , encoding (usually schema-consistent info, though wildly inconsistent info also grabs attention) and retrieval , and they show the perseverance effect (beliefs survive even after the evidence that created them is discredited; first impressions are sticky). The biases of social thought Term Who What it is Self-fulfilling prophecy Robert Merton An expectation makes itself come true by changing behaviour (basis of the Pygmalion / Rosenthal effect). Counterfactual thinking Kahneman & Amos Tversky Imagining "what might have been"; near-misses sting most (the bronze medallist is happier than the silver). Optimistic / unrealistic-optimism bias Neil Weinstein We think bad things are less likely to happen to us than to others. Negativity bias — Negative info weighs more heavily than equally strong positive info. Planning fallacy Kahneman & Tversky We chronically underestimate how long our own tasks will take. Magical thinking — Assumptions defying causality (laws of contagion / similarity; won't eat fudge shaped like dog faeces). Thought suppression & rebound effect Daniel Wegner Trying not to think of something (the "white bear") makes it intrude more; the monitoring process keeps it primed. Overconfidence barrier — More confidence in our judgements than their accuracy warrants. Base-rate fallacy Kahneman & Tversky Ignoring underlying category frequency for vivid case information (engine behind representativeness errors). Conjunction fallacy ("Linda" problem) Tversky & Kahneman Judging a conjunction ("feminist bank teller") as likelier than its component ("bank teller"), logically impossible. False consensus effect Ross et al. Overestimating how many others share our opinions, traits and choices. False uniqueness effect — Underestimating how common our desirable abilities are. Hindsight bias Baruch Fischhoff "I knew it all along", once an outcome is known we see it as inevitable. Framing effect Tversky & Kahneman The same option chosen/rejected by gain ("90% survive") vs loss ("10% die") wording. Confirmation bias — Seeking and weighting belief-consistent evidence, ignoring disconfirming evidence (keeps schemas alive). Illusion of control Ellen Langer Overestimating personal control over chance outcomes (blowing on dice, picking lottery numbers). Gambler's fallacy / hot-hand — Misreading independent random events as due to "even out" or as streaky. Bias blind spot Emily Pronin Seeing bias in others far more readily than in oneself. Sunk-cost fallacy / loss aversion / prospect theory Kahneman & Tversky Honouring past investment; losses loom larger than equivalent gains; choices framed around a reference point. Affect and cognition cut both ways. Mood shapes thought (positive mood broadens thinking, increases heuristic use; we recall mood-congruent material) and thought shapes mood (appraisal of an event determines how you feel). A good mood makes you a lazier, more shortcut-prone thinker. Trap Two near-twins: availability = judged by how easily examples come to mind (recent, vivid, emotional); representativeness = judged by how well it matches a prototype (neglects base rates). "Easy to recall / vivid" → availability; "fits the stereotype/category" → representativeness. All the heuristics-and-biases items trace to Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman. High-yield NIMHANS / clinical map. Wegner's rebound effect is the model behind why "just stop thinking about it" fails in OCD, PTSD intrusions and insomnia, and why acceptance-based therapies (ACT, mindfulness) outperform suppression; pair it with the perseverance effect, which explains why a discredited self-belief ("I'm a failure") persists in depression. Negativity bias + counterfactual thinking underlie depressive rumination ("if only I had…"); depressive realism / pessimistic explanatory style is the opposite of optimistic bias; magical thinking is a named symptom in OCD and schizotypal personality. Cognitive therapy is essentially retraining these automatic biases. 7. Emotion Theory Sequence James-Lange Stimulus → body arousal → you label the emotion ("I tremble, therefore I am afraid") Cannon-Bard Stimulus → arousal AND emotion at the same time (thalamus routes both) Schachter-Singer (two-factor) Arousal + a cognitive label = emotion; same arousal, different label, different emotion Lazarus (appraisal) Cognitive appraisal comes first, then emotion Robert Zajonc Some emotional reactions occur before/without cognition ("preferences need no inferences") Facial-feedback hypothesis (Tomkins; Paul Ekman) Facial expressions feed back and intensify/trigger the felt emotion Ekman: six basic universal emotions (happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, disgust). Components of emotion: physiological arousal, expressive behaviour, conscious experience. Yerkes-Dodson law: performance peaks at moderate arousal (inverted U); harder tasks peak at lower arousal. Robert Plutchik's wheel: eight primary emotions in opposing pairs blending into secondary emotions (joy + trust = love). Dimensional models: Russell's circumplex maps emotion on valence (pleasant–unpleasant) × arousal (high–low). Joseph LeDoux's two roads to fear: a fast "low road" (thalamus → amygdala) for quick reaction, a slow "high road" (via cortex) for accurate appraisal. Cognitive appraisal (Lazarus): primary appraisal (is it relevant/threatening?) then secondary (can I cope?). Display rules: culturally learned norms for when/how to show emotion; basic expressions universal, display rules vary. Emotional intelligence (Peter Salovey & John Mayer; popularised by Daniel Goleman): perceiving, using, understanding, regulating emotion. Trap James-Lange = body first; Cannon-Bard = simultaneous; Schachter-Singer = body + label. This ordering is the single most common emotion-theory exam item. 8. Motivation Instinct theory: behaviour driven by innate biological programs. Drive-reduction (Clark Hull): a need creates a drive; behaviour reduces it to restore homeostasis. Arousal theory: we seek an optimal level of arousal (links to Yerkes-Dodson). Incentive theory: external rewards pull behaviour. Abraham Maslow's hierarchy: physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualisation (later: cognitive, aesthetic, transcendence). Intrinsic vs extrinsic: intrinsic = for its own sake; extrinsic = for a reward. The overjustification effect : paying for an already-enjoyed activity can reduce intrinsic motivation. Self-determination theory (Edward Deci & Richard Ryan): autonomy, competence, relatedness. David McClelland: needs for achievement, affiliation, power (measured via the TAT). ERG theory (Alderfer): Maslow condensed to Existence, Relatedness, Growth; allows frustration-regression. Expectancy theory (Victor Vroom): motivation = expectancy × instrumentality × valence. Goal-setting theory (Locke & Latham): specific, challenging, accepted goals drive performance. Approach-avoidance conflict (Kurt Lewin): approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance, approach-avoidance conflicts. Specific drives: hunger (lateral hypothalamus starts eating, ventromedial stops it; set-point/leptin); arousal/sensation-seeking; achievement motivation (need for achievement vs fear of failure). 9. Intelligence Theorist Model Spearman (1904) Two-factor: general intelligence g + specific s ; invented factor analysis Thurstone (1938) 7 Primary Mental Abilities (no single g) Cattell & Horn Fluid intelligence (Gf, reasoning) vs crystallised (Gc, learned knowledge) J. P. Guilford Structure of Intellect (up to 180 cells); convergent vs divergent thinking Howard Gardner (1983) Multiple intelligences (8): linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalist Robert Sternberg Triarchic: analytical, creative, practical (successful intelligence) Vernon / Carroll (CHC) Hierarchical three-stratum (g → broad → narrow); the dominant modern model Tests: Wechsler (WAIS/WISC, deviation IQ, SD 15), Stanford-Binet (SD 16, SB-5 uses 15), Raven's Progressive Matrices (culture-reduced g). Ratio IQ = (mental age / chronological age) × 100. Flynn effect = rising IQ scores across generations. Heritability estimates are population statistics, not individual destiny. Francis Galton (first to study individual differences, hereditary genius), Binet & Simon (first practical test, mental age), Lewis Terman (Stanford-Binet, longitudinal study of gifted "Termites"). Emotional intelligence (Goleman) broadens the construct beyond academic g. Extremes: intellectual disability (DSM bands; adaptive functioning matters, not just IQ), giftedness, savant syndrome . Heritability & environment: twin/adoption studies; the Flynn effect and stereotype-threat findings show environment matters; reliability/validity and cultural bias are key test-construction concerns. 10.
