Personality Psychodynamic (Freud) Structure: id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle), superego (morality/conscience). Topographic: conscious, preconscious, unconscious (the iceberg). Psychosexual stages: oral → anal → phallic (Oedipus/Electra) → latency → genital; fixation shapes the adult personality. Defence mechanisms: repression, denial, projection, displacement, reaction formation, rationalisation, sublimation, regression (Anna Freud catalogued these). Neo-Freudians Carl Jung: collective unconscious, archetypes, introversion/extraversion. Alfred Adler: inferiority complex, striving for superiority, birth order. Karen Horney: basic anxiety, womb envy (countered Sigmund Freud). Erik Erikson: psychosocial stages (see Development). Trait theories Theorist Model Gordon Allport Cardinal, central, secondary traits Raymond Cattell 16 Personality Factors (16PF), via factor analysis Hans Eysenck Three dimensions: extraversion, neuroticism, psychoticism (PEN) Costa & Robert McCrae Big Five / OCEAN: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism Humanistic & social-cognitive Carl Rogers: self-concept, congruence (real vs ideal self), unconditional positive regard, the fully functioning person. Abraham Maslow: self-actualisation (see Motivation). Albert Bandura: reciprocal determinism (behaviour ↔ person ↔ environment), self-efficacy. Julian Rotter: locus of control (internal vs external). High-yield Assessment: projective tests (Rorschach inkblots, TAT) tap the unconscious; objective inventories (MMPI, 16PF, NEO-PI) are self-report and standardised. 11. Developmental psychology Theorist Stages / idea Jean Piaget (cognitive) Sensorimotor (0–2, object permanence) → preoperational (2–7, egocentrism, no conservation) → concrete operational (7–11, conservation) → formal operational (11+, abstract). Schemas, assimilation, accommodation. Erik Erikson (psychosocial) 8 crisis stages: trust v mistrust → autonomy v shame → initiative v guilt → industry v inferiority → identity v role confusion → intimacy v isolation → generativity v stagnation → integrity v despair. Lawrence Kohlberg (moral) Preconventional (punishment/reward) → conventional (social approval, law and order) → postconventional (social contract, universal ethics). Lev Vygotsky (sociocultural) Zone of proximal development, scaffolding, the social origin of thought (more-knowledgeable other). Sigmund Freud (psychosexual) See Personality. Attachment (John Bowlby; Ainsworth's Strange Situation): secure, insecure-avoidant, insecure-resistant/ambivalent, and disorganised (Main & Solomon). Harry Harlow = contact comfort. Temperament (Alexander Thomas & Stella Chess): easy, difficult, slow-to-warm-up. Nature vs nurture & epigenetics; maturation vs learning; continuous vs stage (discontinuous) views; critical vs sensitive periods. Theory of mind (false-belief / Sally-Anne task, ~4 yrs); Vygotsky vs Piaget on private speech and the social origin of thought. Parenting styles (Diana Baumrind): authoritative, authoritarian, permissive, neglectful. Lifespan: Paul Baltes' lifespan perspective; Kübler-Ross stages of grief; emerging adulthood (Arnett); fluid decline vs crystallised stability in ageing. Moral development: Carol Gilligan's ethic-of-care critique of Kohlberg; Piaget's heteronomous → autonomous morality. Trap Conservation (quantity stays the same despite shape change) appears in concrete operational , not preoperational. Object permanence is the sensorimotor milestone. 12. Consciousness & sleep Sleep stages: NREM 1 (theta, hypnagogic) → NREM 2 (sleep spindles, K-complexes) → NREM 3 (delta, deep/slow-wave) → REM (paradoxical: brain active, body paralysed, dreaming); ~90-minute cycles, REM lengthens toward morning. Circadian rhythm: ~24-hour cycle, governed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus; melatonin from the pineal gland. Dream theories: Sigmund Freud (wish fulfilment, manifest vs latent content); activation-synthesis (Hobson & McCarley, brain makes sense of random REM activity); information-processing/consolidation. Sleep disorders: insomnia, narcolepsy, sleep apnoea, night terrors (NREM) vs nightmares (REM), somnambulism. Altered states: hypnosis, meditation, psychoactive drugs (depressants, stimulants, hallucinogens, opioids) altering consciousness via neurotransmitters. Theories of hypnosis: Hilgard's neodissociation ("hidden observer") vs the social-cognitive/role-enactment view. Functions of sleep: restoration, energy conservation, memory consolidation; sleep deprivation effects. Drug concepts: tolerance, dependence, withdrawal, the reward pathway (dopamine, nucleus accumbens). Consciousness debates: the "hard problem"; the cognitive unconscious; global workspace theory. 13. Stress, coping & health Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome: alarm → resistance → exhaustion. Richard Lazarus & Susan Folkman: primary appraisal (is it a threat?) then secondary appraisal (can I cope?). Problem-focused coping (change the stressor) vs emotion-focused coping (manage the feeling). Physiology: the HPA axis and sympathetic "fight-or-flight" (Cannon); cortisol as the chronic-stress hormone. Type A (competitive, hostile, time-urgent) vs Type B; hostility links to heart disease. Buffers: social support, perceived control, optimism, hardiness (Suzanne Kobasa: commitment, control, challenge). Stressors: Holmes & Rahe Social Readjustment Rating Scale (life-change units); daily hassles vs uplifts (Lazarus); acute vs chronic stress. Tend-and-befriend (Taylor): an alternative to fight-or-flight, oxytocin-linked, more often described in women. Health: psychoneuroimmunology (stress suppresses immunity); the biopsychosocial model; learned optimism (Martin Seligman). 14. Social perception & attribution The problem. To navigate other people we must answer two questions: what are they feeling now (read from nonverbal cues) and why did they do that (attribution). Social perception is how we form impressions and infer causes from limited information. Nonverbal communication Before a word is spoken we read nonverbal channels : facial expressions (Paul Ekman's six basic emotions are largely universal), eye contact (gaze), body language and posture, touch , and paralanguage (tone, pace, pauses). These leak information the person may not mean to send, which is why we often trust the nonverbal over the verbal. Baron's cues to deception : microexpressions (fleeting true feelings flashing before they are masked), interchannel discrepancies (the face says one thing, the hands or voice another), and changes in eye contact and linguistic style. Despite all this, people detect lies barely above chance, because liars control the easy channels and we over-trust the face. Nonverbal "leakage" (Ekman & Friesen): true feelings escape through the channels we control least (legs, feet, voice pitch) while we manage the face. Attribution: explaining behaviour Theory / term Who What it is Attribution theory Fritz Heider We explain behaviour as internal (disposition) or external (situation); the person as "naïve psychologist." Correspondent inference theory Jones & Davis We infer a trait from acts that are freely chosen, unexpected and low in social desirability. Covariation model Harold Kelley Attribution uses consensus, consistency & distinctiveness; high all three → situation/stimulus; low consensus + low distinctiveness + high consistency → the person. Plus the discounting principle (downweight a cause if other plausible causes are present) and the augmenting principle (upweight a cause that produced an act despite obstacles). High-yield Walk Kelley's three Cs. Your friend laughs at a comedian. Consensus: does everyone laugh? Distinctiveness: does she laugh only at this comedian? Consistency: does she laugh every time? High on all three → it's the comedian (external); low consensus + low distinctiveness + high consistency → it's her (internal). Fritz Heider gave the basic internal/external split; Edward E. Jones & Keith Davis asked when an act reveals a true trait; Kelley added the data-driven rule. The two-step attribution model (Gilbert): we first automatically make a dispositional inference, then effortfully correct for the situation, and the correction fails when we are busy or tired, which is why the FAE is so robust. The attributional biases Term Who What it is Fundamental attribution error (correspondence bias) coined by Lee Ross Over-blaming others' character, under-weighting their situation. Actor–observer effect Jones & Richard Nisbett My acts = situation; your acts = your character. Self-serving bias — My success = me; my failure = bad luck/situation. (Better-than-average effect: most rate themselves above average, a statistical impossibility en masse.) Just-world hypothesis Melvin Lerner Belief that people get what they deserve → blaming the victim. Defensive attribution — Blaming a victim more as consequences worsen and as we resemble the victim less, to feel safe ("it couldn't happen to me"). Ultimate attribution error Thomas Pettigrew The FAE applied to groups : an out-group member's bad act is blamed on disposition, their good act explained away as luck/exception. The cognitive cement of prejudice. Facial-feedback hypothesis Tomkins; Paul Ekman Your facial expression feeds back to intensify/trigger the felt emotion. Thin slices Ambady & Robert Rosenthal Surprisingly accurate judgements from very brief (seconds) exposure to behaviour. Impression formation & management Solomon Asch showed first impressions form fast and that some traits are central (swapping "warm" for "cold" transforms the whole impression, while "polite/blunt" barely moves it). The primacy effect means early information weighs most. Baron contrasts Asch's configural / gestalt view (traits fuse into a whole) with Norman Anderson's information-integration / averaging model (we mentally average the weighted values of each trait). We also lean on an implicit personality theory (a lay assumption about which traits go together, "warm people are also generous"), which is how one central trait drags the rest, and on the halo effect (Edward Thorndike: one global positive impression bleeds into ratings of unrelated traits). On the flip side, impression management (self-presentation) is our effort to control the impression others form of us, a theme Erving Goffman framed dramaturgically (life as theatre, front-stage vs back-stage); tactics include self-promotion (look competent), ingratiation (flattery, agreement) and self-deprecation . Trap The attribution swap: FAE (Ross) = judging others (blame the person, ignore their situation); actor–observer (Edward E. Jones & Richard Nisbett) = the gap between explaining your own acts (situation) vs others' acts (character); self-serving = explaining your own outcomes (credit success, dodge blame for failure). Read whose behaviour and whose outcome the stem is about. Separately, Solomon Asch (configural, central traits reorganise the whole) vs Anderson (averaging the weighted trait values). High-yield NIMHANS / clinical map. Depression's negative (pessimistic) attributional style (internal, stable, global for failures) is the mirror image of the self-serving bias, which depressed people lose . The just-world belief explains victim-blaming in trauma work. The FAE is exactly why we pathologise individuals while underrating their situations, the bias clinical formulation tries to correct. Attribution models in order: Fritz Heider (naïve psychologist, internal/external) → Edward E. Jones & Keith Davis (correspondent inference) → Harold Kelley (covariation three Cs). 15. The self The problem. The self is both the thinker and the thing thought about. How do we build a self-concept (content, "who am I"), set our self-esteem (evaluation, "how do I feel about who I am"), and protect that esteem? The recurring finding is that the self is fundamentally social : we know ourselves largely by comparison to, and reflection in, others. Building the self-concept (content side) Term Who What it is Looking-glass self Charles Cooley We build the self-concept from how we imagine we appear to others; the self as a social reflection. The "I" and the "me" William James / G.H. Mead The self as both knower/actor ("I") and object known/evaluated ("me"). Self-reference effect Rogers et al. Information processed in relation to the self is remembered better; the self is a powerful memory organiser. Self-schema Hazel Markus Cognitive generalisations about the self that organise and guide processing of self-relevant information. Possible selves Markus & Nurius Images of what we might become (hoped-for, feared, expected) that motivate and guide behaviour. Self-complexity Patricia Linville Many distinct self-aspects buffer mood swings; a simple self lets one bad domain flood the whole self. Self-concept clarity Jennifer Campbell How clearly, confidently and consistently self-beliefs are defined; low clarity links to low self-esteem. Sociometer theory Mark Leary Self-esteem is an internal gauge of social acceptance/belonging; it drops when we feel rejected. Objective self-awareness theory Duval & Wicklund Focusing attention on the self (a mirror, a camera) makes us compare to standards and feel the gap. Self-regulation & ego depletion Roy Baumeister Self-control draws on a limited resource that fatigues with use (the "strength model"; note replication debate). Measuring and protecting the self Theory / term Who What it is Social comparison theory Leon Festinger We evaluate ourselves by comparison to others (upward = motivating but deflating; downward = self-enhancing). Self-perception theory Daryl Bem When attitudes are weak/ambiguous, we infer them by observing our own behaviour ("I'm eating salad, I guess I like salad"). Self-discrepancy theory E. Tory Higgins Actual vs ideal self → dejection (sadness); actual vs ought self → agitation (anxiety, guilt). Self-monitoring Mark Snyder High self-monitors tailor behaviour to the situation; low ones act from inner attitudes. Self-efficacy Albert Bandura Belief in your capacity to carry out the actions a specific task needs. Self-handicapping Berglas & Jones Setting up an excuse in advance (not studying, drinking before a test) to protect self-esteem from possible failure. Self-verification William Swann We seek feedback confirming our existing self-view, even when negative. Self-affirmation theory Claude Steele Affirming a valued part of the self (in another domain) buffers threats to self-integrity. Spotlight effect Thomas Gilovich Overestimating how much others notice and judge us (the stain on your shirt). BIRGing / CORFing Robert Cialdini Basking in reflected glory ("we won") vs cutting off reflected failure (distancing from losers). Terror management theory Greenberg, Pyszczynski & Solomon Awareness of mortality drives us to defend our cultural worldview and bolster self-esteem. The self across cultures (high-yield NIMHANS contrast) Hazel Markus & Shinobu Kitayama drew the field's biggest cultural distinction: the independent self-construal (individualist/Western, the self defined by internal traits, separate, self-promoting) versus the interdependent self-construal (collectivist cultures including India, the self defined by relationships, roles and group harmony). This explains cultural differences in the FAE (weaker in collectivist cultures), self-serving bias, self-enhancement (lower in East Asian samples) and conformity. India is the textbook collectivist/interdependent case. Trap Two self-discrepancy directions (Higgins): falling short of your ideal self (hopes, what you want to be) → dejection (sad). Falling short of your ought self (duties, what you should be) → agitation (anxious). Ideal→sad, ought→anxious. And dissonance vs self-perception: Festinger involves arousal and a strong prior attitude; Bem (this section) involves no arousal, just calm inference from a weak attitude. High-yield NIMHANS / clinical map. Self-efficacy (Bandura) and self-esteem are workhorses of CBT. Self-discrepancy theory (Higgins) models depression (ideal-self gap) vs anxiety (ought-self gap). Self-verification (Swann) explains why people with low self-esteem resist positive feedback and stay in confirming (even abusive) relationships, a real treatment obstacle. Terror management connects to existential anxiety. Most of these terms are esteem-protecting manoeuvres rather than neutral descriptions; the cooler cognitive exceptions are social comparison (Festinger) and self-perception (Bem). 16. Attitudes & persuasion The problem. An attitude is an evaluation of an object along a like–dislike dimension. The classic ABC structure has three components: A ffective (feelings), B ehavioural (action tendencies), C ognitive (beliefs). The two big questions: do attitudes predict behaviour? and how do you change them? Where attitudes come from, and the implicit/explicit split Attitudes form mostly via low-level learning: classical conditioning (an object paired with positive/negative stimuli, including subliminal conditioning and mere exposure ), instrumental conditioning (attitudes earning approval are reinforced), and observational learning / social comparison (adopting the attitudes of models and reference groups). Twin studies show a partly heritable component. Term What it is Explicit attitudes Conscious, reportable, controllable evaluations. Implicit attitudes Automatic, often unconscious evaluations, measured by the Implicit Association Test (IAT) via reaction times; can diverge from what we say, and predict spontaneous behaviour. Functions of attitudes (Daniel Katz): knowledge (organise the world), utilitarian/instrumental (gain reward, avoid punishment), ego-defensive (protect self-esteem), and value-expressive (state who we are). Changing an attitude requires addressing its function (the same surface attitude may be ego-defensive in one person and value-expressive in another). The attitude–behaviour link For decades the embarrassing answer was "barely". The famous demonstration is the LaPiere study : a researcher toured 1930s America with a Chinese couple and was served almost everywhere, yet most of those same establishments later said by mail they would refuse Chinese guests. The resolution came from Martin Fishbein & Icek Ajzen : attitudes predict behaviour best through intentions , shaped by attitudes plus subjective norms plus (in the planned-behaviour update) perceived behavioural control. Attitudes also predict better when strong, specific, accessible and based on direct experience. Persuasion: how attitudes change Theory / term Who What it is Yale attitude-change approach Carl Hovland Who says what to whom: source (credibility, attractiveness), message and audience factors. Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) Petty & John Cacioppo Persuasion via the central route (thoughtful scrutiny of arguments, when motivated & able) vs the peripheral route (surface cues: attractiveness, length, expert badge). Heuristic-Systematic Model (HSM) Shelly Chaiken Same dual-route idea: systematic (effortful argument analysis) vs heuristic ("experts are right"). Theory of reasoned action / planned behaviour Fishbein & Icek Ajzen Intention (from attitudes + subjective norms + perceived behavioural control) predicts behaviour. Inoculation theory William McGuire A weak counter-argument first "vaccinates" an attitude against later strong attacks. Psychological reactance Jack Brehm Threaten a freedom → people want the forbidden thing more (boomerang effect). Sleeper effect Carl Hovland A low-credibility message has little impact at first but gains force over time as the source is forgotten but the content remembered. Fear appeals — Fear persuades best at moderate levels and only with a clear, doable way to avoid the threat; too much fear triggers denial. Forewarning — Warning people that a persuasion attempt is coming lets them marshal counter-arguments and resist. Need for cognition Cacioppo & Petty A trait, the enjoyment of effortful thinking; high-NFC people are persuaded via the central route, low-NFC via the peripheral. Mere-thought / attitude polarisation Abraham Tesser Merely thinking about an attitude object, without new information, makes the attitude more extreme. Bogus pipeline Jones & Sigall A fake lie-detector that makes people report their true (often less socially desirable) attitudes; a methods trick for measuring real prejudice. LaPiere study Richard LaPiere The classic attitude–behaviour gap: stated prejudice did not match actual service to a Chinese couple. High-yield The dual route, intuitively. When you care and can concentrate (buying a house) you take the central route, weighing real arguments, and the attitude is durable. When you do not care or are distracted (a soft-drink jingle) you take the peripheral route, swayed by who is pretty or how many points were listed, and the attitude is flimsy. ELM (Richard Petty & John Cacioppo) and HSM (Chaiken) are the same insight: central = systematic, peripheral = heuristic, the automatic/controlled split applied to persuasion. Katz's four functions and the sleeper effect are clean single-best-answer items; fear appeals (moderate + efficacy) underpin health-communication design. Cognitive dissonance & consistency theories The most-tested idea in the chapter. When two cognitions clash, or behaviour contradicts an attitude, we feel an unpleasant tension ( dissonance ) and are driven to reduce it, usually by changing the attitude to fit the behaviour . Theory / term Who What it is Cognitive dissonance Leon Festinger Tension from clashing cognitions drives attitude change to reduce it. Insufficient justification / induced compliance Festinger & Carlsmith The $1 group changed their attitude more than the $20 group (less external reward = more dissonance = more internal attitude change). Effort justification Aronson & Mills The harder/more embarrassing the initiation, the more we value the group we joined. Balance theory Fritz Heider We seek consistency among liking relationships (P-O-X triangles; an imbalanced triangle pressures change). Hypocrisy paradigm Aronson et al. Make people publicly advocate a behaviour (e.g. condom use), then remind them of past failures to do it → dissonance drives real behaviour change. Free-choice dissonance Jack Brehm After a hard choice between close options, we boost the chosen and derogate the rejected option ("spreading of alternatives"). High-yield Why $1 beat $20. Participants did a boring task then were paid to tell the next person it was fun. Those paid $20 had a big external reason to lie ("I did it for the money"), so no dissonance, attitude unchanged. Those paid $1 had no good external reason, so the only way to resolve "I said it was fun but I had no reason to lie" was to decide it actually was fun. Less reward, more attitude change. Same logic in effort justification. NIMHANS / clinical: effort justification is one reason expensive/effortful therapy can be valued more (and underlies hazing/cult commitment); reactance (Brehm) explains why heavy-handed advice backfires and is the rationale for motivational interviewing; dissonance is harnessed in attitude-change health interventions. Trap Dissonance vs self-perception: both predict attitude follows behaviour. Leon Festinger (dissonance) = there is arousal/discomfort , applies when the attitude was strong/clear and the behaviour contradicts it. Bem (self-perception) = no arousal , you simply infer the attitude by watching yourself, applies when the attitude was weak or unclear . The deciding clue is whether the stem mentions tension/discomfort (Festinger) or a calm inference (Bem). 17. Stereotyping, prejudice & discrimination The three words kept straight. A stereotype is the cognitive component (a belief about a group's traits). Prejudice is the affective component (a negative feeling toward a group). Discrimination is the behavioural component (unequal treatment). They are the ABC of intergroup bias. Sources of prejudice Theory / term Who What it is Social identity theory Tajfel & Turner Part of our self-esteem comes from group membership → we favour the in-group and derogate the out-group. Minimal group paradigm Henri Tajfel Even arbitrary, meaningless group splits (coin toss, dot-estimation, Klee vs Kandinsky) produce in-group favouritism. Realistic conflict theory Muzafer Sherif Competition over scarce resources breeds intergroup hostility (Robbers Cave); superordinate (shared) goals reduce it. Authoritarian personality Theodor Adorno A rigid, conventional, submissive-to-authority personality (F-scale) prone to prejudice. Right-wing authoritarianism (RWA) Bob Altemeyer Better-validated successor to Adorno: submission to authority + conventionalism + aggression toward sanctioned targets. Social dominance orientation (SDO) Sidanius & Pratto A preference for group-based hierarchy and inequality; predicts prejudice independently of RWA. System justification theory John Jost People are motivated to defend and rationalise the existing social order, even when it disadvantages their own group. Self-image threat & prejudice Fein & Spencer People derogate out-group members more after their own self-esteem is threatened, and doing so restores it. Scapegoat theory (frustration–aggression roots) Frustration is displaced onto a weaker out-group blamed for problems. Integrated Threat Theory (realistic vs symbolic threat) Stephan & Stephan Prejudice is fed by perceived realistic threats (resources, safety) and symbolic threats (values, worldview), plus intergroup anxiety and negative stereotypes. High-yield Identity vs competition vs personality, three engines. Social identity (Henri Tajfel & John Turner): bias arises just from categorising people into us/them, no real conflict needed (minimal-group studies prove arbitrary groups suffice). Realistic conflict (Muzafer Sherif): bias arises from real competition over resources, and Robbers Cave showed shared goals dissolve it. Authoritarian personality (Adorno): bias sits inside a personality type . NIMHANS loves to swap these three. Indian-context applications (caste, religion, language as in-group/out-group lines) fit social identity and realistic conflict. The cognitive machinery of stereotypes Term Who What it is Illusory correlation Hamilton & Gifford Perceiving a link between minority-group membership and rare (negative) behaviour that is not really there. Out-group homogeneity effect — "They're all alike"; we see less variability in out-groups than in our own group. Stereotype threat Steele & Aronson Fear of confirming a negative stereotype about your group depresses your performance on the stereotyped task. Stereotype content model Susan Fiske Groups judged on warmth × competence → four emotions: admiration (warm+competent), envy (cold+competent), pity (warm+incompetent), contempt (cold+incompetent). Subtyping — Filing stereotype-disconfirming individuals into a special "exception" subtype, protecting the overall stereotype. Shifting standards Monica Biernat Judging members of different groups against different, group-based yardsticks ("good… for a woman"). The modern, subtle forms (and the cost to targets) Term Who What it is Modern / subtle (aversive) racism — People who endorse equality still hold automatic negative reactions and discriminate when they can attribute it to something else; bias is implicit, not openly avowed. Hostile vs benevolent sexism Glick & Fiske Two-part "ambivalent sexism": hostile (women seeking power are a threat) plus benevolent (women are wonderful but fragile and need protection). Benevolent sounds positive but still keeps women subordinate. Tokenism — A trivial positive act toward an out-group member used as an excuse to then discriminate; also the strain on a lone "token". Glass ceiling — An invisible barrier keeping qualified members of devalued groups out of top positions. Reducing prejudice Theory / term Who What it is Contact hypothesis Gordon Allport Contact reduces prejudice only if four conditions hold: equal status, common goals, intergroup cooperation, institutional support. Jigsaw classroom Elliot Aronson Cooperative learning where each pupil holds one essential piece of the lesson → forces interdependence, cuts prejudice. A practical application of the contact hypothesis. Common in-group identity model (recategorisation) Gaertner & Dovidio Get rival groups to recategorise "us vs them" into a single inclusive "we" → former out-group members now get in-group warmth. Trap Stereotype threat vs self-fulfilling prophecy: stereotype threat (Steele & Aronson) = the target's own anxiety about confirming the stereotype hurts their performance; self-fulfilling prophecy (Merton) = the perceiver's expectation changes how they treat the target, eliciting the expected behaviour. One is driven from inside the target, the other from the outside perceiver. Hostile vs benevolent sexism (Glick & Fiske): the "nice"-sounding one (cherish and protect) is benevolent, still subordinating. Note Steele appears twice across the syllabus: stereotype threat here and self-affirmation in §15. 18. Attraction, relationships & love The problem. Why do we like and love some people and not others, and what holds relationships together? The chapter moves from the cold predictors of initial attraction to theories of love and then to the economic models of why relationships last or end. Predictors of initial attraction Theory / term Who What it is Propinquity (proximity) effect Leon Festinger, Schachter & Back The closer people live or sit, the more likely they form friendships (the Westgate housing study). Mere-exposure effect Robert Zajonc Repeated exposure to a stimulus, by itself, increases liking for it. Similarity–attraction Donn Byrne We like those with similar attitudes (not "opposites attract"); the "law of attraction". Reward / reinforcement-affect model Byrne & Clore We like people associated with rewards, even when they merely happened to be present when something good occurred. Gain–loss theory of attraction Aronson & Linder We are most attracted to someone whose liking for us increases over time (a gain) and most stung when it decreases (a loss). Matching hypothesis Walster & Berscheid We tend to pair with partners of roughly our own level of physical attractiveness. "What is beautiful is good" Dion, Berscheid & Walster The physical-attractiveness stereotype: we assume good-looking people also have better personalities. Evolutionary mate preferences David Buss Across cultures, men weight youth and attractiveness (fertility cues), women status and resources (provisioning); evolved reproductive strategies (parental investment). Reciprocity of liking — We like those who like us; learning someone likes you boosts your liking for them. Need to belong Baumeister & Leary A fundamental motive to form and maintain lasting positive relationships; its frustration harms health and well-being. High-yield Why proximity and exposure come first. You cannot like someone you never encounter, so propinquity (Leon Festinger's housing study: friendships clustered by who lived nearest stairs and mailboxes) sets the pool; mere exposure (Zajonc) does its quiet work, familiarity breeds liking; only then do similarity (Byrne, the real rule, not "opposites attract") and looks filter further. Critique to keep: the evolutionary mate-preference account (Buss) is heavily tested but also heavily criticised, social-role theory (Eagly & Wood) argues the same sex differences fall out of women's restricted access to resources and power, not genes. Know both sides; NIMHANS likes "which explanation." Theories of love Theory / term Who What it is Triangular theory of love Robert Sternberg Intimacy + passion + commitment combine into 7 types: liking (intimacy only), infatuation (passion only), empty (commitment only), romantic (intimacy+passion), companionate (intimacy+commitment), fatuous (passion+commitment), and consummate (all three). Passionate vs companionate love Hatfield & Berscheid Intense arousal and longing (passionate) vs deep affection, trust and care that lasts (companionate). Two-factor theory of love (misattribution of arousal) Dutton & Aron Arousal from a scary suspension bridge gets relabelled as romantic attraction to the person met there. Adult attachment styles Hazan & Shaver Secure / anxious-ambivalent / avoidant styles carried from infant attachment into romantic love. Four-category attachment model Bartholomew & Horowitz Model-of-self × model-of-other gives secure, preoccupied, dismissing-avoidant and fearful-avoidant styles. Why relationships last or end Theory / term Who What it is Social exchange theory Thibaut & Harold Kelley Relationships weighed as rewards minus costs, against a comparison level (CL) and the comparison level for alternatives (CL-alt). Equity theory Walster / Adams We are happiest when our ratio of inputs to outcomes matches the partner's (over- and under-benefit both cause distress). Investment model Caryl Rusbult Commitment = satisfaction + investment size − quality of alternatives. Accommodation: committed partners inhibit retaliation and respond constructively. Communal vs exchange relationships Clark & Mills Communal partners give based on the other's needs without scorekeeping; exchange partners track reciprocity. Social penetration / self-disclosure Altman & Taylor Relationships deepen as self-disclosure grows in breadth and depth ; reciprocal disclosure builds intimacy. Phases of dissolution Steve Duck Break-ups move through stages: intrapsychic → dyadic → social → grave-dressing (constructing the break-up story). High-yield The two-factor love trick. Dutton & Aron's bridge study is misattribution of arousal in action: men who crossed a high, swaying bridge (arousal from fear) were more attracted to the woman who met them there than men on a safe bridge. Arousal + a label (Schachter–Singer's two-factor theory) = the felt emotion. Baron also covers the dark side: loneliness (the painful gap between desired and actual relationships, a health risk), jealousy (evolutionary sex differences: men fear sexual infidelity, women emotional), and social allergens (a partner's small repeated annoyances accumulating into disgust). NIMHANS / clinical: adult attachment (Cindy Hazan & Phillip Shaver) bridges to Bowlby/Ainsworth; the investment model (Rusbult) is the standard frame for why people stay in unsatisfying or abusive relationships (high investment + low alternatives = high commitment despite low satisfaction). Trap The "who studied liking" cluster: Byrne = similarity · Robert Zajonc = mere exposure · Festinger = propinquity · Robert Sternberg = triangular love · Caryl Rusbult = investment model · Dutton & Aron = misattributed arousal (the bridge). These names rotate as each other's distractors; fix one hook per name. 19. Social influence: conformity, compliance, obedience The three levels. Conformity = changing to match a group with no direct request. Compliance = changing in response to a direct request (the sales techniques). Obedience = changing in response to a direct order from an authority. The levels rise from implicit group pressure to explicit command. Conformity & obedience Term Who What it is Conformity Solomon Asch Going along with a unanimous group's obviously wrong answer (line-judging task); ~33% conformity per trial. Norm formation Muzafer Sherif Used the autokinetic illusion (a still dot of light appears to move) to show groups converge on a shared norm. Informational vs normative influence Deutsch & Gerard We conform to be right (informational, especially when uncertain) vs to be liked/accepted (normative). Obedience to authority Stanley Milgram 65% of ordinary people delivered "lethal" 450V shocks when an authority calmly ordered them to continue. Minority influence / conversion Serge Moscovici A consistent minority can shift the majority via genuine private conversion (often delayed, internalised) rather than mere public compliance. Idiosyncrasy credits Edwin Hollander Conforming early earns "credits" a member can later spend on dissent or innovation without rejection. Social impact theory Bibb Latané Influence on a target = a function of the strength , immediacy and number of sources present. What raises or lowers Asch conformity, and kinds of norms. Conformity rises with group size (up to ~3–4, then plateaus) and unanimity , and collapses the moment one ally/dissenter breaks ranks. Baron separates two kinds of social norm (a Cialdini distinction): Term Who What it is Descriptive norms Robert Cialdini et al. What most people actually do ("everyone litters here"). Tell people what is, and they copy it. Injunctive norms Cialdini et al. What most people approve/disapprove of ("littering is wrong"). More durable for changing behaviour. Mindlessness / the "because" effect Ellen Langer A request with any reason ("...because I have to make copies") gains compliance even when the reason is empty. Symbolic social influence — We are influenced by others even when merely imagined or represented (a mental image of a parent's reaction shapes behaviour). High-yield Muzafer Sherif vs Solomon Asch, the two faces of conformity. Sherif used an ambiguous task (how far did the dot move? nobody knows), so people genuinely looked to others, this is informational influence producing real, internalised norm change. Asch used an unambiguous task (which line is longer? obvious), so people who caved did so to avoid standing out, this is normative influence, often just public compliance. Deutsch & Gerard named the two motives. Compliance techniques Term Who What it is Six principles of influence Robert Cialdini Reciprocity, commitment/consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity. Foot-in-the-door Freedman & Fraser Agreement to a small request first → a bigger one later gets agreed to (via commitment/consistency). Door-in-the-face Robert Cialdini A big request refused first → the smaller real request now looks reasonable (reciprocal concession). Lowballing Robert Cialdini Get a commitment at a good price, then raise the cost; people stick to the deal anyway. That's-not-all technique Jerry Burger Add a bonus or drop the price before the person decides → boosts compliance. Pique technique — An unusual request ("can you spare 37 cents?") disrupts automatic refusal and raises compliance by making people think. Disrupt-then-reframe Davis & Knowles A confusing twist followed by a reframe ("it's 300 pennies… that's a bargain!") boosts compliance. Norm of reciprocity Alvin Gouldner We feel obliged to return favours (the engine behind door-in-the-face and free samples). Agentic vs autonomous state Stanley Milgram People shift from acting on their own values (autonomous) to seeing themselves as an authority's tool, not responsible (agentic state), the mechanism of obedience. Trap Foot-in-the-door vs door-in-the-face: FITD = small → big (Jonathan Freedman & Scott Fraser, via consistency); DITF = big → small (Robert Cialdini, via reciprocal concession). Lowballing = get the yes, then change the deal. That's-not-all = sweeten the offer before the yes. Examiners love swapping the direction. High-yield NIMHANS. Milgram and Asch are perennial: lock the headline numbers (Milgram ~65% to maximum voltage; Asch ~33% conformity per trial, ~75% conformed at least once) and the situational factors that reduce obedience (authority less close/legitimate, peers who rebel, victim more present). Minority influence (Moscovici) via consistency is the standard contrast to majority conformity. Clinically, these explain compliance pressures in institutions and the value of even one dissenting ally. 20. Prosocial behaviour (helping) The problem. Why do we help, when do we fail to, and is helping ever truly selfless? The chapter splits into situational work (the bystander effect: why help fails) and motivational work (egoism vs altruism: why we help at all). When help fails: the bystander effect Term Who What it is Bystander effect & 5-step decision model Latané & John Darley More witnesses → less help. Five steps: notice → interpret as emergency → take responsibility → know how to help → decide to act. (Sparked by the Kitty Genovese case.) Diffusion of responsibility Darley & Bibb Latané "Someone else will do it"; responsibility spreads thin in a crowd (fails step 3). Pluralistic ignorance — Everyone stays calm because no one else looks worried, so no one reads it as an emergency (fails step 2). High-yield Why a crowd freezes you. The five-step model is a chain, and the crowd snaps it at two links. At step 2 (interpret) you look around, see calm faces, and conclude it must not be an emergency, that is pluralistic ignorance . At step 3 (take responsibility) , with many present, each assumes someone else will act, that is diffusion of responsibility . More witnesses make both failures more likely, so paradoxically you are less likely to be helped in a big crowd. Expect a scene with a "which step failed" stem. Why we help: egoism vs altruism Term Who What it is Empathy–altruism hypothesis C. Daniel Batson Feeling empathy for the victim produces genuinely selfless helping, aimed at their welfare, not our own relief. Negative-state relief model Robert Cialdini We help to relieve our own bad mood; helping is ultimately egoistic. Arousal: cost–reward model Piliavin et al. A bystander's unpleasant arousal at seeing distress motivates help; we help when costs of helping are low and costs of not helping are high. Empathic joy hypothesis Smith et al. We help partly for the pleasure of having a positive impact; we want feedback that our help worked. Kin selection / reciprocal altruism Hamilton; Trivers Evolutionary: help relatives (shared genes, kin selection) or those likely to return the favour (reciprocal altruism). Norm of social responsibility — A social norm that we should help those who depend on us, regardless of return. Prosocial / altruistic personality — A cluster (empathy, just-world belief, social responsibility, internal locus, low egocentrism) predicting consistent helping. Volunteerism & the functional approach Clary & Snyder Sustained helping is driven by the personal functions it serves (values, understanding, career, social, esteem, protective). Threat-to-self-esteem / reactions to receiving help Nadler & Fisher Receiving aid can feel demeaning and imply inferiority, so recipients sometimes refuse or resent help, especially from a similar other. What boosts helping: similarity to the victim, seeing a helpful model , feeling gratitude , being in a good mood (the "feel-good, do-good" effect ; guilt also raises helping), and the victim being not responsible for their plight. Helping drops with a hurry (the Good Samaritan study, John Darley & Batson: seminary students late for a talk stepped over a slumped man), diffuse responsibility, and ambiguity. Overjustification (over-rewarding helping can undermine the intrinsic motive); defensive helping (helping an out-group condescendingly to maintain the in-group's status). Trap Why we help, egoism vs altruism: C. Daniel Batson (empathy–altruism) = there is true altruism, born of empathy and aimed at the other's welfare. Robert Cialdini (negative-state relief) and Piliavin (arousal:cost-reward) = we ultimately help to fix our own discomfort, so helping is egoistic. That contrast (selfless vs self-serving motive) is the question. 21. Aggression The first distinction. Aggression is behaviour intended to harm another who does not want to be harmed. Types: hostile aggression (driven by anger, the goal is to hurt, often impulsive) vs instrumental aggression (a cold means to another end, money, status), plus relational aggression (harming through gossip, exclusion, reputation). The chapter traces an arc: from a simple drive theory (frustration always causes aggression), through its cognitive reformulation (frustration only readies aggression, cues pull the trigger), to social learning and integrative models. Theory / term Who What it is Frustration–aggression hypothesis John Dollard, Doob, Miller et al. Original strong form: frustration (a blocked goal) always breeds aggression, and aggression always traces to frustration. Reformulated frustration–aggression Leonard Berkowitz Frustration creates only a readiness (negative affect); aggression follows when aggressive cues are present. Weapons effect Berkowitz & LePage The mere presence of a weapon increases aggression, because the weapon is an aggressive cue. Cognitive-neoassociation Leonard Berkowitz Aversive events (heat, pain, frustration) trigger negative affect that automatically primes a network of anger and fight/flight responses. Social learning of aggression Albert Bandura Aggression is learned by observing and imitating models (the Bobo doll studies). General Aggression Model (GAM) Anderson & Bushman Integrative: person + situation inputs → internal state (arousal, affect, cognition) → appraisal → aggressive (or not) act. Excitation-transfer theory Dolf Zillmann Left-over physiological arousal from one source (exercise, a prior fright) intensifies aggression in a later, unrelated provoking situation. Catharsis hypothesis (Freud / Lorenz roots) The idea that venting "drains" aggression. Largely unsupported ; venting tends to raise later aggression. High-yield The arc in one breath. John Dollard et al. said frustration → aggression, full stop, too rigid. Leonard Berkowitz rescued it: frustration only builds a charge of negative affect ( readiness ); whether it discharges depends on aggressive cues , hence the weapons effect (a gun on the table makes you more aggressive). Bandura's Bobo doll added that we also just copy aggressive models. And the popular belief in catharsis is a myth : venting fuels rather than drains aggression, a high-yield "which is false" item. Social & cultural causes, and reduction Term Who What it is Media violence & desensitisation Anderson, Bushman Repeated violent media raises aggressive thoughts, affect and behaviour and blunts emotional response to real violence; primes aggressive scripts. Culture of honour Nisbett & Cohen In cultures (e.g. the US South) where reputation must be defended, insults trigger far more aggression; aggression is culturally shaped. Heat hypothesis Anderson Higher temperatures reliably increase aggression and violent-crime rates. Alcohol myopia Steele & Josephs Alcohol narrows attention to immediate provoking cues and impairs inhibition, disinhibiting aggression. Hostile attribution bias Kenneth Dodge Aggressive individuals over-read others' ambiguous acts as hostile, then retaliate; central to aggressive children and conduct problems. Displaced & triggered displaced aggression — Aggression aimed at a safer target than the real provoker; a minor provocation from that target then triggers an outsized response. Narcissism / threatened egotism Baumeister & Bushman Inflated, unstable high self-esteem (narcissism), not low self-esteem, predicts aggression when the ego is threatened. Confluence model of sexual aggression Malamuth Sexual coercion arises from the confluence of hostile masculinity and impersonal-sex orientation; violent pornography raises acceptance of aggression toward women. Bullying Dan Olweus Repeated aggression against a less powerful target; involves bullies, victims and bystanders. Reducing aggression. Catharsis does not work. What does: punishment only if prompt, certain and proportionate (or it backfires); incompatible responses (humour, empathy, mild non-aggressive feelings that can't co-exist with anger); apology and mitigating information ; cognitive interventions and exposure to non-aggressive models ; and self-regulation training. Frustration (Freud/Lorenz also gave the older instinct view of aggression). Trap Two Berkowitz ideas kept apart: reformulated frustration–aggression (frustration → readiness, cue → act) and cognitive-neoassociation (aversive events prime an anger network) are both his. Do not confuse excitation-transfer (Zillmann) , where arousal carries over from a prior unrelated event, with the weapons effect, where an external cue triggers aggression. And the catharsis hypothesis is largely disproven , examiners frame it as the false option. High-yield NIMHANS. Determinants of aggression as a list: biological (low serotonin, high testosterone, amygdala/prefrontal function, alcohol disinhibition) and situational/social (heat, provocation, crowding, frustration, media/violent models, culture of honour). The catharsis myth and the weapons effect are classic single-best-answer traps. Dodge's hostile attribution bias is core to the clinical model of conduct disorder and is itself a clean attribution-error item. 22. Groups & individuals The problem. What does the mere presence of, or membership in, a group do to the individual, to effort, self-restraint and decision quality? The chapter pairs opposing effects (presence can boost or sap effort; groups can decide better or worse), and the deciding variable is usually whether you are individually identifiable. A group's structure has four ingredients: roles (expected behaviours for a position), status (rank), norms (shared rules), and cohesiveness (the forces binding members). Presence of others: facilitation vs loafing Term Who What it is Social facilitation Norman Triplett; Robert Zajonc An audience or co-actor boosts performance on easy/well-learned tasks but hurts hard/novel ones (Zajonc: arousal strengthens the dominant response). Evaluation apprehension Nickolas Cottrell It is the fear of being judged , not mere physical presence, that creates the facilitation arousal. Social loafing Bibb Latané, Williams & Harkins People exert less effort in a group when individual output cannot be identified (Ringelmann rope-pull roots). Ringelmann effect Max Ringelmann Per-person pull on a rope falls as the group grows, from coordination loss + reduced effort (historical root of loafing). Process loss vs process gain Ivan Steiner Group output usually falls short of the sum of members' potential because of coordination and motivation losses. Brainstorming productivity loss — Real interacting groups generate fewer ideas than the same number working alone (nominal groups win), due to production blocking and evaluation apprehension. Transactive memory Daniel Wegner Groups develop a shared who-knows-what system, so members offload knowledge and recall more together. Deindividuation Leon Festinger; Philip Zimbardo Anonymity and arousal in a crowd → loss of self-awareness and personal restraint (Stanford prison study). High-yield The first experiment. Norman Triplett (1898) noticed cyclists rode faster racing others than alone, arguably social psychology's first experiment. Robert Zajonc explained it: an audience raises arousal, and arousal strengthens whatever response is dominant , the right one on an easy task (better) but the wrong one on a hard task (worse). Cottrell refined it: the arousal comes from evaluation apprehension , fear of being judged, not bare presence. Group decision-making, conflict & leadership Term Who What it is Group polarisation Moscovici & Zavalloni Group discussion pushes members toward a more extreme version of their initial average leaning. Risky shift James Stoner The earlier-discovered special case: groups often reach riskier decisions than individuals would alone. Groupthink Irving Janis A highly cohesive group suppresses dissent to preserve consensus → defective decisions (Bay of Pigs). Symptoms: illusion of invulnerability, collective rationalisation, belief in the group's morality, stereotyping out-groups, self-censorship, illusion of unanimity, direct pressure on dissenters, mindguards . Remedies: devil's advocate, outside experts, leader withholds opinion, second-chance meetings. Tragedy of the commons / social dilemma Garrett Hardin Individually rational self-interest collectively depletes a shared resource (prisoner's dilemma + commons; cooperation needs trust, communication, sanctions). GRIT Charles Osgood Graduated and Reciprocated Initiatives in Tension-reduction: small, announced, unilateral concessions invite reciprocation and de-escalate conflict. Distributive vs procedural vs transactional justice Adams; John Thibaut & Walker; Tyler Distributive = fairness of outcomes ; procedural = fairness of the process (people accept bad outcomes if the process felt fair, voice, neutrality); transactional = fairness of interpersonal treatment. Great-person / trait theory — Leaders are born with distinguishing traits; weakly supported on its own. Transactional vs transformational leadership Bass; Burns Transactional leaders exchange rewards for performance; transformational leaders inspire and remake followers' values and vision (charisma, intellectual stimulation). Fred Fiedler's contingency model Fred Fiedler Effective leadership depends on the match between leader style (task- vs relationship-oriented, the LPC scale) and situational favourableness. Trap Facilitation vs loafing: social facilitation = others present make you try harder (you are watched and evaluated individually ); social loafing = others present make you try less (your effort is pooled, your individual output hidden ). The deciding variable is whether your individual output is identifiable. Bonus: risky shift is the special case, group polarisation the general rule. Watch the deindividuation attribution: Leon Festinger coined the term, but Philip Zimbardo gave the famous demonstration (Stanford prison). 23. Landmark studies, walked through Social psychology is taught through its classic experiments, and NIMHANS/MET stems often describe a study and ask you to name it, its author or its conclusion. Each landmark below follows the same shape: the question, what they did, what they found, why it matters, and the trap. Learn the design, not just the headline number, because examiners test the procedure ("judged the length of lines" vs "a dot of light that appeared to move") as the giveaway. Triplett (1898) — the first social-psychology experiment Q: does the presence of others change performance? What: Norman Triplett noticed cyclists posted faster times racing others than the clock, then had children wind fishing reels alone vs alongside a co-actor. Found: children wound faster with a co-actor. Matters: widely cited as the first published social-psychology experiment, the seed of social facilitation . Trap: Triplett observed facilitation; Robert Zajonc later explained it (dominant response); Cottrell refined the cause to evaluation apprehension. Sherif (1936) — autokinetic norm formation Q: how do group norms form when reality is ambiguous? What: in a dark room a stationary pinpoint of light appears to move (the autokinetic effect ). Alone, people gave wildly different estimates; in groups they converged on a shared figure, and each kept using it even when later tested alone. Found: a private, internalised norm forms and persists. Matters: the model case of informational social influence . Trap: Muzafer Sherif = ambiguous stimulus, real internal conversion (informational); Solomon Asch = unambiguous, public compliance (normative). The "dot of light" is the tell for Sherif. Asch (1951) — conformity on the line task Q: will people conform to a group that is clearly wrong? What: a single real participant judged which comparison line matched a standard, seated among confederates giving the same wrong answer on critical trials. Found: about 75% conformed on at least one trial; the rate per critical trial was about 33–37% . Conformity rose with group size (up to 3–4, then plateaued) and unanimity , and collapsed the moment a single ally also dissented. Matters: normative pressure can override the plain evidence of one's senses. Trap: lock the two numbers separately and remember one dissenting ally frees the participant, not the size of the majority. Milgram (1963) — obedience to authority Q: how far will ordinary people go in harming another when ordered? What: the "teacher" delivered escalating shocks (15V to 450V , labelled "XXX") to a "learner" (a confederate, never actually shocked) while a calm experimenter issued four scripted prods ("the experiment requires that you continue"). Found: 65% went all the way to 450V. Matters: situational pressure, not sadism, produced obedience. Factors that REDUCED obedience: authority physically absent / by phone; legitimacy undercut (ordinary office vs Yale); victim more present (same room, touch-proximity); and crucially peers who rebelled . Obedience rose when responsibility could be diffused. Trap: headline ~65%; know at least two reducing factors; the agentic state (seeing oneself as the authority's instrument) is the explanatory mechanism. Zimbardo (1971) — the Stanford Prison Experiment Q: do situations and roles, not dispositions, drive cruelty? What: college men were randomly assigned "guards" or "prisoners" in a mock basement prison, meant to run two weeks. Found: guards rapidly became abusive, prisoners passive/distressed; halted after six days . Matters: headline demonstration of deindividuation and the power of assigned roles . Trap: Leon Festinger coined "deindividuation"; Philip Zimbardo demonstrated it. Modern critique (demand characteristics, coached guards, low replicability) is now part of the discussion, a stem may ask what it is criticised for. Festinger & Carlsmith (1959) — $1 vs $20 Q: when does doing something for too little reward change your attitude? What: participants did an excruciatingly boring task, then were paid $1 or $20 to tell a waiting participant it was enjoyable, then privately rated their actual enjoyment. Found: the $1 group rated it more enjoyable. Matters: classic cognitive dissonance via insufficient justification . Trap: the counter-intuitive direction ( less reward → more attitude change) is the whole point; $20 gave an external justification, so no dissonance. Latané & Darley (1968–70) — the bystander effect Q: why do witnesses fail to help? What: two famous variants. In the smoke-filled room study, participants saw smoke seep in; alone, most reported it quickly, but among passive confederates most sat in the haze ( pluralistic ignorance ). In the seizure study, the more bystanders a participant believed were on an intercom, the slower and less likely they were to help ( diffusion of responsibility ). Found: more witnesses → less helping. Matters: formalised as the five-step model . Trap: match the failure to the step; the Kitty Genovese case was the journalistic spark, though its "38 witnesses" detail was later shown to be exaggerated. Darley & Batson (1973) — the Good Samaritan study Q: does being in a hurry suppress helping? What: seminary students walked to give a talk (some on the parable of the Good Samaritan) and passed a man slumped, coughing, in a doorway; the experimenters varied how rushed the student was. Found: being in a hurry was the strongest predictor of not helping; the talk topic barely mattered. Matters: the power of the situation over personal values even in prosocially primed people. Trap: "hurry > piety," situational time pressure beats disposition. Bandura (1961–63) — the Bobo doll Q: is aggression learned by imitation? What: children watched an adult model either attack or ignore an inflatable Bobo doll, then were mildly frustrated and left alone with it. Found: children who saw aggression imitated it (including novel acts and verbal aggression); seeing the model rewarded increased imitation, seeing it punished decreased performance but not learning . Matters: founded social learning theory and the learning/performance distinction. Trap: children learned the aggression regardless of the model's consequences; consequences only changed whether they performed it. Tajfel (1971) — the minimal group paradigm Q: how little does it take to produce in-group bias? What: strangers were split on a trivial basis (Klee vs Kandinsky paintings, or a coin toss), then allocated points to anonymous in-group and out-group members. Found: people favoured their own group though groups were arbitrary, with no prior contact, self-interest or conflict, and would even sacrifice absolute in-group gain to maximise the difference . Matters: the empirical bedrock of social identity theory . Trap: minimal group = bias with no real competition; contrast with Muzafer Sherif's realistic conflict. Sherif (1954) — the Robbers Cave study Q: what creates and cures intergroup hostility? What: at a boys' summer camp, two groups (Eagles, Rattlers) were put into competition for prizes, breeding hostility, then given superordinate goals requiring cooperation (a broken water supply, a stuck truck). Found: competition manufactured prejudice; shared goals dissolved it; mere contact alone did not . Matters: the field demonstration of realistic conflict theory and why the contact hypothesis requires cooperation toward common goals. Trap: it was the superordinate goal , not contact by itself, that reduced hostility. Dutton & Aron (1974) — the shaky-bridge study Q: can arousal from one source be mislabelled as attraction? What: men crossed either a high, swaying suspension bridge (fear arousal) or a low stable bridge, where an attractive female interviewer gave them her number. Found: men from the scary bridge were far more likely to call and rated her more attractive. Matters: misattribution of arousal , an application of Stanley Schachter & Jerome Singer's two-factor theory of emotion to attraction. Trap: the arousal was really fear; participants relabelled it. LaPiere (1934) — attitudes vs behaviour Q: do stated attitudes predict actual behaviour? What: LaPiere toured the US with a young Chinese couple and recorded their treatment at ~250 hotels/restaurants; they were refused only once. Months later he wrote asking whether the same establishments would serve Chinese guests; over 90% said no . Found: a glaring gap between expressed prejudice and real behaviour. Matters: set off decades of work resolved by Martin Fishbein & Icek Ajzen (attitudes predict behaviour through intentions). Trap: LaPiere = the attitude–behaviour gap ; the resolution (intentions, specificity) is the theory-of-reasoned-action line. Other landmark experiments Study Method & finding Harry Harlow (1958) monkeys Infant monkeys preferred a soft cloth "mother" over a wire one with food. Contact comfort drives attachment. Martin Seligman (1967) helplessness Dogs exposed to inescapable shock later failed to escape when they could. Learned helplessness (model of depression). David Rosenhan (1973) "being sane in insane places" Healthy pseudopatients admitted to psychiatric hospitals; diagnoses stuck. Critique of psychiatric labelling. 24. Schools & history of psychology School Core idea & figures Structuralism Break consciousness into elements via introspection. Wilhelm Wundt (first lab, 1879), Edward Titchener. Functionalism What is the mind for ? Adaptive function of behaviour. William James, influenced by Charles Darwin. Psychoanalysis Unconscious drives and early experience. Sigmund Freud. Behaviourism Only observable behaviour; learning by conditioning. John B. Watson, Ivan Pavlov, B. F. Skinner. Gestalt The whole differs from the sum of parts. Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Köhler. Humanistic ("third force") Free will, growth, self-actualisation. Abraham Maslow, Carl Rogers. Cognitive Mental processes as information processing; the "cognitive revolution" (1950s–60s). Ulric Neisser, Miller. Biological / evolutionary Behaviour rooted in the brain, genes, and adaptation. 25. The MCQ traps, collected Method core: experiment = the only design proving causation (manipulate IV, measure DV, random assignment). Correlation ≠ causation (third-variable + directionality). Mediator = the why ; moderator = the when/for whom . Attention selection: Donald Broadbent = early/physical; Anne Treisman = attenuation; Deutsch-Norman = late/meaning; Lavie = depends on load. Cocktail-party effect supports late/attenuation, not Broadbent. Feature search pops out (parallel); conjunction search is serial. Memory: serial position = primacy (LTM) + recency (STM); a delay wipes recency. Anterograde (no new memories, H.M.) vs retrograde (no old). Encoding specificity = Endel Tulving. Conditioning: variable-ratio = highest, most extinction-resistant. Rescorla-Wagner = prediction error, explains blocking. Bobo doll = learning ≠ performance. Emotion order: James-Lange (body first) · Cannon-Bard (simultaneous) · Schachter-Singer (body + label). Availability = ease of recall · representativeness = fit to a prototype (neglects base rates) · anchoring = stuck on a first value. All = Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman. The attribution swap: FAE (Ross) = over-blame others' character · actor–observer (Edward E. Jones & Richard Nisbett) = my acts = situation, your acts = character · self-serving = my success = me, my failure = the situation. Models in order: Fritz Heider → Jones & Keith Davis → Harold Kelley (consensus, consistency, distinctiveness). Self-discrepancy (Higgins): ideal-self gap → dejection (sad); ought-self gap → agitation (anxious). Self cluster: social comparison = Leon Festinger · self-perception = Bem · self-monitoring = Snyder · self-efficacy = Albert Bandura · self-handicapping = Berglas & Jones · self-verification = Swann · self-affirmation = Steele · spotlight = Gilovich · BIRGing = Robert Cialdini · TMT = Greenberg, Pyszczynski & Solomon. Dissonance vs self-perception: Festinger = arousal/discomfort, strong prior attitude; Bem = no arousal, mere inference, weak attitude. $1 > $20 (insufficient justification, Festinger & J. Merrill Carlsmith): less reward = more attitude change. Effort justification = Aronson & Mills. Balance theory = Heider. Persuasion routes: central/systematic vs peripheral/heuristic. ELM = Richard Petty & John Cacioppo; HSM = Chaiken; Yale "who-what-whom" = Carl Hovland; inoculation = McGuire; reactance = Brehm; attitude–behaviour gap = LaPiere; intention model = Martin Fishbein & Icek Ajzen; sleeper effect & functions of attitudes = Hovland / Katz. Prejudice sources: social identity / minimal group = Henri Tajfel (& Turner) · realistic conflict / Robbers Cave = Muzafer Sherif · authoritarian personality (F-scale) = Adorno. Reduction: contact hypothesis (four conditions) = Allport; jigsaw classroom = Aronson; recategorisation = Gaertner & Dovidio. Stereotype cognition: illusory correlation = Hamilton & Gifford · out-group homogeneity · stereotype threat = Steele & Aronson · stereotype content model (warmth × competence) = Fiske. Stereotype threat ≠ self-fulfilling prophecy (target's own fear vs perceiver's expectation). Hostile vs benevolent sexism = Glick & Fiske (benevolent = the "nice"-sounding one). The "who studied liking" cluster: Byrne = similarity · Robert Zajonc = mere exposure · Festinger = propinquity · Robert Sternberg = triangular love · Caryl Rusbult = investment model · Dutton & Aron = misattributed arousal (bridge). Evolutionary mate preferences = Buss (vs Eagly & Wood); dissolution phases = Duck. Conformity: Solomon Asch = unambiguous line task (normative) · Sherif = autokinetic, ambiguous (informational) · Deutsch & Gerard named the two motives · Stanley Milgram = obedience (~65%, agentic state) · Serge Moscovici = minority influence via consistency. Foot-in-the-door vs door-in-the-face: FITD = small→big (Jonathan Freedman & Scott Fraser, consistency); DITF = big→small (Cialdini, reciprocal concession); lowballing = change the deal after the yes; that's-not-all = sweeten before the yes; reciprocity norm = Gouldner. Helping: bystander effect & 5-step model = Bibb Latané & John Darley; crowd failures = pluralistic ignorance (interpret) + diffusion of responsibility (take responsibility). C. Daniel Batson = true altruism (empathy); Cialdini (negative-state relief) and Piliavin (arousal:cost-reward) = egoistic. Kin selection = Hamilton, reciprocal altruism = Trivers. Aggression: frustration–aggression = John Dollard et al.; reformulation + weapons effect = Leonard Berkowitz (& LePage); social learning/Bobo = Bandura; GAM = Anderson & Bushman; excitation-transfer = Zillmann; cognitive-neoassociation = Berkowitz; threatened egotism = Baumeister & Bushman; hostile attribution bias = Dodge; culture of honour = Nisbett & Cohen; catharsis is a myth . Groups: facilitation (Triplett/Zajonc, dominant-response) vs loafing (Latané/Ringelmann, hidden effort); evaluation apprehension = Cottrell; deindividuation = Festinger coined / Zimbardo demonstrated; group polarisation (Moscovici & Marisa Zavalloni) generalises risky shift (Stoner); groupthink = Irving Janis; tragedy of the commons = Hardin; GRIT = Osgood; distributive (outcome) vs procedural (process) justice; transactional vs transformational leadership = Bass. 26. Fast glossary (A–Z) Last-mile recall: every nameable social-psychology term reduced to a single line and its author, alphabetical so you can self-test by covering the right column. If a name fires but the definition doesn't, that is the gap to drill. Term One-line definition (and who) Actor–observer effect My acts → situation, your acts → your character (Edward E. Jones & Richard Nisbett). Agentic state Seeing oneself as an authority's instrument, not the author of the act (Stanley Milgram). Anchoring & adjustment Cling to a first value, adjust too little (Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman). Authoritarian personality Rigid, submissive-to-authority, prejudice-prone; F-scale (Adorno). Availability heuristic Judge likelihood by ease of recall (Tversky & Kahneman). Balance theory We seek consistency in liking-relationships, P-O-X triads (Fritz Heider). Base-rate fallacy Ignore underlying frequencies for vivid cases (Kahneman & Tversky). BIRGing Basking in reflected glory, "we won" (Robert Cialdini). Bystander effect More witnesses → less help; 5-step model (Bibb Latané & John Darley). Catharsis (myth) Venting drains aggression, largely unsupported; it raises it. Cognitive dissonance Tension from clashing cognitions drives attitude change (Leon Festinger). Companionate love Deep affection, trust, care that lasts (Hatfield & Berscheid). Conjunction fallacy Specific conjunction judged likelier than its component, "Linda" (Tversky & Kahneman). Contact hypothesis Contact cuts prejudice if equal status, common goals, cooperation, institutional support (Allport). Correspondent inference Infer a trait from freely chosen, unexpected, low-desirability acts (Jones & Keith Davis). Counterfactual thinking Imagining "what might have been"; near-misses sting most (Kahneman & Tversky). Covariation model Attribution via consensus, consistency, distinctiveness (Harold Kelley). Deindividuation Anonymity + arousal → loss of restraint (Festinger coined; Philip Zimbardo demonstrated). Descriptive vs injunctive norms What people do vs what they approve (Cialdini). Diffusion of responsibility "Someone else will help" in a crowd (Darley & Latané). Discounting / augmenting Downweight a cause if rivals present / upweight a cause acting despite obstacles (Kelley). Door-in-the-face Big refused request → smaller real one, reciprocal concession (Cialdini). Effort justification Harsher initiation → value the group more (Aronson & Mills). Elaboration Likelihood Model Central (argument) vs peripheral (cue) route to persuasion (Richard Petty & John Cacioppo). Empathy–altruism Empathy yields genuinely selfless helping (C. Daniel Batson). Equity theory Happiest when input:outcome ratios match the partner's (Walster/Adams). Evaluation apprehension Fear of being judged, not bare presence, drives facilitation arousal (Cottrell). Excitation-transfer Left-over arousal intensifies later unrelated aggression (Zillmann). False consensus effect Overestimate how many share our views (Ross). Foot-in-the-door Small request first → bigger one later, via consistency (Jonathan Freedman & Scott Fraser). Framing effect Choice flips with gain vs loss wording (Tversky & Kahneman). Frustration–aggression Blocked goals breed aggression; original strong form (John Dollard et al.). Functions of attitudes Knowledge, utilitarian, ego-defensive, value-expressive (Katz). Fundamental attribution error Over-blame others' character, ignore their situation (coined by Ross). Gain–loss theory We like rising liking, dislike falling liking, more than steady (Aronson & Linder). General Aggression Model Person + situation → internal state → appraisal → act (Anderson & Bushman). Group polarisation Discussion amplifies the group's initial leaning (Serge Moscovici & Marisa Zavalloni). Groupthink Cohesion suppresses dissent → bad decisions (Irving Janis). GRIT Announced unilateral concessions de-escalate conflict (Osgood). Halo effect One global positive impression bleeds into specific traits (Edward Thorndike). Hindsight bias "I knew it all along" once the outcome is known (Fischhoff). Hostile attribution bias Read ambiguous acts as hostile, then retaliate (Dodge). Hostile vs benevolent sexism Antagonistic vs patronising-protective; both subordinate women (Glick & Fiske). Idiosyncrasy credits Early conformity buys later licence to dissent (Hollander). Illusory correlation See a link between a minority and rare behaviour that isn't there (Hamilton & Gifford). Implicit attitudes / IAT Automatic evaluations measured by reaction time. Inoculation theory A weak counter-argument vaccinates an attitude (McGuire). Insufficient justification $1 > $20: less reward → more attitude change (Festinger & J. Merrill Carlsmith). Investment model Commitment = satisfaction + investment − alternatives (Caryl Rusbult). Jigsaw classroom Cooperative interdependence cuts prejudice (Aronson). Just-world hypothesis People get what they deserve → victim-blaming (Lerner). Kin selection / reciprocal altruism Help relatives / likely reciprocators (Hamilton; Trivers). LaPiere study The attitude–behaviour gap (LaPiere). Looking-glass self Self built from imagined views of others (Cooley). Lowballing Get the yes, then raise the cost (Cialdini). Matching hypothesis We pair with similar attractiveness levels (Walster & Berscheid). Mere-exposure effect Repeated exposure increases liking (Robert Zajonc). Minimal group paradigm Arbitrary splits produce in-group bias (Henri Tajfel). Minority influence A consistent minority converts the majority privately (Moscovici). Misattribution of arousal Arousal relabelled as attraction, the bridge study (Dutton & Aron). Need to belong Fundamental motive for lasting bonds (Baumeister & Leary). Negative-state relief We help to fix our own bad mood (Cialdini). Obedience to authority ~65% to 450V under orders (Milgram). Out-group homogeneity "They're all alike." Passionate love Intense arousal and longing (Hatfield & Berscheid). Perseverance effect Beliefs survive after the evidence is discredited. Pluralistic ignorance All stay calm because no one else looks worried. Possible selves Hoped-for/feared future selves that motivate (Markus & Nurius). Procedural vs distributive justice Fair process vs fair outcome; process can matter more (Tyler; Adams). Propinquity effect Proximity breeds friendship, Westgate study (Festinger, Stanley Schachter & Back). Reactance Threaten a freedom → want the forbidden more (Brehm). Realistic conflict theory Competition over resources breeds hostility, Robbers Cave (Muzafer Sherif). Representativeness heuristic Judge by resemblance to a prototype, neglect base rates (Tversky & Kahneman). Ringelmann effect Per-person effort falls as group grows (Max Ringelmann). Risky shift Groups decide riskier than individuals; special case of polarisation (Stoner). Schema Mental framework steering attention, encoding, retrieval (Frederic Bartlett; Fiske & Taylor). Self-affirmation Affirm a valued domain to buffer a threat elsewhere (Steele). Self-discrepancy theory Ideal-gap → dejection; ought-gap → agitation (Higgins). Self-efficacy Belief in one's capacity for a task (Albert Bandura). Self-fulfilling prophecy Expectation makes itself come true (Merton). Self-handicapping Pre-set an excuse to protect esteem (Berglas & Jones). Self-monitoring High monitors tailor to the situation, low act on inner attitudes (Snyder). Self-perception theory Infer weak attitudes from your own behaviour (Bem). Self-serving bias Success = me, failure = the situation. Self-verification Seek feedback confirming the existing self-view (Swann). Sleeper effect Low-credibility message gains force as the source is forgotten (Carl Hovland). Social comparison theory We evaluate ourselves against others (Festinger). Social dominance orientation Preference for group hierarchy (Sidanius & Pratto). Social exchange theory Relationships = rewards − costs vs CL and CL-alt (John Thibaut & Kelley). Social facilitation Audience helps easy tasks, hurts hard ones (Norman Triplett; Zajonc). Social identity theory Self-esteem from group → in-group favouritism (Tajfel & John Turner). Social impact theory Influence = strength × immediacy × number (Latané). Social loafing Less effort when individual output is hidden (Latané, Williams & Harkins). Social penetration Relationships deepen via breadth + depth of disclosure (Altman & Taylor). Sociometer theory Self-esteem gauges social acceptance (Leary). Spotlight effect Overestimate how much others notice us (Gilovich). Stereotype content model Warmth × competence → 4 emotions (Fiske). Stereotype threat Fear of confirming a stereotype hurts performance (Steele & Aronson). System justification Motive to defend the existing social order (Jost). Terror management theory Mortality awareness defends worldview & esteem (Greenberg, Pyszczynski & Solomon). That's-not-all technique Sweeten the offer before the decision (Burger). Theory of planned behaviour Intention = attitude + norm + perceived control → behaviour (Martin Fishbein & Icek Ajzen). Thin slices Accurate judgements from seconds of behaviour (Ambady & Robert Rosenthal). Thought-suppression rebound Suppressed thoughts intrude more, the white bear (Wegner). Transactive memory Shared who-knows-what system in groups (Wegner). Transformational leadership Inspire and remake followers' values vs transactional reward-exchange (Bass; Burns). Triangular theory of love Intimacy + passion + commitment → 7 types (Robert Sternberg). Two-step attribution Automatic dispositional inference, then effortful situational correction (Gilbert). Ultimate attribution error FAE applied to out-groups (Thomas Pettigrew). Weapons effect A weapon's mere presence raises aggression (Leonard Berkowitz & LePage). "What is beautiful is good" Attractiveness stereotype (Dion, Berscheid & Walster). Yale attitude-change approach Who says what to whom (Hovland). Mnemonic Last-mile routine: recall → trap discrimination → glossary sweep . Cover the right column above and recover the definition + author for every row; then re-read the §25 trap boxes; then drill the rows that don't fire instantly. That pairing (term recall + lookalike discrimination) is exactly the two skills NIMHANS and MET grade hardest. Quick name-hooks for the most-swapped clusters: Amos Tversky & Kahneman own every heuristic; Leon Festinger = dissonance + social comparison + propinquity (three different things, read the stem); Robert Cialdini = influence principles + door-in-the-face + lowballing + BIRGing + negative-state relief; Steele = self-affirmation AND stereotype threat; Albert Bandura = Bobo doll + self-efficacy + observational learning.

title: Psychological Assessment & Testing
text: Psychological Assessment & Testing A psychological test is a measuring instrument, and like any instrument it must be (a) consistent and (b) accurate. Consistent = reliability . Accurate = validity .
