Everything in this chapter is either a way to estimate reliability, a way to estimate validity, a way to interpret scores against norms, or a real-world test built on those foundations. We measure things we cannot see directly (anxiety, intelligence, personality) by building instruments out of items, like a thermometer made of questions, then deciding things with them: special education, army fitness, diagnosis. This chapter locks the psychometric theory first, then the major intelligence, personality, projective, and clinical instruments, with every author, year, item count, scale, score range, and exam trap in one place. In this book Item analysis & test construction Reliability (the consistency story) Validity (the accuracy story) Norms & standard scores Intelligence theories & IQ mechanics Stanford-Binet family Wechsler family Raven’s Progressive Matrices Kaufman, Cattell CFIT & special-purpose scales Group & infant/developmental scales Indian intelligence tests IQ classification & intellectual disability Objective (self-report) personality tests Projective tests Adjustment, clinical & Indian inventories Aptitude, attitude & interest scales Psychiatric & cognitive rating scales Educational measurement basics Master reference tables & trap list 1. Item analysis & test construction Each test item is a single sensor reading. If a sensor is too easy (everyone passes) it tells us nothing; too hard (no one passes) it tells us nothing; and if it disagrees with the rest of the test, something is wrong with it. That is why every well-built test goes through item analysis. Difficulty index, p The difficulty index is the proportion who got an item right. p = (number correct) / (total attempting) , range 0 to 1. p = 0.50 is the sweet spot for a free-response item because it discriminates the most. For a 4-option MCQ the optimal p is ~0.625 , halfway between chance guessing (0.25) and ceiling (1.00). p above 0.80 = too easy; p below 0.20 = too hard. Both are revision candidates because they cannot separate strong from weak students. Discrimination index, D Do high-scorers on the whole test do better on this item than low-scorers? D = p_upper − p_lower , where p_upper = proportion correct in the top 27% of scorers and p_lower = proportion in the bottom 27%. Range −1 to +1. D above 0.40 = item agrees with the test, a good signal. D near zero = random noise; both groups perform alike. Negative D = the bottom group out-performed the top group: the item is mis-keyed, ambiguous, or has a trick strong test-takers over-think. Trap Read negative discrimination as a mis-keyed / flawed item to discard immediately , NOT as a merely “hard” item. This is asked every cycle. 2. Reliability (the consistency story) Reliability is not about whether a test is correct; it is about whether it is consistent . A bathroom scale that reads 75 kg every time is reliable even if your true weight is 70 (that is a validity problem). A scale bouncing between 60, 90, 80 is unreliable, full stop. If a test is unreliable you cannot trust any single score: the same person retested gives a different answer for reasons unrelated to the trait. You are measuring noise. Definition Classical Test Theory: Observed Score = True Score + Error . Reliability is the proportion of observed-score variance that is true variance, not error. A reliability of 0.80 says 80% signal, 20% noise. There are several reliability methods because there are several ways to think about “consistency”: Across time: test the same person twice (test-retest). Across forms: give two equivalent versions (parallel/alternate forms). Within one administration, across items: check items hang together (split-half, Cronbach alpha, KR-20). Across raters: check two judges agree (Cohen kappa for categorical, ICC for continuous). Test-retest (time stability) Give the test, give it again later, correlate the two scores. High correlation = stable over time. The standard window is two to four weeks . Too long and the trait itself can change (correlation drops, but the test is not at fault); too short and memory carryover inflates the correlation. Split-half + Spearman-Brown Give the test once, split into two halves (often odd vs even items), correlate the halves. By splitting you have halved the test length, and shorter tests are less reliable, so the raw split-half correlation under estimates full-test reliability. Spearman-Brown corrects this: r_full = 2 × r_half / (1 + r_half) . Example: r_half = 0.60 → r_full = 1.20 / 1.60 = 0.75 . Always apply Spearman-Brown after any split. Cronbach alpha Imagine doing every possible split-half and averaging the result: that mean is Cronbach alpha. It is the most common internal-consistency measure for tests with multi-point (e.g. Likert) items. Alpha rises with item count, item homogeneity, and trait variance. Trap Alpha is NOT a measure of unidimensionality. A test can have high alpha and still measure two distinct constructs. The MET loves this. KR-20 (Kuder-Richardson 20) When items are right-or-wrong (dichotomous, 1/0), Cronbach alpha simplifies to KR-20: same idea, adapted for 0/1 items. So “30-item right-wrong vocabulary test, one administration, which reliability?” → KR-20 . Inter-rater: kappa and ICC When humans do the scoring (Rorschach protocols, clinical interviews, essay grades), reliability is about rater agreement. Cohen kappa for categorical decisions (OCD: yes/no), corrects for chance agreement. Kappa ≥ 0.81 = almost-perfect; 0.61–0.80 = substantial. Intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for continuous ratings (a 0–100 severity score); different ICC forms exist depending on whether raters are random or fixed. Trap Kappa is NOT an internal-consistency measure. If a question describes a one-administration internal-structure test, kappa is the wrong answer. Standard Error of Measurement (SEM) SEM is the practical payoff of reliability: the band of error around any single observed score. SEM = SD × √(1 − r_xx) , where SD is the test SD and r_xx its reliability. Example: SD = 20, reliability 0.81 → SEM = 20 × √0.19 = 20 × 0.436 = 8.72 . A score of 100 has a 68% confidence band of roughly 91–109 (±1 SEM). Higher reliability shrinks SEM. SEM is what lets you say two scores differ meaningfully versus fall within the noise band. 3. Validity (the accuracy story) A test can be perfectly reliable yet measure the wrong thing. Validity asks whether the test measures the construct it claims to. The classical model has three broad evidence types; modern theorists (especially Samuel Messick ) fold them all into “construct validity,” but the MET still uses the classical breakdown, so know both. Content validity Does the test cover the domain it claims to? An anxiety scale that asks only about racing heart but ignores worry, restlessness, and sleep is content-deficient. Established by expert panels who rate item-domain coverage; Lawshe’s CVR is the technical formula, but expert judgment is the core. Trap Do not confuse with face validity = whether the test merely looks valid to a layperson taking it. Face validity is the weakest form. A test can have high face validity and poor content validity, or low face validity and rigorous content validity. Criterion validity Does the test correlate with a real-world outcome (the criterion)? Two flavors: Concurrent: criterion measured at the same time. E.g. a new depression scale vs an established gold standard (HAM-D) today. Used when a gold standard already exists. Predictive: criterion measured later. E.g. GRE today predicts graduate GPA two years on. Used to forecast future behaviour. Mnemonic Predictive = Postponed. Concurrent = Current. Construct validity The most abstract form. If the test truly measures Construct X, it should correlate strongly with other measures of X ( convergent ), weakly with unrelated constructs ( discriminant ), and behave as theory predicts study after study ( nomological network ). The classic technique is Campbell & Fiske’s 1959 multitrait-multimethod matrix (MTMM) , which tests convergent and discriminant validity simultaneously by measuring multiple traits with multiple methods. Validity ceiling High-yield Validity cannot exceed the square root of reliability. Max validity coefficient between Test A and B = √(r_xx_A × r_xx_B) . If A is 0.64 reliable and B is 0.81 reliable, max correlation = √(0.64 × 0.81) = 0.72 . Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity; unreliable tests cannot be strongly valid. 4. Norms & standard scores A raw score means nothing alone: “scored 47 on a vocabulary test” tells you nothing until you know what others score. Norms convert raw scores into a frame of reference. The two most useful conversions are percentile ranks and standard scores. Percentile ranks The percentage of the norm group scoring at or below the person’s score. A 75th percentile means 75% scored at or below this person. Easy to interpret but ordinal : the gap between the 50th and 60th percentile is far smaller than between the 90th and 99th. Standard scores These put raw scores on an interval scale with fixed mean and SD: Standard Score = M + (SD × z) , where z is the person’s z-score from the norm group. Memorize these systems cold: Score Mean SD Range / use z 0 1 ~−3 to +3, universal/research T-score 50 10 ~20–80; MMPI family, NEO-PI, Big Five, neuropsych Wechsler IQ (FSIQ/index) 100 15 ~40–160; WAIS, WISC, WPPSI, SB-5 Old Stanford-Binet IQ (1960–1986) 100 16 ~36–164 Stanine 5 2 1–9; achievement/educational tests Sten (Standard Ten) 5.5 2 1–10; 16PF Wechsler subtest scaled 10 3 1–19; subtests inside WAIS/WISC Trap Most-tested swaps: Wechsler IQ SD = 15 vs old Binet SD = 16 . Stanine SD = 2, not 1 . T-score is 50/10, not 100/10 . Sten (16PF) mean 5.5; Stanine (education) mean 5. Normal-curve landmarks: 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD. z = +1 → 84th percentile; z = +2 → 98th percentile. 5. Intelligence theories & IQ mechanics The IQ formula history (memorize the sequence) Mental Age (MA) introduced by Alfred Binet, 1908 revision: the average chronological age that performs at the child’s level. Ratio IQ = (MA / CA) × 100 : William Stern, 1912 ; applied by Terman in the Stanford-Binet 1916. Deviation IQ : Wechsler, 1939 (Wechsler-Bellevue I), comparing the examinee to age-mates via a standardized score with fixed mean & SD. Solved the problem that ratio IQ breaks down past 16 because MA stops climbing linearly. Stanford-Binet switches to deviation IQ in 1960 (Pinneau’s tables), SD = 16. SB-5 (2003) drops SD to 15 to match Wechsler. Trap Do not credit Binet with the IQ formula: Alfred Binet rejected a single global score and wanted a clinical descriptive profile. Stern wrote the ratio formula (1912); Lewis Terman put it into the Stanford-Binet (1916). Theories behind the tests Theorist Year Model One-liner Charles Spearman 1904 Two-factor: g + s All cognitive tests share a general factor g plus task-specific s . Spearman invented factor analysis for this (theory → method, not the reverse). L.L. Thurstone 1938 Primary Mental Abilities (7 PMAs) Verbal Comprehension, Word Fluency, Number, Spatial, Memory, Perceptual Speed, Reasoning. Rejected a single g . Raymond Cattell & John Horn 1966 Gf-Gc Fluid intelligence (Gf, novel reasoning) vs Crystallized (Gc, accumulated knowledge). Gf peaks early adulthood, Gc rises lifelong. Philip E. Vernon 1950 Hierarchical g → v:ed (verbal-educational) + k:m (spatial-mechanical) → minor group factors → specific. J.P. Guilford 1967 Structure of Intellect (SOI) 5 operations × 6 products × 5 contents = 150 abilities ; later expanded to 180 . Introduced divergent vs convergent thinking. Howard Gardner 1983 ( Frames of Mind ) Multiple Intelligences Linguistic, Logical-Mathematical, Musical, Bodily-Kinesthetic, Spatial, Interpersonal, Intrapersonal (7). Naturalist added 1995 → 8. Existential proposed, not confirmed. Robert Sternberg 1985 Triarchic (later Successful Intelligence, 1996) Analytical (componential), Creative (experiential), Practical (contextual). PASS / WICS extensions later. McGrew / Schneider / Carroll 1993 / 1997 / 2018 Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) Integrative hierarchical model: stratum III general factor → 16+ broad abilities (stratum II) → 80+ narrow (stratum I). Underlies WJ-IV, KABC-II, DAS-II. Peter Salovey & John Mayer 1990 / 1997 Four-Branch EI Perceiving, Using, Understanding, Managing emotions. Coined “EI” academically first. Measured by MSCEIT (2002). Daniel Goleman 1995 Emotional Intelligence (popular) 5 domains: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills. Trap Howard Gardner = 8 on Indian exams (7 original + Naturalist 1995); “9” (with Existential) is usually wrong. Charles Spearman invented factor analysis (1904). Guilford SOI = 150 then 180. Cattell appears thrice: 16PF (1949), CFIT (1949), and Gf-Gc with Horn (1966). 6. Stanford-Binet family Origin: Binet-Simon (1905, France) Authors: Alfred Binet & Théodore Simon, commissioned by the French Ministry of Public Instruction to identify children needing special schooling. Year: 1905 (original 30-item graded-difficulty scale, “follow a light” up to “abstract definitions”), revised 1908 (introduced mental age) and 1911 . Did NOT yield IQ. Binet wanted a clinical descriptive profile, not a single number. Stanford revisions (the IQ-formula era) 1916 — Stanford-Binet 1st edition. Lewis M. Terman, Stanford. First English adaptation; ~90 items. Adopted Stern’s ratio IQ = (MA/CA) × 100, mean ≈ 100. Age 2–adult. 1937 — SB-LM (2nd ed.). Terman & Maud Merrill. Two equivalent forms L and M. Still ratio IQ. 1960 — SB-LM revised (3rd ed.). Terman & Merrill. Switched to deviation IQ (Pinneau tables), M = 100, SD = 16 . 1986 — SB-IV (4th ed.). Thorndike, Hagen & Sattler. Hierarchical structure, 4 area scores (Verbal Reasoning, Abstract/Visual Reasoning, Quantitative Reasoning, Short-Term Memory), 15 subtests. Age 2–adult. 2003 — SB-5 (current). Gale H. Roid, Riverside. SD changed to 15 to align with Wechsler. Age range 2–85+. SB-5 structure (the version exam-writers mean today) 10 subtests, 5 factors × 2 domains. 5 factors: Fluid Reasoning (FR), Knowledge (KN), Quantitative Reasoning (QR), Visual-Spatial Processing (VS), Working Memory (WM) — same names across both domains. 2 domains: Verbal (5 subtests) and Nonverbal (5 subtests); each factor has one verbal + one nonverbal subtest. 3 IQ scores: Full-Scale IQ (FSIQ), Verbal IQ (VIQ), Nonverbal IQ (NVIQ). All M = 100, SD = 15. Routing subtests: Object Series/Matrices (nonverbal) and Vocabulary (verbal) set entry difficulty. Admin time: ~45–75 min full; 15–20 min abbreviated. 7. Wechsler family David Wechsler (Bellevue Hospital, NY) built his scales to fix two SB problems: it was age-stratified and clunky for adults, and ratio IQ broke down past 16. His fixes were the deviation IQ (1939) and a point-scale structure where every adult takes the same subtests. Three age bands: WPPSI (Preschool & Primary), ages 2:6–7:7, current WPPSI-IV. Lineage: 1967 → WPPSI-R 1989 → WPPSI-III 2002 → WPPSI-IV 2012 . WISC (Children), ages 6:0–16:11, current WISC-V. Lineage: 1949 → WISC-R 1974 → WISC-III 1991 → WISC-IV 2003 → WISC-V 2014 US (2016 UK, 2019 India). WAIS (Adult), ages 16:0–90:11, current WAIS-IV. Lineage: Wechsler-Bellevue I 1939 (11 subtests, first deviation IQ) → W-B II 1946 → WAIS 1955 → WAIS-R 1981 → WAIS-III 1997 (added Processing Speed, 4-index structure) → WAIS-IV 2008 → WAIS-5 2024 (rolling out; exams still default to WAIS-IV). High-yield All Wechsler FSIQ & index scores: M = 100, SD = 15. All subtest scaled scores: M = 10, SD = 3, range 1–19 . WAIS-IV (the canonical adult answer) Age range: 16:0–90:11. Total subtests: 15 (10 core + 5 supplemental). FSIQ derived from the 10 core subtests. Admin ~60–90 min. 4 index scores: Verbal Comprehension (VCI), Perceptual Reasoning (PRI), Working Memory (WMI), Processing Speed (PSI). Index Subtests (core bold, supplemental italic) VCI Similarities, Vocabulary, Information , Comprehension PRI Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, Visual Puzzles , Figure Weights, Picture Completion WMI Digit Span, Arithmetic , Letter-Number Sequencing PSI Symbol Search, Coding , Cancellation WISC-V (the children’s scale) Age range: 6:0–16:11. Total subtests: 21 (10 primary + 11 secondary, including 5 complementary scored separately). 5 primary indices: Verbal Comprehension (VCI), Visual Spatial (VSI), Fluid Reasoning (FRI), Working Memory (WMI), Processing Speed (PSI). 5 ancillary indices: Quantitative Reasoning (QRI), Auditory Working Memory (AWMI), Nonverbal (NVI), General Ability (GAI), Cognitive Proficiency (CPI). 5 complementary subtests (CHC narrow abilities): Naming Speed Literacy, Naming Speed Quantity, Immediate Symbol Translation, Delayed Symbol Translation, Recognition Symbol Translation. Index Primary subtests VCI Similarities, Vocabulary VSI Block Design, Visual Puzzles FRI Matrix Reasoning, Figure Weights WMI Digit Span, Picture Span PSI Coding, Symbol Search Secondary subtests: Information, Comprehension, Picture Concepts, Arithmetic, Letter-Number Sequencing, Cancellation. Trap WAIS-IV has 4 indices (VCI/PRI/WMI/PSI); WISC-V has 5 (VCI/VSI/FRI/WMI/PSI). The WISC-IV → WISC-V change was splitting old PRI into VSI + FRI . WPPSI-IV (the preschool scale) Age range: 2:6–7:7, split into two batteries. Ages 2:6–3:11: 7 subtests, 3 primary indices (VCI, VSI, WMI) — no FRI/PSI yet (abilities not differentiated). Ages 4:0–7:7: 15 subtests, 5 primary indices (VCI, VSI, FRI, WMI, PSI) — same structure as WISC-V. Primary subtests: Information, Similarities, Block Design, Object Assembly, Matrix Reasoning, Picture Concepts, Picture Memory, Zoo Locations, Bug Search, Cancellation. 8. Raven’s Progressive Matrices Author: John C. Raven. Years: SPM published 1938 (developed 1936), CPM 1947, APM 1943. Nature: nonverbal, multiple-choice, pattern-completion; targets Charles Spearman’s g via eductive (meaning-extracting) reasoning . “Culture-fair”: commonly so described because items are abstract shapes, but cultural loading persists (paper-pencil familiarity, formal schooling). “Culture-reduced” is the more honest phrasing. Used widely in cross-cultural research and India. Version Items Sets Age / use Standard (SPM) 60 5 sets (A, B, C, D, E) × 12 Ages 6–80+, general population Coloured (CPM) 36 3 sets (A, A b , B) × 12 Ages 5–11, elderly, intellectually disabled Advanced (APM) 36 scored + 12 practice (Set I) Set I (12 practice) + Set II (36 scored) Above-average adolescents/adults; SPM ceiling effect Trap SPM = 60, CPM = 36, APM scored = 36 (do not count the 12 practice). The shared 36 on CPM and APM is the classic swap on Indian PG papers. 9. Kaufman, Cattell CFIT & special-purpose scales Kaufman family Authors: Alan S. & Nadeen L. Kaufman. K-ABC (1983) → KABC-II (2004) , ages 3:0–18:11. Built on Alexander Luria’s neuropsychological model (simultaneous + sequential processing); KABC-II added CHC interpretation . Yields two global scores: Mental Processing Index (MPI) for Luria-style use and Fluid-Crystallized Index (FCI) for CHC-style use. 5 scales: Sequential, Simultaneous, Planning, Learning, Knowledge. Designed to reduce verbal/cultural loading and assess minority/ESL children fairly. KAIT (1993): ages 11–85, 10 subtests, separates Fluid vs Crystallized IQ explicitly. KBIT-2 (2004): 2 subtests (Verbal Knowledge + Matrices), ~20 min screen. Trap The original K-ABC (1983) was pure Luria; KABC-II (2004) yields two indices (MPI + FCI) because it supports both Luria and CHC. Cattell’s Culture Fair Intelligence Test (CFIT) Author: Raymond B. Cattell. Year: first 1949, revised 1973. Purpose: measure fluid intelligence (Gf) per Gf-Gc theory with reduced cultural/language loading. 3 scales: Scale 1 (ages 4–8 and ID adults, 8 subtests), Scale 2 (ages 8–13 and average adults, 4 subtests), Scale 3 (ages 14+ and above-average adults, 4 subtests). Scales 2 & 3 subtests (same 4): Series, Classifications, Matrices, Conditions (Topology). Forms A + B for retest. Original M = 100, SD = 24; renormed editions use SD 15 or 16. Special-purpose & nonverbal scales Leiter International Performance Scale — Russell G. Leiter, 1936 → Leiter-R 1997 → Leiter-3 2013 . Fully nonverbal, no language; for deaf, ASD, non-English speakers. Ages 3–75+. Goodenough Draw-A-Man (Florence Goodenough, 1926) → Goodenough-Harris Drawing Test (Harris, 1963) . Children draw a man (and woman + self in Harris); scored on 64–73 body-detail criteria. Ages 3–15. Drawing-based IQ estimate. Slosson Intelligence Test (SIT, 1963; SIT-R3, 2002) — brief individual screen. Differential Ability Scales (DAS-II, Elliott, 2007) — ages 2:6–17:11, CHC-aligned, popular for LD identification. Woodcock-Johnson Cognitive (WJ-IV, 2014) — explicitly CHC; ages 2–90+; GIA + 9 CHC broad abilities. CTONI-2 (Hammill et al., 2009), UNIT-2 (Bracken & McCallum, 2016), WRIT (Glutting et al., 2000), RIAS-2 (Reynolds & Kamphaus, 2015). 10. Group & infant/developmental scales Army tests (WWI) Army Alpha (1917): chaired by Robert M. Yerkes (APA president) with Otis, Lewis Terman, Edward Thorndike, Henry Goddard, Bingham, Whipple. 212 items across 8 subtests (Oral Directions, Arithmetic Problems, Practical Judgment, Synonym-Antonym, Disarranged Sentences, Number Series Completion, Analogies, Information). For literate, English-speaking recruits. Army Beta (1917): same Yerkes committee. 7 subtests (Maze, Cube Analysis, X-O Series, Digit Symbol, Number Checking, Pictorial Completion, Geometrical Construction). For illiterate / non-English recruits; administered via pantomime. Trap Army Alpha = 8 subtests, Army Beta = 7 , Bhatia = 5 . Yerkes was the chair (not Lewis Terman, who was a member but is tied to Stanford-Binet 1916). Other group tests Otis Self-Administering Tests of Mental Ability (Arthur S. Otis, 1922) — civilian descendant of Army Alpha. → OLSAT (current K–12 screen). Wonderlic Personnel Test (1937) — 50 items, 12 minutes , employment screen (famous for NFL combine use). MAB-II (Jackson, 1998) — group-administrable Wechsler-style. Plus CTMM, Henmon-Nelson, CogAT. Infant & developmental scales Bayley Scales of Infant Development (BSID) — Nancy Bayley: BSID-I 1969, BSID-II 1993, Bayley-III 2006 , Bayley-4 2019. Ages 1–42 months . Bayley-III has 5 scales: Cognitive, Language (Receptive + Expressive), Motor (Fine + Gross), Social-Emotional, Adaptive Behavior. Gesell Developmental Schedules — Arnold Gesell, 1940s. Ages 4 weeks–6 years. 5 fields: Adaptive, Gross Motor, Fine Motor, Language, Personal-Social. Yields Developmental Quotient (DQ) = (DA / CA) × 100 . Cattell Infant Intelligence Scale (Psyche Cattell, 1940) — downward extension of Stanford-Binet, ages 2–30 months. Brunet-Lézine (1951) French infant scale; Mullen Scales of Early Learning (1995) birth–68 months; Denver Developmental Screening Test (DDST 1967, Denver-II 1992) screening, ages 0–6. Trap Bayley-III = 1–42 months (not just infants). Gesell to 6 years. Cattell Infant Scale 2–30 months. Stanford-Binet starts at 2. 11. Indian intelligence tests High-yield High-yield for both MET and NIMHANS. Memorize the author-year-count quadruple for each. Bhatia’s Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence Author: Chandra Mohan Bhatia. Year: 1955. Age: originally 11–16, extended to early adulthood. 5 subtests: (1) Koh’s Block Design (10 designs), (2) Alexander’s Pass-Along (8 problems), (3) Pattern Drawing (8 designs), (4) Immediate Memory (digits forward + backward + sentence repetition), (5) Picture Construction (5 pictures). Use: built for the Indian context; performance (nonverbal) orientation suits illiterate and rural populations. Trap Bhatia having 5 subtests is a chronic MCQ trap. The Pass-Along is Alexander’s (1932) , incorporated into Bhatia’s battery — do not say “Bhatia Pass-Along.” Bhatia is 1955 , not 1949 (1949 = WISC and CFIT; 1955 = WAIS and Bhatia). Other Indian instruments Binet-Kamat Test (BKT) — V.V. Kamat, 1934 (Marathi; later Kannada). Ages 3–22, ~80 age-graded tasks. Still used in NIMHANS clinical IQ estimation for Indian children. Malin’s Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC) — Arthur J. Malin, 1969. Ages 6–15. Indian adaptation of WISC (the 1949 original, not WISC-R). 11 subtests. Seguin Form Board — Edouard Seguin (1907 origin), used in India ages 3–7. Nonverbal performance, 10 cut-outs; measures speed of visual-motor coordination. Often misattributed to Indian authors. Mohsin General Intelligence Test (S.M. Mohsin, 1959) — verbal group test, Hindi. Jalota’s Group Test of General Mental Ability (S. Jalota, 1972) — verbal, ages 13+, 100 items. Developmental Screening Test (DST) — Bharath Raj, 1977, ages 0–15. Vineland Social Maturity Scale, Indian adaptation — A.J. Malin, 1965 (Indian Social Quotient). 12. IQ classification & intellectual disability Wechsler IQ classification (current WAIS-IV / WISC-V) IQ range Classification % of population ≥ 130 Very Superior / Extremely High ~2.2% 120–129 Superior / Very High ~6.7% 110–119 High Average ~16.1% 90–109 Average ~50% 80–89 Low Average ~16.1% 70–79 Borderline / Low ~6.7% < 70 Extremely Low (formerly “Mental Retardation”) ~2.2% Intellectual disability severity (DSM-5 / ICD-11) Severity IQ (approx) Profile Mild 50–69 ~85% of ID; academics to ~6th grade; often community-independent with support Moderate 35–49 ~10%; basic communication, supervised work, some self-care Severe 20–34 ~3–4%; limited speech, support for ADLs Profound < 20 ~1–2%; fully dependent Trap DSM-5 downplays IQ cutoffs in favour of adaptive functioning across conceptual, social, and practical domains. The IQ bands are pedagogical, not hard cutoffs. 13. Objective (self-report) personality tests Definition Objective tests use structured items (true/false, Likert, forced-choice) with fixed scoring keys. MCQ-writers attack this area four ways: (1) swap the item count between two tests, (2) swap author/year, (3) ask which scale belongs to which test, (4) ask projective vs objective. Lock the quadruple test → items → scales → author/year cold. MMPI family (Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory) MMPI (original, 1943): Starke R. Hathaway (psychologist) & J. Charnley McKinley (psychiatrist), Univ. of Minnesota. 566 true/false items (550 unique + 16 repeats). Method = empirical criterion-keying : items retained only if they discriminated a diagnostic group from normals, not by face validity — the breakthrough versus older content-based inventories. Norms = “Minnesota normals” (724 hospital visitors), later criticised as a narrow white rural Midwest base, driving the MMPI-2 restandardisation. Clinical cutoff originally T ≥ 70. MMPI-2 (1989 restandardisation; the default version exam-writers mean): 567 true/false items. Age 18+, 6th-grade reading level, 60–90 min. Scored as T-scores (M 50, SD 10) ; clinically significant elevation T ≥ 65 . MMPI-2-RF (2008, Ben-Porath & Tellegen): 338 items; 9 Restructured Clinical (RC) scales + demoralization (RCd) + higher-order scales; common variance of demoralization pulled out so each RC scale is more specific. MMPI-3 (2020, Ben-Porath & Tellegen): 335 items, new norms, 52 scales (H-O, RC, Specific Problem, PSY-5). MMPI-A (adolescent, 1992, Butcher et al.): 478 items, ages 14–18; MMPI-A-RF (2016, 241 items). 10 clinical scales (memorize order; 5 and 0 are the supplementary ones): # Code Name Picks up 1 Hs Hypochondriasis Bodily preoccupation, somatic complaints 2 D Depression Sadness, hopelessness, low morale 3 Hy Hysteria Conversion features, somatic + denial 4 Pd Psychopathic Deviate Authority conflict, antisocial features 5 Mf Masculinity-Femininity Gender-role interest pattern 6 Pa Paranoia Suspiciousness, ideas of reference 7 Pt Psychasthenia Anxiety, obsessional rumination, doubt 8 Sc Schizophrenia Bizarre thought, alienation 9 Ma Hypomania Elevated mood, overactivity, grandiosity 0 Si Social Introversion Social withdrawal vs sociability Validity scales (the L/F/K triad is the high-yield bit): ? (Cannot Say): count of unanswered items; > 30 omissions invalidates the profile. L (Lie): 15 items detecting naive “faking good” (impossibly virtuous claims). High L = unsophisticated impression management. F (Infrequency): 60 items rarely endorsed by normals. High F = random responding, malingering, OR genuine severe pathology (cannot distinguish without more evidence). K (Correction): 30 items measuring subtle defensiveness; added as a correction to 5 clinical scales (1, 4, 7, 8, 9). VRIN (variable inconsistency → random responding), TRIN (all-true/all-false bias), F B (back F — fatigue on later items), F p (F-psychopathology — separates malingering from genuine pathology among inpatients). Interpretation: all scales plotted on one graph in T-units; clinicians read code types (e.g. 2-7/7-2 = anxious-depressed; 4-9 = antisocial acting-out). Single-scale interpretation is discouraged. Trap MMPI-2 = 567 items, 10 clinical scales (Hs D Hy Pd Mf Pa Pt Sc Ma Si), L/F/K validity, T-scores M50/SD10, cutoff T ≥ 65. Don’t confuse with 16PF’s 16 factors or its Sten scores. L = naive faking-good, F = exaggeration/random/severe, K = subtle defensiveness — don’t swap. 16PF (Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire) Author: Raymond B. Cattell (with Tatsuoka & Eber later). Year: 1st ed. 1949; current 5th Edition 1993 . Items: 185 (5th ed.); each 3-choice (agree / ? / disagree), except the reasoning subtest (forced-choice). Age 16+, 35–50 min. Construction: factor analysis of the lexicon — Cattell took Gordon Allport & Henry Odbert’s ~4500 trait words, reduced to ~160 surface traits, factor-analysed to 16 source traits . Scoring: raw → Sten scores (M 5.5, SD 2, range 1–10): 1–3 low pole, 4–7 average, 8–10 high pole. 5 global factors (second-order, close to Big Five): Extraversion, Anxiety, Tough-Mindedness, Independence, Self-Control. Validity indices: Impression Management (IM), Acquiescence (ACQ), Infrequency (INF). Use: normal-population assessment for selection (I/O), career, couples/family counselling. Not a clinical screen. Code Low pole ↔ High pole Code Low pole ↔ High pole A Reserved ↔ Warm M Grounded ↔ Abstracted B Concrete ↔ Abstract reasoning N Forthright ↔ Private C Reactive ↔ Emotionally stable O Self-assured ↔ Apprehensive E Deferential ↔ Dominant Q1 Traditional ↔ Open to change F Serious ↔ Lively Q2 Group-oriented ↔ Self-reliant G Expedient ↔ Rule-conscious Q3 Tolerates disorder ↔ Perfectionistic H Shy ↔ Socially bold Q4 Relaxed ↔ Tense I Utilitarian ↔ Sensitive L Trusting ↔ Vigilant Trap 16PF is NOT the Big Five. 16PF = Raymond Cattell, 185 items, 16 primary + 5 globals, Sten scores. Big Five (OCEAN) = Paul Costa & Robert McCrae (NEO). Gordon Allport & Henry Odbert’s ~4500 trait words is the lexical starting point Cattell factor-analysed — a common stem. NEO Personality Inventory (Five-Factor Model) Authors: Paul T. Costa Jr. & Robert R. McCrae (NIH/National Institute on Aging). Lineage: NEO-PI 1985 → NEO-PI-R 1992 → NEO-PI-3 2010 . Items: 240 (NEO-PI-R / NEO-PI-3), 5-point Likert, 8 items × 30 facets. Short form NEO-FFI / NEO-FFI-3 = 60 items (5 domains only, no facets). Age: 17+ (NEO-PI-3 extended to 12). Forms S (self) and R (observer). Scoring: raw → T-scores; no classic validity scales (assumes honest responding). Dominant trait model in academic psychology since the 1990s. Use: research, occupational selection, therapy planning. Domain 6 facets O — Openness Fantasy, Aesthetics, Feelings, Actions, Ideas, Values C — Conscientiousness Competence, Order, Dutifulness, Achievement Striving, Self-Discipline, Deliberation E — Extraversion Warmth, Gregariousness, Assertiveness, Activity, Excitement-Seeking, Positive Emotions A — Agreeableness Trust, Straightforwardness, Altruism, Compliance, Modesty, Tender-Mindedness N — Neuroticism Anxiety, Angry Hostility, Depression, Self-Consciousness, Impulsiveness, Vulnerability Mnemonic Big Five = OCEAN . NEO has 5 domains × 6 facets = 30 facets . NEO-PI-R/3 = 240 items; NEO-FFI = 60 — don’t confuse long and short forms. EPQ / EPQ-R (Eysenck Personality Questionnaire) Authors: Hans J. & Sybil B.G. Eysenck. Lineage: Maudsley Medical Q (1952) → Maudsley Personality Inventory (MPI, 1959) → Eysenck Personality Inventory (EPI, 1964) → EPQ (1975) → EPQ-R (1985) → EPQ-R Short (1992). Items: EPQ 90; EPQ-R 100 ; Short 48. Yes/No. Age adult; Junior EPQ ages 7–15. PEN dimensions: P — Psychoticism (tough-mindedness, aggression, low empathy; added 1975, the EPI→EPQ move), E — Extraversion (sociability, impulsivity), N — Neuroticism (emotional reactivity), plus L — Lie (social desirability). Biological anchor: Extraversion ↔ cortical arousal (introverts higher baseline), Neuroticism ↔ limbic/ANS reactivity, Psychoticism ↔ dopaminergic function. Eysenck = biology of personality (common MCQ pairing). MBTI (Myers-Briggs Type Indicator) Authors: Katharine Cook Briggs & daughter Isabel Briggs Myers, built on Carl Jung’s Psychological Types (1921). Year: first 1944, commercial 1962 (ETS); current Form M (1998) . Items: Form M = 93 forced-choice ; Form Q = 144 (adds 20 facets); Form G (older) 126. Age 14+. 4 dichotomies → 16 types: E/I (energy direction), S/N (information style), T/F (decision style), J/P (lifestyle/outer-world orientation), e.g. INTJ. Critical: scores are categorical (discrete types), NOT dimensional — the main psychometric criticism. Traits are normally distributed; dichotomisation throws away information; ~50% of takers get a different type on retest within weeks. Use: career counselling, team building, coaching. NOT for clinical diagnosis or selection. MET contrast: “Which test claims discrete types instead of continuous traits?” → MBTI. CPI (California Psychological Inventory) Author: Harrison Gough. Year: 1957 → CPI-434 (1996) → CPI-260 short. Items: 434 / 260, true-false. Scales: 20 “folk-concept” scales (Dominance, Sociability, Empathy, Independence…) under 4 themes (Interpersonal, Self-management, Achievement, Personal Style) + 3 vector scales. Use: explicitly normal populations — the non-clinical complement to MMPI (selection, counselling, leadership). Trap CPI = normal populations (Gough’s “folk concepts”); MMPI = clinical populations. Easy to swap. Other objective inventories on the MET radar Test Items Author / Year What it does PAI (Personality Assessment Inventory) 344, 4-point Leslie Morey, 1991 22 non-overlapping scales (4 validity, 11 clinical, 5 treatment, 2 interpersonal). MMPI’s main rival. HPI (Hogan Personality Inventory) 206 Robert Hogan, 1986 7 primary scales mapped to Big Five for workplace use. MCMI-IV (Millon Clinical Multiaxial) 195, T/F Theodore Millon, 2015 (orig. 1977) 14 personality-disorder + 10 clinical-syndrome scales, DSM-aligned. HEXACO-PI-R 200 (60 brief) Ashton & Lee, 2004 6 factors: Honesty-Humility, Emotionality, eXtraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Openness. 14. Projective tests Definition Projective tests present ambiguous stimuli on the hypothesis that the subject projects unconscious needs, conflicts, and defenses onto them. Less structured scoring, weaker psychometrics, richer clinical material than objective tests. Rorschach Inkblot Test Author: Hermann Rorschach (Swiss psychiatrist). Year: Psychodiagnostik , 1921 (died 1922 at 37, before refining the system). Stimuli: 10 inkblot cards. 5 achromatic (black/grey: I, IV, V, VI, VII), 2 black + red (II, III), 3 fully chromatic (VIII, IX, X). Shorthand: “5 chromatic + 5 achromatic.” Administration: (1) Free Association / Response phase (“What might this be?”); (2) Inquiry phase (where on the blot, and what features — form, colour, shading, movement — made it look that way). Exner Comprehensive System (1974), dominant until 2011: Location: W (whole), D (common detail), Dd (unusual detail), S (white space). Determinants: F (form), M (human movement), FM (animal movement), m (inanimate movement); C (pure colour), FC (form-dominated colour), CF (colour-dominated form); C′ (achromatic colour), T (texture), V (vista), Y (diffuse shading); FD (form-dimension), (2) (pair), r (reflection). Content: H, Hd, A, Ad, An, Bl, Sx, Xy… Popularity: P (common response, e.g. bat/butterfly on card V). Form quality: +, o, u, −. Indices: Erlebnistypus (EB) = M : sum-C (Introversive vs Extratensive vs Ambitent); Lambda (L) = pure-form ratio (high = constricted/defensive); Egocentricity Index = (reflections + pairs)/R; SCZI, DEPI, CDI, S-CON. R-PAS (2011): Meyer, Viglione, Mihura, Erard & Erdberg. Updates Exner norms, drops weak indices, standardises response count (R-Optimised). Increasingly the research standard, but MET still tests Exner. Trap Rorschach = 10 inkblots (not 12, 15, or 20). Determinant trick: FC = form-dominated colour vs CF = colour-dominated. TAT (Thematic Apperception Test) Authors: Henry A. Murray & Christiana D. Morgan, Harvard Psychological Clinic. Year: 1935 (manual 1943). Stimuli: 31 picture cards total — 30 black-and-white ambiguous scenes + 1 blank. 20 cards administered per subject , selected by age (adult/child) and sex (M/F); cards coded e.g. 3BM = card 3 for Boys + Men. Procedure: subject makes up a story for each picture — what led up, what is happening, what characters think/feel, how it ends. Recorded verbatim. Theory: projective hypothesis — subject projects dominant needs (achievement, affiliation, power) and perceived environmental press . Built on Murray’s needs-press theory (Explorations in Personality, 1938). Scoring systems: Murray’s original (code needs + press); SCORS (Westen, 1985, 8 object-relations dimensions); Defense Mechanism Manual (Cramer); David McClelland’s nAch scoring. Indian adaptation: Indian TAT by Uma Choudhury (1960) , culture-adapted scenes. Trap TAT = 31 cards total, 20 administered (not 10, not 20 total). Theory = needs-press . Indian TAT = Uma Choudhury 1960. Other projective tests Test Stimulus Author / Year What it scores CAT (Children’s Apperception Test) 10 animal cards (CAT-A) or 10 human (CAT-H) Leopold & Sonya Bellak, 1949 TAT for children 3–10; animals because young children identify more easily. SAT (Senior Apperception Test) 16 cards Bellak & Bellak, 1973 TAT for older adults — loneliness, dependency, illness. Rosenzweig Picture-Frustration (P-F) 24 cartoon frustration scenes Saul Rosenzweig, 1944 Direction of aggression (extra-/intro-/im-punitive) × type (obstacle-dominance, ego-defense, need-persistence). Holtzman Inkblot Technique (HIT) 45 inkblot cards, 1 response each Wayne Holtzman, 1961 Psychometrically tighter Rorschach alternative (better reliability, parallel forms A & B). Rotter Incomplete Sentences Blank (RISB) 40 sentence stems Julian Rotter, 1950 “I wish…,” “My mother…”; scored for adjustment on a 0–6 scale. Draw-A-Person (DAP / Machover) Draw a person, then opposite sex Karen Machover, 1949 Body image, self-concept. (Goodenough-Harris DAP scores cognitive maturity.) House-Tree-Person (HTP) Draw house, tree, person John Buck, 1948 Combined personality + cognitive screen; symbolic interpretation. Kinetic Family Drawing (KFD) “Draw your family doing something” Burns & Kaufman, 1970 Family dynamics, interaction style. Bender-Visual Motor Gestalt (BVMGT / BG-II) Copy 9 designs (original) / 16 (BG-II) Lauretta Bender, 1938; BG-II 2003 (Brannigan & Decker) Visual-motor maturity; organic brain dysfunction screen. Word Association Test Stimulus words; respond with first word Francis Galton 1879 → Carl Jung 1904–06 → Kent-Rosanoff 1910 Reaction-time anomalies signal “complexes.” Jung’s original projective method. Szondi Test 48 photos of psychiatric patients, sorted by liking Léopold Szondi, 1947 Genetically-driven drive needs. Largely historical. Trap Rosenzweig P-F scores aggression direction × type, NOT needs-press (that’s TAT). HIT = 45 cards, 1 response each, built to fix Rorschach’s reliability. CAT = Bellak 1949, 10 cards. 15. Adjustment, clinical & Indian inventories Beck inventories (all by Aaron T. Beck, Univ. of Pennsylvania; share the 0–3 Likert skeleton) BDI / BDI-II: BDI 1961 (Aaron Beck, Ward, Mendelson, Mock, Erbaugh); BDI-II 1996, 21 items, 0–3 each, total 0–63 , past 2 weeks. Revised to match DSM-IV (added agitation, worthlessness, concentration; removed body image, work difficulty, weight loss, somatic preoccupation). Cutoffs: 0–13 minimal, 14–19 mild, 20–28 moderate, 29–63 severe. 5th–6th-grade reading. Screening/severity, not diagnostic alone. BAI (Beck Anxiety Inventory, 1988): 21 items, 0–3, total 0–63 , past week. Cutoffs: 0–7 minimal, 8–15 mild, 16–25 moderate, 26–63 severe. Loads on somatic anxiety (sweating, dizziness, racing heart) to minimise overlap with depression. BHS (Beck Hopelessness Scale, 1974): 20 true/false items. Measures pessimism about the future; more predictive of eventual suicide than depression severity alone . Cutoff ≥ 9 = elevated risk. BSS / BSI (Beck Scale for Suicide Ideation, 1979 clinician / 1991 self-report): 21 items, 0–2 each. First 5 screen desire to live/die and active/passive ideation; if positive, complete remaining 14. BYI (Beck Youth Inventories, 2001/2005): ages 7–18; 5 scales × 20 items = 100 (Depression, Anxiety, Anger, Disruptive Behavior, Self-Concept). Also CBOCI (Clark-Beck OCD Inventory, 25 items) and Beck Self-Concept Test. Trap BDI-II = 21 items, 0–3, 0–63, past 2 weeks. BAI = 21 items, past week. BHS = 20 T/F. BSS = 21 items, 0–2. BHS (hopelessness) predicts suicide better than BDI severity. Bell’s Adjustment Inventory Author: Hugh M. Bell. Student form 1934, Adult form 1938; Indian adaptations by R.K. Ojha (Hindi) and others. Items: Student form 140 ; Adult form 160 . Yes/No/? format. Areas: Home, Health, Social, Emotional (Student form = 4); Adult form adds Occupational (5). Higher score = poorer adjustment; brackets labelled excellent / good / average / unsatisfactory / very unsatisfactory. Use: screening in school/college counselling, common in Indian masters dissertations (why it persists on MET). Other Indian / adjustment inventories Test Items Author / Year What it does Mooney Problem Check List 288 (adult), 330 (college) Mooney & Gordon, 1950 11 problem areas (Health, Finances, Social…); popular in Indian school-counselling research. Sinha’s Anxiety Scale (SAS) / Comprehensive Anxiety Test (SCAT) 90 A.K.P. & L.N.K. Sinha Indian-normed adult anxiety scale, common in Indian dissertations. Saxena’s Adjustment Inventory ~60 D.N. Saxena Indian school-counselling adjustment scale, sometimes paired with Bell’s. 16. Aptitude, attitude & interest scales Aptitude batteries DAT (Differential Aptitude Test): 8 subtests (Verbal, Numerical, Abstract, Mechanical, Space, Spelling, Language, Perceptual). Bennett, Seashore, Wesman. GATB (General Aptitude Test Battery): nine aptitudes, US Employment Service. Attitude scales Thurstone (1928): equal-appearing intervals; judges scale items 1–11. Likert (1932): summated rating, typically 5-point. Guttman (1944): cumulative — endorsing a stronger item implies endorsing weaker ones. Bogardus: social distance. Osgood semantic differential: bipolar adjectives, 3 factors (evaluation, potency, activity). Interest inventories Strong Interest Inventory: Holland themes (RIASEC) + occupational scales. Kuder Career Search: forced-choice triads. Holland Self-Directed Search: RIASEC = Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising, Conventional. 17. Psychiatric & cognitive rating scales Memorize what each measures and whether it is clinician-rated or self-rated. Scale Measures Type / items BDI-II Depression Self, 21 items HAM-D / HDRS Depression Clinician, 17–21 items MADRS Depression Clinician, 10 items PHQ-9 Depression Self, 9 items BAI Anxiety Self, 21 items HAM-A Anxiety Clinician, 14 items GAD-7 Anxiety Self, 7 items Y-BOCS OCD severity (gold standard) Clinician, 10 items PANSS Schizophrenia (positive + negative) Clinician, 30 items BPRS Brief psychiatric symptoms Clinician, 18 items YMRS Mania Clinician, 11 items MMSE Cognitive screening (general) 30 points, cutoff 23–24 MoCA Mild cognitive impairment 30 points, cutoff 25, more sensitive than MMSE C-SSRS Suicide severity Clinician/interview CAPS-5 PTSD Clinician AUDIT Alcohol use Self Trap Y-BOCS = OCD specifically (not anxiety generally). PANSS = schizophrenia , positive + negative; BPRS is briefer/more general. MMSE = 30 points, cutoff 23–24 ; MoCA more sensitive for mild cognitive impairment. 18. Educational measurement basics Achievement = what you have learned, past (WIAT, school finals). Aptitude = what you can learn, future (DAT, SAT). Intelligence = general cognitive capacity (WAIS, SB). Norm-referenced: compare student to a peer group (ranking, selection). Criterion-referenced: compare to an absolute standard (mastery, licensing). Formative: during learning, low-stakes feedback. Summative: end of unit, high-stakes outcome. 19. Master reference tables & trap list Personality / projective item counts Test Items Author Year MMPI (original) 566 Hathaway & McKinley 1943 MMPI-2 567 Restandardisation team 1989 MMPI-2-RF 338 Ben-Porath & Tellegen 2008 MMPI-3 335 Ben-Porath & Tellegen 2020 MMPI-A 478 Butcher et al. 1992 16PF (5th) 185 Raymond Cattell 1993 NEO-PI-R / NEO-PI-3 240 Paul Costa & Robert McCrae 1992 / 2010 NEO-FFI-3 60 Costa & McCrae 2010 EPQ-R 100 H.J. & S.B.G. Eysenck 1985 MBTI Form M 93 Briggs & Myers 1998 CPI (full) 434 Gough 1957 / 1996 PAI 344 Morey 1991 MCMI-IV 195 Millon 2015 Bell’s Adjustment (student / adult) 140 / 160 Bell 1934 / 1938 BDI-II 21 Beck et al. 1996 BAI 21 Beck et al. 1988 BHS 20 Beck et al. 1974 BSS 21 Beck et al. 1979 / 1991 TAT 31 cards (20 admin) Murray & Morgan 1935 Rorschach 10 inkblots H. Rorschach 1921 CAT 10 cards Bellak 1949 HIT 45 inkblots Holtzman 1961 RISB 40 stems Julian Rotter 1950 Rosenzweig P-F 24 scenes Rosenzweig 1944 Bender-Gestalt 9 designs (BG-II: 16) Bender; BG-II Brannigan & Decker 1938 / 2003 Intelligence test cross-comparison Test Author Year Items / subtests Age Yields Binet-Simon Binet & Simon 1905 30 tasks 3–11 Mental Age (1908+) Stanford-Binet (1st) Lewis Terman 1916 ~90 items 2–adult Ratio IQ, M=100 Stanford-Binet 5 Roid 2003 10 subtests, 5 factors 2–85+ FSIQ/VIQ/NVIQ, M=100, SD=15 WAIS-IV Wechsler / Pearson 2008 15 (10 core + 5 supp) 16:0–90:11 FSIQ + 4 indices (VCI/PRI/WMI/PSI) WISC-V Wechsler / Pearson 2014 21 (10 primary + 11 secondary) 6:0–16:11 FSIQ + 5 indices (VCI/VSI/FRI/WMI/PSI) WPPSI-IV Wechsler / Pearson 2012 7 or 15 2:6–7:7 FSIQ + 3 or 5 indices SPM Raven 1938 60, 5 sets 6–80+ Nonverbal IQ / g CPM Raven 1947 36, 3 sets 5–11, elderly, ID Nonverbal IQ / g APM Raven 1943 12 (Set I) + 36 (Set II) High-IQ adolescents/adults Nonverbal IQ / g Bhatia’s Battery Bhatia 1955 5 subtests 11–16 (Indian) Performance IQ MISIC Malin 1969 11 subtests 6–15 Indian WISC IQ Binet-Kamat Kamat 1934 ~80 tasks 3–22 Indian Binet IQ CFIT R.B. Cattell 1949 3 scales (8/4/4) 4+ Fluid IQ (Gf) KABC-II A. & N. Kaufman 2004 5 scales 3:0–18:11 MPI (Luria) or FCI (CHC) KAIT A. & N. Kaufman 1993 10 subtests 11–85 Fluid + Crystallized IQ Army Alpha Yerkes et al. 1917 212 items, 8 subtests Literate recruits Group verbal IQ Army Beta Yerkes et al. 1917 7 subtests Illiterate recruits Group nonverbal IQ Wonderlic Wonderlic 1937 50 items, 12 min Adult employment IQ proxy Bayley-III Bayley 2006 5 scales 1–42 months Developmental indices Gesell Gesell 1940s 5 fields 4 wk–6 yr DQ = DA/CA × 100 Goodenough-Harris DAM Goodenough → Harris 1926 / 1963 ~73 details 3–15 Drawing IQ estimate Leiter-3 Leiter 2013 10 subtests 3–75+ Nonverbal IQ Numbers-only drill Number What it is 1905 / 1908 / 1912 / 1916 Binet-Simon / Mental Age / Stern ratio IQ / Stanford-Binet 1st (Lewis Terman) 1939 / 1949 / 1955 Wechsler-Bellevue (first deviation IQ) / WISC + CFIT / WAIS + Bhatia 1960 / 2003 SB switches to deviation IQ (SD 16) / SB-5 (SD 15) 60 / 36 / 36+12 SPM items / CPM items / APM (36 scored + 12 practice) 5 / 8 / 7 Bhatia subtests / Army Alpha subtests / Army Beta subtests 4 / 5 WAIS-IV indices / WISC-V primary indices (= SB-5 factors) 10 & 15 / 10 & 21 WAIS-IV core & total subtests / WISC-V primary & total subtests 7 / 8(+1) / 3 / 150–180 Thurstone PMAs / Gardner MI / Sternberg components / Guilford SOI cells 100/15 · 100/16 · 10/3 Wechsler FSIQ · old SB · Wechsler subtest scaled (M/SD) 50/10 · 5.5/2 · 5/2 · 50/12 T-score · Sten · Stanine · Wonderlic items/min Author + year speed drill (personality / projective) Hathaway & McKinley → MMPI (1943). Raymond Cattell → 16PF (1949). Paul Costa & Robert McCrae → NEO. Hans & Sybil Eysenck → EPI (1964), EPQ (1975), EPQ-R (1985). Briggs & Myers → MBTI (1944, commercial 1962). Gough → CPI (1957). Morey → PAI (1991). Millon → MCMI (1977, MCMI-IV 2015). Murray & Morgan → TAT (1935). Hermann Rorschach → Rorschach (1921). Bellak → CAT (1949). Holtzman → HIT (1961). Julian Rotter → RISB (1950). Rosenzweig → P-F (1944). Machover → DAP (1949). Buck → HTP (1948). Bender → Bender-Gestalt (1938). Hugh Bell → Bell’s Adjustment (1934/1938). Aaron Beck → BDI (1961), BHS (1974), BSS (1979), BAI (1988), BDI-II (1996). Uma Choudhury → Indian TAT (1960). High-yield The trap list to memorize cold: Validity ceiling = √reliability. Unreliable tests cannot be strongly valid. Negative discrimination index = mis-keyed item; discard. Cronbach alpha ≠ unidimensionality. Wechsler IQ SD = 15; old Stanford-Binet SD = 16; SB-5 (2003+) SD = 15. Stanine SD = 2, range 1–9. Sten (16PF) M 5.5, SD 2, range 1–10. T-score = 50/10. Predictive = future criterion; Concurrent = same-time. Face validity is weakest; content validity = expert judgment of domain coverage. Kappa is inter-rater, NOT internal consistency. KR-20 is for dichotomous items. MMPI-2 = 567 items, 10 clinical scales, L/F/K validity, T-scores, cutoff T ≥ 65. 16PF = 185 items, 16 factors + 5 globals, Sten, Cattell. NEO = 240 items, OCEAN, 30 facets, Costa & McCrae. NEO-FFI = 60. EPQ-R = 100 items, PEN + Lie; Psychoticism added 1975. MBTI = 16 types, 4 dichotomies, forced-choice, poor retest reliability. CPI = normal populations; MMPI = clinical. Rorschach = 10 inkblots (Exner → R-PAS 2011). TAT = 31 total, 20 admin, needs-press. CAT = Bellak 1949, 10 cards. HIT = 45 cards. Bell’s: Student 140 / 4 areas; Adult 160 / adds Occupational. Beck: BDI-II 21 (0–3, 0–63, 2 weeks); BAI 21 (1 week); BHS 20 T/F (best suicide predictor); BSS 21 (0–2). Indian: TAT = Uma Choudhury 1960; WISC adaptation = MISIC (Malin 1969); Bhatia Battery = C.M. Bhatia 1955 (5 subtests); Binet-Kamat = Kamat 1934. SPM = 60, CPM = 36, APM scored = 36. Bhatia = 5, Army Beta = 7, Army Alpha = 8 subtests. WAIS-IV = 4 indices; WISC-V = 5 (old PRI split into VSI + FRI). Ratio IQ = Stern 1912, applied by Lewis Terman 1916 (not Binet). Howard Gardner = 8 intelligences (Naturalist added 1995). Cattell appears thrice: 16PF, CFIT, Gf-Gc (with Horn). Y-BOCS = OCD; PANSS = schizophrenia; MMSE = 30 points, cutoff 23–24; MoCA more sensitive.

title: Therapy, Counselling & Ethics
text: Therapy, Counselling & Ethics One consolidated chapter for everything the MET / NIMHANS paper tests on treatment: the learning principles that behaviour therapy is built on, the major schools of psychotherapy & counselling (Sharf's frame, school by school, with the third-wave and integrative models folded in), the common therapeutic factors that cut across schools, and professional ethics . Each concept lives in exactly one place. The exam tests four moves: name the theory from its claim; pin the theory to its founder; pin the named technique to its theory; and tell rival theories apart, because that is where the distractor always hides. Learn every technique in its contrast pair . In this book Learning & conditioning: the foundation How to read any theory (the master frame) Psychodynamic approaches Humanistic & existential approaches Behavioural & cognitive approaches Constructivist, feminist & systemic approaches Third-wave, integrative & specialised models Group therapy (Yalom) Common factors & the therapeutic frame Indications quick-map (what to recommend) Professional ethics Master trap list, rosters & glossary High-yield The single most-tested skill is telling near-identical pairs apart: REBT (Ellis) vs Cognitive Therapy (Aaron Beck) , systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) vs flooding , ERP (OCD) vs EMDR (trauma) , cognitive triad (Beck) vs ABC (Albert Ellis) , DBT modules (4) vs ACT hexaflex (6) , and the four family-therapy founders (Bowen / Minuchin / Haley / Satir). And in learning: shaping vs chaining , fading vs extinction , VR vs VI , latent vs insight learning . Master these pairs and most of the section answers itself. 1. Learning & conditioning: the foundation of behaviour therapy Behaviour therapy is applied learning theory, so the vocabulary below is tested both as 1-mark definition traps and as the mechanism behind clinical techniques. Read this orientation once: classical (Pavlovian) conditioning is about stimulus pairings ; operant (Skinnerian) conditioning is about consequences shaping voluntary behaviour ; priming is about one stimulus making a later one easier to process ; and habituation / sensitization are non-associative (a single stimulus, no pairing). When a question mixes the families, the answer is almost always the term whose family matches the stem. Family Terms inside Classical (Pavlovian) phenomena Extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization, discrimination, habituation, sensitization Operant (Skinnerian) shaping tools Shaping, chaining, fading, prompting Operant reinforcement schedules FR, VR, FI, VI Cognitive / social learning Latent learning (Edward Tolman), insight learning (Wolfgang Köhler), observational learning (Albert Bandura) Implicit / cognitive priming Priming (semantic, perceptual, affective) 1.1 Operant shaping tools — shaping, chaining, fading, prompting Shaping (B. F. Skinner): reinforcing successive approximations of a target behaviour the organism does not yet emit . Train a rat to press a lever by reinforcing facing it, then approaching, then touching, then pressing. The defining feature is that the reinforcement criterion changes across trials . Clinically: skill acquisition, autism intervention. Chaining : linking a sequence of already-learned behaviours into a longer chain, where each behaviour is the discriminative stimulus (S D ) for the next and only the final link is reinforced (brushing teeth: pick up brush → wet → paste → brush → rinse → put away). Forward chaining teaches step 1 first; backward chaining teaches the last step first, so the learner always reaches the reinforcer at the natural endpoint (often preferred clinically). Used heavily in ABA / ADL skills training. Prompting : an added antecedent stimulus (verbal, gestural, physical, modelled, visual) that helps the learner emit the right response in the presence of the natural cue. Prompt hierarchy, most → least intrusive: physical → modelling → gestural → verbal → visual/positional . "Least-to-most" vs "most-to-least" prompting are classic vignette distractors. Fading : gradually removing the prompt while transferring stimulus control to the natural cue (teach "ball": full model "say ball" → partial "say buh…" → just holding up the ball). Trap Shaping vs chaining: shaping builds a new behaviour ; chaining links existing behaviours . Fading vs extinction: fading removes the prompt (an antecedent) and transfers stimulus control; extinction removes the reinforcer / UCS and eliminates the behaviour. Prompts are antecedents; reinforcement is a consequence — that distinction has been tested directly. 1.2 Classical conditioning phenomena Extinction : reduction and disappearance of a conditioned response when reinforcement (operant) or the UCS (classical) is no longer presented — Ivan Pavlov's dog stops salivating to the unpaired bell; the ignored tantrum fades. Watch for the extinction burst : a temporary increase in frequency/intensity right after reinforcement is withdrawn, before decline. Extinction does not erase learning. Spontaneous recovery : reappearance of a previously extinguished response after a rest period, with no new conditioning trials — proving extinction is suppression, not unlearning . The recovered response is typically weaker , and re-extinction is faster the second time (savings effect). Distinguish from reinstatement (re-emergence after UCS-alone presentation) and renewal (re-emergence in a new context). Generalization vs discrimination. Generalization = responding similarly to stimuli that resemble the CS / S D (Little Albert, conditioned by John B. Watson & Rosalie Rayner to fear a white rat, also feared a white rabbit, cotton wool, a Santa beard). The generalization gradient : response strength drops with distance from the original CS. Discrimination = responding only to the specific stimulus, taught by differential reinforcement (reinforce in presence of S D , withhold for S Δ ). One-liner: generalization is the default; discrimination is trained. Failure to discriminate underlies many phobias. Note: stimulus generalization (similar CS) ≠ response generalization (different responses to the same CS). 1.3 The four reinforcement schedules Schedule Definition Response pattern Classic example Trap Fixed Ratio (FR) Reinforcement after a fixed number of responses High rate, brief post-reinforcement pause , then burst; step-like record Factory piece-work, paid per 10 units (FR-10) Pause comes after the reinforcer; higher ratios = longer pauses; ratio strain if raised too fast Variable Ratio (VR) Reinforcement after an average number of responses (unpredictable) Highest, steadiest rate; almost no pause Slot machines, fishing, cold-calls — the gambling schedule Most resistant to extinction; "addictive / extremely hard to stop" → VR Fixed Interval (FI) Reinforcement for the first response after a fixed time Scallop — slow after reinforcement, accelerating as the interval ends Checking mail you know arrives at 11am; cramming before a weekly quiz Lowest overall rate of the four; time -based, not response-count (don't confuse with FR) Variable Interval (VI) Reinforcement for the first response after a variable time Steady, moderate rate; no scallop; resistant to extinction Checking phone for a text; pop quizzes Most steady rate. VR is most vigorous . Distinguish by "steady vs vigorous" Mnemonic Ratio = paid per response → high rates. Interval = paid per time → moderate rates. Variable = unpredictable → most resistant to extinction. Fixed = predictable → pause/scallop after reinforcement. Resistance to extinction: VR > VI > FR > FI > continuous (CRF). Continuous reinforcement learns fastest but extinguishes fastest (partial-reinforcement extinction effect). 1.4 Cognitive & social learning Latent learning (Edward Tolman): learning that occurs without reinforcement and without immediate behavioural expression , showing up later once reinforcement appears — proving learning ≠ performance. Tolman & Honzik (1930) rats: a group unreinforced for 10 days, then reinforced from day 11, immediately outperformed the always-reinforced group on day 12. Buzzword: cognitive map (Tolman, 1948, "Cognitive Maps in Rats and Men"); the first big challenge to strict behaviourism. Insight learning (Wolfgang Köhler, Gestalt): sudden understanding of a solution without trial-and-error. Köhler's chimp Sultan (1925) joined two short sticks to reach a banana after a pause — the "aha!" moment. Cognitive, not behaviourist; contrast with Edward Thorndike's trial-and-error / law of effect (puzzle-box cats). Stem says "aha / sudden / no gradual improvement" → insight. Observational learning (Albert Bandura): learning by watching a model ; vicarious reinforcement of the model is enough, no direct reinforcement of the learner required. Bobo doll (1961) : children who watched an adult beat the doll did the same. Four processes (tested): Attention → Retention → Reproduction → Motivation (ARRM) . Vicarious reinforcement/punishment modulate motivation. Bandura's framework = Social Learning Theory (1977) , renamed Social Cognitive Theory (1986) ; home of self-efficacy and reciprocal determinism . 1.5 Priming, habituation & sensitization Priming : exposure to one stimulus (the prime ) unconsciously speeds the response to a later one (the target ) by activating related memory representations — a form of implicit memory. Read NURSE → identify DOCTOR faster than BREAD. Subtypes: semantic (NURSE→DOCTOR), perceptual (briefly flashed word → faster identification), affective (smiling face → positive judgement). It is not classical conditioning (no UCS, reflex or pairing) and not recall (no conscious memory of the prime). Habituation vs sensitization — the simplest, non-associative learning (Kandel's Nobel work on Aplysia). Habituation = a decrease in response to a repeated harmless stimulus (you stop hearing the wall clock; Aplysia's gill-withdrawal weakens with repeated mild touch); mechanism = reduced neurotransmitter release at the sensory-motor synapse. Sensitization = an increase in response after an intense/noxious stimulus (after a loud bang you flinch at every creak); mechanism = heterosynaptic facilitation via serotonergic interneurons → increased NT release. Habituation is stimulus-specific (a new stimulus restores the response → dishabituation ). Mnemonic Habituation says "this is safe, ignore it"; sensitization says "the world is dangerous, react more." Trap Habituation vs sensory adaptation: habituation is in the CNS (learning); sensory adaptation is receptor fatigue (peripheral). Habituation vs extinction: habituation needs only one stimulus with no learning history; extinction requires a previously conditioned association. Latent vs insight: latent = hidden until reinforced (Edward Tolman, rats); insight = sudden "aha" (Wolfgang Köhler, chimps). Observational learning ≠ imitation: imitation is one component; observational learning is the whole 4-stage ARRM process. 2. How to read any theory — the master frame Sharf describes every theory on the same recurring template, and you can predict almost any "which approach" answer from where the theory sits on five axes. The book's chapter frame: (1) history of the originator · (2) theory of personality / view of human nature (how problems develop) · (3) goals of therapy · (4) techniques · (5) the therapeutic relationship · (6) uses / evidence · (7) criticisms. Definition A theory of psychotherapy = a coherent set of assumptions giving the clinician a map of personality, a set of goals , and a set of techniques that follow from the goals. A good theory (Sharf) is precise/clear, comprehensive, parsimonious, useful/applicable, and verifiable/testable. The five predictive axes: View of human nature — determined/pessimistic (psychoanalysis) vs free/optimistic/growth-oriented (person-centred, existential, Adlerian). Behavioural = neutral (a product of learning). Role of the past — past-focused (psychoanalysis, Jungian) vs present/future-focused (behavioural, cognitive, REBT, reality, Gestalt, solution-focused, narrative). Directiveness — highly directive (behaviour therapy, REBT, reality, strategic family) vs non-directive (person-centred, the extreme), with collaborative in between (Aaron Beck, Adlerian, solution-focused). The relationship — the cure itself (person-centred) vs the site of the work via transference (psychoanalysis) vs a collaboration (cognitive, Adlerian, postmodern) vs a means/working alliance (behaviour therapy, REBT). Insight vs action — insight-based (psychoanalysis, Jungian) vs action/doing-based (behavioural, reality, solution-focused, strategic); REBT and Beck use insight into thinking then behavioural action. High-yield The four "forces" / waves (NIMHANS): 1st = psychodynamic ; 2nd = behavioural / cognitive-behavioural ; 3rd = humanistic-existential ; 4th (sometimes-cited) = multicultural / social-justice (and/or transpersonal). Useful for "which wave / force" stems. 3. Psychodynamic approaches 3.1 Psychoanalysis — Sigmund Freud Originator. Sigmund Freud (1856–1939), Viennese neurologist. Working with hysteria (and Breuer's Anna O., source of the "talking cure") he concluded symptoms have hidden unconscious causes. The first systematic theory of psychotherapy, the tradition every later theory reacts to. Personality / how problems develop. Behaviour is driven by instincts (life/Eros, energy = libido ; death/Thanatos) and by an unconscious . The mind has a topographic layout (conscious / preconscious / unconscious) and a structural one: id (pleasure principle, primary process), ego (reality principle, secondary process, mediator), superego (conscience + ego ideal). Personality forms through five psychosexual stages — oral (0–1.5), anal (1.5–3), phallic (3–6: Oedipus/Electra), latency (6–puberty), genital (puberty–adulthood); over/under-gratification → fixation → adult character traits. Problems arise from unconscious conflict and unresolved early childhood; the ego manages anxiety with defence mechanisms (repression the master defence, plus projection, displacement, reaction formation, sublimation, denial, regression, rationalisation — catalogued by Anna Freud). Definition George Vaillant's defence hierarchy: psychotic (denial, distortion) → immature (projection, acting out, regression, somatization) → neurotic (intellectualisation, displacement, reaction formation, repression, isolation of affect) → mature (humour, sublimation, suppression, altruism, anticipation). Goals. Make the unconscious conscious; bring repressed material into awareness so the ego can deal with it; strengthen the ego; resolve childhood conflicts re-enacted in the present. Insight is the engine of change. Techniques. Free association (the fundamental rule, censorship off); dream analysis (the "royal road to the unconscious"; separate manifest from latent content); analysis and interpretation of resistance and transference ; attention to parapraxes (Freudian slips); and working through — repeated re-examination of a conflict across shifting contexts until insight is integrated and behaviour changes (this distinguishes intellectual from emotional/behavioural insight). Relationship. Centres on transference : the client transfers feelings about early figures onto the analyst, and analysing that is the work. The analyst stays relatively neutral (blank-screen); countertransference (the analyst's own reactions) must be monitored. Frequency. Classical psychoanalysis: 3–5×/week, couch, years. Psychoanalytic / psychodynamic therapy: 1–2×/week, face-to-face, months–years. Uses / evidence. Originally neurosis/hysteria; now personality and relational problems. Built on rich but unrepeatable case studies ; modern brief psychodynamic therapy gives more empirical footing. Criticisms. Long, expensive, largely unfalsifiable ; overweighted on sex and the deterministic past; biased sample; little support for the psychosexual stages. Trap Free association + dream analysis + transference = Sigmund Freud. The defining technique is free association; the defining relationship mechanism is the transference. Working through is NOT free association and NOT a single interpretation — it is the repeated re-encounter with the same conflict in shifting contexts until consolidated. Classic MET/NIMHANS distractor. 3.2 The post-Freudian canon Sharf and the cheatsheet both expect you to pin each neo-/post-Freudian to their one signature contribution. Theorist Core contribution Anna Freud Ego psychology; defense mechanisms systematised; child analysis through play Carl Jung Analytical psychology (see 3.3) Alfred Adler Individual psychology (see 3.4) Melanie Klein Object relations; paranoid-schizoid → depressive position; splitting, projective identification; internal objects; play therapy Donald Winnicott Object relations; "good-enough mother," holding environment, true vs false self, transitional object Heinz Kohut Self psychology; narcissistic injury; mirroring/idealising/twinship selfobjects; empathic immersion Karen Horney Basic anxiety; neurotic needs; "tyranny of the should"; feminine-psychology critique of Freud Erik Erikson 8 psychosocial stages (Trust v Mistrust → Integrity v Despair); identity crisis; ego-psychology bridge to lifespan development Harry Stack Sullivan Interpersonal psychiatry; "self-system"; anxiety as interpersonal; influenced IPT Otto Kernberg Transference-Focused Psychotherapy (TFP) for BPD; borderline personality organisation; splitting + identity diffusion 3.3 Jungian analysis — analytical psychology Originator. Carl Gustav Jung (1875–1961), Swiss psychiatrist, Freud's "crown prince" until their 1913 break over the sexual nature of libido. Personality. Jung kept the unconscious but enlarged it and de-sexualised libido into general psychic energy. The psyche = ego (consciousness) + personal unconscious (your own forgotten/repressed material, organised into emotionally charged complexes ) + collective unconscious (an inherited layer shared by all humanity, holding the archetypes : persona, shadow, anima/animus, the self ). Coined introversion / extraversion , added four functions (thinking, feeling, sensing, intuiting) → psychological types . Problems reflect one-sided development and failure of individuation , especially at midlife. Goals. Individuation : integrate conscious and unconscious, persona and shadow, into a balanced self . Techniques. Dream analysis in series with amplification (linking symbols to myth and culture) rather than free association; active imagination (dialoguing with inner images); the word-association test (reveals complexes). Four therapy stages: confession, elucidation, education, transformation. Relationship. A collaborative mutual encounter; both parties are changed by the work. Criticisms. Mystical, obscure, hard to test; collective unconscious and archetypes resist verification (the MBTI descends from his types but has weak psychometrics). Trap Collective unconscious + archetypes + individuation + amplification = Carl Jung, NOT Freud (Freud = personal unconscious only). Dreams: amplification (Jung) vs free association (Freud). 3.4 Adlerian therapy — individual psychology Originator. Alfred Adler (1870–1937), Viennese; broke from Sigmund Freud in 1911 over the sexual emphasis. A major forerunner of humanistic and cognitive therapy. Personality. The one dynamic force is striving for superiority (really, striving for competence/completion). Everyone starts with inferiority ; healthy growth compensates , derailment yields an inferiority complex or over-compensating superiority complex . Each person builds a unique style of life by about age 5; we are pulled by future fictional goals ( fictional finalism ); we are not passive ( creative power of the self ); the mark of health is social interest ( Gemeinschaftsgefühl ). Birth order shapes the style of life. Problems = a mistaken style of life + discouragement / low social interest. Goals. Foster social interest, correct the mistaken style of life and faulty basic mistakes , replace discouragement with encouragement . Techniques. Lifestyle assessment , early recollections (earliest memory reveals the style of life), birth-order analysis, family constellation , encouragement , "the question" ("how would your life be different if you were well?"), acting as if , catching oneself , spitting in the client's soup , and paradoxical intention . Relationship. Egalitarian , collaborative, encouraging. Trap Inferiority/superiority complex · style of life · social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefühl) · birth order · early recollections · encouragement = Alfred Adler. Match the three "wills": will to pleasure = Sigmund Freud, will to power/superiority = Adler, will to meaning = Viktor Frankl. 4. Humanistic & existential approaches 4.1 Existential therapy — May, Yalom, Frankl Originators. A movement, not one founder: Rollo May (brought existentialism to US psychology; existential vs neurotic anxiety, the daimonic, freedom and destiny), Irvin Yalom (the ultimate concerns), Viktor Frankl (logotherapy, forged in the camps). Roots in Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Heidegger, Sartre, Binswanger, Boss. Human nature. No fixed human nature; we are free, responsible, and create ourselves through choices (existence precedes essence). Distress comes from facing, or fleeing, the ultimate concerns / givens of existence . Yalom's four givens: death, freedom (and its responsibility), isolation, meaninglessness. Avoiding these through inauthenticity ("bad faith") produces existential anxiety/guilt. Three modes of being-in-the-world: Umwelt (physical), Mitwelt (social), Eigenwelt (self). Goals. Live authentically , accept freedom and responsibility, confront the givens, find or create meaning . Not symptom removal. Techniques. Deliberately light on technique; the relationship is the method. Frankl's logotherapy is the named exception: paradoxical intention (deliberately wish for the feared thing to break anticipatory anxiety), dereflection (shift attention away from the self/symptom), Socratic dialogue toward meaning. Frankl's three sources of meaning : creative (work/contribution), experiential (love/beauty), attitudinal (stance toward unavoidable suffering). Relationship. A real, authentic I–Thou (Buber) encounter; presence over technique. Uses / criticisms. Grief, terminal illness, life transitions, "existential vacuum." Vague, hard to operationalise; demands an articulate client. Trap Logotherapy · will to meaning · existential vacuum · paradoxical intention · dereflection = Viktor Frankl. The four givens = Irvin Yalom. Rollo May brought existentialism to American therapy. Note: paradoxical intention appears in Frankl AND in Adlerian/strategic work — as a named logotherapy technique it's Frankl; in family work the context decides. 4.2 Person-centred therapy — Carl Rogers Originator. Carl Rogers (1902–1987), American; created client-centred (later person-centred) therapy and pioneered recorded-session research. Human nature. Deeply optimistic : every organism has an innate actualising tendency toward growth. Trouble starts when the child, needing love, takes on conditions of worth ("I'm valued only if…") and distorts/denies experience that doesn't fit the self-concept. The gap between organismic experience and self-concept is incongruence , the source of anxiety. Goals. Reduce incongruence; drop conditions of worth; reconnect with organismic valuing; become a fully functioning person (open to experience, present-living, self-trusting, free, creative). Techniques. Famously non-directive — no diagnosis, no advice, no interpretation. Change comes from the relationship itself . The core triad the therapist provides: congruence/genuineness , unconditional positive regard (UPR) , and empathic understanding . These sit within six necessary and sufficient conditions (1957): two persons in psychological contact ; the client is incongruent/anxious ; the therapist is congruent ; the therapist feels UPR ; the therapist feels empathy ; and the client perceives the empathy and regard. Skills: reflection of feeling, active listening. Outcome marker: self vs ideal-self congruence (the Q-sort ). Mnemonic "EUC" — E mpathy, U PR, C ongruence. Lock the count: six conditions total, of which the therapist supplies three (the core triad), and they are necessary AND sufficient . Trap The core triad (congruence, UPR, empathy) is Carl Rogers ; so are "six necessary and sufficient conditions," "fully functioning person," and "actualising tendency." There is no "interpretation" in Rogers (that's Freud). And note the stem flip: "the relationship is necessary and sufficient" = Rogers; "necessary but not sufficient" = Beck / CBT. 4.3 Gestalt therapy — Fritz Perls Originator. Fritz (Frederick) Perls (1893–1970), with Laura Perls and Paul Goodman. Roots in Gestalt perceptual psychology (figure/ground), psychoanalysis, existentialism. Human nature. A whole person in constant contact with the environment, organising experience into figure (salient now) and ground . Health = staying aware in the here-and-now and completing the cycle of need → contact → satisfaction → withdrawal. Trouble = unfinished business (unexpressed past feelings intruding now) and contact-boundary disturbances : introjection (swallowing others' values whole), projection , retroflection (turning back on the self what you'd do to others), confluence (no boundary), deflection . Perls described five layers of neurosis (phony, phobic, impasse, implosive, explosive). Goals. Restore present awareness ; re-own disowned parts; finish unfinished business; move from environmental support to self-support and integration of polarities. Techniques / experiments. The empty-chair technique (dialogue with an absent person or a part of the self); the two-chair / top-dog vs under-dog dialogue (the moralising "shoulds" tyrant vs the evasive resister within); staying with feeling; exaggeration; the "I take responsibility" exercise; dream work (every dream element = a projected part of the self, acted out rather than interpreted); attention to body language and language ("it" → "I"). Relationship. Active, present-centred, I–Thou dialogic; the therapist may confront and frustrate avoidance. Trap Empty chair · top-dog vs under-dog · here-and-now awareness · unfinished business · figure/ground · layers of neurosis = Gestalt / Perls. Don't assume "chair → couch → Freud"; the empty chair is Gestalt, not psychoanalysis, and not the "miracle question" (SFBT). 5. Behavioural & cognitive approaches 5.1 Behaviour therapy Originators. No single founder. Roots in classical conditioning ( Ivan Pavlov ; John B. Watson & Rosalie Rayner 's Little Albert), operant conditioning ( B. F. Skinner ), social learning ( Albert Bandura ), and clinical pioneers Joseph Wolpe (systematic desensitisation), Hans Eysenck , Arnold Lazarus (later, multimodal therapy). Personality / how problems develop. No deep "personality" structure; behaviour (including symptoms) is learned and maintained by antecedents and consequences. A phobia is a conditioned fear; a habit is a reinforced operant. Strong focus on observable behaviour , the present, and measurement. Begins with a behavioural assessment / functional analysis (A–B–C: antecedent, behaviour, consequence). Goals. Concrete, specific, measurable behavioural change agreed with the client. Technique Mechanism Indication Systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) Reciprocal inhibition : relaxation paired with graded imagined exposure up a fear hierarchy Phobias (classic) In-vivo exposure Real-world graded exposure without relaxation; habituation + extinction Specific phobia, agoraphobia, OCD, PTSD Flooding / implosion Full-intensity exposure with no hierarchy, no relaxation, no escape, until anxiety extinguishes Phobias (less used — dropout) Exposure & Response Prevention (ERP) (Foa, Kozak) Exposure to the obsessional trigger + prevention of the compulsive response OCD — first-line behavioural Tx Aversion therapy Pair the unwanted behaviour with an aversive UCS (covert sensitisation = imaginal version) Paraphilias, substance use (limited evidence + ethical issues) Token economy Operant: secondary reinforcers (tokens) exchanged for primary reinforcers Inpatient/institutional, ID, ADHD classrooms Contingency management Operant: rewards contingent on target behaviour SUDs (esp. stimulant) Behavioural activation (Lewinsohn, Jacobson) Scheduled rewarding/mastery activity; reverses the depressive withdrawal-rumination cycle Depression — comparable to CBT Modeling (Bandura) Observational learning, vicarious reinforcement; participant modeling Phobias, social skills Shaping / chaining Reinforce successive approximations / link existing behaviours (see §1.1) Skill acquisition, autism, ADLs Biofeedback Real-time physiological readouts (EMG, HRV, GSR, EEG) shape autonomic/muscle control Tension headache, migraine, anxiety, incontinence Also: contingency contracting , extinction , relaxation training , assertiveness / social-skills training .
