Relationship. Important but not curative; the therapist is an active teacher / trainer / consultant who forms a working alliance and reinforces progress. Uses / evidence. Phobias, anxiety, OCD, habit disorders, skills deficits, institutional/developmental settings. The strongest empirical evidence base of the classical theories. Criticisms. Can ignore feelings, insight, the relationship and the underlying cause; risk of symptom focus. Trap Systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) vs flooding: desensitisation = graded hierarchy + relaxation (reciprocal inhibition), gentle. Flooding = maximal exposure, no hierarchy, no relaxation. Same idea (exposure), opposite intensity. ERP is the first-line behavioural treatment for OCD (SSRIs = first-line pharmacotherapy); systematic desensitisation is for phobias , not OCD. Token economy = operant/Skinnerian; modeling = Albert Bandura; aversion = pairing with an unpleasant stimulus. 5.2 Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT) — Albert Ellis Originator. Albert Ellis (1913–2007), American; created REBT in the mid-1950s — the first of the cognitive-behavioural therapies (predates Aaron Beck). Personality / how problems develop. It is not events that disturb us but our beliefs about them. Disturbance comes from irrational beliefs — rigid absolutist demands phrased as musts, shoulds, oughts ( musturbation ) — plus their derivatives: awfulising/catastrophising , low frustration tolerance ("I-can't-stand-it-itis") , and global self/other-rating / damnation . The three core irrational demands: "I must do well; others must treat me well; the world must be easy/fair." Definition The A-B-C-D-E model. A = activating event; B = belief (rational or irrational); C = emotional/behavioural consequence. The insight: it is B, not A, that causes C. Therapy adds D = disputing the irrational belief (logical, empirical, pragmatic), leading to E = a new effective philosophy (sometimes A-B-C-D-E-F, F = new feeling). Goals. Identify and dispute irrational beliefs, replace them with flexible preferences, reach deep philosophical change and unconditional self-acceptance . Techniques. Active-directive disputing ; cognitive (cost-benefit analysis); emotive (rational-emotive imagery, shame-attacking exercises , humour, forceful self-statements); behavioural (homework, risk-taking, in-vivo desensitisation, reinforcement). Heavy homework and psychoeducation. Relationship. Warm but secondary; not "necessary" in the Rogerian sense. The therapist is a forceful, active, sometimes blunt teacher/debater who models unconditional acceptance while attacking the beliefs. Criticisms. Confrontational style can clash with some clients/cultures; "rational vs irrational" can be a value judgement. 5.3 Cognitive therapy — Aaron Beck Originator. Aaron T. Beck (1921–2021), American psychiatrist; developed cognitive therapy in the 1960s out of his research on depression (daughter Judith Beck carried it forward). Personality / how problems develop. Emotion and behaviour are shaped by how we interpret events. Early experience lays down schemas (core beliefs) → which generate, in the moment, automatic thoughts (rapid, plausible appraisals just below awareness) → filtered through cognitive distortions : all-or-nothing/dichotomous thinking, overgeneralisation, magnification/minimisation (catastrophising), selective abstraction/mental filter, disqualifying the positive, arbitrary inference, personalisation, labelling, "should" statements, mind-reading/fortune-telling (jumping to conclusions), emotional reasoning. Depression is marked by the cognitive triad : negative view of the self , the world , and the future . Goals. Identify, test and correct distorted thinking; change automatic thoughts and underlying schemas; teach the client to become their own therapist (cognitive restructuring). Techniques. Socratic questioning / guided discovery ; identifying and testing automatic thoughts ( thought records , dysfunctional-thought log); collaborative empiricism (client + therapist treat beliefs as hypotheses and gather evidence); behavioural experiments ; activity scheduling and mastery-and-pleasure ratings; graded task assignment; decatastrophising; downward-arrow to reach core schemas; homework. Relationship. Genuine, warm, collaborative (Carl Rogers' conditions are necessary but not sufficient ); the hallmark is collaborative empiricism — not arguing, but jointly investigating. Uses / evidence. The strongest evidence base of any single approach for depression and anxiety ; foundation of modern CBT ; extended to OCD, PTSD, eating disorders, psychosis (CBTp). Trap REBT (Ellis) vs Cognitive Therapy (Aaron Beck) — the most-tested pair. Albert Ellis = A-B-C(DE) , irrational beliefs , musturbation , disputing ; directive, confrontational, philosophical — the therapist argues the belief is illogical. Beck = automatic thoughts , cognitive distortions , schemas , cognitive triad , collaborative empiricism ; Socratic, gentler — the client tests the thought as a hypothesis against evidence. "Dispute the irrational belief" = Ellis; "test the automatic thought against the evidence" = Beck. The cognitive triad is Beck; the ABC is Ellis — examiners swap these constantly. REBT predates Beck. 5.4 Reality therapy / Choice theory — William Glasser Originator. William Glasser (1925–2013), American psychiatrist; reality therapy in the 1960s, later grounded in choice theory (originally "control theory"). Personality / how problems develop. Behaviour is our best attempt to meet five innate basic needs: survival, love/belonging, power/achievement, freedom, fun. We act to close the gap between what we want (our "quality world") and what we perceive we're getting. Choice theory: we choose nearly all our behaviour and are responsible for it. Total behavior has four inseparable components — acting, thinking, feeling, physiology — and we have the most direct control over acting and thinking (Glasser uses verbs like "depressing," "anxietying"). Problems = irresponsible choices and unsatisfying relationships, not "mental illness." Definition The WDEP system (formalised by Robert Wubbolding): W = explore Wants (needs / quality world); D = examine Doing / current behaviour; E = Evaluation (the client self-evaluates: "is what you're doing getting you what you want?"); P = make a Plan . Plans should be SAMIC (simple, attainable, measurable, immediate, controlled by the client). No excuses, no punishment, no giving up. Relationship. Warm and involved first (build involvement ), then focus on present behaviour and choices; firm but caring, refuses excuses. Trap WDEP · choice theory · total behavior · the five needs = William Glasser (WDEP formalised by Wubbolding). Don't confuse Glasser's five needs with Abraham Maslow's hierarchy, or WDEP with MI's PACE/OARS. Reality therapy is present-focused, NOT past-focused. 6. Constructivist, feminist & systemic approaches 6.1 Solution-Focused Brief Therapy & Narrative therapy These constructivist / postmodern approaches share a premise: reality is socially constructed through language and story, so therapy works on meaning, not a fixed pathology. Both are brief, collaborative, resolutely non-pathologising , and treat the client as the expert . Solution-Focused Brief Therapy (SFBT) — Steve de Shazer & Insoo Kim Berg (Brief Family Therapy Center, Milwaukee; building on MRI brief therapy and Milton Erickson). Core idea: don't analyse the problem, build the solution ; focus on what the client wants and on times the problem is already absent. Signature techniques: the miracle question ("suppose a miracle solved the problem overnight — what would you notice tomorrow?"), exception questions ("when is the problem not happening?"), scaling questions ("on 0–10, where are you, and what is +1?"), the formula first-session task , coping questions , compliments . Rule of thumb: if it works, do more; if not, do something different. 4–8 sessions typical. Narrative therapy — Michael White (Australia) & David Epston (New Zealand) . We live by stories we tell about ourselves; a problem-saturated "dominant story" traps a person. "The problem is the problem; the person is not the problem." Techniques: externalising the problem (talk about "the Anger" or "the OCD" as separate, often by naming it), mapping its influence , finding unique outcomes / sparkling moments (times the person resisted the problem), re-authoring , therapeutic documents/letters , recruiting outsider witnesses / a definitional ceremony. Trap Miracle / exception / scaling questions = SFBT (de Shazer & Berg). Externalising · re-authoring · unique outcomes = Narrative (White & Epston). Both are postmodern and "client-as-expert," but SFBT builds the solution/future while narrative re-writes the story . The "miracle question" is the most-tested single item — it's de Shazer, NOT Gestalt's empty chair. 6.2 Feminist therapy Originators. A movement from the 1960s–70s women's movement (Jean Baker Miller, Carolyn Enns, Laura Brown); often integrated with other approaches. How problems develop. Distress cannot be separated from the social/political context , especially gender-role socialisation and the unequal distribution of power . Much "pathology" in women is a reasonable response to oppression, sexism and trauma. Slogan: "the personal is political." Goals. Symptom relief plus empowerment, self-definition, awareness of how gender-role/power dynamics shaped the problem, and (often) social action. Techniques. Gender-role analysis and intervention; power analysis ; assertiveness training ; reframing/relabelling (move blame from the individual to the social cause); bibliotherapy; therapist self-disclosure; demystifying therapy. Relationship. Deliberately egalitarian — minimise the power differential, treat the client as an equal collaborator. Trap "The personal is political" · gender-role analysis · power analysis · egalitarian relationship = feminist therapy. 6.3 Family systems therapies The unit of treatment shifts from the individual to the system . Drawing on general systems theory and cybernetics , a symptom in one member (the " identified patient ") expresses a dysfunction in the whole family's patterns. Shared concepts: homeostasis (the system resists change), circular causality (a mutual loop, not A→B), feedback loops , boundaries , subsystems . School Founder(s) Signature concepts / techniques Bowenian (multigenerational) Murray Bowen Differentiation of self (separate intellect from emotion, self from family fusion — the central goal); triangulation ; nuclear family emotional system; family projection process; multigenerational transmission; emotional cutoff ; sibling position; the genogram (multigenerational map). Goal: raise differentiation, detriangulate; therapist = calm non-anxious presence. Insight-leaning, slower. Structural Salvador Minuchin Family structure : boundaries (rigid → disengaged ; diffuse → enmeshed ; clear in between), subsystems (spousal/parental/sibling), hierarchy, alignments/coalitions. Joining , mapping, enactment (family plays out the problem in session), boundary-making, unbalancing, reframing. Active, present-focused. Strategic Jay Haley, Cloé Madanes; MRI (Watzlawick, Weakland); Milton Erickson Solve the presenting problem via planned interventions; the symptom serves a function and is maintained by failed "solutions." Directives , paradoxical interventions ( prescribing the symptom ), reframing, ordeals , pretend techniques. Brief, directive, little insight. Experiential / communications (human validation) Virginia Satir (also Carl Whitaker, symbolic) Warm, growth- and communication -focused; self-esteem and congruent communication. The four stress communication stances: placater, blamer, super-reasonable (computer), irrelevant (distractor) , plus the healthy congruent / leveller . Family sculpting , family reconstruction, role play, warmth. Milan systemic Selvini Palazzoli, Boscolo, Cecchin, Prata Circular questioning , hypothesising, neutrality, reflecting team Trap Family-theorist swaps (a top NIMHANS trap): "genogram + differentiation + triangulation" → Bowen ; "boundaries (enmeshed/disengaged) + enactment + joining + subsystems" → Minuchin (structural) ; "directives + paradox / prescribe the symptom" → Jay Haley (strategic) ; "family sculpting + placater/blamer/computer/distractor" → Virginia Satir (experiential) . "Identified patient · homeostasis · circular causality" = family systems generally. 7. Third-wave, integrative & specialised models These are recognition-item favourites ("which of these is a component of ___?"). The trap is always a real concept from a different therapy, so learn the named parts of each. 7.1 Transactional Analysis (TA) — Eric Berne Originator. Eric Berne (1910–1970); popularised in Games People Play . Personality has three ego states : Parent (taught — nurturing or critical), Adult (rational here-and-now processor), Child (felt — spontaneous or adapted). Transactions can be complementary (smooth), crossed (conflict), or ulterior (hidden agenda). Early decisions form a life script ; we exchange strokes (units of recognition); we play repetitive games ("Why Don't You — Yes But") paying off in bad feelings. Four life positions , healthy = "I'm OK–You're OK." Goals: autonomy (awareness, spontaneity, intimacy), strengthen the Adult , rewrite the script via structural / game / script analysis; often contract-based and in groups. 7.2 DBT — Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (Linehan, 1993) Synthesis of behavioural change + Zen acceptance ("dialectics"). Primary target: BPD with chronic suicidality . Four skill modules: mindfulness · distress tolerance · emotion regulation · interpersonal effectiveness. Four treatment modes: individual therapy + group skills training + phone/between-session coaching + therapist consultation team (~1 year). Target hierarchy: life-threatening → therapy-interfering → quality-of-life-interfering behaviours. Mnemonic DBT modules — "My Dog Eats Iguanas": M indfulness, D istress tolerance, E motion regulation, I nterpersonal effectiveness. 7.3 ACT — Acceptance & Commitment Therapy (Hayes) Goal = psychological flexibility , not symptom reduction. The Hexaflex (6 processes): Acceptance · Cognitive Defusion · Self-as-Context · Present-Moment Contact · Values · Committed Action. Each opposed by an inflexibility process (experiential avoidance, fusion, attachment to the conceptualised self, etc.). Underpinned by Relational Frame Theory (RFT) . Techniques: defusion ("I'm having the thought that…"), values clarification, metaphors (passengers on the bus, tug-of-war with a monster). 7.4 Mindfulness-based programmes MBSR — Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (Kabat-Zinn, 1979): 8-week group; body scan, sitting meditation, mindful movement (yoga); chronic pain, stress, anxiety. MBCT — Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (Segal, Williams, Teasdale): 8-week group combining MBSR + cognitive therapy; indication = relapse prevention in recurrent depression (≥3 episodes). Trap MBCT is for preventing relapse , not treating an acute episode. MBSR came first (1979); MBCT added the cognitive layer. 7.5 IPT — Interpersonal Therapy (Klerman & Weissman, 1984) Time-limited (12–16 sessions), originally for MDD; evidence extends to bulimia, postpartum and adolescent depression. Four problem areas (pick one focus): grief · role disputes · role transitions · interpersonal deficits. Deliberately stays in the here-and-now of relationships, not the past. Trap IPT's four areas are NOT "thoughts / feelings / behaviours / body" and NOT "transference." If you see "role dispute / role transition" → IPT. 7.6 Motivational Interviewing (Miller & Rollnick, 1991) A client-centred but directive method to resolve ambivalence and elicit change talk . Spirit — PACE: Partnership, Acceptance, Compassion, Evocation. Processes: Engaging → Focusing → Evoking → Planning. Core skills — OARS: Open questions, Affirmations, Reflections, Summaries. Change talk — DARN-CAT: Desire, Ability, Reason, Need → Commitment, Activation, Taking steps. "Roll with resistance," develop discrepancy, support self-efficacy. Indication: ambivalence, especially SUDs; also weight loss, medication adherence. Pairs naturally with the stages of change. 7.7 Trauma-focused therapies EMDR (Francine Shapiro, 1987): 8-phase protocol pairing brief recall of the trauma memory with bilateral stimulation (eye movements / taps / tones). PTSD (APA, NICE, WHO endorsed). Mechanism debated (working-memory taxation, REM-like processing, dual attention); comparable to trauma-focused CBT. CPT — Cognitive Processing Therapy (Resick & Schnicke): 12-session manualised TF-CBT for PTSD; stuck points → impact statement → Socratic dialogue + worksheets. Prolonged Exposure (Foa): imaginal + in-vivo exposure to trauma memories and avoided stimuli; manualised; equally evidence-based for PTSD. Trap ERP vs EMDR: ERP (exposure + response prevention) = OCD; EMDR (8 phases + bilateral eye movements) = trauma. Different conditions, easily confused. Definition Trauma therapist lineage (high-yield): Pierre Janet (dissociation, traumatic memory, predates Sigmund Freud) · Judith Herman (Complex PTSD; 3-stage recovery: safety → remembrance/mourning → reconnection) · Bessel van der Kolk ("the body keeps the score," somatics, polyvagal) · Edna Foa (Prolonged Exposure; ERP for OCD; emotional processing theory) · Patricia Resick (CPT) · Francine Shapiro (EMDR) · Peter Levine (Somatic Experiencing) · Marsha Linehan (DBT). 7.8 Specialised models for BPD & integration TFP — Transference-Focused Psychotherapy (Otto Kernberg): twice-weekly psychodynamic, here-and-now transference interpretation, "object relations dyads." MBT — Mentalization-Based Treatment (Bateman & Fonagy): builds the capacity to understand one's own and others' mental states; day-hospital and outpatient versions. Integrative / eclectic routes (Sharf): technical eclecticism (pick whatever techniques work, regardless of theory — Lazarus's multimodal therapy , the BASIC ID : Behaviour, Affect, Sensation, Imagery, Cognition, Interpersonal, Drugs/biology); theoretical integration (blend theories into a new whole — Wachtel's cyclical psychodynamics); the common-factors route; and assimilative integration (work from one home theory, importing techniques). Fit the therapy to the client. Trap Ego states (Parent–Adult–Child) · games · scripts · strokes · life positions = TA / Berne. Multimodal therapy / BASIC ID / technical eclecticism = Arnold Lazarus. Don't decide DBT vs ACT on the word "mindfulness" alone — both use it; DBT has 4 modules , ACT has 6 hexaflex processes . 8. Group therapy — Yalom The group is a social microcosm : relationship patterns from outside life replay in the group, and the therapist's job is to surface the here-and-now process. Format: 6–10 members + therapist(s). Bion's basic-assumption groups (dependency, fight-flight, pairing) are influential background. Definition Yalom's 11 therapeutic factors: (1) instillation of hope · (2) universality ("I'm not the only one") · (3) imparting information · (4) altruism · (5) corrective recapitulation of the primary family group · (6) development of socialising techniques · (7) imitative behaviour · (8) interpersonal learning (the engine, paired with here-and-now) · (9) group cohesiveness (the group analogue of the therapeutic alliance) · (10) catharsis · (11) existential factors (responsibility, isolation, meaning, mortality). Trap Tag words social microcosm + here-and-now + interpersonal learning → Irvin Yalom. NOT a Yalom factor: "transference interpretation," "free association," "the miracle question." 9. Common factors & the therapeutic frame Beyond Sharf's schools, NIMHANS leans on the research finding that the schools share more than they differ. High-yield Common factors & the Dodo-bird verdict. Across bona-fide therapies, much outcome is explained by common factors — the therapeutic alliance , empathy, expectancy/hope, a believable rationale + ritual, goal consensus — rather than specific techniques. The " Dodo-bird verdict " (Rosenzweig; championed by Luborsky and Bruce Wampold 's contextual model): "everyone has won and all must have prizes," i.e. all therapies achieve broadly comparable outcomes. The working alliance ( Bordin: bond + goals + tasks ) is the most robust predictor of outcome. Outcome variance (Lambert, Wampold) roughly splits: ~40% client + extra-therapeutic factors · ~30% relationship (alliance) · ~15% expectancy/placebo · ~15% specific technique. Implication: most schools work, mostly via common factors. Specific techniques matter most for specific disorders with strong protocols ( ERP for OCD, exposure for PTSD, behavioural activation for depression ). Definition Stages of change — the Transtheoretical Model (Prochaska & DiClemente): precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance (relapse possible). Match the intervention to the stage — "the client isn't resistant, they're precontemplative." Definition Multicultural counselling competencies (Sue & Sue, the "fourth force"): a competent counsellor has awareness (of own biases/worldview), knowledge (of the client's culture), and skills (culturally appropriate interventions). Watch for cultural encapsulation and etic vs emic . 10. Indications quick-map (what to recommend) Condition First-line psychotherapy MDD (mild–moderate) CBT, behavioural activation, IPT OCD ERP (CBT family); add SSRI if needed Specific phobia In-vivo exposure / systematic desensitisation Social anxiety CBT (Clark & Wells / Heimberg) Panic disorder CBT with interoceptive exposure (Barlow) GAD CBT, applied relaxation, MBCT PTSD Trauma-focused CBT (PE, CPT), EMDR BPD DBT, MBT, TFP, schema therapy (Young) Bulimia / BED CBT-E (Fairburn) Anorexia nervosa (adolescent) FBT (Maudsley) Substance use MI, CBT relapse-prevention (Marlatt), contingency management, 12-step facilitation Schizophrenia (adjunct) CBTp, family interventions (psychoeducation, expressed-emotion work), social skills training Couples Emotionally Focused Therapy (Johnson), Gottman Method, integrative behavioural couple therapy (Christensen, Jacobson) Adolescents — depression IPT-A, CBT Children — anxiety CBT (Coping Cat / Kendall), parent-focused (PCIT) Recurrent depression — relapse prevention MBCT 11. Professional ethics Tested two ways: straight definition ("non-maleficence means ___") or a vignette ("a clinician does X — which principle is violated?"). The four big ones are Beauchamp & Childress's principles ; the rest are the day-to-day rules that fall out of them. Mnemonic The four core principles — "A-B-N-J" / "Auto Brings No Justice": A utonomy · B eneficence · N on-maleficence · J ustice. Principle One line In practice Autonomy Respect the client's right to decide for themselves Informed consent · right to refuse · no coercion Beneficence Act for the client's good Choosing the treatment most likely to help; promoting wellbeing Non-maleficence "First, do no harm" ( primum non nocere ) Not using unproven/harmful methods; staying within competence Justice Fairness — treat like cases alike, distribute resources fairly No discrimination; fair access; equitable waitlists 11.1 Autonomy cluster Informed consent: the client understands the nature, risks, benefits and alternatives, and agrees voluntarily and with capacity . Three pillars: disclosure · capacity · voluntariness. Assent: agreement from someone who can't legally consent (a minor) — you get their assent alongside the parent's consent . Right to refuse / withdraw at any time without penalty. Trap Paternalism = overriding a competent person's choice "for their own good" — the violation of autonomy. Only justified when the person genuinely lacks capacity. Consent vs assent: adults with capacity give consent ; minors give assent (parent consents). 11.2 Confidentiality and its limits Privacy = the client's right; confidentiality = your duty to protect it; privileged communication = the legal protection in court. Limits / when you must break it: risk of serious harm to self or others · suspected child/elder abuse ( mandatory reporting ) · court order. High-yield Duty to warn / protect (Tarasoff): if a client makes a credible threat against an identifiable person, the therapist must act to protect that person — non-maleficence/beneficence to a third party overrides confidentiality. Very common vignette. Confidentiality is not absolute. 11.3 The other named terms Term Means Fidelity Loyalty, keeping promises, being trustworthy and reliable Veracity Truth-telling — honesty about diagnosis/prognosis Competence Practising only within the limits of your training; refer out otherwise Dual / multiple relationship A second role with a client (friend, business, romantic) — a boundary violation Duty of care The legal/ethical obligation to act in the client's best interest Negligence Falling below the accepted standard of care, causing harm (basis of malpractice) Capacity / competence to consent Whether the person can understand and reason about the decision Vulnerability Extra protection owed to those who can't fully protect their own interests (children, severe MI) Termination Planned, gradual; address relapse prevention; leave the door open 11.4 Indian & international context RCI (Rehabilitation Council of India) licenses clinical psychologists and has its own code of ethics . The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 codifies advance directives, nominated representative, right to confidentiality, and consent for persons with mental illness, and decriminalises suicide attempt. The APA Ethics Code is the international reference; its five general principles: beneficence/non-maleficence, fidelity/responsibility, integrity, justice, respect for rights & dignity. Multicultural competence (Sue & Sue): awareness, knowledge, skills. 11.5 Match the scenario to the principle Scenario Principle Therapist uses an untrained technique and the client worsens Non-maleficence (+ competence) Clinician forces medication on a competent, refusing adult Autonomy violated (paternalism) Psychologist dates a current client Fidelity / dual relationship — boundary violation Therapist warns a client's named target of a credible threat Upholds duty to warn (Tarasoff); breaks confidentiality lawfully Same waitlist priority regardless of caste/income Justice Choosing the most evidence-based treatment Beneficence Hiding a poor prognosis from the client Veracity violated Sharing case details at a party Confidentiality violated Getting a 14-year-old's agreement alongside the parent's consent Assent (+ consent) Trap Beneficence vs non-maleficence: do good vs avoid harm. "Withholding a harmful drug" = non-maleficence; "giving a helpful one" = beneficence. Privacy vs confidentiality vs privilege: the right · your duty · court protection. 12. Master trap list, roster & glossary 12.1 The component-to-therapy match table Cover the right column; name the therapy from the cue. If you see this component / cue word… …the therapy is Mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness DBT (Marsha Linehan) Hexaflex · cognitive defusion · self-as-context · values ACT (Hayes) Cognitive triad · automatic thoughts · schema · guided discovery CBT (Aaron Beck) ABC model · irrational belief · dispute · musturbation REBT (Albert Ellis) Empathy · unconditional positive regard · congruence Person-centred (Carl Rogers) PACE · OARS · change talk · DARN-CAT Motivational Interviewing Grief · role dispute · role transition · interpersonal deficit IPT (Klerman & Weissman) Universality · cohesiveness · interpersonal learning · catharsis · social microcosm Group therapy (Irvin Yalom) Empty chair · top-dog/underdog · figure-ground Gestalt (Fritz Perls) Free association · transference · working through · dream analysis Psychoanalysis (Sigmund Freud) Collective unconscious · archetypes · individuation · amplification Carl Jung Early recollections · social interest · style of life · birth order Alfred Adler WDEP (wants, doing, evaluation, planning) · total behavior · five needs Reality therapy (William Glasser) Paradoxical intention · dereflection · will to meaning Logotherapy (Viktor Frankl) The four givens (death/freedom/isolation/meaninglessness) Yalom (existential) 8-week group · relapse prevention in recurrent depression MBCT 8-phase protocol · bilateral eye movements · trauma EMDR (Shapiro) Exposure + response prevention ERP for OCD (Foa) Reciprocal inhibition · fear hierarchy · relaxation pairing Systematic desensitisation (Joseph Wolpe) Miracle question · scaling · exceptions SFBT (de Shazer & Berg) Externalising the problem · re-authoring · unique outcomes Narrative (White & Epston) "Personal is political" · gender-role analysis · power analysis Feminist therapy Differentiation of self · triangles · genogram Bowenian family Family map · enmeshment · joining · enactment Structural family (Salvador Minuchin) Directives · prescribing the symptom · ordeal Strategic family (Jay Haley) Placater/blamer/computer/distractor · family sculpting Experiential family (Virginia Satir) Parent-Adult-Child · games · scripts · "I'm OK–You're OK" Transactional Analysis (Eric Berne) BASIC ID · multimodal · technical eclecticism Lazarus 12.2 The traps that catch everyone Triad vs ABC. Cognitive triad = Aaron Beck; ABC = Albert Ellis. Both CBT-family, easy to swap. REBT (Ellis) vs CT (Beck). Ellis disputes irrational beliefs (directive, confrontational); Beck tests automatic thoughts as hypotheses (collaborative, Socratic). REBT predates Beck. Systematic desensitisation vs flooding. Graded + relaxation (Wolpe) vs intense, no hierarchy, no relaxation. ERP vs EMDR. ERP = OCD; EMDR (8 phases + eye movements) = trauma. DBT (4 modules) vs ACT (6 hexaflex processes). Both use "mindfulness" — don't decide on that word alone. Working through = repeated re-encounter with a conflict until integrated, NOT free association and NOT one interpretation. Empty chair = Gestalt, not psychoanalysis ("chair → couch → Freud" is wrong). Carl Rogers' three core conditions = empathy, UPR, congruence — no "interpretation." Relationship "necessary AND sufficient" = Rogers; "necessary but not sufficient" = Beck/CBT. IPT four areas = grief, role disputes, role transitions, interpersonal deficits (not "thoughts/feelings/behaviours/body"). MI spirit = PACE; skills = OARS. MI is the opposite of confronting/arguing the client out of it. Family swaps: genogram → Bowen; enactment/boundaries → Salvador Minuchin; directives/paradox → Jay Haley; sculpting/stances → Virginia Satir. Paradoxical intention appears in BOTH Frankl (logotherapy) and strategic family therapy — read the stem for context. The three wills: pleasure = Sigmund Freud, power/superiority = Alfred Adler, meaning = Frankl. William Glasser's five needs ≠ Abraham Maslow's hierarchy. 12.3 Founders one-liner roster (technique → who) Technique / concept Who Free association, dream analysis, transference, working through Sigmund Freud (psychoanalysis) Active imagination, dream amplification, word-association test Carl Jung Early recollections, "the question," acting as if, encouragement Alfred Adler Logotherapy, paradoxical intention, dereflection Viktor Frankl The four givens of existence Irvin Yalom Existential vs neurotic anxiety, the daimonic Rollo May Core triad (congruence, UPR, empathy); six conditions; actualising tendency Carl Rogers Empty chair, top-dog/under-dog, awareness work Fritz Perls (Gestalt) Systematic desensitisation, reciprocal inhibition Joseph Wolpe Operant conditioning, token economy roots, functional analysis, shaping B. F. Skinner Modeling / observational learning, self-efficacy Albert Bandura A-B-C(DE), disputing, musturbation Albert Ellis (REBT) Automatic thoughts, schemas, cognitive triad, collaborative empiricism Aaron Beck (cognitive therapy) WDEP, choice theory, total behavior, five needs William Glasser (Wubbolding formalised WDEP) Miracle / exception / scaling questions de Shazer & Berg (SFBT) Externalising, re-authoring, unique outcomes White & Epston (narrative) Gender-role analysis, power analysis, "personal is political" Feminist therapy Genogram, differentiation, triangulation Bowen Enactment, boundaries, joining (structural) Salvador Minuchin Directives, prescribing the symptom (strategic) Jay Haley Family sculpting, the four communication stances Virginia Satir Parent-Adult-Child ego states, games, scripts Eric Berne (TA) Multimodal therapy, BASIC ID, technical eclecticism Lazarus DBT (4 modules) for BPD + chronic suicidality Marsha Linehan ACT, hexaflex, defusion, RFT Hayes PACE, OARS, change talk Miller & Rollnick (MI) EMDR, 8 phases, bilateral stimulation Shapiro Working alliance = bond + goals + tasks Bordin Common factors / Dodo-bird / contextual model Wampold Stages of change (transtheoretical) Prochaska & DiClemente Multicultural competencies (awareness/knowledge/skills) Sue & Sue 4 ethical principles Beauchamp & Childress 12.4 Fast glossary (one line each) Term One-line definition (and who) A-B-C-D-E Activating event → Belief → Consequence → Dispute → Effective new philosophy (Albert Ellis, REBT). Actualising tendency Innate drive of the organism to grow and enhance itself (Carl Rogers). Archetypes Universal inherited images in the collective unconscious (Carl Jung). Automatic thoughts Rapid, plausible negative appraisals just below awareness (Aaron Beck). BASIC ID Multimodal assessment grid: Behaviour, Affect, Sensation, Imagery, Cognition, Interpersonal, Drugs/biology (Lazarus). Boundaries (family) Rules of contact between subsystems; rigid→disengaged, diffuse→enmeshed (Salvador Minuchin). Choice theory We choose nearly all our behaviour to meet five needs (William Glasser). Cognitive distortions Systematic thinking errors (all-or-nothing, overgeneralisation, catastrophising…) (Beck). Cognitive triad Negative view of self, world, future, in depression (Beck). Collaborative empiricism Client + therapist test beliefs as hypotheses with evidence (Beck). Collective unconscious Inherited layer shared by all humanity; holds archetypes (Jung). Common factors / Dodo-bird Shared ingredients (alliance, hope) drive outcome; all therapies roughly equal (Wampold). Conditions of worth "I'm valued only if…"; root of incongruence (Rogers). Core triad Congruence, unconditional positive regard, empathy (Rogers). Defence mechanisms Unconscious ego strategies that reduce anxiety (Freud / Anna Freud; George Vaillant's hierarchy). Dereflection Shift attention away from self/symptom (Viktor Frankl, logotherapy). Differentiation of self Separating intellect from emotion, self from family fusion (Bowen). Disputing Actively challenging irrational beliefs (Ellis). Empty chair Dialogue with an absent person or disowned part of self (Fritz Perls, Gestalt). Enactment Family plays out the problem interaction in session (Minuchin). Exception question "When is the problem absent or less?" (de Shazer, SFBT). Externalising Treat the problem as separate from the person (White, narrative). Extinction burst Temporary surge in a behaviour when reinforcement is first withdrawn (learning). Five basic needs Survival, love/belonging, power, freedom, fun (Glasser). Flooding Intense, prolonged exposure with no hierarchy/relaxation (behaviour therapy). Four givens Death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness (Irvin Yalom). Free association Say whatever comes, censorship off (Freud). Fully functioning person Open, present-living, self-trusting, free, creative (Rogers). Games Repetitive ulterior transactions paying off in bad feelings (Eric Berne, TA). Genogram Multigenerational family map/diagram (Bowen). Hexaflex ACT's six flexibility processes (Hayes). Identified patient The symptom-bearer expressing the system's dysfunction (family systems). Individuation Lifelong integration of the psyche into the self (Jung). Inferiority / superiority complex Paralysing self-doubt / over-compensation (Alfred Adler). Irrational beliefs Rigid absolutist demands (musts/shoulds) (Ellis). Latent learning Learning hidden until reinforcement reveals it; cognitive map (Edward Tolman). Logotherapy Therapy of meaning; will to meaning is primary (Frankl). Manifest vs latent content The remembered dream vs its hidden meaning (Freud). Miracle question "If a miracle solved it overnight, what would you notice?" (de Shazer, SFBT). Modeling Learning a behaviour by observing a model (Albert Bandura). Motivational interviewing Client-centred, directive resolution of ambivalence; OARS, change talk (Miller & Rollnick). Musturbation Rigid demands phrased as musts/shoulds (Ellis). Paradoxical intention Deliberately wish for the feared thing to break anticipatory anxiety (Frankl; also strategic family). Parent-Adult-Child The three ego states (Berne, TA). "Personal is political" Distress is rooted in social/gender power structures (feminist therapy). Power analysis Examining power inequality and how to gain personal power (feminist therapy). Prescribing the symptom Paradox: instruct the family to keep doing it (Jay Haley, strategic). Priming One stimulus speeds processing of a later one; implicit memory (cognitive). Reciprocal inhibition Relaxation displaces anxiety; basis of desensitisation (Joseph Wolpe). Re-authoring Building a new preferred life story (White & Epston, narrative). Scaling question "On 0–10, where are you?" (de Shazer, SFBT). Schema Deep core belief generating automatic thoughts (Beck). Shaping Reinforcing successive approximations of a new behaviour (B. F. Skinner). Social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefühl) Feeling of kinship with humanity; mark of health (Adler). Spontaneous recovery Extinguished response returns after a rest, proving suppression not unlearning (learning). Stages of change Precontemplation→contemplation→preparation→action→maintenance (Prochaska & DiClemente). Style of life Unique pattern built by ~age 5 to pursue goals (Adler). Systematic desensitisation Graded fear hierarchy paired with relaxation (Wolpe). Token economy Earn tokens for target behaviour, exchange for reinforcers (operant/Skinner). Top-dog vs under-dog The "should" tyrant vs the evasive resister within (Perls). Total behavior Acting, thinking, feeling, physiology; we control the first two (Glasser). Transference Client projects feelings about early figures onto the analyst (Freud). Triangulation A third person is drawn in to stabilise two-person tension (Bowen). Unconditional positive regard Non-possessive acceptance/warmth (Rogers). Unfinished business Unexpressed past feelings intruding on the present (Perls). Unique outcomes Moments the person resisted the problem story (White, narrative). WDEP Wants, Doing, Evaluation, Plan (Glasser; Wubbolding). Working alliance Bond + goals + tasks; top predictor of outcome (Bordin).

title: Research Methods & Statistics
text: Research Methods & Statistics One consolidated, exam-ready treatment built from A. K. Singh ( Tests, Measurements and Research Methods in Behavioural Sciences — strong on measurement, test construction, item analysis) and Coolican ( Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology — design, the logic of inference, which test to run). Read the prose and understand why each statistic does what it does; the tables are then just reminders. Trap boxes flag the exact confusions MCQs are built on. Coverage runs MET 2026 depth with NIMHANS M.Phil clinical extensions where the entrance pushes harder. In this book Research design & methodology Variables, confounds, mediation & moderation Validity & threats in a study Sampling Levels of measurement Reliability & validity in measurement Scaling (attitude measurement) Item analysis & test construction Descriptive statistics Distributions, z-scores & the Central Limit Theorem The logic of inference Parametric tests Non-parametric tests Correlation, regression & special coefficients Degrees of freedom — from scratch Qualitative & mixed methods Clinical trials & reporting standards Research ethics Decision table: which test do I use? Collected MCQ traps Worked intuition Fast glossary Research design & methodology Only an experiment (manipulate the IV and randomly assign participants) can establish causation, because randomisation balances out unknown confounds. Everything else can describe and relate, but not prove cause. Experimental hierarchy — by degree of control Design Manipulate IV? Random assignment? Control group? Internal validity True experimental (RCT) Yes Yes Yes High — gold standard for causation Quasi-experimental Yes No (intact/pre-existing groups: classes, wards) Usually yes Moderate — confounds remain Pre-experimental Loosely No Often none Low — e.g. one-group pretest-posttest; many threats Non-experimental (correlational) No — — No causal claim Between- vs within-subjects (and factorial) Between-subjects (independent groups): different people in each condition. No carry-over, but between-person variability is noise and groups may differ to start. Within-subjects (repeated measures): the same people in every condition. Each is their own control, so it is powerful and economical, but risks order/carry-over effects (practice, fatigue) — fixed by counterbalancing . Factorial: two or more IVs crossed, so you can test their interaction (a 2×2 has 4 cells). Specific designs to know Pretest-posttest control group: the classic two-group RCT. Posttest-only control group: avoids pretest sensitisation entirely. Solomon four-group: combines both. Two groups get a pretest, two do not; half of each get treatment. It detects and separates pretest sensitisation (the interaction of pretest and treatment) from the treatment effect itself. Resource-heavy but the most rigorous design for ruling out testing effects. Crossover design: every subject receives both conditions in different order. Single-case designs (ABA, ABAB, multiple baseline): used in behaviour analysis. Non-experimental & epidemiological designs Correlational: measure variables as they are and relate them; no manipulation, so no causal claim. Cross-sectional: one snapshot in time; reports prevalence . Cheap, but cannot show temporality or change. Longitudinal: the same people followed over time; can show change and causal order, but slow, costly, and bleeds participants through attrition . Cohort study: follow exposed and unexposed groups forward in time; reports relative risk . Case-control: start with cases and controls, look back at exposure; reports odds ratio . Case study: deep dive into one person/unit (rich, hypothesis-generating, not generalisable). Observational: watch behaviour in situ — naturalistic vs structured; participant vs non-participant; covert vs overt. Controlling confounds Randomisation — random assignment spreads unknown confounds evenly across groups (the most powerful control). Counterbalancing — vary the order of conditions across subjects to cancel order effects in within-subjects designs. Matching — pair subjects on a key variable (e.g. IQ) before assigning, removing that variable as a confound. Single-blind (participant unaware of condition) and double-blind (participant and experimenter/assessor unaware) — control expectancy and experimenter effects. Trap Random sampling vs random assignment . Random sampling = who gets into the study (drives external validity/generalisability). Random assignment = which condition they go to (drives internal validity/causation). A study can have one without the other. Trap Counterbalancing (fixes order effects in within-subjects designs) vs matching (controls a specific confound variable in between-subjects designs). Variables, confounds, mediation & moderation Independent variable (IV): what the experimenter manipulates or groups by — the presumed cause. Dependent variable (DV): the measured outcome — the presumed effect. Control variable: a variable deliberately held constant. Confound: a variable tied to both the IV and the DV, creating a spurious link and offering a rival explanation. Controlled by randomisation, matching, or statistical adjustment. Extraneous variable: any variable other than the IV that could affect the DV; it becomes a confound only if it also correlates with the IV. Operationalisation: defining a fuzzy construct in concrete, measurable terms (e.g. "anxiety" = score on the GAD-7). Bad operationalisation sinks construct validity. Mediator vs moderator — the high-frequency trap Both are "third variables," but they do opposite jobs: Mediator explains HOW / WHY the IV affects the DV — the mechanism in the causal chain: IV → Mediator → DV . Stress → cortisol → poorer immunity: cortisol mediates. If you control the mediator, the IV–DV link weakens or vanishes. Tested with Baron-Kenny steps or Hayes PROCESS. Moderator changes WHEN / FOR WHOM / HOW STRONGLY the IV affects the DV — it alters the strength or direction of the relationship but is not on the causal path. Therapy works better for women than men: sex moderates therapy → outcome. Statistically a moderator shows up as an interaction term (X × M) in regression. Trap Mediator = mechanism ( how , sits between IV and DV). Moderator = condition ( for whom / when , an interaction). Hook: me diator = me chanism; mo der ator = depends. Validity & threats in a study This is distinct from test validity (covered under measurement). Here we judge the study's conclusions . Internal validity: did the IV really cause the change in the DV, with no confound responsible? Maximised by experimental control and randomisation. External validity: do the findings generalise to other people, settings, and times? Includes population validity (sample → population) and ecological validity (lab → real life). Construct validity (of the study): does the operationalisation actually match the intended construct? Statistical conclusion validity: is the inference about the relationship sound? Threatened by low power, violated assumptions, and p-hacking. There is usually a trade-off : tight lab control boosts internal validity, but the artificial setting can hurt external/ecological validity. Threats to internal validity (Campbell & Stanley) History: an outside event happens during the study and affects the DV. Maturation: participants naturally change over time (grow, tire, heal) regardless of the IV. Testing: taking the pretest itself changes the posttest (practice, sensitisation) — controlled by the Solomon four-group design. Instrumentation: the measuring tool or observer drifts over time. Regression to the mean: people selected for extreme scores drift back toward average on retest, faking an "effect" in pre/post designs without a control. Selection bias: groups differ before the study (the core flaw of non-randomised designs). Attrition (mortality): participants drop out non-randomly, leaving an unrepresentative remainder. Diffusion of treatment: the control group learns from / is contaminated by the experimental group. Hawthorne effect: simply being observed changes behaviour. Demand characteristics: subjects guess the hypothesis and play along. Trap Maturation (internal, natural change within people) vs history (an external event ). And regression to the mean is mistaken for a treatment effect whenever extreme groups are retested without a control group. Sampling A sample stands in for a population. Whether you can generalise depends entirely on how it was drawn. Probability sampling — everyone has a known, non-zero chance Only probability methods let you calculate sampling error and generalise with confidence. Method How Note Simple random Every individual has an equal chance (lottery / random-number table) The benchmark; requires a sampling frame Systematic Pick every k-th person from a list (k = N/n) after a random start Easy, but dangerous if the list has a hidden periodicity matching k Stratified Divide the population into strata (age bands, sex), then sample randomly within each Guarantees representation of each stratum and usually reduces sampling error. Proportionate or disproportionate Cluster Divide into naturally occurring clusters (schools, villages), randomly select whole clusters , study everyone (or many) inside Cheaper over wide areas but higher sampling error. Two-stage = sample within selected clusters Multistage Nest the above (random districts → random schools within → random pupils) National surveys Non-probability sampling — selection chance unknown Convenience: whoever is to hand (the classic undergraduate subject pool). Most prone to bias. Purposive (judgmental): the researcher hand-picks information-rich cases on set criteria. Quota: fill fixed counts per category (50 men, 50 women) but non-randomly within — the non-probability cousin of stratified. Snowball: participants recruit further participants; for hidden/stigmatised populations (e.g. drug users). Trap Stratified vs cluster. Stratified samples randomly within every subgroup (you want all strata in) and lowers error; cluster randomly picks some whole subgroups and skips the rest (you sample groups, for cost) and raises error. Both are probability methods. Trap Sampling error vs sampling bias . Error is the random , unavoidable difference between a sample statistic and the true value from chance alone; it shrinks as n grows and centres on the truth. Bias is a systematic skew from a flawed method (e.g. convenience sampling); it does not shrink with n — a bigger biased sample is just more precisely wrong. Levels of measurement Before any statistic, ask: what kind of numbers am I holding? Stevens (1946) showed that a number can carry four different amounts of information, and the amount you have dictates which statistics are even meaningful . Running a mean on jersey numbers is nonsense not because the arithmetic fails but because the numbers were never on a scale where "average" means anything. This is the single most important idea in the section: the scale chooses the test. The four levels, from least to most information (NOIR) Nominal — labels only Numbers are just names for categories with no order: 1 = male, 2 = female, or blood groups, religion, diagnosis. You can count how many fall in each box and find the mode , but "2 > 1" is meaningless. Permissible: frequencies, proportions, mode, and chi-square on the counts. Ordinal — rank order, unequal gaps Numbers now carry order but the distance between ranks is not equal or known. Finishing 1st, 2nd, 3rd tells you who beat whom, not by how much. Likert agreement, pain 0–10, socio-economic class, IQ classification bands. Because gaps are unequal you should not add or average them, so the centre is the median and spread is described with percentiles. Permissible: median, percentile, Spearman's rho , Mann-Whitney U , and rank-based (non-parametric) tests generally. Interval — equal gaps, no true zero Equal distances mean a degree is a degree everywhere on the scale, so you can finally add, subtract, and take a mean . But zero is arbitrary (0°C is not "no temperature"), so ratios are meaningless : 20°C is not "twice as hot" as 10°C. IQ scores and calendar years sit here. Permissible: mean, SD, t-tests, ANOVA, Pearson's r . Ratio — equal gaps and an absolute zero Zero means none of the thing (0 kg = no weight, 0 ms = no time). Now ratios are valid : 40 kg really is twice 20 kg. Height, weight, reaction time, income, age. All arithmetic plus the geometric mean and coefficient of variation. For test-choice purposes interval and ratio behave identically, which is why people lump them as "scale" or "continuous" data. Level Property added Example Centre Permissible stats Nominal Categories, no order Sex, blood group, diagnosis Mode Frequency, proportion, chi-square Ordinal + Order (unequal gaps) Likert, pain 0–10, SES class Median Median, percentile, Spearman, Mann-Whitney Interval + Equal gaps (no true 0) °C, IQ, calendar year Mean Mean, SD, t, ANOVA, Pearson r Ratio + True zero (ratios valid) Height, weight, RT, age Mean All of the above + geometric mean, CV Mnemonic NOIR — Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio, in increasing order of information. Trap A scale "having numbers" does not make it interval. A 1–5 Likert item is strictly ordinal (the gap from "disagree" to "neutral" need not equal "neutral" to "agree"); only a summed multi-item Likert scale is commonly treated as interval. MCQs love "temperature in Celsius is ratio" — false, no true zero; Kelvin is ratio. And "ordinal data can use the mean" is false — use the median. Reliability & validity in measurement A. K. Singh's home turf. A test score is only as good as its reliability (consistency) and validity (does it measure the intended construct). Reliability — consistency of measurement Reliability asks: if I measured again, would I get the same score? It is a coefficient from 0 to 1 (≥ .70 acceptable for research, ≥ .80–.90 for clinical decisions). Conceptually a score = true score + error; reliability = the proportion of true-score variance in observed scores. Test-retest: same test, same people, two occasions; correlate. Indexes stability over time . Threat: practice/memory effects, real change. Parallel-form (alternate-form): two equivalent versions; correlate. Controls memory effects but you must prove the forms are truly equivalent. Split-half: split the items in two (e.g. odd vs even), correlate the halves. Because you have halved the test, correct upward with the Spearman-Brown prophecy formula (longer tests are more reliable). Internal consistency — Cronbach's alpha (α): the average of all possible split-halves; the standard index of whether the items hang together / measure one thing. Rises with more items and higher inter-item correlations. Acceptable ≈ .70–.95. For dichotomous (right/wrong) items, use KR-20 (Kuder-Richardson). Inter-rater reliability: agreement between observers. Cohen's kappa (κ) for categorical ratings corrects for chance agreement (raw % agreement overstates it); the intraclass correlation (ICC) is used for continuous ratings. High-yield NIMHANS depth on alpha: it is not a measure of unidimensionality, and a high alpha can simply mean you have many items. Above ~.95 suggests redundancy (items are near-duplicates), not excellence. Alpha assumes tau-equivalence; modern psychometrics often prefers McDonald's omega . Always report alpha alongside the construct it indexes. Validity — are you measuring the right thing? Face validity: does it look like it measures the construct, to a layperson? Weakest, most superficial — informally a subset of content validity. Content validity: do the items cover the full domain of the construct (a maths test sampling all topics)? Judged by experts / a blueprint. Criterion validity: does the test correlate with an external criterion? Two flavours by timing — concurrent (criterion measured now , e.g. a new depression scale vs an established one today) and predictive (criterion measured later , e.g. an entrance exam predicting future grades). Construct validity: does it truly tap the theoretical construct? Built from convergent evidence (correlates with measures it should ) and discriminant/divergent evidence (does not correlate with unrelated measures). Includes factorial validity . High-yield Reliability sets a ceiling on validity. A test cannot correlate with anything (be valid) more than it correlates with itself (is reliable). The validity ceiling is max validity = √reliability (assuming a perfectly reliable criterion): r xx = 0.81 → max validity = 0.90. So unreliability caps validity, but the reverse fails — a test can be perfectly reliable yet not valid : a bathroom scale that always reads 5 kg heavy is consistent (reliable) but wrong (invalid). Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. Trap Reliable ≠ valid. Reliability = consistency; validity = accuracy/measuring the intended thing. A test can be reliable but not valid; it cannot be valid without being reliable. Also concurrent (criterion measured now) vs predictive (criterion in the future) — both are criterion validity. Scaling (attitude measurement) Scaling turns attitudes into numbers. Know the logic that distinguishes the four classic methods: Likert (summated rating): respondents rate agreement on a symmetric scale (Strongly disagree … Strongly agree, usually 5 or 7 points); item scores are summed . Easiest to build; individual items are ordinal. Thurstone (equal-appearing intervals): judges first scale many statements for favourability; respondents simply endorse the ones they agree with , and their score is the average scale value of those statements. Aims for interval-level measurement; labour-intensive to construct. Guttman (cumulative / scalogram): items form a hierarchy so that agreeing with a strong item implies agreement with all weaker ones. Unidimensional and reproducible. Semantic differential (Osgood): rate a concept on a series of bipolar adjective pairs (good–bad, weak–strong, fast–slow) on a 7-point line; classically loads onto three dimensions — evaluation, potency, activity (E-P-A) . Trap Thurstone (judges pre-scale statements; you endorse/reject) vs Likert (you rate degree of agreement, items summed) vs Guttman (cumulative hierarchy) vs semantic differential (bipolar adjective pairs). Osgood = semantic differential = evaluation/potency/activity. Item analysis & test construction A. K. Singh's strength: how individual items are evaluated when building a test. After piloting, you examine each item on three indices and keep, revise, or drop it. Item difficulty (p): the proportion of examinees who got the item right . p = 1.0 means everyone passed (too easy); p = 0 means nobody did (too hard). Counter-intuitively, a higher p = an easier item. For maximum discrimination, p ≈ 0.50 is ideal (adjusted upward for guessing on MCQs); keep a spread of difficulties. Discrimination index (D): does the item separate high scorers from low scorers? Split into top and bottom groups (often 27%); D = (proportion correct in upper group) − (proportion correct in lower group) . D ranges −1 to +1; ≥ 0.40 excellent, 0.20–0.39 acceptable, < 0.20 poor. A negative D (low scorers beat high scorers) flags a flawed or mis-keyed item — drop it. Item-total correlation: the correlation between the item score and the total test score (for dichotomous items, a point-biserial). High = the item pulls in the same direction as the test as a whole (good internal consistency); near zero or negative = the item does not belong. Trap Item difficulty is a proportion correct , so a high p = an easy item , not a hard one. And discrimination, not difficulty, is what tells you whether an item separates strong from weak examinees. High-yield NIMHANS depth — IRT basics. Classical test theory (p, D) is sample-dependent: the same item looks "harder" in a weaker group. Item Response Theory (IRT) models the probability of a correct response as a function of latent ability (θ) via an item characteristic curve (ICC) , with item parameters a = discrimination (slope), b = difficulty (location along θ), c = guessing (lower asymptote) — the 1PL/Rasch, 2PL and 3PL models. IRT parameters are (ideally) sample-independent, which is why modern computer-adaptive tests (CAT) are built on it. Descriptive statistics Descriptive statistics summarise the sample in front of you ; they make no claim about a wider population (that is inference). You describe three things about any batch of numbers: where the centre sits ( central tendency ), how spread out it is ( dispersion ), and what shape it has ( skewness, kurtosis ). Central tendency — where the middle is Mean The arithmetic average: add all scores, divide by n. In symbols x̄ = Σx / n . It uses every value, which is its strength and its weakness — every value includes the outliers. One billionaire walking into a room sends the mean income soaring while the median barely moves. Use the mean for roughly symmetric / normal interval-ratio data. Median The middle value when scores are ordered (the 50th percentile). With an even n it is the average of the two middle scores. It ignores the magnitude of extreme scores, so it is robust to outliers and skew . Use it for skewed data (income, reaction times, length of stay) and for ordinal data. Mode The most frequent value. It is the only central-tendency measure usable on nominal data, and a distribution can be bimodal or multimodal (two humps often hints two subgroups are mixed together). Mnemonic Why skew moves them apart: in a symmetric distribution mean = median = mode. In positive (right) skew (long tail of high values, e.g. income) the tail drags the mean up the most, the median less, the mode least, so mode < median < mean . In negative (left) skew it reverses: mean < median < mode . Hook: the mean follows the tail. Trap The order under skew. Positive skew → mean is the largest (mean > median > mode). "Which average is most affected by an outlier?" → the mean . "Which is best for skewed/income data?" → the median . Dispersion — how spread out Range and IQR Range = max − min. One number, crude, fully at the mercy of the two most extreme scores. The Interquartile Range (IQR) = Q3 − Q1 spans the middle 50% of the data, throwing away the outer quarters, so it is robust; it is the box in a box-plot. Variance and SD — the real workhorses To capture spread we measure how far each score sits from the mean. Deviations (x − x̄) sum to zero, so we square them first. The average squared deviation is the variance . Taking the square root returns to the original units — the standard deviation (SD) . Population variance: σ² = Σ(x − μ)² / N Sample variance: s² = Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1) SD = √variance. Population σ = √σ²; sample s = √s². SD is in the same units as the data. What SD actually means: the typical (root-mean-square) distance of a score from the mean. SD = 0 means every score is identical; a larger SD means scores fan out further. In a normal distribution about two-thirds of scores fall within ±1 SD of the mean. It is the default measure of spread because it feeds straight into z-scores, SE, and every parametric test. High-yield Why divide by n − 1 (Bessel's correction)? A sample's own mean sits in the middle of the sample, so deviations from it are a touch too small and would under-estimate the population spread. Dividing by n − 1 (the degrees of freedom) inflates the estimate just enough to make it unbiased. Population formulas use N because μ is fixed and known. The full intuition is in the degrees-of-freedom chapter. Coefficient of variation CV = (SD / mean) × 100%. A unitless relative spread, so you can compare variability across different scales (is weight more variable than height?). Only meaningful on ratio data with a true zero. Shape Skewness Asymmetry. Positive skew = long tail to the right (high values), negative skew = long tail to the left, zero skew = symmetric. Skew is what breaks the normality assumption and pushes you toward the median or a non-parametric test. Kurtosis Tailedness / peakedness relative to the normal curve. Leptokurtic = sharp peak, fat tails (more extreme scores than normal). Platykurtic = flat, thin tails. Mesokurtic = like the normal curve. Mnemonic platy = plateau = flat; lepto = leaping peak. Distributions, z-scores & the Central Limit Theorem The normal (Gaussian) curve A symmetric bell, fully defined by just two numbers: its mean (μ) and SD (σ). Mean = median = mode all sit at the peak. It matters because (a) many natural and psychological variables are roughly normal, and (b) the sampling distribution of the mean becomes normal even when the raw data is not (the CLT, below), which is what lets parametric tests work. High-yield The 68–95–99.7 (empirical) rule. In any normal distribution: ≈ 68% of scores fall within ±1 SD of the mean, ≈ 95% within ±2 SD (more precisely ±1.96 SD), ≈ 99.7% within ±3 SD. So a score 2 SD above the mean beats about 97.5% of the distribution. z-scores — putting everything on one ruler A z-score says how many SDs a value sits from its mean: z = (x − μ) / σ . It standardises any value onto the standard normal distribution (μ = 0, σ = 1), so scores from different scales become comparable and you can read off percentiles from a z-table. A z of +1.5 means "1.5 SDs above average." Standard scores built on z Test-makers rescale z so there are no negatives or decimals, but the information is identical: T-score: mean = 50, SD = 10. Formula T = 50 + 10z . The MMPI uses T-scores; T = 70 → +2 SD → 97.5th percentile (the classic clinical cutoff). Stanine ("standard nine"): range 1–9, mean = 5, SD ≈ 2. Sten ("standard ten"): range 1–10, mean = 5.5, SD = 2. The 16PF uses stens. Wechsler / deviation IQ: mean = 100, SD = 15. Percentile rank: the % of people scoring at or below you — a rank, not a z-score, and not equal-interval (percentiles bunch up near the middle of a normal curve). Trap T-score (mean 50, SD 10) vs Wechsler IQ (mean 100, SD 15) vs sten (mean 5.5, SD 2) vs stanine (mean 5, SD 2). Also: a percentile is a rank, and the gaps between percentiles are not equal — moving from the 50th to 55th percentile is a tiny score change, but 90th to 95th is a big one. Sampling distribution & the standard error Here is the conceptual leap that powers inference. Imagine drawing many samples of size n and writing down each sample's mean. Those means form their own distribution: the sampling distribution of the mean . Its spread is the standard error of the mean (SEM) : SE = SD / √n SE is the typical distance between a sample mean and the true population mean — how wrong your sample mean is likely to be as an estimate. Because of the √n, SE shrinks as the sample grows, but with diminishing returns (to halve the SE you must quadruple n). Trap SD vs SE. SD describes the spread of individual scores ; SE (= SD/√n) describes the spread of sample means and is always smaller. Reporting SE instead of SD makes data look tidier than it is — be sceptical. The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) The CLT states that as sample size n grows, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal distribution regardless of the shape of the underlying population , with mean = μ and SD = σ/√n. This is the foundation of inferential statistics: even on skewed raw data you can use normal-theory (parametric) tests on the mean , provided n is reasonable. Common rule of thumb: n ≥ 30 . Other distributions to recognise t distribution: like the normal but with fatter tails to account for estimating σ from a small sample; shaped by degrees of freedom; → normal as df → ∞. Chi-square (χ²): right-skewed, only positive, for categorical/count data. F distribution: a ratio of two variances; right-skewed; used in ANOVA and regression. Binomial: discrete, counts of successes in n independent trials. Poisson: counts of rare events per fixed interval of time or space. The logic of inference Inference is reasoning from a sample to a population . We can never be certain, so we frame the question as a bet against a default assumption and quantify how surprised we would be by our data if that default were true. Null vs alternative hypotheses Null hypothesis (H₀): the boring default — no effect, no difference, no relationship, status quo (e.g. μ₁ = μ₂, or r = 0). This is what we actually test. Alternative hypothesis (H₁): there is an effect/difference/relationship. Usually what the researcher believes. Two-tailed (any direction) vs one-tailed (a specific direction). We never "accept" H₀ ; we either reject it or fail to reject it. Failing to reject is "not enough evidence," not "proof of no effect." Absence of evidence ≠ evidence of absence. Two ways to be wrong H₀ is true (no real effect) H₀ is false (real effect) Reject H₀ Type I error (α) — false positive Correct — power (1 − β) Fail to reject H₀ Correct (1 − α) Type II error (β) — false negative Type I (α): claiming an effect that is not real. You set this in advance, conventionally α = 0.05. Type II (β): missing an effect that is real. Conventionally kept ≤ 0.20. Power = 1 − β: the probability of detecting a real effect when it exists. Convention: aim for 0.80. Power increases when: sample size n ↑, true effect size ↑, variability (SD) ↓, α made more lenient ↑, and (slightly) using a one-tailed test. There is a tension: lowering α (fewer false positives) raises β (more misses) unless you also raise n. An a priori power analysis sets the sample size before data collection. Trap Type I vs Type II. α = false positive = convicting an innocent (rejecting a true H₀, wrongly rejecting a TRUE null). β = false negative = letting the guilty go (missing a real effect, wrongly retaining a false null). Hook: "Sigh, I missed it" = Type II. The p-value — what it is and is not What it IS: the probability of obtaining data at least as extreme as what you observed, assuming H₀ is true . Small p = "my data would be surprising if there were really no effect," casting doubt on H₀. Decision rule: if p < α → reject H₀ (e.g. p = 0.03 < α = 0.05 → reject). Trap The classic p-value trap. p is NOT the probability that H₀ is true, NOT the probability your result happened "by chance," and NOT the probability you have made an error. It is conditional on H₀. Also p < 0.05 is a convention, not a law of nature, and statistical significance ≠ clinical/practical importance (a trivial effect turns significant with a huge n). Always report effect size alongside p. One-tailed vs two-tailed A two-tailed test asks "is there a difference in either direction?" and splits α into both tails (0.025 each) — the safe default. A one-tailed test asks about a difference in one pre-specified direction, putting all 0.05 in one tail; it has more power but only if you committed to the direction in advance for theoretical reasons. Choosing one-tailed after seeing the data to scrape under 0.05 is p-hacking. Confidence intervals A 95% CI is a range of plausible values for the true parameter. Interpretation: if we repeated the study endlessly, 95% of the intervals built this way would contain the true value. Practical links: if a 95% CI for a difference excludes 0, then p < 0.05; if a 95% CI for a ratio (OR/RR) excludes 1, then p < 0.05. A wider CI means a less precise estimate (small n or high variability). CIs are often more informative than a bare p because they show effect size and precision together. Effect size The p-value tells you whether there is an effect; the effect size tells you how big it is, independent of n. This is why two studies can both be "significant" yet matter very differently. Statistic Used with Benchmarks (small / medium / large) Cohen's d Standardised mean difference (t-tests) 0.2 / 0.5 / 0.8 Hedges' g Like d, corrected for small n Same as d Pearson r Correlation 0.10 / 0.30 / 0.50 r² / eta² (η²) / partial η² Proportion of variance explained (ANOVA) 0.01 / 0.06 / 0.14 Odds ratio (OR) Categorical (case-control) 1.5 / 2.5 / 4.3 High-yield NIMHANS pushes harder — effect size & power analysis. Clinical psychology expects effect sizes, not just p, and an a priori power analysis (e.g. G*Power) before collecting data: fix α (.05), desired power (.80) and the smallest effect worth detecting, then solve for n. After a null result, examine the CI / effect size before concluding "no effect" — you may simply have been underpowered. Cohen's benchmarks are conventions, not laws; in clinical work a "small" effect on suicidality can be hugely important. Parametric tests Parametric tests make assumptions about the population's distribution (chiefly normality) and operate on its parameters (means, variances). When the assumptions hold they are more powerful than their non-parametric cousins — they squeeze more information from the same data. The four parametric assumptions Normality of the DV / of the residuals (the CLT rescues this at large n). Homogeneity of variance — groups have similar spread (checked with Levene's test; Welch's correction if violated). Independence of observations (except where the design pairs them, as in paired/repeated designs). Interval or ratio measurement of the DV. z-test Compares a sample mean to a known population mean when the population SD (σ) is known (rare) or n is very large. Test statistic z = (x̄ − μ) / (σ/√n). In practice we usually do not know σ, which is exactly why the t-test exists. t-tests — comparing one or two means A t-test asks whether a mean difference is big relative to the noise . The general shape is t = (difference in means) / (standard error of that difference) . A big t means the signal dwarfs the noise. We use t rather than z because we estimate the SD from the sample, adding uncertainty (hence the fatter-tailed t distribution, indexed by df). One-sample t: sample mean vs a known/hypothesised value. df = n − 1. Independent-samples t: two separate groups' means (treatment vs control). df = n₁ + n₂ − 2. Assumes equal variances (use Welch's if not). Paired (related) t: two scores from the same or matched subjects (pre vs post, twins). It works on the differences within each pair; df = (number of pairs) − 1. By using each subject as their own control it removes between-person variability, making it more powerful when pairing is sensible. Trap Independent vs paired t. Two different groups → independent . Same people measured twice (or matched pairs) → paired . Using an independent t on paired data throws away the pairing and loses power. ANOVA — comparing three or more means Why not just run many t-tests? Because each test carries a 5% false-positive risk and they pile up ( inflated family-wise Type I error ). ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) tests all means at once with a single test. It works by partitioning variance . Total variability splits into between-groups variance (differences among the group means — the signal, driven by the IV) and within-groups variance (scatter of individuals inside each group — the noise, "error"). The test statistic is the F-ratio : F = between-groups variance / within-groups variance = MS between / MS within If H₀ is true (all means equal), both estimate the same error variance and F ≈ 1. A real effect inflates the numerator, pushing F > 1. A significant F says " at least one mean differs" — it does not say which, so you follow with post-hoc tests . One-way ANOVA: one factor with ≥ 3 levels. Factorial (e.g. two-way) ANOVA: two or more factors at once (drug × dose). Tests each factor's main effect plus their interaction . Repeated-measures ANOVA: the within-subjects version (same people across ≥ 3 conditions/times). Adds the sphericity assumption (equal variances of the differences; corrected with Greenhouse-Geisser). ANCOVA: ANOVA with a continuous covariate statistically removed first (e.g. comparing post-test scores while adjusting for pre-test), which reduces error variance and controls a confound. MANOVA: ANOVA with multiple DVs tested together. High-yield Main effect vs interaction. A main effect is the effect of one factor averaged over the other ("the drug lowered anxiety overall"). An interaction means one factor's effect depends on the level of the other ("the drug helped young patients but not the old") — on a graph, non-parallel lines. Interactions are usually the interesting finding and override simple talk of main effects. Post-hoc tests If the ANOVA F is significant, the omnibus result tells you at least one mean differs but not which. Post-hoc pairwise tests localise the differences while controlling the family-wise error rate. Test When to use Conservatism Tukey HSD All pairwise comparisons, equal n Moderate Bonferroni Few planned comparisons (α/k) Very conservative Scheffé Any contrasts, unequal n Most conservative LSD (Fisher) Only after a significant F Liberal, no protection Dunnett Each group vs a control Moderate Games-Howell Unequal variances Like Tukey Pearson r & linear regression Pearson's r measures the strength and direction of a linear association between two continuous variables, from −1 (perfect negative) through 0 (none) to +1 (perfect positive). r² (coefficient of determination) = the proportion of variance in one variable shared with (explained by) the other; r = .50 → r² = .25 = 25% of variance shared. Linear regression fits a line to predict Y from X, Ŷ = a + bX , where b (slope) is the predicted change in Y per unit X and a is the intercept; the least-squares fit minimises the sum of squared residuals. Multiple regression uses several predictors (Ŷ = a + b₁X₁ + b₂X₂ + …); beware multicollinearity (check VIF). Logistic regression handles a binary outcome, modelling the log-odds and yielding odds ratios. Question Parametric test df / note One mean vs a known value One-sample t n − 1 Two related means (pre/post, matched) Paired t pairs − 1 Two independent group means Independent t n₁ + n₂ − 2 ≥ 3 independent group means One-way ANOVA F; post-hoc if significant ≥ 3 related means (within subjects) Repeated-measures ANOVA sphericity Two factors at once Factorial ANOVA main effects + interaction Compare groups adjusting a covariate ANCOVA covariate removed first Multiple DVs together MANOVA — Linear association, two continuous Pearson r −1 to +1; r² = variance shared Predict continuous Y from X Linear regression Ŷ = a + bX Non-parametric tests Non-parametric ("distribution-free") tests make no assumption of normality and mostly work on ranks rather than raw values, so they suit ordinal data and small or skewed samples. High-yield Use a non-parametric test when: the DV is ordinal (ranks); the data are clearly non-normal and cannot be fixed; there are extreme outliers ; the sample is small so you cannot lean on the CLT; or variances are badly unequal. Cost: less power than the parametric test when the parametric assumptions would have held. Do not pick non-parametric "to be safe" if assumptions hold — you lose power. Parametric counterpart Non-parametric test Use One-sample / paired t Wilcoxon signed-rank One sample vs a value, or paired/related scores — ranks the signed differences (simpler paired) Sign test Uses only the direction (+/−) of each pair's difference; weaker than signed-rank Independent t Mann-Whitney U (= Wilcoxon rank-sum) Two independent groups One-way ANOVA Kruskal-Wallis H ≥ 3 independent groups Repeated-measures ANOVA Friedman test ≥ 3 related conditions Pearson r Spearman's rho (or Kendall's tau) Monotonic association on ranks — Chi-square (χ²) Categorical counts (below) Chi-square (χ²) — for categorical data Chi-square compares the frequencies you observed with the frequencies expected under H₀: χ² = Σ (O − E)² / E . A big χ² means observed counts depart a lot from expectation. Goodness-of-fit: does one categorical variable's distribution match an expected one (e.g. are births evenly spread across months)? Test of independence: are two categorical variables associated (e.g. smoking × diagnosis in a contingency table)? Assumptions: independent observations and expected count ≥ 5 in (almost) every cell. If a 2×2 table has any expected cell < 5, use Fisher's exact test . For paired categorical data (same people, before/after yes-no) use McNemar's test ; for ≥ 3 related categorical measures, Cochran's Q . Trap Wilcoxon signed-rank (paired/related) vs Mann-Whitney U (independent groups) — same pairing logic as paired-vs-independent t. Also Kruskal-Wallis (independent, ≥ 3) vs Friedman (related, ≥ 3). Correlation, regression & special coefficients Correlation is not causation A correlation only says two variables move together. It cannot tell you that X caused Y because of two perennial alternatives: reverse causation (Y → X) and the third-variable (confound) problem (Z drives both). Ice-cream sales correlate with drownings because summer heat drives both. Only a controlled experiment with randomisation licenses a causal claim. Partial correlation Partial correlation measures the association between X and Y after statistically removing the influence of a third variable Z from both.
