If the X–Y correlation collapses once you partial out Z, Z was likely the confound doing the work. Regression vs correlation They share machinery but answer different questions. Correlation is symmetric and unitless — it quantifies how tightly two variables relate (r), with no direction of prediction. Regression is directional — it builds an equation to predict Y from X (Ŷ = a + bX) and its slope b is in real units. r tells you the strength; regression lets you forecast and gives the line. Trap Correlation vs regression. r = strength of association, no units, symmetric (r of X with Y = r of Y with X). Regression = prediction equation with a slope in units, and X→Y is not the same line as Y→X. "r = 0" only rules out a linear relationship — a perfect U-shape has r ≈ 0. And note: r = +0.90 is a strong positive linear association, but r² = 0.81 means 81% of variance explained, NOT 90% . Special correlation coefficients — match the coefficient to the data Pearson r assumes both variables are continuous. When one or both are categorical you switch coefficient: Coefficient Variable 1 Variable 2 Pearson r Continuous Continuous Spearman rho Ordinal (ranks) Ordinal (ranks) Point-biserial True dichotomy (e.g. sex) Continuous Biserial Artificial dichotomy (continuous split into 2) Continuous Phi (φ) True dichotomy True dichotomy (2×2) Tetrachoric Artificial dichotomy Artificial dichotomy For a categorical-categorical association beyond 2×2, use Cramér's V (derived from χ²). Mnemonic "bi-serial" pairs a continuous variable with a dichotomy: point- biserial for a genuine two-category split, plain biserial when a continuous variable was forced into two. Phi vs tetrachoric are the two-dichotomy versions — phi for true categories, tetrachoric when both dichotomies are really continuous underneath. Degrees of freedom — from scratch The one statistics idea everyone memorises as " n − 1 " and almost nobody actually gets . Built from zero with one idea you carry the whole way, so by the end you can look at any test and say why its df is what it is, instead of recalling a formula. Definition Degrees of freedom = how many numbers are still free to be anything, once you have already fixed some fact about them. Every fact you fix (a total, a mean, an estimate) locks one number down, so that number is no longer free. Count the values, subtract the facts you have pinned. That is it — everything below is just this sentence applied. The phrase sounds technical but the idea is everyday. "Freedom" here means freedom to vary — to take any value. A degree of freedom is one independent number you could still change without breaking a rule you have agreed to. The moment a rule forces a number to be one specific value, it has lost its freedom and stops counting. The name comes from physics: a particle moving in 3D space has 3 degrees of freedom (x, y, z); pin it to a tabletop and it has 2; pin it to a wire and it has 1. Each constraint removes one direction it is free to move. Statistics borrows the word exactly. The simplest possible example Forget statistics. I tell you: "I'm thinking of three numbers, and they add up to 10 ." How many can you freely guess? You can pick the first — say 4 . Still free. The second — say 3 . Still free. Now the third is not a guess any more: it must be 3 , because the three must sum to 10. The total forced the last number. Three numbers, one rule (the total), so 2 are free and 1 is forced . Degrees of freedom = 3 − 1 = 2 . The "−1" is the one fact you fixed. If I had said " n numbers with a fixed total," then n − 1 are free and the last is determined. df = n − 1 , not because of a magic rule, but because fixing the total uses up exactly one number's freedom. The last value is the "dependent" one — it has to mop up whatever is needed to satisfy the rule. A degree of freedom is spent by every quantity you estimate In real statistics the "rule you fixed" is almost always this: you calculated a statistic from the data and then reused it. The most common one is the sample mean . To work out how spread out a sample is, you first need its mean — but the mean is computed from the same data . Once you know the mean of n scores, they are no longer all free; they must be consistent with that mean. Five exam scores with a mean of 70 must sum to 350. You are free to set the first four (60, 80, 75, 65 = 280); the fifth must be 70. Four free, one forced. df = 5 − 1 = 4. Definition General rule: df = (number of observations) − (number of parameters you estimated from those observations). Each parameter estimated from the data costs one degree of freedom, because using it imposes one constraint. Estimate one quantity (the mean) → lose 1 df. Estimate two (a slope and an intercept) → lose 2. This single principle predicts the df for every test. Trap df is not "the sample size." It is the sample size minus the estimates you have made. "With n = 20, the t-test df is 20" is wrong: a one-sample t uses the mean, so df = 19. Why sample variance divides by n − 1 (Bessel's correction) Now you can reason it out instead of reciting it. For a whole population you divide by N, because you know the true mean and every score really is free: σ² = Σ(x − μ)² / N . But with a sample you do not know μ. You substitute the sample mean x̄, computed from the very same data, and x̄ sits, by construction, right in the middle of your sample — it hugs your data more tightly than the unknown true mean would. So the deviations from x̄ are, on average, a little too small . Divide by n and you systematically underestimate the real spread. Dividing by n − 1 instead makes the estimate a touch larger, exactly correcting that bias: s² = Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1) . Definition You divide by n − 1 not as a fudge but because only n − 1 of the deviations are free. Once x̄ is fixed, the deviations (x − x̄) must sum to zero, so the last is forced by the other n − 1. There are only n − 1 independent pieces of spread information, so you average over n − 1. High-yield NIMHANS depth — this is Bessel's correction . The estimator s² with n − 1 is unbiased for σ² (its long-run average equals the true variance); dividing by n gives a biased (too small) estimator. Subtlety they probe: s (the SD, the square root) is still slightly biased even after the correction, but s² is unbiased. The correction targets the variance. Degrees of freedom in every test you will meet Just apply "values minus estimates" to each test — it is the same idea every time. t-tests Test df Why (what got fixed) One-sample t n − 1 One group, estimated its mean → lose 1. Paired (dependent) t n − 1 You work on n difference scores and estimate their mean → lose 1 (n = number of pairs). Independent-samples t n₁ + n₂ − 2 Two groups, estimated two means → lose 2. Trap For the paired t with 20 people measured twice, df is not 40 − 2 and not 20. You reduce each pair to one difference score, giving 20 numbers, estimate their mean, so df = 20 − 1 = 19 . One-way ANOVA ANOVA has more than one df because it splits the data into "between groups" and "within groups." Let k = number of groups, N = total people across all groups. Source df Why Between groups k − 1 k group means, but the grand mean fixes one → k − 1 are free. Within groups (error) N − k Each group spends one df on its own mean; k groups → lose k. Total N − 1 N scores, the grand mean fixes one. Check: (k − 1) + (N − k) = N − 1. ✓ High-yield Self-check that always works: between + within = total. If your two df do not add up to N − 1, you have miscounted. The F-ratio is then reported as F(df_between, df_within), e.g. F(2, 27). Chi-square (χ²) Type df Why Goodness of fit k − 1 k categories; the total count is fixed, so the last category's count is forced. Test of independence (r × c table) (r − 1)(c − 1) Row and column totals are fixed, so once you fill (r−1) rows and (c−1) columns, the rest is forced. Picture the 2×2 with all four margin totals fixed: write one cell and the other three are determined by subtraction. So df = (2−1)(2−1) = 1 . Only one cell was ever free. Correlation & regression Analysis df Why Pearson r (significance test) n − 2 You estimate two things to relate x and y — effectively a slope and an intercept → lose 2. Simple linear regression n − 2 The best-fit line has two parameters (slope + intercept); each costs one df. Multiple regression (p predictors) n − p − 1 p slopes + 1 intercept estimated → lose p + 1. Definition The thread through all of it: count the numbers, subtract one for every quantity you had to estimate from them. t with one mean → n − 1. Two means → n₁ + n₂ − 2. A line with two parameters → n − 2. A table with fixed margins → (r−1)(c−1). You never have to memorise these in isolation again. Why df changes the shape of the curve df is not just bookkeeping for picking a critical value — it literally controls the shape of the t and χ² distributions. The t-distribution With small df your estimate of the spread, s, is shaky — built from very few independent deviations, so it can land too low and make results look more impressive than they are. To protect against that, the t-distribution has fatter tails : it demands a bigger t-value before it believes an effect. As df grows, s becomes a trustworthy estimate of σ, the extra caution is no longer needed, and the t-distribution gets thinner and taller until, at large df, it is essentially the normal (z) distribution . That is why a t-table's values shrink down each column toward the z-values as df rises. The χ² distribution χ² is a sum of squared standard-normal pieces, and df is how many independent squared pieces are in the sum. More df = more things added = the distribution shifts right and spreads out. Facts they test: the mean of a χ² distribution equals its df , and its variance equals 2 × df . High-yield NIMHANS depth — the F-distribution (used in ANOVA) is a ratio of two χ²-type quantities, each divided by its own df, which is exactly why F needs two df values, numerator and denominator. Same logic, stacked. Trap The exact df flips MCQs use: (1) "df equals the sample size" — no, df = sample size minus parameters estimated. (2) Population variance uses N; sample variance uses n − 1. (3) Independent t is n₁ + n₂ − 2 , not −1; paired t is n − 1 on the differences . (4) Chi-square independence is (r − 1)(c − 1), a product , not a sum — a 3×4 table is 2 × 3 = 6, not 5. (5) Pearson r and simple regression are n − 2, not n − 1. (6) In ANOVA, between + within df must sum to N − 1. Qualitative & mixed methods Qualitative research studies meaning and experience in words , not numbers. It is inductive (builds theory from data), naturalistic , and treats the researcher as the main instrument. Use it when the question is " how / what is it like / why " rather than "how much"; when the topic is new, sensitive, or poorly understood; or when you want lived experience and context. Approach Aim Hallmark Thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke) Identify patterned themes of meaning 6 phases; flexible, paradigm-free Grounded theory (Glaser & Strauss) Build a theory from the data Constant comparison, theoretical sampling, open→axial→selective coding, saturation Phenomenology / IPA (Husserl, Giorgi; Smith) How individuals make sense of lived experience Small homogeneous sample, bracketing, double hermeneutic Ethnography Describe a culture/community Participant observation, thick description Narrative analysis Make sense of life stories Story structure across a life Content analysis Systematically categorise text Can be qualitative or quantitative (counts codes) Discourse / conversation analysis How language constructs reality / social action Examines power, rhetoric in talk/text Thematic analysis — 6 phases: familiarisation → generating initial codes → searching for themes → reviewing themes → defining & naming themes → writing up. Grounded theory generates theory via constant comparison and stops at saturation (no new categories). IPA is the phenomenology workhorse in clinical psych. Rigour is judged by trustworthiness (Lincoln & Guba): credibility, transferability, dependability, confirmability — paralleling internal validity, external validity, reliability, objectivity. Triangulation (data, investigator, theory, methodological) strengthens findings. Mixed methods Sequential explanatory: quant first, then qual to explain the numbers. Sequential exploratory: qual first to generate hypotheses, then quant to test. Convergent (parallel): both at once, results compared/triangulated. Embedded: one nested inside the other (e.g. qual interviews within an RCT). Trap Bracketing belongs to phenomenology/IPA ; constant comparison to grounded theory ; thick description to ethnography . Grounded theory generates theory, not "describes lived experience" (that is phenomenology). Qualitative sample size is set by saturation , never by power analysis. Clinical trials & reporting standards Clinical trial phases Phase Purpose n Phase 0 Microdosing in humans, pharmacokinetics ~10 Phase I Safety, tolerability, dose-finding 20–100 Phase II Preliminary efficacy + side-effects 100–300 Phase III Confirmatory efficacy vs standard 1000+ Phase IV Post-marketing surveillance Open Blinding: single (subject), double (subject + experimenter), triple (+ analyst). Reduces bias. Allocation concealment ≠ blinding — it concerns who knows the next assignment at the moment of randomisation. Reporting guidelines — match the acronym to the design Acronym For CONSORT Randomised controlled trials PRISMA Systematic reviews + meta-analyses STARD Diagnostic accuracy studies STROBE Observational studies (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) COREQ Qualitative research SPIRIT Trial protocols CARE Case reports TRIPOD Prediction model studies Research ethics Born from abuses (Nazi experiments → Nuremberg Code 1947 ; Tuskegee → the Belmont Report 1979 ; also Milgram and the Stanford Prison study; the Declaration of Helsinki 1964 onwards). The Belmont core principles: respect for persons (autonomy), beneficence (do good, minimise harm), and justice (fair distribution of risk/benefit). Informed consent: participants get the purpose, procedures, risks, benefits and their rights in understandable terms, and agree voluntarily — its four pillars are capacity, voluntariness, disclosure, comprehension. Special protection for vulnerable groups (children, prisoners, those with impaired capacity, pregnant women). Deception & debriefing: deception is permitted only when unavoidable and low-risk, and must be followed by a full debrief explaining the true purpose and undoing any distress. Confidentiality & anonymity: protect identities, store data securely, report in aggregate. Right to withdraw: participants may quit at any time without penalty and withdraw their data. Ethics committee / IRB: an independent board reviews and approves the protocol before data collection; risk tiers run exempt → expedited → full board. Indian context: ICMR National Ethical Guidelines (2017) and the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules (2019). Trap Anonymity (the researcher cannot link data to a person at all) vs confidentiality (the researcher can identify but will not disclose). Deception without a debrief is unethical — the debrief is what (partly) justifies the deception. Decision table: which test do I use? Read it as: what is my DV's data type × how many groups / what design → test. Goal / design Categorical (nominal) DV Ordinal DV / non-normal Interval-ratio DV (normal) One sample vs a known value χ² goodness-of-fit Wilcoxon signed-rank / sign test One-sample t (z if σ known) 2 independent groups χ² independence (Fisher if cell < 5) Mann-Whitney U Independent t 2 related/paired measures McNemar Wilcoxon signed-rank Paired t ≥ 3 independent groups χ² (r × c) Kruskal-Wallis H One-way ANOVA → post-hoc ≥ 3 related measures Cochran's Q Friedman Repeated-measures ANOVA 2 IVs at once log-linear / logistic — Factorial ANOVA (main + interaction) Association between 2 variables φ / Cramér's V (χ²) Spearman rho / Kendall tau Pearson r Predict an outcome Logistic regression Ordinal regression Linear regression Collected MCQ traps Trap Parametric vs non-parametric. Parametric (t, ANOVA, Pearson) needs normality + interval/ratio data and is more powerful when met; non-parametric (Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis, Friedman, Spearman, χ²) is rank/count-based for ordinal, small, or non-normal data. Do not pick non-parametric "to be safe" if assumptions hold — you lose power. Trap Type I vs Type II. Type I (α) = false positive = reject a true H₀ (set, usually .05). Type II (β) = false negative = miss a real effect. Power = 1 − β. "Sigh, I missed it" = II. Trap Reliability vs validity. Reliability = consistency; validity = measures the right construct. Reliable-but-invalid is possible (a scale always 5 kg off); valid-but-unreliable is not (reliability caps validity, max validity = √reliability). Trap Mediator vs moderator. Mediator = mechanism, the how , sits between IV and DV (IV→M→DV). Moderator = condition, the for whom/when , shows up as an interaction. Me-diator = me-chanism. Trap Sampling error vs bias. Error = random, shrinks with n, centres on the truth. Bias = systematic, immune to n — a bigger biased sample is just more precisely wrong. Trap Correlation vs regression. r = strength of linear association, symmetric, unitless. Regression = directional prediction equation (Ŷ = a + bX) with a slope in units. r = 0 only rules out a linear relation (a U-curve has r ≈ 0). Correlation ≠ causation. r = +0.90 → r² = 0.81 = 81% of variance explained, not 90%. Trap Mean vs median under skew. The mean chases the tail. Positive skew → mean > median > mode; use the median for skewed data. The mean is the most outlier-sensitive average. Trap p-value. P(data this extreme | H₀ true), not P(H₀ true) and not "probability it was chance." Significance ≠ importance. Trap SD vs SE. SD = spread of individual scores; SE = SD/√n = spread of sample means, always smaller. Trap Random sampling vs random assignment. Sampling = who gets in (external validity); assignment = which condition (internal validity). Trap Stratified vs cluster sampling. Stratified = random within every subgroup (lowers error); cluster = pick whole subgroups at random (raises error, saves cost). Both are probability methods. Trap ANOVA aftermath. A significant F says "at least one mean differs," not which — run post-hoc (Tukey/Bonferroni/Scheffé) for the pairs. Trap Solomon four-group controls and measures pretest sensitisation. CONSORT = RCT reporting; PRISMA = systematic reviews/meta-analyses; STARD = diagnostic; COREQ = qualitative. Worked intuition What a t actually compares t is a signal-to-noise ratio : the difference between means (signal) divided by the standard error of that difference (noise). If two group means differ by 6 points and the SE of the difference is 2, t = 3 — the gap is three times the typical sampling wobble, so it is hard to dismiss as chance. If the same 6-point gap came with an SE of 6, t = 1 — the gap is no bigger than the noise, so it is unconvincing. Bigger samples shrink the SE (SE = SD/√n), which is why the same mean difference becomes significant as n grows. How ANOVA partitions variance Picture three groups. Total variability in everyone's scores has two sources: scores differ because the group means differ (between-groups, the effect of the IV) and because individuals differ within their own group (within-groups, random error). ANOVA estimates a variance from each source. If the IV does nothing, both estimate the same error variance and their ratio F ≈ 1. If the IV matters, the between-groups estimate balloons and F climbs above 1. Reading F and p You compare your F to the F-distribution at the right df (between, within). A large F lands far in the right tail, giving a small p. p < .05 means: "if all the group means were truly equal, an F this large would happen less than 5% of the time" — surprising enough to reject H₀. But F only flags that something differs; the post-hoc tests and the effect size (η²) tell you which groups and how much. What r² means Square the correlation and you get the proportion of variance shared . r = .60 → r² = .36, so 36% of the variation in Y is accounted for by its linear relationship with X (and 64% is left to other factors). This is why a "moderate" r of .30 looks less impressive once squared (r² = .09 — only 9% of variance), a useful reality check against over-reading correlations. Fast glossary Alpha (α): the Type I error rate you set (usually .05); also Cronbach's α for internal consistency. ANCOVA: ANOVA adjusting for a continuous covariate. ANOVA: compares ≥ 3 means via F = between/within variance. Attrition: non-random dropout, a threat to internal validity. Beta (β): Type II error rate; power = 1 − β. Bias (sampling): systematic error from method; not fixed by larger n. Central Limit Theorem: sampling distribution of the mean → normal as n grows. Chi-square (χ²): Σ(O − E)²/E; test on category counts. Cohen's d: standardised mean-difference effect size (.2/.5/.8). Confidence interval: plausible range for a parameter; 95% CI excluding 0 ↔ p < .05. Confound: third variable tied to both IV and DV. Construct validity: does the test tap the intended construct (convergent + discriminant). Counterbalancing: varying condition order to cancel order effects. Degrees of freedom: values free to vary; shapes t/χ²/F. Discrimination index (D): upper − lower group proportion correct on an item. Effect size: magnitude of an effect, independent of n. Eta squared (η²): proportion of variance explained in ANOVA. External validity: generalisability of findings. F-ratio: between-groups variance / within-groups variance. Internal validity: did the IV really cause the DV. IQR: Q3 − Q1, robust spread. Item difficulty (p): proportion answering an item correctly (high p = easy). Kappa (κ): chance-corrected inter-rater agreement. Kurtosis: peakedness/tailedness (lepto/meso/platy). Likert: summated agreement-rating scale. Mean: arithmetic average; outlier-sensitive. Median: middle value; robust to skew. Mediator: mechanism between IV and DV. Mode: most frequent value; only centre for nominal. Moderator: variable that changes the IV–DV relationship (interaction). Nominal/Ordinal/Interval/Ratio: the four measurement levels (NOIR). Null hypothesis (H₀): no effect/difference — what is tested. p-value: P(data this extreme | H₀ true). Power: 1 − β; chance of detecting a real effect. Reliability: consistency of measurement. r²: proportion of variance shared by two variables. Standard deviation: typical distance from the mean (√variance). Standard error: SD/√n; spread of sample means. Skewness: asymmetry of a distribution. Spearman-Brown: corrects split-half reliability for test length. Type I / Type II error: false positive / false negative. Validity: measuring the intended construct (test) or correctness of conclusions (study). Variance: mean squared deviation from the mean. z-score: (x − μ)/σ; SDs from the mean.

title: DSM-5-TR, the Exam Cut
text: DSM-5-TR, the Exam Cut Every disorder the Indian clinical-psychology entrances actually test, written the way you need it in the hall: the criteria in plain language rather than manual English, the numbers that carry the mark (duration, age of onset, symptom counts, exclusion clauses), and then, under every single disorder, a Comorbidity line and a Differential line. The differential is where papers hide the mark, because the stem almost never asks "what is the definition of X", it describes a person and asks which of four neighbouring diagnoses fits. So read a card as a whole: the criteria tell you what it is, the differential tells you what it is not, and the comorbidity tells you what else to expect sitting on top of it. DSM-5-TR (2022) is used throughout, with the ICD-11 line noted wherever the two systems disagree in a way an examiner can exploit. In this book How DSM-5-TR is built, and how to use it in an exam Neurodevelopmental disorders Schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders Bipolar and related disorders Depressive disorders Anxiety disorders Obsessive-compulsive and related disorders Trauma and stressor-related disorders Dissociative disorders Somatic symptom and related disorders Feeding and eating disorders Elimination disorders Sleep-wake disorders Sexual dysfunctions, gender dysphoria, paraphilias Disruptive, impulse-control and conduct disorders Substance-related and addictive disorders Neurocognitive disorders Personality disorders Section III: the alternative model, culture, and conditions for further study The number sheet: every duration, age and cut-off in one place The differential pairs examiners keep reusing 1. How DSM-5-TR is built, and how to use it in an exam Before any disorder, understand the machine. A surprising number of entrance questions are about the classification system itself rather than about any single disorder, and those are free marks because there is nothing to remember except structure. What DSM is, and what it deliberately is not The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders is published by the American Psychiatric Association . It is a categorical, descriptive, atheoretical nosology. Descriptive means it defines disorders by observable signs and reported symptoms, not by presumed cause. Atheoretical means it deliberately refuses to commit to psychoanalytic, behavioural, or biological explanation, so a clinician of any orientation can use the same code. That neutrality was the single biggest change at DSM-III (1980), which is the edition that introduced explicit operational criteria, the multiaxial system, and the abandonment of the psychoanalytic word "neurosis". If a paper asks which DSM edition marked the turn to operational criteria and reliability, the answer is always DSM-III. Edition timeline, memorise the years DSM-I 1952 (106 categories, "reactions", Meyerian). DSM-II 1968 (182 categories, still psychodynamic language). DSM-III 1980 (265 categories, operational criteria, multiaxial, atheoretical, homosexuality already removed as a diagnosis in 1973 from DSM-II's printing). DSM-III-R 1987. DSM-IV 1994, DSM-IV-TR 2000. DSM-5 2013 (Arabic numeral so it can be revised 5.1, 5.2; multiaxial system abolished; dimensional and spectrum thinking added). DSM-5-TR March 2022 . What changed in the 2022 Text Revision, specifically DSM-5-TR is a text revision, so most of the change is in the explanatory text rather than the criteria. The examinable changes are: One entirely new disorder: Prolonged Grief Disorder , placed in the Trauma and Stressor-Related chapter. This is the highest-yield single fact in the whole TR. Unspecified Mood Disorder was brought back, for presentations where you cannot yet tell depressive from bipolar. Suicidal behaviour and non-suicidal self-injury became separate coded conditions (ICD-10-CM codes) that can be recorded alongside any diagnosis, rather than only being criteria inside borderline personality disorder and depression. Terminology. DSM-5's "Intellectual Disability (Intellectual Developmental Disorder)" was reversed to " Intellectual Developmental Disorder (Intellectual Disability) "; "neuroleptic" was largely replaced by "antipsychotic"; the term "sexual identity" was dropped; "desired gender" became "experienced gender", "cross-sex medical procedure" became "gender-affirming medical procedure", and "natal male/female" became "individual assigned male/female at birth" in Gender Dysphoria. Name and criteria changes inside single disorders (each one is on its card under DSM-5 change): "(Social Phobia)" was dropped from social anxiety disorder and "(Dysthymia)" from persistent depressive disorder ; conversion disorder is now listed as Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (Conversion Disorder) ; the jikoshu-kyofu example became olfactory reference disorder ; in bipolar I, bipolar II and MDD the psychosis exclusion was reworded so that at least one episode must not be superimposed on schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder; mania got its own mild, moderate and severe definitions; and stimulant-induced mild neurocognitive disorder was added. The October 2022 coding update gave prolonged grief disorder its own code ( F43.81 ), replaced the behavioural specifier of major neurocognitive disorder with six named ones (with agitation, anxiety, mood symptoms, psychotic disturbance, other, or without), and added neurocognitive disorder due to unknown aetiology . Culture and racism. Text throughout was rewritten by an Ethnoracial Equity and Inclusion work group; "race" is discussed as a social construct, "racialised" and "ethnoracial" replace older usage, and the impact of racism and discrimination on prevalence and presentation is stated in the text. Prevalence, risk and culture sections were updated across almost every disorder, and ICD-10-CM codes were refreshed. The multiaxial system, and why it is gone DSM-IV-TR used five axes: Axis I clinical disorders, Axis II personality disorders and mental retardation, Axis III general medical conditions, Axis IV psychosocial and environmental problems, Axis V the Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF), a 0 to 100 scale. DSM-5 abolished all of it. Axes I, II and III were merged into a single list of diagnoses; Axis IV was replaced by the ICD Z-codes for psychosocial and contextual factors; Axis V was dropped because the GAF was psychometrically poor (it confounded symptom severity with functioning) and replaced by the WHODAS 2.0 , the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule, a 36-item measure across six domains (cognition, mobility, self-care, getting along, life activities, participation). Trap Questions still ask "on which axis was mental retardation coded?" The answer is Axis II, in DSM-IV-TR, and the correct full answer adds that the multiaxial system no longer exists in DSM-5 or DSM-5-TR and that GAF was replaced by WHODAS 2.0. Answer both halves. The definition of a mental disorder DSM-5-TR defines a mental disorder as a syndrome characterised by clinically significant disturbance in an individual's cognition, emotion regulation, or behaviour that reflects a dysfunction in the psychological, biological, or developmental processes underlying mental functioning. Mental disorders are usually associated with significant distress or disability in social, occupational, or other important activities. Three exclusions are written into that definition and are examined constantly: An expectable or culturally approved response to a common stressor or loss (for example ordinary bereavement) is not a mental disorder. Socially deviant behaviour (political, religious, sexual) and conflicts primarily between the individual and society are not mental disorders, unless the deviance results from a dysfunction in the individual. The disturbance must not be better explained by another condition, including a substance or another medical condition. The clause under almost every disorder Two clauses recur so often that you should assume them unless told otherwise. Clinical significance: "the symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning." Exclusion: "not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition, and not better explained by another mental disorder." When a question gives you a person with symptoms but explicitly says work and relationships are unaffected and they are not bothered, the answer is usually "no diagnosis", not the disorder that matches the symptom list. Categorical versus dimensional, and where DSM-5-TR hedges DSM remains categorical: you either meet criteria or you do not. The known problems with that are heterogeneity (two people with the same diagnosis can share almost no symptoms), arbitrary thresholds (five of nine symptoms is a diagnosis, four is not), high comorbidity (a sign the categories are not carving nature at its joints), and heavy use of "other specified" and "unspecified" residual categories. DSM-5 added dimensional elements without abandoning categories: severity specifiers on almost every disorder, cross-cutting symptom measures, the collapse of autism's subtypes into one spectrum , the collapse of substance abuse and dependence into a single graded substance use disorder , and the Alternative Model for Personality Disorders in Section III. The fully dimensional alternatives you should be able to name are HiTOP (Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology), RDoC (Research Domain Criteria, NIMH, organised by domains such as negative valence and positive valence systems crossed with units of analysis from genes to self-report), and the p-factor (a general psychopathology factor). DSM-5-TR versus ICD-11, the comparisons that get asked Publisher and purpose. DSM is by the American Psychiatric Association, primarily a diagnostic manual for clinicians and researchers. ICD-11 (in effect from 1 January 2022) is by the WHO, is a global public-health statistical classification covering all diseases, is free, and is the system India officially uses for reporting. Structure. ICD-11 uses alphanumeric codes; mental, behavioural and neurodevelopmental disorders sit in Chapter 06. ICD-11 gives prototypical descriptions with flexible boundaries rather than DSM's counted criteria, on the reasoning that counted thresholds create false precision in general medical settings. Disorders that exist in one and not the other. ICD-11 has Complex PTSD , Gaming Disorder , Prolonged Grief Disorder (DSM added it in the TR), Body Integrity Dysphoria , Compulsive Sexual Behaviour Disorder and Olfactory Reference Disorder ; DSM-5-TR does not have Complex PTSD or Gaming Disorder as full diagnoses (internet gaming disorder is in Section III, conditions for further study). DSM has Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder ; ICD-11 folds that presentation into oppositional defiant disorder "with chronic irritability-anger". Personality. ICD-11 abolished the ten categorical personality disorders entirely and replaced them with a single Personality Disorder diagnosis rated mild, moderate or severe, plus five trait domain qualifiers (negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, anankastia) and a borderline pattern qualifier. DSM-5-TR keeps the ten categories in Section II and offers its own trait model only in Section III. Schizophrenia. Both dropped the classical subtypes (paranoid, hebephrenic, catatonic, undifferentiated, residual, simple). ICD-11 requires one month of symptoms; DSM requires six months of total disturbance with at least one month of active-phase symptoms. That six versus one month contrast is one of the most reused questions in the whole syllabus. How to read a vignette fast Four questions, in this order. (1) Duration. Almost every differential in DSM is settled by time: 1 day / 1 month / 6 months / 2 years. Find the duration in the stem first. (2) Onset age. Before 12, before 18, after 60. (3) Is there a substance or medical cause? If the stem mentions steroids, thyroid, stroke, or a drug, that is not decoration. (4) Impairment. If it says functioning is intact, suspect a subthreshold or "no diagnosis" option. 2. Neurodevelopmental disorders Onset in the developmental period, meaning the deficits are present early and are not a decline from a previously normal level. That last phrase is the whole differential against the neurocognitive chapter: neurodevelopmental means never acquired, neurocognitive means acquired and then lost. Intellectual Developmental Disorder (Intellectual Disability) F70-F73 In plain language. The person's reasoning and their ability to run their own life are both below what is expected for their age, and this has been true since childhood. DSM-5 made the important move of deciding severity by adaptive functioning , not by the IQ number, because how well someone copes is what determines the support they need. Deficits in intellectual functions (reasoning, problem solving, planning, abstract thinking, judgment, academic learning, learning from experience), confirmed by clinical assessment and individualised standardised testing. Deficits in adaptive functioning so that the person fails to meet developmental and sociocultural standards for personal independence and social responsibility, across at least one of three domains: conceptual (language, reading, money, time), social (empathy, friendships, gullibility), practical (self-care, job, money management, transport). Onset during the developmental period . Specifiers Severity is the only specifier: mild (F70), moderate (F71), severe (F72) and profound (F73), each judged on adaptive functioning in the conceptual, social and practical domains, not on the IQ score. In mild, difficulties may not be obvious until school age and adults usually manage with some support; in moderate, skills lag markedly behind peers throughout life; in severe, there is little grasp of written language or numbers and support is needed for all daily activities; in profound, skills relate to the physical world rather than symbols and the person depends on others for all daily care, health and safety. There are no subtype or course specifiers. Numbers IQ roughly two standard deviations below the mean, about 65 to 75 allowing for the measurement error band, but severity is graded Mild / Moderate / Severe / Profound on adaptive functioning, not IQ. Prevalence about 1 percent overall, about 6 per 1000 for severe. Male to female roughly 1.6:1 for mild. Course Onset is in the developmental period, and when it is recognised depends on severity: severe forms show delayed motor, language and social milestones within the first 2 years , while mild forms often surface only at school age , when academic demands rise. After early childhood the disorder is usually lifelong and non-progressive , although some genetic causes worsen steadily (Sanfilippo syndrome) or worsen and then stabilise (Rett syndrome), and adults with Down syndrome are at high risk of early Alzheimer's disease. Early and continuing intervention improves adaptive functioning, sometimes enough that the diagnosis no longer applies, and the severity level can change over time. Related Global Developmental Delay is the diagnosis under age 5 when severity cannot yet be reliably assessed; it requires reassessment. Unspecified Intellectual Disability is for over-5s who cannot be assessed because of sensory or physical impairment or severe behaviour. Comorbidity Three to four times the general-population rate of other mental disorders. Commonest: ADHD, autism spectrum disorder, stereotypic movement disorder (with or without self-injury), depressive and bipolar disorders, anxiety disorders, impulse-control disorders. Medically: epilepsy, cerebral palsy, sensory impairment. Differential Major neurocognitive disorder (there the ability was present and was lost; here it was never acquired, though the two can coexist). Specific learning disorder (deficit is confined to one academic domain, general intelligence is normal). Communication disorders (language impaired, non-verbal reasoning intact). Autism (social deficits out of proportion to overall developmental level). Also rule out sensory impairment, deprivation, and poor test-taking due to unfamiliarity with the testing language, which is a real issue in Indian samples. DSM-5 change DSM-5 replaced DSM-IV-TR's mental retardation with intellectual disability (intellectual developmental disorder) and moved it into the new Neurodevelopmental Disorders chapter (it had been coded on Axis II, which went with the multiaxial system). The IQ of about 70 or below criterion was taken out of the criteria (IQ is now discussed in the text), and severity moved from IQ bands to adaptive functioning . DSM-IV's deficits in two of eleven adaptive skill areas became the three domains conceptual, social, practical ; onset before age 18 became onset in the developmental period ; and global developmental delay was added for children under 5. DSM-5-TR (2022): the name was reordered to Intellectual Developmental Disorder (Intellectual Disability) , to line up with ICD-11's disorders of intellectual development , with intellectual disability kept in parentheses. Communication Disorders F80.x In plain language. Five conditions, each about a different part of using language. Language Disorder. Persistent difficulty acquiring and using language across modalities (spoken, written, sign) because of deficits in comprehension or production: reduced vocabulary, limited sentence structure, impaired discourse. Abilities are substantially below age expectation. Onset in the early developmental period. Speech Sound Disorder. Persistent difficulty with speech sound production that interferes with intelligibility. The child is understood poorly, though language content is fine. Childhood-Onset Fluency Disorder (Stuttering). Disturbance in the normal fluency and time patterning of speech: sound and syllable repetitions, prolongations, broken words, audible or silent blocking, circumlocutions, physical tension. Causes anxiety about speaking. Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder. Persistent difficulty with the social use of verbal and non-verbal communication: greeting and sharing information appropriately, changing communication to match the listener or context, following rules of conversation and storytelling (turn taking, rephrasing when misunderstood), and understanding what is not explicitly stated (inference, idiom, humour, metaphor). New in DSM-5. Unspecified Communication Disorder. Specifiers DSM-5-TR gives no subtype, severity or course specifiers for any of the communication disorders (language disorder, speech sound disorder, childhood-onset fluency disorder, social (pragmatic) communication disorder). The one coding rule worth knowing: stuttering that begins after the early developmental period is not childhood-onset fluency disorder but is diagnosed as adult-onset fluency disorder (F98.5). Numbers Stuttering onset usually between ages 2 and 7, with 80 to 90 percent onset by age 6; recovery in about 65 to 85 percent. Social pragmatic communication disorder is rarely diagnosed under age 4 or 5 because the skills are not yet expected. Course Language disorder usually shows first as late talking; once diagnosed from about age 4 it tends to be stable and to persist into adulthood, and receptive deficits carry a worse prognosis than mainly expressive ones. Speech sound disorder usually responds well to treatment and is often not lifelong, but the outlook is poorer when a language disorder coexists, which also raises the risk of specific learning disorder. Stuttering may begin gradually or suddenly, is worsened by anxiety and pressure to communicate, and its severity at age 8 predicts whether it will persist into adolescence and beyond. Social (pragmatic) communication disorder has a variable outcome: some children improve substantially, others stay impaired into adulthood, and early pragmatic deficits can leave lasting difficulties in relationships even after improvement. Comorbidity Specific learning disorder, ADHD, autism spectrum disorder, developmental coordination disorder, social anxiety disorder (especially with stuttering). Differential The examined one is Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder versus Autism Spectrum Disorder . Both have the social communication deficit. Autism additionally requires restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities , and if those are present now or were ever present in the past, the diagnosis is autism, not SPCD. So SPCD is autism's Criterion A without autism's Criterion B, and you must ask about childhood history before settling on it. Also rule out intellectual disability, hearing loss, selective mutism (the child can speak, but does not in specific settings), and normal variation. DSM-5 change DSM-IV-TR already grouped these as Communication Disorders ; DSM-5 moved the group into the new Neurodevelopmental chapter and renamed or merged most of them. DSM-IV-TR's expressive language disorder and mixed receptive-expressive language disorder were merged into a single language disorder ; phonological disorder became speech sound disorder ; stuttering became childhood-onset fluency disorder ; and communication disorder NOS became unspecified communication disorder. Social (pragmatic) communication disorder was newly created , partly for children who would earlier have been called PDD-NOS but who lack restricted, repetitive behaviours. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Autism Spectrum Disorder F84.0 In plain language. Two things together, both from early childhood: the person does not do the ordinary back-and-forth of relating to other people, and the person's behaviour and interests are narrow, repetitive, and sensitive to change. DSM-5 collapsed autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, childhood disintegrative disorder and PDD-NOS into one spectrum, and cut the old triad to a dyad by merging social and communication deficits into one criterion. A. Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across contexts, and all three must be present: (1) deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, from abnormal back-and-forth conversation and failure to share interests or affect through to failure to initiate or respond to social interaction; (2) deficits in non-verbal communicative behaviours, from poorly integrated verbal and non-verbal communication through abnormal eye contact and body language to a total lack of facial expression and gesture; (3) deficits in developing, maintaining and understanding relationships, from difficulty adjusting behaviour to context through difficulty making friends to an absence of interest in peers. B. Restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities , at least two of four : (1) stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, use of objects or speech (lining up toys, echolalia, idiosyncratic phrases); (2) insistence on sameness, inflexible routines, ritualised patterns, extreme distress at small change; (3) highly restricted, fixated interests abnormal in intensity or focus; (4) hyper- or hypo-reactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment (indifference to pain or temperature, adverse response to sounds or textures, excessive smelling or touching, visual fascination with lights or movement). Criterion B4, the sensory criterion, is new in DSM-5. C. Symptoms present in the early developmental period, though they may not fully show until social demands exceed capacity, and may be masked by learned strategies later. D. Clinically significant impairment. E. Not better explained by intellectual disability or global developmental delay; to diagnose both, social communication must be below that expected for general developmental level. Specifiers Severity is coded separately for social communication and for restricted repetitive behaviours, as Level 1 requiring support , Level 2 requiring substantial support , Level 3 requiring very substantial support . Also specify: with or without accompanying intellectual impairment; with or without accompanying language impairment; associated with a known medical, genetic or environmental factor; associated with another neurodevelopmental, mental or behavioural disorder; with catatonia. Numbers Prevalence now reported around 1 in 100 worldwide and higher in US surveillance data (about 1 in 36 in recent CDC estimates). Male to female about 4:1, and girls are under-identified because of camouflaging. Concordance in monozygotic twins is high (roughly 60 to 90 percent for the broader phenotype); heritability is among the highest in psychiatry. Course Signs are usually recognised in the second year of life (12 to 24 months) , earlier if delays are severe and later if subtle; some children show a plateau or regression of social or language skills in the first 2 years, which is rare in other disorders and is a red flag. ASD is not degenerative : symptoms are most marked in early childhood and the early school years, gains usually follow in later childhood, and most improve in adolescence though a small proportion deteriorate. Only a minority of adults live and work independently. The best-established prognostic factors are the presence of intellectual disability and language impairment (functional language by age 5 is a good sign) and additional mental health problems. Comorbidity Around 70 percent have at least one comorbid mental disorder and about 40 percent have two or more. Commonest: intellectual disability, ADHD (DSM-5 for the first time allowed the two to be diagnosed together, DSM-IV forbade it), anxiety disorders (especially specific phobia and social anxiety), depression, OCD, tic disorders, specific learning disorder, developmental coordination disorder, avoidant restrictive food intake disorder, sleep disorders, epilepsy (about 20 to 30 percent), gastrointestinal problems, and known genetic syndromes such as fragile X, tuberous sclerosis and Rett syndrome. Differential Social (pragmatic) communication disorder : no Criterion B, ever. Intellectual disability without autism : social skills are at the level of the mental age, not below it. Rett syndrome : since DSM-5 this is no longer a separate diagnosis but is coded as an associated medical condition; the clue is regression after normal early development, with loss of purposeful hand skills (between 5 and 30 months in the old DSM-IV criteria) followed by hand-wringing, and head growth slowing between 5 and 48 months. Selective mutism : normal social reciprocity outside the feared setting. ADHD : inattention and social intrusiveness without the qualitative social-reciprocity deficit or the repetitive behaviours. Schizophrenia with childhood onset : delusions and hallucinations appear after a period of normal development. Stereotypic movement disorder : stereotypies without the social criterion. Reactive attachment disorder : severe social neglect history, and the social deficit improves once care improves. DSM-5 change DSM-5 merged four DSM-IV-TR pervasive developmental disorders, autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, childhood disintegrative disorder and PDD-NOS , into one autism spectrum disorder , and dropped Rett's disorder . The triad (social interaction, communication, restricted repetitive behaviour) became a dyad , sensory hyper- or hypo-reactivity was added to Criterion B, DSM-IV's onset before age 3 became the early developmental period, and the severity levels and intellectual and language impairment specifiers were introduced. Well-established DSM-IV diagnoses carry over to ASD, and ASD can now be diagnosed with ADHD . DSM-5-TR (2022): Criterion A now reads 'as manifested by all of the following ', making clear that all three social-communication deficits are required. ICD-11 Also uses a single "Autism spectrum disorder" with qualifiers for intellectual and language impairment, so the two systems agree here. ICD-11 kept Rett syndrome out of the mental disorders chapter as well. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder F90.x In plain language. Either the child cannot hold attention, or cannot stay still and cannot wait, or both, to a degree that is out of step with their age and is spoiling their life in more than one place. A. A persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity , with at least six of nine symptoms in the relevant list, present for at least six months , at a level inconsistent with developmental level. From age 17 and older, five of nine is enough. Inattention list (9): careless mistakes and inattention to detail; difficulty sustaining attention; does not seem to listen when spoken to directly; does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish; difficulty organising tasks; avoids tasks requiring sustained mental effort; loses things; easily distracted by extraneous stimuli; forgetful in daily activities. Hyperactivity-impulsivity list (9): fidgets or squirms; leaves seat when remaining seated is expected; runs or climbs inappropriately (in adults, restlessness); unable to play quietly; "on the go" as if driven by a motor; talks excessively; blurts out answers; difficulty waiting turn; interrupts or intrudes. B. Several symptoms present before age 12 . C. Symptoms present in two or more settings (home, school, work, with friends). D. Clear interference with functioning. E. Not occurring exclusively during schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder, and not better explained by another mental disorder. Specifiers Predominantly inattentive presentation , predominantly hyperactive/impulsive presentation , combined presentation . Note the word: DSM-5 says presentation , not subtype, because people move between them over time. Also in partial remission , and severity mild / moderate / severe. Numbers The age-of-onset criterion was raised from 7 in DSM-IV to 12 in DSM-5 , which is the single most examined ADHD fact. Symptom count drops from 6 to 5 at age 17. Prevalence about 5 percent of children and about 2.5 percent of adults. Male to female about 2:1 in children, closer to 1.6:1 in adults; girls present more often with the inattentive picture. Course Excess motor activity is often noticed in toddlers but is hard to separate from normal behaviour before age 4 ; diagnosis is most often made in the primary school years, when inattention becomes more prominent and impairing. Symptoms are fairly stable through early adolescence; hyperactivity declines with age and in adolescents and adults shrinks to fidgetiness or inner restlessness, while inattention, poor planning and impulsivity tend to persist, and a substantial proportion remain impaired into adulthood. Children with ADHD are more likely to develop conduct disorder in adolescence and antisocial personality disorder in adulthood, which raises the risk of substance use disorders; co-occurring conduct problems predict the worst outcome. Comorbidity Oppositional defiant disorder (about half of combined presentation), conduct disorder (about a quarter), specific learning disorder, anxiety disorders, depressive disorders, disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, autism spectrum disorder, tic disorders including Tourette's, substance use disorders in adolescence and adulthood, and antisocial personality disorder in adults. Differential Oppositional defiant disorder : the child refuses because they resist demands, not because they cannot sustain attention. Specific learning disorder : inattention appears only in the academic domain that is hard. Intellectual disability : symptoms must exceed what the mental age predicts. Bipolar disorder : ADHD is chronic and continuous, mania is episodic with a clear change from baseline, and mania brings elevated mood and reduced need for sleep, which ADHD does not. Anxiety : inattention there is driven by worry and rumination. Reactive attachment disorder and medication effects (bronchodilators, thyroid). Also normal high activity in a young child, and an unstimulating classroom. DSM-5 change DSM-5 moved ADHD out of DSM-IV-TR's Attention-Deficit and Disruptive Behavior Disorders grouping into the Neurodevelopmental Disorders chapter. Onset changed from symptoms causing impairment before age 7 to several symptoms present before age 12 ; the cross-setting criterion now needs several symptoms in each setting; examples were added to the items so they fit adolescents and adults; and the threshold for those 17 and older fell to five symptoms. Subtypes became presentations , severity specifiers were added, and autism was removed as an exclusion, so the two can be diagnosed together . DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Specific Learning Disorder F81.x In plain language. A child of ordinary intelligence, taught properly, still cannot read, write or do arithmetic at anything like age level. A. Difficulties learning and using academic skills, with at least one of six symptoms persisting for at least six months despite intervention : inaccurate or slow effortful word reading; difficulty understanding what is read; difficulties with spelling; difficulties with written expression; difficulties mastering number sense, number facts or calculation; difficulties with mathematical reasoning. B. The affected academic skills are substantially and quantifiably below those expected for chronological age and cause significant interference, confirmed by individually administered standardised achievement measures (or, over age 17, a documented history). C. Begin during school-age years, though they may not fully appear until demands exceed capacity. D. Not better accounted for by intellectual disability, uncorrected visual or auditory acuity, other mental or neurological disorders, psychosocial adversity, lack of proficiency in the language of instruction, or inadequate educational instruction. Specifiers With impairment in reading (word reading accuracy, reading rate or fluency, reading comprehension; the alternative term dyslexia is retained in the text), in written expression (spelling accuracy, grammar and punctuation, clarity or organisation; dysgraphia ), or in mathematics (number sense, memorisation of arithmetic facts, accurate or fluent calculation, accurate mathematical reasoning; dyscalculia ). Severity mild / moderate / severe. Numbers Prevalence 5 to 15 percent of school-age children across languages and cultures; about 4 percent in adults. Reading is the commonest domain. DSM-5 abolished the old IQ-achievement discrepancy requirement, which is a favourite question: you no longer need a gap between IQ and achievement, you need low achievement plus failure to respond to intervention. Course Difficulties are usually recognised in the primary school years, once reading, spelling, writing and arithmetic are formally taught, though precursors such as language delay, trouble with rhyming or counting, and poor fine motor skill for writing often appear before school; the diagnosis can only be made after formal education starts . The disorder is lifelong , with a variable course: problems with reading fluency, spelling, written expression and numeracy usually persist into adulthood, where people tend to avoid tasks that demand the weak skill. Outcomes include lower attainment, more school drop-out , unemployment and distress; drop-out and depressive symptoms raise the risk of poor mental health including suicidality, while strong social or emotional support predicts better outcome. Comorbidity ADHD (very high overlap), communication disorders, developmental coordination disorder, autism, anxiety and depressive disorders (secondary to school failure), and conduct problems in adolescence. Differential Normal variation in academic attainment; lack of instruction or schooling disruption, which is common in Indian samples and is an explicit exclusion; intellectual disability (all domains low, not one); ADHD (performance varies with attention and improves with structure); neurocognitive disorder (skills were acquired and lost); psychosocial adversity ; sensory impairment. DSM-5 change DSM-5 merged DSM-IV-TR's separate reading disorder , mathematics disorder and disorder of written expression into a single specific learning disorder , with the affected domain recorded as a specifier and severity specifiers added. The IQ-achievement discrepancy requirement was dropped; instead achievement must be substantially below age expectation and the difficulties must have lasted at least 6 months despite targeted intervention , a response-to-intervention approach. Diagnosis became a clinical synthesis of history, school reports and standardised testing, and the disorder moved to the Neurodevelopmental chapter. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Motor Disorders and Tic Disorders F82, F98.4, F95.x In plain language. Clumsiness that is out of proportion to age, repetitive purposeless movement, and tics. Developmental Coordination Disorder. Acquisition and execution of coordinated motor skills is substantially below age expectation (clumsiness, slowness and inaccuracy in catching, using scissors, handwriting, cycling, sports). It interferes with daily living and academics, begins in the early developmental period, and is not explained by intellectual disability, visual impairment, or a neurological condition affecting movement (cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy). Stereotypic Movement Disorder. Repetitive, seemingly driven and purposeless motor behaviour (hand shaking or waving, body rocking, head banging, self-biting, hitting own body). Onset in the early developmental period, interferes with activities or results in self-injury. Specify with or without self-injurious behaviour , and whether it is associated with a known medical or genetic condition or environmental factor (for example Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, intellectual disability, intrauterine alcohol exposure). Tic disorders. A tic is a sudden, rapid, recurrent, non-rhythmic motor movement or vocalisation. Tourette's Disorder : multiple motor tics and one or more vocal tics , both present at some time during the illness though not necessarily concurrently, persisting for more than 1 year since first tic onset, with onset before age 18 . Persistent (Chronic) Motor or Vocal Tic Disorder : motor or vocal tics but not both, more than 1 year, onset before 18. Provisional Tic Disorder : single or multiple motor and/or vocal tics present for less than 1 year since first onset. Specifiers Developmental coordination disorder has no specifiers. Stereotypic movement disorder : specify with self-injurious behaviour (or behaviour that would cause injury if preventive measures were not used) or without self-injurious behaviour ; specify if associated with a known genetic or other medical condition, neurodevelopmental disorder or environmental factor ; and rate current severity as mild (easily suppressed by a sensory stimulus or distraction), moderate (needs explicit protective measures and behaviour modification) or severe (needs continuous monitoring and protective measures to prevent serious injury). Persistent (chronic) motor or vocal tic disorder : specify with motor tics only or with vocal tics only . Tourette's disorder and provisional tic disorder have no specifiers. Numbers Tics typically begin between ages 4 and 6, peak in severity between 10 and 12, and decline through adolescence. Tourette's prevalence 3 to 8 per 1000 school-age children; male to female 2:1 to 4:1. Coprolalia occurs in only about 10 percent, which is the standard trap because popular culture treats it as the defining feature. Course Developmental coordination disorder is usually not diagnosed before age 5 because motor milestones vary so much; its course is variable but stable over at least a year, and coordination problems persist through adolescence in an estimated 50 to 70 percent . Stereotypic movements usually begin in the first 3 years ; in typically developing children they tend to lessen or can be suppressed, whereas in intellectual disability, especially the self-injurious forms, they can persist for years while changing in form. Tics characteristically wax and wane and shift in location and type over time, worsen with anxiety, excitement and exhaustion, and ease during calm, focused activity; awareness of a premonitory urge usually comes with age. Many adults have much milder tics, but a small proportion have persistently severe or worsening tics, and comorbid ADHD or OCD often causes more impairment than the tics themselves. Comorbidity Tourette's with ADHD (about half) and OCD (roughly a third to a half) is the classic triad. Also anxiety, depression, disruptive behaviour, and learning problems. Developmental coordination disorder co-occurs with ADHD (the old "DAMP" concept), specific learning disorder and autism. Stereotypic movement disorder co-occurs with intellectual disability and autism. Differential Tics versus stereotypies : tics are faster, non-rhythmic, preceded by a premonitory urge and can be briefly suppressed; stereotypies are rhythmic, prolonged, fixed, start earlier (before 3) and are not preceded by an urge. Tics versus compulsions : compulsions are performed in response to an obsession or a rule and aim to prevent something; complex tics can look identical, and the two coexist. Chorea (random, flowing, not suppressible), dystonia (sustained), myoclonus , seizures . Also substance-induced (stimulants) and other medical conditions (Huntington's, post-viral). DSM-5 change DSM-5 placed developmental coordination disorder, stereotypic movement disorder and the tic disorders together as Motor Disorders in the new Neurodevelopmental chapter. DSM-IV-TR's transient tic disorder was renamed provisional tic disorder and lost its 4-week minimum; chronic motor or vocal tic disorder became persistent (chronic) motor or vocal tic disorder with a motor-only or vocal-only specifier; and the rule of no tic-free period longer than 3 months was removed, so tics need only have persisted more than 1 year since first onset. The criteria were standardised across the tic disorders, keeping onset before 18. Stereotypic movement disorder gained the without self-injurious behaviour, associated-condition and severity specifiers. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. 3. Schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders This chapter is arranged along a gradient of psychopathology , from least to most: schizotypal personality disorder, delusional disorder, brief psychotic disorder, schizophreniform disorder, schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder. Everything in it is defined by five domains: delusions, hallucinations, disorganised thinking (speech), grossly disorganised or abnormal motor behaviour including catatonia, and negative symptoms . Learn the five, then learn the durations, because duration is what separates almost every member of this chapter from its neighbour. The duration ladder, the single most examined thing in the chapter Brief psychotic disorder: at least 1 day, less than 1 month, with full return to premorbid functioning. Schizophreniform disorder: at least 1 month, less than 6 months. Schizophrenia: at least 6 months of total disturbance, including at least 1 month of active-phase symptoms. Delusional disorder: at least 1 month of delusions. So: one day, one month, six months. If a stem gives you three months of psychosis, the answer is schizophreniform, and the word "provisional" belongs in the answer if the person has not yet recovered. Delusional Disorder F22 In plain language. One or more fixed false beliefs, for a month or more, and apart from what follows directly from the belief, the person is otherwise entirely normal. The person is not obviously odd, their speech is coherent, they hold down a job. A. One or more delusions of 1 month or longer . B. Criterion A for schizophrenia has never been met. If hallucinations occur they are not prominent and are related to the delusional theme (for example the sensation of insects in delusional parasitosis). C. Apart from the impact of the delusion, functioning is not markedly impaired and behaviour is not obviously bizarre or odd. D. If manic or major depressive episodes have occurred, they have been brief relative to the duration of the delusional periods. E. Not attributable to a substance, another medical condition, or better explained by another disorder such as body dysmorphic disorder or OCD. Subtypes Erotomanic (another person, usually of higher status, is in love with the person), grandiose , jealous (the "Othello syndrome"), persecutory (the commonest), somatic , mixed , unspecified . Also specify with bizarre content . Course specifiers after 1 year: first episode currently in acute episode / in partial remission / in full remission; multiple episodes; continuous. Numbers Lifetime prevalence about 0.2 percent, so it is rare. Onset later than schizophrenia, typically middle to late adult life. The DSM-5 change worth naming: the requirement that delusions be non-bizarre was removed , and "with bizarre content" became a specifier instead. Shared delusional disorder (folie a deux) was also removed as a separate diagnosis; it is now coded as delusional disorder or under other specified schizophrenia spectrum disorder. Course Onset is usually in middle or late adult life , often insidious, and the pattern is variable : the persecutory type in particular tends to be chronic , with the preoccupation waxing and waning; others have full remissions followed by relapse, and some remit within months without recurrence. The diagnosis is generally stable , though a proportion later develop schizophrenia, and overall functioning is usually better than in schizophrenia. Better outcome is associated with good occupational and social adjustment, female sex , onset before 30 , sudden onset , short duration and a clear precipitating factor . Comorbidity Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder (especially where insight is absent), depressive disorders (often secondary to the delusion), and paranoid, schizoid and avoidant personality disorders, which often precede the onset. Differential Schizophrenia (Criterion A met, functioning declines, negative symptoms). OCD with absent insight (the belief grew out of an obsession, and the person has compulsions). Body dysmorphic disorder with absent insight . Paranoid personality disorder (suspiciousness that never reaches delusional conviction, and is lifelong and trait-like). Substance or medication induced , and psychotic disorder due to another medical condition . Major depressive or bipolar disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features (the delusion only exists inside the mood episode). DSM-5 change DSM-5 dropped the requirement that the delusions be non-bizarre ; bizarre delusions are now allowed and recorded with the with bizarre content specifier. Shared psychotic disorder (folie a deux) was removed as a separate diagnosis: if criteria are met it is delusional disorder, otherwise other specified schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorder. The Criterion B note, which in DSM-IV-TR named tactile and olfactory hallucinations related to the delusional theme, now covers hallucinations of any kind provided they are not prominent and related to the delusional theme ; a new exclusion was added for OCD and body dysmorphic disorder with absent insight ; and course specifiers and dimensional severity ratings were introduced. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Brief Psychotic Disorder F23 In plain language. Psychosis that arrives suddenly, lasts days or a few weeks, and then goes completely, leaving the person as they were. A. Presence of one or more of: delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour. At least one must be from the first three (delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech), so catatonia alone does not qualify. B. Duration at least 1 day but less than 1 month , with eventual full return to premorbid level of functioning . C. Not better explained by a depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features or another psychotic disorder, and not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. Specifiers With marked stressor(s) (this is the old brief reactive psychosis ), without marked stressor(s), with peripartum onset (during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum), and with catatonia . Severity rated on the 5 psychotic dimensions, 0 to 4. Numbers Accounts for roughly 9 percent of first-onset psychosis in some series. Twice as common in females. Average age of onset in the mid thirties. Suicide risk is elevated, particularly in the acute phase and in younger patients. Course Onset is sudden , from adolescence or early adulthood onward, sometimes within days of a major stressor or after childbirth. By definition symptoms last at least 1 day and under 1 month, sometimes only a few days, and end in full return to the premorbid level. Relapses can occur and some people are later rediagnosed with schizophrenia or a mood disorder, but for most the outcome in symptoms and social functioning is good. Good prognosis is linked to good premorbid adjustment, a severe precipitating stressor, sudden onset, prominent mood symptoms, confusion or perplexity during the episode, little affective blunting and short duration. Comorbidity Personality disorders, especially borderline, schizotypal, paranoid and histrionic, are frequent precursors. Differential Schizophreniform disorder (a month or more). Substance-induced psychotic disorder , which is the leading practical mimic in a young patient, so ask about cannabis and stimulants and take a urine screen. Psychotic disorder due to another medical condition (delirium, epilepsy, thyrotoxicosis, autoimmune encephalitis). Malingering and factitious disorder . Culturally sanctioned response , such as trance or a possession state that is a normal part of a religious practice, which is explicitly excluded. Bipolar or depressive disorder with psychotic features . Personality disorder with transient stress-related paranoia, especially borderline, where the psychotic-like symptoms are brief, stress-triggered, and recur across a long history. DSM-5 change DSM-5 kept the duration (at least 1 day, less than 1 month, with full return to premorbid functioning) but tightened Criterion A: at least one symptom must now be delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech , whereas DSM-IV-TR accepted grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour alone. The with postpartum onset specifier (within 4 weeks after delivery) was widened to with peripartum onset (during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum), and the with catatonia specifier and dimensional severity ratings were added. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Schizophreniform Disorder F20.81 In plain language. Schizophrenia's symptom picture, but the clock has not run long enough yet. It is a provisional label you use while waiting. A. Same as schizophrenia Criterion A: two or more of delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour, negative symptoms, each present for a significant portion of a 1-month period, with at least one being delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech. B. An episode lasting at least 1 month but less than 6 months . If you are diagnosing while the person is still ill, qualify as "provisional" . C. Schizoaffective and depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features ruled out. D. Not substance or medical. Note that unlike schizophrenia, impaired functioning is not required . Specifiers With good prognostic features requires at least two of: onset of prominent psychotic symptoms within 4 weeks of the first noticeable change in usual behaviour; confusion or perplexity; good premorbid social and occupational functioning; absence of blunted or flat affect. Otherwise, without good prognostic features . Also with catatonia. Numbers Roughly a third recover within the 6 months and keep the diagnosis; about two-thirds progress to schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder. Incidence in developed countries is about a fifth that of schizophrenia. Course Onset and development resemble schizophrenia , typically in late adolescence or early adulthood, but the illness is defined by a time window : if symptoms resolve within 6 months, 'provisional' is dropped and schizophreniform disorder is the final diagnosis; if they reach 6 months, the diagnosis changes to schizophrenia, or to schizoaffective disorder if the mood criteria are met. The four good prognostic features in the specifier ( rapid onset , confusion or perplexity , good premorbid functioning , no flat affect ) mark the cases more likely to recover. In developing countries incidence may be higher, especially of the form with good prognostic features. Comorbidity As for schizophrenia: substance use, depression, anxiety. Differential Brief psychotic disorder (under 1 month). Schizophrenia (6 months or more, including prodrome and residual). Schizoaffective (a full mood episode runs for the majority of the illness). Substance-induced and medical causes. DSM-5 change The duration window ( 1 month to under 6 months ), the 'provisional' rule and the four-item good prognostic features specifier all carried over from DSM-IV-TR. What changed in DSM-5 came with schizophrenia's Criterion A: the single-symptom concession for bizarre delusions or Schneiderian voices was removed, and at least one of the two required symptoms must be delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech . The with catatonia specifier and dimensional severity ratings were added. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Schizophrenia F20.9 In plain language. For at least six months the person has been drifting away from ordinary reality and ordinary functioning, and for at least one of those months they have actively had psychotic symptoms. A. Two or more of the following, each present for a significant portion of time during a 1-month period (or less if successfully treated), and at least one must be (1), (2) or (3) : (1) delusions; (2) hallucinations; (3) disorganised speech (frequent derailment or incoherence); (4) grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour; (5) negative symptoms (diminished emotional expression or avolition). B. Level of functioning in work, interpersonal relations or self-care is markedly below the level achieved before onset (or, with childhood or adolescent onset, failure to achieve the expected level). C. Continuous signs of the disturbance persist for at least 6 months , which must include at least 1 month of Criterion A (active-phase) symptoms , and may include periods of prodromal or residual symptoms, during which the disturbance may show only negative symptoms or two or more Criterion A symptoms in attenuated form. D. Schizoaffective disorder and depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features have been ruled out because either no major mood episodes have occurred concurrently with the active phase, or, if they have, they have been present for a minority of the total duration of the active and residual periods. E. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. F. If there is a history of autism spectrum disorder or a childhood-onset communication disorder, schizophrenia is diagnosed only if prominent delusions or hallucinations , plus the other required symptoms, are also present for at least 1 month. Specifiers Course, only after 1 year of symptoms: first episode currently in acute episode / in partial remission / in full remission; multiple episodes (same three); continuous; unspecified. Also with catatonia . Severity is rated dimensionally 0 to 4 on each of the five psychotic domains. The classical subtypes (paranoid, disorganised or hebephrenic, catatonic, undifferentiated, residual) were deleted in DSM-5 because they had poor reliability, low diagnostic stability and no validity for treatment response. Naming that deletion, and why, is a stock question. Numbers Lifetime prevalence about 0.3 to 0.7 percent. Onset typically early to mid twenties in men, late twenties in women , with a second smaller peak in women after 40. About 5 to 6 percent die by suicide, about 20 percent attempt it. Heritability roughly 80 percent; monozygotic concordance about 45 to 50 percent, dizygotic about 15 percent, one affected parent about 13 percent, both parents about 45 percent.
