Life expectancy is reduced by roughly 15 to 20 years, mostly cardiovascular. The DSM-5 change to name: DSM-IV allowed a single symptom if the delusion was bizarre or the hallucination was a running commentary or two voices conversing (the Schneiderian first-rank concession); DSM-5 removed that special treatment , so two symptoms are always required. Course Psychotic symptoms usually emerge between the late teens and mid thirties , and most people have a gradual prodrome (withdrawal, loss of interest, declining self-care, odd ideas) before frank psychosis, though onset can be abrupt. Most remain chronically ill with relapses and partial remissions and some decline progressively; about 20 percent have a favourable course and few recover completely. Positive symptoms tend to lessen with age, while negative symptoms , which are more closely tied to prognosis, and cognitive deficits persist. Better outcome goes with female sex , later and acute onset , a clear precipitant, good premorbid functioning, prominent mood symptoms, good support and a short duration of untreated psychosis ; WHO studies found better outcome in developing countries , including India. Comorbidity Substance use disorders are the big one, over half, and tobacco use is very high. Also obsessive-compulsive disorder and panic disorder at rates above the general population, schizotypal and paranoid personality disorders (often premorbid), depression, and medical comorbidity: metabolic syndrome, diabetes and cardiovascular disease, driven partly by antipsychotics. Differential Schizoaffective disorder and mood disorder with psychotic features , both settled by the mood-episode arithmetic in Criterion D. Schizophreniform and brief psychotic , settled by duration. Delusional disorder (Criterion A never met, no functional decline). Schizotypal personality disorder (attenuated symptoms, no frank psychosis, lifelong pattern). Obsessive-compulsive disorder with absent insight and body dysmorphic disorder . PTSD (flashbacks and hypervigilance can be mistaken for hallucinations and paranoia, but they are trauma-cued). Autism (Criterion F). Substance-induced psychotic disorder and psychotic disorder due to another medical condition , including temporal lobe epilepsy, delirium, Wilson's disease, SLE, and NMDA-receptor encephalitis. DSM-5 change DSM-5 removed the special status of bizarre delusions and Schneiderian first-rank hallucinations (a running commentary, or voices conversing), which in DSM-IV-TR could satisfy Criterion A alone; now two symptoms are always needed and at least one must be delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech . The five subtypes (paranoid, disorganised, catatonic, undifferentiated, residual) were deleted , catatonia became a specifier, DSM-IV's longitudinal course classifiers were replaced by the new course specifiers, and dimensional severity ratings were added. The 6-month and 1-month durations did not change, and the chapter became Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders . DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. ICD-11 Requires 1 month of symptoms, not six, and does not require functional decline. So the same patient at week five can be schizophrenia under ICD-11 and schizophreniform under DSM-5-TR. That is a favourite comparison question. Schizoaffective Disorder F25.x In plain language. Psychosis and a full mood episode run alongside each other, but the psychosis has also stood alone, without the mood episode, for at least two weeks. That standalone stretch is the whole diagnosis. A. An uninterrupted period of illness during which there is a major mood episode (major depressive or manic) concurrent with Criterion A of schizophrenia . If it is a major depressive episode, depressed mood must be one of the symptoms. B. Delusions or hallucinations for 2 or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode during the lifetime duration of the illness. This is the criterion that defines the disorder. C. Symptoms that meet criteria for a major mood episode are present for the majority of the total duration of the active and residual portions of the illness. D. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. Specifiers Bipolar type (a manic episode is part of the presentation; major depressive episodes may also occur) or depressive type (only major depressive episodes). Also with catatonia, course specifiers after 1 year, and dimensional severity ratings. Numbers Lifetime prevalence about 0.3 percent, roughly a third that of schizophrenia. More common in women, driven by the depressive type. Prognosis sits between schizophrenia and mood disorder, better than schizophrenia and worse than bipolar disorder. Criterion C, the "majority of the total duration" rule, was changed in DSM-5 from a cross-sectional judgment to a lifetime one, so the diagnosis became longitudinal rather than a snapshot. Course Onset is typically in early adulthood but can be anywhere from adolescence to late life; the bipolar type is more common in young adults and the depressive type in older adults. Because the diagnosis rests on the lifetime pattern, many people first diagnosed with another psychotic disorder receive it later as the mood episodes become clear, and some move out of it as mood symptoms fade. The bipolar type is thought to have an outlook nearer bipolar I disorder and the depressive type nearer schizophrenia. Poor premorbid adjustment, insidious onset, no precipitant, early onset, predominant psychotic or negative symptoms, an unremitting course and a family history of schizophrenia predict worse outcome. Comorbidity Substance use disorders, anxiety disorders, and general medical conditions at rates similar to schizophrenia. Differential Two-sided, and this is a guaranteed question. Against schizophrenia : in schizophrenia mood episodes are present for a minority of the illness, in schizoaffective they are present for the majority. Against major depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features : there, the psychosis occurs only during mood episodes, so if you can find two weeks of delusions or hallucinations with no mood episode, it is schizoaffective. Also substance-induced psychotic disorder and psychotic disorder due to another medical condition. DSM-5 change The defining DSM-5 change was Criterion C: DSM-IV-TR required mood symptoms for a substantial portion of the illness, judged largely cross-sectionally, whereas DSM-5 requires a major mood episode for the majority of the total duration of the active and residual illness, judged across the lifetime . This made schizoaffective disorder a longitudinal diagnosis and a narrower one. Criterion A also lost DSM-IV's mixed episode option, since the mixed episode was dropped from DSM-5, and the changes to schizophrenia's Criterion A, the catatonia specifier and dimensional severity ratings apply here too. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Substance/Medication-Induced Psychotic Disorder, and Psychotic Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition Substance-induced: delusions and/or hallucinations that developed during or soon after substance intoxication or withdrawal or exposure to a medication capable of producing them, and are not better explained by an independent psychotic disorder. Evidence for independence would be: symptoms preceded the substance use, or persisted for a substantial period, about 1 month, after acute withdrawal ended. Does not occur exclusively during delirium. Specify onset during intoxication or during withdrawal. Common agents: alcohol, cannabis, amphetamine and other stimulants, cocaine, hallucinogens, inhalants, sedatives; medications: corticosteroids, anticholinergics, L-dopa, isoniazid, interferon. Due to another medical condition: prominent hallucinations or delusions, with evidence from history, examination or labs that the disturbance is the direct pathophysiological consequence of a medical condition, not better explained by another mental disorder, not exclusively during delirium, and causing significant impairment. Specify with delusions or with hallucinations. Classic causes: temporal lobe epilepsy, stroke, brain tumour, traumatic brain injury, Huntington's, Parkinson's, multiple sclerosis, thyroid and parathyroid disease, Cushing's, SLE, B12 deficiency, autoimmune encephalitis, HIV, neurosyphilis. Specifiers Substance/medication-induced : specify with onset during intoxication (criteria for intoxication are met and symptoms develop during it), with onset during withdrawal (criteria for withdrawal are met and symptoms develop during, or shortly after, it) or with onset after medication use (symptoms developed at initiation of a medication, with a change in its use, or during withdrawal from it). The diagnosis is named for the specific substance (for example cannabis-induced psychotic disorder), and its ICD-10-CM code depends on whether there is a comorbid mild , or moderate or severe , use disorder of that substance, or none. Due to another medical condition : specify with delusions (F06.2) or with hallucinations (F06.0) according to which predominates, and record the medical condition's name. For both, current severity may be rated 0 to 4 on the psychosis symptom dimensions, but this is optional. Course A substance/medication-induced psychosis begins during or soon after intoxication, withdrawal or medication exposure and usually clears within days to weeks of abstinence , depending on the substance and its half-life; persistence for about a month after abstinence points to an independent psychotic disorder. A sizeable proportion, especially after cannabis or stimulant -induced psychosis, later develop schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, so follow-up matters. Psychosis due to another medical condition may be a single transient state or may recur with exacerbations of the underlying illness; treating the medical condition often resolves it, but psychotic symptoms can persist long after the medical event. Comorbidity Substance use disorders by definition, and very often a primary psychotic disorder as well, since cannabis and stimulant use are markedly elevated in people with schizophrenia. For the medical form, the comorbidity is the underlying disease itself plus the depression and anxiety that follow it. Differential Delirium is the first thing to exclude, because if consciousness and attention fluctuate, the diagnosis is delirium and not a psychotic disorder. Then a primary psychotic disorder in someone who also happens to use substances, which is settled by timing and by the one-month post-withdrawal rule. DSM-5 change DSM-5 renamed DSM-IV-TR's substance-induced psychotic disorder as substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder , and psychotic disorder due to a general medical condition as psychotic disorder due to another medical condition , the 'general medical condition' wording being dropped across the manual. The core rules carried over: the about 1 month persistence guideline for an independent disorder; the delirium exclusion; and hallucinations the person knows are substance-induced are recorded as intoxication or withdrawal with perceptual disturbances instead. DSM-IV-TR's onset 'during, or within a month of' intoxication or withdrawal was reworded to during or soon after , and optional dimensional severity ratings were added. DSM-5-TR (2022): Criterion B now also covers symptoms that begin after withdrawal from a medication , and with onset after medication use is listed among the onset specifiers. Catatonia F06.1 In plain language. A syndrome of marked psychomotor disturbance, which in DSM-5 stopped being a type of schizophrenia and became something you can attach to many disorders. Requires 3 or more of 12 : stupor (no psychomotor activity, not actively relating to environment), catalepsy (passive induction of a posture held against gravity), waxy flexibility (slight even resistance to positioning by the examiner), mutism , negativism (opposition or no response to instructions or external stimuli), posturing (spontaneous and active maintenance of a posture against gravity), mannerism (odd caricature of normal actions), stereotypy (repetitive, abnormally frequent, non-goal-directed movements), agitation not influenced by external stimuli, grimacing , echolalia , echopraxia . DSM-5 gives three ways to record it: catatonia associated with another mental disorder (used as a specifier for schizophrenia, schizoaffective, brief psychotic, schizophreniform, bipolar and depressive disorders, neurodevelopmental disorders), catatonic disorder due to another medical condition , and unspecified catatonia . Specifiers None of the three catatonia categories has subtypes, severity ratings or course specifiers in DSM-5-TR. Catatonia associated with another mental disorder works the other way round: it is recorded as the with catatonia specifier of the main diagnosis (psychotic, bipolar, depressive, neurodevelopmental or other mental disorders), with the main disorder coded first. Catatonic disorder due to another medical condition is recorded with the name of the medical condition. Unspecified catatonia is used when the underlying mental or medical condition is unclear, full criteria are not met, or information is insufficient, as in an emergency setting. Clinical labels such as malignant , excited or stuporous catatonia are not DSM-5-TR specifiers. Numbers Historically framed as a schizophrenia subtype, but the majority of catatonia in practice occurs in mood disorders , particularly bipolar. Responds to benzodiazepines (lorazepam challenge) and to ECT. Course Catatonia can appear at any age and follows the course of the underlying disorder , so it tends to recur when that disorder relapses; in autism the risk is greatest in adolescence . Untreated, immobility and refusal to eat or drink lead to dehydration, malnutrition, exhaustion and hyperthermia , along with pressure sores, pneumonia and venous thrombosis, and malignant catatonia (with fever and autonomic instability) can be fatal. With prompt treatment the outlook is usually good, better in mood disorders than in chronic schizophrenia, where the response to lorazepam is weaker. Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and raise the risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome, so they are used cautiously. Comorbidity Most commonly a mood disorder, particularly bipolar disorder, then schizophrenia spectrum disorders, autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability. Medically: encephalitis, autoimmune disease, metabolic derangement and drug toxicity. Differential Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, raised CK, following antipsychotic exposure) and malignant catatonia , which overlap dangerously. Non-convulsive status epilepticus , akinetic mutism , locked-in syndrome , severe Parkinsonism , and stupor from a medical or toxic cause. DSM-5 change In DSM-IV-TR catatonia appeared as the catatonic type of schizophrenia , the with catatonic features specifier for mood episodes, and catatonic disorder due to a general medical condition, with different thresholds (two of five symptom clusters in psychotic and mood disorders, only one for a medical cause). DSM-5 deleted the schizophrenia subtype, applied one criteria set (3 of 12 symptoms) in every context, made with catatonia available across psychotic, bipolar, depressive, neurodevelopmental and other disorders, and added unspecified catatonia so it can be diagnosed and treated before the cause is found. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. 4. Bipolar and related disorders DSM-5 pulled the bipolar disorders out of the old "Mood Disorders" chapter and placed them between the psychotic disorders and the depressive disorders, to signal that they bridge the two in symptoms, family history and genetics. Everything here is built from three blocks: the manic episode, the hypomanic episode, and the major depressive episode. The three episode definitions, learn these once Manic Episode A. A distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive or irritable mood AND abnormally and persistently increased goal-directed activity or energy , lasting at least 1 week and present most of the day, nearly every day (or any duration if hospitalisation is necessary). The addition of "increased activity or energy" to Criterion A is a DSM-5 change from DSM-IV, which required mood alone. B. During the mood disturbance, 3 or more of the following ( 4 if the mood is only irritable ), to a significant degree and representing a noticeable change from usual behaviour: inflated self-esteem or grandiosity; decreased need for sleep (feels rested after 3 hours, which is not the same as insomnia); more talkative than usual or pressure to keep talking; flight of ideas or subjective racing thoughts; distractibility; increase in goal-directed activity (social, occupational, sexual) or psychomotor agitation; excessive involvement in activities with a high potential for painful consequences (buying sprees, sexual indiscretion, foolish business investments). The mnemonic is DIG FAST : Distractibility, Indiscretion, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, Sleep deficit, Talkativeness. C. The disturbance is severe enough to cause marked impairment in social or occupational functioning, or to necessitate hospitalisation , or there are psychotic features . Any one of these three makes it mania rather than hypomania. D. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. Note the DSM-5 rule: a full manic episode that emerges during antidepressant treatment or ECT and persists at a fully syndromal level beyond the physiological effect of that treatment counts as a manic episode, and therefore as bipolar I. DSM-IV excluded it. Specifiers These attach to bipolar I when the current or most recent episode is manic. Severity has its own definitions for mania in DSM-5-TR: mild , minimum symptom criteria are met; moderate , a very significant increase in activity or impairment in judgement; severe , almost continual supervision is needed to prevent physical harm to self or others. Psychosis is recorded as mood-congruent (grandiosity, invulnerability, or suspicion that others doubt the person's abilities) or mood-incongruent psychotic features . With mixed features : full manic criteria plus at least 3 depressive symptoms on most days (dysphoria, loss of interest, psychomotor retardation, fatigue, worthlessness or guilt, thoughts of death or suicide); if full mania and full depression are present at the same time, the diagnosis is manic episode with mixed features. Also with anxious distress , with catatonia , with peripartum onset , and in partial or in full remission (full: no significant symptoms for 2 months). With rapid cycling and with seasonal pattern also apply, describing the pattern of episodes over time. Melancholic and atypical features apply only to depressive episodes. Course A manic episode usually begins abruptly , with symptoms escalating over a few days, sometimes after a psychosocial stressor or sleep loss. Untreated, an episode lasts about 3 months (Kaplan and Sadock), which is why treatment is not withdrawn before then; manic episodes are generally briefer and end more abruptly than major depressive episodes. DSM-5 notes that about 60 percent of manic episodes occur immediately before a major depressive episode, so mania often ends by switching into depression. Insight is usually poor during the episode, and people often resist treatment. DSM-5 change Criterion A now requires increased activity or energy alongside the elevated, expansive or irritable mood; DSM-IV required the mood change alone. The DSM-IV mixed episode (full mania and full depression together) was dropped, along with the old exclusion that symptoms must not meet mixed-episode criteria, and replaced by the with mixed features specifier. A fully syndromal manic episode that emerges during antidepressant treatment or ECT and persists beyond the treatment's physiological effect now counts towards bipolar I, where DSM-IV excluded it. DSM-5-TR (2022): the episode criteria are unchanged, but mania-specific severity definitions (taken from DSM-IV) were added, because the general mild-to-severe definitions made no sense for mania, which by definition causes marked impairment. Hypomanic Episode Same Criterion A mood plus energy change, but lasting at least 4 consecutive days . Same list of 7 symptoms, same 3 or 4 threshold. The episode is associated with an unequivocal change in functioning that is uncharacteristic of the person when not symptomatic, and the change is observable by others . The episode is not severe enough to cause marked impairment, does not require hospitalisation, and there are no psychotic features . If any of those three appear, it is by definition mania. Specifiers These attach when the current or most recent episode of bipolar I or II is hypomanic. In bipolar I, a hypomanic episode takes no severity rating and no psychotic-features specifier (psychosis would make it mania); only in partial remission, in full remission or unspecified is added. Specifiers that can attach to the episode: with mixed features (full hypomanic criteria plus at least 3 depressive symptoms on most days), with anxious distress and with peripartum onset . With rapid cycling and with seasonal pattern describe the pattern of episodes over time rather than a single episode. Course Onset is usually rapid , often within a day or two, and hypomanic episodes are generally briefer and more abrupt in onset than major depressive episodes. A hypomanic episode is often immediately preceded or followed by a major depressive episode. Because hypomania feels good and causes no marked impairment, people rarely seek help for it and present instead when depressed; it often comes to light only on direct questioning or from family and friends, which is why bipolar II is so often missed. DSM-5 change Criterion A gained the same requirement of increased activity or energy . The 4-day minimum (as in DSM-IV) was kept; hypomanias of only 2 to 3 days alongside major depressive episodes, or hypomanias with too few symptoms, are placed under other specified bipolar and related disorder . A full hypomanic episode that emerges during antidepressant treatment and persists beyond its physiological effect now counts, with the caution that one or two symptoms (irritability, edginess or agitation after an antidepressant) are not enough. With mixed features can now be applied to hypomania. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Major Depressive Episode 5 or more of 9 symptoms during the same 2-week period, representing a change from previous functioning, and at least one must be (1) depressed mood or (2) loss of interest or pleasure. The nine: (1) depressed mood most of the day nearly every day (in children and adolescents, can be irritable mood ); (2) markedly diminished interest or pleasure in all or almost all activities; (3) significant weight loss or gain (more than 5 percent of body weight in a month) or change in appetite (in children, failure to make expected weight gain); (4) insomnia or hypersomnia; (5) psychomotor agitation or retardation, observable by others , not merely subjective; (6) fatigue or loss of energy; (7) feelings of worthlessness or excessive or inappropriate guilt, which may be delusional; (8) diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness; (9) recurrent thoughts of death, recurrent suicidal ideation without a specific plan, a suicide attempt, or a specific plan. Mnemonic SIG E CAPS plus mood: Sleep, Interest, Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor, Suicide. Specifiers These attach to major depressive disorder or to the depressive episode of bipolar I or II. Severity mild, moderate or severe; with psychotic features , mood-congruent (inadequacy, guilt, disease, death, nihilism, deserved punishment) or mood-incongruent. With melancholic features : loss of pleasure or lack of reactivity, plus 3 of six (distinct quality of mood, worse in the morning, waking at least 2 hours early, marked psychomotor change, significant anorexia or weight loss, excessive guilt). With atypical features : mood reactivity plus 2 of four (weight gain or increased appetite, hypersomnia, leaden paralysis, long-standing rejection sensitivity), and not given if melancholic or catatonic features are present in the same episode. With mixed features : at least 3 manic or hypomanic symptoms. Also anxious distress, catatonia, peripartum onset and remission. Course An episode usually develops over days to weeks , often after a prodrome of anxiety and milder depressive symptoms. Untreated, it typically lasts 6 to 13 months ; treated episodes average about 3 months , and stopping antidepressants before 3 months almost always brings the symptoms back (Kaplan and Sadock). DSM-5 notes that recovery begins within 3 months for about two in five people and within 1 year for about four in five, and that the more recent the onset, the likelier near-term recovery. Most episodes end in full remission with return to previous functioning; a minority leave residual symptoms or become chronic. DSM-5 change The DSM-IV bereavement exclusion was removed; a note now asks the clinician to consider whether a major depressive episode is present in addition to the normal response to a significant loss. Hopeless was added to the examples of subjective depressed mood in Criterion A1. The DSM-IV requirement that the symptoms not meet criteria for a mixed episode was dropped with the mixed episode itself, replaced by the with mixed features specifier. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the episode criteria; it added ICD-10-CM codes to record current or past suicidal behaviour and non-suicidal self-injury . Bipolar I Disorder F31.x In plain language. One manic episode, ever, in a lifetime. That is the entire requirement. Depression is common but is not needed for the diagnosis. Criteria have been met for at least one manic episode . The manic episode may have been preceded by and may be followed by hypomanic or major depressive episodes. The occurrence of the manic and major depressive episode(s) is not better explained by schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia, schizophreniform disorder, delusional disorder, or other specified or unspecified schizophrenia spectrum disorder. Specifiers (these apply across bipolar and depressive disorders): with anxious distress (mild to severe, based on 2 to 5 symptoms); with mixed features (DSM-5 replaced the DSM-IV "mixed episode", which needed full criteria for both mania and depression simultaneously, with a much more usable specifier requiring 3 symptoms of the opposite pole); with rapid cycling (4 or more mood episodes in 12 months); with melancholic features ; with atypical features (mood reactivity, hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis, interpersonal rejection sensitivity); with mood-congruent or mood-incongruent psychotic features ; with catatonia ; with peripartum onset (during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum, which is a much narrower window than the popular usage of "postpartum depression"); with seasonal pattern . Also specify current or most recent episode (manic, hypomanic, depressed, unspecified), severity, psychotic features, and remission status. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 0.6 percent; roughly equal in men and women, though rapid cycling is commoner in women. Mean age of onset about 18. Lifetime suicide risk is roughly 15 times the general population, and bipolar disorder may account for a quarter of all completed suicides. Mania lasting 1 week, hypomania 4 days: those two numbers are asked constantly. Course A first manic episode usually comes in late adolescence or early adulthood but can occur at any age; manic symptoms first appearing in late mid-life or later should prompt a search for a medical or substance cause (for example frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder). The course is recurrent : more than 90 percent of people with a single manic episode go on to have further mood episodes. Most return to full function between episodes, but about 30 percent have severe impairment in work role function. Kaplan and Sadock list as poor prognostic signs poor premorbid occupational status, alcohol dependence, psychotic features, depressive features (especially between episodes) and male sex; good signs are short manic episodes, later age at onset, few suicidal thoughts and few coexisting psychiatric or medical problems. Comorbidity Extremely high. Around three-quarters have a comorbid anxiety disorder (panic disorder, social anxiety, specific phobia); more than half have an alcohol use disorder; ADHD, oppositional defiant and conduct disorder in younger patients; borderline and antisocial personality disorders; migraine; metabolic syndrome. Differential Bipolar II (never a full manic episode). Major depressive disorder (the trap: a person presenting depressed whose past hypomania has never been asked about; always screen). Generalised anxiety, panic, substance use . ADHD (chronic, not episodic, and no decreased need for sleep, and onset before 12). Borderline personality disorder , where mood shifts last hours and are reactive to interpersonal events, versus bipolar where episodes last days to weeks and are autonomous. Schizoaffective and schizophrenia . Substance-induced bipolar and related disorder (stimulants, steroids). Bipolar due to another medical condition (hyperthyroidism, Cushing's, multiple sclerosis, stroke, traumatic brain injury). DSM-5 change DSM-5 moved bipolar disorders out of the single DSM-IV Mood Disorders chapter into their own chapter, Bipolar and Related Disorders , placed between the schizophrenia spectrum and depressive chapters as a bridge between the two. The manic-episode changes carry through: increased activity or energy in Criterion A; the mixed episode replaced by the with mixed features specifier, so 'most recent episode mixed' no longer exists; and persistent antidepressant- or ECT-emergent mania counting as bipolar I. With anxious distress was a new specifier. DSM-5-TR (2022): Criterion B was reworded back towards DSM-IV: at least one manic episode must not be better explained by schizoaffective disorder and must not be superimposed on schizophrenia, schizophreniform, delusional or other psychotic disorder (mania superimposed on these goes to other specified bipolar and related disorder). Mania-specific severity definitions were added, and unspecified mood disorder was restored. Bipolar II Disorder F31.81 In plain language. At least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode, and never a full manic episode. It is not a milder illness, and DSM-5-TR says so explicitly, because the depressive burden is heavier and lasts longer. A. Criteria met for at least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode. B. There has never been a manic episode. C. Not better explained by a schizophrenia spectrum disorder. D. The symptoms of depression, or the unpredictability caused by frequent alternation between periods of depression and hypomania, cause clinically significant distress or impairment. Note that the impairment must come from the depression or the alternation, because if the hypomania itself caused marked impairment it would be mania. Specifiers Specify the current or most recent episode: hypomanic or depressed . Specify if: with anxious distress ; with mixed features ; with rapid cycling (4 or more mood episodes in 12 months, separated by at least 2 months of partial or full remission or by a switch to the opposite pole); with mood-congruent or mood-incongruent psychotic features (these can attach only to the depressive episode, since psychosis during an elevated episode would make it mania); with catatonia ; with peripartum onset ; with seasonal pattern . Course: in partial or in full remission when full criteria for a mood episode are not currently met; severity (mild, moderate, severe) when they are. Bipolar II has a single code (F31.81), so all of these are written out rather than coded. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 0.8 percent. Mean age at onset in the mid twenties, slightly later than bipolar I. People with bipolar II spend more time depressed than people with bipolar I: about half of all weeks in long-term follow-up, against about a third. About 5 to 15 percent go on to have a manic episode, at which point the diagnosis changes to bipolar I permanently. Course It usually begins with a depressive episode , and several depressive episodes often come before the first hypomania is recognised; about 12 percent of people first diagnosed with major depressive disorder are later rediagnosed with bipolar II. The number of lifetime episodes tends to be higher than in major depressive disorder or bipolar I. Most people return to full function between episodes, but at least 15 percent keep some inter-episode dysfunction and about 20 percent pass straight into another episode without recovering in between. About one-third report a lifetime suicide attempt. Comorbidity About 60 percent have three or more co-occurring disorders. Anxiety disorders (about 75 percent), substance use disorders (about 37 percent), eating disorders, especially binge-eating disorder, and personality disorders. Differential Major depressive disorder , the commonest misdiagnosis, because patients present in the depressed phase and do not report hypomania as a problem. Cyclothymic disorder (never a full major depressive episode and never a full hypomanic episode meeting all criteria). Borderline personality disorder . ADHD . Substance-induced states. DSM-5 change Moved with bipolar I into the new Bipolar and Related Disorders chapter. The hypomanic episode now requires increased activity or energy ; a hypomanic episode emerging during antidepressant treatment and persisting beyond the drug's physiological effect counts; and with mixed features can be applied to the hypomanic or the depressive episode. Hypomanias of only 2 to 3 days with depressive episodes go to other specified bipolar and related disorder. The DSM-5 text also stated that bipolar II is not a milder form of bipolar I, because of the time spent depressed and the instability of mood. DSM-5-TR (2022): Criterion C was reworded back towards DSM-IV: at least one hypomanic and at least one major depressive episode must not be better explained by schizoaffective disorder and must not be superimposed on schizophrenia, schizophreniform, delusional or other psychotic disorder. Cyclothymic Disorder F34.0 In plain language. Two years of bobbing up and down, never quite reaching a full hypomanic or a full depressive episode, and never getting a clear two-month stretch of feeling normal. A. For at least 2 years ( 1 year in children and adolescents ), numerous periods with hypomanic symptoms that do not meet criteria for a hypomanic episode and numerous periods with depressive symptoms that do not meet criteria for a major depressive episode . B. During that 2-year period, the hypomanic and depressive periods have been present for at least half the time , and the person has not been without the symptoms for more than 2 months at a time . C. Criteria for a major depressive, manic or hypomanic episode have never been met. D. Not better explained by a schizophrenia spectrum disorder. E. Not substance or medical. F. Clinically significant distress or impairment. Specify with anxious distress . Specifiers The only specifier is with anxious distress (2 or more of: feeling keyed up or tense, unusually restless, difficulty concentrating because of worry, fear that something awful may happen, feeling of losing control). There is no severity rating and no remission specifier, and the episode-based specifiers (mixed features, rapid cycling, psychotic features, peripartum onset, seasonal pattern) cannot apply, because cyclothymia by definition contains no full mood episodes. Numbers Lifetime prevalence 0.4 to 1 percent, equal in men and women, though women present for treatment more. Usual onset in adolescence or early adult life. Risk of progressing to bipolar I or II is roughly 15 to 50 percent. Course Onset is usually insidious , in adolescence or early adult life, and the course is persistent ; it is sometimes regarded as a temperamental predisposition to the other bipolar disorders. Among children with cyclothymic symptoms, mean age at onset is about 6.5 years. When fluctuating hypomanic and depressive symptoms begin late in adult life, bipolar or depressive disorder due to another medical condition (for example multiple sclerosis) must be ruled out first. If a full hypomanic, manic or major depressive episode later occurs, the cyclothymic diagnosis is dropped and replaced by the appropriate disorder. Comorbidity Substance use disorders and sleep disorders. In children, ADHD is a frequent comorbidity. Differential Bipolar II (full episodes have been met). Persistent depressive disorder (only depressive symptoms, no hypomanic periods). Borderline personality disorder , again, where the instability is interpersonally triggered. Rapid cycling bipolar . Substance-induced mood lability. DSM-5 change Moved into the new Bipolar and Related Disorders chapter. DSM-5 tightened the criteria: the hypomanic and depressive periods must be present for at least half the time , and Criterion C now says a major depressive, manic or hypomanic episode has never been met. DSM-IV excluded only major depressive, manic and mixed episodes, and only during the first 2 years , so bipolar I or II could be diagnosed alongside cyclothymia if an episode appeared later; in DSM-5 the cyclothymia diagnosis is dropped instead. With anxious distress became available. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Substance/Medication-Induced Bipolar and Related Disorder, and Bipolar Due to Another Medical Condition A prominent and persistent disturbance in mood, elevated or irritable with or without depressed mood, that developed during or soon after substance intoxication or withdrawal or exposure to a medication capable of producing it, or that is the direct pathophysiological consequence of a medical condition. Common substances: amphetamines and other stimulants, cocaine, phencyclidine, steroids. Common medical causes: Cushing's syndrome, hyperthyroidism, multiple sclerosis, stroke, traumatic brain injury . Remember the DSM-5 rule again: if a fully syndromal manic episode persists beyond the physiological effect of the antidepressant or ECT that triggered it, it is counted as a manic episode and the person has bipolar I, not a substance-induced disorder. Specifiers Substance/medication-induced bipolar and related disorder : specify with onset during intoxication or with onset during withdrawal ; the code also records the substance and whether a mild or a moderate-to-severe use disorder coexists. Bipolar and related disorder due to another medical condition : specify with manic features (full criteria for a manic or hypomanic episode not met), with manic- or hypomanic-like episode (full criteria met except Criterion D for a manic episode or Criterion F for a hypomanic episode), or with mixed features (depressive symptoms are also present but do not predominate). Course Onset follows exposure closely. With stimulants a manic or hypomanic state can appear within minutes to an hour of use and usually resolves over 1 to 2 days; with phencyclidine the picture may begin as a delirium with affective features within hours to a few days; with corticosteroids and some immunosuppressants, mania usually follows several days of use, and higher doses carry more risk. Symptoms should settle once the substance is stopped; persistence for about a month beyond intoxication or withdrawal points to a primary bipolar disorder. The medical form usually begins acutely or subacutely within the first weeks or month of the medical condition, though it can appear with a later relapse or worsening. A first manic episode in later life should raise suspicion of a medical or substance cause. Comorbidity Substance use disorders themselves, plus a primary bipolar disorder in a substantial proportion, since stimulant use is elevated in bipolar disorder. For the medical form, the endocrine or neurological disease and the depression that commonly follows it. Differential Primary bipolar I or II disorder in someone who also uses substances, settled by whether mood symptoms predate use and whether they persist about a month beyond acute intoxication or withdrawal. Delirium . Substance-induced psychotic disorder where psychosis rather than mood predominates. Personality disorders with affective instability. DSM-5 change DSM-IV had single categories, substance-induced mood disorder and mood disorder due to a general medical condition , with specifiers such as 'with manic features', 'with depressive features' and 'with mixed features'. DSM-5 split them by polarity, so the elevated-mood forms now sit in the Bipolar and Related Disorders chapter and the depressive forms in Depressive Disorders, and 'general medical condition' became another medical condition . DSM-5 also added the rule that a persistent, fully syndromal antidepressant- or ECT-emergent mania counts as bipolar I, not as substance-induced. DSM-5-TR (2022): Criterion A of the substance/medication-induced form was reworded to match the medical-condition form, dropping the confusing 'with or without depressed mood' wording, and the timing criterion now also covers symptoms arising after withdrawal from a medication ; the diagnosis itself is unchanged. 5. Depressive disorders DSM-5 added two disorders to this chapter that carry a disproportionate share of exam questions because they are new: Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder and Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder . It also merged dysthymia and chronic major depression into Persistent Depressive Disorder , and removed the bereavement exclusion. Know those four changes and you have most of the chapter's marks. Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder F34.81 In plain language. A child who is angry or irritable almost all of the time, in between frequent explosive outbursts that are far out of proportion to whatever set them off. It was created deliberately to stop children with chronic irritability being diagnosed as paediatric bipolar disorder, which was over-diagnosed in the 2000s in the United States. A. Severe recurrent temper outbursts , verbal or behavioural, grossly out of proportion in intensity or duration to the situation or provocation. B. The outbursts are inconsistent with developmental level . C. Outbursts occur on average 3 or more times per week . D. The mood between outbursts is persistently irritable or angry most of the day, nearly every day, and is observable by others . This inter-episode criterion is what separates it from an ordinary tantrum problem. E. Criteria A to D have been present for 12 or more months , without a period of 3 or more consecutive months free of all of them. F. Present in at least 2 of 3 settings (home, school, with peers) and severe in at least one. G. Diagnosis should not be made for the first time before age 6 or after age 18 . H. By history or observation, the age at onset of criteria A to E is before 10 years . I. There has never been a distinct period lasting more than 1 day during which the full symptom criteria, except duration, for a manic or hypomanic episode have been met. J. The behaviours do not occur exclusively during a major depressive episode and are not better explained by another mental disorder such as autism, PTSD, separation anxiety, or persistent depressive disorder. K. Not attributable to a substance or another medical or neurological condition. Specifiers DSM-5-TR gives no specifiers , subtypes or severity ratings for disruptive mood dysregulation disorder. Numbers The four numbers to hold: outbursts 3 or more times a week , duration 12 months , diagnose only between ages 6 and 18 , onset before 10 . 6-month to 1-year prevalence roughly 2 to 5 percent, commoner in males and in school-age children. Course The course is chronic and non-episodic , which is the defining contrast with bipolar disorder. About half of children with severe, chronic irritability still meet criteria 1 year later. Rates of conversion to bipolar disorder are very low ; the adult outcome is instead unipolar depression and anxiety. Impairment is marked, with disrupted family and peer relationships and poor school performance. Comorbidity Very high. ADHD, oppositional defiant disorder, anxiety disorders and major depressive disorder. Longitudinally, these children tend to develop unipolar depressive and anxiety disorders in adulthood, not bipolar disorder, which is the evidence base the diagnosis was built on. Differential Bipolar disorder is the point of the whole diagnosis: bipolar is episodic with a distinct period of elevated mood and decreased need for sleep, DMDD is persistent and non-episodic . Oppositional defiant disorder shares the irritability, but DMDD requires the severe outbursts and the persistent between-outburst mood; DSM-5 rules that if a child meets criteria for both, only DMDD is diagnosed . Intermittent explosive disorder requires only 3 months and has no persistent inter-episode irritability. ADHD, autism, PTSD, separation anxiety , where the irritability is explained by the other condition. DSM-5 change New in DSM-5 , placed in the depressive disorders chapter rather than with the disruptive, impulse-control and conduct disorders, to curb the over-diagnosis of paediatric bipolar disorder in children with chronic, non-episodic irritability; it grew out of research on severe mood dysregulation . DSM-5 also ruled that it cannot coexist with oppositional defiant disorder (a child meeting both gets only DMDD), intermittent explosive disorder or bipolar disorder , though it can coexist with MDD, ADHD, conduct disorder and substance use disorders. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. ICD-11 Has no DMDD. The same child is coded as oppositional defiant disorder with chronic irritability-anger . Major Depressive Disorder F32.x single, F33.x recurrent In plain language. At least two weeks in which the person is down or has lost all interest, plus enough of the other classic symptoms, and this is a change from how they were. A. Five or more of the nine symptoms of a major depressive episode over the same 2-week period, one of which is depressed mood or anhedonia (list given in the bipolar chapter above). B. Clinically significant distress or impairment. C. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. D. Not better explained by a schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder. E. There has never been a manic or hypomanic episode . Specifiers Single or recurrent episode; mild, moderate, severe; with psychotic features; in partial or full remission. Plus the cross-cutting set: with anxious distress, with mixed features, with melancholic features (loss of pleasure in all activities, lack of reactivity, distinct quality of mood, early morning awakening, marked psychomotor change, excessive guilt, worse in the morning), with atypical features, with mood-congruent or mood-incongruent psychotic features, with catatonia, with peripartum onset, with seasonal pattern. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 7 percent in the United States; lifetime around 15 to 20 percent. Female to male about 2:1 , a ratio that appears at puberty. Peak onset in the twenties. About two-thirds of episodes remit with treatment; recurrence risk after one episode about 50 percent, after two about 70 percent, after three about 90 percent. Course Onset can be at any age, but the likelihood rises sharply at puberty . The course is very variable: some people have long symptom-free intervals between episodes, while others rarely if ever remit. Recurrence risk falls the longer remission lasts, and is higher after a severe episode, in younger people, after several episodes, and when even mild residual symptoms persist, which is one of the strongest predictors. Chronic symptoms raise the likelihood of underlying personality, anxiety and substance use disorders and lower the chance of full recovery. A later switch to bipolar disorder is more likely with mixed features , psychotic features , adolescent onset or a family history of bipolar disorder. Comorbidity Anxiety disorders (panic and generalised anxiety are commonest), substance use disorders, borderline personality disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, eating disorders, and medical illness (post-stroke, post-MI, diabetes, hypothyroidism, cancer, Parkinson's). Differential Bipolar disorders , always screen for past hypomania. Persistent depressive disorder (2 years, milder). Adjustment disorder with depressed mood (identifiable stressor, does not meet full MDE criteria). Bereavement and prolonged grief disorder . Substance-induced depressive disorder (alcohol, sedatives, withdrawal from stimulants; medications: interferon, isotretinoin, some antihypertensives, corticosteroids). Depressive disorder due to another medical condition (hypothyroidism, anaemia, Cushing's, Parkinson's, stroke). Major neurocognitive disorder versus pseudodementia in an older adult. ADHD (distractibility without mood change). Demoralisation and normal sadness . DSM-5 change The bereavement exclusion was removed . In DSM-IV you could not diagnose MDD within 2 months of a death unless there were specific features. DSM-5 dropped that, on the reasoning that grief and depression can coexist and that withholding a diagnosis withheld treatment; a long footnote in the criteria set explains how to distinguish grief (waves of emptiness and yearning, self-esteem preserved, thoughts of joining the deceased) from a major depressive episode (persistent depressed mood, worthlessness, self-critical rumination, suicidal ideation about ending one's own life because of worthlessness). That footnote, and the removal itself, are heavily examined. Also in DSM-5: depressive disorders became a chapter separate from bipolar disorders. New specifiers: with anxious distress and with mixed features ; with postpartum onset became with peripartum onset , now including onset during pregnancy. The DSM-IV chronic specifier (full criteria for 2 years) was absorbed into persistent depressive disorder. DSM-5-TR (2022): Criterion D was reworded back towards DSM-IV: at least one major depressive episode must not be better explained by schizoaffective disorder and must not be superimposed on schizophrenia, schizophreniform, delusional or other psychotic disorder (an episode superimposed on these goes to other specified depressive disorder). It also added prolonged grief disorder (trauma- and stressor-related chapter), now a key differential, and restored unspecified mood disorder . Persistent Depressive Disorder F34.1 In plain language. Depression that has been there for at least two years, most days, at whatever intensity. DSM-5 merged DSM-IV's dysthymic disorder and chronic major depressive disorder into this one label; DSM-5 titled it "persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia)"; DSM-5-TR dropped the bracketed "(dysthymia)". A. Depressed mood for most of the day, for more days than not, for at least 2 years ( 1 year in children and adolescents , where mood may be irritable ). B. While depressed, 2 or more of six: poor appetite or overeating; insomnia or hypersomnia; low energy or fatigue; low self-esteem; poor concentration or difficulty making decisions; feelings of hopelessness. C. During the 2 years, the person has never been without the symptoms in Criteria A and B for more than 2 months at a time . D. Criteria for a major depressive disorder may be continuously present for 2 years. E. There has never been a manic or hypomanic episode, and criteria for cyclothymic disorder have never been met. F. Not better explained by a persistent schizophrenia spectrum disorder. G. Not substance or medical. H. Clinically significant distress or impairment. Specifiers The distinctive ones: with pure dysthymic syndrome (full MDE criteria not met in the preceding 2 years), with persistent major depressive episode (full criteria met throughout the preceding 2 years), with intermittent major depressive episodes, with current episode , and with intermittent major depressive episodes, without current episode . Also early onset ( before 21 ) or late onset (at 21 or after), plus anxious distress, atypical features, remission and severity. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 0.5 percent for persistent depressive disorder and about 1.5 percent for chronic major depressive disorder. Early onset before 21 predicts a worse course and more personality-disorder comorbidity. Course Onset is typically early and insidious , in childhood, adolescence or early adult life, and the course is chronic by definition. When symptoms rise to a major depressive episode they tend to fall back to the lower chronic level rather than clear, and depressive symptoms are much less likely to resolve over a given period than in a discrete major depressive episode. Early onset is also linked to comorbid substance use disorders. Kaplan and Sadock note that about a quarter never attain complete recovery, and that a superimposed major depressive episode ( double depression ) carries a worse prognosis. Comorbidity Compared with MDD, higher rates of anxiety disorders, substance use disorders, and personality disorders , especially cluster B and cluster C. "Double depression", a major depressive episode superimposed on dysthymia, is the classic pattern and is now captured by the intermittent-episodes specifier. Differential Major depressive disorder (episodic rather than 2 years continuous). Cyclothymia (hypomanic periods present). Bipolar II . Psychotic disorders with residual depression. Personality disorders , which may be diagnosed alongside. Depressive disorder due to another medical condition . DSM-5 change New name in DSM-5 , merging DSM-IV dysthymic disorder and chronic major depressive disorder , because no scientifically meaningful difference between them could be found; DSM-5 titled it 'persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia)'. DSM-IV dysthymia required that no major depressive episode occur in the first 2 years; DSM-5 Criterion D allows full major depressive criteria to be present throughout. New specifiers describe the pathway: with pure dysthymic syndrome, with persistent major depressive episode, and with intermittent major depressive episodes, with or without current episode. DSM-5-TR (2022): the bracketed '(dysthymia)' was dropped from the name, because the disorder is broader than DSM-IV dysthymia; the extraneous specifiers were removed, leaving with anxious distress and with atypical features (plus the course, onset, remission and severity specifiers); and a note now says that when major depressive episode criteria are met during the 2 years, major depressive disorder is diagnosed as well . Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder F32.81 In plain language. In the week before the period, mood collapses in a specific patterned way, it lifts within a few days of bleeding starting, and it is gone in the week after. Moved from the DSM-IV appendix into the main text in DSM-5, which is exactly what gets asked. A. In the majority of menstrual cycles, at least 5 symptoms present in the final week before the onset of menses , starting to improve within a few days after the onset of menses , and becoming minimal or absent in the week post-menses . B. One or more of these four must be present: marked affective lability; marked irritability or anger or increased interpersonal conflicts; marked depressed mood, hopelessness or self-deprecating thoughts; marked anxiety, tension, or feelings of being keyed up or on edge. C. One or more of these seven must additionally be present, to reach a total of five: decreased interest in usual activities; subjective difficulty concentrating; lethargy, easy fatigability, marked lack of energy; marked change in appetite, overeating, or specific food cravings; hypersomnia or insomnia; a sense of being overwhelmed or out of control; physical symptoms such as breast tenderness or swelling, joint or muscle pain, bloating or weight gain. D. Significant distress or interference with work, school, usual social activities or relationships. E. Not merely an exacerbation of another disorder. F. Criterion A should be confirmed by prospective daily ratings during at least 2 symptomatic cycles (a provisional diagnosis may be made before that). G. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. Specifiers DSM-5-TR gives no subtypes, severity ratings or other specifiers for premenstrual dysphoric disorder. The one recording rule: until Criterion A has been confirmed by prospective daily ratings over 2 symptomatic cycles, the diagnosis is recorded as provisional . Numbers 12-month prevalence between 1.8 and 5.8 percent of menstruating women when strict prospective ratings are used, which is far below the rate of self-reported premenstrual complaints. Symptoms cease after menopause. Course Onset can occur at any point after menarche , and the course is chronic and cyclical through the reproductive years. Many women report that symptoms worsen as they approach menopause . Symptoms stop after menopause, but cyclical hormone replacement therapy can bring them back. Because the symptoms are tied to ovulatory cycles, they are absent when ovulation is suppressed, as in pregnancy. Comorbidity Major depressive disorder is the commonest, plus anxiety disorders and bipolar disorder. Differential Premenstrual syndrome , which is far more common, needs no affective symptom, and is not as impairing. Premenstrual exacerbation of an existing depressive, bipolar or anxiety disorder, which is Criterion E, and is distinguished by symptoms being present throughout the cycle and simply worsening premenstrually. Dysmenorrhoea (pain starting with menses, not before). Hormonal treatment effects, and thyroid disease. DSM-5 change DSM-IV listed PMDD only in Appendix B (criteria sets for further study) and as an example of depressive disorder not otherwise specified. DSM-5 moved it into the main text as a full depressive disorder, on the strength of the research evidence. The core research criteria were kept: 5 symptoms with at least one affective symptom, timing to the week before menses, and confirmation by prospective daily ratings over 2 symptomatic cycles, with a provisional diagnosis possible before confirmation. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Substance/Medication-Induced Depressive Disorder, and Depressive Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition A prominent and persistent disturbance in mood, predominantly depressed mood or markedly diminished interest or pleasure, that developed during or soon after substance intoxication or withdrawal or medication exposure, or that is the direct pathophysiological consequence of a medical condition. Common substances: alcohol, sedative-hypnotics and anxiolytics (during use), stimulants and cocaine (during withdrawal), opioids. Medications: corticosteroids, interferon-alpha, isotretinoin, reserpine and older antihypertensives, some hormonal contraceptives, varenicline. Common medical causes: hypothyroidism , Cushing's disease, Parkinson's disease, stroke (particularly left frontal), traumatic brain injury, multiple sclerosis, Huntington's, pancreatic carcinoma, vitamin B12 deficiency, obstructive sleep apnoea. Specifiers Substance/medication-induced depressive disorder : specify with onset during intoxication or with onset during withdrawal ; the code also records the substance and whether a mild or a moderate-to-severe use disorder coexists. Depressive disorder due to another medical condition : specify with depressive features (full criteria for a major depressive episode not met), with major depressive-like episode (full criteria met except Criterion C, the substance or medical-cause exclusion), or with mixed features (manic or hypomanic symptoms are also present but do not predominate). Course The substance-induced form begins during use or withdrawal, or soon after exposure to a medication. Once the substance is stopped, depressive symptoms usually remit within days to several weeks , depending on the drug's half-life and any withdrawal syndrome; persistence beyond about 4 weeks after the expected course of withdrawal points to another cause, usually an independent depressive disorder. In the medical form, post-stroke depression often begins acutely , within a day or a few days of the stroke, though sometimes weeks or months later. In Parkinson's and Huntington's disease , depression often appears early and can precede the motor and cognitive impairment. Comorbidity The substance use disorder itself, and, for the medical form, the physical illness plus the anxiety, insomnia and pain conditions that travel with it. A primary depressive disorder frequently coexists, and having one raises the risk of the other. Differential Primary major depressive disorder in someone who also has a medical illness or uses substances. The tests are temporal (did it start with the exposure), dose-related, and whether it resolves when the exposure ends, plus whether the symptom picture is atypical for primary depression. DSM-5 change DSM-IV had single categories, substance-induced mood disorder and mood disorder due to a general medical condition , covering depressive, manic and mixed presentations. DSM-5 split them by polarity, so the depressive forms now sit in the Depressive Disorders chapter and the elevated-mood forms in Bipolar and Related Disorders, and 'general medical condition' became another medical condition . DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. The two other-specified categories worth naming Other Specified Depressive Disorder covers, among others: recurrent brief depression (depressed mood plus 4 other symptoms for 2 to 13 days, at least once a month for 12 months, never meeting criteria for another disorder), short-duration depressive episode (4 to 13 days), and depressive episode with insufficient symptoms . Examiners like recurrent brief depression because the duration is so distinctive. 6. Anxiety disorders DSM-5 broke the old anxiety chapter into three: anxiety disorders proper, obsessive-compulsive and related disorders, and trauma and stressor-related disorders. Inside the anxiety chapter, the big structural changes were that panic disorder and agoraphobia were unlinked into two separate diagnoses (DSM-IV had "panic disorder with agoraphobia" and "agoraphobia without history of panic"), that separation anxiety disorder and selective mutism moved in from the childhood chapter and are no longer restricted to children, and that panic attack became a specifier usable across the whole manual. The chapter is ordered developmentally, by typical age of onset. The 6-month rule Specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia and generalised anxiety disorder all require 6 months or more . In DSM-IV that 6-month requirement applied only to people under 18; DSM-5 extended it to all ages , to stop transient fears being diagnosed. Panic disorder is the exception: it needs 1 month of worry or behaviour change after an attack. Separation anxiety needs 4 weeks in children and adolescents, 6 months or more in adults . Selective mutism needs 1 month , not counting the first month of school. Separation Anxiety Disorder F93.0 In plain language. Fear of being away from the people you are attached to, that is far beyond what is normal for your age, and that shapes what you will and will not do. A. Developmentally inappropriate and excessive fear or anxiety concerning separation from attachment figures, with at least 3 of 8 : recurrent excessive distress when separation is anticipated or occurs; persistent excessive worry about losing attachment figures or about harm befalling them; persistent excessive worry about an untoward event causing separation (getting lost, being kidnapped, having an accident, becoming ill); persistent reluctance or refusal to go out, away from home, to school, to work, because of fear of separation; persistent and excessive fear of or reluctance about being alone or without attachment figures; persistent reluctance or refusal to sleep away from home or to sleep without being near a major attachment figure; repeated nightmares involving the theme of separation; repeated complaints of physical symptoms (headaches, stomach aches, nausea, vomiting) when separation from attachment figures occurs or is anticipated. B. Duration: at least 4 weeks in children and adolescents , typically 6 months or more in adults . C. Clinically significant distress or impairment. D. Not better explained by another disorder such as autism (refusal to leave home because of resistance to change), psychotic disorders (delusions about separation), agoraphobia (refusal to go out without a trusted companion), generalised anxiety disorder (worry about ill health befalling others), or illness anxiety disorder. Specifiers DSM-5-TR gives separation anxiety disorder no subtypes, specifiers or severity ratings . The DSM-IV early onset specifier (onset before age 6) was dropped in DSM-5. If panic attacks occur, the general with panic attacks specifier can be added, as it can to most DSM-5 diagnoses (panic disorder excepted). Numbers The most prevalent anxiety disorder in children under 12, about 4 percent in children, about 1.6 percent in adolescents, and 0.9 to 1.9 percent in adults. DSM-5's change: onset before age 18 is no longer required , so adults can be diagnosed for the first time. Course Onset can be as early as the preschool years , and it often follows a life stress, especially a loss : the death of a relative or pet, an illness, a change of school, parental divorce, a move or immigration. The course runs in periods of exacerbation and remission ; in some people the anxiety and avoidance persist into adulthood, but most affected children are free of impairing anxiety disorders over their lifetimes . Young children who keep attending school do better than adolescents with prolonged school refusal , and childhood separation anxiety is linked to a raised risk of later panic disorder (the basis of Klein's hypothesis ). Comorbidity In children: generalised anxiety disorder and specific phobia. In adults: specific phobia, PTSD, panic disorder, generalised anxiety disorder, social anxiety, agoraphobia, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and personality disorders. Differential Agoraphobia (fear of being unable to escape or get help, not fear of losing the attachment figure). Generalised anxiety disorder (worry is broad, not focused on separation). Autism . Conduct disorder (truancy without fear of separation, so the child leaves home rather than refusing to). School refusal is a behaviour, not a diagnosis, and may arise from separation anxiety, social anxiety, depression, or bullying, which examiners like to test. DSM-5 change DSM-5 moved separation anxiety disorder from "Disorders Usually First Diagnosed in Infancy, Childhood, or Adolescence" into the anxiety disorders chapter, which is now ordered by typical age of onset. It dropped the requirement of onset before age 18 , so adults can be diagnosed. It kept the DSM-IV minimum of 4 weeks for children and adolescents and added a duration of typically 6 months or more for adults , to avoid diagnosing transient fears. The DSM-IV early onset specifier was removed, and the items were reworded to fit adults (for example reluctance to go to work, not only to school). DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Selective Mutism F94.0 In plain language. A child who talks normally at home says nothing at school. It is not that they cannot speak, it is that in specific social settings they do not. A. Consistent failure to speak in specific social situations where there is an expectation for speaking (for example school), despite speaking in other situations. B. Interferes with educational or occupational achievement or with social communication. C. Duration at least 1 month, not limited to the first month of school . D. The failure is not attributable to a lack of knowledge of, or comfort with, the spoken language required (which matters in multilingual Indian classrooms). E. Not better explained by a communication disorder, and does not occur exclusively during autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder. Specifiers DSM-5-TR lists no subtypes, specifiers or severity ratings for selective mutism. Numbers Rare, prevalence 0.03 to 1 percent, and does not vary much by sex or ethnicity. Onset usually before age 5 , though it often comes to attention only on entering school. Course Onset is usually before age 5, but the child often comes to notice only on entering school , when the demand to speak to unfamiliar adults and peers, and to read aloud, rises. Many children outgrow it, though the long-term course is not well studied, and in some the mutism lifts while social anxiety disorder remains. It may last from months to years; children who have not improved by about age 10 tend to have a long-term course and a worse prognosis. Comorbidity Social anxiety disorder is by far the commonest and many researchers regard selective mutism as a variant of it. Also separation anxiety disorder, specific phobia, oppositional behaviour confined to the mute settings, and communication delays. Differential Communication disorders (the difficulty is not situation-specific). Autism . Intellectual disability . Social anxiety disorder (the child may speak, with distress). Normal shyness and the silent period of a child newly immersed in a second language, which is explicitly excluded by Criterion D. DSM-5 change DSM-5 moved selective mutism from "Disorders Usually First Diagnosed in Infancy, Childhood, or Adolescence" into the anxiety disorders chapter, reflecting the view that it is driven by social anxiety. The criteria were essentially unchanged , including the 1-month duration that excludes the first month of school and the exclusion for unfamiliarity with the spoken language. (The older name elective mutism had already been replaced in DSM-IV.) DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Specific Phobia F40.2xx In plain language. One thing, reliably terrifying, avoided or endured with dread, for at least six months, out of proportion to the real danger. A. Marked fear or anxiety about a specific object or situation. In children this may be expressed by crying, tantrums, freezing or clinging. B. The phobic object or situation almost always provokes immediate fear or anxiety. C. It is actively avoided or endured with intense fear or anxiety. D. The fear is out of proportion to the actual danger posed, and to the sociocultural context. E. Persistent, typically lasting 6 months or more . F. Clinically significant distress or impairment. G. Not better explained by another disorder. DSM-5 removed the requirement that the person recognise the fear as excessive or unreasonable; the clinician now judges proportionality. That change also appears in social anxiety disorder and agoraphobia. Specifiers Code by stimulus: animal ; natural environment (heights, storms, water); blood-injection-injury (needles, other medical procedures); situational (aeroplanes, lifts, enclosed places); other (choking, vomiting, in children loud sounds or costumed characters). Numbers 12-month prevalence about 7 to 9 percent, the commonest anxiety disorder. Female to male about 2:1. Median onset between ages 7 and 11. The blood-injection-injury type is the exception you must be able to name: it produces a diphasic vasovagal response , with an initial rise then a sharp fall in heart rate and blood pressure and frequent fainting, whereas every other phobia produces sympathetic arousal only. It also has the strongest family loading, roughly two-thirds of sufferers have an affected relative, and it is treated with applied tension rather than pure relaxation. Course Most specific phobias begin in early childhood , the majority before age 10, although situational phobias tend to start later than animal, natural environment and blood-injection-injury phobias. Onset may follow a traumatic encounter , watching someone else go through one, an unexpected panic attack in the later-feared situation, or information such as heavy news coverage, but many people cannot recall how it began. Phobias that start in childhood and adolescence often wax and wane , whereas those that persist into adulthood are unlikely to remit for most people. In older adults they are less common, more often of the natural environment type, and may show as fear of falling . Comorbidity Most people with one specific phobia have several (the average is three). Comorbid with other anxiety disorders, depression, substance use, and somatic symptom disorder. Specific phobia commonly comes first and predicts later depression. Differential Agoraphobia (fear of two or more of the five agoraphobic situations, and the fear is of not escaping or not getting help). Social anxiety disorder (fear of scrutiny). Separation anxiety . Panic disorder (attacks are unexpected, not cued). OCD (avoidance is driven by an obsession, for example contamination). PTSD (avoidance follows a traumatic event). Illness anxiety disorder . Normal fear, which is proportionate and non-impairing. DSM-5 change DSM-5 dropped the requirement that adults recognise their fear as excessive or unreasonable ; instead the clinician judges whether it is out of proportion to the actual danger and the sociocultural context. The 6-month duration , which DSM-IV applied only to people under 18, now applies at all ages ("typically 6 months or more"), to screen out transient fears. The five stimulus groups were kept (DSM-IV called them types, DSM-5 lists them as specifiers), and blood-injection-injury now has separate codes for fear of blood, of injections and transfusions, of other medical care, and of injury. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Social Anxiety Disorder (formerly Social Phobia) F40.10 In plain language. Fear of being watched and judged, and of doing something humiliating in front of others, that lasts six months and shrinks the person's life. A. Marked fear or anxiety about one or more social situations in which the person is exposed to possible scrutiny by others : social interactions (conversation, meeting unfamiliar people), being observed (eating, drinking), and performing in front of others. In children, the anxiety must occur in peer settings and not just during interactions with adults. B. The person fears they will act in a way, or show anxiety symptoms, that will be negatively evaluated , that is, will be humiliating or embarrassing, will lead to rejection, or will offend others. C. The social situations almost always provoke fear or anxiety. In children this may appear as crying, tantrums, freezing, clinging, shrinking or failing to speak. D. Avoided or endured with intense fear. E. Out of proportion to the actual threat and to the sociocultural context. F. Persistent, typically 6 months or more . G. Significant distress or impairment. H, I, J. Not due to a substance or medical condition, not better explained by another mental disorder, and if another medical condition is present (Parkinson's, obesity, disfigurement from burns or injury) the fear is clearly unrelated or excessive. Specifier Performance only , where the fear is restricted to speaking or performing in public. DSM-5 replaced the DSM-IV "generalized" specifier with this narrower "performance only" one, because the generalised subtype could not be reliably drawn. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 7 percent in the United States, lower in much of Asia (0.5 to 2 percent). Slightly more common in females in community samples, roughly equal in clinical samples. Median onset age 13; about 75 percent onset between 8 and 15. Course Onset may follow a stressful or humiliating experience (being bullied, vomiting during a public speech) or be insidious , growing slowly out of childhood shyness and the temperament of behavioural inhibition . First onset in adulthood is relatively rare and usually follows a stressor or a life change that demands a new social role, such as a promotion. Without treatment the course is usually chronic , often lasting years, and depression and alcohol misuse commonly develop on top of it. Prevalence falls in older age groups. Comorbidity Other anxiety disorders, major depressive disorder (usually later, and social anxiety typically precedes it), substance use disorder, especially alcohol, used as self-medication, body dysmorphic disorder, and avoidant personality disorder , which overlaps so heavily that many argue they are the same construct at different severities. Differential Normal shyness , which is a common trait and only becomes a disorder with impairment. Agoraphobia (the person is comforted by a companion, in social anxiety a companion often makes it worse). Panic disorder (unexpected attacks). Body dysmorphic disorder (fear centres on a perceived physical defect). Autism (social communication skills are deficient, not merely inhibited by anxiety). Major depressive disorder (social withdrawal from anhedonia). Avoidant personality disorder (broader, earlier, more pervasive; often diagnosed together). Taijin kyofusho , the Japanese variant where the fear is of offending or embarrassing others with one's gaze, body odour or blushing, is the standard culture question. DSM-5 change DSM-5 made social anxiety disorder the main name, with social phobia in brackets. The generalised specifier was dropped and replaced by performance only . Adults no longer have to recognise the fear as excessive or unreasonable ; the clinician judges proportion against the sociocultural context. The 6-month duration , previously required only under 18, now applies at all ages. Criterion B was widened from fear of humiliation or embarrassment to include fear of rejection or of offending others , which brings in taijin kyofusho-type presentations. DSM-5-TR (2022) removed the bracketed "(social phobia)" , so the official name is now simply social anxiety disorder ; the criteria that exams test are unchanged. Panic Disorder F41.0 In plain language. Repeated attacks of terror that come out of nowhere and peak within minutes, followed by at least a month of dreading the next one or rearranging life to avoid it. A. Recurrent unexpected panic attacks. A panic attack is an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort that reaches a peak within minutes , during which 4 or more of 13 symptoms occur: palpitations or accelerated heart rate; sweating; trembling or shaking; sensations of shortness of breath or smothering; feelings of choking; chest pain or discomfort; nausea or abdominal distress; feeling dizzy, unsteady, light-headed or faint; chills or heat sensations; paraesthesias; derealisation or depersonalisation ; fear of losing control or going crazy; fear of dying . Culture-specific symptoms such as tinnitus, neck soreness, headache or uncontrollable screaming or crying may be seen but do not count toward the four. B.
