At least one attack has been followed by 1 month or more of one or both: persistent concern or worry about additional attacks or their consequences (losing control, having a heart attack, going crazy); and/or a significant maladaptive change in behaviour related to the attacks (avoiding exercise or unfamiliar situations). C. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition (hyperthyroidism, cardiopulmonary disorders). D. Not better explained by another mental disorder, where the attacks would be expected and cued: social anxiety (social situations), specific phobia (the phobic object), OCD (obsessions), PTSD (trauma reminders), separation anxiety (separation). Specifiers DSM-5-TR gives panic disorder no subtypes, specifiers or severity ratings . The DSM-IV split into panic disorder with agoraphobia and without agoraphobia no longer exists, because agoraphobia is now diagnosed separately. The with panic attacks specifier is not added to panic disorder, since attacks are already part of its criteria; it is attached to other diagnoses instead (for example PTSD with panic attacks). Attacks are described as expected (cued) or unexpected . Numbers 12-month prevalence about 2 to 3 percent in adults and adolescents. Female to male about 2:1. Median onset about age 20 to 24, uncommon before 14 and after 45. A limited-symptom attack has fewer than 4 symptoms. Nocturnal panic attacks, waking from sleep in a panic, occur in a substantial minority and are a favourite MCQ. Panic attack is not a disorder : it is a specifier that can be attached to any DSM-5 diagnosis except panic disorder itself (where the attacks are already part of the criteria), which was the key DSM-5 change alongside the unlinking from agoraphobia. Course Although many people retrospectively date fearful spells back to childhood, the disorder itself usually begins in late adolescence or early adulthood. Untreated, the usual course is chronic but waxing and waning : some people have episodic outbreaks separated by years of remission, others have continuous severe symptoms, and only a minority remit fully without relapse within a few years. The course is often complicated by agoraphobia , other anxiety disorders, depression and substance use, each of which worsens the outlook, whereas good premorbid functioning and a short duration of symptoms point to a better prognosis. Comorbidity Agoraphobia (very high, and now coded as two diagnoses), other anxiety disorders, major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, alcohol use disorder, and medical conditions: mitral valve prolapse, thyroid disease, asthma, COPD, irritable bowel syndrome. Suicidal ideation and attempts are elevated. Differential Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition : hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, vestibular dysfunction, seizure disorders, cardiopulmonary conditions. Substance-induced : caffeine, cannabis, stimulants, alcohol withdrawal. Other anxiety disorders with cued attacks , which is Criterion D. Illness anxiety disorder . PTSD . The clinical rule to state in a written answer: unexpectedness is the defining feature, so ask "was there a trigger?". DSM-5 change DSM-5 unlinked panic disorder from agoraphobia : the DSM-IV diagnoses panic disorder with agoraphobia, panic disorder without agoraphobia, and agoraphobia without history of panic disorder were replaced by two separate diagnoses, both given when both are met. The DSM-IV attack types (situationally bound, situationally predisposed, unexpected) were reduced to expected and unexpected ; the peak became "within minutes" instead of "within 10 minutes" , and the surge can arise from a calm or an anxious state. Panic attack became a specifier usable with any other DSM-5 disorder. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Agoraphobia F40.00 In plain language. Fear of situations you might not be able to get out of, or get help in, if something goes wrong. Not just fear of open spaces, which is the common misreading. A. Marked fear or anxiety about 2 or more of 5 situations: using public transportation; being in open spaces (car parks, marketplaces, bridges); being in enclosed places (shops, theatres, cinemas); standing in line or being in a crowd; being outside of the home alone. The requirement of two or more is a DSM-5 change and is heavily examined. B. The person fears or avoids these situations because of thoughts that escape might be difficult or help might not be available in the event of developing panic-like symptoms or other incapacitating or embarrassing symptoms (falling in the elderly, incontinence). C. The situations almost always provoke fear or anxiety. D. Actively avoided, require the presence of a companion, or are endured with intense fear. E. Out of proportion to the actual danger and the sociocultural context. F. Persistent, typically 6 months or more . G. Significant distress or impairment. H. If another medical condition is present, the fear is clearly excessive. I. Not better explained by another mental disorder. DSM-5 makes it explicit: agoraphobia is diagnosed irrespective of the presence of panic disorder , and if the person meets criteria for both, both diagnoses are given . Specifiers Agoraphobia has no subtypes, specifiers or severity ratings of its own in DSM-5-TR. If panic attacks occur without meeting criteria for panic disorder, the general with panic attacks specifier can be added; if panic disorder criteria are met, both diagnoses are given instead. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 1.7 percent in adolescents and adults. Female to male about 2:1. Mean onset about 17 years, with a second peak after 40. Panic attacks or panic disorder come before the agoraphobia in about 30 percent of community samples and more than 50 percent of clinic samples. Course About two-thirds of cases begin before age 35 , with the greatest risk in late adolescence and early adulthood; first onset in childhood is rare, and onset without preceding panic attacks or panic disorder tends to be later, at about 25 to 29. The course is typically persistent and chronic : complete remission is rare (about 10 percent) unless it is treated , and more severe agoraphobia brings lower remission and higher relapse. Comorbid anxiety, depressive, substance use and personality disorders worsen the course, and a long course raises the risk of secondary depression and substance use. Comorbidity Other anxiety disorders (specific phobia, panic disorder, social anxiety, generalised anxiety), depressive disorders, PTSD, and alcohol use disorder. Differential Specific phobia, situational type : if only one of the five situations is feared, and the fear is not about escape or help, it is specific phobia. Social anxiety disorder (fear of scrutiny, and a companion does not help). Separation anxiety (fear of being away from the attachment figure, and the person is fine outside the home if the figure is present). Major depressive disorder with apathy and withdrawal. Psychotic disorders with persecutory avoidance. Realistic avoidance due to a medical condition such as inflammatory bowel disease or Parkinson's, where the concern is proportionate. DSM-5 change DSM-5 made agoraphobia an independent, codable diagnosis , ending the DSM-IV scheme of panic disorder with agoraphobia and agoraphobia without history of panic disorder. It now requires fear of 2 or more of 5 situation groups, which separates it from situational specific phobia. New criteria require the fear to be out of proportion to the actual danger, judged by the clinician in its sociocultural context, and to last typically 6 months or more . DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Generalised Anxiety Disorder F41.1 In plain language. Six months of worrying about many everyday things, that the person cannot switch off, plus the physical toll of that worrying. A. Excessive anxiety and worry (apprehensive expectation), occurring more days than not for at least 6 months , about a number of events or activities such as work or school performance. B. The person finds it difficult to control the worry . C. The anxiety and worry are associated with 3 or more of 6 symptoms, with at least some present more days than not for the past 6 months ( only 1 item is required in children ): restlessness or feeling keyed up or on edge; being easily fatigued; difficulty concentrating or mind going blank; irritability; muscle tension; sleep disturbance. The mnemonic is WATCHERS or, more simply, remember that muscle tension is the item that best discriminates GAD from other anxiety disorders. D. Significant distress or impairment. E. Not substance or medical (hyperthyroidism). F. Not better explained by another mental disorder. Specifiers DSM-5-TR lists no subtypes, specifiers or severity ratings for generalised anxiety disorder; the general with panic attacks specifier can be added if panic attacks occur. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 2.9 percent in adults, 0.9 percent in adolescents. Female to male about 2:1. Median onset age 30, later than the other anxiety disorders, and onset before adolescence is rare. Course is chronic and fluctuating with low full-remission rates. Course Excessive worry may show early as an anxious temperament , but the disorder itself rarely begins before adolescence, and age at onset is spread across a very broad range. Symptoms wax and wane across the lifespan, moving between full and subthreshold forms. The earlier it begins, the more comorbidity and impairment tend to follow, and younger adults have more severe symptoms than older adults. The content of worry follows age: school and sporting performance in children, the well-being of family and one's own physical health in older adults. Comorbidity Major depressive disorder is the commonest and the overlap is so large that some argue for a combined "distress" construct. Also other anxiety disorders, persistent depressive disorder, substance use, somatic symptom disorder, and the physical conditions worry drives, including irritable bowel syndrome, headaches and insomnia. Differential Non-pathological anxiety , distinguished by controllability, breadth, impairment and physical symptoms. Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition , above all hyperthyroidism . Substance-induced , especially caffeine and stimulant use, and withdrawal states. Social anxiety, OCD, separation anxiety, illness anxiety, anorexia nervosa, PTSD, adjustment disorder , in each of which the worry is confined to a specific theme: scrutiny, obsessions, separation, illness, weight, the trauma, the stressor. Depressive disorders , where rumination is about the past rather than apprehension about the future. DSM-5 change The DSM-5 criteria are essentially unchanged from DSM-IV: 6 months of excessive, hard-to-control worry with 3 of 6 symptoms in adults and 1 in children. The work group's proposals to shorten the duration to 3 months , cut the symptom list and add behavioural criteria (avoidance, reassurance seeking, procrastination) were not adopted . DSM-IV had already absorbed the childhood overanxious disorder into GAD. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Substance/Medication-Induced Anxiety Disorder, and Anxiety Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition Panic attacks or anxiety predominate, developed during or soon after substance intoxication or withdrawal or medication exposure, or are the direct pathophysiological consequence of a medical condition, and are not better explained by an independent anxiety disorder, and do not occur exclusively during delirium. Substances: caffeine (the classic), cannabis, cocaine and amphetamines, hallucinogens, and withdrawal from alcohol, sedatives and opioids. Medications: bronchodilators, thyroid hormone, corticosteroids, decongestants, some antidepressants early in treatment. Medical conditions: hyperthyroidism , phaeochromocytoma , hypoglycaemia, hyperparathyroidism, cardiac arrhythmias, congestive heart failure, pulmonary embolism, COPD and asthma, vestibular dysfunction, seizure disorders. Specifiers Substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder : specify with onset during intoxication , with onset during withdrawal , or with onset after medication use (symptoms beginning when a medication is started, changed or withdrawn). The code also records whether a comorbid substance use disorder is present and whether it is mild or moderate to severe. Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition has no specifiers ; the medical condition is named in the diagnosis (for example anxiety disorder due to phaeochromocytoma) and coded first. Course The substance form begins during or soon after intoxication, withdrawal or medication exposure and usually settles once the substance is stopped ; anxiety that predates the exposure or persists for about a month after acute withdrawal or severe intoxication points to an independent anxiety disorder. The medical form follows the course of the underlying illness and often improves when that is treated, for example when hyperthyroidism is corrected or a phaeochromocytoma removed. Clues to a medical cause are an atypical age at onset or course and no personal or family history of anxiety. Comorbidity The substance use disorder itself, plus primary anxiety and depressive disorders, which are common and often predate the exposure. For the medical form, the underlying disease and the depression that follows it. Differential Primary anxiety disorders in someone who also uses substances or has a medical illness, settled by whether the anxiety predates the exposure and whether it persists about a month past acute withdrawal. Delirium , which excludes the diagnosis. Panic disorder , where attacks are unexpected and not tied to an exposure. Illness anxiety disorder , where the worry is about having a disease rather than a direct physiological effect. DSM-5 change DSM-5 dropped the DSM-IV subtypes (with generalised anxiety, with panic attacks, with obsessive-compulsive symptoms, and for the substance form with phobic symptoms). Obsessive-compulsive presentations moved to the new obsessive-compulsive and related disorders chapter as their own substance-induced and medical diagnoses. The substance form gained the specifier with onset after medication use , and "general medical condition" became "another medical condition" . DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. 7. Obsessive-compulsive and related disorders A new chapter in DSM-5, created because these conditions share repetitive thoughts and behaviours, family loading, neurocircuitry (the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop) and treatment response. Hoarding disorder and excoriation disorder are brand new diagnoses in DSM-5, body dysmorphic disorder moved here from somatoform disorders, and trichotillomania moved here from impulse-control disorders. Every disorder in the chapter carries an insight specifier : with good or fair insight, with poor insight, with absent insight or delusional beliefs. That specifier is the answer to "how does DSM-5 handle a patient whose obsession has become a delusion?": you do not add a psychotic diagnosis, you use the absent-insight specifier. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder F42.2 In plain language. Thoughts that force their way in and will not leave, and acts the person feels driven to perform to make the thoughts tolerable, eating at least an hour a day. A. Presence of obsessions, compulsions, or both . Obsessions are recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges or images that are experienced, at some time during the disturbance, as intrusive and unwanted , and that in most people cause marked anxiety or distress; the person attempts to ignore or suppress them or to neutralise them with some other thought or action. Compulsions are repetitive behaviours (hand washing, ordering, checking) or mental acts (praying, counting, repeating words silently) that the person feels driven to perform in response to an obsession or according to rules that must be applied rigidly ; they are aimed at preventing or reducing anxiety or some dreaded event, but they are not connected in a realistic way to what they are meant to neutralise, or are clearly excessive. B. The obsessions or compulsions are time-consuming (more than 1 hour per day) or cause clinically significant distress or impairment. C. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. D. Not better explained by another mental disorder (see the differential, which DSM lists at unusual length here). Specifiers Insight: good or fair / poor / absent or delusional. Plus tic-related , that is, the individual has a current or past history of a tic disorder, which marks out a distinct subtype with earlier onset, male predominance, more symmetry and ordering symptoms, and a better response to antipsychotic augmentation. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 1.2 percent. Slightly more common in adult women , but males predominate in childhood onset . Mean age at onset 19.5, with about 25 percent by age 14; onset after 35 is unusual. Untreated the course is chronic. Common symptom dimensions: contamination and cleaning; harm obsessions and checking; symmetry, ordering and counting; forbidden or taboo thoughts (aggressive, sexual, religious) with mental rituals. Course Onset is usually gradual , though acute onset occurs, and males start earlier: nearly a quarter of affected males begin before age 10 . Untreated, the course is usually chronic with waxing and waning , some people have an episodic course and a minority deteriorate; remission in untreated adults is low (about 20 percent at 40-year follow-up ), yet about 40 percent of those with childhood or adolescent onset remit by early adulthood. Poorer outcome is linked to yielding to rather than resisting compulsions, poor or absent insight , bizarre compulsions, comorbid depression and schizotypal personality disorder ; good premorbid adjustment, a precipitating event and an episodic course predict a better one. Comorbidity Up to 76 percent have an anxiety disorder, and up to 63 percent a depressive or bipolar disorder, with major depressive disorder commonest. About 30 percent have a lifetime tic disorder. Also obsessive-compulsive personality disorder in roughly a quarter to a third, body dysmorphic disorder, trichotillomania, hoarding, and eating disorders. In children, the sudden-onset presentation after streptococcal infection ( PANDAS , now often subsumed under PANS) is a stock question. Differential Generalised anxiety disorder : worries there are about real-life concerns and are ego-syntonic, obsessions are intrusive, often senseless, and ego-dystonic. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder : a lifelong trait pattern of perfectionism and control, no true obsessions or compulsions , and it is ego-syntonic, so the person sees nothing wrong. This pair is the most reliably examined distinction in the chapter. Body dysmorphic disorder (thoughts confined to appearance). Hoarding disorder (no true obsession; distress arises from discarding). Trichotillomania and excoriation (no obsession precedes the act). Eating disorders (thoughts confined to food and weight). Tics and stereotyped movements (no preceding obsession, and there is a premonitory sensory urge instead). Psychotic disorders (use the absent-insight specifier rather than adding schizophrenia, unless there are other psychotic features). Major depressive disorder (ruminations are mood-congruent and not linked to compulsions). DSM-5 change DSM-5 moved OCD out of the anxiety disorders into a new chapter, Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders , alongside body dysmorphic disorder, trichotillomania and the new hoarding and excoriation disorders. The single DSM-IV with poor insight specifier became three levels (good or fair, poor, absent insight/delusional beliefs ), so a patient with delusional conviction is diagnosed with OCD rather than a psychotic disorder, and a tic-related specifier was added. In the definition of obsessions, "impulses" became "urges" and "inappropriate" became "unwanted" , and the DSM-IV requirement that adults at some point recognise the symptoms as excessive or unreasonable was dropped. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Body Dysmorphic Disorder F45.22 In plain language. The person is convinced some part of how they look is ugly or wrong, other people cannot see it, and they spend hours checking, camouflaging or seeking reassurance. A. Preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others . B. At some point during the course, the person has performed repetitive behaviours (mirror checking, excessive grooming, skin picking, reassurance seeking) or mental acts (comparing their appearance with that of others) in response to the appearance concerns. This criterion was added in DSM-5 . C. Clinically significant distress or impairment. D. The appearance preoccupation is not better explained by concerns with body fat or weight in a person whose symptoms meet criteria for an eating disorder . Specifiers With muscle dysmorphia (the belief that one's build is too small or insufficiently muscular; occurs mostly in males and is the specifier most often asked about), plus the insight specifier. Around a third have absent insight or delusional beliefs. Numbers Point prevalence about 2.4 percent in the United States, 9 to 15 percent in dermatology patients and 7 to 8 percent in cosmetic-surgery patients. Mean age at onset 16 to 17, median 15, with two-thirds onset before 18. Roughly equal in men and women. Suicidal ideation is reported in about 80 percent and attempts in about a quarter, far higher than in OCD, which is a discriminating fact. Course Subclinical appearance concerns typically begin around age 12 or 13 and usually progress gradually to the full disorder, though some people have an abrupt onset. The course is usually chronic , but improvement is likely with evidence-based treatment (SSRIs and CBT). Onset before 18 is linked to more comorbidity, a gradual onset and a higher rate of suicide attempts . Cosmetic surgery and dermatological treatment rarely help and can make the symptoms worse . Comorbidity Major depressive disorder is commonest and usually starts after BDD. Also social anxiety disorder, OCD, substance use disorders (particularly in muscle dysmorphia, with anabolic steroid use), and avoidant personality disorder. Differential Normal appearance concerns and clearly visible defects (which do not qualify). Eating disorders , which is Criterion D. Obsessive-compulsive disorder (the preoccupation is not restricted to appearance). Social anxiety disorder (fear of scrutiny in general, not because of a specific perceived defect). Major depressive disorder (poor self-image without the specific preoccupation and repetitive behaviours). Excoriation disorder (picking without the appearance-defect belief; if picking is to fix a perceived flaw, it is BDD). Gender dysphoria , olfactory reference syndrome (in DSM-5-TR handled under other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder; ICD-11 has it as a full diagnosis). DSM-5 change DSM-5 moved body dysmorphic disorder from the somatoform disorders to the new obsessive-compulsive and related disorders chapter. It added Criterion B (repetitive behaviours or mental acts in response to the concern), the with muscle dysmorphia specifier and the three-level insight specifier. Under DSM-IV a deluded patient could receive both BDD and delusional disorder, somatic type ; DSM-5 records this as BDD with absent insight/delusional beliefs . "Imagined defect" was reworded as perceived flaws that are not observable or appear slight to others, and the exclusion now refers to concerns with body fat or weight in someone who meets criteria for an eating disorder. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Hoarding Disorder F42.3 In plain language. Getting rid of things feels intolerable, so possessions build up until the rooms cannot be used for what rooms are for. New in DSM-5. A. Persistent difficulty discarding or parting with possessions, regardless of their actual value . B. The difficulty is due to a perceived need to save the items and to distress associated with discarding them . C. The difficulty results in the accumulation of possessions that congest and clutter active living areas and substantially compromise their intended use . If living areas are uncluttered, it is only because of the interventions of third parties such as family members, cleaners or authorities. D. Clinically significant distress or impairment, including maintaining a safe environment for self and others . E. Not attributable to another medical condition (brain injury, cerebrovascular disease, Prader-Willi syndrome). F. Not better explained by another mental disorder (obsessions in OCD, decreased energy in major depressive disorder, delusions in schizophrenia, cognitive deficits in major neurocognitive disorder, restricted interests in autism). Specifiers With excessive acquisition (present in about 80 to 90 percent, either buying or acquiring free items), plus the insight specifier. Insight is characteristically poor, and many present only under pressure from family or housing authorities. Numbers Prevalence roughly 2 to 6 percent. Symptoms typically begin between ages 11 and 15, become interfering by the mid twenties and clinically impairing by the mid thirties, and severity increases with each decade of life . Prevalence is roughly three times as high in adults aged 55 to 94 as in those aged 34 to 44. Roughly equal by sex in epidemiological samples, though clinical samples are mostly female. Course Once established, the course is typically chronic , and few people describe a waxing and waning pattern. Many report a stressful or traumatic life event before onset or before a worsening. Indecisiveness is a prominent trait in sufferers and their first-degree relatives, and about half have a relative who hoards. Treatment response is more modest than in OCD and SSRIs help less, with hoarding-focused CBT the best-supported approach; in later life the clutter brings serious risks of fire, falls , poor sanitation and eviction . Comorbidity About 75 percent have a comorbid mood or anxiety disorder, with major depressive disorder in around half. OCD in about 20 percent. ADHD, inattentive presentation, in about 30 percent. Differential OCD , the key one: hoarding in OCD is driven by a classic obsession (contamination fear, fear of harm from discarding, incompleteness), is usually unwanted and distressing rather than pleasurable, and there is no excessive acquisition driven by desire. Major depressive disorder (clutter accumulates from psychomotor retardation and low energy, with no attachment to the objects). Major neurocognitive disorder (accumulation begins after cognitive decline, and is self-neglect rather than saving). Autism . Schizophrenia (delusional reasons). Normal collecting , which is organised, selective and non-impairing. DSM-5 change New in DSM-5 , placed in the new obsessive-compulsive and related disorders chapter. In DSM-IV, hoarding appeared only as a symptom: one of the 8 criteria of obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (inability to discard worn-out or worthless objects), and a presentation of OCD when extreme. DSM-5 made it a separate disorder because most people who hoard have no other OCD symptoms and respond differently to treatment. It carries the with excessive acquisition and insight specifiers. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Trichotillomania (Hair-Pulling Disorder) F63.3 A. Recurrent pulling out of one's hair, resulting in hair loss . B. Repeated attempts to decrease or stop hair pulling. C. Clinically significant distress or impairment. D. Not attributable to another medical condition (a dermatological condition). E. Not better explained by the symptoms of another mental disorder (for example attempts to improve a perceived defect in body dysmorphic disorder). Note what DSM-5 removed from the DSM-IV criteria: the requirements for mounting tension before pulling and pleasure, gratification or relief when pulling , because many patients, particularly those pulling automatically while reading or watching television, do not report them. Specifiers DSM-5-TR lists no subtypes, specifiers or severity ratings for trichotillomania; unlike OCD, body dysmorphic disorder and hoarding disorder, it has no insight specifier . The research distinction between focused and automatic pulling describes style but is not a DSM specifier. Numbers 12-month prevalence 1 to 2 percent. Female to male about 10:1 in adults, roughly equal in children. Onset usually coincides with, or follows, puberty. Sites: scalp commonest, then eyebrows and eyelashes; some pull from pubic, axillary and facial regions. Trichophagia , eating the hair, occurs in a minority and can cause a trichobezoar requiring surgery, which is a favourite MCQ. Course Hair pulling can be seen in infants , where it usually resolves during early development; the disorder proper most often begins at or after puberty. Untreated, the course is usually chronic with waxing and waning , and it may come and go for weeks, months or years at a time; in females symptoms can worsen with hormonal changes such as menstruation and perimenopause. Only a minority remit without relapse within a few years of onset. Onset in early childhood carries a better prognosis than onset after about age 13, which is more often chronic. Comorbidity Major depressive disorder and excoriation disorder , which co-occurs in roughly a fifth to a third. Also OCD, anxiety disorders, and other body-focused repetitive behaviours (nail biting, lip chewing) coded under other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder. Differential Normal hair removal or grooming for cosmetic reasons. Alopecia areata and other dermatological causes, which are distinguished by the pattern; in trichotillomania hairs of varying lengths remain in the affected patch. OCD (pulling in response to an obsession, for example to achieve symmetry). Body dysmorphic disorder (pulling to remove a perceived defect). Stereotypic movement disorder . Psychotic disorder (pulling in response to a delusion or hallucination). DSM-5 change DSM-5 moved trichotillomania from the DSM-IV impulse-control disorders not elsewhere classified into the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders chapter and added the name hair-pulling disorder . It removed the criteria of rising tension before pulling and pleasure, gratification or relief during it, changed "noticeable hair loss" to "hair loss" (since many people camouflage it), and added Criterion B , repeated attempts to decrease or stop. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Excoriation (Skin-Picking) Disorder F42.4 A. Recurrent skin picking resulting in skin lesions . B. Repeated attempts to decrease or stop. C. Clinically significant distress or impairment. D. Not attributable to a substance (cocaine) or another medical condition (scabies). E. Not better explained by another mental disorder (delusions or tactile hallucinations in a psychotic disorder, appearance concerns in body dysmorphic disorder, stereotypies, or intent to self-harm in non-suicidal self-injury). New in DSM-5. Specifiers DSM-5-TR lists no subtypes, specifiers or severity ratings for excoriation disorder, and, as in trichotillomania, there is no insight specifier . Numbers Lifetime prevalence about 1.4 percent or slightly higher; three-quarters or more are female . Most commonly picked sites are the face, arms and hands. Onset most often in adolescence, frequently coinciding with the onset of puberty or with acne. Course is chronic with waxing and waning. Course Onset can be at almost any age, but the disorder most often starts in adolescence and frequently begins with acne or another skin condition. The sites picked shift over time , and for some people it comes and goes for weeks, months or years at a time; without treatment it tends to persist. Complications include scarring , tissue damage and infection that may need antibiotics or occasionally surgery. Shame and camouflage delay help-seeking, and habit reversal training is the best-supported treatment. Comorbidity OCD, trichotillomania, major depressive disorder, and other body-focused repetitive behaviour disorders. Differential Non-suicidal self-injury , where the intent is to relieve emotional pain through harm; in excoriation the intent is to remove an irregularity. Body dysmorphic disorder . Psychotic disorder with delusional parasitosis or formication. Substance-induced , above all methamphetamine and cocaine. Scabies , eczema and other dermatological conditions. DSM-5 change New in DSM-5 : DSM-IV had no category, so skin picking was usually coded as impulse-control disorder not otherwise specified . It was placed in the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders chapter with criteria modelled on trichotillomania: recurrent picking causing skin lesions , repeated attempts to stop , and no requirement of tension or gratification. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Substance-Induced and Medical Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders, and Other Specified Substance/medication-induced , for example the obsessions and compulsions that appear with cocaine or amphetamine use. Due to another medical condition , for example after streptococcal infection, or with basal ganglia lesions, Sydenham's chorea, Huntington's or traumatic brain injury. Other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder is where DSM-5-TR parks several named syndromes examiners like: body-focused repetitive behaviour disorder (nail biting, lip chewing, cheek chewing), obsessional jealousy , olfactory reference disorder (olfactory reference syndrome; listed as jikoshu-kyofu in DSM-5), the belief that one emits a foul or offensive body odour, koro (an episode of sudden intense anxiety that the penis, or in women the vulva and nipples, will recede into the body and cause death), and shubo-kyofu (excessive fear of having a bodily deformity). Specifiers Substance/medication-induced obsessive-compulsive and related disorder : specify with onset during intoxication , with onset during withdrawal , or with onset after medication use . Obsessive-compulsive and related disorder due to another medical condition : specify with obsessive-compulsive disorder-like symptoms , with appearance preoccupations , with hoarding symptoms , with hair-pulling symptoms , or with skin-picking symptoms . Other specified is recorded with the reason (for example "other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder, body-focused repetitive behaviour disorder"); the listed examples not already on this card are body dysmorphic-like disorder with actual flaws and body dysmorphic-like disorder without repetitive behaviours . Unspecified is used when the clinician chooses not to give a reason. Course The substance form begins during or soon after intoxication, withdrawal or medication exposure (stimulants are the classic cause) and usually fades once the substance is stopped; symptoms that predate use or persist for about a month after withdrawal point to primary OCD. The medical form tracks its cause: the post-streptococcal presentation in children begins abruptly and tends to flare again with fresh streptococcal infections, whereas OCD symptoms after stroke, basal ganglia lesions or brain injury follow the lesion. Body-focused repetitive behaviour disorder runs a chronic, fluctuating course like trichotillomania. Koro occurs as acute, usually short-lived episodes, sometimes in epidemics , as in China, South-East Asia and north-east India. Comorbidity Primary obsessive-compulsive disorder, tic disorders and, for the post-streptococcal and basal-ganglia presentations, the neurological condition itself. The named cultural syndromes co-occur with anxiety and depressive disorders. Differential Primary OCD in someone who also uses stimulants, settled by timing and by persistence past withdrawal. Psychotic disorders , where the belief is delusional and unaccompanied by rituals. Body dysmorphic disorder for shubo-kyofu, and delusional disorder, somatic type for olfactory reference syndrome with absent insight. Panic disorder for a koro episode, where the acute anxiety is the presenting feature. DSM-5 change These diagnoses were created in DSM-5 with the new chapter. Obsessive-compulsive presentations caused by substances or medical illness had been the with obsessive-compulsive symptoms subtype of DSM-IV substance-induced anxiety disorder and anxiety disorder due to a general medical condition; they now have their own diagnoses with the new symptom-type specifiers. DSM-5 replaced NOS categories throughout the manual with other specified and unspecified categories, and koro , previously in the DSM-IV glossary of culture-bound syndromes, now appears as a named example here. DSM-5-TR (2022) renamed the jikoshu-kyofu example olfactory reference disorder (olfactory reference syndrome) , the ICD-11 name, because the Japanese label wrongly implied a culture-bound syndrome; its description lists repetitive behaviours such as excessive showering . The other criteria are unchanged. 8. Trauma and stressor-related disorders The one chapter in DSM where an identifiable external event is part of the criteria . It contains the two attachment disorders, acute stress disorder, PTSD, the adjustment disorders, and, new in DSM-5-TR, prolonged grief disorder . Reactive Attachment Disorder F94.1 In plain language. A severely neglected young child who has given up on adults: they do not seek comfort when distressed and do not accept it when it is offered. The internalising half of what DSM-IV called reactive attachment disorder. A. A consistent pattern of inhibited, emotionally withdrawn behaviour toward adult caregivers, shown by both: the child rarely or minimally seeks comfort when distressed, and rarely or minimally responds to comfort when distressed. B. A persistent social and emotional disturbance with at least 2 of 3 : minimal social and emotional responsiveness to others; limited positive affect; episodes of unexplained irritability, sadness or fearfulness that are evident even during non-threatening interactions with adult caregivers. C. The child has experienced a pattern of extremes of insufficient care , shown by at least one of: social neglect or deprivation (persistent lack of having basic emotional needs for comfort, stimulation and affection met); repeated changes of primary caregivers that limit opportunities to form stable attachments (frequent foster placements); rearing in unusual settings that severely limit opportunities to form selective attachments (institutions with high child-to-caregiver ratios). D. The care in Criterion C is presumed to be responsible for the disturbed behaviour in Criterion A. E. Criteria are not met for autism spectrum disorder . F. The disturbance is evident before age 5 . G. The child has a developmental age of at least 9 months . Specifiers Persistent (present for more than 12 months), and severe (all symptoms present at relatively high levels). Numbers Rare, under 10 percent even among severely neglected children, which is an important point: neglect is common, this disorder is not. Developmental age floor of 9 months matters because selective attachments have not formed before then. Course Signs appear between about 9 months and 5 years of age, in children whose neglect has usually been present from the first months of life. The course is driven by the caregiving: once the child is placed in adequate, responsive care (foster care or adoption), the withdrawn, inhibited behaviour usually improves markedly and the child can go on to form selective attachments, so the outcome depends mainly on whether the care is corrected. Without that change, signs may persist for at least several years. Because it is unclear whether RAD occurs in older children, DSM advises caution in making the diagnosis after age 5 . Comorbidity Cognitive and language delays, stereotypies, medical conditions of malnutrition, and depressive symptoms. Differential Autism spectrum disorder , which is Criterion E and is the examined pair: both show social deficits, but autism shows restricted repetitive behaviours, unusual sensory reactivity and language delay in its own pattern and does not require a history of pathogenic care; also, children with RAD improve markedly once caregiving improves, while autism does not remit. Intellectual disability (social behaviour matches mental age, and attachment behaviours are present). Depressive disorders . Disinhibited social engagement disorder , its opposite number. DSM-5 change DSM-IV had a single disorder, reactive attachment disorder of infancy or early childhood , with two subtypes: inhibited and disinhibited . DSM-5 split them: the inhibited subtype became reactive attachment disorder, and the disinhibited subtype became the separate disinhibited social engagement disorder , because the two differ in correlates, course and response to intervention. Both moved out of the childhood-disorders section into the new Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders chapter. DSM-5 also added the developmental age of at least 9 months and the persistent and severe specifiers. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder F94.2 In plain language. The same neglect history, the opposite behaviour: the child is over-friendly with total strangers and will wander off with anyone. DSM-5 split this out from reactive attachment disorder, because unlike RAD it does not require an absence of attachment and does not resolve simply by improving caregiving. A. A pattern of behaviour in which a child actively approaches and interacts with unfamiliar adults , with at least 2 of 4 : reduced or absent reticence in approaching and interacting with unfamiliar adults; overly familiar verbal or physical behaviour that is inconsistent with culturally sanctioned and age-appropriate social boundaries; diminished or absent checking back with the adult caregiver after venturing away, even in unfamiliar settings; willingness to go off with an unfamiliar adult with minimal or no hesitation . B. The behaviours are not limited to impulsivity, as in ADHD, but include socially disinhibited behaviour. C. Same pattern of extremes of insufficient care as in RAD. D. That care is presumed responsible. E. Developmental age of at least 9 months . Specify persistent and severe as above. Specifiers Persistent : the disturbance has been present for more than 12 months . Severe : the child shows all the symptoms of the disorder, each at relatively high levels. These are the same two specifiers that reactive attachment disorder carries; DSM-5-TR gives no subtypes. Numbers Around 20 percent of children in high-risk institutional populations. Unlike RAD, it can persist even after the caregiving environment is corrected and after a secure attachment has formed, which is the fact that justifies the split. Course The neglect is usually present from the first months of life, and there is no evidence that neglect beginning after age 2 produces the disorder. The picture changes with age: indiscriminate approach to strangers in toddlers, attention-seeking in preschoolers, verbal and physical overfamiliarity and inauthentic expression of emotion in middle childhood, and indiscriminate behaviour with conflict in peer relationships in adolescence. Signs are moderately stable, especially if the neglect continues; better caregiving moderates the course, but some children remain symptomatic at least through adolescence. It has not been described in adults . Comorbidity Cognitive and language delay, stereotypies, ADHD, and other signs of severe neglect. Differential ADHD , which is Criterion B: ADHD children are impulsive and intrusive but do not typically show the indiscriminate willingness to go off with a stranger and do not require a neglect history. Williams syndrome , which produces indiscriminate friendliness on a genetic basis. Autism . Normal extraversion , distinguished by the absence of a neglect history and by the intact checking-back behaviour. DSM-5 change New name in DSM-5. It is the old disinhibited subtype of DSM-IV reactive attachment disorder of infancy or early childhood, made a disorder in its own right and placed in the new Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders chapter. The split was justified because this pattern resembles ADHD more than an internalising disorder, can occur in children who have formed attachments, even secure ones , and differs from RAD in correlates, course and response to intervention. Unlike RAD, its criteria contain no before-age-5 rule and no autism exclusion. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder F43.10 In plain language. After a real, severe trauma, the event keeps coming back uninvited, the person avoids everything connected to it, their view of the world and themselves has turned dark, and their nervous system is stuck in alarm, for more than a month. A. Exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence, in one or more of four ways : directly experiencing the event; witnessing it in person as it occurred to others; learning that it occurred to a close family member or close friend (in cases of actual or threatened death, the event must have been violent or accidental ); or experiencing repeated or extreme exposure to aversive details of traumatic events, as with first responders collecting human remains or police repeatedly exposed to details of child abuse. That fourth route does not apply to exposure through electronic media, television, movies or pictures unless the exposure is work-related , which is the single most examined line in the criteria set. DSM-5 deleted the DSM-IV Criterion A2 , which had required the person's response to involve intense fear, helplessness or horror. B. Intrusion , 1 or more of 5 : recurrent, involuntary and intrusive distressing memories (in children over 6, repetitive play expressing themes of the trauma); recurrent distressing dreams (in children, frightening dreams without recognisable content); dissociative reactions such as flashbacks in which the person feels or acts as if the event were recurring (in children, trauma-specific re-enactment in play); intense or prolonged psychological distress at exposure to internal or external cues that symbolise or resemble an aspect of the event; marked physiological reactions to such cues. C. Avoidance , 1 or both : avoidance of, or efforts to avoid, distressing memories, thoughts or feelings about the event; avoidance of, or efforts to avoid, external reminders (people, places, conversations, activities, objects, situations). D. Negative alterations in cognitions and mood , 2 or more of 7 : inability to remember an important aspect of the event, typically due to dissociative amnesia rather than head injury or substances; persistent and exaggerated negative beliefs or expectations about oneself, others or the world ("I am bad", "no one can be trusted", "the world is completely dangerous"); persistent distorted cognitions about the cause or consequences of the event leading the person to blame themselves or others; persistent negative emotional state (fear, horror, anger, guilt, shame); markedly diminished interest or participation in significant activities; feelings of detachment or estrangement from others; persistent inability to experience positive emotions. This whole cluster is new in DSM-5 ; DSM-IV had three clusters, DSM-5 has four. E. Alterations in arousal and reactivity , 2 or more of 6 : irritable behaviour and angry outbursts with little or no provocation, typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression toward people or objects; reckless or self-destructive behaviour (new in DSM-5); hypervigilance; exaggerated startle response; problems with concentration; sleep disturbance. F. Duration of Criteria B, C, D and E is more than 1 month . G. Clinically significant distress or impairment. H. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. Specifiers With dissociative symptoms , which is new in DSM-5 and requires persistent or recurrent depersonalisation (feeling detached from, and as if an outside observer of, one's own mental processes or body) or derealisation (experiencing the surroundings as unreal, dreamlike, distant or distorted). With delayed expression , where full criteria are not met until at least 6 months after the event, though some symptoms may begin immediately. There is also a separate PTSD for children 6 years and younger criteria set, the "preschool subtype", the first developmental subtype in DSM, which needs only one symptom from a combined avoidance-and-negative-cognitions cluster and drops the more verbally demanding items. Numbers Lifetime risk in the United States about 8.7 percent by age 75; 12-month prevalence about 3.5 percent. Rates are much lower in most of Asia, Africa and Latin America, roughly 0.5 to 1 percent. Females are at roughly twice the risk and experience longer duration, partly because of higher exposure to sexual violence. Highest conditional rates follow rape, torture and captivity. Duration threshold 1 month : under a month, consider acute stress disorder. Course Can begin at any age after the first year of life . Symptoms usually start within the first 3 months after the trauma, although full criteria may not be met for months or even years (delayed expression). About half of adults recover completely within 3 months ; others remain symptomatic beyond 12 months, some for decades, and symptoms often flare with reminders, new life stressors or new trauma. Risk of PTSD, and of a longer course, rises with severe or interpersonal, intentional trauma, perceived threat to life, injury, peritraumatic dissociation that persists afterwards, prior trauma or mental disorder, and negative appraisals of the event; social support (for children, family stability) is a protective factor that moderates outcome after trauma. Comorbidity About 80 percent have at least one comorbid disorder. Commonest: major depressive disorder, substance use disorders, other anxiety disorders, bipolar disorder, and in military and veteran samples traumatic brain injury with overlapping symptoms. In children, oppositional defiant and separation anxiety disorders. Differential Acute stress disorder (3 days to 1 month). Adjustment disorder , where either the stressor does not meet Criterion A (divorce, job loss) or it does but the symptom pattern does not meet PTSD criteria. Other specified trauma and stressor-related disorder . Anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorders (intrusions in OCD are not related to a traumatic event). Major depressive disorder (no Criterion B intrusions or Criterion E arousal). Personality disorders , especially borderline, which shares affective instability and interpersonal difficulty. Dissociative disorders . Conversion disorder . Psychotic disorders (flashbacks and reliving versus hallucinations, and this misdiagnosis is common). Traumatic brain injury . Malingering , which must be considered explicitly where compensation or legal proceedings are involved. DSM-5 change DSM-5 moved PTSD out of the anxiety disorders into the new Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders chapter. Criterion A was made explicit (direct, witnessed, learned about, or repeated professional exposure; sexual violence named; media excluded unless work-related) and Criterion A2 (fear, helplessness or horror) was deleted. The three clusters became four : avoidance was separated from numbing, a new negative alterations in cognitions and mood cluster was created, and reckless or self-destructive behaviour was added, taking the symptom count from 17 to 20 . The DSM-IV acute (under 3 months) and chronic (3 months or more) specifiers were dropped, delayed onset became with delayed expression , and the dissociative subtype and separate criteria for children 6 years and younger were added. DSM-5-TR (2022): in the criteria for children 6 years and younger , the note excluding events seen only in electronic media was removed from the witnessing item as redundant , since that item already requires witnessing in person; the adult media exclusion is unchanged. ICD-11 Takes a completely different approach: PTSD is narrowed to three core clusters (re-experiencing in the here and now, avoidance, and a persistent sense of current threat), and a separate diagnosis of Complex PTSD adds three disturbances of self-organisation: affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, and disturbances in relationships . DSM-5-TR has no Complex PTSD; the nearest DSM approximation is PTSD with the dissociative subtype, sometimes alongside a personality-disorder diagnosis. Naming ICD-11 CPTSD and its three extra clusters is one of the highest-yield contrasts in the whole syllabus. Acute Stress Disorder F43.0 In plain language. The same kind of aftermath as PTSD, in the first month, and diagnosed by counting symptoms across all categories rather than requiring a set from each. A. The same exposure criterion as PTSD, with the same four routes and the same media exclusion. B. 9 or more of 14 symptoms from any of five categories, beginning or worsening after the event: intrusion (intrusive memories, distressing dreams, dissociative reactions or flashbacks, intense or prolonged distress or marked physiological reactions to reminders); negative mood (persistent inability to experience positive emotions); dissociative (altered sense of the reality of one's surroundings or oneself, inability to remember an important aspect of the event); avoidance (of internal reminders, of external reminders); arousal (sleep disturbance, irritable behaviour and angry outbursts, hypervigilance, problems with concentration, exaggerated startle response). The key DSM-5 change: DSM-IV required at least three dissociative symptoms; DSM-5 dropped that requirement, because many people develop PTSD without ever dissociating. C. Duration is 3 days to 1 month after trauma exposure . Symptoms typically begin immediately but must persist at least 3 days. D. Clinically significant distress or impairment. E. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition (mild traumatic brain injury) and not better explained by brief psychotic disorder. Specifiers DSM-5-TR lists no specifiers, subtypes or severity ratings for acute stress disorder. There is no dissociative subtype as in PTSD (dissociative symptoms simply count among the 14), and no delayed-expression specifier, since the diagnosis is confined to the first month after the trauma. Numbers The two numbers are 9 of 14 and 3 days to 1 month . Prevalence after trauma varies widely, under 20 percent after events not involving interpersonal assault, higher after assault, rape and mass shootings. Roughly half of those who go on to develop PTSD initially present with acute stress disorder, so it is a poor screening test taken alone. Course Symptoms usually begin immediately after the trauma, but the diagnosis cannot be made until they have lasted 3 days . The disorder may then be a transient stress response that remits within the month , or it may progress to PTSD; symptoms can worsen during that month because of ongoing life stressors or further trauma. Risk is raised by prior mental disorder, high negative affectivity , an avoidant coping style, earlier trauma and female sex, and catastrophic appraisals of the event (exaggerated future harm, guilt, hopelessness) are strongly predictive. Early trauma-focused CBT reduces progression to PTSD, whereas single-session psychological debriefing is not recommended. Comorbidity Prior mental disorders raise risk; depression and pain conditions commonly co-occur; head injury frequently coexists in road traffic and combat contexts. Differential PTSD after a month. Adjustment disorder (stressor does not meet Criterion A, or symptom threshold not met). Panic disorder (unexpected attacks). Dissociative disorders . Traumatic brain injury and postconcussive syndrome . Normal, adaptive acute stress reactions , which is the most important one clinically: transient distress after trauma is expected, and it becomes a disorder only at this symptom count with impairment. DSM-5 change DSM-IV placed acute stress disorder among the anxiety disorders ; DSM-5 moved it to the new Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders chapter. Criterion A now matches PTSD, stating explicitly whether the event was experienced, witnessed or learned about, and Criterion A2 (fear, helplessness or horror) was removed. The biggest change: DSM-IV required three dissociative symptoms ; DSM-5 drops that and accepts any 9 of 14 symptoms across intrusion, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance and arousal, because acute reactions are heterogeneous. The duration window changed from DSM-IV's 2 days to 4 weeks to 3 days to 1 month . DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Adjustment Disorders F43.2x In plain language. A response to an ordinary life stressor that is bigger than you would expect or is clearly wrecking function, but does not amount to any other disorder. A. Development of emotional or behavioural symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor(s) occurring within 3 months of the onset of the stressor. B. These symptoms are clinically significant, shown by one or both of: marked distress that is out of proportion to the severity or intensity of the stressor , taking into account external context and cultural factors; and/or significant impairment in social, occupational or other important areas of functioning. C. The disturbance does not meet criteria for another mental disorder and is not merely an exacerbation of a pre-existing one. D. The symptoms do not represent normal bereavement and are not better explained by prolonged grief disorder. E. Once the stressor or its consequences have terminated, the symptoms do not persist for more than an additional 6 months . Subtypes With depressed mood; with anxiety; with mixed anxiety and depressed mood; with disturbance of conduct; with mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct; unspecified. Also specify acute (under 6 months) or persistent/chronic (6 months or longer, which happens when the stressor itself is enduring). Numbers Very common: 5 to 20 percent of outpatient mental-health caseloads, and up to about 50 percent in hospital psychiatric consultation samples, which makes it the commonest diagnosis in consultation-liaison work. The two numbers to hold: symptoms begin within 3 months of the stressor and resolve within 6 months of the stressor ending. Course After a single acute stressor (losing a job) the reaction usually begins within days and is relatively brief, lasting no more than a few months. If the stressor or its consequences continue (a chronic disabling illness, an ongoing conflict), the disorder can continue too and becomes the persistent (chronic) form. Prognosis in adults is generally good , with most returning to their previous level of functioning. Adolescents take longer to recover and are more likely to go on to develop mood or substance use disorders, so the diagnosis should be revised if a fuller syndrome emerges. Comorbidity Can accompany most medical illnesses, and is associated with increased suicide risk, notably in adolescents and in the medically ill. Differential Major depressive disorder (full criteria met, in which case MDD is diagnosed, not adjustment disorder). PTSD and acute stress disorder (Criterion A trauma and the specific symptom pattern). Personality disorders (long-standing pattern, though a personality disorder can be exacerbated by stress). Normal stress reactions , which is the judgment call: proportionality and impairment. Prolonged grief disorder and uncomplicated bereavement , which is now Criterion D. DSM-5 change DSM-IV gave adjustment disorders a chapter of their own and treated them as a residual category for clinically significant distress that met no other diagnosis. DSM-5 moved them into the new Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders chapter and reconceptualised them as a heterogeneous group of stress-response syndromes following any distressing event, traumatic or not; so a person exposed to a Criterion A trauma who does not meet PTSD or acute stress disorder criteria can receive this diagnosis. The six subtypes were kept, as were the acute and persistent specifiers (DSM-IV called the second one chronic). DSM-5-TR (2022): Criterion D now also excludes presentations better explained by prolonged grief disorder , the new disorder in the same chapter. Prolonged Grief Disorder F43.81 NEW IN DSM-5-TR In plain language. A year or more after a death, the person is still gripped by yearning and preoccupation with the person who died, and their life has not restarted. This is the only new specific disorder in the 2022 Text Revision (unspecified mood disorder and stimulant-induced mild neurocognitive disorder were also added as categories), so treat it as a guaranteed question. A. The death, at least 12 months ago , of a person who was close to the bereaved ( at least 6 months ago for children and adolescents ). B. Since the death, a persistent grief response characterised by one or both of: intense yearning or longing for the deceased; and/or preoccupation with thoughts or memories of the deceased (in children and adolescents, preoccupation may focus on the circumstances of the death). This has been present to a clinically significant degree nearly every day for at least the last month . C. Since the death, 3 or more of 8 symptoms present to a clinically significant degree nearly every day for at least the last month: identity disruption (feeling as though part of oneself has died); a marked sense of disbelief about the death; avoidance of reminders that the person is dead; intense emotional pain (anger, bitterness, sorrow) related to the death; difficulty reintegrating into relationships and activities (problems engaging with friends, pursuing interests, planning for the future); emotional numbness , that is, an absence of or marked reduction in emotional experience; feeling that life is meaningless ; intense loneliness , feeling alone or detached from others. D. Clinically significant distress or impairment. E. The duration and severity of the bereavement reaction clearly exceed expected social, cultural or religious norms for the individual's culture and context. This cultural clause is deliberate and is examinable, because mourning periods differ widely across Indian communities. F. Not better explained by another mental disorder such as major depressive disorder or PTSD, and not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. Specifiers DSM-5-TR gives no specifiers, subtypes or severity ratings for prolonged grief disorder. The difference for children and adolescents is built into Criterion A (6 rather than 12 months since the death) rather than made a specifier, and the with traumatic bereavement specifier of the DSM-5 research version (death by homicide or suicide) was not carried over. Numbers The three that matter: 12 months in adults, 6 months in children and adolescents, and symptoms present nearly every day for at least the last month . Prevalence in bereaved adults is roughly 4 to 10 percent, higher after the death of a child, after violent or unexpected death, and after suicide. Course Grief symptoms usually begin in the first months after the death , but the diagnosis waits for the 12-month (or 6-month) mark because intense early grief is normal and usually softens with time. In prolonged grief disorder it does not: without treatment the yearning and preoccupation tend to persist for years , with impaired work and social functioning, harmful health behaviours such as increased smoking and drinking, worse physical health and raised suicide risk. Heavy dependency on the deceased before the death adds to the risk. It responds to grief-focused psychotherapy (for example Shear's complicated grief treatment) better than to standard treatment for depression. Comorbidity Major depressive disorder, PTSD (especially after violent death), separation anxiety disorder, and substance use disorders. Suicide risk is elevated. Differential Normal grief , distinguished by time course and by whether the person's life has resumed. Major depressive disorder : in PGD the emotional pain is focused on the deceased and yearning is the core, while in depression the low mood is generalised and self-worth is attacked; note that yearning and preoccupation are not criteria for MDD. PTSD : intrusions there are about the traumatic event and carry a sense of current threat, whereas PGD intrusions are about the person and carry longing. Separation anxiety disorder : fear of future separation from living attachment figures, not longing for a dead one. Adjustment disorder , now excluded by Criterion D of that disorder. DSM-5 change DSM-IV-TR had no grief disorder: bereavement was only a V code, and the bereavement exclusion generally barred a diagnosis of major depression in the first 2 months after a death. DSM-5 (2013) removed that exclusion from MDD and placed persistent complex bereavement disorder in Section III, Conditions for Further Study (12 months for adults, 6 months for children, with a traumatic-bereavement specifier); in practice it could be coded only as other specified trauma- and stressor-related disorder. DSM-5-TR (2022) made it a full Section II diagnosis, renamed prolonged grief disorder , in the Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders chapter, with simplified criteria (yearning or preoccupation plus 3 of 8 symptoms), and added it as an exclusion to adjustment disorder. ICD-11 Also has Prolonged Grief Disorder, with a threshold of at least 6 months rather than 12. If a question gives a bereavement of 8 months and asks which system allows the diagnosis, the answer is ICD-11 only. 9. Dissociative disorders Disruption of, or discontinuity in, the normal integration of consciousness, memory, identity, emotion, perception, body representation, motor control and behaviour. DSM-5 placed this chapter immediately after the trauma chapter, without folding it in, to mark the close relationship without asserting that dissociation is always post-traumatic. Dissociative Identity Disorder F44.81 In plain language. Two or more distinct ways of being a self take turns running the person, and there are memory gaps that ordinary forgetting does not explain. A. Disruption of identity characterised by two or more distinct personality states , which in some cultures may be described as an experience of possession . The disruption involves marked discontinuity in sense of self and sense of agency, accompanied by related alterations in affect, behaviour, consciousness, memory, perception, cognition and sensory-motor functioning. These signs and symptoms may be observed by others or reported by the individual , which is a DSM-5 change: DSM-IV required that a state actually take control, DSM-5 permits self-report. B. Recurrent gaps in the recall of everyday events, important personal information, and/or traumatic events that are inconsistent with ordinary forgetting. DSM-5 added everyday events, since DSM-IV limited the amnesia to important personal information. C. Clinically significant distress or impairment. D. The disturbance is not a normal part of a broadly accepted cultural or religious practice . In children, the symptoms are not better explained by imaginary playmates or other fantasy play. E. Not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (blackouts during alcohol intoxication) or another medical condition (complex partial seizures). Specifiers DSM-5-TR has no specifiers or subtypes for dissociative identity disorder. The possession-form presentation is not a subtype; it is written into Criterion A. Presentations that fall short, such as identity disturbance with less than distinct states, or identity change from prolonged and intense coercive persuasion (brainwashing, cult indoctrination, torture, long political imprisonment), are coded as other specified dissociative disorder . Numbers 12-month prevalence about 1.5 percent in one US community sample, with a near-equal sex ratio in that sample though clinical samples are heavily female. Reported rates of childhood abuse and neglect in clinical samples in North America, Europe and Turkey run around 90 percent. Suicide attempts occur in over 70 percent of outpatients with the diagnosis. Course Rooted in overwhelming trauma in childhood , but the full disorder can first appear at almost any age, and the diagnosis is often made only after years of treatment for other conditions. Women predominate in adult clinical samples but not in child clinical samples. Overt decompensation or identity change is often triggered by leaving the traumatising setting , by one's own child reaching the age at which one was abused, by later trauma (even a minor one), or by the death or fatal illness of the abuser. The course is chronic and rarely remits on its own; ongoing abuse, later retraumatisation, comorbid disorders, severe medical illness and delay in appropriate treatment predict a poorer outcome, while phase-oriented trauma treatment (stabilisation, trauma processing, integration) brings improvement. Comorbidity PTSD is nearly universal. Also depressive disorders, substance use disorders, somatic symptom disorder, conversion disorder, eating disorders, sleep disorders, and personality disorders, especially borderline and avoidant. Differential Other specified dissociative disorder , where identity disturbance is less than fully distinct. Major depressive disorder . Bipolar disorder (the rapid shifts here are within-day and identity-linked, not episodic mood). PTSD . Psychotic disorders : voices in DID are typically experienced as coming from inside the head and as belonging to identities, and reality testing is otherwise intact. Borderline personality disorder , which shares identity disturbance and dissociation under stress but lacks the distinct amnesia between states. Seizure disorders , particularly complex partial seizures. Factitious disorder and malingering , which DSM-5-TR discusses at length because of the forensic history around this diagnosis. DSM-5 change The name dissociative identity disorder dates from DSM-IV (1994), replacing multiple personality disorder . DSM-5 changes: Criterion A was broadened to include possession-form experiences and functional neurological (sensory-motor) symptoms, and now states that the identity disruption may be observed by others or self-reported , rather than requiring that identities recurrently take control of behaviour. Criterion B extended the amnesia to gaps in everyday events , not only important personal or traumatic information. The exclusion of broadly accepted cultural or religious practices was added. The dissociative disorders chapter was placed immediately after, but not inside, the trauma chapter. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Dissociative Amnesia F44.0, with fugue F44.1 A. An inability to recall important autobiographical information, usually of a traumatic or stressful nature, that is inconsistent with ordinary forgetting . Note that dissociative amnesia most often consists of localised or selective amnesia for a specific event or events, or generalised amnesia for identity and life history. B. Clinically significant distress or impairment. C. Not attributable to a substance or a neurological or other medical condition. D. Not better explained by DID, PTSD, acute stress disorder, somatic symptom disorder, or major or mild neurocognitive disorder. Specify: with dissociative fugue , that is, apparently purposeful travel or bewildered wandering associated with amnesia for identity or other important autobiographical information. Dissociative fugue is no longer a separate disorder in DSM-5, it is a specifier here. That change is asked frequently. Specifiers With dissociative fugue (coded F44.1 ; without it the code is F44.0): apparently purposeful travel or bewildered wandering associated with amnesia for identity or other important autobiographical information. This is the only formal specifier. The forms of amnesia ( localised, selective, generalised , plus the text descriptions systematised and continuous ) are descriptive, not coded specifiers. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 1.8 percent (1.0 percent in men, 2.6 percent in women) in one US community study. Types to be able to list: localised (no recall of events during a circumscribed period, the commonest), selective (some but not all of the events in a period), generalised (whole life and identity, rare and abrupt), systematised (a specific category of information, for example all memories of one person), and continuous (each new event as it occurs). Course Can occur at any age, from young children (the hardest to assess) to older adults. Generalised amnesia usually has a sudden onset , while localised and selective amnesia often go unnoticed even by the person. Episodes may be single or multiple, and one episode predisposes to further episodes . Memory may return quickly once the person is removed from the traumatic circumstances (for example, combat), or the gaps may persist for long periods, with some memories recovered only years later. Risk and severity rise with the number of adverse childhood experiences , especially physical and sexual abuse, with interpersonal violence, and with more severe, frequent and violent trauma. Comorbidity Depressive disorders, PTSD, conversion disorder, somatic symptom disorder, and personality disorders. Suicide risk is elevated, particularly when memory returns suddenly. Differential Neurocognitive disorders (anterograde deficits predominate, and personal identity is retained until very late). Transient global amnesia (abrupt, anterograde, resolves within 24 hours, older patients, retained identity). Post-ictal and post-traumatic amnesia . Substance-related blackouts . Malingering and factitious disorder , where secondary gain is evident. Normal and age-related forgetting . DSM-5 change DSM-IV listed dissociative fugue as a separate disorder (sudden, unexpected travel away from home with inability to recall one's past, and confusion about identity or assumption of a new one). DSM-5 folded fugue into dissociative amnesia as a specifier , since fugue always involves amnesia for identity or life history. Criterion A was reworded as an inability to recall autobiographical information inconsistent with ordinary forgetting , with a note naming localised or selective amnesia as the usual form and generalised amnesia as the other. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Depersonalisation/Derealisation Disorder F48.1 A. Persistent or recurrent experiences of depersonalisation, derealisation, or both . Depersonalisation : experiences of unreality, detachment, or being an outside observer with respect to one's thoughts, feelings, sensations, body or actions (perceptual alterations, distorted sense of time, unreal or absent self, emotional and/or physical numbing). Derealisation : experiences of unreality or detachment with respect to surroundings (individuals or objects experienced as unreal, dreamlike, foggy, lifeless or visually distorted). B. During these experiences, reality testing remains intact . This is the criterion that separates the disorder from psychosis and is the one examiners test. C. Clinically significant distress or impairment. D. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition (seizures). E. Not better explained by another mental disorder such as schizophrenia, panic disorder, major depressive disorder, acute stress disorder, PTSD, or another dissociative disorder. Specifiers DSM-5-TR has no specifiers or subtypes for depersonalisation/derealisation disorder. Criterion A can be met by depersonalisation alone, derealisation alone, or both, but which one predominates is not coded. Numbers Lifetime prevalence about 2 percent; sex ratio roughly 1:1. Mean age at onset 16, with about 20 percent onset after 20 and only 5 percent after 25; onset after 40 is unusual and should prompt a search for a medical cause. Transient depersonalisation experiences are extremely common in the general population (roughly half of adults report at least one), so the disorder requires persistence and impairment. Course Onset is usually in adolescence and can be extremely sudden or gradual. Episodes last anything from hours or days to weeks, months or years, and the course is often persistent : roughly one-third of cases have discrete episodes, one-third are continuous from the start, and one-third begin episodic and become continuous. Symptoms worsen with stress , worsening mood or anxiety, novel or overstimulating settings, and physical factors such as lighting or lack of sleep. Common precipitants are severe stress, depression, anxiety, panic attacks and drug use (cannabis, hallucinogens, ketamine); childhood emotional abuse and emotional neglect are the most consistent background risk factors, along with a harm-avoidant temperament. Comorbidity Unipolar depressive disorder and anxiety disorders are the commonest; also avoidant, borderline and obsessive-compulsive personality disorders. Differential Panic disorder (depersonalisation only during attacks). Psychotic disorders (reality testing lost). Substance-induced , especially cannabis, ketamine, hallucinogens. Medical causes : temporal lobe epilepsy, migraine, vestibular disease, head injury. PTSD with the dissociative subtype . Major depressive disorder with numbing. DSM-5 change DSM-IV called it depersonalisation disorder , and derealisation occurring without depersonalisation could only be coded as dissociative disorder not otherwise specified. DSM-5 renamed it depersonalisation/derealisation disorder and allowed Criterion A to be met by depersonalisation, derealisation, or both , since the two usually occur together and do not behave as separate conditions. The intact reality-testing criterion was kept. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. 10. Somatic symptom and related disorders The chapter DSM-5 rewrote most radically. DSM-IV's somatisation disorder, hypochondriasis, pain disorder and undifferentiated somatoform disorder were all deleted and replaced. The organising change: DSM-IV defined these disorders by the absence of a medical explanation , which was unreliable and, worse, reinforced mind-body dualism and made patients feel disbelieved. DSM-5 defines them instead by the presence of positive psychological features , namely disproportionate thoughts, feelings and behaviours about the symptoms. Say that sentence in any long-answer question on this chapter. Somatic Symptom Disorder F45.1 A. One or more somatic symptoms that are distressing or result in significant disruption of daily life.
