Note it is one, not the eight-symptom count DSM-IV demanded across four body systems, and the symptom may or may not be medically explained . B. Excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviours related to the somatic symptoms or associated health concerns, shown by at least 1 of 3 : disproportionate and persistent thoughts about the seriousness of one's symptoms; persistently high level of anxiety about health or symptoms; excessive time and energy devoted to these symptoms or health concerns. C. Although any one somatic symptom may not be continuously present, the state of being symptomatic is persistent, typically more than 6 months . Specifiers With predominant pain , which is the replacement for DSM-IV's pain disorder. Persistent (severe symptoms, marked impairment, duration more than 6 months). Severity mild (one Criterion B symptom), moderate (two or more), severe (two or more plus multiple somatic complaints or one very severe symptom). Numbers Prevalence estimated 5 to 7 percent in the general adult population, higher in women. Compare DSM-IV somatisation disorder at under 1 percent: the criteria were loosened deliberately, and the standard criticism to reproduce in an essay is that this risks pathologising normal illness worry in the medically ill. Course There is no age-of-onset rule (DSM-IV somatisation disorder required onset before age 30 ). The course is typically chronic and fluctuating , with symptoms waxing and waning over years. In children the commonest symptoms are recurrent abdominal pain , headache, fatigue and nausea, and a single prominent symptom is more usual than in adults. Persistence is predicted by female sex, older age, fewer years of education, lower socioeconomic status and unemployment , childhood sexual abuse or other adversity, coexisting chronic physical or psychiatric illness, social stress and reinforcing factors such as illness benefits , as well as heightened attention to bodily sensations and attributing them to illness. Comorbidity Depressive and anxiety disorders, PTSD, and genuine medical illness, which frequently coexists. That coexistence is the point: DSM-5 explicitly permits the diagnosis alongside a diagnosed medical condition. Differential Illness anxiety disorder (few or no somatic symptoms, the fear is of having or acquiring an illness). Panic disorder (symptoms are episodic and attack-bound). Generalised anxiety disorder (worry is broader than health). Major depressive disorder . Conversion disorder (loss of function, not distress about a symptom). Delusional disorder, somatic type (fixed, unshakeable belief). Body dysmorphic disorder . OCD with health obsessions. DSM-5 change DSM-5 renamed the chapter from Somatoform Disorders to Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders and replaced somatisation disorder, undifferentiated somatoform disorder, pain disorder and most cases of hypochondriasis with the single somatic symptom disorder. The central shift is from requiring medically unexplained symptoms to requiring positive psychological features (excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviours) about one or more symptoms, explained or not. Pain disorder survives as the with predominant pain specifier, and severity and persistent specifiers were added. Body dysmorphic disorder left the chapter for obsessive-compulsive and related disorders. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Illness Anxiety Disorder F45.21 A. Preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness . B. Somatic symptoms are not present or, if present, are only mild in intensity . If another medical condition is present or there is a high risk of developing one, the preoccupation is clearly excessive or disproportionate. C. There is a high level of anxiety about health , and the person is easily alarmed about personal health status. D. The person performs excessive health-related behaviours (repeatedly checking the body for signs of illness) or exhibits maladaptive avoidance (avoids doctor appointments and hospitals). E. Illness preoccupation has been present for at least 6 months , although the specific illness feared may change. F. Not better explained by another mental disorder. Specify: care-seeking type or care-avoidant type . Specifiers Care-seeking type : medical care, including physician visits or undergoing tests and procedures, is frequently used. Care-avoidant type : medical care is rarely used. There is no severity rating and no insight specifier (DSM-IV hypochondriasis had with poor insight ). Numbers Prevalence 1.3 to 10 percent, roughly equal in men and women. About 75 percent of those who would have been diagnosed with DSM-IV hypochondriasis now fall under somatic symptom disorder because they do have somatic symptoms; the remaining quarter, who have few or no symptoms, become illness anxiety disorder. That reallocation is a stock question. Course Thought to be a chronic and relapsing condition with onset in early and middle adulthood ; it is rare in children. In community samples health anxiety rises with age, and in older adults the fear often centres on memory loss . It may be set off by a major life stress or by a serious health scare that turns out to be benign, and a history of childhood abuse or serious childhood illness predisposes. Kaplan and Sadock list as good prognostic signs: high socioeconomic status, anxiety or depression that responds to treatment, sudden onset , no personality disorder, and no related non-psychiatric medical condition. Comorbidity Anxiety disorders, especially generalised anxiety and panic, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and depressive disorders. Personality disorders in about a fifth. Differential Somatic symptom disorder (prominent somatic symptoms). Generalised anxiety disorder . OCD (obsessions about contracting disease in the future, with compulsions; illness anxiety is about currently having it). Specific phobia of illness . Delusional disorder, somatic type . Major depressive disorder . Adjustment disorder after a genuine diagnosis. DSM-5 change DSM-5 eliminated hypochondriasis , partly because the name was seen as pejorative and unhelpful to the therapeutic relationship. People with health anxiety and significant somatic symptoms are now diagnosed with somatic symptom disorder ; those with high health anxiety and no or only mild symptoms receive the new diagnosis of illness anxiety disorder. The DSM-IV requirement that the fear persist despite appropriate medical evaluation and reassurance and the with poor insight specifier were dropped, and the care-seeking and care-avoidant types were added. The 6-month duration was retained. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (Conversion Disorder) F44.x A. One or more symptoms of altered voluntary motor or sensory function . B. Clinical findings provide evidence of incompatibility between the symptom and recognised neurological or medical conditions . This is positive evidence , for example Hoover's sign (hip extension weakness resolves on contralateral hip flexion against resistance), a tremor that entrains to a tapped rhythm, or tubular visual fields. DSM-5's key change was requiring this positive incompatibility rather than requiring a preceding psychological stressor. C. Not better explained by another medical or mental disorder. D. Causes clinically significant distress or impairment or warrants medical evaluation. Specify symptom type: with weakness or paralysis; with abnormal movement (tremor, dystonic movement, myoclonus, gait disorder); with swallowing symptoms; with speech symptom (dysphonia, slurred speech); with attacks or seizures (psychogenic non-epileptic seizures); with anaesthesia or sensory loss; with special sensory symptom (visual, olfactory or hearing disturbance); with mixed symptoms. Also acute (under 6 months) or persistent (6 months or more), and with or without psychological stressor . Specifiers Symptom type : with weakness or paralysis; with abnormal movement; with swallowing symptoms; with speech symptom; with attacks or seizures ; with anaesthesia or sensory loss; with special sensory symptom; with mixed symptoms. The type sets the code: F44.4 for weakness, movement, swallowing or speech, F44.5 for attacks or seizures, F44.6 for anaesthesia or special sensory symptoms, F44.7 for mixed. Course: acute episode (symptoms present under 6 months) or persistent (6 months or more). Stressor: with psychological stressor (specify the stressor) or without psychological stressor . Numbers Incidence of persistent conversion symptoms about 2 to 5 per 100,000 per year; symptoms are seen in roughly 5 percent of referrals to neurology clinics. Two to three times more common in women . La belle indifference , a bland lack of concern about the deficit, is described classically but is not a criterion and has poor diagnostic value , which is exactly why it is asked. A history of a preceding stressor is also no longer required. Course Onset can occur at any point in life: non-epileptic attacks peak in the third decade and motor symptoms in the fourth . Symptoms may be transient or persistent, and prognosis is better in younger children than in adolescents and adults. Short duration of symptoms and acceptance of the diagnosis predict a good outcome; maladaptive personality traits, comorbid physical disease and receipt of disability benefits predict a poor one. Kaplan and Sadock add acute onset, a clearly identifiable stressor and early treatment as good signs, and note that paralysis, aphonia and blindness carry a better prognosis than tremor and seizures . Comorbidity Depressive and anxiety disorders, PTSD, dissociative disorders (which co-occur frequently), personality disorders, and genuine neurological disease, which co-occurs often, so the presence of epilepsy does not exclude psychogenic non-epileptic seizures. Differential Neurological disease , which requires proper examination, and the historically high misdiagnosis rate has fallen to around 4 percent in modern series. Factitious disorder (deliberate falsification, motive is the sick role). Malingering (deliberate, motive is external gain: compensation, avoiding duty). The distinction from both is that conversion symptoms are not intentionally produced . Somatic symptom disorder (distress about a symptom versus loss of function). Body dysmorphic disorder . Depersonalisation/derealisation . Dissociative disorders . DSM-5 change DSM-IV placed conversion disorder among the somatoform disorders and required that psychological factors (conflicts or stressors) be judged to be associated with the onset, and that the symptom be not intentionally produced or feigned . DSM-5 dropped both requirements: a stressor became a specifier, feigning need not be ruled out, and the emphasis moved to positive clinical findings of incompatibility with neurological disease on examination. It added the name functional neurological symptom disorder in parentheses and replaced DSM-IV's four subtypes (motor, sensory, seizures or convulsions, mixed) with eight symptom types. DSM-5-TR (2022): the order of the names was reversed to Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (Conversion Disorder) ; criteria otherwise unchanged. Psychological Factors Affecting Other Medical Conditions F54 A. A medical symptom or condition (other than a mental disorder) is present. B. Psychological or behavioural factors adversely affect the medical condition in one of four ways: they have influenced the course of the condition, as shown by a close temporal association; they interfere with treatment (poor adherence); they constitute additional well-established health risks; or they influence the underlying pathophysiology, precipitating or exacerbating symptoms or necessitating medical attention. C. Not better explained by another mental disorder. Severity mild to extreme. In DSM-IV, "psychological factors affecting medical condition" sat under Other Conditions That May Be a Focus of Clinical Attention; DSM-5 kept it, added "other" to the name and made it a mental disorder in this chapter. It is the correct label for, say, denial of chest pain delaying treatment, or anxiety worsening asthma. Specifiers Severity: mild , increases medical risk (inconsistent adherence to antihypertensive treatment); moderate , aggravates the underlying medical condition (anxiety aggravating asthma); severe , results in medical hospitalisation or an emergency room visit ; extreme , results in severe, life-threatening risk (ignoring heart attack symptoms). There are no subtypes. Course It can occur at any age , from childhood (where parents or school help corroborate the history) to late life (for example, the stress of caring for an ill spouse). The course follows the medical condition it affects, and the psychological factor may be acute (a stressor that precipitates an asthma attack) or enduring (a habitual coping style of denial, or chronic non-adherence). Prognosis depends on the severity of the medical illness and on how far the factor can be changed, which is why the factor itself, not a separate psychiatric syndrome, is the target of treatment. Comorbidity Depressive and anxiety disorders, adjustment disorder, and the personality traits (hostility, denial, avoidance) that drive the non-adherence. The medical condition itself is the other half of the diagnosis, so cardiovascular disease, asthma, diabetes and cancer are the usual settings. Differential Somatic symptom disorder (there the psychological features attach to symptoms, here they attach to a diagnosed medical condition and worsen it). Adjustment disorder (the medical illness is the stressor causing a psychiatric response, rather than psychological factors worsening the illness). Illness anxiety disorder . DSM-5 change In DSM-IV, psychological factors affecting medical condition was not a mental disorder : it sat in Other Conditions That May Be a Focus of Clinical Attention , with six named types chosen by the kind of factor (mental disorder, psychological symptoms, personality traits or coping style, maladaptive health behaviours, stress-related physiological response, other). DSM-5 made it a mental disorder in the new Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders chapter, renamed it psychological factors affecting other medical conditions, dropped the six types and added the mild to extreme severity specifier. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Factitious Disorder F68.10, imposed on another F68.A Factitious disorder imposed on self. (A) Falsification of physical or psychological signs or symptoms, or induction of injury or disease, associated with identified deception . (B) The person presents themselves to others as ill, impaired or injured. (C) The deceptive behaviour is evident even in the absence of obvious external rewards . (D) Not better explained by another mental disorder such as delusional disorder or another psychotic disorder. Specify single episode or recurrent episodes. Factitious disorder imposed on another (previously factitious disorder by proxy, and the older lay term Munchausen syndrome by proxy). Falsification or induction in another person , associated with identified deception. Note the critical coding rule: the perpetrator, not the victim, receives the diagnosis . The victim is given an abuse diagnosis code. Specifiers Both forms take the same course specifier: single episode or recurrent episodes (two or more events of falsification of illness and/or induction of injury). There are no subtypes or severity ratings; DSM-IV's subtypes by predominantly psychological, predominantly physical, or combined signs and symptoms were dropped. Numbers Prevalence unknown, estimated about 1 percent of hospital inpatients. Commonest in women in the imposed-on-self form and in mothers in the imposed-on-another form; healthcare workers are over-represented. Course Onset is usually in early adulthood , often after a hospitalisation for a medical condition or mental disorder; the imposed-on-another form may begin after the hospitalisation of the person's child or other dependant. The usual course is intermittent episodes ; a single episode, or a persistent unremitting course, is less common. The severe chronic form with wandering between hospitals and pathological lying ( Munchausen syndrome ) has a poor prognosis: these patients rarely accept psychiatric treatment and often leave against medical advice when confronted. In the imposed-on-another form the first priority is the victim's safety . Comorbidity Depressive disorders, substance use disorders, and personality disorders, especially borderline , which is the commonest comorbid personality diagnosis in the imposed-on-self form. In the imposed-on-another form, personality pathology in the perpetrator and genuine iatrogenic harm in the victim. Differential Malingering , which is not a mental disorder in DSM-5 but a V code, "malingering", listed among other conditions that may be a focus of clinical attention. The line is motive: factitious disorder is driven by the internal need to occupy the sick role, malingering is driven by an obvious external incentive (money, drugs, avoiding work, military duty or prosecution). Somatic symptom disorder and conversion disorder , where symptoms are not intentionally produced . Borderline personality disorder , where self-injury is present but is not accompanied by deception about its origin. DSM-5 change DSM-IV gave factitious disorder a chapter of its own , with subtypes by predominant psychological or physical symptoms, and required that the motivation be to assume the sick role . Factitious disorder by proxy appeared only in the DSM-IV appendix of research criteria. DSM-5 moved factitious disorder into Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders , split it into imposed on self and imposed on another (bringing the proxy form into the main text), and replaced inferences about motive with objectively identified deception , evident even without obvious external reward. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; the imposed-on-another form carries its own code, F68.A (introduced in the 2018 ICD-10-CM update), while imposed on self stays F68.10. 11. Feeding and eating disorders DSM-5 merged the childhood feeding disorders with the adult eating disorders into one chapter, added binge-eating disorder as a full diagnosis (it was in the DSM-IV appendix), created avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder to replace "feeding disorder of infancy or early childhood", and loosened anorexia and bulimia in specific ways that are examined constantly. Pica F98.3 children, F50.89 adults A. Persistent eating of non-nutritive, non-food substances over a period of at least 1 month (paper, soap, cloth, hair, string, wool, soil, chalk, talcum powder, paint, gum, metal, pebbles, charcoal, ash, clay, starch, ice). B. The eating is inappropriate to the developmental level of the individual (so it is not diagnosed under a developmental age of about 2 years, when mouthing is normal). C. The eating behaviour is not part of a culturally supported or socially normative practice , which matters because geophagia is normative in some communities. D. If it occurs in the context of another mental disorder (intellectual disability, autism, schizophrenia) or medical condition (pregnancy), it is sufficiently severe to warrant additional clinical attention. Note that unlike the other eating disorders, pica can be diagnosed alongside anorexia and bulimia. Specifiers One specifier only: in remission , used when full criteria were previously met but have not been met for a sustained period of time. DSM-5-TR gives no subtypes and no severity ratings for pica. Age is handled by the code, not by a specifier: there is one ICD-10-CM code for children and another for adults. Course Onset is most often in childhood , though it can begin in adolescence or adulthood. In otherwise typically developing children it usually remits spontaneously with age, whereas in adults it is more likely to occur with intellectual disability , autism or another mental disorder, where it can persist for years; in pregnancy , cravings (for chalk, clay or ice) usually end with the pregnancy. The course can be protracted and the outcome depends on what is eaten: complications include lead poisoning from paint, bezoars (a trichobezoar from swallowed hair) with intestinal obstruction or perforation, parasitic infection from soil, and dental damage. Pica can be fatal , depending on the substance. Comorbidity Intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia, trichotillomania (with trichophagia), excoriation disorder. Medically, iron-deficiency anaemia and zinc deficiency, and in pregnancy. Differential Anorexia nervosa (eating non-food to control appetite). Factitious disorder (swallowing objects for the sick role). Non-suicidal self-injury . Normative cultural practice , which is Criterion C. DSM-5 change DSM-IV placed pica among the feeding and eating disorders of infancy or early childhood , in the chapter for disorders usually first diagnosed in childhood. DSM-5 merged those with the adult eating disorders into one Feeding and Eating Disorders chapter, so pica can be diagnosed at any age . The criteria were kept, with non-food added to non-nutritive, pregnancy and other medical conditions added to the context clause in Criterion D, and an in remission specifier added. The DSM-5 chapter makes the other feeding and eating diagnoses mutually exclusive within an episode, with pica the one exception . DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Rumination Disorder F98.21 A. Repeated regurgitation of food over a period of at least 1 month . Regurgitated food may be re-chewed, re-swallowed or spat out. B. The repeated regurgitation is not attributable to an associated gastrointestinal or other medical condition such as gastro-oesophageal reflux or pyloric stenosis. C. The eating disturbance does not occur exclusively during anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge-eating disorder or ARFID. D. If it occurs in the context of another mental disorder such as intellectual disability, it is severe enough to warrant additional clinical attention. Specifiers One specifier only: in remission , used when full criteria were previously met but have not been met for a sustained period of time. DSM-5-TR gives no subtypes and no severity ratings for rumination disorder. Course Onset can be at any age, but in infants it typically begins between 3 and 12 months . In infants it frequently remits spontaneously , but the course can be protracted, and the resulting malnutrition, weight loss and growth delay make it potentially fatal, particularly in infancy . In older children and adults it may be episodic or continuous until treated . In infants, and in people with intellectual disability or other neurodevelopmental disorders, the regurgitation seems to serve a self-soothing or self-stimulating function, which helps to explain why it persists. Comorbidity Intellectual disability, other neurodevelopmental disorders, and, in infants, neglect and understimulation. In older children and adults it co-occurs with anxiety and with the other feeding and eating disorders. Differential Gastrointestinal conditions (reflux, gastroparesis, pyloric stenosis), which are Criterion B. Bulimia nervosa (regurgitation there is part of purging after a binge, in the service of weight control). DSM-5 change DSM-IV listed rumination disorder among the feeding and eating disorders of infancy or early childhood . DSM-5 moved it into the single Feeding and Eating Disorders chapter so that it can be diagnosed at any age , stated that regurgitated food may be re-chewed, re-swallowed or spat out , extended the Criterion C exclusion to binge-eating disorder and ARFID as well as anorexia and bulimia, and added an in remission specifier. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID) F50.82 In plain language. The person does not eat enough, but not because of any concern about weight or shape. That last clause is the whole diagnosis. New in DSM-5, replacing DSM-IV's feeding disorder of infancy or early childhood, and applicable at any age. A. An eating or feeding disturbance, for example apparent lack of interest in eating or food, avoidance based on the sensory characteristics of food, or concern about aversive consequences of eating (fear of choking or vomiting after a choking episode), that persistently fails to meet appropriate nutritional and/or energy needs, associated with 1 or more of 4 : significant weight loss or failure to achieve expected weight gain or faltering growth in children; significant nutritional deficiency ; dependence on enteral feeding or oral nutritional supplements ; marked interference with psychosocial functioning . B. Not better explained by lack of available food or by an associated culturally sanctioned practice (so famine, poverty and religious fasting are excluded). C. The disturbance does not occur exclusively during anorexia or bulimia , and there is no evidence of a disturbance in the way one's body weight or shape is experienced . D. Not attributable to a concurrent medical condition or better explained by another mental disorder; where it occurs alongside one, it exceeds what is routinely associated and warrants additional clinical attention. Specifiers One specifier only: in remission , used when full criteria were previously met but have not been met for a sustained period of time. There are no severity ratings, and the three presentations named in Criterion A ( apparent lack of interest in eating or food, avoidance based on sensory characteristics , and concern about aversive consequences ) are examples, not formal subtypes . Course Restriction from lack of interest in eating usually begins in infancy or early childhood , and sensory-based avoidance usually appears in the first decade; both can persist into adulthood. Avoidance driven by fear of aversive consequences (choking, vomiting) can begin at any age , often abruptly after a frightening episode. Long-term data are scant, but sensory-based restriction tends to be stable and long-standing , and adults who still have it may function relatively normally. There is no good evidence that ARFID leads on to anorexia nervosa or another eating disorder. Comorbidity Anxiety disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder, autism spectrum disorder (the sensory-based presentation in particular), ADHD, and intellectual disability. Differential Anorexia nervosa , settled by Criterion C: no body-image disturbance and no fear of fatness in ARFID. Specific phobia of choking or vomiting, which can be an alternative label when the food restriction is not the focus. Depression and psychotic disorders with reduced appetite. Normal picky eating , which is common and does not cause nutritional or psychosocial harm. Medical causes: coeliac disease, food allergy, oesophageal disorders, inflammatory bowel disease. DSM-5 change New in DSM-5. It replaced and broadened DSM-IV's feeding disorder of infancy or early childhood , which required onset before age 6 and a persistent failure to eat adequately with failure to gain weight or significant weight loss over at least 1 month. ARFID has no age limit , does not require weight loss (significant nutritional deficiency, dependence on enteral feeding or supplements, or marked psychosocial interference are each enough), and is separated from anorexia by the absence of any disturbance in how body weight or shape is experienced . DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Anorexia Nervosa F50.01 restricting, F50.02 binge-eating/purging A. Restriction of energy intake relative to requirements, leading to a significantly low body weight in the context of age, sex, developmental trajectory and physical health. Significantly low weight is defined as less than minimally normal, or, for children and adolescents, less than that minimally expected. B. Intense fear of gaining weight or of becoming fat, or persistent behaviour that interferes with weight gain , even though at a significantly low weight. That second clause is a DSM-5 addition, added because many patients, particularly in Asian samples, deny the fear but act on it. C. Disturbance in the way one's body weight or shape is experienced, undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation, or persistent lack of recognition of the seriousness of the current low body weight. DSM-5 removed the amenorrhoea criterion that DSM-IV required (three consecutive missed cycles), because it excluded males, premenarchal girls, postmenopausal women and women on hormonal contraceptives, and because those who met all criteria except amenorrhoea did not differ clinically. This deletion is the most examined single fact about anorexia. Subtypes and severity Restricting type : during the last 3 months, no recurrent episodes of binge eating or purging; weight loss is accomplished by dieting, fasting and/or excessive exercise. Binge-eating/purging type : during the last 3 months, recurrent episodes of binge eating or purging (self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives, diuretics or enemas). Severity for adults is by BMI : mild BMI at or above 17 , moderate 16 to 16.99 , severe 15 to 15.99 , extreme below 15 . Also in partial or full remission. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 0.4 percent among young females; female to male about 10:1. Peak onset in adolescence and young adulthood; onset before puberty or after 40 is unusual. It has one of the highest mortality rates of any mental disorder , with a crude mortality rate around 5 percent per decade, from medical complications and from suicide. Physical signs to be able to list: amenorrhoea, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, lanugo hair, dry skin, hypercarotenaemia, osteopenia, leukopenia, raised cortisol, low T3, and in purging patients hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, dental enamel erosion, parotid enlargement and Russell's sign (calluses on the dorsum of the hand). Watch for refeeding syndrome , above all hypophosphataemia, on rapid nutritional restoration. Course Usually begins in adolescence or young adulthood , often after a period of changed eating or a stressful life event such as leaving home. The course is highly variable: some recover after a single episode , some fluctuate between weight restoration and relapse, and some run a chronic course over many years; most remit within about 5 years of presentation, and in long-term follow-up roughly half recover fully, a third improve with residual symptoms and a fifth stay chronically ill. Crossover from the restricting to the binge-eating/purging type is common, and a minority cross over to bulimia nervosa. Worse outcome goes with later onset, longer duration, lower weight, purging and comorbidity , while adolescent onset and a short duration before treatment predict a better outcome. Comorbidity Major depressive disorder (very high), obsessive-compulsive disorder (especially the restricting type), social anxiety disorder, alcohol and substance use disorders (especially binge-purge type), and personality disorders (obsessive-compulsive with restricting, borderline with binge-purge). Differential Bulimia nervosa , and the rule to state is simple: if criteria for anorexia are met, anorexia takes precedence , so a person who binges and purges but is significantly underweight has anorexia, binge-eating/purging type, not bulimia. ARFID (no body-image disturbance). Avoidant, depressive or psychotic causes of weight loss . Body dysmorphic disorder . Medical causes of weight loss: coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, hyperthyroidism, malignancy, tuberculosis, HIV, superior mesenteric artery syndrome. DSM-5 change DSM-5 deleted the amenorrhoea criterion . It rewrote Criterion A from refusal to maintain a minimally normal body weight, with its guideline of less than 85 percent of expected weight , to restriction of energy intake leading to a significantly low body weight, so both the word refusal (which implies intent) and the numerical cut-off went. Criterion B gained or persistent behaviour that interferes with weight gain . The two subtypes are now judged over the last 3 months , and BMI-based severity and partial and full remission specifiers were added. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Bulimia Nervosa F50.2 A. Recurrent episodes of binge eating , defined by both: eating, in a discrete period (for example within any 2-hour period), an amount of food that is definitely larger than what most individuals would eat in a similar period under similar circumstances; and a sense of lack of control over eating during the episode. B. Recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviours to prevent weight gain: self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives, diuretics or other medications, fasting, or excessive exercise. C. Both the binge eating and the compensatory behaviours occur, on average, at least once a week for 3 months . DSM-IV required twice a week for 3 months, so the frequency threshold was halved in DSM-5. That halving is examined. D. Self-evaluation is unduly influenced by body shape and weight. E. The disturbance does not occur exclusively during episodes of anorexia nervosa. Severity By average number of episodes of inappropriate compensatory behaviour per week: mild 1 to 3, moderate 4 to 7, severe 8 to 13, extreme 14 or more . DSM-5 also deleted the purging and non-purging subtypes . Numbers 12-month prevalence 1 to 1.5 percent among young females; female to male about 10:1. Peak onset in late adolescence and young adulthood, slightly later than anorexia. Weight is typically normal or overweight , which is why it goes undetected for years. Crude mortality about 2 percent per decade. Course Usually begins in adolescence or young adulthood ; onset before puberty or after 40 is uncommon, and the binge eating frequently starts during or after a diet . The course may be chronic or intermittent , with remissions alternating with recurrences, and disturbed eating persists for several years in many clinic patients, although over long-term follow-up symptoms diminish in many people, with or without treatment. Remission lasting more than 1 year predicts a better long-term outcome. Crossover to anorexia nervosa occurs in a minority ( 10 to 15 percent ), and some people keep bingeing but stop compensating, so that they then meet criteria for binge-eating disorder. Comorbidity Depressive and bipolar disorders, anxiety disorders, substance use disorders in about 30 percent (alcohol and stimulants), and borderline personality disorder in a substantial minority. Self-harm and suicide risk are elevated. Differential Anorexia nervosa, binge-eating/purging type , distinguished by significantly low body weight, and anorexia takes precedence. Binge-eating disorder (binges without compensatory behaviour). Kleine-Levin syndrome and other neurological causes of hyperphagia. Major depressive disorder with atypical features (overeating without the loss-of-control quality and without compensation). Borderline personality disorder , where binge eating may be one of several impulsive behaviours. DSM-5 change DSM-5 halved the frequency threshold from twice a week to once a week for 3 months and deleted the purging and non-purging subtypes . It added severity by weekly episodes of compensatory behaviour (mild 1 to 3, moderate 4 to 7, severe 8 to 13, extreme 14 or more) and in partial remission and in full remission specifiers, and bulimia now sits in the combined Feeding and Eating Disorders chapter. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Binge-Eating Disorder F50.81 In plain language. Binges without the compensating. Promoted from the DSM-IV research appendix to a full DSM-5 diagnosis, which is the fact examiners want. A. Recurrent episodes of binge eating, defined exactly as in bulimia (large amount, discrete period, loss of control). B. The binge-eating episodes are associated with 3 or more of 5 : eating much more rapidly than normal; eating until feeling uncomfortably full; eating large amounts of food when not feeling physically hungry; eating alone because of feeling embarrassed by how much one is eating; feeling disgusted with oneself, depressed, or very guilty afterward. C. Marked distress regarding binge eating is present. D. The binge eating occurs, on average, at least once a week for 3 months . E. The binge eating is not associated with recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviour and does not occur exclusively during bulimia nervosa or anorexia nervosa. Severity By binge episodes per week: mild 1 to 3, moderate 4 to 7, severe 8 to 13, extreme 14 or more . Numbers 12-month prevalence about 1.6 percent in adult females and 0.8 percent in adult males, so it is the commonest eating disorder and has the least skewed sex ratio (roughly 2:1 rather than 10:1). It occurs across normal-weight, overweight and obese individuals. Obesity is not a mental disorder in DSM-5 and is not the same as binge-eating disorder, a distinction that gets tested. Course Typically begins in adolescence or young adulthood , though it can start later, and people seeking treatment are usually older than those with anorexia or bulimia. In bulimia, dieting usually comes before the binges; in many people with binge-eating disorder it is the other way round, the binge eating comes first and dieting follows . The course is relatively persistent , comparable to bulimia in severity and duration, but remission rates are higher than for anorexia or bulimia, both naturally and with treatment. Crossover to other eating disorders is uncommon . Comorbidity Bipolar disorders, depressive disorders, anxiety disorders and, to a lesser degree, substance use disorders. Medically: obesity, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes. Differential Bulimia nervosa (compensatory behaviour present). Obesity without binge eating , where overeating is not in discrete episodes and lacks the loss-of-control quality and the distress. Major depressive disorder with atypical features . Bipolar disorder in an episode with increased appetite. Prader-Willi syndrome and other medical hyperphagia. DSM-5 change DSM-IV had binge-eating disorder only in Appendix B (criteria sets for further study), so in practice it was diagnosed as eating disorder not otherwise specified. DSM-5 made it a full diagnosis , lowered the threshold from at least 2 days a week for 6 months to at least once a week for 3 months (counting episodes rather than days), and added severity and remission specifiers. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. 12. Elimination disorders Enuresis F98.0 A. Repeated voiding of urine into bed or clothes, whether involuntary or intentional. B. The behaviour is clinically significant, shown by a frequency of at least twice a week for at least 3 consecutive months , or by clinically significant distress or impairment. C. Chronological age is at least 5 (or the equivalent developmental level). D. Not attributable to a substance (a diuretic, an antipsychotic) or another medical condition (diabetes, spina bifida, a seizure disorder). Specify: nocturnal only (the commonest, "monosymptomatic enuresis"), diurnal only (also called urinary incontinence), or nocturnal and diurnal . Primary (continence never achieved) and secondary (onset after a period of established continence) are course types described in the text, not specifiers. Specifiers Nocturnal only : passage of urine only during night-time sleep; the commonest subtype, also called monosymptomatic enuresis . Diurnal only : passage of urine during waking hours, also called urinary incontinence ; it is commoner in girls and is divided into an urge incontinence group (sudden urgency, detrusor instability) and a voiding postponement group (the child consciously defers the urge until wetting results). Nocturnal and diurnal : a combination of the two, also called non-monosymptomatic enuresis . There is no severity specifier. Primary and secondary are course types described in the DSM-5-TR text, not formal specifiers. Numbers Prevalence about 5 to 10 percent at age 5, 3 to 5 percent at age 10, and about 1 percent at 15 and above. Spontaneous remission is roughly 5 to 10 percent per year. Commoner in boys for the nocturnal form. Treatment of choice is the bell-and-pad urine alarm (classical conditioning), with desmopressin as pharmacological backup. Course Primary enuresis (continence never established) is, by definition, present from age 5; secondary enuresis (onset after a period of established continence) most often begins between 5 and 8 years , frequently after a psychosocial stressor, but can start at any age. The two types do not differ in their rates of comorbid mental disorders. The natural course is steady spontaneous remission , so most children are dry by adolescence , and diurnal enuresis is uncommon after age 9. Treatment shortens the course: the bell-and-pad alarm gives the more durable result, whereas relapse is common when desmopressin is stopped. Comorbidity Encopresis, sleepwalking and sleep terrors, ADHD, and developmental delays. Secondary enuresis frequently follows a psychosocial stressor such as the birth of a sibling, school entry, or family disruption. Differential Urinary tract infection, diabetes mellitus and insipidus, seizure disorder, neurogenic bladder, structural urological abnormalities, and obstructive sleep apnoea, all Criterion D. DSM-5 change DSM-5 created a new stand-alone chapter, Elimination Disorders , for enuresis and encopresis, which DSM-IV had placed among the disorders usually first diagnosed in infancy, childhood or adolescence. The criteria themselves were not significantly changed : the same age floor of 5, the same frequency of twice a week for 3 consecutive months (or distress or impairment), and the same three subtypes. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Encopresis F98.1 A. Repeated passage of faeces into inappropriate places (clothing, floor), whether involuntary or intentional. B. At least one such event per month for at least 3 months . C. Chronological age is at least 4 (or the equivalent developmental level). D. Not attributable to a substance (laxatives) or another medical condition except through a mechanism involving constipation. Specify: with constipation and overflow incontinence (the commoner form, with a palpable faecal mass and loose overflow soiling), or without constipation and overflow incontinence (more often associated with oppositional defiant disorder or conduct disorder). Specifiers With constipation and overflow incontinence : there is evidence of constipation on examination or by history. This is the commoner form; the faeces are typically poorly formed, leakage ranges from occasional to continuous and happens mostly by day, and the soiling resolves once the constipation is treated . Without constipation and overflow incontinence : no evidence of constipation; the faeces are usually of normal form, soiling is intermittent, and stool may be deposited in a prominent place, which links this type with oppositional defiant disorder or conduct disorder . There is no severity specifier, and primary versus secondary encopresis is a course distinction in the text, not a specifier. Numbers About 1 percent of 5-year-olds; more common in males . Note the two age floors: enuresis 5, encopresis 4. Course Primary encopresis means faecal continence was never established; secondary means soiling began after a period of continence, often after a stressor such as starting school or the birth of a sibling. Inadequate or inconsistent toilet training and psychosocial stress predispose to it, and in the constipation type a cycle of painful defecation, withholding, rectal distension and loss of rectal sensation keeps it going. Encopresis can persist for years with intermittent exacerbations , but it rarely continues beyond adolescence. Outcome is better in the constipation type once the bowel is cleared and regular toileting is established, and worse when the soiling is deliberate and part of oppositional or conduct problems. Comorbidity Enuresis, which co-occurs frequently, plus oppositional defiant disorder and conduct disorder in the without-constipation form, and ADHD. Chronic constipation with painful defecation is the usual physical driver, and shame and social withdrawal follow. Differential Hirschsprung's disease, hypothyroidism, anal fissure with retention, spinal cord lesions, and dietary causes of chronic constipation. DSM-5 change Moved with enuresis into the new Elimination Disorders chapter in DSM-5; DSM-IV had it among the disorders usually first diagnosed in infancy, childhood or adolescence. The criteria were not significantly changed : age at least 4, at least one event a month for at least 3 months, and the same two subtypes, with and without constipation and overflow incontinence . DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. 13. Sleep-wake disorders DSM-5 abandoned DSM-IV's split into primary sleep disorders, sleep disorders related to another mental disorder, and those due to a general medical condition, because that split forced a causal judgment clinicians could not reliably make. The DSM-5 approach is to diagnose the sleep disorder in its own right alongside any coexisting condition, on the reasoning that insomnia and depression have a bidirectional relationship and that the sleep problem needs treating either way. Say that in an essay. Insomnia Disorder F51.01 A. A predominant complaint of dissatisfaction with sleep quantity or quality, associated with 1 or more of 3 : difficulty initiating sleep; difficulty maintaining sleep, with frequent awakenings or problems returning to sleep; early-morning awakening with inability to return to sleep. B. Clinically significant distress or impairment. C. The sleep difficulty occurs at least 3 nights per week . D. Present for at least 3 months . E. Occurs despite adequate opportunity for sleep. F. Not better explained by, and does not occur exclusively during, another sleep-wake disorder. G. Not attributable to a substance. H. Coexisting mental disorders and medical conditions do not adequately explain the predominant complaint. Specify: with non-sleep disorder mental comorbidity, with other medical comorbidity, with other sleep disorder; and episodic (1 to 3 months), persistent (3 months or more), recurrent (two or more episodes within a year). Specifiers Comorbidity specifiers: with non-sleep disorder mental comorbidity (including substance use disorders), with other medical comorbidity , and with other sleep disorder . Course specifiers: episodic , symptoms lasting at least 1 month but less than 3 months; persistent , symptoms lasting 3 months or longer; recurrent , two or more episodes within the space of 1 year. There is no severity specifier. Because the full diagnosis needs 3 months, insomnia of under 3 months that otherwise meets the criteria (acute or short-term insomnia) is coded as other specified insomnia disorder . Numbers The exam numbers are 3 nights a week for 3 months . About one third of adults report insomnia symptoms, 10 to 15 percent have daytime impairment, and 6 to 10 percent meet full criteria. Commoner in women (about 1.44:1) and increases with age. First-line treatment is CBT-I (stimulus control, sleep restriction, sleep hygiene, cognitive restructuring, relaxation), not hypnotics. Course Insomnia can begin at any age, but the first episode is most common in young adulthood ; in women new-onset insomnia often appears at menopause and may outlast the other menopausal symptoms, and late-life onset usually accompanies other health problems. It may be situational (days to a few weeks, resolving with the stressor), episodic and recurrent with stressful events, or persistent , with chronicity rates of about 45 to 75 percent over 1 to 7 years of follow-up. Persistence is explained by perpetuating factors in Spielman's 3P model (predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating): conditioned arousal in bed, worry about sleep, and habits such as napping and spending longer in bed. Persistent insomnia raises the later risk of major depressive disorder , hypertension and myocardial infarction. Comorbidity Depressive, bipolar and anxiety disorders (insomnia is both a risk factor for and a residual symptom of depression), substance use disorders, and medical conditions with pain. Differential Normal sleep variation and short sleepers . Situational or acute insomnia (under 3 months). Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders , particularly delayed sleep phase type, where the person sleeps well if allowed their own schedule. Restless legs syndrome and breathing-related sleep disorders . Substance-induced sleep disorder (caffeine, alcohol rebound, stimulants). Narcolepsy . DSM-5 change DSM-IV's primary insomnia was renamed insomnia disorder , and DSM-IV's insomnia related to another mental disorder and sleep disorder due to a general medical condition (insomnia type) were dropped: the primary versus secondary distinction was abandoned , so insomnia is diagnosed in its own right and coexisting conditions are recorded with specifiers. The minimum duration rose from 1 month to 3 months , a frequency of 3 nights a week was added, early-morning awakening was named as a symptom, and non-restorative sleep on its own no longer qualifies. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Hypersomnolence Disorder and Narcolepsy F51.11, G47.4xx Hypersomnolence disorder. Self-reported excessive sleepiness despite a main sleep period of at least 7 hours, with at least one of: recurrent periods of sleep or lapses into sleep within the same day; a prolonged main sleep episode of more than 9 hours per day that is non-restorative; difficulty being fully awake after abrupt awakening ( sleep inertia or sleep drunkenness). Occurs at least 3 times per week for at least 3 months , with distress or impairment. Narcolepsy. Recurrent periods of an irrepressible need to sleep, lapsing into sleep, or napping occurring within the same day, at least 3 times per week over the past 3 months , plus at least 1 of 3 : (1) episodes of cataplexy , meaning, in long-standing disease, brief episodes of sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone with retained consciousness precipitated by laughter or joking, or, in children or within 6 months of onset, spontaneous grimaces or jaw-opening episodes with tongue thrusting or global hypotonia without an emotional trigger; (2) hypocretin-1 (orexin) deficiency in CSF, at or below one third of control values; (3) nocturnal polysomnography showing REM sleep latency of 15 minutes or less, or a multiple sleep latency test with mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less and two or more sleep-onset REM periods. Specifiers Hypersomnolence disorder : specify with mental disorder , with medical condition , or with another sleep disorder ; acute (less than 1 month), subacute (1 to 3 months) or persistent (more than 3 months); and severity by the number of days a week with difficulty maintaining daytime alertness, mild 1 to 2 , moderate 3 to 4 , severe 5 to 7 . Narcolepsy subtypes in DSM-5-TR: with cataplexy or hypocretin deficiency (type 1) ; without cataplexy and either without hypocretin deficiency or hypocretin unmeasured (type 2) ; and each of these due to a medical condition . Narcolepsy severity: mild , cataplexy less than once a week and naps needed only once or twice a day; moderate , cataplexy once daily or every few days, disturbed night sleep and multiple daily naps; severe , drug-resistant cataplexy with multiple attacks a day, nearly constant sleepiness and disturbed night sleep. Numbers Narcolepsy prevalence about 0.02 to 0.04 percent. Typical onset in adolescence or the early twenties. Strong association with HLA-DQB1*06:02 and with loss of hypothalamic hypocretin-producing neurons. The classic tetrad to name: excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic (or hypnopompic) hallucinations . Note that only sleepiness plus one of the three objective or cataplexy criteria is required; sleep paralysis and hallucinations are not criteria in DSM-5. Course Hypersomnolence disorder usually begins in late adolescence or early adulthood (mean onset 17 to 24 years), builds up gradually over weeks to months, and then runs a persistent and stable course unless treated; people are typically diagnosed 10 to 15 years after the first symptoms. Narcolepsy usually begins in childhood, adolescence or young adulthood, with suggested peaks at 15 to 25 and 30 to 35 years, and onset may be abrupt or gradual. Sleepiness is nearly always the first symptom , and cataplexy follows, usually within the first few years. Once established, narcolepsy is lifelong , although severity is highest after abrupt onset in children and lessens with age or treatment, so that cataplexy occasionally disappears. Comorbidity Depressive disorders (which frequently precede or follow hypersomnolence), bipolar disorder, substance use disorders, and, in narcolepsy specifically, obesity, obstructive sleep apnoea, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression and anxiety, plus the social impairment that comes from cataplexy in public. Differential Sleep deprivation and insufficient sleep syndrome , the commonest cause of daytime sleepiness. Obstructive sleep apnoea hypopnoea . Major depressive disorder with hypersomnia . Substance effects . Kleine-Levin syndrome (recurrent hypersomnia with hyperphagia and hypersexuality in young males). Cataplexy specifically must be distinguished from syncope, atonic seizures and conversion . DSM-5 change DSM-IV's primary hypersomnia was renamed hypersomnolence disorder , its primary versus secondary split was replaced by specifiers for coexisting conditions, and the duration rose from 1 month to 3 months (at least 3 times a week). Narcolepsy was redefined around its biology: DSM-IV required daily sleep attacks for 3 months plus cataplexy or REM intrusions (hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations, sleep paralysis), whereas DSM-5 requires sleepiness plus cataplexy, hypocretin deficiency , or polysomnography/MSLT evidence, so sleep paralysis and hallucinations are no longer criteria . DSM-5 also added narcolepsy subtypes and severity ratings. DSM-5-TR (2022) regrouped the narcolepsy subtypes, in line with ICSD-3, into type 1 (with cataplexy or hypocretin deficiency) and type 2 (without), each also codable as due to a medical condition. Breathing-Related Sleep Disorders, Circadian Rhythm Disorders, and Parasomnias Obstructive Sleep Apnoea Hypopnoea. Either polysomnographic evidence of at least 5 obstructive apnoeas or hypopnoeas per hour of sleep plus nocturnal breathing symptoms (snoring, snorting, gasping, breathing pauses) or daytime sleepiness and fatigue; or polysomnographic evidence of 15 or more events per hour regardless of symptoms. Severity by apnoea-hypopnoea index: mild under 15, moderate 15 to 30, severe over 30. Also Central Sleep Apnoea and Sleep-Related Hypoventilation . Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders. A persistent pattern of sleep disruption due to an alteration of the circadian system or a misalignment between the endogenous rhythm and the required schedule. Types: delayed sleep phase (the commonest in adolescents; a familial form exists), advanced sleep phase (older adults), irregular sleep-wake type , non-24-hour sleep-wake type (common in blind individuals), and shift work type . Jet lag type was removed in DSM-5. Non-REM Sleep Arousal Disorders. Recurrent episodes of incomplete awakening from sleep, usually during the first third of the major sleep episode (that is, from slow-wave, N3 sleep), accompanied by either sleepwalking or sleep terrors . The person has no or little dream imagery recalled, is relatively unresponsive during the episode, and has amnesia for it . Sleep terrors involve abrupt terror arousals with a panicky scream, intense fear and autonomic arousal. Nightmare Disorder. Repeated occurrences of extended, extremely dysphoric and well-remembered dreams, usually involving threats to survival, security or physical integrity, generally occurring during the second half of the major sleep episode (that is, from REM sleep). On awakening the person rapidly becomes oriented and alert . REM Sleep Behaviour Disorder. Repeated episodes of arousal during sleep associated with vocalisation and/or complex motor behaviours, arising during REM sleep and therefore usually more than 90 minutes after sleep onset, more frequent in the later portions of the sleep period. Upon awakening the person is completely awake, alert and not confused . Requires either REM sleep without atonia on polysomnography, or a history suggestive of the disorder plus an established synucleinopathy diagnosis. Highly examinable point: RBD is a prodrome of the alpha-synucleinopathies , so a large majority of cases eventually convert to Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies or multiple system atrophy. Restless Legs Syndrome. An urge to move the legs, usually accompanied by or in response to uncomfortable sensations, with all three features: the urge begins or worsens during periods of rest or inactivity; is partially or totally relieved by movement; is worse in the evening or at night. Occurs at least 3 times per week for at least 3 months. Associated with iron deficiency , pregnancy and renal failure. Substance/Medication-Induced Sleep Disorder , with insomnia, daytime sleepiness, parasomnia or mixed types. Specifiers Obstructive sleep apnoea hypopnoea : severity by apnoea-hypopnoea index, mild under 15 , moderate 15 to 30 , severe over 30 . Central sleep apnoea : idiopathic , Cheyne-Stokes breathing , or comorbid with opioid use , with severity graded by the frequency of breathing disturbances and the extent of oxygen desaturation and sleep fragmentation. Sleep-related hypoventilation : idiopathic , congenital central alveolar , or comorbid , with severity graded by the degree of hypoxaemia and hypercarbia during sleep and evidence of end-organ impairment. Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders : the five types plus unspecified ; delayed and advanced phase types may be familial ; all may be episodic (1 to under 3 months), persistent (3 months or longer) or recurrent (two or more episodes within 1 year). Non-REM arousal disorder : sleepwalking type (with sleep-related eating or sleep-related sexual behaviour , sexsomnia) or sleep terror type . Nightmare disorder : during sleep onset ; with an associated non-sleep disorder, medical condition or other sleep disorder; acute (1 month or less), subacute (over 1 and under 6 months), persistent (6 months or more); severity mild under one a week, moderate weekly but not nightly, severe nightly. REM sleep behaviour disorder and restless legs syndrome have no specifiers. Course Obstructive sleep apnoea follows a J-shaped age curve: a first peak at 3 to 8 years , when tonsils and adenoids are large for the airway, a fall in later childhood, then a rise through midlife with weight gain and, in women, after menopause; it is chronic unless treated and may level off after 65. Delayed sleep phase type usually starts in adolescence and can persist for years with exacerbations, advanced sleep phase type usually starts in later adulthood (earlier in familial cases), and shift work type resolves when a normal daytime schedule resumes. Non-REM arousal disorders are commonest in childhood and diminish with age; new onset in an adult should prompt a search for a cause such as obstructive sleep apnoea, nocturnal seizures or medication. Nightmares often begin at 3 to 6 years but peak in prevalence and severity in late adolescence or early adulthood. REM sleep behaviour disorder usually begins after 50 , mostly in men, and is progressive , with most idiopathic cases eventually developing a synucleinopathy, often many years later. Restless legs syndrome usually begins in the second or third decade and becomes more prevalent with age until about 60; familial cases begin younger and progress more slowly. Comorbidity Obstructive sleep apnoea with obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and depression. Circadian disorders with depressive disorders and, in the delayed phase type, adolescence itself. Non-REM arousal disorders with other parasomnias, enuresis and, in adults, obstructive sleep apnoea acting as the arousal trigger. REM sleep behaviour disorder with the alpha-synucleinopathies and with antidepressant use, which can unmask it. Restless legs syndrome with iron deficiency, pregnancy, renal failure, depression and ADHD. The differential that gets asked Sleep terrors versus nightmares. Sleep terrors: first third of the night, non-REM slow-wave sleep, marked autonomic arousal, the person is inconsolable and unresponsive, there is amnesia for the episode, and dream recall is minimal. Nightmares: second half of the night, REM sleep, the person wakes fully and can describe the dream vividly, and there is no amnesia and no confusion. Sleep terrors versus RBD. RBD occurs in REM, later in the night, the behaviour enacts a recalled dream, the person is instantly alert afterwards, and it is a disorder of older men that predicts Parkinson's. Nocturnal panic attacks also wake the person from non-REM sleep, but they are fully alert and there is no amnesia. Nocturnal seizures are stereotyped and brief. DSM-5 change DSM-IV's single breathing-related sleep disorder was split into three: obstructive sleep apnoea hypopnoea , central sleep apnoea and sleep-related hypoventilation , with polysomnographic thresholds. Circadian rhythm sleep disorder became circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders : jet lag type was removed , and advanced sleep phase , irregular sleep-wake and non-24-hour types were added. DSM-IV's separate sleepwalking disorder and sleep terror disorder were merged into non-REM sleep arousal disorders . REM sleep behaviour disorder and restless legs syndrome , previously only examples under parasomnia NOS and dyssomnia NOS, became full diagnoses . DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. 14. Sexual dysfunctions, gender dysphoria, paraphilic disorders Sexual Dysfunctions F52.x In plain language. A problem in the ability to respond sexually or to experience sexual pleasure, that has lasted at least six months and causes distress. DSM-5 made three structural changes: it became gender-specific where the evidence supported that, it added a minimum duration of about 6 months and a frequency requirement of 75 to 100 percent of occasions to almost every dysfunction, and it merged several DSM-IV categories. Delayed Ejaculation. Marked delay in, infrequency of, or absence of ejaculation on almost all or all (75 to 100 percent) partnered sexual occasions, without the person desiring the delay. Erectile Disorder. At least one of three on almost all or all occasions: marked difficulty obtaining an erection, marked difficulty maintaining one until completion, or a marked decrease in erectile rigidity. Female Orgasmic Disorder. Marked delay in, infrequency of, or absence of orgasm, and/or markedly reduced intensity of orgasmic sensations, on almost all or all occasions. Female Sexual Interest/Arousal Disorder. Lack of, or significantly reduced, sexual interest or arousal, shown by at least 3 of 6 : absent or reduced interest in sexual activity; absent or reduced sexual or erotic thoughts or fantasies; no or reduced initiation of sexual activity and typically unreceptive to a partner's attempts to initiate; absent or reduced sexual excitement or pleasure during sexual activity in almost all encounters; absent or reduced sexual interest or arousal in response to any internal or external sexual or erotic cues; absent or reduced genital or non-genital sensations during sexual activity in almost all encounters. This diagnosis merged DSM-IV's female hypoactive sexual desire disorder and female sexual arousal disorder, on the evidence that desire and arousal are not separable in women. Male Hypoactive Sexual Desire Disorder. Persistently or recurrently deficient or absent sexual or erotic thoughts or fantasies and desire for sexual activity, judged by the clinician taking into account age and context. Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disorder. Persistent or recurrent difficulties with 1 or more of 4 : vaginal penetration during intercourse; marked vulvovaginal or pelvic pain during vaginal intercourse or penetration attempts; marked fear or anxiety about vulvovaginal or pelvic pain in anticipation of, during, or as a result of vaginal penetration; marked tensing or tightening of the pelvic floor muscles during attempted vaginal penetration. This merged DSM-IV's vaginismus and dyspareunia , because the two could not be reliably distinguished. That merger is the most-asked fact in this section. Premature (Early) Ejaculation. A persistent or recurrent pattern of ejaculation during partnered sexual activity within approximately 1 minute following vaginal penetration and before the person wishes it, on almost all or all (75 to 100 percent) occasions. Substance/Medication-Induced Sexual Dysfunction , and Other Specified / Unspecified Sexual Dysfunction . All the specific dysfunctions above (not the substance/medication-induced one) require duration of approximately 6 months , clinically significant distress, and that the dysfunction is not better explained by a non-sexual mental disorder, severe relationship distress (partner violence) or other significant stressors, and is not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. Specify: lifelong or acquired; generalised or situational; and severity mild, moderate or severe. DSM-5 deleted the DSM-IV subtypes "due to psychological factors" versus "due to combined factors". Specifiers Every specific dysfunction is specified lifelong (present since the person became sexually active) or acquired (began after a period of relatively normal sexual function), and all except genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder also generalised (not limited to certain partners, situations or types of stimulation) or situational . Female orgasmic disorder adds never experienced an orgasm under any situation . Severity is mild, moderate or severe , rated by the distress the symptoms cause, except in premature (early) ejaculation , which is rated by latency: mild within about 30 seconds to 1 minute of vaginal penetration, moderate within about 15 to 30 seconds, severe before or at the start of sexual activity or within about 15 seconds. Substance/medication-induced sexual dysfunction takes onset specifiers (during intoxication, during withdrawal, after medication use) and severity by the share of sexual occasions affected: mild 25 to 50 percent , moderate 50 to 75 percent , severe 75 percent or more . Numbers The two to remember across the whole group: 6 months minimum duration and 75 to 100 percent of occasions . Sexual aversion disorder was deleted in DSM-5 for lack of evidence and rare use. Course Onset defines the first specifier: lifelong dysfunctions are present from the first sexual experiences, while acquired ones begin after a period of normal function, often with a medical illness, a medication, relationship difficulty or a life stage. Erectile disorder and delayed ejaculation become much more common with age, especially after 50, and acquired erectile disorder is often linked to vascular disease or diabetes, for which it can be an early marker. Lifelong premature (early) ejaculation starts with the first sexual experiences and tends to persist, whereas the acquired form appears later in life, often with erectile problems, prostatitis or thyroid disease. In women, desire and arousal fluctuate with age, relationship and life events (pregnancy, menopause), and the first orgasm can come at any point from before puberty to well into adulthood. Lifelong genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder usually comes to notice at first attempted intercourse, tampon use or gynaecological examination, whereas acquired cases often follow childbirth or menopause. Prognosis with sex therapy (Masters and Johnson's sensate focus , the stop-start and squeeze techniques, graded vaginal dilators) is generally good, and poorer when relationship conflict or depression goes unaddressed. Comorbidity Depressive and anxiety disorders, relationship distress, and, medically, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, prostate surgery, and pelvic floor pathology. Antidepressants, particularly SSRIs, are a leading iatrogenic cause and should always be asked about. Differential Substance and medication effects (SSRIs, antipsychotics, antihypertensives, alcohol, opioids). Another medical condition (diabetic neuropathy, vascular disease, endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, hypogonadism, hyperprolactinaemia). Another mental disorder , especially depression. Relationship distress and interpersonal factors , including partner violence, which are explicit exclusions. Inadequate sexual stimulation and lack of knowledge, which is common and is not a disorder. DSM-5 change DSM-5 split DSM-IV's single Sexual and Gender Identity Disorders chapter into three: Sexual Dysfunctions, Gender Dysphoria and Paraphilic Disorders. It added gender-specific diagnoses where the evidence supported them, added the approximately 6-month duration and, for most, the 75 to 100 percent of occasions threshold, and dropped the due to psychological factors versus due to combined factors subtypes. In women, hypoactive sexual desire disorder and female sexual arousal disorder merged into female sexual interest/arousal disorder , while in men desire problems became male hypoactive sexual desire disorder ; vaginismus and dyspareunia merged into genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder ; sexual aversion disorder was deleted. Male orgasmic disorder was renamed delayed ejaculation , male erectile disorder became erectile disorder , and premature ejaculation became premature (early) ejaculation with a new 1-minute latency criterion. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Gender Dysphoria F64.x In plain language. Distress arising from a marked incongruence between the gender a person experiences themselves to be and the one they were assigned at birth. DSM-5 renamed DSM-IV's Gender Identity Disorder to Gender Dysphoria to shift the diagnostic focus from identity itself to the distress , precisely so that being transgender is not framed as a disorder. That renaming and its rationale is the whole examinable point. In adolescents and adults. A marked incongruence between one's experienced or expressed gender and assigned gender, of at least 6 months duration, with at least 2 of 6 : a marked incongruence between experienced gender and primary and/or secondary sex characteristics; a strong desire to be rid of one's primary and/or secondary sex characteristics; a strong desire for the primary and/or secondary sex characteristics of the other gender; a strong desire to be of the other gender; a strong desire to be treated as the other gender; a strong conviction that one has the typical feelings and reactions of the other gender. Plus clinically significant distress or impairment. In children. Duration at least 6 months, with at least 6 of 8 , and Criterion A1 is mandatory : a strong desire to be of the other gender or an insistence that one is the other gender. The remaining seven cover cross-dressing preference, cross-gender roles in make-believe play, preference for the toys and activities stereotypically used by the other gender, preference for playmates of the other gender, rejection of the toys and activities typical of one's assigned gender, dislike of one's sexual anatomy, and a desire for the primary or secondary sex characteristics matching one's experienced gender. Specify: with a disorder/difference of sex development ; and, for adolescents and adults, posttransition , meaning the person has transitioned to full-time living in the desired gender and has undergone or is preparing for at least one gender-affirming medical procedure. DSM-5-TR updated the language here: "desired gender" became "experienced gender", "cross-sex medical procedure" became "gender-affirming medical procedure", "natal male/female" became "individual assigned male/female at birth". Specifiers With a disorder/difference of sex development (the DSM-5-TR wording; DSM-5 said disorder of sex development), for example congenital adrenal hyperplasia or androgen insensitivity syndrome; the sex-development condition is coded as well. This one is available for both the child and the adolescent/adult criteria. Posttransition , for adolescents and adults only: the individual has transitioned to full-time living in the experienced gender (with or without legal change of gender) and has undergone or is preparing for at least one gender-affirming medical procedure or treatment regimen , namely regular gender-affirming hormone treatment or surgery confirming the experienced gender. Posttransition is used where continuing treatment supports the new gender role, even if the dysphoria itself has eased. There are no severity specifiers . Numbers Prevalence estimates in adults range roughly 0.005 to 0.014 percent for individuals assigned male at birth and 0.002 to 0.003 percent for those assigned female, though these come from clinic attendance and undercount. In children referred to clinics, rates of persistence into adolescence and adulthood have historically been reported as low for those assigned male and higher for those assigned female, but the figures are contested and the DSM-5-TR text is careful about them. Course Two trajectories are described. In early-onset gender dysphoria, gender-nonconforming behaviour and statements usually appear between 2 and 4 years and continue into adolescence and adulthood; in late-onset gender dysphoria, it emerges around puberty or much later in life. Childhood dysphoria does not always persist, and persistence rates differ by assigned sex and are contested (see Numbers), but dysphoria that persists or intensifies in early adolescence, when secondary sex characteristics develop, is much more likely to continue into adulthood. Mental-health outcomes are better with family and social acceptance, and worse with stigma, rejection and discrimination (minority stress), which contribute substantially to the high rates of depression and suicidality. Comorbidity Anxiety and depressive disorders, notably high rates of suicidality, driven substantially by stigma, family rejection and discrimination (the minority stress framework, which DSM-5-TR names). Autism spectrum disorder co-occurs at rates above the population base rate. Differential Non-conformity to gender roles , which is explicitly not a disorder. Transvestic disorder (cross-dressing for sexual arousal, with no incongruence of gender identity). Body dysmorphic disorder . Schizophrenia with delusions of belonging to another gender, which is rare. Other clinical presentations such as the desire for castration or penectomy without a wish to change gender identity, which does not meet the criteria for gender dysphoria. DSM-5 change DSM-5 renamed DSM-IV's Gender Identity Disorder as Gender Dysphoria , moving the focus from identity to distress , and gave it its own chapter, separate from the sexual dysfunctions and paraphilias. Gender replaced sex (assigned gender, experienced gender, or some alternative gender), DSM-IV's two criteria (cross-gender identification and discomfort with one's sex) were merged into one Criterion A, a 6-month duration was added, children and adolescents/adults got separate criteria sets, and in children the strong desire to be the other gender (A1) became mandatory . A physical intersex condition, an exclusion in DSM-IV, became the specifier with a disorder of sex development ; posttransition was added; the sexual-orientation specifier was dropped. DSM-5-TR (2022) changed wording only: desired gender became experienced gender , cross-sex became gender-affirming medical procedure, natal male/female became individual assigned male/female at birth , and the specifier became disorder/difference of sex development . ICD-11 Went further: it removed gender incongruence from the mental disorders chapter altogether and placed it in a new chapter on conditions related to sexual health, in order to retain access to care while removing the mental-illness framing. That contrast between DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 is high-yield. Paraphilic Disorders F65.x In plain language. A paraphilia is an intense and persistent sexual interest in something other than genital stimulation or preparatory fondling with phenotypically normal, physically mature, consenting human partners. A paraphilic disorder is a paraphilia that is currently causing distress or impairment to the individual, or whose satisfaction has entailed personal harm or risk of harm to others . DSM-5's central move was to separate the two: a paraphilia by itself is not a mental disorder . Say that sentence in any answer on this chapter. The eight named disorders: Voyeuristic Disorder (observing an unsuspecting person who is naked, disrobing or engaging in sexual activity; the individual must be at least 18 ); Exhibitionistic Disorder (exposure of one's genitals to an unsuspecting person; specify whether sexually aroused by exposing to prepubertal children, physically mature individuals, or both); Frotteuristic Disorder (touching or rubbing against a non-consenting person); Sexual Masochism Disorder (being humiliated, beaten, bound or otherwise made to suffer; specify with asphyxiophilia); Sexual Sadism Disorder (the physical or psychological suffering of another person); Pedophilic Disorder ; Fetishistic Disorder (use of non-living objects or a highly specific focus on non-genital body parts; the criteria explicitly exclude articles of clothing used in cross-dressing, which would be transvestic disorder, and devices designed for genital stimulation); Transvestic Disorder (cross-dressing; specify with fetishism or with autogynephilia). All require the arousal pattern over a period of at least 6 months , plus either the person having acted on the urges with a non-consenting person, or the urges causing clinically significant distress or impairment. Pedophilic Disorder specifically: over at least 6 months, recurrent, intense sexually arousing fantasies, sexual urges or behaviours involving sexual activity with a prepubescent child or children (generally age 13 or younger) ; the person has acted on these urges, or they cause marked distress or interpersonal difficulty; and the person is at least 16 years old and at least 5 years older than the child. The criteria exclude an individual in late adolescence involved in an ongoing sexual relationship with a 12 or 13 year old. Specify exclusive or non-exclusive type; sexually attracted to males, females, or both; and whether limited to incest. Every paraphilic disorder except pedophilic disorder can be specified in a controlled environment (where opportunity is restricted, for example institutional settings) and in full remission (no distress, impairment or acting out for at least 5 years while in an uncontrolled environment).
