Specifiers Two course specifiers apply to seven of the eight: in a controlled environment (living in an institution or other setting where opportunities to act on the urges are restricted) and in full remission (for at least 5 years in an uncontrolled environment, no distress or impairment and, for the disorders involving non-consenting people, no acting on the urges). Pedophilic disorder takes neither ; instead specify exclusive type (attracted only to children) or non-exclusive type , sexually attracted to males, females or both , and limited to incest . Disorder-specific specifiers: exhibitionistic , aroused by exposing to prepubertal children , to physically mature individuals , or to both ; sexual masochism , with asphyxiophilia (arousal from restricted breathing); fetishistic , body part(s) , non-living object(s) or other ; transvestic , with fetishism (aroused by fabrics, materials or garments) or with autogynephilia (aroused by thoughts or images of oneself as female). Voyeuristic, frotteuristic and sexual sadism disorders have only the two course specifiers. There are no severity ratings . Numbers The three that get asked: pedophilic disorder requires the person to be at least 16 and at least 5 years older than the child, and the child to be generally 13 or younger ; voyeuristic disorder requires the person to be at least 18 ; all require 6 months . Paraphilic disorders are far more common in males; the male to female ratio for most is very high. Course Paraphilic interests usually first appear around puberty or in adolescence , and most of the disorders present in late adolescence or early adulthood. The underlying paraphilia tends to be lifelong (DSM-5 says this explicitly of pedophilia), but the distress, impairment and propensity to act tend to decline with age , in parallel with the general fall in sexual drive. In transvestic disorder the erotic arousal to cross-dressing may fade over time while cross-dressing continues as a comfort behaviour, and some individuals later develop gender dysphoria. Kaplan and Sadock's prognostic factors: a poor prognosis goes with early onset, a high frequency of acts, no guilt or shame, and substance misuse ; a better prognosis goes with a history of conventional sexual relationships alongside the paraphilia, high motivation to change, and self-referral rather than referral by a legal agency. Comorbidity Multiple paraphilias frequently coexist in the same individual. Also substance use disorders, depressive and anxiety disorders, ADHD, and antisocial personality disorder, particularly with the coercive paraphilias. Differential A paraphilia without distress, impairment or harm , which is not a disorder. Conduct disorder and antisocial personality disorder , where the offending is part of a broader antisocial pattern rather than paraphilic arousal. Substance intoxication and major neurocognitive disorder , particularly frontotemporal, where disinhibited sexual behaviour appears late in life without a lifelong pattern. Manic episode . Intellectual disability . Fetishistic versus transvestic disorder is the classic pair: if the clothing is used in cross-dressing, it is transvestic. DSM-5 change DSM-5 gave the paraphilias their own chapter, renamed Paraphilic Disorders , and added disorder to every name (fetishism became fetishistic disorder, pedophilia became pedophilic disorder) to mark the new rule that a paraphilia is necessary but not sufficient : Criterion A identifies the paraphilia and Criterion B (distress, impairment, or harm or risk of harm to others) makes it a disorder. New specifiers were added: in a controlled environment and in full remission (not for pedophilic disorder), with asphyxiophilia , the exhibitionistic target specifiers, and the fetishistic focus specifiers. Transvestic fetishism became transvestic disorder , no longer restricted to heterosexual males, and its DSM-IV specifier with gender dysphoria was replaced by two new ones, with fetishism and with autogynephilia . Fetishistic disorder now includes non-genital body parts (partialism, formerly paraphilia NOS). Proposals for hebephilia and paraphilic coercive disorder were rejected. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. 15. Disruptive, impulse-control and conduct disorders Conditions involving problems in the self-control of emotions and behaviour that violate the rights of others or bring the individual into significant conflict with societal norms or authority figures. DSM-5 placed antisocial personality disorder in this chapter as well as in the personality disorders chapter, dual-listing it, because it belongs conceptually to both. Oppositional Defiant Disorder F91.3 A. A pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behaviour, or vindictiveness lasting at least 6 months , with at least 4 symptoms from any of these three categories, exhibited during interaction with at least one individual who is not a sibling. DSM-5 grouped the eight symptoms into these three types, which is a change from DSM-IV's flat list, and it added the sibling exclusion. Angry/irritable mood: often loses temper; is often touchy or easily annoyed; is often angry and resentful. Argumentative/defiant behaviour: often argues with authority figures or, for children and adolescents, with adults; often actively defies or refuses to comply with requests from authority figures or with rules; often deliberately annoys others; often blames others for their mistakes or misbehaviour. Vindictiveness: has been spiteful or vindictive at least twice within the past 6 months. Frequency rule, which is a DSM-5 addition and is examinable: for children under 5 , the behaviour should occur on most days for at least 6 months; for those 5 and older , at least once per week for at least 6 months (except the vindictiveness item). B. Associated with distress in the individual or others in their immediate social context, or it impacts negatively on social, educational, occupational or other areas of functioning. C. Not occurring exclusively during the course of a psychotic, substance use, depressive or bipolar disorder, and criteria for disruptive mood dysregulation disorder are not met . DSM-5 removed the DSM-IV exclusion that prohibited diagnosing ODD alongside conduct disorder, so the two can now be diagnosed together. Severity: mild (symptoms confined to one setting), moderate (two settings), severe (three or more settings). Specifiers DSM-5-TR gives ODD only a current severity rating, and it is graded by the number of settings , not the number of symptoms: mild , symptoms confined to only one setting (at home, at school, at work or with peers); moderate , some symptoms present in at least two settings; severe , some symptoms present in three or more settings. Pervasiveness is used because it is an important indicator of severity, and it is not unusual for symptoms to appear only at home and only with family members. There are no onset subtypes and no remission specifiers for ODD; the childhood-onset and adolescent-onset types belong to conduct disorder. Numbers Prevalence about 1 to 11 percent, averaging around 3.3 percent. Commoner in males before adolescence (about 1.4:1); the sex difference is not consistently found in adolescents and adults. First symptoms usually appear in the preschool years, and rarely later than early adolescence. Course After an onset in the preschool to early-adolescent years, ODD often precedes conduct disorder , especially the childhood-onset type, but many children with ODD never go on to develop conduct disorder. The two symptom groups predict different futures: the defiant, argumentative and vindictive symptoms carry most of the risk for conduct disorder , while the angry/irritable mood symptoms carry most of the risk for later anxiety and depressive disorders . Children and adolescents with ODD are at increased risk, as adults, of antisocial behaviour, impulse-control problems, substance misuse, anxiety and depression. Comorbidity ADHD is the most frequent, and conduct disorder. Also anxiety disorders, major depressive disorder, and substance use disorders in adolescence. ODD is a well-established risk factor for later anxiety and depression, not only for conduct disorder. Differential Conduct disorder : ODD's defiance is directed at authority and involves no serious violation of others' basic rights or major societal norms, while conduct disorder involves aggression to people and animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness or theft, and serious rule violations. Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder : if criteria for both are met, only DMDD is diagnosed . ADHD : non-compliance driven by inattention and impulsivity, and children with ADHD alone are not typically spiteful or vindictive. Intermittent explosive disorder (high rates of anger but with serious aggression toward others, and no persistent defiance). Depressive and bipolar disorders with irritability. Normal developmental oppositionality in toddlers and adolescents, which is why the frequency and duration rules exist. DSM-5 change DSM-5 moved ODD out of the DSM-IV grouping of attention-deficit and disruptive behaviour disorders (under disorders usually first diagnosed in infancy, childhood or adolescence) into the new chapter Disruptive, Impulse-Control and Conduct Disorders . The eight symptoms were kept but grouped into three types (angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behaviour, vindictiveness) to show that ODD has both emotional and behavioural components. DSM-5 also removed the exclusion of conduct disorder , added the frequency guidance (most days under age 5, at least weekly from age 5), added the not-a-sibling clause, and added the severity rating by number of settings . DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Intermittent Explosive Disorder F63.81 A. Recurrent behavioural outbursts representing a failure to control aggressive impulses, shown by either : (1) verbal aggression (temper tantrums, tirades, verbal arguments or fights) or physical aggression toward property, animals or other individuals , occurring twice weekly, on average, for 3 months , where the physical aggression does not result in damage or destruction of property and does not result in physical injury to animals or other individuals; or (2) three behavioural outbursts involving damage or destruction of property and/or physical assault involving physical injury against animals or other individuals occurring within a 12-month period . B. The magnitude of aggressiveness expressed is grossly out of proportion to the provocation or to any precipitating psychosocial stressors. C. The outbursts are not premeditated and are not committed to achieve some tangible objective such as money, power or intimidation. That impulsivity criterion is what separates it from instrumental aggression in conduct disorder or antisocial personality disorder. D. Cause marked distress or impairment, or are associated with financial or legal consequences. E. Chronological age is at least 6 (or the equivalent developmental level). F. Not better explained by another mental disorder, and not attributable to another medical condition or a substance. In children aged 6 to 18, aggressive behaviour occurring as part of an adjustment disorder should not be given this diagnosis. Specifiers DSM-5-TR lists no specifiers, subtypes or severity ratings for intermittent explosive disorder. The two Criterion A routes (A1, frequent verbal or non-damaging, non-injurious physical aggression, twice weekly on average for 3 months; A2, three damaging or injurious outbursts within 12 months) are alternative ways of meeting the diagnosis, not subtypes to be recorded. Numbers The two pathways are the exam point: twice weekly for 3 months of non-destructive aggression, or 3 destructive or injurious outbursts in 12 months . Minimum age 6 . 12-month prevalence about 2.7 percent in the United States, commoner in those under 35 to 40 and in males. Onset is most commonly in late childhood or adolescence, rarely after 40. Course After an onset in late childhood or adolescence, the disorder is usually chronic and persistent , continuing for many years, and the course may be episodic , with recurrent periods of outbursts. Each outburst has a rapid onset with little or no prodrome, typically lasts less than 30 minutes , and is commonly set off by a minor provocation from a close intimate or associate. A history of physical and emotional trauma in the first two decades of life is the main recognised environmental risk factor, and the outbursts bring repeated social, occupational, financial and legal consequences. Comorbidity Depressive, anxiety and substance use disorders. Also ADHD, conduct disorder, oppositional defiant disorder, and antisocial and borderline personality disorders. Differential Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder : DMDD requires persistent negative mood between outbursts, and IED does not, and DMDD needs 12 months and an onset before 10. Antisocial and borderline personality disorders , where aggression occurs but is part of a wider pattern, and the level of impulsive aggression is lower than in IED. The DSM-5 note that allows IED as an additional diagnosis, when the outbursts exceed what is usual and need separate clinical attention, names ADHD, conduct disorder, ODD and autism spectrum disorder . Conduct disorder (aggression is often premeditated and instrumental). Delirium, major neurocognitive disorder, personality change due to another medical condition . Substance intoxication or withdrawal . Adjustment disorder in children, an explicit exclusion. DSM-5 change DSM-IV placed IED among the impulse-control disorders not elsewhere classified and required discrete episodes resulting in serious assaultive acts or destruction of property . DSM-5 moved it to the new Disruptive, Impulse-Control and Conduct Disorders chapter and widened it: verbal aggression and non-destructive, non-injurious physical aggression now count, with explicit frequency thresholds (the two Criterion A routes). It also specified that outbursts are impulsive and/or anger-based , required marked distress, impairment, or financial or legal consequences, set a minimum age of 6 , and clarified the relation to ADHD, DMDD and other childhood disorders. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the IED criteria; a September 2022 update added impairing emotional outbursts to the other conditions that may be a focus of clinical attention (not a mental disorder). Conduct Disorder F91.x A. A repetitive and persistent pattern of behaviour in which the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate societal norms or rules are violated, with at least 3 of 15 criteria in the past 12 months from any of the four categories below, with at least 1 criterion present in the past 6 months . Aggression to people and animals: often bullies, threatens or intimidates; often initiates physical fights; has used a weapon that can cause serious physical harm (a bat, brick, broken bottle, knife, gun); has been physically cruel to people; has been physically cruel to animals; has stolen while confronting a victim (mugging, purse snatching, extortion, armed robbery); has forced someone into sexual activity. Destruction of property: has deliberately engaged in fire setting with the intention of causing serious damage; has deliberately destroyed others' property other than by fire setting. Deceitfulness or theft: has broken into someone else's house, building or car; often lies to obtain goods or favours or to avoid obligations (cons others); has stolen items of nontrivial value without confronting a victim (shoplifting, forgery). Serious violations of rules: often stays out at night despite parental prohibitions, beginning before age 13; has run away from home overnight at least twice while living in the parental or surrogate home, or once without returning for a lengthy period; is often truant from school, beginning before age 13. B. Clinically significant impairment in social, academic or occupational functioning. C. If the individual is 18 or older, criteria are not met for antisocial personality disorder . Specifiers Childhood-onset type (at least one symptom before age 10), adolescent-onset type (no symptoms before age 10), unspecified onset . Severity mild, moderate, severe. And the DSM-5 addition that is asked most: with limited prosocial emotions , requiring at least 2 of 4 characteristics persistently over at least 12 months in more than one relationship or setting: lack of remorse or guilt ; callous, lack of empathy ; unconcerned about performance at school or work; shallow or deficient affect . This specifier operationalises the callous-unemotional trait and marks a more severe, more stable and more heritable variant with a worse treatment response. Numbers The arithmetic to hold: 3 of 15 in 12 months, 1 in the past 6 months , and the childhood-onset cut at age 10 . 12-month prevalence 2 to 10 percent, median about 4 percent. Substantially commoner in males. Childhood-onset type is male-predominant, more aggressive, and has a worse prognosis, with a higher likelihood of progressing to antisocial personality disorder; adolescent-onset type is more equally distributed by sex and often desists. Course Onset can be as early as the preschool years, but the first significant symptoms usually appear between middle childhood and middle adolescence , onset after age 16 is rare , and ODD is a common precursor of the childhood-onset type. Symptoms escalate with development: less severe behaviours (lying, shoplifting) tend to emerge first and the most severe (rape, theft while confronting a victim) last. The course is variable, and in the majority the disorder remits by adulthood , especially with adolescent onset and fewer, milder symptoms. Childhood onset , more numerous and severe symptoms, limited prosocial emotions and accompanying ADHD predict persistence into antisocial personality disorder, criminality and substance use disorders, and CD also raises the adult risk of mood, anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorders. Comorbidity ADHD and oppositional defiant disorder, both very common. Also specific learning disorder, anxiety disorders, depressive and bipolar disorders, and substance use disorders. Differential Oppositional defiant disorder (defiance without rights violations). ADHD (impulsive disruptive behaviour without rule violations). Intermittent explosive disorder (aggression only, and impulsive, without the deceit, theft and rule-breaking). Depressive and bipolar disorders with irritability and aggression confined to mood episodes. Adjustment disorder with disturbance of conduct . Antisocial personality disorder in those 18 and over, which is Criterion C. DSM-5 change DSM-5 moved conduct disorder from the DSM-IV section of disorders usually first diagnosed in infancy, childhood or adolescence into the new Disruptive, Impulse-Control and Conduct Disorders chapter. The criteria (3 of 15 in 12 months, at least 1 in the past 6 months) and the childhood-onset, adolescent-onset and unspecified-onset subtypes were kept largely unchanged . The one major addition is the descriptive specifier with limited prosocial emotions , for those who meet full criteria and also show callous-unemotional traits. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Pyromania and Kleptomania F63.1, F63.2 Pyromania. Deliberate and purposeful fire setting on more than one occasion ; tension or affective arousal before the act; fascination with, interest in, curiosity about, or attraction to fire and its situational contexts (paraphernalia, uses, consequences); pleasure, gratification or relief when setting fires, witnessing them, or participating in their aftermath. The fire setting is not done for monetary gain, as an expression of sociopolitical ideology, to conceal criminal activity, to express anger or vengeance, to improve one's living circumstances, in response to a delusion or hallucination, or as a result of impaired judgment (as in major neurocognitive disorder, intellectual disability or substance intoxication). Not better explained by conduct disorder, a manic episode, or antisocial personality disorder. Kleptomania. Recurrent failure to resist impulses to steal objects that are not needed for personal use or for their monetary value ; increasing sense of tension immediately before the theft; pleasure, gratification or relief at the time of committing the theft; the stealing is not committed to express anger or vengeance and is not in response to a delusion or a hallucination ; and it is not better explained by conduct disorder, a manic episode or antisocial personality disorder. Specifiers DSM-5-TR lists no specifiers, subtypes or severity ratings for either pyromania or kleptomania . For kleptomania, the three course patterns described in the text (sporadic, episodic, chronic) are descriptions only, not codable specifiers. Numbers Both are rare. Kleptomania prevalence roughly 0.3 to 0.6 percent, and about 4 to 24 percent of people arrested for shoplifting; female to male about 3:1 . Pyromania is rarer still, and is male-predominant . The critical exam point for both: the great majority of shoplifters and fire setters do not have these disorders, because ordinary theft is for gain and ordinary arson is for revenge, insurance or concealment. Course Pyromania : there are too few data to establish a typical age at onset, and a link between fire setting in childhood and pyromania in adulthood has not been documented; although juvenile fire setting is a major problem, pyromania in childhood appears to be rare. Fire-setting incidents are episodic and may wax and wane in frequency, and the long-term course is unknown. Kleptomania : age at onset is variable but it often begins in adolescence ; it can also begin in childhood or adulthood, and rarely in late adulthood. Three courses are described: sporadic (brief episodes with long periods of remission), episodic (protracted periods of stealing alternating with remission) and chronic with some fluctuation. It may continue for years despite multiple convictions for shoplifting. Comorbidity Kleptomania: obsessive-compulsive disorder, bipolar and depressive disorders, anxiety disorders, eating disorders (particularly bulimia nervosa), substance use disorders, and other impulse-control disorders. Pyromania: substance use disorders, gambling disorder, depressive and bipolar disorders, and other impulse-control disorders. Differential Ordinary theft or arson (motive is gain, revenge or concealment). Malingering , feigning kleptomania to avoid prosecution. Manic episode , psychotic disorders , antisocial personality disorder , conduct disorder , major neurocognitive disorder and intellectual disability , all explicit exclusions. DSM-5 change Both were moved from the DSM-IV chapter Impulse-Control Disorders Not Elsewhere Classified into the new DSM-5 chapter Disruptive, Impulse-Control and Conduct Disorders , alongside ODD, intermittent explosive disorder, conduct disorder and antisocial personality disorder (listed in both this chapter and the personality disorders chapter). Their old neighbours were rehoused: pathological gambling became gambling disorder in the addictive disorders chapter, and trichotillomania moved to obsessive-compulsive and related disorders. The criteria for pyromania and kleptomania themselves were essentially unchanged, apart from updated terms (major neurocognitive disorder and intellectual disability in the pyromania exclusions). DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. 16. Substance-related and addictive disorders The two DSM-5 changes to lead with: substance abuse and substance dependence were merged into a single Substance Use Disorder rated mild, moderate or severe, and Gambling Disorder was moved into this chapter , making it the first and only behavioural addiction recognised as a full DSM diagnosis. Alongside those, the criterion of recurrent legal problems was deleted and craving was added as a new criterion. Substance Use Disorder, the general criteria set F1x.x0 In plain language. The same eleven criteria apply to every substance class. They fall into four groups: impaired control, social impairment, risky use, and pharmacological criteria. Impaired control (4): (1) the substance is taken in larger amounts or over a longer period than was intended; (2) there is a persistent desire or unsuccessful efforts to cut down or control use; (3) a great deal of time is spent in activities necessary to obtain, use, or recover from the substance; (4) craving , or a strong desire or urge to use. Social impairment (3): (5) recurrent use resulting in a failure to fulfil major role obligations at work, school or home; (6) continued use despite persistent or recurrent social or interpersonal problems caused or exacerbated by the effects of the substance; (7) important social, occupational or recreational activities are given up or reduced because of use. Risky use (2): (8) recurrent use in situations in which it is physically hazardous; (9) use is continued despite knowledge of having a persistent or recurrent physical or psychological problem that is likely to have been caused or exacerbated by it. Pharmacological (2): (10) tolerance , defined by either a need for markedly increased amounts to achieve intoxication or the desired effect, or a markedly diminished effect with continued use of the same amount; (11) withdrawal , shown by the characteristic withdrawal syndrome for that substance, or by taking the substance (or a closely related one) to relieve or avoid withdrawal symptoms. Important qualification: tolerance and withdrawal occurring during appropriate medical treatment with prescribed medications such as opioid analgesics, sedatives or stimulants do not count as criteria. Severity: mild 2 to 3 symptoms, moderate 4 to 5 , severe 6 or more , within a 12-month period. That grading replaces the DSM-IV abuse/dependence dichotomy. Specify: in early remission (none of the criteria, except craving, met for at least 3 months but less than 12 months), in sustained remission (at least 12 months), on maintenance therapy , in a controlled environment . Specifiers Severity , by the number of criteria within 12 months: mild 2 to 3 , moderate 4 to 5 , severe 6 or more . Remission , after full criteria were previously met: in early remission , no criteria met for at least 3 months but less than 12 months ; in sustained remission , none met for 12 months or longer ; in both, craving is the one criterion allowed to persist. Two additional specifiers: in a controlled environment , where access to the substance is restricted (closely supervised substance-free jails, therapeutic communities, locked hospital units); and on maintenance therapy , which exists only for opioid use disorder (methadone, buprenorphine, naltrexone) and tobacco use disorder (for example, nicotine replacement). Numbers Two symptoms is the diagnostic threshold , and the severity bands 2 to 3, 4 to 5, 6 or more, all within 12 months. Early remission is 3 to 12 months, sustained remission 12 months or more. The 10 substance classes DSM-5 recognises: alcohol; caffeine; cannabis; hallucinogens (phencyclidine and other hallucinogens); inhalants; opioids; sedatives, hypnotics and anxiolytics; stimulants (amphetamine-type substances, cocaine, other); tobacco; and other or unknown substances. Note that caffeine has no use disorder in DSM-5, only intoxication, withdrawal, and caffeine-related conditions, with caffeine use disorder placed in Section III for further study. That asymmetry is examined. Course Substance use usually starts in adolescence , and use disorders typically emerge in the late teens and twenties ; for alcohol, onset of the use disorder peaks in the late teens to mid-20s, and most people who develop alcohol-related disorders do so by their late 30s. The course is characteristically chronic and relapsing , with alternating remission and relapse, and relapse is commonest in the first months after stopping. Clinic patients with long, severe histories are not the typical case, however: many people with milder disorders remit without treatment , often as adult roles accumulate. Worse outcome goes with early onset of use , a family history of substance use disorder, comorbid conduct disorder or antisocial personality disorder and other psychiatric disorders, and polysubstance use. Comorbidity Extremely high with depressive, bipolar, anxiety and psychotic disorders, PTSD, ADHD, conduct disorder and antisocial and borderline personality disorders. Multiple substance use disorders commonly co-occur. Differential Non-pathological substance use , including heavy use that produces no criteria. Substance-induced mental disorders , which are separate diagnoses (substance-induced psychotic, bipolar, depressive, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, sleep, sexual dysfunction, delirium and neurocognitive disorders). Independent primary mental disorders , distinguished by symptoms preceding substance use or persisting about a month beyond acute withdrawal. DSM-5 change DSM-5 abolished the DSM-IV split between substance abuse (1 of 4 criteria) and substance dependence (3 of 7) and merged them into one substance use disorder : 11 criteria, a threshold of 2 , and mild, moderate and severe grades. The abuse criterion of recurrent legal problems was dropped and craving was added . The "with physiological dependence" subtype and polysubstance dependence were eliminated, early remission now starts at 3 months rather than 1 month, the full versus partial remission distinction went, and "on agonist therapy" became on maintenance therapy . The chapter was renamed Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders to admit gambling disorder, amphetamine and cocaine were combined as stimulants , and nicotine became tobacco . DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Intoxication and withdrawal syndromes worth knowing cold Alcohol intoxication: slurred speech, incoordination, unsteady gait, nystagmus, impairment in attention or memory, stupor or coma. Alcohol withdrawal: within hours to a few days of cessation, with 2 or more of autonomic hyperactivity, increased hand tremor, insomnia, nausea or vomiting, transient hallucinations or illusions, psychomotor agitation, anxiety, generalised tonic-clonic seizures. Specify with perceptual disturbances . Delirium tremens typically appears 48 to 96 hours after the last drink and is a medical emergency. Related conditions to name: Wernicke's encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency: confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) and Korsakoff's syndrome (anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation), coded in DSM-5 as alcohol-induced major neurocognitive disorder, amnestic-confabulatory type . Opioid intoxication: pupillary constriction plus drowsiness or coma, slurred speech, impairment in attention or memory; severe overdose produces respiratory depression. Opioid withdrawal: dysphoric mood, nausea or vomiting, muscle aches, lacrimation or rhinorrhoea, pupillary dilation , piloerection, sweating, diarrhoea, yawning, fever, insomnia. It is intensely unpleasant but not usually life-threatening, which is the standard contrast with alcohol and sedative withdrawal, both of which can kill. Stimulant (cocaine, amphetamine) intoxication: tachycardia or bradycardia, pupillary dilation , elevated or lowered blood pressure, perspiration or chills, nausea or vomiting, weight loss, psychomotor agitation or retardation, muscular weakness, respiratory depression, chest pain, cardiac arrhythmias, confusion, seizures, dyskinesias, dystonias or coma. Withdrawal: dysphoric mood plus fatigue, vivid unpleasant dreams, insomnia or hypersomnia, increased appetite, psychomotor retardation or agitation, that is, the "crash". Cannabis intoxication: conjunctival injection, increased appetite, dry mouth, tachycardia. Cannabis withdrawal is new in DSM-5: irritability or anger, nervousness or anxiety, sleep difficulty, decreased appetite or weight loss, restlessness, depressed mood, plus at least one physical symptom such as abdominal pain, tremor, sweating, fever, chills or headache. Caffeine intoxication: recent consumption usually in excess of 250 mg, with 5 or more of restlessness, nervousness, excitement, insomnia, flushed face, diuresis, gastrointestinal disturbance, muscle twitching, rambling flow of thought and speech, tachycardia or cardiac arrhythmia, periods of inexhaustibility, psychomotor agitation. Caffeine withdrawal, new in DSM-5: headache, marked fatigue or drowsiness, dysphoric mood or irritability, difficulty concentrating, flu-like symptoms. Tobacco withdrawal: irritability, anxiety, difficulty concentrating, increased appetite, restlessness, depressed mood, insomnia, following at least several weeks of daily use. Hallucinogen Persisting Perception Disorder: re-experiencing, following cessation of hallucinogen use, of one or more of the perceptual symptoms experienced while intoxicated, for example geometric hallucinations, false perceptions of movement in the peripheral visual fields, flashes of colour, intensified colours, trails of images of moving objects, positive afterimages, halos around objects, macropsia and micropsia. Specifiers The one recurring specifier is with perceptual disturbances : hallucinations with intact reality testing , or auditory, visual or tactile illusions, occurring in the absence of a delirium . It applies to alcohol withdrawal , sedative, hypnotic or anxiolytic withdrawal , and opioid, stimulant and cannabis intoxication ; hallucinations without intact reality testing point instead to a substance-induced psychotic disorder. Stimulant intoxication and withdrawal also name the agent (amphetamine-type substance, cocaine or other stimulant). The other syndromes on this card (alcohol intoxication, opioid withdrawal, cannabis withdrawal, caffeine intoxication and withdrawal, tobacco withdrawal, hallucinogen persisting perception disorder) have no specifiers. Two gaps are examinable: there is no tobacco intoxication diagnosis, and no withdrawal diagnosis for hallucinogens or inhalants . Course Alcohol : withdrawal begins as blood alcohol falls sharply, usually 4 to 12 hours after drinking stops or is reduced, peaks on the second day and improves markedly by the fourth or fifth day , though milder anxiety, insomnia and autonomic symptoms can linger for 3 to 6 months ; fewer than 10 percent ever develop dramatic symptoms such as withdrawal delirium, and fewer than 3 percent have seizures. Opioids : heroin withdrawal starts 6 to 12 hours after the last dose (2 to 4 days for long-acting methadone), peaks within 1 to 3 days and subsides over 5 to 7 days . Stimulants : the crash after a binge, within hours to several days, brings lassitude, depression and hunger needing several days of rest, and depressive symptoms with suicidal ideation are the most serious risk. Cannabis : withdrawal begins within 24 to 72 hours, peaks in the first week and lasts about 1 to 2 weeks, though sleep difficulty can last over 30 days. Caffeine : withdrawal begins 12 to 24 hours after the last dose, peaks at 1 to 2 days and lasts 2 to 9 days. Tobacco : withdrawal begins within 24 hours, peaks at 2 to 3 days and lasts 2 to 3 weeks. Comorbidity Every intoxication and withdrawal syndrome sits on top of a substance use disorder, and multiple substance use disorders usually travel together (alcohol with tobacco, opioids with sedatives). Add depressive, anxiety, psychotic and neurocognitive disorders, PTSD, ADHD and antisocial and borderline personality disorders, plus the medical load: liver disease, pancreatitis, cardiomyopathy, hepatitis C and HIV. Differential The first question in every case is delirium , which changes the management. Then, for each picture: opioid versus stimulant intoxication is settled at the pupil (constricted versus dilated). Alcohol or sedative withdrawal versus opioid withdrawal is settled by danger (seizures and delirium tremens can kill, opioid withdrawal is miserable but rarely lethal). Withdrawal versus a primary anxiety or depressive disorder is settled by timing and by whether it clears within about a month of abstinence. Wernicke-Korsakoff versus dissociative amnesia is settled by the ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confabulation. DSM-5 change DSM-5 merged amphetamine and cocaine into one stimulant class with shared intoxication and withdrawal criteria, renamed nicotine withdrawal tobacco withdrawal , and folded phencyclidine into the hallucinogen class. Two withdrawal syndromes became official diagnoses: cannabis withdrawal (absent from DSM-IV) and caffeine withdrawal (in the DSM-IV appendix for further study). DSM-IV's alcohol-induced persisting amnestic disorder became alcohol-induced major neurocognitive disorder, amnestic-confabulatory type . Intoxication and withdrawal are now coded according to whether a use disorder (mild, or moderate to severe) coexists. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Gambling Disorder F63.0 In plain language. The only behavioural addiction in DSM-5. It was moved out of the impulse-control disorders (where DSM-IV called it "pathological gambling") into the substance-related and addictive disorders chapter, on evidence of shared reward circuitry, tolerance-like escalation, withdrawal-like states and comparable comorbidity. A. Persistent and recurrent problematic gambling behaviour leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, shown by 4 or more of 9 in a 12-month period: needs to gamble with increasing amounts of money to achieve the desired excitement (a tolerance analogue); is restless or irritable when attempting to cut down or stop (a withdrawal analogue); has made repeated unsuccessful efforts to control, cut back or stop; is often preoccupied with gambling; often gambles when feeling distressed (helpless, guilty, anxious, depressed); after losing money, often returns another day to get even ( chasing losses ); lies to conceal the extent of involvement; has jeopardised or lost a significant relationship, job, or educational or career opportunity; relies on others to provide money to relieve desperate financial situations (a bailout). B. The gambling behaviour is not better explained by a manic episode . Specify: episodic or persistent; in early remission (3 to 12 months with no criteria met) or in sustained remission (12 months or more); severity mild 4 to 5 , moderate 6 to 7 , severe 8 to 9 criteria. Note the DSM-5 change: the DSM-IV criterion of having committed illegal acts such as forgery, fraud, theft or embezzlement to finance gambling was deleted , and the threshold was lowered from 5 of 10 to 4 of 9 . Specifiers Episodic : meeting criteria at more than one time point, with symptoms subsiding between periods of gambling disorder for at least several months . Persistent : continuous symptoms, meeting criteria for multiple years . In early remission : after full criteria were met, none met for at least 3 months but less than 12 months ; in sustained remission : none met for 12 months or longer . Unlike the substance use disorders, there is no craving exception (there is no craving criterion) and no "in a controlled environment" or "on maintenance therapy" specifier. Current severity : mild 4 to 5 criteria, moderate 6 to 7 , severe 8 to 9 . Numbers Past-year prevalence about 0.2 to 0.3 percent; lifetime about 0.4 to 1.0 percent, and higher in men (about 0.6 percent) than women (about 0.2 percent). Men tend to start earlier and to have problems with strategic forms such as sports betting and card games; women start later, progress faster (the "telescoping" effect) and more often use non-strategic forms such as slot machines and bingo. Course Gambling disorder can begin in adolescence or young adulthood , but in others it first appears in middle or even older adulthood. It generally develops over years , with a gradual increase in both the frequency of gambling and the size of wagers , and milder forms can progress to severe ones; progression is faster in women. Gambling may be regular or episodic, and the disorder may be persistent or go into remission , which is what the episodic, persistent and remission specifiers capture. Gambling that begins in childhood or early adolescence raises the risk of the disorder, and the main complications are debt, damaged relationships and work, and suicidal behaviour . Comorbidity Substance use disorders, particularly alcohol and tobacco, depressive and bipolar disorders, anxiety disorders, ADHD, and antisocial personality disorder. Suicide risk is markedly elevated. Differential Non-disordered social or professional gambling . Manic episode , which is Criterion B: a person who gambles heavily only while manic has bipolar disorder, and if the gambling predates and outlasts the mood episodes, both diagnoses are given. Antisocial personality disorder . Other medical conditions : dopamine agonists used for Parkinson's disease produce impulse-control behaviours including gambling, and that iatrogenic cause is a favourite MCQ. DSM-5 change DSM-5 renamed pathological gambling as gambling disorder and moved it from the impulse-control disorders not elsewhere classified into the renamed Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders chapter, as its only non-substance (behavioural) addiction. The illegal acts criterion was dropped, the threshold fell from 5 of 10 to 4 of 9 , a 12-month time frame was set, and the episodic/persistent, remission and severity specifiers were introduced. Internet gaming disorder was placed in Section III for further study. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. ICD-11 Recognises Gaming Disorder , online and offline, as a full diagnosis. DSM-5-TR does not: Internet Gaming Disorder sits in Section III as a condition for further study. Do not confuse the two systems here. 17. Neurocognitive disorders The chapter that used to be "Delirium, Dementia, Amnestic and Other Cognitive Disorders". DSM-5 replaced the word dementia with Major Neurocognitive Disorder , partly because "dementia" carries stigma and partly because it was not used for younger adults with acquired impairment from HIV or head injury. It also created Mild Neurocognitive Disorder as a new diagnosis, to capture the pre-dementia stage that the literature calls mild cognitive impairment, so that early intervention becomes possible. Amnestic disorder was absorbed into these categories. Every NCD is then given an aetiological subtype , so you diagnose twice: the syndrome, then the cause. The six cognitive domains DSM-5 works from Complex attention (sustained, divided, selective, processing speed); executive function (planning, decision making, working memory, responding to feedback, inhibition, mental flexibility); learning and memory (immediate memory, recent memory including free recall, cued recall and recognition memory, very-long-term memory, implicit learning); language (expressive, including naming, word finding, fluency, grammar and syntax, and receptive); perceptual-motor (visual perception, visuoconstructional, perceptual-motor, praxis, gnosis); social cognition (recognition of emotions, theory of mind). Social cognition is new in DSM-5 and its inclusion is what allows the behavioural-variant frontotemporal presentation to be captured. Learn all six by name. Delirium F05 In plain language. Attention and awareness break down over hours or days, they wax and wane through the day, and there is a medical cause behind it. A. A disturbance in attention (reduced ability to direct, focus, sustain and shift attention) and awareness (reduced orientation to the environment). B. The disturbance develops over a short period of time, usually hours to a few days , represents an acute change from baseline , and tends to fluctuate in severity during the course of a day . C. An additional disturbance in cognition (memory deficit, disorientation, language, visuospatial ability or perception). D. The disturbances in A and C are not better explained by another pre-existing, established or evolving neurocognitive disorder, and do not occur in the context of a severely reduced level of arousal such as coma. E. Evidence from history, physical examination or laboratory findings that the disturbance is a direct physiological consequence of another medical condition, substance intoxication or withdrawal, exposure to a toxin, or multiple aetiologies. Specify: substance intoxication delirium, substance withdrawal delirium, medication-induced delirium, delirium due to another medical condition, delirium due to multiple aetiologies. Also acute (hours to days) or persistent (weeks to months), and hyperactive , hypoactive or mixed level of activity. Specifiers Aetiology : substance intoxication delirium (diagnosed instead of plain intoxication when the attention and cognitive disturbance predominates and warrants clinical attention), substance withdrawal delirium , medication-induced delirium (a medication taken as prescribed), delirium due to another medical condition , and delirium due to multiple aetiologies . Duration : acute , lasting a few hours or days; persistent , lasting weeks or months. Level of activity : hyperactive (agitation, mood lability, refusal to cooperate with care), hypoactive (sluggishness and lethargy approaching stupor), or mixed (normal psychomotor activity despite disturbed attention and awareness, or activity that fluctuates rapidly). Attenuated delirium syndrome is the standard example of other specified delirium. Numbers Prevalence in the general community about 1 to 2 percent, rising to 14 percent in those over 85. On admission to hospital 14 to 24 percent; incidence during hospitalisation 6 to 56 percent; 70 to 87 percent of older patients in intensive care and up to 60 percent in nursing homes at some point. The hypoactive subtype is the commonest in older adults and is routinely missed, being mistaken for depression, which is a classic exam and clinical trap. Course Onset is acute , over hours to days, sometimes after a prodrome of restlessness, anxiety, irritability or disturbed sleep, and symptoms fluctuate through the day, often worsening at night. Most people recover fully , with or without treatment, and early recognition and correction of the cause shortens the episode; untreated, delirium can progress to stupor, coma, seizures or death. Prognosis is worst in the old and the medically ill: mortality in hospital is high, and as many as 40 percent die within a year of diagnosis, particularly those with malignancy or other serious illness. In older hospitalised patients delirium is also followed by functional decline and a higher risk of institutional placement . Comorbidity Pre-existing major or mild neurocognitive disorder is the single largest risk factor, and delirium superimposed on dementia is extremely common. Also polypharmacy, sensory impairment, infection, dehydration, hip fracture and post-operative states. Differential Major neurocognitive disorder , and this is the pair to be able to draw as a table: delirium is acute onset with a fluctuating course, impaired attention and consciousness , disturbed sleep-wake cycle, frequent visual hallucinations , and is usually reversible ; dementia is insidious in onset with a progressive course, attention and consciousness are preserved until late , hallucinations are less common early, and it is usually irreversible . Psychotic disorders and bipolar or depressive disorders with psychotic features , in which delusions and hallucinations occur without the acute attentional disturbance and fluctuation. Acute stress disorder . Malingering and factitious disorder . DSM-5 change DSM-IV defined delirium by a disturbance of consciousness (reduced clarity of awareness of the environment); DSM-5 replaced this with a disturbance in attention and awareness . It kept the exclusion of a pre-existing, established or evolving neurocognitive disorder (dementia in DSM-IV), added that the disturbance must not occur in a severely reduced level of arousal such as coma , and introduced the acute/persistent and hyperactive/hypoactive/mixed specifiers. The DSM-IV chapter "Delirium, Dementia, and Amnestic and Other Cognitive Disorders" became Neurocognitive Disorders . DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Major and Mild Neurocognitive Disorder, the syndrome criteria Major NCD, Criterion A: evidence of significant cognitive decline from a previous level of performance in one or more of the six cognitive domains, based on both (1) concern of the individual, a knowledgeable informant, or the clinician that there has been a significant decline, and (2) a substantial impairment in cognitive performance , preferably documented by standardised neuropsychological testing or, in its absence, another quantified clinical assessment. The conventional benchmark is performance 2 or more standard deviations below appropriate norms, that is, at or below the 3rd percentile. Major NCD, Criterion B: the cognitive deficits interfere with independence in everyday activities , that is, at a minimum the person requires assistance with complex instrumental activities of daily living such as paying bills or managing medications. Mild NCD, Criterion A: evidence of modest cognitive decline , conventionally 1 to 2 standard deviations below norms, that is, between the 3rd and 16th percentiles. Mild NCD, Criterion B: the cognitive deficits do not interfere with independence in everyday activities, though greater effort, compensatory strategies or accommodation may be required. That independence line is the entire major-versus-mild distinction, and it is asked constantly. C. The deficits do not occur exclusively in the context of a delirium. D. The deficits are not better explained by another mental disorder such as major depressive disorder or schizophrenia. Specify: the aetiological subtype, and without behavioural disturbance or with behavioural disturbance (psychotic symptoms, mood disturbance, agitation, apathy or other behavioural symptoms), for major and mild NCD alike (for major NCD this became six named specifiers in the October 2022 update, see Specifiers below), plus severity mild (difficulties with instrumental activities of daily living such as housework and managing money), moderate (difficulties with basic activities such as feeding and dressing), severe (fully dependent). Specifiers Aetiological subtype , always recorded: Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal degeneration (frontotemporal lobar degeneration in DSM-5), Lewy body disease, vascular disease, traumatic brain injury, substance/medication use, HIV infection, prion disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, another medical condition, multiple aetiologies, or unspecified, with unknown aetiology added by the October 2022 update; for five of these, probable or possible is added. For major NCD , current severity : mild (difficulty with instrumental activities such as housework and managing money), moderate (difficulty with basic activities such as feeding and dressing), severe (fully dependent). Behavioural specifiers: DSM-5 and the March 2022 printing of DSM-5-TR used with or without behavioural disturbance ; from 1 October 2022 an APA update replaced these, for major NCD, with with agitation , with anxiety , with mood symptoms , with psychotic disturbance , with other behavioural or psychological disturbance (for example, apathy) and without accompanying behavioural or psychological disturbance . Mild NCD keeps the simple with/without behavioural disturbance. Course Onset and course follow the cause. The neurodegenerative causes (Alzheimer's, frontotemporal, Lewy body) begin insidiously and progress gradually , moving over years from mild through moderate to severe major NCD; vascular NCD is classically stepwise or static between events; NCD after traumatic brain injury is worst soon after the injury and then static or improving; substance-induced NCD may partly recover with sustained abstinence. Mild NCD is often, but not always, a stage on the way: in clinic samples of mild cognitive impairment roughly 10 to 15 percent a year progress to dementia, while others stay stable or improve, especially when depression, medication or another reversible cause lies behind the decline. Age is the strongest risk factor: major NCD affects about 1 to 2 percent at age 65 and as many as 30 percent by 85 . Comorbidity Depression and anxiety are extremely common at the mild stage, when insight is retained, and apathy, agitation and psychosis appear as the disorder progresses; DSM-5 captures these with the with behavioural disturbance specifier. Delirium is superimposed frequently. Add the vascular risk load (hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation), sensory impairment, falls and malnutrition. Differential Delirium , which must be excluded first (Criterion C). Major depressive disorder , that is, depressive pseudodementia. Normal ageing , which is why Criterion A2 asks for standardised testing. Intellectual disability , where the ability was never acquired rather than lost. Schizophrenia with cognitive impairment, distinguished by the lifelong history. Malingering and factitious disorder where compensation or litigation is in play. DSM-5 change DSM-5 replaced the DSM-IV chapter "Delirium, Dementia, and Amnestic and Other Cognitive Disorders" with Neurocognitive Disorders . Dementia and amnestic disorder were subsumed under major NCD (the word dementia may still be used), and a less severe level, mild NCD , became a diagnosis (DSM-IV had placed mild neurocognitive disorder only in its appendix for further study). Memory impairment is no longer required : DSM-IV dementia demanded memory loss plus aphasia, apraxia, agnosia or executive disturbance, whereas DSM-5 needs decline in any one of six domains (complex attention, executive function, learning and memory, language, perceptual-motor, social cognition). DSM-5-TR (2022): criteria unchanged, but an October 2022 update coded severity for major NCD, replaced its behavioural specifier with six specific ones (with agitation, with anxiety, with mood symptoms, with psychotic disturbance, with other behavioural or psychological disturbance, and without), and added major or mild NCD due to unknown aetiology . The aetiological subtypes, with what distinguishes each Alzheimer's disease. Insidious onset and gradual progression , with early and prominent impairment in learning and recent memory . Probable Alzheimer's requires evidence of a causative genetic mutation from family history or genetic testing, or all three of: clear evidence of decline in memory and learning plus at least one other domain; steadily progressive gradual decline without extended plateaus; and no evidence of mixed aetiology. Otherwise possible . It is the commonest cause of major NCD, accounting for roughly 60 to 80 percent of cases. Pathology: extracellular beta-amyloid plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau , with early atrophy in the medial temporal lobe and hippocampus and a cholinergic deficit arising from the nucleus basalis of Meynert. Genetics: APOE e4 raises risk for late onset; mutations in APP (chromosome 21), presenilin 1 (chromosome 14) and presenilin 2 (chromosome 1) cause early-onset autosomal dominant disease, and people with Down syndrome almost all develop Alzheimer pathology by their forties because of the extra copy of APP on chromosome 21. Frontotemporal NCD. Insidious onset and gradual progression with either a behavioural variant (3 or more of: behavioural disinhibition, apathy or inertia, loss of sympathy or empathy, perseverative, stereotyped or compulsive/ritualistic behaviour, hyperorality and dietary changes, plus prominent decline in social cognition and/or executive ability) or a language variant (primary progressive aphasia, with prominent decline in speech production, word finding, object naming, grammar or word comprehension). Learning, memory and perceptual-motor function are relatively spared , which is the discriminator against Alzheimer's. Onset is typically earlier, in the fifties and sixties. Pathology: tau or TDP-43 inclusions; Pick bodies in the classic Pick's disease form. NCD with Lewy Bodies. Core diagnostic features: fluctuating cognition with pronounced variations in attention and alertness ; recurrent well-formed and detailed visual hallucinations ; and spontaneous features of parkinsonism, with onset subsequent to the development of cognitive decline . Suggestive features: meeting criteria for REM sleep behaviour disorder, and severe neuroleptic sensitivity , which is a safety point as well as an exam point. The conventional one-year rule : if cognitive decline begins at least a year before parkinsonism, it is NCD with Lewy bodies; if motor signs clearly precede cognition by more than a year, it is major NCD due to Parkinson's disease. Vascular NCD. The clinical features are consistent with a vascular aetiology, shown by either onset of the deficits temporally related to one or more cerebrovascular events , or evidence of decline that is prominent in complex attention, including processing speed, and in frontal-executive function . There is evidence of cerebrovascular disease from history, physical examination and/or neuroimaging sufficient to account for the deficits. Course is classically stepwise rather than smoothly progressive, with focal neurological signs. The second commonest cause of major NCD, and it frequently coexists with Alzheimer pathology as a mixed dementia. NCD due to Traumatic Brain Injury. There is evidence of a TBI with one or more of: loss of consciousness, post-traumatic amnesia, disorientation and confusion, or neurological signs. The NCD presents immediately after the injury or immediately after recovery of consciousness and persists past the acute post-injury period. Substance/Medication-Induced NCD. The impairments do not occur exclusively during delirium and persist beyond the usual duration of intoxication and acute withdrawal. Alcohol is the leading cause; specify persistent where deficits continue after an extended period of abstinence. NCD due to HIV Infection. Documented HIV infection, with a pattern that is not better explained by secondary brain disease such as progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy or cryptococcal meningitis. Typically subcortical, with slowed processing and executive difficulty. NCD due to Prion Disease. Insidious onset with rapid progression, plus motor features such as myoclonus or ataxia, or biomarker evidence. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is the archetype, and rapid progression over months is the discriminator. NCD due to Parkinson's Disease. Insidious onset and gradual progression in an individual with established Parkinson's disease , where the disturbance is not attributable to another condition. Probable requires both no evidence of mixed aetiology and Parkinson's disease clearly preceding the onset of the NCD; possible if only one is met. NCD due to Huntington's Disease. Insidious onset and gradual progression, with either clinically established Huntington's or risk based on family history or genetic testing. Autosomal dominant, caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion on chromosome 4 ; presents with chorea , and cognitive change is early and executive. NCD due to Another Medical Condition and due to Multiple Aetiologies , plus Unspecified NCD . Specifiers Every subtype is diagnosed as major or mild , with the severity and behavioural specifiers from the syndrome card. Probable versus possible applies to five. Alzheimer's : for mild NCD, probable needs genetic evidence (testing or family history); without it, possible needs all three of clear decline in memory and learning, steadily progressive gradual decline without extended plateaus, and no evidence of mixed aetiology. Frontotemporal : probable needs a causative genetic mutation or disproportionate frontal and/or temporal involvement on neuroimaging. Lewy body : probable with two core features, or one suggestive plus at least one core; possible with one core, or one or more suggestive. Vascular : probable needs neuroimaging evidence of significant parenchymal injury, a temporal link to documented cerebrovascular events, or clinical plus genetic evidence (for example, CADASIL). Parkinson's : probable when there is no mixed aetiology and Parkinson's disease clearly precedes the NCD. Substance/medication-induced : name the substance and specify persistent ; alcohol-induced major NCD is amnestic-confabulatory type (Korsakoff) or nonamnestic-confabulatory type . Course Alzheimer's : insidious onset, usually late in life (early-onset cases in the 40s or 50s are more often linked to causative mutations), with gradual decline, sometimes with brief plateaus, through severe dementia to death; survival after diagnosis averages about 10 years , and death most often follows aspiration. Frontotemporal : commonly presents in the 50s , and decline is faster and survival shorter than in typical Alzheimer's disease. Lewy body : insidious and gradually progressive, but often preceded by acute confusional episodes (delirium) triggered by illness or surgery, and REM sleep behaviour disorder can precede the cognitive decline by years. Vascular : stepwise or fluctuating, with plateaus or partial improvement, though small-vessel disease can progress gradually. Traumatic brain injury : deficits are greatest just after the injury, and after mild TBI symptoms usually resolve within days to weeks, typically fully by 3 months; repeated injuries raise the risk of lasting decline. Prion disease is the fastest, with most people dying within a year, while substance-induced NCD may improve with sustained abstinence and HIV NCD with antiretroviral treatment. Comorbidity Each subtype carries its own load. Alzheimer's with depression and later psychosis and agitation. Vascular with stroke, hypertension, diabetes and post-stroke depression. Lewy body with REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression, orthostatic hypotension and severe antipsychotic sensitivity. Frontotemporal with motor neurone disease in a subset, and with the highest rate of being misdiagnosed as a primary psychiatric disorder. Traumatic brain injury with PTSD, substance use and chronic pain. Substance-induced with the substance use disorder itself and with Wernicke-Korsakoff. The differential that decides marks Alzheimer's versus frontotemporal: memory first versus behaviour or language first, later onset versus earlier onset, insight lost early in FTD. Alzheimer's versus Lewy body: steady decline versus fluctuating attention, visual hallucinations early in Lewy body, parkinsonism, neuroleptic sensitivity, REM sleep behaviour disorder. Alzheimer's versus vascular: smooth progression versus stepwise, memory-first versus executive-and-speed-first, focal signs and imaging. Any dementia versus delirium: onset, course, and attention. Any dementia versus depressive pseudodementia: in depression the onset is more abrupt and datable, the person complains loudly of memory loss rather than concealing it, answers "I don't know" rather than confabulating, effort is poor but performance improves with encouragement, and there is a mood history. Any dementia versus normal ageing , which is Criterion A2 and the reason for standardised testing. DSM-5 change DSM-IV had dementia of the Alzheimer's type (with early-onset , at 65 or below, and late-onset subtypes), vascular dementia, dementia due to HIV disease, head trauma, Parkinson's, Huntington's, Pick's and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, and substance-induced persisting dementia and amnestic disorder. DSM-5 gave each aetiological subtype its own criteria , for both major and mild NCD; named frontotemporal lobar degeneration (absorbing Pick's disease) and Lewy body disease as subtypes; renamed head trauma traumatic brain injury and Creutzfeldt-Jakob prion disease ; introduced the probable/possible distinction; and dropped the early/late-onset subtypes of Alzheimer's. DSM-5-TR (2022) added stimulant-induced mild NCD , and an October 2022 update added major or mild NCD due to unknown aetiology . 18. Personality disorders An enduring pattern of inner experience and behaviour that deviates markedly from the expectations of the individual's culture , is pervasive and inflexible , has an onset in adolescence or early adulthood , is stable over time , and leads to distress or impairment. The pattern must be manifest in 2 or more of four areas: cognition (ways of perceiving and interpreting self, other people and events), affectivity (the range, intensity, lability and appropriateness of emotional response), interpersonal functioning , and impulse control . Learn that general criteria set, because a question that asks "what are the general diagnostic criteria for a personality disorder" is asking for exactly those four areas plus the pervasiveness, stability, onset and exclusion clauses. DSM-5 kept the ten categorical disorders in three clusters unchanged from DSM-IV; the alternative dimensional model sits in Section III. The three clusters Cluster A, the odd or eccentric: paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal. Cluster B, the dramatic, emotional or erratic: antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic. Cluster C, the anxious or fearful: avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive. The clusters have limited validity and high co-occurrence, and DSM-5 says so; that criticism is worth stating when you list them. Cluster A: Paranoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal F60.0, F60.1, F21 Paranoid Personality Disorder. A pervasive distrust and suspiciousness of others such that their motives are interpreted as malevolent, beginning by early adulthood, with 4 or more of 7 : suspects without sufficient basis that others are exploiting, harming or deceiving them; is preoccupied with unjustified doubts about the loyalty or trustworthiness of friends or associates; is reluctant to confide in others because of unwarranted fear that the information will be used maliciously against them; reads hidden demeaning or threatening meanings into benign remarks or events; persistently bears grudges; perceives attacks on their character or reputation that are not apparent to others and is quick to react angrily or to counterattack; has recurrent suspicions, without justification, regarding the fidelity of a spouse or sexual partner. Schizoid Personality Disorder. A pervasive pattern of detachment from social relationships and a restricted range of expression of emotions , with 4 or more of 7 : neither desires nor enjoys close relationships, including being part of a family; almost always chooses solitary activities; has little if any interest in having sexual experiences with another person; takes pleasure in few if any activities; lacks close friends or confidants other than first-degree relatives; appears indifferent to the praise or criticism of others; shows emotional coldness, detachment or flattened affectivity. Schizotypal Personality Disorder. A pervasive pattern of social and interpersonal deficits marked by acute discomfort with, and reduced capacity for, close relationships, plus cognitive or perceptual distortions and eccentricities of behaviour , with 5 or more of 9 : ideas of reference (excluding delusions of reference); odd beliefs or magical thinking that influences behaviour and is inconsistent with subcultural norms (superstitiousness, belief in clairvoyance, telepathy or a sixth sense; in children and adolescents, bizarre fantasies or preoccupations); unusual perceptual experiences including bodily illusions; odd thinking and speech (vague, circumstantial, metaphorical, overelaborate or stereotyped); suspiciousness or paranoid ideation; inappropriate or constricted affect; behaviour or appearance that is odd, eccentric or peculiar; lack of close friends or confidants other than first-degree relatives; excessive social anxiety that does not diminish with familiarity and tends to be associated with paranoid fears rather than negative judgments about self. Note that schizotypal is dual-listed , appearing in both the personality disorders chapter and the schizophrenia spectrum chapter, because it is genetically related to schizophrenia. Specifiers DSM-5-TR gives no specifiers, subtypes or severity ratings for paranoid, schizoid or schizotypal personality disorder. The one recordable qualifier is premorbid : if criteria were met before the onset of schizophrenia, the diagnosis is recorded as, for example, paranoid personality disorder (premorbid) . Severity enters only through the Section III Alternative Model for Personality Disorders , which rates the Level of Personality Functioning from 0 (little or no impairment) to 4 (extreme impairment) alongside pathological trait domains; of these three, only schizotypal is kept among that model's six named disorders. Course All three are evident by early adulthood and may be foreshadowed in childhood and adolescence by solitariness, poor peer relationships, social anxiety, underachievement at school, hypersensitivity, and peculiar thoughts, language or fantasies, so that such children are seen as odd and teased. The course is usually chronic , and these individuals seldom seek help for the personality pattern itself. Under stress, all three can show very brief psychotic episodes lasting minutes to hours. Paranoid and schizoid personality may be the premorbid antecedent of delusional disorder or schizophrenia. Schizotypal has a relatively stable course , with only a small proportion going on to schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder, and, with obsessive-compulsive personality disorder, it is among the types least likely to soften with age. Comorbidity Cluster A disorders co-occur with each other, with depressive disorders, and with schizophrenia spectrum disorders in relatives. Schizotypal carries the highest risk of transition to a psychotic disorder. Differential Schizoid versus schizotypal: both are socially isolated, but schizotypal adds the cognitive and perceptual oddness, which schizoid lacks. Schizoid versus avoidant: the avoidant person wants relationships but fears rejection, the schizoid person does not want them. That pair is asked more often than any other in the personality chapter. Paranoid personality versus delusional disorder: suspiciousness that never reaches delusional conviction. Autism spectrum disorder , which can look schizoid but includes restricted repetitive behaviours and has a developmental onset. Schizophrenia in prodrome or residual phase . Personality change due to another medical condition and substance effects. DSM-5 change The Section II criteria for all ten personality disorders were carried over from DSM-IV unchanged . The changes were structural: the multiaxial system was abolished , so personality disorders are no longer recorded on a separate Axis II ; an Alternative Model for Personality Disorders was placed in Section III; and schizotypal personality disorder was dual-listed , with its criteria in the personality disorders chapter and a listing in the schizophrenia spectrum chapter. In the schizoid and schizotypal exclusions, pervasive developmental disorder became autism spectrum disorder . DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Cluster B: Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic F60.2, F60.3, F60.4, F60.81 Antisocial Personality Disorder. A pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others , occurring since age 15, with 3 or more of 7 : failure to conform to social norms with respect to lawful behaviours, as shown by repeatedly performing acts that are grounds for arrest; deceitfulness, as shown by repeated lying, use of aliases or conning others for personal profit or pleasure; impulsivity or failure to plan ahead; irritability and aggressiveness, as shown by repeated physical fights or assaults; reckless disregard for the safety of self or others; consistent irresponsibility, as shown by repeated failure to sustain consistent work behaviour or honour financial obligations; lack of remorse, as shown by being indifferent to or rationalising having hurt, mistreated or stolen from another. B. The individual is at least 18 . C. There is evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15 . D. The antisocial behaviour does not occur exclusively during schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. Those three age-related clauses (since 15, at least 18, conduct disorder before 15) are the most examined arithmetic in the chapter. Borderline Personality Disorder. A pervasive pattern of instability of interpersonal relationships, self-image and affects, and marked impulsivity , with 5 or more of 9 : frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment (not including the self-harm in criterion 5); a pattern of unstable and intense interpersonal relationships characterised by alternating between extremes of idealisation and devaluation ( splitting ); identity disturbance, that is, a markedly and persistently unstable self-image or sense of self; impulsivity in at least two areas that are potentially self-damaging (spending, sex, substance abuse, reckless driving, binge eating), not including the self-harm in criterion 5; recurrent suicidal behaviour, gestures or threats, or self-mutilating behaviour; affective instability due to a marked reactivity of mood, with episodic dysphoria, irritability or anxiety usually lasting a few hours and only rarely more than a few days ; chronic feelings of emptiness; inappropriate intense anger or difficulty controlling anger; transient, stress-related paranoid ideation or severe dissociative symptoms . Histrionic Personality Disorder. A pervasive pattern of excessive emotionality and attention seeking , with 5 or more of 8 : is uncomfortable in situations in which they are not the centre of attention; interaction with others is often characterised by inappropriate sexually seductive or provocative behaviour; displays rapidly shifting and shallow expression of emotions; consistently uses physical appearance to draw attention to self; has a style of speech that is excessively impressionistic and lacking in detail; shows self-dramatisation, theatricality and exaggerated expression of emotion; is suggestible, that is, easily influenced by others or circumstances; considers relationships to be more intimate than they actually are. Narcissistic Personality Disorder. A pervasive pattern of grandiosity in fantasy or behaviour, need for admiration and lack of empathy , with 5 or more of 9 : has a grandiose sense of self-importance; is preoccupied with fantasies of unlimited success, power, brilliance, beauty or ideal love; believes they are special and unique and can only be understood by, or should associate with, other special or high-status people or institutions; requires excessive admiration; has a sense of entitlement; is interpersonally exploitative; lacks empathy; is often envious of others or believes that others are envious of them; shows arrogant, haughty behaviours or attitudes. Specifiers DSM-5-TR gives no specifiers, subtypes or severity ratings for antisocial, borderline, histrionic or narcissistic personality disorder. In particular, Section II has no psychopathy specifier ; the callous-unemotional specifier with limited prosocial emotions belongs to conduct disorder only. The Section III Alternative Model keeps antisocial, borderline and narcissistic (histrionic is dropped), rates severity on the Level of Personality Functioning Scale (0 to 4), and offers one named specifier, antisocial personality disorder with psychopathic features (low anxiousness, low withdrawal, high attention seeking). Numbers Borderline prevalence about 1.6 percent in the community, rising to about 6 percent in primary care, 10 percent in psychiatric outpatients and 20 percent in inpatients; roughly 75 percent of clinical cases are female, though community samples are closer to even. About 8 to 10 percent die by suicide , which is roughly 50 times the general population rate. Antisocial personality disorder prevalence about 0.2 to 3.3 percent, strongly male-predominant, and much higher in prison populations. Narcissistic 0 to 6.2 percent, with 50 to 75 percent male. Histrionic about 1.84 percent. Course All four are evident by adolescence or early adulthood. Antisocial : the course is chronic but the disorder may become less evident or remit with age, particularly by the fourth decade of life , most clearly for criminal behaviour; child abuse or neglect, erratic parenting or inconsistent discipline make it more likely that conduct disorder evolves into it. Borderline : the commonest pattern is chronic instability in early adulthood , with impairment and suicide risk greatest in the young-adult years and waning with age; most become more stable in relationships and work in their 30s and 40s , and in outpatient follow-up as many as half no longer meet full criteria after about 10 years , although intense emotions and impulsivity are often lifelong. Narcissistic : narcissistic traits are common in adolescents and do not by themselves mean the disorder will follow; affected adults adjust poorly to the physical and occupational limits of ageing. Histrionic : little systematic course data exist. Comorbidity Borderline: depressive and bipolar disorders, substance use disorders, eating disorders (especially bulimia), PTSD, ADHD, and other personality disorders. Antisocial: substance use disorders, anxiety and depressive disorders, gambling disorder, somatic symptom disorder, and other Cluster B disorders. Narcissistic: depressive disorders, anorexia nervosa, substance use disorders (particularly cocaine), and other personality disorders. Differential Borderline versus bipolar II , the one that decides marks: borderline mood shifts last hours and are reactive to interpersonal events , especially perceived abandonment, while bipolar episodes last days to weeks , are relatively autonomous, and bring changes in sleep need and goal-directed activity; borderline also has chronic emptiness, identity disturbance and self-harm as the stable trait background. Borderline versus histrionic : both seek attention, but borderline adds self-destructiveness, angry disruptions of relationships and chronic emptiness. Narcissistic versus antisocial : both are exploitative, but antisocial adds impulsivity, aggression, deceit for material gain and a conduct-disorder history, while narcissistic exploitation serves admiration and status. Antisocial versus adult antisocial behaviour (a V code, where the behaviour is not part of a personality disorder, for example professional criminality without the broader pattern). Personality change due to another medical condition and substance use disorders , in which the behaviour appears only in the context of use. DSM-5 change The Section II criteria for antisocial, borderline, histrionic and narcissistic personality disorders were carried over from DSM-IV unchanged ; the changes were structural: Axis II was abolished with the multiaxial system, and the Alternative Model for Personality Disorders was added in Section III (without histrionic). Antisocial personality disorder is now dual-listed , with its criteria in the personality disorders chapter and a listing in the Disruptive, Impulse-Control and Conduct Disorders chapter, reflecting its continuity with conduct disorder.
