DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. Cluster C: Avoidant, Dependent, Obsessive-Compulsive F60.6, F60.7, F60.5 Avoidant Personality Disorder. A pervasive pattern of social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy and hypersensitivity to negative evaluation , with 4 or more of 7 : avoids occupational activities that involve significant interpersonal contact because of fears of criticism, disapproval or rejection; is unwilling to get involved with people unless certain of being liked; shows restraint within intimate relationships because of the fear of being shamed or ridiculed; is preoccupied with being criticised or rejected in social situations; is inhibited in new interpersonal situations because of feelings of inadequacy; views self as socially inept, personally unappealing or inferior to others; is unusually reluctant to take personal risks or to engage in any new activities because they may prove embarrassing. Dependent Personality Disorder. A pervasive and excessive need to be taken care of that leads to submissive and clinging behaviour and fears of separation, with 5 or more of 8 : has difficulty making everyday decisions without an excessive amount of advice and reassurance from others; needs others to assume responsibility for most major areas of their life; has difficulty expressing disagreement with others because of fear of loss of support or approval; has difficulty initiating projects or doing things on their own because of a lack of self-confidence in judgment or abilities rather than a lack of motivation or energy; goes to excessive lengths to obtain nurturance and support from others, to the point of volunteering to do things that are unpleasant; feels uncomfortable or helpless when alone because of exaggerated fears of being unable to care for themselves; urgently seeks another relationship as a source of care and support when a close relationship ends; is unrealistically preoccupied with fears of being left to take care of themselves. Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder. A pervasive pattern of preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism and mental and interpersonal control, at the expense of flexibility, openness and efficiency , with 4 or more of 8 : is preoccupied with details, rules, lists, order, organisation or schedules to the extent that the major point of the activity is lost; shows perfectionism that interferes with task completion, for example being unable to complete a project because their own overly strict standards are not met; is excessively devoted to work and productivity to the exclusion of leisure activities and friendships, not accounted for by obvious economic necessity; is overconscientious, scrupulous and inflexible about matters of morality, ethics or values, not accounted for by cultural or religious identification; is unable to discard worn-out or worthless objects even when they have no sentimental value; is reluctant to delegate tasks or to work with others unless they submit to exactly their way of doing things; adopts a miserly spending style toward both self and others, money being viewed as something to be hoarded for future catastrophes; shows rigidity and stubbornness. Specifiers DSM-5-TR gives no specifiers, subtypes or severity ratings for avoidant, dependent or obsessive-compulsive personality disorder. In the Section III Alternative Model , avoidant and obsessive-compulsive personality disorders are kept among its six named disorders, with severity rated on the Level of Personality Functioning Scale (0 to 4), while dependent personality disorder is dropped and would be described there as personality disorder, trait specified . Numbers Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is the most prevalent personality disorder in the general population, roughly 2.1 to 7.9 percent, and is about twice as common in males. Avoidant about 2.4 percent, roughly equal by sex. Dependent about 0.5 to 0.6 percent, and it is diagnosed more often in females, which DSM-5-TR flags as possibly reflecting sex bias in diagnosis rather than true prevalence. Course All three are evident by early adulthood . Avoidant : avoidance often starts in infancy or childhood as shyness, isolation and fear of strangers and new situations; in most children this shyness gradually dissipates, but those who develop the disorder become increasingly shy and avoidant in adolescence and early adulthood , when new relationships matter most, and in adults the disorder tends to become less evident or remit with age. Dependent : chronic physical illness or separation anxiety disorder in childhood or adolescence may predispose to it, and it should be diagnosed with great caution, if at all, in children and adolescents, for whom dependent behaviour may be developmentally appropriate; loss of the supporting relationship is a common trigger for depression. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder , with schizotypal, is among the types least likely to remit with age , unlike antisocial and borderline. Comorbidity Avoidant with social anxiety disorder (very high), depressive and bipolar disorders, and dependent and borderline personality disorders. Dependent with depressive, anxiety and adjustment disorders. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder with obsessive-compulsive disorder in a minority, hoarding disorder, eating disorders and depressive disorders. Differential Avoidant versus social anxiety disorder : overlapping to the point that many argue they are the same dimension, with avoidant being earlier, more pervasive and involving a more global sense of inadequacy; DSM-5 permits both diagnoses together. Avoidant versus schizoid , as above, decided by whether the person desires relationships. Avoidant versus dependent : both are clinging and fear rejection, but the avoidant person avoids relationships until certain of acceptance, while the dependent person rushes into them and clings. OCPD versus OCD : OCPD has no true obsessions or compulsions and is ego-syntonic , OCD has intrusive ego-dystonic obsessions with ritualised compulsions; they can coexist, and only about a quarter to a third of OCD patients have OCPD. OCPD versus hoarding disorder : the miserly and object-retention criteria overlap, and if hoarding is prominent, hoarding disorder should be diagnosed as well. DSM-5 change The Section II criteria for avoidant, dependent and obsessive-compulsive personality disorders were carried over from DSM-IV unchanged , so the changes are structural: personality disorders left the abolished Axis II , and the Section III Alternative Model kept avoidant and obsessive-compulsive but dropped dependent. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder stayed in the personality disorders chapter when OCD moved out of the anxiety disorders into the new Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders chapter. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. The other three personality diagnoses Personality Change Due to Another Medical Condition. A persistent personality disturbance that represents a change from the individual's previous characteristic pattern , with direct pathophysiological evidence of a medical cause, not better explained by another mental disorder, and not occurring exclusively during delirium. Specify labile, disinhibited, aggressive, apathetic, paranoid, other, combined or unspecified type. Classic causes: frontal lobe lesions, epilepsy, traumatic brain injury, tumour, Huntington's, multiple sclerosis, endocrine disease. The Phineas Gage case is the standard illustration. Other Specified Personality Disorder and Unspecified Personality Disorder , used for presentations with mixed features or where criteria for no single disorder are fully met. This category is heavily used in practice, which is itself one of the standard criticisms of the categorical system. Specifiers Personality change due to another medical condition is subtyped by the predominant feature: labile (affective lability), disinhibited (poor impulse control, for example sexual indiscretions), aggressive , apathetic (marked apathy and indifference), paranoid (suspiciousness or paranoid ideation), other , combined (more than one feature predominates) and unspecified . In children, the change must be a marked deviation from normal development or a significant change in usual behaviour lasting at least 1 year . Other specified personality disorder requires the clinician to record the reason (for example, "mixed personality features"); unspecified personality disorder is used when the reason is not given or information is insufficient. Course Personality change due to another medical condition begins after the causative illness or injury, and its course follows that condition: after a static insult such as a stroke or traumatic brain injury the change may persist or partly improve; with progressive disease such as Huntington's disease or an enlarging tumour it tends to worsen; and when the cause is treatable, as with some endocrine disorders, it may lessen once the cause is treated. Other specified and unspecified personality disorder follow the general personality disorder course: onset traceable to at least adolescence or early adulthood , and a stable pattern of long duration . Comorbidity Personality change due to another medical condition sits alongside the causative disease and, very often, depression, apathy and the family distress the change produces. The other specified and unspecified categories carry the same comorbid load as the specific disorders they resemble: mood, anxiety and substance use disorders above all. Two rules that answer many questions Age. Personality disorders may be diagnosed in individuals under 18 only if the features have been present for at least 1 year , with the single exception that antisocial personality disorder cannot be diagnosed before age 18 under any circumstances. Culture. The pattern must deviate from the expectations of the individual's own culture , so a habit of deference or of family interdependence that is normative in an Indian joint family is not evidence of dependent personality disorder. Both rules are examinable and both are commonly missed. DSM-5 change In DSM-IV, personality change due to a general medical condition sat in the chapter of mental disorders due to a general medical condition not elsewhere classified; DSM-5 renamed it personality change due to another medical condition and placed it in the personality disorders chapter , with the same subtypes. DSM-IV's personality disorder not otherwise specified was replaced by other specified personality disorder and unspecified personality disorder , as with every NOS category in DSM-5, and the Section III Alternative Model offers personality disorder, trait specified as its counterpart. DSM-5-TR (2022): no change to the criteria that exams test; text and codes updated. 19. Section III: the alternative model, culture, and conditions for further study DSM-5 is organised in three sections. Section I is the introduction, the definition of a mental disorder, and the use of the manual. Section II is the diagnostic criteria and codes, the operational manual you actually diagnose from. Section III is "Emerging Measures and Models": assessment measures, the cultural formulation, the alternative model for personality disorders, and conditions for further study. Knowing that three-part structure, and knowing which things live in Section III rather than Section II, is worth easy marks. The Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders (AMPD) A hybrid dimensional-categorical model, proposed for research and placed in Section III because the field could not agree to replace the categories outright. It has two criteria: Criterion A: level of personality functioning , rated on the Level of Personality Functioning Scale across four elements grouped in two domains. Self : identity and self-direction . Interpersonal : empathy and intimacy . Rated 0 (little or no impairment) to 4 (extreme impairment); moderate impairment or greater, that is a rating of 2 or more, is required for a personality disorder. Criterion B: pathological personality traits , in 5 broad domains subdivided into 25 facets : negative affectivity (versus emotional stability), detachment (versus extraversion), antagonism (versus agreeableness), disinhibition (versus conscientiousness), and psychoticism (versus lucidity). Notice that four of the five are maladaptive variants of the Big Five , with openness replaced by psychoticism, and this mapping is exactly what examiners ask for. The trait measure is the PID-5 , the Personality Inventory for DSM-5. The model retains only six specific personality disorders: antisocial, avoidant, borderline, narcissistic, obsessive-compulsive and schizotypal , plus personality disorder, trait specified for everything else. The four dropped from the alternative model are paranoid, schizoid, histrionic and dependent. The Cultural Formulation and the DSM-5-TR treatment of culture The Outline for Cultural Formulation asks for: cultural identity of the individual; cultural conceptualisations of distress; psychosocial stressors and cultural features of vulnerability and resilience; cultural features of the relationship between the individual and the clinician; and overall cultural assessment. The Cultural Formulation Interview (CFI) is a 16-question semi-structured interview, with an informant version and 12 supplementary modules, new in DSM-5. DSM-5 replaced the DSM-IV term culture-bound syndromes with three more precise concepts: cultural syndromes (clusters of symptoms that co-occur in a specific cultural group), cultural idioms of distress (ways of expressing distress that may not refer to specific symptoms, for example "thinking too much"), and cultural explanations or perceived causes (explanatory models, for example nervios , maladi moun ). That three-way replacement is a stock question. The named cultural concepts to be able to list: ataque de nervios (Latino, uncontrollable shouting, crying, trembling, heat in the chest rising to the head, often after a family stressor), dhat syndrome (South Asian, anxiety and somatic complaints attributed to semen loss in urine), khyal cap or wind attacks (Cambodian), kufungisisa ("thinking too much", Zimbabwe), maladi moun (Haitian, sent sickness), nervios , shenjing shuairuo (Chinese neurasthenia), susto (fright-induced illness, Latin America), taijin kyofusho (Japanese, fear of offending others through one's appearance or behaviour). Dhat, koro and possession states are the ones most likely to appear in an Indian entrance paper. Conditions for Further Study, the Section III list Not official diagnoses. If a question offers one of these as an answer for "which is a DSM-5 diagnosis", it is a distractor. They are: attenuated psychosis syndrome ; depressive episodes with short-duration hypomania ; persistent complex bereavement disorder (superseded in DSM-5-TR by prolonged grief disorder in Section II, so this one has effectively been promoted and renamed); caffeine use disorder ; internet gaming disorder ; neurobehavioural disorder associated with prenatal alcohol exposure ; suicidal behaviour disorder and non-suicidal self-injury (both of which DSM-5-TR converted into coded conditions that can be recorded alongside any diagnosis, so they too moved forward). Other conditions that may be a focus of clinical attention These are the Z codes , and they are not mental disorders . They include relational problems, abuse and neglect, educational and occupational problems, housing and economic problems, problems related to the social environment, problems related to crime or interaction with the legal system, and other health service encounters. Three that are examined specifically: malingering , adult antisocial behaviour and child or adolescent antisocial behaviour , borderline intellectual functioning , bereavement (uncomplicated) , age-related cognitive decline , and non-adherence to medical treatment . If a question asks "is malingering a mental disorder in DSM-5?", the answer is no, it is a condition that may be a focus of clinical attention. 20. Almost every differential question in the syllabus is decided by one of these numbers. tension then relief Gambling disorder vs manic episode Gambling confined to mood episodes is bipolar disorder Delirium vs major NCD Acute and fluctuating with impaired attention and consciousness, versus insidious and progressive with attention preserved Major vs mild NCD Independence in everyday activities lost, versus retained with extra effort Alzheimer's vs frontotemporal NCD Memory first and later onset, versus behaviour or language first and earlier onset with memory relatively spared Alzheimer's vs Lewy body NCD Fluctuating attention, early well-formed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, neuroleptic sensitivity, RBD Alzheimer's vs vascular NCD Gradual versus stepwise; memory-first versus processing-speed and executive-first with imaging evidence Dementia vs pseudodementia Complains of memory loss, "I don't know" answers, datable onset, mood history, improves with encouragement Schizoid vs avoidant PD Does not want relationships, versus wants them but fears rejection Schizoid vs schizotypal PD Schizotypal adds cognitive and perceptual oddness Borderline vs histrionic PD Self-destructiveness, chronic emptiness and angry ruptures in borderline Narcissistic vs antisocial PD Exploitation for admiration and status, versus for material gain with a conduct disorder history Avoidant vs dependent PD Avoids relationships until certain of acceptance, versus rushes in and clings The DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR change list, in one paragraph Multiaxial system abolished, GAF replaced by WHODAS 2.0. Schizophrenia subtypes deleted and the Schneiderian single-symptom concession removed. Autism's four disorders collapsed into one spectrum, triad reduced to a dyad, sensory criterion added. ADHD onset age raised from 7 to 12 and the symptom count reduced to 5 at age 17. Specific learning disorder's IQ-achievement discrepancy requirement abolished. Bereavement exclusion removed from major depressive disorder. DMDD and PMDD added; dysthymia and chronic MDD merged into persistent depressive disorder. Panic disorder and agoraphobia unlinked, agoraphobia now needs 2 of 5 situations, panic attack becomes a universal specifier, and the 6-month rule extended to all ages. A new obsessive-compulsive and related disorders chapter with hoarding and excoriation added and insight specifiers throughout. A new trauma and stressor-related chapter, with PTSD gaining a fourth cluster, losing Criterion A2, gaining a dissociative subtype and a preschool subtype. Dissociative fugue demoted to a specifier. Somatoform disorders rebuilt around positive psychological criteria, with somatisation disorder, hypochondriasis and pain disorder deleted and vaginismus and dyspareunia merged. Anorexia's amenorrhoea criterion deleted, bulimia's frequency halved, binge-eating disorder and ARFID added. Substance abuse and dependence merged into a graded substance use disorder, legal problems deleted, craving added, gambling disorder moved in as the first behavioural addiction. Dementia renamed major neurocognitive disorder, mild NCD created, social cognition added as a sixth domain. Personality disorders unchanged in Section II, with the alternative dimensional model in Section III. Then, in DSM-5-TR 2022: prolonged grief disorder added, unspecified mood disorder restored, suicidal behaviour and non-suicidal self-injury given codes, and the whole text revised for cultural and ethnoracial accuracy. Built for Sihan · DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022), exam cut for the MET, NIMHANS, IHBAS, RML, CIP, SGT and Amity clinical psychology entrances · criteria are paraphrased in plain language for study, not reproduced verbatim, so check the manual itself for the exact wording before any clinical use.

title: Psychological Tests: Authors, Versions, Items and Subtests
text: Psychological Tests: Authors, Versions, Items and Subtests Every psychological test the Indian clinical psychology entrances (RCI MA, NIMHANS, IHBAS, RML, JSS, CIP, Amity) keep asking about, one table per test: full name, who built it and when, the current edition and the ones before it, publisher, age range, number of items, every subtest, scale or index, how it is scored and normed, what it measures, its Indian adaptation, and the trap examiners set on it. Each family opens with a from-scratch explanation of how that kind of test works and closes with a comparison table. Where a count or a year genuinely differs between sources, the table says so instead of guessing: an honest "uncertain" is worth more in the hall than a confident wrong number. In this book Intelligence tests (international) Performance tests and Indian intelligence tests Developmental, adaptive behaviour and social maturity scales Objective personality inventories Aptitude, interest, creativity and attitude measures Projective techniques Neuropsychological tests and batteries Clinical rating scales and symptom inventories Structured diagnostic interviews and the mental status examination Index of every test in this book 1. Intelligence tests (international) An intelligence test is a standardised set of tasks, given in exactly the same way to everyone, whose scores are compared with a large reference group (the norm sample ) of people of the same age. The test does not measure "intelligence" directly; it samples behaviour (defining words, copying block patterns, repeating digits) that theory and data say depends on general reasoning ability. The score tells you where a person stands relative to age-mates, which is why the same raw score means something very different at age 7 and at age 70. The modern story starts in Paris. The French government wanted a way to identify children who would not profit from ordinary schooling, and Alfred Binet and Theodore Simon (1905) produced the first practical intelligence scale: 30 tasks arranged in rough order of difficulty. In the 1908 revision Binet and Simon grouped tasks by the age at which typical children pass them, which gave the idea of a mental age (MA) : a child who passes the tasks typical of 8-year-olds has an MA of 8, whatever their actual age. A third revision followed in 1911. Mental age alone is awkward, because being 2 years behind means far more at age 4 than at age 14. The German psychologist William Stern (1912) proposed dividing mental age by chronological age (CA), giving a "mental quotient". Lewis Terman (1916) , in the Stanford revision of the Binet scale at Stanford University, multiplied this by 100 and called it the intelligence quotient : ratio IQ = (MA / CA) x 100 . A 10-year-old with an MA of 12 has a ratio IQ of 120. The ratio IQ breaks down in adolescence and adulthood, because mental age stops growing in the late teens while chronological age keeps rising, so an ordinary 40-year-old would get an absurdly low "IQ". David Wechsler (1939) , working at Bellevue Hospital in New York, solved this with the deviation IQ . Instead of a ratio, the person's score is converted to a standard score that shows how far they sit from the mean of their own age group, on a scale with mean 100 and standard deviation (SD) 15 . An IQ of 115 now means "1 SD above the age mean" (about the 84th percentile) at any age. Every major modern test uses deviation scores. Within Wechsler batteries, individual subtests are reported as scaled scores with mean 10 and SD 3 . Theoretical frameworks evolved alongside: Charles Spearman's (1904) general factor g , Raymond Cattell's (1941, 1963) fluid (Gf) versus crystallised (Gc) intelligence, John Horn's extensions, and John Carroll's (1993) three-stratum model, which merged into the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) model that now organises the indices of the Wechsler, Stanford-Binet and KABC-II. Definition Ratio IQ = (mental age / chronological age) x 100 (Stern 1912 idea, Lewis Terman 1916 formula and name). Deviation IQ = a standard score locating the person relative to same-age peers, mean 100, SD 15 on Wechsler tests (Wechsler 1939). Scaled score = subtest standard score, mean 10, SD 3. T score = mean 50, SD 10. z score = mean 0, SD 1. Exam trap "Who coined IQ?" Stern proposed the quotient (MA/CA) in 1912; Terman added the x 100 and popularised the term "IQ" in the 1916 Stanford-Binet. Wechsler introduced the deviation IQ for adults. The 1960 Stanford-Binet Form L-M also switched to a deviation IQ, but with SD 16 , not 15. Alfred Binet himself never used the IQ. How to read age ranges in this book: Wechsler-style notation "16:0 to 90:11" means 16 years 0 months up to 90 years 11 months. WAIS-IV: Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fourth Edition The WAIS-IV is the standard individually administered adult intelligence test worldwide and the one most often named in Indian entrance papers. The examiner gives a series of subtests (verbal questions, block puzzles, digit repetition, symbol copying), converts each raw score to an age-scaled score, and combines these into four index scores and a Full Scale IQ. Interpretation moves from the global score (FSIQ) to the indices to individual subtests, looking for statistically significant strengths and weaknesses. The fourth edition is the one that dropped the old Verbal IQ and Performance IQ in favour of four indices. Field Detail Full name Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fourth Edition Author(s), year David Wechsler (original Wechsler-Bellevue Intelligence Scale, 1939). WAIS-IV (2008) was developed by the publisher's research team after Wechsler's death (1981), still under his name. Versions Wechsler-Bellevue Form I (1939), Wechsler-Bellevue Form II (1946), WAIS (1955), WAIS-R (1981), WAIS-III (1997), WAIS-IV (2008), WAIS-5 (2024, see next entry) Publisher Pearson (formerly The Psychological Corporation) Age range 16:0 to 90:11 Items Item counts are per subtest (they differ widely, and testing stops at discontinue rules); a single total item count is not a meaningful or standard figure. 15 subtests in all. Subtests / scales / indices 10 core subtests : Verbal Comprehension: Similarities, Vocabulary, Information. Perceptual Reasoning: Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, Visual Puzzles. Working Memory: Digit Span (forward, backward and the new sequencing task), Arithmetic. Processing Speed: Symbol Search, Coding. 5 supplemental subtests : Comprehension (VCI), Picture Completion and Figure Weights (PRI), Letter-Number Sequencing (WMI), Cancellation (PSI). Figure Weights, Letter-Number Sequencing and Cancellation are normed only for ages 16 to 69. 4 indices : Verbal Comprehension Index (VCI), Perceptual Reasoning Index (PRI), Working Memory Index (WMI), Processing Speed Index (PSI). Full Scale IQ (FSIQ) from the 10 core subtests. Optional composites : General Ability Index (GAI = VCI + PRI subtests, less affected by working memory and speed) and Cognitive Proficiency Index (CPI = WMI + PSI subtests). New in WAIS-IV: Visual Puzzles, Figure Weights, Cancellation. Dropped from WAIS-III: Object Assembly and Picture Arrangement. Scoring and norms FSIQ and indices mean 100, SD 15; subtest scaled scores mean 10, SD 3. US standardisation sample 2,200. FSIQ 130 and above: very superior; 69 and below: extremely low (WAIS-IV classification labels). Measures General intellectual ability (g) and four broad abilities: verbal reasoning and knowledge, nonverbal and fluid reasoning, working memory, processing speed Indian adaptation Pearson has marketed an India edition with Indian norms (reported as WAIS-IV INDIA); year and sample details uncertain. In routine Indian practice, especially for certification, the older Indian performance scale WAPIS (Ramalingaswamy, 1974) and Indian norms of other tests are still widely used. Exam trap WAIS-IV has no VIQ or PIQ (those ended with WAIS-III). It has 4 indices, not 5 (5 primary indices belong to WISC-V and WAIS-5). The core-versus-supplemental split is 10 + 5 = 15 . Comprehension and Picture Completion are supplemental in WAIS-IV, while Visual Puzzles is core. GAI is built from VCI and PRI; CPI from WMI and PSI: examiners swap these. WAIS-5: Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fifth Edition The WAIS-5 is the 2024 revision of the adult Wechsler. Its main structural change is to bring the adult test into line with WISC-V: the old Perceptual Reasoning Index is split into a Visual Spatial Index and a Fluid Reasoning Index , giving five primary indices. It was designed for both paper and digital (Q-interactive tablet) administration and shortened the subtests needed for an FSIQ. Because it is very new, Indian clinics and most Indian textbooks still teach WAIS-IV; treat WAIS-5 details below as current but verify against the manual. Field Detail Full name Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fifth Edition Author(s), year David Wechsler (original scale 1939); WAIS-5 developed by Pearson's research team, published 2024 Versions WAIS-5 (2024); previous: WAIS-IV (2008), WAIS-III (1997), WAIS-R (1981), WAIS (1955), Wechsler-Bellevue (1939) Publisher Pearson Age range 16:0 to 90:11 Items Per subtest; total subtest count reported as about 20 across primary, secondary and complementary groupings (exact count and grouping: uncertain, check the manual) Subtests / scales / indices 5 primary indices : Verbal Comprehension (VCI), Visual Spatial (VSI), Fluid Reasoning (FRI), Working Memory (WMI), Processing Speed (PSI). New subtests (as reported): Running Digits, Set Relations, Spatial Addition (Spatial Addition previously appeared in the Wechsler Memory Scale, WMS-IV), and Digit Span is split into separately scored tasks such as Digit Sequencing (details uncertain). Retained subtests include Similarities, Vocabulary, Information, Block Design, Visual Puzzles, Matrix Reasoning, Figure Weights, Arithmetic, Coding, Symbol Search. Which older subtests (for example Comprehension, Picture Completion, Cancellation, Letter-Number Sequencing) were dropped or moved: uncertain. FSIQ is derived from a reduced set of about 7 subtests (exact composition uncertain). Ancillary indices such as GAI and CPI are available. WISC-V: Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fifth Edition The WISC-V is the children's version of the Wechsler, used for school-age assessment of intellectual disability, giftedness and specific learning disorder. It was the first Wechsler to split perceptual reasoning into separate visual-spatial and fluid reasoning indices, producing five primary indices. Subtests are organised in three tiers (primary, secondary, complementary), and the FSIQ comes from just 7 primary subtests, which shortens testing. Testing starts with two routing subtests that estimate the person's level so that later subtests begin at the right difficulty. It is valued for its very wide age range and good floor and ceiling, useful in assessing both intellectual disability and high giftedness. John Raven designed it to measure Charles Spearman's g , specifically eductive ability (making meaning out of confusion, seeing relations), as distinct from reproductive ability (recalling learned information), which he measured with the companion Mill Hill Vocabulary Scale. Items get "progressively" harder within each set, hence the name. Field Detail Full name Raven's Progressive Matrices: Standard (SPM), Coloured (CPM), Advanced (APM) Author(s), year John C. Performance tests and Indian intelligence tests A performance test is an intelligence test in which the person responds by doing something with materials (arranging blocks, fitting shapes into a board, sliding pieces, drawing) rather than by answering in words. Performance tests developed for three reasons. First, the US Army testing programme of World War I (the Army Alpha for literate recruits and the Army Beta for illiterate and non-English-speaking recruits, Robert Yerkes and colleagues, 1917) showed that verbal tests unfairly penalise people without schooling or language. Second, clinicians needed tests for deaf, speech-impaired and non-English-speaking children. Third, verbal and performance tasks seemed to tap partly different abilities: W. P. Alexander (1935) argued for a "practical" factor (F) beyond g, and Wechsler built both Verbal and Performance scales into his tests. India needed performance tests for the same reasons, even more acutely: at independence most of the population was not literate, the country has dozens of languages, and verbal Western tests are culturally loaded. Indian psychologists therefore did two things: they adapted Western tests (Binet-Kamat from the Stanford-Binet; MISIC from the WISC; WAPIS from the WAIS; Indian norms for Raven's and the Draw-a-Man), and they assembled batteries of existing performance tests with Indian norms (the Bhatia Battery). Many of these instruments date from the 1930s to 1970s and use old norms, a limitation examiners like to ask about, yet they remain in daily use in Indian clinics and are named in the government guidelines for certifying intellectual disability. High yield Indian adaptation pairs to memorise: Binet-Kamat (V. V. Kamat) from Stanford-Binet; MISIC (A. J. Malin, Nagpur) from WISC; WAPIS (P. Ramalingaswamy) from WAIS performance scale; Malin's VSMS (A. J. Malin, Nagpur) from Doll's Vineland; DASII (Pramila Phatak, Baroda) from Bayley; Bhatia Battery (C. M. Bhatia) is an Indian battery of mostly Western performance tests. Bhatia Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence C. M. Bhatia assembled five tests, four performance tests and one memory test, and standardised them on Indian school children so that intelligence could be assessed without depending on literacy or a particular language. The tests are given individually with materials, and the scores are converted into an overall index. It remains one of the most-asked Indian tests in entrance MCQs, usually as "name the five subtests" or "who developed it". Kohs Block Design Test The person is given coloured cubes and a printed design card and must arrange the blocks so that their top faces reproduce the design. Wechsler borrowed it as the Block Design subtest, which is still one of the best single measures of g in the Wechsler batteries and is sensitive to right parietal brain damage. Developmental, adaptive behaviour and social maturity scales An IQ test asks "how well can this person reason when tested?". A developmental scale asks "has this infant or young child reached the milestones expected for their age?", and an adaptive behaviour scale asks "how well does this person actually manage everyday life: dressing, eating, communicating, getting along with others, handling money?". These questions matter because intellectual disability is defined by two criteria, deficits in intellectual functioning and deficits in adaptive functioning, both beginning in the developmental period. A child can score 65 on an IQ test yet function independently at home and school; under DSM-5 that child may not meet criteria. Most developmental and adaptive scales are completed by observation and informant interview (usually a parent or caregiver) rather than by testing the person directly, which makes them usable with infants and with severely disabled people who cannot be tested. Scores are typically expressed as an age equivalent (developmental age, social age) and a quotient: Developmental Quotient (DQ) = developmental age / chronological age x 100 , and Social Quotient (SQ) = social age / chronological age x 100 . Modern scales (Vineland-3, Bayley-4) use deviation standard scores with mean 100, SD 15 instead. A further distinction is screening versus diagnostic assessment . Screening tests (Denver II, TDSC) are short, used on many children (for example in paediatric clinics), and only flag children who need further evaluation; they do not give a diagnosis or a reliable quotient. Diagnostic scales (Bayley, Gesell schedules, DASII) take longer and give a quantified developmental level. Definition Adaptive behaviour : the conceptual, social and practical skills people learn and perform in their everyday lives (AAIDD definition). Social age (SA) : the age level of a person's social competence on the VSMS. SQ = SA / CA x 100. DQ = developmental age / CA x 100. VSMS: Vineland Social Maturity Scale (Doll) Edgar Doll, at the Vineland Training School in New Jersey, wanted to measure what intelligence tests missed: how far a person can look after themselves and take part in social life. The VSMS is a list of everyday competencies arranged in order of the age at which they are typically achieved (from "crows, laughs" in infancy to managing others' affairs in adulthood). An informant who knows the person well is interviewed, each item is marked as habitually performed or not, and the total gives a social age and a social quotient. It was the first standardised adaptive behaviour scale. Field Detail Full name Vineland Social Maturity Scale Author(s), year Edgar A. Gesell's maturational theory (development unfolds according to an inner biological timetable) shaped the whole field, and the Bayley, Denver and Indian DST all borrow from his items. Classifying intellectual disability: IQ ranges, adaptive criteria and Indian certification Older systems classified intellectual disability (formerly "mental retardation") mainly by IQ ranges, roughly 2, 3, 4 and 5 SD below the mean of 100. DSM-IV-TR (2000) used overlapping bands (for example "50 to 55 up to about 70") to allow for measurement error. DSM-5 (2013) made a major change: the diagnosis still requires IQ about 2 SD below the mean (approximately 65 to 75, that is 70 plus or minus 5 for measurement error), but severity (mild, moderate, severe, profound) is now defined by adaptive functioning in three domains (conceptual, social, practical), not by IQ. ICD-11 (2019, in force 2022) uses "disorders of intellectual development" with mild, moderate, severe, profound and provisional categories, based on standardised tests where available (mild about 2 to 3 SD below the mean; moderate 3 to 4 SD; severe and profound more than 4 SD, separated from each other only by adaptive behaviour). In India, intellectual disability is one of the 21 disabilities under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016 ; "benchmark disability" is 40 percent or more, which gives access to reservations and benefits. The government guidelines for assessment (Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment; a 2018 gazette notification under the RPwD Act replaced earlier guidelines) use standardised Indian tests to obtain an IQ and a social quotient (SQ, from VSMS) for children and adults, and a DQ for young children (with "global developmental delay" for children under 5). Certification is by a medical board that includes a clinical psychologist. Objective personality inventories An objective personality inventory is a self-report questionnaire. The person reads a fixed set of statements ("I often feel tense", "I like going to parties") and answers in a fixed format (true/false, yes/no, a 3, 4 or 5 point agreement scale, or a forced choice between two statements). It is called "objective" not because the person is being objective about themselves, but because the scoring is objective: two scorers with the same answer sheet always get the same score, unlike a projective test where interpretation depends on the clinician. The weakness is the mirror image of the strength: the person can see what is being asked, so they can fake good, fake bad, answer carelessly, or simply agree with everything (acquiescence). This is why the serious clinical inventories carry validity scales that check how the test was taken before any clinical scale is read. There are three classic ways to build an inventory, and examiners love to ask which test used which. Rational (logical or content) keying: the author writes items that obviously reflect the trait, based on theory or clinical judgement. Example: Woodworth Personal Data Sheet, Bell Adjustment Inventory, the MMPI-2 content scales, the Taylor Manifest Anxiety Scale (items chosen by clinicians' judgement). Empirical criterion keying: the author does not care what an item seems to mean; an item is kept only if it statistically separates a criterion group (say, diagnosed depressed patients) from normals. The item "I prefer a shower to a bath" could land on a scale purely because the groups answered it differently. Examples: MMPI (1943), CPI, Strong Vocational Interest Blank. Factor-analytic construction: the author gives a large item pool to many people and lets factor analysis reveal which items cluster into dimensions. Examples: Raymond B. Cattell's 16PF, Hans Eysenck's EPI/EPQ, J. P. Guilford's inventories, and the Big Five tradition (NEO-PI-R). Many modern tests mix methods; the MMPI-2 Restructured Clinical scales, for instance, were built by factor analysis inside an empirically keyed instrument, and Theodore Millon's MCMI combined theory, internal consistency and external validation (a "sequential" approach). The first personality inventory was the Woodworth Personal Data Sheet (Robert S. Woodworth, 1917, published 1919), built during World War I to screen US army recruits for "shell shock" proneness (emotional instability). It had about 116 yes/no questions (sources give 116; treat the exact count as uncertain) drawn from psychiatric symptom lists, so it was rationally keyed. Every later inventory is a descendant of this idea of a "paper psychiatric interview". High yield First personality inventory: Woodworth Personal Data Sheet (1917). Classic empirically keyed test: MMPI (Hathaway and McKinley, 1943). Classic factor-analytic tests: 16PF (Raymond Cattell), EPQ (Hans Eysenck), NEO-PI-R (Paul Costa and Robert McCrae). "Sane man's MMPI" or the test for normal people built the empirical way: CPI (Gough). MMPI: Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory The MMPI was built at the University of Minnesota hospitals to give psychiatrists a quick, standardised aid to diagnosis. Starke R. Hathaway (a psychologist) and J. Charnley McKinley (a neuropsychiatrist) wrote about 1,000 statements, administered them to diagnosed patient groups and to normal visitors to the hospital (the "Minnesota normals"), and kept items that separated each patient group from normals: this is pure empirical criterion keying . The person answers True or False (or Cannot Say). Scores are converted to T scores and interpreted mainly as code types , the two or three highest elevated clinical scales (for example a "2-7" code: depressed and anxious), because the scales turned out to be poor at pure diagnosis but rich in correlates. MBTI: Myers-Briggs Type Indicator The MBTI turns Carl Gustav Jung's Psychological Types (1921) into a questionnaire. Jung described two attitudes (extraversion and introversion) and four functions (thinking, feeling, sensing, intuition). Katharine Cook Briggs and her daughter Isabel Briggs Myers added a fourth preference, Judging versus Perceiving, and sort each person into one of 16 types (e.g. INTJ). Items are mostly forced-choice between two words or two statements. It is popular in career counselling and team building, and is intended for normal people, not for diagnosis. EPPS: Edwards Personal Preference Schedule Allen L. Edwards showed that people answer inventory items largely according to how socially desirable the item sounds. To neutralise this, he paired statements of roughly equal social desirability, each tapping a different need from Henry Murray's (1938) need system, and made the person choose one: a forced-choice format. Because every choice for one need is a choice against another, the scores are ipsative : they show the relative strength of needs within one person and always sum to the same total, so they cannot properly be compared between people. Q-sort: Q-technique and the California Q-set In a Q-sort the person sorts a deck of cards, each carrying a descriptive statement ("I am a submissive person"), into piles from "most like me" to "least like me", with a fixed number of cards per pile so the result forms a quasi-normal distribution (commonly 9 piles). William Stephenson (1953) introduced this Q-technique : instead of correlating tests across people (R-technique), it correlates people (or the same person under different instructions) across items. Carl Rogers and his colleagues (John Butler and Gerard Haigh, 1954) used it to measure the gap between the real self and the ideal self : the correlation between the two sorts rose during successful client-centred therapy. Jack Block's California Q-set is a standard 100-item deck sorted by an observer (clinician) to describe someone's personality. Aptitude, interest, creativity and attitude measures This family covers tests that are not about psychopathology or global intelligence. An aptitude test estimates a person's potential to learn or succeed in a specific area in future (mechanical work, clerical work, numerical tasks); an achievement test , by contrast, measures what has already been learned. Because general intelligence tests give one broad score, guidance psychologists wanted multiple aptitude batteries that give a profile of separate abilities, which grew out of factor analysis (L. L. Thurstone's Primary Mental Abilities, 1938). The DAT and GATB are the two classic batteries. Interest inventories ask what a person likes or dislikes (activities, school subjects, occupations), on the logic that people are happier and stay longer in work that matches their interests. Two construction routes matter: the empirical route (Edward K. Strong Jr.: compare the answers of people successfully employed in an occupation with "people in general") and the homogeneous or rational route (G. Frederic Kuder's broad interest areas; John L. Holland's six RIASEC types). Creativity tests rest on J. P. Guilford's distinction (presidential address to the APA, 1950; Structure of Intellect model, 1956/1967) between convergent thinking , finding the single correct answer, and divergent thinking , producing many varied answers to an open problem. Divergent production is scored for fluency (number of responses), flexibility (number of different categories), originality (statistical rarity) and elaboration (amount of detail). Attitude scales measure an evaluative disposition towards an object (a group, the church, an institution). The classic scaling methods differ in how statements are chosen and how a score is formed: Thurstone uses judges to place statements on an interval scale, Likert sums agreement ratings, Guttman builds a cumulative ladder, Emory Bogardus measures social distance, and Osgood maps connotative meaning. Implicit measures (the IAT) try to bypass self-report altogether. High yield Aptitude = future potential; achievement = past learning. Strong = empirical occupational keying; Kuder = forced-choice triads, ipsative; Holland = RIASEC hexagon (used inside the Strong as General Occupational Themes). Divergent thinking scoring: fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration (FFOE). DAT: Differential Aptitude Tests The DAT was built for educational and vocational guidance of secondary school students: rather than one IQ, it gives a profile of eight abilities so that a counsellor can say, for example, "strong mechanical and spatial, weak verbal". Each subtest is a timed multiple-choice test. The sum of Verbal Reasoning and Numerical Ability works as an index of scholastic aptitude (general academic ability). Thurstone scale: method of equal-appearing intervals Louis L. Thurstone and Ernest J. Chave (1929, The Measurement of Attitude , on attitude toward the church) first wrote a large pool of opinion statements. Many judges (around 300 in the original work) sorted each statement into 11 piles from most unfavourable to most favourable, without giving their own opinion. Each statement's scale value is the median pile it was placed in; its ambiguity is the spread of judges' placements (the interquartile range, Q). Statements with low ambiguity and evenly spaced scale values (commonly about 20 to 22) form the final scale. A respondent simply ticks the statements they agree with, and their score is the median (or mean) scale value of those statements. Projective techniques Every test in the earlier sections of this book works the same way: the item is clear, the possible answers are fixed, and the score is a count of how many answers fall in a keyed direction. A projective technique turns that logic upside down. The stimulus is deliberately ambiguous (an inkblot, a vague picture, half a sentence, a blank sheet of paper), the instructions are minimal ("What might this be?", "Tell me a story", "Finish the sentence"), and there is no right answer. Because the stimulus itself contains so little structure, whatever structure appears in the response is assumed to come from the person: their needs, fears, conflicts, defences, ways of perceiving and ways of organising experience. That assumption is called the projective hypothesis . Definition The projective hypothesis states that when a person is asked to impose meaning or organisation on an ambiguous, relatively unstructured stimulus, the response reflects the person's own enduring personality: their perceptual style, needs, motives, conflicts and defences. The less structured the stimulus, the more the response is determined by the person rather than by the stimulus. 6.0.1 Where the idea came from The word "projection" comes from Sigmund Freud, who described it in the 1890s (in his papers on paranoia, 1894 to 1896, and most fully in the Schreber case, 1911) as a defence mechanism : an unacceptable impulse or feeling of one's own is attributed to someone else ("I hate him" becomes "he hates me"). Freud also allowed a broader, non-defensive sense in which people generally read their inner world into the outer world. Projective testing borrowed the broader sense. A person who tells a story about a boy sadly staring at a violin is not necessarily defending against anything; they are simply organising an ambiguous picture using their own concerns. The phrase "projective methods" was coined by Lawrence K. Frank (1939) in his paper "Projective methods for the study of personality" in the Journal of Psychology . Frank argued that personality is a dynamic process of organising experience, and that the best way to see it is to give a person a "field" with little cultural structure and watch how they structure it, the way an X-ray reveals an inner structure without opening the body. Frank grouped together techniques that already existed: Hermann Rorschach's inkblots (1921), Carl Jung's word association (1910), and Christiana Morgan and Henry Murray's Thematic Apperception Test (1935). Henry Murray (1938, Explorations in Personality ) supplied the motivational theory (needs and press) that most storytelling techniques still use. 6.0.2 Why ambiguity matters, and what the techniques share Projective techniques share five features: (1) an ambiguous or unstructured stimulus; (2) a task that allows an almost unlimited variety of responses; (3) a disguised purpose, so the person usually does not know how the answer will be interpreted, which makes faking harder; (4) a global, holistic interpretation aiming at the whole personality rather than a single trait; and (5) heavy reliance on the trained clinician's judgement. They grew out of the psychodynamic tradition, which explains why so many of them talk about unconscious conflict, psychosexual stages and defence. In modern language many authors prefer the term performance-based personality tests (or "free-response measures") because the person performs a task in front of you and you observe how they do it, which is less theory-laden than "projection". 6.0.3 Gardner Lindzey's five-way classification (1959) Gardner Lindzey (1959) , in "On the classification of projective techniques" ( Psychological Bulletin ), sorted projective tests by the kind of response they require. This is the classification Indian MCQs ask about most often, and it appears in Anne Anastasi's and Frank Freeman's textbooks. Association : the person responds to a stimulus with the first word, image or percept that comes to mind. Examples: Rorschach Inkblot Test, Holtzman Inkblot Technique, Somatic Inkblot Series, Word Association Test (Francis Galton, Jung, Kent-Rosanoff), Hand Test. Construction : the person must create or construct a product, typically a story, from a picture. Examples: Thematic Apperception Test, Children's Apperception Test, Senior Apperception Technique, Roberts Apperception Test, Blacky Pictures, Make-A-Picture-Story. Completion : the person completes an unfinished stimulus. Examples: Rotter Incomplete Sentences Blank, Sacks Sentence Completion Test, Rosenzweig Picture-Frustration Study (completing a cartoon speech balloon), story completion methods. Choice or ordering : the person chooses among, or arranges in order, a set of alternatives according to some criterion (liking, appropriateness, attractiveness). Examples: Szondi Test (choose liked and disliked photographs), Tomkins-Horn Picture Arrangement Test, and picture-arrangement variants of the TAT. Expression : the person freely expresses themselves through a medium, and the manner (style) of production matters as much as the product. Examples: Draw-A-Person, House-Tree-Person, Kinetic Family Drawing, finger painting, play techniques, psychodrama, Bender Gestalt used projectively. Lowenfeld's World and Mosaic techniques are placed by different authors under expression or construction. Memory hook "A Clever Child Can Express" : Association, Construction, Completion, Choice/ordering, Expression. Then attach one anchor test to each: Rorschach (A), TAT (Construction), Sentence completion (Completion), Szondi (Choice), Draw-A-Person (Expression). 6.0.4 The reliability and validity problem Projective tests have been criticised since the 1950s, and you must be able to explain both sides. Standardisation : many techniques have several competing administration and scoring systems (the Rorschach had five major American systems before 1974; the TAT still has no single official system), so two clinicians may not be giving the same test. Reliability : interscorer reliability is acceptable only when a structured coding system is used (Exner's Comprehensive System, R-PAS, the Rotter ISB). Test-retest reliability is hard to estimate because stories and percepts change from occasion to occasion. Split-half reliability is usually not meaningful because cards are not equivalent items. Validity : global, intuitive interpretation has poor validity. Classic studies by Loren and Jean Chapman (1967, 1969) showed illusory correlation : clinicians "saw" relationships (for example big eyes in a drawing and paranoia) that did not exist in the data, because the signs matched their expectations. Specific, empirically keyed variables fare better: Joni Mihura and colleagues' 2013 meta-analysis in Psychological Bulletin found good validity for some Rorschach variables (especially those indexing thought disorder and perceptual accuracy) and poor validity for others, which shaped R-PAS. Norms : norms are often small, old, or American; cultural influence on content (what is "popular" or "normal") is large, which matters directly in India. Examiner effects : the examiner's behaviour, sex, rapport and even seating position influence responses (Exner seated the examiner side by side to reduce cueing). In their favour : they are hard to fake in a socially desirable direction, they bypass reading ability, they give rich idiographic material for case formulation, and they can reveal thought disorder and perceptual distortion that a self-report questionnaire, which depends on insight, cannot. High yield Frank 1939 coined the term; Sigmund Freud supplied the concept of projection; Murray supplied needs and press; Lindzey 1959 supplied the five categories. Projective = unstructured stimulus, unlimited response, disguised purpose, global interpretation. Main weakness: reliability and validity; main strength: resistance to faking and access to unconscious or unreportable material. Rorschach: Rorschach Inkblot Test The Rorschach is the best-known projective technique and the prototype of the "association" category. Hermann Rorschach, a Swiss psychiatrist working at Herisau, published it in his 1921 monograph Psychodiagnostik , based on about 400 subjects; he died in 1922, aged 37, before he could develop it further. The person is shown 10 symmetrical inkblots one at a time and asked "What might this be?" (the response or free association phase ); the examiner records every response verbatim, then goes back through each response in the inquiry phase to find out where on the blot the person saw it (location) and what about the blot made it look that way (determinants). Rorschach's own insight was that how a person sees (whole versus detail, form versus colour, movement) is more informative than what they see, so the test is fundamentally a test of perception and problem-solving under ambiguity, not just a content test. The 10 cards Colour group Cards Notes Achromatic (black, white and grey only) I, IV, V, VI, VII 5 cards. Card V (bat or butterfly) is the "easiest" popular; Card IV is often called the "father card" and Card VII the "mother card" in older lore (folk interpretation, not validated). Black and red (achromatic plus red) II, III 2 cards. The red was thought to provoke "colour shock". Fully chromatic (multi-coloured pastels) VIII, IX, X 3 cards. Card VIII has the most popular animal response (the side pink animals). Scoring (coding) categories, built up from scratch Location (where on the blot): W = whole blot; D = common detail (a frequently used area); Dd = unusual detail (a rarely used area); S = white space (always coded together with W, D or Dd, for example WS). Developmental quality (DQ) adds how well the parts are integrated: + (synthesised), o (ordinary), v/+ and v (vague). Determinants (what feature of the blot produced the percept): F = form (shape) alone; M = human movement; FM = animal movement; m = inanimate movement; chromatic colour : FC (form dominant, colour secondary), CF (colour dominant), C (pure colour, no form), Cn (colour naming); C' = achromatic colour (black, white, grey used as colour); T = texture (shading felt as touch, fur); V = vista (shading felt as depth); Y = diffuse shading (light-dark without texture or depth); FD = form dimension (depth from size or perspective, not shading); Fr / rF = reflection; (2) = pair. Shading and achromatic codes also take FT/TF, FV/VF, FY/YF, FC'/C'F forms depending on whether form dominates. Form quality (how well the percept fits the blot): in the Comprehensive System + (superior, elaborated), o (ordinary, common and accurate), u (unusual but acceptable), - (minus, distorted). Poor form quality (high X-%) indexes perceptual distortion and reality-testing problems. Content : H (whole human), (H) (fictional human), Hd (human detail), A, Ad, An (anatomy), Bl (blood), Sx (sex), Xy (X-ray), Na (nature), Bt (botany), Cg (clothing), Fd (food), Fi (fire), Ex (explosion), Art, Ay (anthropology), Cl (clouds), Ge (geography), Hh (household), Ls (landscape), Sc (science), Id (idiographic) and so on. Populars (P) : responses given very frequently in the normative sample. The Comprehensive System lists 13 populars (for example a bat or butterfly on Card V, two humans on Card III, the animals on the sides of Card VIII). Z (organisational activity) : a weighted score given when a person organises parts of the blot into a meaningful relationship; ZSum and Zd (ZSum minus the expected ZSum) index the efficiency of information scanning (overincorporation versus underincorporation). Special scores (Comprehensive System): cognitive slippage codes DV, INCOM, DR, FABCOM, ALOG, CONTAM (Level 1 and Level 2) summed as WSum6; plus AB, AG, COP, MOR, PER, CP, PSV and the later GHR/PHR (good and poor human representation). Five classical American scoring systems (before Exner) Rorschach's early death left the method without an owner, and five American schools developed in parallel: Samuel J. Beck (from his 1937 monograph onward; strongly empirical and normative), Bruno Klopfer ( The Rorschach Technique , with Douglas Kelley, 1942; phenomenological, introduced "testing the limits"), Zygmunt Piotrowski ( Perceptanalysis , 1957; known for his organic signs), Marguerite Hertz (Cleveland; frequency tables of form level), and David Rapaport and Roy Schafer (with Merton Gill, Diagnostic Psychological Testing , 1945 to 1946; psychoanalytic ego psychology; Schafer 1954 on psychoanalytic interpretation). John Exner's survey of these systems in the late 1960s found that they used different administration, codes and interpretations, so research results could not be compared. That problem is why the Comprehensive System was built. Exner CS: Rorschach Comprehensive System John E. Exner Jr. combined the empirically best-supported elements of the five American systems into one standardised method, published in 1974 as The Rorschach: A Comprehensive System (Volume 1). Administration was fixed: examiner seated side by side with the client, the single standard question "What might this be?", a response phase followed by an inquiry phase, and verbatim recording. Responses are coded, and the codes are tallied into a Structural Summary , a page of frequencies, ratios, percentages and derived indices that is interpreted against normative data. Exner (who died in 2006) set a minimum of 14 responses : protocols with R under 14 were considered unreliable and the person was asked to give more. The minimum R is 14 in the Comprehensive System; in R-PAS the target is 18 to 28. SCZI was renamed and revised as PTI; an MCQ may describe PTI as a "schizophrenia index" in older terms. R-PAS: Rorschach Performance Assessment System R-PAS was developed after Exner's death by members of his research council, who wanted to keep only variables with solid empirical support (drawing on the Mihura et al. 2013 meta-analysis) and to fix the biggest practical problem of the CS: the huge variation in the number of responses, which distorts almost every other score. Its key administrative change is R-Optimised administration : the person is asked to give two, maybe three responses per card; if they give only one, the examiner prompts for another, and if they give four, the examiner pulls the card back ("prompt and pull"). This keeps most protocols in the target range of about 18 to 28 responses . Results are reported as standard scores (mean 100, SD 15) against an international normative sample, on two pages of variables. Holtzman (one response per card) is a third, separate approach. HIT: Holtzman Inkblot Technique Wayne H. Holtzman (with Joseph Thorpe, Jon Swartz and E. Wayne Herron) built the HIT in 1961 specifically to answer the psychometric criticisms of the Rorschach. Instead of 10 cards with a variable number of responses, it has many more cards and allows only one response per card , so every person contributes the same number of responses and each card can be treated like a test item. It has two parallel forms (A and B) of 45 cards each, which makes test-retest and alternate-form reliability possible, something the Rorschach cannot offer. Responses are scored on 22 standardised variables with norms. Field Detail Full name Holtzman Inkblot Technique (HIT) Author(s), year Wayne H. Holtzman, with Joseph S. Thorpe, Jon D. Swartz and E. SIS: Somatic Inkblot Series The Somatic Inkblot Series is a set of inkblots deliberately drawn to suggest body parts, internal organs and anatomical images , so that the person's responses reveal body image, somatic preoccupation and the emotional meaning attached to the body. It was developed by Wilfred A. Cassell, an American psychiatrist, starting around 1980, and is used in psychosomatic medicine and with patients who express distress through bodily symptoms. Like the Rorschach, it is an association technique, but the stimuli are not neutral: they are built to "pull" bodily content. TAT: Thematic Apperception Test The TAT is the prototype of the "construction" category. The person is shown pictures of people in ambiguous situations and asked to tell a dramatic story for each: what led up to the scene, what is happening now, what the characters are thinking and feeling, and how it ends. The theory (Henry Murray's personology, 1938) is that the storyteller identifies with a central character, the hero , and attributes to the hero their own needs (internal motives, for example need for achievement, affiliation, aggression, autonomy) while describing press (forces in the environment acting on the hero, for example rejection, danger, nurturance). The combination of a need and a press, with its outcome, is a thema . "Apperception" (a term from Johann Friedrich Herbart) means perceiving something in the light of past experience and existing mental contents, which is exactly what the test exploits. Field Detail Full name Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) Author(s), year Christiana D. Morgan and Henry A. Murray, 1935 ("A method for investigating fantasies", Harvard Psychological Clinic); manual by Murray, 1943 Versions 1935 original set; third and final revision of cards published with the 1943 Harvard manual (this is the set still used) Publisher Harvard University Press Age range Mainly adolescents and adults (commonly from about 14 years); children are better tested with the CAT; sources differ on the lower limit Items 31 cards : 30 pictures plus 1 blank card (card 16) . Cards are coded by number and letters: B (boys), G (girls), M (adult males), F (adult females), e.g. 3BM, 6GF, 12M. 11 cards are universal (no letter), for example 1 (boy with violin), 2, 4, 5, 10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 19, 20. Classically 20 cards per person in 2 sessions of 10 (cards 1 to 10, then the more unusual 11 to 20, at least a day apart); in practice clinicians use 8 to 12 selected cards Subtests / scales / indices No subtests. Murray's need-press analysis (needs, press, thema, outcome, hero). Later scoring systems: Leopold Bellak's (1947 onward), David McClelland and John Atkinson's need for achievement scoring (1953), Phebe Cramer's Defense Mechanism Manual, Drew Westen's SCORS (Social Cognition and Object Relations Scale) Scoring and norms No single official norm system; mostly qualitative or content-coded. "20" is the number classically given to one person, in two sessions. Card 1 is the boy with the violin. Authors are Morgan AND Murray (1935); the 1943 manual is Murray's. Murray's theory term is press (environment), not "pressure". The Indian TAT is by Uma Chowdhury, not by Udai Pareek (Pareek adapted the Rosenzweig P-F). CAT: Children's Apperception Test Leopold Bellak and Sonya Sorel Bellak created the CAT in 1949 because young children found the TAT's adult human scenes hard to identify with. Following a suggestion attributed to Ernst Kris, they used animals in human-like situations (for example chicks eating at a table with a large hen in the background; a lion with a pipe and cane), on the idea that children identify more readily with animals and that animal pictures are less threatening. The pictures target feeding, sibling rivalry, parental relations, aggression, toilet training and fears of being alone at night. RISB: Rotter Incomplete Sentences Blank Sentence completion is the prototype of the "completion" category. The person is given sentence stems ("I like...", "My father...", "I regret...") and asked to complete each with their real feelings. Julian B. Rotter and Janet E. Rafferty (1950) made it one of the most psychometrically respectable projectives by providing an objective scoring manual that rates each completion for conflict versus positive adjustment, giving a total overall adjustment score. Because the stems are semi-structured, it is the least ambiguous projective, and its purpose is fairly transparent. P-F Study: Rosenzweig Picture-Frustration Study Saul Rosenzweig built the P-F Study from his own frustration-aggression theory. Each item is a cartoon of two people in a mildly frustrating everyday situation: one person says something frustrating, and the other person's speech balloon is empty. The respondent writes the first reply that comes to mind, which is assumed to show how they typically react to frustration. It is a "completion" technique, semi-projective and fairly structured, and is scored objectively on two dimensions: direction of aggression and type of reaction. WAT: Word Association Test (Galton, Jung, Kent-Rosanoff) The word association method is the oldest projective technique. A list of stimulus words is read aloud one at a time, and the person replies with the first word that comes to mind while the examiner times the reaction. Francis Galton (1879) first tried it on himself with 75 words to study the contents of the mind. Carl Gustav Jung (Studies in Word Association, 1904 to 1910; his 1909 to 1910 Clark University lectures) turned it into a clinical tool with a list of 100 stimulus words , using disturbances in responding, called complex indicators , to detect emotionally charged "complexes": prolonged reaction time, failure to respond, repeating the stimulus word, misunderstanding the word, perseveration, very personal or odd responses, clang associations, and failure to reproduce the original answer on a second run (the reproduction test). Jung also combined it with the psychogalvanic (skin conductance) response. Grace H. Kent and Aaron J. Rosanoff (1910) took the opposite, normative route: 100 neutral common words with frequency tables of responses from 1,000 normal adults, so that a response could be scored as common or idiosyncratic, used originally to distinguish psychotic from normal subjects. Field Detail Full name Word Association Test (Jung's association method; Kent-Rosanoff Free Association Test) Author(s), year Francis Galton, 1879; Carl Jung, 1904 to 1910 (100-word list); Grace Kent and Aaron Rosanoff, 1910; David Rapaport's 60-word list (1946) used diagnostically Versions Jung list, Kent-Rosanoff list, Rapaport list; many local translations Publisher Kent-Rosanoff published in American Journal of Insanity (1910); no single commercial publisher Age range Older children to adults Items Galton 75 words; Jung 100; Kent-Rosanoff 100; Rapaport 60 Subtests / scales / indices Jung: complex indicators, reaction time. Kent-Rosanoff: common versus individual (idiosyncratic) responses using frequency tables Scoring and norms Reaction time (in seconds), response content, frequency norms (Kent-Rosanoff from 1,000 normal adults) Measures Emotional complexes (Jung); commonality of thought, thought disorder (Kent-Rosanoff) Indian adaptation Hindi and other Indian language word lists have been constructed by individual researchers; standard adaptation uncertain Exam trap Carl Jung's list (complex indicators, reaction time, emotional complexes) versus Kent-Rosanoff (frequency tables, normality versus psychosis, 1,000 normals). Both have 100 words and both date from around 1910, so examiners ask which one had norms (Kent-Rosanoff) and which one detected complexes (Jung). The originator of word association is Francis Galton (1879), not Jung. Wundt used association in the laboratory too, but the clinical method is Jung's. DAP: Draw-A-Person (Machover) In the Draw-A-Person, the person is given a blank sheet and a pencil and asked to "draw a person"; afterwards they are asked to draw a person of the opposite sex, and then questioned about the drawings. Karen Machover (1949, Personality Projection in the Drawing of the Human Figure ) proposed the body-image hypothesis : the drawn figure represents the drawer's own body image and self-concept, so features like size, placement on the page, line pressure, erasures, omissions and the treatment of specific body parts (eyes, hands, mouth) are read as signs of personality and conflict. Neuropsychological tests and batteries A neuropsychological test is a standardised task that samples one cognitive function (attention, memory, language, visuospatial skill, executive control, motor speed) so that the clinician can infer how well the brain systems underlying that function are working. The logic is borrowed from neurology: a lesion in a particular brain region produces a particular pattern of failures, so a carefully chosen set of tasks can reveal whether the brain is affected, which functions are impaired and spared, and how the person fails. Clinically, these tests are used in dementia, head injury, stroke, epilepsy, tumours, schizophrenia and other psychiatric disorders with cognitive deficits, ADHD and learning disorders, and for rehabilitation planning and capacity decisions. Historical "organicity" testing. From the 1930s to the 1960s, clinical psychologists were mostly asked one crude question: "Is this patient organic (brain damaged) or functional (psychiatric)?" Single tests were used as general screens for "organicity": the Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test (Lauretta Bender, 1938), the Benton Visual Retention Test (Arthur Benton, 1946) and the Memory-for-Designs Test (Frances Graham and Barbara Kendall, 1946; manual 1960). The assumption was that brain damage is a single, unitary thing that any sensitive test will detect. That assumption is now known to be wrong: brain damage varies by location, size, speed of onset and age, and a right parietal stroke and a left frontal tumour produce very different profiles. Modern neuropsychology therefore asks about specific functions, not "organicity" in general, although the old screening tests remain popular in Indian clinics and in MCQs. Three approaches to assessment. (1) The fixed battery approach gives every patient the same, fixed set of tests, scored against norms, with summary indices. Examples are the Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Battery (Ward Halstead, 1947; Ralph Reitan) and the Luria-Nebraska Neuropsychological Battery (Charles Golden and colleagues, 1980). Strengths: comprehensive, good for research and for comparing patients; weaknesses: long (often 6 to 8 hours for the Halstead-Reitan) and not tailored to the referral question. (2) The flexible battery approach chooses a core set of tests and then adds tests depending on the referral question and on what the first results show (most clinicians work this way today; the NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery is usually used as a flexible, domain-based set). (3) The process approach , developed by Edith Kaplan and colleagues at the Boston Veterans Administration Hospital (the "Boston Process Approach", from the 1970s and 1980s), argues that how a person reaches a score matters more than the score itself. Two patients may both score 20 on a copying task, one because of poor planning (piecemeal, fragmented copy, typical of right hemisphere or frontal damage) and the other because of missing details within an intact outline (typical of left hemisphere damage). The process approach records strategies, errors, time per item and the order of drawing. Products of this approach include the WAIS-R as a Neuropsychological Instrument (WAIS-R NI , Kaplan, Fein, Morris and Delis, 1991), the California Verbal Learning Test and the Delis-Kaplan Executive Function System (D-KEFS , Dean Delis, Edith Kaplan and Joel Kramer, 2001). Luria's qualitative approach. The Russian neuropsychologist Alexander Romanovich Luria (1902 to 1977) did not use norms or total scores. He saw every complex behaviour as a functional system built from several links located in different brain areas, and he organised the brain into three functional units : (1) the unit for regulating tone and waking (brainstem and reticular formation), (2) the unit for receiving, analysing and storing information (posterior cortex: occipital, temporal, parietal), and (3) the unit for programming, regulating and verifying activity (frontal lobes). By watching exactly where a function broke down (syndrome analysis), Luria inferred which link was damaged. His methods were collected and published in English by the Danish psychologist Anne-Lise Christensen (1975) as Luria's Neuropsychological Investigation ; Golden and colleagues later standardised Christensen's items into the Luria-Nebraska battery. Domains to know. Orientation and general cognition (MMSE, MoCA, ACE-III); attention and speed (Digit Span, Trail Making A, Stroop word and colour pages, digit vigilance, cancellation); memory (WMS, PGI Memory Scale, Rey AVLT, CVLT, Rey complex figure recall, Benton Visual Retention Test); language (Boston Naming Test, Token Test, verbal fluency, BDAE, WAB); visuospatial and constructional skill (Bender-Gestalt, Rey figure copy, clock drawing, block design); executive function (WCST, Trail Making B, Stroop interference, Tower of London, verbal fluency); motor (finger tapping, grip strength, grooved pegboard); and severity or staging scales (GCS, CDR, GDS, Hachinski). Definition Executive functions are the higher-order control processes, mainly supported by the prefrontal cortex and its circuits, that let a person plan, start, shift, inhibit, monitor and adjust goal-directed behaviour. Classic tests: WCST (set shifting), Stroop (inhibition), Trail Making B (switching), Tower of London (planning), verbal fluency (generation and strategic retrieval). Bender-Gestalt: Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test The person copies simple geometric designs (dots, lines, curves, overlapping shapes) printed one per card, on a blank sheet, with no time limit and no eraser restrictions in most versions. The idea, drawn from Gestalt psychology, is that perceiving a design as an organised whole and reproducing it requires integrating visual perception with motor output (visual-motor integration); children's copies mature with age, and brain damage, intellectual disability or emotional disturbance distort the copies in characteristic ways (rotation, fragmentation, perseveration, overlapping difficulty, closure problems). Scoring systems count these errors (Pascal and Suttell for adults, Koppitz for children) or rate each drawing globally (Bender-Gestalt II). It is quick (about 10 minutes), non-verbal and culture-light, which is why it became one of the most used tests in the world and is part of the Indian PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction. BVRT: Benton Visual Retention Test The BVRT is a test of visual memory and visual perception in which the person looks at a card showing one to three geometric figures and then draws them from memory (or copies them). Each design typically has two large main figures and one small peripheral figure, so the test is sensitive both to memory loss and to unilateral spatial neglect (consistently missing the peripheral figure on one side). Because three equivalent forms exist, the test can be repeated (for example before and after treatment) with less practice effect. Two scores are obtained: the number correct (0 to 10) and the error score , with errors classified into six types; the expected score is adjusted for the person's estimated premorbid IQ and age.
