HRB: Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Battery The Halstead-Reitan is the classic fixed battery : a set of tests given to everyone in the same way, designed to detect brain damage and to suggest its lateralisation (left vs right) and whether it is focal or diffuse. Ward Halstead, working at the University of Chicago, studied patients with frontal lobe lesions and developed a set of tests of what he called "biological intelligence" (as distinct from psychometric IQ). His student Ralph Reitan, at Indiana University, selected the tests that best separated brain-damaged from control patients, added several, and validated the battery over decades. Interpretation uses four methods together: level of performance (cut-offs), pattern of performance across tests, pathognomonic signs (for example aphasia), and comparison of the right and left sides of the body. LNNB: Luria-Nebraska Neuropsychological Battery The Luria-Nebraska is an attempt to combine Alexander Luria's rich qualitative items with American psychometric standardisation. Charles Golden and his colleagues at the University of Nebraska took the items in Anne-Lise Christensen's (1975) compilation of A. R. Luria's bedside methods, fixed the administration, and scored each item 0 (normal), 1 (borderline) or 2 (clearly abnormal). Items are grouped into clinical scales, and scale totals are converted to T scores where higher means more impairment . A "critical level", adjusted for age and education, marks the T score above which a scale is considered impaired. It takes about 2 to 3 hours, much shorter than the Halstead-Reitan, but it was criticised (for example by Spiers, 1981, and Adams, 1980) for being heavily verbal and for straying from Luria's qualitative spirit. The examiner reads 15 common nouns (List A) and the person recalls as many as possible, five times in a row; this produces a learning curve . Then an interference list (List B) is read once and recalled, after which the person tries List A again without hearing it (sensitive to interference and forgetting). After a 20 to 30 minute delay there is another free recall and usually a recognition trial. CVLT: California Verbal Learning Test The CVLT is a list-learning test built on the process approach. Its list looks like a shopping list: 16 words from 4 semantic categories (for example fruits, tools, clothing, spices), presented in mixed order. The examiner can therefore see whether the person spontaneously groups words by category ( semantic clustering , an active, frontal-dependent strategy) or just recalls them in the order heard ( serial clustering , a more passive strategy). It also measures cued recall (giving the category name), recognition, intrusions and repetitions, so it gives a detailed picture of why memory fails. ROCF: Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure Test The person first copies a complex, abstract line drawing (a large rectangle with diagonals, a cross, triangles, circles and other details), then draws it from memory, without warning, after a short delay and again after about 30 minutes. The copy shows visuoconstructional ability and planning or organisation (does the person start with the big rectangle and fit details in, or build the figure piece by piece?), while the recall trials measure visual memory. Because it is hard to verbalise, it is often treated as a test of right hemisphere (non-verbal) memory, and the organisation of the copy is sensitive to executive dysfunction. WCST: Wisconsin Card Sorting Test The WCST is the classic test of set shifting and abstract reasoning. Four stimulus cards are placed in front of the person (one red triangle, two green stars, three yellow crosses, four blue circles), and the person must match each response card to one of them. The examiner does not say what the rule is, only "right" or "wrong" after each card. The hidden rule is colour first, then form, then number, and after 10 consecutive correct matches the examiner silently changes the rule. A healthy person notices the "wrong" feedback and shifts; a patient with dorsolateral prefrontal dysfunction tends to keep sorting by the old rule ( perseveration ). Brenda Milner (1963) showed this deficit in patients with frontal lobe excisions, which made the WCST the iconic "frontal lobe" test, although damage elsewhere can also impair it. TMT: Trail Making Test The Trail Making Test is a paper-and-pencil task in which the person draws lines to connect circles in order as fast as possible. Part A uses numbers only (1 to 25), so it mainly measures visual scanning, attention and psychomotor speed. Part B alternates numbers and letters (1, A, 2, B, 3, C and so on), so the person must keep two sequences in mind and switch between them, which adds working memory and set shifting (an executive demand). Errors are pointed out immediately and the time keeps running, so the score is completion time in seconds. Comparing B with A (B minus A, or B/A ratio) removes the effect of simple speed and isolates the switching cost. TOL: Tower of London The Tower of London is a planning task: the person must rearrange coloured balls on pegs to match a goal picture in the minimum number of moves, thinking the moves through before acting. The standard apparatus has three pegs of unequal length that hold 1, 2 and 3 balls respectively, and three balls (red, green, blue). Tim Shallice designed it to study patients with frontal lobe lesions, who make more moves, break rules and plan less before starting. Digit Span The examiner reads strings of digits at a rate of one per second, and the person repeats them; the strings grow by one digit until the person fails both trials of a length. In Digits Forward the person repeats in the same order (simple auditory attention and short-term span; normal adult span about 7, plus or minus 2, after George Miller, 1956). In Digits Backward the person reverses the order, which requires holding and manipulating information (working memory; normal adult span about 5). WAIS-IV added Digit Span Sequencing (repeat in ascending numerical order). It appears in the WAIS, WISC, original WMS, PGI Memory Scale and many screening tools. Digit span is typically preserved in pure amnesia (short-term store intact) even when long-term memory is severely impaired. BNT: Boston Naming Test The Boston Naming Test is a confrontation naming test: the person sees black-and-white line drawings, from very common objects (bed, tree) to rare ones (abacus, trellis), and must name each one. If the person misperceives the picture, a semantic (stimulus) cue is given; if they still cannot name it, a phonemic cue (the first sound) is given. Naming difficulty (anomia) is present in almost all aphasias and in Alzheimer's disease, and whether the phonemic cue helps can separate retrieval failure from loss of the word's meaning. It is a naming test, not a comprehension test (comprehension = Token Test). Token Test The Token Test measures auditory comprehension of spoken commands that grow in length and grammatical complexity, using plastic tokens that differ in shape (circles and squares), colour (five colours) and size (large and small). Commands range from "Touch the red circle" to "Put the red circle on the green square" and "Before touching the yellow circle, pick up the red square". Because the vocabulary is tiny and concrete, failure reflects difficulty processing language structure and verbal working memory, not vocabulary, so it is very sensitive to mild receptive language problems in aphasia. BDAE and WAB: Boston Diagnostic Aphasia Examination and Western Aphasia Battery These are comprehensive aphasia batteries used by speech-language pathologists and neuropsychologists to describe a patient's language profile and classify the aphasia syndrome. Both assess spontaneous speech (fluency, grammar, paraphasias), auditory comprehension, repetition, naming, reading and writing. The combination of fluency, comprehension and repetition maps onto classic syndromes: Broca's (non-fluent, comprehension relatively spared, repetition poor), Wernicke's (fluent, comprehension poor, repetition poor), conduction (fluent, comprehension good, repetition poor), transcortical types (repetition preserved), global and anomic aphasia. MMSE: Mini-Mental State Examination The MMSE is a 5 to 10 minute bedside screening test of global cognition, the most widely used cognitive screen in the world. It covers orientation, registration and recall of three words, attention (serial sevens or spelling WORLD backwards), naming, repetition, a three-stage command, reading, writing a sentence and copying intersecting pentagons. It was designed to be quick and to cover "only the cognitive aspects of mental functions", hence "mini". It is strongly affected by education and language and has a ceiling effect, so it misses mild cognitive impairment and is insensitive to executive deficits. CDT: Clock Drawing Test The person is asked to draw a clock face with all the numbers and set the hands to a specified time, classically "ten past eleven" (which forces the person to inhibit the pull of the "10" towards the number 10 and place the minute hand at 2). Drawing a clock requires comprehension, planning, visuospatial organisation, number knowledge, abstract representation of time and inhibition, so it is a fast, education-light screen for both visuospatial and executive dysfunction. Hemineglect shows as numbers crowded on one side. It is used alone, inside MoCA, and in the Mini-Cog (Soo Borson and colleagues, 2000: 3-word recall plus clock). The clinician scores the best response in three areas: eye opening, verbal response and motor response, and adds them. For GCS think " 4 eyes, 5 words (jive), 6 moves ": E4 V5 M6. 8. Clinical rating scales and symptom inventories A rating scale gives a number to how much of a symptom a person has. A diagnostic interview answers a yes/no question (does this person meet criteria for disorder X?). A rating scale answers "how much?" (how severe is the depression today, and has it come down since last month?). This is why rating scales are the workhorses of drug trials, outcome monitoring and audit, while diagnosis rests on interviews and clinical judgement. Most of the scales below were built in a burst between about 1959 and 1990, when psychopharmacology needed a way to show that a drug reduced symptoms more than a placebo did. The first split to learn is who does the rating . In a clinician-rated (observer-rated) scale, a trained interviewer asks questions, observes the patient and assigns the score: HAM-D, HAM-A, MADRS, BPRS, PANSS, SANS, SAPS, YMRS, Y-BOCS, CARS, ISAA, CIWA-Ar and CGI all work this way. In a self-report inventory, the person reads the items and marks the answers: BDI, BAI, PHQ-9, GAD-7, Zung SDS, GHQ, SCL-90-R, AUDIT and EPDS. Clinician ratings can capture things the patient cannot report (blunted affect, poverty of speech, lack of insight) and work with patients who cannot read; self-reports are cheap, fast and capture inner states (guilt, hopelessness) without interviewer bias, but depend on literacy, honesty and insight. A third group is informant-rated (parent or teacher): CBCL, Conners scales, M-CHAT-R/F, and the ADI-R interview of a parent. The second split is purpose . A screening tool is short and sensitive, meant to pick out possible cases in a population (GHQ-12, PHQ-9, GAD-7, AUDIT, CAGE, M-CHAT-R/F, EPDS): a positive screen means "assess further", never "diagnosis made". A severity or outcome measure tracks how bad symptoms are and how they change with treatment (HAM-D, MADRS, PANSS, Y-BOCS, YMRS, CIWA-Ar, CGI). A diagnostic instrument maps symptoms onto criteria (SCID, MINI, ADOS-2 together with ADI-R; see section 9). A disability measure rates functioning rather than symptoms (IDEAS, WHODAS 2.0, GAF, DAQ). Examiners love asking "which of these is a screening instrument?" and "which is clinician-rated?", so file every scale on both axes. Definition Anchor points are the written descriptions attached to each score on an item (for example, on HAM-D item 1, "0 = absent ... 4 = patient reports virtually only these feeling states in spontaneous verbal and non-verbal communication"). Well-defined anchors are what make two raters agree (inter-rater reliability). Sensitivity to change is the ability of a scale to move when the patient improves; MADRS was built specifically to be more sensitive to change than HAM-D. 8.1 Psychosis and schizophrenia BPRS: Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale The BPRS is the grandparent of modern psychosis ratings. John Overall and Donald Gorham (1962) wanted a short scale that could quickly measure change in hospitalised patients on the new antipsychotic drugs. After a semi-structured interview of about 20 minutes, the clinician rates each symptom on a 7-point severity scale. Some items are rated from what the patient says (anxiety, guilt), others from observation (blunted affect, motor retardation, mannerisms). It covers positive symptoms, negative symptoms, mood and anxiety, so it is a broad "general psychopathology" measure rather than a schizophrenia-only scale. GAF: Global Assessment of Functioning (and WHODAS 2.0) The GAF is a single 0 to 100 style rating of a person's overall psychological, social and occupational functioning, with descriptive anchors every 10 points (for example 91 to 100 superior functioning, 41 to 50 serious symptoms such as suicidal ideation or serious impairment, 1 to 10 persistent danger of hurting self or others). DSM-5 (2013) dropped the multiaxial system and the GAF because it mixed symptoms with disability and had poor reliability, and recommended the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0 (WHODAS 2.0) instead. Structured diagnostic interviews and the mental status examination In the 1960s and 1970s studies such as the US-UK Diagnostic Project (1972) showed that psychiatrists in New York and London gave different diagnoses to the same patients, mostly because they asked different questions and used different definitions ( information variance and criterion variance ). Two fixes followed. Operational criteria (Feighner criteria 1972, Research Diagnostic Criteria 1978, then DSM-III 1980) fixed the definitions. Structured interviews fixed the questions, so that every patient is asked the same things in the same order, and the answers are scored against the criteria. Interviews sit on a continuum. A fully structured interview (DIS, CIDI, DISC) has fixed wording and fixed coding, so it can be given by trained lay interviewers in large epidemiological surveys, but it cannot use clinical judgement. A semi-structured interview (SCID, SCAN, K-SADS, IPDE) gives required questions but lets the clinician probe, rephrase and judge whether a symptom is really present, so it needs clinically trained interviewers. A brief structured interview (MINI) trades depth for speed. The mental status examination , at the end of this section, is not a test at all: it is the clinician's systematic, here-and-now observation of the patient, and every clinical psychology viva expects you to know its headings cold. SCID-5: Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 The SCID is a semi-structured interview, administered by a clinician, that walks through the DSM criteria module by module (mood episodes, psychotic symptoms, substance use, anxiety, OCD, trauma, and so on), with suggested questions on the left and the DSM criterion beside them. The interviewer rates each criterion as absent, subthreshold or present, using judgement. The SCID-5 comes in several versions for different purposes, which is a favourite exam question. History tells you what has happened over months and years; the MSE records what the clinician observes and elicits now, during the interview . It is cross-sectional (one point in time), and it is written descriptively, in the patient's own words where possible, rather than with labels alone ("he said, 'my neighbours are poisoning my food'" is better than "persecutory delusions" by itself). Indian teaching (following Fish's Clinical Psychopathology and Indian textbooks such as Niraj Ahuja's) usually uses the order below. Learn the headings, then what goes under each. Memory hook " A ll P atients R eally S hould M ake T heir P sychiatrist C arefully I nquire": Appearance and behaviour, Psychomotor activity, Rapport, Speech, Mood and affect, Thought, Perception, Cognition, Insight (with judgement under cognition). 1. General appearance and behaviour What a stranger would notice: apparent age versus stated age, build, grooming and hygiene, dress (appropriate to weather and setting, or bizarre, or provocative), facial expression, eye contact, posture, gait, any physical abnormalities, tics, tremors or mannerisms. Behaviour includes attitude towards the examiner (cooperative, guarded, hostile, seductive, evasive, apathetic) and any abnormal behaviour during the interview (hallucinatory behaviour such as muttering or looking at empty corners, social withdrawal, disinhibition). Examples: unkempt and dishevelled in severe depression, schizophrenia or dementia; flamboyant, colourful, over-decorated in mania. 2. Psychomotor activity The amount and speed of movement. Increased : restlessness, pacing, hand-wringing (agitation, typical of agitated depression or anxiety), overactivity (mania), akathisia (drug-induced restlessness). Decreased : psychomotor retardation (slow movements, long pauses; depression), stupor (no movement or speech despite clear consciousness). Catatonic signs belong here: waxy flexibility (limbs stay where the examiner places them), posturing , negativism , echopraxia (copying movements), automatic obedience , mannerisms (purposeful-looking but odd movements) and stereotypies (repetitive, non-goal-directed movements). 3. Rapport Whether a working emotional connection can be established: "rapport established with ease", "established with difficulty", or "could not be established". Rapport is often hard with paranoid, negativistic or severely withdrawn patients; a strikingly "glass wall" or "praecox feeling" (the examiner's sense of being unable to reach the patient, described in schizophrenia by H. C. Rümke, 1941) was classically noted. Eye contact (maintained, avoided, staring) is usually recorded here or under appearance. 4. Speech Speech is described as an act, separately from the thought it carries. Record: rate (rapid, slow), volume (loud, soft), tone and prosody (monotonous or modulated), quantity (talkative, or poverty of speech with brief answers), reaction time (latency before answering, prolonged in depression), spontaneity (speaks spontaneously or only in reply), pressure (rapid, hard to interrupt: mania), relevance and coherence (answers to the point or not; understandable or not), and abnormalities such as stuttering, dysarthria (articulation problem, often neurological), aphasia, mutism, neologisms, echolalia (repeating the examiner's words) and clang associations (words linked by sound). 5. Mood and affect This is the most tested distinction in the MSE. Mood is the patient's pervasive and sustained emotional state, reported by the patient (subjective): "How have you been feeling in your spirits?" "Low, doctor, very low." It is recorded in the patient's own words, often alongside the clinician's description (Indian case formats write "subjective" and "objective" mood). Affect is the observable, moment-to-moment expression of emotion, seen by the examiner in face, voice and gesture. The classic analogy: mood is the climate , affect is the weather . Affect is described along several dimensions: Quality : what emotion is shown (sad, anxious, irritable, euphoric, perplexed). Range : how many different emotions are shown during the interview. Full (normal), restricted or constricted (reduced range), blunted (severe reduction in intensity), flat (virtually no expression). Reactivity : whether affect shifts appropriately with the topic or with the examiner's humour (reduced in melancholic depression). Appropriateness (congruence): whether affect matches the content of thought. Inappropriate or incongruent affect, for example laughing while describing a parent's death, is classically seen in schizophrenia. A second, separate question is whether mood is congruent with the delusions (mood-congruent versus mood-incongruent psychotic features). Stability : stable versus labile (rapid, unprovoked shifts, as in mania, organic states, pseudobulbar affect). Intensity and communicability (whether the examiner can empathise with it). Definition Other mood terms: euthymia (normal mood), dysphoria (unpleasant mood), euphoria (exaggerated well-being), elation (euphoria with increased motor activity), exaltation (intense elation with grandiosity), ecstasy (intense rapture), alexithymia (difficulty identifying and describing one's emotions, Peter Sifneos 1973), anhedonia (loss of pleasure). 6. Thought Indian MSE formats divide thought into four parts: Stream (tempo and continuity) : how fast and how smoothly thoughts flow. Flight of ideas (rapid thoughts with abrupt shifts, but connections understandable: mania), pressure of thought , retardation or slowing (depression), thought block (sudden stopping of thought mid-sentence, the patient cannot explain why: schizophrenia), perseveration (persistent repetition of the same response; organic conditions), circumstantiality (delay in reaching the goal through excessive irrelevant detail, but the goal is reached) and tangentiality (the goal is never reached) are sometimes placed here and sometimes under form. Form : the organisation and logical connection of thoughts, i.e. formal thought disorder. Loosening of associations (Eugen Bleuler, 1911: ideas shift between unrelated topics), derailment , knight's move thinking , word salad (incoherent mixture of words), neologisms (new words), overinclusion (Norman Cameron, 1938: inability to keep conceptual boundaries), concrete thinking , illogicality , and Schneider's descriptions (derailment, substitution, omission, fusion, drivelling). Content : what the patient thinks about. Delusions (fixed, false, unshakeable beliefs out of keeping with sociocultural background: persecutory, reference, grandiose, guilt, nihilistic, jealousy, erotomanic, somatic, infidelity), overvalued ideas (Carl Wernicke, 1900: strongly held but understandable beliefs that dominate life, e.g. in anorexia), obsessions , preoccupations , phobias , hypochondriacal ideas , and always suicidal and homicidal ideation , which must be asked about directly. Possession : whether the patient experiences thoughts as their own. In obsessions , thoughts are recognised as one's own though unwanted (ego-dystonic). In passivity of thought , a Schneiderian first-rank symptom, ownership is lost: thought insertion (thoughts put in by an outside agency), thought withdrawal (thoughts taken out), thought broadcasting (thoughts spread so others know them). 7. Perception Abnormal perceptual experiences, with the modality always specified. Hallucinations are perceptions without an external stimulus, experienced as real and in external space: auditory (most common in schizophrenia; second-person commenting/commanding, or third-person voices discussing the patient, a first-rank symptom, and audible thoughts, Gedankenlautwerden), visual (common in organic and delirious states), olfactory and gustatory (temporal lobe lesions, also depression), tactile (formication in cocaine and alcohol withdrawal), somatic and kinaesthetic. Illusions are misperceptions of a real stimulus. Pseudohallucinations are perceived in inner subjective space and recognised as not real (definitions differ between Karl Jaspers' and later usage). Hypnagogic (falling asleep) and hypnopompic (waking) hallucinations can be normal. Also record depersonalisation (feeling oneself unreal or detached) and derealisation (the surroundings feel unreal). 8. Cognitive functions (higher mental functions) Cognition is tested by direct bedside tasks. Formal tests such as the MMSE (Folstein, Folstein and McHugh, 1975) or the Hindi Mental State Examination (HMSE, Ganguli et al., 1995) can supplement it. Consciousness : alert, drowsy, clouded, stuporose or comatose (often recorded first). Orientation : to time (day, date, month, year, time of day), place and person . Orientation to time is lost first in organic states and orientation to person last; disorientation strongly suggests an organic condition such as delirium or dementia. Attention and concentration : attention is the ability to focus on a task; concentration is the ability to sustain that focus. Tests: serial 7s (subtract 7 from 100 repeatedly: 93, 86, 79, 72, 65; record errors and time taken), serial 3s from 20 if 7s are too hard, months of the year or days of the week backwards, and digit span (forward digit span of about 7 plus or minus 2 in normal adults; backward span is usually one or two fewer, with sources giving slightly different normal values). Digit span is strictly a test of attention and immediate registration rather than memory. Memory : immediate (registration and recall within seconds, e.g. repeating digits or three words straight away), recent (events of the past hours or days: what did you eat this morning, how did you come here; plus recall of the three words after about 5 minutes, which tests recent memory/new learning), recent past (past few months: news events) and remote (years ago: date of marriage, schooling, verified with relatives). Remote memory is typically preserved longest in dementia (Ribot's law, Théodule Ribot, 1881: recent memories are lost before older ones). General information and intelligence : fund of knowledge appropriate to education and culture (name of the Prime Minister, capital cities, recent major events), simple arithmetic, and a clinical estimate of whether intelligence is average, above or below. The questions must be adjusted for the patient's education and background. Abstraction (abstract thinking) : the ability to move from concrete instances to general concepts. Proverb interpretation ("What does 'a rolling stone gathers no moss' mean?") and similarities ("How are an apple and a banana alike?" Abstract answer: both are fruits; concrete answer: both are round, or "you can eat them"). Concrete thinking appears in schizophrenia, organic disorders and intellectual disability; proverb responses are strongly influenced by culture and education, so interpret with caution. Judgement : the ability to assess a situation and act appropriately. Personal judgement (realistic plans for one's own future, e.g. what will you do after discharge), social judgement (behaviour in social situations, observed during the interview and from history) and test judgement (responses to hypothetical situations: "What would you do if you found a stamped, addressed envelope on the road?" or "if you saw a fire in a cinema hall?"). 9. Insight Insight is the patient's awareness and understanding of their own illness: whether they recognise that they are ill, that the illness is psychological, and that they need treatment. A widely taught six-point grading appears in Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry and is reproduced in many Indian textbooks and case formats. It is a textbook teaching convention rather than a validated scale, and wording varies slightly between editions and sources: Complete denial of illness. Slight awareness of being sick and needing help, but denying it at the same time. Awareness of being sick but blaming it on others, on external factors or on organic (physical) factors. Awareness that illness is caused by something unknown in oneself. Intellectual insight : admission that one is ill and that symptoms or failures in adjustment are due to one's own irrational feelings or disturbances, but without applying this knowledge to future experiences. True emotional insight : emotional awareness of one's own motives and feelings and those of important people in one's life, which can lead to basic changes in behaviour. Structured measures of insight also exist, for example the Schedule for Assessment of Insight (Anthony David, 1990), which rates three components: recognition of illness, relabelling of unusual experiences as pathological, and treatment adherence; and the Scale to Assess Unawareness of Mental Disorder (SUMD; Xavier Amador et al., 1993). Exam trap Intellectual insight is grade 5, not the highest : the patient "knows" but does not change behaviour. Only true emotional insight (grade 6) produces change. Grade 3 (aware but blames external or organic causes) is a common choice for patients with somatisation or alcohol use. If a question cites the six grades, it is following Kaplan and Sadock; do not attribute the grading to Karl Jaspers or Fish. 9.2 MSE summary and traps MSE heading What is recorded Key examples / tests Appearance and behaviour Grooming, dress, attitude, eye contact, abnormal behaviour Unkempt in depression; colourful dress in mania; hallucinatory behaviour Psychomotor activity Amount and speed of movement Agitation, retardation, catatonic signs (waxy flexibility, posturing) Rapport Ease of establishing contact Difficult in paranoid, withdrawn patients Speech Rate, volume, tone, quantity, reaction time, coherence Pressure of speech (mania), poverty of speech, mutism Mood Subjective, sustained emotional state Recorded in patient's own words Affect Observed, moment-to-moment expression Range, reactivity, appropriateness, stability (labile), intensity Thought Stream, form, content, possession Flight of ideas, thought block, loosening, delusions, thought insertion Perception Hallucinations, illusions, depersonalisation Third-person auditory hallucinations (first-rank) Cognition Consciousness, orientation, attention, memory, information, abstraction, judgement Serial 7s, digit span, 3-word recall, proverbs, similarities, envelope test Insight Awareness of illness and need for treatment Six grades (Kaplan and Sadock convention) Exam trap Mood is subjective and sustained; affect is objective and momentary.
