title: Requested Topics
text: Requested Topics Five topics you asked for by name, each written to be learned cold from this page alone: the diathesis-stress model and its descendants, Eugen Bleuler's four A's and how the idea of schizophrenia was built, the theory of planned behaviour, every kind of brain scan an examiner can ask about, and the nine concepts you asked about after the NIMHANS paper on 31 May (dissociation, desensitization, habit reversal, flashbulb memory, paradoxical intention, ICD-11 gender incongruence, the gunas, dharana and Kegels). Theorists and years sit inside the explanations where they belong, the exam traps are flagged as you go, and each chapter closes with a self-check written the way the entrance papers write their questions. In this book The diathesis-stress model Bleuler's four A's and the history of the schizophrenia concept The theory of planned behaviour Types of brain scanning and imaging tests NIMHANS 31 May: the nine you asked about (Qs 36-41, gunas, dharana, Kegels) 1. The diathesis-stress model Why do two people who go through the same divorce, the same job loss or the same childhood poverty end up so differently, one with a major depressive episode and the other with a bad few months? And why do identical twins, who share all their genes, so often differ on whether they develop schizophrenia? The diathesis-stress model is psychology's oldest and most widely used answer to both questions. It is less a single theory than a template for explaining how a disorder comes about, and almost every modern theory of depression, anxiety and psychosis is built on it. Definition A diathesis is a predisposition or vulnerability to a disorder that a person carries before the disorder appears. The word comes from the Greek diathesis , meaning "disposition" or "arrangement" (from diatithenai , to arrange or dispose), and was used in older medicine for a constitutional tendency to a disease (for example the "gouty diathesis"). The diathesis-stress model states that a disorder develops when a diathesis is combined with sufficient stress (an adverse environmental event or condition), and that neither the diathesis alone nor the stress alone is usually sufficient. 1.1 The core idea, built from scratch Think of three ingredients: The diathesis : something relatively enduring that the person brings to the situation. It can be biological (genes, neurodevelopmental damage, a reactive stress hormone system), psychological (a negative thinking style, dysfunctional schemas, a personality trait such as neuroticism) or social and developmental (early loss, insecure attachment). It is usually latent : you cannot see it in daily behaviour until something activates it. The stress : an environmental challenge, usually after the diathesis is in place. Classic examples are negative life events (bereavement, failure, migration), chronic strain (poverty, caregiving, a hostile family) and biological insults (cannabis use, infection, sleep loss). The interaction : the outcome depends on the combination . A high-diathesis person may break down after a modest stressor; a low-diathesis person may need an extreme stressor, or may never break down at all. The statistical word for this is interaction : the effect of stress on outcome is not the same for everyone, it depends on (is "moderated by") the level of diathesis. In plain words, stress hurts the vulnerable much more than the non-vulnerable. This is why the model is often written as vulnerability x stress rather than vulnerability + stress. Exam trap The diathesis is the predisposition , never the stressor. If an option says "diathesis refers to the precipitating life event", it is wrong. The stressor is the precipitant (trigger); the diathesis is the predisposing factor. In the familiar "4 P" case formulation, diathesis maps onto predisposing factors and stress onto precipitating (and sometimes perpetuating) factors. 1.2 History: from Meehl to Zubin and Spring Paul E. Meehl (1962): schizotaxia, schizotypy, schizophrenia The modern model is usually traced to Paul E. Meehl (1962) , whose presidential address to the American Psychological Association was published in the American Psychologist as "Schizotaxia, schizotypy, schizophrenia". Meehl proposed a chain of three levels: Schizogene : Meehl hypothesised a single dominant gene (the "schizogene") as the inherited starting point. This specific single-gene claim has not been supported; schizophrenia is now understood as highly polygenic. Schizotaxia : the gene produces a subtle neural integrative defect , a fault in how the nervous system integrates information (Meehl spoke of a defect he called "hypokrisia" at the level of neuronal functioning). Schizotaxia is purely the inherited neurological vulnerability. Schizotypy : almost any schizotaxic person, growing up in any ordinary social learning environment, develops a characteristic personality organisation called schizotypy: cognitive slippage (mild thought disorder), anhedonia, interpersonal aversiveness and ambivalence. Schizotypy is learned on top of schizotaxia. Schizophrenia : only a minority of schizotypes decompensate into clinical schizophrenia, and this happens when they meet adverse environmental conditions (Meehl, writing in 1962, gave the much-criticised example of a "schizophrenogenic" mother). Most schizotypes remain compensated for life. In his later reformulation (Meehl, 1990) he gave rough figures, often quoted as about 10 percent of the population being schizotypal in his sense and about 10 percent of those developing clinical schizophrenia. Treat these as Meehl's speculative estimates, not epidemiological facts. Exam trap Schizotaxia = inherited neural integrative defect (biology). Schizotypy = the personality organisation that develops from it through social learning (psychology). Schizotypal personality disorder = a DSM diagnostic category (DSM-III, 1980, onward), partly inspired by the schizotypy concept and by the Danish adoption studies of relatives of people with schizophrenia, but not the same thing as Paul Meehl's schizotypy. Also note: in ICD-10 schizotypal disorder sits in the schizophrenia chapter (F21), whereas DSM places schizotypal personality disorder among personality disorders and also lists it in the schizophrenia spectrum chapter. David Rosenthal (1970): popularising the term The exact phrase "diathesis-stress" is often credited to David Rosenthal (1970) , in his book Genetic Theory and Abnormal Behavior , which used it to summarise the genetic and environmental evidence on schizophrenia, including the Danish adoption studies he ran with Seymour Kety and others. Who used the phrase first is uncertain; sources differ, so the safe statement is that Rosenthal popularised it. Joseph Zubin and Bonnie Spring (1977): the vulnerability-stress model Joseph Zubin and Bonnie Spring (1977) , in "Vulnerability: a new view of schizophrenia" ( Journal of Abnormal Psychology ), restated the idea in a form that is still the standard textbook diagram. Their key claims: Vulnerability is the enduring trait ; schizophrenia itself is not permanent. What a person carries for life is the vulnerability, not the illness. Episodes are time-limited . An episode occurs when stress pushes the person above their personal vulnerability threshold ; when the stress subsides the person tends to return to their premorbid level. This was a deliberate challenge to the Kraepelinian assumption of inevitable deterioration. Inborn vs acquired vulnerability . Inborn vulnerability lies in the genes and internal environment (neurophysiology). Acquired vulnerability comes from traumas, specific diseases, perinatal complications, family experiences, adolescent peer interactions and other life events. Moderators . Whether stress tips someone over also depends on their social network, ecological niche and premorbid personality. Graphically, Zubin and Spring plotted vulnerability against challenging events: a curved threshold line divides a "well" zone from an "episode" zone. A highly vulnerable person crosses the line with little stress; a person with low vulnerability needs a great deal. Memory hook Zubin and Spring = 1977 , the same year as George Engel's biopsychosocial model (1977) and one year before Kety. Remember "seven-seven: vulnerability and biopsychosocial were born together". But they are different ideas: Engel's model is a general philosophy of medicine (biology, psychology and social context all matter for every illness); the diathesis-stress model is a specific causal claim that a pre-existing vulnerability interacts with later stress. 1.3 Refinements: what form does the interaction take? Scott Monroe and Anne Simons (1991) Scott M. Monroe and Anne D. Simons (1991) , "Diathesis-stress theories in the context of life stress research: implications for the depressive disorders" ( Psychological Bulletin ), is the classic critical review. Their main points: Most theories had been vague about how diathesis and stress combine. Researchers needed to specify the form of the relationship rather than just say "both matter". Stress must be measured carefully . Self-report checklists confound the stressor with the person's reaction to it. They favoured interview-based, contextual ratings of life events (in the tradition of George Brown and Tirril Harris's Life Events and Difficulties Schedule) and the distinction between independent events (outside the person's control, such as an earthquake) and dependent events (partly produced by the person, such as a breakup after repeated arguments). Diathesis and stress are not always independent . The diathesis may shape which stressors the person meets, and stress may change the diathesis over time (a dynamic rather than fixed diathesis). Forms of the model (Ingram and Luxton, 2005) Rick Ingram and David Luxton (2005), in a widely cited chapter on vulnerability-stress models, organised the possible forms. The terms below are the ones exam setters lift: Form What it claims Dichotomous diathesis The diathesis is either present or absent (as in Paul Meehl's single gene). Without it, no amount of stress produces the disorder. Quasi-continuous diathesis The diathesis varies in degree (as with polygenic risk or a graded cognitive style). The more diathesis, the less stress needed. Ipsative (additive) model Diathesis and stress are inversely related: they add up, and disorder appears once the sum crosses a threshold. A very strong diathesis may need almost no stress, and an extreme stressor may produce disorder even in someone with little diathesis. Zubin and Spring's diagram is of this kind. Threshold (interactive) model Stress has an effect only once the diathesis (or stress) passes a certain level; below it, stress makes little difference. The exact labels vary between textbooks, so in an MCQ go by the description rather than the label alone. Stress generation (Constance Hammen, 1991) Constance Hammen (1991) , studying women with depression, showed that depressed people experience more dependent stressful events (especially interpersonal conflicts) than controls, but not more independent ones. In other words, people with a depressive diathesis partly generate their own stress. This breaks the simple assumption that stress just "happens to" the vulnerable person and is a key reason Monroe and Simons called for a dynamic model. Kindling (Robert Post, 1992) Robert M. Post (1992) , in the American Journal of Psychiatry , borrowed the term "kindling" from epilepsy research. In mood disorders the first episodes are usually triggered by major life stress, but later episodes need less and less stress, and eventually may occur almost spontaneously. The diathesis itself is being changed (sensitised) by earlier episodes. Monroe and Kate Harkness (2005) later distinguished two readings: stress sensitisation (smaller stressors become enough) and stress autonomy (episodes occur without stress). Kindling is a related idea, not a version of the original diathesis-stress model: it describes a diathesis that grows over time. 1.4 Examples of diatheses Cognitive diatheses in depression Aaron T. Beck (cognitive theory, 1967 onward): early experience lays down dysfunctional schemas (for example "I am worthless unless I am loved"). They stay latent until a congruent stressor (a rejection) activates them, producing the negative cognitive triad (self, world, future). Beck (1983) added the personality diatheses sociotropy (dependence on relationships) and autonomy (dependence on achievement and independence), with the congruency hypothesis : sociotropic people are vulnerable to interpersonal loss, autonomous people to failure. Hopelessness theory , Lyn Abramson, Gerald Metalsky and Lauren Alloy (1989) , Psychological Review : the diathesis is a negative inferential style , a tendency to explain negative events with stable and global causes, to infer negative consequences, and to infer negative things about oneself. When such a person meets negative events, they are likely to become hopeless, and hopelessness is the proximal sufficient cause of a subtype, "hopelessness depression". This is an explicit diathesis-stress theory, and it revised the earlier learned helplessness reformulation (Abramson, Martin Seligman and Teasdale, 1978). A genetic example: Caspi et al. (2003) and what happened next Avshalom Caspi, Terrie Moffitt and colleagues (2003) , in Science , used the Dunedin (New Zealand) birth cohort and reported that people carrying one or two short alleles of the serotonin transporter promoter polymorphism ( 5-HTTLPR ) were more likely to become depressed after stressful life events than people with two long alleles. It became the textbook example of a gene x environment (G x E) interaction, that is, a molecular diathesis-stress effect. The story did not hold up well. Neil Risch and colleagues (2009) , a meta-analysis in JAMA , found no evidence that 5-HTTLPR moderated the stress-depression link (stress itself strongly predicted depression). A 2011 meta-analysis by Karg and colleagues, using broader inclusion, did report support, so the literature was contested for a while. Then Richard Border and colleagues (2019) , in the American Journal of Psychiatry , tested historical depression candidate genes, including 5-HTTLPR and its interaction with stress, in very large samples and found no support. The lesson for exams: Caspi et al. is the classic G x E example, but it is now regarded as a failed replication story, and polygenic approaches have replaced single candidate genes. Schizophrenia examples Copenhagen high-risk study : begun in 1962 by Sarnoff Mednick and Fini Schulsinger . Children of mothers with schizophrenia (high genetic risk) and matched controls were followed from childhood. Among the high-risk children, those who later developed schizophrenia were more likely to have had obstetric complications and disruptive early rearing (for example separation from the mother), a diathesis-stress pattern where acquired insults act on a genetic predisposition. Finnish Adoptive Family Study of Schizophrenia , led by Pekka Tienari : adopted-away children of mothers with schizophrenia spectrum disorders were compared with adoptees of mothers without them, and the adoptive families' functioning was rated independently. High genetic risk raised the rate of schizophrenia spectrum disorders mainly when the adoptive family was rated as disturbed (dysfunctional communication); in healthy adoptive families the high-risk adoptees did about as well as controls (Tienari et al., 2004, British Journal of Psychiatry ). This is one of the cleanest human demonstrations of genotype x rearing environment interaction. A cousin: Barlow's triple vulnerability theory David H. Barlow (2000, 2002) explained anxiety and related emotional disorders through three vulnerabilities: a generalised biological vulnerability (heritable negative affect, neuroticism), a generalised psychological vulnerability (an early sense that events are uncontrollable and unpredictable) and a specific psychological vulnerability (learning that particular objects or bodily sensations are dangerous, which explains why one person develops panic disorder and another social anxiety). Stress activates these vulnerabilities. It is a diathesis-stress model with the diathesis split into three layers. 1.5 Differential susceptibility: the challenge to diathesis-stress The diathesis-stress model assumes that "vulnerable" people only ever do worse: in a good environment they are at best equal to everyone else. Jay Belsky (1997) proposed, on evolutionary grounds, that some children are simply more plastic (more responsive to rearing) than others. Because parents cannot know which rearing strategy will pay off in an unpredictable future, natural selection would favour having some offspring who are highly shaped by the environment and others who are not. Belsky and Michael Pluess (2009) , in "Beyond diathesis stress: differential susceptibility to environmental influences" ( Psychological Bulletin ), reviewed evidence that the same traits once called vulnerabilities (difficult or negatively emotional infant temperament, certain dopamine and serotonin gene variants, high physiological reactivity) make people do worse in adverse environments but better in supportive ones. The slogan is "for better and for worse" , in contrast to diathesis-stress, which is only "for worse". Biological sensitivity to context : W. Thomas Boyce and Bruce J. Ellis (2005) , Development and Psychopathology , argued that high stress reactivity (autonomic and adrenocortical) reflects heightened sensitivity to context, both harmful and protective. They proposed a U-shaped relation: highly reactive children are over-represented in both very stressful and very protective early environments. Orchid vs dandelion children : a metaphor drawn from the Swedish expression maskrosbarn ("dandelion child", one who thrives anywhere). Dandelion children do reasonably well in almost any environment; orchid children wilt under neglect but flourish spectacularly with good care. Boyce popularised it in his book The Orchid and the Dandelion (2019). Vantage sensitivity : Pluess and Belsky (2013) , Psychological Bulletin , described the positive half on its own: some individuals benefit more than others from positive experiences and interventions (for example psychotherapy or school programmes). Vantage resistance is the failure to benefit. Diathesis-stress describes the negative pole, vantage sensitivity the positive pole, and differential susceptibility combines both. Seeing the difference: the crossover interaction Plot environment quality on the x axis (adverse on the left, supportive on the right) and outcome (well-being, higher is better) on the y axis. Draw one line for the "vulnerable" or "susceptible" group and one for the comparison group. A. Diathesis-stress B. Differential susceptibility Adverse Supportive Adverse Supportive Environment quality Environment quality Well-being Well-being gap only at adverse end lines cross Vulnerable / susceptible Non-vulnerable / less susceptible Panel A (diathesis-stress) : the lines fan out toward the adverse end and converge at the supportive end. In a good environment the vulnerable do as well as everyone else; the diathesis only shows under stress. This is an ordinal (non-crossing) interaction. Panel B (differential susceptibility) : the susceptible line is steeper and crosses the other line. Susceptible people do worst in bad environments and best in good ones. This is a disordinal (crossover) interaction. To claim differential susceptibility, researchers must show the crossover point lies within the realistic range of environments, and that the "better" side is real, not just noise (Glenn Roisman and colleagues, 2012, proposed formal statistical tests for this). Feature Diathesis-stress Differential susceptibility What the trait is A vulnerability (risk factor) A plasticity or sensitivity factor Effect in adverse environment Worse outcome Worse outcome Effect in supportive environment Same as others (no advantage) Better than others Shape of interaction Ordinal, fan-shaped Crossover Key names Paul Meehl 1962, Rosenthal 1970, Zubin and Spring 1977, Monroe and Simons 1991 Belsky 1997, Boyce and Ellis 2005, Belsky and Pluess 2009, Pluess and Belsky 2013 (vantage sensitivity) 1.6 Clinical implications Prevention : if the diathesis can be identified early (family history, high-risk mental states, a negative cognitive style), stress exposure can be reduced or coping strengthened before a first episode. Clinical high-risk (prodromal) services for psychosis rest on this logic. Relapse prevention : in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, medication is understood as lowering biological vulnerability, while psychosocial work reduces stress. Relapse signature plans teach patients and families to spot early warning signs after a stressor. Stress management and coping : problem-solving training, sleep regularity, avoiding cannabis and other drugs, and building social support all aim at the stress side or at the moderators that Zubin and Spring listed. Cognitive therapy : Aaron Beck's therapy tries to modify the diathesis itself (the schemas) so that future stressors do less damage; mindfulness-based cognitive therapy targets the kindling-like reactivation of depressive thinking in recurrent depression. Family expressed emotion (EE) : George W. Brown, J. L. T. Birley and John Wing (1972) , building on Brown's earlier work in the 1950s and 1960s, showed that people with schizophrenia discharged to families high in criticism, hostility or emotional over-involvement relapsed more often. Christine Vaughn and Julian Leff (1976) replicated this using the Camberwell Family Interview and found the risk was greatest when high-EE contact was long (more than about 35 hours a week face to face) and medication was not taken. High EE is an environmental stressor acting on a biological vulnerability. Family psychoeducation and behavioural family therapy (for example Ian Falloon's work) lower EE and reduce relapse. Indian relevance: EE studies in north India (Chandigarh, by N. N. Wig, Leff and colleagues in the 1980s, linked to the WHO Determinants of Outcome study) found that high EE was less common in Indian families than in London samples, one proposed reason for the better course of schizophrenia observed in developing-country WHO centres. High yield Paul Meehl 1962 (schizotaxia, schizotypy, schizophrenia; schizogene). Rosenthal 1970 (popularised "diathesis-stress"). Zubin and Spring 1977 (vulnerability model; episodes time-limited; inborn vs acquired vulnerability). Monroe and Simons 1991 ( Psychological Bulletin review of diathesis-stress and life stress). Hammen 1991 (stress generation). Post 1992 (kindling). Abramson, Metalsky and Alloy 1989 (hopelessness theory). Caspi 2003 (5-HTTLPR x stress), Risch 2009 and Border 2019 (failed). Belsky 1997, Belsky and Pluess 2009 (differential susceptibility). Boyce and Ellis 2005 (biological sensitivity to context). Pluess and Belsky 2013 (vantage sensitivity). Brown, Birley and Wing 1972; Vaughn and Leff 1976 (expressed emotion). Exam trap (1) Diathesis = predisposition, not trigger. (2) Schizotaxia (neural defect) vs schizotypy (personality organisation) vs schizotypal personality disorder (DSM category). (3) Zubin and Spring is 1977 , not 1962 (Meehl) or 1970 (Rosenthal). (4) In Zubin and Spring, the vulnerability is permanent, the episode is time-limited. (5) Engel's biopsychosocial model (1977) is not the diathesis-stress model. (6) Differential susceptibility is "for better and for worse"; diathesis-stress is "for worse only". (7) Stress generation (Hammen) means dependent events increase, not independent ones. (8) Kindling is Post (1992), borrowed from epilepsy research. Self-check The term "diathesis" in the diathesis-stress model refers to: a the precipitating life event b a pre-existing predisposition or vulnerability c the coping response to stress d the residual symptoms after an episode ✓ Answer: (b) a pre-existing predisposition or vulnerability Diathesis-stress model (vulnerability x stress) The concept What it is A diathesis is a predisposition or vulnerability that a person carries before the disorder appears; the Greek word means "disposition". How it works The stressor is the precipitant (trigger). Disorder develops when diathesis and enough stress combine; neither alone is usually sufficient. Exam tip In the "4 P" formulation, diathesis maps onto predisposing factors and stress onto precipitating factors. Why the other options are wrong (a) the precipitating life event That is the stressor , the precipitant or trigger; swapping it with the diathesis is the classic trap. (c) the coping response to stress The person's reaction once stress arrives; coping can soften the outcome but is not the pre-existing vulnerability. (d) the residual symptoms after an episode These come after an episode, whereas the diathesis is present before any disorder appears. In Meehl's (1962) model, the inherited neural integrative defect is called: a schizotypy b schizotaxia c schizoid personality d schizophreniform state ✓ Answer: (b) schizotaxia Paul E. Meehl, APA presidential address (1962) The concept Meehl's chain Meehl proposed that an inherited schizogene produces schizotaxia , a subtle neural integrative defect: purely the inherited neurological vulnerability. What grows on it Through ordinary social learning, a schizotaxic person develops schizotypy , the personality organisation built on it. Only a minority of schizotypes decompensate into schizophrenia. Exam tip Schizotaxia = biology (neural defect); schizotypy = psychology (personality). Schizotypal personality disorder is a separate DSM category. Why the other options are wrong (a) schizotypy Meehl's name for the personality organisation (cognitive slippage, anhedonia, interpersonal aversiveness, ambivalence) learned on top of the defect; the near-identical name is the trap. (c) schizoid personality A DSM personality disorder category (detachment, restricted emotion), not one of the levels in Meehl's chain. (d) schizophreniform state Echoes Langfeldt's schizophreniform states (acute onset, good prognosis), now a DSM duration category of 1 to 6 months; not an inherited defect. "Vulnerability: a new view of schizophrenia", which proposed that episodes are time-limited while vulnerability is enduring, was written by: a Paul Meehl, 1962 b David Rosenthal, 1970 c Joseph Zubin and Bonnie Spring, 1977 d Scott Monroe and Anne Simons, 1991 ✓ Answer: (c) Joseph Zubin and Bonnie Spring, 1977 Joseph Zubin and Bonnie Spring (1977) The concept The paper Zubin and Spring (1977), in the Journal of Abnormal Psychology , restated diathesis-stress as the vulnerability-stress model , still the standard textbook diagram. Key claims Vulnerability is the enduring trait. An episode occurs when stress pushes a person above their threshold and is time-limited, a challenge to Kraepelin's assumption of inevitable deterioration. Memory hook "Seven-seven": Zubin and Spring share 1977 with Engel's biopsychosocial model , but the two are different ideas. Why the other options are wrong (a) Paul Meehl, 1962 Wrote "Schizotaxia, schizotypy, schizophrenia", the earlier APA address at the root of the model, not the vulnerability paper. (b) David Rosenthal, 1970 Popularised the phrase "diathesis-stress" in Genetic Theory and Abnormal Behavior , drawing on the Danish adoption studies; he did not write this paper. (d) Scott Monroe and Anne Simons, 1991 Wrote the classic Psychological Bulletin review asking how diathesis and stress combine, focused on depression rather than schizophrenia. Hammen's (1991) finding that depressed women experience more dependent, interpersonal stressful events is known as: a kindling b stress generation c vantage sensitivity d expressed emotion ✓ Answer: (b) stress generation Constance Hammen (1991), stress generation The concept What it is Stress generation : people with a depressive diathesis partly generate their own stress, so they meet more dependent events, especially interpersonal conflicts. The key contrast They do not meet more independent events (outside their control, such as an earthquake). A dependent event is partly produced by the person, such as a breakup after repeated arguments. Why it matters It breaks the idea that stress just happens to the vulnerable person, one reason Monroe and Simons called for a dynamic model. Why the other options are wrong (a) kindling Robert Post's (1992) idea, borrowed from epilepsy research, that later mood episodes need less and less stress. (c) vantage sensitivity Pluess and Belsky (2013): some people benefit more than others from positive experiences, the positive pole of differential susceptibility. (d) expressed emotion Family criticism, hostility or emotional over-involvement that predicts relapse in schizophrenia (Brown, Birley and Wing, 1972; Vaughn and Leff, 1976). In the hopelessness theory of Abramson, Metalsky and Alloy (1989), the diathesis is: a the short allele of 5-HTTLPR b a negative inferential style attributing negative events to stable, global causes c high expressed emotion in the family d sociotropy ✓ Answer: (b) a negative inferential style attributing negative events to stable, global causes Abramson, Metalsky and Alloy (1989), hopelessness theory The concept The diathesis The cognitive diathesis is a negative inferential (attributional) style: explaining negative events with stable and global causes, inferring negative consequences and negative things about oneself. How it works When such a person meets negative events they become hopeless , the proximal sufficient cause of "hopelessness depression". It is an explicit diathesis-stress theory ( Psychological Review ). Background It revised the learned helplessness reformulation of Abramson, Seligman and Teasdale (1978). Why the other options are wrong (a) the short allele of 5-HTTLPR A genetic candidate from Caspi et al. (2003), later not supported (Border et al., 2019); a gene, not a cognitive style. (c) high expressed emotion in the family A family-environment stressor that predicts relapse, mainly in schizophrenia; it is stress acting on the person, not their own diathesis. (d) sociotropy Beck's (1983) personality diathesis of dependence on relationships, which leaves people vulnerable to interpersonal loss; a different theory. The large 2019 study by Border and colleagues concluded that 5-HTTLPR x stress effects on depression: a were strongly confirmed b were confirmed only in women c were not supported d were larger than the main effect of stress ✓ Answer: (c) were not supported Richard Border and colleagues (2019) The concept The background Caspi et al. (2003), using the Dunedin cohort, reported that short 5-HTTLPR alleles raised depression risk after stressful life events: the textbook G x E example. What Border found Border et al. (2019), in the American Journal of Psychiatry , used very large samples and found no support for historical candidate gene or candidate G x E hypotheses. Exam tip Caspi is now a failed replication story (Risch 2009 was also negative); polygenic approaches have replaced single candidate genes. Why the other options are wrong (a) were strongly confirmed The opposite of the finding: strong confirmation was Caspi's 2003 claim, which the large studies did not replicate. (b) were confirmed only in women A subgroup claim the study did not make; its headline was no support for the interaction. (d) were larger than the main effect of stress Reverses the real pattern: stress itself strongly predicted depression (Risch 2009), while the gene x stress interaction did not hold. A trait that predicts worse outcomes in adverse environments and better outcomes in supportive environments, compared with others, best fits: a the diathesis-stress model b differential susceptibility c the kindling hypothesis d the biopsychosocial model ✓ Answer: (b) differential susceptibility Belsky (1997); Belsky and Pluess (2009) The concept What it is Differential susceptibility : some people are more plastic, so the same trait makes them do worse in adverse environments but better in supportive ones, "for better and for worse". The graph The susceptible line is steeper and crosses the other: a crossover (disordinal) interaction. Diathesis-stress gives only a fan-shaped ordinal one. Who Belsky (1997) proposed it on evolutionary grounds; Belsky and Pluess (2009) reviewed the evidence in Psychological Bulletin . Why the other options are wrong (a) the diathesis-stress model "For worse" only: vulnerable people do worse under stress, but in a supportive environment they do no better than others. (c) the kindling hypothesis Post's (1992) idea that later mood episodes need less stress; about recurrence, not environment quality. (d) the biopsychosocial model Engel's (1977) general philosophy that biology, psychology and social context all matter; it makes no crossover prediction. "Biological sensitivity to context" was proposed by: a Belsky and Pluess (2009) b Boyce and Ellis (2005) c Caspi and Moffitt (2003) d Ingram and Luxton (2005) ✓ Answer: (b) Boyce and Ellis (2005) W. Thomas Boyce and Bruce J. Ellis (2005) The concept The idea Boyce and Ellis (2005), in Development and Psychopathology , argued that high stress reactivity (autonomic and adrenocortical) reflects heightened sensitivity to context , both harmful and protective. Key prediction A U-shaped relation: highly reactive children are over-represented in both very stressful and very protective early environments. Popular version Boyce later popularised the orchid vs dandelion metaphor in The Orchid and the Dandelion (2019). Why the other options are wrong (a) Belsky and Pluess (2009) Wrote "Beyond diathesis stress" in Psychological Bulletin , the review of differential susceptibility : a close cousin with a different label. (c) Caspi and Moffitt (2003) Reported the 5-HTTLPR x stress interaction in the Dunedin cohort, the classic gene x environment example. (d) Ingram and Luxton (2005) Organised the forms of vulnerability-stress models (dichotomous, quasi-continuous, ipsative, threshold), not this idea. Which component is NOT one of the classic dimensions of expressed emotion rated on the Camberwell Family Interview that predict relapse? a critical comments b hostility c emotional over-involvement d thought broadcasting ✓ Answer: (d) thought broadcasting Kurt Schneider's first-rank symptoms The concept Why this one Thought broadcasting (one's thoughts escape and are known to others) is a Schneiderian first-rank symptom in the patient, not an EE dimension. What EE is Expressed emotion (EE) rates relatives' attitudes toward the patient; critical comments, hostility and emotional over-involvement predict relapse. Who showed it Brown, Birley and Wing (1972) showed it; Vaughn and Leff (1976) replicated it using the Camberwell Family Interview. Why the other options are not the answer (a) critical comments A core EE dimension: the relative's critical remarks about the patient, counted on the Camberwell Family Interview. (b) hostility A core EE dimension: rejection of the patient as a person, beyond criticism of specific behaviour. (c) emotional over-involvement A core EE dimension: over-protective, self-sacrificing or exaggerated emotional responses by the relative. Robert Post's (1992) kindling hypothesis proposes that in recurrent mood disorder: a each later episode needs more stress than the first b later episodes need less stress and may become autonomous c stress plays no role at any stage d episodes are caused only by independent life events ✓ Answer: (b) later episodes need less stress and may become autonomous Robert M. Post (1992), kindling hypothesis The concept What it is Post borrowed kindling from epilepsy research. First mood episodes are usually triggered by major life stress; later ones need less and less, and may occur almost spontaneously. Why Earlier episodes sensitise the system, so the threshold for later episodes falls: the diathesis itself grows over time. Two readings Monroe and Harkness (2005) split it into stress sensitisation (smaller stressors become enough) and stress autonomy (episodes occur without stress). Why the other options are wrong (a) each later episode needs more stress than the first The exact reverse of kindling: the threshold falls, not rises, as episodes recur. (c) stress plays no role at any stage Wrong from the start: first episodes are usually triggered by major life stress. (d) episodes are caused only by independent life events Kindling says later episodes need little or no stress, so no particular kind of life event is required. 2. Bleuler's four A's and the history of the schizophrenia concept "Schizophrenia" is a little over a century old as a word, and the concept has been reshaped three or four times since. Entrance examiners love this history because it is full of near-identical names, years one apart and symptom lists that sound alike. The way to keep it straight is to see each figure as answering a different question: Emil Kraepelin asked "what is the course?", Eugen Bleuler asked "what is the underlying psychological disturbance?", and Schneider asked "which symptoms can be reliably recognised and used for diagnosis?" 2.1 Before Kraepelin: the pieces Bénédict Augustin Morel (France) used the term démence précoce ("early dementia") for young people who showed early mental deterioration. The usual dates given are 1852 (Études cliniques) and 1860 (Traité des maladies mentales); sources differ on which is the "first" use. Morel worked within his theory of hereditary degeneration . Ewald Hecker (1871) described hebephrenia , an illness beginning in adolescence with silly, incongruous behaviour and rapid deterioration (the name had been suggested earlier by his teacher Karl Ludwig Kahlbaum). Karl Ludwig Kahlbaum (1874) described catatonia ("tension insanity"), with motor symptoms such as stupor, posturing and waxy flexibility. Paranoid states (with delusions as the main feature) were described by several authors as separate conditions. 2.2 Emil Kraepelin: dementia praecox Emil Kraepelin , working in Heidelberg and later Munich, revised his textbook ( Psychiatrie ) repeatedly. He used the Latin term dementia praecox in the 4th edition (1893) , at first for a narrower group among the "degenerative" processes. In the 6th edition (1899) he consolidated hebephrenia, catatonia and paranoid dementia into one disease, dementia praecox, on the grounds that, despite different symptoms, they shared: early onset (praecox = early, typically adolescence or young adulthood), and a deteriorating course ending in a characteristic weakening of mind (the "dementia"). In the same edition he set this against manic-depressive insanity , which ran an episodic course with good recovery between episodes. This Kraepelinian dichotomy (dementia praecox vs manic-depressive insanity, separated by course and outcome) still underlies the split between schizophrenia spectrum and mood disorder chapters in DSM and ICD. Kraepelin's method was longitudinal: he grouped patients by how the illness unfolded over years, recorded on his famous index cards (Zählkarten), rather than by any single symptom. Later editions (the 8th, 1909 to 1915) added further subforms such as simple dementia praecox. Exam trap Emil Kraepelin did not coin the French "démence précoce" (that is Morel). He did not coin "schizophrenia" (that is Bleuler). What Kraepelin did was unify hebephrenia, catatonia and paranoid forms under "dementia praecox" (consolidated in the 6th edition, 1899) and separate it from manic-depressive insanity. If a question asks who first described catatonia, the answer is Kahlbaum (1874); hebephrenia, Hecker (1871). 2.3 Eugen Bleuler: from dementia praecox to "the group of schizophrenias" Eugen Bleuler (1857 to 1939) was director of the Burghölzli , the psychiatric hospital of the University of Zurich, from 1898; Carl Gustav Jung worked there under him. Bleuler lived alongside his patients and was influenced by the associationist psychology of the day and by Sigmund Freud's ideas, which he applied to the content of psychotic symptoms. He introduced the word "schizophrenia" in a lecture in 1908 (to the German Psychiatric Association, Berlin). His great monograph, Dementia Praecox oder Gruppe der Schizophrenien ("Dementia praecox, or the group of schizophrenias"), appeared in 1911 as part of Gustav Aschaffenburg's handbook of psychiatry. It was translated into English only in 1950 , by Joseph Zinkin . Why rename it? "Schizophrenia" comes from Greek schizein (to split) and phren (mind). Bleuler meant the splitting (loosening) of the psychic functions from one another: thought, emotion and will no longer work together as a coherent whole, so a patient might describe a tragedy while smiling. He did not mean a "split personality" in the sense of multiple identities (that is dissociative identity disorder, a completely different condition). He also rejected Emil Kraepelin's name because his own patients showed that the illness was: not always a dementia : many did not deteriorate to a final weakened state, and some recovered, and not always praecox : onset could be later in life. The phrase "group of schizophrenias" shows that he already saw it as a heterogeneous group of conditions, not a single disease. 2.4 The four A's, one by one Eugen Bleuler did not use the phrase "four A's" himself; it is a teaching mnemonic added later by textbook writers to summarise his fundamental symptoms . Each is explained below with a clinical picture. 1. Associations (loosening of associations) For Bleuler this was the central disturbance. In normal thinking, ideas follow one another guided by a goal (the "determining tendency"). In schizophrenia the threads that link ideas are broken, so thoughts follow chance, sound or private links. Example: asked "How are you sleeping?", a patient replies, "Sleep is a bed of roses, roses are red, the Red Army marches at night, I keep watch." Modern terms that descend from this include derailment, tangentiality, incoherence and, in its mildest form, Meehl's "cognitive slippage". Bleuler also included thought blocking (sudden stopping of the train of thought). 2. Affect (affective disturbance) Emotional expression becomes flattened (blunted) or incongruous (inappropriate) to the content of thought. Example: a young man reports, without visible emotion, that his mother died last week, or laughs while describing being persecuted. Bleuler stressed that the inner emotional life might be less impoverished than it looks; what is lost is the integration between feeling and the rest of the mind. 3. Ambivalence Bleuler coined this word too. It means the simultaneous presence of contradictory feelings, wishes or thoughts toward the same object, both held at full strength without resolution. He described three forms: affective ambivalence : loving and hating the same person at the same moment; ambitendency (volitional ambivalence): wanting and not wanting to do something at once, so the patient starts to shake hands, withdraws, extends the hand again; intellectual ambivalence : thinking "I am a man" and "I am not a man" at the same time. Ordinary mixed feelings are not what he meant: in schizophrenia the opposites coexist without the normal pressure to reconcile them. 4. Autism Bleuler coined "autism" (Greek autos , self), around 1910 to 1911 (sources differ on the very first use), for the withdrawal from external reality into an inner world of fantasy , with "autistic thinking" governed by wishes and private logic rather than by reality. Example: a patient sits for hours absorbed in an inner drama, treating reality as less important than the inner world. The word was later borrowed by Leo Kanner (1943) , "Autistic disturbances of affective contact", and Hans Asperger (1944) , "autistic psychopathy", for a developmental condition of childhood. That borrowing is why the same word now names a completely different disorder. Memory hook A ssociations, A ffect, A mbivalence, A utism. None of the four is a hallucination or a delusion. Eugen Bleuler thought the dramatic "positive" symptoms were the surface; the real illness was the loosening underneath. 2.5 Two different axes: fundamental vs accessory, primary vs secondary This is the single most confused point in Bleuler questions, so build it slowly. Eugen Bleuler classified symptoms in two separate ways . Axis 1: fundamental (basic) vs accessory symptoms (a diagnostic axis) Fundamental symptoms are present, at least to some degree, in every case and at every stage, and are characteristic of schizophrenia. They are therefore what the diagnosis rests on. They include the four A's, and Bleuler also listed further fundamental disturbances (of attention, will, the "person" or sense of self, and schizophrenic "dementia" in his special sense). Accessory symptoms may or may not be present, come and go, and also occur in other illnesses. They include hallucinations, delusions , catatonic symptoms, certain disturbances of memory, speech and writing, and acute syndromes. They are often what brings the patient to hospital, yet for Bleuler they were not essential to the diagnosis. Axis 2: primary vs secondary symptoms (a theoretical, causal axis) Primary symptoms are the direct product of the underlying disease process , which Bleuler presumed to be organic. The chief primary symptom in his account was the loosening of associations (along with some others he thought organic, such as certain disturbances of consciousness and physical signs). Secondary symptoms are the person's psychological reactions to the primary disturbance and to their life situation, shaped by complexes and wishes. Much of the clinical picture, including autism, much of the affective change, hallucinations and delusions, was secondary in this sense. Because these are different axes, a symptom can be fundamental but secondary : autism is present in every case (fundamental) yet Bleuler regarded it as a psychological consequence (secondary). Hallucinations are accessory and secondary . Loosening of associations is fundamental and primary . Symptom Fundamental or accessory? Primary or secondary? Loosening of associations Fundamental Primary (the core) Autism Fundamental Largely secondary Hallucinations Accessory Secondary Delusions Accessory Secondary Catatonic symptoms Accessory Mostly secondary in his account Exam trap "Primary" is not a synonym for "fundamental", and "secondary" is not a synonym for "accessory". Many guidebooks blur them; when an MCQ asks specifically about Eugen Bleuler's primary symptom, the safest answer is loosening (disturbance) of associations. When it asks which are accessory , choose hallucinations and delusions. A fifth and sixth A? Some textbooks add Attention (Bleuler did discuss attentional disturbance among fundamental symptoms) and Avolition (or abulia, loss of will) as a fifth and sixth A. These are later teaching extensions, not part of the classic four. Do not confuse them with Nancy Andreasen's negative symptom domains on the SANS (1982): affective flattening, alogia, avolition-apathy, anhedonia-asociality and attention, sometimes called "the five A's of negative symptoms". If a question says "Bleuler's four A's", stick to associations, affect, ambivalence and autism. 2.6 Bleuler's influence: a broad concept and the US-UK gap Because Eugen Bleuler's fundamental symptoms were subtle and not tied to deterioration, his concept was broad : mild, latent and "simple" cases with no hallucinations or delusions could qualify. This broad view became dominant in the United States (helped by psychoanalytic psychiatry and by Harry Stack Sullivan and others), whereas British and European psychiatry stayed closer to Emil Kraepelin and Schneider. US-UK Diagnostic Project (John E. Cooper, Robert Kendell, Barry Gurland and colleagues, 1972, Psychiatric Diagnosis in New York and London ): New York hospital psychiatrists diagnosed schizophrenia far more often than London psychiatrists, including many patients London would have called manic-depressive or personality disordered. When the project team rated the same patients with a standardised interview (the Present State Examination), most of the difference disappeared. The gap was in diagnostic habits , not in the patients. International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia (IPSS) , WHO (1973): nine centres, including Agra in India . Seven centres shared a broadly similar core concept; Washington and Moscow used much broader concepts. The IPSS and its successor, the WHO Determinants of Outcome study (with Chandigarh as an Indian centre), also suggested a better course in developing-country centres. These findings pushed psychiatry toward operational criteria (Feighner criteria 1972, Research Diagnostic Criteria 1978, DSM-III 1980) that narrowed the American concept and leaned on Schneider's symptoms. 2.7 Kurt Schneider: first-rank symptoms Kurt Schneider (Heidelberg) took a pragmatic route. Whatever the underlying process, which symptoms are both easy to recognise and highly characteristic ? He set these out in Klinische Psychopathologie (first edition 1950, developed from earlier work in the late 1930s), translated into English by M. W. Hamilton in 1959 . In the absence of organic brain disease, the presence of a first-rank symptom (FRS) was to be taken as strongly suggestive of schizophrenia. Christopher S. Mellor (1970) later gave the standard operational definitions. The commonly cited list of 11 : Audible thoughts ( Gedankenlautwerden , also "thought echo" or écho de la pensée ): hearing one's own thoughts spoken aloud. Voices arguing or discussing the patient in the third person. Voices commenting on the patient's actions ("now she is picking up the cup"). Somatic passivity : bodily sensations experienced as imposed by an outside agency. Thought withdrawal : thoughts are taken out of the mind by an outside force. Thought insertion : thoughts that are not one's own are put into the mind. Thought broadcasting (diffusion): one's thoughts escape and are known to others. Made feelings : emotions imposed from outside. Made impulses (drives) : urges imposed from outside. Made volitional acts : actions controlled by an outside agency. Delusional perception : a normal perception is given a sudden, delusional, self-referent meaning (for example, "the traffic light turned red, so I knew I had been chosen to save the world"). This is a two-stage process: normal percept, then unconnected delusional meaning. Items 4 and 8 to 10 together are often grouped as passivity experiences (delusions of control); items 5 to 7 as thought alienation ; items 1 to 3 as third-person auditory hallucinations . Second-rank symptoms were other features that could support the diagnosis but were less specific: other kinds of hallucination, sudden delusional ideas (delusional notions), perplexity, depressive or euphoric mood changes and emotional blunting. These occur in many disorders. High yield FRS are not pathognomonic. Later studies found them in a proportion of patients with mania and other psychoses, and a substantial minority of people with schizophrenia never show any. ICD-10 gave FRS heavy weight. DSM-IV allowed a single Criterion A symptom to suffice if delusions were bizarre or hallucinations were a running commentary or two voices conversing. DSM-5 (2013) dropped this special weighting (and the classic subtypes), so these symptoms now count like any other Criterion A symptom. 2.8 After Schneider: positive and negative symptoms, Crow, Langfeldt Gabriel Langfeldt (Norway, 1939) separated "true" process schizophrenia (insidious, poor prognosis) from schizophreniform states (acute onset, clear precipitant, good prognosis). The term survives as DSM's schizophreniform disorder, though now defined by duration (1 to 6 months), not prognosis. Timothy Crow (1980) proposed two syndromes. Type I : positive symptoms, acute, good response to neuroleptics, presumed dopamine (D2) excess, reversible, no intellectual impairment. Type II : negative symptoms, chronic, poor drug response, structural brain change (ventricular enlargement), intellectual impairment, poorer outcome. Nancy Andreasen built rating scales for negative (SANS, 1982) and positive (SAPS, 1984) symptoms and, with Olsen (1982), positive, negative and mixed subtypes. The negative symptom concept looks back to Eugen Bleuler's fundamental symptoms, and the positive concept to Schneider's FRS. The terms "positive" and "negative" symptoms themselves go back to the neurologist John Hughlings Jackson in the 19th century. 2.9 Kraepelin vs Bleuler vs Schneider Feature Emil Kraepelin Eugen Bleuler Kurt Schneider Key term Dementia praecox Schizophrenia ("group of schizophrenias") First-rank symptoms Key dates 4th ed 1893 (term); 6th ed 1899 (consolidated) 1908 lecture (word coined); 1911 monograph; English 1950 (Zinkin) Klinische Psychopathologie 1950; English 1959 Basis for diagnosis Course and outcome (early onset, deterioration) Underlying psychological disturbance (fundamental symptoms) Specific, easily recognised symptoms Core features Hebephrenic, catatonic and paranoid forms with deterioration Four A's: associations, affect, ambivalence, autism 11 FRS (thought alienation, passivity, third-person voices, delusional perception) Status of hallucinations and delusions Common features Accessory (not essential) Certain specific forms are first rank Prognosis view Pessimistic (deterioration) Variable; recovery possible Not the basis for diagnosis Width of concept Moderate Broad Narrow Main legacy Dichotomy with manic-depressive illness Name; negative and cognitive symptom tradition; broad US concept ICD-10 and DSM-III to DSM-IV criteria; Present State Examination 2.10 Manfred Bleuler and long-term outcome Eugen Bleuler's son Manfred Bleuler , also director of the Burghölzli, personally followed a cohort of patients for more than two decades (the usually quoted figure is 208 patients), published in German in 1972 and in English in 1978. He found that the course was far less uniformly bad than Emil Kraepelin had held: a substantial minority recovered (often quoted as about a quarter), many reached a stable outcome after the first years, and steady progression to severe "end states" was uncommon. The exact percentages vary between secondary sources, so learn the direction of the finding rather than a single number. Do not confuse father and son: Eugen coined schizophrenia and autism; Manfred did the long-term outcome study. Exam trap (1) Bleuler coined both schizophrenia and autism ; Kanner (1943) and Asperger (1944) borrowed autism. (2) 1908 = the word introduced in a lecture; 1911 = the monograph; 1950 = English translation. Read which event the question names. (3) The four A's do not include hallucinations or delusions; those are accessory. (4) Ambivalence is the umbrella; ambitendency is its volitional form (and is listed among catatonic motor signs in modern texts). (5) Schizophrenia does not mean split personality. (6) Fundamental/accessory and primary/secondary are different axes. (7) Morel = démence précoce; Emil Kraepelin = dementia praecox; Hecker = hebephrenia (1871); Kahlbaum = catatonia (1874). (8) Schneider's FRS number 11 in the usual list; delusional perception is the only delusion among them. (9) Manfred Bleuler, not Eugen, ran the long-term outcome study. Self-check The term "schizophrenia" was first introduced by Eugen Bleuler in: a 1899 b 1908 c 1911 d 1950 ✓ Answer: (b) 1908 Eugen Bleuler, 1908 lecture (German Psychiatric Association, Berlin) The concept The three dates Bleuler used the word in a 1908 lecture ; the monograph, Dementia Praecox oder Gruppe der Schizophrenien , followed in 1911 and the English translation (Joseph Zinkin) in 1950 . The word From Greek schizein (to split) and phren (mind): the splitting of thought, emotion and will from one another, not a split personality . Exam tip Read which event the question names: 1908 = word introduced , 1911 = monograph, 1950 = English edition. Why the other options are wrong (a) 1899 Not a Bleuler date; 1899 is Kraepelin's 6th edition, which consolidated dementia praecox . (c) 1911 The year of the monograph Dementia Praecox oder Gruppe der Schizophrenien , not the first use of the word. (d) 1950 The English translation by Joseph Zinkin, and also the year of Schneider's Klinische Psychopathologie ; far too late for the coinage. Which of the following is NOT one of Bleuler's four A's? a Ambivalence b Autism c Auditory hallucinations d Associations ✓ Answer: (c) Auditory hallucinations Eugen Bleuler, fundamental vs accessory symptoms The concept The four A's Associations, Affect, Ambivalence, Autism : a later teaching mnemonic for Bleuler's fundamental symptoms , present in every case and at every stage. Why this one Hallucinations were accessory symptoms for Bleuler: they come and go and occur in other illnesses, so the diagnosis does not rest on them. Why the other options are not the answer (a) Ambivalence One of the four: contradictory feelings, wishes or thoughts toward the same object held at once; Bleuler coined the word. (b) Autism One of the four: withdrawal from external reality into an inner world of fantasy; Bleuler coined this word too. (d) Associations One of the four, and the central one: loosening of associations , the chief primary symptom in Bleuler's account. (c) 8th edition, 1913 Came well after the consolidation (the 8th edition ran 1909 to 1915) and added further subforms such as simple dementia praecox. A patient reaches out to shake the doctor's hand, withdraws it, then extends it again, repeatedly. This is best described as: a echopraxia b ambitendency c waxy flexibility d thought blocking ✓ Answer: (b) ambitendency Eugen Bleuler, ambivalence (volitional form) The concept What it is Ambitendency is the volitional form of Bleuler's ambivalence : wanting and not wanting to act at once, so the patient starts to shake hands, withdraws, then extends the hand again. The other forms Bleuler also described affective ambivalence (loving and hating the same person) and intellectual ambivalence ("I am a man" and "I am not a man"). Exam tip Ambivalence is the umbrella; ambitendency is also listed among catatonic motor signs in modern texts. (d) thought blocking Sudden stopping of the train of thought, which Bleuler grouped with association disturbance; it affects thinking, not movement. According to Bleuler, the primary symptom, a direct product of the disease process, was: a delusions b autism c loosening of associations d hallucinations ✓ Answer: (c) loosening of associations Eugen Bleuler, primary vs secondary symptoms The concept Two axes Bleuler sorted symptoms twice: fundamental vs accessory (diagnostic) and primary vs secondary (causal). Primary means a direct product of the presumed organic disease process. Why this one Loosening of associations was his chief primary symptom: both fundamental and primary, the core of the illness. Exam tip Autism was fundamental but largely secondary; delusions and hallucinations were accessory and secondary. Primary is not a synonym for fundamental. Why the other options are wrong (a) delusions Accessory and secondary: a psychological reaction to the primary disturbance, not its direct product. (b) autism Fundamental but largely secondary: present in every case, yet a psychological consequence of the loosening; the classic trap. (d) hallucinations Accessory and secondary, like delusions; they often bring the patient to hospital but are not the core process. Exam tip The first-rank voices are third-person : audible thoughts, voices arguing or discussing the patient, and voices commenting on actions. (c) Emotional blunting Also second rank; it belongs with Bleuler's affect disturbance and later negative symptoms, not Schneider's first-rank list. (d) Second-person command hallucinations Not first rank: Schneider's voices are third-person (arguing, discussing or commenting); command hallucinations in the second person do not qualify. The borrowing Kanner (1943) and Asperger (1944) borrowed it for a developmental condition of childhood, which is why one word now names two different disorders. Why the other options are wrong (a) Leo Kanner Borrowed the word in 1943 ("Autistic disturbances of affective contact") for a childhood developmental condition; he did not coin it. (b) Hans Asperger Borrowed it in 1944 ("autistic psychopathy"); the trap is that his name is now tied to the childhood condition. (d) Emil Kraepelin Unified dementia praecox (1899) and judged by course; he coined neither "schizophrenia" nor "autism", both Bleuler's words.
