The finding The course was far less uniformly bad than Kraepelin held: a substantial minority recovered , many stabilised after the first years, and steady decline to severe end states was uncommon. Exam tip Do not confuse father and son : Eugen coined schizophrenia and autism; Manfred ran the long-term outcome study. Why the other options are wrong (a) Eugen Bleuler His father, who coined "schizophrenia" and "autism" and also directed the Burghölzli; the shared surname is the trap. (c) Gabriel Langfeldt Norwegian psychiatrist (1939) who separated process schizophrenia from good-prognosis schizophreniform states. (d) Kurt Schneider Heidelberg psychiatrist who listed the 11 first-rank symptoms , a diagnostic contribution, not an outcome study. 3. The theory of planned behaviour The theory of planned behaviour (TPB) is the most widely used model in social and health psychology for predicting what people will actually do. To understand why it exists you have to start with an embarrassing problem that social psychology faced in the middle of the twentieth century: attitudes, the field's favourite concept, did not seem to predict behaviour. 3.1 The attitude-behaviour problem Gordon Allport (1935) had called attitude "the most distinctive and indispensable concept" in social psychology, on the assumption that if you know how a person feels about something you can predict how they will act toward it. Two pieces of evidence shook that assumption. Richard LaPiere (1934), "Attitudes vs. actions". Between 1930 and 1932 LaPiere travelled across the United States with a young Chinese couple at a time of strong anti-Chinese prejudice. They visited hotels, auto camps and restaurants (the commonly cited total is 251 establishments) and were refused service only once. About six months later LaPiere mailed a questionnaire to the same establishments asking "Will you accept members of the Chinese race as guests?" Of those who replied, roughly 92% said no. The stated attitude (rejection) and the actual behaviour (acceptance) were almost opposite. The study has methodological problems (the person answering the letter was probably not the person at the front desk, the couple were well dressed and accompanied by a white professor, and a letter about "the Chinese race" is a far more abstract target than a particular polite couple), but it became the classic demonstration of the gap. Allan Wicker (1969). Wicker reviewed several dozen studies that had measured both attitudes and overt behaviour and concluded that the relationship was weak: correlations rarely exceeded about .30 and the typical value was around .15. He even suggested that the attitude concept might be abandoned. A correlation of .15 means attitudes explain only about 2% of the variance in behaviour. 3.2 The rescue: the principle of compatibility Icek Ajzen and Martin Fishbein (1977, Psychological Bulletin ) argued that attitudes do predict behaviour, but only when both are measured at the same level of specificity. They originally called this the principle of correspondence ; Ajzen later relabelled it compatibility . Any behaviour has four elements, remembered as TACT : Target (toward what), Action (what is done), Context (where), and Time (when). LaPiere measured a general attitude ("the Chinese race") and tried to predict a highly specific act (serving this couple, in this hotel, on this evening). A general attitude toward religion will not predict whether you attend a particular temple next Sunday, but it will predict a broad aggregate of religious behaviours across many occasions. Conversely, a specific attitude ("my attending the temple this Sunday") predicts that specific act well. When attitude and behaviour measures are compatible, correlations rise substantially. Definition Principle of compatibility (Icek Ajzen and Martin Fishbein, 1977): an attitude predicts a behaviour well only when both are defined at the same level of generality on Target, Action, Context and Time. General attitudes predict aggregated behaviour; specific attitudes predict specific acts. 3.3 The Theory of Reasoned Action (TRA) Martin Fishbein and Icek Ajzen set out the Theory of Reasoned Action in Belief, Attitude, Intention, and Behavior: An Introduction to Theory and Research (1975), building on Fishbein's earlier expectancy-value work on attitudes in the 1960s. Ajzen and Fishbein then presented it for applied readers in Understanding Attitudes and Predicting Social Behavior (1980). The word "reasoned" does not mean people are perfectly logical; it means behaviour follows reasonably from the information and beliefs a person holds. The TRA has a simple chain: Behavioural intention is the immediate antecedent of behaviour. Intention is the person's readiness or plan to perform the act ("I intend to exercise three times this week"). Intention is determined by two things: the attitude toward the behaviour and the subjective norm . Attitude toward the behaviour is the person's overall positive or negative evaluation of performing the behaviour. It is built by an expectancy-value rule: for each salient outcome, multiply the strength of the belief that the behaviour leads to that outcome (behavioural belief, b ) by the evaluation of that outcome ( e ), and sum: A B = Σ b i e i . Example: "Exercising will reduce my weight" (very likely, +3) × "reducing my weight is" (very good, +3) = +9; add up across outcomes like "exercising will tire me" and "exercising will take time from study". Subjective norm is the perceived social pressure to perform or not perform the behaviour. It is built from normative beliefs (what I think specific important others, called referents, want me to do: parents, spouse, doctor) multiplied by motivation to comply with each referent, then summed: SN = Σ n j m j . The relative weight of attitude and subjective norm varies across behaviours and people. For some acts (choosing a career in a joint family) the norm dominates; for others (choosing a flavour of ice cream) attitude dominates. Everything else (personality, demographics, general attitudes toward objects) is treated as an external variable : it influences behaviour only indirectly by shaping these beliefs. The limit of the TRA: volitional control. The TRA works for behaviours fully under volitional control, where intending is enough to act. Many important behaviours are not like that. You may fully intend to quit smoking, lose weight or attend therapy but lack the skill, money, time, transport or cooperation of others. For such behaviours intention alone predicts poorly. This is the gap the TPB was built to fill. 3.4 The Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) Icek Ajzen extended the TRA in a book chapter, "From intentions to actions: A theory of planned behavior", in Julius Kuhl and Jürgen Beckmann (Eds.), Action Control: From Cognition to Behavior (Springer, 1985). The fully developed and most cited statement is Ajzen (1991), "The theory of planned behavior", Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes , 50, 179 to 211. Note that the TPB is Ajzen's theory alone; Martin Fishbein was co-author of the TRA, not of the TPB papers. The single addition is perceived behavioural control (PBC) : the person's perception of how easy or difficult it will be to perform the behaviour. Like the other constructs it rests on beliefs. Control beliefs ( c ) are beliefs about the presence of factors that can help or hinder (time, money, skill, a nearby gym, a supportive partner), and each is weighted by its perceived power ( p ) to facilitate or inhibit the behaviour: PBC = Σ c k p k . The two routes of PBC. PBC works in two ways, and examiners love this point: Indirect route, via intention. People form stronger intentions to do things they believe they can do. If I think quitting is impossible for me, I will hardly intend to quit. Direct route, to behaviour. PBC also predicts behaviour directly, but only to the extent that PBC is an accurate reflection of actual behavioural control . Here PBC acts as a proxy for actual control (real skills, resources, opportunities). Two people with equally strong intentions to exercise will differ in success if one actually has a gym and free time; PBC captures part of that difference. When perceptions are unrealistic (little information, a new behaviour, changed circumstances) the direct path weakens. Ajzen (1991) also suggested that PBC moderates the intention-behaviour link (intentions translate into behaviour more strongly when control is high), though in practice most studies test only additive paths. Link to self-efficacy. Ajzen explicitly noted that PBC is most compatible with Albert Bandura's (1977) concept of self-efficacy , "beliefs in one's capability to organise and execute the courses of action required" (from Bandura's 1977 Psychological Review paper, "Self-efficacy: Toward a unifying theory of behavioral change"). Later research showed PBC items split into two factors: self-efficacy / perceived capacity (ease or difficulty, confidence) and perceived controllability / autonomy (whether it is up to me). Self-efficacy items usually predict intention better. High yield TPB = TRA + perceived behavioural control. Three belief bases feed three constructs: behavioural beliefs → attitude toward the behaviour; normative beliefs → subjective norm; control beliefs → PBC. These three → intention → behaviour, plus a direct PBC → behaviour path that works only insofar as PBC mirrors actual control. Theory of planned behaviour (Ajzen, 1985, 1991) Behavioural beliefs × outcome evaluations Normative beliefs × motivation to comply Control beliefs × perceived power Attitude toward the behaviour Subjective norm Perceived behavioural control (PBC) Intention Behaviour Actual control (skills, resources) direct path (proxy) Figure: the TPB. Solid arrows are the main causal paths; the dashed arrow is the direct PBC → behaviour path, which holds only to the extent PBC reflects actual control. Delete the bottom row (control beliefs, PBC, actual control) and you have the TRA. 3.5 Later extensions Descriptive vs injunctive norms. The subjective norm in the TRA and TPB is essentially injunctive : what others think I ought to do. Robert Cialdini and colleagues (Cialdini, Reno and Kallgren, 1990, the "focus theory of normative conduct", tested with littering studies) distinguished this from the descriptive norm : what others actually do. Seeing a littered car park makes people litter more (descriptive), even if they know littering is disapproved (injunctive). TPB researchers later added descriptive norms and found they add predictive power. The Reasoned Action Approach (RAA). Martin Fishbein and Icek Ajzen (2010), Predicting and Changing Behavior: The Reasoned Action Approach , unified the TRA and TPB. The RAA keeps attitude, perceived norm and PBC, but splits each into two subcomponents: attitude into instrumental (useful/useless) and experiential (pleasant/unpleasant); perceived norm into injunctive and descriptive ; PBC into capacity and autonomy . Fishbein died in 2009, before the book appeared. 3.6 How good is the evidence? Two meta-analyses are quoted in almost every textbook. Treat the exact numbers as the commonly cited figures: Christopher Armitage and Mark Conner (2001) , British Journal of Social Psychology , about 185 independent studies: the TPB explained about 39% of the variance in intention and about 27% of the variance in behaviour . PBC added significantly to the prediction of intention over attitude and subjective norm. Subjective norm was the weakest predictor. Prediction of self-reported behaviour was better than prediction of objectively measured behaviour. Paschal Sheeran (2002) , European Review of Social Psychology , a meta-analysis of meta-analyses: the average intention-behaviour correlation was about .53, meaning intentions explain about 28% of the variance in behaviour . This leaves a large intention-behaviour gap : Sheeran showed most of the gap comes from "inclined abstainers", people who intend to act but do not. 3.7 Applications in health psychology The TPB has been applied to condom use, smoking initiation and cessation, exercise, diet, alcohol use, breast and cervical screening, medication adherence and help-seeking. In India it is a natural fit for public health behaviours such as handwashing with soap, vaccination uptake (including COVID-19 and childhood immunisation), toilet use under sanitation campaigns, tobacco and gutka cessation, and mental health help-seeking. A clinical psychologist might use it to understand why a patient with depression does not attend follow-up: is it attitude ("therapy will not help"), norm ("my family thinks seeing a psychiatrist is shameful"), or PBC ("the hospital is two buses away and I cannot take leave")? Each points to a different intervention. How a TPB questionnaire is built (Icek Ajzen's recommended procedure): Define the behaviour in TACT terms ("washing hands with soap before every meal at home over the next two weeks"). Elicitation study. In a small sample from the target population, ask open-ended questions: What are the advantages/disadvantages of doing this? Who would approve/disapprove? What would make it easier/harder? The most frequently mentioned answers become the modal salient beliefs . Main questionnaire. Build items for each belief and each direct construct, typically on 7-point scales. Direct attitude uses semantic differential pairs ("For me, washing hands before meals is: bad 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 good; unpleasant ... pleasant; harmful ... beneficial"). Belief strength items are often scored from 1 to 7 or from -3 to +3; evaluations and motivation to comply are usually bipolar. Measure behaviour later (prospective design), ideally objectively. Analyse with hierarchical regression or structural equation modelling. 3.8 Criticisms "Time to retire". Falko Sniehotta, Justin Presseau and Vera Araújo-Soares (2014), in Health Psychology Review , argued that the TPB has limited predictive validity, that its constructs often do not change behaviour when targeted in interventions, and that it is too static. Icek Ajzen published a reply defending it. Rationality bias. The model assumes deliberate, conscious processing. It neglects emotion, impulse, and automatic processes. Past behaviour and habit. Past behaviour often predicts future behaviour better than TPB variables and adds variance beyond them, which suggests habit (automatic responding cued by context) is missing from the model. Self-report and common method variance inflate correlations; objective behaviour is predicted less well. Intention-behaviour gap. Even strong intentions often fail. Sufficiency assumption. Ajzen allowed extra predictors in principle, and many have been added (moral norm, anticipated regret, self-identity), which weakens the claim that three constructs are enough. Bridging the gap: implementation intentions. Peter Gollwitzer (1999, American Psychologist ) distinguished goal intentions ("I intend to do X") from implementation intentions , "if-then" plans that link a situation to a response: "If it is 7 am on a weekday, then I will walk for 20 minutes around the park." Such plans delegate control to situational cues and help close the intention-behaviour gap. Gollwitzer and Sheeran's (2006) meta-analysis is often cited for a medium-to-large effect. 3.9 Comparison with other health behaviour models Model Origin Core constructs Proximal predictor Key point for exams Theory of Reasoned Action Martin Fishbein and Icek Ajzen, 1975; 1980 Attitude toward the behaviour, subjective norm Intention Only for volitional behaviours Theory of Planned Behaviour Icek Ajzen, 1985; 1991 Attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioural control Intention (plus PBC directly) Adds PBC to TRA Health Belief Model Godfrey Hochbaum, Irwin Rosenstock and colleagues, US Public Health Service, 1950s (built to explain poor uptake of free tuberculosis X-ray screening) Perceived susceptibility, perceived severity, perceived benefits, perceived barriers, cues to action; self-efficacy added later (Rosenstock, Strecher and Becker, 1988) No intention construct; beliefs predict action directly "Cues to action" is unique to the HBM Protection Motivation Theory Ronald Rogers, 1975 (revised 1983) Threat appraisal (severity, vulnerability, rewards of maladaptive response) and coping appraisal (response efficacy, self-efficacy, response cost) Protection motivation (functions like intention) Built to explain fear appeals 3.10 Exam traps Exam trap TPB = TRA + PBC. Options that say TPB added "subjective norm" or "intention" are wrong; those were already in the TRA. The TRA is Fishbein and Icek Ajzen (1975); the TPB is Ajzen alone. Exam trap Years: TPB first proposed 1985 (book chapter in Kuhl and Beckmann), fully developed 1991 (OBHDP journal). Both answers can appear; "proposed" points to 1985, "the classic paper" to 1991. TRA: 1975 (and 1980). Reasoned Action Approach: 2010. Exam trap Subjective norm is perceived social pressure , not the actual opinions of others and not the actual behaviour of others (that is the descriptive norm). Attitude is toward the behaviour ("my quitting smoking"), not toward the object ("cigarettes"). PBC is perceived, not actual control ; it predicts behaviour directly only as a proxy for actual control. Memory hook "A-S-P before I-B": Attitude, Subjective norm, PBC come before Intention, then Behaviour. Beliefs underneath: Behavioural, Normative, Control ("BNC"). 3.11 Self-check The construct added by the theory of planned behaviour to the theory of reasoned action is: a Subjective norm b Behavioural intention c Perceived behavioural control d Attitude toward the object ✓ Answer: (c) Perceived behavioural control Icek Ajzen (1985, 1991) The concept The gap The theory of reasoned action (Fishbein and Ajzen, 1975) works only for behaviours under full volitional control , where intending is enough to act. The addition Icek Ajzen added perceived behavioural control (PBC), how easy or hard the person thinks the act will be, to handle behaviours not under full volitional control. Exam tip TPB = TRA + PBC . The TPB is Ajzen's alone (1985 chapter, 1991 paper); Fishbein co-authored only the TRA. Why the other options are wrong (a) Subjective norm Already in the TRA: perceived social pressure from important others, one of its two determinants of intention. (b) Behavioural intention Already in the TRA as the immediate antecedent of behaviour; the TPB kept it rather than added it. (d) Attitude toward the object Not a construct of either theory: both use attitude toward the behaviour , not toward the object. In TPB, the immediate antecedent of behaviour is: a Attitude b Intention c Normative belief d Self-efficacy ✓ Answer: (b) Intention Ajzen, theory of planned behaviour (1991) The concept What it is Intention is the person's readiness or plan to perform the act; it is the proximal determinant of behaviour in both the TRA and the TPB. The chain Attitude, subjective norm and PBC feed intention, which leads to behaviour. Memory hook: "A-S-P before I-B" . The caveat PBC may also act directly on behaviour, but only insofar as it mirrors actual control (skills, resources). Why the other options are wrong (a) Attitude One step back: attitude toward the behaviour feeds intention, which then drives behaviour. (c) Normative belief Two steps back: normative beliefs, weighted by motivation to comply, build the subjective norm. (d) Self-efficacy Bandura's (1977) concept, which Ajzen called most compatible with PBC; it is not the TPB's proximal predictor. Normative beliefs are weighted by: a Outcome evaluation b Perceived power c Motivation to comply d Response efficacy ✓ Answer: (c) Motivation to comply Fishbein and Ajzen, theory of reasoned action (1975) The concept The formula Subjective norm = Σ normative belief × motivation to comply (SN = Σ n j m j ). The parts A normative belief is what a specific important other (a referent : parent, spouse, doctor) wants me to do; motivation to comply is how much I want to go along with that person. The pattern Each construct is beliefs × weights, summed: behavioural beliefs × outcome evaluation, normative beliefs × motivation to comply, control beliefs × perceived power. Why the other options are wrong (a) Outcome evaluation Weights behavioural beliefs to build attitude toward the behaviour (A B = Σ b i e i ). (b) Perceived power Weights control beliefs to build perceived behavioural control (PBC = Σ c k p k ). (d) Response efficacy From Protection Motivation Theory (Rogers, 1975): the belief that the recommended action works, part of coping appraisal. LaPiere's (1934) study is famous for showing: a Cognitive dissonance after forced compliance b A discrepancy between stated attitudes and actual behaviour c Conformity to group pressure d The mere exposure effect ✓ Answer: (b) A discrepancy between stated attitudes and actual behaviour Richard LaPiere (1934), "Attitudes vs. actions" The concept The study LaPiere toured the US (1930 to 1932) with a young Chinese couple; of about 251 establishments visited, only one refused them service. The twist About six months later, establishments that had served the Chinese couple were asked by letter; roughly 92% of replies said they would refuse Chinese guests, a stark attitude-behaviour gap . Why it happened Ajzen and Fishbein (1977) explained it with compatibility : a general attitude ("the Chinese race") cannot predict a specific act (serving this couple). Why the other options are wrong (a) Cognitive dissonance after forced compliance Festinger's dissonance theory; the classic forced-compliance study is Festinger and Carlsmith (1959). (c) Conformity to group pressure Asch's line-judgement studies showed conformity to group pressure; LaPiere's study involved no group pressure. (d) The mere exposure effect Zajonc's finding (1968) that repeated exposure alone increases liking; unrelated to attitude-behaviour consistency. The principle of compatibility requires attitude and behaviour to match on: a Target, action, context and time b Valence, intensity, centrality and accessibility c Cognition, affect and conation d Severity, susceptibility, benefits and barriers ✓ Answer: (a) Target, action, context and time Icek Ajzen and Martin Fishbein (1977), Psychological Bulletin The concept The principle An attitude predicts a behaviour well only when both are measured at the same level of specificity on TACT : Target, Action, Context, Time . Example A general attitude toward religion will not predict attending a particular temple next Sunday, but it does predict an aggregate of religious behaviours. Name note Ajzen and Martin Fishbein first called it the principle of correspondence ; Ajzen later relabelled it compatibility. Why the other options are wrong (b) Valence, intensity, centrality and accessibility Dimensions describing the attitude itself (its direction and strength), not the four elements of a behaviour. (c) Cognition, affect and conation The classic tripartite (ABC) model of attitude components, not the elements of the behaviour. (d) Severity, susceptibility, benefits and barriers Core constructs of the Health Belief Model (Hochbaum, Rosenstock and colleagues, 1950s). PBC is expected to predict behaviour directly when: a Subjective norm is weak b PBC accurately reflects actual control c The behaviour is fully volitional d Attitudes are negative ✓ Answer: (b) PBC accurately reflects actual control Ajzen, theory of planned behaviour (1985, 1991) The concept What PBC is Perceived behavioural control (PBC) is how easy or hard a person thinks the behaviour will be. It is the one construct Ajzen added to the TRA. The direct path PBC predicts behaviour directly, not only through intention, but only to the extent it accurately reflects actual control (real skills, resources, opportunities). The direct path works because PBC serves as a proxy for actual control. Exam tip When perceptions are unrealistic (little information, a new behaviour, changed circumstances) the direct path weakens . Why the other options are wrong (a) Subjective norm is weak The strength of the subjective norm bears on intention, not on the direct PBC path; what matters is how accurate PBC is, not how weak the other predictors are. (c) The behaviour is fully volitional Fully volitional behaviour is the TRA's territory, where intending is enough to act; PBC was added for behaviours not under full volitional control. (d) Attitudes are negative Attitude valence is irrelevant here: attitudes feed intention, and whether they are positive or negative does not decide if PBC predicts behaviour directly. Ajzen considered PBC most similar to: a Rotter's locus of control b Bandura's self-efficacy c Seligman's learned helplessness d Festinger's dissonance ✓ Answer: (b) Bandura's self-efficacy Bandura, self-efficacy (1977) The concept The link Ajzen explicitly linked PBC to Bandura's (1977) self-efficacy : beliefs in one's capability to organise and execute the courses of action required. Not locus of control Ajzen distinguished PBC from generalised locus of control : PBC is about one specific behaviour, not a general expectancy that holds across situations. Later research PBC items split into two factors: self-efficacy (ease, confidence) and perceived controllability (whether it is up to me). Why the other options are wrong (a) Rotter's locus of control Julian Rotter's generalised expectancy of internal vs external control; the main trap, because Ajzen explicitly distinguished PBC from it. (c) Seligman's learned helplessness Martin Seligman's passivity after repeated uncontrollable aversive events, a model of depression; not what Ajzen compared PBC to. (d) Festinger's dissonance Leon Festinger's cognitive dissonance (1957): tension from holding inconsistent cognitions; an attitude-change theory, unrelated to perceived control. According to the commonly cited meta-analysis by Armitage and Conner (2001), TPB explains approximately what percentage of variance in behaviour? a 10% b 27% c 39% d 60% ✓ Answer: (b) 27% Armitage and Conner meta-analysis (2001) The concept The figures Armitage and Conner (2001) , about 185 studies: the TPB explained about 27% of the variance in behaviour and about 39% in intention. Why behaviour is lower Behaviour sits further down the chain than intention, and the intention-behaviour gap cuts prediction. Self-reported behaviour was predicted better than objectively measured behaviour. Key note PBC added to the prediction of intention over attitude and subjective norm; subjective norm was the weakest predictor. Why the other options are wrong (a) 10% Too low; the TPB does far better than the weak attitude-behaviour link Wicker (1969) reported (typical correlation about .15, about 2% of variance). (c) 39% The trap: 39% is the variance explained in intention , not behaviour, in the same meta-analysis. (d) 60% Too high; neither figure in the meta-analysis comes close, intention at 39% or behaviour at 27%. "If I finish dinner, then I will take my tablet immediately" is an example of: a A descriptive norm b A cue to action c An implementation intention d A control belief ✓ Answer: (c) An implementation intention Gollwitzer, implementation intentions (1999) The concept What it is Peter Gollwitzer (1999) separated goal intentions ('I intend to do X') from implementation intentions : if-then plans that link a situation to a response. Why it works The plan hands control to a situational cue (finishing dinner), so the act follows almost automatically. That is how if-then plans bridge the intention-behaviour gap . Spot it The ' If X, then I will Y ' wording is the giveaway. Why the other options are wrong (a) A descriptive norm What others actually do ( Cialdini and colleagues, 1990), as in a littered car park making people litter; a social norm, not a personal plan. (b) A cue to action A Health Belief Model construct: a trigger such as a symptom, reminder or media message that prompts action, not a self-made if-then plan. (d) A control belief A TPB belief about factors that help or hinder the behaviour (time, money, skill), feeding PBC ; a belief, not a plan. Which model includes "cues to action"? a Theory of reasoned action b Theory of planned behaviour c Health belief model d Protection motivation theory ✓ Answer: (c) Health belief model Health Belief Model (Hochbaum, Rosenstock, 1950s) The concept The model The Health Belief Model came from Hochbaum, Rosenstock and colleagues at the US Public Health Service in the 1950s, built to explain poor uptake of free tuberculosis X-ray screening. Its constructs Perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits and barriers, plus cues to action ; self-efficacy was added later (Rosenstock, Strecher and Becker, 1988). Exam tip Cues to action are a Health Belief Model construct, unique to the HBM . The HBM also has no intention construct. Why the other options are wrong (a) Theory of reasoned action Fishbein and Ajzen (1975): attitude toward the behaviour and subjective norm lead to intention; no cues to action. (b) Theory of planned behaviour Ajzen (1985, 1991): the TRA plus perceived behavioural control; still no cues to action. (d) Protection motivation theory Ronald Rogers (1975): threat appraisal and coping appraisal, built to explain fear appeals; no cues to action. 4. Types of brain scanning and imaging tests Clinical psychology entrance papers ask about brain imaging in two ways: "which technique measures what" and "who invented it, when". To answer both you need a small set of organising ideas first. 4.1 The organising ideas Structural vs functional imaging. Structural (anatomical) methods show what the brain looks like: size and shape of regions, tumours, strokes, atrophy, enlarged ventricles. CT, structural MRI and DTI are structural. Functional methods show what the brain is doing: electrical activity, blood flow, oxygenation, glucose metabolism, receptor binding. EEG, MEG, fMRI, PET, SPECT and fNIRS are functional. The question to ask is: does the image change when the person changes what they are thinking? If yes, it is functional. Spatial vs temporal resolution. Spatial resolution is how precisely you can say where something is (millimetres). Temporal resolution is how precisely you can say when it happened (milliseconds to minutes). Methods that measure electrical or magnetic signals directly (EEG, MEG) are fast (milliseconds) but poor at localisation. Methods that measure blood flow or metabolism (fMRI, PET, SPECT, fNIRS) are slow, because blood responds over seconds, but fMRI and PET localise better. This is the spatial-temporal trade-off , and it is the most examined idea in this topic. Invasive vs non-invasive. Invasive methods break the skin or enter the body: injecting a radioactive tracer (PET, SPECT), injecting contrast through an arterial catheter (angiography), or placing electrodes on or in the brain (intracranial recording). EEG, MEG, MRI, fMRI and fNIRS are non-invasive. Ionising radiation. X-rays and gamma rays carry enough energy to knock electrons off atoms and can damage DNA, so exposure is limited, especially in children and pregnancy. CT and angiography use X-rays; PET and SPECT use gamma-emitting radioactive tracers. MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves, and EEG, MEG and fNIRS use no ionising radiation at all. 4.2 Historical precursors: pneumoencephalography and cerebral angiography Feature Pneumoencephalography (PEG) Cerebral angiography Full name Pneumoencephalography (air encephalography); ventriculography when air is put directly into the ventricles Cerebral angiography; modern form is digital subtraction angiography (DSA) Inventor / key people and year Walter Dandy, Johns Hopkins: ventriculography 1918, pneumoencephalography 1919 Egas Moniz (António Egas Moniz), Lisbon, 1927; DSA developed in the late 1970s to early 1980s What it measures, physical principle CSF is drained (usually by lumbar puncture) and replaced with air; air is radiolucent, so the ventricles and subarachnoid spaces stand out on plain X-ray Radio-opaque contrast dye is injected into the arteries (now via a catheter from the femoral artery) and X-rays are taken as it flows, showing the vessels. DSA subtracts a pre-contrast image so only the vessels remain Structural or functional Structural (indirect: shape of ventricles) Structural (vascular anatomy), with some flow information Spatial resolution Poor by modern standards Very high for vessels (sub-millimetre) Temporal resolution Not applicable Seconds (can follow contrast flow) Radiation / invasive X-rays; highly invasive and very painful (severe headache, vomiting) X-rays; invasive (arterial catheter); small risk of stroke Clinical and research uses Historically, localising tumours and showing ventricular enlargement; early schizophrenia studies (W. Jacobi and H. Winkler, 1927, reported ventricular enlargement) Aneurysms, arteriovenous malformations, vessel stenosis; DSA is still the gold standard and is used for interventional treatment (coiling, thrombectomy) Limits Obsolete since CT and MRI Invasive; shows vessels, not brain tissue; increasingly replaced for diagnosis by CT and MR angiography Exam trap Egas Moniz won the 1949 Nobel Prize for prefrontal leucotomy (psychosurgery), not for angiography, although angiography is arguably his more lasting contribution. Angiography always needs contrast dye ; plain X-ray cannot see blood vessels. 4.3 Computed tomography (CT / CAT) Feature CT Full name Computed tomography; older name computerised axial tomography (CAT scan) Inventor / key people and year Allan Cormack developed the mathematics in papers of 1963 and 1964; Godfrey Hounsfield built the scanner at EMI, and the first clinical brain scan was performed on 1 October 1971 at Atkinson Morley's Hospital, London (with radiologist James Ambrose). Hounsfield and Cormack shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine What it measures, physical principle An X-ray tube rotates around the head; detectors measure how much the beam is attenuated along many angles; a computer reconstructs cross-sectional slices from these projections. Brightness reflects tissue density (X-ray attenuation) Structural or functional Structural (perfusion CT adds limited functional information) Spatial resolution Good, roughly 0.5 to 1 mm in modern scanners; poorer soft-tissue contrast than MRI Temporal resolution Not used for brain activity; a head scan takes seconds Radiation / invasive Ionising radiation (X-rays); non-invasive unless iodinated contrast is injected Clinical and research uses First-line in acute stroke (to exclude haemorrhage before thrombolysis), head injury, acute haemorrhage, skull fractures, calcification, hydrocephalus; useful when MRI is contraindicated Limits Radiation; poor for posterior fossa (bone artefact), small lesions, early ischaemic stroke and white matter disease; poorer grey/white matter contrast than MRI Hounsfield units (HU) put attenuation on a fixed scale: water = 0 , air = -1000 , dense bone roughly +1000 (values for bone vary, roughly +400 to above +1000). Fat is negative (around -100), CSF near 0, brain around +20 to +40. Acute blood is hyperdense (bright, roughly +50 to +80 HU, values approximate) because clotted blood is concentrated; over days to weeks it becomes isodense and then hypodense. An acute ischaemic infarct may be invisible on CT in the first hours, then appears hypodense (dark). This is why CT in stroke is used mainly to rule out bleeding. Memory hook On CT, "white is dense": bone and fresh blood bright, air and CSF dark. CT = X-rays; "CAT" is just the old name for the same scan. 4.4 Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) Feature MRI Full name Magnetic resonance imaging (originally nuclear magnetic resonance imaging; "nuclear" was dropped to avoid confusion with radioactivity) Inventor / key people and year NMR physics: Felix Bloch and Edward Purcell (1946). Raymond Damadian reported in 1971 ( Science ) that tumour tissue has different relaxation times and claimed priority for the idea of MR scanning. Paul Lauterbur published the first MR image using magnetic field gradients in 1973 ( Nature ); Peter Mansfield developed the mathematics for fast imaging and echo-planar imaging (1977). Lauterbur and Mansfield shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine; Damadian's exclusion was publicly contested What it measures, physical principle Hydrogen nuclei (protons, mostly in water and fat) align in a strong magnetic field (typically 1.5 or 3 tesla). A radiofrequency pulse tips them; as they relax back they emit a radio signal. Different tissues relax at different rates (T1, T2), and gradients encode position Structural or functional Structural (fMRI, DTI and MRS are special MRI techniques) Spatial resolution Very good, about 1 mm routinely, sub-millimetre at high field Temporal resolution Not applicable for structural scans (a sequence takes minutes) Radiation / invasive No ionising radiation; non-invasive (gadolinium contrast optional) Clinical and research uses Tumours, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy foci (e.g. hippocampal sclerosis), posterior fossa, dementia (hippocampal atrophy), early stroke (diffusion-weighted imaging), volumetric research in psychiatry Limits Contraindicated with pacemakers (unless MR-conditional), cochlear implants, ferromagnetic aneurysm clips, metallic foreign bodies (e.g. in the eye); noisy, claustrophobic, slow, expensive; patient must stay still T1 vs T2. On T1-weighted images CSF is dark , fat is bright and white matter is brighter than grey matter: T1 looks like the anatomy textbook and is used for anatomy and volumetric measurement. On T2-weighted images CSF is bright and most pathology (oedema, inflammation, demyelination, tumour) is bright because it contains extra water: T2 is used to find lesions. FLAIR (fluid-attenuated inversion recovery) is a T2-type image with the CSF signal suppressed, so CSF is dark while lesions stay bright; this makes periventricular multiple sclerosis plaques easy to see. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) shows an acute ischaemic infarct within minutes, far earlier than CT. Memory hook "T2 = H 2 O bright": water (CSF) is white on T2. "World War 2": water white on T2. 4.5 Functional MRI (fMRI) Feature fMRI Full name Functional magnetic resonance imaging, usually BOLD fMRI Inventor / key people and year Seiji Ogawa described blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) contrast in 1990 (rat studies, PNAS ). John Belliveau published a human functional MRI study using injected contrast in 1991; the first human BOLD studies appeared in 1992 (groups including Kenneth Kwong, Ogawa and Peter Bandettini) What it measures, physical principle Deoxyhaemoglobin is paramagnetic and distorts the local magnetic field, lowering the MR signal; oxyhaemoglobin is diamagnetic and does not. When neurons become active, blood flow increases more than oxygen use, so the local concentration of deoxyhaemoglobin falls and the signal rises Structural or functional Functional Spatial resolution Good, about 1 to 3 mm Temporal resolution Moderate, seconds; the haemodynamic response peaks about 4 to 6 s after neural activity and lasts 10 to 20 s Radiation / invasive No radiation, no injection; non-invasive Clinical and research uses Cognitive neuroscience; pre-surgical mapping of language and motor areas; resting-state connectivity in psychiatric disorders Limits Indirect measure (blood, not neurons); slow; sensitive to head motion; noisy scanner; same contraindications as MRI; results are relative (task vs baseline), not absolute Why "indirect"? fMRI does not record neurons firing. It records a vascular response that follows neural activity. Nikos Logothetis and colleagues (2001) found the BOLD signal tracks local field potentials (synaptic input and local processing) better than spiking output. The haemodynamic response function may show a small initial dip, a peak at about 4 to 6 s, and a post-stimulus undershoot. Designs. In a block design the participant alternates long blocks (e.g. 20 to 30 s) of task and rest; it gives strong signal. In an event-related design brief single trials are presented and the response to each is modelled; this allows randomised trials and sorting by behaviour (e.g. remembered vs forgotten items). Resting-state fMRI measures spontaneous slow fluctuations while the person lies quietly: Bharat Biswal (1995) showed that left and right motor cortices fluctuate together at rest. Marcus Raichle and colleagues (2001, PNAS , "A default mode of brain function") named the default mode network (medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate/precuneus, inferior parietal lobule), which is more active at rest and during self-referential thought and deactivates during external tasks. DMN abnormalities are reported in depression, schizophrenia, autism and Alzheimer's disease. Exam trap fMRI measures blood oxygenation (the ratio of oxygenated to deoxygenated haemoglobin), not neuronal firing, glucose use or electrical activity. And it is deoxy haemoglobin that is paramagnetic. 4.6 Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) Feature DTI Full name Diffusion tensor imaging (a form of diffusion MRI) Inventor / key people and year Peter Basser, James Mattiello and Denis Le Bihan, 1994; Le Bihan had introduced diffusion MRI in the mid 1980s What it measures, physical principle Water molecules diffuse more easily along axons than across them, because myelin and membranes restrict movement. DTI measures the direction and degree of this diffusion in each voxel Structural or functional Structural (white matter microstructure and connectivity) Spatial resolution About 2 mm Temporal resolution Not applicable Radiation / invasive None; non-invasive Clinical and research uses White matter integrity in traumatic brain injury, multiple sclerosis, schizophrenia, ageing; surgical planning to avoid major tracts Limits Crossing fibres confuse the tensor model; tractography can produce false tracts; cannot show direction of signal flow Fractional anisotropy (FA) ranges from 0 (diffusion equal in all directions, isotropic, as in CSF) to 1 (diffusion in a single direction). High FA indicates organised, intact white matter (e.g. corpus callosum); reduced FA is reported in many disorders. Tractography follows the principal diffusion direction from voxel to voxel to reconstruct fibre pathways such as the arcuate fasciculus. 4.7 Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) MRS uses the same scanner but, instead of an image, produces a spectrum showing the concentration of chemicals in a chosen region (a "voxel"). Common peaks: N-acetylaspartate (NAA) , a marker of neuronal integrity that falls with neuronal loss; choline (membrane turnover, raised in tumours); creatine (energy metabolism, used as a reference); myo-inositol (glial marker); lactate (anaerobic metabolism); and glutamate/glutamine (often reported together as Glx) and GABA with special sequences. It is non-invasive, has no radiation, and is used in psychiatry research (e.g. glutamate in schizophrenia, GABA in depression). Its limits are low spatial resolution (voxels of a few cubic centimetres) and low signal. 4.8 Positron emission tomography (PET) Feature PET Full name Positron emission tomography Inventor / key people and year Earlier positron imaging by Gordon Brownell and William Sweet (1950s, Boston). The modern tomographic PET scanner was developed at Washington University, St Louis, by Michael Phelps, Edward Hoffman and Michel Ter-Pogossian, 1973 to 1975. 18 F-FDG was synthesised at Brookhaven by Tatsuo Ido and Alfred (Al) Wolf with colleagues, about 1976 to 1978 (sources differ on the exact year); the first human FDG brain images were made at the University of Pennsylvania (Abass Alavi, Martin Reivich) in 1976. FDG built on Louis Sokoloff's deoxyglucose method (published 1977) What it measures, physical principle A tracer labelled with a positron-emitting isotope is injected. Each positron travels a millimetre or so, meets an electron and annihilates , producing two 511 keV gamma photons travelling in opposite directions. Detectors in a ring register both photons simultaneously (coincidence detection) and the computer locates the source along that line Structural or functional Functional (metabolism, blood flow, receptor binding, protein deposits) Spatial resolution Moderate, about 4 to 5 mm clinically (better in research scanners) Temporal resolution Poor, tens of seconds (water) to many minutes (FDG uptake takes about 30 to 45 minutes) Radiation / invasive Ionising radiation; invasive (intravenous injection of a radioactive tracer) Clinical and research uses Dementia (temporoparietal hypometabolism in Alzheimer's disease), epilepsy focus (interictal hypometabolism), tumours; receptor studies, e.g. 11 C-raclopride for dopamine D2/D3 receptors and dopamine release, and amyloid PET (Pittsburgh compound B, reported in 2004) and tau PET Limits Radiation limits repeat scans; short-lived isotopes ( 15 O about 2 min, 11 C about 20 min, 18 F about 110 min) often need an on-site cyclotron; expensive; poor temporal resolution FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose) is a glucose analogue: it is taken up by active cells and phosphorylated but cannot be metabolised further, so it becomes trapped, and its concentration reflects regional glucose metabolism. With 15 O-labelled water, PET measures regional cerebral blood flow and was the main tool for cognitive activation studies in the 1980s and early 1990s before fMRI. 4.9 Single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) Feature SPECT Full name Single photon emission computed tomography (also SPET) Inventor / key people and year David Kuhl and Roy Edwards, University of Pennsylvania, early 1960s (emission tomography reported around 1963) What it measures, physical principle A tracer emitting single gamma photons is injected; a gamma camera rotating around the head records them, and tomographic slices are reconstructed. No positrons, no annihilation, no coincidence detection Structural or functional Functional (mainly regional cerebral blood flow; also dopamine transporter) Spatial resolution Lower than PET, roughly 8 to 10 mm Temporal resolution Poor (minutes); but because HMPAO is fixed in the brain within minutes of injection, it gives a "snapshot" of flow at the moment of injection, useful for injecting during a seizure Radiation / invasive Ionising radiation; invasive (injection) Clinical and research uses Regional cerebral blood flow with 99m Tc-HMPAO or 99m Tc-ECD; ictal SPECT in epilepsy; dementia differential; DaTscan ( 123 I-ioflupane) images the dopamine transporter to distinguish Parkinsonian syndromes and dementia with Lewy bodies from essential tremor or Alzheimer's disease Limits Lower resolution and less quantitative than PET SPECT is cheaper and more widely available than PET because its isotopes (technetium-99m, half-life about 6 hours, from a generator) last longer and do not need an on-site cyclotron. That is why it is common in hospitals that cannot afford PET. Exam trap PET = positrons , which annihilate into two photons (511 keV each). SPECT = single photons . PET has better resolution; SPECT is cheaper. Both use radioactive tracers. 4.10 Electroencephalography (EEG) and event-related potentials (ERPs) Feature EEG Full name Electroencephalography Inventor / key people and year Richard Caton recorded electrical activity from animal brains in 1875. Hans Berger, Jena, made the first human recording in 1924 and published in 1929 ("Über das Elektrenkephalogramm des Menschen"); alpha is still called the "Berger rhythm". The 10-20 electrode system was introduced by Herbert Jasper in 1958 What it measures, physical principle Scalp electrodes record voltage differences produced by the summed postsynaptic potentials of large populations of synchronously active, parallel-oriented cortical pyramidal neurons Structural or functional Functional Spatial resolution Poor (centimetres); the skull smears the signal and the "inverse problem" means many source configurations fit the same scalp pattern Temporal resolution Excellent, milliseconds Radiation / invasive None; non-invasive; cheap and portable Clinical and research uses Epilepsy diagnosis, sleep staging (polysomnography), encephalopathy and delirium (diffuse slowing), brain death assessment, monitoring anaesthesia; ERP research on attention, memory and language Limits Poor localisation; mainly sees superficial cortex; artefacts from eye movements and muscle Rhythms (boundaries vary slightly between sources): Delta , about 0.5 to 4 Hz: deep (slow-wave) sleep, infants; in an awake adult suggests pathology. Theta , about 4 to 8 Hz: drowsiness, light sleep, children; frontal midline theta during concentration. Alpha , about 8 to 13 Hz: relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed, maximal over occipital regions; blocked by eye opening (alpha blocking). Beta , about 13 to 30 Hz: alert, active thinking; increased by benzodiazepines. Gamma , above about 30 Hz: feature binding, perception. In the 10-20 system electrodes are placed at 10% or 20% of the distance between skull landmarks (nasion, inion, preauricular points); letters denote region (Fp, F, C, T, P, O), odd numbers the left hemisphere, even numbers the right, and "z" the midline (Fz, Cz, Pz). ERPs are small voltage changes time-locked to a stimulus, extracted by averaging many trials. Key components: Contingent negative variation (CNV) : W. Grey Walter and colleagues (1964), a slow negative shift between a warning signal and an imperative stimulus, reflecting expectancy and preparation. P300 (P3) : Samuel Sutton, Margery Braren, Joseph Zubin and E. Roy John (1965), a positive wave about 300 ms after a rare, task-relevant stimulus in an oddball paradigm; reflects context updating; reduced amplitude in schizophrenia. Mismatch negativity (MMN) : Risto Näätänen, Anthony Gaillard and Sirkka Mäntysalo (1978), an automatic response to a deviant sound in a repetitive sequence, even without attention; reduced in schizophrenia. N400 : Marta Kutas and Steven Hillyard (1980), a negativity about 400 ms after a semantically unexpected word ("He spread the warm bread with socks"). 4.11 Magnetoencephalography (MEG) Feature MEG Full name Magnetoencephalography Inventor / key people and year David Cohen, 1968 (first recording of the alpha rhythm's magnetic field, with an induction coil); in 1972 Cohen recorded with a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device, developed by James Zimmerman and colleagues) What it measures, physical principle The same neuronal currents that produce EEG also produce tiny magnetic fields (femtotesla range, billions of times weaker than the Earth's field). SQUID sensors cooled in liquid helium detect them inside a magnetically shielded room Structural or functional Functional Spatial resolution Better than EEG (a few millimetres for favourable sources), because magnetic fields pass through skull and scalp without being smeared Temporal resolution Excellent, milliseconds Radiation / invasive None; non-invasive Clinical and research uses Localising epileptic foci and eloquent cortex before surgery; language and auditory research Limits Very expensive; few centres; best for tangential sources (in sulcal walls) and nearly blind to radial sources (on gyral crowns) and deep sources; head must stay still Because EEG sees both radial and tangential sources but MEG mainly tangential ones, the two are complementary. Newer optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs) work without liquid helium and may make wearable MEG possible. 4.12 Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) Feature fNIRS Full name Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (also optical imaging, NIRS) Inventor / key people and year Frans Jöbsis, 1977 ( Science ), showed near-infrared light could monitor tissue oxygenation through the intact skull; functional brain studies developed in the early 1990s What it measures, physical principle Near-infrared light (about 650 to 950 nm) passes through scalp and skull; oxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin absorb it differently, so detectors a few centimetres from the source estimate changes in both Structural or functional Functional (haemodynamic, like fMRI) Spatial resolution Poor to moderate (about 1 to 3 cm) Temporal resolution Sampling is fast, but the haemodynamic signal itself is slow (seconds) Radiation / invasive None; non-invasive Clinical and research uses Infants and children, people who cannot lie in a scanner, naturalistic tasks (walking, conversation), bedside monitoring; it is cheap and portable and tolerant of movement Limits Reaches only the outer cortex (about 1 to 2 cm depth); no deep structures; scalp blood flow and hair interfere 4.13 Not imaging: TMS, the lesion method and intracranial recording Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) was introduced by Anthony Barker and colleagues in Sheffield in 1985. A coil held over the scalp produces a brief, strong magnetic pulse that induces an electrical current in the cortex underneath, depolarising neurons. Single pulses over motor cortex cause a muscle twitch (motor evoked potential); repetitive TMS (rTMS) can raise or lower cortical excitability for a while. It stimulates the brain; it does not image it. Its research value is causal: a temporary "virtual lesion" tests whether a region is necessary for a task. Clinically, rTMS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is approved for treatment-resistant depression (US FDA clearance 2008), and it is used in Indian centres including NIMHANS (details of individual services not verified here). The lesion method infers function from what is lost after brain damage (Paul Broca's patient "Tan", 1861; Phineas Gage, 1848; H.M., 1953). It is causal but depends on accidents of nature, and lesions rarely respect functional boundaries. Intracranial recording (electrocorticography from grids on the cortex, or depth electrodes, in epilepsy surgery patients) gives both excellent temporal and excellent spatial resolution but is highly invasive and done only for clinical reasons. Exam trap TMS uses a magnet, like MRI and MEG, but it is a stimulation technique, not an imaging technique. If asked which option is "not a neuroimaging method", TMS (or ECT, or tDCS) is the answer. 4.14 Master comparison table Method Structural / functional What is measured Spatial resolution Temporal resolution Ionising radiation Pneumoencephalography Structural Air-filled ventricles on X-ray Poor Not applicable Yes Angiography / DSA Structural (vascular) Contrast-filled vessels on X-ray Very high (vessels) Seconds Yes CT Structural X-ray attenuation (density) About 0.5 to 1 mm Not applicable Yes MRI Structural Proton relaxation (T1, T2) About 1 mm Not applicable No DTI Structural Water diffusion along axons About 2 mm Not applicable No MRS Neurochemical Metabolite concentrations Low (cm voxels) Minutes No fMRI Functional Blood oxygenation (BOLD) About 1 to 3 mm Seconds No PET Functional Positron tracer: glucose, flow, receptors, amyloid About 4 to 5 mm Minutes Yes SPECT Functional Single-photon tracer: blood flow, dopamine transporter About 8 to 10 mm Minutes Yes EEG / ERP Functional Scalp electrical potentials Poor (cm) Milliseconds No MEG Functional Magnetic fields of neuronal currents Better than EEG (mm to cm) Milliseconds No fNIRS Functional Oxy/deoxyhaemoglobin by light absorption About 1 to 3 cm, surface only Seconds No TMS Neither (stimulation) Induces cortical current About 1 cm Milliseconds No High yield Best temporal resolution: EEG and MEG (milliseconds). Best spatial resolution among non-invasive functional methods: fMRI. Only invasive methods (intracranial recording) give both. Radiation: CT, angiography, PET, SPECT. No radiation: MRI family, EEG, MEG, fNIRS. 4.15 Imaging in psychiatry Schizophrenia: enlarged lateral ventricles. Eve Johnstone, Timothy Crow, Christopher Frith and colleagues (1976, The Lancet ) showed on CT that chronic schizophrenia patients had larger lateral ventricles than controls. This was the first CT demonstration and revived interest in brain structure in schizophrenia (pneumoencephalography studies from 1927 had hinted at it). Later MRI work added reduced hippocampal, temporal and grey matter volume. Hypofrontality. Reduced frontal activity in schizophrenia was first described by David Ingvar and Göran Franzén (1974) using xenon-133 regional cerebral blood flow, before PET; it was later reported in PET studies (e.g. Monte Buchsbaum and colleagues, early 1980s) and in fMRI during working memory tasks, though findings are inconsistent. Dopamine. PET with raclopride showed increased amphetamine-induced dopamine release in schizophrenia (mid-1990s studies) and is used to estimate antipsychotic D2 occupancy (therapeutic window about 65% to 80%, commonly cited). OCD. PET studies (Lewis Baxter and colleagues, 1987) reported hypermetabolism in the orbitofrontal cortex and caudate nucleus, which decreased after successful treatment with medication or behaviour therapy; this supports the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit model. Depression. Reduced activity in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and altered subgenual cingulate activity (target of deep brain stimulation by Helen Mayberg, 2005). Dementia. MRI hippocampal atrophy and FDG-PET temporoparietal hypometabolism in Alzheimer's disease; amyloid PET to detect plaques. Indian context. NIMHANS, Bengaluru, has a dedicated neuroimaging and interventional radiology department with MRI and is a major centre for psychiatric neuroimaging research (for example, MRI studies in schizophrenia and OCD), and it offers clinical neuromodulation (rTMS, tDCS, ECT). Exact current scanner types and whether PET is available on campus were not verified, so do not rely on this paragraph for a specific factual MCQ. 4.16 Exam traps Exam trap CT uses X-rays, not magnets. CAT = computerised axial tomography = CT (same scan). MRI uses no ionising radiation (magnetic field plus radio waves). Its danger is metal, not radiation. fMRI measures blood oxygenation , not neuronal firing directly. PET-FDG measures glucose metabolism. PET uses positrons (two 511 keV photons); SPECT uses single photons . EEG: best temporal, poor spatial. fMRI: better spatial, poor temporal. MEG vs EEG: both milliseconds; MEG localises better and is less distorted by the skull, but sees mainly tangential sources and is far costlier. TMS is not an imaging technique. Angiography needs contrast dye. Egas Moniz: angiography 1927, Nobel 1949 for leucotomy. Nobel pairings: CT = Hounsfield and Cormack (1979); MRI = Lauterbur and Mansfield (2003), not Damadian. Berger: first human EEG 1924, published 1929. Do not confuse the two years. T1: CSF dark. T2: CSF bright. FLAIR: T2 with CSF made dark. 4.17 Self-check Which technique has the best temporal resolution? a PET b fMRI c EEG d SPECT ✓ Answer: (c) EEG Spatial-temporal resolution trade-off The concept What it is Temporal resolution is how precisely a method says when something happened. EEG records electrical activity directly, in milliseconds . Why the others are slow PET, fMRI and SPECT depend on slow haemodynamic or metabolic changes, because blood responds over seconds. The trade-off EEG is fast but poor at localisation (centimetres); fMRI localises better but is slow. Why the other options are wrong (a) PET Tracer imaging of metabolism, blood flow or receptors; temporal resolution is poor, tens of seconds to minutes ( FDG uptake takes about 30 to 45 minutes). (b) fMRI Best spatial resolution among non-invasive functional methods, but the BOLD response peaks about 4 to 6 s after activity, so it resolves seconds, not milliseconds. (d) SPECT Single-photon tracer imaging of blood flow; temporal resolution is poor ( minutes ), and spatial resolution is lower than PET. The BOLD signal in fMRI depends mainly on the magnetic properties of: a Oxyhaemoglobin b Deoxyhaemoglobin c Glucose d Gadolinium ✓ Answer: (b) Deoxyhaemoglobin Seiji Ogawa, BOLD contrast (1990) The concept The physics Deoxyhaemoglobin is paramagnetic : it distorts the local magnetic field and lowers the MR signal. Oxyhaemoglobin is diamagnetic and does not. Why activity raises it Active neurons draw more blood flow than the oxygen they use, so local deoxyhaemoglobin decreases and the BOLD signal rises. Key note fMRI measures blood oxygenation, an indirect index of neural activity, not neuronal firing. Why the other options are wrong (a) Oxyhaemoglobin Diamagnetic , so it barely affects the field; the trap is that it rises during activity, but the signal change comes from losing deoxyhaemoglobin. (c) Glucose Glucose metabolism is what FDG-PET measures; glucose plays no magnetic role in the BOLD signal. (d) Gadolinium An optional injected contrast agent for structural MRI; BOLD fMRI needs no injection and uses the blood's own haemoglobin. The first clinical CT scan was performed by: a Paul Lauterbur, 1973 b Godfrey Hounsfield, 1971 c Egas Moniz, 1927 d Michael Phelps, 1975 ✓ Answer: (b) Godfrey Hounsfield, 1971 Godfrey Hounsfield, EMI (1971) The concept The first scan Godfrey Hounsfield built the CT scanner at EMI . The first clinical brain scan was on 1 October 1971 at Atkinson Morley's Hospital, London , with radiologist James Ambrose. Maths and prize Allan Cormack developed the mathematics (1963, 1964); Hounsfield and Cormack shared the 1979 Nobel Prize. How CT works A rotating X-ray beam measures attenuation from many angles and a computer rebuilds slices; brightness reflects tissue density . Why the other options are wrong (a) Paul Lauterbur, 1973 Lauterbur published the first MR image using magnetic field gradients (1973), not a CT scan; he shared the 2003 Nobel with Peter Mansfield. (c) Egas Moniz, 1927 Moniz developed cerebral angiography in Lisbon (1927); his 1949 Nobel was for prefrontal leucotomy, not imaging. (d) Michael Phelps, 1975 Phelps helped develop the modern PET scanner at Washington University, St Louis (1973 to 1975), not CT. On a T2-weighted MRI, cerebrospinal fluid appears: a Dark b Bright c Invisible d Same as bone ✓ Answer: (b) Bright MRI relaxation: T1 vs T2 weighting The concept How MRI contrast works Hydrogen nuclei in water and fat are tipped by a radiofrequency pulse and relax at different rates, T1 and T2 , depending on the tissue. The T2 rule Water is bright on T2-weighted images, so CSF is bright, and so is most pathology (oedema, demyelination); that is why T2 is used to find lesions. T1 and FLAIR CSF is dark on T1 and on FLAIR , a T2-type image with the CSF signal suppressed. Hook: ' T2 = H 2 O bright '. Why the other options are wrong (a) Dark That is CSF on T1-weighted images and on FLAIR; the classic swap of the two weightings. (c) Invisible CSF always shows on MRI, bright or dark depending on weighting; no standard sequence makes it vanish . (d) Same as bone Cortical bone has almost no mobile protons, so it is dark on both T1 and T2; CSF on T2 is the opposite, bright. Which of the following involves no ionising radiation? a CT b PET c SPECT d MRI ✓ Answer: (d) MRI MRI physics: magnetic field and radio waves The concept What ionising means Ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays) carries enough energy to knock electrons off atoms and can damage DNA. Why MRI is safe here MRI uses a magnetic field and radiofrequency pulses, neither of them ionising. Its danger is metal (pacemakers, aneurysm clips), not radiation. Why the other options are wrong (a) CT Builds slices from X-ray attenuation, and X-rays are ionising. (b) PET Injects a positron-emitting radioactive tracer whose annihilation gives gamma photons , so it is ionising. (c) SPECT Injects a gamma-emitting radioactive tracer (e.g. technetium-99m ), so it involves ionising radiation. Coincidence detection of two 511 keV photons is the basis of: a SPECT b PET c MEG d CT ✓ Answer: (b) PET PET physics: positron annihilation, coincidence detection The concept How it works An injected tracer emits a positron , which travels about a millimetre, meets an electron and annihilates. Positron annihilation yields two 511 keV photons travelling in opposite directions. Coincidence detection A detector ring registers both photons at once ( coincidence detection ), and the computer places the source on the line between them. Common tracer FDG , a glucose analogue, gets trapped in active cells, so PET maps regional glucose metabolism. Why the other options are wrong (a) SPECT Uses single photons and a rotating gamma camera: no positrons, no annihilation, no coincidence detection; the classic PET/SPECT swap. (c) MEG Detects the tiny magnetic fields of neuronal currents with SQUID sensors; no tracer and no photons. (d) CT Measures X-ray attenuation from an external tube rotating around the head; the radiation does not come from a tracer inside the body. Fractional anisotropy is a measure derived from: a MRS b DTI c fNIRS d ERP ✓ Answer: (b) DTI Basser, Mattiello and Le Bihan, DTI (1994) The concept What DTI measures Water diffuses more easily along axons than across them, because myelin and membranes restrict it. DTI measures the direction and degree of this diffusion in each voxel. What FA is Fractional anisotropy (FA) runs from 0 (equal in all directions, as in CSF) to 1 (one direction only); it indexes directional water diffusion. Reading it High FA means organised, intact white matter (e.g. corpus callosum); reduced FA is reported in many disorders. Why the other options are wrong (a) MRS Magnetic resonance spectroscopy gives a spectrum of chemical concentrations (NAA, choline, creatine) in a voxel, not diffusion direction. (c) fNIRS Uses near-infrared light to estimate oxy- and deoxyhaemoglobin changes in outer cortex; it has no diffusion measure. (d) ERP Event-related potentials are averaged EEG voltage changes time-locked to a stimulus (P300, N400); electrical, not white matter structure. Which of these is NOT a neuroimaging technique? a MEG b fNIRS c TMS d SPECT ✓ Answer: (c) TMS Anthony Barker, TMS, Sheffield (1985) The concept What TMS does TMS (Anthony Barker and colleagues, Sheffield, 1985) uses a coil to send a brief magnetic pulse that induces current in the cortex, depolarising neurons. Why it is not imaging It stimulates cortex rather than recording or imaging it; its research value is causal, a temporary virtual lesion . Exam trap TMS uses a magnet like MRI and MEG, but in a 'not neuroimaging' question TMS (or ECT, or tDCS) is the answer. Why the other options are not the answer (a) MEG A real imaging method: magnetoencephalography records the tiny magnetic fields of neuronal currents with SQUID sensors, at millisecond resolution. (b) fNIRS A real imaging method: near-infrared light estimates oxy- and deoxyhaemoglobin changes in outer cortex, a haemodynamic signal like fMRI. (d) SPECT A real imaging method: a gamma-emitting tracer and rotating gamma camera image regional cerebral blood flow . The P300 component was first described by: a Kutas and Hillyard, 1980 b Sutton and colleagues, 1965 c Näätänen and colleagues, 1978 d Grey Walter and colleagues, 1964 ✓ Answer: (b) Sutton and colleagues, 1965 Sutton, Braren, Zubin and John (1965) The concept What P300 is The P300 (P3) is a positive ERP wave about 300 ms after a rare, task-relevant stimulus in an oddball paradigm ; it reflects context updating. Who found it Samuel Sutton , Margery Braren, Joseph Zubin and E. Roy John described it in 1965. Clinical note P300 amplitude is reduced in schizophrenia . Why the other options are wrong (a) Kutas and Hillyard, 1980 Kutas and Hillyard (1980) described the N400 , a negativity about 400 ms after a semantically unexpected word ('warm bread with socks'). (c) Näätänen and colleagues, 1978 Näätänen and colleagues (1978) described the mismatch negativity (MMN), an automatic response to a deviant sound, even without attention. (d) Grey Walter and colleagues, 1964 Grey Walter and colleagues (1964) described the contingent negative variation (CNV), a slow negative shift between a warning and an imperative stimulus. Enlarged lateral ventricles in schizophrenia were first demonstrated on CT by: a Johnstone and colleagues, 1976 b Ingvar and Franzén, 1974 c Baxter and colleagues, 1987 d Raichle and colleagues, 2001 ✓ Answer: (a) Johnstone and colleagues, 1976 Johnstone, Crow, Frith and colleagues, The Lancet (1976) The concept The finding Eve Johnstone , Timothy Crow , Christopher Frith and colleagues (1976, The Lancet ) showed on CT that chronic schizophrenia patients had larger lateral ventricles than controls. Why it mattered It was the first CT demonstration and revived interest in brain structure in schizophrenia; pneumoencephalography studies from 1927 had only hinted at it. Why the other options are wrong (b) Ingvar and Franzén, 1974 Ingvar and Franzén (1974) described hypofrontality , reduced frontal blood flow in schizophrenia, using xenon-133 before PET; not ventricles, not CT. (c) Baxter and colleagues, 1987 Baxter and colleagues (1987) reported the OCD PET findings: orbitofrontal and caudate hypermetabolism that fell after successful treatment. (d) Raichle and colleagues, 2001 Raichle and colleagues (2001) named the default mode network , more active at rest; a functional finding, not a CT one. 5. The full why page with 27 questions, the trap under every wrong option, is at missed-concepts , and the same 27 are a mock in the Tests app. 5.1 Vaillant's ladder of defences (Q36: dissociation) George Vaillant ( Adaptation to Life , 1977), working from the Harvard Grant Study, ranked the defences Sigmund and Anna Freud (1936) described into four levels by maturity. Your Q36 asked where dissociation sits: neurotic . Level Defences What it means I. Psychotic Delusional projection, psychotic denial (of external reality), distortion Reality testing lost; psychosis, dreams, early childhood II. Immature Projection, schizoid fantasy, hypochondriasis, passive aggression, acting out Normal in adolescence; in adults, personality disorders and substance misuse III. Neurotic Repression, displacement, reaction formation, intellectualization (isolation, undoing), dissociation (neurotic denial) Private distress, reality testing intact, the person functions IV. Mature Altruism, humour, sublimation, suppression , anticipation Healthy adults; predicted better health, work and marriage in the Grant Study The DSM-IV Defensive Functioning Scale (1994) uses seven levels instead; dissociation is at the mental inhibitions (compromise formation) level, with repression, displacement, intellectualization, isolation of affect, reaction formation and undoing. Same neighbours, same verdict. Exam trap Suppression is conscious and mature; repression is unconscious and neurotic. Projection is immature, but delusional projection is psychotic. Dissociation is not immature, however dramatic dissociative disorders look. 5.2 Systematic desensitization and its neighbours (Q37) Joseph Wolpe, Psychotherapy by Reciprocal Inhibition (1958). Principle: reciprocal inhibition (a term from Charles Sherrington): a response incompatible with anxiety, made in the presence of the feared stimulus, weakens the stimulus-anxiety bond. That is counterconditioning. Steps: (1) relaxation training (Edmund Jacobson's progressive relaxation, 1938); (2) anxiety hierarchy rated on SUDS, 0 to 100 (Wolpe, 1969); (3) imagine each scene while relaxed, moving up only when calm. Forerunner: Mary Cover Jones (1924), little Peter and the rabbit. Technique What is done Mechanism Systematic desensitization Relaxation paired with a graded hierarchy, usually imagined Counterconditioning In vivo desensitization Same, with the real stimulus Counterconditioning Flooding Most feared stimulus at full strength, no escape, until anxiety falls Extinction Implosive therapy (Stampfl and Levis, 1967) Flooding in imagination, exaggerated scenes with psychodynamic themes Extinction Aversion therapy Unwanted behaviour paired with an emetic or a shock Classical conditioning of an aversion Exposure and response prevention (Meyer, 1966) Face the obsession's trigger, block the compulsion (OCD) Extinction plus blocking negative reinforcement Exam trap Reciprocal inhibition is the principle; systematic desensitization is the technique. 'Gradual' and 'relaxation' mean desensitization; 'full intensity' and 'no escape' mean flooding. 5.3 Habit reversal training (Q38: awareness training) Nathan Azrin and Gregory Nunn (1973). For tics, Tourette's and body-focused repetitive behaviours: trichotillomania, skin picking, nail biting, also stuttering. Original package, four phases: Awareness training : response description, response detection, early warning (the urge or first movement), situation awareness. Your Q38. Competing response training : a physically incompatible, inconspicuous action (clench fists for hair pulling) held about a minute, or three minutes in the original, or until the urge passes. Habit control motivation : inconvenience review, social support, public display. Generalization training : rehearsing the routine across situations, often in imagination. Simplified HRT (Raymond Miltenberger, Wayne Fuqua and Douglas Woods, 1998): awareness training, competing response training, social support. CBIT (John Piacentini and colleagues, 2010) is HRT plus function-based work, first-line for tics. Exam trap HRT is not the treatment for OCD (that is ERP), even though trichotillomania and excoriation sit in DSM-5's obsessive-compulsive and related chapter. Negative practice (Knight Dunlap, 1932), performing the habit on purpose until fatigue, is the opposite idea. 5.4 Flashbulb memory (Q39: confidence) Vivid, detailed memories of the circumstances in which you heard shocking news. Canonical details: place, ongoing activity, informant, own feeling, others' feeling, aftermath. Study Event Finding Roger Brown and James Kulik (1977) Kennedy assassination, 1963 Coined the term; proposed a special 'Now Print!' mechanism (Livingston, 1967) Ulric Neisser and Nicole Harsch (1992) Challenger explosion, 1986 Re-tested about 2.5 years later: accuracy poor, about a quarter wrong on every major detail, confidence still high Jennifer Talarico and David Rubin (2003) 9/11, against an everyday memory Both lost consistency at the same rate; only flashbulb memories kept vividness and belief in accuracy. 'Confidence, not consistency' Kathy Pezdek (2003) 9/11 Most students 'remembered' seeing the first plane hit live on TV; that footage aired only the next day William Hirst and colleagues (2009, 2015) 9/11, national sample Consistency dropped in year one, then levelled off; confidence stayed high Why vivid: emotional arousal at encoding (amygdala boosting hippocampal consolidation, James McGaugh) plus heavy rehearsal through media and retelling. No special mechanism needed. Exam trap Subjective confidence is very high and stays high; accuracy (consistency) falls like any memory. 'Confidence falls in step with accuracy' is wrong. 5.5 Paradoxical intention and Frankl's toolkit (Q40) Viktor Frankl, logotherapy, the 'third Viennese school' after Sigmund Freud and Alfred Adler. Primary motive: the will to meaning. Lack of meaning: existential vacuum, noogenic neurosis. Technique Targets Instruction Paradoxical intention (first described 1939) Anticipatory anxiety, fear of a symptom Intend or wish for the feared thing, with humour: 'try to stay awake', 'show them how much you can sweat' Dereflection Hyper-reflection, excessive self-watching Turn attention away from yourself, to the partner, a task, a meaning Socratic dialogue Loss of meaning Questioning that helps the client find meaning Neighbours: negative practice (Knight Dunlap, 1932: perform the habit on purpose until fatigue); symptom prescription in family therapy (Milton Erickson, Jay Haley, Paul Watzlawick, 1974); for insomnia, stimulus control (Richard Bootzin, 1972: get up if not asleep in about 20 minutes) and sleep restriction (Arthur Spielman, 1987: limit time in bed). Exam trap 'Doing the opposite of the goal to reach the goal' is paradoxical intention. 'Stop watching yourself' is dereflection. Sensate focus is William Masters and Virginia Johnson (1970), not Viktor Frankl. 5.6 Gender incongruence: where it sits now (Q41) System Name Where Key point ICD-10 Gender identity disorders, F64 (transsexualism F64.0, dual-role transvestism F64.1, GID of childhood F64.2) Chapter V, mental and behavioural Framed as a mental disorder ICD-11 (adopted 2019, in force 1 Jan 2022) Gender incongruence: HA60 adolescence or adulthood, HA61 childhood Chapter 17, Conditions related to sexual health No distress needed; code kept for access to care DSM-III (1980) Transsexualism; GID of childhood Mental disorder DSM-IV (1994) Gender identity disorder Mental disorder Identity itself labelled DSM-5 (2013), DSM-5-TR (2022) Gender dysphoria Own chapter Distress or impairment; 6 months; 2 of 6 (adults), 6 of 8 (children) Also moved to ICD-11 Chapter 17: sexual dysfunctions (HA00 to HA03) and sexual pain-penetration disorder (HA20). Stayed in Chapter 6: paraphilic disorders (6D30 to 6D3Z). Sleep-wake disorders moved out of the mental chapter to Chapter 7. Exam trap Gender incongruence was relocated, not deleted. ICD-11 says gender incongruence; DSM-5 says gender dysphoria. 5.7 The three gunas (the Bavisha question) From Samkhya (Kapila; Ishvarakrishna's Samkhya Karika ) and the Bhagavad Gita (chapters 14, 17, 18). Prakriti, matter including the mind, is made of three gunas, always present together; the dominant one shapes the person. Purusha is pure consciousness, the witness. Guna Quality In a person Clinical mapping Sattva Light, clarity, balance Calm, truthful, content, wise Mental health Rajas Activity, passion Restless, ambitious, craving, angry, greedy Anxiety, agitation, mania Tamas Darkness, heaviness, inertia Dull, lethargic, withdrawn, deluded, oversleeping Depression, apathy Bavisha, jobless, stressed, not eating, unable to act: shutdown, so tamas alone . Research measure: the Vedic Personality Inventory (David Wolf, 1998). Exam trap Yama is a limb of yoga (ethical restraints), not a guna or a state, so 'yama' and 'both yama and tamas' are wrong. Stressed and racing would be rajas; stuck and inert is tamas. 5.8 Patanjali's eight limbs (dharana) Yoga Sutras: yoga is 'chitta vritti nirodhah', stilling the mind's fluctuations (1.2). The eight limbs, ashtanga (2.29). Mnemonic: Yogis Never Argue, Peaceful People Don't Disturb Silence. # Limb Meaning 1 Yama Restraints: ahimsa, satya, asteya, brahmacharya, aparigraha 2 Niyama Observances: shaucha, santosha, tapas, svadhyaya, ishvara pranidhana 3 Asana Posture, steady and comfortable (2.46) 4 Pranayama Breath regulation 5 Pratyahara Withdrawal of the senses (2.54) 6 Dharana Concentration: binding the mind to one point (3.1) 7 Dhyana Meditation: unbroken flow of that focus (3.2) 8 Samadhi Absorption, only the object remains (3.3) Dharana + dhyana + samadhi on one object = samyama (3.4). Limbs 1 to 5 are bahiranga (outer), 6 to 8 antaranga (inner). Jnana yoga is a path in the Gita (with karma and bhakti), not a limb. Exam trap Senses in is pratyahara; mind fixed on one point is dharana; focus flowing on its own is dhyana. Pranayama before pratyahara, dharana before dhyana. 5.9 Kegels and the pelvic floor Arnold Kegel, American gynaecologist, 1948: exercises for urinary incontinence after childbirth. Target: the pelvic floor , mainly the levator ani and its pubococcygeus (PC) part, running from the pubic bone to the tailbone and supporting the bladder, bowel and uterus. Method: squeeze and lift for a few seconds, relax, repeat in sets. Uses : stress urinary incontinence, postpartum recovery, pelvic organ prolapse, incontinence after prostate surgery, faecal incontinence.
