Early biofeedback : Kegel's perineometer, a pressure gauge the patient watched. Biofeedback types: EMG (tension headache, pelvic floor), thermal (migraine, Raynaud's), GSR (arousal), heart rate variability, EEG or neurofeedback (ADHD, epilepsy). Sex therapy : part of directed masturbation for female orgasmic disorder (Joseph LoPiccolo and W. Charles Lobitz, 1972); an add-on for premature ejaculation; pelvic floor relaxation with graded dilators for vaginismus. Exam trap Bed-wetting in a child is not a Kegel problem. First-line is the enuresis alarm, the bell-and-pad (O. Hobart Mowrer and Willie Mae Mowrer, 1938), or desmopressin. Squeezing the buttocks or abdomen is not a Kegel. 5.10 Self-check: your nine Which type of defence mechanism is dissociation? a Mature b Immature c Neurotic d Conscious ✓ Answer: (c) Neurotic George Vaillant, Adaptation to Life (1977) The concept The ladder George Vaillant (1977), working from the Harvard Grant Study, ranked defences into four levels: psychotic, immature, neurotic , mature. Where it sits Dissociation (neurotic denial) is neurotic, alongside repression, displacement, reaction formation and intellectualization: private distress, reality testing intact. Exam trap Dissociation is not immature, however dramatic dissociative disorders look. The DSM-IV Defensive Functioning Scale puts it at the mental inhibitions level, same neighbours. Why the other options are wrong (a) Mature The top level: altruism, humour, sublimation, suppression, anticipation, seen in healthy adults; dissociation is not among them. (b) Immature Projection, schizoid fantasy, hypochondriasis, passive aggression, acting out; the trap, because dissociative disorders look dramatic. (d) Conscious Not one of Vaillant's levels; the one conscious defence, suppression , is classed as mature. A technique in which a response that inhibits anxiety is paired with an anxiety-provoking stimulus, step by step, to break the conditioned link between that stimulus and anxiety is: a Systematic desensitization b Flooding c Aversion therapy d Exposure and response prevention ✓ Answer: (a) Systematic desensitization Joseph Wolpe, reciprocal inhibition (1958) The concept The principle Joseph Wolpe (1958): by reciprocal inhibition , a response incompatible with anxiety, made in the presence of the feared stimulus, weakens the stimulus-anxiety bond. That is counterconditioning. The steps Relaxation training, an anxiety hierarchy rated on SUDS (0 to 100), then each scene imagined while relaxed, moving up only when calm. Systematic desensitization is this package. Exam tip 'Gradual' plus 'relaxation' means desensitization. Reciprocal inhibition is the principle ; systematic desensitization is the technique . Why the other options are wrong (b) Flooding The most feared stimulus at full strength, no escape, until anxiety falls; works by extinction , not step-by-step pairing with relaxation. (c) Aversion therapy Pairs the unwanted behaviour with an emetic or a shock to condition an aversion ; it adds discomfort rather than inhibiting anxiety. (d) Exposure and response prevention Meyer (1966), for OCD: face the obsession's trigger and block the compulsion; extinction , with no anxiety-inhibiting response paired in. In habit reversal training (HRT), the technique used to make the person aware of the habit is: a Competing response training b Social support c Generalization training d Awareness training ✓ Answer: (d) Awareness training Azrin and Nunn, habit reversal training (1973) The concept What HRT is Habit reversal training (Nathan Azrin and Gregory Nunn, 1973) treats tics and body-focused repetitive behaviours such as trichotillomania and nail biting. Awareness training Awareness training makes the person notice the habit: response description, response detection, early warning (the urge or first movement), situation awareness. Other phases Competing response training, habit control motivation and generalization training complete the original four-phase package. Why the other options are wrong (a) Competing response training The next phase: a physically incompatible, inconspicuous action (clench fists for hair pulling) held until the urge passes; it replaces the habit rather than detecting it. (b) Social support Part of habit control motivation in the original package (and of simplified HRT): others encourage the person; it motivates , it does not build awareness. (c) Generalization training Rehearsing the routine across situations, often in imagination, so the skill transfers ; not the awareness step. The subjective confidence people have in their flashbulb memories is: a Low, because the event was emotionally shocking b Very high, and it stays high even as accuracy falls c Moderate, and in line with how accurate the memory is d High at first, then falls in step with accuracy ✓ Answer: (b) Very high, and it stays high even as accuracy falls Neisser and Harsch (1992); Talarico and Rubin (2003) The concept What it is Flashbulb memories are vivid memories of where you were when you heard shocking news; Brown and Kulik (1977) coined the term. The finding Neisser and Harsch (1992, Challenger) found accuracy poor about 2.5 years on, confidence still high; Talarico and Rubin (2003, 9/11): 'confidence, not consistency'. Why Emotional arousal at encoding plus heavy rehearsal make them vivid, so confidence is very high, and it stays high even as accuracy falls. Why the other options are wrong (a) Low, because the event was emotionally shocking The opposite: the shock makes these memories feel vivid and certain, so confidence is high , not low. (c) Moderate, and in line with how accurate the memory is The core finding is a mismatch : confidence stays high while accuracy (consistency) falls like any memory. (d) High at first, then falls in step with accuracy The trap: accuracy falls but confidence does not follow it; Hirst and colleagues found confidence stayed high while consistency dropped. An intervention in which the person deliberately does, or wishes for, the very opposite of the therapeutic goal in order to reach that goal is: a Paradoxical intention b Dereflection c Negative practice d Reciprocal inhibition ✓ Answer: (a) Paradoxical intention Viktor Frankl, logotherapy (first described 1939) The concept What it is Paradoxical intention (Viktor Frankl , first described 1939): the person intends or wishes for the feared thing, with humour, e.g. 'try to stay awake'. What it targets Anticipatory anxiety , the fear of a symptom: wishing for the symptom removes the fear that feeds it. Exam tip 'Doing the opposite of the goal to reach the goal' is paradoxical intention; 'stop watching yourself' is dereflection . Why the other options are wrong (b) Dereflection Frankl's other technique: turning attention away from yourself to a partner, task or meaning, for hyper-reflection ; no wishing for the opposite. (c) Negative practice Knight Dunlap (1932): performing the unwanted habit on purpose until fatigue; it repeats the habit itself rather than wishing for the opposite of a goal. (d) Reciprocal inhibition Wolpe's principle behind systematic desensitization: an anxiety-incompatible response weakens the stimulus-anxiety bond; a principle, not a paradoxical instruction. In ICD-11, gender incongruence is placed in: a Chapter 6, Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders b Chapter 5, Endocrine, nutritional or metabolic diseases c Chapter 17, Conditions related to sexual health d Nowhere: it was removed from ICD-11 altogether ✓ Answer: (c) Chapter 17, Conditions related to sexual health ICD-11 (adopted 2019, in force 1 Jan 2022) The concept Where it sits In ICD-11 , gender incongruence (HA60 adolescence or adulthood, HA61 childhood) is in Chapter 17, Conditions related to sexual health. Why it moved It is no longer framed as a mental disorder and needs no distress, but the code was kept for access to care . ICD-10 had gender identity disorders (F64) in Chapter V. Exam trap Relocated, not deleted. ICD-11 says gender incongruence; DSM-5 says gender dysphoria. Why the other options are wrong (a) Chapter 6, Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders The mental disorders chapter, its old home in ICD-10 (Chapter V, F64); ICD-11 moved it out, though paraphilic disorders stayed in Chapter 6. (b) Chapter 5, Endocrine, nutritional or metabolic diseases A distractor: gender incongruence concerns identity, not hormones , and moved to the sexual health chapter, not the endocrine one. (d) Nowhere: it was removed from ICD-11 altogether The trap: it was relocated, not deleted ; the code was kept for access to care. Bavisha lost her job. Since then she is stressed, has stopped eating properly and cannot get herself to do anything. According to yogic philosophy, the main issue she is dealing with is: a Yama alone b Tamas alone c Both yama and tamas d Rajas alone ✓ Answer: (b) Tamas alone Samkhya and the Bhagavad Gita: the three gunas The concept The gunas In Samkhya and the Bhagavad Gita, prakriti (matter including the mind) is made of three gunas : sattva (clarity), rajas (activity), tamas (inertia); the dominant one shapes the person. Why tamas Tamas is darkness, heaviness, inertia (dull, lethargic, withdrawn), mapping to depression. Bavisha, jobless, not eating and unable to act, is in shutdown: tamas alone. Exam tip Stressed and racing would be rajas ; stuck and inert is tamas. Why the other options are wrong (a) Yama alone Yama is the first limb of Patanjali's yoga ( ethical restraints such as ahimsa, satya), not a guna or a state of mind. (c) Both yama and tamas Fails because yama is a limb of yoga, not a guna, so it cannot pair with tamas as her state. (d) Rajas alone Activity and passion (restless, craving, angry; maps to anxiety , agitation); 'stressed' tempts, but she is inert, not racing. Which of the eight limbs of yoga is concentration, directing the mind's energy to a single point? a Pratyahara b Jnana c Dhyana d Dharana ✓ Answer: (d) Dharana Patanjali, Yoga Sutras 3.1 The concept The eight limbs Patanjali's Yoga Sutras list eight limbs (ashtanga): yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana , dhyana, samadhi. What dharana is Dharana, the sixth limb, is concentration : binding the mind to one point (3.1). It opens the three inner limbs. Exam tip Senses in is pratyahara ; mind fixed on one point is dharana; focus flowing on its own is dhyana . Why the other options are wrong (a) Pratyahara The fifth limb, withdrawal of the senses (2.54), the step just before concentration. (b) Jnana Not a limb: jnana yoga is the path of knowledge in the Gita, alongside karma and bhakti. (c) Dhyana The seventh limb, meditation : an unbroken flow of that focus (3.2); dharana comes first, dhyana continues it. Kegel exercises strengthen which part of the body? a The abdominal (core) muscles b The pelvic floor muscles c The lower back (lumbar) muscles d The gluteal (buttock) muscles ✓ Answer: (b) The pelvic floor muscles Arnold Kegel, gynaecologist (1948) The concept What Kegels are Arnold Kegel , an American gynaecologist, introduced the exercises in 1948 for urinary incontinence after childbirth. The target They strengthen the pelvic floor , mainly the levator ani and its pubococcygeus (PC) part, which runs from pubic bone to tailbone and supports the bladder, bowel and uterus. Method and uses Squeeze and lift for a few seconds, relax, repeat in sets; used for stress urinary incontinence , postpartum recovery and prolapse. Why the other options are wrong (a) The abdominal (core) muscles Worked by core exercises such as crunches or planks; squeezing the abdomen is not a Kegel. (c) The lower back (lumbar) muscles Worked by back-extension exercises; Kegels do not involve the lumbar spine . (d) The gluteal (buttock) muscles Squeezing the buttocks is a common mistake, not a Kegel; the PC muscle lies deeper, in the pelvic floor.

title: Blatt & Spitz — Anaclitic vs Introjective Depression
text: Blatt & Spitz — Anaclitic vs Introjective Depression Abnormal · Mood disorders · Exam-grade · Built 2026-06-07 Why this page exists: Both Sidney Blatt and René Spitz showed up on the NIMHANS paper . That makes them high-yield, not edge cases. This is the focused one-pager; the same content folds into the Abnormal book's mood-disorders chapter. The single biggest trap is below: there are two different "anaclitic depressions" (one infant, one adult) and they get conflated constantly. THE TRAP, up front: "Anaclitic depression" means two different things depending on who said it. René Spitz's anaclitic depression = an infant syndrome caused by separation from the mother (clinical/developmental observation, 1946). Sidney Blatt's anaclitic depression = an adult depression subtype / personality configuration centred on dependency (theory of depression, 1974). Both come from the same root word "anaclitic" = leaning on / depending on (Greek anaklinein , to lean upon). Same word, different age group, different theorist. If a stem mentions infants/separation → Spitz. If it mentions an adult dependency-vs-self-criticism split → Blatt. 0. Which textbook are they actually in? Your direct question — which book covers Sidney Blatt and René Spitz. Straight answer: neither sits in the six you've got loaded. Schultz (history & systems), Baron (intro), Pinel (biopsych), Eysenck, Sharf (counselling), AK Singh (general/experimental) — none of them carry Blatt's typology or Spitz's infant depression properly. They're psychodynamic / developmental, so they fall in the Abnormal + Developmental gap . Here's where they really live: Topic Primary source (the theorist) Standard textbook you'd cite for it Blatt — anaclitic vs introjective depression; two-polarities model; DEQ Blatt, Experiences of Depression (2004); Polarities of Experience (2008); orig. paper Blatt (1974) Abnormal/clinical texts under mood-disorders → psychodynamic theories : Barlow & Durand, Abnormal Psychology (psychological dimensions of mood disorders) and Sadock & Sadock, Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry (psychodynamic theories of depression). Also surfaces in personality texts beside Aaron Beck's sociotropy/autonomy. Spitz — anaclitic depression in infants; hospitalism; foundling-home study Spitz, The First Year of Life (1965); orig. papers Spitz (1945 hospitalism; 1946 anaclitic depression) Developmental psychology texts under attachment / maternal deprivation (alongside John Bowlby, Harry Harlow, Mary Ainsworth), and abnormal/clinical texts under childhood disorders / failure to thrive. Barlow & Durand touches it in the mood/attachment material; classic developmental texts (e.g. Berk, Development Through the Lifespan ) carry the deprivation studies. Bottom line: for the MET, treat both as Abnormal + Developmental material, not personality-theory or biopsych. The cleanest single home is Barlow & Durand (mood disorders) for Blatt and any developmental/attachment chapter for Spitz. That's why they're not turning up when you revise from the six — this page is their home until the full Abnormal book lands in the Library. 1. The Word: "Anaclitic" Anaclitic = leaning on / dependent on another for support. From Greek anaklinein ("to lean upon"). Freudian root: anaclitic object-choice = choosing a love object on the model of the person who fed/protected you (mother), i.e. love based on dependency, vs narcissistic object-choice (loving someone like yourself). So "anaclitic depression" in both René Spitz and Sidney Blatt = a depression organised around dependency and loss of the caregiving/loved other . 2. Blatt — Two-Polarities (Two-Configurations) Model Sidney J. Blatt (Yale) argued that personality develops along two fundamental, lifelong coordinates / developmental lines : Line Also called What it is about Anaclitic Relatedness (interpersonal) Establishing and maintaining close, satisfying relationships — intimacy, trust, mutuality. Introjective Self-definition (identity) Establishing a stable, coherent, realistic, positive sense of self — autonomy, identity, self-worth. Core claim: Normal personality development is a dialectic — the two lines develop in reciprocal, synergistic interaction. You need relatedness to define a self, and a self to relate. Maturity = a balance of both. Blatt, 1974 (and refined through 1992, 2004/2008 Polarities of Experience ). Psychopathology = a one-sided, exaggerated over-development of one line at the expense of the other. You compensate on one axis because the other is distorted. Two corresponding configurations of depression fall out of this (next section). 3. Blatt's Two Types of Depression Anaclitic depression (dependent) Introjective depression (self-critical) Polarity Relatedness disturbed Self-definition disturbed Core theme Loss of the other / fear of abandonment Loss of self-worth / failure to meet standards Felt experience Helplessness, weakness, loneliness, emptiness, depletion; longing to be loved, cared for, fed, protected Guilt, worthlessness, inferiority, failure, self-criticism; feeling one has not lived up to expectations Central fear Being abandoned / unloved Loss of approval / recognition , disapproval of a harsh conscience Superego / conscience Not the main driver Harsh, punitive superego ; perfectionism Developmental tie Oral, early dependency; disrupted attachment Later, autonomy/achievement; self-evaluation What they seek Closeness, reassurance, being taken care of Achievement, control, perfection, approval TRAP: Don't map "anaclitic = sad" and "introjective = guilty" too crudely. The cleaner split: anaclitic depression is about the relationship (losing the other) ; introjective depression is about the self (failing the self/standards) . Dependency vs self-criticism. 3.1 How Blatt's split lines up with other two-factor depression models Examiners love asking which models are "the same idea under different names." Sidney Blatt's anaclitic/introjective parallels: Author Dependency / relatedness pole Self-criticism / self-definition pole Blatt Anaclitic Introjective Aaron Beck Sociotropy Autonomy Arieti & Bemporad Dominant other Dominant goal Bakan Communion Agency Sigmund Freud (work/love) Love (Lieben) Work (Arbeiten) One-liner: Blatt = Beck's sociotropy/autonomy from a psychoanalytic angle. Anaclitic ≈ sociotropic; introjective ≈ autonomous. 3.2 The measure Depressive Experiences Questionnaire (DEQ) — Sidney Blatt, D'Afflitti & Quinlan (1976). Yields the factors Dependency (anaclitic) and Self-Criticism (introjective) — plus an Efficacy factor. If a question names the DEQ → it's Blatt's anaclitic/introjective framework. 3.3 Therapeutic change — the two types improve through different mechanisms Sidney Blatt did not just describe the two types, he tied them to how people get better in therapy (his reanalysis of the Menninger Psychotherapy Research Project , and later work on therapeutic action): Anaclitic (dependent) Introjective (self-critical) What drives improvement The therapeutic relationship itself — feeling held, cared for, securely attached to the therapist Insight & interpretation — understanding, mastery, cognitive/interpretive work More responsive to Supportive, relational elements of treatment Interpretive, insight-oriented elements Changes shown most in Quality of interpersonal relationships Self-concept, cognitive functioning, reduced self-criticism Exam line: Blatt's two types improve through different mechanisms — anaclitic patients respond to the relationship , introjective patients respond to insight . (This is why the model matters for treatment matching, not just diagnosis.) 3.4 Perfectionism and suicide — the dangerous pole Sidney Blatt's later signature work was on perfectionism , especially self-critical perfectionism (the introjective pole taken to the extreme). Key paper: Blatt (1995), "The Destructiveness of Perfectionism" ( American Psychologist ) — he linked harsh, self-critical perfectionism to severe depression, poor treatment response, and suicide . He drew on high-achieving people who died by suicide despite outward success: the relentless inner standard, never "good enough," is lethal. TRAP / high-yield: Between the two types it is the introjective / self-critical one that carries the higher suicide risk — the self-punishing, perfectionistic route. Anaclitic = clings and seeks care; introjective = turns the attack inward. 4. Spitz — Anaclitic Depression (the infant syndrome) René Spitz (1887–1974), Austrian-American psychoanalyst, studied infants in institutions and foundling homes. Anaclitic depression (Spitz, 1946): a syndrome in infants roughly 6–18 months old who, after forming a good, normal attachment to the mother , are separated from her for a prolonged period (about 3 months) with no adequate substitute caregiver . Course: at first the infant protests/cries and clings; then withdraws, becomes weepy, apprehensive, sad, refuses contact ; loses appetite and weight, develops insomnia ; motor/cognitive development slows and regresses; becomes susceptible to infection; a frozen, dejected expression. Reversibility: if the mother (or an adequate substitute) is returned within ~3–5 months , the infant typically recovers . The key is that the infant had a good relationship and then lost it — it is a depression of loss , not of never-having-had. "Anaclitic" because the depression follows the loss of the love object on whom the infant was anaclitically (dependently) leaning . Spitz anaclitic depression in one line: good attachment → prolonged separation (~3 months) in mid-infancy → withdrawal, weight loss, developmental arrest → reversible if the mother comes back in time . 4.1 The bridge to attachment theory — protest → despair → detachment René Spitz's observations of the infant's reaction to separation (first protest/crying and clinging , then the withdrawn, weepy, despairing anaclitic-depression phase ) prefigure John Bowlby's three-stage separation sequence : Stage Bowlby (separation response) Spitz's parallel 1 Protest — crying, searching, clinging, anger Initial protest/clinging at separation 2 Despair — withdrawal, sadness, hopelessness The anaclitic-depression phase: weepy, withdrawn, dejected 3 Detachment — apparent indifference, defensive shutdown Slides toward the deeper deterioration if loss persists The chain examiners love: emotional bond > physical provision; separation produces protest → despair → detachment ; early deprivation leaves lasting effects. Spitz is one of the founding maternal-deprivation studies, feeding straight into Bowlby (separation/loss), Harry Harlow (the cloth vs wire monkeys — contact comfort over food), and Mary Ainsworth (Strange Situation / attachment types). 5. Spitz — Hospitalism (the severe, often irreversible deprivation) Hospitalism (René Spitz, 1945): the extreme, prolonged deterioration — physical, cognitive, emotional — of infants raised in institutions (foundling homes) under severe emotional / maternal deprivation , even when physical and nutritional needs are met and hygiene is good. Spitz's classic comparison: Foundling Home — infants cared for by overworked nurses (about one nurse to seven infants), almost no individual mothering. Despite clean, hygienic, well-fed conditions, infants showed catastrophic decline : severe developmental delay, marasmus (wasting), high susceptibility to infection, and a very high mortality rate . Nursery (a women's prison) — infants cared for by their own mothers . These infants thrived and developed normally. Conclusion: it is maternal/emotional contact , not just food and hygiene, that infants need. Emotional deprivation alone produces devastating, often irreversible harm. Linked downstream to marasmus (failure to thrive / wasting) and to John Bowlby's maternal deprivation work and Harry Harlow's monkeys. 6. Spitz: Anaclitic Depression vs Hospitalism Anaclitic depression Hospitalism Year 1946 1945 Deprivation Partial — lost a mother it had Total / prolonged emotional deprivation, often never had mothering Precondition A prior good attachment , then separation Institutional rearing with no individual mother figure Reversibility Reversible if mother returns within ~3–5 months Often irreversible ; marasmus, high mortality Severity Serious but recoverable Most severe; can be fatal TRAP: Both are René Spitz, both are infants, both are emotional deprivation. The dividing line is partial & reversible (anaclitic depression) vs total & often irreversible (hospitalism) . Hospitalism is the worse, institutional one with the high death rate. 7. The Master Comparison (Blatt vs Spitz on "anaclitic") René Spitz — anaclitic depression Sidney Blatt — anaclitic depression Who Infants (~6–18 months) Adults What kind of construct A clinical syndrome from real separation A personality configuration / subtype of adult depression Cause Actual loss of the mother Over-development of the relatedness line; dependency vulnerability Paired with Hospitalism (the severe form) Introjective (self-critical) depression Year / work 1946 1974, DEQ 1976 Memory hook: Spitz = small (infants) , anaclitic vs hospitalism . Blatt = big (adults) , anaclitic vs introjective . Same word "anaclitic," different theorist, different age. 8. High-Yield MCQ Lines Anaclitic = leaning on / dependent (Greek, to lean upon). René Spitz, 1946: anaclitic depression = infant separated from an attached mother for ~3 months → withdrawal, weight loss, developmental arrest; reversible if she returns in time . Spitz, 1945: hospitalism = institution-reared infants, severe emotional deprivation despite good physical care → marasmus, high mortality, often irreversible . Spitz's foundling-home vs nursery study showed emotional/maternal contact matters more than food & hygiene. Sidney Blatt's two-polarities model: personality develops along relatedness (anaclitic) and self-definition (introjective) lines, in a dialectic. Blatt's anaclitic depression = dependency, helplessness, fear of abandonment, longing to be cared for. Blatt's introjective depression = self-criticism, guilt, worthlessness, harsh superego, failure to meet standards. Blatt ≈ Aaron Beck: anaclitic ≈ sociotropy, introjective ≈ autonomy. Also Arieti's dominant-other vs dominant-goal; Bakan's communion vs agency. Measure of Blatt's types = Depressive Experiences Questionnaire (DEQ) (1976): Dependency, Self-Criticism, Efficacy. Therapeutic change differs by type: anaclitic patients improve via the relationship , introjective patients via insight/interpretation (Blatt, Menninger reanalysis). Higher suicide risk = introjective / self-critical perfectionist. Blatt (1995), "The Destructiveness of Perfectionism." Spitz prefigures John Bowlby: protest → despair → detachment; founding maternal-deprivation study (with Harry Harlow, Mary Ainsworth, Bowlby). Do not confuse Spitz's infant anaclitic depression with Blatt's adult anaclitic depression subtype. 9. 30-Second Recall Script "Anaclitic" = leaning/dependent. Two theorists, two age groups. Spitz (infants): anaclitic depression (1946) is an infant who had a good mother, lost her ~3 months in mid-infancy, withdrew, lost weight, stopped developing — reversible if she comes back; hospitalism (1945) is institution-reared infants with total emotional deprivation despite food & hygiene — marasmus, high death rate, often irreversible (foundling home vs prison nursery study). Sidney Blatt (adults): personality grows along two lines — relatedness (anaclitic) and self-definition (introjective) — in a dialectic; pathology = lopsided over-development of one. Anaclitic depression = dependency, abandonment fear, wanting care; introjective depression = self-criticism, guilt, harsh superego, failing one's standards. Maps onto Aaron Beck's sociotropy/autonomy. Measured by the DEQ . The two types even improve differently in therapy — anaclitic via the relationship , introjective via insight ; and the introjective/self-critical perfectionist carries the higher suicide risk (Blatt, "Destructiveness of Perfectionism," 1995). René Spitz's separation reaction prefigures Bowlby's protest → despair → detachment . Built 2026-06-07 — focused one-pager off the NIMHANS-tested Blatt + Spitz questions. Folds into the Abnormal book's mood-disorders chapter. Pair with the Barlow & Durand and Ahuja abnormal pages. Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS Prep

title: Unit 3 – Psychometrics & Test Construction
text: Unit 3 – Psychometrics & Test Construction The science of measuring the mind: how a psychological test is built, scored and judged. This book teaches the four scales of measurement, the anatomy of a good item and how to analyse one, the full reliability and validity families with their formulae, the meaning of norms and standard scores, and the major families of real tests – intelligence, neuropsychological, personality, interest and aptitude – together with where and why each is applied (education, occupation, military, clinic). It closes with the M.Phil-style exam questions folded in. Sourced from Rodrick Prashanth's Unit 3 decks (Areas of testing, Applications of testing, Interest & aptitude tests, Item writing & item analysis, Reliability/Validity/Norms, Scales) and the M.Phil question bank, deepened to NIMHANS clinical depth. In this book Scales of measurement & attitude scaling Item writing & item analysis Reliability Validity Norms & standard scores Areas of testing: intelligence & creativity Areas of testing: neuropsychological assessment Areas of testing: personality assessment Interest & aptitude tests Applications of testing Structured personality-test construction M.Phil exam questions 1. Scales of measurement & attitude scaling The one idea. Before you can measure a psychological attribute you must decide what kind of number you are assigning. S. S. Stevens' four levels of measurement – nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio – form a ladder: each rung adds one mathematical property and therefore unlocks one more legitimate statistic. Choosing the wrong scale is the commonest hidden error in test interpretation: you cannot average ranks, and you cannot say one IQ is "twice" another. The four levels Level Allows categorising Allows ranking (order) Equal intervals True (absolute) zero Example Nominal Yes – – – Diagnosis codes, gender, jersey numbers Ordinal Yes Yes – – Rank in class, Likert agree/disagree, race finishing order Interval Yes Yes Yes – Temperature in °C, IQ scores, calendar years Ratio Yes Yes Yes Yes Reaction time, weight, number of errors, age Why each property matters. A nominal scale only labels – the numbers are names, so the only legitimate operations are counting frequencies and the mode. An ordinal scale adds order, so you can take a median and percentiles, but the gaps between ranks are unequal (the difference between 1st and 2nd is not the same "amount" as between 2nd and 3rd). An interval scale adds equal spacing, so you can finally add, subtract and compute a mean and standard deviation; but its zero is arbitrary (0°C is not "no temperature"). A ratio scale adds a true zero meaning total absence of the attribute, so ratios become meaningful: 40 errors is genuinely twice 20 errors. High-yield Memorise the ladder of properties: N ominal = categorise; O rdinal = + order; I nterval = + equal intervals; R atio = + true zero. Each level permits everything the levels below it permit, plus one more. Mnemonic NOIR (French for "black") gives the order of increasing power: N ominal → O rdinal → I nterval → R atio. Trap Interval vs ratio. Both have equal intervals; only ratio has a true zero. IQ and Celsius temperature are interval – an IQ of 0 does not mean "no intelligence," so you cannot say IQ 140 is "twice as smart" as IQ 70. Kelvin temperature and reaction time are ratio. Attitude scales Attitude measurement applies these principles to subjective opinion. The deck names four classic formats: Scale Structure Key feature Likert scale Five ordered responses on an agree/disagree or approve/disapprove continuum (e.g. Strongly Agree → Strongly Disagree) Summative; the most widely used attitude format. Strictly ordinal, though usually treated as interval in practice. Guttman scale Items ordered by intensity; a respondent who endorses one statement also endorses all milder statements on the same continuum Cumulative / unidimensional. "Check the statement from each group that is most true of you." Semantic differential (Osgood) A set of bipolar adjective scales (Healthy – Unhealthy, Pleasant – Unpleasant) anchoring a 7-point line Measures the subjective meaning and affective reaction to a concept; classic dimensions are Evaluation, Potency, Activity. Stapel scale A single ( unipolar ) adjective with 10 categories from −5 to +5, no neutral zero A one-adjective alternative to the semantic differential; forces a direction. Trap Semantic differential vs Stapel. Semantic differential uses bipolar adjective pairs with a neutral midpoint; the Stapel scale uses a single (unipolar) adjective on a −5 to +5 line with no neutral point . Guttman is cumulative (endorsing a strong item implies endorsing the weaker ones); Likert is summative. 2. Item writing & item analysis The one idea. A test is only as good as its items. Item construction is part craft (writing clear, unambiguous questions) and part statistics (keeping the items that actually discriminate among people and dropping those that do not). Item analysis is the set of empirical methods for that pruning. Guidelines for item writing (DeVellis, 2012) Define clearly what you want to measure before writing anything. Generate an item pool larger than the final test, so weak items can be discarded. Avoid exceptionally long items – length adds reading load, not information. Keep reading difficulty appropriate to the intended respondents. Avoid "double-barrelled" items that pack two ideas into one statement ("I feel anxious and depressed") – the respondent cannot answer cleanly. Mix positively and negatively worded items to counter acquiescence (yea-saying) response bias. Item formats & correction for guessing The dichotomous format scores an item 0 or 1 (true/false, right/wrong). The polytomous format gives each item more than two alternatives. In a multiple-choice item, the incorrect alternatives are called distractors ; it is usually best to write three or four good distractors per item, and three distractors are about as effective as five in most cases. Because a low-ability test-taker can score by guessing, scores are sometimes adjusted by a correction for guessing : Definition Corrected score = R − W/(n − 1) , where R = number of right responses, W = number of wrong responses, and n = number of choices per item. The formula subtracts an estimate of how many "right" answers were really lucky guesses. Mathematical treatments summarise the mean, the reliability from the binomial distribution, and a guessing threshold – the chance that a low-ability test-taker will reach each score. Personality and attitude measures, by contrast, do not score responses right or wrong; they quantify a characteristic of the response using formats such as Likert, the category scale, and the Q-sort. Item difficulty (p) Item difficulty is defined by the proportion of people who get the item correct – confusingly, a higher p means an easier item. The optimal difficulty level lies roughly halfway between 100% correct and the chance level. Worked example for a four-choice item (chance = .25): Half the difference between 1.00 and chance: (1.00 − 0.25)/2 = 0.75/2 = 0.375 Add chance back: 0.375 + 0.25 = 0.625 Shortcut: (chance + 1.00)/2 = (0.25 + 1.00)/2 = 0.625 A good test, however, needs items at many difficulty levels, because it must discriminate across the whole range of ability. For most tests, items in the range .30 to .70 maximise the information they give about differences between individuals. Some achievement tests deliberately load on harder items to identify high-ability candidates. Trap High p = EASY item, not hard. p = .90 means 90% passed it (easy); p = .20 means only 20% passed (hard). The "optimum" .625 for a 4-choice item already builds in the chance correction – for a true/false item (chance .50) the optimum is (.50 + 1.00)/2 = .75. Item discrimination Item discriminability asks whether the people who did well on a particular item also did well on the test as a whole. There are two classic approaches: The extreme-group (discrimination index) method. Compare a high-scoring group (e.g. top third of the class) with a low-scoring group (bottom third). Find the proportion in each group who got the item correct; the difference between these proportions is the discrimination index (D) . The closer D is to 1.0, the better the item. A negative D (the weak students passed it more often than the strong ones) is a red flag. The point-biserial method. The correlation between a dichotomous variable (passed/failed the item) and a continuous variable (total test score) is the point-biserial correlation , used here as an index of discriminability. On a short test, correlating an item with the total score is problematic because the item itself inflates the total, so an item-remainder (item-total minus that item) score is used – e.g. on a six-item test, correlate passing item 1 with the score from items 2–6. If the value is negative or low, drop the item. Item characteristic curves & Item Response Theory An item characteristic curve (ICC) graphs total test score on the X-axis against the proportion of examinees passing that item on the Y-axis. A good item's curve rises steeply across the ability range. Newer approaches, collectively Item Response Theory (IRT) , give each item its own ICC describing the probability of a correct response given the ability level of the test-taker . IRT models use one, two, or three parameters: difficulty, discriminability, and a guessing parameter (the probability that the lowest-ability test-takers answer correctly). Because a computer can identify exactly which items pin down a given ability level, IRT enables computer-adaptive testing : the test-taker is not forced through items far above or below their level, sparing time and embarrassment. High-yield Two pillars of item analysis: difficulty (p) = proportion correct (high = easy, optimum ~.625 for 4-choice); discrimination = does the item separate strong from weak test-takers (discrimination index D = difference in pass rates between high and low groups; point-biserial = item–total correlation). IRT generalises this to per-item curves and powers adaptive testing. Criterion-referenced tests A criterion-referenced test compares performance against a defined standard of learning rather than against other people. You first specify objectives precisely (what the programme should achieve), then evaluate items by giving the test to two groups – one that has had the learning unit and one that has not. The resulting frequency polygon looks like a V : low scorers (left) are the un-taught group, high scorers (right) the taught group. The bottom of the V is the antimode (least frequent score), which is taken as the cutting score – the point of decision separating those who have mastered the unit from those who have not. Trap Norm-referenced vs criterion-referenced. Norm-referenced compares you to others (percentile rank). Criterion-referenced compares you to a fixed standard ("80% correct = pass"); item variability is deliberately minimal, which is why traditional reliability formulae are inappropriate for them. 3. Reliability The one idea. Reliability is consistency of measurement. A reliable test gives much the same result on repeated, equivalent measurement. Reliability is never all-or-none; it is a matter of degree, expressed as a coefficient between 0.0 and 1.0. Classical (true-score) theory Classical test theory says any observed score is the sum of a true score and error: X = T + e , where T comes from factors that contribute to consistency and e from factors that contribute to inconsistency . Sources of measurement error: item selection, test administration, and test scoring. There is also systematic measurement error , where (unknown to the developer) the test consistently measures something other than the intended trait; the model becomes X = T + e s + e u (systematic + unsystematic error). Assumptions of the classical model: measurement errors are random; the mean error of measurement = 0; true scores and errors are uncorrelated (r Te = 0); errors on different tests are uncorrelated (r 12 = 0). It follows that the variance of obtained scores is the variance of true scores plus the variance of error: σ 2 X = σ 2 T + σ 2 e . Definition The reliability coefficient (r XX ) is the ratio of true-score variance to total score variance: r XX = σ 2 T / σ 2 X = σ 2 T / (σ 2 T + σ 2 e ) . It ranges from 0.0 (all error) to 1.0 (all true score). The families of reliability Reliability splits into temporal stability (test–retest, alternate-forms) and internal consistency (split-half, coefficient alpha), plus interscorer reliability for subjectively scored tests. Test–retest reliability The most straightforward method: administer the identical test twice to the same heterogeneous, representative sample and correlate the scores. Practice, maturation or schooling may raise the second score, but as long as the two sets of scores are strongly correlated, such effects do not threaten test–retest reliability. Psychometricians treat test–retest as the gold-standard approach. Its error source is changes over time . Alternate-forms (parallel-forms) reliability Two forms of a test are independently built to the same specifications (often item-by-item), so they share statistical and normative properties. Administer both to the same group and correlate. This shares features with test–retest (two administrations with a gap) but adds item-sampling differences as an extra source of error variance; alternate forms are also expensive to construct. Immediate alternate-forms isolates item sampling; delayed alternate-forms adds change over time. Split-half reliability Administer the test once , split it into two equivalent halves, and correlate the half-scores. The challenge is splitting the test into truly equivalent halves; since items are often ordered by difficulty (first half easier), the standard solution is to compare odd items vs even items . Because a half-test is shorter (and shorter tests are less reliable), the half-test correlation must be stepped up to a full-test estimate with the Spearman-Brown formula : Definition r SB = 2r hh / (1 + r hh ) , where r hh is the half-test reliability and r SB the estimated full-test reliability. Example: a half-test reliability of .70 corrects to a full-test reliability of about .82 . Split-half estimates are generally similar to, but often a little higher than, test–retest estimates. Its error sources are item sampling and the particular nature of the split. Coefficient alpha (Cronbach, 1951) Rather than rely on one arbitrary split, Lee Cronbach proposed averaging across all possible splits. Coefficient alpha can be thought of as the mean of all possible split-half coefficients, each corrected by Spearman-Brown. Definition r α = [N/(N−1)] × (1 − Σσ 2 j / σ 2 ) , where N = number of items, σ 2 j = variance of one item, Σσ 2 j = sum of item variances, and σ 2 = variance of total scores. Like all reliability estimates, α ranges 0.00–1.00. Alpha is traditionally read as an index of unidimensionality – how far the scale measures a single factor. But beware: alpha rises with the number of items, so a high alpha can occur even with several dimensions if there are many items. This is exactly why psychometricians still treat test–retest as essential. Kuder-Richardson (KR-20) Coefficient alpha is the general case of an earlier formula by G. Frederic Kuder and Marion Richardson (1937): KR-20 . KR-20 applies to the special case where each item is scored 0 or 1 (dichotomous). Coefficient alpha extends the Kuder-Richardson method to items that are not scored 0/1 – for example an attitude scale where examinees choose strongly agree / agree / disagree / strongly disagree. Interscorer (inter-rater) reliability Some tests leave much to the examiner's judgment in assigning scores – projective tests, and tests of moral development and creativity fall here. A sample of tests is scored independently by two or more examiners and the pairs of scores are correlated. Interscorer reliability supplements the other estimates but does not replace them; you would still assess test–retest or another type in a subjectively scored test. (In behavioural observation, a common convention is that two observers should agree at r ≥ 0.80, or 80% inter-rater agreement for interval recording.) Synopsis of reliability methods Method No. of forms No. of sessions Main source(s) of error Test–retest 1 2 Changes over time Alternate-forms (immediate) 2 1 Item sampling Alternate-forms (delayed) 2 2 Item sampling + changes over time Split-half 1 1 Item sampling + nature of the split Coefficient alpha 1 1 Item sampling + test heterogeneity Interscorer 1 1 Scorer differences Special circumstances Unstable characteristics. When the trait itself changes fast (e.g. an electrodermal measure of emotional reactivity), test and retest must be nearly instantaneous to give an accurate reliability index. Speed vs power tests. A speed test has uniform, easy items where the score depends on how many you finish in the time – its reliability must come from test–retest or from two separately timed half-tests (with Spearman-Brown), not from an ordinary single-session split-half. A power test gives ample time but is hard enough that no one gets a perfect score. Restriction of range. Reliability is spuriously low if estimated on a homogeneous sample (e.g. estimating an IQ test's reliability by retesting only college students). Criterion-referenced tests. Their score variability is minimal by design, so traditional reliability approaches are simply inappropriate. High-yield Match the method to the error it isolates: test–retest = stability over time; alternate-forms = item sampling (+ time if delayed); split-half / alpha / KR-20 = internal consistency; interscorer = scorer disagreement. KR-20 = dichotomous items; alpha = its general (any-scoring) form. Speed tests must NOT use single-session split-half. 4. Validity The one idea. Validity is whether the inferences drawn from a test are appropriate, meaningful and useful – classically, whether the test measures what it purports to measure. Modern theory treats validity as a unitary concept, with the traditional "types" being different lines of evidence rather than separate validities. The three traditional categories are content, criterion-related, and construct validity. Trap Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. A bathroom scale that reads 5 kg too heavy every time is perfectly reliable yet invalid. A test can be reliable and still measure the wrong thing; but a test that is not reliable cannot be valid. The validity coefficient is in fact capped by reliability (see below). Content validity Content validity is the degree to which the items are representative of the universe of behaviour the test was meant to sample – fundamentally a sampling question. The test's items are a sample from a larger population of possible items; if the sample is representative, the test has content validity. Developers must also specify the relevant universe of responses . Content validity is hardest to ensure for ill-defined traits, where it rests on the considered opinion of expert judges. Quantifying content validity. Two expert judges rate each item on a 4-point relevance scale; ratings are dichotomised into weak (1–2) vs strong (3–4) relevance and entered in a 2×2 agreement table. The coefficient of content validity = D / (A + B + C + D) , where D is the cell where both judges rated the item strongly relevant. Example: on a 100-item test both judges agreed 87 items were strongly relevant, giving 87/(4+4+5+87) = .87. Definition Face validity is whether a test merely looks valid to users, examiners and especially examinees. It is a matter of social acceptability, not a technical form of validity . Criterion-related validity Demonstrated when a test effectively estimates performance on an outcome measure (the criterion ). The test score is useful only insofar as it predicts the criterion accurately (e.g. a college entrance exam that predicts later GPA). Two sub-types differ by timing : Concurrent validity – criterion measures obtained at about the same time as the test scores. Correlations between a new test and an established test are typical evidence; the instrument must measure the same construct as the criterion test. Predictive validity – criterion measures obtained in the future (months or years later, like college grades predicted from an entrance exam). When a test is used for prediction, a regression equation is developed. A criterion must be reliable, appropriate, and free of criterion contamination (the criterion must not be influenced by the test itself). Crucially, the validity coefficient is bounded by reliability: Definition The theoretical upper limit of the validity coefficient is the square root of (test reliability × criterion reliability): r xy ≤ √(r xx · r yy ) . The standard error of estimate (SE est ) is the margin of error expected in the predicted criterion score. Trap Concurrent vs predictive. The only difference is timing of the criterion. "Same time" = concurrent; "later" = predictive. Both are species of criterion-related validity. Construct validity A construct is a theoretical, intangible trait on which people differ (leadership ability, overcontrolled hostility, depression, intelligence, psychopathy). Construct validity is the appropriateness of inferences about the underlying construct. All constructs share two features: there is no single external referent that can validate them (they cannot be fully operationalised), yet a network of interlocking suppositions can be derived from theory. Many theorists regard construct validity as the unifying concept for all validity evidence. Construct-validity studies fall into several categories: (1) test homogeneity – whether items/subtests are homogeneous and measure a single construct (select items correlating highly with the total score); (2) developmental changes – whether scores change with age as theory predicts (older children should know more vocabulary); (3) theory-consistent group differences – high-construct people score high; (4) theory-consistent intervention effects – scores move correctly after an intervention; (5) convergent and discriminant validation ; (6) factor analysis ; (7) classification accuracy . Convergent validity – the test correlates highly with other tests sharing the same construct. Discriminant validity – the test does not correlate with measures from which it should differ. When several traits are each measured by several methods and all pairs are correlated, the result is a multitrait-multimethod (MTMM) matrix (Campbell & Fiske) – the classic design for showing convergent and discriminant validity simultaneously. Factor analysis identifies the minimum number of factors needed to account for the intercorrelations among a battery of tests; you administer the battery to several hundred subjects and analyse the correlation matrix. Classification accuracy matters for screening tests – e.g. the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), whose validity hinges on correctly classifying people as cases or non-cases. High-yield Three validity families: content (representative sampling of the item universe; quantified by expert-judge agreement), criterion-related (predicts an outcome – concurrent = now, predictive = later), and construct (measures the theoretical trait; the unifying concept; convergent = correlates with similar, discriminant = doesn't correlate with different; MTMM matrix; factor analysis). Face validity is "looks valid" and is NOT real validity. 5. Norms & standard scores The one idea. A raw score (e.g. "32 correct") is meaningless on its own. Norms give a frame of reference by describing how a representative standardisation (normative) sample performed, so an individual's score can be located relative to others. The deck title for the reliability material was "Reliability, Validity and Norms"; this section teaches the norm concepts at the depth NIMHANS expects. The normative sample Norms are only as good as the sample they come from. A good standardisation sample is large, representative of the population for whom the test is intended, and current (norms go stale – the Flynn effect means IQ norms drift over decades). Norms can be national, local, or subgroup-specific (by age, grade, sex). A test like the Henmon-Nelson provides two sets of norms – one by age, one by grade. Percentile ranks A percentile rank is the percentage of the norm group scoring at or below a given raw score (a percentile rank of 70 means you did as well as or better than 70% of the sample). Percentiles are intuitive and require only an ordinal scale, but they are not equal-interval : near the middle of a normal distribution, scores pile up, so a few raw-score points span many percentile points; at the extremes, large raw differences move the percentile little. A percentile band (used by the Kuhlmann-Anderson) reports a range, like a confidence interval, to remind the user that any single score has measurement error. Trap Percentile rank is not a percentage-correct score. 70th percentile means "better than 70% of people," not "70% of items correct." And percentiles are ordinal, so do not average them – the gap between the 50th and 55th percentile is much smaller in raw terms than the gap between the 90th and 95th. Standard scores Standard scores re-express a raw score in standard-deviation units, putting different tests on a common, equal-interval metric. Standard score Mean SD Notes / where used z-score 0 1 The basic standard score: z = (X − M) / SD . Can be negative; carries decimals. T-score 50 10 z rescaled (T = 50 + 10z) to avoid negatives/decimals. Used by the MMPI and many personality scales. Deviation IQ 100 15 (Wechsler) Wechsler's solution; replaced the old ratio IQ (MA/CA × 100). Stanford-Binet historically used SD 16. Stanine 5 ~2 "STAndard NINE": a single-digit 1–9 scale dividing the distribution into nine bands. Coarse but compact. Sten 5.5 2 "Standard TEN": a 1–10 scale used by Cattell's 16PF. Why standard scores beat percentiles for arithmetic: because they are equal-interval (built on the underlying normal curve), you can legitimately average them and compare across tests. In a normal distribution, about 68% of scores fall within ±1 SD, 95% within ±2 SD, and 99.7% within ±3 SD – the rule that lets you convert any z to a percentile and back. Mnemonic Means and SDs to memorise: z = 0, 1 · T = 50, 10 · IQ = 100, 15 · stanine = 5, 2 (1–9) · sten = 5.5, 2 (1–10). T-score → "Ten" SD; IQ → "fifteen". Definition The deviation IQ (Wechsler) expresses intelligence as a standard score with mean 100, SD 15: it locates a person relative to their own age group , fixing the flaw of the old ratio IQ (mental age ÷ chronological age × 100), which broke down in adulthood because mental age plateaus. High-yield Raw scores are uninterpretable; norms supply meaning. Percentile rank = % scoring at or below (intuitive but ordinal, not equal-interval). Standard scores (z, T, deviation IQ, stanine, sten) are equal-interval and comparable across tests. 68–95–99.7 within ±1/2/3 SD. Wechsler IQ: mean 100, SD 15. 6. Areas of testing: intelligence & creativity The one idea. Intelligence has never had one agreed definition – each theorist measured what they conceived. The major individual tests (Wechsler, Stanford-Binet) operationalise these ideas, and creativity tests extend the toolkit to divergent thinking. Definitions of intelligence (who said what) Theorist Intelligence is… Spearman (1904, 1923) A general ability involving the eduction of relations and correlates (the basis of his "g"). Binet & Simon (1905) The ability to judge well, understand well, reason well. Lewis Terman (1916) The capacity to form concepts and grasp their significance. Pintner (1921) The ability to adapt adequately to relatively new situations in life. Thorndike (1921) The power of good responses from the point of view of truth or fact. Thurstone (1921) The capacity to inhibit instinctive adjustments, imagine alternatives, and realise modified adjustments in behaviour. Wechsler (1939) The aggregate or global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally, and deal effectively with the environment. Humphreys (1971) The entire repertoire of acquired skills, knowledge, learning sets and generalisation tendencies available at one time. Jean Piaget (1972) The superior forms of organisation/equilibrium of cognitive structuring used for adaptation. Robert Sternberg (1985/86) The capacity to automatise information processing and emit contextually appropriate behaviour in response to novelty (meta-, performance, and knowledge-acquisition components). Hans Eysenck (1986) Error-free transmission of information through the cortex. Howard Gardner (1986) The ability to solve problems or fashion products valued within one or more cultural settings. Ceci (1994) Multiple innate abilities that develop or atrophy depending on motivation and exposure. Sattler (2001) Intelligent behaviour reflects the survival skills of the species. The Wechsler tests From the 1930s, David Wechsler at Bellevue Hospital built instruments that defined adult intelligence testing. The first, the Wechsler-Bellevue Intelligence Scale (1939), drew on the Binet scales and the Army Alpha and Beta tests. It was designed to fix flaws of earlier tests: items had no appeal for adults; too many emphasised mere word manipulation; instructions stressed speed over accuracy; and reliance on mental age was irrelevant to adults. Wechsler's corrections: a test designed specifically for adults; performance items added to balance verbal questions; reduced emphasis on speed; and a new deviation IQ method (score relative to one's own age group) rather than the ratio IQ. He split the scale into Verbal and Performance sections, hoping large V–P differences would aid psychiatric diagnosis. The three modern Wechsler tests are WAIS-IV (adults), WISC-IV (children), and WPPSI-IV (preschool). Common features: 13–15 subtests and an empirically based breakdown into composite/index scores plus a Full Scale IQ. Where the originals gave only Verbal IQ and Performance IQ, the WISC-IV and WAIS-IV now yield four index scores: Verbal Comprehension, Perceptual Reasoning, Working Memory, and Processing Speed . The WPPSI-IV (ages 4:0–7:7) adds a fifth, Fluid Reasoning . Other intelligence tests Stanford-Binet, Fifth Edition (SB5) – lineage to the Binet-Simon 1905 scale; the oldest, most prestigious pedigree. Built so each of five factors is assessed in two domains (nonverbal and verbal). The five factors (from Carroll, 1993; Alan Baddeley, 1986) are fluid reasoning, knowledge, quantitative reasoning, visual-spatial processing, and working memory ; crossing 5 factors × 2 domains gives 10 subtests. Detroit Tests of Learning Aptitude-4 (DTLA-4) – revision of a 1935 instrument; individually administered, ages 6–17; 10 subtests forming 16 composites (general intelligence, optimal level, and 14 ability areas). Cognitive Assessment System-II (CAS-II) – ages 5–17; explicitly built on the PASS theory (Planning, Attention, Simultaneous, Successive) of intelligence. Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test-2 (KBIT-2) – a brief screening test with a Verbal/Crystallised scale (Verbal Knowledge, Riddles) and a Nonverbal/Fluid scale (Matrices). Its brevity suits research and signalling the need for fuller assessment. Creativity Most definitions stress novelty and usefulness of the product, and treat creativity as a kind of process. Kaufman (2012) factor-analysed 94 items into five factors – Self/Everyday, Scholarly, Performance, Mechanical/Scientific, and Artistic creativity – producing the Kaufman Domains of Creativity Scale (K-DOCS) . Classic creativity tests: Remote Associates Test (RAT) (Mednick, 1962) – a timed 40-minute paper-and-pencil test indexing the remoteness of verbal associations (find a word linking three cues, e.g. rat–blue–cottage → "cheese"). Critics (Osche, 1990) say it is more a measure of verbal intelligence than of general creativity. Composite Creative Personality Scale (Harrington, 1975) – 42 self-checked adjectives. Guilford's Structure of Intellect (SOI) model parcelled intelligence into 150 factors; from the operations dimension came divergent thinking . J. P. Guilford's experimental divergent-thinking measures (Alternate Uses, Consequences, Ideational Fluency) were standardised as the Christensen-Guilford Fluency Tests . Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT) – loosely based on Guilford; two parallel forms (A, B) and two parts (Verbal, Figural). Verbal scoring uses Fluency (number of relevant ideas), Originality (inventiveness), and Flexibility (range of categories). Figural scoring adds Abstractness of Titles, Elaboration, and Resistance to Premature Closure. High-yield Wechsler = deviation IQ + V/P split → four indices (VC, PR, WM, PS). SB5 = 5 factors × 2 domains = 10 subtests. CAS-II = PASS theory. Creativity's signature construct is J. P. Guilford's divergent thinking ; the TTCT scores Fluency, Originality, Flexibility (+ Elaboration on the figural part). 7. Areas of testing: neuropsychological assessment The one idea. Neuropsychological tests map cognition onto brain function across discrete domains – orientation, attention, memory, language, spatial ability, and executive function. The Mental Status Examination (MSE) is the loosely structured interview that usually precedes other assessment; it describes the patient's orientation, memory, thought, feeling and judgment and is the psychological equivalent of the general physical exam. By domain Sensory input. Reitan-Klove Sensory-Perceptual Examination (unilateral/bilateral stimulation in touch, hearing, vision – especially diagnostic if errors cluster on one side of the body); Finger Localization Test (identify touched fingers without sight). Attention & concentration. Test of Everyday Attention (TEA) (Robertson et al., 1994/96) measures sustained, selective, divided attention and attentional switching, with three parallel versions. The Continuous Performance Test (CPT) (Rosvold et al., 1956) measures sustained attention/vigilance – errors of omission (failing to respond to a target) and errors of commission (responding to a non-target). Digit Span and Serial Subtractions also index attention. Learning & memory. Wechsler Memory Scale-IV (WMS-IV) – nine subtests (seven for the Standard Battery) yielding five indices (Immediate Memory, Delayed Memory, Auditory Memory, Visual Memory, Visual Working Memory). Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (RAVLT) – descended from Claparede's free-recall of a 15-word list; five learning trials, an interference list, immediate recall, then a recognition trial. Wide Range Assessment of Memory and Learning-2 (WRAML-2) – first comprehensive memory scale for children (5–17, norms now to 90); three indices (Verbal Memory, Visual Memory, Attention/Concentration). Language. Standardised aphasia screening tests resemble the brief clinical exam but add objective, precise scoring; their weakness is missing subtle aphasia. Spatial & manipulatory ability. Bender Visual-Motor Gestalt Test (BGT) – design copying; the original nine cards, BGT-II adds seven; assembly tests (Benton 3-D Block Construction, forms A and B). Executive functions (logical analysis, conceptualisation, reasoning, planning, flexibility). Porteus Mazes ; Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) – sort 64 cards (1–4 symbols: triangle, star, cross, circle; in red, green, yellow, blue) by an unknown principle, told only "right"/"wrong" as you go (sensitive to perseveration and set-shifting); Lezak's Tinkertoy Test – build anything from 50 pieces, scored 21–112 (pieces used, mobility, symmetry, naming); promising for Alzheimer's assessment. Screening for alcohol use disorders CAGE – four questions: C utting down, A nnoyed by criticism, G uilty about drinking, E ye-opener in the morning. More effective for screening men than women. TWEAK – developed specifically for women: T olerance, W orried friends/relatives, E ye-opener, A mnesia, feeling the need to K ut down. Mnemonic Alcohol screens: CAGE (Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener) for general/men; TWEAK for women. WCST → executive/set-shifting; CPT → sustained attention (omission vs commission errors); RAVLT → verbal learning over 5 trials. 8. Areas of testing: personality assessment The deck groups personality inventories by their method of construction (the next section unpacks the four strategies in full). Key instruments named: Theory-guided inventories Personality Research Form (PRF) (Jackson) – expands Murray's needs; short forms A/B and long forms AA/BB (440 true–false items); the long form gives 20 personality scores plus two validity scores (Infrequency, Desirability). State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI) – current Form Y; distinguishes transient state anxiety from stable trait anxiety. Factor-analytically derived inventories Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ) – measures three dimensions: Psychoticism (P), Extraversion (E), Neuroticism (N) , plus a Lie (L) validity scale; 90 yes/no items (age 16+); Junior EPQ has 81 items (ages 7–15). Comrey Personality Scales (CPS) – 180 items, 8 trait scales (Trust, Orderliness, Social Conformity, Activity, Emotional Stability, Extraversion, Mental Toughness, Empathy) plus Validity Check (V) and Response Bias (R). Also factor-derived: 16PF and the NEO-FFI (Big Five). Criterion-keyed inventories: the MMPI The MMPI (1943) was a 566-item true–false inventory built for psychiatric diagnosis; the MMPI-2 (1989) restandardised it. Its four classic validity scales: Cannot Say (?) – total items omitted or double-marked. L (Lie) – 15 items scored "false"; endorsing personal virtue rarely seen in the culture flags faking-good. F (Infrequency) – 60 items endorsed by normals ≤10% of the time; reflects serious maladjustment, but very high F can also mean poor reading, random responding, faking-bad, or a "cry for help". K – a subtle defensiveness scale (30 items) detecting normal-looking profiles from defensive patients. High-yield MMPI validity scales = ? (Cannot Say), L (Lie), F (Infrequency), K (defensiveness) . EPQ measures P-E-N + Lie. STAI separates state (now) from trait (enduring) anxiety. 9. Interest & aptitude tests The one idea. Interest inventories measure what a person likes (vocational preferences), distinct from aptitude tests which measure what a person can learn to do . Both feed career counselling and personnel selection. History of interest inventories The first item pool of interest activities was assembled in a 1919 seminar by Clarence S. Yoakum at Carnegie Institute of Technology – a 1,000-item pool built by rational sampling to represent the whole domain of interests. Many later inventories grew from it: the Occupational Interest Inventory (Freyd, 1922–23), Interest Report Blank (Cowdery, 1926), General Interest Survey (Kornhauser, 1927), Vocational Interest Blank (Strong, 1927) , Purdue Interest Report (Remmers, 1929), Interest Analysis Blank (Hubbard, 1930), and the Minnesota Interest Inventory (Paterson et al., 1930). The earliest inventories used the atheoretical, empirical method of contrast groups : people with similar interests cluster together and can be differentiated from dissimilar groups. This logic underlies the Strong Interest Inventory (Harmon, Hansen, Borgen & Hammer, 1994), the Career Assessment Inventory (Johansson, 1975/1986), and the Campbell Interest and Skill Survey (CISS) (Campbell, Hyne & Nilsen, 1992). Theories of vocational interest Anne Roe (1956) and John Holland (1959) drew on J. P. Guilford's factor analysis, which found seven interest factors : (a) mechanical, (b) scientific, (c) social welfare, (d) aesthetic expression, (e) clerical, (f) business, and (g) outdoor work. Holland's theory of vocational personality (RIASEC). From data with the Vocational Preference Inventory (VPI) and other inventories, Holland proposed that people can be classed into six types (or combinations): R ealistic, I nvestigative, A rtistic, S ocial, E nterprising, C onventional. The types arrange on a hexagon in R-I-A-S-E-C order: adjacent types (e.g. Realistic–Investigative, Enterprising–Conventional) are more related than opposite types (e.g. Realistic–Social, Artistic–Conventional). His theory spawned the Self-Directed Search (SDS) , the ACT Interest Inventory, the Career Decision-Making System-Revised (CDM-R; Harrington & O'Shea, 1993), and the General Occupational Themes of the Strong Interest Inventory. Mnemonic Holland's hexagon: RIASEC – " R ealistic I nvestigators A nd S ocial E nterprising C onventionals." Adjacent = similar; opposite = dissimilar. Current inventories Major current interest inventories include the Vocational Preference Inventory (Holland, 1985), the Self-Directed Search, various forms of the Kuder , the Strong Interest Inventory, the Career Assessment Inventory, the Jackson Vocational Interest Survey (JVIS) (Jackson, 1977), the unisex ACT Interest Inventory (UNIACT; Lamb & Prediger, 1981), and the Vocational Interest Inventory. Campbell Interest and Skill Survey (CISS) profile has three scale types: 7 Orientation Scales (the major interest factors from statistical clustering), 29 Basic Scales (homogeneous content clusters such as Sales, Supervision, Adult Development, International Activities, Science, Woodworking, Military/Law Enforcement), and 60 Occupational Scales (built by E. K. Strong's empirical method of contrast groups, surveying successful, satisfied workers in 60 occupations). A distinctive CISS feature is reporting both interest and self-reported skill . Aptitude test batteries Aptitude tests predict future learning/performance and rely heavily on criterion-related validity (contrast with achievement tests, which look backward at what has been learned and rest on content validity). Major multiple-aptitude batteries (also covered in the applications deck) include the General Aptitude Test Battery (GATB) , the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery (ASVAB) , the Differential Aptitude Test (DAT) , and the Employee Aptitude Survey. Specialised aptitude tests include the Bennett Mechanical Comprehension Test (mechanical aptitude via pictures of belts and flywheels; forms S and T), the Minnesota Spatial Relations Test and Revised Minnesota Paper Form Board (spatial), the Crawford Small Parts Dexterity Test and Purdue Pegboard (motor/dexterity), and the Minnesota Clerical Test (Number and Name Comparison, scored for speed with errors penalised). High-yield Interest inventories built by the empirical method of contrast groups (Strong, CISS, CAI). Holland's RIASEC hexagon is the most-tested vocational theory. CISS scales = 7 Orientation + 29 Basic + 60 Occupational. Aptitude predicts future ability (criterion-related validity); achievement measures past learning (content validity). 10. Applications of testing The one idea. The same psychometric machinery serves very different settings – schools, employers, the military, and the clinic. Each setting privileges a different kind of validity evidence. Testing in education Achievement tests measure the effects of a specific programme of instruction and represent a terminal evaluation of training; their validity is mostly content-related . Aptitude tests reflect the cumulative influence of everyday experience and predict subsequent performance, relying on criterion-oriented evidence. Group achievement tests: Stanford Achievement Test (10th ed., K–12); Metropolitan Achievement Test (MAT-8, renormed 2000, with Braille/large-print/audio versions). Group mental ability tests: Kuhlmann-Anderson (KAT, 8th ed., 8 levels, nonverbal at lower levels, scores as deviation IQs or percentile bands); Henmon-Nelson (single g score, norms by age and by grade, low ceiling, caution below 80 or above 130); Cognitive Abilities Test (CogAT, verbal/quantitative/nonverbal, good for poor readers and ESL, sensitive to giftedness). Graduate/professional entrance: GRE (verbal GRE-V, quantitative GRE-Q, analytical GRE-A – essay since 2002; overpredicts younger, underpredicts older students; prone to grade inflation); Miller Analogies Test (strictly verbal, 120 analogies in 60 minutes, has an age bias); LSAT (reading comprehension, logical reasoning, analytical reasoning). Early childhood / readiness: Metropolitan Readiness Tests (6th ed.); Boehm Test of Basic Concepts (relational concepts). School readiness = prerequisite skills enabling the learner to profit from instruction. Occupational / personnel selection I/O psychology emphasises criterion-related validity for selection – tests should correlate strongly with the criterion of job performance. Guion noted the difficulty of predicting complex behaviour (partly situation-dependent) from simple tests. Autobiographical data via a Biographical Information Blank, scored by empirical keying : contrast a successful and an unsuccessful group, find which biodata items discriminate, and weight them. Employment interview: reliability assessed by correlating different interviewers; prone to halo bias (rating high/low on all dimensions from a global impression); panel interviews raise reliability. Cognitive ability tests: general (Wonderlic Personnel Test – 50 items in 12 minutes, a speeded test, points added for those 30+; Shipley, Wesman); mechanical (Bennett); clerical (Minnesota Clerical Test); the multiple-aptitude GATB (12 tests, 9 factors, 3 composites). Personality in selection: most personality–proficiency correlations are negligible, but specific criteria predict better, and the Big Five (especially Conscientiousness) show useful operational validity (corrected for sampling error, range restriction, criterion unreliability). The CPI predicts managerial potential; the Inwald Personality Inventory and MMPI screen law enforcement; the Hogan Personality Inventory (built on the Big Five) predicts performance across settings. The added unique information a test gives is its incremental validity . Integrity tests: attitudes toward theft + overt admissions; overt vs personality-based types. Work samples (a miniature replica of the job) and situational exercises (the white-collar equivalent, for managerial selection). Military The ASVAB is used across the U.S. armed services – a multiple-aptitude battery for grades 11–12 with 10 subtests (general science, arithmetic reasoning, word knowledge, paragraph comprehension, numerical operations, coding speed, auto/shop, mathematics knowledge, mechanical comprehension, electronics information) grouped into academic, occupational, and overall composites. Clinical & counselling The WAIS and Stanford-Binet are staples; clinicians also do profile analysis – examining the pattern of subtest scores via three procedures: evaluating scatter (V–P differences, subtest variation), interpreting features against base-rate data , and matching score patterns to clinical syndromes (Alzheimer's, learning disability, anxiety). Later research found little significance in scatter and favoured combining objective scores with qualitative clinical interpretation. Specific learning disability is diagnosed when there is a severe discrepancy between intellectual ability and achievement, and the child is not achieving commensurate with age and ability despite appropriate education. Tools: Kaufman Test of Educational Achievement; Woodcock-Johnson; Stanford-Binet, K-ABC, Wechsler scales (for global index + qualitative deficits). Dynamic assessment deliberately departs from standardised administration – " testing the limits " and learning-potential assessment using a test–teach–test format. Behavioural assessment From the behavioural movement (1960s–70s), many clinicians shifted to directly assessing the target behaviour (motor responses, physiological responses like heart rate, and verbal reports). Lang & Lazovik's (1963) classic desensitisation paper introduced three still-used strategies: the Fear Survey Schedule (FSS) (50 fears rated 1–7), the Behavioural Avoidance Test (BAT) (motor approach to a phobic object), and the Fear Thermometer (rate discomfort 1–10). Behavioural assessment is integrated with treatment and formalised as the single-case experimental design . Four basic measurement approaches for ongoing behaviour: Method What it records Note Permanent products A lasting trace/result of behaviour (blood alcohol level, weight loss, a wet bed) Behaviour is inferred from the product; minimal observer time, high inter-rater agreement, but no guarantee the behaviour was performed appropriately. Event recording Tally the rate of the target behaviour Only for behaviours with clear beginning and end points; low-frequency behaviours need longer periods. Duration recording How long the behaviour lasts (per occurrence, cumulative, or % of total time) Requires discrete limits. Interval recording (time sampling) Whether the behaviour occurs in chosen time intervals For behaviours with unclear limits/rate; high inter-rater reliability; cannot distinguish frequency from duration within an interval. For inter-rater reliability, behavioural assessors use two observers; a primary observer and an independent checker who rates one-third to one-half of periods. By convention, a Pearson correlation ≥ 0.80, or 80% inter-rater agreement (interval recording), is acceptable. High-yield Setting → favoured validity: achievement/education = content; aptitude & personnel = criterion-related. Personnel: empirical keying, halo bias, incremental and operational validity. Behavioural assessment's four recording methods: permanent products, event, duration, interval (time sampling). 11. Structured personality-test construction The one idea. There are four strategies for building a structured (objective) personality test, grouped into deductive (logical-content, theoretical) and empirical (criterion-group, factor-analytic). Knowing which test was built by which strategy is a perennial exam target. Deductive strategies Logical-content strategy Items are written whose content logically taps the trait. Examples: Woodworth Personal Data Sheet – the first personality inventory; a "paper-and-pencil psychiatric interview" giving a single global score. Items endorsed by ≥25% of normals were excluded (to cut false positives); only symptoms occurring twice as often in a neurotic group as in normals were kept. Bell Adjustment Inventory – multidimensional: Home, Health, Social, Vocational/Occupational, Economic, Emotional functioning. Bernreuter Personality Inventory – ages 13+, six traits (introversion, confidence, sociability…). Mooney Problem Checklist (1950) – a list of problems recurring in case histories and students' written statements. Theoretical strategy Items are derived from a personality theory. Edwards Personal Preference Schedule (EPPS) – based on Murray's (1938) need system (achievement, deference, exhibition…); Edwards selected 15 needs and, to combat social-desirability response bias, paired items of comparable desirability in a forced-choice format. Choosing between two needs yields an ipsative score (relative, not absolute). A consistency scale repeats 15 item pairs.
