A design-thinking workflow The notes use the design-thinking arc: Empathize → Ideate (and beyond): Brainstorming rules: defer judgment; encourage wild ideas; build on others' ideas; go for quantity; diverge and converge; brainstorm often. Mash-up : connect two unrelated ideas into one (the IDEO "node" school desk). Reframing the problem : e.g. "the elevator is too slow" (solution: new lift/upgrade motor) reframed as "the wait is annoying" (solution: play music, put up TV screens). Reframing as "How might we…?" questions (e.g. "How might we make bathrooms safe for the elderly?") opens new solution spaces. 4. Thinking Thinking is the manipulation of mental representations of information. The representations may be words, visual images, sounds, or abstract symbols; thinking transforms them into new forms to reach goals, solve problems, reason, and decide. Mental images Thought can use mental images : representations in the mind that resemble the object or event represented. Classic findings (Kosslyn; Shepard & Metzler) show mental images behave like physical ones: the eye takes longer to scan a large mental image just as it does a large real one, and we can mentally rotate images, with larger rotations taking proportionally longer (mental-rotation experiments). This implies mental images preserve spatial, analog properties of the real thing. Concepts A concept is a mental category that groups objects, events, or people sharing common properties. Concepts let us organise complex phenomena into simpler, usable categories so we don't treat every new instance as wholly unique. Some concepts can be defined by a clear set of properties (e.g. geometric shapes such as a square: a figure with four equal sides and four right angles summing to 360°), but most everyday concepts are fuzzier and are better captured by prototypes . Prototypes A prototype is the most typical, representative example of a concept. Because real categories vary so much (think of the variation among "dogs", from a chihuahua to a Great Dane: both have fur, four legs, a tail, but the similarities end there), we judge category membership by closeness to the prototype rather than by a rigid definition. Propositions A proposition is a meaningful unit of knowledge that expresses a single idea or relationship and that can be judged true or false. Much of our knowledge is stored as networks of propositions linking concepts. Propositional thought is typically expressed in language. Language and thinking The relationship between language and thought is a central question. The linguistic-relativity (Whorfian) hypothesis holds that the language we speak shapes how we perceive and think about the world (e.g. the number of colour terms a language has may influence how speakers categorise colour). The stronger claim, that language wholly determines thought, is largely rejected; the milder claim, that language can influence thought, retains support. Either way, language is the chief vehicle through which propositional thinking is encoded and communicated. 5. Concepts & categorization The fundamental unit of symbolic knowledge is the concept : an idea about something that provides a means of understanding the world. We use stored concepts to think, solve problems, and make decisions. Categorization is the process by which concepts are organised: a category is itself a concept that points out equivalences among other concepts based on shared features or similarity to a prototype. A category is a class of similar things that share either an essential core or some similarity in perceptual, biological, or functional properties. The classical (feature-based) view The classical view holds that all instances of a concept share fundamental defining features, and those features are individually necessary and collectively sufficient for membership. Its assumptions: concepts are lists of features; membership is clear-cut (in or out); and all members are created equal . This view fits scientific taxonomies and artificial concepts : it lets us correctly categorise atypical objects (bats as mammals, tomatoes as fruits, coconuts as nuts). Definition Necessary and sufficient features : a feature is necessary if every member must have it; a set is sufficient if having all of them guarantees membership. The classical view says category features are both. Why the classical view fails: graded structure Semantic memory generally does not use necessary-and-sufficient rules. Real categories are loose and fuzzy , and members vary in how well they fit ( graded membership ). Related principles: Central tendency : there is a mental core/centre where the best members live. Typicality effect : items differ in how typical they are judged to be (a robin is a "better" bird than a penguin). Novick (2003) found airplanes' rated typicality as vehicles spiked for about a month after the 9/11 attacks, then returned to baseline, showing typicality is context-sensitive. Family resemblance (Wittgenstein): members share some features without any one feature being shared by all. Correlated attributes : real-world features co-occur (things with wings often also have beaks). Trap Artificial vs natural concepts. Artificial concepts can be clearly defined by rules (a tomato is a fruit by botanists' criteria). Natural concepts have no fixed defining features, are "fuzzy around the edges", yet more accurately reflect the messy natural world. Probabilistic theories: prototype vs exemplar Probabilistic theories assume categories form by accumulating probabilities and likelihoods across experience: Prototype theory : a category is summarised by a prototype , an average of all your experiences with members: a central, idealised representation that may match no individual member. A typical example is judged quickly because it is highly similar to the prototype . Exemplar theory : we store many specific exemplars (individual encountered instances). A typical example is judged quickly because it resembles many stored exemplars . The two often make the same predictions and can be hard to distinguish. Chin-Parker & Ross (2004) oriented learners to either "diagnostic" features (must-have, classical-flavoured) or "prototypical" features (typically-present); people later showed sensitivity only to the feature type they had learned with, suggesting both kinds of representation are used depending on the task. High-yield Prototype = one averaged ideal you compare against. Exemplar = many remembered specific instances you compare against. Both are probabilistic and both explain typicality effects. Problems with probabilistic theories Circularity problem : how does memory know which experiences to average into a category without already knowing what the category is? Ad hoc categories (Barsalou): people generate categories on the fly without prior experience (e.g. "things to grab from a burning house"). These show graded structure, have a prototype, and exhibit typicality effects, yet are conjured by context (gray is more like white in the context of hair colour but more like black in the context of clouds), revealing how flexible semantic memory is. Explanation-based (theory) view and essentialism The explanation-based view says semantic categories are essentially theories of the world we create to explain why things are the way they are: structures we impose on the world, which may or may not reflect how the world actually is. (A shoe and a brick can share a category, "things to pound a nail with if you don't have a hammer", while a shoe and a sock fall in different categories.) People use causal relations among members to infer the internal structure of new members. Embodied cognition (Borghi, Glenberg & Kaschak, 2004): perspective shapes concept use. People told "you are driving a car" responded faster to interior parts (speedometer); those told "you are washing a car" responded faster to exterior parts (trunk). Psychological essentialism : people treat category members as if they share an underlying, often invisible essence , and categorise based on beliefs (right or wrong) about that essence, even where no real essence exists (e.g. "TOOL"). 6. Reasoning Reasoning draws conclusions from premises or evidence. It is not encapsulated (enclosed/isolated): it is woven through a wide array of cognitive functions, and even visual perception contains elements of reasoning. Two forms of reasoning Deductive reasoning : from general premises to a necessarily valid (or invalid) conclusion, assuming the premises are true . Top-down; truth-preserving. Inductive reasoning : testing the truth of general statements from specific observations. Bottom-up; the engine of theory formation ; conclusions are probable, not certain. Syllogisms A syllogism is a three-statement logical form: two premises taken to be true, then a conclusion based on them. The two premises state a class-inclusion (subset–superset) relation among abstract elements A, B, C; they are the major premise and minor premise ; the third statement is the conclusion . Abstract form: All A are B; All B are C; Therefore all A are C. Crucially, the truth of the premises is separate from the validity of the argument . A syllogism can be valid yet have a false premise (and thus a false conclusion). Applying syllogisms to the real world is a two-step process : (1) determine whether the syllogism is valid ; (2) if valid, determine the empirical truth of the premises. The four types of premises are: universal affirmative (All A are B), universal negative (No A are B), particular affirmative (Some A are B), and particular negative (Some A are not B). Definition Valid = the conclusion follows logically from the premises (structure). True = the statement matches reality (content). A valid argument can be untrue; a true statement can sit in an invalid argument. Belief bias Belief bias is the tendency to accept believable conclusions and reject unbelievable ones, irrespective of logical validity. Evans et al. (1983) showed that accepting invalid conclusions as valid was dramatically more common when the conclusion was believable than when it was unbelievable. Example trap: "All poodles are animals; all animals are wild; therefore all poodles are wild", logically valid in form, but rejected because the premise is false and the conclusion unbelievable. Euler circles and how to test a syllogism Euler circles (diagrams showing class relations) help determine whether a syllogism holds. Performance improves when people draw diagrams or generate specific examples, but only if they actively try to find an interpretation that makes the syllogism false . Formally, evaluating a conclusion by the predicate calculus requires three steps: (1) consider all possible interpretations of premises and conclusion; (2) consider all possible combinations of meanings of the major and minor premises; (3) check whether all possible meanings of the conclusion are consistent with all possible combinations of the premises. If a single interpretation of the conclusion fails to follow from a single possible combination of premise meanings, no valid conclusion may be drawn. Common errors and their causes Ceraso & Provitera (1971): people correctly identify a valid conclusion only about three-quarters of the time, and often endorse a conclusion as valid when one cannot say for certain. Systematic patterns: When the major premise is a universal affirmative (all) and the minor is a particular affirmative (some) , people overwhelmingly accept a " some " conclusion (and likewise when both are "some"). When both premises are universal negatives , people often accept a " no " conclusion. Three reasons for these errors: cognitive constraints (memory limits), illicit conversion (illegitimately reversing the terms of a premise), and meaning & knowledge (belief bias). Conditional reasoning A conditional-reasoning problem has two parts: a conditional clause ("if P then Q") and some evidence about P or Q. The "if" clause is the antecedent (P); the "then" clause is the consequent (Q). The task: decide what follows logically. For "If it rains, the streets will be wet", the four cases are P, not-P, Q, not-Q: Conditional Evidence given Conclusion Validity Name If P, then Q P (affirm antecedent) Therefore Q Valid Modus ponens If P, then Q Not P (deny antecedent) No conclusion Invalid (denying antecedent) If P, then Q Q (affirm consequent) No conclusion Invalid (affirming consequent) If P, then Q Not Q (deny consequent) Therefore not P Valid Modus tollens People handle modus ponens easily but find modus tollens (denying the consequent) much harder. Example of the affirming-the-consequent error: "If Susan is angry, then I am upset; I am upset; therefore Susan is angry" (invalid). Errors fall into three broad categories: form errors (illicit conversion / reversing conditions), search errors ( confirmation bias : searching only for positive, confirming evidence), and memory-related errors (memory limits; we tend to use mental models rather than formal logic). High-yield Only two valid conditional inferences: modus ponens (affirm antecedent → affirm consequent) and modus tollens (deny consequent → deny antecedent). The two invalid forms are affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent . 7. Problem solving Problem solving is the process used when you want to reach a specified goal but the solution is not immediately obvious, because you are missing information and/or it is unclear how to reach the goal (Bassok & Novick, 2012). Every problem has three components : the initial state (the situation at the start), the goal state (the situation when solved), and the obstacles (restrictions that make it hard to move from initial to goal state). Understanding the problem (representation) Constructing a well-organised mental representation of the problem is crucial. Understanding involves: paying attention to the relevant information; using various methods of representing the problem (diagrams, symbols); and using situated and embodied cognition . (Classic catch: the "bus driver" word problem that buries the simple question, "What is the driver's name?", under irrelevant boarding figures, illustrating how attention to the right information governs success.) Algorithms vs heuristics Algorithm : a method that will always produce a solution, though it can be inefficient (e.g. exhaustive search ). Guarantees success but can be slow. Heuristic : a general rule that is usually right. Faster but not guaranteed. Example: the anagrams LSSTNEUIAMYOUL and IPMHYLOD can be cracked by exhaustive search (guaranteed but slow) or by a heuristic (reject implausible consonant clusters like LT, TN). The heuristic is quick but may misfire: in the second anagram, ignoring the "LY" combination would be a mistake. Trap Algorithm = always works, may be slow. Heuristic = usually works, faster, not guaranteed. Exhaustive search is the prototypical algorithm. Specific heuristics Analogy : use the solution to a similar earlier problem to solve a new one (the Wright brothers modelled airplane wings on bird wings). The big challenge is to find the problem isomorph , the abstract puzzle underneath, a set of problems with the same underlying structure and solution but different surface details. People fail when they fix on surface features rather than structural features; they use analogy correctly more often after solving several structurally similar problems first. Means-ends analysis : identify the "ends" then the "means" to reach them. Two components: break the main problem into subproblems (each with a defined initial and goal state), and work to reduce the distance between initial and goal state for each subproblem. Sometimes solving requires temporarily increasing the distance (moving "away" from the goal), which people are reluctant to do. Hill-climbing : consistently choose the alternative that appears to lead most directly toward the goal. Useful when you can see only the immediate next step, but it can lead you astray, because it ignores indirect routes with greater long-term payoff (e.g. taking a job right after college for immediate salary when a graduate degree would yield more in the long run). Gestalt insight, functional fixedness, and mental set The Gestalt tradition emphasised sudden insight : a problem is restructured and the solution appears whole. Two classic blocks (covered in detail in section 8) are functional fixedness (Karl Duncker's candle problem) and mental set (Luchins' water-jar problem), both arising from over-reliance on top-down processing. 8. Factors influencing problem solving Effective problem solving needs an ideal blend of top-down (knowledge-driven) and bottom-up (data-driven) processing. Experts use top-down processing well, leaning on knowledge, memory, and strategy. But mental set and functional fixedness interfere precisely because they rely too heavily on top-down processing. Three factors dominate: expertise, mental set, and functional fixedness. Expertise An expert shows consistently exceptional skill on representative tasks in an area, with superior long-term memory and a detailed conceptual structure. Experts differ from novices on several dimensions: Dimension Experts vs novices Knowledge base Broader, deeper; detailed, specific schemas. Memory Better but very domain-specific : chess experts recall ~50,000 "chunks" (familiar piece arrangements) and far outperform novices on real game positions, but are only slightly better on random arrangements. Strategies Approach novel problems systematically (novices are haphazard); use the means-ends heuristic effectively; emphasise structural similarity in analogies (novices are distracted by surface similarity). Speed & accuracy Much faster and more accurate; operations become automatic; on tasks like anagrams they may use parallel rather than serial processing. Metacognition Better at judging problem difficulty, allocating time, and recovering from errors, but they underestimate how long novices will need (novices judge their own difficulty more accurately). Mental set Mental set (Luchins' water-jar problem ): individuals keep using the same solution that worked on previous problems even when an easier method exists; they close the mind prematurely. Top-down processing is over-active. EEG work shows people have greater changes in event-related potentials (ERPs) on trials where they break a set. Mental set is linked to Carol Dweck's (2006) mindset concept: a fixed mindset (intelligence is fixed; effort won't help; give up on improving) hampers flexible problem solving, whereas a growth mindset (abilities can be cultivated; seek challenges) supports it. Functional fixedness Functional fixedness (Karl Duncker's candle problem ) is the tendency to assign fixed functions to objects, so we fail to see other useful features. Like mental set, it occurs when top-down processing is over-active, but it concerns physical objects rather than problem-solving strategies. Objects normally have fixed functions (a screwdriver tightens screws; a coin buys things), and in daily life, with many tools available, fixedness rarely handicaps us. It bites when we apply a fixed function too rigidly: if you have no screwdriver, a coin can substitute, but functional fixedness keeps you from seeing it. Trap Mental set vs functional fixedness. Mental set = stuck on a strategy/method (water-jar). Functional fixedness = stuck on an object's usual function (candle/box of tacks). Both stem from excessive top-down processing. 9. Decision making Decision making vs problem solving (Gilhooly, 1996): the two overlap (decision making requires some problem solving, and problem solving requires deciding which strategy to use), but differ in emphasis. In problem solving the focus is on selecting actions and generating options ; in decision making the options are usually already presented and you choose among them without the load of option-generation. Classical (normative) decision theory Early "economic man/woman" models assumed decision makers are: fully informed about all options and outcomes, infinitely sensitive to subtle distinctions, and fully rational . The refined version, subjective expected utility (SEU) theory , predicts people reach well-reasoned decisions by: considering all known alternatives; using the maximum available information; carefully (if subjectively) weighing costs/risks against benefits; calculating the probability of outcomes; and applying sound reasoning to maximise utility (subjective value) given probability. Definition Expected utility = the subjective value (utility) of an outcome weighted by its probability. Normative theory says a rational chooser picks the option with the highest expected utility. Bounded rationality and satisficing In the 1950s Herbert Simon (1957) challenged unlimited rationality. We are not irrational, but show bounded rationality : rational within limits of information, time, and cognitive capacity. His key strategy is satisficing : rather than computing the option that maximises gains across the whole universe of options, we consider options one by one and pick the first that is "satisfactory", just good enough to meet a minimum level of acceptability. Elimination by aspects Amos Tversky (1972) extended bounded rationality with elimination by aspects , used when there are far more alternatives than we can reasonably weigh: focus on one aspect (attribute), set a minimum criterion, and eliminate every option failing it; pick a second aspect, set a criterion, eliminate more; continue this sequential process until one option remains. In practice we often combine elimination-by-aspects or satisficing to narrow the field to a few options, then apply more thorough strategies. (The notes also reference Galotti's general phases of decision making.) High-yield SEU (maximise utility × probability) is the normative ideal; satisficing (first "good enough" option) and elimination by aspects (sequential attribute cut-offs) are Simon's and Amos Tversky's descriptive , bounded-rationality alternatives. 10. Decision-making styles Rowe & Boulgarides (1983) proposed a Cognitive-Contingency model of decision styles, combining a person's cognitive complexity with their value orientation (concern for task vs people). It is distinct from leadership/managerial style and is measured by the Decision Style Inventory (DSI) : 20 questions (five per each of four factors), ~10 minutes, self-scoring, with over 90% face validity and over 70% test-retest reliability, taken by 7,000+ people. The four-force model and the decision process The four-force model gives the contextual variables (echoing Kurt Lewin): the individual's reaction to the work environment , the people in the organisation, the task/function , and the individual's personal needs . The simplified decision process has three phases: (1) perception/filtering of stimuli (the "information style", subject to overload and bias); (2) cognition (problem solving, negotiation, heuristics, analysis, evaluation, risk-taking); and (3) action (where managerial/leadership behaviour is most overt; power, persuasion, motivation). The two axes and four styles The DSI matrix crosses cognitive complexity (vertical: low = few/rigid rules, high need for structure; high = integrates diverse cues, high tolerance for ambiguity) with value orientation (horizontal: task/technical focus = "left brain"; people/social focus = "right brain"). This yields four styles: Style Complexity × value Characteristics Directive Low complexity, task-oriented Low tolerance for ambiguity; focus on technical problems; high need for power; uses limited information and few alternatives; emphasises speed and action; aggressive, authoritarian, short-range, tight controls; very effective at getting results. Analytic High complexity, task-oriented Abstract thinker; high tolerance for ambiguity; uses considerable information; careful examination of alternatives; optimises solutions; enjoys challenges; innovative; prefers written reports; seeks variety. Conceptual High complexity, people-oriented Wants elaborate, broad treatment of problems; considers many alternatives; systems perspective; future-oriented; highly creative; values quality, openness, shared goals; needs praise; independent; prefers loose control. Behavioural Low complexity, people-oriented Deep concern for fellow employees; strong need for affiliation; supportive, good listener, receptive, communicates easily; warm; accepts loose control; prefers meetings to reports; uses little data; short-range, people-oriented. Individuals have one or more dominant styles and one or more back-up styles; few people change their basic style over time, but shifts occur under stress or information overload . The signature finding: under stress all styles tend to shift toward Directive (e.g. high analytics shift to directive). The directive style "explodes" when stressed; the analytic is the "cool cucumber" who turns directive; the conceptual becomes erratic (diverges rather than converges); the behavioural avoids the issue. Style also shifts with age/maturity (older managers more considerate; younger people lower on directive, higher on behavioural). Applications: training, reorganisation/job matching, personnel selection, career planning, and creativity development. Mnemonic The four DSI quadrants: D-A-C-B = D irective (task, simple), A nalytic (task, complex), C onceptual (people, complex), B ehavioural (people, simple). Under stress, everyone drifts toward Directive . 11. Heuristics in decision making Daniel Kahneman won the 2002 Nobel Prize in economics for this work. With Amos Tversky he proposed that a small number of heuristics guide human judgment under uncertainty. The classics: representativeness , availability , and anchoring and adjustment , plus the framing effect. The representativeness heuristic We judge that a sample is likely if it is similar (representative) to the population it came from. Asked which coin-toss sequence is more likely, T H H T H T or H H H T T T, most pick the first because it "looks random", though both are equally probable. The danger: it is so persuasive that people ignore statistics they should use, especially sample size and base rates. Small-sample fallacy (Daniel Kahneman & Amos Tversky, 1972): asked whether a small hospital (~15 births/day) or large hospital (~45 births/day) is more likely to report a day with >60% boys, most say "equal", but a small sample more easily yields extreme proportions. We forget that deviations from population proportions are likelier in small samples, which fuels stereotyping from a handful of group members. A remedy: meet many members of the target group. Base-rate fallacy (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973): we ignore how often something occurs in the population. Given a description matching the stereotype of a computer-science student (Tom W), people judge by representativeness and ignore the base rate even when it is provided. Conjunction fallacy (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983): by the conjunction rule the probability of two events together cannot exceed the probability of either alone. Yet people judge "bank teller AND feminist" more probable than "bank teller", because "feminist" is representative of the described person (single, outspoken, philosophy major, social-justice activist). Traced directly to representativeness. High-yield Representativeness breeds three errors: the small-sample fallacy (ignoring sample size), the base-rate fallacy (ignoring population frequency), and the conjunction fallacy (rating A&B more likely than A). The availability heuristic We estimate frequency or probability by how easily relevant examples come to mind. Easy retrieval feels like high frequency, even when retrieval ease is uncorrelated with true frequency, biasing decisions. Influencing factors: Recency : recent items come to mind faster, so we overrate them. MacLeod & Campbell (1992): people made to recall pleasant past events later judged pleasant future events more likely; the reverse for unpleasant events. Familiarity : familiar items inflate frequency estimates. Brown & Siegler (1992): during a period when El Salvador was constantly in the news and Indonesia rarely, students estimated similar populations for the two countries, although Indonesia's population was ~35 times larger. Illusory correlation : believing two variables are related (e.g. a group has certain traits) when accurate tabulation shows no significant relationship, a stereotyping mechanism driven by what's available in memory. A helpful counterpart is the recognition heuristic , which can actually improve accuracy (recognised options are sometimes the better bet). The anchoring and adjustment heuristic We start from a first approximation (the anchor ) and adjust insufficiently from it. The anchor restricts our search for relevant information to numbers near it, even when the anchor is arbitrary. Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman's product demonstration: estimating 8×7×6×… vs 1×2×3×… (descending vs ascending) gave median estimates of 2,250 vs 512 , driven purely by the first (anchor) number. Anchoring also corrupts confidence intervals : people's 98% intervals contain the true answer only ~60% of the time (over-confidence), as Slovic et al. (1974) illustrate with a chained estimate of US car imports anchored on rough early figures. Englich & Mussweiler (2001): experienced trial judges' sentences were swayed by an obviously unqualified "prosecutor's" demand, 28 months after a 12-month demand vs 36 months after a 34-month demand. The framing effect The framing effect shows that the outcome of a decision depends on (a) the background context and (b) the wording of the question. Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman (1981) "Asian disease" problem: framed as lives saved , 72% chose the certain Program A (saving 200 for sure) over the risky Program B (one-in-three chance of saving 600), people were risk-averse for gains . Framed as deaths , only 22% chose the certain Program C (400 die for sure) and 78% chose the risky Program D, people were risk-seeking for losses , even though the four programs are statistically equivalent. Background context matters too: 88% would re-buy a lost theatre ticket when a $10 bill was lost (different mental account), but only 46% when the $10 ticket itself was lost. This asymmetry, risk-averse for gains and risk-seeking for losses, plus reference-dependence and loss aversion, is the heart of Kahneman & Tversky's prospect theory , the descriptive alternative to expected-utility theory. High-yield Prospect theory / framing : identical outcomes drive opposite choices depending on wording. People are risk-averse for gains ("lives saved" → take the sure thing) and risk-seeking for losses ("deaths" → gamble). Losses loom larger than equivalent gains (loss aversion). Trap Don't conflate the heuristics. Representativeness = "is it similar to the category?" (ignores base rates). Availability = "how easily do examples come to mind?" (recency/familiarity). Anchoring = "start from a number and adjust too little." Framing = "the wording/reference point flips the choice."

title: Unit 7 — Personality, Emotion & Motivation
text: Unit 7 — Personality, Emotion & Motivation The whole of personality from first principles — the psychodynamic founders (Sigmund Freud, Carl Jung, Alfred Adler) and the neo-Freudians, the trait and type measurers (Gordon Allport, Cattell's 16PF, Eysenck's PEN, the Big Five and beyond), the humanistic-existential self (Abraham Maslow, Carl Rogers, May), and the behavioural / social-cognitive theorists (Albert Bandura, Julian Rotter, Walter Mischel, Martin Seligman, Kelly) — then how personality is assessed, and finally the affective and developmental engine behind it: theories of emotion, stress and the GAS, theories of motivation, attachment and emotional-social development, and the exploratory/sensation-seeking drive. Built from the Unit 7 source decks and taught to NIMHANS/MET depth, losing no named theorist or term. In this book Freud & the psychoanalytic approach Neo-Freudians: Jung, Adler, Horney, ego & object relations Erikson & lifespan identity Trait & type approaches Humanistic: Maslow & Rogers Existential: Rollo May Behavioural & social-cognitive: Bandura, Rotter, Mischel Cognitive approaches: Kelly, Lewin, Seligman, Kohlberg Assessment of personality Emotion & its physiology; theories of emotion Stress, the GAS & conflict Theories of motivation Emotional & social development Attachment Exploratory behaviour, curiosity & sensation seeking Fast glossary (A–Z) 1. Freud & the psychoanalytic approach The one idea. Sigmund Freud saw the psychological world as a series of opposing tensions (for example the tension between selfishness and society). Underlying every tension were inner pressures that strive for relief. The motor of the whole system is instinct : the German term is Trieb — a driving force or impulse. Instincts are the basic elements of personality, the motivating forces that drive behaviour and determine its direction. Instincts and motivation Life instincts (Eros). Serve the survival of the individual and the species by satisfying needs for food, water, air and sex. They are oriented toward growth and development. The psychic energy of the life instincts is the libido (Latin for desire/lust). Cathexis. The libido can be attached to, or invested in, objects — Sigmund Freud called this cathexis . Death instincts (Thanatos). In opposition to the life instincts, Freud postulated a destructive/death instinct. One component is the aggressive drive — the wish to die, turned outward against objects other than the self. Levels of personality (the topographic model) Level What it holds Conscious All sensations and experiences in immediate awareness. Preconscious / subconscious The storehouse of memories that can be brought to awareness. Unconscious The most important level and the major portion of personality; holds instincts, drives, desires and emotionally charged memories. The structure of the mind (the structural model) Id — operates on the pleasure principle ; strives solely to satisfy desires and reduce inner tension. It can only act through reflex or through wish-fulfilling hallucinatory/fantasy experience, which Sigmund Freud called primary-process thought . Ego — based on the reality principle ; the structure that develops to deal with the real world using perception, recognition, judgement and memory ( secondary-process thought ). Superego — based on the morality principle ; represents society's demands. Through praise/punishment children learn good and bad: punished behaviours form the conscience ; praised behaviours form the ego-ideal . When the ego and especially the superego do not do their job, elements of the id slip out as parapraxes — mistakes that reveal the unconscious. Freudian slips (errors in speech or writing) are more common when a person is tired or distracted, because defences are down and unconscious impulses surface. Psychosexual stages of development Stage Age Erogenous zone / conflict Fixation outcome Oral 0–1 Mouth; pleasure from sucking; id dominant Oral-incorporative (optimism, dependency) vs oral-aggressive/sadistic (pessimism, hostility, aggressiveness) from painful teething Anal 1–3 Toilet training interferes with gratification from defecation Anal-aggressive (hostile, sadistic) vs anal-retentive (stubborn, stingy, hoarding, rigid, compulsively neat, obstinate) Phallic 4–5 Incestuous fantasies; Oedipus/Electra complex; castration anxiety; superego develops Phallic character — strong narcissism Latency 5–puberty Sublimation of the sex instinct — Genital Adolescence–adulthood Sex-role identity, adult social relationships Genital type — finds satisfaction in love and work (work = acceptable sublimation of id impulses) Definition Fixation. An arresting of part of the libido at an earlier psychosexual stage because of excessive frustration or gratification, leaving a characteristic adult personality pattern. Anxiety and the defence mechanisms For Sigmund Freud, anxiety is a feeling of fear and dread without an obvious cause. He proposed three types: reality anxiety (fear of tangible dangers), neurotic anxiety (id–ego conflict), and moral anxiety (id–superego conflict). When anxiety builds, the ego deploys defence mechanisms : Defence What it does Repression Unconscious denial of the existence of something that causes anxiety Denial Denying an external threat or traumatic event Reaction formation Expressing an id impulse that is the opposite of the true one Projection Attributing a disturbing impulse to someone else Regression Retreating to an earlier, less frustrating period and acting childishly Rationalization Reinterpreting behaviour to make it more acceptable, less threatening Displacement Shifting id impulses from a threatening/unavailable object to an available substitute Sublimation Diverting instinctual energy into socially acceptable behaviours Mnemonic Three anxieties map to the three conflicts: Reality = external world; Neurotic = id vs ego; Moral = id vs superego. "RNM = world, ego, conscience." 2. Neo-Freudians: Jung, Adler, Horney, ego & object relations Carl Jung — analytical psychology Jung divided the psyche into three parts: Conscious ego — the conscious aspect of personality; embodies the sense of self. Personal identity (ego) develops around age 4. Personal unconscious — thoughts/feelings not currently conscious, including material that is merely unimportant now and material actively repressed because it is ego-threatening. Collective unconscious — a deeper, transpersonal layer made of powerful emotional symbols, the archetypes — emotional patterns common to all people, formed from the beginnings of human time, that predispose us to react in predictable ways to recurring stimuli. Common archetypes Anima (the female element in a man) and animus (the male element in a woman). Persona (Latin for "mask") — the socially acceptable front we present to others. Shadow — the dark, unacceptable side: shameful desires and motives we would rather not admit. Self — represents unity, integration and harmony of the total personality; striving toward this wholeness is the ultimate goal of life (involves balancing all parts). Mother — generativity and fertility, evoked by an actual or figurative mother figure. Hero — the strong, good force that battles the enemy to rescue another. Its opposite is the demon (cruelty and evil). Complexes, libido and energy A complex is a group of emotionally charged feelings, thoughts and ideas organised around a particular theme (e.g. power, status) in the personal unconscious. Its strength is set by its libido ("value"); complexes may be conscious or unconscious, and those out of conscious control can intrude on consciousness. Jung substantiated complexes with his word-association test , measuring response delays, respiration, galvanic skin response and memory on retest. Jung used libido in two ways: a diffuse general life energy , and (like Sigmund Freud) a narrower psychic energy that fuels the psyche — but for Jung this is not necessarily sexual . Three principles of psychic energy: opposition (conflict between opposing tendencies generates energy), equivalence (energy withdrawn from one activity is transferred elsewhere), and entropy (a tendency toward balance/equilibrium — the ideal is equal distribution over all structures). Functions, attitudes and individuation Functions: rational (judging) = thinking & feeling; irrational (perceiving) = sensing & intuiting. Attitudes: extroversion (libido directed at the external world) and introversion (inward focus). Two attitudes × four functions = eight psychological types , the basis of the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) . Individuation — psychological health from integrating all conscious and unconscious facets. Steps: confront the unconscious → dethrone the persona → accept our dark sides → accept our anima/animus → transcend. Alfred Adler — individual psychology Carl Jung coined "complex," but the inferiority complex is Adler's. Overwhelming helplessness can produce it; a person may fabricate a compensating superiority complex . Spoiling and neglect by parents can both cause inferiority feelings. A central core of personality is the striving for superiority (perfection striving). Organ inferiority — everyone is born with some physical weakness; at this "weak link" disease takes root and the body tries to compensate elsewhere. Adler also added an aggression drive and the masculine protest (both boys and girls strive to become independent of, and equal to, the powerful adults around them; drives can be expressed directly or reversed). Fictional finalism — people strive toward imagined future goals ("fictional goals"). Three fundamental life tasks everyone must address: occupational (career), societal (friendship/social networks; expressed through social interest — the innate potential to cooperate toward personal and societal goals), and love (finding a life partner). Birth order Position Adlerian profile First-born "Dethroned" by a sibling; becomes a good organiser, conscientious, scrupulous, authoritarian and conservative (or a pseudo-parent) Second-born Born into rivalry; optimistic, competitive, ambitious — repeated failure can damage self-esteem Last-born Most pampered; driven to surpass older siblings, develops fast, often a high achiever — but over-pressure can breed a lazy, defeatist attitude Only child Matures early (more time with adults); never learned to share or compete; keenly disappointed if abilities go unrecognised Style of life — a unique character structure through which each of us strives for perfection, created by the creative power of the self . Basic styles: dominant/ruling (extreme types attack others, become sadists/delinquents/sociopaths; less virulent become alcoholics, drug addicts or suicides), getting (dependent, expects to receive), avoiding (sidesteps problems to avoid failure), and the healthy socially useful type. Karen Horney Rejected Freud's penis envy ; argued women's inferiority feelings stem from upbringing and an overemphasis on securing a man's love. Proposed womb envy — men's unconscious envy of women's ability to bear children. Childhood is dominated by the safety need (security and freedom from fear). Security depends on parents; lack of warmth and affection weakens it. Basic anxiety — a child's feeling of being alone, helpless and insecure, arising from problems in the parental relationship. In reaction, the person settles into one of three modes of relating: passive , aggressive or withdrawn styles. Aspects of the self: the Real Self (inner core, our potential for self-realisation, damaged by parental neglect), the Despised Self (perceptions of inferiority based on others' negative evaluations), and the Ideal Self (a "tyranny of the should" — a composite of all our shoulds). Alienation from the Real Self breeds neurosis and an interpersonal coping strategy; these ideas led to modern "possible selves." Neurotic needs / neurotic trends — irrational defences against anxiety that become permanent personality features, grouped into three categories of behaviour and attitude toward oneself and others (the basis of the moving-toward / against / away grouping). Ego psychology & object relations Anna Freud brought the ego into focus, emphasising the social environment while keeping the ego linked to id and superego. Heinz Hartmann (1894–1970), sometimes called the founder of ego psychology : the ego is neither controlled by the id nor fully autonomous; it can direct self-preserving but short-term-unpleasant behaviour and functions independently to cope with society's demands. Object relations theories — "object relations" = the mental representation of significant others. The self is socially constructed through specific interpersonal interactions, not emerging purely through biological development. Margaret Mahler — studied symbiosis: some children could not form emotional ties (shutting off from the world); symbiotic psychotic children formed ties so strong they could not form a sense of self. Healthy ties with the mother (the normal symbiotic child) are vital. Melanie Klein — studied the infant's reaction to the removal of the mother's breast (the first source of satisfaction); the infant blames the mother, then resolves the conflict by understanding the mother's love is not just her breast. Extended by Stephen Mitchell into the relational perspective . Heinz Kohut — extended Alfred Adler and Klein: a key problem for anxious people is fear of losing an important love object (often the parent), which can produce narcissistic personality disorder (feeling powerless and dependent yet projecting bravado and self-aggrandisement). 3. Erik Erikson — lifespan identity & identity crises Where Sigmund Freud held personality fixed by age 5–6, Erikson argued that identity formation is a lifelong process . Personality (he focused on identity ) develops through eight stages ; the outcome of each stage depends partly on the previous one, and successful negotiation of each ego crisis is essential for optimal growth. His first five stages parallel Freud's psychosexual stages. Stage (crisis) Approx. age Favourable outcome / virtue Trust vs Mistrust 0–1 (oral) Hope Autonomy vs Shame & Doubt 1–3 (anal) Will Initiative vs Guilt 3–5 (phallic) Purpose Industry vs Inferiority 6–11 (latency) Competence Identity vs Role Confusion Adolescence (genital) Fidelity Intimacy vs Isolation Young adulthood Love Generativity vs Stagnation Middle adulthood Care Ego Integrity vs Despair Old age Wisdom High-yield Erik Erikson = psychoSOCIAL and lifelong (eight stages), against Sigmund Freud's biological, childhood-fixed psychoSEXUAL five. The adolescent crisis is identity vs role confusion ; the term identity crisis is Erikson's. 4. Trait & type approaches Jung's extroversion–introversion (as a trait) & the MBTI For Carl Jung, extroversion = an orientation toward things outside oneself; introversion = turning inward to explore one's feelings. The MBTI , based on Jung, measures introversion/extroversion plus three sub-scales: Sensation–Intuition (realism vs imagination), Thinking–Feeling (logical/objective vs personal/subjective), and Judgment–Perception (structured/judgmental vs flexible/perceptive). Gordon Allport — trait psychology "Personality is the dynamic organization within the individual of those psychophysical systems that determine … characteristic behavior and thought" (Allport, 1961). Allport considered personality discrete/discontinuous — almost two personalities, one for childhood (driven by primitive urges/reflexes) and one for adulthood (more psychological). Traits are predispositions to respond similarly to different stimuli; they are real, cause behaviour, can be shown empirically, are interrelated, and vary with the situation. Individual traits (later relabelled personal dispositions ) are unique to a person; common traits are shared by many (e.g. members of a culture). Three grades: cardinal traits (the most pervasive, powerful, dominating traits), central traits (the handful of outstanding traits describing a person), and secondary traits (least important, displayed inconspicuously and inconsistently). Functional autonomy — the motives of mature, healthy adults are no longer functionally connected to the prior experiences in which they first appeared. Perseverative functional autonomy governs low-level routine behaviours; propriate functional autonomy governs values, self-image and lifestyle (the proprium = the ego/self). Propriate functioning follows three principles: organising the energy level, mastery and competence, and propriate patterning (striving for consistency and integration). Allport described seven stages of development of the proprium from infancy to adolescence. Raymond Cattell — 16PF Defined traits as relatively permanent reaction tendencies, the basic structural units of personality. Distinguished common traits (in everyone to some degree) from unique traits (in one or a few). Used source traits (the underlying factors, obtained by factor analysis) to derive 16 basic personality factors , assessed by the Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire (16PF) . Three data sources: Q-data (self-report questionnaires), T-data (objective test/observational data from controlled test situations), and L-data (life-record data, e.g. school records). Hans Eysenck — the PEN model Using factor analysis Eysenck identified three dimensions: E — Extraversion vs introversion; N — Neuroticism vs emotional stability; P — Psychoticism vs impulse control (superego functioning). Biologically, extraverts have a lower base level of cortical arousal than introverts, so they actively seek excitement and stimulation; introverts shy away because their cortical arousal is already high. Trap Hans Eysenck's arousal logic is counter-intuitive: extraverts are under -aroused and seek stimulation; introverts are over -aroused and avoid it. Raymond Cattell = 16 factors; Eysenck = 3 (PEN); the Big Five = 5 . McCrae & Costa — the Five-Factor Model (Big Five / OCEAN) Emerged from extensive factor analyses of personality-describing adjectives and of personality tests/scales: O — Openness (to experience/culture/intellect): imaginative, witty, original, artistic vs shallow, plain, simple. C — Conscientiousness (lack of impulsivity; early research called it "Will"): cautious, dependable, persevering, organised vs careless, disorderly, undependable. E — Extroversion (surgency): energetic, enthusiastic, dominant, sociable, talkative vs shy, retiring, submissive, quiet. A — Agreeableness : friendly, cooperative, trusting, warm vs cold, quarrelsome, unkind. N — Neuroticism (emotional instability): nervous, high-strung, tense, volatile, moody, worrying vs calm, contented. Mnemonic OCEAN = Openness, Conscientiousness, Extroversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism. Extensions of the trait model Ashton & Lee — HEXACO : a six-factor model adding Honesty-Humility (H) to Emotionality, eXtraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness and Openness. Paulhus & Williams — the Dark Triad (2002): Narcissism (extreme selfishness, inflated sense of one's abilities, constant need for admiration), Machiavellianism (the need to manipulate others through cunning, deceit and unscrupulous behaviour), and Psychopathy (callous, insensitive, egocentric, antisocial, takes advantage of others using charm and often violence). Type approaches The idea of types is that there are discrete classes of people. Types are usually just the first step toward a fuller understanding of traits. The classic application is the assessment of people prone to heart disease — Type A versus Type B (see Stress). The motivational approach to traits — Henry Murray Henry Murray proposed needs related to personality, including the need for Achievement (n Ach), Affiliation (n Aff), Power (n Power) and Exhibition (n Exh). 5. Humanistic approach: Maslow & Rogers Abraham Maslow — the hierarchy of needs Maslow proposed a hierarchy of five innate needs that activate and direct behaviour, described as instinctoid (having a hereditary component). From strongest/lowest to weakest/highest: physiological → safety → belongingness and love → esteem → self-actualization . Lower needs must be at least partially satisfied before higher needs become influential. Outside the hierarchy sit the cognitive needs : the need to know and the need to understand. Self-actualization — the highest need: the maximum realisation and fulfilment of one's potentials, talents and abilities. Lower needs are deficit (deficiency, D) needs — failing to satisfy them produces a deficit/crisis; higher needs are growth (being, B) needs — their satisfaction improves health, happiness, contentment, fulfilment and longevity, but failing them produces no crisis. Physiological/safety needs arise in infancy; belongingness/esteem in adolescence; self-actualization not until midlife. The study of self-actualizers Self-actualizers run on metamotivation (B-motivation / Being-motivation) — concerned with fulfilling potential; others run on D-motivation (Deficiency) — striving to make up for something lacking. Metaneeds are states of being (goodness, uniqueness, perfection) rather than specific goal objects; failing to satisfy them produces metapathology . Conditions for self-actualization: freedom from social/self constraints, not distracted by lower needs, security in self-image and relationships (able to love and be loved), and realistic self-knowledge. Barriers: lower needs unmet; inadequate education or improper child-rearing (the ideal is a balance of permissiveness and regulation); and the Jonah complex — fear that maximising our potential will lead to a situation we cannot cope with. Self-actualization requires courage, discipline and self-control. Carl Rogers — self / actualization theory The goal of life is self-actualization , an innate tendency toward growth, part of a larger actualizing tendency spanning all physiological and psychological needs. The organismic valuing process evaluates experiences by how well they serve the actualizing tendency: growth-promoting experiences are sought, hindering ones avoided. Positive regard — the need for acceptance, love and approval, especially from the mother in infancy. Unconditional positive regard is granted freely; conditional positive regard ties love to behaviour. Internalised, regard becomes positive self-regard . Conditions of worth (akin to the Freudian superego) — seeing ourselves as worthy only under conditions acceptable to our parents; we avoid perceptions opposing them. Incongruence develops between the self-concept and threatening behaviours; we defend against anxiety by denying threatening parts of the experiential field. The fully functioning person (peak of development): awareness of all experiences with no conditions to defend against, the ability to live fully in each moment, trust in oneself, a sense of freedom and personal power, and creativity and spontaneity. Self-Determination Theory (Deci & Ryan) A contemporary outgrowth of Abraham Maslow's self-actualization. People have an innate tendency to express their interests and develop their capabilities, facilitated by focusing on intrinsic motivation (doing an activity for the interest and challenge of the activity itself). SDT specifies three basic needs whose satisfaction yields well-being: competence (mastering difficult tasks), autonomy (basing one's actions on one's own interests, needs and values) and relatedness (a close connection with others). 6. Existential approach: Rollo May Being-in-the-world (Dasein) — existentialists take a phenomenological approach: we exist in a world best understood from our own perspective. Dasein (German, "to exist there") expresses the basic unity of person and environment. Alienation — the illness of our time, in three areas: separation from nature, lack of meaningful interpersonal relations, and alienation from one's authentic self. We experience three simultaneous modes: Umwelt (the environment, biological drives, natural law), Mitwelt (relations with other people), and Eigenwelt (our relationship with our self). Nonbeing — awareness of self as a living, emerging being leads to dread of not being (nonbeing/nothingness). Death is the most obvious avenue, but nonbeing also appears as blind conformity or generalized hostility. Anxiety — arises when one's existence or a value identified with it might be destroyed. Freedom cannot exist without anxiety. Normal anxiety is proportionate to the threat and can be confronted consciously; neurotic anxiety is disproportionate, involves repression and is managed by blocking off awareness. Guilt — arises when we deny our potentialities, fail to perceive others' needs, or ignore our dependence on nature. Both anxiety and guilt are ontological (about the nature of being). Three forms of ontological guilt correspond to the three modes: separation guilt (Umwelt — separation from nature), guilt of Mitwelt (inadequacy with others), guilt of Eigenwelt (denial/failure of one's own potentialities). Intentionality — the structure that gives meaning to experience and lets people make decisions about the future. Care is an active state in which something matters, the opposite of apathy; without care there is no love, and care is also the source of will ("the capacity to organize one's self so that movement toward a goal may take place"). Four forms of love (Western tradition): Sex (biological release of sexual tension), Eros (psychological desire for procreation/creation through enduring union, built on care and tenderness — the salvation of sex), Philia (intimate non-sexual friendship that takes time to grow), and Agape (altruistic, disinterested esteem for the other's welfare). Eros is built on philia; philia needs agape. Freedom and destiny — healthy people both assume their freedom and face their destiny. Freedom of doing (existential freedom) = acting on one's choices; freedom of being (essential freedom) = the inner possibility of changing. Destiny = "the design of the universe speaking through the design of each one of us"; within its boundaries we have the power to choose, but it does not permit any change we wish. The power of myth — myths are the stories that unify a society; for May they are archetypal patterns comparable to Carl Jung's collective unconscious. Psychopathology — for May, apathy and emptiness (not anxiety and guilt) are the malaise of modern times; disturbed people deny their destiny, lose their freedom, and erect neurotic symptoms to renounce freedom. He saw psychopathology as a lack of communication . 7. Behavioural & social-cognitive: Bandura, Rotter, Mischel B. F. Skinner — the behavioural baseline The strict behavioural view treats personality as a set of learned response tendencies shaped by reinforcement and punishment, with no need to invoke inner traits — the backdrop against which Albert Bandura, Julian Rotter and Walter Mischel added cognition. Albert Bandura — social/observational learning Observational learning (modelling). Rather than reinforcing ourselves for each action, we learn through vicarious reinforcement — observing others' behaviour and its consequences. Learning can occur through observation/example, not only direct reinforcement. The Bobo doll experiment. Preschool children watched an adult hit and kick an inflatable Bobo doll while shouting "Sock him in the nose!"; left alone with the doll they imitated the aggression. The experimental group was about twice as aggressive as a control group not exposed to the model. Watching a model perform usually-suppressed behaviour is disinhibition (an online form is trolling ). Three factors influencing modelling: characteristics of the models (those similar in appearance/sex/age and of high status are more effective; simple behaviours are imitated more readily than complex ones); characteristics of the observers (people low in self-confidence/self-esteem imitate more); and the reward consequences (seeing a model rewarded or punished affects imitation). Four processes of observational learning: attentional → retention → production → incentive/motivational processes. Self-reinforcement — administering rewards/punishments to oneself for meeting one's own standards. Self-efficacy — our feeling of adequacy, efficiency and competence in coping with life. Low self-efficacy → feeling helpless and unable to control events; high → believing one can deal effectively with situations. Four sources of self-efficacy : performance attainment (mastery experiences), vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion, and physiological/emotional arousal — each suggesting a way to raise efficacy (reachable goals, good models, encouragement, and managing arousal through diet/stress reduction/exercise). Walter Mischel — the person-situation debate Mischel challenged the consistency of broad traits across situations (the person–situation debate ), arguing behaviour is highly situation-specific. His later Cognitive-Affective Personality System (CAPS) reframes personality as stable if…then behavioural signatures — a person behaves consistently within similar situations even if they look inconsistent across different ones. Julian Rotter — social learning & locus of control Behaviour depends on both outcome expectancy (how strongly we expect performance to bring a positive result) and reinforcement value (how much we value the expected reinforcement). The set of relevant behaviours available is the behaviour potential . Generalized vs specific expectancies. Specific expectancies attach a reward to a behaviour in a particular situation; generalized expectancies span a group of situations and give the stable, situationally consistent characteristics we call personality. Out-of-character behaviour can arise from specific expectancies. Rotter described six psychological needs developing out of biological needs: recognition-status, dominance, independence, protection-dependency, love and affection, and physical comfort. Reinforcement value is judged relative to other available reinforcers; behaviour potential, outcome expectancy and reinforcement value combine into the psychological situation . Locus of control (LOC). An internal LOC is the generalized expectancy that one's own actions lead to desired outcomes; an external LOC attributes outcomes to chance or powerful others. Later work found three orthogonal dimensions: internality , luck/chance and powerful others . Internals are more achievement-oriented and higher achievers; externals are less independent and more likely to be depressed and stressed. 8. Cognitive approaches: Kelly, Lewin, Seligman, Kohlberg Roots: Gestalt and Kurt Lewin Gestalt psychology (influential in 1920s Germany): humans seek meaning, organise sensations into meaningful perceptions, and complex stimuli are not reducible to the sum of their parts. Kurt Lewin — came out of the Gestalt tradition but focused on personality and social psychology. His field theory (1935) centres on the life space — all internal and external forces acting on an individual — and on contemporaneous causation (behaviour is caused at the moment of its occurrence by all influences present then). Cognitive styles — field dependence/independence (Witkin, Solomon Asch). Field-dependent people are heavily influenced by salient but irrelevant context, are more holistic/intuitive, and are more sensitive to social/interpersonal contexts; field-independent people are more analytical, restructure problems more, and are guided more by internalised aspects. George Kelly — personal construct theory Each person has a unique system of constructs used to understand and predict behaviour (their own and others'). Constructive alternativism — we are not controlled by our constructs; we are free to revise or replace them with alternatives. The theory is presented in scientific form, organised into a fundamental postulate and 11 corollaries . (Kelly is associated with the person-as-scientist metaphor and the Role Construct Repertory / "Rep" Test.) Martin Seligman — explanatory styles, learned helplessness & learned optimism Explanatory style — cognitive personality variables capturing one's habitual way of interpreting events. The optimistic style perceives even neutral events positively and finds eventual positives in negatives; the pessimistic style focuses on the negative potential. Optimism is associated with better outcomes, especially under challenge. Defensive pessimism (Julie Norem) — in risky situations a person reduces anxiety and improves performance by anticipating a poorer outcome; excessive optimism can be maladaptive when failure chances are high. Learned helplessness (Seligman, 1975) — repeated exposure to unavoidable punishment leads an organism to accept later punishment even when it becomes avoidable. In the classic study, dogs given inescapable shocks later failed to escape when escape was possible. Learned optimism — training people to think differently about themselves and their situations, developing the healthier responses of the optimistic style. Lawrence Kohlberg — moral development Kohlberg (1969) described three levels of moral reasoning, each with two stages: Level Stages Reasoning I. Preconventional (typical ages 4–10; external controls) 1. Orientation toward punishment & obedience; 2. Instrumental purpose & exchange Obey rules to avoid punishment (ignoring motive, focusing on physical form/consequences) or to serve self-interest ("you scratch my back"), following the golden rule instrumentally II. Conventional (usually after age 10; internalised authority standards) 3. Maintaining mutual relations, approval of others ("Am I a good boy/girl?"); 4. Social concern & conscience ("What if everybody did it?") Want to please and help others, judge intentions and develop ideas of a "good person"; later value duty, respect for authority and maintaining the social order III. Postconventional (morality of autonomous moral principles) 5. Morality of contract, individual rights & democratically accepted law; 6. Universal ethical principles Think in rational terms valuing the majority's will and society's welfare; recognise that human need can conflict with law; ultimately act on internalised principles of right, fairness and justice regardless of others' opinions, condemning themselves if they fail 9. Assessment of personality Freudian assessment techniques Free association — the patient says whatever comes to mind ("daydreaming out loud"). Catharsis = the expression of emotions expected to reduce disturbing symptoms; resistance = a blockage or refusal to disclose painful memories. Dream analysis — dreams symbolically represent repressed desires, fears and conflicts. The manifest content = the actual events of the dream; the latent content = the hidden symbolic meaning. Across the theories — how each measures personality Carl Jung — the word-association test (response delay, respiration, GSR, retest memory) to detect complexes; the MBTI derived from his types. Raymond Cattell — the 16PF , with Q-data, T-data and L-data. Hans Eysenck — questionnaires measuring the PEN dimensions. Robert McCrae & Paul Costa — the Big Five via factor-analysed self-report scales. Zuckerman — the Sensation Seeking Scale (SSS) , a 40-item paper-and-pencil questionnaire (see §15). Murray — needs (n Ach etc.) classically assessed with projective methods (the Thematic Apperception Test). High-yield Type A vs Type B is the canonical type assessment (heart-disease proneness). 16PF = Raymond Cattell, PEN = Hans Eysenck, OCEAN = Robert McCrae & Paul Costa, MBTI = Jung-derived, SSS = Zuckerman, word-association = Carl Jung. 10. Emotion & its physiology; theories of emotion Emotion is the "feeling" aspect of consciousness, with three elements: a certain physical arousal , a certain behaviour that reveals the feeling outwardly, and an inner awareness of the feeling. The physiology of emotion Arousal is created by the sympathetic nervous system : heart rate increases, breathing quickens, pupils dilate, the mouth dries. Different emotions show different physiological signatures: sadness, anger and fear raise heart rate more than disgust; disgust raises skin conductance more than happiness; anger shows vascular signs such as higher diastolic blood pressure compared with fear. The amygdala (in the limbic system, on each side of the brain) is associated with emotions such as fear and pleasure in humans and animals. Other subcortical and cortical areas — notably the frontal lobes — also process emotion: positive emotions are associated with the left frontal lobe, negative feelings (sadness, anxiety, depression) with the right frontal lobe. The endocrine response (hormonal secretions) and autonomic arousal can be triggered by a fast "low road" (thalamus → amygdala) and a slower "high road" (thalamus → cortex → amygdala). Theories of emotion Theory Sequence (snarling dog → ?) Key claim Common-sense Stimulus → conscious fear → ANS arousal "I'm shaking because I'm afraid." Feeling comes first, then the body. James-Lange Stimulus → ANS arousal & body changes → conscious fear "I'm afraid because I'm shaking." The bodily response comes first and is the emotion. Cannon-Bard Stimulus → subcortical (thalamic) activity → arousal AND fear simultaneously "I'm shaking and feeling afraid at the same time." Physiological arousal and the felt emotion occur together, independently. Schachter-Singer (two-factor / cognitive arousal) Stimulus → ANS arousal + cognitive label → fear Emotion = physiological arousal plus a cognitive interpretation/label of that arousal. Lazarus (cognitive-mediational) Stimulus → cognitive appraisal → arousal + emotion "This dog is dangerous and that makes me afraid." A cognitive appraisal must come first. Facial-feedback Stimulus → facial expression → bodily response/emotion Facial muscle movements feed back to produce or intensify the felt emotion. Trap James-Lange = body first , then feeling; Cannon-Bard = body and feeling together (thalamic); Schachter-Singer = arousal + label ; Lazarus = appraisal first. Don't confuse Schachter-Singer (label after arousal) with Lazarus (appraisal before arousal). 11. Stress, the GAS & conflict Hans Selye — the General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) Selye, the founder of stress research, studied the sequence of physiological reactions the body uses to adapt to a stressor — the general adaptation syndrome (GAS) , in three stages: Alarm. The sympathetic nervous system is activated; the adrenal glands release hormones that increase heart rate, blood pressure and blood-sugar supply, producing a burst of energy. Reactions such as fever, nausea and headache are common. Resistance. As stress continues, the body settles into sympathetic activity, continuing to release stress hormones to fight off or resist the stressor; early alarm symptoms lessen and the person may actually feel better. One stress hormone, noradrenaline (norepinephrine) , affects the brain's processing of pain, producing a kind of analgesia (so a person under stress may not feel hitting an arm or shin). Exhaustion. When the body's resources are gone, exhaustion occurs, which can lead to stress-related diseases (high blood pressure, weakened immune system) or, without outside help, the death of the organism. Personality differences in stress (the Type theory of cardiac risk) Type Profile Health link Type A Workaholic, competitive, ambitious, hates wasting time, easily annoyed More likely to have health issues (e.g. heart disease), especially the more hostile the person Type B More easygoing, slower to anger, less competitive or driven Less likely to have health issues Type C Pleasant and at peace but finds it difficult to express emotions, especially negative ones Associated with cancer Type H ("hardy") Looks like Type A but thrives on stress via three factors: commitment, control, and seeing stressors as a challenge Less prone to heart disease Mnemonic The three C's of hardiness (Type H): Commitment, Control, Challenge. Conflict: sources and types Whenever you are torn between competing, incompatible desires, goals or actions, you are in conflict : Approach–approach — attraction to two or more desirable goals; least stressful. Avoidance–avoidance — a choice between two or more undesirable situations; more stressful. Approach–avoidance — a single goal/event has both positive and negative aspects; can be most stressful . Multiple approach–avoidance (e.g. double approach–avoidance ) — common in daily life when decisions affect two or more goals each with pros and cons. 12. Theories of motivation Motivation is the process by which activities are started, directed and continued so that physical or psychological needs/wants are met. Intrinsic vs extrinsic. Intrinsic = actions rewarding or satisfying in and of themselves; extrinsic = actions performed because they lead to an external outcome. Instinct approach. Instincts are biologically determined, innate patterns of behaviour. The older view is criticised because instincts are mainly descriptions , not explanations ; but the idea that some behaviour is hereditary remains important. Drive-reduction (Clark Hull). A need is a requirement for something essential to survival; a need creates psychological tension (a drive ) and physical arousal, and satisfying the need reduces the drive/tension (toward homeostasis ). Primary drives involve survival needs (hunger, thirst) and maintain homeostasis; secondary (acquired) drives are learned through experience or conditioning (money, social approval). Psychological-needs / McClelland. Some theories highlight learned psychological needs: need for achievement (nAch) , need for affiliation (nAff) , and need for power (nPow) . Dweck suggests need for achievement is linked to a person's view of self (fixed vs changeable mindset) and locus of control. Arousal theory. People have an optimal level of tension/arousal they work to maintain (the Yerkes-Dodson law — an inverted-U where performance peaks at moderate arousal). The need for stimulation usually settles at a moderate level but ranges low to high ( sensation seeking ). Incentive approach. Based partly on principles of learning: incentives are things that attract or lure people into action, most often through their rewarding properties (motivation pulled from outside, not just pushed by internal drives). Humanistic. Based primarily on Abraham Maslow's hierarchy — basic needs must be met before higher levels can be reached (other versions differ in number of levels and focus). Self-determination theory. Similar to Maslow's hierarchy: three universal needs — autonomy, competence and relatedness — must be met for well-being. High-yield Match the theorist: drive-reduction = Clark Hull; arousal/optimal-arousal = Yerkes-Dodson (inverted-U); nAch/nAff/nPow = David McClelland; hierarchy = Abraham Maslow; autonomy/competence/relatedness = Self-Determination (Edward Deci & Richard Ryan). Drives push from inside; incentives pull from outside. 13. Emotional & social development Emotional expression & self-conscious emotions Self-conscious emotions — embarrassment, shame, guilt, envy and pride — each involves some damage to, or enhancement of, the sense of self. Self-evaluative emotions (shame, guilt, pride) require both self-recognition (recognising oneself in a mirror/photo) and an understanding of rules or standards for evaluating one's conduct. Parents socialize emotions by modelling positive emotions, attending to infants' pleasant feelings, and being less responsive to negative displays. Emotional self-regulation Begins by the end of the first year and develops slowly: toddlers move from depending on others to regulating emotions on their own; grade-schoolers comply with culturally defined emotional display rules (suppressing unacceptable emotions and outwardly replacing them with the called-for feeling). Social referencing — by 8–10 months, infants use others' emotional expressions to infer the meaning of ambiguous situations. Emotional competence has three components: competent emotional expressivity (frequent positive, infrequent negative displays), emotional knowledge (correctly identifying others' feelings and their causes), and emotional regulation (adjusting one's arousal to an appropriate intensity to achieve goals). Each component is related to children's social competence . Temperament & development (Thomas & Chess; Rothbart) Temperament is a person's tendency to respond in predictable ways to environmental events, influenced by genetic and environmental factors; negatively-toned attributes are shaped more by nonshared environmental influences (aspects siblings do not share). Mary Rothbart & John Bates' dimensions: fearful distress, irritable distress (frustration/anger), positive affect (sociability), activity level, attention span/persistence, and rhythmicity (regularity of bodily functions). Temperamental attributes (activity level, irritability, sociability, fearfulness) are moderately stable over time, including behavioral inhibition (withdrawal from unfamiliar people/situations). Alexander Thomas & Stella Chess grouped these into profiles: Easy — even-tempered, typically positive mood, open and adaptable; regular, predictable habits. Difficult — active, irritable, irregular in habits. Slow-to-warm-up — inactive, somewhat moody, slow to adapt; responds to novelty in mildly (not intensely) negative ways. Difficult and slow-to-warm-up children are at greater risk of adjustment problems, depending on the goodness-of-fit between parenting and the child's temperament. Social development & person perception Age trends in how children perceive others: Children younger than 7–8 describe others in the same concrete, observable terms they use for the self. Behavioral comparisons phase — grade-schoolers form impressions by comparing/contrasting overt behaviours. Psychological constructs phase — later, they rely on stable traits to describe patterns. Psychological comparisons phase — young adolescents compare/contrast people on abstract psychological dimensions; by 14–16 they know situational influences can make a person act "out of character." Theories of social-cognitive development — Selman Robert Selman's role-taking theory (1980): the growth of role-taking skills underlies a mature understanding of self and others, tested with the Holly dilemma (an 8-year-old who promised her father not to climb trees, but is the only one who can rescue a kitten stuck in a tree). Social influences — equal-status contacts with friends and peers are crucial: they contribute indirectly by fostering role-taking (children must compromise to keep play going) and directly by providing experiences of what others are like. Jean Piaget assumed equal-status peer contact is an important contributor to social perspective-taking. 14. Attachment Attachment (John Bowlby, 1969) is the strong affectional tie we feel with the special people in our lives. Infants form reciprocal affectional ties to caregivers during the first year; parents' bonding strengthens as they gear behaviour to the infant's social signals and establish synchronized routines. The phases of attachment Asocial phase (0–6 weeks). Phase of indiscriminate attachment (6 weeks–7 months). Phase of specific attachments (7–9 months) — the first true attachments; the attachment object becomes a secure base for exploration . Phase of multiple attachments (9–18 months). Theories of attachment Psychoanalytic and learning theories were discredited because feeding plays less of a role in human attachment than they expected. Cognitive-developmental — attachments depend on cognitive development: infants must recognise that familiar companions have permanence (object permanence), since a stable relationship is hard to form with someone who seems to cease to exist when out of view. Harry Harlow & Zimmerman — infant monkeys separated at birth and raised with a wire surrogate or a cloth surrogate spent time with the wire mother only while feeding but ran to the cloth mother when upset or afraid — showing contact comfort is a more powerful contributor to attachment than feeding/hunger reduction. Ethological theory — Konrad Lorenz : young goslings followed almost any moving object (their mother, a duck, even a human), a behaviour he called imprinting . Imprinting is automatic (no teaching needed), occurs only within a narrowly delimited critical period after hatching, and is irreversible.
