In humans, infants inherit attributes that maintain contact and elicit caregiving — Lorenz's "kewpie doll" appearance (large forehead, chubby cheeks, soft rounded features) makes infants seem cute/lovable, and smiling/babbling reinforces caregiving. Attachment-related fears Stranger anxiety and separation anxiety stem from infants' wariness of strange situations and their inability to explain who strangers are or where absent companions have gone. Both usually decline in the second year as toddlers mature and venture from their secure bases to explore. Attachment quality — Ainsworth's Strange Situation The Strange Situation (Mary Ainsworth, 1978) assesses attachment quality in 1- to 2-year-olds. Four classifications: Classification Behaviour Secure Actively explores while alone with mother; may be upset by separation but greets her warmly on return and seeks contact that alleviates distress; outgoing with strangers when mother is present. Resistant (ambivalent) Stays close, explores little; very distressed at departure; ambivalent on return — angry, resists physical contact; very wary of strangers even when mother is present. Avoidant Little distress on separation; turns away from / ignores mother even when she tries to gain attention; often sociable with strangers but may avoid them too. Disorganized / disoriented (Main & Solomon, 1990) A confusing combination of resistant and avoidant patterns; on reunion may seem dazed, freeze, or approach then abruptly move away — confusion about whether to approach or avoid the caregiver. Cultural variation. The distribution of classifications varies across cultures and reflects child-rearing differences — for example Japanese mothers emphasize social routines more and exploration less than American mothers, and seek to promote the infant's amae (a state of total dependence on the mother and a presumption of her love and indulgence). Factors influencing attachment security & later development Caregiving hypothesis — sensitive, responsive caregiving → secure attachments; inconsistent, neglectful, over-intrusive or abusive caregiving → insecure attachments. Environmental stressors (poverty, a stormy marriage) also contribute. Caregiving may determine whether attachment is secure or insecure. Temperament hypothesis — infant characteristics and temperament may influence attachment by shaping caregiver–infant interactions; child temperament may determine the kind of insecurity shown when caregiving is insensitive. Internal working models — cognitive representations of self, others and relationships, constructed from interactions with caregivers; often stable over time and shaping reactions to people and challenges for years. Secure attachment predicts later intellectual curiosity and social competence. Parents' working models correspond closely to their children's. Working models can change : a secure history is no guarantee of positive adjustment, nor insecurity a certain indicator of poor outcomes. 15. Exploratory behaviour, curiosity & sensation seeking Zuckerman's sensation seeking Sensation seeking is the need for varied, novel, complex and intense sensations and experiences, and the willingness to take physical, social, legal and financial risks for the sake of such experience. Measured by the Sensation Seeking Scale (SSS) , a 40-item paper-and-pencil questionnaire. Four components Thrill and adventure seeking — desire for physical activities involving speed, danger, novelty and defiance of gravity (parachuting, scuba diving, bungee jumping). Experience seeking — novel experiences through travel, music, art or a nonconformist lifestyle with similar people. Disinhibition — release through uninhibited social activities (risky sex, impulsiveness, aggressiveness, antisocial behaviour). Boredom susceptibility — aversion to repetition, routine work and predictable people; restless discontent when exposed to them. Good vs bad sensation seeking Good sensation seeking — non-impulsive, socialized; chiefly the thrill-and-adventure-seeking component. Bad sensation seeking — impulsive, unsocialized; high scores on disinhibition, experience seeking and boredom susceptibility, plus high scores on Hans Eysenck's psychoticism scale. Characteristics of sensation seekers Age — younger people seek adventure, risk and novelty more than older people. Gender — men score higher on thrill-and-adventure seeking, disinhibition and boredom susceptibility (and higher overall sensation seeking with lower impulse control); women score higher on experience seeking. Racial/cultural — Asians scored lower on the SSS than people in Western countries; white subjects scored higher than non-whites. Risk-taking groups — three types of risk takers were identified: antisocial , adventurous , and prosocial risk takers. Antisocial (drug addicts, criminals) and adventurous (mountain climbers, sky divers) scored significantly higher on the SSS than prosocial risk takers (police, firefighters). Skydivers, firefighters, riot-control police, bungee jumpers and race-car drivers all score high. Behavioural differences — high sensation seekers are more likely than low to use and sell illicit drugs (and earlier), drink alcohol, shoplift and commit delinquent behaviour; more had tattoos and body piercings; at work they scored lower on job performance, were less likely to form social relationships at work, and less likely to try to obtain information from co-workers or supervisors. Personality correlates SSS scores (especially disinhibition) relate to Hans Eysenck's extraversion and to the asocial tendencies of psychoticism . High scores correlate with extraversion as described by Carl Jung and measured by the MBTI . No correlation was found between sensation seeking and neuroticism . High SSS scorers show high autonomy : they openly express emotions, are assertive, nonconforming and confirmed risk takers, acting independently of social conventions and others' needs. Self-regulation (Bandura, applied to exploration) When people have high self-efficacy , are confident in their reliance on proxies , and possess solid collective efficacy , they have considerable capacity to regulate their own behaviour. Albert Bandura (1994) held that people use both reactive and proactive strategies. External factors provide a standard for evaluating our behaviour and the means for reinforcement. Internal factors : self-observation (monitoring our own performance, even if attention is not complete or accurate); judgmental processes (regulating behaviour through cognitive mediation, comparing performance against personal standards rather than others' conduct, weighing the value of the activity and the performance attribution of causes); and self-reaction (responding positively or negatively to our own behaviour depending on how it measures up to personal standards). 16. Fast glossary (A–Z) Term Meaning Agape May's altruistic, disinterested love; esteem for the other's welfare. Amae Japanese state of total dependence on the mother and presumption of her indulgence. Archetype Carl Jung's inherited emotional symbol in the collective unconscious (persona, shadow, anima/animus, self, mother, hero). Basic anxiety Karen Horney: a child's feeling of being alone, helpless and insecure. Behaviour potential Julian Rotter: the likelihood of a behaviour given expectancy and reinforcement value. Cannon-Bard Arousal and emotion occur simultaneously via thalamic activity. Cardinal/central/secondary Gordon Allport's three grades of trait dominance. Cathexis Sigmund Freud: investment of libido in an object. Conditions of worth Carl Rogers: seeing oneself as worthy only under parent-acceptable conditions. Constructive alternativism Kelly: freedom to revise/replace one's constructs. Dark Triad Paulhus & Williams: narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy. Dasein "To exist there"; being-in-the-world (existentialism). Drive-reduction Clark Hull: need → drive/tension → behaviour → reduction (homeostasis). Eros/Philia/Sex/Agape May's four forms of love. Explanatory style Martin Seligman: optimistic vs pessimistic habitual interpretation of events. Field dependence Witkin: reliance on salient context vs analytical field independence. Fictional finalism Alfred Adler: striving toward an imagined future goal. Functional autonomy Allport: adult motives detached from their original source. GAS Hans Selye: alarm → resistance → exhaustion. Goodness-of-fit Match between a child's temperament and parenting demands. HEXACO Ashton & Lee's six factors (adds Honesty-Humility). Id/Ego/Superego Pleasure / reality / morality principle. Imprinting Konrad Lorenz: automatic, critical-period, irreversible following response. Individuation Jung: integration of conscious and unconscious into wholeness. Inferiority complex Adler's term for pervasive feelings of helplessness. Internal working model John Bowlby: cognitive representation of self/others/relationships. James-Lange Emotion follows the bodily response ("afraid because shaking"). Jonah complex Abraham Maslow: fear of one's own potential/greatness. Lazarus Cognitive appraisal precedes emotion and arousal. Learned helplessness Seligman: accepting avoidable punishment after inescapable punishment. Libido Freud: sexual psychic energy; Jung: general (not necessarily sexual) life energy. Locus of control Rotter: internal (own actions) vs external (chance/powerful others). MBTI Jung-derived type inventory (E/I, S/N, T/F, J/P). Metamotivation Maslow's B-motivation of self-actualizers (vs D-motivation). nAch / nAff / nPow David McClelland's needs for achievement, affiliation, power. OCEAN Big Five: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extroversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism. Object relations Mental representations of significant others (Margaret Mahler, Melanie Klein, Heinz Kohut). Organismic valuing process Rogers: judging experiences by how well they serve actualization. Parapraxis Freudian slip revealing the unconscious. PEN Hans Eysenck: Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism. Penis envy / womb envy Freud's concept; Horney's male-counterpart rebuttal. Positive regard Rogers: need for acceptance/love; unconditional vs conditional. Proprium Allport's term for the ego/self. Psychosexual stages Freud: oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital. Reinforcement value Rotter: how much one values an expected reinforcement. Schachter-Singer Two-factor emotion: arousal + cognitive label. Self-determination Edward Deci & Richard Ryan: autonomy, competence, relatedness. Self-efficacy Albert Bandura: belief in one's competence to cope; four sources. Sensation Seeking Scale Zuckerman's 40-item SSS; four components. Social interest Adler: innate potential to cooperate toward shared goals. Social referencing Using others' expressions to interpret ambiguous situations (8–10 months). Source traits Raymond Cattell's underlying factors behind the 16PF. Strange Situation Mary Ainsworth: secure, resistant, avoidant, disorganized. Style of life Adler: dominant, getting, avoiding, socially useful. Temperament types Alexander Thomas & Stella Chess: easy, difficult, slow-to-warm-up. Type A/B/C/H Cardiac-risk personality types (H = hardy: commitment, control, challenge). Yerkes-Dodson Inverted-U arousal–performance law; optimal arousal level. Word-association test Jung's method for detecting complexes.

title: Unit 8 — Social Psychology
text: Unit 8 — Social Psychology How the presence, behaviour and existence of other people shape what we think, feel and do: the field's history and grand theories, how we read other people, how groups push us into conformity, obedience and compliance, what happens inside groups, how leaders lead, why we help and why we harm, the roots of prejudice and intergroup conflict, and how all of it is applied to health, the law and the environment. Built file-by-file from the Rodrick Prashanth source decks and deepened to NIMHANS / MET clinical-psychology depth, preserving every named theorist, study, term and proposition. In this book History of social psychology Theories of social psychology Social perception Group & social influence Group dynamics Leadership styles Prosocial behaviour Aggression Theories of intergroup relationship Applying social psychology 1. History of social psychology The one idea. Social psychology is the scientific study of how the actual, imagined or implied presence of others influences an individual's thoughts, feelings and behaviour. Its history is a chain of named "firsts" and named "founders", and the paper loves to test who did what, in what year. The foundation (late 19th to early 20th century) Figure Year Contribution Norman Triplett 1897–1898 Credited with the first research article in social psychology . He noticed cyclists raced faster against others than against a clock, and designed a careful controlled experiment to study it. This is the origin of social facilitation . Max Ringelmann 1880s (published 1913) Found individuals performed worse on simple tasks such as rope-pulling when working with others. This is the origin of social loafing (the "Ringelmann effect"). William McDougall 1908 Published an early social psychology textbook; helps establish the field. Edward Ross 1908 American who published a founding social psychology text the same year. Floyd Allport 1924 His textbook is taken as establishing social psychology as a distinct experimental field. Trap Norman Triplett = social facilitation (first article, 1897–98). Max Ringelmann = social loafing (1880s, published 1913). Don't swap them. Establishing the field as a discipline is attributed to McDougall (1908), Ross (1908) and Floyd Allport (1924). 1930s–1950s: the field finds its problems 1936: Gordon Allport (younger brother of Floyd, the 1924 textbook author) and others formed the Society for the Psychological Study of Social Issues (SPSSI) . Muzafer Sherif published groundbreaking experimental research on social influence (the autokinetic-effect norm-formation studies). Kurt Lewin fled the Nazis and emigrated to the US in the early 1930s. His central contribution: behaviour is a function of the interaction between the person and the environment (the interactionist perspective ), often written B = f(P, E) . 1950s: Gordon Allport (1954) published The Nature of Prejudice . Solomon Asch (1951) demonstrated how willing people are to conform to an obviously wrong majority. Leon Festinger introduced two landmark theories: social comparison (1954, how people learn about themselves by comparing to others) and cognitive dissonance (1957, how attitudes change through one's own behaviour). 1960s–1990s: crisis and pluralism Stanley Milgram's obedience research (early/mid 1960s) linked the post-WWII era to the coming era of social revolution, showing individuals' vulnerability to the destructive commands of authority. Strong disagreements of the period (the "crisis of social psychology") were largely a reaction against the dominant method of the day, the laboratory experiment . Mid-1970s onward = an era of pluralism: laboratory and field experiments used side by side; a "hot" perspective (emotion and motivation) alongside a "cold" perspective (cognition); and the rise of international, cross-cultural and multicultural perspectives. Social psychology in a new century Social cognition dominated the final quarter of the field's first century: the study of how people perceive, remember and interpret information about themselves and others. Social neuroscience emerged as a subfield studying the relationship between neural and social processes. Behavioural genetics (the study of how genes affect behaviour) triggered research on, e.g., whether aggression is heritable and the role of genes in sexual orientation. Evolutionary psychology uses evolutionary principles to understand behaviour (e.g., asking how the psychological mechanisms underlying jealousy may have evolved from natural-selection pressures). Increasing emphasis on testing the universal generality vs cultural specificity of theories via cross-cultural and multicultural research. High-yield Norman Triplett (facilitation, first article) · Max Ringelmann (loafing) · McDougall/Ross 1908 + Floyd Allport 1924 (founding) · Lewin B = f(P,E) · Muzafer Sherif (norm formation) · Solomon Asch 1951 (conformity) · Leon Festinger 1954 social comparison / 1957 dissonance · Milgram 1960s (obedience) · Gordon Allport 1954 Nature of Prejudice . New century: social cognition, social neuroscience, behavioural genetics, evolutionary psychology, cross-cultural work. 2. Theories of social psychology The grand frameworks the field uses to explain social behaviour. Learn each by its core construct and its named author. Field theory (Kurt Lewin) Lewin, whose name is most associated with field theory , was a student of the founders of the Gestalt movement. Others (Edward Tolman 1932, Wheeler 1940, Karl Lashley 1929, Brunswik 1949) have been called field theorists, but none dealt specifically with social behaviour, so Lewin is taken as the best representative. Six principal attributes of field theory: (1) use of a constructive method ; (2) a dynamic approach; (3) emphasis on psychological processes; (4) analysis based on the situation as a whole ; (5) a distinction between systematic and historical issues; (6) a mathematical representation of the psychological situation (Lewin favoured topology ). Definition Life space = the person plus the psychological environment as it exists for him: the totality of all psychological factors influencing the individual at any given moment. A thing "exists" in the life space if it has demonstrable effects . Kurt Lewin held that the properties of the field at the present time are the only determinants of behaviour (an ahistorical orientation). Regions / life spheres: major parts of the life space (needs, profession, family, friendships), further differentiated into smaller units. Differentiation depends on age, intelligence and experience. Two added dimensions: fluidity (how distinguishable and how permeable regions are) and the reality–irreality dimension (reality = objective aspects; irreality = imagery, fantasy, hopes and fears; the psychological future has both a level of reality, "what is expected", and irreality, "hopes and fears"). Behaviour = locomotion: behaviour is any change in the life space, conceived as a locomotion of the person within it (bodily or psychological). The space of free movement is limited by barriers (boundaries that resist locomotion). Force: "that which causes change" (Lewin, 1936), with direction, strength and point of application (vector + arrow). The combination of all forces on a point is the resultant force . Valence describes whether a goal region is attractive (positive) or repulsive (negative); the strength of force is a function of valence and psychological distance. The change of force strength with distance is the goal gradient (it rises faster as one nears a negative goal than a positive one). Types of force: driving, restraining, induced (from another's wishes), own-need, and impersonal (situational requirements). Tension systems: tension is aroused when a person accepts task completion as a goal; it is discharged by completing the task and seeks equilibrium with neighbouring regions. This explains why incompleted tasks are recalled and resumed more than completed ones (the Zeigarnik effect ). Substitute satisfaction can discharge tension; its effectiveness depends on similarity, difficulty, and permeability of boundaries. Cognitive dissonance (Leon Festinger, 1957) Follows Heider's balance theory and the consistency tradition: the core principle is the tendency toward cognitive consistency . Two cognitions are dissonant if, considered alone, the obverse of one would follow from the other; consonant if one follows from the other. Four sources of dissonance: logical inconsistency; cultural mores; opinion generality (a specific opinion clashing with a more general one); past experience. Magnitude depends on the importance of the elements and the weighted proportion of relevant cognitions that are dissonant; the maximum possible dissonance equals the total resistance to change of the least resistant element. Consequences: dissonance is uncomfortable and motivates reduction; the person also actively avoids dissonance-increasing information. Decisions: dissonance is an inevitable consequence of decision; post-decision dissonance grows with the importance of the decision, the attractiveness of the unchosen option, and the cognitive overlap of the options. Forced compliance: public compliance without private change. The smaller the reward/punishment (just sufficient to elicit compliance), the greater the dissonance, hence the greater the attitude change. Selective exposure is curvilinearly related to dissonance: moderate dissonance maximises information seeking/avoidance. Social support: dissonance from disagreement varies with the number of agreeing others, importance of elements, relevance and attractiveness of the disagreer, and extent of disagreement. Trap Less-leads-to-more. In forced compliance, a smaller incentive produces more attitude change (you can't blame the small reward, so you change your attitude instead). This is the opposite of a reinforcement prediction, and is the classic dissonance exam item. Psychodynamic approach: Freud's group psychology Sigmund Freud viewed society as the product of the individual personalities within it. Four major works: Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego (1922), Civilization and its Discontents (1930), Totem and Taboo (1913), and The Future of an Illusion . Core ideas: society inhibits and represses instinctual impulses; the family is the fundamental agent of socialisation and the prototype for all later social relationships; groups form as a re-enactment of the individual's libidinal ties to parents ; social justice arises from envy and hostility among members; law and religion protect society against man's aggressive and sexual impulses. Rapaport's (1959) metapsychological points of view on Freud's system: the empirical (subject matter is behaviour), the Gestalt (all behaviour is the total expression of all structures and forces), the genetic (mental phenomena have historical antecedents; earlier behaviour can be reactivated), the dynamic (all behaviour is ultimately drive-determined, primarily a broad sexual/libidinal drive), the economic (behaviour regulated by distribution and flow of psychic energy), the structural (id/ego/superego intervene between arousal and investment), and the adaptive (behaviour is shaped by, and shapes, external and bodily reality). Sociobiological theory (Edward O. Wilson, 1975) In Sociobiology: The New Synthesis , Wilson outlined a framework for the biological basis of social behaviour. As a branch of evolutionary biology, it uses demographic parameters and population genetics to predict social organisation across species. Its key contribution is ultimate causation (the selective forces operating over generations) as distinct from proximate causation (mechanisms within an individual's lifetime). Sociobiology differs from evolutionary psychology : both use ultimate causal explanations, but evolutionary psychology models the underlying information-processing circuitry (cognitive programs) , whereas sociobiology steps straight from selective forces to behaviour without specifying the cognitive programs. Social cognitive theory (Albert Bandura) Began as Social Learning Theory (SLT) in the 1960s; became Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) in 1986. Learning occurs in a social context through the dynamic, reciprocal interaction of person, environment and behaviour . Constructs: reciprocal determinism , behavioural capability (knowledge + skill to perform), observational learning (modelling), reinforcements , expectations (and expectancies , the subjective value of outcomes), and self-efficacy (added when SLT became SCT; confidence in one's ability to perform a behaviour). High-yield Self-efficacy is the construct added when Social Learning Theory became Social Cognitive Theory (1986). The first five constructs (reciprocal determinism, behavioural capability, observational learning, reinforcements, expectations) were already in SLT. 3. Social perception Social perception = the process through which we seek to know and understand other people: how we learn about others, communicate without words, attribute causes, and form impressions. Nonverbal communication To understand others' emotional states we rely on nonverbal communication ("an unspoken language of facial expressions, eye contact, and body movements and postures"). The basic channels are: Facial expressions — the primary channel of emotion. Eye contact — high contact signals liking/interest; staring = continued steady gaze regardless of the recipient's response (often a sign of hostility). Body language — cues from posture, position and movement of the body. Touching — can induce positive reactions when appropriate, negative when not. Paralanguage / paralinguistic cues — tone and inflection of voice (not the words themselves). Body chemistry — even subtle olfactory cues (e.g., menstrual-cycle chemical changes) can be transmitted to others. Definition Facial feedback hypothesis: the facial expressions we show not only reflect our internal feelings but feed back to influence our subjective emotional experience. Evidence: participants given Botox (which paralyses facial muscles) reported less negative reaction to negative film clips and less positive reaction to mildly positive clips than those given Restylane (a non-paralysing control). Recognising deception Microexpressions: fleeting facial expressions lasting only a few tenths of a second. Interchannel discrepancies: inconsistencies between cues from different channels (liars struggle to control all channels at once). Eye contact: liars often blink more and show more dilated pupils. Exaggerated facial expressions: e.g., smiling more broadly than usual. Linguistic style: when lying, the pitch of the voice often rises, response latency increases, and speakers start–stop–restart sentences more. Attribution: understanding causes of behaviour Attribution = our efforts to understand the causes behind others' (and sometimes our own) behaviour. Jones & Davis (1965): correspondent inference theory We are most likely to conclude that behaviour reflects stable traits (reach a correspondent inference ) when the behaviour: is freely chosen ; yields distinctive, non-common effects (effects caused by one specific factor but not others); and is low in social desirability . Kelley's theory of causal attribution (covariation model) To answer "why?" we focus on three kinds of information: Dimension Meaning Consensus Extent to which other people react to the same stimulus in the same way (higher = more people react alike). Consistency Extent to which this person reacts the same way to the stimulus on other occasions / over time. Distinctiveness Extent to which this person reacts differently to other, different stimuli. Other dimensions of causal attribution concern whether causes are stable over time and controllable . People who believe strongly in God, or whose culture accepts complex causality, more often attribute improbable but important events to "what was meant to be" (fate). The level of interpretation we use is action identification : low-level interpretations focus on the action itself, higher-level on its ultimate goals. Sources of attributional bias Correspondence bias / Fundamental Attribution Error (FAE): the tendency to explain others' actions as stemming from dispositions even when situational causes are present. Reasons: dispositional causes are more salient ; we give situational causes insufficient weight; we begin by assuming behaviour reflects character, then under-correct for the situation. Actor–observer effect: we attribute our own behaviour to external/situational causes but others' behaviour to internal causes. Self-serving bias: we attribute positive outcomes to internal causes and negative ones to external causes (especially strong for negative events). Trap FAE = bias about others (over-attribute to disposition). Actor–observer = the self–other split (own behaviour situational, others' dispositional). Self-serving = the good–bad split for one's own outcomes (success internal, failure external). Distinguish all three. 4. Group & social influence Social influence = efforts by one or more persons to change the behaviour, attitudes or feelings of others. It can even be symbolic (occurring when others are not present and make no direct attempt). The three main forms are conformity , compliance and obedience . Social facilitation and social loafing Social facilitation: the tendency to perform simple/well-learned tasks better when others are present; more precisely, the strengthening of dominant (most likely) responses in the presence of others (on some tasks the presence of others hinders performance). Robert Zajonc: increased arousal enhances performance on easy tasks (dominant response correct) but promotes incorrect responding on complex tasks (dominant response wrong) — e.g., people do worse on hard anagrams when anxious. Why? Nickolas Cottrell → evaluation apprehension (we wonder how observers are judging us). Sanders, Baron & Moore → distraction–conflict ("driven by distraction": attention conflict overloads cognition, causing arousal). Zajonc → mere presence produces arousal even without evaluation or distraction. Social loafing: the tendency to exert less effort when pooling efforts toward a common goal than when individually accountable. Free riders benefit from the group but give little in return. High-yield The reconciling rule: when being observed increases evaluation concern, social facilitation occurs; when being lost in a crowd decreases evaluation concern, social loafing occurs. Loafing is reduced when the task is challenging/appealing/involving, when members see others as unable to contribute, when high effort is seen to bring rewards, and when members are friends or feel indispensable. Conformity Definition Conformity = changing attitudes/behaviour to adhere to existing social norms (rules indicating how we should behave). Acceptance = conformity that involves both acting and believing in accord with social pressure. Solomon Asch first systematically studied conformity: participants judged which of three comparison lines matched a standard. When confederates gave identical wrong answers, real participants tended to give the same wrong answer; three-quarters conformed at least once . Philip Zimbardo's Stanford Prison study showed the powerful impact of norms attached to social roles : participants came to behave like real guards and prisoners. Two motives for conformity: normative social influence (the desire to be liked) and informational social influence (the desire to be right/accurate). Factors: cohesiveness , group size , and the type of norm operating ( descriptive = what most people do; injunctive = what is approved/expected). Emotional contagion: we catch others' emotions; if they are dissimilar to us in important ways, we may show counter-contagion (opposite emotions). Nonconformity is encouraged by the desire to attract a mate, by power (powerful people depend less on others and take others' perspectives less), and by the desire to be unique. Minority influence: minorities can sway majorities by being consistent , avoiding appearing rigid/dogmatic, and arguing a position consistent with current social trends. Compliance (Robert Cialdini) Cialdini studied "compliance professionals" and identified six basic principles of compliance : friendship/liking, commitment/consistency, scarcity, reciprocity, authority, social validation (consensus) . Tactic Underlying principle How it works Ingratiation Friendship/liking Get others to like us (flattery, self-promotion, improved appearance, positive nonverbal cues, small favours, incidental similarity ) so they agree more readily. Foot-in-the-door Commitment/consistency Begin with a small request, then escalate to a larger one. Lowball Commitment/consistency An offer is changed to make it less attractive after the person has accepted. Door-in-the-face Reciprocity Begin with a large request; when refused, retreat to the smaller one actually desired all along. That's-not-all Reciprocity Offer additional benefits before the person decides. Playing hard to get Scarcity Suggest a person/object is scarce and hard to obtain. Deadline technique Scarcity Tell targets they have only limited time to take advantage of an offer. Trap Foot-in-the-door (small → large) is based on consistency ; door-in-the-face (large → small) is based on reciprocity . Lowball and foot-in-the-door both start small but lowball involves changing the deal after acceptance . Obedience (Stanley Milgram, 1963, 1965, 1974) The clearest, most dramatic evidence for obedience. Teacher-participants were told to increase shock strength each time the "learner" erred (the learner never actually received shocks). When teachers hesitated, the experimenter used graded prods : "Please continue"; "The experiment requires that you continue"; "It is absolutely essential that you continue"; "You have no other choice; you must go on." Reasons for destructive obedience: Transfer of responsibility onto the experimenter (the authority figure, not the participant, would be responsible). Badges/signs of authority that remind people of the norm "obey the people in charge". Immediacy of the victim: when the victim was unseen/unheard, obedience was higher. Gradual escalation of orders yields more obedience than sudden escalation; situations move quickly. Social power (French & Raven, 1959) Power = the capacity to influence others while resisting their attempts to influence you. John French and Bert Raven (1959) identified five bases of social power (reward, coercive, legitimate, referent, expert); Raven (1965, 1993) later added a sixth (informational power). Persuasion Persuasion = changing attitudes through messages. Most persuasive communicators are credible, physically attractive , and seem not to be trying to persuade. Fear appeals that are too frightening tend not to work; positively framed messages are often more effective. Definition Elaboration-Likelihood Model (ELM): persuasion occurs by two routes. The central route (systematic processing) involves careful attention to message content (argument strength matters), used when motivation and capacity are high. The peripheral route (heuristic processing) uses mental shortcuts and peripheral cues (communicator attractiveness/expertise), used when ability, capacity or motivation is low. Electronic word-of-mouth (eWoM) persuasion depends on communicator credibility, consistency among reviewers, and consistency with prior beliefs. Resistance to persuasion is increased by: reactance (negative reaction to threats to personal freedom, which can boomerang into greater opposition), forewarning (knowing someone will try to change us), selective avoidance , active counterarguing , and attitude inoculation (exposure to weak attacks so refutations are ready for stronger ones). Ego-depletion from prior self-regulation undermines our ability to resist persuasion (and makes us less honest). 5. Group dynamics A group = a collection of people perceived to be bonded together in a coherent unit to some degree. Types and structure of groups Common-bond groups: face-to-face interaction; members bonded to each other . Common-identity groups: face-to-face interaction often absent; members linked via the category rather than each other. Entitativity: the extent to which a group is perceived as a coherent whole. Entitative groups interact often, are important to members, share goals, and are similar in important ways. Key components of groups: Component Meaning Status Gained for many reasons (physical characteristics to conformity to norms); higher for prototypical or senior members; high-status members are more idiosyncratic/variable and report conforming less . Roles Sets of behaviours expected of those in particular positions; powerful when internalised as part of identity; enacting a role well can feel authentic. Norms Rules/expectations about how members should behave. Feeling rules govern emotions (in collectivist groups: maintain harmony even at personal cost; in individualist groups: value standing out). Cohesiveness All forces causing members to remain. Cohesive groups have solidarity, see themselves as homogeneous, support and cooperate with ingroup members, pursue group over individual goals, have high morale, and perform better. An outgroup/competitive threat increases cohesion. Group development and socialisation Bruce Tuckman (1965) five-stage developmental sequence: forming (orientation), storming (conflict over goals/practices), norming (consensus, cohesion, common identity), performing (smooth functioning, shared norms), adjourning (the group dissolves). Moreland & Levine's group socialisation model: three basic processes ( evaluation, commitment, role transition ) leading to five phases. Transition criteria often become formalised as rites of passage / initiation rites serving three functions: symbolic, apprenticeship, loyalty elicitation . Costs and benefits of joining: benefits include self-knowledge, progress toward goals, enhanced status, and a means of social change (when a politicised collective identity forms). Costs include loss of personal freedom and demands on time/energy/resources. After painful initiations people justify their effort and show increased positive attitudes toward the group. A schism (splintering into factions) causes emotional distress and loss of identification. Coordination, cooperation and fairness Cooperation = working together for shared goals; often fails because of social dilemmas (individuals gain by defection, but if all defect everyone loses). Negative interdependence (one's gain = another's loss) lowers cooperation. Conflict = perceiving that others have taken or will take actions incompatible with one's interests; faulty attribution can drive it. Bargaining and superordinate goals (goals both sides seek that tie their interests together) reduce conflict. Perceived fairness has three forms: distributive justice (fairness of outcomes/share of rewards), procedural justice (fairness of the procedures used to distribute), and transactional justice (how the treatment is delivered — whether distributors explain/justify decisions and show respect). Group decision-making Group polarization: groups make more extreme decisions than individuals. Two reasons: members want views more prototypical (hence more extreme) than average; and persuasive arguments in discussion shift members further in the dominant direction. Groupthink (Irving Janis): a tendency for highly cohesive groups to assume they can do no wrong and to reject information contrary to the group's view. Groups also reject criticism more from outgroup than ingroup members. Hidden-profile / shared-information bias: members fail to share unique information; discussion focuses on what everyone already knows. A remedy is to keep members unaware of others' views before discussion. Brainstorming does not produce more creativity than individuals working alone; but debate about ideas does stimulate more creative idea production. Deindividuation Definition Deindividuation = a psychological state of reduced self-awareness brought on by external conditions such as being an anonymous member of a large crowd, encouraging unrestrained, antisocial action. It is especially likely when people are in a large group, physically anonymous, and aroused/distracted. The diminished self-awareness and self-restraint increase responsiveness to the immediate situation (negative or positive). Deindividuation is less likely when self-awareness is high. High-yield Polarization = more extreme. Groupthink = cohesive groups suppress dissent (Irving Janis). Deindividuation = anonymity/arousal → reduced self-awareness → unrestrained behaviour. Brainstorming in groups is not more creative than individuals alone. 6. Leadership styles Leadership = getting group members to achieve the group's goals. Trait and situational perspectives Great person theory: attributes effective leadership to innate or acquired individual characteristics. The best Big Five predictors of effective leadership are being extraverted, open to experience, and conscientious . Situational perspective: different styles are effective in different situations; the interaction of leader behaviour and situational factors matters. Lewin's classic leadership styles Style Behaviour Autocratic Organised activities, gave orders, was aloof, focused exclusively on the task. Democratic Called for suggestions, discussed plans, behaved like an ordinary member. Laissez-faire Left the group to its own devices, intervened minimally. The two leadership dimensions (Ohio State, LBDQ) The Leader Behaviour Description Questionnaire (LBDQ) drew a distinction between two dimensions: initiating structure (define objectives and organise members' work toward them — task-oriented ) and consideration (concern for subordinates' welfare and harmonious relationships — relationship-oriented ). A single person can be high on both , and such a person is a particularly effective leader. Contingency theories Fred Fiedler's contingency theory: measures leadership style with the Least Preferred Coworker (LPC) scale (rate the person you least like working with on dimensions like pleasant–unpleasant, friendly–unfriendly). Effectiveness is contingent on three situational dimensions, in descending importance: (1) leader–member relations , (2) task structure , (3) position power (intrinsic authority of the leader's position). Normative decision theory (NDT): focused on leadership in group decision-making; identifies three strategies — autocratic (no subordinate input), consultative (input sought, leader decides), group decision-making (leader and subordinates as equal partners). Effectiveness is contingent on leader–subordinate relations and task clarity/structure. Path–goal theory: a leader's main function is to motivate followers by clarifying the paths to their goals; also classifiable as a transactional leadership theory. It distinguishes two LBDQ behaviours: structuring (most effective when followers are unclear about goals/how to reach them — new, difficult, ambiguous tasks; backfires as "meddling" when tasks are well understood) and consideration (most effective when the task is boring/uncomfortable, but not when followers are already engaged and motivated, where it can seem distracting). High-yield Fred Fiedler = LPC scale + three situational dimensions (leader–member relations > task structure > position power). Ohio State LBDQ = initiating structure (task) vs consideration (relationship). Path–goal = a transactional theory; structuring helps unclear tasks, consideration helps boring tasks. 7. Prosocial behaviour Definition Prosocial behaviour = actions by individuals that help others with no immediate benefit to the helper. Motives for helping Empathy–altruism hypothesis: because of empathy, we help those in need out of empathic concern. Empathy = the capacity to experience others' emotional states, feel sympathy, and take their perspective, with three components: emotional empathy (sharing feelings), a cognitive component ( empathic accuracy , perceiving thoughts/feelings accurately), and empathic concern (concern for another's well-being). Negative-state relief model: we help to relieve and reduce our own negative emotional discomfort. Empathic joy hypothesis: helping stems from the positive reactions recipients show, and the positive feelings this induces in helpers. Competitive altruism: we help to increase our own status and reputation. Kinship selection theory: we help relatives because it increases the chance our genes are passed on. Reciprocal altruism theory: we help non-relatives because helping is usually reciprocated, indirectly aiding our own survival. Defensive helping: helping to reduce the threat an outgroup poses to one's ingroup. Responding to emergencies: the bystander effect A bystander's response can range from apathy to heroism. Because of diffusion of responsibility , the more bystanders present, the less likely each is to help and the greater the delay (the bystander effect ). Pluralistic ignorance is the tendency to do nothing because, not knowing what is happening, each bystander relies on others' (inactive) cues. The bystander effect is weaker among people who belong to the same group. Definition John Darley & Latané (1968) five-step decision model: whether a bystander helps depends on five sequential decisions — (1) notice the event, (2) interpret it as an emergency, (3) assume responsibility , (4) know how to help , and (5) decide to implement the help. Failing any step means no help is given. Factors and emotions in helping We help those similar to us more (similarity mostly affects the emotional , not the cognitive, component of empathy); we help those we like and those not responsible for their need. Helping is increased by exposure to prosocial models and by playing prosocial video games (which prime prosocial thoughts). Gratitude increases helping by enhancing helpers' self-worth and self-efficacy. Positive feelings increase helping; negative feelings tend to reduce it (though both can enhance or inhibit depending on the situation). Feelings of elevation (being inspired by others' kind acts) increase helping. Empathy is weaker across group boundaries. Three types of perspective taking : "imagine other", "imagine self", and fantasy (empathy for a fictional character). Factors that reduce helping: social exclusion (reduces capacity for empathy), darkness /anonymity, and putting an economic value on one's time . Reactions to being helped: positive when help seems to stem from the helper's positive feelings ( autonomous motivation ); far less positive when help seems forced ( controlled motivation ). Low-status group members are reluctant to receive help from high-status groups, especially when seeking equality. 8. Aggression Definition Aggression = behaviour directed toward the goal of harming another living being who is motivated to avoid such treatment. Theoretical perspectives Drive theories (Leonard Berkowitz 1989; Feshbach 1984): aggression stems from externally elicited drives to harm. The most famous is the frustration–aggression hypothesis (John Dollard, Doob, Miller, O. Hobart Mowrer & Sears, 1939), which made two sweeping claims: (1) frustration always leads to some form of aggression, and (2) aggression always stems from frustration. Both are now considered false: frustration is a strong elicitor only under limited conditions. Social learning perspective (Albert Bandura, 1997): we are not born with aggressive responses; we acquire them through direct experience or observation of others . General Aggression Model (GAM) (Anderson & Bushman, 2002): two input classes — situational factors (frustration, provocation, aggressive models, discomfort) and person factors (irritability, pro-violence attitudes, hostile attribution tendency, aggression-related skills). These act through three processes: arousal , affective states (hostile feelings), and cognitions (hostile thoughts). Depending on appraisals and restraining factors, the person then engages in thoughtful or impulsive action. Causes of aggression Provocations: actions perceived as stemming from malicious intent — condescension (a very powerful source), harsh/unjustified criticism (especially personal criticism), and teasing . Excitation-transfer theory: heightened arousal can increase aggression if it persists beyond its original situation and is misattributed as anger in a new context. Social exclusion: rejection initiates a hostile cognitive mind-set, making us perceive ambiguous actions as hostile. Media violence increases aggression via priming of aggressive thoughts, weakening of restraints, and desensitization . Violent video games increase aggressive cognition, affect and behaviour, and reduce empathy/prosocial behaviour (people play them for competence and mastery, not the violent content). Cultural, personality and situational factors Cultures of honor: cultures with strong norms that aggression is appropriate in response to insults to one's honor; impact especially apparent for sexual jealousy. Evolutionary view: men feel jealousy over sexual infidelity (paternal uncertainty), women over emotional infidelity (need for mate's assistance in child rearing); manhood is "precarious" and threats to it may trigger aggression to restore it. TASS model (Traits As Situational Sensitivities): personality traits interact with situational factors; personal traits enhance aggression only when situational factors (e.g., provocation) are above threshold , and individual differences are eliminated when the situation is strong (high provocation). Type A behaviour pattern: more irritable and aggressive than Type B; more likely to engage in hostile aggression (prime objective = harming the victim) but not more instrumental aggression (aggression to attain other goals such as resources or praise). Narcissism: overinflated self-worth; react with exceptionally high aggression to ego-threatening feedback; view themselves as victims of others' transgressions. Gender: males are more aggressive overall, but the difference is highly situation-dependent and eliminated under strong provocation. Males use more direct aggression, females more indirect ; gender differences are smaller and more complex than once thought. Situational determinants: high temperatures increase aggression up to a point (then decline); alcohol increases aggression in both sexes (reduces information-processing capacity). Bullying and reducing aggression Bullying = repeated assault on others with little/no power to retaliate. Motives: holding power, being part of a "tough" high-status group, and feeling better about oneself. Among boys, power and group motives predict bullying (not feeling depressed); for girls, all three motives do. Few children are solely bullies or victims; many switch roles. Bullies make hostile/dispositional attributions ; bullies and bully-victims favour responding with aggression and have lower self-esteem . Cyberbullying = repeated online assaults (insults, exclusion, blackmail). Reducing aggression: Punishment works only when it is prompt, certain, strong, and perceived as justified . Catharsis hypothesis (venting reduces aggression) is mainly false — venting tends to increase subsequent aggression. Self-affirmation (bolstering self-esteem) can reduce aggression in high-narcissism people by preventing ego threats from triggering aggression. Trap The frustration–aggression hypothesis (John Dollard et al., 1939) and the catharsis hypothesis are both classic "this is now considered FALSE" exam items. Hostile aggression (harm is the goal) vs instrumental aggression (harm is a means to another goal) is a frequent distinction. 9. Theories of intergroup relationship How relations between groups produce prejudice, conflict and collective action. Minimal group experiments & Social Identity Theory (Tajfel) Henri Tajfel and associates set out to define an intergroup situation where social categorisation occurs on a trivial criterion but none of the usual conditions of intergroup conflict are present. The conditions were: no face-to-face interaction, complete anonymity of group membership, no instrumental/rational link between criteria and rewards, no utilitarian value of the rewards to the subject, and a number of allocation options. The first minimal group experiment (Tajfel, 1970): 64 British schoolboys (14–15) did a dot-estimation task and were assigned (actually randomly) to "overestimator/underestimator" or "more/less accurate" groups. They allocated real money to anonymous in-group and out-group members (identified only by code numbers) via a matrix offering strategies: Fairness (F) , Maximum Joint Profit (MJP) , Maximum In-group Profit (MIP) , and Maximum Difference in favour of the in-group (MD) . Result: subjects favoured the in-group, endorsing a combination of MD and MIP most often — even at the expense of absolute in-group profit. Tajfel concluded that mere social categorisation produces discriminatory intergroup behaviour without any of the normal conditions of conflict. Definition Social Identity Theory (Henri Tajfel & John Turner): people are motivated to maintain or achieve a positive self-identity . Three central processes: social categorisation (segmenting the world to impose order and provide a locus of self-identification), social identity (the part of the self-concept derived from group membership, with its value and emotional significance), and social comparison (comparing in-group to out-group, drawing on Festinger's 1954 theory). The goal is positive psychological group distinctiveness : an identity perceived as distinct and positive vis-à-vis relevant comparison groups. Negative social identity → dissatisfaction → (if cognitive alternatives are perceived) attempts to change the situation. Social change and social mobility A strategy for social change is embarked upon only when cognitive alternatives to the existing situation are perceived, which depends on two factors: stability–instability (can the hierarchy be changed?) and legitimacy–illegitimacy (is the situation just?). A disadvantaged group perceiving cognitive alternatives may: be absorbed into the dominant group, redefine the negatively evaluated characteristic, create new dimensions of comparison, or directly compete. Social mobility assumes the system is flexible and permeable, permitting free movement of individuals. Relative deprivation theory Definition Relative deprivation = a perceived discrepancy between attainments ("what is") and expectations/entitlements ("what ought to be"). It is always relative to other conditions; deprivation is not absolute. James Davies (1969) J-curve model: when attainments suddenly fall short of rising expectations, relative deprivation is acute, producing collective unrest — "revolutions of rising expectations". Gary Runciman (1966) distinguished egoistic relative deprivation (deprivation relative to similar individuals) from fraternalistic relative deprivation (comparison with dissimilar others / other groups). They are independent. Walker & Mann (1987) : fraternalistic deprivation predicts willingness for militant protest; egoistic deprivation predicts personal stress symptoms (headaches, indigestion, sleeplessness). Fraternalistic deprivation translates into protest only with: strong ingroup identification, belief that action is feasible, perceptions of injustice (procedural injustice especially potent), and a particular ingroup–outgroup comparison. Social protest and collective action Response to deprivation often involves sustained social protest. Sympathisers hold supportive attitudes that don't automatically become behaviour; they can be mobilised into activists . Klandermans views protest as intergroup behaviour occurring in "multiorganisational fields" , with four steps to participation: becoming part of the mobilisation potential, becoming a target of mobilisation attempts, developing motivation to participate, and overcoming barriers to participation. Realistic conflict theory (Muzafer Sherif) A key feature of intergroup behaviour is ethnocentrism , whose origins (Sherif 1962) lie in the nature of intergroup relations: where groups compete over scarce resources , relations become conflictual and ethnocentric. Tested in the famous Robber's Cave experiments (field experiments at summer camps, 1949/1953/1954): Phase 1: boys arrived and formed friendships in camp-wide activities. Phase 2: camp split into two groups (breaking friendships); isolated groups developed their own norms and status differences. Phase 3: intergroup competitions generated fierce hostility that generalised beyond the contests. Phase 4: introducing superordinate goals (desired by both but unachievable alone) gradually improved relations through cooperation. Cooperation, competition and social dilemmas Dilemma Structure Prisoner's dilemma Two guilty suspects questioned separately; each can confess for immunity. If both confess = moderate sentence; if neither = light sentence. A "two-person, mixed-motive, non-zero-sum game" (a zero-sum game = one's gain is always the other's loss). Trucking game Two players run trucking companies; a short shared one-lane route causes repeated head-on conflict and wasted time arguing. Commons dilemma An n-person prisoner's dilemma: cooperation by all benefits all, competition by all harms all. The classic example (100 farmers, 100-cow common) yields the tragedy of the commons when each adds an extra cow. Equity theory Equity theory specifies conditions for intergroup conflict and its resolution. Justice = a socially defined standard for evaluating resource distribution. People define justice from inputs (contributions: attributes, abilities, efforts) and outcomes (tangible/intangible rewards or punishments). For justice, outcomes need not be equal; the ratio of outcomes to inputs must be equal (Ox/Ix = Oy/Iy). Walster, Berscheid & Walster (1973) revised the formula to permit negative inputs/outcomes (using absolute values). Perceived inequity causes psychological distress; equity can be restored by actual restoration (changing real inputs/outcomes) or psychological restoration (cognitively distorting the perceived inputs/outcomes). Balance theory (Fritz Heider, 1946) The p-o-x (balance) theory : originally about the sentiments of a person (p) toward another (o) and an impersonal object (x) belonging to o; later expanded to general interpersonal relations. Heider proposed two relation types: unit relations (U / not-U: elements seen as belonging together or not, governed by Gestalt factors of similarity, proximity, common fate, good continuation, set, past experience) and sentiment relations (L / DL: liking, admiring vs disliking, rejecting). Balance in dyads: balanced when both relations are positive or both negative; imbalanced when one is positive and one negative. Balance in triads: balanced when all three relations are positive, or when two are negative and one positive; imbalanced when one is negative and two positive; ambiguous when all three are negative. (Always judged from p's viewpoint .) Consequences of the balance tendency: preference for balanced states, induction of new relations to produce balance, and pressure to change imbalanced states (by altering either sentiment or unit relations). Mnemonic Triad balance = "multiply the signs to +." A triad is balanced when the product of the three signs is positive (+++ or +−−). One negative + two positives gives a product of −, which is imbalanced and feels uncomfortable. Social exchange theory (George Homans, 1961) Homans explained elementary face-to-face interaction as the psychological exchange of rewards (positive reinforcements) and costs (negative reinforcements) between two persons. He limited the theory to behaviour that is social, directly reacted to by the other party (not a third party), and actual (not a mere norm). His unit of analysis was the elementary face-to-face social interchange ; the dyad and small group are the building blocks of larger social units. Three descriptive terms : activity , sentiment , interaction ; two key variables : quantity (frequency) and value (degree of reinforcement). Homans' propositions of human exchange: Success: the more often an action is rewarded, the more likely it is performed (a derivative of Thorndike's law of effect). Stimulus: the more similar present stimuli are to past rewarded ones, the more likely the action (stimulus generalisation / secondary reinforcement). Value: the more valuable the result, the more likely the action. Deprivation–satiation: the more often a reward has recently been received, the less valuable further units become. Aggression–approval (5a/5b): unexpected non-reward/punishment → anger and aggression; expected (or greater-than-expected) reward → pleasure and approving behaviour. Rationality: a person chooses the action whose value × probability of success is greatest. Rule of distributive justice: a person in exchange expects rewards proportional to costs, and net profits proportional to investments; evaluations of "just return" are based on past exchange experience, which sets up an expected "exchange rate". High-yield Henri Tajfel = social identity / minimal groups (MD & MIP). Muzafer Sherif = realistic conflict / Robber's Cave / superordinate goals. Fritz Heider = balance (p-o-x). George Homans = social exchange (rewards/costs, six propositions). Davies = J-curve; Runciman = egoistic vs fraternalistic relative deprivation; Walster et al. = equity ratio. The contact hypothesis & reducing prejudice Prejudice (a negative attitude toward an outgroup) is reduced by intergroup contact under favourable conditions (the contact hypothesis , traced to Gordon Allport's 1954 Nature of Prejudice ): equal status, common goals, cooperation, and institutional support. Robber's Cave demonstrated that contact alone was insufficient — superordinate goals requiring cooperation were what reduced hostility. 10. Applying social psychology How social-psychological principles are applied to clinical/health work, the law, and the environment. Social psychology in clinical / health settings Illusory correlations: the tendency to see correlations where none exist. Clinicians may perceive illusory correlations during diagnosis; hindsight explanations breed overconfidence; erroneous diagnoses can be self-confirming because interviewers seek and recall confirming information. This underscores the need for rigorous testing of intuitive conclusions and statistical prediction. Depressive realism: mildly depressed people make more accurate (rather than self-serving) judgments. Depressed people have a negative, pessimistic attributional/explanatory style , attributing failure to stable, global, internal causes. Depression is a vicious circle in which negative thoughts elicit self-defeating behaviours. Loneliness (common in individualistic societies) and shyness (a form of social anxiety marked by self-consciousness) are similar vicious circles in which negative feelings elicit off-putting behaviour. Loneliness can prompt nostalgia, which reminds people of social connections. Health psychology studies how people decide they are ill, explain symptoms, and seek/follow treatment, and the links among illness, stress and a pessimistic explanatory style. Therapy and social relations Consistent with the attitudes-follow-behaviour principle, several therapies prescribe action: we can influence feelings indirectly through behaviour. The vicious circle of depression/loneliness/anxiety can be broken at any point — by changing the environment, training constructive behaviour, or reversing negative thinking ( social skills training and explanatory-style therapy ). Improvements are best maintained when people attribute them to internal factors under their continued control rather than to the treatment program. Changing clients' attitudes requires persuasion ; therapists act as expert, trustworthy communicators. Social relations and health: close, supportive relationships lower risk of illness and premature death and foster happiness (e.g., married adults report being happier and are at less risk for depression), partly by helping people confide intimate emotions. Social psychology in law Eyewitness testimony accuracy is impaired by many factors. Assertive witnesses are more likely to be believed, although assertiveness does not reflect actual certainty. The human eye is not a video camera. Misinformation effect: incorporating misleading post-event information into one's memory so the false information is believed true. Repeated retelling lets errors creep in. To reduce errors, let witnesses recount without interruption and encourage them to visualise the scene and their emotional state. Juror judgments: with ambiguous evidence, jurors interpret it through preconceived biases and sympathise with attractive/similar defendants. Pretrial publicity and inadmissible evidence often influence jurors despite judicial instruction (especially when the admonition comes after an impression is formed). Lawyers use jury consultants ; disqualifying death-penalty opponents itself produces a biased jury. Group deliberation can entrench and polarise views, though it may make jurors more lenient when evidence is weakly incriminating. Social psychology and the environment Humanity can prepare for a sustainable future by increasing technological efficiency, creating incentives, and changing actions and attitudes to control population and moderate consumption. People in rich nations report greater happiness than those in poor nations, yet materialism fails to satisfy , explained by two principles: the adaptation-level phenomenon (adapting to a level of stimulation and reacting only to changes from it) and social comparison (evaluating oneself against others). To build a satisfying, sustainable future, individuals and societies can promote close relationships, belief-based social networks, positive thinking habits, and engaging activity ( flow ). High-yield Applied themes: illusory correlation + self-confirming diagnosis (clinical judgment); depressive realism + pessimistic explanatory style (stable/global/internal); attitudes-follow-behaviour therapy + internal attribution of improvement; misinformation effect + eyewitness fallibility (law); adaptation-level + social comparison + flow (environment/well-being).

title: Unit 9 — Human Development & Intervention
text: Unit 9 — Human Development & Intervention The arc of a human life and the clinical work built on top of it: how development proceeds from conception to old age across every domain and theory (Sigmund Freud, Erik Erikson, Jean Piaget, Lev Vygotsky, the learning and information-processing views), how language and motor skills unfold, what it means for behaviour to become abnormal and how disorders are described and classified, the full landscape of psychotherapies (psychoanalytic, person-centred, Gestalt, existential, behavioural, REBT/CBT, transactional, family/systems), and the biological and socioemotional theories of successful aging. Built from Rodrick Prashanth's MET source decks and taught to NIMHANS clinical depth, losing no named theorist, term, or stage. In this book Developmental processes, domains & periods Theories of development Piaget's cognitive stages Vygotsky & information-processing Sensorimotor & motor development Language: components, theories, periods The concept of abnormality Describing & assessing disorders Classification (DSM & ICD) & causes Psychoanalytic therapy Person-centred, Gestalt & existential Behaviour therapy REBT & Beck's cognitive therapy Transactional analysis Family & systems therapy Successful aging: biological theories Socioemotional aging & late-life disorders 1. Developmental processes, domains & periods The one idea. Developmental science studies change and stability across the lifespan. Scientists care not only about how people change but about the underlying stability or constancy of personality and behaviour over time. Two kinds of change Quantitative change — a change in number or amount : growth in height, weight, vocabulary, aggressive behaviour, or frequency of communication. Qualitative change — a change in kind, structure, or organisation . Not "more of the same" but a different form altogether. Three domains of development Change and stability occur in various domains (dimensions) of the self. Scientists discuss them separately but treat development as a single unified process . Domain What changes Physical development Growth of body and brain; change or stability in sensory capacities, motor skills, and health. Cognitive development Change or stability in mental abilities: learning, attention, memory, language, thinking, reasoning, and creativity. Psychosocial development Change and stability in emotions, personality, and social relationships. Periods of the lifespan The division of the lifespan into periods (infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, old age) is a social construction : a concept about the nature of reality based on societally shared perceptions or assumptions, not a fixed biological fact. High-yield Quantitative = change in amount (height, vocabulary). Qualitative = change in kind/structure . Three domains: physical, cognitive, psychosocial. Lifespan periods are a social construction . 2. Theories of development The psychoanalytic viewpoint — Freud Sigmund Freud concluded that human development is a conflictual process : as biological creatures we have basic sexual and aggressive instincts that must be served, yet society dictates that many of these drives be restrained. The ways parents manage these urges in the first few years play a major role in shaping personality. Freud held personality was fixed in childhood — essentially formed by age 5 or 6. Psychosexual stages of development Stage Age Characteristics Fixation outcomes Oral 0–1 Mouth is the primary erogenous zone; pleasure from sucking; id is dominant . Oral incorporative (taking in) — optimism, dependency. Oral aggressive/sadistic (during teething) — pessimism, hostility, aggressiveness. Anal 1–3 Toilet training (external reality) interferes with gratification from defecation. Anal aggressive — defecates to defy parents; basis for hostile/sadistic adult behaviour. Anal retentive — stubborn, stingy, hoarding; rigid, compulsively neat, obstinate, overly conscientious. Phallic 4–5 Incestuous fantasies; Oedipus and Electra complex ; castration anxiety; superego development. Phallic character shows strong narcissism . Latency 5–puberty Period of sublimation of the sex instinct. — Genital Adolescence–adulthood Development of sex-role identity and adult social relationships. Genital type finds satisfaction in love and work , work being an acceptable outlet for sublimation of id impulses. Erikson's theory of psychosocial development Erik Erikson renounced Sigmund Freud's idea of fixity, arguing that identity formation is a lifelong process . Personality (Erikson focused on identity ) develops through eight stages as life unfolds. The outcome of each stage depends on the outcome of the previous one, and successful negotiation of each ego crisis is essential for optimal growth. He used Freud's psychosexual stages as his basis; his first five stages reflect ego crises tied to Freud's stages. Trap Sigmund Freud: personality fixed by age 5–6 , five psychosexual stages. Erik Erikson: identity is lifelong , eight psychosocial stages built on Freud's first five. Don't merge the two. The learning viewpoint — Watson & the operant view John B. Watson believed that well-learned associations between external stimuli and observable responses (called habits ) are the building blocks of development. From this perspective children do not progress through distinct biologically dictated stages; development is a continuous process of behavioural change shaped by each person's unique environment, and may differ dramatically from person to person. Operant learning theory claims development depends on external stimuli (reinforcers and punishers) rather than internal forces such as instincts, drives, or maturation. Modern developmentalists agree habits can emerge and disappear over a lifetime depending on their positive or negative consequences. The cognitive viewpoint — Jean Piaget Piaget (1950) defined intelligence as a basic life process that helps an organism adapt to its environment . As children mature they acquire ever more complex cognitive structures. A cognitive structure — what Piaget called a scheme (or schema ) — is an organised pattern of thought or action used to cope with or explain some aspect of experience. Cognitive development occurs neither solely through maturation nor solely through learning : through interaction with the environment, psychological structures become reorganised. Infants are born with simple schemata such as sucking and grasping . Definition Assimilation = actively organising new information so it fits with what is already perceived and thought. Accommodation = changing what is already perceived or thought so it fits new information. Learning occurs through these two basic mental operations. 3. Piaget's cognitive stages Jean Piaget described four stages through which all of us pass. Each new experience requires cognitive organisation or reorganisation in a mental structure (schema). Sensorimotor stage (0–2 years) Infants know the world through senses and motor action, building from inborn reflexes (sucking, grasping) toward intentional behaviour and, eventually, object permanence and mental representation. Preoperational stage (2–7 years) Marked by the appearance of the symbolic function — the ability to make one thing (a word or object) stand for or represent something else. The knowledge that an entity can stand for something other than itself is representational insight . Language is the most obvious symbolism; pretend (symbolic) play blossoms in the early preoperational period. 2½-year-olds lack dual representation — the ability to think about an object in two different ways at the same time. Deficits in preoperational reasoning Animism — attributing life and lifelike qualities to inanimate objects. Egocentrism — viewing the world from one's own perspective; difficulty recognising another's point of view. Centration — attending to one aspect of a situation to the exclusion of others (contrast with decentration). Lack of conservation — failure to recognise that properties of an object/substance do not change when its appearance is altered superficially. Lack of reversibility — inability to reverse or negate an action by mentally performing the opposite (negation). Theory of Mind (ToM) ToM develops during the preoperational period: children's developing concepts of mental activity — an understanding that humans are cognitive beings whose mental states are not always shared with or accessible to others. The most frequently used tool is the false-belief task , where the child must infer that another person does not possess knowledge that the child possesses (holds a false belief). Children usually make an egocentric response . Concrete-operational stage (7–11 years) Can solve conservation problems. Mental seriation — mentally arranging items along a quantifiable dimension (height, weight). Transitivity — recognising necessary relations among elements in a series (if A > B and B > C, then A > C). Horizontal décalage — Jean Piaget's term for uneven cognitive performance: inability to solve certain problems even though one can solve similar problems requiring the same operations (e.g., solving some conservation tasks but not others). Formal-operational stage (11–12 years and beyond) Formal operations are mental actions performed on ideas and propositions . The benchmark is hypothetico-deductive reasoning . Such thinkers are not restricted to previously acquired facts but can generate hypotheses , and can think inductively (from specific observations to broad generalisations). For them, what is possible is more important than what is real . Mnemonic Some People Can Fly — Sensorimotor, Preoperational, Concrete-operational, Formal-operational. Conservation arrives at concrete ; abstract hypotheticals arrive at formal . 4. Vygotsky & the information-processing viewpoint Vygotsky's sociocultural theory Lev Vygotsky focused on how culture — the beliefs, values, traditions, and skills of a social group — is transmitted across generations. Cognitive growth is a socially mediated activity : children acquire new ways of thinking through cooperative dialogues with more knowledgeable members of society . He rejected the notion that all children progress through the same universal stages, arguing the new skills children master are often specific to their culture rather than universal structures. Four interrelated levels of analysis Microgenetic — changes over very brief periods (seconds, minutes, days). Ontogenetic — development of the individual over their lifetime. Phylogenetic — development over evolutionary time. Sociohistorical — changes that have occurred in one's culture and the values, norms, and technologies its history generated. Core constructs Tools of intellectual adaptation — each culture provides children tools that let them use basic mental functions more adaptively. Zone of proximal development (ZPD) — the range of tasks too complex to be mastered alone but accomplishable with guidance and encouragement from a more skilful partner . Scaffolding — the process by which an expert, instructing a novice, responds contingently to the novice's behaviour so the novice gradually increases understanding. Less able children elicit more support than more capable children. Guided participation — adult–child interactions in which children's cognitions are shaped as they participate with or observe adults in culturally relevant activities (e.g., learning weaving or hunting without formal schooling). Contrast with context-independent learning ("knowledge for knowledge's sake") that prepares children for formal schooling. Trap Jean Piaget = child as a lone scientist discovering through self-directed interaction; universal stages. Lev Vygotsky = child as a social apprentice ; learning is mediated by culture and more skilful partners (ZPD, scaffolding); skills are culture-specific. The information-processing viewpoint The human mind is likened to a computer into which information flows, is operated on, and is converted to output (answers, inferences, solutions). Theorists view cognitive development as age-related changes in the mind's hardware (brain and peripheral nervous system) and software (mental processes such as attention, perception, memory, and problem-solving strategies). Crucially, development is a continuous process that is not stage-like — involving small quantitative rather than large qualitative changes. 5. Sensorimotor & motor development Basic trends of locomotor development Cephalocaudal — development proceeds head downward (head, neck, upper extremities precede legs and lower extremities). Proximodistal — development proceeds centre outward (trunk and shoulders before hands and fingers). Three views of motor sequencing/timing Viewpoint Claim Maturational Motor development is the unfolding of a genetically programmed sequence in which nerves and muscles mature in a downward and outward direction. Experiential (practice) Maturation is necessary but not sufficient ; infants physically capable of sitting/crawling/walking won't be proficient without opportunities to practise. Dynamical systems Each new skill is a construction that emerges as infants actively reorganise existing motor capabilities into new, more complex action systems; a real world of interesting objects and events gives infants reasons (purposes, motives) to reach, sit, crawl, walk, and run. New patterns are at first tentative, inefficient, uncoordinated, then become smooth and coordinated. Fine motor development — voluntary reaching & manipulatory skills Newborns come equipped with a grasping reflex and make uncoordinated prereaches (primitive thrusts) at objects in the visual field.
