By 2 months, reaching/grasping may seem to deteriorate as the reflexive palmar grasp disappears and prereaching occurs less often. From 3 months, voluntary reaching is a learned motor skill that does not simply "unfold"; infants make in-flight corrections, improving in accuracy. By ~4–5 months, an infant able to sit and reach inward across the body can grasp interesting objects with both hands. The palmar grasp (clumsy, claw-like grip allowing little tactile exploration) is replaced near the end of the first year by the ulnar grasp . The pincer grasp (thumb + forefinger) transforms the child from a fumbler into a skilful manipulator; by 16 months they use thumbs and forefingers to lift and explore. By the end of the second year they scribble with a crayon, copy a simple line, and build towers of five or more blocks. Fingering activity may be the primary method by which 4- to 6-month-olds gain information about objects, since unimanual grasping is still poor. 6. Language: components, theories & periods Definition Language = a small number of individually meaningless symbols (sounds, letters, gestures) combined by agreed-on rules to produce an infinite number of messages. Communication = the process by which one organism transmits information to and influences another. Vocables = unique patterns of sound a prelinguistic infant uses to represent objects, actions, or events. Five components of language Component What it covers Phonology The sound system of a language and rules for combining sounds to produce meaningful units. Phonemes = the basic units of sound used in a spoken language. Morphology The basic units of meaning. Morphemes = smallest meaningful language units. Free morphemes stand alone (e.g., "dog"); bound morphemes cannot stand alone but change meaning when attached to a free morpheme. Semantics The expressed meaning of words and sentences. Syntax The structure of a language; rules specifying how words and grammatical markers combine into meaningful sentences. Pragmatics Principles underlying effective, appropriate use of language in social contexts; involves sociolinguistic knowledge (culturally specific rules for how language should be structured and used). Theories of language development Learning theorists (empiricist) — language is obviously learned. Emphasise imitation and reinforcement . B. F. Skinner : adults shape a child's speech by selectively reinforcing babbling that resembles words, then withhold reinforcement until the child combines words into longer grammatical utterances. Social-learning theorists add that children acquire much linguistic knowledge by listening to and imitating older companions. Nativists — language acquisition is a biologically programmed activity, possibly involving specialised processing that operates most efficiently early in childhood. Evidence: linguistic universals . Noam Chomsky proposed a language acquisition device (LAD) — an inborn linguistic processor activated by verbal input, containing a universal grammar (rules common to all languages). Dan Slobin proposed an inborn language-making capacity (LMC) — cognitive/perceptual abilities specialised for language learning. The sensitive-period hypothesis was prompted by observations that child aphasics often recover lost language without therapy, whereas adult aphasics usually require extensive therapy. Interactionists — language acquisition reflects a complex interplay among biological predispositions, cognitive development, and the unique linguistic environment ( not a dedicated LAD or LMC). Like nativists they believe children are biologically prepared, but the preparation is a powerful, slowly maturing human brain. Elizabeth Bates (1999) argued grammatical speech arises out of social necessity as vocabularies grow beyond 100–200 words. Adults give children repeated opportunities to learn that conversing involves turn-taking, that things have names, and proper ways to ask and answer. Definition Child-directed speech (motherese) = the short, simple, high-pitched, often repetitive sentences adults use with young children. Adults provide negative evidence — responding to ungrammatical speech in ways that subtly signal an error: expansions (responding with a grammatically improved form) and recasts (responding with a nonrepetitive, grammatically correct statement). Periods of language development Prelinguistic period. Infants are well prepared: sensitive to intonational cues from birth, able to discriminate a wider variety of phonemes than adults. They begin cooing at ~2 months, babbling at about 6–7 months, and by 7–10 months are already segmenting others' speech into phrases and wordlike units. They learn turn-taking and that gestures communicate. Receptive language is ahead of productive language. Holophrase (one-word) period. Infants speak in holophrases (one-word utterances that carry a whole sentence's meaning) and expand vocabulary one word at a time, mostly about moving/manipulable objects. A vocabulary spurt (naming explosion) occurs between 18 and 24 months. Western children mostly develop a referential style; a smaller number, and many from social-harmony cultures, adopt an expressive style. Toddlers use social/contextual cues to fast map words, aided by processing constraints (object scope constraint, mutual exclusivity, lexical context, syntactic bootstrapping), and make semantic errors of overextension and underextension . Telegraphic period. At 18–24 months toddlers produce two- and three-word sentences called telegraphic speech (omitting grammatical markers and smaller words). These follow word-order rules and express consistent semantic relations ; toddlers grow sensitive to pragmatic constraints and sociolinguistic prescriptions (e.g., politeness in requests). Preschool period (ages 2–5). Language becomes much more adult-like. Children add grammatical morphemes (-s plural, -ed past, -ing progressive, articles, prepositions, auxiliaries), may overregularise , and learn transformational grammar (turning declaratives into questions, negations, imperatives, relative clauses, compound sentences). Middle childhood & adolescence. A period of refinement: subtle exceptions to grammatical rules, complex syntax, rapid vocabulary growth, growing metalinguistic awareness , and much better referential communication skills. 7. The concept of abnormality (psychopathology) No single indicator is sufficient in and of itself to define abnormality. The more a person has difficulties across the following areas, the more likely they have a mental disorder. Seven indicators of abnormality Suffering — psychological pain or distress. Maladaptiveness — behaviour that interferes with well-being and functioning. Statistical deviancy — being statistically rare or atypical. Violation of the standards of society — breaking social/moral norms. Social discomfort — making others uneasy. Irrationality and unpredictability . Dangerousness — to self or others. Definition DSM-5 mental disorder = a syndrome present in an individual that involves clinically significant disturbance in behaviour, emotion regulation, or cognitive functioning, reflecting a dysfunction in biological, psychological, or developmental processes necessary for mental functioning. 8. Describing & assessing disorders Epidemiology & prevalence terms Mental health epidemiology studies the distribution of mental disorders across settings or population groups (epidemiology more broadly studies the distribution of diseases, disorders, and health-related behaviours). Term Meaning Point prevalence Estimated proportion of actual, active cases of a disorder at a given point in time. 1-year prevalence Everyone who experienced the disorder at any point throughout the entire year. Lifetime prevalence Number of people who have had a disorder at any time in their lives (even if now recovered). Incidence Number of new cases over a given period (typically 1 year). Lower than prevalence because it excludes preexisting cases. Comorbidity Presence of two or more disorders in the same person. Especially high in people with severe forms; in the NCS-R study, half of those with a disorder rated as serious had two or more additional disorders. Other descriptions of disorders Sex ratio — percentage of males vs females with the disorder; and age of onset , which differs across disorders. Course — most disorders follow an individual pattern: chronic (lasting a long time, sometimes a lifetime, e.g., schizophrenia); episodic (recovery within months then recurrence, e.g., mood disorders); time-limited (improves without treatment in a short period). Onset — acute (sudden) vs insidious (gradual, over an extended period). Prognosis — the anticipated course of a disorder. The mental status examination (MSE) Systematic observation of an individual's behaviour across five categories : Appearance and behaviour — general appearance, gait, grooming, posture, facial expression. Thought processes — rate/flow of speech (continuity of speech), delusions, hallucinations, obsessions. Mood and affect — mood is the predominant feeling state; affect is the feeling state accompanying what we say at a given point, judged "appropriate" or "inappropriate". Intellectual functioning — attention, concentration, memory. Sensorium — general awareness of surroundings; orientation to place, time, and person. Trap Mood vs affect: mood is the sustained, predominant feeling state (the "climate"); affect is the moment-to-moment expressed feeling (the "weather"), rated as appropriate or inappropriate. Prevalence vs incidence: prevalence counts all active cases; incidence counts only new cases. Culture-specific disorders (culture-bound syndromes) are recognised patterns of distress tied to particular cultural contexts, reminding clinicians that the expression of abnormality is shaped by culture. 9. Classification (DSM & ICD) & causes of disorders History & the two major systems The 19th-century German physician Emil Kraepelin was the first modern theorist to develop a comprehensive classification model on the basis of distinctive features (symptoms) of abnormal behaviour patterns. DSM — Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, published by the American Psychiatric Association; an outgrowth of Kraepelin's work. Introduced in 1952 ; the latest, DSM-5 , was published in 2013 . Used widely in the United States. ICD — International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, published by the WHO; now in its 11th revision (ICD-11) . A compendium of both mental and physical disorders and the most widely used diagnostic manual worldwide. DSM-5 vs DSM-IV — major changes Dispensed with the multiaxial framework. The old five axes comprised: Axis I & II — inventory of mental disorders; Axis III — medical conditions and diseases; Axis IV — psychosocial and environmental problems/sources of stress affecting functioning; Axis V — a rating scale (GAF) of overall level of functioning. Adopted a dimensional component. DSM-5 did not abandon the categorical model but expanded it to include a dimensional component for many disorders. New, reclassified, and consolidated disorders: Asperger's disorder and autistic disorder reclassified under autism spectrum disorder . Trichotillomania (hair-pulling) moved from impulse-control disorders to Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders . Pathological (compulsive) gambling moved from impulse-control to Substance Use and Addictive Behaviors . PTSD moved from anxiety disorders to a new category, Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders . Causes of disorders — the diathesis-stress model Definition Diathesis = a predisposition toward developing a disorder, deriving from biological, psychological, or sociocultural causal factors. Stress = the response/experience to demands perceived as taxing or exceeding one's personal resources. Many disorders develop when a stressor operates on a person who has a diathesis (vulnerability) . The model accounting for both is the diathesis-stress (stress-diathesis) model . Protective factors such as intelligence and inoculation to stress reduce the chances of disorder. Two kinds exist: the integrative stress-diathesis model and the additive stress-diathesis model. 10. Psychoanalytic therapy Goals & process The two goals of Freudian psychoanalytic therapy are to make the unconscious conscious and to strengthen the ego so behaviour is based more on reality and less on instinctual cravings or irrational guilt. Analysts assume an anonymous, nonjudgmental "blank-screen" stance , avoiding self-disclosure and maintaining neutrality to foster a transference relationship in which clients make projections onto them. Analysis of transference is the very essence of therapeutic work. Counter-transference — the therapist projecting feelings onto the client — is detrimental and to be avoided. Six basic techniques Technique What it is Maintaining the analytic framework The range of procedural/stylistic factors: analyst's relative anonymity, neutrality and objectivity, regularity and consistency of meetings, starting/ending on time, clarity on fees, basic boundary issues. Free association Clients say whatever comes to mind, however painful, silly, trivial, illogical, or irrelevant. Gives access to the unconscious. Interpretation The analyst points out, explains, and even teaches the meanings of behaviour in dreams, free association, resistances, defences, and the therapeutic relationship. Functions: enable the ego to assimilate new material and speed up uncovering further unconscious material. Dream analysis Key procedure for uncovering unconscious material and giving insight into unresolved problems. During sleep defences are lowered and repressed feelings surface. Analysis of resistance Resistance is anything that works against the progress of therapy — the client's reluctance to bring repressed unconscious material to awareness. Analysis of transference The transference situation is valuable because its manifestations let clients re-experience feelings that would otherwise be inaccessible. 11. Person-centred, Gestalt & existential therapy Person-centred therapy (Carl Rogers) Rogers held that three therapist attributes create a growth-promoting climate: Congruence — genuineness, realness. Unconditional positive regard — acceptance and caring. Accurate empathic understanding — deeply grasping the subjective world of another. The actualizing tendency is a directional process of striving toward realization, fulfilment, autonomy, and self-determination. Goals: help clients achieve greater independence and integration, and increase congruence. It is the therapist's attitude , not knowledge/theories/techniques, that facilitates change; the therapist is a catalyst . Immediacy (addressing what is going on between client and therapist) is highly valued. Offshoots: Motivational Interviewing (MI) by William R. Miller and Stephen Rollnick (early 1980s), a humanistic, client-centred, modestly directive approach matched to the stages of change (precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance); and Person-Centred Expressive Arts Therapy (Natalie Rogers). Gestalt therapy (Fritz Perls) Arnie Beisser (1970) proposed the paradoxical theory of change : authentic change occurs more from being who we are than from trying to be who we are not. Key concepts: Holism — "Gestalt" is German for a whole/completion, a form that cannot be separated into parts without losing its essence. Field theory — the organism must be seen in its environment/context as part of a constantly changing field; emphasis on the figure (most salient experience) vs the ground (out of awareness). Therapists practise "attending to the obvious" via gestures, tone, demeanour. Figure-formation process — how the individual organises experience moment to moment as something emerges from the background into focal attention. Organismic self-regulation — equilibrium is "disturbed" by the emergence of a need, sensation, or interest. Contact & resistances to contact — contact is made by seeing, hearing, smelling, touching, moving; boundaries both connect and separate. Resistances ("contact boundary phenomena"): introjection (uncritically accepting others' beliefs), projection (disowning aspects of self by assigning them to the environment), retroflection (turning back on ourselves what we'd do to others, or doing to ourselves what we'd want others to do), deflection (distraction/veering off), confluence (blurring the self–environment differentiation). The NOW — phenomenological inquiry attends to what is occurring now; therapists ask " what " and " how " questions, rarely "why". Unfinished business — uncompleted figures leave unexpressed feelings (resentment, rage, pain, anxiety, grief, guilt). The impasse (stuck point) occurs when external support is unavailable; the therapist accompanies clients through it without rescuing or frustrating them. Energy and blocks to energy — blocked energy manifests as bodily tension, restricted voice, shallow breathing, avoiding contact. Goal: greater awareness and with it greater choice (increased awareness is itself curative). Therapists work within I/Thou dialogue in a here-and-now framework, attending to body language and speech habits ("It" talk, "You" talk, questions, language that denies power, metaphors). Miriam Polster (1987) described a three-stage integration sequence: discovery, accommodation, assimilation . Gestalt techniques Experiments vs exercises — exercises are ready-made techniques; experiments grow out of the client–therapist interaction (the cornerstone of experiential learning). Confrontation — inviting clients to examine incongruities, especially verbal–nonverbal gaps. Internal dialogue exercise — the top dog (righteous, authoritarian, "shoulds"/"oughts", the critical parent) vs the underdog (victim: defensive, apologetic, helpless, feigning powerlessness). Empty-chair technique — given by Jacob Moreno (founder of psychodrama); a vehicle for role reversal . Future projection , making the rounds , the reversal exercise , the rehearsal exercise , the exaggeration exercise , staying with the feeling , and Gestalt dream work (acting out the dream in the present; each part is a projection of the self). Existential therapy The existential tradition balances the limits and tragic dimensions of human existence against its possibilities. Schneider and Krug (2010) name three values: the freedom to become within limits; the capacity to reflect on the meaning of our choices; the capacity to act on those choices. Sartre (1971) called the failure to accept personal responsibility inauthenticity . Existential guilt grows from a sense of incompleteness — awareness of having evaded a commitment or chosen not to choose. Authenticity is living true to one's own evaluation of a valuable existence — the courage to be who we are. Four ways of being (Dasein) Umwelt — the biological world / environment. Mitwelt — "with-world"; the area of human relationships. Eigenwelt — "own-world"; the relationship individuals have with themselves. Überwelt — relationship with spiritual/religious values (added by van Deurzen; the first three were introduced by Binswanger). Irvin Yalom (1980) distinguished three types of isolation : interpersonal (distance from others), intrapersonal (separating parts of oneself via defences), and existential (being separated from the world — a profound aloneness). Other themes: meaning and meaninglessness (Viktor Frankl emphasised the search for meaning) and self-transcendence (rising above immediate situation and self-interest). Authenticity is the basic goal ; for May, "the aim of therapy is that the patient experiences his existence as real" — May (1958) asked not "How are you?" but " Where are you?" Phases: initial (clarifying assumptions about the world), middle (examining the source/authority of one's value system), and final (putting self-knowledge into action). 12. Behaviour therapy Foundations — four major areas of development Area Key ideas Classical conditioning UCS → UCR; UCS + NS → UCR; CS → CR. Learning by association. Operant conditioning Positive & negative reinforcement ; positive & negative punishment ; schedules of reinforcement (intermittent vs fixed; ratio vs interval). Social learning theory Triadic reciprocal interaction (environmental factors, personal factors, individual behaviour); self-efficacy . Cognitive behaviour therapy Emphasises the interaction among affective, behavioural, and cognitive dimensions. Basic characteristics & assumptions Focus on observable behaviour, current determinants, learning experiences that promote change , tailoring strategies to the individual, and rigorous assessment/evaluation. Based on the principles and procedures of the scientific method ; uses functional assessment (behavioural analysis) . Clients assume an active role ; BT is action-oriented and educational. Insight may not be necessary for behaviour change. The focus is on assessing overt and covert behaviour directly, identifying the problem, and evaluating change; treatment is individually tailored. Definition Functional assessment / behavioural analysis uses the ABC model — A ntecedents, B ehaviours, C onsequences — to identify the events that influence or are functionally related to a behaviour. Techniques & procedures Applied behaviour analysis (ABA) — operant techniques applied across settings: positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, extinction (withholding reinforcement from a previously reinforced response), positive punishment, negative punishment. Relaxation training — Jacobson (1938) developed progressive muscle relaxation ; used for stress, anxiety, asthma, headache, hypertension, insomnia, irritable bowel syndrome, panic disorder. Exposure therapies — systematic confrontation with a feared stimulus (imaginal or in vivo/live). Variants of systematic desensitization: in vivo exposure (exposure to actual events), self-managed in vivo exposure (clients expose themselves when a therapist can't be present), and flooding — intense, prolonged exposure ( in vivo flooding to actual stimuli; imaginal flooding in the client's imagination). Systematic desensitization — based on classical conditioning, developed by Joseph Wolpe . Clients imagine successively more anxiety-arousing situations while engaging in a behaviour (relaxation) that competes with anxiety, becoming gradually desensitized . Steps (McNeil & Kyle, 2009): relaxation training → development of the anxiety hierarchy → systematic desensitization proper . Also used for anger, asthmatic attacks, insomnia, motion sickness, nightmares, sleepwalking. Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) — a form of exposure therapy combining imaginal flooding, cognitive restructuring, and rapid rhythmic eye movements / bilateral stimulation for traumatic stress; developed by Francine Shapiro (2001) . Social skills training — psychoeducation, modeling, reinforcement, behavioural rehearsal, role playing, feedback; includes anger management and assertion training . Self-modification (self-management) programs — basic steps (Watson & Tharp, 2007): selecting goals → translating goals into target behaviours → self-monitoring (behavioural diary) → working out a plan for change → evaluating the action plan. Strategies include self-monitoring, self-reward, self-contracting, stimulus control, and self-as-model. Advantage: treatment can be extended to the public. Multimodal therapy (Arnold Lazarus) — an open system encouraging technical eclecticism , grounded in social learning and cognitive theory. Personality is divided into seven areas — BASIC I.D. : B ehaviour, A ffective responses, S ensations, I mages, C ognitions, I nterpersonal relationships, D rugs (biological functions, nutrition, exercise). Premise: breadth is often more important than depth . 13. REBT & Beck's cognitive therapy Albert Ellis's Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy (REBT) The basic assumption is that people contribute to their own psychological problems by the way they interpret events. Cognitions, emotions, and behaviours interact significantly with a reciprocal cause-and-effect relationship. REBT's basic hypothesis: our emotions stem mainly from our beliefs, evaluations, interpretations, and reactions . CBT (combining cognitive and behavioural principles in a short-term approach) has generated more empirical research than any other psychotherapy model. The focus is on working with thinking and acting rather than primarily expressing feelings; therapy is an educational process . View of emotional disturbance & the three basic musts It is our own repetition of early-indoctrinated irrational thoughts that keeps dysfunctional attitudes alive. Blame is at the core of most emotional disturbance. We escalate desires and preferences into dogmatic shoulds , musts , and oughts . The three basic irrational "musts" : "I must do well and win the approval of others for my performances." "Other people must treat me considerately, fairly, kindly, and exactly the way I want." "I must get what I want, when I want it; and I must not get what I don't want." High-yield ABCDEF framework: A (activating event) → B (belief about A) → C (emotional/behavioural consequence) → D (disputing intervention) → E (effective new philosophy) → F (new feeling). The disputing process has three components: detecting, debating, discriminating . Cognitive restructuring = replacing faulty cognitions with constructive beliefs (monitor self-talk, identify maladaptive self-talk, substitute adaptive self-talk). Goals (Ellis, 2001b): help clients achieve unconditional self-acceptance (USA) and unconditional other-acceptance (UOA) . Techniques span three classes: cognitive (disputing irrational beliefs, cognitive homework, changing one's language, psychoeducation, coping self-statements, cost-benefit analysis); emotive (rational emotive imagery, humour, role playing, shame-attacking exercises, forceful self-statements/self-dialogue); and behavioural (operant conditioning, self-management, systematic desensitization, relaxation, modeling, real-life behavioural homework). Aaron Beck's Cognitive Therapy (CT) Beck developed CT from his research on depression , observing that depressed clients had a negative bias in interpreting life events, producing cognitive distortions. CT sees problems as stemming from commonplace processes: faulty thinking, incorrect inferences from inadequate information, and failing to distinguish fantasy from reality. Assumptions: internal communication is accessible to introspection; clients' beliefs have highly personal meanings; these meanings can be discovered by the client. Cognitive distortions (logical errors) Arbitrary inferences — conclusions without supporting evidence; includes catastrophizing . Selective abstraction — conclusions based on an isolated detail. Overgeneralization — extreme beliefs from a single incident applied to dissimilar settings. Magnification and minimization — perceiving a situation as greater or lesser than it deserves. Personalization — relating external events to oneself without basis. Labeling and mislabeling — defining identity by past imperfections/mistakes. Dichotomous thinking — either-or, all-or-nothing extremes. The frequent question is " Where is the evidence for ___? " The Socratic (inductive) questioning method leads the client through questions to become aware of thoughts, identify distortions, and find adaptive replacements. Automatic thoughts are personalised notions triggered by particular stimuli that lead to emotional responses. In depression, Beck described the cognitive triad : a negative view of (1) themselves, (2) experience (interpreting in a negative manner — selective abstraction), and (3) the future (gloomy projections). Beck (1967) designed the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) . In family work, CT emphasises schema (core beliefs) and "family schemata". Trap Albert Ellis (REBT) centres on irrational beliefs / the three musts and disputing (the D in ABCDEF), with a directive, even confrontational style. Aaron Beck (CT) centres on cognitive distortions and the cognitive triad , using collaborative Socratic questioning ("where is the evidence?"). Both restructure cognition; the flavour differs. 14. Transactional Analysis (Eric Berne) TA is a psychological theory developed by Eric Berne in the 1960s explaining why we think, act, and feel as we do. Philosophical assumptions: People are OK; everyone has the capacity to think; people decide their own destiny, and these decisions can be changed. Ego-state model (PAC) & transactions An ego-state is a set of related behaviours, thoughts, and feelings. We all have three: Parent, Adult, Child . Adult — thinking, feeling, behaving in response to the here-and-now, using all available resources. Parent — behaving, thinking, feeling as one's parents did. Child — returning to ways of behaving/thinking/feeling as one did as a child. Capital letters P, A, C indicate ego-states; small letters p, a, c indicate real-life parents, adults, children. Structural analysis uses the PAC model to understand personality. A transaction is the exchange of communications between the ego-states of two people; transactional analysis proper analyses sequences of transactions. Complementary transactions (ego-states sympathetic to one another) are effective; crossed transactions occur when a response comes from a different ego-state than expected. Any signal of recognition is a stroke . Decisional model, life-script & games TA holds that self-defeating behaviour follows strategies decided in childhood — the best way of surviving then. Because the person is responsible for these early decisions, she can redecide . Each of us writes a life-story ; the unaware version is the life-script . Parents give script-messages (how to be / not to be); negative messages are injunctions . Script analysis shows how people unawarely set up or solve problems. Distorting one's perception so it fits the script is redefining ; selectively ignoring information is discounting . Permitted childhood feelings used to cover authentic feelings are racket feelings ; storing one instead of expressing it is saving a stamp ; a game is a repetitive sequence where both parties end up with racket feelings. Symbiosis is where a person and partner together display only three ego-states (one supplies Parent and Adult, the other Child). Therapy & autonomy Eric Berne urged that the proper goal is not insight but cure , progressing through four stages: social control → symptomatic relief → transference cure → script cure . The goal of personal change is autonomy , whose components are awareness, spontaneity, and the capacity for intimacy . Client and therapist enter a contract (mutual consent, valid consideration, competency, lawful object). Therapy involves closing escape hatches (an unconditional decision never to kill/harm self or others or go crazy). The therapist's crucial function is to give permission, protection, and potency . Three schools: Classical (strengthen Adult), Redecision (do so from a Child ego-state), Cathexis (emphasis on Child as well as Adult; the client also assumes a Parent role). 15. Family & systems therapy General systems theory Feedback — the communication pattern within the units of a system, in two basic patterns: linear and circular . Two types: negative feedback (equilibrium is achieved) and positive feedback (change occurs in the system). Homeostasis — systems tend to seek stability and equilibrium; a family regulates itself to maintain stability, achieved through feedback from its units. Equifinality — many different ways to reach the same destination (related to complexity). Pathological communication patterns (schizophrenia research) Double bind — Gregory Bateson, Jackson, Jay Haley & Weakland (1956): a person receives two related but contradictory messages, one often clear and the other unclear (nonverbal), creating a "no-win" paradox. Marital schism & skew — Lidz and colleagues: marital schism = undermining the worth of the other parent by competing for the children's sympathy; marital skew = one parent's psychological disturbance dominates the home while the other accepts it, distorting reality for the children. Bowen's intergenerational (family systems) theory Based on the individual's ability to differentiate intellectual functioning from feelings . Eight core concepts: Differentiation of self — being able to separate one's intellectual processes from one's feeling processes. Triangulation — when two people are under stress they bring in a third member to dilute the anxiety/tension. Nuclear family emotional systems — when partners have relatively low differentiation, they may project their stress onto a child (the family projection process ). Family projection process — projecting parental stress onto one child. Emotional cutoff — managing unresolved attachment by emotional distance. Multigenerational transmission process — after six or seven generations of increasingly fused couples, an observer could find highly dysfunctional families vulnerable to stress and lacking differentiation. Sibling position — Bowen believed birth order affects functioning within the family. Societal regression — the broader lack of differentiation between thoughts and feelings at a societal level. Techniques: evaluation interview (any combination of members; a single member can suffice if willing to work on differentiating their own feelings rather than blaming others), genograms , interpretation (information from genograms interpreted so members understand dynamics; the therapist maintains objectivity to see patterns reflecting the family of origin), and detriangulation (Bowen worked with the healthiest, most differentiated member to make changes; he tried to separate parts of a triangle directly). Structural family therapy (Salvador Minuchin) Traces to the early 1960s with delinquent boys from poor families at the Wiltwyck School in New York. Central idea: an individual's symptoms are best understood from interactional patterns within a family. Goals: (1) reduce symptoms of dysfunction; (2) bring about structural change by modifying transactional rules and establishing more appropriate boundaries. Structural-strategic approaches were the most-used models; interventions became synonymous with the systems approach — joining, boundary setting, unbalancing, reframing, ordeals, paradoxical interventions, and enactments . Concepts Family structure — rules developed over years determining who interacts with whom (temporary or long-standing). Family subsystems — husband–wife, parents–children, siblings. Boundary permeability — rules about who participates in interactions and how. Alignments and coalitions — alignments = ways members join with or oppose each other; coalitions = alliances against another member. Minuchin uses triangle more specifically than Bowen: a coalition where "each parent demands that the child side with him against the other parent". Techniques Family mapping — diagrams of current ways families relate. Enactment — instructing the family to act out a conflict so the therapist works with it in the present. Intensity — repeating the message or changing interaction length to facilitate change. Changing boundaries — rearranging seating, changing distance, unbalancing the structure (e.g., siding with a parent in an enmeshed family to restore parental power). Reframing — offering a different explanation so a constructive change can occur. Trap Bowen vs Salvador Minuchin: Bowen is intergenerational (differentiation of self, eight concepts, genograms, detriangulation across generations). Minuchin is structural and present-focused (family structure, subsystems, boundaries, enactment, unbalancing). Both use "triangle", but Minuchin means it more narrowly (a parent–parent–child coalition). 16. Successful aging: biological theories Definition Life span = the upper boundary of life, the maximum number of years an individual can live (for humans ~120–125 years). Life expectancy = the number of years that will probably be lived by the average person born in a particular year. Genes matter for reaching extreme old age, but other factors do too; what usually contributes to surviving into the 100s is the ability to cope successfully with stress . Genetic-programming theories Theory Claim Cellular clock theory (Leonard Hayflick, 1977) Cells can divide a maximum of ~75–80 times (the Hayflick limit ); ability to divide decreases with age. The answer to why cells stop may lie at the tips of chromosomes — telomeres (DNA sequences that cap chromosomes) shorten with each division; after ~70–80 replications they are dramatically reduced and the cell can no longer reproduce. Injecting the enzyme telomerase can substantially extend cell life. Programmed senescence theory Aging results from the sequential switching on and off of certain genes. Senescence is the time when age-associated deficits become evident. Immunological theory A programmed decline in immune-system function leads to increased vulnerability to infectious disease and thus to aging and death. Hormonal stress theory Aging in the body's hormonal system can lower resilience to stress and increase disease likelihood. The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is a main regulatory system for responding to stress; with aging, stress hormones remain elevated longer than in youth. Prolonged elevations are linked to cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes, and hypertension. Variable-rate theories Free-radical theory — normal metabolism produces unstable oxygen molecules ( free radicals ) that ricochet around cells, damaging DNA and other structures, leading to disorders including cancer and arthritis. Wear-and-tear theory — cells and tissues have vital parts that simply wear out. Rate-of-living theory — the greater an organism's rate of metabolism, the shorter its life span. Autoimmune theory — the immune system becomes confused and attacks the body's own cells. 17. Socioemotional aging & late-life disorders Theories of socioemotional development in aging Theory Core idea Disengagement theory To cope effectively, older adults should gradually withdraw from society. Older adults develop increasing self-preoccupation, decrease emotional ties, and show less interest in society's affairs; by disengaging they were believed to enjoy enhanced life satisfaction. (Largely discredited but examinable.) Activity theory The more active and involved older adults are, the more likely they are to be satisfied with their lives; many achieve greater satisfaction by continuing their middle-adulthood roles into late adulthood. Socioemotional selectivity theory (Laura Carstensen) Older adults become more selective about social networks: placing high value on emotional satisfaction, they spend more time with familiar, rewarding individuals and consciously decrease total social contacts. Two classes of goals: (1) knowledge-related and (2) emotional. Selective Optimization with Compensation (SOC) (Paul Baltes & colleagues) Successful aging is linked with three factors: Selection (reduced capacity requires reducing performance in most life domains), Optimization (maintaining performance in some areas through continued practice and new technologies), and Compensation (when tasks demand a level beyond current potential — e.g., memorising fast, reacting quickly when driving — older adults compensate, especially under high mental/physical demand). High-yield Disengagement = withdraw. Activity = stay engaged. Socioemotional selectivity (Carstensen) = prune to emotionally rewarding relationships. SOC (Paul Baltes) = Select, Optimize, Compensate. Mental problems in old age Definition Dementia = the general term for physiologically caused cognitive and behavioural decline sufficient to affect daily life. Alzheimer's disease (AD) — a progressive, degenerative brain disorder. The brain shows excessive neurofibrillary tangles (twisted masses of collapsed protein fibres) and large waxy chunks of amyloid plaque (nonfunctioning tissue formed in the spaces between neurons by an abnormal variant of the protein beta amyloid ). Parkinson's disease — the second most common disorder involving progressive neurological degeneration, characterised by tremor, stiffness, slowed movement, and unstable posture .

title: Unit 10 — Emerging Areas
text: Unit 10 — Emerging Areas The newer frontiers of applied psychology, built directly from the Unit 10 source: the psychology of gender and the schools of feminism , feminist psychology and feminist therapy with their critique of traditional treatment, the workplace barriers women face, the psychology of poverty , the positive-psychology science of wellbeing and self-growth (eudaimonia vs hedonia, the major wellbeing models, character strengths and post-traumatic growth), and cyberpsychology (online disinhibition and internet addiction). Every named area, model and theorist in the file is reproduced and taught to NIMHANS depth. In this book Issues of gender Types of feminism Feminist psychology Workplace barriers: glass ceiling & relatives Feminist therapy Issues in traditional therapies Empowerment & feminist techniques The psychology of poverty Wellbeing & self-growth Models of wellbeing Character strengths & virtues Post-traumatic growth Cyberpsychology 1. Issues of gender The one distinction to never blur. The whole topic rests on separating two words the public uses interchangeably. Sex is the biological distinction between male and female, fixed at conception by the chromosomes: the male karyotype is XY and the female karyotype is XX . Gender is the culturally constructed categorisation of maleness and femaleness, that is, the social meanings of masculinity and femininity . Sex is given by biology; gender is built by culture. Definition Gender = the culturally constructed categorisation of maleness and femaleness (masculinity / femininity). Sex = the biological distinction of male (XY chromosome) and female (XX chromosome). Gender stereotypes A gender stereotype is a widely held belief about the abilities, personality traits, and social behaviour of females and males (the source attributes this definition to Weiten, 2001 ). Stereotypes are not the same as differences that actually exist; they are beliefs about the sexes, which may be exaggerated, inaccurate, or self-fulfilling. They feed the discrimination patterns described later in this book (glass ceiling, maternal wall, etc.). Minimalist vs maximalist views of gender differences How big are the psychological differences between men and women? The field splits into two camps: Maximalists believe in huge, fundamental differences between men and women. On this view the sexes are deeply, qualitatively distinct. Minimalists believe there are few fundamental differences between them. On this view the apparent gaps are small, situational, or socially produced rather than essential. Trap Maximalist = MAXimum difference; minimalist = MINimum difference. Maximalists emphasise large, fundamental sex differences; minimalists emphasise that the genuine fundamental differences are few. Do not confuse the camps because the names sound technical. High-yield Sex = biological (XY male, XX female). Gender = cultural construction of masculinity/femininity. Gender stereotype = widely held belief about males'/females' abilities, traits and social behaviour (Weiten, 2001). Maximalists = big differences; minimalists = few fundamental differences. 2. Types of feminism The source lists five branches of feminism . Each answers the same question, "what is the root of women's oppression and how do we end it?", in a different way. Learn them by their diagnosis and their strategy , because that is what is tested. Branch Core idea / diagnosis Strategy Liberal feminism Works within the structure of mainstream society. Its roots reach back to social-contract theory of government, the idea instituted by the American Revolution. Integrate women into the existing structure (equal access, equal rights) rather than overthrow it. Radical feminism Seen by many as the "undesirable" element of feminism, yet it is actually the breeding ground for many of the ideas that other branches shape and pound out. Holds that women's oppression is the deepest, original oppression. Tackle the root system of male domination (patriarchy) directly; the source ties consciousness raising to this branch. Socialist feminism The result of Marxism meeting radical feminism . Marxism recognises that women are oppressed and attributes the oppression to the capitalist / private-property system . The only way to end women's oppression is to overthrow the capitalist system . Cultural feminism Retreated to vanguardism , working instead to build a women's culture . Some of this effort has had real social benefit. Create and value a distinct women's culture rather than fight for integration. Eco-feminism Much more spiritual than political or theoretical in nature. May or may not be wrapped up with Goddess worship and vegetarianism . Its basic tenet: a patriarchal/hierarchical society will exploit its resources without regard to long-term consequences, as a direct result of the attitudes fostered in such a society. Link the domination of women to the domination of nature; resist both. Mnemonic " L iberals L obby (work within), R adicals R oot out patriarchy, S ocialists S mash capitalism, C ultural C reates a women's culture, E co links women & E arth." — L-R-S-C-E. High-yield Socialist feminism = Marxism + radical feminism , blames the capitalist/private-property system. Radical feminism is the "breeding ground" of feminist ideas and is the home of consciousness raising . Liberal feminism = integration within the system. Eco-feminism = spiritual, links patriarchy to environmental exploitation. 3. Feminist psychology Feminist psychology aims to understand the individual within the larger social and political aspects of society . Its defining move is to refuse to study a person in isolation: a woman's distress is read against the background of her social and political situation, not just her internal makeup. Key figures named in the source Karen Horney — Feminine Psychoanalysis. Horney challenged Freud from within psychoanalysis, replacing his "penis envy" account of female development with a social and cultural reading of women's psychology. She is the named author of a feminine psychoanalysis , foregrounding women's experience rather than treating it as a deviation from a male standard. Edward Strecker — "Mom-ism". Strecker is associated with the concept of Mom-ism , a (controversial, mother-blaming) idea critiqued within feminist psychology for pathologising motherhood and women's roles. Consciousness raising Consciousness raising is closely tied with radical feminism . It aims to weed out discrimination and segregation based on sex , and it maintains a key radical-feminist claim: women's oppression is not a by-product of capitalist oppression but a "primary cause" in its own right. In other words, against socialist feminism (which traces oppression back to capitalism), consciousness raising treats the oppression of women as primary, not derivative. Trap Both socialist feminism and consciousness raising mention capitalism, but they take opposite sides. Socialist feminism says women's oppression comes from capitalism. Consciousness raising (radical) insists it is not a by-product of capitalism but a primary cause . High-yield Feminist psychology = understand the individual within the larger social and political context. Karen Horney = feminine psychoanalysis ; Edward Strecker = "Mom-ism" ; consciousness raising = radical feminism, oppression of women as a primary cause . 4. Workplace barriers: the glass-ceiling family The source gives four named "invisible barrier" effects that describe how discrimination keeps women out of, or trapped in, particular places in the labour market. They are routinely tested as a matching set, so learn each by its precise location and mechanism. Effect What it describes Glass ceiling effect When women can't reach higher ranks, pay or positions because of discrimination, limiting beliefs, etc. The barrier is at the top , invisible but real. Maternal wall The stereotypes and forms of discrimination encountered by working mothers and by mothers seeking employment . Bias triggered specifically by motherhood. Sticky floor effect A discriminatory employment pattern that keeps workers, mainly women, in the lower ranks of the job scale . The barrier is at the bottom ; they cannot rise off the floor. Glass-cliff effect When a woman is promoted to a leadership role of an organisation that is about to collapse , set up to be a scapegoat for the failure. A precarious, high-risk promotion. Trap Ceiling vs floor vs cliff. Glass ceiling = blocked at the top . Sticky floor = stuck at the bottom . Glass cliff = promoted, but onto a failing organisation so she takes the blame. Maternal wall = bias specifically against mothers . Mnemonic Top blocked = ceiling ; bottom stuck = floor ; promoted-to-fall = cliff ; mother-penalty = wall . 5. Feminist therapy Feminist therapy is a type of therapy based on viewing individuals within their sociocultural context . It carries the central commitment of feminist psychology into the consulting room: the client's problems are understood against her social and cultural situation, not treated as purely intrapsychic faults. Two features that define the approach Not just for women. Feminist therapy is not confined to women ; it addresses gender-role conformities for clients of any gender, that is, the costs of rigidly conforming to prescribed gender roles. An egalitarian relationship. The client–therapist relationship is meant to be as egalitarian as possible , with both sides communicating on equal ground and sharing experiences . The therapist deliberately flattens the usual power hierarchy of treatment, which is itself a therapeutic statement about power. High-yield Feminist therapy = individuals understood within their sociocultural context ; not confined to women (it addresses gender-role conformity in general); the therapeutic relationship is deliberately egalitarian , with shared, equal-ground communication. 6. Issues in traditional therapies Feminist therapy arose as a critique of biases built into traditional therapy. The source names three problems. Gender bias Many traditional therapies assume that women should follow sex-roles in order to be mentally healthy . They treat gender differences as entirely biologically based and therefore encourage female clients to be submissive, expressive, and nurturant in order to achieve fulfillment . Mental health is thus equated with conformity to a feminine role. Androcentrism Androcentrism means treating being male as the norm . Feminine traits are then viewed as a deviation from the norm and as a deficiency on the part of women . The male is the yardstick; the female is measured as a falling-short of it. Definition Androcentrism = taking the male as the standard/norm, so that feminine traits appear as a deviation from, and a deficiency relative to, that norm. Intrapsychic assumptions Traditional therapy locates the trouble inside the client. As a result, therapists tend to blame clients for their symptoms, even when the client may in fact be coping admirably in a difficult and oppressive situation , and they may pathologise normal responses to oppressive environments . A reasonable reaction to an unjust situation gets relabelled as the client's disorder. Trap The intrapsychic assumption is the engine of victim-blaming: it treats a healthy reaction to an oppressive environment as a personal pathology. Feminist therapy's correction is the slogan "the personal is political" — relocate the problem from inside the person to the social situation. 7. Principles of empowerment & feminist techniques Principles of empowerment Feminist therapy works from three empowerment principles: Personal is political. A client's private distress is connected to wider social and political conditions; her problems are not purely individual failings. Egalitarian relationships. Therapy models equal power between client and therapist rather than expert-over-patient. Value the female perspective. Women's experiences and ways of knowing are treated as valid and valuable, not as deviations to be corrected. Techniques Sex-role analysis — a critique of cultural conditioning : examining how the client has been shaped by the gender roles society imposed on her, and what those roles cost her. Power analysis — examining power differentials : making visible the unequal power between the client and others (partners, employers, institutions) and how it bears on her difficulties. Assertiveness training — teaching the client to express needs and set boundaries, countering the trained submissiveness that gender bias rewards. The source also flags poverty alongside these techniques, signalling that material deprivation is part of the social context feminist therapy must address, which leads to the next major area. High-yield Empowerment principles: personal is political , egalitarian relationships , value the female perspective . Techniques: sex-role analysis (critique of cultural conditioning), power analysis (examining power differentials), assertiveness training . 8. The psychology of poverty Poverty is a condition in which a person or community is deprived of, or lacks, the essentials for a minimum standard of wellbeing and life . It is an emerging area for psychology because deprivation shapes development, stress, health and mental disorder, and because the intrapsychic-assumption trap above (blaming individuals for circumstance) bites hardest here. Types of poverty Type Meaning Absolute poverty The scarcity of basic food, clean water, health, shelter, education and information . People in absolute poverty struggle to survive and suffer many child deaths from preventable diseases like malaria, cholera and water-contamination-related diseases . Relative poverty Defined from a social perspective : living standard compared to the economic standard of the surrounding population . It is therefore a measure of income inequality , often measured as the percentage of the population with income below some fixed proportion of median income . Situational poverty A temporary poverty caused by an adverse event such as an environmental disaster, job loss, or severe health problem. Generational poverty Poverty handed down from one generation to the next . It is more complicated because there is no easy escape : people are trapped and cannot access the tools needed to get out. The source quotes Jensen (2009) : it "occurs in families where at least two generations have been born into poverty… not equipped with the tools to move out of their situation." Rural poverty Occurs in rural areas with population below 50,000 , where there are fewer job opportunities, less access to services, less support for disabilities, and fewer quality education opportunities. Urban poverty Occurs in metropolitan areas with population over 50,000 . Marked by limited access to health and education, inadequate housing and services, a violent and unhealthy environment due to overcrowding, and little or no social-protection mechanism. Trap Absolute vs relative poverty. Absolute = lacking the basics for survival (food, water, shelter), an objective threshold. Relative = below the standard of those around you, a measure of inequality tied to median income. And note the population line: rural < 50,000 , urban > 50,000 . High-yield Six types: absolute (no basics), relative (below surrounding standard = inequality, vs median income), situational (temporary, from an adverse event), generational (handed down, ≥2 generations born into it — Arthur Jensen 2009), rural (pop < 50,000), urban (pop > 50,000). 9. Wellbeing & self-growth This is the positive-psychology heart of the unit: instead of asking what makes people ill, it asks what makes life good and what helps people flourish. It opens with the two great traditions of what "wellbeing" even means. Two conceptions of wellbeing Eudaimonic wellbeing Hedonistic wellbeing Equates wellbeing with The cultivation of personal strengths and contribution to the greater good , acting in accordance with one's deeper nature and values. Pleasure and happiness . Key features Acting in accordance with one's inner nature and deeply held values ; the realization of one's true potential ; the experience of purpose or meaning in life . Maximising positive feeling and enjoyment, minimising pain. Definition Eudaimonic wellbeing = wellbeing as living in line with one's true nature and values, realising one's potential, and finding meaning. Hedonistic wellbeing = wellbeing as pleasure and happiness. Mnemonic " Hedon ist chases the feeling (pleasure/happiness); eudaimon chases the fulfilment (meaning/potential/values)." The two F's tell them apart. 10. Models of wellbeing The source lists four wellbeing models. Learn the named author and the component list of each. The holistic view of wellbeing A holistic model treats wellbeing as multi-domain. The source names the domains as emotional, intellectual, spiritual, occupational, social, and physical wellness . Health is not just absence of illness but balance across all these domains. Subjective wellbeing — Diener's tripartite model Subjective wellbeing (SWB) consists of three components (Ed Diener's tripartite model): Cognitive evaluation of life satisfaction (a judgement of how one's life is going); Presence of positive affect ; Relative absence of negative affect . SWB is the standard operationalisation of the hedonic tradition: a satisfied judgement plus lots of good feeling and little bad feeling. Carol Ryff's Six-Factor Model of Psychological Well-Being The Six-Factor Model of Psychological Well-Being was developed by Carol Ryff . It identifies six factors that contribute to an individual's psychological wellbeing, contentment and happiness. This is the leading eudaimonic model. The six factors are: Autonomy Environmental Mastery Personal Growth Positive Relations with Others Purpose in Life Self-Acceptance Mnemonic Ryff's six: " A utonomy, E nvironmental mastery, P ersonal growth, P ositive relations, P urpose, S elf-acceptance" → A-E-P-P-P-S ("A-E and three P's and S"). PERMA model — Seligman The PERMA model was given by Martin Seligman and has five measurable elements : P ositive emotions E ngagement R elationships M eaning and purpose A ccomplishment Trap Don't cross the authors: Ed Diener = the tripartite subjective wellbeing model (life satisfaction + positive affect + low negative affect). Ryff = the six-factor psychological wellbeing model. Martin Seligman = PERMA (five elements). Ryff has SIX factors; PERMA has FIVE. High-yield Ed Diener → SWB, 3 parts (life-satisfaction cognition + positive affect + relative absence of negative affect). Ryff → 6 factors (Autonomy, Environmental Mastery, Personal Growth, Positive Relations, Purpose in Life, Self-Acceptance). Martin Seligman → PERMA (Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, Accomplishment). Holistic view = 6 wellness domains. 11. Character strengths & virtues Character Strengths and Virtues (CSV) is described as a groundbreaking handbook that compiles the work of researchers to create a classification system for widely valued positive traits . It is, in effect, positive psychology's answer to the diagnostic manual: instead of cataloguing disorders, it catalogues what is best in people. (CSV was authored by Christopher Peterson and Martin Seligman; it is often called the "un-DSM".) The system contains 6 classes of virtues that are made up of 24 character strengths . The six virtue classes are universally valued across cultures, and the 24 strengths are the measurable routes to expressing them. High-yield Character Strengths and Virtues = a classification of widely valued positive traits, structured as 6 virtues built from 24 character strengths . Think of it as the positive-psychology counterpart to the DSM. 12. Post-traumatic growth Post-traumatic growth (PTG) is the counterpart to PTSD: the same struggle that can break a person can, far more often, change them for the better. The source stresses the asymmetry: most trauma survivors report growth after their experience , while only a few develop PTSD . Definition Post-traumatic growth (a term coined by Tedeschi and Calhoun ) = the positive psychological change experienced as a result of the struggle with highly challenging life circumstances . The five areas of post-traumatic growth Appreciation of life — a renewed sense of the value of being alive. Relating to others — deeper, closer relationships. Personal strength — a sense of "if I survived that, I am stronger than I knew." New possibilities — new paths, goals and opportunities open up. Spiritual, existential or philosophical change — a transformed worldview or faith. Trap PTG is not simply the absence of PTSD, and it does not mean the trauma was good. It is genuine positive change that grows out of the struggle with adversity. Note the key statistic the source emphasises: growth is the common outcome; PTSD is the rare one. High-yield PTG coined by Tedeschi & Calhoun = positive psychological change from struggling with highly challenging circumstances. Five areas: appreciation of life, relating to others, personal strength, new possibilities, spiritual/existential/philosophical change . Most survivors grow; only a few develop PTSD. 13. Cyberpsychology Cyberpsychology studies the psychological effects of the internet and digital technology on human behaviour. The source focuses on two phenomena: why people behave badly online (online disinhibition) and how internet use becomes a disorder (internet addiction). Online disinhibition Cyberbullying occurs due to a phenomenon called online disinhibition : people say and do things online that they would not say or do face-to-face, because the usual social brakes are loosened. The anonymity, invisibility and distance of the screen lower the inhibitions that normally restrain hostile behaviour. The source credits Suler with identifying the areas (components) of online disinhibition. Definition Online disinhibition (Suler) = the loosening or abandonment of the social restrictions and inhibitions that would normally be present in face-to-face interaction, occurring when people are online. It is the mechanism behind cyberbullying . Internet addiction disorder (IAD) The source states that the APA has included internet addiction as a disorder in DSM-5 , and lists four components essential for a diagnosis of IAD : Excessive internet use — using the internet far more than intended, losing track of time. Withdrawal — feelings of tension, anger or depression when access is denied. Tolerance — needing more and more (better equipment, more hours, more content) to get the same satisfaction. Adverse consequences — negative effects on work, relationships, health and functioning. Mnemonic The four IAD components map onto the classic addiction tetrad: E-W-T-A — E xcessive use, W ithdrawal, T olerance, A dverse consequences. Trap The source follows the deck's claim that internet addiction was "included as a disorder in DSM-5." In the actual DSM-5, only Internet Gaming Disorder appears, and only in Section III as a condition for further study , not as a fully recognised diagnosis. For this paper, answer per the source (four components: excessive use, withdrawal, tolerance, adverse consequences) but know the real DSM-5 nuance. High-yield Cyberbullying is driven by online disinhibition (areas identified by Suler ). Internet addiction disorder has four diagnostic components: excessive internet use, withdrawal, tolerance, adverse consequences .

title: Research Methods & Statistics
text: Research Methods & Statistics How psychological knowledge is made and judged: the philosophical paradigms beneath every study, the quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods that grow from them, the experimental and non-experimental designs that license (or block) causal claims, and the statistical tests that decide whether a result is real. This book moves from epistemology to inference, builds every parametric test (t, F) from the logic of sampling distributions, extends them to MANOVA and ANCOVA, and closes with the distribution-free family. It is prioritised for MET 2026 and NIMHANS clinical psychology, with assumptions, degrees of freedom and a "which test when" decision table you can recite under pressure. In this book Paradigms & methods of research Research designs & sampling Hypothesis testing & inference Parametric test: the t-test ANOVA & experimental designs MANOVA & ANCOVA Non-parametric tests "Which test when" decision guide 1. Paradigms & methods of research The one idea behind the section. Before any method is chosen, a researcher already holds a paradigm : a way of thinking about and conducting research, a philosophy that guides how the research might be done. Method is downstream of philosophy. Two scientists can study the same phenomenon and reach different designs because they answer two prior questions differently: what is real ( ontology ) and how can we know it ( epistemology ). Definition Ontology = the nature of reality (is there one objective reality, or many constructed realities?). Epistemology = the nature of knowledge and the relationship between the knower and what is known (can the researcher stand apart from what is studied, or are they entangled with it?). Together they shape both the data-collection process and the analysis. The four research paradigms Learn each by its stance on reality, on the researcher, and on the kind of knowledge it produces. Paradigm Ontology / epistemology Typical methods Goal Positivism One objective reality exists and can be measured directly; researcher is detached and value-free Experiments, structured measurement, statistics Discover universal laws; explain and predict Post-positivism Objective reality exists but can only be known imperfectly and probabilistically ; all observation is theory-laden Quantitative methods with a plan fixed before the study; falsification Approximate truth through repeated, fallible testing Constructivism / interpretivism Reality is socially and personally constructed ; multiple realities; knower and known are inseparable Open-ended interviews, observation, narrative documents kept in text form Understand meaning from the participant's perspective Critical / transformative Reality is shaped by power, history, economics; knowledge is political Critical ethnography, participatory and emancipatory designs Expose and change unjust structures; empower Trap Positivism vs post-positivism. Both are "objective-reality" paradigms and both drive quantitative work. The shift is that positivism claims we can know reality directly and with certainty, while post-positivism (the modern stance behind most quantitative social science) says we can only know it imperfectly : every measurement is fallible, theory-laden, and provisional, so we falsify rather than prove. In exam phrasing, "quantitative research = post-positivist approach" and "qualitative research = constructivist approach". Quantitative vs qualitative vs mixed methods The paradigm choice cascades into a whole research stance. The table is high-yield because the paper tests the cascade directly. Feature Quantitative (post-positivist) Qualitative (constructivist) Plan A specific plan is developed prior to the study; tight structure Less structure on specific guidelines; general guidelines only; emergent design Data "Objective": easily classified or quantified (age, gender, test scores, recovery time) "Subjective": interpreted differently by different people (perceptions of pain, feelings about work) Collection Structured interviews / questionnaires, observations, records; scored reliably with little training Open-ended interviews, observation, narrative documents (diaries); data kept in text form Analysis Inferential statistics to generalise from sample to population Coding of themes , assigning meaning to words or images Strength Results across many studies can be combined into a large body of evidence Depth; tools for data, analysis and interpretation that quantitative work lacks Mixed methods. When the two paradigms are blended so that one sets the stage for or leads to the other , the approach is mixed methods. It rests on the pragmatic approach, which focuses on methodological rather than philosophical concerns and combines qualitative and quantitative methods, using exploratory and confirmatory methods. This widens the options for data collection, analysis tools and interpretation. Trap Using two methods in the same study but discussing them separately is not mixed methods, it is just "two methods being used". Mixed methods requires genuine integration where one paradigm feeds the other. Qualitative methods of research, in depth NIMHANS expects you to name each qualitative tradition and its signature. Observation. Being present in a situation and recording one's impressions. The primary research instrument is the self , consciously gathering sensory data. Problems: the enormous complexity of human behaviour, the impossibility of a complete record, and the subjectivity of the researcher. Types: structured (schedules predetermine the categories of behaviour/talk to be observed, e.g. Flanders' Interaction Analysis Categories, FIAC), unstructured (broad decisions made in advance, seen through the researcher's own socio-culturally constructed values), shadow studies (tracking one participant), and participant observation (the researcher joins and participates, gaining unique insight but risking distraction from the research purpose). Survey method. Studies large and small populations (universes) by selecting and studying samples to discover relative incidence, distribution and interrelations of variables. Variables = sociological facts (sex, income, religious/political affiliation, SES), opinions and attitudes. Factual "face-sheet information" is recorded on a face sheet. Uses interviews, schedules and questionnaires; other types include the panel technique (same respondents re-interviewed over time), telephone surveys (high speed, low cost) and mail questionnaires (cheap but poor response rate, cannot check answers). Researchers use a flow plan : objectives → statement of problem → sample and sampling plan → construction of the schedule/instrument → data collection → coding and tabulation → analysis and interpretation → report. Advantages : wide scope, accurate. Disadvantages : does not penetrate below the surface, demanding of time and money, can lift the respondent out of his social context and invalidate results. Phenomenology. The study of lived human phenomena within everyday social contexts, from the perspective of those who experience them. Direct approach : the detached researcher shines a light on the foreground, studying participants' mental representations (rooted in Husserl , whose starting point is a conscious actor separated from a world of objects). Indirect approach : the involved, connected observer immerses in the everyday world and lights up the background (rooted in Heidegger , who saw us as first and foremost immersed in the world, aiming to deepen understanding of "what it is to be"). Grounded theory. A theory- generating methodology; the end product is an integrated theoretical formulation. The researcher does not enter with a predefined theory. Coding sequence: open coding (concept identification, text broken apart line-by-line) → axial coding (weaving data back together, grouping concepts into categories) → selective coding (constructing the single most representative core category ). Key constructs: theoretical sampling (data gathering directed by emerging concepts), saturation (no new concepts/properties emerge; data become repetitive), and memo writing (records of the analyst's evolving thoughts). The theory is a co-construction between researcher and participants. Field studies. Ex post facto scientific inquiries into relations among variables in real social structures; the researcher does not manipulate any independent variable. Two types: exploratory (seeks "what is", discovers significant variables and relations, lays groundwork for later hypothesis testing) and hypothesis-testing . Strong in realism, social significance, strength of variables, theory orientation and heuristic quality; weakest in its ex-post-facto character (weaker statements of relation than experiments), plethora of variables, lack of precision, and practical problems (feasibility, cost, sampling, time). Focus group. A small but demographically diverse group whose reactions are studied in guided/open discussion (market research, political analysis); peer groups and professional teams work better than strangers. Problems: pecking orders, histories and animosities, confusion about purpose, and convenience/purposive sampling (not representative). Not an effective way of measuring attitudes; it is a social process in which participants co-produce an account specific to that time and place. Ethnography. Literally "writing about people"; treats people as meaning-makers and aims to describe how a culture "ticks". Tends to focus on a limited range of cases (often one setting), with strong links to anthropology (proper ethnography = participant observer in everyday life). Critical ethnographers link the "micro" (participants' meanings) to the "macro" (structural and political dimensions). Demands reflexivity (a research diary) and openness to reformulating the problem. Narrative inquiry / life history. Concerned with the production, interpretation and representation of storied accounts of lived experience. A life story becomes a life history when the researcher adds analysis of the social, historical, political and economic context. The life-history inquiry is a dialogic event co-constructed over time. Research ethics Whatever the paradigm, ethical conduct is non-negotiable. Core principles tested at NIMHANS level: Informed consent — voluntary participation with full disclosure of purpose, procedures and risks; a code of practice has to be established in advance. Confidentiality and anonymity — protecting identity and data; especially hard in focus groups. Beneficence and non-maleficence — maximise benefit, minimise harm; this is why withdrawing a successful treatment in a reversal (ABAB) design can be considered unethical in clinical settings, motivating multiple-baseline designs. Right to withdraw without penalty at any time. Debriefing — explaining the study afterwards, especially when deception was used. Justice — fair selection of participants; no exploitation of vulnerable groups. High-yield Paradigm cascade: positivism/post-positivism → quantitative → objective data → inferential statistics ; constructivism → qualitative → subjective data → thematic coding ; pragmatism → mixed methods . Ontology = nature of reality; epistemology = nature of knowledge. Husserl = direct phenomenology; Heidegger = indirect. Grounded theory codes open → axial → selective and stops at saturation. 2. Research designs & sampling A design is the structure that decides what you can conclude. The single most important question is whether the design supports a causal claim, and that turns on two features: an active (manipulated) independent variable and random assignment . The family of designs Design Active IV? Random assignment? Causal claim? True (randomised) experiment Yes Yes Yes — the gold standard Quasi-experiment Yes No (intact groups) Weak; confounds not fully ruled out Correlational No (measured, not manipulated) No No — association only Descriptive No No No — "what is", no comparison True (randomised) experimental approach Has random assignment of participants to intervention and comparison groups and an active, manipulated independent variable; the groups' scores on the dependent variable are compared. Criteria: (1) the IV must be active, i.e. manipulatable, with the experimenter able to set several levels; (2) participants are randomly assigned, so each has an equal chance of any group, and after assignment but before intervention the groups are assumed equivalent in all other respects including demographics. A study can have a weak sampling procedure and still be a true experiment (random assignment, not random sampling, is what makes it experimental). The researcher controls extraneous variables to maximise the IV's effect. Types of true-experimental designs: Posttest-only control-group design — randomise to two groups, treat one, measure both after. Pretest–posttest control-group design — measure before and after in both groups. Solomon four-group design — combines the two above to detect and control for pretest sensitisation (whether being pretested changes the effect). Randomised experimental design with matching — match participants on a relevant variable, then randomly assign within pairs. Within-subjects (crossover) design — each participant receives every condition. Quasi-experimental approach Has an active IV but no random assignment ; participants are already in intact groups, so the researcher has less control. The design's strength depends on how much control the investigator actually has over manipulating the IV. Categories: Pre-experimental designs (quasi-experiments with major limitations, no feasible comparison group or pretest): one-group posttest-only, one-group pretest–posttest, posttest-only non-equivalent groups. Pretest–posttest designs with a non-equivalent comparison group. Time-series designs — repeated measures before and after intervention, no random assignment; single-group and multiple-group time-series. Single-subject (small-n) designs (see ANOVA section). Variables and validity Independent variable (IV) = the presumed cause; dependent variable (DV) = the measured effect. Extraneous variable = any variable other than the IV that could affect the DV; a confound is an extraneous variable that systematically varies with the IV. Internal validity = the degree to which the design supports a causal claim (threatened by history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, regression to the mean, selection, attrition). External validity = generalisability to other people, settings and times. Sampling Sampling decides external validity (generalisation), whereas random assignment decides internal validity (causation). Do not confuse the two. Probability (random) sampling Non-probability sampling Simple random — every member has equal, independent chance Convenience — whoever is available Systematic — every k-th member from a list Purposive — chosen for a characteristic the researcher wants Stratified — split into strata, sample within each (proportionate or disproportionate) Quota — fill preset category counts non-randomly Cluster / multistage — sample naturally occurring groups, then within them Snowball — participants recruit further participants Trap Random sampling ≠ random assignment . Random sampling (drawing the sample from the population) supports generalisation ; random assignment (allocating participants to conditions) supports causal inference . A true experiment requires random assignment but can survive a weak (non-random) sample. Focus groups and field studies use convenience/purposive sampling, so they cannot claim a representative sample. 3.
