The journal The Indian Psychological Association was formed in 1925 and launched the Indian Journal of Psychology in 1926. Departments at Madras and Pune came later. Why the other options are wrong (1) (b) → (a) → (c) → (e) → (d) Puts Madras before the Indian Journal of Psychology; the journal (1926) came first, before the Madras department was set up. (3) (b) → (c) → (a) → (d) → (e) Places Madras before Mysore and the journal last; Mysore (1924) and the journal (1926) both came before Madras and Pune. (4) (a) → (b) → (e) → (c) → (d) Starts with Mysore, but Calcutta University had the first psychology department in India, before Mysore. Choose the odd one for the pattern of sympathetic activation during emotions. 1 Increased heart rate 2 Pupil constriction 3 Increased breathing rate 4 Lowered skin resistance ✓ Answer: (2) Pupil constriction Walter Cannon, sympathetic fight-or-flight response The concept Why this one In emotion the sympathetic branch dilates the pupils to let in more light. Pupil constriction is a parasympathetic effect, so it is the odd one out. How it works The sympathetic system prepares the body for fight or flight : faster heart and breathing, more sweating, blood sent to the muscles, digestion slowed. Exam tip Lowered skin resistance means more sweat on the skin; this is the galvanic skin response recorded by the polygraph. Old key This page used to show (3) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are not the answer (1) Increased heart rate A faster heartbeat pumps more blood to the muscles; it is a classic sympathetic sign and fits the pattern. (3) Increased breathing rate Faster breathing brings in more oxygen for action; it is a sympathetic effect and fits the pattern. (4) Lowered skin resistance Sympathetic activation of sweat glands lowers skin resistance (raises skin conductance); it fits the pattern and is what the polygraph records. A psychological currency that permits deviation from the group is called: 1 Conformity 2 Obedience 3 Idiosyncrasy credit 4 Compliance ✓ Answer: (3) Idiosyncrasy credit Edwin Hollander, idiosyncrasy credit The concept Why this one Idiosyncrasy credit is the goodwill a member earns by conforming and contributing to the group. It can later be 'spent' to deviate without being rejected. How it works Leaders and high-status members build up credits over time, so the group accepts their new ideas. A newcomer who deviates early has no credit and is punished. Exam tip Edwin Hollander's idea explains how an accepted leader can bring change: first conform, then innovate. Why the other options are wrong (1) Conformity Changing one's behaviour or beliefs to match group norms; it is the opposite of deviating, not a credit that allows it. (2) Obedience Following a direct command from an authority figure, as in Stanley Milgram's studies; it involves no store of credit. (4) Compliance Going along with a direct request (foot-in-the-door, door-in-the-face), often without private agreement; it is not a licence to deviate. Which of the following is excluded from Berkowitz's frustration-aggression hypothesis? 1 Frustration always leads to aggression. 2 Social rules may inhibit aggression. 3 Frustration may result in other behaviour than aggression. 4 Cognitive factors can override aggression. ✓ Answer: (1) Frustration always leads to aggression. Leonard Berkowitz, revised frustration-aggression hypothesis The concept Why this one The original 1939 hypothesis of John Dollard, Neal Miller and colleagues said frustration always leads to aggression . Leonard Berkowitz dropped this claim. What Berkowitz said Frustration produces negative affect (anger) and a readiness to aggress. Whether aggression follows depends on aggressive cues, learning, social rules and thinking. Exam tip In his later cognitive neoassociation model, higher-order thinking (appraisal, attribution) can restrain or redirect the urge to aggress. Old key This page used to show (4) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are not the answer (2) Social rules may inhibit aggression. Included: norms and fear of punishment can hold back aggression even when a person is frustrated, which the revised view accepts. (3) Frustration may result in other behaviour than aggression. Included: frustration can lead to other responses such as withdrawal or problem solving, so aggression is only one possible outcome. (4) Cognitive factors can override aggression. Included: in Berkowitz's cognitive neoassociation model, appraisal and higher-order thinking can override the first aggressive urge. Choose the correct sequence of events following prolonged stress. (a) Corticotropin releasing factor (b) Adrenocorticotrophic hormone (c) Cortisol (d) Immune suppression Choose the correct option: 1 (a) → (b) → (c) → (d) 2 (d) → (c) → (a) → (b) 3 (a) → (c) → (d) → (b) 4 (b) → (c) → (a) → (d) ✓ Answer: (1) (a) → (b) → (c) → (d) Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis The concept Correct order (a) The hypothalamus releases CRF → (b) the anterior pituitary releases ACTH → (c) the adrenal cortex releases cortisol → (d) prolonged high cortisol suppresses the immune system. How it works Cortisol raises blood sugar and damps inflammation. That helps in the short term, but when stress lasts it lowers lymphocyte activity and resistance to infection. Exam tip This is the slow HPA axis ; the fast route is the sympathetic-adrenal medullary system releasing adrenaline. Link it to Hans Selye's general adaptation syndrome. Old key This page used to show (3) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (2) (d) → (c) → (a) → (b) Starts with immune suppression, which is the end result of the chain; CRF must come first to start the hormonal cascade. (3) (a) → (c) → (d) → (b) Puts cortisol before ACTH, but the adrenal cortex releases cortisol only after ACTH from the pituitary reaches it. (4) (b) → (c) → (a) → (d) Starts with ACTH, but the pituitary releases ACTH only after the hypothalamus sends CRF. Imaginal disputation by using the ability of a client to imagine is a method of: 1 REBT 2 Existential Confrontation 3 Gestalt therapy Confrontation 4 Mindfulness ✓ Answer: (1) REBT Albert Ellis, rational emotive behaviour therapy The concept Why this one Imaginal disputation is an REBT technique: the client imagines a troubling event and, while still imagining it, disputes the irrational belief behind the upset. How it works In rational emotive imagery the client pictures the worst case, feels the unhealthy emotion, then changes the self-talk so it becomes a healthy one (concern instead of anxiety). Exam tip Albert Ellis's ABCDE: Activating event, Belief, Consequence, Disputing , Effect. Disputing can be cognitive, imaginal or behavioural. Using Hull's theory, Taylor conceptualized that anxiety is an emotionally based drive and therefore high anxious subjects on Taylor's Manifest Anxiety Scale (MAS) should be conditioned faster than low anxious subjects. The study verified the hypothesis. This provides evidence for: 1 Concurrent validity of MAS 2 Construct validity of MAS 3 Convergent validity of MAS 4 Lack of validity for MAS ✓ Answer: (2) Construct validity of MAS Janet Taylor's MAS; construct validation (Anne Anastasi) The concept Why this one The MAS was built on Clark Hull's drive theory. Showing that high scorers condition faster, as the theory predicts, supports the scale as a measure of the construct anxiety-as-drive. What it is Construct validity is how far a test measures a theoretical trait. It is shown by deriving predictions from the theory and testing them, often experimentally. Exam tip Concurrent validity = correlation with a criterion measured at the same time. Convergent validity = high correlation with other measures of the same trait (Campbell and Fiske). Why the other options are wrong (1) Concurrent validity of MAS Correlating the MAS with a criterion measured at the same time, such as clinicians' ratings; no theory-based experimental prediction is involved. (3) Convergent validity of MAS Shown by high correlations with other anxiety tests; this study tested a prediction from drive theory, not overlap with other tests. (4) Lack of validity for MAS The prediction was confirmed, so the result supports the scale; lack of validity would follow only if high and low scorers conditioned alike. During the 1960s, Hoffman and others criticised the college entrance examination and other nationally administered educational tests, and argued that: (a) These favour shrewd and nimble witted (b) These are over concerned with the expression of skill than the quality of thought behind the answer (c) These favour subtle, creative and more profound persons (d) These carry a bad effect in recognition of merit. Choose the correct option: 1 only (a) is correct 2 (a) and (d) are correct 3 only (c) is correct 4 (c) and (d) are correct ✓ Answer: (2) (a) and (d) are correct Banesh Hoffman, The Tyranny of Testing (1962) The concept Why this one Banesh Hoffman argued that multiple-choice tests favour the shrewd and nimble-witted (a) and have a bad effect on education and the recognition of merit (d). Why others false (b) twists his point: he said the tests score only the chosen answer, ignore the quality of thought behind it and neglect skill in expression. (c) is the reverse: he said they penalise the subtle, creative, more profound person. Context His attack on the multiple-choice format fed the 1960s debate on standardised testing that Anne Anastasi reviews. Old key This page used to show (3) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (1) only (a) is correct (a) is true, but (d) is also one of Hoffman's charges: that such tests harm education and the recognition of merit. (3) only (c) is correct (c) inverts Hoffman: he said the tests penalise the subtle, creative and profound candidate, not favour them. (4) (c) and (d) are correct (d) is true but (c) is false; Hoffman held that creative, profound thinkers are the ones these tests penalise. Match the following diseases with their corresponding descriptions. List I: (a) Parkinson's Disease; (b) Huntington's Disease; (c) Alzheimer's Disease; (d) Korsakoff Syndrome List II: (i) Movement disorder associated with cognitive deficits; (ii) Progressive motor disorder associated with severe dementia; (iii) Progressive decline in memory starting with selective forgetting; (iv) A form of dementia caused by deficiency of vitamin Thiamine Choose the correct option from those given below: 1 (a)-(ii), (b)-(i), (c)-(iv), (d)-(iii) 2 (a)-(i), (b)-(iv), (c)-(iii), (d)-(ii) 3 (a)-(i), (b)-(ii), (c)-(iii), (d)-(iv) 4 (a)-(ii), (b)-(iii), (c)-(iv), (d)-(i) ✓ Answer: (3) (a)-(i), (b)-(ii), (c)-(iii), (d)-(iv) Neurodegenerative and amnesic disorders (John Pinel) The concept Correct pairs (a) Parkinson's = (i) movement disorder with cognitive deficits; (b) Huntington's = (ii) progressive motor disorder with severe dementia; (c) Alzheimer's = (iii) progressive memory decline starting with selective forgetting; (d) Korsakoff = (iv) thiamine deficiency dementia. Arrange the Ego Strengths in correct sequence according to Erikson's stages of development. 1 Hope → purpose → competence → fidelity → love → care → wisdom → will 2 Will → hope → purpose → competence → fidelity → care → wisdom → love 3 Hope → will → purpose → competence → fidelity → love → care → wisdom 4 Purpose → hope → will → fidelity → competence → care → wisdom → love ✓ Answer: (3) Hope → will → purpose → competence → fidelity → love → care → wisdom Erik Erikson, psychosocial stages and basic virtues The concept Correct order Hope (trust vs mistrust) → will (autonomy vs shame) → purpose (initiative vs guilt) → competence (industry vs inferiority) → fidelity (identity vs role confusion) → love (intimacy vs isolation) → care (generativity vs stagnation) → wisdom (integrity vs despair). What they are Erik Erikson called each ego strength the basic virtue that emerges when a stage crisis is resolved well. Exam tip Memory aid: 'Hope Will Purposely Compete For Love, Care and Wisdom'. The Generational Digital or Gen D factor: (a) pertains to reversal of power hierarchy in terms of digital technology (b) pertains to imparting knowledge downward to the younger generation (c) calls for psychoeducation of parents and caregivers on digital technology usage (d) calls for the adolescent psychoeducation on digital technology usage Choose the correct option: 1 Only (a) 2 Only (b) 3 (a) and (c) 4 (b) and (d) ✓ Best answer: (3) (a) and (c) Generational digital divide (Gen D factor) The concept Why this one The Gen D factor describes a reversal of the usual hierarchy : the young know digital technology better than their parents (a). So the remedy targets the adults: psychoeducation of parents and caregivers (c). Why others false (b) is the traditional direction of teaching; with digital technology, knowledge flows upward from child to parent. (d) misses the point, since the gap lies with the adults who must guide and monitor use. Not certain Gen D is a niche term from writing on digital media, not a standard textbook; if (c) is read as a separate recommendation rather than part of the idea, option (1) is the runner-up. Involvement of the frontal lobe in intelligence can be understood in terms of which of the following sequences? 1 Frontal lobe → Focusing attention internally → Working memory → General reasoning 2 Frontal lobe → Focusing attention internally → Response selection → General reasoning 3 Frontal lobe → Short term memory → Working memory → General reasoning 4 Frontal lobe → Response selection → Working memory → General reasoning ✓ Best answer: (1) Frontal lobe → Focusing attention internally → Working memory → General reasoning Michael Kane and Randall Engle, executive attention The concept Why this one The prefrontal cortex lets a person hold attention on internal representations and block distraction. This controlled attention sets working memory capacity, which in turn predicts general (fluid) reasoning . How it works Michael Kane and Randall Engle argue that working memory capacity is largely executive attention ; John Duncan found lateral frontal cortex active across high-g tasks. Exam tip Short-term memory is passive storage; working memory adds active control. That is why working memory tasks correlate more strongly with g. Not certain The chain comes from research papers rather than one standard textbook; option (4), with response selection as the frontal step, is the runner-up because the frontal lobe also selects responses. Old key This page used to show (4) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (2) Frontal lobe → Focusing attention internally → Response selection → General reasoning Response selection is a frontal output function, but the route to reasoning runs through working memory, which this chain leaves out. (3) Frontal lobe → Short term memory → Working memory → General reasoning Short-term memory is passive storage, not the frontal contribution; the frontal lobe adds attentional control, which turns storage into working memory. (4) Frontal lobe → Response selection → Working memory → General reasoning Response selection is a frontal function, but the link from frontal lobe to working memory is internally focused attention, not picking responses. Which of the following are the two major symptoms of Alzheimer's disease? 1 Neurofibrillary tangles and Amyloid plaques 2 Collateral sprouting and cerebral ischemia 3 Amyloid plaques and cerebral ischemia 4 Neurofibrillary tangles and collateral sprouting ✓ Answer: (1) Neurofibrillary tangles and Amyloid plaques Alois Alzheimer; plaques and tangles The concept Why this one The two defining brain signs of Alzheimer's disease are amyloid plaques (clumps of beta-amyloid between neurons) and neurofibrillary tangles (twisted tau threads inside neurons). How it works Plaques and tangles first build up in the medial temporal lobe (entorhinal cortex, hippocampus), which is why memory goes first. Acetylcholine neurons of the basal forebrain are also lost. Exam tip Alois Alzheimer first described plaques and tangles; traditionally a definite diagnosis needs them to be found at autopsy . Old key This page used to show (2) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (2) Collateral sprouting and cerebral ischemia Collateral sprouting is regrowth of axon branches after injury, and cerebral ischaemia is loss of blood supply (stroke); neither is an Alzheimer's hallmark. (3) Amyloid plaques and cerebral ischemia Plaques are a hallmark, but ischaemia (blocked blood flow) causes stroke and vascular dementia, not Alzheimer's disease. (4) Neurofibrillary tangles and collateral sprouting Tangles are a hallmark, but collateral sprouting is a recovery process after neural damage, not a sign of Alzheimer's. Which of the following are the advantages of fMRI over PET scan? (a) Nothing has to be injected into the body (b) Provides both structural and functional information of the same image (c) Produces three-dimensional images of activity over the entire brain Choose the correct option: 1 Only (a) and (b) 2 Only (a) and (c) 3 Only (b) and (c) 4 (a), (b) and (c) ✓ Answer: (4) (a), (b) and (c) John Pinel, Biopsychology: fMRI versus PET The concept Why this one John Pinel lists the advantages of fMRI over PET: nothing is injected , it gives structural and functional information in the same image, its spatial resolution is better, and it can produce 3-D images of activity over the whole brain. So (a), (b) and (c) are all true. How it works fMRI tracks the BOLD signal, the rise in oxygenated blood in active areas. PET needs a radioactive tracer injected into the blood. Exam tip PET keeps one strength: with labelled ligands it can image specific chemicals and receptors . Old key This page used to show (3) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (1) Only (a) and (b) (a) and (b) are right, but (c) is also an fMRI advantage Pinel lists: 3-D images of activity across the whole brain. (2) Only (a) and (c) (a) and (c) are right, but (b) is too: fMRI shows structure and function in the same image, while PET shows only activity. (3) Only (b) and (c) (b) and (c) are right, but (a) is the most cited advantage: fMRI needs no injected radioactive tracer. Feminist theory helped in: 1 dealing with gender inequality 2 understanding sexual preferences 3 human growth and development 4 gender issues ✓ Best answer: (1) dealing with gender inequality Feminist theory and feminist therapy (Gerald Corey) The concept Why this one Feminist theory began as a challenge to gender inequality : unequal power, rights and opportunities for women. In therapy its slogan is 'the personal is political'. How it works Feminist therapists such as Jean Baker Miller look at how gender-role socialisation and oppression shape distress, and aim for an egalitarian therapist-client relationship. Exam tip Gerald Corey lists empowerment , valuing women's experience and social change among its goals. Not certain Option (4) 'gender issues' is broad and also true; (1) is chosen because challenging gender inequality is the defining aim of feminist theory. Why the other options are wrong (2) understanding sexual preferences Sexual preferences are studied in sexology and research on sexual orientation; feminist theory centres on power and gender, not sexual preference. (3) human growth and development Human development is the field of developmental psychology (Jean Piaget, Erik Erikson); feminists such as Carol Gilligan criticised such theories for male bias but did not build them. (4) gender issues Very broad; feminist theory does deal with gender issues, but its specific contribution is exposing and challenging gender inequality. "Value of behaviour to the organism, its evolutionary history, and its causation in terms of stimulus, hormonal and neurological events" has been an area of study of which of the following? 1 Evolutionary psychology 2 Psychoanalysis 3 Ethology 4 Instinct Psychology ✓ Answer: (3) Ethology Niko Tinbergen, four questions of ethology The concept Why this one Ethology , the biological study of animal behaviour in natural settings, asks about a behaviour's survival value , its evolutionary history and its immediate causes (stimuli, hormones, nerves). How it works Niko Tinbergen's four questions : causation (mechanism), development, function (survival value) and evolution. Konrad Lorenz and Karl von Frisch shared the 1973 Nobel Prize with him. Exam tip Classic ethology terms: fixed action pattern , sign stimulus, imprinting. Why the other options are wrong (1) Evolutionary psychology Evolutionary psychology (David Buss, Leda Cosmides) explains human mental mechanisms as adaptations; it does not study hormonal and neural causes of animal behaviour. (2) Psychoanalysis Sigmund Freud's psychoanalysis studies unconscious conflict and childhood experience, not evolutionary history or hormonal causes of behaviour. (4) Instinct Psychology William McDougall's instinct psychology listed inborn instincts as the motives of behaviour; it did not study evolutionary history or neural causation. Which part of the brain is responsible for transferring information from Short Term Memory to Long Term Memory? 1 Amygdala 2 Hypothalamus 3 Hippocampus 4 Cerebellum ✓ Answer: (3) Hippocampus Hippocampal consolidation; patient H.M. (Brenda Milner) The concept Why this one The hippocampus consolidates new information, moving it from short-term into long-term memory. Evidence Patient H.M. (Henry Molaison) lost both hippocampi in epilepsy surgery. His short-term memory and old memories stayed, but he could not form new long-term declarative memories ( anterograde amnesia ). Exam tip Amygdala = emotional memory; cerebellum = motor skills and conditioned reflexes; hypothalamus = drives such as hunger and thirst. Why the other options are wrong (1) Amygdala The amygdala adds emotional weight to memories, especially fear; it does not transfer general information into long-term memory. (2) Hypothalamus The hypothalamus regulates hunger, thirst, temperature, sex and the pituitary; it is not the memory consolidation centre. (4) Cerebellum The cerebellum handles motor coordination, procedural skills and eyeblink conditioning, not consolidation of declarative facts. For becoming a good basketball player, one must use: 1 Algorithms 2 Heuristics 3 Concepts 4 Prototypes ✓ Answer: (2) Heuristics Heuristics versus algorithms in problem solving The concept Why this one Basketball needs split-second decisions in a changing game, so a player relies on heuristics : quick rules of thumb learned from experience, such as 'pass when double-teamed'. What it is An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure that guarantees a solution but is slow. A heuristic is a shortcut that is fast and usually works, though it can fail. Exam tip Gerd Gigerenzer's gaze heuristic (keep the angle of gaze to the ball constant) explains how fielders catch a ball without computing its path. Why the other options are wrong (1) Algorithms Algorithms are exhaustive step-by-step procedures that guarantee an answer, as in maths; they are far too slow for fast, changing game situations. (3) Concepts Concepts are mental categories that group objects and ideas; they organise knowledge but are not a strategy for split-second play. (4) Prototypes Prototypes are the most typical examples of a concept (Eleanor Rosch); they help with categorising, not quick decisions in a game. Which of the following is the most common anti-obesity hormone? 1 Leptin 2 Orexin 3 Insulin 4 Ghrelin ✓ Answer: (1) Leptin Leptin, the fat-cell satiety hormone The concept Why this one Leptin is released by fat cells in proportion to body fat. It acts on the hypothalamus to cut food intake and raise energy use, so it is called the anti-obesity hormone. Evidence ob/ob mice cannot make leptin and become very obese; leptin injections make them eat less and lose weight. Exam tip Most obese people have high leptin but are leptin resistant , so leptin does not cure common obesity. Ghrelin from the stomach is the hunger hormone. Old key This page used to show (3) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (2) Orexin Orexin (hypocretin) from the lateral hypothalamus promotes wakefulness and food seeking; its loss causes narcolepsy, and it does not fight obesity. (3) Insulin Insulin from the pancreas lowers blood glucose and promotes fat storage; it also signals satiety, but it is not the main anti-obesity hormone. (4) Ghrelin Ghrelin is released by an empty stomach and stimulates hunger; it is the hunger hormone, the opposite of an anti-obesity signal. Arrange the following in sequence as per Atkinson and Shiffrin's model of memory when the information is processed. (a) Short term memory (b) Elaborative rehearsal (c) Long term memory (d) Attention (in Sensory memory) (e) Sensory memory 1 (d) → (e) → (a) → (b) → (c) 2 (e) → (a) → (d) → (b) → (c) 3 (e) → (d) → (a) → (b) → (c) 4 (d) → (e) → (a) → (b) → (c) ✓ Answer: (3) (e) → (d) → (a) → (b) → (c) Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin, multi-store model (1968) The concept Correct order (e) Sensory memory holds all input briefly → (d) attention selects part of it → (a) short-term memory → (b) elaborative rehearsal links it to meaning → (c) long-term memory. Which of the following is the explanation of the Premack principle? 1 A primary reinforcement is thought of as being related to an organism's survival 2 A secondary reinforcer acquires reinforcing value because of pairing with a primary reinforcer 3 All responses are potential reinforcers 4 A more frequently occurring activity can be used to reinforce an activity that occurs less often ✓ Answer: (4) A more frequently occurring activity can be used to reinforce an activity that occurs less often David Premack, Premack principle The concept Why this one David Premack showed that a high-probability behaviour can reinforce a low-probability one: 'finish your homework, then you can play'. How it works Reinforcers are treated as activities, not things. Whatever a person prefers to do can be made contingent on a less preferred activity. Exam tip Also called Grandma's rule . Its refinement, response deprivation theory, says any activity restricted below its usual level can act as a reinforcer. Why the other options are wrong (1) A primary reinforcement is thought of as being related to an organism's survival Describes a primary reinforcer such as food or water, which satisfies a biological need without any learning. (2) A secondary reinforcer acquires reinforcing value because of pairing with a primary reinforcer Describes a secondary (conditioned) reinforcer such as money or praise, which gains value from pairing with primary reinforcers. (3) All responses are potential reinforcers Overstates the idea: an activity reinforces only a less probable activity, so reinforcing power depends on relative probability, not on simply being a response. Arrange in sequence the network of auditory pathways. (a) Auditory Nerve (b) Cochlear Nuclei (c) Superior Olives (d) Lateral Lemniscus (e) Inferior Colliculi (f) Medial Geniculate Nuclei (g) Primary Auditory Cortex Choose the correct sequence: 1 (a) → (c) → (b) → (d) → (e) → (g) → (f) 2 (a) → (b) → (c) → (d) → (e) → (f) → (g) 3 (b) → (a) → (d) → (c) → (g) → (e) → (f) 4 (f) → (g) → (e) → (d) → (c) → (b) → (a) ✓ Answer: (2) (a) → (b) → (c) → (d) → (e) → (f) → (g) Ascending auditory pathway (Pinel, Carlson) The concept Correct order (a) Auditory nerve → (b) cochlear nuclei (medulla) → (c) superior olives → (d) lateral lemniscus → (e) inferior colliculi (midbrain) → (f) medial geniculate nuclei (thalamus) → (g) primary auditory cortex (temporal lobe). How it works The superior olive is the first point where input from both ears meets, so it compares timing and loudness between the ears to locate sounds. Exam tip Medial geniculate = hearing; lateral geniculate = vision. Old key This page used to show (1) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (1) (a) → (c) → (b) → (d) → (e) → (g) → (f) Puts superior olives before cochlear nuclei and cortex before the medial geniculate; auditory nerve fibres end in the cochlear nuclei first, and the thalamus relays to cortex. (3) (b) → (a) → (d) → (c) → (g) → (e) → (f) Starts with the cochlear nuclei and puts cortex before the colliculi; the auditory nerve comes first, and the cortex is the final stop. (4) (f) → (g) → (e) → (d) → (c) → (b) → (a) Lists the pathway backwards, from thalamus to nerve; hearing signals ascend from the auditory nerve to the cortex. Escalation of commitment involves the following sequence of steps. (a) Occurrence of loss (b) Self-Justification (c) Strengthening by external factor (d) Rational expectation of positive outcome Choose the correct option: 1 (d) → (a) → (c) → (b) 2 (d) → (a) → (b) → (c) 3 (a) → (b) → (c) → (d) 4 (a) → (b) → (d) → (c) ✓ Answer: (2) (d) → (a) → (b) → (c) Barry Staw, escalation of commitment (Greenberg and Baron) The concept Correct order (d) A project starts with a rational expectation of a positive outcome → (a) losses occur → (b) the decision maker carries on out of self-justification , not wanting to admit an error → (c) external factors (political pressure, public commitment) strengthen commitment further. What it is Escalation of commitment is the tendency to keep investing in a failing course of action, 'throwing good money after bad' (Barry Staw). Exam tip Remedies: set limits in advance, let different people make the first and later decisions, and review progress regularly. Old key This page used to mark this question as withdrawn. That key does not line up with this paper, so it is answered here like the rest. Why the other options are wrong (1) (d) → (a) → (c) → (b) Puts external pressure before self-justification; the first reaction to early losses is the personal need to justify the decision, with outside forces added later. (3) (a) → (b) → (c) → (d) Starts with the loss; escalation begins with a sound decision based on a rational expectation of success, before any loss occurs. (4) (a) → (b) → (d) → (c) Starts with the loss and puts the rational expectation in the middle; the positive expectation comes first and leads to the initial decision. Client: "I really don't have much to say (tapping foot)." Counsellor: "Do you know you are tapping your foot?" Client: "No. I guess I am feeling some impatience (pause). Even more, some confused." Here the counselor is: 1 Trying to create awareness in the client 2 Being a little too harsh 3 Making an effort to understand the client's behaviour at a deeper level 4 Trying to create both awareness and deeper understanding ✓ Best answer: (1) Trying to create awareness in the client Fritz Perls, Gestalt awareness technique The concept Why this one The counsellor simply points to a nonverbal act the client has not noticed (foot tapping). Bringing an unnoticed behaviour into focus is awareness work. How it works In Gestalt therapy (Fritz Perls), awareness of what one is doing right now is itself healing. The counsellor reflects the body cue and the client discovers the feeling behind it (impatience, confusion). Exam tip Gestalt asks 'what' and 'how' and stays in the here and now ; it does not interpret causes or ask 'why'. Not certain The client's reply does reach a deeper grasp of his feelings, so (4) is defensible, but the counsellor's own move only points out the behaviour, which is awareness work. Old key This page used to show (4) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (2) Being a little too harsh The question is gentle and non-judgemental; it neither blames nor attacks the client, so it is not harsh. (3) Making an effort to understand the client's behaviour at a deeper level Probing the deeper meaning or causes of behaviour is interpretation, as in psychoanalysis; this counsellor does not interpret, the client finds the feeling himself. (4) Trying to create both awareness and deeper understanding The deeper understanding comes from the client, not from any interpretation by the counsellor; the counsellor's own move is only to raise awareness. The Phi-Phenomenon is best seen between which of the following time intervals? 1 50 to 350 milliseconds 2 110 to 320 milliseconds 3 30 to 200 milliseconds 4 215 to 375 milliseconds ✓ Answer: (3) 30 to 200 milliseconds Max Wertheimer, apparent motion (1912) The concept Why this one When two lights flash one after the other, movement is seen between them when the gap is about 30 to 200 ms , best at about 60 ms. How it works Gap under about 30 ms: the lights look simultaneous . Gap over about 200 ms: they look successive , two separate flashes. In between, one light seems to move: the phi phenomenon . Exam tip Phi is apparent movement , the basis of films and neon signs. Max Wertheimer's study of it, with Wolfgang Köhler and Kurt Koffka, started Gestalt psychology . Why the other options are wrong (1) 50 to 350 milliseconds Starts above the 30 ms threshold and runs well past 200 ms, where the two flashes are seen as separate (succession), not as movement. (2) 110 to 320 milliseconds Leaves out the optimal gap of about 60 ms and runs past 200 ms, where the flashes look successive. (4) 215 to 375 milliseconds Lies almost wholly above 200 ms, where the two lights are seen one after the other with no movement. Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A): Philosophically the word pragmatism emphasizes result rather than methods. Reason (R): A pragmatic view of science accepts a methodological approach to knowledge. In the light of the above two statements, choose the correct option: 1 Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A) 2 Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A) 3 (A) is true, but (R) is false 4 (A) is false, and (R) is true ✓ Best answer: (3) (A) is true, but (R) is false Charles Peirce, William James, John Dewey: pragmatism The concept Assertion True. Pragmatism (William James, John Dewey) judges an idea by its practical consequences : what works is true. Results matter more than the route taken. Reason False as stated. A pragmatic view of science does not commit to one fixed method; it is method-pluralist and uses whatever approach answers the question. Exam tip Pragmatism is the usual philosophy behind mixed-methods research: the research question, not the method, comes first. Not certain If R is read as pragmatists such as Charles Peirce valuing the method of science, R is true but does not explain A, giving (2). Why the other options are wrong (1) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A) R is not true as stated, and a stress on a fixed method could not explain a philosophy that puts results ahead of methods. (2) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A) Needs R to be true; pragmatism does not tie knowledge to one methodological approach, so R fails. (4) (A) is false, and (R) is true A is the standard definition of pragmatism (truth judged by practical results), so A cannot be false. Double standards of mental health with regard to adult females: (a) depicted adult female behaviour as less socially desirable and healthy (b) had set up barriers against the advancement of women in non-traditional roles (c) pertain to the changing dual personality of women in the current scenario (d) pertain to the identification of the general standards of healthy behaviour with men only Choose the correct option: 1 Only (d) is correct 2 Only (c) is correct 3 Only (a) and (b) are correct 4 (a), (b) and (c) are correct ✓ Answer: (3) Only (a) and (b) are correct Inge Broverman and colleagues (1970) The concept Why this one In the study by Inge Broverman and colleagues, clinicians rated a healthy woman as less healthy and less socially desirable than a healthy adult, so (a) is true. Such a double standard also discourages women from non-traditional roles, so (b) is true. What they found Clinicians' picture of a healthy adult (sex unspecified) matched their picture of a healthy man . A healthy woman was seen as more submissive, less independent and more emotional. Why not (c), (d) (c) 'dual personality' is not part of the concept. The adult standard did match the male one, but (d) alone leaves out the core finding (a), so the best set is (a) and (b). Why the other options are wrong (1) Only (d) is correct The adult standard did align with the male one, but (d) alone misses the core finding that female behaviour was rated less healthy and desirable. (2) Only (c) is correct (c) is not part of the concept; the double standard is about clinicians' stereotyped judgements, not a changing dual personality of women. (4) (a), (b) and (c) are correct Includes (c), which is false; the double standard concerns stereotyped clinical judgements, not a dual personality of women. Consider the three types of investigation in psychological research written in alphabetical order: (a) Controlled laboratory experiments; (b) Ex post facto studies; and (c) Field experiment Arrange them in descending order in terms of their ability to control secondary variance usually. 1 (a), (c), (b) 2 (a), (b), (c) 3 (c), (a), (b) 4 (b), (c), (a) ✓ Answer: (1) (a), (c), (b) Fred Kerlinger, control of extraneous variance The concept Why this one The laboratory experiment controls extraneous (secondary) variance best, the field experiment next, and the ex post facto study least. Correct order (a) laboratory experiment: variables manipulated, setting controlled, random assignment → (c) field experiment: manipulation and randomisation in a real setting with less control → (b) ex post facto: no manipulation, no random assignment. Exam tip Fred Kerlinger's MAXMINCON : maximise systematic variance, minimise error variance, control extraneous variance. Control falls as realism rises. Old key This page used to show (4) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (2) (a), (b), (c) Puts ex post facto second, but it has no manipulation or random assignment, so it controls extraneous variance least, below the field experiment. (3) (c), (a), (b) A field experiment runs in a natural setting with many uncontrolled influences, so it cannot beat the laboratory experiment. (4) (b), (c), (a) This is the ascending order (least to most control), the reverse of what is asked. There are many mnemonic devices to help a person memorize lists of words and vocabulary items. Identify the correct device series. (a) Categorical Clustering (b) Interactive Images (c) Recognition (d) Pegword System (e) Method of Loci Choose the correct option: 1 (a), (b) and (c) 2 (b), (c) and (d) 3 (c), (d) and (e) 4 (a), (b), (d) and (e) ✓ Answer: (4) (a), (b), (d) and (e) Robert Sternberg, mnemonic devices in cognitive psychology The concept Why this one Categorical clustering , interactive images , the pegword system and the method of loci are all mnemonic devices; recognition is a way of retrieving, not a device. What each does Clustering groups items by category; interactive images link items in one vivid scene; pegwords hook items onto rhymes (one is a bun); loci place items along a familiar route. Exam tip Other devices: acronyms, acrostics and the keyword system (for foreign vocabulary). Recognition and recall are memory measures. Old key This page used to show (2) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (1) (a), (b) and (c) Includes recognition, which is a retrieval task (picking the right item from choices), not a technique for encoding lists. (2) (b), (c) and (d) Includes recognition, a memory test rather than a mnemonic, and leaves out clustering and the method of loci. (3) (c), (d) and (e) Includes recognition, which is a way of testing memory, and leaves out clustering and interactive images. If you move a book from your desk to a shelf, you know the form of the book is not changing. It may be because of which of the following? 1 Linear perspective 2 Relative size 3 Shape constancy 4 Size constancy ✓ Best answer: (3) Shape constancy Perceptual constancy: shape constancy The concept Why this one As you carry the book its image on the retina changes from a rectangle to a trapezoid, yet you still see a rectangle. Keeping form stable is shape constancy . What it is Perceptual constancy lets us see objects as stable despite changing retinal images: shape, size, brightness and colour constancy. Exam tip Shape: form stays the same (an opening door). Size: an object does not seem to shrink as it moves away (a friend walking off). Not certain Moving the book also changes its distance, so size constancy (4) can be argued, but the stem asks about its form, which is shape. Old key This page used to show (4) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are not the answer (1) Linear perspective A monocular depth cue: parallel lines seem to meet in the distance; it signals depth, not a stable form. (2) Relative size A depth cue: the smaller of two similar objects looks farther away; it does not keep form constant. (4) Size constancy Keeps an object's perceived size stable as distance changes; the stem asks about form, which is shape constancy. Arrange the following stages of moral development in sequence of their emergence as an individual grows up. (a) Morality of interpersonal cooperation (b) Universal ethical principle orientation (c) Social order maintaining orientation (d) Instrumental Purpose Orientation Choose the correct option: 1 (d) → (a) → (b) → (c) 2 (d) → (a) → (c) → (b) 3 (a) → (b) → (d) → (c) 4 (b) → (c) → (d) → (a) ✓ Answer: (2) (d) → (a) → (c) → (b) Lawrence Kohlberg, stages of moral development The concept Why this one Lawrence Kohlberg 's stages run from self-interest to approval to law and order to universal principles: (d) → (a) → (c) → (b). Correct order Stage 2 instrumental purpose (preconventional) → Stage 3 interpersonal cooperation , good boy/nice girl → Stage 4 social order maintaining , law and order (both conventional) → Stage 6 universal ethical principles (postconventional). Exam tip Stage 1 is punishment and obedience; Stage 5 is social contract. Three levels, two stages each. Old key This page used to show (1) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (1) (d) → (a) → (b) → (c) Puts universal ethical principles (Stage 6) before social order maintaining (Stage 4), reversing the last two steps. (3) (a) → (b) → (d) → (c) Starts with Stage 3 and puts Stage 6 second; instrumental purpose (Stage 2) must come first. (4) (b) → (c) → (d) → (a) Almost reversed: universal ethical principles is the highest stage, reached last if at all. Beta endorphin is mobilized from the Pituitary Gland during stress in approximately the same quantities as: 1 Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) 2 Corticotrophin releasing factor (CRF) 3 Epinephrine 4 Dopamine ✓ Answer: (1) Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) co-release The concept Why this one Beta endorphin and ACTH are cut from the same precursor molecule, pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) , in the anterior pituitary, so stress releases them together in roughly equal amounts. How it works Stress → hypothalamus releases CRF → anterior pituitary splits POMC → ACTH (drives cortisol from the adrenal cortex) plus beta endorphin (pain relief). Exam tip This is the basis of stress-induced analgesia : the body's own opioids blunt pain during emergencies. Why the other options are wrong (2) Corticotrophin releasing factor (CRF) Made by the hypothalamus, not the pituitary; it triggers the release of ACTH and beta endorphin rather than being released with them. (3) Epinephrine Released by the adrenal medulla under sympathetic control, not split from POMC in the pituitary. (4) Dopamine A neurotransmitter of reward and movement pathways; it is not split from POMC alongside beta endorphin. Which of the following are the elements of the Language Acquisition Process? (a) Phonemes (b) Morphemes (c) Syntax (d) Pragmatics Choose the correct option: 1 (a), (c) and (d) only 2 (b), (c) and (d) only 3 (a), (b) and (c) only 4 (a), (b) and (d) only ✓ Best answer: (3) (a), (b) and (c) only Structure of language: phonemes, morphemes, syntax The concept Why this one A child acquires language by mastering its structural units: phonemes (basic sounds), morphemes (smallest units of meaning) and syntax (rules for ordering words). How it builds Sounds (cooing, babbling) → words made of morphemes → word combinations governed by syntax (telegraphic speech) → full sentences. Pragmatics Pragmatics is the social use of language (turn taking, politeness); it is about using language in context rather than one of its structural building blocks. Not certain All four belong to language development; texts that count pragmatics as an element could support (1), (2) or (4), but the three structural units are the usual set. Old key This page used to show (2) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (1) (a), (c) and (d) only Drops morphemes, the smallest units of meaning, and adds pragmatics, which is the social use of language rather than a structural unit. (2) (b), (c) and (d) only Drops phonemes, the basic sound units that babbling and first words are built from, and adds pragmatics instead. (4) (a), (b) and (d) only Drops syntax, the grammar rules for combining words, which is central to acquiring language, and adds pragmatics. The core emphasis of developmental psychology is represented by which of these sets of pairs? 1 Individual v/s shared and stability v/s change 2 Young v/s old and stability v/s change 3 Individual v/s shared and young v/s old 4 Cross-sectional v/s longitudinal and self-esteem v/s self-doubt ✓ Best answer: (1) Individual v/s shared and stability v/s change Lifespan developmental psychology, core issues The concept Why this one Developmental psychology asks how people change and how they stay stable over the lifespan, and which patterns are shared by everyone versus individual to each person. How it works Shared (normative) pattern: most babies walk around one year. Individual differences: timing and style vary with genes and experience. Stability versus change: does a shy toddler stay shy? Exam tip Other core issues: nature versus nurture , continuity versus discontinuity (stages), critical versus sensitive periods. Not certain Both (1) and (2) contain stability versus change; (2) works only if the age span is treated as a core issue, which standard texts do not do. Old key This page used to show (2) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (2) Young v/s old and stability v/s change The age range the field covers is not a theoretical issue; only stability versus change fits here. (3) Individual v/s shared and young v/s old Young versus old describes age groups, not a core issue, and the pair leaves out stability versus change. (4) Cross-sectional v/s longitudinal and self-esteem v/s self-doubt Research designs (cross-sectional, longitudinal) plus a personality theme; neither pair is the field's core emphasis. Which of the following schools of Buddhism focuses on collective freedom from suffering and feeling the ways of enlightenment? 1 Nirvana 2 Theravada Buddhism 3 Mahayana Buddhism 4 Vajrayana Buddhism ✓ Answer: (3) Mahayana Buddhism Mahayana Buddhism, bodhisattva ideal The concept Why this one Mahayana ('great vehicle') stresses liberation for all beings. Its ideal is the bodhisattva , who delays final nirvana to help others reach enlightenment. Contrast Theravada stresses individual liberation by one's own effort; its ideal is the arhat . Vajrayana is the tantric school of Tibet. Exam tip Collective, compassion-based liberation → Mahayana; individual path → Theravada; ritual, mantra and tantra → Vajrayana. Old key This page used to show (1) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (1) Nirvana This is the goal itself, the end of craving and suffering, not a school of Buddhism. (2) Theravada Buddhism The older school of Sri Lanka and South-East Asia; it stresses individual liberation through one's own effort (the arhat ideal). (4) Vajrayana Buddhism The tantric school of Tibet using mantras, rituals and a guru; it grew out of Mahayana but is known for esoteric practice. The three psychologists who illustrated the diversity of approaches to functional psychology at Columbia were: 1 Harvey Carr, James McKeen Cattell and E.L. Thorndike 2 James Angell, Harvey Carr and James McKeen Cattell 3 E.L. Thorndike, R.S. Woodworth and James Angell 4 James McKeen Cattell, E.L. Thorndike and R.S. Woodworth ✓ Answer: (4) James McKeen Cattell, E.L. Thorndike and R.S. Woodworth James McKeen Cattell, E. L. Thorndike, Robert S. Woodworth The concept Why this one At Columbia University functionalism was loose and practical: James McKeen Cattell (mental tests), Edward Thorndike (law of effect) and Robert Woodworth (dynamic psychology). Chicago vs Columbia The formal Chicago school of functionalism was led by John Dewey, James Angell and Harvey Carr. Exam tip Robert Woodworth added the organism to S-R, giving S-O-R, and stressed motivation in his dynamic psychology. Woodworth and James Angell Includes James Angell, who made functionalism a formal school at the University of Chicago, not Columbia. Match the following types of memories with their features. List I: (a) Non-declarative memory; (b) Echoic memory; (c) Semantic memory; (d) Episodic memory List II: (i) Type of declarative memory containing general knowledge of language and information; (ii) Type of declarative memory containing personal information not readily available to others; (iii) Type of LTM for skills, procedures, habits etc.; (iv) Auditory sensation lasting only for 2 to 4 seconds Choose the correct option from those given below: 1 (a)-(i), (b)-(ii), (c)-(iii), (d)-(iv) 2 (a)-(ii), (b)-(iii), (c)-(iv), (d)-(i) 3 (a)-(iii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(i), (d)-(ii) 4 (a)-(iv), (b)-(iii), (c)-(ii), (d)-(i) ✓ Answer: (3) (a)-(iii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(i), (d)-(ii) Endel Tulving (episodic, semantic); Ulric Neisser (echoic) The concept Correct pairs (a) Non-declarative = (iii) LTM for skills, procedures, habits; (b) Echoic = (iv) auditory sensation lasting 2 to 4 seconds; (c) Semantic = (i) general knowledge of language and facts; (d) Episodic = (ii) personal events not readily available to others. (4) (a)-(iv), (b)-(iii), (c)-(ii), (d)-(i) Pairs non-declarative with auditory sensation and semantic with personal events; non-declarative holds skills, semantic holds general knowledge. Match the following elements of the Immune System with their respective functions. List I: (a) Neutrophils; (b) Immunoglobulins; (c) NK (Natural Killer) cells; (d) CD4 List II: (i) Yield Marshalls; (ii) Cytotoxic action; (iii) Phagocytic action; (iv) Antibody action Choose the correct option: 1 (a)-(iv), (b)-(ii), (c)-(iii), (d)-(i) 2 (a)-(iii), (b)-(i), (c)-(ii), (d)-(iv) 3 (a)-(iii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(ii), (d)-(i) 4 (a)-(ii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(i), (d)-(iii) ✓ Answer: (3) (a)-(iii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(ii), (d)-(i) Psychoneuroimmunology: immune cell functions The concept Correct pairs (a) Neutrophils = (iii) phagocytic action; (b) Immunoglobulins = (iv) antibody action; (c) NK cells = (ii) cytotoxic action; (d) CD4 = (i) marshals that direct the response. Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A): Culture encompasses lifestyles, values, practices and goals which provide distinct identities to people and community. Reason (R): Culture always acts as a constraint in the growth of a community. In the light of the above two statements, choose the correct option: 1 Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A) 2 Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A) 3 (A) is true, but (R) is false 4 (A) is false, but (R) is true ✓ Answer: (3) (A) is true, but (R) is false Cultural psychology: culture as a shared way of life The concept Assertion True. Culture is a shared design for living (values, beliefs, practices, goals) that gives a group its distinct identity . Reason False. Culture can limit some choices, but it also enables growth by passing on knowledge, skills and support; 'always a constraint' is wrong. Exam tip Absolute words such as always or never in a Reason often signal that it is false. Why the other options are wrong (1) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A) R is false, since culture also enables growth, and a false Reason cannot explain the Assertion. (2) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A) Needs R to be true; culture is not always a constraint, it also supports and enables a community's growth. (4) (A) is false, but (R) is true A is a standard definition of culture, so it is true; R is the false statement. Eleven rural, eleven semi-urban and eleven urban students were thoroughly interviewed and ranked (using a pooled sample of N = 33) for their communication skills. Which one of the following statistical techniques would be appropriate to explore the groupwise difference in communication? 1 Friedman's test 2 Kruskal-Wallis H test 3 Rank difference correlation 4 One-way ANOVA for independent samples ✓ Answer: (2) Kruskal-Wallis H test Kruskal-Wallis one-way analysis of variance by ranks The concept Why this one Three independent groups (rural, semi-urban, urban) with ranked (ordinal) data call for the Kruskal-Wallis H test , the non-parametric version of one-way ANOVA. How it works Rank all 33 students together, sum the ranks in each group, then H = [12 / N(N + 1)] × Σ(R 2 /n) - 3(N + 1), tested against chi-square with k - 1 = 2 df. Exam tip Two independent groups → Mann-Whitney U ; related samples → Wilcoxon (two) or Friedman (three or more). Old key This page used to show (3) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (1) Friedman's test For three or more related (repeated or matched) samples; these are three separate groups of students. (3) Rank difference correlation Spearman's rho measures the relationship between two sets of ranks, not differences between groups. (4) One-way ANOVA for independent samples Needs interval scores with roughly normal distributions; ranked data call for its non-parametric version, Kruskal-Wallis. Which of the following norms suggest to people how they ought to behave? 1 Social responsibility norms 2 Reciprocity norms 3 Prescriptive norms 4 Proscriptive norms ✓ Answer: (3) Prescriptive norms Social norms: prescriptive versus proscriptive The concept Why this one Prescriptive norms tell people what they ought to do (help a friend, say thank you). Contrast Proscriptive norms tell people what they ought not to do (do not steal). Together they make up a group's rules of conduct. Exam tip Descriptive norms describe what most people actually do; injunctive norms state what is approved or disapproved (Robert Cialdini). Old key This page used to show (1) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (1) Social responsibility norms A specific helping norm: help those who depend on us; it is one example of a rule, not the general class of 'ought' norms. (2) Reciprocity norms A specific norm (Alvin Gouldner) that we should help, and not harm, those who have helped us; it is one example, not the category. (4) Proscriptive norms These say what people should not do, forbidding behaviour rather than suggesting how one ought to behave. Which of the following are motivators for helping others? (a) Attitudes (b) Empathy (c) Personal distress (d) Norms and values Choose the correct option: 1 (a), (b) and (c) 2 (a), (b) and (d) 3 (a), (c) and (d) 4 (b), (c) and (d) ✓ Answer: (4) (b), (c) and (d) C. Daniel Batson, empathy versus personal distress The concept Why this one People help out of empathy (concern for the victim), personal distress (to relieve their own upset) and norms and values (social responsibility, reciprocity, moral values). Attitudes are not a standard helping motive. How it works C. Daniel Batson's empathy-altruism view: empathic concern gives an altruistic motive. Personal distress gives an egoistic motive: help to reduce one's own arousal, as in Jane Piliavin's arousal cost-reward model. Exam tip When escape is easy, distressed people often leave instead of helping; empathic people help anyway. Old key This page used to show (2) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. Which part of the neuron is covered by the Myelin sheath? 1 Whole of Axon 2 Parts of Axon 3 Whole of Dendrite 4 Parts of Dendrites ✓ Answer: (2) Parts of Axon Myelination by Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes The concept Why this one Myelin wraps the axon in segments, not end to end. Between the segments are bare gaps called nodes of Ranvier , and the axon hillock and terminal buttons are also uncovered. How it works Myelin is a fatty insulating layer made by Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system and oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system. The impulse jumps from node to node ( saltatory conduction ), which makes it much faster. Exam tip Myelin covers the axon only, and only in parts. Dendrites receive input and are not myelinated. Loss of myelin in the CNS causes multiple sclerosis . Old key This page used to show (3) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. (4) Parts of Dendrites No part of a dendrite carries myelin; myelin insulates axons only, to speed up the action potential. Which of the following are the main biases in the attribution process? (a) Fundamental attribution error (b) Actor-observer effect (c) Situational influence (d) Self-serving bias Choose the correct option: 1 (a), (b) and (c) 2 (a), (b) and (d) 3 (b), (c) and (d) 4 (a), (c) and (d) ✓ Answer: (2) (a), (b) and (d) Lee Ross; Edward Jones and Richard Nisbett The concept Why this one The three classic attribution biases are the fundamental attribution error, the actor-observer effect and the self-serving bias, so (a), (b) and (d) are right. Actor-observer effect (Edward Jones and Richard Nisbett): we blame the situation for our own acts but dispositions for others' acts. Which of the following are true as per Brentano's concept of Phenomenology? (a) Outer objects can be perceived only (b) Mental experiences can be perceived only (c) Feelings and willing be combined in one category (d) Outer objects can be both perceived and experienced Choose the best option: 1 (c) and (d) are correct 2 (a) and (c) are correct 3 (b), (c) and (d) are correct 4 (a) and (b) are correct ✓ Best answer: (3) (b), (c) and (d) are correct Franz Brentano, act psychology (1874) The concept Why this one Franz Brentano held that mental acts can only be perceived inwardly, never observed as objects, while outer (physical) objects can be both perceived and observed. He also merged feeling and willing into one class. So (b), (c) and (d). Act psychology In Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint (1874), Brentano said psychology studies mental acts , not contents. Every act is intentional : it is directed at an object (I see something, I judge something). Three classes He sorted acts into ideating (presenting), judging , and loving and hating ; the last class joins feeling and willing, which is why (c) is true. (2) (a) and (c) are correct Pairs (c) with (a), but Brentano did not limit outer objects to mere perception; unlike mental acts, they can also be observed. (4) (a) and (b) are correct Leaves out (c), the surest Brentano claim: he merged feeling and willing into a single class of loving and hating. The phenomenon where bystanders assume that nothing is wrong in an emergency because no one looks concerned is called: 1 Diffusion of responsibility 2 Pluralistic ignorance 3 Prosocial behaviour 4 Bystander effect ✓ Answer: (2) Pluralistic ignorance Bibb Latané and John Darley, bystander intervention The concept Why this one Pluralistic ignorance is when each bystander looks at the others, sees calm faces, and wrongly concludes there is no emergency. Everyone hides their own worry, so the whole group misreads the situation. Where it fits In Bibb Latané and John Darley 's model, a bystander must notice the event, interpret it as an emergency , take responsibility, decide how to help, and act. (3) Prosocial behaviour Any voluntary act that benefits others, such as helping; it is the outcome bystander research studies, not this error of interpretation. Match the following types of aggression with their description. List I: (a) Hostile Aggression; (b) Emotional Aggression; (c) Instrumental Aggression; (d) Thanatos List II: (i) An instinctual drive involving aggressive action towards death; (ii) Injury in which the goal is to obtain something of value; (iii) An act stemming from feelings of anger and aimed at inflicting pain; (iv) Injury or harm that is carried out for the explicit goal of hurting someone Choose the correct option from those given below: 1 (a)-(i), (b)-(ii), (c)-(iii), (d)-(iv) 2 (a)-(ii), (b)-(iii), (c)-(iv), (d)-(i) 3 (a)-(iii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(i), (d)-(ii) 4 (a)-(iii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(ii), (d)-(i) ✓ Answer: (4) (a)-(iii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(ii), (d)-(i) Types of aggression; Sigmund Freud's Thanatos The concept Correct pairs (a) Hostile aggression = (iii) act stemming from anger and aimed at inflicting pain; (b) Emotional aggression = (iv) harm carried out with the explicit goal of hurting someone; (c) Instrumental aggression = (ii) injury used to obtain something of value; (d) Thanatos = (i) instinctual drive towards death. In a newly developed adjustment inventory using a 'Yes/No' format, there were some positively worded items ('Yes' response indicating adjustment) and some negatively worded items ('No' response indicating adjustment). Test developers follow this practice to offset the effects of: 1 Acquiescence 2 Faking 3 Random responding 4 Socially desirable responding ✓ Answer: (1) Acquiescence Acquiescence response set; balanced keying The concept Why this one Acquiescence is the tendency to say 'Yes' or agree regardless of content. Mixing positively and negatively keyed items ( balanced keying ) means a yes-sayer gains on some items and loses on others, so the bias cancels out. What it is Acquiescence is a response set : a style of answering that distorts scores whatever the item content. It is common in Yes/No and agree/disagree formats. (3) Random responding Answering without reading the items; it is detected by infrequency or consistency scales, not offset by reversing item wording. Which of the following statements are correct? (a) Dilthey opposed reductionism (b) Dilthey opposed psychophysical parallelism (c) Dilthey rejected the positivistic approaches to experimental psychology (d) Dilthey rejected the idea of description Choose the correct option: 1 (a), (b) and (d) are correct 2 (a), (c) and (d) are correct 3 (b) and (c) are correct 4 (a), (b) and (c) are correct ✓ Answer: (4) (a), (b) and (c) are correct Wilhelm Dilthey, descriptive psychology (1894) The concept Why this one Wilhelm Dilthey opposed reducing mental life to elements or physiology (a), rejected the hypotheses of explanatory psychology such as psychophysical parallelism (b), and rejected positivist experimental psychology as the model for the human sciences (c). Why (d) is false Dilthey did not reject description; he called for a descriptive and analytic psychology that describes lived experience as a connected whole (1894). According to social impact theory, the effect of majority on minority rests on three of the following. (a) Majority's strength (b) Minority's will (c) Immediacy (d) Number of persons Choose the correct option: 1 (a) (b) (c) 2 (a) (c) (d) 3 (b) (c) (d) 4 (b) (d) (a) ✓ Answer: (2) (a) (c) (d) Bibb Latané, social impact theory (1981) The concept Why this one In Bibb Latané 's social impact theory , influence depends on the strength (status, power) of the source, its immediacy (closeness in space and time) and the number of people. In the light of the above two statements, choose the correct option: 1 Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A) 2 Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A) 3 (A) is true, but (R) is false 4 (A) is false, but (R) is true ✓ Best answer: (2) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A) Marvin Zuckerman, sensation seeking The concept Assertion True. (3) (A) is true, but (R) is false R is true: thrilling or frightening activity triggers sympathetic arousal and epinephrine release from the adrenal medulla. Match the following leadership styles with their characteristics. List 1: (a) Directive; (b) Supportive; (c) Participative; (d) Achievement oriented List 2: (i) Leader consults subordinates thereby permitting them to participate in decision making; (ii) Leader sets challenging goals and seeks improvement in performance; (iii) Leader provides specific guidance by establishing work schedules and rules; (iv) Leader establishes good relations with subordinates and satisfies their needs Choose the correct option from those given below: 1 (a)-(i), (b)-(ii), (c)-(iii), (d)-(iv) 2 (a)-(ii), (b)-(iii), (c)-(iv), (d)-(i) 3 (a)-(iii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(i), (d)-(ii) 4 (a)-(iv), (b)-(i), (c)-(ii), (d)-(iii) ✓ Answer: (3) (a)-(iii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(i), (d)-(ii) Robert House, path-goal theory of leadership (1971) The concept Correct pairs (a) Directive = (iii) specific guidance, schedules and rules; (b) Supportive = (iv) good relations and attention to needs; (c) Participative = (i) consults subordinates in decisions; (d) Achievement-oriented = (ii) sets challenging goals and seeks improvement. What it is In Robert House 's path-goal theory , the leader clears the path to goals and raises followers' belief that effort leads to rewards. The best style depends on the followers and the task. Exam tip Path-goal theory draws on Victor Vroom's expectancy theory . Directive suits ambiguous tasks; supportive suits stressful or boring tasks.
