Dr. X, as a therapist, felt a sense of complete understanding towards a father client whose children behaved exactly the way his own children used to behave. This is: 1 Empathy 2 Jumping to conclusion 3 Warmth and genuineness 4 Sympathy ✓ Best answer: (4) Sympathy Carl Rogers, empathy versus sympathy The concept Why this one Dr X's understanding comes from his own past, not from the client's frame of reference. Feeling with a client because 'I have been through the same' is sympathy , which shades into over-identification . Empathy Carl Rogers defined empathy as sensing the client's private world 'as if' it were your own, without losing the 'as if' quality. An empathic therapist never assumes complete understanding. Why it matters Sympathy can lead the therapist to project his own experience onto the client and miss what is unique in this father's situation. This links to countertransference . Not certain Many would read 'complete understanding' as empathy (1); but understanding drawn from the therapist's own matching life, not the client's frame of reference, is sympathy or over-identification. Why the other options are wrong (1) Empathy Understanding the client's world from the client's frame of reference while staying separate; claiming complete understanding through one's own experience goes beyond it. (2) Jumping to conclusion A cognitive error of judging on too little evidence; the item describes a felt emotional closeness, not a hasty inference. (3) Warmth and genuineness Warmth (unconditional positive regard) and genuineness (congruence) are Rogers' other core conditions; they concern acceptance and honesty, not a feeling of shared experience. Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A): MRI provides images of brain activity rather than brain images. Reason (R): Results in MRI are obtained from the measurement of waves that hydrogen atoms emit when they are activated by radio-frequency waves in a magnetic field. In the light of the above two statements, choose the correct option: 1 Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A) 2 Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A) 3 (A) is true, but (R) is false 4 (A) is false, but (R) is true ✓ Answer: (4) (A) is false, but (R) is true Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) versus fMRI The concept Assertion False. Standard MRI gives high-resolution pictures of brain structure . Images of brain activity come from fMRI (or PET). Reason True. In MRI a strong magnetic field lines up hydrogen atoms ; a radio-frequency pulse knocks them out of line, and the waves they give off as they realign are measured to build the image. Exam tip Structure: CT, MRI. Activity: PET, fMRI (the BOLD signal , based on oxygenated blood flow), EEG. Why the other options are wrong (1) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A) A is false: plain MRI shows brain structure; it is functional MRI that tracks activity through changes in blood oxygen. (2) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A) A is false, so this cannot be right: structural MRI images anatomy, not activity. (3) (A) is true, but (R) is false The reverse is true: A is false (MRI shows structure) and R is true (hydrogen atoms emit the measured waves). Read the following paragraph and answer questions 91 to 95. The experimental psychologist wanted to explore whether noise adversely affects reaction time (RT). She also wanted to explore whether the stress level would moderate the effect of noise. She varied noise at three levels: low (30 decibels), moderate (60 decibels) and high (90 decibels). She varied stress at two levels: low and high. From the initial pool of college students, subjects were randomly assigned to different groups. However, a few subjects could not turn up to the laboratory due to vacation. In all, two hundred and ninety-seven subjects participated in the experiment. Each subject, in each group, was tested for simple RT, disjunctive RT, and choice RT. The theory and preliminary analyses indicated the three types of RT were moderately correlated. The covariance matrices, showing the covariances among the three types of RT, were found to be quite similar for all the groups. The multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) results were computed to explore the group differences in means. As the most common practice is, four test criteria (Pillai's criterion, Wilks' criterion, Hotelling's criterion, and Roy's criterion) were obtained. Among the different results obtained in this work, one interesting finding was that stress moderated the effect of noise level on reaction time. Q.91 Which of the following test criteria is more appropriate than the others? 1 Roy's criterion 2 Wilks' criterion 3 Hotelling's criterion 4 Pillai's criterion ✓ Best answer: (4) Pillai's criterion Pillai's trace, robust MANOVA criterion The concept Why this one Dropouts left 297 subjects in 6 cells, and 297 ÷ 6 = 49.5, so the cell sizes are unequal . Pillai's criterion (Pillai's trace) is the most robust of the four to unequal n and assumption violations, so it is the safest choice. The four criteria All four test whether group centroids differ on the combined DVs. With 1 df (stress, 2 levels) they give the same F; noise and the interaction have 2 df, so the four can differ. When to use which Wilks' lambda : the usual default. Roy's largest root : most powerful when groups differ on one dimension, least robust. Pillai's trace: advised by Barbara Tabachnick and Linda Fidell when cells are unequal, samples small or homogeneity doubtful. Not certain Wilks' criterion (2) is the most widely reported default and is fine once covariance matrices are homogeneous; Pillai's is preferred here only because the dropouts make the cells unequal. Old key This page used to show (2) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (1) Roy's criterion Roy's largest root uses only the first discriminant dimension; powerful when groups differ on one dimension but the least robust, so a poor choice with unequal cells. (2) Wilks' criterion Wilks' lambda is the most commonly reported criterion, but it is less robust than Pillai's trace when cell sizes are unequal, as here after the dropouts. (3) Hotelling's criterion Hotelling's trace (Hotelling-Lawley) behaves much like Wilks' lambda and is less robust than Pillai's trace to unequal cell sizes. The design employed in the above study can best be labelled as: 1 Randomized six group design with a single factor 2 Balanced factorial design 3 Unbalanced factorial design 4 Unbalanced factorial design with a covariate ✓ Answer: (3) Unbalanced factorial design Factorial design with unequal cell sizes The concept Why this one Two IVs are crossed, noise (3 levels) × stress (2 levels), giving a 3 × 2 factorial design with 6 cells. With 297 subjects, 297 ÷ 6 = 49.5, so the cells cannot be equal: the design is unbalanced . Balanced vs unbalanced Balanced means every cell has the same n. Dropouts (here, students away on vacation) make cell sizes unequal, which complicates the sums of squares and calls for robust tests. Why no covariate A covariate is a variable measured before treatment and statistically controlled (ANCOVA). The three RT measures are dependent variables, not covariates. Old key This page used to show (2) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (1) Randomized six group design with a single factor There are six groups, but they come from two crossed factors (noise and stress), so it is factorial; a single-factor design could not test the noise × stress interaction. (2) Balanced factorial design Balanced needs equal n in every cell; 297 subjects cannot be split equally into 6 cells (49.5 each), and dropouts are reported. (4) Unbalanced factorial design with a covariate No covariate was measured or controlled; simple, disjunctive and choice RT are the dependent variables analysed by MANOVA. Which one of the following conclusions can be confidently drawn from the above study? 1 Main effect of noise is significant 2 Main effect of stress is significant 3 Noise × Stress interaction is significant 4 The main effects of noise, stress and interaction effect are significant ✓ Answer: (3) Noise × Stress interaction is significant Interaction (moderation) in a factorial design The concept Why this one The passage says stress moderated the effect of noise on RT. Moderation means the effect of one IV changes across levels of another, which is a significant noise × stress interaction . What it is A main effect is the overall effect of one factor averaged over the other; an interaction exists when the lines for one factor are not parallel across levels of the other. Exam tip A significant interaction says nothing about whether the main effects are significant. The passage reports only the interaction, so that is all we can conclude. Why the other options are wrong (1) Main effect of noise is significant The passage never reports the main effect of noise; with a significant interaction the main effect may or may not be significant, and would need qualifying. (2) Main effect of stress is significant No result for the main effect of stress is given; stress is said only to moderate the noise effect, which is an interaction. (4) The main effects of noise, stress and interaction effect are significant Only the interaction is reported; claiming all three effects are significant goes beyond the evidence in the passage. The above information suggests that: 1 the assumption of homogeneity of covariance matrices is not satisfied 2 the assumption of homogeneity of covariance matrices is satisfied 3 covariances among Dependent Variables (DV) are zero 4 the assumption of homogeneity of variances is not tenable ✓ Answer: (2) the assumption of homogeneity of covariance matrices is satisfied Homogeneity of covariance matrices (Box's M test) The concept Why this one The passage says the covariance matrices of the three RTs were quite similar for all the groups . That is exactly the MANOVA assumption of homogeneity of covariance matrices , so it is satisfied. What it is It is the multivariate version of ANOVA's equal-variance assumption: each group should have the same variance on each DV and the same covariances between DVs. It is usually checked with Box's M test . Exam tip Box's M is very sensitive in large samples, so a strict level such as .001 is often used. If it is violated and cells are unequal, report Pillai's criterion . Old key This page used to show (1) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (1) the assumption of homogeneity of covariance matrices is not satisfied The opposite: covariance matrices that are quite similar across groups mean the homogeneity assumption holds, not fails. (3) covariances among Dependent Variables (DV) are zero The three RTs were moderately correlated, so their covariances are clearly not zero. (4) the assumption of homogeneity of variances is not tenable Similar covariance matrices also have similar variances on their diagonals, so equal variances are tenable too. Which one of the following reasons best justifies the application of MANOVA in the present work? 1 There are several groups and more than one Independent Variable (IV) 2 More than one Dependent Variable (DV) has been employed 3 More than one Dependent Variable with moderate intercorrelations has been employed 4 The moderating effect of stress on the effect of noise on RT can be demonstrated only through MANOVA ✓ Answer: (3) More than one Dependent Variable with moderate intercorrelations has been employed Rationale for MANOVA: moderately correlated DVs The concept Why this one MANOVA is best justified when there are several DVs that are moderately correlated , as the three RTs are here. It tests group differences on their combined pattern and controls the Type I error of many separate ANOVAs. Why moderate If the DVs are uncorrelated , separate ANOVAs do the job. If they are very highly correlated, they are redundant ( multicollinearity ) and MANOVA loses power. Exam tip Number of IVs decides whether a design is factorial ; number of DVs decides whether the analysis is multivariate . ANOVA: one DV. MANOVA: two or more DVs. Old key This page used to show (4) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (1) There are several groups and more than one Independent Variable (IV) Several groups and more than one IV justify a factorial design, which a factorial ANOVA handles with a single DV. (2) More than one Dependent Variable (DV) has been employed More than one DV is needed but not enough: uncorrelated DVs could be analysed by separate ANOVAs, so the moderate correlation is the real reason. (4) The moderating effect of stress on the effect of noise on RT can be demonstrated only through MANOVA Moderation is the interaction term and can be tested by a factorial ANOVA on each DV; MANOVA is not the only way. Read the following paragraph and answer questions 96 to 100. A leading business school in the city had a view that its students must attain total proficiency in English language usage. As an initial step, the school authorities decided to develop a brief language usage test. The project incharge wrote 30 items. Each item had five alternative answers, one of which was correct. He administered these 30 items to a sample of 250 students. For item analysis, item-remainder correlations were computed. The item analysis retained 25 items. The twenty-five item version was administered to a fresh sample of 300 students. Three reliability coefficients were computed: split-half reliability coefficient, Kuder-Richardson (K-R) reliability coefficient, and Cronbach alpha. The Cronbach alpha was found to be 0.7. The test-retest reliability was also computed with a time-interval of eight weeks in two administrations, using the same sample. The test-retest correlation was found to be 0.26, significant at the .001 level. The school authorities, pleased with the efforts of the project incharge, asked him to add similar items and develop a 75-item version. Q.96 The above information provides evidence for: (a) Unsatisfactory test-retest reliability (b) Satisfactory test-retest reliability (c) Acceptable internal consistency reliability (d) Unacceptable internal consistency reliability Choose the correct option: 1 (a) and (c) 2 (a) and (d) 3 (b) and (c) 4 (b) and (d) ✓ Answer: (1) (a) and (c) Reliability benchmarks (Jum Nunnally's 0.70 rule) The concept Why this one A test-retest r of 0.26 is far too low, so (a). Cronbach's α of 0.70 meets the usual minimum for a new test, so (c). Hence (a) and (c). Working Shared variance = r² = 0.26² ≈ 0.07, so only about 7% of score variance is stable over eight weeks. Significance at .001 comes from the large N: t = 0.26 × √298 ÷ √(1 - 0.0676) ≈ 4.6, which only shows r is not zero. Benchmarks Statistical significance is not adequacy. A reliability of about 0.70 is acceptable for early research ( Jum Nunnally ), while good ability tests usually show test-retest coefficients of 0.80 or more. Old key This page used to show (3) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (2) (a) and (d) (a) is right, but α = 0.70 is at the accepted minimum for a new test, so internal consistency is acceptable, not unacceptable. (3) (b) and (c) r = 0.26 explains only about 7% of variance; its significance reflects the large sample of 300, not satisfactory stability. (4) (b) and (d) Both parts are reversed: test-retest r = 0.26 is unsatisfactory, and α = 0.70 is acceptable. Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A): The computation of K-R reliability is questionable in the above study. Reason (R): K-R reliability is suitable for tests with dichotomous items. In the light of the above two statements, choose the correct option: 1 Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A) 2 Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A) 3 (A) is true, but (R) is false 4 (A) is false, but (R) is true ✓ Answer: (4) (A) is false, but (R) is true G. Frederic Kuder and Marion Richardson (1937), KR-20 The concept Assertion False. Each item has five options but only one is correct, so it is scored right = 1, wrong = 0 . Every item is therefore dichotomous , and K-R is exactly the right formula. Reason True. KR-20 (and KR-21) were built for items scored 0/1: KR-20 = (k ÷ (k - 1)) × (1 - Σpq ÷ s X ²), where pq is each item's variance. Exam tip The number of answer options does not decide this; the scoring does. Rating-scale or partial-credit items need Cronbach's alpha instead. Old key This page used to show (2) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (1) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A) A is false: five-option items scored right or wrong are dichotomous, so using K-R here is fully appropriate. (2) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A) A is false: the number of answer choices does not matter; scoring each item as correct (1) or incorrect (0) makes it dichotomous. (3) (A) is true, but (R) is false The reverse: R is true (K-R suits dichotomously scored items) and A is false. If the project incharge developed a 75-item version by adding similar items, what would be the expected Cronbach alpha? 1 0.700 2 0.824 3 0.875 4 0.931 ✓ Answer: (3) 0.875 Spearman-Brown prophecy formula The concept Why this one Going from 25 to 75 similar items lengthens the test by a factor of n = 75 ÷ 25 = 3 . The Spearman-Brown prophecy formula predicts the new reliability. Working r new = nr ÷ (1 + (n - 1)r) = (3 × 0.7) ÷ (1 + 2 × 0.7) = 2.1 ÷ 2.4 = 0.875 . Exam tip Longer tests are more reliable, with diminishing returns , as long as the added items are parallel. Halving the test (n = 0.5) would drop 0.7 to 0.35 ÷ 0.65 ≈ 0.54. Why the other options are wrong (1) 0.700 Leaves α unchanged; adding parallel items raises reliability, so tripling the length must push it above 0.70. (2) 0.824 This is what doubling gives: (2 × 0.7) ÷ (1 + 0.7) = 1.4 ÷ 1.7 ≈ 0.824. The test is tripled, not doubled. (4) 0.931 Overshoots: reaching 0.931 would need a test nearly six times as long (about 145 items); tripling gives 2.1 ÷ 2.4 = 0.875. Which one of the following correlations is most suitable for computing item-remainder correlations? 1 Tetrachoric Correlations 2 Phi Coefficient 3 Contingency Coefficient 4 Point biserial Correlation ✓ Answer: (4) Point biserial Correlation Point-biserial correlation in item analysis The concept Why this one An item-remainder correlation relates each item, scored 0/1 (a true dichotomy: right or wrong), with the total of the remaining items, a continuous score. Dichotomous with continuous → point-biserial r . Formula r pb = ((M p - M q ) ÷ s t ) × √(pq), where M p and M q are the mean remainder scores of those who passed and failed the item. Why 'remainder' The item is removed from the total first, so it is not correlated with itself. This stops the item-total correlation from being inflated, which matters most in short tests. Old key This page used to show (3) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (1) Tetrachoric Correlations Tetrachoric r is for two variables both artificially dichotomised from underlying normal continua; the remainder score here is continuous. (2) Phi Coefficient Phi is for two true dichotomies, such as pass/fail on two items; it suits item-item, not item-remainder, correlation. (3) Contingency Coefficient The contingency coefficient C is for two categorical variables in a chi-square table; it does not fit a continuous remainder score. Consider the three reliability coefficients computed in the above study: (a) split-half reliability coefficient; (b) K-R reliability coefficient; and (c) Cronbach alpha. Which one of the following is true in the above context? 1 All the three reliability coefficients would be the same 2 All the three reliability coefficients would be different 3 (b) and (c) would be the same, but (a) can be different 4 (a) and (b) would be the same, but (b) can be different ✓ Answer: (3) (b) and (c) would be the same, but (a) can be different Lee Cronbach (1951): alpha equals KR-20 for 0/1 items The concept Why this one For items scored 0/1, each item's variance is pq , so Cronbach's α reduces exactly to KR-20 ; both equal 0.70 here. A split-half coefficient depends on how the test is split, so it can differ. Working α = (k ÷ (k - 1)) × (1 - Σs i ² ÷ s X ²). Put s i ² = p i q i for dichotomous items and you get KR-20: (k ÷ (k - 1)) × (1 - Σpq ÷ s X ²). Split-half Split-half correlates two halves (e.g. odd vs even items) and steps it up with Spearman-Brown. Lee Cronbach showed α is the mean of all possible split-half coefficients, so any single split may be higher or lower. Exam tip KR-20 = α for dichotomous items. KR-21 assumes all items are equally difficult and gives a value equal to or lower than KR-20. Old key This page used to show (1) here, from a key that does not line up with this paper. See below for why it is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (1) All the three reliability coefficients would be the same Split-half reliability depends on the particular split and can differ; only KR-20 and α are mathematically identical for 0/1 items. (2) All the three reliability coefficients would be different K-R (KR-20) and Cronbach's α cannot differ here: with dichotomous items α reduces exactly to KR-20. (4) (a) and (b) would be the same, but (b) can be different Garbled and wrong: the split-half coefficient is the one that can differ, while K-R and α must be equal for 0/1 items. 4. No official answer key was ever found for it, so every answer below is worked out from the standard textbooks and checked against a second, separate solve. Trap These answers are worked out, not an official key. Mr A approached the therapist for anger management. After Mr A narrated an incident in which he experienced anger, which of the following is the most appropriate way of further questioning at the initial level? 1 Could you please tell me why did you get angry? 2 Could you please explain what made you angry? 3 Please help me understand whom did you get angry at 4 Please explain how did you feel when you were angry ✓ Best answer: (2) Could you please explain what made you angry? Counselling skills: open, non-judgemental questioning The concept Why this one What made you angry is an open, non-blaming question about the trigger of the anger, the first thing anger work needs to map. How it works Anger management (for example Raymond Novaco's stress inoculation approach) starts by finding the provoking situations , then the thoughts, body signals and actions that follow. Exam tip Skilled interviewers avoid why questions early on: they sound accusing and invite excuses or intellectualising. Not certain Exploring feelings first, option (4), is also defensible in a client-centred frame, but anger is already the named feeling, so the trigger question comes first. Why the other options are wrong (1) Could you please tell me why did you get angry? A why question; it sounds like an accusation, makes the client defensive and invites justifications rather than a description of the trigger. (3) Please help me understand whom did you get angry at A narrow question about the target person only; it misses the situation, thoughts and events that sparked the anger. (4) Please explain how did you feel when you were angry Asks about the feeling, but the client has already said it was anger; feelings work usually follows once the trigger is clear. Which of the following are true for bootstrapping? (a) It involves a large number of sub-samples. (b) It does not rely on assumptions about the population. (c) It is applicable in case of nonmetric data only. (d) It is based on sample data only. Select the correct option 1 Only (a) and (b) 2 Only (a), (b) and (c) 3 Only (a), (b) and (d) 4 Only (b), (c) and (d) ✓ Answer: (3) Only (a), (b) and (d) Bradley Efron, bootstrap resampling The concept Why this one Statements (a), (b) and (d) are true. The bootstrap draws thousands of resamples with replacement from the one observed sample to estimate a statistic's sampling distribution. How it works The sample stands in for the population, so no assumption such as normality is needed; the spread of the resampled statistics gives the standard error and confidence interval. Why (c) is false It works with any data, including metric (interval and ratio) data such as means, correlations and regression weights. Why the other options are wrong (1) Only (a) and (b) Misses (d): the bootstrap is built only from the observed sample data, with no outside population values, so (d) is also true. (2) Only (a), (b) and (c) Includes (c), which is false, since bootstrapping is widely used with metric data; it also leaves out the true (d). (4) Only (b), (c) and (d) Drops the true (a), the many resamples that define the method, and adds the false (c). In Torrance Test of Creative Thinking (figural), picture construction activity is scored for which of the following? (a) Fluency (b) Flexibility (c) Originality (d) Elaboration Select the correct option 1 Only (a) and (b) 2 Only (c) and (d) 3 Only (b), (c) and (d) 4 (a), (b), (c) and (d) ✓ Answer: (2) Only (c) and (d) E. Paul Torrance, TTCT Figural scoring The concept Why this one In picture construction the child makes only one picture from a given shape, so there is nothing to count for fluency or flexibility; it is scored for originality and elaboration . Test layout E. Paul Torrance's figural test has three activities: picture construction, picture completion and lines or circles . The last two give many responses, so fluency can also be scored there. Exam tip Fluency = number of ideas; flexibility = number of categories; originality = statistical rarity; elaboration = amount of added detail. Why the other options are wrong (1) Only (a) and (b) Fluency and flexibility need many responses to count, but picture construction yields a single drawing, so neither is scored there. (3) Only (b), (c) and (d) Flexibility counts the categories across many responses; with only one picture it cannot be scored in this activity. (4) (a), (b), (c) and (d) All four are scored across the figural test as a whole, but not in the single-picture construction activity. Arrange the following in correct sequence of development of emotional expressions: (a) Self-conscious emotions emerge but depend on monitoring and encouragement of adults (b) Expression of happiness increases while interacting with familiar people (c) Anger and happiness increase in frequency and intensity (d) Self-conscious emotions are clearly linked to self-evaluation Select the correct option: 1 (b) (a) (c) (d) 2 (b) (c) (a) (d) 3 (b) (c) (d) (a) 4 (c) (b) (a) (d) ✓ Answer: (2) (b) (c) (a) (d) Laura Berk, milestones of emotional development The concept Correct order (b) first 6 months: happiness is expressed more with familiar people → (c) 7 to 12 months: anger (and fear) rise in frequency and intensity → (a) 18 months to 2 years: self-conscious emotions appear but depend on adult monitoring → (d) early childhood: they become tied to self-evaluation . Why this order Basic emotions come first. Self-conscious emotions (shame, guilt, pride, embarrassment) need a sense of self , which appears in the second year; judging oneself by inner standards comes later. Exam tip Self-conscious emotions are first guided by adults' reactions , then by the child's own standards. Why the other options are wrong (1) (b) (a) (c) (d) Puts adult-dependent self-conscious emotions (a) before the rise in anger (c), but anger intensifies late in the first year, well before self-conscious emotions appear. (3) (b) (c) (d) (a) Places self-evaluation (d) before the adult-dependent stage (a); children first rely on adults' reactions and only later judge themselves by their own standards. (4) (c) (b) (a) (d) Starts with rising anger (c), but greater happiness with familiar people (b) appears earlier, in the first six months along with the social smile. Limbic system, basal ganglia and corpus striatum are parts of which section of the brain? 1 Midbrain 2 Hindbrain 3 Telencephalon 4 Diencephalon ✓ Answer: (3) Telencephalon Divisions of the brain: telencephalon The concept Why this one The telencephalon is the largest part of the forebrain. It contains the cerebral cortex, the limbic system and the basal ganglia , whose main part is the corpus striatum. Brain divisions Forebrain = telencephalon + diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus). Midbrain = mesencephalon (tectum, tegmentum). Hindbrain = metencephalon (pons, cerebellum) + myelencephalon (medulla). Exam tip Limbic system and basal ganglia → telencephalon; thalamus and hypothalamus → diencephalon . Why the other options are wrong (1) Midbrain The midbrain (mesencephalon) holds the tectum (superior and inferior colliculi) and the tegmentum with the substantia nigra, not the limbic system or striatum. (2) Hindbrain The hindbrain holds the medulla, pons and cerebellum, which control vital functions, posture and balance. (4) Diencephalon The diencephalon is the thalamus and hypothalamus, the other half of the forebrain; the basal ganglia do not sit there. Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements. Assertion (A): Focus group involves an unstructured interview. Reason (R): Focus group involves interaction among participants moderated by the researcher, as a source of data. Choose the correct answer from the options given below: 1 Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A) 2 Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A) 3 (A) is true but (R) is false 4 (A) is false but (R) is true ✓ Best answer: (1) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A) Focus group method (moderated group interview) The concept Assertion True. A focus group is an unstructured interview with a small group (often 6 to 10 people), run by a moderator in a natural, conversational way. Reason True. The data come from the group interaction : people react to, build on and challenge each other, with the researcher acting as moderator. Link R explains A: because the interaction itself is the data, the moderator keeps the format open instead of working through a fixed list of questions. Not certain Many methods texts call focus groups semi-structured because the moderator uses a topic guide, which would make A doubtful and favour (4). Why the other options are wrong (2) Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A) R is not a side fact; the reliance on free participant interaction is exactly why the focus group interview is left unstructured. (3) (A) is true but (R) is false R is true: interaction among participants, guided by a moderator, is the defining source of focus group data. (4) (A) is false but (R) is true A is true in the usual definition: the focus group is a nonstructured, natural group interview, not a fixed questionnaire. Psychometric tests of creativity like the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking measure creativity in terms of: 1 Person 2 Product 3 Process 4 Persuasion ✓ Best answer: (3) Process E. Paul Torrance; Mel Rhodes' four Ps of creativity The concept Why this one Divergent-thinking tests such as the TTCT treat creativity as a thinking process : E. Paul Torrance defined it as sensing problems or gaps, forming and testing ideas, and communicating the results. The four Ps Mel Rhodes sorted creativity into person (traits), process (thinking), product (outputs) and press (environment). Psychometric divergent-thinking tests fall under process. Exam tip Fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration are indices of the divergent-thinking process, scored from the responses. Not certain Because TTCT scores are counted from the responses produced, some texts describe it as a product measure, which would make (2) the answer. Which one of the following is the correct answer for the experiment conducted at the University of California at Santa Barbara, in which individuals running on a jogging path speeded up as they came upon a woman seated on the grass facing them rather than sitting with her back turned? 1 Distraction conflict 2 Presence of co-actor 3 Evaluation apprehension 4 Free riders ✓ Answer: (3) Evaluation apprehension Charles Worringham and David Messick, jogging-path study The concept Why this one Joggers sped up only when the woman faced them and could watch them, not when her back was turned; her presence was the same, so the boost came from concern about being evaluated . What it is Evaluation apprehension (Nickolas Cottrell) holds that others arouse us because we worry about how they will judge us, and this arousal strengthens dominant, well-learned responses such as running. Exam tip Robert Zajonc = mere presence arousal; Cottrell = evaluation apprehension ; Robert Baron = distraction-conflict . Why the other options are wrong (1) Distraction conflict Robert Baron's distraction-conflict theory says an audience splits attention between task and observers; it does not explain why facing versus turning away made the difference. (2) Presence of co-actor Means someone doing the same task alongside you, as in Norman Triplett's racing cyclists; the woman was sitting on the grass, not jogging. (4) Free riders Group members who slack off and benefit from others' effort, a feature of social loafing when individual output cannot be identified. Which one of the following is NOT a characteristic of attention? 1 Processing capacity and selectiveness 2 Automatic processing 3 Initial detection of stimuli 4 Control ✓ Answer: (3) Initial detection of stimuli Features of attention: capacity, selectivity, control, automaticity The concept Why this one Initial detection of stimuli is the job of sensation , the receptors registering energy from the world; attention works on that input afterwards by selecting what gets further processing. Exam tip Sensation = detecting; perception = interpreting; attention = selecting and focusing limited mental resources. Why the other options are not the answer (1) Processing capacity and selectiveness Fits: attention is a limited-capacity resource, so it must select some inputs and ignore others, as Donald Broadbent's filter model proposed. (2) Automatic processing Fits: practised tasks run with little attentional effort; Walter Schneider and Richard Shiffrin contrasted such automatic processing with effortful controlled processing. (4) Control Fits: attention can be directed voluntarily (top-down) or captured by salient stimuli (bottom-up), so control of attention is a core feature. What is the theoretical approach called which attempts to explain completely the phenomenon of one field of study in terms of the dynamics of a more basic field? 1 Interactionism 2 Reductionism 3 Pragmatism 4 Compliant solution ✓ Answer: (2) Reductionism Reductionism, philosophy of science The concept Why this one Reductionism explains a phenomenon completely in terms of a more basic field, for example explaining depression entirely by neurotransmitters, or behaviour entirely by physiology. How it works Psychology is reduced to biology, biology to chemistry, chemistry to physics; critics reply that whole systems show emergent properties their parts lack, the Gestalt point that the whole differs from the sum of its parts. Why the other options are wrong (1) Interactionism Holds that two factors, such as mind and body or person and situation, influence each other; it does not reduce one field to another. (3) Pragmatism The philosophy of William James and John Dewey that judges ideas by their practical consequences and usefulness. (4) Compliant solution Karen Horney's compliant (self-effacing) solution is a neurotic trend of moving toward people to win love and approval; it is not a theory of explanation. According to Adler, which of the following is used by the neurotic to escape from problems? 1 Depreciation 2 Self-accusation 3 Distancing 4 Safeguarding strategies ✓ Best answer: (3) Distancing Alfred Adler, safeguarding through distance The concept Why this one Alfred Adler said neurotics escape life's tasks (work, love, friendship) by keeping a distance from them. He called this withdrawal , or safeguarding through distance. Four forms Moving backward (retreating to a safer, younger way of living), standing still (not moving at all), hesitating (putting things off) and constructing obstacles (a small barrier to blame). The bigger picture Distancing is one of three safeguarding tendencies that protect a fragile self-esteem: excuses ('Yes, but'), aggression (depreciation, accusation, self-accusation) and withdrawal. Not certain Some keys may pick (4), the umbrella term, since all three kinds are safeguarding strategies; but the one that is itself an escape from problems is distancing. (2) Self-accusation Using guilt and self-torment to hurt the people close to you; another aggressive safeguarding tendency, not a way of escaping. (4) Safeguarding strategies The umbrella term for all three kinds (excuses, aggression, withdrawal); they protect self-esteem, and the one that escapes problems is distancing. Which among the following are the assumptions on which Binet developed his first test of intelligence? (a) Mental competence increases over the childhood years (b) A child's relative standing in mental development compared to his age group will remain constant as the child grows. (4) (b) and (d) only Statement (d) contradicts the age-scale idea: Binet's items are graded precisely because competence increases, not decreases, across childhood. On a Wechsler-type Adult Intelligence Scale, having normally distributed scores, a subject had a percentile rank of 84. His deviation IQ would be: 1 84 2 85 3 115 4 120 ✓ Answer: (3) 115 David Wechsler's deviation IQ, mean 100, SD 15 The concept Why this one On a normal curve about 84% of scores fall below +1 SD (50% below the mean plus 34% between the mean and +1 SD). Wechsler scales use mean 100 and SD 15 , so IQ = 100 + 15 = 115 . Working z = (IQ - 100) / 15. Percentile 84 gives z = +1, so IQ = 100 + (1 × 15) = 115. Exam tip Percentiles 16, 50, 84 and 98 match Wechsler IQs of about 85, 100, 115 and 130 . (2) 85 That IQ is 1 SD below the mean, which corresponds to the 16th percentile, not the 84th. (4) 120 That IQ is about 1.33 SD above the mean, roughly the 91st percentile. First make a small request; when the person complies, make another large request. This concept is based on which compliance technique? 1 Foot-in-the-door 2 Door-in-the-face 3 Lowball 4 That's-not-all ✓ Answer: (1) Foot-in-the-door Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser, foot-in-the-door The concept Why this one The foot-in-the-door technique starts with a small request; once the person agrees, a larger related request is more likely to be accepted. When acetylcholine links up on the post-synaptic side, it generates a depolarisation. What do you call it? 1 Inhibitory Post-synaptic Potential 2 Excitatory Post-synaptic Potential 3 End plate potential 4 End plate potential and Inhibitory Post-synaptic Potential ✓ Best answer: (3) End plate potential End plate potential at the neuromuscular junction The concept Why this one When acetylcholine from a motor neuron binds nicotinic receptors on the muscle's motor end plate, the resulting depolarisation is called the end plate potential (EPP). Exam tip EPP = depolarisation at a muscle fibre; EPSP = small graded depolarisation at a neuron; IPSP = hyperpolarisation. (4) End plate potential and Inhibitory Post-synaptic Potential Pairs a depolarisation with an IPSP, which is a hyperpolarisation; one event cannot be both. The interaction of sensory impulses indicates the complexity of stimulation and therefore the difficulties in predicting behaviour. Behaviour is seldom a function of only one stimulus; rather it is a function of many stimuli. The above explanation is based on which learning theory? 1 Guthrie's theory 2 Pavlov's theory 3 Hull's theory 4 Tolman's theory ✓ Answer: (3) Hull's theory Clark Hull, afferent neural interaction postulate The concept Why this one The passage is Clark Hull's postulate on the interaction of sensory impulses (afferent neural interaction): stimuli arriving together modify one another, so behaviour reflects a pattern of many stimuli. Why the other options are wrong (1) Guthrie's theory Contiguity theory: a stimulus pattern present during a movement will, on recurrence, produce that movement, learned in one trial; Edwin Guthrie set out no such postulate. (4) Tolman's theory Purposive behaviourism: learning through expectancies and cognitive maps, as Edward Tolman argued, not through interacting sensory impulses. Match List-I with List-II: List-I (Concept): (a) Big-C creativity; (b) Little-C creativity; (c) Mini-C creativity; (d) Pro-C creativity List-II (Description): (i) Creativity of eminence; (ii) Creativity of everyday life recognised by others; (iii) Subjective and personal form of day-to-day creativity; (iv) Professional creativity which has not attained the status of eminence Select the correct option: 1 (a)-(i); (b)-(ii); (c)-(iii); (d)-(iv) 2 (a)-(ii); (b)-(i); (c)-(iv); (d)-(iii) 3 (a)-(iii); (b)-(iv); (c)-(i); (d)-(ii) 4 (a)-(iv); (b)-(iii); (c)-(ii); (d)-(i) ✓ Answer: (1) (a)-(i); (b)-(ii); (c)-(iii); (d)-(iv) James Kaufman and Ronald Beghetto, Four C model of creativity The concept Correct pairs (a) Big-C = (i) creativity of eminence; (b) Little-c = (ii) everyday creativity recognised by others; (c) Mini-c = (iii) subjective, personal creativity; (d) Pro-c = (iv) professional creativity not yet eminent. Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements.
