Which of the following is useful for testing univariate normality of distribution? (A) Q-Q plot (B) Shapiro-Wilk test (C) Jarque-Bera test (D) Scatter plot 1 A and B only 2 B and D only 3 A, B and D only 4 A, B and C only ✓ Answer: (4) A, B and C only Tests of univariate normality The concept Why this one A Q-Q plot , the Shapiro-Wilk test and the Jarque-Bera test all check whether a single variable follows a normal distribution. A scatter plot needs two variables, so it cannot test univariate normality. How each works A Q-Q plot puts the data's quantiles against normal quantiles, and points on a straight line mean normality; Shapiro-Wilk compares ordered scores with expected normal scores, and Jarque-Bera tests whether skewness and kurtosis match a normal curve. Exam tip A significant Shapiro-Wilk or Jarque-Bera result (p below .05) means the data depart from normality. Scatter plots are used to check linearity and homoscedasticity between two variables. Why the other options are wrong (1) A and B only Q-Q plot and Shapiro-Wilk are correct, but the list is incomplete: the Jarque-Bera test also tests univariate normality from skewness and kurtosis. (2) B and D only Shapiro-Wilk fits, but a scatter plot shows the relationship between two variables, and the Q-Q plot and Jarque-Bera test are left out. (3) A, B and D only Wrongly includes the scatter plot , a bivariate graph for linearity, and leaves out the Jarque-Bera test, which checks skewness and kurtosis against the normal curve. Which is the correct sequence of speech and language development according to Vygotsky? (A) Naive (B) Primitive (C) Egocentric (D) Ingrowth 1 A, B, C, D 2 B, A, C, D 3 A, B, D, C 4 B, A, D, C ✓ Answer: (2) B, A, C, D Lev Vygotsky, Thought and Language (1934) The concept Why this one Lev Vygotsky described four stages of speech: primitive (natural), naive psychology, egocentric speech and ingrowth. That is B, A, C, D. Correct order (B) Primitive: crying, babbling and other pre-intellectual sounds; (A) Naive: words used correctly before their logic is grasped; (C) Egocentric: talking aloud to guide one's own actions; (D) Ingrowth: speech goes inward as silent inner speech . Exam tip For Vygotsky, egocentric speech does not simply die out, as Jean Piaget thought; it turns into inner speech that guides thinking. Why the other options are wrong (1) A, B, C, D Puts naive psychology before the primitive stage, but the primitive (natural) stage of crying and babbling is the starting point in Vygotsky's scheme. (3) A, B, D, C Starts with naive instead of primitive and puts ingrowth before egocentric speech, when inner speech grows out of egocentric speech. (4) B, A, D, C Gets the first two stages right but reverses the last two: egocentric speech comes first and only later turns inward as ingrowth (inner speech). Match List I with List II. List I (Types of Reliability): (A) Test-retest (B) Alternate Form (delayed) (C) Coefficient alpha (D) Cohen's Kappa. List II (Source of Error Variance): (I) Content heterogeneity (II) Inter-scorer differences (III) Time sampling (IV) Content sampling and time sampling. Choose the correct answer from the options given below: 1 A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III 2 A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-III 3 A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II 4 A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I ✓ Answer: (3) A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II Anne Anastasi, sources of error variance in reliability The concept Why this one Each reliability method picks up a different source of error : test-retest catches time sampling , delayed alternate forms catch content and time sampling, alpha catches content heterogeneity , and Cohen's kappa catches inter-scorer differences. Correct pairs (A) Test-retest = (III) Time sampling; (B) Alternate form (delayed) = (IV) Content sampling and time sampling; (C) Coefficient alpha = (I) Content heterogeneity; (D) Cohen's kappa = (II) Inter-scorer differences. How it works Delayed alternate forms change both the items and the occasion, so two errors enter. Cohen's kappa measures agreement between two raters beyond chance, so its error is scorer disagreement. Why the other options are wrong (1) A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III Gives test-retest the double error of delayed alternate forms and pairs Cohen's kappa with time sampling; kappa is about agreement between raters , not occasions. (2) A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-III Uses time sampling twice, for alpha and kappa; coefficient alpha reflects item heterogeneity and kappa reflects inter-scorer differences. (4) A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I Gets A and B right but swaps C and D: coefficient alpha reflects content heterogeneity , while inter-scorer differences belong to Cohen's kappa. Which of the following are involved in decreased food intake and weight loss? (A) Insulin (B) Leptin (C) Cholecystokinin (D) Orexin 1 A and B only 2 A, B and C only 3 A, B and D only 4 B, C and D only ✓ Answer: (2) A, B and C only Satiety signals: leptin, insulin, cholecystokinin The concept Why this one Leptin, insulin and cholecystokinin (CCK) all act as satiety signals that lower food intake. Orexin does the opposite: it increases hunger and eating. How it works Leptin from fat cells and insulin from the pancreas tell the hypothalamus how much fat the body stores, so high levels cut long-term intake. CCK is released by the gut during a meal and ends the meal sooner. Exam tip Eating up: ghrelin , orexin, neuropeptide Y; eating down: leptin, insulin (in the brain), CCK. Leptin-deficient ob/ob mice become very obese. Why the other options are wrong (1) A and B only Leaves out cholecystokinin, a gut hormone released during a meal that signals fullness and shortens the meal. (3) A, B and D only Includes orexin (hypocretin), a lateral hypothalamic peptide that increases food intake and wakefulness, and leaves out CCK, which reduces intake. (4) B, C and D only Leaves out insulin, which acts in the brain as a long-term satiety signal, and wrongly includes orexin, which stimulates eating. Jensen put forward the 'Regression' argument to account for which of the following? 1 To understand inter-generation changes in intelligence 2 To understand intra-generation changes in intelligence 3 To understand group differences in intelligence 4 To understand the role of genetics in intelligence ✓ Answer: (3) To understand group differences in intelligence Arthur Jensen, regression to the mean argument The concept Why this one Arthur Jensen used the regression argument in the debate on Black-White IQ differences in the USA, so it was meant to account for group differences in intelligence. How it works Children of very bright parents score closer to the average than their parents ( regression to the mean ). Jensen argued that children of high-IQ Black and White parents regress towards different group means, and took this as evidence for a partly genetic group difference. Exam tip Critics replied that regression towards different group means is expected whatever causes the gap, so it does not prove a genetic cause. Why the other options are wrong (1) To understand inter-generation changes in intelligence Rising IQ scores across generations is the Flynn effect , described by James Flynn; Jensen's regression argument dealt with differences between racial groups. (2) To understand intra-generation changes in intelligence Changes within one generation, such as IQ gains with age or schooling, were not its target; the argument compared groups. (4) To understand the role of genetics in intelligence Too broad: Jensen did hold that genes matter, but the regression argument was used specifically to explain the gap between groups. List I: (A) Happiness results from experiences of personal expressiveness (B) Happiness is self-realization, meaning the expression and fulfilment of inner potentials (C) Happiness reflects an individual's own judgement about the quality of his or her life (D) Happiness results from the fulfilment of three basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence and relatedness. List II: (I) Ryan & Deci (II) Diener (III) Aristotle (IV) Waterman. Choose the correct answer from the options given below: 1 A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV 2 A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II 3 A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I 4 A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III ✓ Answer: (3) A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I Eudaimonic and hedonic views of well-being The concept Why this one Alan Waterman linked happiness to personal expressiveness , Aristotle to self-realisation (eudaimonia), Ed Diener to one's own judgement of life, and Richard Ryan and Edward Deci to three basic needs. Correct pairs (A) Personal expressiveness = (IV) Waterman; (B) Self-realisation = (III) Aristotle; (C) Own judgement of life quality = (II) Diener; (D) Autonomy, competence, relatedness = (I) Ryan and Deci. Two traditions Hedonic views stress pleasure and life satisfaction (Diener's subjective well-being); eudaimonic views stress living true to one's potential (Aristotle, Waterman, and Ryan and Deci's self-determination theory). Why the other options are wrong (1) A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV Gives self-realisation to Diener and the three basic needs to Waterman; the three needs come from Ryan and Deci's self-determination theory . (2) A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II Gives personal expressiveness to Aristotle and life judgement to Ryan and Deci; judging one's own life quality is Diener's subjective well-being . (4) A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III Gives personal expressiveness to Diener and the three needs to Aristotle; autonomy, competence and relatedness come from Ryan and Deci. Match List I with List II. List I: (A) The theory that an individual's self-concept is derived partly from membership in a group (B) The theory that prejudice arises from a real conflict of interest between groups (C) The theory that all societies are organised in group hierarchies and sustained through discrimination (D) The most important social perspective in social psychology. List II: (I) Realistic group conflict theory (II) Social Dominance theory (III) Social Identity theory (IV) Interdependence theory. Choose the correct answer from the options given below: 1 A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV 2 A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I 3 A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV 4 A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I ✓ Best answer: (1) A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV Henri Tajfel, Muzafer Sherif, Jim Sidanius, Harold Kelley The concept Why this one Option (1) gets C and D right and only swaps the labels of A and B, the likeliest copying slip. Correct pairs (A) Self-concept from group membership = Social identity theory (Henri Tajfel, John Turner); (B) Real conflict of interest = Realistic group conflict theory (Muzafer Sherif); (C) Hierarchies kept by discrimination = Social dominance theory (Jim Sidanius, Felicia Pratto); (D) = Interdependence theory (John Thibaut, Harold Kelley). Not certain As printed no option fits the true pairs A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV; option 1 fits if I and III were swapped in copying, and option 2 (also two pairs right) is the runner-up. Why the other options are wrong (2) A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I Gets A and C right but gives real conflict of interest to interdependence theory, when it is realistic group conflict theory (Muzafer Sherif). (3) A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV Gives the hierarchy description to social identity theory and real conflict to social dominance theory; only D is right. (4) A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I Gives self-concept to social dominance theory and hierarchies to interdependence theory; self-concept from groups is Tajfel and Turner's social identity theory . The enhancement of dominant responses is strongest when people think they are being evaluated. What is the correct sequence of this theory? (A) Evaluation apprehension (B) Well learned (C) Presence of others (D) Increased arousal (E) Social facilitation 1 B, A, C, D, E 2 D, A, B, E 3 A, B, C, D, E 4 A, C, D, B, E ✓ Best answer: (4) A, C, D, B, E Nickolas Cottrell, evaluation apprehension; Robert Zajonc, drive theory The concept Why this one Option (4) gets the core chain right: arousal boosts the dominant (well-learned) response , giving social facilitation . Strictly, the presence of others comes before evaluation apprehension. Correct order (C) Presence of others → (A) evaluation apprehension (worry about being judged) → (D) increased arousal → (B) the well-learned, dominant response becomes more likely → (E) social facilitation on easy tasks. What it is Robert Zajonc said the mere presence of others raises arousal. Nickolas Cottrell added that the effect is strongest when the others can evaluate us; blindfolded onlookers produced little effect. Not certain The textbook chain is C, A, D, B, E (presence of others comes first), which no option prints; option 4 only swaps the first two steps, while option 1 wrongly starts with the well-learned response. Why the other options are wrong (1) B, A, C, D, E Starts with the well-learned response, but the dominant response is the result of arousal, near the end of the chain, not its trigger. (2) D, A, B, E Lists only four steps, leaves out the presence of others, and starts with arousal, when arousal follows evaluation apprehension. (3) A, B, C, D, E Puts the well-learned response before the presence of others and arousal; in the theory, arousal comes first and then strengthens the dominant response. Which technique of studying the brain involves injecting the patient with radioactive glucose? 1 EEG 2 MRI 3 PET 4 CT ✓ Answer: (3) PET Positron emission tomography (PET) The concept Why this one In a PET scan the patient receives radioactive glucose or a similar tracer. Busy brain areas use more glucose, so they show up as active on the scan. How it works Detectors pick up the positrons given off by the tracer and a computer builds a colour map of activity. PET shows brain function , not just structure. Exam tip Structure: CT, MRI. Function: PET, fMRI (blood oxygen, no injection), EEG (electrical activity). Why the other options are wrong (1) EEG EEG records the brain's electrical activity through electrodes on the scalp; nothing is injected. (2) MRI MRI uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to image brain structure; no radioactive tracer is used. (4) CT CT combines many X-ray images taken from different angles to show brain structure, not glucose use. Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R. Assertion A: The NEO-PI-R does not have a response style scale. Reason R: NEO-PI-R developers argued that adjustment of social desirability leads to a reduction in validity. In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below: 1 Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A 2 Both A and R are correct and R is NOT the correct explanation of A 3 A is correct but R is not correct 4 A is not correct but R is correct ✓ Answer: (1) Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A Paul Costa and Robert McCrae, NEO-PI-R The concept Assertion True. The NEO-PI-R by Paul Costa and Robert McCrae has no lie, faking or social desirability scale, unlike the MMPI with its L, F and K scales. Reason True. Costa and McCrae argued that socially desirable answers often reflect real traits, so correcting scores for social desirability makes them less valid, not more. Why R explains A They left a response style scale out of the test precisely because they believed such corrections lower validity . Why the other options are not the answer (2) Both A and R are correct and R is NOT the correct explanation of A R is not a side fact: it is the stated reason why the authors chose not to build a response style scale into the test. (3) A is correct but R is not correct R is true: Costa and McCrae did argue that adjusting scores for social desirability reduces validity. (4) A is not correct but R is correct A is true: the NEO-PI-R has no formal response style or validity scale like the MMPI's L, F and K. Which of the following are comprised in executive functions? (A) Planning (B) Attention (C) Set shifting (D) Declarative memory 1 A, B and C only 2 A, B and D only 3 A, C and D only 4 B, C and D only ✓ Answer: (1) A, B and C only Executive functions of the prefrontal cortex The concept Why this one Executive functions are the control processes that run goal-directed behaviour: planning , controlling attention and set shifting . Declarative memory is a memory store, not a control process. What it is They depend mainly on the prefrontal cortex . Common tests are the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (set shifting), Tower of London (planning) and Stroop (inhibition and attention). Exam tip Akira Miyake's model names three core executive functions: shifting , updating of working memory and inhibition . Why the other options are wrong (2) A, B and D only Includes declarative memory, the conscious memory for facts and events that depends on the hippocampus, and leaves out set shifting, a core executive function. (3) A, C and D only Leaves out attention control and wrongly includes declarative memory, which is a long-term memory system, not an executive process. (4) B, C and D only Leaves out planning, a classic executive function, and includes declarative memory, which is stored knowledge rather than control. Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R. Assertion A: According to Classical Test Theory (CTT) total variance is equal to the sum of true variance and error variance. Reason R: Error variance and true variance are independent of each other as per CTT. In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below: 1 Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A 2 Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A 3 A is correct but R is not correct 4 A is not correct but R is correct ✓ Answer: (1) Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A Classical test theory, X = T + E The concept Assertion True. In classical test theory an observed score is true score plus error (X = T + E), and total variance splits as σ 2 X = σ 2 T + σ 2 E . Reason True. CTT assumes error is random and uncorrelated with true scores. Why R explains A The variance of a sum equals the sum of the variances plus twice their covariance . Because T and E are independent, the covariance is zero, so total variance is simply true plus error variance. Why the other options are wrong (2) Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A R is the very condition that makes A hold: without zero covariance between true and error scores, an extra covariance term would appear. (3) A is correct but R is not correct R is true: independence of true and error scores is a core assumption of classical test theory. (4) A is not correct but R is correct A is true: in classical test theory total variance equals true variance plus error variance. What is the retention without conscious recollection of skills and dispositions called? 1 Iconic memory 2 Implicit memory 3 Explicit memory 4 Semantic memory ✓ Answer: (2) Implicit memory Daniel Schacter, implicit memory The concept Why this one Implicit memory is retention shown in behaviour without conscious recollection, such as skills, habits and conditioned dispositions. Examples Riding a bicycle, typing, or feeling uneasy near dogs after a bite. Priming is also implicit: an earlier exposure speeds later recognition without awareness. Exam tip Amnesic patients such as H.M. (Henry Molaison) lose explicit memory but still learn new skills such as mirror drawing, showing the two systems are separate. Why the other options are wrong (1) Iconic memory Iconic memory is the brief visual sensory store, lasting under a second, shown by George Sperling's partial report studies. (3) Explicit memory Explicit (declarative) memory is the opposite: facts and events that are consciously recalled. (4) Semantic memory Semantic memory , named by Endel Tulving, is consciously accessible general knowledge such as word meanings and facts, a part of explicit memory. Arrange in sequence what Yerkes described commonly takes place in "insight learning". (A) Sharpening and frequent recurrent attention to the goal (B) Trial (C) Survey/Inspection (D) Attitude of concentrated attention (E) Critical point 1 B, C, A, D, E 2 B, D, C, A, E 3 C, D, B, A, E 4 B, C, A, E, D ✓ Answer: (3) C, D, B, A, E Robert Yerkes, insight in great apes The concept Why this one Robert Yerkes , watching apes solve problems, saw them first survey the situation, pause in concentrated attention, try a response, keep attending to the goal, and finally reach a critical point of sudden solution. Correct order (C) Survey/inspection → (D) attitude of concentrated attention → (B) trial → (A) sharpening and recurrent attention to the goal → (E) critical point, after which the act is readily repeated. Exam tip Insight learning is linked with Wolfgang Köhler 's chimpanzee Sultan, who joined sticks and stacked boxes to reach bananas. Insight is sudden, transfers well and is not blind trial and error. Why the other options are wrong (1) B, C, A, D, E Starts with trial, but in Yerkes' account the animal first surveys and inspects the problem; trial comes only after concentrated attention. (2) B, D, C, A, E Starts with trial before survey; trial comes third, after inspection and a pause of concentrated attention. (4) B, C, A, E, D Starts with trial and puts the critical point before concentrated attention; the critical point, the sudden solution, is the last step. Who among the following is credited with proposing the investment theory of creativity? 1 Getzels and Jackson 2 Kaufman 3 Wallach and Kogan 4 Sternberg ✓ Answer: (4) Sternberg Robert Sternberg and Todd Lubart, investment theory The concept Why this one Robert Sternberg and Todd Lubart proposed the investment theory : creative people 'buy low and sell high', backing unpopular ideas and moving on once they become accepted. How it works Creativity needs six resources working together: intellectual abilities, knowledge, thinking styles, personality, motivation and environment. Exam tip Sternberg also gave the triarchic theory of intelligence and the triangular theory of love. Why the other options are wrong (1) Getzels and Jackson Jacob Getzels and Philip Jackson studied gifted school pupils and showed that high creativity and high IQ were only weakly related. (2) Kaufman James Kaufman, with Ronald Beghetto, proposed the Four C model of creativity (mini-c, little-c, Pro-c, Big-C). (3) Wallach and Kogan Michael Wallach and Nathan Kogan tested children's creativity in a relaxed, game-like, untimed setting and found it fairly separate from intelligence. Which of the following principle is violated when a psychologist intentionally misrepresents his research results? 1 Beneficence 2 Fidelity and responsibility 3 Integrity 4 Confidentiality ✓ Answer: (3) Integrity APA Ethics Code, Principle C: Integrity The concept Why this one APA Principle C, Integrity , asks psychologists to promote accuracy, honesty and truthfulness. Knowingly misrepresenting results is dishonest, so it breaks integrity. What it is The APA Ethics Code has five general principles : (A) Beneficence and non-maleficence, (B) Fidelity and responsibility, (C) Integrity, (D) Justice, (E) Respect for people's rights and dignity. Exam tip Making up data is fabrication ; presenting others' work as one's own is plagiarism ; both are research misconduct. Why the other options are wrong (1) Beneficence Principle A, beneficence and non-maleficence, is about benefiting clients and avoiding harm, not about honesty in reporting. (2) Fidelity and responsibility Principle B, fidelity and responsibility, is about building trust and accepting professional responsibility towards clients and society. (4) Confidentiality Confidentiality is a specific standard about protecting client information, not one of the five general principles, and it is not about falsifying results. In multiple approach-avoidance conflict, one has to choose between which of the following? 1 Two goals possessing both negative and positive aspects 2 More than two goals; each having both positive and negative aspects 3 More than two goals; one having negative aspects and others having positive valences 4 More than two goals; at least one having positive aspects while others may have negative aspects ✓ Answer: (2) More than two goals; each having both positive and negative aspects Kurt Lewin, types of motivational conflict The concept Why this one In a multiple approach-avoidance conflict there are more than two options and each has both attractive and unattractive features, for example choosing between three job offers. Conflict types Approach-approach : two attractive goals; avoidance-avoidance : two unpleasant ones; approach-avoidance: one goal with good and bad sides; double approach-avoidance: two goals, each with both sides. Exam tip Kurt Lewin described the basic types. Approach-avoidance conflicts often cause vacillation, because avoidance rises faster than approach as the goal comes near. Why the other options are wrong (1) Two goals possessing both negative and positive aspects This is a double approach-avoidance conflict: only two goals, each with good and bad sides. (3) More than two goals; one having negative aspects and others having positive valences Wrongly gives only one goal negative features; in the multiple form, every option has both positive and negative sides. (4) More than two goals; at least one having positive aspects while others may have negative aspects Allows some goals to be purely positive or purely negative; in multiple approach-avoidance every option has both sides. Match List I with List II. List I: (A) Cancer that originates in the blood-forming cells such as stem cells (B) Cancer of the epithelial tissue, cells that line the outer and inner surface of the body such as skin, stomach etc. (C) Cancer that arises from the cells in connective tissue such as bone, muscles (D) Cancer of the sympathetic system which is one of the rare types of cancer. Which of the following characterise the hardy person? (A) He is high on sense of commitment (B) He is more likely to act to 'cover-up' (C) He doesn't avoid problems, yet he is often angry (D) He is always under the control of his life and events 1 A and C only 2 A and D only 3 A and B only 4 A, B and D only ✓ Answer: (2) A and D only Suzanne Kobasa, hardiness (commitment, control, challenge) The concept Why this one Suzanne Kobasa found that hardy people combine commitment , a sense of control over life events, and seeing change as a challenge. A is commitment; D, read as being in control of one's life, is control. What it is Hardiness buffers stress: highly stressed executives high in hardiness fell ill less often. Hardy people use active, transformational coping instead of avoiding or denying problems. Exam tip Remember the three Cs: commitment, control, challenge. Hostility and anger belong to the toxic core of the Type A pattern, not to hardiness. Why the other options are wrong (1) A and C only Statement C is false: hardy people face problems, but frequent anger and hostility mark the Type A pattern, which raises heart disease risk. (3) A and B only Statement B is false: covering up or denying problems is avoidant coping, the opposite of the active coping hardy people use. (4) A, B and D only Commitment and control fit, but statement B does not: hardy people face and transform problems rather than covering them up. A researcher is studying the group process of software startup developers by staying with them for six months. Which of the following is used by her? 1 Grounded theory 2 Ethnography 3 Narrative analysis 4 Phenomenological research ✓ Answer: (2) Ethnography Ethnography, John Creswell's five qualitative approaches The concept Why this one Ethnography studies the shared patterns of a culture-sharing group through long fieldwork , living with and observing the group. Staying six months with a startup team to study its group process fits exactly. How it works The main method is participant observation , backed by interviews and field notes. It grew out of anthropological fieldwork. Exam tip John Creswell's five approaches: narrative (one person's story), phenomenology (lived experience), grounded theory (build a theory), ethnography (a culture-sharing group), case study (a bounded case). Why the other options are wrong (1) Grounded theory Grounded theory (Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss) aims to build a new theory from data through coding and constant comparison, not to describe a group's culture. (3) Narrative analysis Narrative analysis studies the life stories of one or a few individuals and retells them in time order. (4) Phenomenological research Phenomenological research describes the shared lived experience of a phenomenon, such as grief, across several people, mainly through in-depth interviews. What do you call the neurological procedure involving the implantation of a medical device under the skin in the chest that sends electrical impulses to electrodes surgically placed in a specific location in the brain? 1 Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) 2 Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) 3 Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) 4 Vagus Nerve Stimulation (VNS) ✓ Answer: (1) Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) Deep brain stimulation (DBS) The concept Why this one In deep brain stimulation a pulse generator, like a pacemaker, is placed under the skin of the chest and wired to electrodes implanted deep in the brain. Uses It is used for Parkinson's disease , essential tremor and dystonia, and is being studied for severe, treatment-resistant OCD and depression. A common target is the subthalamic nucleus. Exam tip Chest device + electrodes in the brain = DBS; chest device + wire to a neck nerve = VNS ; magnetic coil on the scalp = rTMS. Why the other options are wrong (2) Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) rTMS is non-invasive: a magnetic coil held against the scalp induces currents in the cortex, and nothing is implanted. (3) Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) ECT passes a brief current through scalp electrodes under anaesthesia to cause a controlled seizure; nothing is implanted. (4) Vagus Nerve Stimulation (VNS) VNS also uses a chest pulse generator, but its wire goes to the vagus nerve in the neck, not to electrodes inside the brain. According to Lazarus, what comes between the stimulus and the emotional response to that stimulus to mediate? 1 Physiological reactions 2 Labeling 3 Social and situational cues 4 Cognitive appraisal ✓ Answer: (4) Cognitive appraisal Richard Lazarus, cognitive appraisal theory The concept Why this one Richard Lazarus held that emotion depends on how we judge an event. This cognitive appraisal sits between the stimulus and the emotional response. How it works Primary appraisal asks whether the event is relevant, harmful or threatening; secondary appraisal asks whether I can cope. Reappraisal updates the judgement. Exam tip Lazarus debated Robert Zajonc , who claimed that feeling can come before thinking (affective primacy). Why the other options are wrong (1) Physiological reactions Physiological reactions come first in the James-Lange theory , where emotion is the perception of bodily changes. (2) Labeling Labelling of arousal is the central step in Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer's two-factor theory . (3) Social and situational cues In the two-factor theory, Schachter and Singer said people use social and situational cues to label unexplained arousal; Lazarus stressed appraisal of the event's meaning instead. Several types of heuristics have been identified by researchers. Which of these are included in it? (A) Lexicographic strategy (B) Satisficing strategy (C) Mental set (D) Elimination by aspects 1 A, B and C only 2 A, B and D only 3 A, C and D only 4 B, C and D only ✓ Answer: (2) A, B and D only Decision heuristics: Herbert Simon, Amos Tversky The concept Why this one The lexicographic strategy , satisficing and elimination by aspects are short-cut decision rules, that is, heuristics. Mental set is a problem-solving block, not a decision heuristic. How each works Lexicographic: choose the option that is best on the single most important attribute; satisficing (Herbert Simon): take the first option that is good enough; elimination by aspects (Amos Tversky): drop options that fail on one attribute at a time. Exam tip Mental set is shown in Abraham Luchins' water jar problems: people keep using a method that worked before even when a simpler one exists. Why the other options are wrong (1) A, B and C only Includes mental set, a fixed way of approaching problems that blocks new solutions, and leaves out elimination by aspects. (3) A, C and D only Leaves out satisficing, Herbert Simon's rule of taking the first good-enough option, and wrongly includes mental set. (4) B, C and D only Leaves out the lexicographic strategy and wrongly includes mental set, which is a barrier to problem solving. Which one of the following is the correct description of Old Fashioned Racism? 1 A contemporary form of antagonism towards a racial group based on prejudice and values rather than on self-interest 2 Beliefs in racial superiority, segregation and formal discrimination 3 Attitude towards a racial group, combining egalitarian social values and negative emotion resulting in avoidance of that group 4 Well learned sets of association that can be automatically activated, uncontrollable and unintentional ✓ Answer: (2) Beliefs in racial superiority, segregation and formal discrimination John McConahay, old-fashioned versus modern racism The concept Why this one Old-fashioned racism is open, blatant prejudice: beliefs in racial superiority , support for segregation and formal, legal discrimination. How it differs After the civil rights era open racism became socially unacceptable and gave way to subtler forms such as modern racism , measured by John McConahay's Modern Racism Scale. Exam tip Blatant = old-fashioned; values not self-interest = symbolic; egalitarian values plus avoidance = aversive; automatic associations = implicit . Why the other options are wrong (1) A contemporary form of antagonism towards a racial group based on prejudice and values rather than on self-interest This describes symbolic racism (David Sears), a modern form rooted in values such as individualism rather than personal self-interest. (3) Attitude towards a racial group, combining egalitarian social values and negative emotion resulting in avoidance of that group This describes aversive racism (Samuel Gaertner and John Dovidio): egalitarian beliefs plus hidden negative feelings that lead to avoidance. (4) Well learned sets of association that can be automatically activated, uncontrollable and unintentional This describes implicit prejudice or stereotypes: automatic associations, measured with tools like the Implicit Association Test. Match List I with List II. List I (Description): (A) A laboratory device for testing depth in infants and young animals (B) Refers to the differences in two eyes' location of corner angles (C) Refers to two points which fall on non-corresponding retinal positions one nearer and the other farther (D) Perceptional adaptability to adjust to an artificially displaced visual field. List II (Concept): (I) Perceptual adaptation (II) Horizontal disparity (III) Vertical disparity (IV) Visual cliff. Choose the correct answer from the options given below: 1 A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV 2 A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I 3 A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II 4 A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I ✓ Answer: (4) A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I Eleanor Gibson and Richard Walk, visual cliff; binocular disparity The concept Why this one The visual cliff tests depth perception in infants and perceptual adaptation is adjusting to a displaced visual field; only option (4) has both. B and C are the two kinds of binocular disparity. Correct pairs (A) Depth test for infants = (IV) Visual cliff; (B) Different positions of corners and angles in the two eyes = (III) Vertical disparity; (C) Points on non-corresponding retinal positions, nearer or farther = (II) Horizontal disparity ; (D) Adjusting to a displaced field = (I) Perceptual adaptation. How it works Eleanor Gibson and Richard Walk found most crawling infants would not cross the 'deep' side of the cliff. Horizontal disparity is the main cue for stereopsis , and people wearing prism goggles that shift the visual field soon adapt their reaching. Why the other options are wrong (1) A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV Puts perceptual adaptation on the infant depth test and the visual cliff on the displaced field; the visual cliff is Gibson and Walk's infant depth test. Which one of the following branches of philosophy of science deals with the question of existence? 1 Post-positivism 2 Structuralism 3 Ontology 4 Scientific realism ✓ Answer: (3) Ontology Ontology, the study of being The concept Why this one Ontology is the branch of philosophy that asks what exists and what kinds of things are real. In science it asks which entities (atoms, minds, traits) truly exist. Three questions Ontology asks "what is there?"; epistemology asks "how do we know it?"; methodology asks "how do we study it?". Exam tip Research paradigms are compared on these three. Positivism assumes one real world (realist ontology); constructivism assumes reality is socially built (relativist ontology). Why the other options are wrong (1) Post-positivism A research paradigm holding that reality exists but can only be known imperfectly, so claims are probabilistic and open to falsification; it is a position, not the branch about existence. (2) Structuralism A school of thought that breaks things into basic elements or underlying structures (Edward Titchener in psychology), not the philosophical study of existence. (4) Scientific realism A specific position within the debate, not a branch: it holds that the unobservable entities of successful theories, such as electrons or genes, really exist. Which of the following is the correct response pattern for the semantic differential test to measure a trait 'active'? 1 I am active: SA A N D SD 2 I am active: True/False 3 Choose one: Active-Trusting 4 Active...Neutral...Passive ✓ Answer: (4) Active...Neutral...Passive Charles Osgood, semantic differential (1957) The concept Why this one Charles Osgood's semantic differential rates a concept on a line between two bipolar adjectives , such as active and passive, usually with seven steps and a neutral middle. How it works Ratings group into three factors: evaluation (good to bad), potency (strong to weak) and activity (active to passive). "Active versus passive" is an activity scale. Exam tip Opposite adjectives with steps between = Osgood ; strongly agree to strongly disagree = Likert ; true or false = inventory format such as the MMPI. Why the other options are wrong (1) I am active: SA A N D SD This is the Likert (summated ratings) format: agreement with a statement on five steps from strongly agree to strongly disagree. (2) I am active: True/False A dichotomous true/false item format, as used in inventories such as the MMPI, not a scale between two opposite adjectives. (3) Choose one: Active-Trusting Active and trusting are not opposites, so this is a forced choice between two unrelated traits, not a bipolar semantic scale. Which approach focussed on the nature of a task and its influence on a person's ability in solving problems? 1 Associationist approach 2 Information processing approach 3 Gestalt approach 4 Behaviourist approach ✓ Best answer: (2) Information processing approach Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, information processing approach The concept Why this one Allen Newell and Herbert Simon analysed the task environment : the structure of the task sets what the solver must represent and which moves are possible. How it works The solver builds a problem space (start state, goal state, operators) and searches it with heuristics such as means-end analysis , limited by working memory capacity. Exam tip Associationist = trial and error, habit strength; Gestalt = restructuring and insight; information processing = task analysis, problem space and computer simulation (General Problem Solver). Not certain Gestalt psychologists also stressed how the structure of a problem shapes its solution (restructuring, functional fixedness), so (3) is the runner-up. Why the other options are wrong (1) Associationist approach Explains problem solving as trial and error that strengthens stimulus-response bonds (Edward Thorndike), so it focuses on learned habits rather than the structure of the task. (3) Gestalt approach Wolfgang Köhler, Max Wertheimer and Karl Duncker stressed perceptual restructuring, sudden insight and blocks such as functional fixedness, not a formal analysis of the task. (4) Behaviourist approach Treats problem solving as responses shaped by reinforcement history and ignores how the solver mentally represents the task. Match List I with List II. List I: (A) Pratibha (B) Prajna (C) Vak (D) Bhavas. List II: (I) Samkhya philosophy (II) Nyaya Vaisesika (III) Tantrik tradition (IV) Patanjali Yoga system. Choose the correct answer from the options given below: 1 A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III 2 A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III 3 A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I 4 A-I, B-IV, C-II, D-III ✓ Answer: (3) A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I Classical Indian philosophical systems (darshanas) and Tantra The concept Correct pairs (A) Pratibha = (II) Nyaya Vaisesika ; (B) Prajna = (IV) Patanjali Yoga system; (C) Vak = (III) Tantrik tradition; (D) Bhavas = (I) Samkhya philosophy. Pratibha and prajna Pratibha is a flash of intuitive knowledge that arises without the senses, discussed in Nyaya Vaisesika as the knowledge of seers. Prajna in the Yoga Sutras is insight wisdom reached in samadhi. Vak and bhavas In Tantra, vak (speech) unfolds in levels from para to vaikhari (spoken word). In Samkhya , the eight bhavas are dispositions of buddhi: virtue, knowledge, detachment, power and their opposites. Why the other options are wrong (1) A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III Every pair is wrong: pratibha belongs to Nyaya Vaisesika, prajna to Yoga, vak to the Tantrik tradition and the bhavas to Samkhya. (2) A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III Gets pratibha and prajna right but swaps the last two: vak belongs to the Tantrik tradition and the bhavas to Samkhya. (4) A-I, B-IV, C-II, D-III Only prajna (Yoga) is right; pratibha is Nyaya Vaisesika, vak is Tantrik and the bhavas are Samkhya. In the famous experiment by Schachter and Singer involving epinephrine, what was found to govern the emotions? 1 Perceptual cues only 2 Social appraisal only 3 Both cognitive appraisal and physiological arousal 4 Both cognitive and social appraisal ✓ Answer: (3) Both cognitive appraisal and physiological arousal Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer, two-factor theory (1962) The concept Why this one In Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer's two-factor theory , emotion needs both physiological arousal and a cognitive label (appraisal) explaining why one is aroused. The experiment Participants got epinephrine . Those not told about its side effects took on the mood of a euphoric or angry stooge, labelling their arousal from the situation; informed participants blamed the drug and copied less. Exam tip James-Lange = bodily change first, then emotion; Cannon-Bard = both at once via the thalamus; Schachter-Singer = arousal plus label. Why the other options are wrong (1) Perceptual cues only Cues from the situation guided the labelling, but on their own they did not produce emotion; arousal from the drug was also needed. (2) Social appraisal only The stooge's behaviour supplied the cue for labelling, but the theory also requires physiological arousal, so social appraisal alone is not enough. (4) Both cognitive and social appraisal Leaves out the bodily factor; the core claim is that arousal must be present and then explained cognitively. Who among the following has laid emphasis on examining the relationship of culturally specific practices with development? 1 Piaget 2 Fodor 3 Vygotsky 4 Kohlberg ✓ Answer: (3) Vygotsky Lev Vygotsky, sociocultural theory The concept Why this one Lev Vygotsky argued that development cannot be separated from its cultural and social context: the tools, language and practices of a culture shape how children think. Key ideas Children learn through interaction with more skilled people within the zone of proximal development , supported by scaffolding . Higher mental functions appear first between people, then within the child. Exam tip Piaget = child as lone scientist passing universal stages; Vygotsky = child as apprentice whose path depends on culture. Why the other options are wrong (1) Piaget Jean Piaget proposed universal stages driven by the child's own exploration and gave culture only a minor role. (2) Fodor Jerry Fodor is a philosopher of mind known for the modularity of mind and the language of thought, not cultural development. (4) Kohlberg Lawrence Kohlberg proposed universal stages of moral reasoning and has been criticised for underplaying cultural variation. Mr A is very good at discriminating between progressive and regressive ways of behaviour. His choices are clearly perceived by him and adequately symbolised. According to Rogers, these are the characteristics of which of the following? (A) Individual tendency towards 'growth' (B) Tendency to 'self actualise' (C) His constructive creativity (D) His self-affirmation 1 A and C only 2 A, C and D only 3 A and B only 4 B only ✓ Answer: (3) A and B only Carl Rogers, actualising tendency The concept Why this one Carl Rogers held that the forward-moving growth tendency, the drive to self-actualise , works only when choices are clearly perceived and adequately symbolised. A person must tell progressive from regressive behaviour to actualise. What it is The actualising tendency is the one master motive to maintain and enhance the organism, moving it towards greater differentiation, autonomy and maturity. Exam tip Denied or distorted experience ( incongruence ) blurs this choice; congruence lets the person see and take the growth path. Why the other options are wrong (1) A and C only Includes (C) and drops (B); Rogers ties clear symbolisation of choices to the tendency to self-actualise, not to creativity as such. (2) A, C and D only Adds (C) and (D) and drops (B); creativity and self-affirmation are not what Rogers links to telling progressive from regressive behaviour. (4) B only Self-actualising is right, but Rogers describes it as the forward-moving growth tendency, so (A) belongs with it. For an intelligence test in an educational setting, which of the following difficulty value shows maximum discrimination? 1 0.8 2 0.6 3 0.5 4 0.3 ✓ Answer: (3) 0.5 Item difficulty index and discrimination The concept Why this one An item passed by 50% (p = 0.5) splits the group into two equal halves, giving the largest number of pass-fail contrasts between people, so it discriminates most. How it works Item difficulty p is the proportion who answer correctly. At p = 1.0 or 0 everyone gets the same result, so the item tells you nothing about differences. Exam tip Anne Anastasi: for maximum differentiation choose items near p = 0.5 . With guessing on multiple choice the optimum rises to about (1 + chance)/2, for example 0.625 for four options. Why the other options are wrong (1) 0.8 An easy item: 80% pass, so it only separates the weakest fifth from the rest and makes fewer distinctions between people. (2) 0.6 Close to the optimum and near the value adjusted for guessing on four-option items, but without that adjustment 0.5 discriminates more. (4) 0.3 A hard item: only 30% pass, so most people fail it and it separates fewer pairs of test takers. Making decisions by the use of mental short cuts that focus on one aspect of a problem, while ignoring others refers to which one of the following? 1 Framing 2 Belief perseverance 3 Heuristics 4 Mental set ✓ Answer: (3) Heuristics Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, heuristics The concept Why this one Heuristics are mental shortcuts or rules of thumb that give fast answers by using only part of the information, so they can bias decisions. Examples Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described availability (judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind), representativeness (judging by resemblance to a prototype) and anchoring. Exam tip Heuristic = quick but error-prone; algorithm = step-by-step method that guarantees a solution but is slow. Why the other options are wrong (1) Framing The effect of how options are worded (as gains or as losses) on the choice people make, shown by Tversky and Kahneman. (2) Belief perseverance Clinging to a belief even after the evidence for it has been discredited. (4) Mental set A tendency to keep using a strategy that worked before even when a better one exists, as in Abraham Luchins' water jar problems. Which of the following are the parts of mental logic theories of reasoning? (A) A set of inference schemas (B) Accumulation of concepts (C) A reasoning program (D) A set of pragmatic principles 1 A, B and C only 2 A, B and D only 3 A, C and D only 4 B, C and D only ✓ Answer: (3) A, C and D only Martin Braine and David O'Brien, mental logic theory The concept Why this one Mental logic theories, such as that of Martin Braine and David O'Brien, have three parts: a set of inference schemas , a reasoning program that applies them, and pragmatic principles that shape how premises are understood. How it works People are assumed to carry abstract rules such as modus ponens in the head; the program chains them to reach conclusions, while pragmatic principles handle context and wording. Exam tip Mental logic (Braine; Lance Rips' PSYCOP) = rules of inference; mental models (Philip Johnson-Laird) = imagined scenarios of the premises. Why the other options are wrong (1) A, B and C only Includes (B) and drops (D); accumulation of concepts is not a component, while pragmatic principles are. (2) A, B and D only Includes (B) and drops (C); the reasoning program that applies the schemas is a core part of the theory. (4) B, C and D only Drops (A), the inference schemas that are the heart of any mental logic theory, and adds (B), which is not a part. In which sequence, according to Piaget, are the following cognitive milestones achieved? (A) Object permanence (B) Reversibility (C) Abstraction (D) Centration 1 A, B, C, D 2 C, A, B, D 3 D, A, B, C 4 A, D, B, C ✓ Answer: (4) A, D, B, C Jean Piaget, stages of cognitive development The concept Correct order (A) Object permanence , sensorimotor (0 to 2 years) → (D) Centration , preoperational (2 to 7) → (B) Reversibility , concrete operational (7 to 11) → (C) Abstraction, formal operational (11 onwards). (4) 58 Subtracts 2 from a single group; df = n - 2 applies when testing a correlation, not a paired t-test. Which of the following is true about Hypovolemia? Which is true about coefficient alpha? Which of the following are considered in favour of scientific realism? (A) Corroboration (B) Empiricism (C) Miracle argument (D) Selective optimism 1 A and B only 2 B and D only 3 B and C only 4 A, C and D only ✓ Answer: (4) A, C and D only Hilary Putnam's no-miracles argument; selective realism The concept Why this one Corroboration, the no-miracles argument and selective optimism are all moves realists make. In depth perception, what kind of images are used? 1 Uni-dimensional image 2 Two-dimensional images 3 Three-dimensional images 4 Four-dimensional images ✓ Answer: (2) Two-dimensional images Depth perception from two-dimensional retinal images The concept Why this one The image on each retina is flat, two-dimensional . In the independent groups' design, selective subject loss occurs because of which of the following? (A) Subjects are lost differently across conditions (B) Subject characteristics are responsible for subject loss (C) Subjects are lost uniformly across conditions (D) Subject characteristics are independent of subject loss 1 A and B only 2 A and C only 3 B and D only 4 C and D only ✓ Answer: (1) A and B only John Shaughnessy and Eugene Zechmeister, Research Methods in Psychology The concept Why this one Selective subject loss happens when participants drop out differently across conditions (A) and a subject characteristic linked to the outcome causes the dropout (B). The independent variable is then confounded . Contrast Mechanical subject loss (equipment failure, experimenter error) has nothing to do with the person, so it does not bias the groups. Why the other options are wrong (2) A and C only C contradicts A: loss spread evenly across conditions leaves the groups comparable, so it is not selective loss. (3) B and D only D is the opposite of B: if subject characteristics were unrelated to dropping out, the loss would not bias the groups. Immediately after an action potential, the cell does not produce another action potential due to 1 Absolute refractory period 2 Relative refractory period 3 Resting state 4 Active state ✓ Answer: (1) Absolute refractory period Absolute refractory period of the neuron The concept Why this one During the absolute refractory period , about 1 to 2 milliseconds after a spike, no stimulus of any strength can trigger another action potential. What follows Next comes the relative refractory period , when only a stronger-than-normal stimulus can fire the cell because the membrane is briefly hyperpolarised. Exam tip Refractory periods make action potentials travel one way down the axon and set a ceiling on firing rate. Why the other options are not the answer (2) Relative refractory period Here a second spike is possible, but only with a stronger-than-normal stimulus, because the membrane is briefly hyperpolarised. (3) Resting state At rest (about -70 mV) the neuron is ready to fire; firing is not blocked. (4) Active state Not a technical stage; the active phase is the action potential itself, not the period that follows it. In Bronfenbrenner's model, which one of the following systems is independent of cultural bias? 1 Micro system 2 Meso system 3 Exo system 4 Macro system ✓ Best answer: (1) Micro system Urie Bronfenbrenner, ecological systems theory The concept Why this one The microsystem is the child's immediate, face-to-face setting: family, school, peers. List I: (A) Efficacy (B) Tolerance (C) Downregulation (D) Withdrawal. List II: (I) Response activated when drugs bind with a receptor (II) Repeated exposure with less activation of receptors (III) Compensatory reduction in receptor availability (IV) Unpleasant physiological responses. Choose the correct answer from the options given below: 1 A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV 2 A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV 3 A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I 4 A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III ✓ Answer: (2) A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV Drug-receptor pharmacology terms The concept Correct pairs (A) Efficacy = (I) response activated when the drug binds the receptor; (B) Tolerance = (II) less receptor activation after repeated exposure; (C) Downregulation = (III) compensatory reduction in receptor availability; (D) Withdrawal = (IV) unpleasant physiological responses. Which one of the following is considered as correct for Poverty Gap? 1 Gap between Rich and Poor 2 Gap between developed and developing nations 3 Difference between poverty line and actual income level of all those living below that line 4 Gap in the infrastructure facilities between developed nations ✓ Answer: (3) Difference between poverty line and actual income level of all those living below that line Poverty gap, a measure of poverty depth The concept Why this one The poverty gap is the shortfall between the poverty line and the actual income of each person below it, added up or averaged across the population. How it works If the line is 100 and a person earns 70, the gap is 30. The poverty gap index averages these shortfalls over the whole population (the non-poor count as zero) as a share of the line. Exam tip The headcount ratio tells how many people are poor; the poverty gap tells how poor they are. Why the other options are wrong (1) Gap between Rich and Poor This is income inequality, measured by tools such as the Gini coefficient, not the poverty gap. (2) Gap between developed and developing nations This is the development divide between rich and poor countries, not a measure of individual poverty. (4) Gap in the infrastructure facilities between developed nations This is an infrastructure or development gap between countries; the poverty gap concerns individual incomes below the poverty line. Which of the following is correct about this? 1 The father represses the curiosity 2 Such change is permanent 3 It is the most modifiable response 4 It is conditioned hostility ✓ Best answer: (4) It is conditioned hostility Classical conditioning and stimulus generalisation The concept Why this one The son learned hostility towards the punishing father, and it has spread to other authority figures. Exam tip Learned emotional responses can be weakened by extinction or counter-conditioning, so calling such a change permanent goes too far. (3) It is the most modifiable response A broad attitude learned early and generalised to all superiors is usually resistant to change, not the most modifiable kind of response. Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R. Assertion A: The obtained t-value will follow the theoretical t-distribution if the underlying assumptions are fulfilled. Reason R: The application of t-test makes an assumption of heterogeneity of variance. In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below: 1 Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A 2 Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A 3 A is correct but R is not correct 4 A is not correct but R is correct ✓ Answer: (3) A is correct but R is not correct William Gosset ('Student'), t-test assumptions The concept Assertion A is true: the computed t follows the theoretical t distribution for its degrees of freedom only when the test's assumptions hold, so its p-values are then accurate. Reason R is false: the independent t-test assumes homogeneity of variance (equal population variances), not heterogeneity. Other assumptions The data should come from normal populations and the observations should be independent; Levene's test checks equal variances. Exam tip When variances are unequal, use Welch's t-test , which adjusts the degrees of freedom. Why the other options are wrong (1) Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A R is false: the t-test assumes equal (homogeneous) variances, so it cannot explain A. (2) Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A R is false, not true: heterogeneity of variance violates the t-test's assumption of equal variances. (4) A is not correct but R is correct A is correct: when normality, independence and equal variances hold, the sampling distribution of t matches the theoretical t distribution. Client: (Silent and shifting nervously in her chair. She is facing the counselor, but her eyes scan anxiously about). Counselor: "It must be difficult for you to decide what you are going to do here with me." This counselor response is an example of: 1 Dealing with content speculated to be motivating the non-verbal behaviour by the counselor 2 Encouraging the client to deal with non-verbal behaviour 3 Encouraging the client to understand the feelings 4 Reflection of feelings ✓ Best answer: (1) Dealing with content speculated to be motivating the non-verbal behaviour by the counselor Responding to client nonverbal behaviour (counselling skills) The concept Why this one The counsellor does not name the behaviour or a feeling. Instead the counsellor speculates about the content behind it, that the client is unsure what to do in the session, and responds to that. The choices A counsellor can respond to nonverbal behaviour by ignoring it, by inviting the client to look at it ('What are you feeling as you shift in your chair?'), or by addressing what seems to be motivating it. A teacher engages students in hands-on, inquiry-based and relevant learning activities in his class. What does this illustrate? (A) Application of the law of exercise (B) Application of the law of effect (C) Creating intrinsic motivation (D) Creating extrinsic motivation 1 B only 2 B and C only 3 A and C only 4 C only ✓ Answer: (4) C only Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, intrinsic motivation The concept Why this one Hands-on, inquiry-based, relevant tasks make learning interesting in itself, so students work because they want to. (3) A and C only C is right, but A, Edward Thorndike's law of exercise, concerns strengthening bonds through repetition and drill, not inquiry or relevance. What do you call the attention that is drawn automatically to a stimulus without the intention of the participant? 1 Divided attention 2 Shadowing 3 Endogenous attention 4 Exogenous attention ✓ Answer: (4) Exogenous attention Michael Posner, exogenous vs endogenous orienting The concept Why this one Exogenous attention is captured automatically, bottom-up, by a salient stimulus such as a sudden flash or a loud noise, whatever the person intends. Contrast Endogenous attention is voluntary and top-down: you direct it on purpose, to serve a goal or follow a cue such as an arrow. Exam tip In Michael Posner 's cueing task, a flash at the target location works fast and automatically; a central arrow works more slowly and needs intention. Why the other options are wrong (1) Divided attention This means spreading attention across two or more tasks at once, as in driving while talking; it concerns capacity, not automatic capture. (2) Shadowing This is the dichotic listening technique of repeating one ear's message aloud, used by Colin Cherry to study selective attention. (3) Endogenous attention The opposite: voluntary, goal-directed (top-down) attention, which needs the participant's intention. Which one of the following terms denotes that there are qualities of experience that cannot be explained in terms of combinations of traditional kinds of sensations? 1 Zeitgeist 2 Tropism 3 Gestalt Qualitaten 4 Conarium ✓ Answer: (3) Gestalt Qualitaten Christian von Ehrenfels, form qualities (1890) The concept Why this one Christian von Ehrenfels coined Gestaltqualitäten (form qualities). A melody stays the same tune in a new key though every note has changed, so the whole is not a sum of sensations. Why it matters This challenged the structuralism of Wilhelm Wundt and Edward Titchener, which built experience from elementary sensations. It paved the way for Gestalt psychology (Max Wertheimer, Wolfgang Köhler, Kurt Koffka). Exam tip Gestalt motto: the whole is different from the sum of its parts. Why the other options are wrong (1) Zeitgeist Means 'spirit of the times', the intellectual climate of an era, a term Edwin Boring used in his history of psychology. (2) Tropism In Jacques Loeb's work, an automatic, forced orientation of an organism towards or away from a stimulus such as light. (4) Conarium The old name for the pineal gland, which René Descartes saw as the point where mind and body interact. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is released by which of the following? 1 Adrenal cortex 2 Adrenal medulla 3 Anterior pituitary 4 Posterior pituitary ✓ Answer: (4) Posterior pituitary Hypothalamus and posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) The concept Why this one ADH ( vasopressin ) is made by neurons in the hypothalamus, travels down their axons and is released into the blood from the posterior pituitary . (3) Anterior pituitary Makes and releases its own hormones, such as growth hormone, ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH and prolactin, under control of hypothalamic releasing hormones. Which of the following dimensions are essential to be mastered in multicultural counseling, as per McFadden's transcultural perspective? Which one of the following models proposes that there are three major functional units of the brain: focussing on sustaining attention; receiving and storing information; and planning and self-monitoring? 1 PASS model 2 Kar and Parrila's model 3 Atkinson and Shiffrin model 4 Hunt's model ✓ Answer: (1) PASS model J. Das, Jack Naglieri and John Kirby is built on Alexander Luria 's three functional units of the brain. The three units Unit 1 (brainstem, reticular system): arousal and attention . Which of the following are the components of Metacognition? Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R. Who among the following conducted one of the most famous and controversial experiments in the area of obedience? 1 Sherif 2 Asch 3 Milgram 4 Cialdini ✓ Answer: (3) Milgram Stanley Milgram, obedience studies at Yale (1963) The concept Why this one Stanley Milgram had participants, as 'teachers', give what they thought were rising electric shocks to a 'learner'. Teplov, while discussing strong/weak nervous systems, believed that the point of 'transmarginal inhibition' is the point beyond which: 1 The magnitude of response decreases as stimulus intensity decreases 2 The magnitude of response increases as stimulus intensity decreases 3 The magnitude of response increases irrespective of stimulus intensity decrease/increase 4 The magnitude of response decreases irrespective of stimulus intensity decrease/increase ✓ Best answer: (2) The magnitude of response increases as stimulus intensity decreases Boris Teplov, after Ivan Pavlov's law of strength The concept Why this one Below the threshold of transmarginal inhibition , response grows with stimulus intensity. Beyond it the relation reverses: stronger stimuli give weaker responses, so lowering intensity makes the response rise, as (2) says. How it works Ivan Pavlov saw transmarginal (protective) inhibition as the nervous system shielding itself from overload. Boris Teplov measured strength of the nervous system by how high this threshold lies. Strong vs weak A strong nervous system tolerates intense stimulation before inhibition sets in; a weak one is more sensitive and reaches the point sooner. Not certain The options look garbled: the real idea is that response falls as intensity rises, which (2) states in reverse, while (1) would be right if its second 'decreases' was meant to be 'increases'. Why the other options are wrong (1) The magnitude of response decreases as stimulus intensity decreases Below the threshold, response falls when intensity falls; that is the ordinary law of strength, not what happens beyond transmarginal inhibition. (3) The magnitude of response increases irrespective of stimulus intensity decrease/increase Beyond the threshold, response still depends on intensity, but inversely; it does not keep rising whatever the stimulus does. (4) The magnitude of response decreases irrespective of stimulus intensity decrease/increase Response does not fall whatever happens: beyond the threshold it falls when intensity rises but recovers when intensity is lowered. Which of the following were considered to be appropriate for psychological study by Wundt? (A) Analysis of cultural products (B) Higher mental processes (C) The totality of psychological phenomena (D) Self-observation (E) Physiological type of experimentation 1 B, C and D only 2 B, C, D and E only 3 A, D and E only 4 A, C, D and E only ✓ Best answer: (4) A, C, D and E only Wilhelm Wundt, experimental psychology and Völkerpsychologie The concept Why this one Wilhelm Wundt defined psychology as the study of the whole content of immediate experience (C). List I: (A) Aggression (B) Anti-Social Aggression (C) Prosocial Aggression (D) Sanctioned Aggression. Arrange the pairings of US and CS in classical conditioning in terms of onset of US in relation to CS, starting from the earliest. (A) Backward (B) Simultaneous (C) Delayed (D) Trace 1 A, B, C, D 2 D, B, C, A 3 C, D, B, A 4 D, C, A, B ✓ Answer: (1) A, B, C, D Pavlovian conditioning: CS-US timing procedures The concept Correct order Backward (US comes before the CS) → Simultaneous (US starts with the CS) → Delayed (US starts while the CS is still on) → Trace (US starts only after the CS has ended). How it works The conditioned stimulus (CS) is the signal and the unconditioned stimulus (US) is the event it predicts. Moving from backward to trace, the US arrives later and later relative to CS onset. Exam tip Delayed conditioning usually gives the strongest learning; trace weakens as the gap grows; backward conditioning is the weakest and often produces inhibition. Why the other options are wrong (2) D, B, C, A Puts trace first, but in trace conditioning the US arrives only after the CS has ended, so its onset is the latest, not the earliest. (3) C, D, B, A Starts with delayed and ends with backward, nearly reversing the order; backward is the only procedure in which the US comes before the CS. (4) D, C, A, B Places trace and delayed ahead of backward and simultaneous, when those two have the earliest US onset. The Door in the Face Technique is based on which tactic of compliance? 1 Tactics based on reciprocity 2 Tactics based on commitment or consistency 3 Tactics based on friendship or liking 4 Tactics based on scarcity ✓ Answer: (1) Tactics based on reciprocity Robert Cialdini, door-in-the-face technique The concept Why this one In the door-in-the-face technique a large request is refused, then the asker retreats to a smaller one. Classic example Robert Cialdini 's team asked students to counsel young offenders two hours a week for two years (refused), then to take them on a two-hour zoo trip; far more agreed than when asked for the zoo trip alone.
