Why the other options are wrong (2) Tactics based on commitment or consistency This group covers foot-in-the-door and lowball, which build on an earlier small yes, not on a refused large request. (3) Tactics based on friendship or liking This group covers ingratiation, flattery and self-presentation, which work by making the target like the requester. (4) Tactics based on scarcity This group covers playing hard to get and the deadline technique, which make an offer seem rare or short-lived. Cognitive theory contends that dependency behaviours arise from and are maintained by cognitive distortions and maladaptive thought processes. Which of the following are associated with cognitive distortions? (A) Availability (B) Hindsight bias (C) Flexible attribution (D) Illusion of control 1 A, B, C and D 2 A, B and C only 3 B, C and D only 4 C and D only ✓ Answer: (1) A, B, C and D Cognitive model of gambling and other dependencies The concept Why this one All four are recognised cognitive distortions in problem gambling and other dependencies. Each keeps the person believing that carrying on will pay off. Availability, hindsight Availability : vivid, easily recalled wins seem more common than they are. Hindsight bias : after an outcome the person feels it was predictable, so they trust their future predictions. Attribution, control Flexible attribution : wins are credited to skill, losses blamed on bad luck or near misses. Illusion of control (Ellen Langer): belief that one can influence chance outcomes. Exam tip Add the gambler's fallacy (a win is 'due' after a run of losses) to the same list. Why the other options are wrong (2) A, B and C only Leaves out illusion of control, the best known gambling distortion, in which a person believes skill or rituals can sway chance outcomes. (3) B, C and D only Leaves out availability: vividly remembered wins feel more frequent than they are, which feeds continued gambling or use. (4) C and D only Leaves out availability and hindsight bias, both standard distortions that make wins seem common and outcomes seem predictable. What does 'Absolute Poverty' mean? 1 Poverty in terms of absolute number of people 2 Poverty in terms of prevailing price level 3 Poverty in terms of absolute level of unemployment 4 Basic minimum calorie requirement ✓ Answer: (4) Basic minimum calorie requirement Indian poverty line, minimum calorie norm The concept Why this one Absolute poverty means income too low to meet basic needs. In India it has been measured by the money needed for a minimum calorie intake : 2,400 kcal per person per day in rural areas and 2,100 in urban areas. Absolute vs relative Relative poverty compares a person's income with others in the same society; absolute poverty uses a fixed minimum standard, however others live. Exam tip The poverty line is the money value of that minimum consumption basket; people below it are counted as absolutely poor. Why the other options are wrong (1) Poverty in terms of absolute number of people The number of poor people is the headcount, a way of counting poverty, not its meaning; absolute poverty refers to a fixed minimum standard of living. (2) Poverty in terms of prevailing price level Prices are used to turn the minimum consumption basket into a money poverty line, but absolute poverty itself is defined by the minimum needs. (3) Poverty in terms of absolute level of unemployment Unemployment is a cause and correlate of poverty, not the definition of absolute poverty. In cognitive therapy by Ellis, arrange the sequence of the following after recognising the activating event. (A) Discriminating the new emotional/behavioural consequences (B) Recognising the emotional/behavioural consequences of belief (C) Understanding the corresponding beliefs (D) Challenging and counteracting these beliefs (E) Recognising new feelings 1 B-C-A-E-D 2 C-B-D-A-E 3 C-B-A-E-D 4 B-C-D-A-E ✓ Best answer: (4) B-C-D-A-E Albert Ellis, REBT ABCDE model The concept Correct order After the activating event : recognise the emotional and behavioural consequences (B), find the beliefs behind them (C), dispute the beliefs (D), discriminate the new consequences (A), recognise new feelings (E). So B-C-D-A-E. Why consequence first The client arrives with the upsetting feeling, so the therapist assesses the consequence first and then looks for the corresponding irrational belief that produced it. How it works Albert Ellis held that events do not upset us directly; our irrational beliefs about them do. Disputing those beliefs produces a more effective outlook and healthier feelings. Exam tip ABCDEF = Activating event, Belief, Consequence, Disputing, Effect (new effective philosophy), new Feelings, as set out by Gerald Corey. Not certain Read by the letters of the ABC model, the belief comes before the consequence, which gives C-B-D-A-E, option (2), the runner-up. Why the other options are wrong (1) B-C-A-E-D Starts right with consequences then beliefs, but leaves disputing to the end, when disputing must come before any new consequences or feelings appear. (2) C-B-D-A-E Puts the belief first, the literal letter order of ABC; in practice the therapist starts from the upsetting consequence and then finds the corresponding belief. (3) C-B-A-E-D Puts the belief first and places the new consequences and feelings before disputing, when they are the result of disputing. Match List I with List II. List I (Sources of Personal Efficacy by Bandura): (A) Performance accomplishment (B) Vicarious experiences (C) Verbal persuasion (D) Emotional arousal. List II (Therapeutic processes): (I) Live models, symbolic modelling (II) Attribution, relaxation biofeedback, symbolic desensitisation (III) Participant modelling, performance exposure (IV) Suggestion, exhortation, self-instruction. Choose the correct answer from the options given below: 1 A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I 2 A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV 3 A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV 4 A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II ✓ Answer: (4) A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II Albert Bandura, self-efficacy theory (1977) The concept Correct pairs (A) Performance accomplishment = (III) participant modelling, performance exposure; (B) Vicarious experience = (I) live and symbolic modelling; (C) Verbal persuasion = (IV) suggestion, exhortation, self-instruction; (D) Emotional arousal = (II) attribution, relaxation biofeedback, symbolic desensitisation. How it works Self-efficacy is the belief that one can carry out a behaviour. Albert Bandura named four sources of it, and each therapy raises efficacy through one of them. Exam tip Performance accomplishments (mastery experiences) are the strongest source, because they rest on one's own success. Why the other options are wrong (1) A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I Gives vicarious experience the arousal methods (II) and emotional arousal the modelling methods (I); watching models is the vicarious source. (2) A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV Swaps the first two sources: participant modelling is a performance method, while live and symbolic modelling are vicarious; it also swaps persuasion and arousal. (3) A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV Every pair is wrong: relaxation and biofeedback lower emotional arousal, live models are vicarious, and suggestion and exhortation are verbal persuasion. Who believed that meaning in life can be uncovered by creative, experiential and attitudinal values? 1 Rollo May 2 Victor Frankl 3 Friedrich Nietzsche 4 Jean Paul Sartre ✓ Answer: (2) Victor Frankl Viktor Frankl, logotherapy The concept Why this one Viktor Frankl said meaning is found three ways: creative values (what we give the world through work or deeds), experiential values (what we take from it, such as love or beauty) and attitudinal values (the stand we take toward unavoidable suffering). Background Frankl, a concentration camp survivor, founded logotherapy and saw the will to meaning as the main human motive (Man's Search for Meaning). Exam tip Attitudinal values remain even when nothing can be changed: a person can still choose their attitude to suffering. Why the other options are wrong (1) Rollo May American existential psychologist who wrote on anxiety, love and will and the courage to create, not on the three value routes to meaning. (3) Friedrich Nietzsche German philosopher of the will to power and the Übermensch; Frankl quoted his line that one who has a why to live can bear almost any how. (4) Jean Paul Sartre French existentialist who held that existence precedes essence and that we create meaning through free choice, not through three types of value. Which of the following is an attitude measure that places a single adjective in the centre of an even number of numerical values? 1 Edwards scale 2 Thurstone scale 3 Stapel scale 4 Semantic differential scale ✓ Answer: (3) Stapel scale Jan Stapel, unipolar rating scale The concept Why this one The Stapel scale puts one adjective (say 'Friendly') in the middle of a column of numbers, usually +5 to -5 with no zero. The respondent picks how well the word describes the object. How it differs It is a one-pole version of the semantic differential , so there is no need to find an exact opposite adjective for each item. Exam tip Stapel = single adjective, even number of points (10). Semantic differential = two bipolar adjectives at the ends of a usually seven-point line. Why the other options are wrong (1) Edwards scale Allen Edwards is known for the scale discrimination technique, which blends Thurstone and Likert methods, and for work on social desirability; no central adjective is used. (2) Thurstone scale Louis Thurstone's method of equal-appearing intervals has judges rate statements on an 11-point scale; respondents then endorse statements of known scale value. (4) Semantic differential scale Charles Osgood's tool places the object between two opposite adjectives (good to bad) on a usually seven-point scale, not one adjective in the centre. Total cholesterol is determined by adding which of the following values? 1 HDL + LDL 2 HDL + LDL + 30% of VLDL 3 HDL + LDL + 10% of VLDL 4 HDL + LDL + 20% of Triglycerides ✓ Answer: (4) HDL + LDL + 20% of Triglycerides Friedewald formula: VLDL cholesterol = triglycerides ÷ 5 The concept Why this one Total cholesterol is the cholesterol carried in HDL , LDL and VLDL . VLDL cholesterol is estimated as triglycerides ÷ 5, that is 20% of triglycerides (in mg/dL). How it works Labs use the same relation rearranged, the Friedewald formula : LDL = total cholesterol - HDL - (triglycerides ÷ 5). Exam tip High LDL ('bad') raises the risk of coronary heart disease ; high HDL ('good') protects against it. Why the other options are wrong (1) HDL + LDL Leaves out VLDL cholesterol, which carries part of the blood's cholesterol, so this sum would underestimate the total. (2) HDL + LDL + 30% of VLDL VLDL counts in full, not as 30%; the one-fifth rule applies to triglycerides, which are used to estimate VLDL. (3) HDL + LDL + 10% of VLDL Same error: the whole VLDL value counts; only triglycerides are scaled, by one fifth, to estimate it. What is the correct sequence of transformation in integral yoga? (A) Transformation of physical (B) Transformation of subconscient (C) Transformation of mind (D) Transformation of vital (E) Transformation of inconscient 1 C, D, A, B, E 2 A, C, D, B, E 3 A, D, C, B, E 4 C, A, D, B, E ✓ Answer: (1) C, D, A, B, E Sri Aurobindo, Integral Yoga The concept Correct order Mind (C) → vital (D) → physical (A) → subconscient (B) → inconscient (E). How it works In Sri Aurobindo 's Integral Yoga the higher consciousness descends from above, so the parts of the being change from the top down: first the mind, then the vital (life force, desires, emotions), then the body, and lastly the hidden subconscient and inconscient bases. Exam tip The deeper the level, the later and harder its change; the inconscient is the last and most resistant. Why the other options are wrong (2) A, C, D, B, E Starts with the physical, but in Integral Yoga the body is among the last parts to change; the descent begins with the mind. (3) A, D, C, B, E Reverses mind, vital and physical, working upward from the body, whereas Aurobindo's transformation works downward from the mind. (4) C, A, D, B, E Puts the physical before the vital, but the vital (desires and emotions) lies between mind and body and is transformed before the body. What comprises haptic perception? (A) Shape (B) Size (C) Volume (D) Identity 1 A, B and C only 2 A, C and D only 3 B, C and D only 4 A, B and D only ✓ Best answer: (4) A, B and D only James J. Gibson, active touch; Susan Lederman and Roberta Klatzky The concept Why this one Haptic perception is perception by active touch: the hand moves over an object. It gives the object's shape and size and lets us recognise what it is (its identity), often within a couple of seconds without looking. How it works Hand movements combine skin input with kinaesthetic information from muscles and joints. Susan Lederman and Roberta Klatzky described exploratory procedures: contour following for shape, lateral motion for texture, pressure for hardness. Exam tip Tactile (passive) perception = touch applied to a still hand; haptic = active exploration, the distinction drawn by James J. Gibson. Not certain Volume can also be judged by enclosing an object in the hand, so (1) is defensible; the item seems to follow a definition listing shape, size and identity. Why the other options are wrong (1) A, B and C only Drops identity, yet recognising what an object is by touch alone (haptic object recognition) is a main function of haptic perception. (2) A, C and D only Drops size, which active touch judges directly, for example from how far the fingers spread around an object. (3) B, C and D only Drops shape, the property most clearly given by haptic exploration, especially by tracing an object's contours with the fingers. Which neurotransmitter is helpful in synaptic plasticity? 1 Acetylcholine 2 Glutamate 3 GABA 4 Dopamine ✓ Answer: (2) Glutamate Timothy Bliss and Terje Lømo, long-term potentiation The concept Why this one Glutamate , the brain's main excitatory transmitter, drives long-term potentiation (LTP) , the best studied form of synaptic plasticity, especially in the hippocampus. How it works When the cell is depolarised enough to remove the magnesium block, glutamate opens NMDA receptors . Calcium flows in and triggers changes, such as extra AMPA receptors, that strengthen the synapse. Exam tip The NMDA receptor is a coincidence detector (it needs glutamate and depolarisation together), a cellular version of Donald Hebb's rule. Why the other options are wrong (1) Acetylcholine The transmitter at the neuromuscular junction and in attention and memory circuits (lost in Alzheimer's disease); LTP itself depends mainly on glutamate. (3) GABA The main inhibitory transmitter; it opposes the depolarisation that NMDA-dependent plasticity needs. (4) Dopamine Signals reward and prediction error and can modulate plasticity, but it does not directly induce LTP. What is the correct sequence of the Decision Making Perspective of Pro-social behaviour to help a person in distress? (A) Taking personal responsibility (B) Weighing the cost and benefits (C) Perceiving a need (D) Deciding how to help 1 A, C, B, D 2 B, A, C, D 3 A, B, C, D 4 C, A, B, D ✓ Answer: (4) C, A, B, D Shelley Taylor, Letitia Peplau, David Sears: decision model of helping The concept Correct order Perceiving a need (C) → taking personal responsibility (A) → weighing costs and benefits (B) → deciding how to help (D), then acting. How it works A bystander must first notice the event and interpret it as an emergency, then feel personally responsible , then judge whether the rewards of helping outweigh the costs, and only then choose what to do. Exam tip Diffusion of responsibility blocks the second step: the more bystanders, the less each feels responsible (Bibb Latané and John Darley's bystander studies). Why the other options are wrong (1) A, C, B, D Puts responsibility before noticing the need; no one can take responsibility for a problem they have not yet perceived. (2) B, A, C, D Starts by weighing costs and benefits, which comes only after the need is perceived and responsibility accepted. (3) A, B, C, D Puts taking responsibility first and perceiving the need third; the model begins with noticing and interpreting the situation. Comprehension (Q91-Q95): A researcher wanted to predict academic achievement using Intelligence Test-A (IT-A), Intelligence Test-B (IT-B), Type of school (rural/urban), and conscientiousness as predictors, using multiple regression analysis on data from 200 students. The OLS estimator was used. For the entire model F = 8.9, p < .01. In individual predictor analysis, IT-B was the insignificant predictor. A suitable test indicated homoscedasticity. The model R² = 0.64 and adjusted R² = 0.59. Both intelligence tests are significantly correlated with the criterion variable and with each other. What is indicated by R² in the passage? 1 64% variance is explained 2 80% variance is explained 3 32% variance is explained 4 36% variance is explained ✓ Answer: (1) 64% variance is explained Coefficient of determination (R²) The concept Why this one R² , the coefficient of determination, is the share of criterion variance explained by all predictors together. R² = 0.64, so 0.64 × 100 = 64% of the variance in academic achievement is explained. Adjusted R² Adjusted R² (0.59) corrects for the number of predictors and sample size, so it is slightly smaller; 59% is the better estimate for the population. Exam tip Unexplained variance = 1 - R² = 0.36 (36%). The multiple correlation R = √0.64 = 0.80. Why the other options are wrong (2) 80% variance is explained This is the multiple correlation R (√0.64 = 0.80) read as a percentage; variance explained uses the squared value, R². (3) 32% variance is explained Half of R²; nothing in the conversion halves R², which reads directly as 64%. (4) 36% variance is explained This is 1 - R², the share of variance the predictors leave unexplained. Which of the following is correct about the residual variance in the passage? 1 It is correlated with the predictor variable 2 It is correlated with the criterion variable 3 It is systematically distributed 4 It is randomly distributed ✓ Answer: (4) It is randomly distributed OLS regression assumptions, homoscedastic residuals The concept Why this one The test showed homoscedasticity : residuals spread equally at every level of the predicted score. With the OLS assumptions met, residuals are randomly distributed around zero with no pattern. What residuals are A residual is observed minus predicted score (Y - Ŷ). OLS picks the weights that make the sum of squared residuals smallest, and by construction leaves residuals uncorrelated with the predictors. Exam tip A funnel or curve in the residual plot signals heteroscedasticity or non-linearity, that is, systematic error. Why the other options are wrong (1) It is correlated with the predictor variable OLS residuals are uncorrelated with every predictor by construction; any such correlation would mean the model had missed predictable variance. (2) It is correlated with the criterion variable Residuals are part of the criterion score, so some overlap with it is built in; the assumption that matters is that they show no systematic pattern. (3) It is systematically distributed A systematic pattern, such as a funnel or curve, would signal heteroscedasticity or a mis-specified model, the opposite of what the test found. What kind of a variable is 'type of school' in the passage? 1 Moderator variable 2 Mediator variable 3 Dummy variable 4 Quasi-continuous variable ✓ Answer: (3) Dummy variable Dummy coding of categorical predictors The concept Why this one Type of school has two categories (rural, urban). To enter it in a regression it is coded 0 and 1 (rural = 0, urban = 1), which makes it a dummy variable . How it works The weight of a dummy variable is the difference in predicted achievement between urban and rural students, other predictors held constant. A variable with k categories needs k - 1 dummies. Exam tip A moderator changes the strength of an X-Y link (tested with an interaction term); a mediator carries the effect from X to Y. The passage tests neither. Why the other options are wrong (1) Moderator variable That role changes the strength or direction of a predictor-criterion link and is tested with an interaction term; school type here is simply one more predictor. (2) Mediator variable That role lies on the causal path from predictor to criterion (X → M → Y); the passage does not model school type that way. (4) Quasi-continuous variable That label fits variables with many ordered values, like rating scale totals; rural/urban has just two unordered categories. Which of the following is the reason for the insignificance of IT-B? 1 Heteroscedasticity 2 Poor predictive power 3 Small sample size 4 Multicollinearity ✓ Answer: (4) Multicollinearity Multicollinearity in multiple regression The concept Why this one IT-B correlates with achievement but also with IT-A. Once IT-A is in the model, IT-B adds little unique variance and its standard error inflates, so its weight is not significant. This is multicollinearity . How it works Regression weights reflect each predictor's unique contribution . When two predictors overlap, the variance they share is not credited to either one. Exam tip Check it with the variance inflation factor (VIF) or tolerance; VIF above 10 (tolerance below 0.1) is a common warning sign. Why the other options are wrong (1) Heteroscedasticity Ruled out: the passage says a suitable test showed homoscedasticity. (2) Poor predictive power IT-B is significantly correlated with achievement, so on its own it does predict; it loses significance only because its variance overlaps with IT-A. (3) Small sample size 200 students for four predictors is ample, and the other predictors reached significance in the same sample. Which of the following is the df for F for the entire model? 1 4; 195 2 4; 199 3 3; 196 4 3; 199 ✓ Answer: (1) 4; 195 F-test degrees of freedom in regression The concept Why this one For the whole model, df 1 (regression) = k = number of predictors = 4 , and df 2 (residual) = N - k - 1 = 200 - 4 - 1 = 195 . How it works F = mean square regression ÷ mean square residual, each mean square being its sum of squares divided by its df. Total df = N - 1 = 199 = 4 + 195. Exam tip The extra 1 subtracted in the residual df is for the intercept. Why the other options are wrong (2) 4; 199 199 is the total df (N - 1); the residual df must also lose one df for each of the four predictors. (3) 3; 196 There are four predictors (IT-A, IT-B, school type, conscientiousness), not three, so df 1 = 4 and df 2 = 195. (4) 3; 199 Uses three predictors and the total df; the model has four predictors, and the residual df is 195. Comprehension (Q96-Q100): A psychologist developed a scale measuring warmth and competence dimensions. She factor-analysed 25 items to retain 20 items, choosing Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA). Bartlett's test = 237.8, p < .001. The overall Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure was 0.89. Principal Components Analysis (PCA) was used to extract components. The first eight eigenvalues were 9.9, 6.5, 1.6, 1.00, 0.85, 0.83, 0.82 and 0.79. Factors were retained on the basis of the scree plot and rotated using the varimax criterion. Three items showed cross-loadings, eighteen items loaded on only one factor, and the remaining items did not load on any factor. The Bartlett's test results in the above study suggested that: 1 The population correlation matrix is not an identity matrix 2 The population correlation matrix is an identity matrix 3 The sample correlation matrix is not an identity matrix 4 The sample correlation matrix is an identity matrix ✓ Answer: (1) The population correlation matrix is not an identity matrix Bartlett's test of sphericity The concept Why this one Bartlett's test of sphericity tests the null hypothesis that the population correlation matrix is an identity matrix. Here the value is 237.8, p What it is An identity matrix has 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere, meaning no item correlates with any other. Then there would be no common factors to extract. Exam tip A significant Bartlett test plus KMO above 0.6 (here 0.89) shows the data suit factor analysis. Why the other options are wrong (2) The population correlation matrix is an identity matrix This is the null hypothesis, which the significant result (p (3) The sample correlation matrix is not an identity matrix Significance tests make inferences about the population; the sample matrix is observed directly and is almost never exactly an identity matrix. (4) The sample correlation matrix is an identity matrix The test concerns the population, not the sample, and the significant result points away from an identity matrix, not towards one. Which of the following is correct for the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin test? (A) It is a test of sampling adequacy (B) Chi-square test is used to test the significance (C) Values smaller than 0.5 are desirable (D) Smaller partial correlation leads to high KMO 1 A only 2 A and B only 3 A and D only 4 B, C and D only ✓ Answer: (3) A and D only Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure of sampling adequacy The concept Why this one A is true: KMO is a measure of sampling adequacy . D is true: KMO compares simple correlations with partial correlations , so small partials give a high KMO. Why B, C false B: KMO is an index from 0 to 1 with no chi-square test; chi-square belongs to Bartlett's test . C: values below 0.5 are unacceptable; higher is better. How it works KMO = Σr² ÷ (Σr² + Σpartial r²). When items share common factors, partial correlations are small and KMO nears 1. The passage's 0.89 is 'meritorious' on Henry Kaiser 's labels. Why the other options are wrong (1) A only A is true but incomplete: D is also true, because KMO rises as partial correlations shrink relative to simple correlations. (2) A and B only B is false: KMO is a descriptive index from 0 to 1; the chi-square significance test belongs to Bartlett's test of sphericity. (4) B, C and D only B and C are false: KMO has no chi-square test, and values below 0.5 make the data unacceptable for factor analysis; it also omits the true statement A. Which of the following is correct in case of the three items having cross-loading? 1 They have excellent validity 2 They are conceptually sound items 3 The scale has poor reliability 4 They should not be retained in the final scale ✓ Answer: (4) They should not be retained in the final scale Louis Thurstone, simple structure The concept Why this one A cross-loading item loads substantially on two or more factors, so it does not measure one dimension cleanly. In scale building such items are usually dropped . Simple structure Louis Thurstone's simple structure asks that each item load highly on one factor and near zero on the rest; varimax rotation aims at this. Exam tip Items that load on no factor , like the remaining items in the passage, are also deleted. Why the other options are wrong (1) They have excellent validity Cross-loading weakens construct validity, because the item does not clearly belong to warmth or to competence. (2) They are conceptually sound items An item that loads on two dimensions is conceptually ambiguous, not sound; its wording probably taps both constructs. (3) The scale has poor reliability Cross-loading is a problem of factorial validity for three items; by itself it says nothing about the reliability of the whole scale. In the above example, what percentage of the variance would be explained by the first unrotated factor? 1 9.9 2 39.6 3 65.6 4 72.0 ✓ Answer: (2) 39.6 Variance explained = eigenvalue ÷ number of variables The concept Why this one In PCA each standardised item contributes 1 unit of variance, so total variance = number of items analysed = 25 . Variance explained = eigenvalue ÷ items × 100 = 9.9 ÷ 25 × 100 = 39.6% . What an eigenvalue is An eigenvalue is the sum of squared loadings of all items on a component, that is, how much of the total variance it captures. Exam tip Rotation (varimax) redistributes variance among the retained factors, which is why the question asks about the unrotated factor. Why the other options are wrong (1) 9.9 This is the eigenvalue itself, not a percentage; it must be divided by the 25 items to give the share of total variance. (3) 65.6 This is the cumulative variance of the first two components: (9.9 + 6.5) ÷ 25 = 16.4 ÷ 25 = 65.6%. (4) 72.0 This is the cumulative variance of the first three components: (9.9 + 6.5 + 1.6) ÷ 25 = 18 ÷ 25 = 72%. Using the Kaiser-Guttman criterion, how many factors would be retained in the above study? 1 4 2 8 3 2 4 3 ✓ Answer: (4) 3 Louis Guttman and Henry Kaiser, eigenvalue-greater-than-one rule The concept Why this one The Kaiser-Guttman criterion keeps components with eigenvalues greater than 1 . Only 9.9, 6.5 and 1.6 exceed 1, so 3 factors are kept; the fourth value, 1.00, is not greater than 1. Why 1 A component with an eigenvalue below 1 explains less variance than a single standardised item , so it is not worth keeping. Exam tip The rule often keeps too many factors; the scree plot (Raymond Cattell) and parallel analysis are better guides. Here the sharp drop after 6.5 points to two factors, warmth and competence. Why the other options are wrong (1) 4 Counts the eigenvalue of exactly 1.00, but the criterion keeps only values greater than 1, so the fourth component is dropped. (2) 8 This is just the number of eigenvalues reported; four of them are below 1 and one is exactly 1. (3) 2 This is what the scree plot suggests (the elbow after 6.5) and fits the two-dimension theory, but the Kaiser-Guttman count is 3.

title: Statistics and Research Methods for Clinical Psychology Entrances
text: Statistics and Research Methods for Clinical Psychology Entrances Everything from scales of measurement (Stanley Smith Stevens, 1946) to MANCOVA, factor analysis and item response theory, then the whole of research methods (designs, validity, single-case, qualitative, trials, ethics), built from scratch, with a diagram on every idea that has a shape. This is a book, not a cheat sheet. Every concept is built from the ground up: what the thing is, why it exists, the formula with every symbol named, a worked example with real numbers, the assumptions it stands on, what breaks it, and who invented it. Read it cold and you will understand statistics and research design, not just recognise the words. Part I (sections 1 to 17) is statistics; Part II (sections 18 to 27) is research methods. The 64 diagrams are drawn from the actual functions or from real numbers, so the normal curve really is a normal curve, the F distribution really is an F distribution, and every single-case graph, time series and forest plot is computed. 27 sections 64 diagrams 60+ named statisticians 100+ research-methods names Every test with its assumptions Built for IHBAS · CIP · RML · JSS · DIMHANS · Amity · SGT · NIMHANS 1 · Variables and scales of measurement 2 · Frequency distributions and graphs 3 · Central tendency 4 · Dispersion 5 · Skewness and kurtosis 6 · The normal curve and standard scores 7 · Probability, sampling and the sampling distribution 8 · Hypothesis testing, errors, power, effect size 9 · The t tests 10 · ANOVA 11 · ANCOVA, MANOVA, MANCOVA 12 · Correlation 13 · Regression 14 · Non-parametric tests 15 · Psychometrics 16 · Which test to use 17 · Formula sheet and who-did-what index Part II: Research methods 18 · The research process: science, problems, hypotheses and variables 19 · Validity of a study and the control of extraneous variables 20 · Experimental and quasi-experimental designs 21 · Non-experimental designs: correlational, developmental and epidemiological 22 · Single-subject (small-N) designs 23 · Collecting the data: observation, interviews, questionnaires and scaling 24 · Qualitative and mixed-methods research 25 · Clinical trials, evidence and meta-analysis 26 · Research ethics 27 · Which design to use, the research-methods name index, and the traps How to use this book. First pass: read sections 1 to 8 straight through, because everything later is built on them. Second pass: sections 9 to 14 are the test family; do not memorise formulas, memorise the question each test answers and the assumptions it needs , because that is what entrance papers ask. Third pass: section 15 (psychometrics) is worth as many marks as ANOVA in most of these papers and is usually the least prepared. Section 16 is the decision tree; if you can walk it without looking, you can answer any "which test would you apply" item. Section 17 is the night-before page. Part II (sections 18 to 27) is research methods: read 18 to 20 in order, because validity and the threats in 19 are the language every design in 20 to 22 is judged in; 23 to 26 can be read in any order; 27 is the which-design tree, the name index and the traps. 1 Variables and scales of measurement Statistics is a set of tools for one job: getting from what you observed in a handful of people to a defensible statement about people in general. Everything in this book is either describing what you have (descriptive statistics) or generalising beyond what you have (inferential statistics). Keep that split in your head; it is the first line of a hundred exam answers. 1.1 The vocabulary you cannot skip Term Meaning Symbol Population The entire set of people or observations you actually want to talk about. Usually hypothetical and never fully measured. N Sample The subset you actually measured. Statistics exists because samples are all you ever get. n Parameter A number describing the population . Fixed, unknown, written with Greek letters. μ, σ, ρ, π Statistic A number describing the sample . Known, varies from sample to sample, written with Roman letters. M or X̄, s, r, p Variable Any characteristic that takes more than one value. X, Y Constant A characteristic that takes only one value in your study. – Datum / data A single recorded observation / the set of them. Xᵢ The rule that generates half the notation questions: Greek letters are for populations, Roman letters are for samples. μ is the population mean, M (or X̄) is the sample mean. σ is the population SD, s is the sample SD. ρ (rho) is the population correlation, r is the sample correlation. β is the population regression weight, b is the sample one. Types of variable Independent variable (IV): the one the experimenter manipulates or selects. The presumed cause. Also called the predictor (in regression) or the factor (in ANOVA). Its values are called levels . Dependent variable (DV): the one you measure. The presumed effect. Also called the criterion or the outcome. Extraneous variable: anything else that could affect the DV. Controlled by randomisation, matching, holding constant, or statistically (ANCOVA). Confounding variable: an extraneous variable that actually varies systematically with the IV , so its effect is inseparable from the IV's. A confound is an extraneous variable that got away. Mediator: the variable through which the IV acts (X → M → Y). Explains how or why . Tested by Baron and Kenny's (1986) steps or by Sobel / bootstrapped indirect effects. Moderator: a variable that changes the strength or direction of the X–Y relation. Explains when or for whom . Statistically, a moderator is an interaction . Discrete variable: takes only separate whole values (number of children, number of hospital admissions). Continuous variable: can take any value in a range; between any two values another is possible (reaction time, IQ). Measured to a limit of precision, with real limits of ±half the smallest unit: a reported weight of 62 kg means 61.5 to 62.5. Trap: mediator and moderator are the single most confused pair in research-methods sections. Mediator = the mechanism, sits between IV and DV in the causal chain. Moderator = the condition, sits outside and changes the size of the effect. "Stress causes depression through rumination" is mediation. "Stress causes depression more strongly in people with low social support" is moderation. 1.2 The four scales of measurement (S. S. Stevens, 1946) Stanley Smith Stevens , Harvard psychophysicist, published "On the theory of scales of measurement" in Science in 1946. The four-scale taxonomy is his, and it is the single most examined single fact in the statistics section of every one of these papers. Learn it perfectly. Scale What it does Properties Examples Permissible central tendency Permissible statistics Nominal (categorical) Names / labels only. Numbers are arbitrary tags. Identity / difference only. No order, no equal intervals, no true zero. Gender, diagnosis, blood group, jersey numbers, marital status, religion Mode only Frequencies, percentages, mode, χ², phi, contingency coefficient, Cramér's V Ordinal (ranks) Orders cases, but the gaps between ranks are unequal and unknown. Identity + order. No equal intervals, no true zero. Socio-economic status, ranks in a class, Likert-type agreement, Mohs hardness, stage of illness, birth order Mode and median Median, percentiles, quartile deviation, Spearman ρ, Kendall τ, Mann–Whitney U, Kruskal–Wallis Interval Equal units, but the zero point is arbitrary. Identity + order + equal intervals. No absolute zero. Temperature in °C or °F, calendar years, IQ scores, most psychological test scores, z scores Mode, median and mean Mean, SD, Pearson r, t test, ANOVA, regression, factor analysis Ratio Equal units and a true zero meaning "none of it". All four properties. Ratios are meaningful. Height, weight, reaction time, number of errors, income, age, kelvin temperature Mode, median, mean, geometric and harmonic mean Everything, plus coefficient of variation and ratio statements Mnemonic: NOIR (French for black), in order of increasing information: N ominal, O rdinal, I nterval, R atio. Each scale keeps all the properties of the ones before it and adds one. Any statistic legal at a lower scale stays legal at a higher one; the reverse is never true. The two traps that are asked every year. (1) Temperature in Celsius is interval, not ratio , because 0°C is the freezing point of water, not the absence of heat; 40°C is not "twice as hot" as 20°C. Temperature in kelvin is ratio. (2) IQ is interval, not ratio. There is no IQ of zero meaning "no intelligence", so a person with IQ 140 is not twice as intelligent as one with 70. Strictly, IQ is arguably only ordinal, but for exam purposes it is treated as interval. Why the scale decides everything downstream. The scale of your DV is the first branch of the which-test decision tree. Nominal DV means frequencies means chi-square. Ordinal DV means ranks means the non-parametric family. Interval or ratio DV means the mean and the SD are meaningful, which means the parametric family (t, ANOVA, Pearson, regression) becomes available. If you can name the scale you have already narrowed the answer to about four tests. Two more scales worth knowing Absolute scale: a counting scale where the unit is one and cannot be changed (number of children). Some texts treat it as a fifth, strongest scale. Interval-like ordinal (quasi-interval): Likert items are ordinal per item, but a summed Likert scale of many items is conventionally treated as interval. Say this explicitly if asked; examiners like the nuance. 2 Frequency distributions and graphs Raw data is unreadable. The first act of every analysis is to impose order on it, and the tool for that is the frequency distribution. 2.1 Building a grouped frequency distribution Find the range: R = highest score − lowest score (some texts add 1 for the "inclusive range"). Choose the number of class intervals: conventionally 10 to 20. Too few hides the shape, too many defeats the purpose. Find the class interval width (i): i = R / (number of intervals), rounded to a convenient number (2, 3, 5, 10). Set the intervals so they are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, and start the lowest interval at a multiple of i. Tally and count. Term Definition Example (interval 50–59) Apparent (written) limits The limits as printed. 50 and 59 Exact / real limits The true boundaries, extending half a unit each way. Used in all computation. 49.5 and 59.5 Class interval (i) Upper real limit − lower real limit. 59.5 − 49.5 = 10 Midpoint (lower limit + upper limit) / 2. Assumed to represent every score in the interval. 54.5 Cumulative frequency (cf) Running total of frequencies up to the top of that interval. – Relative frequency f / N, usually expressed as a proportion or percentage. – 2.2 The graphs Histogram bars touch: the variable is continuous Frequency polygon midpoints joined, anchored to the baseline 50% → median Ogive (cumulative frequency) always S-shaped; read percentiles off it Same grouped frequency distribution, three standard graphs. A bar diagram differs from a histogram in one way: its bars have gaps, because the variable is categorical. The three graphs of a frequency distribution. Graph Built from Used for Distinguishing feature Bar diagram Categories on X, frequency on Y Nominal or ordinal data Bars have gaps between them, because the categories are discrete Histogram Class intervals on X, frequency on Y Continuous, grouped data Bars touch , because the variable is continuous. Area is proportional to frequency Frequency polygon Midpoints joined by straight lines Comparing two or more distributions on one axis Anchored to the baseline at both ends; area under it equals the histogram's area Frequency curve A smoothed frequency polygon Showing the underlying shape Smooth, no corners; the theoretical limit as N → ∞ and i → 0 Ogive (cumulative frequency curve) Cumulative frequency plotted at the upper real limit Reading percentiles and the median straight off the graph Always S-shaped and never decreasing. The score at 50% cumulative frequency is the median Pie chart Proportions as sectors of a circle Parts of a single whole, nominal data Each 1% = 3.6° Stem-and-leaf plot (Tukey) Leading digits as stems, trailing as leaves Small datasets Shows the shape and preserves every original value Box plot (Tukey) Five-number summary Comparing groups, spotting outliers and skew Built entirely from ranks, so extreme scores cannot distort it Scatterplot / scattergram Paired X and Y values as points Correlation and regression The only honest way to see a relationship before computing r Lower whisker Q1 − 1.5×IQR Q1 (25th %ile) Median (Q2) Q3 (75th %ile) Upper whisker Q3 + 1.5×IQR Outliers Interquartile range, IQR = Q3 − Q1 (semi-interquartile range or quartile deviation Q = IQR/2) Tukey's box-and-whisker plot. Everything in it is a rank statistic, so it is unaffected by extreme scores , that is why it is paired with the median, not the mean. Box plot (John Tukey, 1977): the five-number summary drawn. Reading a box plot for skew: if the median line sits nearer the bottom of the box and the upper whisker is longer, the distribution is positively skewed. Nearer the top with a longer lower whisker means negative skew. A centred median with equal whiskers means symmetry. 3 Central tendency A measure of central tendency is a single value that best represents the whole distribution: the point around which the scores cluster. There are three you must know cold, and two more worth naming. 3.1 The mean (arithmetic average) Definition: the sum of all scores divided by the number of scores. The balance point of the distribution. Formulas. Ungrouped sample mean: M = ΣX / n . Population mean: μ = ΣX / N . Grouped data: M = ΣfXᵐ / N , where Xᵐ is the midpoint of each interval and f its frequency. Assumed-mean (short) method: M = A + (Σfd / N) × i , where A is any assumed mean, d = (Xᵐ − A)/i, and i is the class interval. Worked example Scores: 4, 7, 7, 9, 13. ΣX = 40, n = 5, so M = 40 / 5 = 8 . The six mathematical properties of the mean (each one is an exam item) The sum of deviations about the mean is exactly zero: Σ(X − M) = 0. This is what "balance point" means, and it is why you must square deviations to get a usable measure of spread. The sum of squared deviations about the mean is a minimum: Σ(X − M)² is smaller than Σ(X − any other value)². This is the least squares property , and it is the reason regression, ANOVA and the variance are all built on the mean. Adding a constant c to every score adds c to the mean. Multiplying every score by c multiplies the mean by c. The mean is affected by every single score , so one extreme score moves it. It is not resistant. The mean of a combined group is the weighted mean: Mᵗ = (n₁M₁ + n₂M₂) / (n₁ + n₂). The mean is the most reliable measure across repeated samples , that is, it has the smallest standard error, which is why inferential statistics is built on it. Trap: the mean cannot be computed from an open-ended distribution ("60 and above"), because the top interval has no midpoint. In that situation you must use the median. 3.2 The median Definition: the value that divides the ordered distribution into two equal halves. The 50th percentile, the 2nd quartile, the 5th decile. Formulas. Ungrouped, n odd: the ((n+1)/2)th score. Ungrouped, n even: the mean of the (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th scores. Grouped: Md = L + [(N/2 − cf) / f] × i , where L is the exact lower limit of the median class, cf the cumulative frequency below it, f the frequency of the median class and i the interval width. Worked example Scores 4, 7, 7, 9, 13 (n = 5, odd): the (5+1)/2 = 3rd score, so Md = 7 . Add a sixth score of 40: ordered 4, 7, 7, 9, 13, 40; median = (7 + 9)/2 = 8 , while the mean jumps from 8 to 13.3. That single comparison is the whole argument for the median. Properties The sum of absolute deviations from the median is a minimum: Σ|X − Md| is smaller than about any other point. (The mean minimises squared deviations; the median minimises absolute ones.) It is a positional average, so it is unaffected by extreme scores : it is robust or resistant. It can be computed for open-ended distributions and for ordinal data. It cannot be manipulated algebraically the way the mean can, so it is not used in inferential statistics. 3.3 The mode Definition: the most frequently occurring score. The point of maximum density. Grouped formula (crude vs. exact). Crude mode = midpoint of the interval with the highest frequency. Exact (King's) formula: Mo = L + [(f₁ − f₀) / (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × i . Empirical relation for a moderately skewed distribution (Karl Pearson): Mo = 3Md − 2M , equivalently M − Mo = 3(M − Md) . A distribution can have no mode, one mode ( unimodal ), two ( bimodal ), or many ( multimodal ). A bimodal distribution usually means two different populations have been pooled, and that is a substantive finding, not a nuisance. It is the only measure of central tendency usable with nominal data. It is the least stable across samples and the least used inferentially. A rectangular or uniform distribution has no mode at all. 3.4 Choosing between them Use the... When Because Mean Data are interval or ratio, distribution roughly symmetrical, and you intend to do further statistics on it Most reliable, uses all the data, algebraically tractable, required by t, ANOVA and regression Median Distribution is skewed, there are outliers, the distribution is open-ended, or the data are ordinal Resistant to extreme scores; still meaningful when the mean is misleading Mode Data are nominal, or you specifically want the most typical or most common case The only legal option at nominal level; identifies the actual peak Classic applied example: income. Income distributions are strongly positively skewed, so the mean income of a country is dragged up by a few very rich people, and the median income is the honest description of the typical person. Same logic for hospital length of stay, reaction times, and number of therapy sessions attended. Two extra means worth naming Geometric mean: the nth root of the product of n scores. Used for rates of change, growth rates and ratio data. GM ≤ AM always. Harmonic mean: n divided by the sum of the reciprocals. Used for averaging rates and, in statistics, for computing the effective sample size in unequal-n ANOVA and post hoc tests. HM ≤ GM ≤ AM always. 4 Dispersion Two distributions can have the same mean and be completely different. Central tendency without dispersion is half a description. Measures of dispersion (variability, scatter, spread) tell you how far the scores stray from the centre. 4.1 Range R = highest score − lowest score. Simplest, crudest, and completely determined by the two most extreme scores, which are also the two least reliable ones. Unstable across samples. Useful only as a quick indication. 4.2 Quartile deviation (semi-interquartile range) Q = (Q₃ − Q₁) / 2 , where Q₁ is the 25th percentile and Q₃ the 75th. The interquartile range (IQR) is Q₃ − Q₁; the quartile deviation is half of it. It covers the middle 50% of scores, so it is unaffected by extreme values. It is the partner of the median : report Md and Q together, always. 4.3 Average deviation (mean deviation) AD = Σ|X − M| / N. The average distance of scores from the mean, ignoring sign. Uses all scores, which is a step up from the range, but the absolute-value operator makes it algebraically useless, so it disappeared from inferential statistics. It is minimised when taken about the median , not the mean. 4.4 Variance and standard deviation Definition: the standard deviation is the root-mean-square deviation from the mean. It is, quite literally, the typical distance a score sits from the mean, in the original units. The variance is its square. Formulas. Population variance: σ² = Σ(X − μ)² / N · population SD: σ = √[Σ(X − μ)² / N] Sample variance (unbiased estimate): s² = Σ(X − M)² / (n − 1) · sample SD: s = √[Σ(X − M)² / (n − 1)] Computational (raw-score) form: s² = [ΣX² − (ΣX)²/n] / (n − 1) The numerator Σ(X − M)² has its own name: the sum of squares (SS) . Remember that, because the whole of ANOVA is bookkeeping about sums of squares. Worked example Scores 4, 7, 7, 9, 13; M = 8. Deviations: −4, −1, −1, +1, +5. (They sum to 0, as they must.) Squared: 16, 1, 1, 1, 25. SS = 44. s² = 44 / (5 − 1) = 11.0 · s = √11 = 3.32 . If these five were the whole population: σ² = 44/5 = 8.8, σ = 2.97. Note that dividing by n gives a smaller , biased-downward answer. 4.5 Degrees of freedom: why n − 1 The idea. Degrees of freedom is the number of values in a calculation that are free to vary once the constraints are imposed. To compute the sample variance you must first compute M from the same data. That fixes one thing: the deviations must sum to zero. So if n = 5 and you know four of the deviations, the fifth is forced. Only 4 of the 5 are free. Hence df = n − 1. The consequence. Dividing SS by n gives a variance estimate that is systematically too small, because the sample mean is always closer to the sample's own scores than the population mean is. Dividing by n − 1 corrects the downward bias, and is called Bessel's correction . It makes s² an unbiased estimator of σ². Degrees of freedom for every test you will meet One-sample t: df = n − 1 · Independent t: df = n₁ + n₂ − 2 · Paired t: df = n(pairs) − 1 One-way ANOVA: df between = k − 1, df within = N − k, df total = N − 1 Two-way ANOVA: df A = a − 1, df B = b − 1, df A×B = (a−1)(b−1), df within = N − ab Repeated measures: df treatment = k − 1, df subjects = n − 1, df error = (k−1)(n−1) Pearson r significance: df = n − 2 · Simple regression: df = n − 2 · Multiple regression: df = n − k − 1 χ² goodness of fit: df = k − 1 · χ² independence: df = (r − 1)(c − 1) A general principle: df = number of observations − number of parameters you had to estimate from the data. 4.6 Coefficient of variation CV = (s / M) × 100. A relative, unit-free measure of dispersion, so it lets you compare the variability of two things measured in different units (heights in cm vs. weights in kg), or two groups with very different means. It requires a ratio scale with a meaningful zero, so it must not be used on IQ or on Celsius temperature. 4.7 Properties of the standard deviation Adding a constant to every score leaves the SD unchanged (the whole distribution shifts, the spread does not). Multiplying every score by c multiplies the SD by |c| and the variance by c². The SD is in the same units as the original scores; the variance is in squared units. That is why you report SD and analyse variance. Variances add; standard deviations do not. This is the reason ANOVA partitions variance . The SD is the most reliable measure of dispersion across repeated samples, and it is the one used in every inferential formula. It is affected by every score, including extreme ones. On badly skewed data, report the quartile deviation with the median instead. Recap of sections 1 to 4: Stevens's four scales (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio) determine which statistics are legal. A frequency distribution and its graphs (histogram, polygon, ogive, box plot) show you the shape. Central tendency locates it: the mean is the balance point and minimises squared deviations, the median is the 50th percentile and resists outliers, the mode is the peak and the only option at nominal level. Dispersion measures how wide it is: range, quartile deviation (partner of the median), average deviation, and the standard deviation (partner of the mean), whose squared numerator SS and denominator n − 1 are the foundation of everything that follows. 5 Skewness and kurtosis Central tendency gives the location, dispersion gives the width. The third and fourth properties of a distribution are its shape : how lopsided it is (skewness) and how peaked it is (kurtosis). Formally these are the third and fourth moments about the mean; the first moment is zero by definition and the second is the variance. 5.1 Skewness Mo Md M Negative skew Mean < Median < Mode long tail to the LEFT Sk < 0 Mo = Md = M Normal (symmetrical) Mean = Median = Mode no tail Sk = 0 Mo Md M Positive skew Mode < Median < Mean long tail to the RIGHT Sk > 0 Skewness. Mo = mode, Md = median, M = mean. The name of the skew follows the tail, not the hump. The mean is dragged furthest because it is the only one of the three that uses every score's value. Definition: the degree of asymmetry of a distribution. A distribution is skewed when one tail is longer than the other. Positive (right) skew Symmetrical Negative (left) skew Tail Long tail to the right, towards high scores Both tails equal Long tail to the left, towards low scores Order Mode < Median < Mean Mode = Median = Mean Mean < Median < Mode Sk > 0 = 0 < 0 Bulk of scores Low; a few very high scores stretch it out Centred High; a few very low scores stretch it out Test example A very difficult test: most people score low A well-constructed test of average difficulty A very easy test: most people score high (a ceiling effect) Real examples Income, reaction time, number of psychiatric admissions, symptom counts in a normal population Height, IQ in the general population Age at death, scores on a mastery test, life satisfaction in a healthy sample The rule that unlocks every skew item: the skew is named for the tail , not the hump, and the mean is always dragged furthest into the tail , because the mean is the only one of the three that uses each score's actual value. So the mean is always on the tail side of the median, and the mode is always at the hump. Get the mean's position and the whole ordering falls out. Formulas. Pearson's first coefficient of skewness: Sk = (M − Mo) / s Pearson's second coefficient (used when the mode is unstable): Sk = 3(M − Md) / s Bowley's quartile coefficient: Sk = (Q₃ + Q₁ − 2Md) / (Q₃ − Q₁) , bounded between −1 and +1 Moment coefficient: g₁ = m₃ / s³ , where m₃ is the third moment about the mean = Σ(X − M)³/N Interpretation rule of thumb: |Sk| under 0.5 is approximately symmetrical, 0.5 to 1.0 is moderately skewed, over 1.0 is substantially skewed. Another common working rule: skew is a problem if it exceeds twice its own standard error. What causes skew, and what to do about it Floor effect: the measure cannot go below a limit and most people are at it. Produces positive skew. Common with symptom counts and error counts in healthy samples. Ceiling effect: the measure cannot go above a limit and most people are at it. Produces negative skew. Common with easy tests. Selection: studying only the extreme end of a population. Transformations to fix positive skew: square root (mild), logarithm (moderate), reciprocal (severe). For negative skew, reflect the variable first (subtract each score from the maximum + 1), then apply the same transformation. Or switch to a non-parametric test , which does not care about the shape. 5.2 Kurtosis Leptokurtic (Ku > 3, excess > 0) Mesokurtic (normal, Ku = 3, excess = 0) Platykurtic (Ku < 3, excess < 0) All three have the same mean and the same total area. They differ in peakedness and tail weight. Excess kurtosis = Ku − 3. Leptokurtic = tall and thin with fat tails; platykurtic = flat and broad. Kurtosis: the peakedness of the distribution. Definition: the degree of peakedness of a distribution relative to the normal curve, and equivalently the heaviness of its tails. Type Shape Ku (moment) Excess kurtosis (Ku − 3) Tails Leptokurtic Tall, thin, sharply peaked ("lepto" = slender, think a leaping narrow peak) > 3 Positive Fat: more extreme scores than a normal curve Mesokurtic The normal curve itself ("meso" = middle) = 3 0 Normal Platykurtic Flat, broad, blunt ("platy" = flat, think a plateau or a platypus) < 3 Negative Thin: fewer extreme scores; in the limit, a rectangular distribution Formula. Moment coefficient of kurtosis g₂ = m₄ / s⁴ , where m₄ = Σ(X − M)⁴/N. Percentile-based: Ku = Q / (P₉₀ − P₁₀) , which equals 0.263 for a normal curve. Most software reports excess kurtosis, so a printed value of 0 means normal, not flat. Trap: SPSS and most statistical software report excess kurtosis (already minus 3). So a reported kurtosis of 0.00 means mesokurtic (normal), while a reported 3.00 means strongly leptokurtic. Exam questions almost always use the raw moment version where normal = 3. Read the question for which convention it wants. Testing normality formally Test Who Use Read it as Shapiro–Wilk Samuel Shapiro and Martin Wilk, 1965 The most powerful normality test for small to moderate n (under about 50, usable to 2000) Non-significant (p > .05) = normal. You want it to fail Kolmogorov–Smirnov Andrey Kolmogorov and Nikolai Smirnov Compares the sample cumulative distribution to the normal one; better for larger n (with the Lilliefors correction) Non-significant = normal Skewness / kurtosis z tests – Divide the coefficient by its standard error |z| > 1.96 means significant departure at .05 Q–Q plot / P–P plot – Visual check Points on the straight diagonal = normal The large-n paradox. Shapiro–Wilk and K–S become so powerful with large n that they flag trivial, harmless departures from normality as significant. With n over about 300, trust the histogram, the Q–Q plot and the skew and kurtosis values instead of the p value, and remember that the central limit theorem has already protected you. 6 The normal curve and standard scores The normal curve was derived by Abraham de Moivre in 1733 as the limit of the binomial, developed by Pierre-Simon Laplace , and applied to measurement error by Carl Friedrich Gauss (hence "Gaussian"). The percentages are fixed properties of the curve, which is why one z score converts into every other standard score. 6.1 Properties of the normal probability curve Bell-shaped and perfectly symmetrical about the mean. Skewness = 0. Mean = median = mode , all at the centre. Asymptotic: the tails approach the X axis but never touch it, so the curve extends from −∞ to +∞. Any score has a non-zero probability. Unimodal , with a single maximum ordinate at the mean. The maximum ordinate is 0.3989 (that is, 1/√2π) when expressed in z units. Mesokurtic: kurtosis = 3, excess kurtosis = 0. Total area under the curve = 1.00 (or 100%), which is why areas can be read as probabilities. Points of inflection (where the curve changes from concave-down to concave-up) lie exactly at ±1σ. It is completely defined by two parameters: μ and σ . Change μ and the curve slides; change σ and it widens or narrows. The standard normal curve is the special case with μ = 0 and σ = 1. The quartile deviation Q = 0.6745σ, and the average deviation AD = 0.7979σ. 6.2 The area percentages (memorise these exactly) Band Area inside Area in each tail μ ± 1σ 68.26% (34.13% each side) 15.87% μ ± 2σ 95.44% (adds 13.59% each side) 2.28% μ ± 3σ 99.74% (adds 2.14% each side) 0.13% μ ± 1.96 σ 95.00% exactly 2.5% (this is where α = .05 two-tailed comes from) μ ± 2.58 σ 99.00% exactly 0.5% (this is where α = .01 two-tailed comes from) μ ± 1.645 σ 90.00% 5% (the one-tailed .05 critical value) The three numbers that carry the most marks: 68 – 95 – 99.7 for 1, 2 and 3 SD, and 1.96 and 2.58 as the exact 95% and 99% cut-offs. Every confidence interval and every z test in the paper comes out of these. 6.3 z scores Definition: a z score expresses a raw score as the number of standard deviations it lies above or below the mean. z = (X − M) / s (sample) · z = (X − μ) / σ (population) · to go back: X = M + z·s Worked example A student scores 85 on a test with M = 70 and s = 10. z = (85 − 70)/10 = +1.5 . From the table, the area below z = 1.5 is .9332, so the student is at the 93rd percentile and beat 93% of the group. A second student scores 60: z = −1.0, area below = .1587, so the 16th percentile . Properties of a z distribution The mean of a set of z scores is always 0 and the SD always 1 . Converting to z is a linear transformation. Standardising does not change the shape of the distribution. A skewed distribution converted to z scores is still exactly as skewed. This is the most frequently missed point about z scores. z scores make scores from different tests comparable, which is the whole reason they exist. Roughly 99.7% of z scores fall between −3 and +3. Trap: "z transformation normalises a distribution." False. It standardises it (fixes M = 0, s = 1) but leaves the shape untouched. To actually change the shape into a normal one you need a normalised standard score , which is computed from percentile ranks via the area table, not from the linear z formula. Normalised T scores and stanines are of this second kind. 6.4 The derived standard scores Score Mean SD Formula from z Where you meet it z 0 1 – The base currency of all standard scores T score (McCall) 50 10 T = 50 + 10z MMPI, MCMI, most clinical inventories.
