Had this clinic given those 100 patients eight weeks of a useless herbal remedy and run a one-group pretest–posttest study, it would have reported a 7.6-point "improvement" with a large effect size and a tiny p value. That is the danger. Regression to the mean contaminates any study that selects people because they are extreme , which in clinical work is nearly every study, since people seek treatment when their symptoms are at their worst. Untreated improvement in clinical samples: part of the "improvement" in uncontrolled case series, and part of the placebo response in drug trials, is regression. Matching across different populations: if a treatment group from a low-scoring population is matched on pretest with a control group from a higher-scoring population, each matched group regresses toward its own population mean on retest, manufacturing a spurious difference. Donald Campbell and Albert Erlebacher (1970) showed how this could make the American Head Start compensatory education programme look harmful. Reward and punishment: Daniel Kahneman ( Thinking, Fast and Slow , 2011) recalled Israeli Air Force flight instructors who were convinced that praise after an excellent landing made the next one worse and criticism after a bad landing made the next one better. Both were regression: an exceptional landing is usually followed by a more ordinary one, whatever the instructor says. How to control regression. Not by matching, and not by testing more people. The cure is a control group drawn from the same extreme pool and formed by random assignment : both groups regress equally, and only the difference between them reflects treatment. Other safeguards: use highly reliable measures; take two baseline measurements, selecting on the first and using the second as the pretest; and never interpret improvement in a group selected for extremity without a control. 19.4 Threats to external validity Campbell and Stanley (1963) listed four factors that limit generalisation (they called them "factors jeopardising external validity or representativeness"): Reactive or interaction effect of testing (pretest sensitisation): the pretest may make participants more or less responsive to the treatment, so the result holds only for pretested people. A pretest questionnaire about stigma may sensitise participants to an anti-stigma film; unpretested audiences in the real world would not respond as strongly. The Solomon four-group design was built to detect exactly this. Interaction of selection and treatment: the treatment works only for the kind of people who happened to be sampled. A mindfulness programme tested on motivated, educated, urban volunteers may not work for rural patients with low literacy. Reactive effects of experimental arrangements: the experimental setting itself (being observed, the laboratory, knowing one is in a study) produces effects that will not occur outside it. The Hawthorne effect and demand characteristics (19.5) are the classic cases. Multiple-treatment interference: when the same participants receive several treatments, the effects of earlier ones persist and interfere with later ones, so the result applies only to people who received that sequence. This is the external-validity face of the carry-over problem in within-subject designs (19.7). Cook and Campbell (1979) restated external validity threats as interactions of the treatment with selection, setting and history : the effect may hold only for these people, only in this kind of setting, or only at this point in time (a programme evaluated before smartphones may not work after them). Shadish, Cook and Campbell (2002) generalised this to interactions of the causal relationship with units, treatment variations, outcomes and settings. The common remedies are random sampling from the target population (section 7.2), heterogeneous samples and settings, field replication and, ultimately, meta-analysis across many studies (section 25). 19.5 Reactivity and bias: participants and experimenters People who know they are being studied do not behave like people who do not, and researchers who know what they expect do not observe like researchers who do not. Any influence that systematically distorts results is a bias . Behaviour changed by the act of measuring it is reactivity . Both threaten the construct and external validity of a study, and, when they differ between groups, its internal validity. Participant effects The Hawthorne effect. Between 1924 and 1932 the Western Electric Company's Hawthorne Works near Chicago studied worker productivity (later associated with Elton Mayo, and written up by Fritz Roethlisberger and William Dickson in Management and the Worker , 1939). In the illumination experiments output rose when lighting was increased, but also in the control group, and sometimes when the light was dimmed. The interpretation that output rose because the workers knew they were being studied was named the Hawthorne effect by Henry A. Landsberger ( Hawthorne Revisited , 1958): participants change their behaviour because they know they are being observed, independent of the intervention. Reanalyses (Steven Levitt and John List, 2011) found the original data much weaker than the legend, but the term is established. Martin T. Orne , "On the social psychology of the psychological experiment: with particular reference to demand characteristics and their implications" ( American Psychologist , 1962). Demand characteristics are the totality of cues in an experimental situation (rumours, the instructions, the setting, the procedure, the experimenter's manner) that convey the hypothesis to participants and so influence their behaviour. Orne showed how powerful the role of "experimental subject" is: participants given page after page of random numbers to add, and told to tear up each completed sheet and continue, kept going for hours. Orne proposed quasi-controls to detect demand: a careful post-experimental inquiry , a pre-inquiry (asking people to imagine they were in the study and predict their behaviour) and simulators (participants asked to fake being hypnotised or treated, to see whether the "effect" can be produced by role-playing alone). Good-subject effect: Orne's observation that most participants want to help science and the experimenter, so they try to work out the hypothesis and confirm it. Evaluation apprehension: Milton J. Rosenberg (1965): participants are anxious to be judged favourably (as psychologically healthy, intelligent, normal) and behave so as to look good. Stephen Weber and Thomas Cook (1972) classified participant roles as good , negativistic (deliberately working against the hypothesis, sometimes called the "screw-you" effect), faithful (scrupulously following instructions) and apprehensive . Social desirability: the tendency to answer in the way that will be viewed favourably by others, a major bias in self-report (Allen L. Edwards, 1957; the Marlowe–Crowne Social Desirability Scale, Douglas Crowne and David Marlowe, 1960). Controlled by anonymity, forced-choice items matched for desirability, lie or validity scales, and indirect measures (section 23). John Henry effect (19.2) and novelty effect : a new treatment, gadget or app produces improvement partly because it is new and exciting; the effect fades as the novelty wears off, so short trials overestimate benefit. Placebo and nocebo A placebo (Latin, "I shall please") is an inert treatment (sugar pill, sham procedure) given so that expectation is held constant between groups; the placebo effect is improvement produced by the expectation of treatment and the ritual of care. Henry K. Beecher 's "The Powerful Placebo" ( JAMA , 1955) pooled 15 studies and reported about 35% of patients satisfactorily relieved by placebo. Later analyses (Asbjørn Hróbjartsson and Peter Gøtzsche, 2001) showed much of that was natural recovery and regression to the mean, though placebo responses on subjective outcomes such as pain are real. The nocebo effect (Latin, "I shall harm"), named by Walter Kennedy in 1961, is the reverse: negative expectations produce symptoms, as when patients warned of headaches report more headaches on placebo. Experimenter effects Oskar Pfungst (1907) investigated Clever Hans , a Berlin horse owned by Wilhelm von Osten that apparently answered arithmetic questions by tapping its hoof. Pfungst showed that Hans answered correctly only when the questioner knew the answer and was visible: the horse was reading tiny, involuntary cues (a slight lift of the head or relaxation of posture when the correct number of taps was reached). Nobody was cheating; the cue was unconscious. Clever Hans is the founding example of the experimenter expectancy effect , and the reason for blind testing. Robert Rosenthal made the experimenter expectancy effect a research programme. In Rosenthal and Kermit Fode (1963) , students were each given rats to train in a maze; some were told their rats were specially bred "maze-bright", others "maze-dull". The rats were in fact randomly assigned from the same stock, yet the "bright" rats learned faster, presumably because of differences in how the students handled and observed them. In Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson's Pygmalion in the Classroom (1968) , teachers at an elementary school were told that a test had identified certain children (actually chosen at random, about 20%) as "bloomers" who would show an intellectual spurt; after about eight months those children, especially in the first and second grades, had gained more IQ points than their classmates. This Pygmalion or Rosenthal effect is the self-fulfilling prophecy in the classroom. Later replications found the effect real but smaller and less consistent than the 1968 study suggested. Keep the sources of expectancy apart. Demand characteristics (Orne): cues that make the participant guess and play to the hypothesis. Experimenter expectancy (Robert Rosenthal; Clever Hans): the experimenter's expectation leaks into the participant's behaviour or into the recording of it. Hawthorne effect : change because one is observed . Placebo effect : change because one expects to be treated . John Henry effect : the control group competes. The past-paper answer to "a double-blind study is used to minimise the impact of" is both experimenter bias and expectancy effects . 19.6 Techniques of control Control means holding constant, or otherwise neutralising, the influence of extraneous variables so that only the IV differs between conditions (a past paper defined it as "the process of holding constant the possible influence" of extraneous variables). Fred N. Kerlinger , in Foundations of Behavioral Research (1964 and later editions), summed up the aim of design in the MAXMINCON principle : max imise systematic (experimental) variance, by making the levels of the IV as different as possible; min imise error variance, by reliable measurement and controlled conditions; and con trol extraneous systematic variance, by the techniques below. Ronald A. Fisher 's The Design of Experiments (1935) gave the three classic principles of experimental design: randomisation , replication (more than one unit per condition, so error can be estimated) and local control (blocking similar units together). Randomisation Random assignment (randomisation) gives every participant an equal chance of being placed in any condition, typically by computer-generated random numbers. It is the most powerful control technique because it equalises groups, within the limits of chance, on every extraneous variable at once, known and unknown, measured and unmeasured: severity, motivation, genes, life events. It is the defining feature of a true experiment and the main protection against selection bias and confounding. With small samples chance imbalance remains possible, which is why trials use block and stratified randomisation and keep the sequence hidden from recruiters ( allocation concealment , section 25). Random selection and random assignment are different things. Random selection (random sampling, section 7.2) decides who gets into the study ; it makes the sample representative and buys external validity . Random assignment decides which condition each participant receives ; it makes the groups equivalent and buys internal validity . A study can have either without the other. Most clinical trials use a convenience sample of consenting patients (no random selection) but assign them randomly (strong internal validity, limited generality); a national survey uses random selection but assigns nobody to anything (representative, but no causal claim). Past papers: "randomisation is not possible in" purposive sampling (it refers to selection); "the principle that ensures every participant has an equal chance of being assigned to any group" is randomisation ; "the main reason for randomly assigning subjects" is to make the groups as similar as possible so the only systematic difference is the treatment. Population everyone you want to generalise to Random selection Sample (n = 20) Random assignment Treatment group e.g. group CBT Control group e.g. treatment as usual compare at posttest differ only by the IV buys EXTERNAL validity the sample represents the population buys INTERNAL validity groups start equal, so a difference is due to the IV Random selection decides who enters the study (external validity); random assignment decides who gets which condition (internal validity). Matching In matching , participants are paired on a variable known to affect the DV (baseline severity, IQ) and the members of each pair are placed in different conditions, ideally by random assignment within the pair (the matched-pairs approach, combining matching with randomisation). It reduces error variance and guarantees balance on the matched variable. Its problems: you can match only on variables you know about and can measure; matching on several at once soon becomes impossible and discards participants; without random assignment every unmatched variable can still differ; and matching groups from different populations creates regression artefacts (19.3). Elimination and holding constant An extraneous variable can be eliminated (a sound-proof room removes noise) or held constant (only right-handed participants, only first-episode patients, always 10 a.m., the same experimenter and instructions), so it cannot differ between conditions. The cost is external validity: the result strictly applies only to people and conditions like those. Building it into the design, and statistical control Instead of removing a variable, make it a factor: a 2 (treatment vs control) × 2 (male vs female) factorial design measures the effect of sex and its interaction with treatment instead of leaving it as noise (section 10.4). When the variable is a nuisance, this is blocking : participants are grouped into homogeneous blocks (mild, moderate, severe) and randomly assigned within each, so block-to-block variation leaves the error term (the randomised block design , Fisher's local control). A variable that cannot be controlled by design can be measured and removed statistically: ANCOVA (section 11.2) adjusts posttest means for a covariate such as pretest severity, and partial correlation (12.5) and multiple regression (13.3) remove a third variable's influence. Statistical control is weaker than randomisation: it adjusts only for what was measured, and only as well as it was measured. Participants as their own controls In a within-subjects (repeated-measures) design every participant experiences every condition, so stable individual differences drop out of the error term and power rises (sections 9.4 and 10.5). The price is order effects (19.7). Blinding Single-blind: the participants do not know which condition they are in. Controls participant expectancy, placebo responses and demand. Double-blind: neither the participants nor the people administering the treatment and assessing the outcome know who is in which condition. Controls participant expectancy and experimenter bias . Triple-blind: additionally, those analysing the data (and in trials the monitoring committee) do not know which coded group is which until the analysis is done. In psychotherapy trials the therapist and patient cannot be blind to the therapy delivered, so the realistic standard is a blind outcome assessor (single-blind assessment). Other procedural controls Deception and cover stories: a plausible false account of the purpose keeps participants from guessing the hypothesis, reducing demand characteristics; ethically permissible only when necessary, low-risk and followed by debriefing (section 26). Standardised instructions and procedures: every participant receives the same script, timing and setting, which reduces both error variance and experimenter influence. Automation: presenting stimuli and recording responses by computer removes experimenter cues and recording errors. Unobtrusive (non-reactive) measures , where ethical, to reduce reactivity. Placebo controls hold expectation constant in drug trials. In psychotherapy research the equivalent is the attention-placebo (attention control) condition: participants receive the same amount of therapist contact and a credible rationale without the active ingredient, so that any advantage of the real therapy cannot be due to attention, warmth or expectancy alone. A wait-list control controls for time, history and maturation but not for attention or expectancy. Technique What it controls Main limitation Random assignment All participant variables, known and unknown; selection bias Can fail by chance in small samples Matching The matched variables only Unknown variables uncontrolled; loss of participants; regression artefacts Elimination / holding constant The variable held constant Reduces generality Blocking / factorial inclusion The blocked variable, and its interaction with the IV Needs more participants and cells Statistical control (ANCOVA) Measured covariates Only what was measured; assumes homogeneous regression slopes Within-subjects design All stable individual differences Order and carry-over effects Counterbalancing Order (position) effects Fails with asymmetric carry-over Blinding Expectancy, placebo, experimenter bias Often impossible for therapists and patients in psychotherapy Placebo / attention control Expectancy, attention, the ritual of treatment Hard to make a credible psychological placebo 19.7 Order effects and counterbalancing When the same participants serve in several conditions, the order in which they meet the conditions can affect their scores. Section 10.5 introduced these briefly; here they are treated properly. Practice effects: performance improves with repetition (familiarity with the task, warming up). Fatigue effects: performance declines with time and repetition (tiredness, boredom). Carry-over effects: the effect of one condition persists into the next (a drug still active, a strategy still in use, a mood still lingering). Sensitisation: after experiencing several conditions, participants work out what is being varied and guess the hypothesis. Practice and fatigue are position effects : they depend on where in the sequence a condition falls, whichever condition it is. Carry-over is a sequence effect : it depends on which condition came before. In psychophysics the same logic applies to primacy and recency effects and to the order of ascending and descending series, and the standard answer to "primacy and recency effects in a psychophysics experiment are controlled by" is counterbalancing . The counterbalancing schemes Complete counterbalancing: use every possible order, with equal numbers of participants in each. With n conditions there are n! orders: 2 conditions give 2, 3 give 6, 4 give 24, 5 give 120. Practical only for small n. Partial (incomplete) counterbalancing: use a subset of orders chosen so that position effects still balance out. Latin square: n orders, arranged so that each condition appears exactly once in each ordinal position (and once in each row). It balances position (practice and fatigue) but not sequence: in the simple cyclic square A is always immediately followed by B. Balanced Latin square ( Williams design , after E. J. Williams, 1949): additionally, each condition immediately precedes and follows every other condition exactly once , which balances first-order carry-over. For an even number of conditions n rows suffice; for an odd number two squares (2n rows) are needed. ABBA (reverse) counterbalancing: each participant receives the conditions in one order and then in the reverse (A B B A), so that each condition has the same average position. It assumes practice effects are linear ; if most practice happens early, ABBA fails. Randomised orders: each participant receives an independently randomised order. Simple and effective with many participants or many trials; with few participants imbalance can remain. Latin square (cyclic) position of each condition 1st 2nd 3rd 4th Group 1 A B C D Group 2 B C D A Group 3 C D A B Group 4 D A B C Each condition once in every position: 4 orders but A always comes just before B, B before C ... Balanced Latin square Williams design (1949) 1st 2nd 3rd 4th Group 1 A B D C Group 2 B C A D Group 3 C D B A Group 4 D A C B Every position once, and every condition follows every other exactly once odd number of conditions: 2n rows Complete counterbalancing 3 conditions: 3! = 6 orders Order 1 A B C Order 2 A C B Order 3 B A C Order 4 B C A Order 5 C A B Order 6 C B A All possible orders 4 conditions: 24 orders 5 conditions: 120 orders so only for 2 to 4 conditions Three ways to counterbalance: a cyclic Latin square balances position only, a balanced (Williams) Latin square also balances which condition follows which, and complete counterbalancing uses all n! orders. Why counterbalancing works, and when it fails. Counterbalancing does not remove order effects; it spreads them equally across conditions , so they add the same amount to every condition mean and cancel in the comparison (they still inflate error variance, and order can be entered as a factor to measure it). That logic requires the order effect to be symmetric : doing A first must help B exactly as much as doing B first helps A. When carry-over is asymmetric (differential), counterbalancing fails, a problem E. C. Poulton and P. R. Freeman (1966) documented as "unwanted asymmetrical transfer". Examples: participants taught an imagery mnemonic in condition A will keep using it in the "rote rehearsal" condition B, but not the reverse; a drug with a long half-life contaminates the placebo period that follows it; insight, once gained, cannot be unlearned. The remedies are a washout period between conditions (standard in crossover drug trials) or abandoning the within-subjects design for a between-subjects design. Recap of section 19: validity of a study (not of a test, section 15.3) has four types (Cook and Campbell, 1979; Shadish, Cook and Campbell, 2002): statistical conclusion, internal (Campbell's sine qua non), construct and external; internal and external trade off. External validity splits into population and ecological validity (Bracht and Glass, 1968); ecological validity is Brunswik's term stretched to mean real-world realism; Aronson and Carlsmith (1968) separated mundane from experimental realism. Campbell and Stanley's (1963) eight internal threats: history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, statistical regression, selection, experimental mortality, selection–maturation interaction; Cook and Campbell added ambiguous temporal precedence, diffusion, compensatory equalisation, compensatory rivalry (John Henry) and resentful demoralisation, the last four moved to construct validity in 2002. A control group controls history, maturation, testing and instrumentation; only random assignment controls selection. Regression to the mean (Francis Galton, 1886): in our simulation (r = .60) the untreated top 10% fell from 67.8 to 60.2. External threats: pretest sensitisation, selection × treatment, reactive arrangements, multiple-treatment interference. Reactivity: Hawthorne (named by Landsberger, 1958), demand characteristics (Orne, 1962), evaluation apprehension (Rosenberg, 1965), placebo (Beecher, 1955), nocebo (Kennedy, 1961); expectancy: Clever Hans (Pfungst, 1907), Robert Rosenthal and Fode (1963), Pygmalion (1968). Control: MAXMINCON (Kerlinger); randomisation, replication, local control (Fisher, 1935); random assignment buys internal validity, random selection external; matching, holding constant, blocking, ANCOVA, own controls, blinding, placebo and attention controls. Counterbalance order effects: n! orders, Latin square, balanced Latin square (Williams, 1949), ABBA, random orders; asymmetric carry-over defeats them all. 20 Experimental and quasi-experimental designs A research design is the plan that decides who is studied, what is done to them, when they are measured and what they are compared with. Section 19 listed the threats that can make a conclusion wrong; this section ranks the designs by how many of those threats each one rules out, from the true experiment (a causal claim), through the quasi-experiment (a cautious one), down to the pre-experimental designs (mostly none). Section 21 covers designs that manipulate nothing. 20.1 What makes an experiment Manipulation. The researcher deliberately changes the independent variable (IV): CBT for some patients and not others. A variable you merely measure (gender, diagnosis, childhood trauma) is not manipulated, and a study built on it is not an experiment however controlled it looks. Control. Everything except the IV is held constant or balanced: same assessor, instructions and timing, and a control group treated identically except that it does not receive the IV (the experimental group does). Random assignment. Every participant has an equal chance of landing in any condition, decided by a random process, not by the researcher, clinician or participant. It balances the groups on every variable at once, including ones nobody thought of, so any remaining difference is chance, which is exactly what the significance test (section 8) allows for. Random assignment is not random sampling. Random sampling (section 7.2) decides who gets into the study and protects external validity. Random assignment decides which condition each person goes to and protects internal validity. Most clinical trials randomly assign a convenience sample: strong internal, limited external validity. A survey can have a perfect random sample and no assignment at all. Ronald A. Fisher built the logic of the modern experiment at the Rothamsted agricultural station and set it out in The Design of Experiments (1935). His three principles are asked by name: randomisation , replication (several units per treatment, so that error can be estimated) and local control (grouping similar units into blocks to remove their differences from error). The randomised block, Latin square and factorial designs below are all his. 20.2 What a causal claim needs: three criteria, Mill's methods and MAXMINCON Three conditions must hold before you can say X causes Y. They go back to John Stuart Mill 's A System of Logic (1843) and are stated the same way in modern texts such as William R. Shadish, Thomas D. Cook and Donald T. Campbell (2002). Criterion Meaning How an experiment secures it 1. Covariation X and Y vary together The groups differ significantly on the DV 2. Temporal precedence The cause comes before the effect X is applied first and Y measured afterwards, so the order is known by construction 3. Elimination of alternative explanations (non-spuriousness) No third variable or artefact could produce the covariation Random assignment plus a control group removes the threats of section 19 A correlational study can meet the first, sometimes the second, rarely the third; that gap is why correlation does not imply causation (section 12.1). Mill's methods of induction. Of Mill's five methods, two are the logic of all design. The method of agreement : if every case showing the effect shares only one circumstance, that circumstance is probably the cause (weak, because the shared factor may not be the only one). The method of difference : if a case with the effect and a case without it differ in only one circumstance, that circumstance is the cause. This is the logic of the experiment : experimental and control groups made identical except for X. The other three are the joint method of agreement and difference, the method of residues (subtract the effects of known causes; what remains belongs to the remaining cause) and the method of concomitant variation (Y changes in degree whenever X does), which is the logic of correlation. Kerlinger's MAXMINCON. Fred N. Kerlinger , in Foundations of Behavioral Research (1964), reduced the purpose of design to the control of variance, in one acronym (Indian guides also write Max-Min-Con or Max-Kon-Min). Instruction Which variance How MAXimise Systematic (experimental) variance produced by the IV; Indian texts call it primary variance Make the levels of the IV as different as possible (a full course of CBT, not one session); deliver it well MINimise Error variance: individual differences and measurement error Reliable measures (section 15.2), standardised procedures, within-subjects or blocked designs CONtrol Extraneous systematic variance from other variables; also called secondary variance Randomisation, elimination (hold constant), matching, building the variable in as a factor or block, ANCOVA (section 11.2) It is the F ratio in words. F = between-groups variance / within-groups variance (section 10.1). Maximising systematic variance enlarges the numerator, minimising error shrinks the denominator, and controlling extraneous variance stops a confound impersonating the treatment in the numerator. In the item "maximisation of ____, minimisation of ____, control of ____ variance", the answer is primary, error, secondary . 20.3 Reading and writing Campbell and Stanley's notation Donald T. Campbell and Julian C. Stanley wrote "Experimental and quasi-experimental designs for research on teaching" as a chapter of N. L. Gage's Handbook of Research on Teaching (1963), reprinted as a book in 1966. They described 16 designs (3 pre-experimental, 3 true experimental, 10 quasi-experimental) and rated each against 8 threats to internal validity and 4 to external validity (section 19), using a compact notation. X = exposure to the treatment; a blank where X would be = no treatment (different treatments: X₁, X₂). O = an observation or measurement of the DV, numbered O₁, O₂ ... R = random assignment, written at the start of each row. Each row is one group; left to right is time; symbols in the same vertical column happen at the same time. A dashed line between rows = groups not equated by randomisation (intact groups). Later authors write NR at the start of such rows, and C for assignment by a cut-off score. "Thirty inpatients with schizophrenia are randomly split; both groups are rated on the PANSS; one receives eight weeks of social skills training; both are rated again" is written R O₁ X O₂ over R O₃ O₄, the pretest-posttest control group design. If ward A got the training and ward B did not, the R's disappear and a dashed line separates the rows. To place any design, ask in order: is there an R, is there a row without X, and is there an O before X? Campbell and Stanley's (1963) notation for the three pre-experimental, three true experimental and three of their ten quasi-experimental designs. Their numbering (1 to 16) is shown before each name. 20.4 Pre-experimental designs Campbell and Stanley called these "pre-experimental" because they cannot rule out rival explanations. Examiners ask exactly which threats each one fails, and they are the designs most hospital audits and student projects use without realising it. Design 1, the one-shot case study (X O). A group is treated, then measured once. A deaddiction centre runs a new relapse-prevention group and reports that craving scores at the end are "low". Low compared with what? With no pretest and no comparison group, there is no comparison at all. It fails history, maturation, selection and mortality ; Campbell and Stanley said such studies have "such a total absence of control as to be of almost no scientific value", and that piling up careful detail on one group is the "error of misplaced precision"; the effort would be better spent on a comparison group. Design 2, the one-group pretest-posttest design (O X O). Twenty patients with panic disorder score 31 on the Beck Anxiety Inventory, receive ten sessions of CBT, and score 18. The fall could be history (anything else that happened in between), maturation (spontaneous remission), testing (the pretest changed the posttest), instrumentation (a stricter rater or changed scale), or regression (marked "?": if patients were enrolled because they scored extremely high, they drift towards the mean anyway); the selection-maturation interaction is also uncontrolled. It does control selection and mortality, because the same people are compared with themselves. Design 3, the static-group comparison (X O over a dashed line over O). Students at a college with a mindfulness programme are compared on stress with students at a college without one. Measuring both groups at the same time controls history, testing, instrumentation and regression (maturation "?"). The decisive weakness is selection : the colleges may have differed before the programme. Mortality and the selection-maturation interaction are also uncontrolled. Where textbooks disagree. Campbell and Stanley (1963) call these three "pre-experimental". Shadish, Cook and Campbell (2002) dropped the label and treat them as the weakest quasi-experiments ("designs without a control group", "without a pretest"). If the question names Campbell and Stanley or offers "pre-experimental", choose it. 20.5 True experimental designs All three use random assignment and a control group , and Campbell and Stanley rate all three as controlling all eight internal threats. They differ in what they do about the pretest. Design 4, the pretest-posttest control group design (R O X O over R O O), is the classic randomised controlled trial. History, maturation, testing, instrumentation and regression act equally on both groups and cancel in the comparison; randomisation removes selection; the pretest checks that randomisation worked, shows who dropped out, and adds precision when used as a covariate (ANCOVA, section 11.2). Its one weakness is external: the interaction of testing and X (pretest sensitisation), because the pretest may make people more responsive to the treatment. The wrong statistic. Running a paired t test inside each group and concluding "the treatment group changed significantly and the control group did not" is the error Campbell and Stanley singled out. Compare the groups directly: ANCOVA on posttests, a t test on gain scores, or the group × time interaction in a mixed ANOVA (section 10.5). Design 6, the posttest-only control group design (R X O over R O). Randomisation already makes the groups equivalent within the limits the significance test allows for, so the pretest is not essential; most of Fisher's agricultural experiments had none. Dropping it removes testing effects and pretest sensitisation and is necessary when a pretest is impossible or would reveal the purpose. The price: no check on initial equivalence, no covariate, no view of who dropped out, and larger groups are needed. Analysis: independent t (section 9.3) or one-way ANOVA. Design 5: the Solomon four-group design Richard L. Solomon proposed it in "An extension of control group design" ( Psychological Bulletin , 1949). Campbell and Stanley wrote that it "deservedly has higher prestige" than design 4 and "represents the first explicit consideration of external validity factors". It is designs 4 and 6 run side by side, all four groups randomly assigned: Group Pretest Treatment Posttest Role 1 O₁ X O₂ Experimental group of design 4 2 O₃ – O₄ Control group of design 4 3 – X O₅ Experimental group of design 6 4 – – O₆ Control group of design 6 What it controls: everything design 4 controls, plus pretest sensitisation (the reactive or interaction effect of testing, testing × X), which it not only avoids but measures , along with the main effect of testing. That is the answer to "the Solomon four-group design is used to control for ...". The comparisons. The effect of X is replicated four ways: O₂ > O₁, O₂ > O₄, O₅ > O₆ and O₅ > O₃; if all agree, the inference is much stronger. O₄ vs O₆ isolates the effect of the pretest alone, and comparing O₆ with the pretest means O₁ and O₃ shows the combined effect of maturation and history. The analysis. No single test uses all six sets of scores, because groups 3 and 4 have no pretest. Campbell and Stanley set the pretests aside and run a 2 × 2 factorial ANOVA on the four posttests : pretested (yes/no) × treated (yes/no) (section 10.4). Column means give the main effect of X, row means the main effect of pretesting, and the interaction is pretest sensitisation. If both pretest effects are negligible, an ANCOVA of O₂ vs O₄ with the pretest as covariate adds precision. Worked example. Undergraduates are randomly assigned to four groups to test a 20-minute anti-stigma film; the DV is an attitude-to-mental-illness scale (higher = more accepting). Pretest means O₁ = O₃ = 58; posttest means O₂ = 72, O₄ = 60, O₅ = 66, O₆ = 59. Main effect of the film = (72 + 66)/2 − (60 + 59)/2 = 9.5 . Main effect of pretesting = (72 + 60)/2 − (66 + 59)/2 = 3.5 . The film's effect is 12 points in pretested students but 7 in unpretested ones, an interaction of 5 : the stigma questionnaire primed students to take the message to heart. Testing alone (O₄ − O₆) = 1; maturation plus history (O₆ − 58) = 1. In the real world nobody fills in a questionnaire before the film, so expect about 7 points; design 4 alone would have reported 12. The Solomon four-group design (Richard L. Solomon, 1949): four randomly assigned groups, and the 2 × 2 analysis of posttest means that Campbell and Stanley (1963) recommend, with the worked numbers from the text. Its cost: four groups instead of two, roughly double the participants ("more than double effort", said Campbell and Stanley), and an awkward analysis. It is worth it mainly when sensitisation is a real risk: attitude change, health education, prejudice reduction. Read it as rules. A control group measured at the same time controls history, testing and instrumentation. Random assignment controls selection and its interactions. A pretest creates the testing × X problem, escaped only by design 6 and the unpretested half of design 5. No design fully settles selection × X (generalising beyond the kind of people studied); that needs random sampling or replication. 20.6 Who gets what: between, within, mixed, matched and blocked designs Between-subjects Within-subjects (repeated measures) Mixed (split-plot) Definition Each participant experiences one condition Each participant experiences every condition At least one between and one within factor Example CBT vs waiting list Reaction time under placebo, low and high dose Group (CBT vs control) × time (pre, post, follow-up): the standard trial For No order or carryover effects; the only option when a treatment cannot be undone Fewer participants; each person is their own control, so individual differences leave the error term and power rises A clean group comparison plus the power of repeated measures; the group × time interaction is the treatment effect Against More participants; individual differences inflate error Order effects (practice, fatigue, carryover, sensitisation), controlled by counterbalancing (section 19) Some problems of both; sphericity needed for the within factor Statistics Independent t (9.3), ANOVA (10.2, 10.4) Paired t (9.4), repeated-measures ANOVA (10.5), Wilcoxon, Friedman (14.3) Mixed ANOVA (10.5) "Split-plot" is Fisher's agricultural term: whole plots got one treatment (between) and each plot was split into subplots for a second (within). Matched-groups design. Participants are paired on a variable strongly related to the DV (baseline severity, IQ), and one member of each pair is randomly assigned to each condition; the analysis treats the pair as the unit (paired t). Matching equates the groups on the matched variable and cuts error variance, but only on that variable. Matching intact groups without randomisation is dangerous: matched people are atypical of their own populations and regress towards different means on retest, producing a spurious effect. Matching supplements randomisation; it never replaces it. Randomised block design (RBD). Fisher's local control made concrete: participants are grouped into blocks homogeneous on a nuisance variable (severity, hospital), and randomly assigned to all treatments within each block, so block differences are removed from error. With t treatments and b blocks, error df = (t − 1)(b − 1) : four relaxation techniques across five severity blocks gives 3 × 4 = 12. A repeated-measures design is the case in which each person is a block. Latin square as a design. A t × t arrangement that controls two nuisance variables at once (rows, for example participants; columns, for example order), with each treatment once in every row and column. Its main use is counterbalancing order (section 19); it reappears below as the counterbalanced quasi-experiment. Error df = (t − 1)(t − 2) , so 6 for a 4 × 4 square. It assumes the treatments do not interact with the row and column variables. 20.7 Factorial and nested designs A factorial design studies two or more IVs (factors) at once, every level of each combined with every level of the others: "more than one IV, levels combined in a systematic manner". 2 × 3 = two factors (count the numbers), with 2 and 3 levels (read the numbers), and 6 cells (multiply). 2 × 2 × 3 = three factors, 12 cells. With k factors there are 2 k − 1 effects: two factors give 2 main effects + 1 interaction; three factors give 3 main + 3 two-way + 1 three-way = 7. Therapy (CBT vs counselling) × medication (none, low, high) for depression is a 2 × 3 with six cells. A main effect is one factor's effect averaged over the other; an interaction means one factor's effect depends on the level of the other (CBT helps a lot without medication but adds little at high dose). The statistics are in section 10.4. Why factorial designs are efficient. Every participant contributes to every main effect, so one study answers several questions; Fisher (1935) showed that a factorial experiment estimates several factors, and their interactions, with the same number of trials needed to estimate one factor alone to the same precision. Only a factorial design can reveal an interaction , often the clinically important finding. And testing one factor across levels of another shows how general its effect is. The cost: cells multiply fast, and three-way interactions are hard to read. Nested designs. In a nested (hierarchical) design each level of one factor occurs within only one level of another, instead of being crossed with all. Therapists 1 to 3 deliver only CBT and therapists 4 to 6 only interpersonal therapy: therapists are nested within therapy. Pupils within classrooms and patients within wards are the everyday cases. You cannot test the interaction of the nested factor with the factor it sits in, and therapist differences are partly confounded with the therapy comparison, so the nested factor is modelled as a random factor (multilevel models). Campbell and Stanley make the same point about assigning whole classrooms: the classroom, not the pupil, becomes the unit of analysis. 20.8 Quasi-experimental designs A quasi-experiment keeps manipulation (or a clearly timed intervention) and a comparison but lacks random assignment . Campbell and Stanley (1963) gave it its name; the standard extended work is Thomas D. Cook and Donald T. Campbell , Quasi-Experimentation: Design and Analysis Issues for Field Settings (1979), updated by Shadish, Cook and Campbell (2002). Randomisation is often impossible: patients are already on wards, a policy changes for a whole district, or withholding treatment would be unethical. The strategy is to add design features (pretests, comparison groups, many time points) until each specific rival explanation becomes implausible. Nonequivalent control group design (design 10) O X O over a dashed line over O O: two intact groups, both pretested and posttested, one treated. One ward of a government mental hospital introduces a token economy; a similar ward continues usual care; both are rated before and after six months. It is design 4 without the R, and the pretest makes it far better than the static-group comparison: you can see how unequal the groups were and analyse change. Main effects of history, maturation, testing and instrumentation are controlled; what remains are interactions with selection : Selection-maturation: the groups were changing at different rates anyway (an acute ward improves faster than a chronic one). Selection-history (local history): an event affected one group only (ward A got a new charge nurse). Selection-instrumentation: the scale behaves differently in the two groups (a ceiling effect in the better ward). Selection-regression: the treated group was chosen because it scored extremely, so it regresses towards the mean while the comparison does not. Interrupted time-series design (design 7) O O O O X O O O O: one unit measured many times before and after an intervention. The pre-intervention points show the series' level, trend and bounce, so the change at X is judged against what the series was already doing; that answers maturation, testing and regression. An effect can be a change in level (an immediate step), in slope (the trend bends), or both, analysed by segmented regression or ARIMA models. Donald T. Campbell and H. Laurence Ross's (1968) study of the Connecticut crackdown on speeding, introduced after a record year of road deaths in 1955, is the classic: the next year's fall looked like success, but the longer series showed how unstable yearly totals were and that a record year is usually followed by a lower one (regression to the mean). History is the main remaining threat: another event at the same moment as X. If a new consultant took over the ward in week 25 of panel A, the step would look identical. Next is instrumentation : a new protocol often brings a new definition of an "incident" or a new form, producing a step with no change in behaviour. Seasonal cycles (examinations, festivals, monsoon admissions) can mimic or hide an effect in a short series. Multiple (controlled) time series (design 14) adds a comparison series from a similar unit that did not receive X (the next ward, a neighbouring state, as Campbell and Ross used). If both series drop at week 25, history is the likely cause; if only the treated one drops, history becomes implausible. In a switching-replications variant, the comparison unit receives X later, so the effect must appear twice at two different times. Regression discontinuity design (design 16) Donald L. Thistlethwaite and Donald T. Campbell (1960) introduced it as "an alternative to the ex post facto experiment", asking whether public recognition in the National Merit Scholarship programme affected students' later plans and achievements. Recognition went to students above a cut-off on a qualifying score, so they would have done better anyway. Their solution: assign by a strict cut-off on a quantitative pre-measure , plot the outcome against that pre-measure, and look for a discontinuity (jump) in the regression line exactly at the cut-off. Notation: C O X O over C O O, where C = assignment by cut-off. A District Mental Health Programme clinic screens adults with the PHQ-9 (0 to 27). Places are scarce, so the rule is strict: 15 or more is offered eight sessions of CBT, below 15 is not; everyone is reassessed at three months. Treated patients started more depressed and are still worse on average at follow-up, so the naive comparison says therapy did harm. But on each side, follow-up rises smoothly with intake score. Fit a line to each side: with no effect the two lines would meet at the cut-off as one line; if CBT works, the treated line drops there, and the drop is the effect. 0 5 10 15 20 25 0 5 10 15 20 25 PHQ-9 screening score at intake PHQ-9 three months later cut-off: 15 or more gets CBT no therapy offered The jump at the cut-off is the treatment effect gap between the two lines: −4.0 PHQ−9 points (simulated true effect −4.0) Blue line, fitted to untreated people: slope 0.71; dashed part shows where treated people would have been without CBT Orange line, fitted to treated people: slope 0.80 Naive comparison of means (treated minus untreated): +2.2 says CBT made people worse, because they started worse Regression discontinuity computed from 260 simulated patients: separate regression lines on each side of the cut-off, and the vertical gap between them at the cut-off estimates the effect of CBT for people near a score of 15. Why it is the strongest quasi-experiment. The assignment rule is completely known, so it can be modelled exactly, which is what a nonequivalent group design lacks. Regression to the mean does not bias it, because both sides regress along the same line. Ethically it is attractive: treatment goes to those who need it most. What breaks it. (1) The cut-off must be obeyed; clinicians nudging 14s up to 15 make it "fuzzy". (2) The shape of the relation must be right; a curve fitted with straight lines can fake a jump. (3) The estimate applies only near the cut-off. (4) It needs many more participants than a randomised trial for the same power. Natural experiments and counterbalanced designs In a natural experiment the "treatment" is assigned by nature, policy or accident in a way plausibly unrelated to the outcome. In the Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944–45 a blockade caused famine in the western Netherlands for a sharply bounded period; Ezra Susser and colleagues (1996) found that people conceived at its height had about twice the risk of schizophrenia. Nobody could ethically starve pregnant women, but history did, for a precisely dated window. Natural experiments remain quasi-experiments: they are only as good as the argument that exposure was "as if random". In a counterbalanced (rotation) design (design 11), intact groups that cannot be randomised each receive every treatment, in orders arranged as a Latin square, so that differences among groups and among occasions are balanced out of the treatment comparison. Its weaknesses are carryover (multiple-treatment interference) and treatment-by-group interactions. Its single-group cousin, the equivalent time-samples design (design 8: X₁O X₀O X₁O X₀O), is the ancestor of the ABAB designs of section 22. Laboratory experiment Field experiment Control of extraneous variables High Lower Internal validity Higher Lower External (ecological) validity Lower: artificial tasks and settings Higher Demand characteristics High: people know they are studied (Martin T. Orne, 1962) Low Ethics Consent straightforward Covert manipulation raises consent problems (section 26) Example Stanley Milgram's (1963) obedience studies at Yale Irving Piliavin, Judith Rodin and Jane Piliavin (1969): a confederate collapsed in New York subway trains to see who helped "The advantage of field experiments over laboratory experiments" is higher external validity ; internal validity and ease of control are the laboratory's. Kurt Lewin 's field theory held that behaviour is a function of person and environment, B = f(P, E) ( Principles of Topological Psychology , 1936), so behaviour stripped of its natural field may not be the same behaviour. With Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White (1939) he created autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire leadership climates in boys' clubs, an early field experiment, and in 1946 he coined action research . Analogue studies investigate a clinical question under conditions that resemble but are not the real clinical situation: non-clinical or sub-clinical participants (students with high spider fear instead of patients with phobia), a standardised short treatment, a laboratory setting, or analogue measures such as role-plays. Peter J. Lang and A. David Lazovik's (1963) test of systematic desensitisation with snake-fearful students is the classic. Strengths: control, randomisation, easy recruitment, fewer ethical problems. Weakness: generalisation to real patients, who are more severe, comorbid and differently motivated. The exam answer to "analogue research involves" is research on healthy, non-clinical populations . Simulation reproduces the essential features of a real situation artificially: Philip Zimbardo's Stanford Prison Experiment (1971) simulated a prison, Orne's "simulators" faked hypnosis as a control for demand characteristics, simulated patients are used in interviewing research, and computer (Monte Carlo) simulation, as in this book's computed diagrams, shows how a method behaves when the truth is known. Simulation buys control and safety at the cost of realism. Recap of section 20: an experiment needs manipulation, control and random assignment (Ronald A. Fisher's randomisation, replication and local control, 1935); a causal claim needs covariation, temporal precedence and elimination of alternatives (John Stuart Mill, 1843, whose method of difference is the experiment). Fred N. Kerlinger's MAXMINCON: maximise systematic (primary), minimise error, control extraneous (secondary) variance. Donald T. Campbell and Julian C. Stanley (1963): R, X, O, dashed line for nonequivalent groups; 16 designs (3 pre-experimental, 3 true, 10 quasi) against 8 internal and 4 external threats. One-shot case study (X O) is uninterpretable; one-group pretest-posttest (O X O) fails history, maturation, testing and instrumentation; static-group comparison fails selection and mortality. Pretest-posttest control group controls all internal threats but not pretest sensitisation; posttest-only control group avoids it; Richard L. Solomon's (1949) four-group design measures it through a 2 × 2 ANOVA on posttests (pretested × treated), at about double the cost. Within-subjects designs gain power but need counterbalancing; mixed (split-plot) designs are the standard trial; RBD error df = (t − 1)(b − 1), Latin square (t − 1)(t − 2). A 2 × 3 factorial has two factors and six cells and is the only way to see interactions; nested factors sit inside others. Quasi-experiments (Thomas D. Cook and Campbell, 1979) lack random assignment: nonequivalent control group (selection interactions remain), interrupted time series (history and instrumentation remain; a comparison series helps), regression discontinuity (Donald L. Thistlethwaite and Campbell, 1960; the jump at the cut-off is the effect), natural experiments and counterbalanced designs. Field experiments trade internal for external validity; analogue studies use non-clinical participants. 21 Non-experimental designs: correlational, developmental and epidemiological In a non-experimental design the researcher manipulates nothing and assigns nobody. Variables are measured as they already exist, and the question is whether, how strongly and in what pattern they go together. Clinical psychology cannot do without these designs: age, sex, diagnosis, childhood trauma, poverty and brain injury cannot be assigned, and many things that could be assigned (neglect, substance use) must not be. Non-experimental designs describe, predict and generate hypotheses; they support a causal claim only through the slow accumulation of evidence described in 21.7. 21.1 Correlational designs A correlational design measures two or more variables in the same people and quantifies how they covary, with r, regression or their relatives (sections 12 and 13). Sleep quality and depressive symptoms are measured in 300 college students; r = −.45. It can tell you that the variables are related, how strongly, in what direction and in what shape, and it allows prediction : knowing X improves your guess about Y. It cannot, on its own, tell you why, because of two problems (section 12.1). The directionality problem (reverse causation): does poor sleep cause depression, or depression cause poor sleep? A single correlation is symmetrical and cannot say. The third-variable problem (spurious correlation): a third variable may cause both. Heavy social media use and depression in adolescents may both be driven by loneliness or family conflict. Partial correlation (section 12.5) removes third variables you measured ; it cannot remove the ones you did not. The cross-lagged panel design A partial answer to the directionality problem is to measure both variables on the same people at two (or more) times. Donald T. Campbell and Julian C. Stanley (1963) proposed the name "cross-lagged panel correlation", and Donald Pelz and Frank Andrews (1964) developed the same idea. Six correlations result: two synchronous (A and B at time 1; A and B at time 2), two stabilities or autocorrelations (A with itself, B with itself) and two cross-lagged correlations (A₁ with B₂, B₁ with A₂). The logic is temporal precedence: if A causes B, early A should predict later B better than early B predicts later A. Time 1: age 8 Time 2: age 18 TV violence (A₁) TV violence (A₂) Aggression (B₁) Aggression (B₂) stability r = .05 stability r = .40 synchronous r = .20 synchronous r = .05 r(A₁, B₂) = .30 r(B₁, A₂) = .02 Logic: if A causes B, the lag from A to later B should exceed the lag from B to later A. Here .30 > .02, so the pattern favours TV violence → aggression. All values are illustrative. A cross-lagged panel design: two variables measured on the same people at two times. The two diagonal (cross-lagged) correlations are compared; the synchronous and stability correlations are the context they must be read in. The classic application is Leonard D. Eron, L. Rowell Huesmann, Monroe M. Lefkowitz and Leopold O. Walder (1972), "Does television violence cause aggression?": in their Columbia County sample, boys' preference for violent television at about age 8 predicted their aggression ten years later better than early aggression predicted later viewing preference. The method has known weaknesses. David A. Kenny (1975) showed that unequal stabilities or changing reliabilities can by themselves make one cross-lag larger, and a third variable acting on both can still produce the pattern. Today panel data are analysed with cross-lagged panel models in structural equation modelling (section 13.6), which estimate each path while controlling for the stabilities. 21.2 Survey research Fred N. Kerlinger 's definition ( Foundations of Behavioral Research , 1964) is the one examiners quote: survey research studies large and small populations by selecting and studying samples drawn from them, to discover the relative incidence, distribution and interrelations of sociological and psychological variables. Kerlinger classed surveys as non-experimental. So a survey can tell you how common something is (incidence, prevalence), how it is spread across groups (distribution) and what goes with what (interrelations), but not the causal factors of an event , which is the answer to "survey research does NOT ...". A census is a survey of the whole population; a sample survey studies a sample (section 7.2). Type Who is measured, and when Example Main problem Cross-sectional survey One sample, one occasion A prevalence survey of exam anxiety in Class 12 students A snapshot: no change, no time order Trend study Different samples from the same population at several times (repeated cross-sections) The National Family Health Survey rounds (NFHS-1 to NFHS-5) Shows population change, not individual change Cohort study (survey sense) Different samples from the same cohort (people born or entering in the same period) at several times Samples of the 1990 birth cohort surveyed in 2010 and 2020 Change within a generation, but not within individuals Panel study The same individuals at every wave The same 2,000 students surveyed every year of college Attrition and panel conditioning (being surveyed changes later answers) Surveys are collected face-to-face, by telephone, by post, or online, each mode trading cost against response rate, coverage and social desirability; the design of questionnaires, interviews and scales is in section 23. Whatever the mode, the two big threats are coverage and non-response bias (the people who answer differ from those who do not) and self-report bias . Placing a typical M.Phil or MA dissertation. A single online questionnaire (Google Forms, shared through WhatsApp and Instagram) given once to about 250 college students recruited by convenience and snowball sampling, measuring, say, social media use, loneliness and depressive symptoms, and analysed with Pearson correlations and a binary logistic regression predicting probable depression (PHQ-9 of 10 or more), is a cross-sectional correlational survey design : non-experimental, quantitative, one time point, non-probability sample. Say exactly that in a viva. Its honest limitations are the ones in this section: no temporal order and no causal inference (the odds ratios from the logistic regression, section 13.5, are adjusted associations , and "predict" means only statistical prediction); possible third variables; common-method variance because every measure is self-report on one occasion; and limited external validity because the sample is convenience-based and limited to people online. 21.3 Ex post facto (causal-comparative) research Ex post facto means "from after the fact". Kerlinger defined it as systematic empirical inquiry in which the scientist does not have direct control of the independent variables, because their manifestations have already occurred or because they are inherently not manipulable; inferences about relations are made, without direct intervention, from the concomitant variation of independent and dependent variables. In practice the researcher starts from groups that already differ on the IV and compares them on the DV, which is why it is also called causal-comparative research. Adolescents who were bullied at school vs those who were not, compared on social anxiety; children of a parent with schizophrenia vs controls, compared on attention. Why it is not an experiment, however carefully done. There is no manipulation and no random assignment. The decisive problem is self-selection : people end up in the groups for reasons of their own, and those reasons may themselves cause the DV. People who practise yoga daily and report less anxiety may have chosen yoga because they were calmer, healthier or wealthier to begin with. Matching and ANCOVA can equate the groups on measured variables only; the rest of the selection differences remain. Reverse causation is also open (social anxiety may attract bullying). Survey research is ex post facto in this sense, which is exactly why it cannot isolate causes. 21.4 Developmental designs Developmental questions are about change with age . The difficulty is that age never travels alone. Every observation has an age , a cohort (the generation, defined by year of birth) and a time of measurement (the year of testing, carrying that period's history), and the three are locked together: age = time of measurement − year of birth . Fix any two and the third is fixed, so a simple design can never separate all three. Cross-sectional design: different age groups tested at one time . Quick and cheap, no attrition or practice effects. But age differences are confounded with cohort differences : 70-year-olds and 30-year-olds tested in 2026 differ in schooling, nutrition and technology as well as in age, and it shows age differences , not age changes or individual trajectories. This is the answer to "a disadvantage of cross-sectional studies is ...". Longitudinal design: one cohort tested repeatedly as it ages. It shows real age changes and individual differences in change, and the order of events. But age changes are confounded with time of measurement (a change between 2010 and 2020 might come from the era, not from ageing), and it suffers attrition (selective drop-out, usually of the less healthy), practice effects from repeated testing, ageing instruments, cost, and results that arrive after a career. It describes one cohort only. Time-lag design: people of the same age tested at different times (18-year-olds in 2000, 2010 and 2020). Age is held constant; cohort and time of measurement are confounded . It answers questions like "are today's adolescents more anxious than earlier generations at the same age?" K. Warner Schaie , "A general model for the study of developmental problems" ( Psychological Bulletin , 1965), set out the age-cohort-time model and three sequential designs that combine simple ones so that two of the three factors can be separated (with an assumption about the third): Cohort-sequential: two or more cohorts followed longitudinally over the same ages ; separates age and cohort, assuming no time-of-measurement effect. Time-sequential: the same age range tested cross-sectionally at two or more times; separates age and time of measurement, assuming no cohort effect. Cross-sequential: two or more cohorts tested at the same times ; separates cohort and time of measurement, assuming no age effect. Schaie's own Seattle Longitudinal Study , begun in 1956 as his doctoral work and repeated at seven-year intervals with new cohorts added, is the model sequential study. Earlier, Richard Q. Bell (1953) had proposed "convergence", an accelerated longitudinal design in which several cohorts are followed for a short span and the overlapping segments are joined into one long curve, which is the cohort-sequential idea. Its designs are the same logic in a medical vocabulary: the IV is called the exposure and the DV the outcome . Prevalence and incidence Measure Definition Example Point prevalence Existing cases at one point in time ÷ population at that time Proportion of adults with a current depressive episode on the survey day Period prevalence People who were cases at any time during a period (e.g. the past 12 months) ÷ population 12-month prevalence of alcohol use disorder Lifetime prevalence People who have ever been cases, including recovered ones ÷ population Has ever met criteria for panic disorder Incidence (cumulative incidence, risk) New cases during a period ÷ people at risk (free of the disorder) at the start New cases of postpartum depression within a year of delivery Incidence rate (incidence density) New cases ÷ total person-time at risk 12 new cases per 1,000 person-years Prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration (for a fairly rare, stable condition). Schizophrenia has a low incidence but lasts long, so its prevalence is high relative to incidence; a brief adjustment disorder can have high incidence and low point prevalence. Incidence is what you need for causes (who becomes ill); prevalence is what you need for service planning (how many are ill now). India's National Mental Health Survey 2015–16 (NIMHANS), a cross-sectional prevalence study of adults in 12 states, reported a lifetime prevalence of any mental morbidity of 13.7% and a current prevalence of 10.6% (excluding tobacco use disorder). The four core designs A cross-sectional (prevalence) study measures exposure and outcome in a population sample at the same time. It gives prevalence and associations quickly, but cannot show which came first, and it over-represents long-lasting cases (people who recover or die quickly are less likely to be caught on survey day). A cohort study starts with people who are free of the outcome, classifies them by exposure, and follows them to see who develops the outcome. It gives incidence directly and so the relative risk , establishes temporal order, and can study several outcomes of one exposure. In a prospective cohort the researcher starts now and follows people into the future (the Framingham Heart Study, from 1948; Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill's British Doctors Study of smoking, from 1951). In a retrospective (historical) cohort both exposure and outcome have already happened, but the analysis still runs forward, from exposure recorded in old files to outcome recorded later: school records from 2005 that noted bullying, linked to clinic records in 2025. Cohort studies are slow and expensive, need very large samples for rare outcomes, and lose people to attrition. A case-control study runs the other way. It starts from the outcome : cases who have the disorder and controls who do not, as similar as possible otherwise (often matched on age and sex). It then looks back for differences in past exposure. Doll and Hill's 1950 comparison of lung cancer patients with controls, which found far more smokers among the cases, is the landmark. It is fast, cheap and the most efficient design for rare disorders (autism, early-onset psychosis, suicide), since you begin with the few cases instead of waiting for them, and it can examine many exposures at once. Its weaknesses: it cannot give incidence or relative risk, only the odds ratio ; choosing proper controls is hard (hospital controls bring Berkson's bias , Joseph Berkson, 1946); and it is vulnerable to recall bias : mothers of children with a developmental disorder search their memories of pregnancy far harder than mothers of typical children. A nested case-control study is carried out inside an existing cohort: every case that arises is compared with a sample of cohort members who were still free of the outcome at that time. Exposure data (stored blood, early questionnaires) were collected before the outcome, which removes recall bias, and only a fraction of the stored material has to be analysed. Cohort studies run from exposure to outcome, either forwards from now (prospective) or through old records (retrospective); case-control studies run backwards from outcome to exposure; a cross-sectional study takes both at one moment. Retrospective is not the same as case-control. A retrospective cohort uses past data but reasons from exposure to outcome; a case-control study reasons from outcome to exposure. The question "the British Doctors were questioned about smoking in 1951 and followed for decades: what design?" is a prospective cohort (observational, not experimental). "Rare outcome plus past exposure" signals case-control. Ecological studies and the ecological fallacy An ecological study uses groups (districts, states, countries) as the units: suicide rates against unemployment rates across Indian states, for example, using National Crime Records Bureau data. The ecological fallacy is drawing conclusions about individuals from a correlation between group averages. William S. Robinson (1950) gave the classic demonstration with 1930 US census data: across the 48 states, the percentage of foreign-born residents correlated +.53 with the literacy rate, yet at the individual level being foreign-born correlated −.11 with literacy. Immigrants had settled in states whose native-born populations were highly literate. A state-level correlation, even a strong one, says nothing certain about the people inside the states. (The reverse error, generalising from individuals to groups, is the atomistic fallacy.) 21.6 Measuring association: relative risk, odds ratio and attributable risk Arrange any exposure-outcome study as a 2 × 2 table with cells a (exposed, ill), b (exposed, well), c (unexposed, ill), d (unexposed, well). Risk in a group = ill ÷ everyone in that group: a/(a+b) for exposed, c/(c+d) for unexposed. Relative risk (risk ratio), RR = risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed. Needs incidence, so it comes from cohort studies and trials. Odds = ill ÷ well within a group: a/b and c/d. Odds ratio, OR = (a/b)/(c/d) = ad/bc . The only measure available from a case-control study, and the one logistic regression produces (section 13.5). Reading them: RR or OR = 1 means no association ; above 1, the exposure is associated with more of the outcome (a risk factor); below 1, with less (protective). A 95% confidence interval that includes 1 means the association is not significant. Risk difference (attributable risk) = risk in exposed − risk in unexposed: the excess cases due to the exposure, on an absolute scale. Attributable risk percent in the exposed = risk difference ÷ risk in exposed. Population attributable risk percent = (overall risk − risk in unexposed) ÷ overall risk: the share of all cases in the population that would disappear if the exposure did. Worked example. A cohort of 1,000 adults whose childhood records noted trauma (200 exposed) or not (800 unexposed) is assessed for depression. 60 of the 200 exposed and 80 of the 800 unexposed are depressed. Risk in exposed = 60/200 = 0.30; risk in unexposed = 80/800 = 0.10. RR = 0.30/0.10 = 3.0 : those exposed to childhood trauma were three times as likely to be depressed. Odds in exposed = 60/140 = 0.429; odds in unexposed = 80/720 = 0.111. OR = (60 × 720)/(140 × 80) = 43,200/11,200 = 3.86 . Risk difference = 0.30 − 0.10 = 0.20 : 20 extra cases per 100 exposed people (number needed to harm = 1/0.20 = 5). Attributable risk percent in the exposed = 0.20/0.30 = 67% : two-thirds of the depression among the exposed is attributable to the exposure, if the association is causal. Overall risk = 140/1,000 = 0.14, so PAR% = (0.14 − 0.10)/0.14 = 29% . OR = (60 × 360) / (80 × 70) = 3.86: the same OR. A 'risk' from that table (60/130) would be meaningless, because the researcher chose how many controls to take. Risk exposed = a/(a+b) = 60/200 = 0.30 unexposed = c/(c+d) = 80/800 = 0.10 Relative risk RR = 0.30/0.10 = 3.0 Odds exposed = a/b = 60/140 = 0.429 unexposed = c/d = 80/720 = 0.111 Odds ratio OR = ad/bc = 3.86 Impact risk difference = 0.30 − 0.10 = 0.20 AR% in exposed = 0.20/0.30 = 67% PAR% = (0.14 − 0.10)/0.14 = 29% OR (3.86) is larger than RR (3.0) because depression is common here (30% vs 10%). Worked 2 × 2 table: childhood trauma and adult depression. Risk ratio 3.0, odds ratio 3.86, risk difference 0.20 (20 extra cases per 100 exposed); the case-control sample recovers the same odds ratio. Why the OR is bigger than the RR here, and why case-control studies use it. The OR exaggerates the RR whenever the outcome is common; when the outcome is rare (roughly under 10% in both groups), b ≈ a + b and d ≈ c + d, so OR ≈ RR. That is the rare disease assumption , and it is why case-control studies of rare disorders report ORs as estimates of relative risk. The OR survives case-control sampling because it is symmetrical: the odds of exposure among cases divided by the odds of exposure among controls equals the odds of illness among the exposed divided by the odds among the unexposed, so sampling all cases and only some controls leaves it unchanged (3.86 in the figure), whereas any "risk" from that table depends on how many controls the researcher decided to take. From association to causation: the Bradford Hill criteria Austin Bradford Hill , in "The environment and disease: association or causation?" (1965), listed nine "viewpoints" for judging whether an observed association is causal. He insisted they were aids to judgement, not a checklist, and that none except temporality is indispensable. Viewpoint Question Applied to childhood trauma and adult depression Strength Is the association large? RR = 3 is stronger than most confounders could produce Consistency Is it repeated in different places, samples and designs? Found in cohort and case-control studies across countries Specificity Does the exposure lead to one particular outcome? Weak here: trauma predicts many disorders (Hill himself said this one is often absent) Temporality Does the exposure come first? The trauma was recorded in childhood: the only essential criterion Biological gradient Is there a dose-response relation? More types or longer duration of trauma, higher risk Plausibility Is there a plausible mechanism? Stress-system (HPA axis) sensitisation, negative schemas Coherence Does it fit what else is known? Consistent with stress-diathesis models Experiment Does removing or reducing the exposure reduce the outcome? Prevention and early-intervention evidence Analogy Do similar exposures have similar effects? Early adversity in animal studies 21.7 Descriptive designs: observation, case study and archival research Naturalistic observation records behaviour in its natural setting without intervening: children's play in an anganwadi, interaction on a psychiatric ward. It gives high ecological validity and is often the first step in a new area, but it is open to reactivity (people behave differently when watched) and observer bias, and it cannot explain what it records. Sampling, coding and observer reliability are covered in section 23. A case study is an intensive, usually long-term study of one person, family, group or institution, using interviews, observation, tests and records. It is idiographic (aimed at understanding the particular), in the sense Wilhelm Windelband (1894) distinguished from the nomothetic search for general laws, a distinction Gordon W. Allport (1937) brought into psychology. It is the right design for rare phenomena, for generating hypotheses, for disconfirming a universal claim with one counter-example, and for illustrating a treatment. Its limits: no control, no generalisation to others, and heavy reliance on the investigator's interpretation and on retrospective reports. (Small-N designs that add experimental control to the single case are section 22.) Case Who reported it What it is remembered for Anna O.
