Strengths: easy to construct and to answer, applicable to any concept, gives a multidimensional picture, and a self versus ideal-self pair of profiles is a ready index of self-esteem. Weaknesses: some adjective pairs do not fit some concepts ("heavy–light" for a person with diabetes); respondents may reach the extremes or the midpoint by style; the polarity of pairs should be alternated so that the favourable adjective is not always on the left (to break acquiescence and position sets). The figure aligns all favourable poles on the left only for reading. Bogardus social distance scale Emory S. Bogardus (1925) measured prejudice as the degree of intimacy a person will accept with members of a group. Respondents mark the closest relationship they would accept: (1) to close kinship by marriage; (2) to my club as personal chums; (3) to my street as neighbours; (4) to employment in my occupation; (5) to citizenship in my country; (6) as visitors only to my country; (7) would exclude from my country. Accepting a close relationship implies accepting the more distant ones, so the scale is cumulative (Guttman-type) and ordinal. It is still used for attitudes to castes, religions, migrants and people with mental illness. Paired comparisons and rank order In the method of paired comparisons every stimulus is paired with every other and the respondent chooses the preferred (or more favourable) one in each pair. With n stimuli there are n(n − 1)/2 pairs: 10 stimuli need 45 judgements, 20 need 190, which is the method's practical limit. The proportion of times each stimulus is preferred is converted to a scale position using Thurstone's law of comparative judgment, giving an interval scale of preference. The rank-order method asks the respondent to order all stimuli at once, which is quicker but yields only ordinal data and becomes unreliable in the middle of long lists. Q-sort William Stephenson introduced Q-technique in 1935 and set it out in The Study of Behavior: Q-Technique and Its Methodology (1953). Ordinary (R-technique) factor analysis correlates tests across many people; Q-technique correlates persons (or one person's different sorts) across many items. The respondent sorts a deck of cards, each with a statement ("I am a responsible person", "I often feel insecure"), into piles from "most like me" to "least like me", with a forced, roughly normal distribution (a fixed number of cards in each pile, typically 9 or 11 piles, with few at the extremes and many in the middle). Because the distribution is fixed, everyone's sort has the same mean and spread, so the method describes the relative importance of traits within one person (ipsative measurement) rather than comparing people's absolute levels. Carl Rogers made it famous in psychotherapy research: in Psychotherapy and Personality Change (Rogers and Dymond, 1954), clients sorted the same statements twice, once for the self and once for the ideal self , and the correlation between the two sorts (John Butler and Gerard Haigh's self–ideal correlation) rose after client-centred therapy, the operational measure of reduced self-ideal discrepancy (incongruence). Jack Block's California Q-set (1961) is the best-known standard deck. Sociometry and the sociogram Jacob L. Moreno , founder of psychodrama, introduced sociometry in Who Shall Survive? (1934), from work with girls at the Hudson training school in New York. In the sociometric test each member of a group names the people they would choose (and sometimes reject) as companions for an activity: "Whom would you like to sit next to?", "Whom would you like in your project group?". The choices are drawn as a sociogram , with people as circles and choices as arrows, which shows the group's structure: stars (chosen by many), isolates (chosen by none), mutual pairs , chains , cliques and rejectees . Teachers and school counsellors use it to identify isolated and rejected children; it measures patterns of attraction, choice and social distance within a group, not personality or intelligence. Visual analogue, forced-choice and checklist methods Visual analogue scale (VAS): a line, usually 100 mm , with anchors only at the ends ("no pain" … "worst pain imaginable"; "not at all anxious" … "extremely anxious"). The respondent marks the line and the score is the distance in mm. Quick, sensitive to small changes, language-light and repeatable many times a day (craving, pain, mood), but each scale is a single item and needs some abstract understanding. Forced-choice method: the respondent must choose between two or more statements, usually matched for social desirability, so that the "good-looking" answer is not obvious. It reduces social desirability and leniency, but produces ipsative scores (a high score on one trait forces lower scores on others), which complicates comparison between people. Edwards Personal Preference Schedule is the textbook example. Checklist method: the respondent (or an observer) ticks every adjective or statement that applies, as in Harrison Gough's Adjective Check List or symptom checklists. Fast and simple, but it records presence or absence, not degree, and the number ticked depends on how many items the respondent tends to tick. Thurstone's respondents only agree or disagree; it is Likert's respondents who rate degree of agreement. 23.7 Other sources of data Psychophysiological measures These record bodily activity that accompanies psychological states: electrodermal activity (EDA, the older galvanic skin response or GSR, first described by Charles Féré and Ivan Tarchanoff around 1888 to 1890), which rises with sweat-gland activity under arousal; heart rate and heart-rate variability; blood pressure; respiration; electromyography (EMG, muscle tension, used in biofeedback); electroencephalography (EEG, first recorded in humans by Hans Berger, 1929 ) and event-related potentials, with millisecond timing but poor spatial resolution; and brain imaging, especially fMRI , which tracks the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal described by Seiji Ogawa (1990), with good spatial but poor temporal resolution. Their place: they are hard to fake and are not filtered through language or self-presentation, and they suit arousal, anxiety and emotion research, biofeedback and lie detection (the polygraph). But they measure arousal, not a specific emotion (fear, anger and excitement look alike on GSR), are sensitive to movement, temperature and medication, need costly equipment, and usually confine the person to a laboratory. They complement self-report and observation rather than replacing them. Archival and secondary data Archival research analyses records that already exist: hospital case files, school records, court and police records, census data, newspapers, letters and diaries, social media posts. The classic is Émile Durkheim's Suicide (1897) , built entirely from official statistics. Indian examples include National Crime Records Bureau suicide statistics, the National Family Health Survey and the National Mental Health Survey of India (2015–16) carried out by NIMHANS. Archival data are cheap, often huge, longitudinal and non-reactive , but they were collected for other purposes by other people, so variables may be missing or defined differently, accuracy cannot be checked, and recording practices change over time (a "rise" in recorded suicides may reflect better reporting). Experience sampling and ecological momentary assessment The experience sampling method (ESM) , developed by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi and Reed Larson in the late 1970s and 1980s, signals participants (originally with pagers, now with smartphone apps) at random moments several times a day to record what they are doing, where, with whom and how they feel. It produced Csikszentmihalyi's research on flow and Larson's studies of adolescents' daily moods. Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) , the term of Arthur Stone and Saul Shiffman (1994), applies the same idea in clinical and health research: craving and lapses in smokers, mood swings in bipolar disorder, panic attacks, pain. Because reports are made in the moment and in the person's natural environment, they reduce retrospective recall bias and have high ecological validity, at the cost of burden on participants, missed prompts and reactivity. Diaries Diary methods ask people to record events, symptoms or feelings at regular times (end of each day) or whenever an event happens: sleep diaries in insomnia, headache diaries, food and mood diaries, the thought records of CBT, a parent's ABC (antecedent–behaviour–consequence) chart of tantrums. They capture sequences and context close to the time of occurrence, but depend on compliance and honesty, and paper diaries are often back-filled just before the appointment. Unobtrusive (non-reactive) measures Eugene Webb, Donald Campbell, Richard Schwartz and Lee Sechrest (1966) , Unobtrusive Measures: Nonreactive Research in the Social Sciences , catalogued ways of measuring behaviour without the person knowing, so reactivity is impossible. Physical traces are either erosion measures (wear: the floor tiles around the hatching-chick exhibit at Chicago's Museum of Science and Industry had to be replaced far more often than elsewhere, indexing its popularity) or accretion measures (deposits: litter, empty bottles in a hostel's bins, graffiti, the number of cigarette butts). Others are archival records , simple observation by an unseen observer, and contrived observation with hidden hardware. Webb and colleagues argued that because every method has its own bias, a finding should be checked by several methods whose biases differ, which they called triangulation. Projective methods Projective techniques (Hermann Rorschach's inkblots, 1921; Christiana Morgan and Henry Murray's Thematic Apperception Test, 1935; sentence completion, draw-a-person) present ambiguous stimuli on the theory that people project their own needs and conflicts into their responses. As data-collection methods they are indirect and hard to fake but depend heavily on scorer judgement, so inter-scorer reliability (section 15.2) is the first thing to check. Raymond B. Cattell's three media of data classify all of the above: L-data (life record: observable behaviour in everyday life, ratings by others, records such as school grades), Q-data (questionnaire: self-report of one's own characteristics) and T-data (objective test: behaviour in a controlled test situation whose purpose the person cannot easily see). 23.8 Primary and secondary, quantitative and qualitative, and triangulation Primary data are collected first-hand by the researcher for the present study (the interviews, observations and questionnaires above). Secondary data were collected by someone else for another purpose and are re-used: census tables, NFHS datasets, hospital registers, a previous trial's data. Secondary analysis is cheap and fast and allows very large or historical samples, but the researcher controls neither the variables nor the quality. Meta-analysis (section 25) is a systematic analysis of secondary data. Quantitative data are numbers (counts, ratings, scores) suited to statistical analysis; qualitative data are words, images and observations analysed for meaning, themes and patterns (section 24). Most methods in this section can produce either: an interview can be fully structured with coded answers or completely open; observation can be a coding scheme or rich field notes. Structured methods trade depth for comparability; unstructured methods trade comparability for depth. Because every method has a characteristic error (reactivity in observation, interviewer bias in interviews, response sets in questionnaires, non-specificity in physiology, unknown accuracy in archives), the strongest research combines methods whose errors differ. This is triangulation : if a child's improvement shows up in observed behaviour, in the teacher's ratings and in the parent's interview, no single method's bias can explain it. The same idea underlies the multitrait–multimethod logic of section 15.3 and the mixed-methods designs of section 24, where Norman Denzin's (1970) four types of triangulation (data, investigator, theory and methodological) are explained. Recap of section 23: observation is naturalistic or controlled, participant or non-participant, overt or covert; Gold's (1958) four roles run from complete participant to complete observer, trading insider understanding (and the risk of going native) against detachment. Reactivity is reduced by habituation, observer bias by blinding, observer drift by recalibration. Behaviour is sampled by time, event (Dawe, 1934) or situation and recorded continuously, in anecdotal or running records, checklists, rating scales or coding schemes such as Bales's 12-category Interaction Process Analysis (1950). Interviews are structured (DIS, CIDI, MINI), semi-structured (SCID, PSE/SCAN, K-SADS) or unstructured, and carry interviewer bias (Rice, 1929). Good items are never double-barrelled, leading, loaded, doubly negative or jargon; pilot first; low response rates mean non-response bias. Response sets (Cronbach, 1946) include acquiescence (cure: balanced keying), social desirability (Edwards, 1957; Marlowe–Crowne, 1960; cure: anonymity, forced choice, lie scales), extreme and midpoint responding and faking. Rating errors: halo (Edward Thorndike, 1920), leniency, severity, central tendency, logical, contrast, proximity. Thurstone (1928, 1929): judges, 11 piles, median scale value, Q for ambiguity. Likert (1932): summated ratings, ordinal per item, interval in total. Guttman (1944): cumulative, CR ≥ .90. Osgood (1957): semantic differential, E P A. Bogardus (1925): social distance. Paired comparisons: n(n − 1)/2. Stephenson's Q-sort (1953) gave Rogers the self–ideal correlation; Jacob Moreno's sociogram (1934) shows stars and isolates. Other sources: psychophysiology, archives, ESM/EMA, diaries, unobtrusive measures (Webb and colleagues, 1966). Data are primary or secondary, quantitative or qualitative, and strongest when triangulated. 24 Qualitative and mixed-methods research Sections 19 to 22 ask "how much?" and "does X cause Y?". Many clinical questions cannot be answered with numbers. What is it like to hear a voice nobody else hears? Why does a family take a son with psychosis to a temple for two years before a hospital? What do patients mean when they say they have "tension"? Qualitative research exists for these questions, and the entrance papers test it as recall: which approach goes with which founder, the order of coding, the six phases of thematic analysis, Lincoln and Guba's criteria, the mixed-methods designs. 24.1 What qualitative research is, and why it exists Qualitative research studies meaning, experience, process and context , using words, images and observed action as data, analysed by interpretation rather than counting. Meaning: a diagnosis of schizophrenia can mean "a treatable illness" to a psychiatrist and "the daughters of this family will not marry" to a grandmother. Experience: how panic, caring or recovery is lived from the inside. Process: how something unfolds over time, such as deciding to seek help. Context: how family, caste, ward or law shape all of this. The work is naturalistic : it studies people where the phenomenon happens, not in a laboratory. Its logic is inductive and bottom-up. A quantitative study deduces a hypothesis from theory and tests it (the hypothetico-deductive cycle of section 18); a qualitative study starts with an open question and builds concepts, themes or a theory out of the data. Many describe the reasoning as abductive (Charles Sanders Peirce's term): moving between data and ideas to find the most plausible explanation. The researcher is the instrument : the interviewer's questions, rapport and interpretations produce the data, which Yvonna Lincoln and Egon Guba (1985) called the "human instrument". Because this instrument cannot be standardised, qualitative work replaces standardisation with reflexivity , an open account of how the researcher's background and position shaped the study. The design is emergent : questions and sampling may change as the study proceeds, which would be fatal in an experiment and is a strength here. The roots. Wilhelm Dilthey (1883) argued that the natural sciences explain (Erklären) while the human sciences must understand meaning from the inside (Verstehen), which Max Weber made a method of sociology. Symbolic interactionism , the name Herbert Blumer coined in 1937 for the ideas of George Herbert Mead , holds that people act toward things on the basis of the meanings those things have for them, meanings that arise in social interaction and are modified through interpretation. Phenomenology (24.5) and ethnomethodology (24.8) are the other roots. Qualitative work mostly sits in the constructivist / interpretivist paradigm (and the critical paradigm), quantitative work in positivism / post-positivism , and mixed methods in pragmatism ; the paradigms are laid out in section 18. Qualitative work is also idiographic (studying the particular case in depth) rather than nomothetic (seeking general laws across people). Wilhelm Windelband drew that distinction in 1894 and Gordon Allport (1937) brought it into psychology, preferring the idiographic. Experiments are the nomothetic method. Feature Quantitative research Qualitative research Aim Measure, test hypotheses, estimate effects, generalise Understand meaning, experience, process and context in depth Typical question How many? How much? Does X cause Y? What is it like? How does it happen? What does it mean? Logic Deductive, theory-testing, top-down Inductive or abductive, theory-generating, bottom-up Paradigm Positivist / post-positivist Constructivist / interpretivist, critical Design Fixed in advance Emergent and flexible Sampling Probability sampling; size from power analysis (section 8) Purposive or theoretical sampling of information-rich cases; size from saturation Data Numbers from standardised instruments Words, images, observed action: transcripts, field notes, documents Researcher Detached; a source of bias to be controlled The instrument; involved; made transparent by reflexivity Analysis Statistical, after data collection Interpretive coding into categories and themes, often during data collection Quality criteria Internal and external validity, reliability, objectivity Trustworthiness: credibility, transferability, dependability, confirmability (24.12) Generalisation Statistical: sample to population Transferability to similar settings, or analytic generalisation to theory How the papers ask it. "Which does not apply to qualitative research?" An emphasis on objective truth (the role of language, understanding of processes and concern for individuality all do apply). "Which does not go with symbolic interactionism, meaning and phenomenology?" The researcher's authority : qualitative work privileges participants' meanings. "A critical feature of qualitative research?" Data collected in a context-specific setting, with bottom-up evidence , not standardised tools or probability samples. "Which is quantitative: case study, ethnography, survey, grounded theory?" Survey. "Nomothetic study belongs to?" The experimental method. When to choose it: a new or poorly understood topic; a question about meaning, experience or process; a sensitive subject or marginalised group whose voice is the point; building a questionnaire or intervention that fits a culture; explaining puzzling numbers. What it cannot do is estimate prevalence, size a treatment effect, or generalise statistically. 24.2 Sampling in qualitative research Probability sampling (section 7.2) aims at a sample that represents a population. Qualitative research wants information-rich cases : people who have lived the experience and can talk about it in depth. The phrase belongs to Michael Quinn Patton (1990), who catalogued the strategies of purposive (purposeful) sampling. Because selection is deliberate, the chance of selection is unknown, which is why "randomisation is not possible in purposive sampling" is a correct exam statement. Purposive strategy What you choose Clinical example Maximum variation Cases as different as possible on what matters; patterns that survive the variety are convincing Carers of people with schizophrenia: urban and rural, rich and poor, parents and spouses Homogeneous Cases alike on key features, to study one experience in depth (standard in IPA and focus groups) First-time mothers aged 20 to 30 with postpartum depression, from one district Typical case The ordinary instance, to show what is normal A typical patient's route through a district hospital OPD Extreme or deviant case Unusual successes or failures that reveal what makes the difference People who recovered fully from first-episode psychosis with no follow-up care Critical case A case that allows logical generalisation: "if it happens here, it will happen anywhere" If a well-staffed teaching hospital cannot deliver CBT to inpatients, a rural centre will not Criterion Every case meeting a set criterion All patients who dropped out after one therapy session last year Snowball / chain referral Participants lead you to further participants Hidden or stigmatised groups: people who inject drugs, families who hide an ill member Convenience Whoever is available Patton calls it the least desirable strategy: neither purposeful nor strategic Theoretical sampling belongs to grounded theory (24.6). Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss (1967) defined it as data collection controlled by the emerging theory: after analysing the first interviews, you choose whom to interview next in order to develop the categories you have found. If early data suggest that "fear of neighbours knowing" delays help-seeking, you next sample families living anonymously in a city to see how that category behaves. The difference from purposive sampling is timing and basis : purposive sampling is planned in advance from the question; theoretical sampling is decided during the study from the analysis. Theoretical saturation (Glaser and Strauss, 1967) is reached when new data add no new properties to the categories of the theory. Data saturation , in wider use, means new interviews bring no new information or themes. In a widely cited test, Greg Guest, Arwen Bunce and Laura Johnson (2006) found that in a fairly homogeneous sample almost all themes had appeared within 12 interviews and the main ones within 6. How sample size is decided. Never by power analysis. Instead by saturation; by information power ( Kirsti Malterud and colleagues, 2016: the more relevant information each participant holds, given the study's aim, sample specificity, use of theory, quality of dialogue and analysis strategy, the fewer participants you need); by the conventions of the approach; and by practicality. Rules of thumb: IPA uses 3 to 10 homogeneous participants (Smith and colleagues suggest about 3 for a student project); John Creswell cites 5 to 25 for phenomenology (from Donald Polkinghorne, 1989) and 20 to 30 for grounded theory; ethnography studies one group; a case study one or a few cases; focus-group studies run three or four groups per type of participant (Richard Krueger's rule of thumb). Exact definitions. Purposive sampling: deliberate selection of information-rich cases, planned in advance. Theoretical sampling: selection directed by the emerging theory during analysis. Theoretical saturation: new data add no new properties to the categories. Data saturation: new data add no new information or themes. 24.3 Collecting qualitative data In-depth interviews. The workhorse is the semi-structured interview (interview formats are compared in section 23). The interviewer follows a topic guide of open questions ("Tell me about the time you first noticed something was wrong") and uses probes ("What was that like?", "Can you give me an example?", "What does tension feel like?"), avoids leading questions, and lets silences work. Interviews are audio-recorded with consent and transcribed verbatim ; the transcript is the data. Steinar Kvale (InterViews, 1996) contrasted the interviewer as miner , digging out knowledge already there, with the interviewer as traveller , co-constructing knowledge in conversation. Focus groups. A focus group is a moderated discussion of a focused topic in which the interaction between participants is itself the data. It descends from the focused interview of Robert K. Merton and Patricia Kendall (1946), developed at Columbia University to study audience reactions to wartime propaganda films and radio, and expanded with Marjorie Fiske into The Focused Interview (1956). Size: usually about 6 to 10 participants, for about 1 to 2 hours; usually homogeneous on the key characteristic, because people speak more freely among peers. Moderator: introduces the topic, keeps it focused, draws out quiet members, restrains dominant ones, and does not give their own views; an assistant takes notes. Group dynamics: the strength is synergy (one comment sparks another; shared norms and vocabulary become visible). The weakness is dominance, conformity and groupthink, social desirability, and reluctance to disclose stigmatised experiences before neighbours. The unit of analysis is the group. Good for shared views, norms and language, and generating questionnaire items; poor for life histories, sensitive disclosures, or measuring how common a view is. Example: four focus groups with ASHA workers to learn how they recognise and talk about depression in new mothers, before writing a screening tool in the local language. Other sources. Participant observation is the core of ethnography; its roles and recording are covered in section 23. Documents (case files, letters, policies, newspaper reports, online forum posts) are naturally occurring data, produced without the researcher. Visual methods include photo-elicitation (photographs as interview prompts; John Collier, 1957) and photovoice (participants photograph their own lives and discuss the pictures; Caroline Wang and Mary Ann Burris, 1997). Diaries (written, audio, video) capture experience close to when it happens and across weeks, reducing recall bias. 24.4 The coding vocabulary Almost every qualitative analysis works by coding : attaching short labels to segments of data so that segments with similar meaning can be gathered, compared and interpreted. These terms are used as distractors across all the approaches. Term Meaning Code A word or short phrase capturing the meaning of a data segment ("hiding the illness") Category A group of related codes at a higher level of abstraction (the grounded-theory term): "hiding the illness", "avoiding weddings" and "fear of gossip" become "managing stigma" Theme A pattern of shared meaning across the data set, organised around a central idea that matters for the research question (Braun and Clarke). An interpretation, not a topic heading Memo A note the analyst writes about a code, category or emerging idea; memos record the analysis and become the draft of the theory (central in grounded theory) Codebook The list of codes, each with a definition, inclusion and exclusion rules and an example, so several coders can code consistently In vivo code A code in the participant's own words: "my mind is not in my control" A priori vs emergent A priori (deductive) codes are set before analysis, from theory or the interview guide; emergent (inductive) codes are created from the data Semantic vs latent Semantic codes stay with the explicit meaning; latent codes interpret underlying ideas and assumptions CAQDAS Computer-assisted qualitative data analysis software: NVivo , ATLAS.ti , MAXQDA . It stores, codes, retrieves and links data and memos; it does not analyse 24.5 Phenomenology and interpretative phenomenological analysis Edmund Husserl founded phenomenology (Logical Investigations, 1900–1901; Ideas, 1913) with the slogan "back to the things themselves": describe experience exactly as it appears to consciousness. Consciousness is always consciousness of something ( intentionality , from his teacher Franz Brentano). His method is the epoché or bracketing : suspending one's assumptions and theories about the phenomenon so it can be described freshly, and then seeking its essence , the invariant structure that makes the experience what it is. His student Martin Heidegger (Being and Time, 1927) replied that we are always already being-in-the-world , with a fore-structure of understanding, so we can never fully bracket ourselves out: all understanding is interpretation . That made phenomenology hermeneutic , developed further by Hans-Georg Gadamer (Truth and Method, 1960) and his hermeneutic circle : the parts are understood through the whole and the whole through the parts. Descriptive (transcendental) phenomenology Interpretive (hermeneutic) phenomenology Philosopher Husserl Heidegger, Gadamer Researcher Brackets assumptions; a detached describer Cannot bracket fully; uses their own understanding, made explicit Goal The essential structure (essence) of the experience An interpretation of what the experience means, in context Research methods Giorgi; Colaizzi; Clark Moustakas (1994) Max van Manen (1990); IPA Aim and data. Phenomenology asks: what is the lived experience of this phenomenon, and what is its essential structure? Data are long, open interviews with people who have lived it ("Please describe, in as much detail as you can, a time when you...") or written first-person accounts. Amedeo Giorgi (Psychology as a Human Science, 1970), at Duquesne University, turned Husserl's philosophy into the descriptive phenomenological psychological method . Holding the attitude of bracketing throughout, the researcher (1) reads the whole description for a sense of the whole ; (2) divides it into meaning units ; (3) transforms each unit into psychologically sensitive language; and (4) synthesises them into a general structure of the experience. Paul Colaizzi (1978) gave the seven steps most used in nursing and Indian clinical theses: Read all participants' descriptions to acquire a feeling for them. Extract significant statements . Formulate meanings for each. Organise the meanings into clusters of themes . Integrate the results into an exhaustive description . Reduce it to the fundamental structure of the phenomenon. Return to the participants to validate the findings (a member check), a step Giorgi's method does not include. Example study question: "What is the lived experience of mothers caring for an adult son with schizophrenia in a joint family?" The output is a structure of the experience: constant vigilance, grief for the son who was, being judged by relatives. Phenomenology in psychiatry is different. Karl Jaspers (General Psychopathology, 1913) brought phenomenology into psychiatry as descriptive psychopathology : the clinician empathically describes the patient's subjective experience and separates the form of a symptom from its content . That is a way of examining a patient. Phenomenological research (Husserl, Giorgi, Colaizzi, IPA) is a method for studying lived experience across participants. Detached or involved? One paper asked which approach of phenomenology uses "uninvolved, objective observation" and which "involved observation", with the labels direct and indirect . These labels are not standard in the main qualitative textbooks and are not used consistently, so anchor on the substance: detached, bracketed description = Husserl, descriptive phenomenology ; involved, interpretive understanding = Heidegger, hermeneutic phenomenology . "Semi-direct" is not a category at all. Interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA) Jonathan A. Smith introduced interpretative phenomenological analysis in health psychology in 1996 and set it out fully with Paul Flowers and Michael Larkin in 2009 (second edition 2022). It was born inside psychology, not philosophy, and is now the most used phenomenological method in clinical and health psychology. IPA rests on three pillars. Phenomenology: it studies how people experience and make sense of major life events. Hermeneutics: it is openly interpretive, and its signature idea is the double hermeneutic : the participant is trying to make sense of their world, and the researcher is trying to make sense of the participant trying to make sense of their world. Idiography: each case is analysed in detail on its own terms before comparison across cases. Samples are small, purposive and homogeneous ; data are semi-structured interviews. The analysis (Smith, Flowers and Larkin, 2009): Reading and re-reading the first transcript. Initial noting : descriptive, linguistic and conceptual comments. Developing emergent themes . Searching for connections across emergent themes (superordinate themes). Moving to the next case , trying to bracket the previous case's ideas. Looking for patterns across cases : a table of master (group) themes. The 2022 edition renamed the products: experiential statements , personal experiential themes (per case) and group experiential themes (across cases). Example study question: "How do young women make sense of their recovery from anorexia nervosa?" Six women, analysed case by case. IPA versus descriptive phenomenology. Descriptive phenomenology (Husserl, Giorgi, Colaizzi) brackets and seeks the essence . IPA interprets (double hermeneutic), stays idiographic and claims no universal essence. "Double hermeneutic", "idiographic" or "Jonathan Smith" means IPA; "epoché", "essence", "meaning units", "significant statements" or "seven steps" means descriptive phenomenology. 24.6 Grounded theory Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss published The Discovery of Grounded Theory in 1967, after studying how hospital staff and dying patients in California handled the knowledge that a patient was dying (Awareness of Dying, 1965). They objected to sociology that only tested "grand theories" (Talcott Parsons): theory should be generated from data by systematic comparison. Strauss brought the Chicago school's symbolic interactionism; Glaser brought Columbia's rigour (Paul Lazarsfeld's methods, Robert Merton's middle-range theory). Aim. Grounded theory is the approach whose output is a theory : an explanation of a process (a "substantive" theory of, say, help-seeking for psychosis), built inductively. It starts with no hypothesis, and classic grounded theory even delays the literature review so as not to force the data into existing ideas. Its tools are simultaneous data collection and analysis ; the constant comparative method (each new incident is compared with earlier ones coded the same way, then with categories, then categories with each other; the signature of the approach); theoretical sampling and saturation (24.2); memo writing ; theoretical sensitivity (Glaser, 1978), the analyst's ability to see what matters theoretically; and the core category , the central concept to which all others relate. The three coding stages examiners ask about come from Anselm Strauss and Juliet Corbin (Basics of Qualitative Research, 1990): Open coding: break the data apart line by line, label concepts, and group them into categories with properties and dimensions. Axial coding: put the data back together by relating categories to subcategories around the "axis" of a category, using a coding paradigm (conditions, actions and interactions, consequences). "Weaving the data back together around groups of concepts" is axial coding. Selective coding: choose one core category and relate every other category to it, integrating the theory into one storyline. Constant comparison and memo writing run through every stage 1 Raw data 2 Open coding 3 Axial coding 4 Selective coding interview transcripts field notes diaries, documents sleepless nights hiding it neighbours talking blaming myself temple visits hospital is far money running out carrying the burden managing stigma searching for a cure CORE CATEGORY protecting the family's name Do new data add new properties? NO Theoretical saturation: stop and write the theory YES Theoretical sampling: go back to the field for the people and settings the weak categories need Each loop: collect, code, compare, write memos, ask again. Strauss and Corbin (1990): open, axial, selective. Glaser: substantive (open, selective) then theoretical coding. The grounded-theory coding funnel: many open codes are woven into a few axial categories and then integrated around one core category, while theoretical sampling sends the analyst back to the field until new data add nothing new (theoretical saturation). The split. Glaser kept the classic version: substantive coding (open, then selective once a core category appears) followed by theoretical coding , which models how the substantive codes relate using "coding families" such as his six Cs (causes, contexts, contingencies, consequences, covariances, conditions). In Emergence vs Forcing (1992) he attacked Strauss and Corbin's paradigm for forcing data into preset categories instead of letting theory emerge . Kathy Charmaz (Constructing Grounded Theory, 2006) then founded constructivist grounded theory : theory is not discovered in the data but constructed by researcher and participants together, so reflexivity is essential. She codes in two main phases, initial (line-by-line, often in gerunds such as "hiding", "waiting") and focused , then theoretical. Her own studies of chronic illness described the "loss of self". Version Founders Coding Stance Classic (Glaserian) Glaser and Strauss 1967; Glaser 1978, 1992 Substantive (open → selective), then theoretical Theory emerges; do not force Straussian Strauss and Corbin 1990 Open → axial → selective Procedural; a coding paradigm guides analysis Constructivist Charmaz 2006 Initial → focused (→ theoretical) Theory is co-constructed Example study question: "How do families in rural Karnataka move from first noticing psychotic symptoms to reaching a psychiatrist?" Early open codes ("consulting the elders", "trying the temple first") become categories; theoretical sampling then seeks families who went straight to hospital; a core category such as "protecting the family's name" organises a theory of delayed help-seeking. Grounded-theory traps. (1) The order is open → axial → selective , from Strauss and Corbin (1990) , not the 1967 book. (2) Open coding fractures, axial reassembles, selective finds the core category. (3) Grounded theory generates theory; it neither tests theory nor merely describes lived experience (that is phenomenology). (4) Its signature words are constant comparison, theoretical sampling, memos, core category . (5) Sampling stops at theoretical saturation , not at a number fixed in advance. 24.7 Ethnography, case study and narrative research Ethnography Bronislaw Malinowski created modern fieldwork by living among the people of the Trobriand Islands , off New Guinea, during the First World War (1915–1918), learning their language and joining daily life; Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922) set the goal of grasping "the native's point of view". The linguist Kenneth Pike (1954) coined emic and etic from phon emic and phon etic . Clifford Geertz (The Interpretation of Cultures, 1973) made thick description the aim of interpretive ethnography, borrowing the phrase from the philosopher Gilbert Ryle . Ethnography (Greek: writing about a people) is the study and written description of a culture or social group from the inside, through long immersion in its natural setting: how does this group live, and what do its beliefs, rules and practices mean to its members? Its main method is participant observation , with informal interviews, documents and artefacts, over months or years. Emic vs etic: an emic account uses insiders' own categories; an etic account uses the outsider's analytic categories, which allow comparison across cultures. "Tension" or "dhat" as idioms of distress in North India are emic; "generalised anxiety disorder" is etic. John Berry (1969) warned against an imposed etic , forcing one culture's categories on another. Thick description: Ryle's example is that a twitch of the eyelid and a conspiratorial wink are physically identical, so a "thin" description cannot tell them apart; a thick description records the context and layers of meaning that make it a wink. It is also Lincoln and Guba's technique for transferability (24.12). Key informants are insiders who know the culture and explain it (a senior ward attendant); gatekeepers control access (a medical superintendent). Field notes: jottings in the field, written up the same day, keeping description separate from interpretation. Over-identifying with the group is going native . The most famous psychiatric ethnography is Erving Goffman 's Asylums (1961), from a year of fieldwork at St Elizabeths Hospital, Washington, DC, which described the mental hospital as a total institution that strips inmates of their former identities. David Rosenhan's covert pseudo-patient study (1973) is discussed under ethics in section 26. Example study question: "How do patients, families and priests understand and manage mental illness at a temple healing centre in South India?" Months of participant observation, key informants among priests and long-staying families, thick description of daily rituals. Ethnography vs phenomenology vs grounded theory. Ethnography studies a culture or group ; phenomenology an experience (its essence); grounded theory a process (a theory). "The research method that writes about people and cultures" is ethnography . Emic = insider, etic = outsider ; thick description is Geertz's, after Ryle. Case study research A case study investigates one case (a person, family, ward, programme or event), or a few, in depth and in context, using several sources of evidence. Robert K. Yin (Case Study Research: Design and Methods, 1984) defined it as an empirical inquiry into a contemporary phenomenon within its real-life context, especially when the boundary between phenomenon and context is unclear. Yin's case studies are exploratory, descriptive or explanatory ; single or multiple ; holistic or embedded (sub-units inside the case). Evidence from documents, records, interviews, observation and artefacts should converge . Multiple cases follow replication logic (like repeating an experiment), not sampling logic, so case studies support analytic generalisation to theory, not statistical generalisation to a population. Robert E. Stake (The Art of Case Study Research, 1995) gave the typology examiners like: an intrinsic case is studied because it is interesting in itself (a patient with a unique presentation); an instrumental case is a means to understand a wider issue (one district team, studied to understand task-sharing in primary care); a collective case study uses several instrumental cases together (four district teams). Josef Breuer and Sigmund Freud's Anna O. (1895), Freud's Little Hans (1909) and the amnesic patient H.M. (William Scoville and Brenda Milner, 1957) are classic clinical case studies; case studies as a non-experimental design also appear in section 21. Case study is not a single-case experiment. A case study describes and interprets, with no manipulated variable and no baseline. A single-case experimental design (ABAB, multiple baseline; section 22) measures one person repeatedly while introducing and withdrawing treatment, so it supports causal inference. "N = 1" alone does not tell you which it is. Narrative research and life history Narrative research starts from the idea that people make sense of their lives by telling stories , and studies what is told, how it is plotted, and what the telling does. Jerome Bruner (1986) distinguished paradigmatic (logical-scientific) from narrative modes of thought. Arthur Frank (The Wounded Storyteller, 1995) described three illness narratives: restitution ("I was ill, I was treated, I am back to normal"), chaos (no sequence, no control) and quest (illness as a journey that changes the self). William Labov , first with Joshua Waletzky (1967), gave a structural model of oral narrative: abstract, orientation, complicating action, evaluation, resolution, coda. Data come from a narrative interview that opens with one generative request ("Tell me the story of your illness, from wherever you think it began") and then interrupts as little as possible, and from diaries and autobiographies. The analysis keeps each story whole (sequence, turning points, how narrators position themselves) rather than cutting it into codes across people. A life history covers a whole life set in its social and historical context; the classic is William I. Thomas and Florian Znaniecki's The Polish Peasant in Europe and America (1918–1920), built from letters and a long autobiography. Example study question: "How do survivors of a suicide attempt story their lives in the following year?" Narrative research is not narrative therapy (Michael White and David Epston, 1990), which helps clients re-author their stories as a treatment. 24.8 Language as data: discourse analysis, conversation analysis and ethnomethodology These approaches treat language not as a window onto inner states but as action : talk and text do things (blame, excuse, diagnose, resist) and construct versions of reality. Ethnomethodology. Harold Garfinkel (Studies in Ethnomethodology, 1967) coined the word for the study of the methods ordinary people use to produce and make sense of everyday social order. These methods are taken for granted, so he exposed them with breaching experiments : students behaved as polite lodgers in their own homes for fifteen minutes to an hour, or demanded clarification of ordinary remarks ("How are you?" "How am I in what sense: my health, my finances, my studies?"). The bewilderment and anger that followed revealed the background expectations everyone silently relies on. Its main offspring is conversation analysis. Conversation analysis (CA) was developed by Harvey Sacks , Emanuel Schegloff and Gail Jefferson ; their paper "A simplest systematics for the organization of turn-taking for conversation" (1974) is its founding text. CA studies the fine structure of naturally occurring talk , transcribed in the Jefferson system (pauses in tenths of a second, overlaps, emphasis, intonation). Its core concepts are turn-taking (speakers change over at transition-relevance places with little gap or overlap); adjacency pairs (a first part makes a particular second part expected: question and answer, greeting and greeting, invitation and acceptance or refusal); preference organisation (preferred responses come quickly and plainly, dispreferred ones late, hedged and with accounts); and repair (how troubles of speaking and hearing are fixed). Clinically, Rosemarie McCabe and colleagues (2002) showed in recorded consultations that when patients with psychosis tried to talk about their psychotic experiences, psychiatrists hesitated and steered the talk away. Discourse analysis (DA) is a family. In psychology the key text is Jonathan Potter and Margaret Wetherell , Discourse and Social Psychology: Beyond Attitudes and Behaviour (1987). They showed that people's expressed "attitudes" vary with what their talk is doing, so attitudes are better studied as things people do in talk than as stable inner states. The analysis attends to function, variation and construction , and to interpretative repertoires : recurrent, culturally available ways of talking about a topic. Derek Edwards and Potter extended this into discursive psychology (1992). Foucauldian discourse analysis , after the philosopher Michel Foucault (Madness and Civilization, 1961; Discipline and Punish, 1975), works at a larger scale: how discourses backed by institutions construct objects such as "the mentally ill", offer subject positions such as "patient" or "dangerous person", and carry power/knowledge . Conversation analysis Discourse analysis (Potter and Wetherell) Foucauldian discourse analysis Data Naturally occurring talk, finely transcribed Interviews, talk, texts Texts, policies, case notes, media Question How is this interaction organised turn by turn? What is this talk doing, with which repertoires? How do discourses construct objects and subjects, with what power effects? Signature terms Turn-taking, adjacency pair, repair Interpretative repertoire, function, variation Subject position, power/knowledge Clinical question How do CBT therapists and clients handle disagreement over homework? How do students talk about "depression" versus "tension"? How do case notes construct the "non-compliant patient"? Language-approach traps. Turn-taking, adjacency pairs = conversation analysis (Sacks, Schegloff, Jefferson). Interpretative repertoires = Potter and Wetherell. Power, subject positions = Foucauldian. Breaching experiments = Garfinkel's ethnomethodology, and despite the name they are not laboratory experiments. 24.9 Thematic, content and framework analysis The approaches so far are methodologies , each with its own philosophy, sampling logic and output. These three are methods of analysis usable within several frameworks. Virginia Braun and Victoria Clarke , "Using thematic analysis in psychology" (Qualitative Research in Psychology, 2006), turned a loosely described practice into a clear method; it is among the most cited papers in psychology. They later called their version reflexive thematic analysis , to separate it from "coding reliability" versions that count coder agreement (Richard Boyatzis, 1998) and from codebook versions such as framework analysis. Thematic analysis identifies, analyses and reports patterns of meaning ( themes ) across a data set. Its advantage is flexibility : it is not tied to one theory, so it can be inductive or deductive , semantic or latent , realist or constructionist, which makes it the usual first method for students. The six phases, in order: Familiarising yourself with the data: transcribing, reading and re-reading, noting initial ideas. Generating initial codes systematically across the whole data set and collating the extracts for each. Searching for themes: collating codes into candidate themes. Reviewing themes against the coded extracts and then the entire data set; drawing a thematic map. Defining and naming themes: refining what each theme is about and the overall story. Producing the report: vivid extracts tied back to the question and the literature. 1 Familiarising with the data notes on first ideas 2 Generating initial codes codes collated with extracts 3 Searching for themes candidate themes 4 Reviewing themes a thematic map 5 Defining and naming themes a name and definition each 6 Producing the report analytic narrative Phase 4 re-reads the whole data set: do the themes fit it? Solid arrows give the usual order. Dashed arrows are the expected loops back: the analysis is recursive, not linear (Braun and Clarke, 2006). Writing goes on in every phase. Braun and Clarke's six phases of thematic analysis (2006). The numbered order is the usual path, but the dashed loops are part of the method: analysts return to earlier phases whenever a later phase shows that codes or themes do not yet fit. In later writing Braun and Clarke slightly relabelled the phases (for example "generating initial themes", "developing and reviewing themes") and stressed three points: themes are actively generated by the researcher, not "emerging"; the researcher's subjectivity is a resource , so inter-coder agreement scores are unnecessary in reflexive TA; and a theme is a pattern of shared meaning , not a topic summary such as "experiences of medication". Example study question: "How do clinical psychology trainees experience their first psychiatric placement?" Codes such as "feeling like an impostor" and "watching restraint" are developed into themes such as "learning to hold distress". Content analysis began as a quantitative method. Bernard Berelson (1952) defined it as "a research technique for the objective, systematic and quantitative description of the manifest content of communication": categories are fixed in advance, trained coders count their occurrence, and inter-coder reliability is checked (Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff's alpha). Its questions follow Harold Lasswell's (1948) "who says what, to whom, in which channel, with what effect". Qualitative content analysis keeps the systematic, rule-based categorising but interprets meaning, including latent content; Hsiu-Fang Hsieh and Sarah Shannon (2005) distinguished conventional (inductive categories), directed (categories from theory) and summative (counting keywords, then interpreting their use) versions. Quantitative content analysis Qualitative content analysis Reflexive thematic analysis Output Frequencies, statistics A systematic category system Interpreted themes Content Manifest Manifest and latent Semantic and latent Coder agreement Essential Often checked Not used; reflexivity instead Example Count how often newspaper suicide reports name the method Categorise what helpline callers ask for Themes in carers' accounts of burden Framework analysis was developed by Jane Ritchie and Liz Spencer (1994) at Social and Community Planning Research in London (now NatCen) for applied policy research . Its five stages are familiarisation , identifying a thematic framework , indexing , charting (summarising the data into a matrix of cases by themes) and mapping and interpretation . The matrix makes comparison across cases and stakeholder groups, and auditing, easy, which is why health-services researchers like it. Example study question: "How do ASHA workers, primary-care doctors and families view a new depression-screening programme?" One row per participant, grouped by stakeholder; one column per theme. Analysis-method traps. The six phases: familiarise, code, search for themes, review , define and name , report; codes come before themes and searching before reviewing. Berelson (1952) = quantitative content analysis of manifest content. Charting and a matrix = framework analysis. Thematic analysis is a flexible method ; IPA and grounded theory are methodologies with built-in philosophies. 24.10 Action research, participatory research and Q-methodology Kurt Lewin coined "action research" in "Action research and minority problems" (1946): research that studies a social situation while changing it , with the people involved, in "a spiral of steps, each of which is composed of a circle of planning, action, and fact-finding about the result of the action". The popular wording plan → act → observe → reflect comes from Stephen Kemmis and Robin McTaggart's later version of the spiral. Each cycle produces a change and evidence about it, and the reflection feeds the next plan, so the process is a spiral . It is usually done by practitioners in their own setting. Example: a ward team wants to reduce physical restraint. Cycle 1: plan de-escalation training and post-incident debriefs; run them for two months; record restraint episodes and interview staff; reflect on what helped. Cycle 2 revises the debrief, and so on. Participatory action research (PAR) makes the people affected co-researchers who share power over the questions, methods and use of findings, with the aim of empowerment and social change. Its roots include Paulo Freire (Pedagogy of the Oppressed, written in 1968) and Orlando Fals-Borda in Colombia; in health it is called community-based participatory research . Photovoice is a common PAR tool. Example: service users and carers co-design and evaluate a peer-support group in a district mental health programme. Q-methodology: a bridge. William Stephenson (1935) proposed correlating persons instead of tests: "Q" factor analysis as opposed to the usual "R" factor analysis of variables (section 15.5). Each participant sorts a set of statements into a forced, roughly normal grid from "most disagree" to "most agree"; the sorts are factor-analysed by person , and each factor is a shared viewpoint that the researcher interprets qualitatively. Carl Rogers used Q-sorts to track the gap between real and ideal self across therapy (Rogers and Rosalind Dymond, 1954). Because it uses statistics to reveal subjectivity , it is often called a bridge between qualitative and quantitative work. The Q-sort as a scaling technique is in section 23. 24.11 Telling the approaches apart Approach Key names Question it answers Typical sample Signature words Descriptive phenomenology Husserl; Giorgi 1970; Colaizzi 1978 What is the essence of this lived experience? In Fourth Generation Evaluation (1989), Guba and Lincoln added authenticity criteria, which have no quantitative parallel. Trustworthiness (qualitative) Parallel quantitative idea How you earn it Credibility truth value Internal validity prolonged engagement, triangulation, member checking, peer debriefing, negative cases Transferability applicability External validity thick description of setting and sample, so readers judge the fit to their own setting Dependability consistency Reliability audit trail of every decision; an external inquiry audit of the process Confirmability neutrality Objectivity audit trail back to the raw data; reflexive journal; triangulation Authenticity, added by Guba and Lincoln (1989): fairness and ontological, educative, catalytic and tactical authenticity. It has no quantitative parallel. Lincoln and Guba's (1985) trustworthiness criteria, the conventional criterion each one parallels, and the main techniques for achieving it. Credibility (parallels internal validity) is confidence that the findings truly represent participants' realities. Transferability (parallels external validity) is whether findings apply elsewhere; the researcher cannot prove it, but supplies enough thick description for readers to judge. Dependability (parallels reliability) means the process is consistent and documented well enough to be audited. Confirmability (parallels objectivity) means the findings are shaped by the data rather than the researcher's bias and can be traced back to the data. Authenticity covers fairness (all viewpoints represented) and ontological, educative, catalytic and tactical authenticity (the research enlarged participants' understanding and enabled action). Norman K. Denzin (The Research Act, 1970; the 1978 second edition is the one usually cited) distinguished four types: data triangulation (several sources, varied by time, space and person: patients, carers and nurses on the same ward in different months); investigator triangulation (several researchers code the data); theory triangulation (reading the data through more than one theory, say stigma theory and explanatory models); and methodological triangulation (several methods, within one method type or between methods: interviews plus observation plus case-record review). The idea is older and quantitative: Donald Campbell and Donald Fiske's (1959) case for measuring every construct by more than one method (multiple operationism, the logic of the multitrait-multimethod matrix in section 15.3). The inter-coder agreement debate. Approaches that treat coding as measurement (quantitative content analysis, codebook TA) report agreement statistics such as kappa. Interpretive approaches (reflexive TA, IPA, constructivist grounded theory) reject them: agreement may only mean shared bias, and one analyst's interpretation is legitimate if transparent and well evidenced. A common middle path is to double-code part of the data and discuss disagreements, without a coefficient. Member checking has critics too: participants may reasonably reject an interpretation pitched at a level they were never asked to reach. Other frameworks and reporting. Clinical psychologists also meet Lucy Yardley 's (2000) four principles (sensitivity to context; commitment and rigour; transparency and coherence; impact and importance) and Robert Elliott, Constance Fischer and David Rennie 's (1999) publication guidelines. COREQ (Allison Tong, Peter Sainsbury and Jonathan Craig, 2007) is a 32-item checklist for interview and focus-group studies in three domains: research team and reflexivity, study design, and analysis and findings. SRQR (Bridget O'Brien and colleagues, 2014) has 21 items and covers all qualitative designs. They sit alongside CONSORT and PRISMA (section 25). Trustworthiness traps. Learn the pairs as a block: credibility–internal validity, transferability–external validity, dependability–reliability, confirmability–objectivity . Member checking serves credibility ; thick description transferability ; the audit trail dependability and confirmability . Transferability is judged by the reader, not proved by the researcher. Denzin's four triangulations are data, investigator, theory, methodological . 24.13 Mixed-methods research Mixed-methods research collects and analyses both quantitative and qualitative data in one study or programme and integrates them, so the combination answers the question better than either alone. Integration is the defining feature: a survey and some interviews reported in separate chapters is a multimethod study, not a mixed-methods one. The usual philosophical justification is pragmatism : the question, not a paradigm, decides the methods. John W. Creswell and Vicki L. Plano Clark , Designing and Conducting Mixed Methods Research (2007; second edition 2011; third 2018), gave the standard classification. The 2007 edition named four designs (triangulation, embedded, explanatory, exploratory); 2011 named six (convergent parallel, explanatory sequential, exploratory sequential, embedded, transformative, multiphase); 2018 reduced the core to three (convergent, explanatory sequential, exploratory sequential), treating the rest as complex designs built on them. Why mix. The original rationale was triangulation : if methods with different weaknesses converge, the answer is more trustworthy. That is Campbell and Fiske's multiple operationism (section 15.3) applied to whole methods. Jennifer Greene, Valerie Caracelli and Wendy Graham (1989) listed five purposes: triangulation (convergence), complementarity (elaboration), development (one method informs the next, as in building a questionnaire), initiation (finding paradoxes that reframe the question) and expansion (breadth). Notation. Janice Morse (1991) introduced the shorthand: capitals ( QUAN , QUAL ) mark the dominant strand, lower case ( quan , qual ) a supplementary one; + means concurrent and → sequential. Later writers added brackets, as in QUAN(qual) , for an embedded strand. Convergent (parallel) QUAN + QUAL RCT scores and patient interviews collected together, then compared Explanatory sequential QUAN → qual a survey finds poor uptake of tele-therapy; interviews then ask why Exploratory sequential QUAL → quan caregiver interviews build a burden scale, which a large survey then validates Embedded QUAN(qual) a few interviews nested inside a CBT trial to explain how it works QUAN QUAL Merge and compare Interpret QUAN first, priority qual explains it Interpret results pick whom to interview QUAL first Build a tool quan tests it Interpret the tool may be a scale, items or an intervention QUAN: randomised trial qual before qual during qual after Interpret The four mixed-methods designs most papers ask about (after Creswell and Plano Clark), with Morse's notation and a clinical example. Capitals show the dominant strand, the arrow shows sequence, and + shows strands run at the same time.
