Egger's regression test (Matthias Egger, George Davey Smith and colleagues, 1997) puts a number on asymmetry: regress each study's standardised effect (d/SE) on its precision (1/SE). With no small-study bias the line passes through the origin; an intercept significantly different from zero signals asymmetry. Trim and fill (Sue Duval and Richard Tweedie, 2000) estimates how many studies are missing, "trims" the asymmetric small studies to find the true centre, then "fills" in their mirror images on the empty side and recomputes the pooled effect. Caution: asymmetry is a small-study effect , not proof of publication bias. Small trials may genuinely find bigger effects (more severe or more selected patients, more enthusiastic investigators, lower quality), and real heterogeneity or chance can also produce it. Funnel tests have little power with fewer than about 10 studies. 25.14 The Dodo bird verdict, and the criticisms of meta-analysis In 1936 Saul Rosenzweig , in "Some implicit common factors in diverse methods of psychotherapy", argued that very different therapies seem to work about equally well because they share common factors (a relationship, an explanation, a hopeful healer). He borrowed a line from the Dodo in Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland , who judges a race and declares: "Everybody has won, and all must have prizes." In 1975 Lester Luborsky, Barton Singer and Lise Luborsky reviewed comparative studies of psychotherapies ("Is it true that 'everyone has won and all must have prizes'?") and found that most comparisons showed no significant difference: the Dodo bird verdict . Bruce Wampold and colleagues' 1997 meta-analysis of direct comparisons between bona fide therapies found differences close to zero, and Wampold's The Great Psychotherapy Debate (2001) built a contextual model in which common factors (alliance, empathy, expectations, a credible rationale) do most of the work, an idea rooted in Jerome Frank's Persuasion and Healing (1961) and Edward Bordin's (1979) working alliance. The counter-position, from the empirically supported treatments movement: specific treatments matter for specific disorders (exposure for obsessive-compulsive disorder, phobias and PTSD); comparative trials are too small to detect modest differences; and researcher allegiance colours comparative results. Exams ask for the verdict itself: different bona fide therapies tend to produce roughly equivalent outcomes, attributed to common factors such as the therapeutic alliance and empathy. Do not confuse two "1950s to 1970s" debates. Hans Eysenck (1952) asked whether psychotherapy works at all (spontaneous remission); Smith and Glass (1977) answered with meta-analysis: yes, d ≈ 0.68. The Dodo bird verdict asks whether one therapy works better than another ; Rosenzweig (1936) and Luborsky and colleagues (1975) answered: mostly not. (A parallel to Eysenck in social work: Joel Fischer's 1973 review "Is casework effective?" concluded that it had not been shown to be.) The standard criticisms of meta-analysis Criticism What it says Standard reply Apples and oranges It mixes studies too different to combine: different therapies, patients, outcome measures Define the question and the inclusion criteria tightly; test whether the differences matter with subgroup analysis and meta-regression (if the question is about fruit, pooling apples and oranges is legitimate) Garbage in, garbage out Pooling many poor studies gives a precise but wrong answer (Eysenck's "mega-silliness" objection) Rate every study's risk of bias; run sensitivity analyses with only high-quality studies; GRADE the certainty File drawer / publication bias The studies found are a biased sample of those done Search grey literature and registries; funnel plot, Egger's test, trim and fill (25.13) Non-independence One study contributes several effect sizes (Smith and Glass had 833 from 375 studies), over-weighting it One effect per study, or multilevel (three-level) meta-analysis Ecological (aggregation) fallacy A moderator that explains differences between studies need not apply to individuals Individual participant data meta-analysis 25.15 The replication crisis and open science John Ioannidis (2005) had argued in "Why most published research findings are false" that small studies, small effects and flexible analyses make most significant findings in some fields false positives. Then, in 2011, Daryl Bem published nine experiments in a leading social psychology journal claiming evidence of precognition using standard methods (if standard methods can "prove" the impossible, the methods are the problem); the fraud of Diederik Stapel came to light (section 26); and Joseph Simmons, Leif Nelson and Uri Simonsohn (2011), in "False-positive psychology", showed that combining a few common, undisclosed choices (which of two outcomes to report, adding participants after peeking, adding a covariate, dropping a condition) could raise the real false-positive rate from the nominal 5% to about 61% . They called this flexibility researcher degrees of freedom , and illustrated it with a real experiment "showing" that listening to "When I'm Sixty-Four" made people younger. The Open Science Collaboration (2015), a project of some 270 researchers coordinated by Brian Nosek , published "Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science" in Science . They repeated 100 studies from three leading psychology journals (2008 issues). 97% of the original studies had significant results; only 36% of the replications did. The replications' mean effect size was about half the originals' (r = .20 vs .40); 47% of original effect sizes fell within the replication's 95% confidence interval, and 39% of effects were subjectively rated as replicated. The usual exam answer is " about 36% (roughly one-third) replicated ". Questionable research practices (QRPs) Practice What it is p-hacking Trying analyses (outcomes, covariates, exclusions, transformations, subgroups) until p < .05, then reporting only that one HARKing (Norbert Kerr, 1998) H ypothesising A fter the R esults are K nown: presenting a post hoc hypothesis as if it had been predicted in advance Optional stopping Checking significance as data come in and stopping when p dips below .05; each peek is another chance of a Type I error (section 8) Selective reporting (outcome switching) Reporting only the measures, conditions or studies that "worked"; the within-study version of the file drawer Flexible exclusion of outliers Deciding which participants to drop after seeing which choice gives significance Rounding p values Reporting p = .054 as "p < .05" Leslie John, George Loewenstein and Drazen Prelec (2012) surveyed about 2,000 academic psychologists and found such practices were widespread and widely regarded as defensible. Andrew Gelman and Eric Loken (2013) added that p-hacking need not be deliberate: when analysis decisions depend on the data, a researcher who runs only one test is still walking a " garden of forking paths ". QRPs are not fabrication (section 26), but they produce the same result: false findings in the literature. The open-science remedies Preregistration: a time-stamped, public plan written before data collection (hypotheses, sample size and stopping rule, primary outcome, analysis plan), on the Open Science Framework, AsPredicted, or for trials a registry such as CTRI or ClinicalTrials.gov. Deviations are allowed but must be declared, which kills HARKing and hidden p-hacking. Exploratory analyses remain welcome, labelled as exploratory. Registered reports: the journal peer-reviews the introduction, methods and analysis plan before the data exist; if approved, it gives in-principle acceptance , and the paper is published whatever the results. This removes publication bias at source. First launched by the journal Cortex in 2013 (Chris Chambers). Open data, materials and code , so others can check the analysis and repeat the study (APA Standard 8.14 already requires sharing data for verification, section 26). Adequate power: a priori power analysis and larger samples (section 8), often through multi-site collaborations. Replication: direct (exact, close) replication repeats the original procedure as closely as possible; conceptual replication tests the same hypothesis with different methods. A field needs both. Institutions: the Center for Open Science (founded 2013 by Brian Nosek and Jeffrey Spies), the reporting guidelines of 25.9, and journals' transparency standards. Recap of section 25: the RCT is the gold standard for treatment questions because random allocation balances known and unknown confounders and a control group absorbs remission, regression and expectancy; Lind (1747) ran the first controlled trial, the MRC streptomycin trial (1948, Bradford Hill) the first modern RCT. Allocation is simple, block or stratified; allocation concealment hides the next assignment from recruiters (prevents selection bias, always possible), blinding hides the actual assignment afterwards (single, double, triple; psychotherapy can blind only assessors). Waitlist and no-treatment controls control only for time, attention-placebo for common factors, active comparators answer "which is better"; dismantling removes a component (Jacobson 1996), additive designs add one. Designs: parallel, crossover (washout; fails with carryover), cluster (design effect), factorial; superiority vs non-inferiority (CI above −Δ) vs equivalence (CI within ±Δ); efficacy (explanatory, manualised) vs effectiveness (pragmatic; Martin Seligman 1995). Drug phases: 0 microdose, I safety and dose in healthy volunteers, II efficacy in patients, III confirmatory RCTs before approval, IV post-marketing surveillance; India: CDSCO/DCGI under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules 2019, registration on CTRI (ICMR 2007, mandatory 2009). Analyse by intention-to-treat ; avoid LOCF. NNT = 1/ARR , rounded up; relative risk reductions flatter rare-event benefits. Report with CONSORT (2010: 25 items plus flow diagram; 2025: 30 items), PRISMA, STROBE, STARD, CARE, COREQ, SPIRIT, TREND, SCRIBE. Evidence-based practice (Sackett 1996) integrates research, clinical expertise and patient values (APA 2006); Division 12 ESTs are well-established or probably efficacious. Glass coined meta-analysis (1976); Smith and Glass (1977) answered Hans Eysenck (1952) with d = 0.68 from 375 studies. Pool by inverse-variance weights, fixed or random effects; heterogeneity by Q and I² (25/50/75%); read the forest plot's squares, CIs and diamond. Publication bias (Robert Rosenthal's file drawer, fail-safe N) shows as funnel asymmetry, tested by Egger's regression, corrected by trim and fill. Dodo bird verdict (Rosenzweig 1936; Luborsky 1975): bona fide therapies perform about equally. Replication crisis: 36% of 100 replications significant (Open Science Collaboration 2015), driven by p-hacking, HARKing (Kerr 1998), optional stopping and researcher degrees of freedom (Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn 2011); remedies are preregistration, registered reports, open data and well-powered replication. 26 Research ethics Every design in sections 18 to 25 involves doing something to people (or animals) for the sake of knowledge rather than for their own immediate good. Research ethics is the set of principles, codes and laws that decides when that is acceptable and on what conditions. It did not grow out of philosophy seminars; almost every rule in it was written in response to a specific scandal. So this section begins with the history, then distils the principles, then turns them into the practical questions an ethics committee will ask about your study: consent, deception, confidentiality, risk, inducements, fairness, animals, honesty in publication. 26.1 Why research ethics exists: the history The Nazi experiments and the Nuremberg Code (1947) During the Second World War, German physicians carried out lethal experiments on concentration camp prisoners: immersion in freezing water and exposure to simulated high altitude to study survival, deliberately infected wounds to test drugs, and twin studies at Auschwitz. At the Doctors' Trial in Nuremberg (United States v. Karl Brandt et al.), 23 defendants, most of them physicians, were tried; seven were executed. The verdict of August 1947 set out ten principles for permissible medical experiments, the Nuremberg Code , drawing partly on a memorandum by the American physician Leo Alexander. The Nuremberg Code's ten points , in brief: (1) "The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential" (legal capacity, free choice without force or coercion, enough knowledge and understanding); (2) the experiment must yield results for the good of society unobtainable by other means; (3) it must rest on prior animal work and knowledge of the disease; (4) it must avoid all unnecessary physical and mental suffering; (5) no experiment where death or disabling injury is expected; (6) risk must never exceed the humanitarian importance of the problem; (7) proper preparations and facilities to protect the subject; (8) only scientifically qualified persons may conduct it; (9) the subject must be free to end the experiment at any time; (10) the scientist must stop if continuing is likely to cause injury, disability or death. The Declaration of Helsinki (1964 onwards) The Nuremberg Code was a court's verdict, and doctors outside Germany tended to treat it as a rule for barbarians, not for them. The medical profession's own statement came from the World Medical Association : the Declaration of Helsinki , adopted in June 1964 at its General Assembly in Helsinki. It distinguished research combined with patient care from non-therapeutic research, and it has been revised repeatedly: 1975 (Tokyo, which introduced review by an independent committee ), 1983, 1989, 1996, 2000 (Edinburgh), 2008 (Seoul, which required trial registration), 2013 (Fortaleza), and most recently October 2024 (Helsinki), a revision that speaks of research "participants" rather than "subjects". Helsinki is the source of the rules on placebo controls (26.12) and on the primacy of the participant's welfare over the interests of science and society. Tuskegee, the National Research Act (1974) and the Belmont Report (1979) From 1932 to 1972 the US Public Health Service ran the "Tuskegee Study of Untreated Syphilis in the Negro Male" in Macon County, Alabama. About 600 poor Black men were enrolled, 399 with latent syphilis and 201 without. They were told they were being treated for "bad blood", were given free meals, transport and burial insurance, and were never told their diagnosis. When penicillin became the standard cure in the 1940s, it was deliberately withheld, and the men were steered away from treatment, so that the natural course of the disease could be observed to death. A Public Health Service employee, Peter Buxtun, raised objections internally for years; the story broke through the journalist Jean Heller of the Associated Press in July 1972, and the study ended that year. (US President Bill Clinton formally apologised in 1997.) Public outrage produced the National Research Act (1974) , which required institutional review of federally funded research and created the National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research . The Commission's best-known product, named after the Belmont Conference Center in Maryland where it was drafted, is the Belmont Report : completed in 1978 and published in the US Federal Register in April 1979 . Its three principles (26.2) became the basis of US regulation, codified in 1991 as the Common Rule (the Federal Policy for the Protection of Human Subjects, 45 CFR 46, adopted by 15 federal departments and agencies; revised version in force from January 2019). The Common Rule requires review by an institutional review board (IRB) of at least five members, including at least one scientist, one non-scientist and one member not affiliated with the institution. Henry K. Beecher , a Harvard anaesthetist, showed in 1966 ("Ethics and clinical research", New England Journal of Medicine ) that abuse was not confined to Nazis or to one government project: he described 22 ethically questionable studies published in mainstream journals by respected investigators. The international, developing-country perspective came from the Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences (CIOMS) , working with the World Health Organization: proposed guidelines in 1982, revised in 1993 and 2002, and replaced in 2016 by the International Ethical Guidelines for Health-related Research Involving Humans , with particular attention to research in low-resource settings. studies and scandals (above the line) international codes and laws (below) India (below) 1930 1940 1950 1920 Little Albert 1932–72 Tuskegee syphilis study 1939 Monster Study 1947 Nuremberg Code 1950 1960 Tuskegee, continued to 1972 1956–71 Willowbrook 1963 Milgram obedience 1970 Tearoom Trade 1971 Stanford Prison 1953 APA's first ethics code 1959 the 3 Rs (animals) 1964 Declaration of Helsinki 1974 National Research Act 1990 2000 2010 2020 1998 Wakefield MMR paper 2011 Stapel fraud exposed 2014 Facebook contagion study 1979 Belmont Report 1980 ICMR policy statement 1991 Common Rule 2002 APA Ethics Code 2007 CTRI launched 2017 ICMR guidelines; MHCA 2019 NDCT Rules 2024 Helsinki revised A timeline of research ethics: the studies that provoked reform sit above each line, and the codes, reports and laws written in response sit below it (India in teal). 26.2 The Belmont principles, and the ethical theories behind every code The Belmont Report reduced the field to three principles , each with an application . This mapping is the single most examined fact in research ethics. Belmont principle Its application What the researcher does Respect for persons autonomy; protect those with diminished autonomy Informed consent information, comprehension, voluntariness Consent form and process Assent plus parental permission Representative if capacity is impaired Right to withdraw, no penalty Beneficence do no harm; maximise benefits, minimise harms Risk-benefit assessment systematic and justified, reviewed by a committee Ethics committee review Least risky design that works Debriefing and follow-up Confidential data handling Justice fair sharing of the burdens and benefits of research Selection of subjects fair procedures and fair outcomes No easy targets (poor, prisoners, captive students) for risky work Do not exclude groups who would benefit from the results Each Belmont principle has one application: respect for persons requires informed consent, beneficence requires a risk-benefit assessment, and justice requires fair selection of participants. Respect for persons: two convictions. Individuals should be treated as autonomous agents , and persons with diminished autonomy (children, people with severe mental illness or dementia, prisoners) are entitled to protection. Application: informed consent , which Belmont says has three elements: information , comprehension and voluntariness . Beneficence: two rules, "do not harm", and "maximise possible benefits and minimise possible harms". Application: a systematic assessment of risks and benefits , which the review committee checks. Justice: fairness in who bears the burdens of research and who receives its benefits. Application: fair selection of subjects . Tuskegee is the textbook violation: the burdens fell on poor Black men, while the knowledge served others. Four principles and two ethical theories In the same year, Tom Beauchamp and James Childress published Principles of Biomedical Ethics (1979), which gave clinical ethics its four principles ("principlism"): respect for autonomy , non-maleficence (do no harm), beneficence (do good) and justice . The difference from Belmont is that beneficence is split into two. The ICMR's 2017 guidelines (26.4) use exactly these four. A frequent question asks which list is the "four pillars of principle-based ethics": beneficence, non-maleficence, justice and respect for autonomy (not "integrity", not "respect" alone). Approach Core idea In research ethics Deontological (duty-based; Immanuel Kant) Some acts are right or wrong in themselves, whatever their consequences; people must never be used merely as a means Deceiving or harming a participant is wrong even if the knowledge gained is valuable; the spirit of Diana Baumrind's (1964) critique of Stanley Milgram's obedience study (1963; 26.9) Utilitarian / consequentialist (Jeremy Bentham, John Stuart Mill) The right act produces the greatest good for the greatest number: a cost-benefit judgement The risk-benefit analysis of ethics committees; Milgram's own defence (valuable knowledge, little lasting harm) 26.3 Professional codes: the APA Ethics Code and the BPS The American Psychological Association adopted its first ethics code in 1952, published in 1953 as Ethical Standards of Psychologists , the first such code in psychology and, unusually, built empirically from critical incidents that members described. The current version is the Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct , adopted in 2002 (effective June 2003) and amended in 2010 and 2016 (the 2016 amendment, effective January 2017, concerned Standard 3.04 and the prohibition on psychologists' participation in torture). A draft revised code was released for public comment in December 2024 but, as of this writing, the 2002 code with its 2010 and 2016 amendments remains in force. Structure of the APA code. An introduction and preamble; five General Principles (A to E), which are aspirational (ideals, not enforceable rules); and ten sections of Ethical Standards , which are enforceable : 1 Resolving Ethical Issues, 2 Competence, 3 Human Relations, 4 Privacy and Confidentiality, 5 Advertising and Other Public Statements, 6 Record Keeping and Fees, 7 Education and Training, 8 Research and Publication , 9 Assessment, 10 Therapy. General Principle Meaning A. Beneficence and Nonmaleficence Strive to benefit those you work with and take care to do no harm; guard against misuse of your influence B. Fidelity and Responsibility Establish relationships of trust; be aware of professional and scientific responsibilities to society; manage conflicts of interest C. Integrity Accuracy, honesty and truthfulness in science, teaching and practice; where deception may be justified, a serious obligation to consider its consequences and correct mistrust D. Justice Fairness: all persons are entitled to equal access to the benefits of psychology and to equal quality of processes and services E. Respect for People's Rights and Dignity Privacy, confidentiality and self-determination; special safeguards for people whose capacity for autonomous decisions is impaired; respect for cultural and individual differences Count and contents. "How many General Principles?" Five. "Which is NOT one of them?" Look for an intruder such as Equity , Competence or Confidentiality (competence and confidentiality are Standards 2 and 4, not General Principles). Note also that Principle A is one principle with two names, and E is "Respect for People's Rights and Dignity", not "autonomy". Standard 8: Research and Publication Standard Title What it requires 8.01 Institutional Approval Obtain approval where required (IRB or ethics committee) and conduct the research as approved 8.02 Informed Consent to Research Tell participants the purpose, duration and procedures; their right to decline and to withdraw; consequences of declining or withdrawing; foreseeable risks, discomfort or adverse effects; prospective benefits; limits of confidentiality; incentives; whom to contact. For intervention research also: the experimental nature of the treatment, what the control group will get, how assignment is made, available alternatives, and costs 8.03 Informed Consent for Recording Voices and Images in Research Consent before recording, except naturalistic observation in public places, or when deception is used (consent then sought at debriefing) 8.04 Client/Patient, Student, and Subordinate Research Participants Protect them from adverse consequences of declining or withdrawing; when research is a course requirement or earns extra credit, offer an equitable alternative activity 8.05 Dispensing With Informed Consent for Research Only where research would not reasonably be assumed to create distress or harm and involves normal educational practices in educational settings; only anonymous questionnaires, naturalistic observations or archival research where disclosure would not put participants at risk and confidentiality is protected; or job/organisational effectiveness studies with no risk to employability; or where law or regulations permit 8.06 Offering Inducements for Research Participation Avoid excessive or inappropriate financial or other inducements likely to coerce participation 8.07 Deception in Research Strict conditions (26.6) 8.08 Debriefing Promptly give participants information about the nature, results and conclusions, and correct misconceptions; if delay is justified, reduce the risk of harm; if harm occurred, take steps to minimise it 8.09 Humane Care and Use of Animals in Research 26.10 8.10 Reporting Research Results Do not fabricate data; correct significant errors once discovered 8.11 Plagiarism Do not present others' work or data as your own 8.12 Publication Credit Authorship only for work actually performed or substantially contributed; order reflects contribution; a student is usually first author of a multi-authored article based substantially on their dissertation 8.13 Duplicate Publication of Data Do not publish previously published data as original 8.14 Sharing Research Data for Verification Do not withhold data from competent professionals who want to verify claims by reanalysis 8.15 Reviewers Respect the confidentiality and proprietary rights of material submitted for review In Britain, the British Psychological Society publishes a separate Code of Human Research Ethics (2010, revised 2014 and 2021) built on four principles: respect for the autonomy, privacy and dignity of individuals, groups and communities; scientific integrity ; social responsibility ; and maximising benefit and minimising harm . Do not confuse these with the four principles of the BPS's general Code of Ethics and Conduct : respect, competence, responsibility and integrity. 26.4 Research ethics in India The ICMR guidelines The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) issued India's first statement in 1980 ( Policy Statement on Ethical Considerations Involved in Research on Human Subjects ), then the Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research on Human Subjects (2000), the Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research on Human Participants (2006), and the current National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants (2017) . The 2017 guidelines apply to behavioural and social science research in health, which includes clinical psychology. ICMR 2017: four basic principles : respect for persons (autonomy), beneficence, non-maleficence and justice. These expand into 12 general principles : (1) essentiality, (2) voluntariness, (3) non-exploitation, (4) social responsibility, (5) ensuring privacy and confidentiality, (6) risk minimisation, (7) professional competence, (8) maximisation of benefit, (9) institutional arrangements, (10) transparency and accountability, (11) totality of responsibility, (12) environmental protection. The 2017 guidelines classify research by risk, and the category decides the type of ethics review: ICMR risk category Meaning and examples Usual review Less than minimal risk Harm nil or not expected: anonymous data, public-domain data, meta-analysis Exemption from review (decided by the committee, not the researcher) Minimal risk No greater than in routine daily life or routine tests: questionnaires, interviews, history taking, observation, urine or saliva samples Expedited review (chair, member secretary and one or two members) Minor increase over minimal risk (low risk) Routine research on children, research on people unable to consent, delaying or withholding a proven treatment in a control or placebo arm, small blood samples, social and psychological risks Full committee review More than minimal risk (high risk) Interventional studies with drugs, devices or invasive procedures Full committee review Research involving deception must always go to full committee review under ICMR 2017, which describes a two-step procedure: initial consent, then debriefing after participation. Ethics committees ICMR 2017 (all biomedical and health research) New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules 2019, Rule 7 (drug trials) Size Preferably 7 to 15 members At least 7 members (CDSCO registration sets a maximum of 15) Independence Preferably 50% from outside the institution; chairperson from outside; member secretary from the institution At least 50% not affiliated with the institution; chairperson from outside; member secretary from the institution Members Basic medical scientist (preferably a pharmacologist for drug research), clinician, legal expert, social scientist / philosopher / ethicist / theologian, lay person from the community Must include at least one lay person, one woman, one legal expert and one independent member (social scientist, NGO representative, philosopher, ethicist or theologian) Gender "Adequate representation of age and gender" At least one woman Quorum At least 5, including at least one non-affiliated member (preferably the lay person) At least 5 members of the specified categories Registration Committees reviewing biomedical and health research register with the Department of Health Research Committees reviewing drug trials register with the Central Licencing Authority (CDSCO); valid 5 years Other Indian law and bodies Clinical trial registration: on CTRI (launched by ICMR 2007, mandatory since 2009; section 25.6). Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI): a statutory body under the RCI Act, 1992 (under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment), which registers clinical psychologists and other rehabilitation professionals. Section 21 of the Act lets the Council prescribe standards of professional conduct, etiquette and a code of ethics, framed as regulations in 1998; misconduct can lead to removal from the register. Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, Section 99 (Research): research on persons with mental illness needs their free and informed consent . If a person cannot give it but does not resist, interventional research needs permission from the State Mental Health Authority , which may allow research on the consent of the nominated representative only if the research cannot be done on people able to consent, is necessary to promote the mental health of the population represented, aims at knowledge relevant to their mental health needs, discloses all interests, and has ethics committee approval. Case notes may be used for research without consent if anonymity is secured. Consent can be withdrawn at any time. Data protection: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs digital personal data in India; for international studies, the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, applied from 2018) may also apply. Mandatory reporting: the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 requires anyone who learns of child sexual abuse to report it, and penalises failure to report. This overrides research confidentiality (26.7). 26.5 Informed consent in practice 1 Approval Ethics committee or IRB approves the protocol first 2 Recruitment No pressure or undue inducement; equitable alternative 3 Information Purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, confidentiality, rights 4 Consent Capacity checked; assent + parent for minors; signed form 5 Participation Free to withdraw at any time, without penalty 6 Debriefing Dehoaxing: reveal any deception; desensitising: undo harm 7 Data choices Offer withdrawal of data; answer questions; resources 8 Protection Coded, secure data; report in aggregate; share results consent is a process: re-check it if the study or the person's capacity changes Deception (APA 8.07) is explained as early as feasible, no later than the end of data collection. The participant's path from approval to debriefing: consent is obtained before participation, withdrawal stays open throughout, and any deception is undone at debriefing. Informed consent is a person's voluntary agreement to take part, given with enough information to decide and the capacity to understand it. It is a process , not a signature: the information sheet is discussed, questions are answered, and consent is renewed if the study changes or the person's capacity fluctuates (as in relapsing psychosis or bipolar disorder). Three conditions What it means Threatened by Competence (capacity) The person can understand the information, appreciate how it applies to them, reason about it and communicate a choice Childhood, intellectual disability, dementia, acute psychosis, intoxication Information and comprehension All material facts are disclosed in a language and at a level the person understands Jargon, English-only forms for non-English speakers, long legal documents, low literacy Voluntariness The choice is free of coercion and undue influence Power relationships (teacher and student, doctor and patient, warden and prisoner), large payments, fear of losing treatment Elements of the information (combining APA 8.02, Belmont and ICMR): the purpose ; the procedures and what is experimental; the expected duration ; foreseeable risks and discomforts ; expected benefits to the participant or to others; alternatives (especially treatment alternatives in a clinical trial); how confidentiality will be protected and its limits ; that participation is voluntary ; the right to withdraw at any time without penalty or loss of benefits (including the clinical care they would otherwise receive); any incentives or compensation; and a contact person for questions about the study and about participants' rights. Consent is normally written; oral consent (witnessed and recorded) is used for people who cannot read; a waiver of consent is possible only for minimal-risk research that could not otherwise be done (APA 8.05; decided by the committee). Children: assent and parental permission Minors cannot give legal consent, so research needs permission (consent) from a parent or legal guardian plus the child's own assent : affirmative agreement appropriate to the child's age. Mere failure to object is not assent, and a child's refusal should normally be respected even if the parent agrees (unless the research offers a direct benefit unavailable elsewhere). This follows the principle in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) that children can express their views, including assent and dissent. ICMR 2017 is specific: no documentation of assent is needed below 7 years ; verbal assent , recorded in the presence of the parents, from 7 to 12 ; written assent (with parental signature) from 12 to 18 . Adults with impaired capacity Capacity is decision-specific and can fluctuate, so it is assessed for this decision at this time, not assumed from a diagnosis. A person with schizophrenia is not automatically incapable. Where capacity is absent, consent comes from a legally acceptable (authorised) representative (ICMR) or, under the Mental Healthcare Act, through the nominated representative with State Mental Health Authority permission (26.4), and the person's own assent or dissent is still sought. The research should be possible only in this population and carry low risk, and consent is sought from the person directly if they regain capacity. Vulnerable groups People whose ability to protect their own interests is reduced need additional safeguards: children ; prisoners and others in custody; people with severe mental illness or cognitive impairment; pregnant women (risk to the fetus); the terminally ill; economically and socially disadvantaged people; and anyone in a dependent or hierarchical relationship with the researcher: students in the researcher's own class , employees, patients of the treating clinician, members of the armed forces. ICMR 2017 also lists sexual minorities and sex workers, and tribal populations. Safeguards include independent recruiters (a student should not be asked by their own teacher in class), extra committee scrutiny, an equitable alternative to participation for students (APA 8.04), and a guarantee that refusing will not affect grades or treatment. Active and passive consent; consent online Active (opt-in) consent: a parent or participant must positively agree, usually by returning a signed form. The standard. Passive (opt-out) consent: participation is assumed unless the parent returns a refusal; sometimes used in school surveys. It raises response rates and reduces bias against non-responding families, but non-return may mean the letter never reached home, so committees allow it only for minimal-risk research. Online research: consent is typically a click-through information page; the researcher cannot see whether it was read, cannot easily verify age or identity, and cannot ensure debriefing if the participant closes the window (so debriefing information is shown at exit). Data from public social media posts raise questions of whether "public" means "consented"; verbatim quotes can be traced by a search engine, so they are paraphrased. The Association of Internet Researchers publishes guidelines on these issues. 26.6 Deception and debriefing Some questions cannot be studied if participants know the hypothesis: conformity, obedience, bystander intervention, the effect of expectations. Psychology therefore permits deception, under strict conditions. APA Standard 8.07, Deception in Research. (a) Psychologists do not conduct a study involving deception unless they have determined that its use is justified by the study's significant prospective scientific, educational or applied value and that effective non-deceptive alternative procedures are not feasible . (b) Psychologists do not deceive prospective participants about research that is reasonably expected to cause physical pain or severe emotional distress . (c) Any deception that is an integral feature of the design is explained as early as is feasible , preferably at the end of the person's participation and no later than the end of data collection , and participants are permitted to withdraw their data . Active deception (deception by commission): telling participants something false, e.g. a cover story about the study's purpose, false feedback on a test, a fake shock generator, a confederate posing as a participant. Passive deception (deception by omission): withholding information, e.g. not mentioning the real hypothesis, or not saying that a second "unrelated" study is part of the first. Generally regarded as less serious, but still requires justification. Cover story: the false explanation of the study's purpose that keeps the real hypothesis hidden (Milgram's "effects of punishment on learning"). Confederate (stooge): a member of the research team who pretends to be a participant or bystander and behaves according to a script (the unanimous majority in Solomon Asch's 1951 line-judging study; Milgram's "learner"). Debriefing Debriefing is the conversation after participation in which the researcher explains the true nature and purpose of the study, answers questions and makes sure the participant leaves no worse off. David Holmes (1976) , in two papers in the American Psychologist , named its two components: Dehoaxing: revealing the deception and convincing the participant that the false information was false (for example, that the "learner" received no shocks and the personality feedback was invented). Desensitising: helping participants deal with any negative feelings or self-knowledge the study produced (for example, that they were willing to shock someone), by explaining that most people behave the same way and that their behaviour reflects the situation, not a defect in them. Holmes reviewed the evidence and concluded that, done carefully, both were effective. But Lee Ross, Mark Lepper and Michael Hubbard (1975) showed a problem: participants given false feedback about their ability kept part of the false belief even after being told the feedback was fake ( belief perseverance ). Simply announcing "it was fake" (outcome debriefing) was not enough; it worked better when the researcher also explained the process by which false beliefs persist. This is process debriefing , now the recommended standard: discuss the participant's experience, explain the deception and why it was needed, explain how such beliefs persist, check for distress, and offer withdrawal of data and contact details. Debriefing is good practice even when no deception was used. Informed consent vs debriefing. Informed consent comes before participation and tells people enough to decide whether to take part; debriefing comes after and tells them everything, including what was concealed. "The principle under which participants are given full information about all aspects of the study after it is done" is debriefing. Debriefing does not retroactively make an unjustified deception acceptable. 26.7 Confidentiality, anonymity and privacy Anonymity Confidentiality Definition Nobody, not even the researcher , can link the data to the person; no identifying information is collected The researcher knows who gave the data but promises not to disclose it to others, and reports only in a form that cannot identify anyone Example An online survey with no names, emails or IP addresses recorded A longitudinal study that must contact the same people again; a therapy trial; a recorded interview Follow-up possible? No Yes Can you withdraw a person's data later? No, it cannot be found Yes, through the code The classic trap. A study cannot be both anonymous and longitudinal, and a face-to-face interview is never anonymous: the researcher has seen the person. Promising "anonymity" when you mean "confidentiality" is itself an ethical error. Privacy is a third, broader idea: the person's right to control access to themselves and their information, which can be violated even when data stay confidential (covert observation of private behaviour, 26.12). Keeping data confidential Coding (pseudonymisation): replace names with ID numbers and keep the key linking codes to names separately, locked or encrypted, with access limited to named researchers. Secure storage: password-protected, encrypted devices; locked cabinets for paper; a stated retention period and secure destruction afterwards. Reporting in aggregate: group statistics, no small cells that identify individuals (the only woman psychiatrist in a district hospital), altered details in case descriptions, pseudonyms in qualitative quotes. Limits of confidentiality Confidentiality is not absolute, and its limits must be stated in the consent process (APA 8.02). Researchers may have to break it when there is a serious and imminent risk of harm to the participant (active suicidal intent) or to others ; the US case Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California established a duty to warn (1974) and then a broader duty to protect (1976) identifiable potential victims of a client's violence. Breaches are also required by law : mandatory reporting of child abuse (POCSO in India), court orders and subpoenas, and certain notifiable conditions. A study screening adolescents for self-harm must therefore have a written plan for what happens when a participant discloses suicidal intent. 26.8 Risk and benefit, the right to withdraw, inducements, and fair selection Minimal risk (US Common Rule, 45 CFR 46.102): "the probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort anticipated in the research are not greater in and of themselves than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests." ICMR 2017 uses essentially the same definition and adds categories below and above it (26.4). Risks in psychological research are rarely physical. They include psychological harm (anxiety, guilt, lowered self-esteem, re-traumatisation when interviewing survivors), social harm (stigma if a diagnosis or sexual orientation is exposed), legal harm (disclosure of drug use) and economic harm (loss of a job). Benefits include direct benefit (a trial treatment), indirect benefit (monitoring, information), and the value of the knowledge to society. The ethics committee's risk-benefit analysis asks whether the risks are minimised (the least risky design that can answer the question), whether they are reasonable in relation to the expected benefits, and whether safeguards (screening, distress protocols, stopping rules, data monitoring) are in place. The right to withdraw without penalty, at any time and without giving reasons, is in every code since Nuremberg (point 9). In practice it also means participants can ask for their data to be removed (until it is anonymised or published), and that withdrawal must not cost them anything they were entitled to, such as their usual clinical treatment. Milgram's prods ("you have no other choice, you must go on") are the classic violation. Inducements and coercion. Coercion is an explicit or implicit threat of harm for not participating (a prisoner fearing loss of parole, a patient fearing loss of care, a student fearing a lower grade). Undue inducement is an offer so large that it distorts judgement about risk. Reasonable payment for time and reimbursement of travel are acceptable; the larger the payment relative to the person's income, the more the committee worries, which is a real issue in low-income settings. Course credit is acceptable only if an equitable, non-research alternative is offered (APA 8.04) and the instructor does not know who declined. Fair selection (justice) cuts both ways. Risky research must not be loaded onto convenient, powerless groups (prisoners, institutionalised children, the poor, captive students), as at Tuskegee and Willowbrook. But excluding groups (women, children, older adults, people with comorbidity, non-English speakers) from research also harms them, because treatments then go untested in the very people who will receive them. 26.9 The famous ethically controversial studies Study Researcher(s), year What happened The ethical issue Little Albert John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner, 1920 An infant ("Albert B.", about 9 months old at baseline, 11 months when conditioning began) was conditioned to fear a white rat by pairing it with a loud noise; the fear generalised to other furry objects Deliberately induced fear in an infant; never deconditioned (he left the hospital); consent from a mother who worked at the hospital is questionable Monster Study Wendell Johnson; carried out by his graduate student Mary Tudor, University of Iowa, 1939 22 children at an orphans' home in Iowa; some children who spoke normally were repeatedly told their speech was defective and that they stuttered ("negative therapy") Harm to vulnerable children (orphans), deception, lasting speech and psychological problems; kept quiet until 2001; Iowa paid a settlement in 2007 Tuskegee syphilis study US Public Health Service, 1932–1972 399 Black men with syphilis (and 201 controls) observed untreated for 40 years; told they had "bad blood"; penicillin withheld No informed consent, deception, withholding effective treatment, exploitation of a poor minority (injustice); led to the National Research Act and Belmont Willowbrook hepatitis studies Saul Krugman, Willowbrook State School, New York, 1956–1971 Children with intellectual disabilities were deliberately infected with hepatitis to study the disease and test gamma globulin Harm to a vulnerable group; coerced consent : when the school was "full", places were available only in the hepatitis unit for children whose parents agreed Obedience to authority Stanley Milgram, Yale, published 1963 40 men told to give increasing "shocks" to a learner (a confederate) for errors; 26 of 40 (65%) went to the maximum 450 V ; experimenter's prods ("The experiment requires that you continue") Deception; severe stress (sweating, trembling, nervous laughter; three had full seizures); pressure undermining the right to withdraw. Critique by Diana Baumrind (1964) ; Milgram replied that he had dehoaxed everyone and that in a follow-up 84% were glad to have taken part and 1.3% sorry Tearoom Trade Laud Humphreys, 1970 Covert participant observation of men having impersonal sex in public toilets, acting as "watchqueen" (lookout); noted licence plates, traced addresses, and a year later interviewed the men at home in disguise as part of a "social health survey" No consent, deception, invasion of privacy , risk of exposure when homosexuality was criminalised Stanford Prison Experiment Philip Zimbardo, Stanford, August 1971 24 male students randomly assigned to be guards or prisoners in a mock prison; planned for two weeks, stopped after six days after guards became abusive and prisoners broke down; ended after Christina Maslach objected Harm and humiliation; prisoners led to believe they could not leave (right to withdraw); Zimbardo's dual role as researcher and "prison superintendent". Later critiques (Thibault Le Texier, 2019) also question its demand characteristics Maternal deprivation in monkeys Harry Harlow, University of Wisconsin, 1950s–1960s ("The Nature of Love", 1958); later isolation chamber ("pit of despair") work with Stephen Suomi, early 1970s Infant rhesus monkeys separated from mothers, raised with wire or cloth surrogates or in total isolation; showed contact comfort mattered more than feeding Severe, lasting suffering in animals; central to the growth of animal welfare and the 3 Rs Facebook emotional contagion Adam Kramer, Jamie Guillory and Jeffrey Hancock, published 2014 ( PNAS ) The News Feeds of 689,003 users were manipulated for one week in January 2012 to show fewer positive or fewer negative posts; users' own posts shifted slightly in the same direction No specific informed consent (only the platform's terms of service), no debriefing, attempts to alter mood; the journal published an editorial expression of concern Why Stanley Milgram is the hardest case. Diana Baumrind argued that the stress and the loss of dignity were not justified, that the laboratory setting made subjects especially trusting, and that the experience could harm their self-image and trust in authority. Milgram answered that the outcome was not predictable (psychiatrists he surveyed had expected almost nobody to go to the end), that everyone was dehoaxed and reconciled with the "learner", that most were glad to have taken part, and that the knowledge was important. Under APA 8.07(b) (no deception about research expected to cause severe emotional distress) the original study could not be approved today; Jerry Burger's 2009 partial replication stopped at 150 V, the point at which the learner first demands to be let out. 26.10 Animal research Animals cannot consent, so the ethics of animal research is about justification and welfare. William Russell and Rex Burch , in The Principles of Humane Experimental Technique (1959), proposed the framework every committee now uses, the 3 Rs : R Meaning Example Replacement Use non-animal methods wherever possible Cell cultures, computer models, human volunteers, recorded data Reduction Use the minimum number of animals that gives a valid answer Power analysis, better designs, sharing animals and data between studies Refinement Minimise pain, distress and lasting harm; improve welfare Anaesthesia and analgesia, humane end points, enriched housing, trained handlers APA Standard 8.09 requires psychologists to acquire, care for, use and dispose of animals in line with the law, under the supervision of a psychologist trained in their care; to minimise discomfort, infection, illness and pain; to subject animals to pain, stress or privation only when an alternative procedure is unavailable and the goal is justified by its scientific, educational or applied value; to perform surgery under appropriate anaesthesia; and, when an animal's life must be ended, to do so rapidly and with minimal pain. Reporting of animal studies follows the ARRIVE guidelines (section 25.9). India. Animal experiments are regulated under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 (Section 15) and the Breeding of and Experiments on Animals (Control and Supervision) Rules, 1998 , through the Committee for the Purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CPCSEA) . Every establishment needs an Institutional Animal Ethics Committee (IAEC) . In January 2023 the committee was renamed the Committee for Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CCSEA) , under the Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying; question papers still use "CPCSEA". The Indian committee also stresses a " fourth R ", rehabilitation and after-care of animals once experiments end. 26.11 Research misconduct, authorship and publication ethics Research misconduct = FFP (US federal definition, 2000): fabrication (making up data or results), falsification (manipulating materials, equipment or processes, or changing or omitting data, so the record misrepresents the research) and plagiarism (appropriating another person's ideas, processes, results or words without credit), in proposing, performing, reviewing or reporting research. It excludes honest error and differences of opinion . Questionable research practices (p-hacking, HARKing; section 25.15) are a grey zone short of FFP that does similar damage. Famous cases Sir Cyril Burt (British educational psychologist, died 1971): reported a correlation of .771 between the IQs of identical twins reared apart, unchanged to three decimals as his sample grew from 21 to 53 pairs. Leon Kamin (1974) pointed out the implausibility; the journalist Oliver Gillie (1976) alleged fraud and that two co-authors could not be traced; Burt's biographer Leslie Hearnshaw (1979) concluded he had fabricated data. Later authors (Robert Joynson 1989, Ronald Fletcher 1991) defended him, so the case is usually described as a controversy ; the data are no longer used. Diederik Stapel (social psychologist, Tilburg University, Netherlands): exposed in 2011 after junior colleagues reported him; an investigation (final report 2012) found he had fabricated data in dozens of publications, often handing "collected" data sets to students. He has about 58 retractions. The case fed directly into the replication crisis (25.15). Andrew Wakefield (1998, The Lancet ): a paper on 12 children suggesting a link between the MMR vaccine and autism; found to be dishonest and unethical (including invasive procedures on children without proper approval), retracted in 2010, and Wakefield was struck off the UK medical register. Vaccination rates fell for years afterwards: misconduct with a public-health cost. Plagiarism and publication ethics Forms of plagiarism: copying verbatim without quotation marks and citation; patchwriting or mosaic plagiarism (stitching together lightly altered phrases from sources); paraphrasing ideas without credit; collusion (submitting jointly produced work as individual work); ghost-writing (submitting work someone else wrote); self-plagiarism (recycling your own published text as new). Correct citation is not plagiarism ; that is the usual "which is NOT" answer. Duplicate publication (publishing the same data twice as original, APA 8.13) and salami slicing (splitting one study into many thin papers) inflate the evidence base and can double-count participants in meta-analyses. Authorship must reflect real contribution (APA 8.12). The International Committee of Medical Journal Editors requires all four: substantial contribution to conception, design, data collection or analysis; drafting or critically revising the paper; approving the final version; and accepting accountability for the work. Gift (honorary) authorship (adding a head of department who did nothing) and ghost authorship (omitting someone, such as a company writer, who did write it) both violate this. Minor contributors go in the acknowledgements. Conflicts of interest: financial (industry funding, consultancy, shares in a test or app) and non-financial (allegiance to one's own therapy, 25.14) must be declared; drug-company-funded trials are more likely to report results favouring the sponsor's product. Correcting the record: errors are corrected (APA 8.10) and seriously flawed papers retracted. Data sharing for verification (8.14) and preregistration make all of this easier to detect. 26.12 The ethics of particular designs Withdrawal (reversal) designs (ABAB, section 22): returning to baseline means withdrawing a treatment that is working , for example stopping a successful intervention for a child's self-injury. This is acceptable for brief periods with mild behaviours, but for dangerous behaviours the ethical alternative is a multiple-baseline design , which never removes the treatment. Waitlist and no-treatment controls (25.3): delaying treatment is justified when the delay is short, the condition is not dangerous, waitlisted people are monitored and can be moved to treatment ("rescue" or escape rules) if they deteriorate, and treatment is offered at the end. A waitlist is not acceptable for a person at high suicide risk. Placebo controls when an effective treatment exists: the Declaration of Helsinki allows a placebo or no-intervention control only where no proven intervention exists , or where there are compelling, scientifically sound methodological reasons and the participants will not face additional risk of serious or irreversible harm. Otherwise the new treatment should be compared with the best proven one (an active comparator, or "add-on" designs where everyone receives standard care). ICMR 2017 classes delaying or withholding a proven treatment in a control or placebo arm as a "minor increase over minimal risk", which needs full committee review. Equipoise: randomising patients is ethical only when there is genuine uncertainty in the expert community about which arm is better; Benjamin Freedman (1987) called this clinical equipoise . If accumulating evidence clearly favours one arm, an independent data and safety monitoring board stops the trial early. Covert observation (section 23): observing people without their knowledge avoids reactivity but violates consent and possibly privacy. It is acceptable for anonymous behaviour in genuinely public places (APA 8.05 and 8.03), and controversial in private or semi-private settings: Humphreys' tearooms, or David Rosenhan's (1973) pseudopatients ("On being sane in insane places"), who deceived psychiatric hospital staff to gain admission. Qualitative research and the researcher relationship (section 24): in-depth interviews create intimacy, so participants may disclose more than they intended; consent is treated as an ongoing process consent , renegotiated during the study. Interviews about trauma, abuse or suicide need a distress protocol (pause, stop, referral). A clinician who interviews their own patients holds a dual role that can make refusal feel risky and blur research with therapy. Rich description of a small community can reveal identities even with pseudonyms (deductive disclosure), so details are altered and quotes checked. Reflexivity (section 24) includes reflecting on these power relationships. Recap of section 26: research ethics was written in response to scandals. The Nazi experiments produced the Nuremberg Code (1947; 10 points; "the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential"); the profession answered with the World Medical Association's Declaration of Helsinki (1964; latest revision October 2024). Tuskegee (US Public Health Service, 1932–72) led to the National Research Act (1974) and the Belmont Report (1979): respect for persons → informed consent (information, comprehension, voluntariness); beneficence → assessment of risks and benefits; justice → fair selection of subjects; then the Common Rule (1991; IRBs) and CIOMS guidelines. Beauchamp and Childress (1979) gave four principles (autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence, justice); deontology judges acts by duty, utilitarianism by cost-benefit. The APA Ethics Code (first 1953; current 2002, amended 2010 and 2016) has five aspirational General Principles (A beneficence and nonmaleficence, B fidelity and responsibility, C integrity, D justice, E respect for people's rights and dignity) and enforceable Standards; Standard 8 covers research (8.01 approval to 8.15 reviewers; 8.07 deception, 8.08 debriefing, 8.09 animals). In India, the ICMR National Ethical Guidelines (2017 ; earlier 1980, 2000, 2006) give four basic and 12 general principles and four risk levels; ethics committees have 7 to 15 members, half from outside, with a lay person, legal expert and social scientist, and under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules 2019 at least one woman; trials register on CTRI; RCI regulates clinical psychologists; Mental Healthcare Act 2017 Section 99 requires free and informed consent (or State Authority permission). Consent needs competence, information and voluntariness, with assent plus parental permission for children (ICMR: verbal 7 to 12, written 12 to 18). Deception is allowed only with significant value, no alternative, no pain or severe distress, and early explanation (APA 8.07); debriefing means dehoaxing and desensitising (Holmes 1976), ideally process debriefing. Anonymity means even the researcher cannot identify participants; confidentiality means the researcher can but will not tell, within stated limits (risk of harm, Tarasoff, POCSO). Minimal risk = no more than daily life or routine tests; the right to withdraw is absolute; avoid coercion and undue inducement; select participants fairly. Know the controversial studies (Little Albert 1920, Monster Study 1939, Tuskegee, Willowbrook, Milgram 1963 and Diana Baumrind 1964, Tearoom Trade 1970, Stanford Prison 1971, Harry Harlow, Facebook 2014), the 3 Rs (Russell and Burch 1959; CPCSEA, now CCSEA), misconduct as fabrication, falsification and plagiarism (Burt, Stapel, Wakefield), honest authorship, and the ethics of withdrawal designs, waitlists, placebo controls, covert observation and qualitative relationships. 27 Which design to use, the research-methods name index, and the traps This section closes Part II the way sections 16 and 17 close Part I. It gives you a decision walk that ends in a design name, a one-line lookup table for the way papers describe designs, an index of every name in sections 18 to 26, and the confusable pairs that cost the most marks. Nothing here is new; each line points back to the section where it is taught properly. 27.1 Which design to use Almost every "which design is this?" or "which design should the researcher use?" item is a single path through five questions. Ask them in order. First, what kind of question is it? There are six kinds. To describe asks what is there and how common it is: how many college students in Bengaluru screen positive for depression? To relate or predict asks whether two variables go together: is childhood trauma associated with adult depression? To establish cause asks whether changing X changes Y: does CBT reduce BDI scores more than waiting? To study one person's change asks whether an intervention works for this particular client: does a token economy reduce this boy's tantrums? To understand meaning asks what an experience is like or how a process unfolds: what is it like to care for a son with schizophrenia? To pool studies asks what the whole body of evidence says: across 40 trials, how large is the effect of CBT for panic? The kind of question settles the family of design before anything else. Second, for description: once or over time? One measurement of a population at one moment is a cross-sectional survey , which gives prevalence. Measuring the same people repeatedly is a longitudinal (panel) design, which shows change within people. If age differences are the point, remember that a cross-sectional comparison of age groups confounds age with cohort and a longitudinal one confounds age with time of measurement; the sequential designs of K. Warner Schaie (1965), which follow several cohorts over time, disentangle them (section 21). Third, for relationships: where do you start? If you start from the outcome (people who already have a rare disorder, plus matched controls) and look back for exposures, it is a case-control study, the design of choice for rare outcomes, and it yields an odds ratio. If you start from the exposure and follow exposed and unexposed people forward to see who develops the outcome, it is a cohort study, which yields incidence and relative risk (prospective if followed from now, retrospective if reconstructed from old records). If you simply measure both variables on the same people, it is correlational . When the "independent variable" has already happened and cannot be manipulated (abuse, divorce, a head injury), and groups are compared on it after the fact, the design is called ex post facto (causal-comparative). None of these can prove causation on its own; for that, observational researchers use Austin Bradford Hill 's (1965) nine viewpoints (strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment, analogy). Fourth, for cause: can you manipulate, and can you randomise? If you cannot manipulate the IV, you are back to ex post facto or a natural experiment. If you can manipulate it and can randomly assign people to conditions, you have a true experiment (section 20.5): the posttest-only or pretest-posttest control group design, or the Solomon four-group design (Richard L. Solomon, 1949) when you fear that the pretest itself sensitises people to the treatment; with two or more IVs, a factorial design; in a clinical treatment test, a randomised controlled trial with blinding and intention-to-treat analysis (section 25). If you can manipulate but cannot randomise, you have a quasi-experiment (section 20.8): intact groups give the nonequivalent control group design ; many observations before and after an intervention give an interrupted time series ; and a cut-off score that decides who is treated gives a regression discontinuity design (Donald L. Thistlethwaite and Donald T. Campbell, 1960). Random assignment, not manipulation, is the line between true and quasi-experiments. Fifth, one case or many? If the question is about one person's change and you can take repeated measurements, use a single-case experimental design (section 22). If the treatment can be withdrawn and the behaviour is reversible, the ABAB reversal design is the strongest. If withdrawal is unethical or the behaviour will not reverse (a skill once learned), use a multiple-baseline design across behaviours, settings or participants. If the goal is reached in steps (cigarettes cut from 20 to 15 to 10 a day), use a changing-criterion design; to compare two treatments quickly in one client, an alternating-treatments design. If you only want to describe one person richly, without manipulation, it is a case study (sections 21 and 24). For questions of meaning, choose the qualitative approach by its object (section 24): phenomenology or IPA for lived experience, grounded theory for a theory of a process, ethnography for a culture, and mixed methods when you need numbers and meaning together. To pool many studies, do a systematic review and, where the studies are similar enough, a meta-analysis (section 25). 1 What is the question? 2 Then ask 3 Design (section) Cross-sectional survey (21) Longitudinal / panel study (21) Sequential design, Schaie (21) Describe what is there, how common? Work left to right: the kind of question, then the one or two questions that split it, then the design and the section that teaches it. Most "which design is this?" items in the entrance papers are a single path through this tree. The five questions, in order. 1. What kind of question? Describe, relate, cause, one person's change, meaning, or pooling studies. 2. Can the IV be manipulated? No means non-experimental (correlational, ex post facto, cohort, case-control). 3. Can people be randomly assigned? Yes means a true experiment; no means a quasi-experiment. 4. One case or many? One person with repeated measurement means a single-case design; many means a group design. 5. Is time a dimension? Once means cross-sectional; repeatedly means longitudinal; several cohorts over time means sequential. Answer those and only one design is left standing. If the question says ..., the answer is ...
