Cognitive Psychology If behaviorism had banished the mind from psychology, the cognitive revolution of the 1950s and 1960s brought it back. Behaviorists had refused to study internal mental events on the grounds that they could not be directly observed. Cognitivists countered that the mind could be studied scientifically and indirectly , by inferring internal processes from carefully measured behavior, just as physicists infer unseen particles from their effects. Drivers of the Cognitive Revolution Several developments converged to reinstate the mind as a legitimate object of study: Chomsky's 1959 critique of Skinner's Verbal Behavior : Noam Chomsky argued that language is generative (we produce sentences never heard before), that children acquire it too fast and too well to be explained by reinforcement, and that humans possess an innate Language Acquisition Device (LAD) and a transformational grammar . This devastating review is often taken as the symbolic launch of the revolution. The computer / information-processing metaphor : the mind came to be seen as an information processor that takes input, encodes, stores, retrieves, and outputs, mirroring a computer. Shannon's information theory , which gave psychology a formal vocabulary for measuring information. The 1956 "annus mirabilis" : George Miller's paper "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two" ; Allen Newell and Herbert Simon's Logic Theorist (an early AI program); and the Dartmouth conference that christened "artificial intelligence." Earlier groundwork by Frederic Bartlett , whose 1932 work on schemas showed that memory is reconstructive, not photographic. Definition Information-processing model: the view that the mind operates like a computer, handling information through a sequence of stages: input, encoding, storage, retrieval, and output. Ulric Neisser and the Naming of the Field Ulric Neisser's 1967 textbook Cognitive Psychology named and consolidated the discipline, earning him the title "father of cognitive psychology." The Information-Processing Model of Memory The dominant framework was a set of stage models , debating whether processing is serial (one step at a time) or parallel . The landmark Atkinson-Shiffrin multi-store model (1968) proposed three stores: Store Capacity Duration Sensory register Very large Fraction of a second Short-term / working memory 7 ± 2 items ~15-30 seconds Long-term memory Essentially unlimited Potentially permanent Refinements followed. Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch (1974) replaced the passive short-term store with an active working memory comprising a central executive directing two subsystems, the phonological loop (verbal/acoustic information) and the visuospatial sketchpad (visual and spatial information), with an episodic buffer added later (2000) to integrate them. Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart (1972) offered an alternative levels of processing framework: memory depends not on which store but on how deeply material is encoded (shallow surface processing versus deep semantic processing). In attention, Donald Broadbent proposed the influential filter (bottleneck) model , in which a filter selects one channel of incoming information for further processing. Key Figures and Allied Lines George Miller quantified short-term capacity at seven plus or minus two "chunks." Herbert Simon and Allen Newell pioneered the study of problem-solving , building the General Problem Solver (GPS) and introducing bounded rationality (the idea that human reasoning is rational but limited by information and capacity). Jerome Bruner , also a founder of the field, advanced discovery learning and three modes of representation : enactive (action-based), iconic (image-based), and symbolic (language-based). Jean Piaget is often placed here as the great cognitive-developmental theorist. Later, Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed that judgment relies on heuristics (mental shortcuts) such as availability, representativeness, and anchoring , extending Simon's bounded rationality into the study of cognitive bias. Cognitive psychology also yielded clinical fruit: Aaron Beck's cognitive therapy, built on the cognitive triad (negative views of self, world, and future) and systematic cognitive distortions , and Albert Ellis's Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT) with its ABC model (Activating event, Beliefs, Consequences). Definition Schema: a mental framework or organized knowledge structure that guides how we perceive, interpret, and remember information. Connectionism and the Cognitive Science Turn From the 1980s, connectionism / parallel distributed processing (PDP) modeled cognition through networks of simple interconnected units, inspired by the brain rather than the serial computer. The field broadened into cognitive science (uniting psychology, linguistics, computer science, and philosophy) and then into cognitive neuroscience , which uses brain imaging to ground mental processes in neural activity. Legacy Cognitive psychology is the dominant paradigm in psychology today and the theoretical foundation of CBT , the most empirically supported family of psychotherapies. High-yield Cognitive revolution drivers: Chomsky's 1959 critique of B. F. Skinner, the computer/information-processing metaphor, Shannon's information theory, and the 1956 events (Miller, Allen Newell & Herbert Simon, Dartmouth AI). Ulric Neisser, 1967 named the field. Miller: 7 ± 2. Atkinson-Shiffrin: three stores, sensory register, short-term, long-term. Trap Distinguish cognitive psychology (the experimental science of mental processes, founded by Ulric Neisser, Miller, Jerome Bruner, etc.) from cognitive therapy (the clinical treatment founded by Aaron Beck). And remember it was Noam Chomsky's critique of B. F. Skinner , not Skinner himself, that helped launch the revolution. Indian Psychology & Eastern Systems 9.1 Orientation: What "Indian Psychology" Means Western academic psychology grew out of physiology and philosophy in 19th-century Europe and defined itself as the empirical study of behaviour and mental processes, with health understood largely as the absence of pathology. Indian psychology is a different enterprise altogether. It is indigenous , rooted in philosophy and spiritual practice (the Vedas, Upanishads, and the great darshanas), and its goal is not the removal of symptoms but self-realization and liberation ( moksha ) and the deliberate transformation of consciousness . Where Western psychology asks "how does the mind work?", Indian psychology asks "who is the knower behind the mind, and how is one freed?" The "self" here is not the ego or personality but a deeper witnessing consciousness. Indian thought is traditionally divided into nine systems ( darshanas , literally "ways of seeing"). The six orthodox systems are called āstika because they accept the authority of the Vedas; the heterodox ( nāstika ) systems reject Vedic authority. The six orthodox darshanas are conventionally studied in three allied pairs. Pair Systems Core emphasis Logic + Atomism Nyaya & Vaisheshika Valid knowledge (pramanas) and logic; atomistic metaphysics of substance Cosmology + Practice Samkhya & Yoga Dualism of consciousness and matter; the disciplined path to liberation Ritual + Knowledge Mimamsa & Vedanta Vedic ritual action (karma-kanda); ultimate reality and the self (jnana-kanda) The three heterodox (nāstika) systems are Buddhism , Jainism , and Charvaka (a materialist, empiricist school that denied the soul and afterlife). For psychology, the most heavily examined systems are Samkhya, Yoga, Vedanta, and Buddhism. 9.2 Samkhya: Purusha, Prakriti, and the Three Gunas Samkhya , attributed to the sage Kapila , is the oldest of the systems and supplies the conceptual backbone for much of Indian psychology. It is a dualism of two ultimate, eternal realities. Purusha is pure consciousness, the passive witness (sakshi); it is many (each being has its own Purusha), changeless, and does nothing. Prakriti is primordial matter or nature, the active, unconscious source of everything mental and physical. Bondage arises when Purusha mistakenly identifies with the activities of Prakriti; liberation ( kaivalya , "aloneness") comes from discriminating the two. Prakriti is composed of three gunas (strands or qualities) held in equilibrium until evolution begins. From their disturbance unfolds a fixed sequence of evolutes : first mahat / buddhi (cosmic intellect, the faculty of discrimination), then ahamkara (the ego, the "I-maker"), then manas (mind, the coordinating sense), and from these the five sense-organs, five action-organs, five subtle elements (tanmatras), and five gross elements. Note that buddhi, ahamkara, and manas together form the inner instrument (antahkarana); they are all material, not consciousness itself. Definition Guna = a constituent quality or "strand" of Prakriti (nature). The three gunas (sattva, rajas, tamas) are present in everything; what differs is their proportion. A person's temperament, mood, food, and even thoughts are classified by which guna dominates. The three gunas are the single most-tested idea in Indian psychology, so learn them cold. Guna Quality Mental state / personality Example Sattva Purity, light, harmony, balance, clarity Calm, wise, content, disciplined, compassionate A serene, clear-thinking meditator Rajas Activity, passion, restlessness, energy Driven, anxious, craving, agitated, ambitious A restless, competitive striver Tamas Inertia, darkness, dullness, heaviness Lethargic, confused, dull, depressed, negligent A sluggish, apathetic person High-yield The three gunas : Sattva = purity/light/balance, Rajas = activity/passion/restlessness, Tamas = inertia/darkness/dullness. All of nature is a mixture of the three; personality is governed by which dominates. This item appears on virtually every Indian entrance. Memory hook Gunas in descending "energy quality": S-R-T = Saint, Restless, Tired . The Saint is sattvic (calm/pure), the Restless one is rajasic (driven), the Tired one is tamasic (dull/inert). 9.3 Yoga: Patanjali and the Eight Limbs The Yoga system, set out in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras , shares Samkhya's metaphysics but adds Ishvara (a special Purusha, a focus for devotion) and supplies the practical method for stilling the mind. Its central object is the chitta (mind-stuff), whose constant fluctuations are the chitta vrittis (mental modifications). The defining aphorism is "Yogah chitta vritti nirodhah" : yoga is the cessation (restraint) of the modifications of the mind. When the vrittis are stilled, the witness (Purusha) rests in its own nature. Definition Chitta vritti = a modification or wave in the mind-stuff (thoughts, perceptions, memories, emotions). Moksha / kaivalya = liberation, the final goal: the witnessing self freed from identification with mind and matter, ending the cycle of suffering and rebirth. The path is Ashtanga Yoga , the eight limbs: Yama — ethical restraints (non-violence, truth, non-stealing, continence, non-greed) Niyama — personal observances (purity, contentment, discipline, study, surrender) Asana — steady, comfortable posture Pranayama — regulation of breath / vital energy Pratyahara — withdrawal of the senses from their objects Dharana — concentration (fixing attention on one point) Dhyana — meditation (sustained, uninterrupted flow of attention) Samadhi — absorption / union, the goal High-yield "Yogah chitta vritti nirodhah" (yoga = stilling the mind's modifications) and the eight limbs in order: Yama, Niyama, Asana, Pranayama, Pratyahara, Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi . Examiners love asking for the sequence or for which limb is "sense-withdrawal" (Pratyahara) versus "concentration" (Dharana). Memory hook Eight limbs: "Young Novices Are Pretty Punctual During Daily Sadhana." Y-N-A-P-P-D-D-S. The last three (Dharana-Dhyana-Samadhi) practised together are called samyama . Patanjali names five kleshas (afflictions) that bind the mind: avidya (ignorance, the root of the rest), asmita (egoism / I-am-ness), raga (attachment to pleasure), dvesha (aversion to pain), and abhinivesha (clinging to life, fear of death). Yoga also describes four states of consciousness : jagrat (waking), swapna (dream), sushupti (deep dreamless sleep), and turiya ("the fourth", pure witnessing consciousness underlying the other three). Samadhi itself has grades, broadly samprajnata (with an object / seed) maturing into asamprajnata (objectless / seedless, nirbija) absorption. 9.4 Vedanta: Brahman, Atman, and the Five Sheaths Vedanta ("the end of the Vedas", based on the Upanishads) culminates in the Advaita (non-dual) teaching of Adi Shankara . Its claim is radical: there is only one reality, Brahman , and the individual self, Atman , is identical with it. The appearance of a separate world and separate selves is maya (illusion / superimposition). Liberation is not attaining something new but realizing what was always true, summed up in the great saying (mahavakya) "Tat Tvam Asi" , "Thou art That." Vedanta analyses the person as five concentric koshas (sheaths) covering the Atman, from grossest to subtlest: Kosha Sheath of Level Annamaya Food (the physical body) Gross Pranamaya Vital energy / breath Subtle Manomaya Mind (sensory-emotional) Subtle Vijnanamaya Intellect / discernment Subtle Anandamaya Bliss Causal (innermost) Trap Do not confuse Samkhya with Advaita Vedanta . Samkhya is dualist (two realities: Purusha + Prakriti) and is atheistic / non-theistic (no creator God needed). Advaita Vedanta is non-dualist (only Brahman is real; the world is maya). And while Samkhya is non-theistic, Yoga takes the same metaphysics but adds Ishvara , so Yoga is theistic. "Dualism = Samkhya, non-dualism = Advaita" is the line examiners test. 9.5 Buddhist Psychology Buddhism is a nāstika system but one of the most psychologically sophisticated. Its core is the Four Noble Truths : Dukkha — life involves suffering / unsatisfactoriness Samudaya — the cause of suffering is craving / attachment (tanha) Nirodha — suffering can cease (nirvana) Magga — the way to cessation is the Eightfold Path The Noble Eightfold Path covers right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration (grouped as wisdom, ethical conduct, and mental discipline). Three "marks of existence" frame Buddhist psychology: anicca (impermanence, nothing is fixed), dukkha (unsatisfactoriness), and anatta (no-self, there is no permanent, unchanging soul, directly opposing the Hindu Atman). The person is only a bundle of five skandhas (aggregates): form (rupa), sensation (vedana), perception (samjna), mental formations (samskara), and consciousness (vijnana). Experience arises through dependent origination (pratitya-samutpada): every state conditions the next in a chain, so there is no independent self at the centre. Trap Anatta (Buddhism) vs Atman (Vedanta). Vedanta affirms an eternal self (Atman = Brahman); Buddhism denies any permanent self (anatta / anatman). This direct opposition is a favourite MCQ. Buddhist practice of mindfulness ( sati ) and insight meditation ( vipassana ) has had an enormous modern clinical impact: it is the root of MBSR (Kabat-Zinn's Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction), MBCT (Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy for relapse prevention in depression), and the mindfulness/acceptance components of DBT and ACT. This is the clearest bridge between Eastern systems and contemporary evidence-based therapy. 9.6 Clinical Relevance and the Modern Indian Psychology Movement Several Indian constructs map directly onto clinical and personality psychology: Triguna model in assessment. The sattva-rajas-tamas scheme is used as an indigenous personality framework; Indian inventories such as the Vedic Personality Inventory and various Triguna scales measure a person's guna profile, an alternative to Western trait models. The self. Indian thought distinguishes the ego/personality from a deeper witnessing self, and tends toward a collectivistic, relational, embedded self, contrasting with the bounded, individualistic Western self. The Purusharthas , the four legitimate aims of life: dharma (duty / righteousness), artha (wealth / livelihood), kama (pleasure / desire), and moksha (liberation). A balanced, integrated life pursues all four, with moksha as the highest. The Bhagavad Gita's psychology. The Gita offers three complementary paths (yogas): Karma yoga (the path of action), Bhakti yoga (the path of devotion), and Jnana yoga (the path of knowledge). Its central teaching, nishkama karma (desireless / non-attached action, acting fully but renouncing attachment to the fruits), is widely cited for stress regulation and resilience. The modern Indian psychology movement seeks to recover these ideas as a scientific psychology. An early landmark is Jadunath Sinha's multi-volume Indian Psychology (cognition, emotion, will), which systematically extracted psychological content from the classical texts. Contemporary scholars (for example those associated with the Pondicherry / Sri Aurobindo tradition and the broader "indigenous psychology" movement) continue to develop Indian frameworks of consciousness, well-being, and self-realization as a complement to, not merely a translation of, Western psychology. High-yield Lock in the founder-text-system links: Samkhya = Kapila (Purusha/Prakriti, gunas); Yoga = Patanjali (Yoga Sutras, eight limbs, kleshas); Advaita Vedanta = Shankara (Brahman/Atman, maya, koshas); Buddhism = Four Noble Truths (anatta, anicca, skandhas). Plus the four Purusharthas (dharma-artha-kama-moksha) and the Gita's nishkama karma . 10. The Schools Side by Side: Timeline, Comparison, and Traps Everything above is one argument: each school is a reply to the one before it. Use the three tools in this section to lock the whole map down before the exam. First the timeline (who came when), then the comparison grid (what each school took as the object of study, its method, and its view of the person), then the trap recap (the swaps examiners set most often). 10.1 Timeline of the schools Era School Founder / key date Core move 1879 Structuralism Wilhelm Wundt (Leipzig lab); Edward Titchener systematised Analyse the contents of consciousness into elements via introspection 1890s-1900s Functionalism James (1890); Dewey's Reflex Arc (1896) Ask what consciousness is for : adaptation, applied psychology 1900s Psychoanalysis Sigmund Freud (Interpretation of Dreams, 1900) The dynamic unconscious drives behaviour 1912 Gestalt Max Wertheimer (phi phenomenon) Perception grasps organised wholes , not elements 1913 Behaviorism John B. Watson (manifesto); Pavlov, B. F. Skinner Study only observable behaviour ; learning by conditioning 1950s-60s Humanistic (Third Force) Maslow, Carl Rogers The whole, free, growth-seeking person 1956-67 Cognitive Miller (1956), Ulric Neisser (1967), Noam Chomsky The mind as an information processor ; mind back in science Ancient, ongoing Indian psychology Kapila, Patanjali, Shankara, Buddha Transform / transcend the mind toward liberation (moksha) 10.2 The comparison grid School Object of study Method View of the person Structuralism Structure/contents of conscious experience Analytic introspection (trained observers) A mind built of sensory elements Functionalism Functions of mind; what it does Varied; objective + applied, animal studies An organism adapting to its environment Gestalt Perceptual organisation, wholes Phenomenological experiment An active organiser of experience Behaviorism Observable behaviour (S-R) Controlled experiment; conditioning A blank slate shaped by environment Psychoanalysis The unconscious; drives and conflict Free association, dream analysis, case study Driven by unconscious instincts and early childhood Humanistic The whole person, subjective experience Phenomenology; the therapeutic relationship Free, dignified, striving toward self-actualization Cognitive Mental processes (memory, attention, thought) Controlled experiment; inference from behaviour; modelling An active information processor Indian psychology Consciousness and the self behind the mind Introspection, meditation, disciplined practice (sadhana) A witnessing consciousness seeking liberation High-yield The one-line spine of the whole unit: Structuralism = structure of consciousness; Functionalism = function of consciousness; Gestalt = organised wholes; Behaviorism = observable behaviour; Psychoanalysis = the unconscious; Humanism = the whole free person; Cognitive = information processing; Indian = liberation of consciousness. If you can say which "object of study" each school claimed, you can place any theorist or term. 10.3 The "forces" of psychology A common exam shorthand calls the major clinical traditions "forces": the first force is psychoanalysis, the second force is behaviorism, the third force is humanistic/existential psychology, and the fourth force is usually given as transpersonal (or, in some texts, multicultural) psychology. The cognitive revolution is sometimes folded in as part of a "cognitive-behavioural" mainstream rather than counted as a separate force. 10.4 Trap recap: the swaps examiners set They bait you with The correct answer "Who founded structuralism?" Edward Titchener coined and built it; Wilhelm Wundt founded experimental psychology (voluntarism) Structuralism vs functionalism Structuralism = what/structure ; functionalism = why/function Insight learning vs trial-and-error Insight = Wolfgang Köhler (sudden reorganisation); trial-and-error = Edward Thorndike (gradual) Gestalt psychology vs Gestalt therapy Wertheimer/Köhler/Koffka (perception) vs Fritz Perls (psychotherapy), unrelated Classical vs operant conditioning Classical = involuntary, antecedent elicits (Ivan Pavlov); operant = voluntary, consequence controls (B. F. Skinner) Negative reinforcement = punishment? No. Negative reinforcement increases behaviour by removing an aversive Personal vs collective unconscious Personal/dynamic = Sigmund Freud ; collective + archetypes = Carl Jung Inferiority complex; basic anxiety Inferiority/superiority = Alfred Adler ; basic anxiety = Karen Horney Psychosexual vs psychosocial stages Psychosexual = Freud ; psychosocial (8 stages, lifelong) = Erik Erikson Self-actualization vs individuation Self-actualization = Abraham Maslow ; individuation/self-realization = Jung Cognitive psychology vs cognitive therapy Science of mind = Neisser/Miller ; therapy = Aaron Beck (and Ellis's REBT) Samkhya vs Advaita Vedanta Samkhya = dualist (Purusha + Prakriti); Advaita = non-dualist (only Brahman) Atman vs anatta Eternal self (Atman) = Vedanta ; no-self (anatta) = Buddhism Memory hook If you remember nothing else, remember the chain of rebellions and one signature name per school: Wilhelm Wundt (structure), James/Dewey (function), Max Wertheimer (wholes), Watson/Skinner (behaviour), Sigmund Freud (unconscious), Maslow/Rogers (the person), Ulric Neisser (information), Patanjali (liberation). Eight names, eight schools, one century of argument, plus the timeless Indian thread.

title: Systems & Theories — Answer Explanations
text: Systems & Theories — Answer Explanations Every one of the 119 questions from the Systems & Theories mock, written out the way the test screen shows them: the correct answer and the theorist it belongs to up top, the concept built from scratch below, then each wrong option nailed to whose idea it actually is. Read it straight through to lock in who owns what, or jump to a school and skim the answer lines. Companion to the Systems & Theories teaching book and the mock itself. In this book History & Schools (19) Psychodynamic (36) Behavioural / Learning (13) Humanistic / Gestalt (21) Cognitive / Consciousness (12) Indian Psychology (18) History & Schools Q1 What do Herman Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud share in common? a Each of them worked independently and were pioneers in the field of psychology b Each of them founded a formal psychology laboratory c Each of them developed novel observational methods to study how the mind works d (a) and (c) ✓ Answer: (d) (a) and (c) Ebbinghaus, Galton and Freud, late nineteenth-century pioneers The concept Why (d) Two separate claims, (a) and (c), are each fully true of all three men, and stopping at one undersells what they share. The era All three belong to the late nineteenth-century emergence of psychology as a science, when the study of mind broke away from pure philosophy and physiology and began to use real methods. Independent pioneers (a) Hermann Ebbinghaus (Germany, memory research), Francis Galton (England, differential psychology) and Sigmund Freud (Austria, psychoanalysis) worked in different countries and traditions and never collaborated. Yet each launched a brand-new line of inquiry on his own initiative. Novel methods (c) None merely speculated. Ebbinghaus created the nonsense-syllable technique, with himself as sole subject, to chart the forgetting curve , bringing Wilhelm Wundt 's experimental rigour to memory; Galton measured individual differences (questionnaires, twin studies, mental tests, correlation), seeding psychometrics and behaviour genetics; Freud used free association and dream interpretation to probe the unconscious, opening the dynamic/clinical tradition parallel to the academic labs. Exam tip When two single options are each independently true and a 'both' choice exists, the 'both' choice usually wins, so never stop at the first correct-looking answer. Panwar key Herman Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud, all 3 of them worked independently and were pioneers in the field of psychology. And they developed novel observational methods to study how the mind works. Why the other options are wrong (a) Each of them worked independently and were pioneers in the field of psychology True of all three (independent, pioneering originality), but only half of what they share: it ignores (c)'s equally true point about new observational methods. True but incomplete, so (d) is the complete answer. (b) Each of them founded a formal psychology laboratory Founding a formal lab belongs to Wilhelm Wundt (first lab, Leipzig in 1879 ), the standard distractor. None of the three did: Hermann Ebbinghaus self-experimented, Galton ran an anthropometric measurement station, Sigmund Freud worked clinically. (c) Each of them developed novel observational methods to study how the mind works Fully true of all three (nonsense syllables, correlation, free association), but it covers only their methodological side and leaves out (a)'s independent pioneering, so the combined (d) is more complete. Q2 In which year the first mental hospital in the USA was opened? a 1693 b 1753 c 1793 d 1547 ✓ Answer: (b) 1753 Pennsylvania Hospital, Philadelphia, backed by Benjamin Franklin (1753) The concept Why 1753 In 1753 the Pennsylvania Hospital in Philadelphia, the first hospital in the United States, opened its doors and admitted patients with mental illness from the very start. Before 1753 In the colonial era there was no organised system of care: people with mental illness were confined at home, jailed or left to wander. No public institution received them, and madness was explained in moral and supernatural rather than medical terms. What came after 1753 opens the institutional and moral-treatment story, the move from neglect toward treatment, that later runs through Philippe Pinel 'unchaining' patients in France, William Tuke's York Retreat in England and Dorothea Dix 's mid-nineteenth-century reform crusade across America. General, not asylum Championed by Benjamin Franklin and physician Thomas Bond , it cared for the sick poor of all kinds, and several of its earliest patients were mentally ill. So organised care began inside a general hospital; purpose-built facilities such as the Williamsburg asylum (1773), often called the first American hospital solely for the mentally ill, came later. Exam tip First U.S. hospital equals 1753, Philadelphia, with mental patients among its first admissions: a general hospital, not the later dedicated asylums. Panwar key The first hospital in the U.S. opened its doors in 1753 in Philadelphia. While it treated a variety of patients, six of its first patients suffered from mental illness. Why the other options are wrong (a) 1693 Far too early: the American colonies had no public hospital of any kind then, and care of the mentally ill was entirely informal (home confinement or jail). A near-miss late-seventeenth-century decoy. (c) 1793 A real Philadelphia date, but it marks the catastrophic yellow-fever epidemic , not a hospital founding: right city, wrong event. The Pennsylvania Hospital had already been open forty years by then. (d) 1547 The year London's Bethlem Hospital (the infamous 'Bedlam') was granted to the City and became a dedicated asylum, in England , not the USA. Famous, but an English date: wrong by country. Q3 Who established the first laboratory for experimental study of psychology? a Galton b Weber c Wundt d Jung ✓ Answer: (c) Wundt Wilhelm Wundt, Leipzig laboratory (1879) The concept Why Wundt Wilhelm Wundt opened the first laboratory devoted to the experimental study of psychology, conventionally treated as the founding moment of psychology as an independent science. Before 1879 The mind belonged to two parent disciplines: philosophy , reasoning from the armchair, and physiology , studying the body's sensory and nervous machinery (Weber, Fechner, Helmholtz). No separate discipline examined mental processes through controlled experiment. The Leipzig lab Wundt fused the two at the University of Leipzig in 1879 , Germany, measuring conscious experience under controlled conditions: timing reactions to stimuli (mental chronometry) and training observers to report sensations by introspection . His legacy With students (Edward Titchener, Hall, Cattell and others) who carried the method across Europe and America, he is the father of experimental psychology ; his school is structuralism , later systematised by Titchener. He is the hinge between pre-scientific philosophy of mind and the later schools (functionalism, behaviourism, Gestalt, psychoanalysis, the cognitive era), each defined by agreeing with or revolting against his programme. Exam tip Lock the trio: Wundt, 1879, Leipzig. For who founded the first psychology lab or made psychology experimental, answer Wundt, not the physiologists or differential-psychology figures around him. Panwar key Wilhelm Wundt opened the first laboratory of psychology in 1879, in Leipzig, Germany. Why the other options are wrong (a) Galton Francis Galton , same era: mental testing, individual differences, an 'anthropometric laboratory' (a tempting word-match). But that was a measurement station gathering public data, not an experimental lab for consciousness, and came after Leipzig. (b) Weber Ernst Weber , a physiologist: his sensory thresholds (Weber's law, the just-noticeable difference) fed experimental psychology. However, he studied sensation as physiology and founded no psychology lab; he is a precursor to Wilhelm Wundt. (d) Jung Carl Jung , a psychoanalyst who founded analytical psychology in the early twentieth century. Born 1875, only four years before the Leipzig lab, he worked in the clinical/depth tradition and founded no experimental laboratory. Q4 American Psychological Association (APA) was founded in: a 1892 b 1893 c 1896 d 1897 ✓ Answer: (a) 1892 G. Stanley Hall, Clark University (July 1892) The concept Why 1892 The American Psychological Association was founded in July 1892 at Clark University , Worcester, Massachusetts, when a small group of psychologists met to create a national society advancing psychology as a science and profession. First president G. Stanley Hall was its driving force and first president. He studied in Wundt's Leipzig tradition, opened one of the first U.S. psychology labs (Johns Hopkins), founded the first American psychology journal and trained many early psychologists. The 1890s American psychology came of age and detached from philosophy and physiology. The science born in Wundt's Leipzig lab in 1879 had crossed the Atlantic; William James had published Principles of Psychology (1890); structuralism and emerging functionalism competed; labs multiplied on American campuses. Why it mattered Practitioners needed a shared organisation for standards, communication and annual meetings. The APA filled that role, marking psychology's professional, institutional phase, and is now the largest professional psychology body in the world. Exam tip Lock in APA, 1892, Clark University, Hall as first president. Watch the year: do not blur the founding with later annual meetings, the first formal convention or later expansions. Panwar key The American Psychological Association was formed in July 1892 at Clark University, Worcester, Massachusetts, United States. Why the other options are wrong (b) 1893 A deliberate off-by-one decoy next to the true year, catching anyone who recalls 'early 1890s' but not the exact digit. The APA was founded in 1892; the one-year gap is the whole trap. (c) 1896 The year Lightner Witmer opened the first psychological clinic (University of Pennsylvania), launching clinical psychology. A real 'first', but a different one from the APA founding. (d) 1897 Five years after the 1892 founding, a later year offered to muddy the timeline. There is no major APA-founding event in 1897; it only catches those unsure whether it was the early or late 1890s. Q5 What is true about Structuralism? a Aim was to create a "periodic table" of the "elements of sensations" b Aim was to understand the nature of consciousness c Aim was to study the behaviour and not mind d all the above ✓ Answer: (a) Aim was to create a "periodic table" of the "elements of sensations" Wundt and Titchener's structuralism The concept Why (a) The signature ambition of structuralism was a mental equivalent of chemistry's periodic table, cataloguing the basic elements of sensation . The school Founded by Wilhelm Wundt in his 1879 Leipzig laboratory and systematised by his English-born American student Edward Titchener , it was the first formal school after psychology became a science. The chemistry model As complex substances reduce to a finite set of chemical elements, complex conscious experience should reduce to irreducible mental elements: sensations, images and affective feelings. Disciplined observers isolated them by trained introspection , reporting the raw contents of awareness (quality, intensity, duration) under controlled conditions. The aim was analytic and descriptive: dissect consciousness into atoms and arrange them in an orderly table. Its fall Historically this was psychology's first attempt to look like a hard science. It was challenged by functionalism (what the mind is for, not what it is made of), then largely swept aside by behaviourism , which rejected the study of consciousness; its failure (introspective reports proved unreliable and irreproducible between laboratories) helped trigger both. Exam tip Structuralists did care about consciousness generally, but the question rewards the unique goal: reducing consciousness to elemental sensations. So (a) beats the vaguer (b), and the behaviourist-flavoured (c) is simply wrong. Panwar key Structuralism was the first approach to understanding psychology after the field was born. The aim was to understand and be able to well describe the structures of which the human mind is formed. It also aimed at creating a table of elements of sensations like the periodic table in chemistry. Why the other options are wrong (b) Aim was to understand the nature of consciousness Loosely true, a 'safe' choice, but too broad: it describes the general territory, not structuralism's distinctive aim, the 'periodic table of sensations' in (a). Nor can it fold into 'all the above', since (c) is false. (c) Aim was to study the behaviour and not mind That is behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner), which rejected introspection and consciousness: the opposite of structuralism, which studied the mind by introspection. Studying behaviour alone is false here, and that falsity also sinks (d). (d) all the above Only correct if every bundled statement is true, and (c) (behaviour not mind) flatly contradicts structuralism. One false member kills an 'all of the above' choice. Q6 According to John Dewey, ____ is the connection between sensory stimuli and motor responses. a Efferent arc b Reflex arc c Association arc d Dynamic arc ✓ Answer: (b) Reflex arc John Dewey, The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology (1896) The concept Why reflex arc In his 1896 paper The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology , John Dewey took the reflex arc , the supposed connection between sensory stimulus and motor response, as his explicit subject and target of criticism. What it is In physiology, a stimulus excites a sensory ( afferent ) pathway that connects through the nervous system to a motor ( efferent ) pathway, producing a response; it is usually drawn as a one-way stimulus-then-response chain. Historical place The paper is a founding statement of American functionalism (the Chicago school) and an early shot against stimulus-response (S-R) psychology, which would harden into behaviourism under John B. Watson. S-R treated stimulus and response as separate basic building blocks stitched together. Dewey's critique That carving is artificial: sensation and movement are phases of one continuous, coordinated act of adaptation, and the response loops back to reshape how the next stimulus is perceived (the child reaching for the candle flame is one organised act). Physiology implies a unity of coordinated action, which the old psychology wrongly split. This stress on the whole adaptive act, function over fixed elements, makes the paper functionalist and a bridge toward organism-centred and Gestalt-flavoured thinking. Exam tip The term Dewey defined and then criticised is the reflex arc; his contribution was rejecting its fragmentation in favour of a unified, functional act. Panwar key John Dewey's Education theory based on his concept of functional psychology, focused on action and application. It went against the traditional concept of stimulus-response. Dewey through his theory argued that the neural circuitry of the reflex arc was being misinterpreted by behaviourist psychology which was using stimulus and response as basic units. Physiology implied a unity of coordinated action, but psychology was treating 'stimulus' and 'response' as separable. Why the other options are wrong (a) Efferent arc Only the outgoing motor limb (efferent: carrying signals away from the centre toward the muscles), so it sounds plausible. John Dewey discussed the whole afferent-to-efferent loop; picking the half-term misses it. (c) Association arc Not a term John Dewey used; there is no such structure in his reflex-arc paper. It borrows the respectable word 'association' (from associationist psychology) to fake a technical concept: a pure fabrication distractor. (d) Dynamic arc Not a recognised Dewey concept either. It appeals because John Dewey argued the act is dynamic and continuous, not static, so the examiner turns his spirit into a plausible false label; he named the reflex arc. Q7 According to Titchener, Introspection is a highly specialised form of ______ in which the psychologist attempts to study his own consciousness scientifically. a Self perception b Self thinking c Attention d Self observation ✓ Answer: (d) Self observation Edward Titchener, structuralist introspection The concept Why self observation Edward Titchener framed introspection as a highly specialised form of self-observation in which the psychologist studies his own consciousness scientifically. Background Wundt's English-born student, he carried German laboratory psychology to America and founded structuralism at Cornell in the 1890s. Its aim, inherited from Wundt's 1879 Leipzig programme, was to reduce mental life to elemental sensations, images and affective states. How it works Reaching those elements needs a disciplined inward look, not watching behaviour from outside: a comparatively neutral, systematic act of observing the self , unlike casual everyday reflection. Trained observers ('reagents') reported an experience's quality, intensity, duration and clearness, avoiding the stimulus error : naming the object ('an apple') instead of the bare sensation ('a round red patch with these brightness and hue qualities'). Its weakness Historically this method was structuralism's fatal vulnerability: it proved unreliable and irreproducible, with different labs reporting different 'elements'. That let behaviourism (John B. Watson, 1913) dismiss it as unscientific and shift psychology to observable behaviour. Exam tip Titchener's introspection is self-observation made rigorous, a controlled report of conscious contents rather than ordinary thinking, perceiving or merely attending. So the answer is self observation, not attention, self-perception or self-thinking. Panwar key According to Titchener, Introspection is a highly specialised form of self observation in which the psychologist attempts to study his own consciousness scientifically. Self-observation is the relatively neutral approach to study the self and was used by Edward Tichener. Why the other options are wrong (a) Self perception The term from Daryl Bem's 1960s self-perception theory (we infer our attitudes by observing our behaviour), a social-psychology concept from another era. Edward Titchener's method directly reported the contents of consciousness instead. (b) Self thinking Not a recognised term in structuralism's account of introspection, just a loose echo of an inward act. Edward Titchener set his method apart from ordinary thinking, which is itself a conscious content to be observed. (c) Attention A real, central topic in early experimental psychology (focusing consciousness on a stimulus), but it is an object of study the observer reports on, not the act of self-observation Edward Titchener called introspection. Q8 The aim of Functionalism was to study ______ as it functions in adapting the ______ to its environment. a Organism, Mind b Mind, Organism c Thinking, Organism d Attention, Individual ✓ Answer: (b) Mind, Organism William James, Dewey and Angell's functionalism The concept Why (b) The classic aim of functionalism was to study the mind as it functions in adapting the organism to its environment. The contrast Structuralism (Wundt's Leipzig lab, Titchener at Cornell), the first force, asked what the mind is made of , breaking consciousness into elemental sensations by introspection. Functionalism, the distinctively American second force, led in spirit by William James at Harvard and developed by John Dewey and James Angell at the University of Chicago around the turn of the twentieth century, asked what it is for . Darwin's influence Charles Darwin's evolution drove the shift: if every biological feature aids survival, mental processes (perceiving, remembering, feeling, willing) must serve an adaptive purpose too. The guiding question became practical and biological: how do mental processes help a living creature meet the demands of its surroundings and survive? Mind serves organism So the mind is what is studied and the organism is what it serves. This imported Darwinian thinking into psychology and later seeded evolutionary psychology and applied psychology (education, industry, mental testing). Exam tip The order of the blanks is the test: functionalism studies the mind functioning to adapt the organism to its environment, not the reverse. Panwar key Functionalism was an early approach after the idea of Cartesian duality was popular. The aim was to study the mind as it functions in adapting the organism to its environment. Why the other options are wrong (a) Organism, Mind The right two words in reversed order, the trap for careless readers who skip checking the slots. Making the organism adapt the mind inverts functionalism's logic and its Darwinian, survival-serving role for mental processes. (c) Thinking, Organism Too narrow: thinking is one obvious mental activity, but functionalism's declared object was the mind broadly, the whole sweep of mental processes serving adaptation. Substituting one faculty is also historically inaccurate. (d) Attention, Individual Both real terms, but attention is just one specific mental process, not functionalism's overarching subject, and 'individual' does not match the biological framing of an organism adapting to its environment. Both blanks mismatch. Q9 ______ of the American Psychological Association represents Health Psychology. a Division 16 b Division 38 c Division 47 d Division 98 ✓ Answer: (b) Division 38 APA Division 38, Society for Health Psychology The concept Why 38 Division 38 of the APA is designated for Health Psychology , now formally called the Society for Health Psychology. How the APA works The American Psychological Association (founded 1892, the institutional milestone in psychology becoming a profession) is split into numbered divisions, each a distinct specialty or interest area. The numbers roughly track chartering order, not importance, so they are essentially arbitrary labels. What it covers The psychological side of physical health and illness: how behaviour, stress, beliefs and emotions affect the onset and course of disease, how to promote healthy behaviour, and how psychologists work in healthcare to prevent, treat and manage illness and disability. Background Health psychology emerged in the 1970s alongside behavioural medicine. It rests on George Engel 's biopsychosocial model (1977): health and illness arise from biological, psychological and social factors together, a direct challenge to the older purely biomedical model it helped overturn. The APA recognises clinical health psychology as a professional specialty, with Division 38 as its organisational home. Exam tip A pure memory item: Division 38 equals Health Psychology. Anchor 38 firmly and do not let it slide into the neighbouring numbered divisions. Panwar key Division 38 of the American Psychological Association represents Health Psychology. Under APA (American Psychological Association) clinical health psychology is a professionally recognized specialty that investigates and implements clinical services across diverse populations and settings to promote health and well-being and to prevent, treat and manage illness and disability. Why the other options are wrong (a) Division 16 The Division of School Psychology , serving children and education systems. A real, well-known division, hence a strong decoy, but it has nothing to do with physical health and illness. (c) Division 47 The Society for Sport, Exercise and Performance Psychology . Exercise and fitness feel close to 'health', but this distinct division focuses on athletic performance, not the biopsychosocial study of illness (Division 38). (d) Division 98 A pure fabrication: no APA division numbered that high represents health psychology. The large, round-feeling number catches anyone without firm recall who gambles high; the real designation is Division 38. Q10 Which of the following historical perspectives gave rise to the evolutionary perspective? a behaviourism b Structuralism c Psychoanalysis d Functionalism ✓ Answer: (d) Functionalism William James and the Chicago school's functionalism The concept Why functionalism The evolutionary perspective grew directly out of functionalism 's central question: what mental processes are for . Functionalism Founded in spirit by William James and developed by the Chicago school (John Dewey, Angell), it arose in late-nineteenth-century America against structuralism. Where structuralism dissected the contents of consciousness, functionalism, shaped by Charles Darwin's evolution, asked how consciousness helps an organism adapt and survive, putting adaptation , purpose and survival value at the heart of explanation. Evolutionary psychology A modern perspective that crystallised in the late twentieth century (Tooby, Cosmides, Buss), it explains behaviours and mental traits as products of natural selection : how a tendency improved survival and reproduction in ancestral environments. The bridge is function and adaptive value, which it reframes as inherited, gene-based adaptations. The other schools Structuralism (Wilhelm Wundt, Edward Titchener) catalogued what consciousness contains ; psychoanalysis (Freud) used unconscious drives and childhood conflict; behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner) used stimulus-response links learned from the environment in a single lifetime. None put inherited adaptive function at the centre. Exam tip Functionalism, with its Darwinian adaptive emphasis, seeded the modern evolutionary perspective. Panwar key Functionalism paved the way for the understanding and interpreting human evolution and behaviour from a perspective that focused on the functionality aspect of thought and behaviour, the choices and the fears that people make and have. Why the other options are wrong (a) behaviourism Behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner) studied conditioned responses and banned inner states and adaptive 'purpose'. Biological-sounding and scientific, but its environment-driven learning opposes the evolutionary stress on inherited, naturally selected traits. (b) Structuralism Structuralism (Wilhelm Wundt, Edward Titchener) catalogued elemental sensations and ignored purpose, function and survival value: the opposite of adaptive thinking. It provoked functionalism as a reaction rather than seeding the evolutionary view. (c) Psychoanalysis Psychoanalysis (Freud) explored unconscious drives, childhood conflict and instinctual energy; 'instinct' makes it feel biological. But it explains behaviour by intrapsychic conflict and developmental history, not naturally selected adaptive function. Q11 Who is the most associated with the techniques of introspection? a Wundt b James c Watson d Wertheimer ✓ Answer: (a) Wundt Wilhelm Wundt, Leipzig laboratory (1879) The concept Why Wundt Wilhelm Wundt made introspection the signature method of the first scientific psychology, so he is the figure most identified with it. What it meant Not casual self-reflection but a trained, controlled, almost experimental procedure ( experimental self-observation ). Observers got a precise, repeatable stimulus and reported the immediate contents of consciousness (quality, intensity, duration) under standardised lab conditions, with trials repeated to check reliability. Background Wundt founded the first psychology lab at the University of Leipzig in 1879 , Germany, psychology's birth as a science, and built structuralism around this method, breaking experience into elements on analogy with chemistry. His student Edward Titchener carried it to America and refined it (the stimulus error ), but Wundt is its originator. The other founders William James (functionalism) was sceptical of rigid introspection; John Watson (behaviourism, 1913) rejected it as unscientific, demanding observable behaviour; Max Wertheimer (Gestalt) studied whole perceptual forms. Indeed, introspection's unreliability between labs gave behaviourism its opening. Exam tip Wundt, introspection, the Leipzig 1879 lab and structuralism form one cluster: when introspection is named, default to Wundt. Panwar key Wilhelm Wundt, the founder of modern psychology, a proponent of the structuralist perspective, used the technique of introspection to understand and interpret the human mind. He started the first psychology laboratory in Leipzig, Germany. Why the other options are wrong (b) James William James , same generation, used and discussed introspection, but founded functionalism and criticised Wilhelm Wundt and Edward Titchener's rigid, element-hunting version, preferring a naturalistic study of the 'stream of consciousness'. (c) Watson John Watson is linked to introspection for the opposite reason: his 1913 behaviourist manifesto rejected it as unscientific and unverifiable, demanding observable behaviour. Choosing him reverses the relationship; he is its great opponent. (d) Wertheimer Max Wertheimer founded Gestalt psychology , which studied whole perceptual organisations ('the whole is greater than the sum of its parts') and reacted against the atomistic, element-by-element approach introspection served. Q12 Which among the following branches of Psychology specifically studies behaviour in relation to genetic inheritance? a Evolutionary Psychology b Development Psychology c Health Psychology d Experimental Psychology ✓ Answer: (a) Evolutionary Psychology Darwin-based evolutionary psychology (Cosmides, Tooby, Buss) The concept Why this one Evolutionary psychology is the branch that specifically explains behaviour in relation to genetic inheritance and the action of natural selection. Roots It applies Charles Darwin's nineteenth-century theory of evolution to the mind, treating psychological traits as products of the selection pressures our ancestors faced. Conceptually it descends from functionalism (William James, Chicago school), which first asked what mental processes are for ; it grounded that in genetics, crystallising in the late twentieth century through Leda Cosmides, John Tooby and David Buss. Core idea Tendencies that improved survival and reproduction passed down through the genes , so present-day behaviour carries inherited adaptations from the ancestral 'environment of evolutionary adaptedness'. Fusing psychology with biology, it asks why an emotion, mate preference or fear exists by reconstructing the adaptive problem it solved: ancestral environment, then naturally selected genes, then an inherited tendency. The others Developmental psychology studies change across the lifespan, health psychology studies behaviour and illness, and experimental psychology names a method, not a content area. Exam tip When a question ties behaviour to genes, heredity or natural selection, the answer is evolutionary psychology: heredity and adaptation are its defining lens. Panwar key Evolutionary psychology is a scientific discipline that approaches human behaviour through a lens that incorporates the effects of evolution. It combines the science of psychology with the study of biology. It specifically studies behaviour in relation to genetic inheritance. Why the other options are wrong (b) Development Psychology Developmental psychology studies change across the lifespan, infancy to old age, and touches genes via nature-nurture. But it weighs nature and nurture over time; 'in relation to genetic inheritance' points to evolutionary psychology. (c) Health Psychology Health psychology studies how stress, behaviour and beliefs affect physical health and illness, using the biopsychosocial model. 'Biology' makes it feel gene-related, but it is about health behaviour and illness, not inherited traits. (d) Experimental Psychology Experimental psychology is defined by its method (controlled laboratory experiments), usable on memory, perception, learning and more, not by any subject matter. It sounds rigorous, but choosing it confuses a methodology with a content focus. Q13 Which among the following Schools of Thought used Introspection as a method of analysis? a Functionalism b behaviourism c Structuralism d Psychoanalysis ✓ Answer: (c) Structuralism Wundt and Titchener's structuralism The concept Why structuralism Structuralism is the school of thought built on introspection as its method of analysis. The school Founded by Wilhelm Wundt in his 1879 Leipzig laboratory, when psychology became an independent science, and systematised by his English-born student Edward Titchener at Cornell, it was the first formal school. Its chemistry-borrowed aim was to reduce mental life to basic elements (sensations, images, affective feelings), like a periodic table of the mind. Why introspection You cannot reach those elements by watching behaviour from outside; you must look inward in a disciplined way. Introspection gave a trained, systematic report of one's raw conscious contents under controlled conditions, describing bare qualities (intensity, duration, quality) rather than the object that caused them, so avoiding the stimulus error . The other schools Behaviourism (John B. Watson, around 1913) rejected introspection as unscientific; functionalism (James, John Dewey) used broader observation and applied work; psychoanalysis (Freud) used free association and dream analysis to reach the unconscious. Indeed, introspection's unreliability between labs discredited structuralism and opened the door to behaviourism. Exam tip Introspection is the structuralist tool: when a question pairs a school with introspection, choose structuralism. Panwar key It has often been claimed that Wilhelm Wundt, the father of experimental psychology and founder of structuralism, was the first to adopt introspection to experimental psychology. The focus of structuralism was on reducing mental processes down into their most basic elements. The structuralists used techniques such as introspection to analyse the inner processes of the human mind. Why the other options are wrong (a) Functionalism Functionalism (James, John Dewey), same era, also studied consciousness, but asked what it is for in adaptation and used varied methods (naturalistic observation, mental testing, applied work) rather than strict laboratory introspection. (b) behaviourism Behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner) is famous for rejecting introspection: Watson called it unscientific and studied observable behaviour alone. Choosing it reverses the relationship; it is introspection's chief opponent. (d) Psychoanalysis Psychoanalysis (Freud) used inward-looking clinical techniques, free association and dream analysis , to uncover the unconscious: a depth approach quite unlike controlled laboratory introspection on conscious sensory elements. Q14 Who among the following is credited with the book titled Principles of Psychology? a Wilhelm Wundt b William James c B.F. Skinner d None of the above ✓ Answer: (b) William James William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890) The concept Why James William James wrote the landmark two-volume The Principles of Psychology , published in 1890. Background Psychology was born in 1879 in Wundt's Leipzig lab and crossed the Atlantic within a decade; James, at Harvard , became its leading American voice. Trained first as a physician before turning to physiology, psychology and philosophy, he set up an early demonstration lab in the United States and inspired functionalism (what the mind is for ), a Darwinian counterweight to the structuralism of Wilhelm Wundt and Titchener. The book A synthesis of more than a decade of his thinking, it became the foundational American textbook of the discipline, shaping generations; it was so vast that he later issued a condensed version, nicknamed 'Jimmy'. Key ideas It introduced the stream of consciousness (experience as a continuous flowing whole, challenging the structuralists' sensory atoms), habit as the 'flywheel of society', the James-Lange theory of emotion (we feel afraid because we tremble, not the reverse) and a pioneering treatment of the self . These made James the bridge between the new laboratory science and a broader, practical, biologically minded psychology. Exam tip Lock the link: James, The Principles of Psychology , 1890. Take care not to credit Wundt, whose similar text was Principles of Physiological Psychology (1873-74); the English Principles of Psychology is James's. Panwar key The Principles of Psychology is an 1890 book about psychology by William James, an American philosopher and psychologist who trained to be a physician before going into psychology. Why the other options are wrong (a) Wilhelm Wundt Wilhelm Wundt wrote Principles of Physiological Psychology , an almost identical title the examiner exploits. But it has the extra word 'Physiological' and is structuralist/experimental; the plain Principles of Psychology (1890) is William James's. (c) B.F. Skinner B.F. Skinner belongs to a later era and behaviourism ; his works were on operant conditioning, such as The Behavior of Organisms (1938) and Science and Human Behavior . He wrote no Principles of Psychology . (d) None of the above Wrong because William James clearly and famously wrote The Principles of Psychology in 1890; with a correct named author among the options, the catch-all cannot be right. Q15 Who among the following was the first female president of the American Psychological Association (APA)? a Margaret Floy Washburn b Leta Stetter Hollingworth c Karen Horney d Mary Calkins ✓ Answer: (d) Mary Calkins Mary Whiton Calkins, first female APA president (1905) The concept Why Calkins Mary Whiton Calkins was the first woman to serve as president of the American Psychological Association , taking office as its 14th president in 1905. The era At the turn of the twentieth century American psychology, fresh from Wundt's Leipzig revolution, was institutionalising itself through the APA (founded 1892), university labs and doctoral programmes, almost entirely under men. Her training She studied under William James (the functionalist) and Hugo Munsterberg at Harvard and completed every doctoral requirement; James reportedly called her examination the finest he had seen. Yet Harvard refused her the degree because she was a woman. Her work Despite that, she invented the paired-associate technique for memory (items learned in pairs so one cues recall of the other, still used today), ran one of the first psychology labs at a women's college (Wellesley), and built a systematic psychology of the self anticipating later self and personality theory. Her 1905 election broke the gender barrier at the top of organised American psychology, a milestone comparable in symbolic weight to the field's founding firsts. Exam tip First female APA president equals Calkins, 1905. Do not confuse her with Margaret Floy Washburn : first woman psychology PhD (1894, under Edward Titchener), and in 1921 the second female APA president. Panwar key Mary Whiton Calkins was the 14th President of APA and the first woman to serve in that office. Why the other options are wrong (a) Margaret Floy Washburn The twin-trap: the first woman to earn a psychology PhD (1894), and an APA president, but only the second woman to be one, in 1921. The first female president was Calkins (1905). (b) Leta Stetter Hollingworth A genuine pioneer in the psychology of women (debunking 'variability' myths) and of gifted children, but never APA president. She rewards partial knowledge of early women in the field while still being wrong. (c) Karen Horney A famous neo-Freudian in the psychoanalytic tradition, challenging Freud on feminine psychology, working largely in Germany and then the USA as a clinician and theorist. She never served as APA president. Q16 Given below are two statements, first labelled assertion (A) and the other labelled as reason (R). Indicate your answer using the codes given below: Assertion (A): Fritz perls was a proponent of the gestalt perspective. Reason (R): Gestalt focuses on the wholeness of individuals' experiences in the present moment. a If (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation (A) b If (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation (A) c If (A) is true but (R) is false d If (R) is true but (A) is false ✓ Answer: (a) If (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation (A) Fritz Perls, with Laura Perls and Paul Goodman, Gestalt therapy The concept Why (a) Both statements are true, and the reason correctly explains the assertion: present-moment wholeness is exactly why Fritz Perls is classed as Gestalt rather than simply humanistic. The assertion Perls, together with Laura Perls and Paul Goodman, founded Gestalt therapy in the mid-twentieth century, so he was a proponent of the Gestalt perspective. Gestalt roots Gestalt psychology (Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Kohler) began as a theory of perception: 'the whole is more than the sum of its parts', with experience organised into meaningful wholes. Historically it arose in early-twentieth-century Germany as a reaction against the atomism of structuralism. Into therapy Perls transplanted this principle into therapy : present-moment awareness , the here-and-now, and integrating fragmented parts of the self, rather than excavating the past as psychoanalysis did. Trained in psychoanalysis before breaking from it, he carried wholeness into the humanistic 'third force' of the 1950s and 60s, alongside Carl Rogers and Abraham Maslow. Exam tip Gestalt therapy is often loosely grouped with humanistic-existential approaches, but wholeness-in-the-present marks it as Gestalt, so R is the criterion for A, not an incidental truth. When both are true and R states the principle justifying A, R is the correct explanation. Panwar key Fritz Perls is generally regarded as a proponent of the gestalt perspective and not humanistic because his Gestalt ideas focused on the wholeness of individuals' experiences in the present moment, ... Why the other options are wrong (b) If (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation (A) Keeps both true but denies the link, as if they were two unrelated facts. Present-moment wholeness is not a coincidental fact about Gestalt but the very reason Perls counts as Gestalt, not just humanistic. (c) If (A) is true but (R) is false R is not false: present-moment wholeness accurately describes the Gestalt approach. This baits anyone who doubts the 'here-and-now wholeness' characterisation, which is precisely correct. (d) If (R) is true but (A) is false A is firmly true: Fritz Perls founded Gestalt therapy. This tempts students who wrongly file Perls under humanistic or existential psychology, but his core identity is Gestalt. Q17 Herman von Helmholtz (1821-94): a He was a proponent of the just noticeable difference b He gave the trichromatic theory of colour vision c He proposed the concept of the unconscious d He gave the law of effect ✓ Answer: (b) He gave the trichromatic theory of colour vision Hermann von Helmholtz, Young-Helmholtz trichromatic theory The concept Why (b) Hermann von Helmholtz (1821 to 1894) is credited with developing the trichromatic theory of colour vision. How it works The eye must encode a vast range of colours from light. Building on Thomas Young (hence the Young-Helmholtz theory ), it holds that colour vision rests on three types of cones, each most sensitive to short, medium or long wavelengths (roughly blue, green, red); any colour arises from their relative activation, so three primaries can reproduce the visible spectrum. Ewald Hering's opponent-process theory later complemented it at a different stage of the visual system. Background He was a nineteenth-century physician-physicist of the physiological tradition, the parent discipline that, with philosophy, gave birth to scientific psychology in 1879. With Weber, Fechner and Muller he was a pre-Wundt precursor whose precise sensory measurement showed mental and neural processes could be quantified, making an experimental psychology conceivable. Nerve speed Beyond colour, he was the first to measure the speed of nerve conduction , showing it is finite and measurable rather than instantaneous. That opened the study of reaction time and mental chronometry, running from Wilhelm Wundt's lab to modern cognitive psychology. Exam tip Helmholtz equals the trichromatic (Young-Helmholtz) theory, three cone types. Do not attach the just-noticeable difference (Weber and Fechner) or the law of effect (Edward Thorndike) to him. Panwar key Herman von Helmholtz boasts a wide range of achievements. Indeed, you will still find his color theory of vision in psychology textbooks. His work paved the way for others to investigate the psychological significance of the time taken to react to a stimulus (reaction time or response latency). This approach remains important in modern psychology. Why the other options are wrong (a) He was a proponent of the just noticeable difference The jnd and Weber's law belong to Ernst Weber and Gustav Fechner , founders of psychophysics . All three were nineteenth-century German sensory scientists, so contributions get swapped; Helmholtz's signature is colour vision and nerve speed. (c) He proposed the concept of the unconscious The unconscious is Sigmund Freud's construct (with roots in Schopenhauer and Hartmann). Helmholtz did write about 'unconscious inference' in perception, but that narrow idea is not the Freudian dynamic unconscious meant here. (d) He gave the law of effect Edward Thorndike 's law from his puzzle-box experiments: satisfying consequences strengthen responses. A cornerstone of learning theory from another era and tradition (American connectionism/behaviourism), unrelated to Helmholtz's colour vision. Q18 Which one of the following branches of philosophy of science deals with the question of existence? a Post-positivism b Structuralism c Ontology d Scientific realism ✓ Answer: (c) Ontology Ontology, the study of being The concept Why ontology Among the branches of the philosophy of science, ontology is the one that deals with the question of existence. What it is The branch of metaphysics concerned with what exists, the nature of being , and the kinds and structures of entities that make up reality. From the Greek ontos (being) and logos (study), it asks what sorts of things exist, how they are categorised and what it means to be real. Its sister branch Epistemology (from episteme , knowledge) asks instead how we can know reality and what counts as valid knowledge. In research methodology the two found every paradigm and shape method choice: your ontological stance concerns the reality studied (one objective reality, the realist view, or a socially constructed one, the relativist view); your epistemological stance, how you can know it. Why it matters The pairing underlies the split in the human sciences between positivist research (objective reality, measured experimentally) and interpretivist research (constructed meaning, understood qualitatively), running through psychology's century-long debate about imitating the natural sciences. Exam tip Post-positivism and scientific realism are positions within the philosophy of science (largely epistemological or metaphysical stances), and structuralism is a school of thought. Existence and being equal ontology; knowing equals epistemology. Panwar key Ontology, as a branch of philosophy, is the science of what is, of the kinds and structures of objects. In simple terms, ontology seeks the classification and explanation of entities. Ontology concerns claims about the nature of being and existence. Why the other options are wrong (a) Post-positivism The successor to positivism: it accepts an external reality but holds our knowledge of it is always fallible and theory-laden. That is an epistemological stance (how we know), not a branch studying what exists. (b) Structuralism In psychology, Wilhelm Wundt and Edward Titchener's school analysing the structure of consciousness; in linguistics/anthropology, a separate movement. Either way a school or method, not a branch about being: a familiar-word trap. (d) Scientific realism The position that successful scientific theories truly describe a mind-independent world, unobservables included. It touches existence, a clever trap, but it is a stance on whether theories track reality, not the branch studying being. Q19 Who is often referred to as the "Founder of Modern Psychology in India"? a Girindra Shekhar Bose b Narendra Nath Sen Gupta c Amitosh Mukherjee d M.V. Gopalswamy ✓ Answer: (b) Narendra Nath Sen Gupta Narendra Nath Sen Gupta, University of Calcutta (1916) The concept Why Sen Gupta Narendra Nath Sen Gupta is regarded as the founder of modern psychology in India, having established the country's first independent psychology department. Before him Scientific psychology was born in Wundt's Leipzig lab in 1879 and spread out from Germany. In India the mind was treated within philosophy and classical speculative traditions (Vedanta, Samkhya, Yoga), with no Western-style experimental discipline. What he did Trained at Harvard (under figures such as Hugo Munsterberg) in the experimental lab approach, he founded India's first independent department of psychology and first psychology lab at the University of Calcutta in 1916 , the Calcutta milieu that would soon host India's psychoanalytic movement. That shift from armchair philosophy to laboratory-based experimental study along Western lines is what 'modern' means in his title. Later work He co-authored an early Indian psychology textbook with Radhakamal Mukerjee and helped train and work alongside the next generation, including the psychoanalyst Girindra Shekhar Bose. Exam tip Lock in Sen Gupta, first department and lab, University of Calcutta, 1916. Take care not to credit M.V. Gopalswamy , who founded the Mysore department and did important applied and experimental work, but later. Panwar key Narendra Nath Sen Gupta is regarded as the founder of modern psychology in India. He established the first independent department of psychology in India at the University of Calcutta in 1916. Why the other options are wrong (a) Girindra Shekhar Bose The father of psychoanalysis in India , founder of the Indian Psychoanalytic Society and a noted correspondent of Sigmund Freud: foundational, but in a different stream. The first experimental department is Sen Gupta's distinction. (c) Amitosh Mukherjee Not a recognised founder of modern Indian psychology; a plausible Bengali-sounding name for those who know the discipline began in Calcutta. There is no documented 'founder' claim attached to it, unlike Sen Gupta's record. (d) M.V. Gopalswamy A real pioneer who founded the psychology department at the University of Mysore and advanced applied and experimental psychology in India. But it came after Calcutta's 1916 department, so the founder title is Sen Gupta's. Psychodynamic Q20 Select the incorrect pair: a Jung: Extroversion-Introversion b Kohlberg: Formal operations c Adler: Ruling Dominant Type d Ellis: Rational Emotive Therapy ✓ Answer: (b) Kohlberg: Formal operations Jean Piaget's formal operations, not Kohlberg's moral stages The concept Why (b) Formal operations belongs to Jean Piaget , not Lawrence Kohlberg , whose name is tied to moral development, so this is the incorrect pair. Piaget's stages In the cognitive-developmental tradition (outside the psychodynamic schools, yet tested beside them), Piaget, the Swiss genetic epistemologist , mapped four invariant cognitive stages: sensorimotor (0-2), preoperational (2-7), concrete operational (7-11) and formal operational (roughly 11+), where abstract, hypothetical, propositional reasoning emerges. Kohlberg's stages At Harvard in the 1950s-70s, Kohlberg applied Piaget's stage logic to moral reasoning : three levels, each split into two stages: preconventional (obedience, self-interest), conventional (approval, law-and-order) and postconventional (social contract, universal ethical principles). Why they get swapped Kohlberg was Piaget's heir; both used hierarchical, sequence-fixed stages driven by qualitative reorganization of thought, so a swap almost looks right. But formal operations is how we think abstractly; Kohlberg's stages are how we judge right and wrong . Exam tip Historically the options mix schools: Carl Jung (analytical psychology) and Alfred Adler (individual psychology) split off from Sigmund Freud, and Albert Ellis founded a cognitive-behavioural therapy in the 1950s; only the Kohlberg-Piaget mismatch is broken. Any pairing that gives Kohlberg a Piagetian term is the incorrect pair. Panwar key Kohlberg is associated with Moral Development theory, whereas "Formal Operations" is a concept developed by Jean Piaget. Why the other options are not the answer (a) Jung: Extroversion-Introversion True: Carl Jung , founder of analytical psychology and the most famous Freud defector, coined the introversion-extroversion attitude dimension in Psychological Types (1921). A correct pair cannot be the answer. (c) Adler: Ruling Dominant Type True: Alfred Adler , founder of Individual Psychology, described a fourfold typology: the Ruling/Dominant type plus the getting, avoiding and socially useful types. It is less rehearsed than Sigmund Freud's structures, but correct. (d) Ellis: Rational Emotive Therapy True: Albert Ellis founded Rational Emotive Therapy (later REBT) in the 1950s, the first major cognitive therapy. It lures students who confuse Ellis with Aaron Beck, but the link is accurate. Q21 Who published the mechanism of hysteria in 1893? a Freud and Charcot b Freud and Breuer c Freud and Adler d Freud and Jung ✓ Answer: (b) Freud and Breuer Sigmund Freud and Josef Breuer, Preliminary Communication (1893) The concept Why (b) The 1893 paper on the mechanism of hysteria was the joint work of Sigmund Freud and the senior Viennese physician Josef Breuer , issued as their Preliminary Communication and expanded in 1895 into Studies on Hysteria . Background This is the prehistory of psychoanalysis, the moment before Freud's mature system existed, when he was still a neurologist working with an older mentor. Hysteria meant physical symptoms (paralysis, blindness, mutism, fits) with no organic cause; Breuer and Freud argued these were the bodily conversion of repressed emotional trauma . The Anna O. case Breuer's patient Anna O. (Bertha Pappenheim) found her symptoms eased when she traced each one back to the forgotten memory that triggered it; she called this the talking cure or chimney-sweeping, and Breuer labelled it catharsis . The seed claim: 'hysterics suffer mainly from reminiscences', meaning blocked affect, denied normal discharge, converts into symptoms. Where it leads The collaboration supplied the raw ideas (the unconscious, repression, cure through verbal recall) that Freud built into psychoanalysis proper before Breuer, uneasy with the sexual emphasis, fell away. Charcot comes before (Freud's 1885-86 Paris training in hypnosis); the great defectors Alfred Adler and Jung come over a decade after , breaking from a theory that did not yet exist in 1893. Exam tip The 1893 hysteria work and the Anna O. case belong to Breuer , the bridge figure between hypnosis-era medicine and psychoanalysis. Panwar key In 1893, Sigmund Freud, along with Viennese physician Joseph Breuer, published their studies on hysteria. Why the other options are wrong (a) Freud and Charcot Jean-Martin Charcot , the great Parisian neurologist at the Salpetriere, taught Freud about hysteria and hypnotic suggestion in 1885-86. He came before the Vienna work and did not co-author the 1893 paper; that was Josef Breuer. (c) Freud and Adler Alfred Adler joined Freud's Wednesday circle only around 1902 and broke away in 1911 to found Individual Psychology. He had no part in the 1890s hysteria studies, which predate his arrival by roughly a decade. (d) Freud and Jung Carl Jung began corresponding with Freud only in 1906 and broke from him by 1913. The most celebrated collaborator-turned-defector, he was a teenager in 1893 and played no part in the hysteria research with Breuer.
