Q22 Reports on sexual behaviour of men was published by a Sigmund Freud b Alfred Kinsey c Anna Freud d Karen Horney ✓ Answer: (b) Alfred Kinsey Alfred Kinsey, the Kinsey Reports (1948, 1953) The concept Why (b) The landmark reports on human sexual behaviour were empirical survey works, not theory, produced by Alfred Kinsey and his team at Indiana University. Background They sit outside the psychodynamic tradition, in mid-twentieth-century empirical sexology , a deliberate break from the armchair, moralistic and psychoanalytic treatment of sex. Kinsey was a zoologist (originally a gall-wasp taxonomist) who brought large-scale, quantitative biological data-collection to a taboo subject. The two volumes Sexual Behaviour in the Human Male (1948) and Sexual Behaviour in the Human Female (1953) rest on thousands of confidential face-to-face interviews. Co-authors were Wardell Pomeroy , Clyde Martin and (female volume) Paul Gebhard ; the publisher was W.B. Saunders. Kinsey scale The Kinsey scale , a 0-to-6 continuum from exclusively heterosexual to exclusively homosexual, reframed orientation as a spectrum rather than two fixed boxes. The data showed behaviours assumed rare were widespread, making the reports scandalous and foundational and helping launch modern sex research, later continued by William Masters and Virginia Johnson. Exam tip Theory versus measurement: Sigmund Freud theorized about sexuality from the clinic (libido, psychosexual stages); Kinsey measured it through surveys. Who reported on (counted, surveyed) sexual behaviour is Kinsey, the empiricist, not any psychoanalyst. Panwar key The Kinsey Reports are two scholarly books on human sexual behaviour, Sexual Behaviour in the Human Male (1948) and Sexual Behaviour in the Human Female (1953), written by Alfred Kinsey, Wardell Pomeroy, Clyde Martin, and (for Sexual Behaviour in the Human Female) Paul Gebhard and published by W.B. Saunders. Why the other options are wrong (a) Sigmund Freud The psychoanalyst who made sexuality central (libido, psychosexual stages), but he theorized from individual clinical cases and never produced statistical, interview-based survey reports. 'Reports' signals empirical data: Alfred Kinsey's domain. (c) Anna Freud Sigmund's daughter, who pioneered child psychoanalysis and systematized the ego defence mechanisms . The famous surname tempts, but her work was defences and child analysis, not large-scale sexual-behaviour surveys. (d) Karen Horney A neo-Freudian known for basic anxiety and for challenging Freud on feminine psychology (penis envy versus womb envy). She wrote about sex-linked psychology, but produced theory, not survey reports of sexual behaviour. Q23 Who is the father of Psychoanalysis? a Bernheim b Sigmund Freud c Adler d Jung ✓ Answer: (b) Sigmund Freud Sigmund Freud, founder of psychoanalysis The concept Why (b) Sigmund Freud is universally credited as founder of psychoanalysis , the theory and treatment method that defines the first force of depth psychology. The model Psychoanalysis is both a model of the mind and a therapy . As a model, the mind is largely unconscious , behaviour is driven by instinctual urges (sexual and aggressive), and personality is structured into id, ego and superego . The therapy It brings repressed unconscious conflicts into awareness through free association , dream interpretation (dreams as the 'royal road to the unconscious') and analysis of resistance and transference. Freud, an Austrian neurologist in Vienna, built this from his 1890s clinical work on hysteria and set out the dream theory in The Interpretation of Dreams (1900). Historically He is the trunk of the psychodynamic tree: early loyalists, then the great defectors Alfred Adler (Individual Psychology, broke away 1911) and Carl Jung (Analytical Psychology, broke away ~1913), then the neo-Freudians (Karen Horney, Erich Fromm, Harry Stack Sullivan), ego psychologists and object-relations theorists. Every one of those schools is a reaction to Freud, which is why he, not his successors, is 'the father'. Exam tip Bernheim was a hypnosis-and-suggestion figure who influenced Freud but founded nothing of the sort; Adler and Jung each founded a rival school under a different name. The single originator of psychoanalysis, the parent theory they all defined themselves against, is Freud. Panwar key Sigmund Freud is best known as the creator of the therapeutic technique known as psychoanalysis. The Austrian-born psychiatrist greatly contributed to the understanding of human psychology in areas such as the unconscious mind, sexuality, and dream interpretation. He is regarded as the father of psychoanalysis. Why the other options are wrong (a) Bernheim Hippolyte Bernheim of the Nancy school championed hypnotic suggestion and influenced the young Freud's thinking. He worked in the hypnosis tradition and never created psychoanalysis; he is upstream of it, not its author. (c) Adler An early member of Freud's circle who broke away in 1911 to found Individual Psychology (social urges, inferiority). Founding a rival school is not founding psychoanalysis, which was Freud's. (d) Jung Once Freud's anointed heir, he split off around 1913 to found Analytical Psychology (collective unconscious, archetypes). A distinct school; the parent theory of psychoanalysis belongs to Freud alone. Q24 Freud published The Interpretation of Dreams in: a 1900 b 1898 c 1902 d 1904 ✓ Answer: (a) 1900 Sigmund Freud, Die Traumdeutung (dated 1900) The concept Why (a) 1900 is the official publication date on Freud's The Interpretation of Dreams ( Die Traumdeutung ). The wrinkle The book physically appeared in early November 1899 , but the Leipzig-Vienna publisher Franz Deuticke post-dated it to 1900 so it would read as heralding the new century. The canonical exam answer is 1900, even though Panwar notes the 4 November 1899 printing. What it says The founding text of the mature psychoanalytic theory of the unconscious, where Sigmund Freud moved from the hysteria collaboration with Breuer into a system of his own. Core claim: dreams are wish-fulfilments and the 'royal road to the unconscious'. It let him study the unconscious in healthy people, not only patients, and made dream analysis a central pillar of technique. Dream-work Manifest content (the dream as consciously remembered) and latent content (the hidden, often forbidden wish) are linked by the dream-work : condensation , displacement and symbolization turn the unacceptable wish into an acceptable image. This is early, pre-structural Freud; the id-ego-superego scheme came later, in 1923. Exam tip The book is dated 1900 and its thesis is that dreams are disguised wish-fulfilments. Remembering the dawn-of-the-century post-dating protects you against the 1898 and even 1899 distractors. Panwar key Sigmund Freud published The Interpretation of Dreams on November 4th, 1899. The publication date is dated 1900. Why the other options are wrong (b) 1898 Predates the book: in 1898 Freud was still doing the self-analysis and dream-collection that fed it. The writing began in the late 1890s, but the published, dated work is 1900. (c) 1902 Two years too late. 1902 is when Freud gained his professorship and the Wednesday Psychological Society began forming, real milestones, but not the dream book's date. (d) 1904 Four years too late, nearer The Psychopathology of Everyday Life (1901) or later works. A pure distance distractor, plausible only with no anchor for the turn-of-the-century date. Q25 Children with organic defects and those born into minority groups are likely to develop ____. a Superiority complex b Inferiority complex c Compensation d Fictional goals ✓ Answer: (b) Inferiority complex Alfred Adler, Individual Psychology The concept Why (b) In Alfred Adler's Individual Psychology, real disadvantages such as organic defects (bodily weakness or 'organ inferiority') or minority-group marginalization can intensify ordinary inferiority feelings into a chronic, disabling complex. Background Adler was the first major defector from Sigmund Freud, breaking away in 1911 to replace the sexual drive with a social, goal-directed psychology. Everyone begins life small, weak and dependent, giving a universal feeling of inferiority that in the healthy case drives striving for superiority (or perfection), the push toward mastery and competence. The complex When the feeling becomes overwhelming, it hardens into an inferiority complex , a fixed sense of inadequacy that blocks functioning instead of fuelling it. Adler's three childhood risk roots are organ inferiority / physical defect , pampering and neglect ; marginalized or minority children fall under the neglected, disadvantaged category because their handicap can feel insurmountable. Compensation The linked idea is compensation and overcompensation , the attempt to offset the weakness, which can mask itself as a superiority complex. Exam tip A normal inferiority feeling is universal and motivating; an inferiority complex is the pathological, stuck version. Defect and minority disadvantage point to that complex, not to healthy striving or its overcompensated superiority mask. Panwar key Adler in his school of Individual Psychology explains the concept of overcompensation that can lead to the development of an inferiority complex. This is a lack of self-esteem where the person is unable to rectify his feelings of inferiority. According to Adler, the hallmark of an inferiority complex is that persons are always striving to find a situation in which they excel. This drive is due to their overwhelming feelings of inferiority. There are two components of these feelings of inferiority: primary and secondary. Why the other options are wrong (a) Superiority complex Adler's overcompensated mask over deep inferiority, a secondary defence layered on top and causally downstream. What such children 'develop' from their handicap is the inferiority complex itself. (c) Compensation Adler's healthy striving mechanism , the effort to offset a weakness through growth or skill. It names the corrective response, not the disabling deficit state the disadvantage produces. (d) Fictional goals Adler's fictional finalism: people are pulled forward by an imagined future ideal that guides the style of life. Real Adlerian theory, but about teleological motivation, not how defect or minority status breeds inadequacy. Q26 Jung disagreed with Freud on the nature of the unconscious, arguing that it exists on two levels ____ and ____. a Collective and individual b Anima and animus c Extroversion and introversion d Intuitive and perceptive ✓ Answer: (a) Collective and individual Carl Jung, Analytical Psychology The concept Why (a) Carl Jung split the unconscious into a personal (individual) unconscious and a deeper collective unconscious ; that second layer is the point on which he broke from Sigmund Freud. Freud vs Jung Freud's unconscious is wholly personal : repressed memories and forbidden wishes acquired in one's own lifetime. Jung, Freud's designated heir until their 1913 split that birthed Analytical Psychology , kept that layer as the personal unconscious , holding forgotten and suppressed experiences unique to the person. The collective layer Beneath it lies the collective unconscious , inherited and shared by all humanity, a psychic deposit of the species' evolutionary and ancestral history. Its contents are the archetypes , universal predisposing patterns and images (the shadow, the anima/animus, the wise old man, the great mother) that recur across myths, religions and dreams. Background Jung's reading of comparative religion, Eastern philosophy (Buddhism, Hinduism) and alchemy shaped this view, which is why Freud, the rationalist, rejected it as mystical. All four options are real Jungian terms, so you must tell the levels from the contents or dimensions . Exam tip The personal/individual unconscious is yours alone and acquired in your lifetime; the collective unconscious is universal and inherited. Two levels of the unconscious in Jung means personal/individual and collective. Panwar key Jung, like Freud, also divided the human psyche into three parts. But in Jung's view the unconscious was divided into the personal unconscious and the collective unconscious. The personal unconscious includes memories (both recalled and suppressed) and the collective unconscious holds our experiences as a species or knowledge that we are born with. Jung's take on the human psyche was inspired by his studies into Eastern philosophy and religion such as Buddhism and Hinduism. Why the other options are wrong (b) Anima and animus Archetypes : the inner feminine within a man and the inner masculine within a woman, which reside inside the collective unconscious. They are contents of the deep layer, not its two structural levels . (c) Extroversion and introversion Jung's two attitude types from Psychological Types (1921), describing the direction of psychic energy. A conscious personality dimension, not divisions of the unconscious. (d) Intuitive and perceptive Echo Jung's psychological functions (thinking, feeling, sensation, intuition) and the later MBTI-style preferences built on him. They describe modes of orienting to the world, not the layered structure of the unconscious. Q27 In a psychoanalytic practice, where the patient relaxes on a couch and freely tells whatever comes into his/her mind is called a Dreaming b Narration c Free association d Story telling ✓ Answer: (c) Free association Freud, classical psychoanalytic technique The concept Why (c) Free association is Freud's defining technique: the patient reclines and reports whatever enters the mind, uncensored. The goal Psychoanalysis aims to surface repressed material from the unconscious . Direct questioning fails because the patient's defences guard the painful content; free association sidesteps them by having the patient voice every thought, image and feeling as it arises, however trivial, embarrassing, illogical or irrelevant. Why it works It rests on psychic determinism : mental life is never random, so a chain of seemingly stray associations is steered by unconscious conflicts, and following it leads back to the repressed root. Historically Freud developed free association to replace hypnosis , the cathartic-hypnotic method he took from Charcot in Paris and his colleague Josef Breuer in Vienna; hypnosis was unreliable and made patients parrot the analyst's suggestions, while free association let patients 'speak for themselves'. Points where the patient hesitates, blanks, blushes or changes subject signal resistance , and associations often expose transference . Exam tip Couch plus an uncensored stream of thought equals free association, the core royal route (alongside dream interpretation) into the unconscious in classical psychoanalysis. Panwar key Free association is the expression of the content of consciousness without censorship as an aid in gaining access to unconscious processes. This technique is used in psychoanalysis (and also in psychodynamic theory) which was originally devised by Sigmund Freud out of the hypnotic method of his mentor and colleague, Josef Breuer. Freud described it as a phenomenon in which the patients spoke for themselves, rather than repeating the ideas of the analyst. Why the other options are wrong (a) Dreaming Links to dream interpretation , the other great psychoanalytic route to the unconscious. But dreaming is a sleeping mental event analysed afterward, not the waking, on-the-couch technique of speaking every thought aloud. (b) Narration Not a defined psychoanalytic technique, just an everyday word for telling an account. Free association is precisely un structured and uncensored, the opposite of a coherent narrative. (d) Story telling Not the technical term either: a story is organized, sequenced and edited, whereas free association demands a deliberately disorganized, unedited flow. That absence of structure is what lets repressed links surface. Q28 Karen Horney's conception of feelings of pervasive loneliness and helplessness that are the foundation of neurosis is called a Innate anxiety b Existential anxiety c Basic anxiety d Neurotic anxiety ✓ Answer: (c) Basic anxiety Karen Horney, neo-Freudian theory of neurosis The concept Why (c) Karen Horney used exactly the phrase basic anxiety for the pervasive loneliness and helplessness she placed at the foundation of neurosis. Who she was A leading neo-Freudian , trained in psychoanalysis but rejecting Sigmund Freud's biological, libido-and-instinct account in favour of social and relational causes. She also challenged Freud's view of feminine psychology, replacing 'penis envy' with male 'womb envy'. Where it comes from Basic anxiety arises in childhood when the parent-child environment goes wrong: domination, indifference, erratic or hostile behaviour, lack of respect for the child's individual needs, or no genuine warmth and guidance. The child feels small, isolated and helpless in a potentially hostile world, and this insecure foundation later breeds neurosis . Neurotic trends To cope, the person adopts rigid strategies, the three neurotic trends : moving toward people (compliance, self-effacement, seeking approval), against people (aggression, control, need to dominate) or away from people (detachment, withdrawal). The healthy person uses all three flexibly; the neurotic clings compulsively to one. Exam tip 'Basic anxiety' is Horney's specific named concept , learned from disturbed early relationships, distinct from Freud's drive-based 'neurotic anxiety' and the philosophers' 'existential anxiety'. Pervasive childhood helplessness as the origin of neurosis, tied to Horney, means basic anxiety. Panwar key Psychoanalytic theorist Karen Horney developed one of the best-known theories of neurosis. She believed that neurosis resulted from basic anxiety caused by interpersonal relationships. According to Horney, basic anxiety (and therefore neurosis) could result from a variety of situations including direct or indirect domination, indifference, erratic behaviour, lack of respect for the child's individual needs, and lack of real guidance. Why the other options are wrong (a) Innate anxiety Not a Horney term; it contradicts her thesis. Karen Horney insisted basic anxiety is learned from childhood interpersonal experience, not biologically inborn; 'innate' is exactly what she argued against. (b) Existential anxiety A concept from existential and humanistic psychology (Rollo May, Irvin Yalom, drawing on Kierkegaard and Heidegger): dread of meaninglessness, freedom and death. A different school, not Horney's foundation-of-neurosis term. (d) Neurotic anxiety Sigmund Freud's term: the ego's fear that the id's impulses will break through and overwhelm it. The strongest decoy, but drive-based and intrapsychic, not Horney's relationally caused basic anxiety. Q29 The Ego is sometimes described as the ____ because it directs energies supplied by the Id. a Executive b Superordinate c Subordinate d Congruence ✓ Answer: (a) Executive Sigmund Freud, structural model (1923) The concept Why (a) Freud described the ego as the executive of personality, the agency that directs and manages the psychic energy supplied by the id. The structural model Freud's 1923 structural model is the mature phase of his theory, succeeding the topographical (conscious/unconscious) scheme. The id is the primitive reservoir of instinctual energy demanding immediate gratification on the pleasure principle; the superego is the internalized moral code, conscience plus ego-ideal. The ego's job The ego sits between them, faces reality and runs on the reality principle through secondary process thinking: it satisfies the id only in realistic, safe, socially acceptable ways while honouring the superego. Weighing costs and benefits, delaying gratification, testing reality and deciding when and how desires are discharged is an executive function , like a manager allocating resources it does not generate. The key mechanism The ego has no libido of its own ; it borrows energy from the id and channels it, and directing energy it did not produce earns the 'executive' label. Historically this mediator-ego launched the ego psychology school (Anna Freud, Heinz Hartmann, Erik Erikson), which expanded its autonomous, adaptive functions. Exam tip The id supplies the drive, the superego supplies the rules, and the ego executes , balancing both against the constraints of reality. Panwar key The ego, according to Freud, operates based on the reality principle, which strives to satisfy the id's desires in realistic and socially appropriate ways. The reality principle weighs the costs and benefits of an action before deciding to act upon or abandon impulses, so as it tries to balance the actions of Id and superego, it performs the executive function. Why the other options are wrong (b) Superordinate Implies the ego ranks above id and superego. Sigmund Freud's ego does not dominate; it serves and balances three masters (id, superego, reality), often anxiously. 'Executive' means managing, not outranking. (c) Subordinate Wrongly demotes the ego to a servile role. It does borrow its energy from the id, but functionally it is the managing, directing structure, so this inverts its actual status. (d) Congruence A Rogerian / humanistic term for the match between self-concept and lived experience, from a completely different school. It has no Freudian meaning for the ego. Q30 According to Sigmund Freud, the id operates on a Pleasure principle b Reality principle c Unconscious mind d Conscious mind ✓ Answer: (a) Pleasure principle Sigmund Freud, the id and the pleasure principle The concept Why (a) Freud held that the id operates entirely on the pleasure principle . What the id is The oldest, most primitive of the three structures in Freud's structural model, present from birth and wholly unconscious . It houses the instinctual drives (Eros and, later, Thanatos) and is the source of all psychic energy, the libido . How it works The pleasure principle demands every wishful impulse be satisfied immediately , regardless of consequence, logic, morality or external reality; getting it feels like pleasure, being blocked like rising tension or 'unpleasure' to be discharged at once. The id uses primary process thinking (primitive, illogical, irrational, timeless, fantasy-oriented) and can even hallucinate the desired object (wish-fulfilment) to relieve tension. Example and context The newborn who cries the instant it is hungry is pure id on the pleasure principle, with no capacity to wait. Placing it in the psychodynamic arc, the id-ego-superego triad belongs to Freud's 1923 structural revision and seeds the later ego-psychology tradition. Exam tip The id runs on the pleasure principle and primary process; the ego runs on the reality principle and secondary process, delaying gratification to fit the real world. Panwar key The id operates on the pleasure principle (Freud, 1920) which is the idea that every wishful impulse should be satisfied immediately regardless of the consequences. When the id achieves its demands, we experience pleasure; when it is denied we experience 'unpleasure' or tension. The id engages in primary process thinking, which is primitive, illogical, irrational, and fantasy oriented. Why the other options are wrong (b) Reality principle Governs the ego , the realistic, delaying, consequence-weighing agency, not the id. The strongest decoy as the matched opposite term, but assigning it to the id reverses Sigmund Freud's scheme. (c) Unconscious mind A region or level of the psyche in the topographical model, not a 'principle'. The id genuinely is entirely unconscious, but a location is not the principle it runs on. (d) Conscious mind Also a level of awareness, not an operating principle, and doubly wrong: the id has no conscious component. It confuses 'where the id lives' with 'how the id works'. Q31 According to Sigmund Freud, wars and violence are evidence of a Life instinct b Libido c Death instinct d None of these ✓ Answer: (c) Death instinct Sigmund Freud, Thanatos in Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920) The concept Why (c) Freud interpreted wars and violence as expressions of the death instinct . Dual instincts This is Freud's late, post-First-World-War dual-instinct theory, a darkening of psychoanalysis after he witnessed mass slaughter. Against the earlier sex-centred picture, Eros , the life instinct, gathers the sexual and self-preservative urges, is fuelled by libido , and binds, builds and sustains life. Thanatos Opposed to it stands Thanatos , the death instinct, introduced in Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920): 'the goal of all life is death', a pull back toward an earlier, inorganic, tensionless state. Since the organism cannot simply annihilate itself, it is typically turned outward as aggression, cruelty, war and violence; turned inward , it can surface as self-harm, depression, masochism or suicide. Reception This pessimistic view, deepened in Civilization and Its Discontents (1930) and his exchange with Einstein on 'Why War?', was controversial and largely rejected by the neo-Freudians and even by Freud's own daughter's ego-psychology successors. Exam tip Libido and the life instinct concern preservation, bonding and pleasure; aggression, destruction and war trace to the death instinct ( Thanatos ). 'Wars and violence' is the textbook signal for it, not Eros or libido. Panwar key The concept of the death instinct was initially described in Beyond the Pleasure Principle, in which Freud proposed that 'the goal of all life is death.' Freud believed that people typically channel their death instincts outwards. Aggression, for example, arises from the death instinct. Sometimes these instincts towards destruction can be directed inwards, however, which can result in self-harm or suicide. Why the other options are wrong (a) Life instinct Eros drives survival, sexuality, bonding and creation, the constructive opposite of the forces behind war. The natural counterpart in the dual-instinct pair, but the wrong pole: Eros builds and unites, war expresses Thanatos. (b) Libido The energy of Eros , the sexual/life-instinct drive, and Sigmund Freud's most famous energetic term. It fuels the life instinct, not aggression; destructiveness is the work of the death instinct. (d) None of these Wrong because Freud explicitly attributed aggression and war to the death instinct in Beyond the Pleasure Principle and later works. He plainly committed to a clear answer. Q32 Errors in speech that reflect unconscious thoughts or impulses is a Defense Mechanism b Freudian slips c Cognitive Distortion d Speech disorder ✓ Answer: (b) Freudian slips Sigmund Freud, The Psychopathology of Everyday Life (1901) The concept Why (b) Errors of speech that betray unconscious thoughts are exactly what a Freudian slip is. What it is Sigmund Freud's own technical term is parapraxis (German Fehlleistung ): a slip of the tongue, pen or memory that is never random but always meaningful. It rests on psychic determinism : mental life is fully caused, so even a trivial verbal mistake comes from a repressed wish, impulse or thought leaking past the ego's censorship into everyday behaviour. Examples A person who intends one word but substitutes another tied to what they secretly feel, or who 'forgets' a name linked to an uncomfortable association, has exposed unconscious content. Background In The Psychopathology of Everyday Life (1901) Freud treated slips, lapses, bungled actions and forgetting as windows into the unconscious, alongside dreams and jokes as everyday counterparts of the clinical symptom. Placing it historically, this is early-Freud material, the same turn-of-the-century project as the dream book, showing the unconscious works in normal people, not only patients. Exam tip A defence mechanism is an unconscious anxiety-management strategy and a cognitive distortion is a faulty thinking pattern from a rival (cognitive) school; neither is specifically a speech error revealing the unconscious. 'Errors in speech reflecting unconscious impulses' means the Freudian slip. Panwar key Freudian slips are the slipping of unconscious thoughts and impulses in regular speech. Defense mechanism is unconscious, cognitive distortion is asynchronicity in thoughts and behaviour. Why the other options are wrong (a) Defense Mechanism An unconscious ego strategy that wards off anxiety (repression, projection, denial and so on). It is unconscious, but it is a general protective manoeuvre, not specifically a slip of the tongue, which is the parapraxis. (c) Cognitive Distortion Biased thinking patterns (catastrophizing, all-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralization) from the cognitive therapy of Aaron Beck and Albert Ellis , a different tradition. Conscious-level reasoning errors, not unconscious verbal leaks. (d) Speech disorder Stuttering, articulation or fluency impairment: an organic, neurological or developmental condition. A literal-minded decoy; such errors have a physical or developmental cause, not an unconscious psychological one. Q33 According to Jung, the archetype representing the feminine side of males is called: a Animus b Shadow c Persona d Anima ✓ Answer: (d) Anima Carl Jung, Analytical Psychology The concept Why (d) In Carl Jung's analytical psychology the anima is the unconscious feminine archetype carried within a man. Archetypes Archetypes are universal, inherited patterns in the collective unconscious , the deep stratum shared across humanity that was Jung's great divergence from Sigmund Freud. Among them is a contrasexual pair: every man holds an inner feminine image, the anima, and every woman an inner masculine image, the animus. What the anima does It carries a man's unconscious feminine qualities (feeling, relatedness, receptivity, mood, eros) and shapes how he relates to women, often by projection onto a partner, and to his own emotional life. Integrating it is essential to individuation , uniting conscious and unconscious into a balanced, whole Self; a man who denies his anima stays one-sided, prey to moods he cannot own. Related archetypes The shadow is the repressed, instinctual dark side (loosely like Freud's id); the persona is the social mask presented to meet external demands. Placing Jung historically, he was Freud's heir until their 1913 break founded Analytical Psychology, trading Freud's sexual drive for a symbolic, spiritual, lifelong model of growth. Exam tip Anima is the feminine-within-the-male; animus is the masculine-within-the-female. The feminine side of a male is the anima, not the animus. Panwar key Anima is the female side of the male. Animus is the male side of the female, shadow is nearly analogous to Freud's Id and Persona is the facade that a person assumes to balance between the internal needs and the external demands. Why the other options are wrong (a) Animus The exact reverse archetype: the unconscious masculine image within a woman . The strongest decoy, since anima and animus are near-twins differing only by direction; the feminine side of a male is the anima. (b) Shadow The repressed, instinctual, often darker side of the psyche, roughly like Sigmund Freud's id. A core Jungian archetype, but about disowned instinct and 'darkness', not gender. (c) Persona The social mask worn to satisfy external demands and present an acceptable face to the world. It concerns the public self, not an inner gendered archetype. Q34 According to psychoanalytic perspective, the terms gratification, irrational and impulsive are related to: a Id b Ego c Superego d Defense Mechanism ✓ Answer: (a) Id Sigmund Freud, structural model (1923) The concept Why (a) Gratification, irrationality and impulsiveness are the defining qualities of the id . What the id is The most primitive of Sigmund Freud's three personality structures in the 1923 structural model, wholly unconscious and present from birth. It stores the instinctual drives, supplies all psychic energy (the libido ) and runs on the pleasure principle , demanding immediate gratification of every urge regardless of logic, morality, reality or consequence. How it works Its mode is primary process thinking : irrational, illogical, timeless, impulsive and fantasy-driven, even hallucinating the wished-for object to discharge tension. It has no contact with the external world and cannot tolerate delay, which is why 'gratification, irrational, impulsive' maps onto it so cleanly. Contrast The ego is partly conscious, runs on the reality principle and secondary process, and rationally delays gratification to fit the world; the superego is the internalized moral conscience and ego-ideal that judges right and wrong. A defence mechanism is a tactic the ego uses against anxiety, not a personality structure at all. Exam tip 'Immediate gratification, irrational, impulsive, instinctual, pleasure' points at the id; 'realistic, planning, delay, mediating' at the ego; 'moral, ideal, conscience' at the superego. Panwar key According to psychoanalytic perspective, the Id is the seat of the unconscious where the irrational desires and drives are stored, it works on the pleasure principle and demands immediate gratification of needs. Why the other options are wrong (b) Ego Runs on the reality principle, mediating realistically among id, superego and the external world, the opposite of impulsive gratification. The central decision-maker, but its hallmark is delay and realism. (c) Superego The moral conscience and ego-ideal that restrains the id and punishes transgressions with guilt. Moralistic and inhibiting, the antithesis of irrational immediate gratification. (d) Defense Mechanism Ego strategies (repression, projection, etc.) that manage anxiety: processes, not the impulsive drive structure. Unconscious like the id, but the question describes the instinctual seat of impulses. Q35 According to Jung, the archetype representing the masculine side of females is called: a Animus b Shadow c Persona d Anima ✓ Answer: (a) Animus Carl Jung, Analytical Psychology The concept Why (a) In Carl Jung's analytical psychology the animus is the unconscious masculine archetype present within a woman. Archetypes Jung held that the collective unconscious , the inherited, species-wide stratum that was his decisive break from Sigmund Freud, contains universal archetypes. Among them is a contrasexual pair: each woman carries an inner masculine image, the animus, just as each man carries an inner feminine image, the anima. What the animus does It embodies a woman's unconscious masculine qualities (assertiveness, logic, the drive toward opinion, judgment and action) and colours how she relates to men, often via projection, and to her own initiative and authority. Becoming aware of and integrating it is part of individuation , unifying conscious and unconscious into a whole Self; left unexamined, it can show as rigid, dogmatic, argumentative opinionatedness. Related archetypes The shadow is the repressed, instinctual dark side (loosely like Freud's id); the persona is the outward social mask. Placing Jung historically, he founded Analytical Psychology after his 1913 split from Freud, substituting a symbolic, spiritual, growth-oriented model for Freud's sexual-drive theory. Exam tip Animus is the masculine-within-the-female; anima is the feminine-within-the-male. The masculine side of a female is the animus: the exact mirror of the anima question, so keep the direction straight. Panwar key Animus is the male side of the female, shadow is nearly analogous to Freud's Id and Persona is the facade that a person assumes to balance between the internal needs and the external demands. Anima is the female side of the male. Why the other options are wrong (b) Shadow The repressed, instinctual dark side of the psyche, roughly like Sigmund Freud's id. A core Jungian archetype, but about disowned instinct and 'darkness', not gender. (c) Persona The public mask worn to satisfy social demands and present an acceptable face. A famous Jungian term, but about the outward social self, not an inner gendered archetype. (d) Anima The exact reverse archetype: the unconscious feminine image within a man . The strongest decoy, since the two differ only in direction; the masculine side of a female is the animus. Q36 Alfred Adler proposed that humans are motivated by a Conscious drives b Neurotic needs c Empathic understanding d Social urges ✓ Answer: (d) Social urges Alfred Adler, Individual Psychology (1911) The concept Why (d) Alfred Adler broke from Sigmund Freud and argued that humans are motivated fundamentally by social, not sexual, forces. The split An early member of Freud's Vienna circle, Adler left in 1911 to found Individual Psychology , rejecting Freud's grounding of motivation in libido and instinctual sexual and aggressive drives. He recast the person as an inherently social being whose strivings unfold within, and are oriented toward, a community. Striving and social interest His central motive is striving for superiority (or perfection/completion), the push from a felt inferiority toward competence and mastery, always in a social context. Crucially, healthy striving is governed by social interest ( Gemeinschaftsgefuhl ), an innate but cultivable sense of belonging and concern for others: the well-adjusted channel it into socially useful goals, the maladjusted chase personal superiority at others' expense. Other ideas Adler also stressed birth order , the unique goal-directed style of life and the creative self . Together these make him the forerunner of the more socially and culturally oriented neo-Freudians (Karen Horney, Erich Fromm, Harry Stack Sullivan) who followed. Exam tip Freud says sex and instinct drive us; Adler says social urges , belonging and striving for superiority within community. When the named motivator is Adler's, the answer is social urges. Panwar key Adler deviated from the Freudian theory where he focused on the social aspect of an individual's life. He established that individuals are motivated by social urges and not sexual impulses as Freud stated. Why the other options are wrong (a) Conscious drives Too vague; it does not name Adler's specific claim. Adler did stress more conscious, goal-directed striving than Sigmund Freud's deep unconscious, but his distinctive answer to what motivates us is the social dimension. (b) Neurotic needs Karen Horney's concept: her ten compulsive interpersonal strategies condensed into the three neurotic trends. A fellow social-minded neo-Freudian, but this is her account of pathology, not Adler's theory of normal motivation. (c) Empathic understanding A therapeutic stance from Carl Rogers' humanistic, person-centred approach, a different force of psychology. It concerns how a therapist relates to a client, not what drives human behaviour. Q37 'Many mental disorders can be traced to unconscious urges or impulses and to the struggle over their expression that takes place in the hidden depths of human personality'. The above statement is related to which one of the following perspectives? a Gestalt b Humanistic c Social Learning d Psychodynamic ✓ Answer: (d) Psychodynamic Psychodynamic perspective, from Sigmund Freud and successors The concept Why (d) The statement locates mental disorder in unconscious urges and the inner struggle over expressing them, the signature claim of the psychodynamic perspective. What it holds Growing from Sigmund Freud and his successors, it holds that much of mental life is unconscious and personality runs on perpetual conflict between instinctual drives (id), morality (superego) and reality (ego). Socially unacceptable wishes are pushed out of awareness by repression and other defence mechanisms, but the buried drives keep pressing for discharge. Symptoms Symptoms and disorders are compromise formations , the visible result of the hidden tug-of-war between forbidden impulses and the forces holding them down. 'Hidden depths of human personality' and 'struggle over their expression' are pure psychodynamic language. Now the rivals Humanistic (Carl Rogers, Abraham Maslow): blocked self-actualization and incongruence, stressing growth, choice and the present, not buried conflict. Social learning (Bandura): observation, modeling and reinforcement, not the dynamic unconscious or the past. Gestalt : perceptual organization, present awareness and the structuring of wholes; each rival downplays what this statement foregrounds. Exam tip Any statement tracing disorder to unconscious impulses and intrapsychic conflict over their expression is psychodynamic, the only one of the four that makes the buried, conflicted unconscious the cause of pathology. Panwar key The psychodynamic approach to human personality states that the undesirable thoughts and socially unacceptable impulses and desires are pushed to the unconscious. The struggle of expression of these is looked at as the causing factor of mental disorders and issues. The Humanistic and Social learning approaches do not consider the influence of the past. Gestalt does not consider the influence of unconscious urges. Why the other options are wrong (a) Gestalt Concerns perceptual organization and the apprehension of wholes ('the whole is other than the sum of its parts'); its therapy offshoot stresses present-moment awareness. It posits no unconscious drives causing disorder. (b) Humanistic Attributes problems to blocked self-actualization, conditions of worth and incongruence between self and experience. It deliberately rejects the dark, conflict-ridden unconscious in favour of growth and choice. (c) Social Learning Explains behaviour through observation, imitation, modeling and reinforcement, with no dynamic unconscious or repressed impulses. It locates causes in the observable environment and learning history, not 'the hidden depths of personality'. Q38 The defence mechanism involving an intellectual reason to justify a certain action connected only in the mind of the person after the behaviour is completed is: a Denial b Repression c Rationalisation d Projection ✓ Answer: (c) Rationalisation Named by Ernest Jones (1908); catalogued by Anna Freud (1936) The concept Why (c) Rationalisation is the only listed defence that supplies an after-the-fact intellectual justification: a reason the person builds in their own mind only once the behaviour is already complete . Begin with defences A defence mechanism is an unconscious strategy the ego uses to reduce the anxiety that erupts when a forbidden id-impulse, or an ugly truth about oneself, threatens to reach awareness. It belongs to classical psychoanalysis , the first force of depth psychology, founded by Sigmund Freud in fin-de-siecle Vienna in the 1890s and 1900s. History Freud sketched the defences, but his daughter Anna Freud systematised them in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936), pivoting the movement from Freud's drive-focus toward the ego psychology school (later Heinz Hartmann). Rationalisation was named by Freud's English follower Ernest Jones in 1908; historically, later ego psychologists refined this defence family, sharpening the line between self-deceiving justification and honest reasoning. How it works It manufactures a plausible, logical, socially acceptable explanation that masks the real, often unconscious, motive: a student who failed says 'the questions were unfair' rather than admit not studying; a person who overpays calls it 'an investment'. The emotional verdict comes first and reasoning is recruited to defend it, like a lawyer arguing a case already decided. The key is sequence : the action happens for hidden reasons, then the mind invents an acceptable cause the person genuinely believes, protecting self-esteem. Exam tip Building a coherent argument makes it a relatively mature, secondary defence that demands a fair degree of intelligence, unlike cruder, primitive defences such as denial or projection that simply block or expel reality. It gives self-serving reasons after the behaviour is completed, swapping the true motive for a respectable one. Panwar key Denial is denying the reality altogether, repression is involved in almost all defense mechanisms, projection is projecting the negative aspect of self onto others. Rationalisation is a secondary and much more mature defence mechanism and requires a decent amount of intelligence by explaining the reasons to justify one's actions. Why the other options are wrong (a) Denial A primitive, early defence (also catalogued by Anna Freud): flatly refusing to acknowledge a painful external reality, e.g. insisting a terminal diagnosis is wrong. It blocks reality wholesale rather than inventing a justification for a completed act. (b) Repression The master defence Sigmund Freud called the cornerstone of psychoanalysis: pushing threatening thoughts, memories or impulses out of consciousness and keeping them there. It underlies almost every other defence, but buries material rather than building an excuse. (d) Projection Attributing one's own unacceptable impulses or feelings to others ('I'm not angry, you are'), on the same Freudian defence roster. It hides a true motive too, but externalises a feeling rather than justifying one's own finished action. Q39 An investment of psychic energy in an object or person is a Displacement b Cathexis c Instinct d Repression ✓ Answer: (b) Cathexis Sigmund Freud, economic metapsychology The concept Why (b) Cathexis is Sigmund Freud's precise term for the investment of psychic energy (libido) into an object, person or mental image. Where it belongs Freud's metapsychology, developed in Vienna across the 1890s to 1920s, had three angles: topographic (conscious, preconscious, unconscious), structural (id, ego, superego) and economic , which treats the mind as a system distributing a quantity of energy. Cathexis belongs to this third, economic view, the energy-accounting side of classical psychoanalysis . How it works Begin with the economic premise: the psyche runs on a finite pool of mental energy that can attach to mental representations. When the id desires something, it binds energy to that thing's image; the stronger the cathexis, the more the person is drawn to it, so it measures how much an object 'matters'. When the actual object is unavailable, energy goes into a mental representation of it; picture a grieving person whose libido stays bound to the lost loved one ( Mourning and Melancholia , 1917), or the infant who first cathects the mother's breast. Word and opposite Freud's German word was Besetzung ('occupation' or 'filling'), rendered by his English translator James Strachey as the Greek-derived 'cathexis' (from kathexis , a holding or retaining). The opposite, anticathexis (counter-cathexis), is the ego's expenditure of energy to dam up or restrain an id impulse from reaching consciousness, the energetic basis of repression ; the more energy spent holding an impulse down, the less is free for living. Exam tip This drive-economic, almost hydraulic vocabulary was later de-emphasised by the neo-Freudians and object-relations theorists, who put real relationships in place of abstract energy, yet it remains foundational. Cathexis is the investment of psychic/libidinal energy in an object or person, the basic currency of Freud's energy theory of mind. Panwar key According to Freud, when the object of desire is not available, individuals tend to invest psychic energy in creating a mental image of that object. This is termed as cathexis. Why the other options are wrong (a) Displacement A defence mechanism redirecting an impulse from a threatening target onto a safer substitute (the kicked-dog example). It too 'moves' energy, but concerns which target receives a feeling, not the act of investing energy. (c) Instinct The bodily source of psychic energy (Freud's Trieb ), a demand on the mind for work; Eros and Thanatos are the major drives. It supplies the energy; cathexis is the act of binding it to an object. (d) Repression The ego's defence of pushing unacceptable material out of awareness, maintained energetically by anticathexis. It describes blocking and forgetting, not the positive attachment of energy to an object or person. Q40 A woman reflecting her anger from her husband onto her child is an example of a Projection b Reaction Formation c Sublimation d Displacement ✓ Answer: (d) Displacement Sigmund Freud; listed by Anna Freud (1936) The concept Why (d) The woman redirects an emotion away from its true, threatening target onto a safer substitute: that is displacement . Background A classic ego-defence from classical psychoanalysis , the first force of depth psychology, first described by Sigmund Freud in Vienna and formally listed by his daughter Anna Freud in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936). That work helped found the ego psychology school, which shifted attention from the id's drives to the ego's coping machinery. How it works Recall that defences are the ego's unconscious tactics for managing anxiety from feelings it cannot safely express. In displacement the impulse is not denied, reversed or transformed; only its target is swapped, because the original object is too dangerous, too powerful or unavailable. Here venting at the husband feels risky to the marriage, so the wife discharges the anger onto her child, who poses no threat and cannot retaliate. Examples The worker scolded by the boss goes home and kicks the dog: the affect travels down a chain from the powerful to the powerless. On Freud's account the same mechanism also fuels dream symbolism (emotional weight shifts from a significant image to a trivial one) and phobias , where dread attaches to a substitute object. Exam tip Distinguish it from projection (attributing your own feeling to someone else) and sublimation (rechanneling the impulse into something socially valuable); both change more than the address. Displacement keeps the emotion intact and fully recognisable and only moves it to a safer, substitute target. Panwar key Displacement is the defense mechanism in which an emotion/feeling, usually the ones which are anxiety provoking or stressful about a stressor, is directed towards or onto other objects or persons which is less threatening. In this case, the woman displaces her anger for her husband towards her child, thus indulging in displacement. Why the other options are wrong (a) Projection Attributing one's own unacceptable feelings to another person: here the wife would claim her child or husband is the angry one. It externalises the emotion's ownership rather than relocating its target . (b) Reaction Formation Converts an unacceptable impulse into its conscious opposite, e.g. exaggerated tenderness toward someone you actually resent. It flips anger into love; the wife is still openly angry, just at the wrong target. (c) Sublimation Rechannels a sexual or aggressive impulse into a socially valued activity (sport, surgery, art), considered the most mature defence. Here the anger is simply dumped on a substitute person, not transformed into anything constructive or admired. Q41 The neo-Freudian include: a Hans Eysenck, Karen Horney, Albert Bandura b Carl Roger, Sigmund Freud, Alfred Adler c Carl Jung, Karen Horney, Alfred Adler d Alfred Adler, Albert Bandura ✓ Answer: (c) Carl Jung, Karen Horney, Alfred Adler Jung, Horney and Adler, the textbook neo-Freudian trio The concept Why (c) Carl Jung , Karen Horney and Alfred Adler are classic neo-Freudians: they accepted Sigmund Freud's insight of an unconscious mind but substantially revised his system. Every other set smuggles in at least one non-neo-Freudian or, in (b), Freud himself. The arc Picture psychodynamic thought in order. Freud built psychoanalysis in Vienna from the 1890s and gathered a circle; his most gifted early disciples broke away over doctrine: Adler in 1911 and Jung in 1913, the two great 'defectors', each founding a rival school. A second wave of neo-Freudians followed in the 1930s and 1940s, many of them emigres shaped by social and cultural concerns. Kept and dropped They kept the unconscious, the formative power of early childhood, intrapsychic conflict and defence-like processes. They downplayed or rejected Freud's heavy emphasis on the sexual drive (libido) as the single engine of personality, raising social, cultural and interpersonal forces in its place. The trio Adler stressed striving for superiority and compensation for inferiority feelings (Individual Psychology); Jung introduced the collective unconscious and archetypes (Analytical Psychology). Horney , culturally minded and proto-feminist, emphasised basic anxiety from disturbed early relationships and rejected Freud's penis-envy, countering it with 'womb envy'. Erik Erikson (psychosocial stages) and Harry Stack Sullivan (interpersonal theory) are also neo-Freudians, so the group is broader than three. Exam tip Neo-Freudians kept the unconscious but traded Freud's sexual emphasis for social and cultural determinants. Panwar key Four notable neo-Freudians include Alfred Adler, Erik Erikson, Carl Jung and Karen Horney. Why the other options are wrong (a) Hans Eysenck, Karen Horney, Albert Bandura Eysenck was a trait and biological theorist (extraversion, neuroticism, psychoticism); Bandura founded social-learning/social-cognitive theory (observational learning, self-efficacy). Only Horney is genuinely neo-Freudian, so two of the three belong to other schools. (b) Carl Roger, Sigmund Freud, Alfred Adler Carl Rogers is a humanistic (third-force) psychologist, and Sigmund Freud is the original the neo-Freudians revised, so he cannot count among his own successors. Only Adler is correctly neo-Freudian. (d) Alfred Adler, Albert Bandura Bandura belongs to social-learning theory, a learning-based rather than psychodynamic tradition. Adler is indeed neo-Freudian, but one non-neo-Freudian name spoils the set, and the list is incomplete next to the correct trio. Q42 Research has begun to show some support for which of Freud's concepts? a The existence of an id, ego and superego b The order of the psychosexual stages c The concepts of an unconscious mind d The existence of the Oedipus Complex ✓ Answer: (c) The concepts of an unconscious mind Sigmund Freud's unconscious mind, now backed by cognitive science The concept Why (c) Of Sigmund Freud 's claims, the unconscious mind is the one modern empirical research has begun to support. His later structural ideas (id, ego, superego, the fixed order of psychosexual stages, the Oedipus complex) are hard to operationalise and resist falsification, so they have little backing; Karl Popper attacked psychoanalysis on exactly this ground. Freud's starting point Freud built classical psychoanalysis in Vienna on the late-19th-century insight that conscious awareness is only 'the tip of the iceberg'. His early topographic model split the mind into conscious, preconscious and unconscious, with the unconscious as the engine of everything. This founding premise of the psychodynamic tradition was kept even by the defectors Alfred Adler and Carl Jung and the later neo-Freudians. What research shows Cognitive science , which arose in the mid-20th century partly in reaction against psychoanalysis, independently vindicated the claim that much mental activity occurs outside awareness. Research on implicit memory , automatic processing, priming, subliminal perception and selective attention shows perception, judgement, emotion and behaviour are routinely shaped by information we never consciously register. The nuance This cognitive 'adaptive unconscious' is not Freud's seething reservoir of repressed sexual and aggressive wishes held down by active censorship; it is a set of efficient, automatic information-processing routines that exist for speed, not defence. So research supports the existence of unconscious processing, not Freud's dynamic, motivated account; still, the conscious mind is only a sliver of mental life. Exam tip Of Freud's ideas, the existence of unconscious mental processing has growing empirical support; his structural and stage-based claims remain largely unsupported. Panwar key Research on attention, consciousness and memory points out that there are many things in the human mental system that are out of our conscious awareness. These provide support to Freud's idea of the unconscious mind. Why the other options are wrong (a) The existence of an id, ego and superego Freud's structural model ( The Ego and the Id , 1923): iconic as a metaphor, but hypothetical agencies that cannot be directly measured or falsified, so research support is exactly what it lacks. (b) The order of the psychosexual stages A developmental sequence (oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital) Freud tied to libido. It sounds testable, but developmental research has not confirmed the stages or their adult-personality consequences. (d) The existence of the Oedipus Complex Freud's claim of universal childhood desire for the opposite-sex parent and rivalry with the same-sex parent. Among his most disputed ideas: criticised cross-culturally (e.g. by Malinowski ) and empirically unverified. Q43 Which structure of the personality, according to Freud, works on the reality principle? a Id b Ego c Superego d Libido ✓ Answer: (b) Ego Sigmund Freud's structural model (The Ego and the Id, 1923) The concept Why (b) In Sigmund Freud 's structural model , the ego is the structure that operates on the reality principle. Picture the three parts as a permanent three-way negotiation. Background The model comes from The Ego and the Id (1923), a later, mature phase of classical psychoanalysis that revised Freud's earlier topographic (conscious/unconscious) map. It went on to give rise to the ego psychology school of Anna Freud and Heinz Hartmann. Id and superego The id is the primitive drive system, present from birth and wholly unconscious; on the pleasure principle it demands immediate, total gratification with no regard for consequences, logic or morality. The superego is internalised moral authority: the conscience (which punishes) and the ego-ideal (which sets aspirations), formed around ages 3 to 6 through identification with the same-sex parent at the close of the Oedipal phase. It runs on a moral, idealistic principle, pushing for perfection and inflicting guilt on transgression. The ego Between these, and pressed by external reality, the ego is the executive manager: it still satisfies the id's urges, but only in realistic, safe, socially acceptable ways. It delays gratification, postpones discharge, weighs consequences through secondary-process (logical, planful) thinking and engineers compromises; it spans the conscious, preconscious and unconscious levels and deploys defence mechanisms when the conflict threatens to overwhelm it. Later ego psychologists enlarged it from mere referee to an autonomous, adaptive agency with 'conflict-free' functions. Exam tip Id = pleasure principle, superego = morality and ideals, ego = reality principle , the rational mediator that adapts impulses to the real world. Panwar key According to Freudian theory of personality, the ego works on the reality principle, balancing between the id that works on the pleasure principle and the superego that works on the moral principle. Why the other options are wrong (a) Id Runs on the pleasure principle , demanding immediate gratification regardless of reality, logic or morality. It is the impulse the ego must restrain, the opposite of reality testing. (c) Superego Runs on a moral (idealistic) principle, enforcing conscience and the ego-ideal and generating guilt. Like the ego it opposes the raw id, but it pursues moral perfection, not realistic adaptation. (d) Libido The psychic/sexual energy of the drives: core Freudian vocabulary, but not a structure of personality at all. The question asks for a structure (id, ego or superego); libido is the energy they invest. Q44 Sigmund Freud began his career as a a Neurologist b Psychiatrist c Psychoanalyst d Philosopher ✓ Answer: (a) Neurologist Sigmund Freud, trained in neurology; studied under Charcot (1885-86) The concept Why (a) Sigmund Freud 's medical training and first career were in neurology and neuroanatomy, long before psychoanalysis existed. 'Psychiatrist' and 'psychoanalyst' describe what he became , not where he began . Early career Freud qualified in medicine in Vienna in 1881 and worked under the physiologist Ernst Brucke in the great German physicalist tradition, studying the anatomy and physiology of the nervous system (nerve cells of fish and humans) and even researching cocaine as a possible anaesthetic. He then practised as a clinical neurologist treating 'nervous' disorders and wrote monographs on aphasia and on cerebral palsy in children, all within organic medicine. The turn In 1885-86 a travelling grant took him to Paris to study under Jean-Martin Charcot , the leading neurologist of the age, who used hypnosis to investigate and treat hysteria : dramatic physical symptoms (paralyses, blindness, contractures) with no detectable organic cause. Watching symptoms appear and dissolve under suggestion shook Freud's purely physical outlook and turned him toward psychological causation. Building psychoanalysis Back in Vienna, with his older colleague Josef Breuer on cases such as Anna O. (Bertha Pappenheim, who coined the phrase 'talking cure'), he developed the cathartic method, then free association, and gradually built psychoanalysis , the founding act of the psychodynamic tradition. The arc that follows (Freud, then the defectors Alfred Adler in 1911 and Carl Jung in 1913, then the neo-Freudians) springs from this neurological start. His abandoned Project for a Scientific Psychology (1895) even tried to ground the mind in neurons before he turned to a purely psychological model. Exam tip Freud started as a neurologist and neuroanatomist, was trained in hysteria under Charcot in Paris, and only afterward invented psychoanalysis. Panwar key Sigmund Freud began his medical career as a neuroanatomist and neurologist before he established the theory and techniques of Psychoanalysis. He was trained in neurology under Jean Charcot. Why the other options are wrong (b) Psychiatrist Freud treated mental disorders but was not trained or board-certified in psychiatry, the specialty of diagnosing and treating mental illness; he approached the mind from the nervous system. Where he ended up, not how he began. (c) Psychoanalyst The role Freud himself created : psychoanalysis did not exist as a discipline until he built it in the late 1890s and after. You cannot begin a career in a field not yet invented. (d) Philosopher He engaged sweeping ideas on civilisation, religion and the mind and was read like one, but began as a working medical scientist (neurologist, neuroanatomist); his philosophical-style theorising came much later, always framed as science. Q45 ________ was the proponent of Individual Psychology. a Horney b Jung c Adler d Erikson ✓ Answer: (c) Adler Alfred Adler, who broke from Freud in 1911 The concept Why (c) Alfred Adler founded the school known as Individual Psychology ; the other three are tied to other movements. His place in history An Austrian physician, Adler was among the earliest, most prominent members of Freud's Vienna Psychoanalytic Society, even its president for a time. He broke away in 1911 when his emphasis on aggression and inferiority clashed with Sigmund Freud's emphasis on sexuality, becoming the first major 'defector' from classical psychoanalysis . He is a founding figure of the more socially minded branch of depth psychology that the neo-Freudians later extended. The name The Latin individuum means 'undivided': the person is an indivisible, unified, goal-directed whole, unlike Freud's psyche as a battleground of warring parts (id, ego, superego). Adler rejected Freud's primacy of the sexual drive and his backward-looking, deterministic stress on early fixation. Core ideas The central motive is the striving for superiority , a forward-pulling, teleological drive toward growth, mastery, competence and completeness, from a felt 'minus' to a felt 'plus'. It arises partly as compensation for the universal feelings of inferiority of childhood smallness, weakness and dependence on adults. He also stressed the style of life (a unique, self-created pattern toward a private, fictional final goal) and social interest ( Gemeinschaftsgefuhl ), the sense of community and concern for others' welfare that he made the yardstick of mental health. Exam tip Adler = Individual Psychology, a holistic, future-oriented theory centred on striving for superiority and compensation for inferiority. Panwar key Alfred Adler was an Austrian psychiatrist and the proponent of Individual Psychology. He held that human thought and behaviour are individual man's striving for superiority and power, partly in compensation for his feeling of inferiority. Why the other options are wrong (a) Horney A neo-Freudian whose own system centred on basic anxiety from disturbed early relationships and three neurotic interpersonal trends (moving toward, against and away from people). Karen Horney shares Adler's social outlook but did not found this school. (b) Jung Founder of Analytical Psychology (collective unconscious, archetypes, introversion/extraversion, individuation). Carl Jung is the other great Freud defector of the same era, but his school's name and content differ from Adler's. (d) Erikson An ego psychologist known for the eight psychosocial stages spanning the lifespan. Like Adler, Erik Erikson broadens psychoanalysis toward social factors, but he founded no such school and belongs to a later generation. Q46 Inferiority complex was suggested by : a Carl Jung b Harry Stack Sullivan c Erik Erikson d Alfred Adler ✓ Answer: (d) Alfred Adler Alfred Adler, Individual Psychology The concept Why (d) Alfred Adler introduced the inferiority complex , the cornerstone of his Individual Psychology . His place in history An Austrian physician and senior member of Freud's Vienna circle, Adler broke with classical psychoanalysis in 1911 over Sigmund Freud's insistence on the sexual drive, the first great defector of the psychodynamic movement. Across the 1910s and 1920s he built his own neo-Freudian system in which inferiority and compensation, not libido, are the motor of personality. Normal inferiority Begin with his premise: inferiority feelings are universal , since every child starts small, weak and dependent on more capable adults, so baseline inadequacy is normal and even motivating . He first spoke medically of organ inferiority (a weak organ the body compensates for), then generalised it into a psychological law. Healthy people compensate by striving toward competence, mastery and superiority, turning weakness into a spur. The complex An inferiority complex is the pathological outcome when those feelings become exaggerated, fixed and overwhelming: a deep, disabling inadequacy and insecurity the person cannot move past or turn into useful effort, from actual or imagined physical or psychological deficiency (perception matters as much as fact). It can drive maladaptive overcompensation (an aggressive grab for power and dominance) or a brittle, defensive superiority complex that masks the doubt with boasting and contempt. Exam tip The inferiority complex, a basic feeling of inadequacy from real or imagined deficiency, was Adler's, not Jung's, Sullivan's or Erikson's. It flows from his ideas of compensation and striving for superiority, and is now one of psychology's most borrowed everyday terms. Panwar key The term 'inferiority complex' was coined in the 1920s by French psychologist Alfred Adler. It is "a basic feeling of inadequacy and insecurity, deriving from actual or imagined physical or psychological deficiency." Why the other options are wrong (a) Carl Jung Founder of Analytical Psychology (collective unconscious, archetypes, word-association test) and a contemporaneous Freud defector. Jung did coin 'complex' in the association-test context, but the inferiority complex is Adler's term. (b) Harry Stack Sullivan An American neo-Freudian whose interpersonal theory centred relationships and anxiety ('self-system', significant others). His focus on insecurity overlaps thematically, but the inferiority complex predates him and belongs to Alfred Adler. (c) Erik Erikson Used 'inferiority' as the negative pole of his fourth psychosocial stage, industry vs. inferiority (school age), borrowing the everyday term. The clinical concept itself was coined by Alfred Adler. Q47 In Freud's theory which portion of personality is concerned with the immediate gratification of primitive needs : a Only Id b Only Ego c Both id and ego d Both Id and Superego ✓ Answer: (a) Only Id Sigmund Freud's id, run on the pleasure principle (1923) The concept Why (a) In Sigmund Freud 's structural model the id is the single agency devoted to the immediate gratification of primitive needs. Every option that adds the ego or the superego fails, because those two restrain gratification rather than seek it. Its place in the system The structural model comes from The Ego and the Id (1923), the mature stage of classical psychoanalysis that superseded Freud's earlier conscious/unconscious topographic map. The later ego psychology school of Anna Freud and Heinz Hartmann was built on it. Take the three structures in turn. The id The id is present from birth, entirely unconscious , and the original reservoir from which the other structures differentiate; it holds the basic biological drives: hunger, thirst, sex (Eros) and aggression (Thanatos). On the pleasure principle it demands needs be met instantly and completely, with zero tolerance for tension or delay and no concern for reality, logic, time or morality. When that is impossible it uses primary process thinking , conjuring a wish-fulfilling mental image of the desired object, as the hungry infant hallucinates the breast. Ego and superego The ego grows out of the id later, under the pressure of reality, precisely to restrain and channel it; it works on the reality principle through secondary process (logical, planful) thinking, negotiating, postponing and finding safe outlets. The superego , formed around ages 3 to 6 through identification at the close of the Oedipal stage, holds internalised morality and the ego-ideal and actively opposes raw gratification, punishing it with guilt. Exam tip Only the id seeks immediate gratification of primitive needs, because only it operates on the pleasure principle. Panwar key Id refers to unconscious psychic energy that works to satisfy basic urges, needs, and desires. The Id operates based on the pleasure principle, which demands immediate gratification of needs. Why the other options are wrong (b) Only Ego The ego works on the reality principle , using secondary-process thinking to delay gratification and fit urges to real-world constraints. It is the active 'doer' that gets needs met, but by negotiating and postponing, not instantly. (c) Both id and ego Adding the ego spoils it: the ego restrains immediate gratification rather than demanding it. Id and ego work closely and the ego serves the id's ultimate aims, but their methods are opposite. (d) Both Id and Superego The superego is the internalised conscience and ego-ideal; it opposes primitive gratification and punishes it with guilt. Both are partly unconscious and pressure the ego, but the superego pulls toward moral restraint, the reverse of pleasure-seeking. Q48 The concept of 'Collective Unconscious' has been introduced by which of the following Psychologists? a Karen Horney b Alfred Adler c Carl Jung d Sigmund Freud ✓ Answer: (c) Carl Jung Carl Jung, Analytical Psychology (broke with Freud in 1913) The concept Why (c) The collective unconscious is Carl Jung 's signature contribution and the centrepiece of his school, Analytical Psychology . It sets that school apart from Freudian psychoanalysis and from the more socially focused neo-Freudians like Karen Horney and Adler. His place in history Jung was Sigmund Freud's close associate, once his anointed heir and the first president of the International Psychoanalytic Association, until their painful 1913 break . With Alfred Adler (who had left in 1911) he became one of the two great defectors from classical psychoanalysis , then built a distinct depth psychology of his own. Two kinds of unconscious Both men used the word 'unconscious' but meant different things. Freud's unconscious is personal : the individual's own repressed wishes, conflicts and forgotten experiences, acquired in one lifetime. Jung agreed this layer exists just below consciousness, but argued for a deeper stratum beneath it not built from personal history at all. The collective layer The collective unconscious is inherited and shared by the whole species, an inborn psychic substrate common to humanity, the precipitate of ancestral experience laid down over evolutionary time. Its contents are the archetypes , universal primordial images and organising patterns: the Mother , the Shadow (the disowned dark self), the Anima and Animus (the contra-sexual inner figure), the Wise Old Man and the unifying Self . Jung's evidence was their recurrence across the myths, religions, fairy tales, art and dreams of cultures with no historical contact, and in the fantasies of psychotic patients who could not have learned them. Exam tip The personal unconscious is yours alone; the collective unconscious is inherited, shared by all humans, populated by archetypes, and Jung's idea. Panwar key Collective unconscious refers to structures of the unconscious mind which are shared among beings of the same species. It was a term coined by Carl Jung. Why the other options are wrong (a) Karen Horney A neo-Freudian focused on basic anxiety and the social and cultural roots of neurosis. Horney too revised Sigmund Freud, but her interpersonal, culture-oriented work has nothing like an inherited, species-wide unconscious. (b) Alfred Adler Founder of Individual Psychology, stressing inferiority feelings and striving for superiority. Adler was Jung's fellow Freud-defector of the same period, but his goal-directed, social system has no collective, archetype-filled unconscious. (d) Sigmund Freud Originated the unconscious, but specifically the personal unconscious of repressed individual material. The strongest distractor, yet Freud never proposed an inherited, collective layer; that was exactly the kind of departure that led Jung to break from him. Q49 According to Freud's stages of psychosexual development, the oedipus complex corresponds to ________. a Anal b Phallic c Genital d Latency ✓ Answer: (b) Phallic Sigmund Freud's psychosexual stages: the phallic stage, ages 3 to 6 The concept Why (b) Sigmund Freud located the Oedipus complex in the phallic stage, before latency and well before the genital stage. The theory In psychosexual development , a core pillar of classical psychoanalysis, personality forms through a fixed, universal sequence of stages, each defined by the erogenous zone where libido (pleasure-seeking energy) is focused. Too little or too much gratification at a stage produces lifelong fixation . Walk the stages The oral stage (0-1) centres on the mouth, sucking and biting, and the anal stage (1-3) on control and release of the bowels in toilet training. In the phallic stage, roughly ages 3 to 6, libido shifts to the genitals and the child becomes aware of sexual difference. Then come latency (about age 6 to puberty: urges go dormant and energy goes into schooling, skills and same-sex friendships) and the genital stage at puberty (mature, reciprocal sexuality). The complex During the phallic stage the child unconsciously desires the opposite-sex parent and feels rivalry, even hostility, toward the same-sex parent: the Oedipus complex in boys (named for the Greek myth, with castration anxiety , the fear of paternal retaliation), and what is sometimes labelled the Electra complex in girls (a term Carl Jung, not Freud, popularised; Freud spoke of penis envy). It is resolved by identification with the same-sex parent: the child renounces the impossible desire and takes the rival 'inside', absorbing that parent's standards, prohibitions and values. So the superego crystallises, making this stage pivotal for moral and gender-role development. Exam tip Oedipus complex = phallic stage (ages 3-6), resolved by identification, which builds the superego. Panwar key Oedipus complex is the complex of emotions aroused in a young child, typically around the age of four, by an unconscious sexual desire for the parent of the opposite sex and wish to exclude the parent of the same sex. It corresponds to the phallic stage. Why the other options are wrong (a) Anal Ages 1-3: toilet training and control of elimination; fixation yields 'anal-retentive' or 'anal-expulsive' traits. It sits just before the phallic stage, too early for the genital focus and parental rivalry the Oedipal conflict needs. (c) Genital Begins at puberty and concerns mature, reciprocal sexual relationships outside the family. Its name sounds sexual, but by puberty the complex was long resolved through identification; this stage comes after the Oedipal period. (d) Latency About age 6 to puberty, when sexual urges go dormant and energy is sublimated into learning and same-sex friendships. It follows the resolution of the Oedipus complex, so the complex has already passed. Q50 The defence mechanism that involves 'evolving logical and socially acceptable explanations after the occurrence to behaviour that were actually driven by internal unconscious motives' is called as ________. a Sublimation b Projection c Rationalisation d Displacement ✓ Answer: (c) Rationalisation Ernest Jones (1908); catalogued by Anna Freud (1936) The concept Why (c) Rationalisation constructs logical, socially acceptable explanations after the fact for behaviour actually driven by hidden unconscious motives. Background It is an ego-defence from classical psychoanalysis , the founding force of depth psychology, first sketched in Sigmund Freud's circle: his English follower Ernest Jones introduced the term in 1908. Anna Freud later catalogued it in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936), the text that anchored the ego psychology school. How it works Recall that defence mechanisms are the ego's unconscious tactics for managing anxiety from forbidden id-impulses, superego guilt or unflattering truths about the self. Rationalisation works by substitution of motive : the real, embarrassing or unacceptable reason, which would wound self-esteem if admitted, is hidden behind a respectable justification the person genuinely believes rather than cynically invents. Crucially it is retroactive : the act comes first for unconscious reasons, then the mind supplies a tidy, plausible account, so the logic follows the behaviour instead of guiding it. Examples and maturity Classic cases are 'sour grapes' (dismissing the unattainable as undesirable, from Aesop's fable) and its mirror, 'sweet lemons' (insisting a poor outcome was what you wanted all along); overpaying for a luxury becomes 'an investment', shouting at a child 'discipline for their own good'. Building a coherent narrative takes real cognitive effort, so it counts as a relatively mature and intellectual defence, unlike primitive, reality-denying defences such as denial or projection. Exam tip Rationalisation hides the true unconscious motive behind a logical, socially acceptable justification produced after the behaviour has occurred.
