Panwar key Rationalisation is a defence mechanism which permits an individual to deal with emotional conflicts, or internal or external stressors, by devising reassuring or self-serving logical and socially acceptable but incorrect explanations for his or her own, or others' thoughts, actions, or feelings, which cover up other motives. Why the other options are wrong (a) Sublimation Channels unacceptable sexual or aggressive impulses into socially valued activities (art, sport, surgery); reckoned the most mature defence. It turns the impulse into action rather than producing after-the-fact explanations . (b) Projection Attributes one's own unacceptable feelings or motives to others ('she's the one who's hostile'). It disguises an unconscious motive too, but relocates the feeling onto someone else instead of justifying one's own behaviour. (d) Displacement Redirects an impulse from a threatening target onto a safer substitute (anger at the boss vented on the family). It changes the target of a feeling, not the reason given for behaviour. Q51 Which of the following is not associated with the 'inferiority complex'? a Certainty in decision making b Lack of self-worth c Overcompensation d Hopelessness ✓ Answer: (a) Certainty in decision making Alfred Adler's inferiority complex (Individual Psychology) The concept Why (a) Certainty and confidence in making decisions mark a secure, self-assured person who trusts their own judgement, the very opposite of the inferiority complex . Three options describe the complex and one its absence: a 'find the odd one out' item. Its place The inferiority complex is the signature idea of Alfred Adler 's Individual Psychology. This Austrian physician became the first major defector from Sigmund Freud's classical psychoanalysis in 1911, putting inferiority and compensation, rather than libido, at the centre of personality. (The printed key's aside about Carl Jung and the word-association test is incidental and slightly garbled; the complex itself is firmly Adler's.) Feeling vs complex Inferiority feelings are universal and even motivating, the normal childhood experience of being small and dependent. A complex develops when they become exaggerated, fixed and disabling: a deep, persistent sense of inadequacy and insecurity, a felt 'not good enough', from real or imagined physical or psychological deficiency. Its features Its hallmarks cluster around self-doubt and its fallout: lack of self-worth, hopelessness and overcompensation. People with the complex typically show indecisiveness , hesitation, dependence on others' approval and avoidance, not crisp decisiveness. Exam tip Inferiority complex means inadequacy, low self-worth, hopelessness and overcompensation, never the confident certainty of secure decision making. Panwar key Carl Jung created the word association test in the middle of the 20th century to unravel the subconscious. The inferiority complex involves feelings of inadequacy, lack of self-worth, overcompensation and hopelessness, not certainty in decision making. Why the other options are not the answer (b) Lack of self-worth True: it is the emotional heart of the complex, the felt conviction of being inadequate, 'less than' or lesser. In a 'which is NOT' item, picking a genuine feature is the trap. (c) Overcompensation True: the classic Adlerian behavioural response, an exaggerated, sometimes aggressive striving (for power, status or perfection) to mask inadequacy, which can harden into a brittle, boastful superiority complex . It sounds confident, but it belongs to the complex. (d) Hopelessness True: it follows when the person feels permanently unable to measure up and stops believing effort will help, the sense of never closing the gap. A real correlate, included to bait a wrong pick. Q52 Which of the following does NOT characterise the Ego-defence mechanisms? a Having certain adaptive value b Pushing painful experiences out of consciousness c Result in distorted view of reality d Rational unconscious protective measures ✓ Answer: (d) Rational unconscious protective measures Anna Freud, The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936) The concept Why (d) The word rational makes this option false: ego-defence mechanisms are precisely NOT rational. 'Rational' implies conscious, reasoned, deliberate problem-solving (closer to a healthy coping strategy), whereas defences are automatic, reality-bending and hidden from the self. Their place in the system Defence mechanisms are a core concept of classical psychoanalysis , the founding force of depth psychology, sketched by Sigmund Freud across his career. His daughter Anna Freud catalogued them systematically in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936), launching the ego psychology tradition by turning the spotlight from the id's drives onto the ego's coping apparatus. What they are By the structural model they are the ego's automatic, unconscious strategies for coping with anxiety from conflict among the id, the superego and external reality. Above all they operate unconsciously , outside deliberate control or awareness. Three options name genuine features (first, adaptive value; second, pushing pain out of awareness; third, distorting reality), and spotting them isolates the false one. Exam tip Ego-defence mechanisms are unconscious, reality-distorting, somewhat adaptive coping devices, but they are not rational, deliberate measures. Panwar key The ego-defence mechanisms operate to cope from overwhelming situations. It provides a distorted view of reality, are unconscious and push painful experiences into the unconscious. These are not necessarily rational. Why the other options are not the answer (a) Having certain adaptive value True: used in moderation, defences shield the ego and preserve functioning under acute stress, which is why Freud, Anna Freud and later ego psychologists treated them as normal, not purely pathological. (b) Pushing painful experiences out of consciousness True: this is the core action of repression , which Freud called the cornerstone on which the whole structure of psychoanalysis rests; it is the foundational defence and the parent of the others. (c) Result in distorted view of reality True: defences protect the ego by editing, denying, reversing or rearranging uncomfortable truths rather than confronting them honestly. A defining property, the odd one out only if misread. Q53 The re-channeling of sexual or aggressive impulses in a socially acceptable direction is known as : a Displacement b Overcompensation c Projection d Sublimation ✓ Answer: (d) Sublimation Sigmund Freud (Civilization and Its Discontents, 1930); Anna Freud (1936) The concept Why (d) Sublimation re-channels unacceptable sexual or aggressive impulses into socially acceptable, constructive outlets; it is the textbook example of 'rechanneling' rather than blocking. Its place in history It is an ego-defence from classical psychoanalysis , the founding force of depth psychology, introduced by Sigmund Freud . He saw it not merely as a personal coping device but as the wellspring of art, science and civilisation itself, a theme of Civilization and Its Discontents (1930), where culture is bought by renouncing and redirecting instinct. Anna Freud later included it among the defences she formally catalogued in 1936, within the ego psychology tradition. How it works Recall that the ego must manage id-impulses that society forbids. Sublimation does not bury, deny, reverse or merely relocate them; it transforms them, redirecting the drive-energy (libido or aggression) into valued or admired activities. Aggression becomes competitive sport, debate or a surgeon's incisive precision; the sexual drive becomes artistic creation or scientific curiosity; raw impulse becomes genuine achievement. Why it is healthiest Freud judged it the healthiest, most mature and adaptive defence because it allows real instinctual satisfaction while serving the social good, a win-win rather than a disguise or distortion of reality; it is often the only defence judged unequivocally healthy. Distinguish it from displacement (shifting an emotion onto a safer target without making it socially valuable) and projection (expelling one's own impulses onto others), which both leave the impulse essentially untransformed. Exam tip Sublimation re-channels sexual or aggressive impulses into socially acceptable, constructive activity, the most mature of the defences. Panwar key Sublimation is the channeling of unacceptable feelings, desires, and impulses, often of a sexual or aggressive nature, into positive, socially approved activity. Sublimation is one of Anna Freud's original defense mechanisms. Why the other options are wrong (a) Displacement Shifts an impulse from a threatening target onto a safer substitute (anger at the boss taken out on the family). The closest distractor, but it changes only the target , without making the discharge socially constructive. (b) Overcompensation An Adlerian concept, not a Freudian defence: the exaggerated effort to overcome felt inferiority, sometimes producing a superiority complex. It belongs to Adler's Individual Psychology and concerns inferiority, not re-channeling sexual or aggressive impulses. (c) Projection Attributes one's own unacceptable sexual or aggressive impulses to other people ('he's the aggressive one'). It externalises the impulse onto someone else rather than converting it into constructive activity. Q54 A socially acceptable reason for actions that are really based on motives believed to be socially unacceptable is known as ________. a rationalisation b reaction formation c sublimation d displacement ✓ Answer: (a) rationalisation Ernest Jones (1908); listed by Anna Freud (1936) The concept Why (a) Rationalisation supplies a socially acceptable reason for actions whose real motives are socially unacceptable. Contrast reaction formation (impulse into its conscious opposite), sublimation (impulse into valued activity) and displacement (feeling onto a safer target): only rationalisation invents an acceptable cover story . Its place in the system It is an ego-defence of classical psychoanalysis , the founding force of depth psychology, rooted in Sigmund Freud 's account of the mind; his English follower Ernest Jones coined the term in 1908. Anna Freud later listed it in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936), the founding work of the ego psychology school. How it works Recall that defences are the ego's unconscious devices for warding off anxiety from forbidden id-impulses, superego guilt or unflattering truths about the self. By substitution of motive , the genuine, embarrassing or unacceptable reason is replaced in the mind by a plausible, logical, respectable one. Because the person sincerely believes it rather than knowingly lying, self-esteem is preserved, the true driver stays hidden from the self, and the justification is 'consciously tolerable', even admirable or superior. Examples A manager who fires an employee out of personal dislike calls it 'a budget decision'; a person who lashes out was 'only being honest'; a student who cheats argues 'everyone does it'. Building a coherent, plausible narrative makes it a relatively mature, intellectual defence rather than a primitive one, and it is among the most common in everyday life because it feels so reasonable from the inside. Exam tip Rationalisation justifies socially unacceptable motives with a socially acceptable, logical-sounding reason. Panwar key Rationalisation is a defense mechanism in which controversial behaviours or feelings are justified and explained in a seemingly rational or logical manner to avoid the true explanation, and are made consciously tolerable, or even admirable and superior, by plausible means. Why the other options are wrong (b) reaction formation Expresses the conscious opposite of one's true unacceptable feeling (exaggerated kindness to someone you secretly hate, moral crusading against an impulse you harbour). It masks a motive but flips the feeling instead of justifying the behaviour. (c) sublimation Channels unacceptable sexual or aggressive impulses into valued activity such as art or sport; the most mature defence. It shares 'socially acceptable' but transforms the impulse into action , not into a reason for an action. (d) displacement Redirects an impulse from a dangerous target onto a safer one (kicking the dog after a bad day at work). It changes the target of a feeling rather than fabricating an acceptable justification for a motive. Q55 Who among the following is considered as the proponent of Word Association Test to understand the unconscious conflicts in an individual? a Henry Murray b Carl Jung c Sigmund Freud d Donald Winicott ✓ Answer: (b) Carl Jung Carl Jung, at the Burgholzli clinic in Zurich (early 1900s) The concept Why (b) Carl Jung developed the Word Association Test as a tool for uncovering unconscious conflicts, one of the first attempts to bring measurement to the study of the unconscious. Its place in history Jung devised it in the early 1900s at the Burgholzli psychiatric clinic in Zurich under Eugen Bleuler , during his close collaboration with Sigmund Freud and well before their 1913 break. It later became foundational to Analytical Psychology , the depth psychology he built after leaving Freud. The procedure Picture it: the examiner reads a standard list of stimulus words one at a time, and the respondent replies with the very first word that comes to mind. Jung measured the content and, crucially, the reaction time and objective signs of emotional disturbance: hesitation, an unusually long pause, a bizarre or absent answer, misunderstanding or repetition of the stimulus word, even physiological arousal recorded with a galvanometer (an early lie-detector-style measure of skin response). What it reveals Where disturbances clustered around particular themes, Jung inferred an emotionally charged complex , a cluster of repressed, conflict-laden ideas and feelings snagging the smooth flow of association; this is where the everyday word 'complex' comes from. This rigorous, measurable work first won Freud's admiration and drew the two men together. It offered an early, semi-objective, partly quantitative route into the unconscious, anticipating later projective and reaction-time methods. Exam tip The Word Association Test, using reaction times to stimulus words to expose unconscious complexes, was Jung's creation. Panwar key Carl Jung created the word association test at the beginning of the 20th century to unravel the subconscious. Jung wanted to understand its manifestations and find appropriate channels to analyze it. Why the other options are wrong (a) Henry Murray Developed the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), where respondents tell stories about ambiguous pictures, and the needs/press theory (personology). Also a projective probe of unconscious motives, but not the structured stimulus-word/reaction-time method. (c) Sigmund Freud Accessed the unconscious through free association (an open-ended flow with no fixed word list) and dream analysis. The shared goal makes him the strongest distractor, but the formal, timed test was Carl Jung's. (d) Donald Winicott A British object-relations theorist known for the 'good-enough mother', the holding environment, transitional objects and, clinically, the Squiggle Game with children. Winnicott is a depth-psychology figure linked to child play techniques, not any word-association test. Behavioural / Learning Q56 Which ONE of the following theorists developed the concept of self-efficacy that has been used as a cognitive-behavioural theoretical explanation for how people change? a Aaron Beck b Albert Ellis c Albert Bandura d B.F. Skinner ✓ Answer: (c) Albert Bandura Albert Bandura, social-cognitive theory (from the 1960s) The concept Why (c) Albert Bandura coined and developed self-efficacy : a person's belief in their own capacity to organize and execute the actions needed to manage a situation or accomplish a specific task. Crucially it measures confidence in deploying skill, not actual skill, and it is task-specific rather than global. The theory Bandura embedded it in his social-cognitive theory : behaviour emerges from a three-way interplay of personal factors (beliefs, expectations), behaviour and environment, a loop he called reciprocal determinism . In Systems and Theories Behaviourism, founded by John B. Watson (1913) as a revolt against introspection, split into Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning, Edward Thorndike's connectionism and B. F. Skinner's radical operant behaviourism, all of which ignored inner mental events. Working from the 1960s, Bandura is the great bridge figure: he kept learning and observable behaviour but reintroduced cognition (expectations, beliefs, self-reflection), at the hinge between strict behaviourism and the cognitive revolution. Four sources Efficacy beliefs grow from mastery experiences (past successes, the strongest source), vicarious experiences (watching similar others succeed, tied to his observational-learning research), verbal persuasion (encouragement) and one's physiological and affective state (arousal read as nerves or readiness). High self-efficacy means harder goals, persistence through setbacks and rebound from failure; low self-efficacy breeds avoidance and early surrender. So shifting a belief about one's capability can shift action even before skill improves, which made it a leading cognitive-behavioural explanation for change. Exam tip Self-efficacy is a task-specific belief about one's ability to perform (Bandura), distinct from self-esteem, a global judgement of self-worth. Panwar key Psychologist Albert Bandura has defined self-efficacy as one's belief in one's ability to succeed in specific situations or accomplish a task. One's sense of self-efficacy can play a major role in how one approaches goals, tasks, and challenges. Why the other options are wrong (a) Aaron Beck The father of cognitive therapy : the cognitive triad (negative views of self, world, future), schemas and automatic thoughts. Also a cognitive-behavioural account of change, but Beck targeted distorted thinking, not belief in one's own task capability. (b) Albert Ellis Created REBT and the ABC model : an Activating event plus irrational Beliefs produce emotional Consequences. The shared first name 'Albert' is the trap; Ellis targeted irrational beliefs and disputing them, not self-efficacy. (d) B.F. Skinner Developed operant conditioning , reinforcement schedules and the Skinner box. The archetypal learning theorist, but his radical behaviourism deliberately excluded internal beliefs, and self-efficacy is exactly such an internal cognitive construct. Q57 ____ proposed that animals have the capacity to develop a mental representation, a cognitive map, of the place. a Tolman b Harlow c Kohler d Gould ✓ Answer: (a) Tolman Edward C. Tolman, purposive behaviourism (1930s-1940s) The concept Why (a) Edward C. Tolman proposed that animals form an internal mental representation, a cognitive map , of their environment. In Systems and Theories He worked in the 1930s-1940s, inside the strict behaviourism that John B. Watson founded in 1913 and that Clark Hull and others formalized as pure stimulus-response (S-R) learning driven only by reinforcement. Tolman broke ranks from the inside: he accepted the study of observable behaviour but insisted that intervening variables (purposes, expectancies, cognitive maps) sit between stimulus and response. His purposive behaviourism (or molar behaviourism) makes him a forerunner of the cognitive revolution that overturned behaviourism in the 1950s-60s. The maze studies Hungry rats explored a maze with no food reward; strict reinforcement theory predicted they would learn nothing. Yet once food was introduced, these previously unrewarded rats solved the maze almost immediately, matching rats rewarded from the start. Tolman concluded they had silently built a cognitive map, an internal picture of the maze's spatial layout, during their reward-free wandering. Latent learning The learning had occurred but stayed hidden until a motive (hunger plus reward) gave reason to display it: latent learning . It directly refuted the claim that learning requires reinforcement, showing behaviour can be guided by internal representations rather than mechanical S-R chains. Exam tip Tolman = cognitive map + latent learning + purposive behaviourism: learning can occur without reinforcement and be stored mentally, the seed of the cognitive turn against pure S-R psychology. Panwar key Tolman's experiments with rats demonstrated that organisms can learn even if they do not receive immediate reinforcement. Tolman placed hungry rats in a maze with no reward; as the unreinforced rats explored, they developed a cognitive map, a mental picture of the layout of the maze. When food was later placed in the maze, they navigated it as quickly as the rewarded group. This is known as latent learning. Why the other options are wrong (b) Harlow Ran rhesus-monkey studies (wire vs cloth surrogate mothers) showing contact comfort , not feeding, drives attachment . Harry Harlow is a tempting animal-learning name, but his work was the emotional basis of attachment, not spatial maps in mazes. (c) Kohler Gestalt psychologist Wolfgang Kohler showed insight learning in chimpanzees (Sultan stacking boxes for a banana, the sudden 'aha'). Like Tolman he opposed trial-and-error S-R accounts, but insight is sudden perceptual restructuring, not a stored spatial map. (d) Gould Linked in some texts to animal navigation and honeybee research, which superficially resembles spatial mapping. However, the cognitive map and the latent-learning maze paradigm are credited to Edward Tolman. Q58 ____ is defined by Rotter as "the potentiality of any behaviour occurring in any given situation as calculated in relation to any single reinforcement or set of reinforcements". a Behaviour potential b Expectancy c Reinforcement value d Punishment value ✓ Answer: (a) Behaviour potential Julian Rotter, social-learning theory (1950s) The concept Why (a) Julian Rotter defined behaviour potential as exactly this: the potentiality of any behaviour occurring in a given situation, calculated in relation to a single reinforcement or set of reinforcements. In Systems and Theories Rotter is a major social-learning theorist of the 1950s who, like Albert Bandura, sits at the bridge between strict behaviourism and cognitive psychology. Pure behaviourists (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner) predicted behaviour from external reinforcement alone; Rotter kept reinforcement central but added cognition , predicting behaviour from the meeting of the person's expectations and the perceived situation, not from drives or reinforcement history alone. This cognitive-behavioural emphasis is why he, Bandura and later cognitive theorists are seen as moving psychology past pure S-R determinism. Four variables Behaviour potential is the likelihood a response will occur in a specific situation, judged relative to the reinforcement it is expected to bring. Expectancy is the subjective probability the behaviour will actually produce that reinforcement. Reinforcement value is how much the person prefers that outcome over alternatives, and the psychological situation is the context as the person perceives it. The formula Behaviour potential is a function of expectancy and reinforcement value, so a high-potential behaviour is one the person both expects to pay off and strongly values the payoff from. Rotter is equally famous for locus of control , the belief that outcomes flow from one's own actions (internal) or from luck and powerful others (external), itself a kind of generalized expectancy. Exam tip Behaviour potential is the predicted likelihood of acting ; expectancy is the belief the act will be rewarded ; reinforcement value is how much that reward is wanted . Panwar key Behaviour potential, one of the four principles given by Rotter, is the likelihood of the occurrence of a behaviour. It is calculated in relation to any single reinforcement or set of reinforcements. Why the other options are wrong (b) Expectancy A genuine Rotter variable, hence the strongest trap: the subjective probability that a behaviour will lead to a reinforcement, an input to the formula. The quoted definition describes the output, the likelihood of the behaviour itself. (c) Reinforcement value Also a real Rotter variable: how much the person prefers a particular reinforcer over others, the outcome's desirability. The quoted definition concerns the potential for the behaviour to occur , so this confuses value with potential. (d) Punishment value Not one of Rotter's four named constructs at all, but a manufactured term mirroring 'reinforcement value'. His framework is built on reinforcement (expectancy, reinforcement value, behaviour potential, psychological situation). Q59 In ____ a stimulus which is originally neutral may become reinforcing by being associated with a reinforcing stimulus. a Primary reinforcement b Secondary reinforcement c Discrimination d Generalization ✓ Answer: (b) Secondary reinforcement B.F. Skinner's operant conditioning (1930s-50s) The concept Why (b) In secondary reinforcement an originally neutral stimulus becomes reinforcing by being paired with a stimulus that already reinforces. In Systems and Theories Reinforcement is the engine of operant conditioning , built by B.F. Skinner in the 1930s-50s as an extension of Thorndike's Law of Effect. This is the heart of behaviourism, founded by John B. Watson in 1913, and it stands opposite Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning (which pairs stimuli to elicit reflexes); secondary reinforcement is one way neutral stimuli gain motivational power within the operant line. Two kinds of reinforcer First separate the two. A primary reinforcer satisfies a biological need on its own with no learning (food, water, warmth, relief from pain); its power is innate. A secondary or conditioned reinforcer starts neutral with no inherent reward value and gains its power only by repeated association with a primary (or already-established) reinforcer. Examples and mechanism The classic example is money : it cannot be eaten or drunk, yet it reliably buys primary rewards; praise, grades, tokens and the clicker in animal training work the same way. It depends on contiguity : the closer in time the pairing, the more reinforcing value is absorbed, and a secondary reinforcer can in turn condition further neutral stimuli. The principle underlies token-economy programmes in clinical and educational settings, where tokens (secondary) are exchanged for primary rewards. Exam tip A primary reinforcer is rewarding innately ; a secondary (conditioned) reinforcer is rewarding only through learned association with a primary one. Panwar key The secondary reinforcement is the process in which a neutral stimulus acquires the ability to influence the future probability of a particular response by virtue of being paired with another stimulus that naturally enhances such probability. The proximity in time with the primary reinforcer makes the secondary reinforcer effective. Why the other options are wrong (a) Primary reinforcement Innately reinforcing and needs no learning (food, water, warmth, relief from pain). The natural opposite: the question's stimulus is 'originally neutral... becomes reinforcing by being associated', a learned, conditioned process. (c) Discrimination Learning to respond to one stimulus but not to a similar one (responding differently to different stimuli). It concerns which stimuli trigger a response, not how a neutral stimulus gains reinforcing power. (d) Generalization Responding similarly to stimuli that resemble the original conditioned stimulus, the mirror of discrimination. It describes the spread of a response across similar cues, not the conversion of a neutral stimulus into a reinforcer. Q60 The aim of ____ is characteristically forthright and objective: "given the stimulus, to be able to predict the response, and given the response to be able to predict the antecedent stimulus". a Structuralism b Behaviourism c Functionalism d Gestalt School ✓ Answer: (b) Behaviourism John B. Watson, who launched behaviourism (1913) The concept Why (b) Predicting the response from the stimulus, and the stimulus from the response, is the defining forthright, objective goal of behaviourism . In Systems and Theories John B. Watson launched behaviourism in 1913 with 'Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It' (the behaviourist manifesto), a sharp revolt against introspection . The schools before it looked inward: structuralism (Wilhelm Wundt, Edward Titchener) analysed conscious experience, functionalism (William James) studied the purpose of mind, and psychoanalysis probed the unconscious. Core claims Watson rejected consciousness, mind and soul as private and unscientific: psychology must be a purely objective natural science of observable, measurable, outwardly visible behaviour. Its unit of analysis is the stimulus-response (S-R) bond , the lawful link between an environmental input and a measurable behavioural output. Under strict determinism behaviour is fully caused by external stimuli, so the stimulus predicts the response and the response reveals the antecedent stimulus; that two-way predictability is the quoted aim, serving prediction and control . What came later The school was extended by Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning, Thorndike's Law of Effect and especially B. F. Skinner's operant conditioning, before the cognitive revolution of the 1950s-60s reintroduced internal mental processes. Exam tip Behaviourism studies observable S-R relations and aims at prediction and control, deliberately excluding the inner conscious states that structuralism and functionalism examined. Panwar key Behaviourism is the school that came in response to the internally-oriented psychoanalytic school and propounded the idea that behaviour is caused by external stimuli. It believes in strict determinism where, 'given the stimulus, to be able to predict the response, and given the response to be able to predict the antecedent stimulus'. Why the other options are wrong (a) Structuralism Wilhelm Wundt and Edward Titchener broke conscious experience into basic elements (sensations, feelings) through trained introspection . It is the very inward-looking school behaviourism rebelled against, the opposite of predicting observable S-R links. (c) Functionalism William James's school studied the purpose of mental processes in helping organisms adapt to their environment. It too was scientific and American, but it still concerned mind and consciousness serving adaptation, not deterministic S-R prediction. (d) Gestalt School Max Wertheimer, Wolfgang Kohler and Kurt Koffka stressed holistic perception: 'the whole is greater than the sum of its parts'. It explicitly opposed S-R reductionism; its concern is organized perception, not two-way S-R predictability. Q61 Bandura noted that most behaviour occurs in the absence of external rewards and punishment so that most behaviour stems from a negative reinforcement b self-regulation c reciprocal dualism d behavioural determinism ✓ Answer: (b) self-regulation Albert Bandura, self-regulation (social-cognitive theory) The concept Why (b) Albert Bandura held that most behaviour occurs without external reward or punishment, so it must stem from internal, self-generated control: self-regulation . Background In Systems & Theories, behaviourism (founded by John B. Watson in 1913, radicalized by B. F. Skinner) explained behaviour purely by external reinforcement and punishment. Bandura's social-cognitive theory (1960s onward) is the great bridge to the cognitive turn: it accepts learning and observable behaviour, but sees people as active agents who guide their own conduct, not mere reactors to outside reinforcement. That is why he noticed everyday behaviour persists with no external reinforcer, a fact pure operant theory struggles to explain. How it works Self-regulation is governing one's behaviour through internally set standards and self-administered consequences, in three steps: self-observation (monitoring one's own actions), judgement (comparing them against a personal standard or goal) and self-response (rewarding or sanctioning oneself with pride, satisfaction or self-criticism). Because these consequences are self-produced , not delivered by the environment, behaviour is sustained without external reward, explaining the bulk of human action. Related ideas Self-regulation works alongside self-efficacy , the belief in one's ability to achieve goals; both are cognitive elements that separate Bandura from strict behaviourists. His whole model rests on reciprocal determinism , the mutual, three-way influence of person, behaviour and environment, replacing the one-way environmental control of classic behaviourism. Exam tip Self-regulation is internal control through self-set standards and self-reward; external reinforcement (which Bandura said is usually absent) comes from outside the person. Panwar key Self-regulation and self-efficacy are two elements of Bandura's theory that rely heavily on cognitive processes. They represent an individual's ability to control their behaviour through internal reward or punishment, in the case of self-regulation, and their beliefs in their ability to achieve desired goals as a result of their own actions, in the case of self-efficacy. Why the other options are wrong (a) negative reinforcement A Skinnerian operant process: removing an aversive stimulus to strengthen a behaviour (e.g. taking a painkiller to end pain). Real, but an external consequence, exactly what Bandura said is usually absent. (c) reciprocal dualism A fabricated term made to sound like Bandura's real reciprocal determinism (the mutual influence of person, behaviour, environment). Misnamed, and in any case not the source of behaviour the question asks for. (d) behavioural determinism One-way control of behaviour by the environment, the classic behaviourist stance Bandura explicitly moved beyond. His point is that behaviour comes from internal self-direction, so this contradicts him. Q62 Behaviour, emitted spontaneously or voluntarily, that operate on the environment to change is called: a Opposition principle b Behaviour potential c Operant behaviour d Personal disposition ✓ Answer: (c) Operant behaviour B. F. Skinner, operant behaviour (radical behaviourism, 1930s) The concept Why (c) Operant behaviour is B.F. Skinner's name for behaviour emitted spontaneously or voluntarily that operates on the environment to produce change; because it operates on the environment, he called it operant. Background In Systems & Theories, Skinner was a radical behaviourist working from the 1930s, extending Thorndike's Law of Effect within the behaviourist movement John B. Watson founded in 1913. His operant conditioning deliberately contrasts with Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning, which deals with reflexes elicited by stimuli. Two kinds Respondent behaviour is reflexive and elicited automatically by a preceding stimulus (Pavlov's salivation to a tone): the basis of classical conditioning . Operant behaviour is not pulled out by a known stimulus but emitted freely; the organism acts on its surroundings, and the consequences decide whether it recurs: the basis of operant conditioning . How it works Behaviour is shaped by its consequences: reinforcement (positive or negative) raises the future probability of the response, punishment lowers it. In the operant chamber (Skinner box) a rat's lever-press for food is the textbook operant; Skinner also developed shaping (reinforcing successive approximations) and schedules of reinforcement, and this voluntary, consequence-driven view became the core of modern behaviour therapy. Exam tip Respondent behaviour is elicited by a stimulus and involuntary; operant behaviour is emitted voluntarily and controlled by its consequences. Panwar key Operant behaviour is voluntary rather than elicited and is contingent upon the environment change. Why the other options are wrong (a) Opposition principle Not a recognised behaviourist term for emitted, environment-operating behaviour: an invented label with no real referent in B. F. Skinner's or any standard learning framework. (b) Behaviour potential Julian Rotter's social-learning concept: the likelihood of a behaviour occurring given a particular reinforcement. It names a predicted probability , not a class of voluntary, environment-operating behaviour , which is Skinner's operant. (d) Personal disposition Gordon Allport's trait concept: a unique trait that characterizes an individual's personality structure. It belongs to trait/personality theory, not learning theory, so it has nothing to do with conditioned or emitted behaviour. Q63 J.B. Watson, the founder and father of behaviouristic school of psychology defined 'Psychology' as the science of ______. a Soul b Consciousness c Mind d behaviour ✓ Answer: (d) behaviour John B. Watson, behaviourist manifesto (1913) The concept Why (d) John B. Watson , founder and father of the behaviourist school, defined psychology as the science of behaviour , not of soul, mind or consciousness. Earlier definitions In Systems & Theories, the definition evolved. Ancient and philosophical thinkers studied the soul (from psyche ); Wilhelm Wundt (first laboratory, 1879) and Edward Titchener made it the study of the conscious mind through introspection , the structuralist programme; functionalism (William James) shifted focus to the purpose of mind. Watson's revolt In 1913 his behaviourist manifesto, the founding revolt against introspection, rejected all of these: soul, mind and consciousness are private, cannot be objectively observed or measured by an outsider, so have no place in a true natural science. Psychology must study publicly observable behaviour, its data being stimulus-response (S-R) pairs: humans and animals understood entirely through links between environmental stimuli and measurable responses. His stance Watson was radical , dismissing all reference to inner mental life, and stressed environment and conditioning over heredity (his 'give me a dozen healthy infants' claim). Ivan Pavlov, Edward Thorndike and especially B. F. Skinner later extended his programme, before the cognitive revolution reintroduced mind. Exam tip Watson defined psychology as the science of observable behaviour , deliberately excluding the unobservable soul, mind and consciousness of earlier definitions. Panwar key Watson was a radical behaviourist and rejected the ideas of soul, mind and consciousness. He was of the opinion that humans can be understood in terms of stimulus-response pairs. Why the other options are wrong (a) Soul The oldest, philosophical way of defining psychology (from the Greek psyche ). A tempting 'origins' answer, but Watson explicitly rejected the soul as unobservable and unscientific: the antithesis of his definition. (b) Consciousness The structuralist definition (Wilhelm Wundt, Edward Titchener), studied through introspection. It was the leading scientific definition just before Watson, but it is precisely the school he revolted against. (c) Mind The mentalistic definitions Watson dismissed. 'Mind' feels like psychology's natural subject, but he argued the mind is private and unmeasurable, replacing it with observable behaviour. Q64 John B. Watson is best known as the founder of a Behaviourism b Functionalism c Rationalism d Structuralism ✓ Answer: (a) Behaviourism John B. Watson, American psychologist, behaviourist manifesto (1913) The concept Why (a) John B. Watson , an American psychologist, is universally regarded as the founder and father of the behaviourist school. Background In Systems & Theories, the dominant approaches of the early 1900s all looked inward: structuralism (Wilhelm Wundt, Edward Titchener) analysed conscious experience through introspection; functionalism (William James) studied the purpose of mental processes in adaptation; Freudian psychoanalysis probed the unconscious. The manifesto In 1913 Watson published 'Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It', the behaviourist manifesto : psychology should abandon consciousness and introspection and become the objective science of observable behaviour, studied as stimulus-response relations. He framed it partly against psychoanalysis, which he judged speculative and unscientific, and partly against the introspective structuralists. Key ideas He stressed conditioning and the power of environment over heredity , claiming he could shape any healthy infant into any specialist (doctor, lawyer, beggar, thief) given control of its upbringing; his Little Albert study showed conditioned fear in a child. His founding act was later extended by Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning, Edward Thorndike's connectionism and especially B. F. Skinner's operant conditioning, before the cognitive turn of the 1950s-60s. Exam tip Watson founded behaviourism , the science of observable behaviour; structuralism and functionalism both still studied inner conscious experience. Panwar key John Watson, an American psychologist is regarded as the founder of behaviourism. He proposed this approach to psychology in response to Freudian Psychoanalysis. He regarded that behaviourism is the science of observable behaviour. Why the other options are wrong (b) Functionalism Led by William James (with John Dewey and Angell), studying the function of mind in adaptation. Like behaviourism it is American and practical, but it came earlier and still studied consciousness; Watson did not found it. (c) Rationalism A philosophical epistemology : knowledge comes mainly from reason, not the senses (René Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz). It belongs to philosophy, not psychology, and is nothing Watson founded. (d) Structuralism Founded by Wilhelm Wundt and Edward Titchener , analysing conscious experience via introspection. It is the school Watson directly opposed: he rejected and replaced it, he did not found it. Q65 If you express an attitude to a friend who then provides positive reinforcement, your attitude is likely to be ________. a Weakened b Strengthened c Both a and b d None of the above ✓ Answer: (b) Strengthened B.F. Skinner, positive reinforcement (operant conditioning) The concept Why (b) Positive reinforcement , by definition, increases the future likelihood of the behaviour it follows, so an attitude that earns approval becomes stronger. Background In Systems & Theories, reinforcement is the central mechanism of operant conditioning , developed by B.F. Skinner in the behaviourist tradition John B. Watson founded in 1913, building on Thorndike's Law of Effect. The behaviourist insight here: attitudes, like other learned responses, are shaped by their consequences. Key terms A reinforcer is any consequence that raises the probability the preceding behaviour will recur. Positive means a pleasant stimulus is added (praise, approval, money, attention), not that the outcome is morally good; reinforcement always means the behaviour increases . Applied here Your friend's approval is a positive reinforcer, so expressing and holding that attitude is rewarded, strengthened and more likely to recur. Contrast negative reinforcement , which also increases behaviour but by removing an unpleasant stimulus, and punishment (positive or negative), which decreases it; students often wrongly read 'positive' and 'negative' as good and bad instead of addition and subtraction. Exam tip Reinforcement of either kind always strengthens behaviour; only punishment or extinction weakens it. 'Positive' simply means a pleasant stimulus was added. Panwar key Positive reinforcement would lead to an increase in the occurrence of the behaviour preceding it. Hence, the attitude expressed in the above case are likely to be strengthened. Why the other options are wrong (a) Weakened The effect of punishment (adding an aversive or removing a pleasant consequence) or extinction (withholding reinforcement), not reinforcement. Positive reinforcement by definition increases behaviour, so this is the wrong direction. (c) Both a and b A single positive reinforcer cannot both strengthen and weaken the same response; reinforcement reliably strengthens . This catches students who are unsure of the direction and hedge. (d) None of the above A definite, correct option is present: strengthening is exactly what positive reinforcement produces, so (b) is precisely right. Q66 The law of effect was formulated by ________. a Thorndike b Skinner c Pavlov d Watson ✓ Answer: (a) Thorndike Edward L. Thorndike, Law of Effect (puzzle-box cats) The concept Why (a) Edward L. Thorndike formulated the Law of Effect , the foundational principle linking behaviour to its consequences. Background In Systems & Theories, Thorndike worked around 1898-1911, as functionalism gave way to the behaviourist era. His connectionism (learning as strengthening stimulus-response bonds, or 'connections') is a crucial bridge that fed directly into John B. Watson's behaviourism (1913) and especially B. F. Skinner's operant conditioning. The puzzle box A hungry cat in a latched puzzle box , food visible outside, had to act (press a lever, pull a loop) to escape and reach the food. At first it struggled randomly, but over repeated trials escape time fell as the successful action was selected and useless ones dropped out: trial-and-error learning (learning by selecting and connecting). The laws Law of Effect: responses followed by a satisfying consequence are 'stamped in' and become more likely; those followed by discomfort are 'stamped out'. He also proposed the Law of Exercise (connections strengthen with practice or use, weaken with disuse) and the Law of Readiness . This anticipated Skinner's operant conditioning, where reinforcement and punishment shape voluntary behaviour, and stands beside Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning as a twin pillar of learning theory. Exam tip The Law of Effect and trial-and-error puzzle-box learning belong to Thorndike; Skinner later built on it but did not formulate it. Panwar key Edward Thorndike initially proposed that humans and animals acquire behaviours through the association of stimuli and responses. He gave the Law of Effect, which specifies that any time a behaviour is followed by a positive consequence, that behaviour is likely to recur. Why the other options are wrong (b) Skinner The most tempting trap: his operant conditioning is the direct heir of the Law of Effect. But Skinner extended and renamed it (reinforcement, schedules); Thorndike stated the original law from puzzle-box cat studies before Skinner's work. (c) Pavlov Discovered classical conditioning , the reflexive pairing of a neutral stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus (the salivating dogs). That is involuntary respondent learning, not the consequence-based Law of Effect. (d) Watson Founded behaviourism in 1913 and championed conditioning; however, his contribution was the behaviourist programme and S-R methodology . Edward Thorndike had already stated the Law of Effect from his puzzle-box experiments. Q67 Who was the first to propose and establish Psychology as the scientific study of behaviour? a R.S. Woodworth b J.B. William c Wilhelm Wundt d N.L. Munn ✓ Answer: (d) N.L. Munn N.L. Munn per the key; conceptually John B. Watson (1913) The concept Why (d) The book credits N.L. Munn , author of widely used introductory psychology textbooks, with defining psychology as the scientific study of behaviour. His textbooks popularized this behaviour-centred definition for generations of students, which is why the key attributes it to him. The lineage In Systems & Theories, psychology's definition moved from the study of the soul , to the conscious mind under Wilhelm Wundt (first psychology laboratory, 1879; father of experimental psychology), to observable behaviour. The nuance The strict science-of-behaviour definition is historically the achievement of the behaviourist school: John B. Watson in 1913 insisted psychology study only observable, measurable behaviour and abandon introspection, and Edward Thorndike, Ivan Pavlov and B. F. Skinner carried it forward. Watson originated the stance conceptually; Munn is credited for the definitional statement in textbook form. Hold both in mind for the exam. Exam tip Wundt made psychology the science of conscious mind ; the science-of- behaviour definition belongs to the behaviourist line, credited in this key to Munn and conceptually originated by Watson in 1913. Panwar key According to the book's key, N.L. Munn is credited here. (Note: It is John B. Watson who first defined psychology strictly as the science of behaviour in 1913; the official answer is kept as printed.) Why the other options are wrong (a) R.S. Woodworth Known for dynamic psychology and the S-O-R model (adding the Organism between stimulus and response), plus a famous textbook. A textbook author of the same era, but not the one credited with first defining psychology as the science of behaviour. (b) J.B. William A garbled, non-existent name, likely a scrambling of 'J.B. Watson' and 'William James'. It matches no real founder of this definition: a typographic lure, not a genuine candidate. (c) Wilhelm Wundt Founded experimental psychology in 1879 and defined it as the study of consciousness via introspection, the tempting 'first/founder' answer. His subject was the conscious mind, not behaviour. Q68 The 'instinct theory' of motivation was developed by whom? a Sigmund Freud b William James c William McDougall d Abraham Maslow ✓ Answer: (c) William McDougall William McDougall (1871-1938), instinct theory of motivation The concept Why (c) William McDougall developed and systematized the instinct theory of motivation . Background In Systems & Theories, McDougall (1871-1938) was a British-American psychologist, key to social psychology and purposive (hormic) psychology . Working in the early 1900s as behaviourism rose, he argued against it that behaviour is fundamentally goal-directed, not mechanical; his is one of the earliest formal motivation theories, predating the drive-reduction theories of Clark Hull and the humanistic theories of Abraham Maslow. What an instinct is Begin with the key term: an instinct is an inborn, inherited disposition that energizes and directs behaviour toward a goal without needing to be learned. A set of innate instincts drives all purposive conduct, and each has three parts: cognitive (perceiving the relevant object), affective or emotional core (e.g. fear tied to the instinct of flight) and conative (the impulse to act toward the goal). Catalogue and critique He listed instincts such as flight (fear), curiosity, pugnacity (anger), reproduction and the parental/protective instinct, each paired with an emotion; because instincts supply both the energy and direction of behaviour, they are the prime movers of human action. Critics later said naming a separate instinct for every behaviour explained nothing ( circular reasoning ), which pushed the field toward drive and incentive theories. Exam tip The formal instinct theory of motivation is McDougall's, not James's, Freud's or Maslow's. Panwar key William McDougall developed the instinct theory of motivation by emphasizing that human behavior is largely goal-directed and rooted in inherited instincts. He proposed that instincts provide both the energy and direction for behavior, making them fundamental motivators of human action. Why the other options are wrong (a) Sigmund Freud Built a psychoanalytic instinct/drive theory around Eros (life/sexual, libido) and Thanatos (death). Same word 'instinct', but a depth-psychology account of unconscious drives, not a systematic catalogue of inherited motivational instincts. (b) William James Did write extensively on human instincts in his Principles of Psychology , and shares the first name 'William'. However, the formal theory (cognitive-affective-conative structure) is McDougall's, far fuller than James's descriptive list. (d) Abraham Maslow Proposed the hierarchy of needs , a humanistic motivation theory of ascending needs (physiological to self-actualization). A motivation theory, but not an instinct theory, and from a different, later school. Humanistic / Gestalt Q69 Which of the following perspectives of psychology is most concerned with the individuals reaching their maximum potential? a behavioural b Cognitive c Humanistic d Psychoanalysis ✓ Answer: (c) Humanistic Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers, humanistic third force (1950s) The concept Why (c) Of the four major systems, only humanism makes the drive to reach one's maximum potential the organising centre of its whole model of the person. The other forces In Systems & Theories, the first force , psychoanalysis (Sigmund Freud), explained people through unconscious drives, repressed conflict and early childhood, casting human nature as conflicted. The second force , behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner), reduced the person to learned stimulus-response links and reinforcement histories, refusing to study inner life; the cognitive view, a later development, studies how the mind encodes, stores and retrieves information. The third force Against the pessimism and determinism of the first two forces, Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers launched humanistic psychology in the 1950s, joined by Rollo May. Its premise: human nature is fundamentally positive and growth-oriented, and every person carries an innate push to become the fullest version of themselves. Key concepts Maslow called this self-actualization , the apex of his hierarchy of needs; Rogers described the fully functioning person , guided by an actualizing tendency . Humanism studies the whole individual, conscious experience and free will, valuing subjective striving over external control: an artist who creates not for reward but to express their deepest capacities is self-actualizing. Exam tip Humanistic psychology, the third force , is built around self-actualization and reaching one's full potential; neither the cognitive (information processing) nor the behavioural (conditioning) school fits. Panwar key Humanistic psychology believes in the positivity of human nature and is based on the ideas of self-actualization (realising and reaching one's full potential) and a fully functioning individual. Why the other options are wrong (a) behavioural The second force (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner): action explained purely by observable stimulus-response learning and reinforcement, ignoring inner mental life. It has no concept of inner growth; the person is shaped from outside, not striving from within. (b) Cognitive Studies how the mind processes information: attention, memory, perception, language and thinking. It does concern the inner mind, unlike behaviourism, but its focus is mental mechanics, not personal fulfilment or self-actualization. (d) Psychoanalysis Sigmund Freud's first force : behaviour traced to unconscious conflict, repressed drives and early experience, a markedly less optimistic view. Its aim is resolving buried conflict, not realising positive potential. Q70 Who is the founder of Positive Psychology? a Howard Gardner b Steve Pinker c Bandura d Seligman ✓ Answer: (d) Seligman Martin Seligman, APA president (1998), with Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi The concept Why (d) Martin Seligman is recognised as the founder of modern positive psychology as a scientific discipline. The crucial distinction is between coining a phrase and launching a field. Who coined it The term first appeared in Abraham Maslow's 1954 book Motivation and Personality , but stayed a passing label within the humanistic tradition. In Systems & Theories, humanistic psychology (the third force, Maslow and Carl Rogers) first insisted on studying strengths rather than pathology, but was criticised for lacking scientific rigour and hard data; positive psychology is its empirical heir. Launching the field During his 1998 term as president of the American Psychological Association , Seligman made human strengths and well-being his theme, arguing psychology had spent decades fixated on disorder while neglecting what makes life worth living. With Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (originator of flow , the state of absorbed engagement), he defined it as the scientific study of positive human functioning and flourishing across individual, relational and institutional levels. What set him apart His insistence on the scientific method : measuring happiness, optimism, character strengths and engagement empirically, not only theorising. Concrete products: learned optimism (a reversal of his earlier 'learned helplessness' research) and the PERMA model of well-being. Exam tip Maslow coined the term within humanism; Seligman is the founder who built positive psychology into a rigorous empirical science. Panwar key Martin Seligman and Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi define positive psychology as "the scientific study of positive human functioning and flourishing on multiple levels." Martin Seligman is a pioneer of Positive Psychology (the term itself was coined by Abraham Maslow), not simply because he has a systematic theory about why happy people are happy, but because he uses the scientific method to explore it. Why the other options are wrong (a) Howard Gardner Famous for the theory of multiple intelligences (linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical and others), which challenged the single-IQ view. A major modern psychologist on positive human capacities, but his domain is intelligence and cognition. (b) Steve Pinker Cognitive scientist, linguist and popular author (Steven Pinker) on language, the mind and evolutionary psychology ( The Language Instinct ). He writes optimistically about human progress but neither coined nor founded positive psychology. (c) Bandura Founded social-cognitive theory , with self-efficacy and observational learning (the Bobo doll studies). Self-efficacy is a positive, strength-focused construct, but his framework is social-cognitive learning theory, not positive psychology. Q71 Which psychology emerged as the fourth force? a Experiential b Behaviouristic c Transpersonal d Psychoanalytic ✓ Answer: (c) Transpersonal Abraham Maslow and others, fourth force (around 1968) The concept Why (c) Transpersonal psychology is the school explicitly named the fourth force in psychology. The numbering In Systems & Theories the forces are a historical sequence: first, psychoanalysis (Sigmund Freud), unconscious drives and early conflict; second, behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner), observable, conditioned responses; third, humanistic psychology (Abraham Maslow, Carl Rogers, May), growth, free will and self-actualization, a reaction against the determinism of the first two. The fourth force Around 1968 , Maslow was among those who announced a fourth force for experiences the first three could not capture: spirituality, transcendence, mystical states and peak experiences beyond the individual ego. 'Trans-personal' means 'beyond the personal': the self can extend past ordinary identity into a wider, sometimes spiritual, awareness, like the unity reported in deep meditation. Link to humanism Maslow helped found both; the fourth force grew out of the third when humanists found self-actualization sometimes opened onto transcendent experiences their framework could not explain. Yet the two are counted as separate forces. Exam tip Transpersonal psychology is the fourth force, distinct from psychoanalysis, behaviourism and humanism, and defined by transcendence and spiritual experience. Panwar key In 1968 Maslow was among the people who announced transpersonal psychology as a "fourth force" in psychology, in order to distinguish it from the three other forces of psychology: psychoanalysis, behaviourism and humanistic psychology. Why the other options are wrong (a) Experiential Not one of the named forces. The word echoes humanistic and Gestalt language about lived, present experience, but no historically numbered 'force' carries this name. (b) Behaviouristic The second force (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner), not the fourth. It studies observable, conditioned behaviour and explicitly rejects the inner and spiritual phenomena of the transpersonal fourth force, so it is doubly wrong. (d) Psychoanalytic The first force (Sigmund Freud), not the fourth. It does explore hidden, non-conscious mind, but that is the personal unconscious, not transcendence beyond the ego. Q72 Maslow considers physiological and safety needs truly as a Higher needs b Lower needs c Greatest potency needs d Transformational needs ✓ Answer: (b) Lower needs Abraham Maslow, hierarchy of needs (1943) The concept Why (b) In Maslow's framework, physiological and safety needs sit at the very base of the pyramid: the basic, lower tier. Background In Systems & Theories, Abraham Maslow , a founder of humanistic psychology (the third force, with Carl Rogers), offered a humanistic alternative to behaviourist drive-reduction and Freudian instinct theory. His 1943 paper A Theory of Human Motivation arranged human motives in an ascending hierarchy. The pyramid Picture a five-level pyramid: at the bottom physiological needs (food, water, sleep, warmth), then safety needs (security, shelter, stability). The lower four levels (physiological, safety, social, esteem) are deficiency needs (D-needs): they arise from deprivation and create tension until satisfied. The top level, self-actualization, is a growth need (B-need, for Being), driven by the desire to develop rather than fill a lack. Prepotency Under prepotency , lower needs must be reasonably met before higher ones motivate, which is exactly why these are called lower: a starving person is preoccupied with food long before reputation or growth. Calling them 'lower' is about position, not importance; they are in fact the most urgent. Exam tip Physiological and safety needs are the lower, basic deficiency needs at the foundation of Maslow's hierarchy. Panwar key Maslow's hierarchy is most often displayed as a pyramid. The lowest levels of the pyramid are made up of the most basic needs. Needs at the bottom of the pyramid are basic physical requirements including the need for food, water, sleep, and warmth. Physiological, security, social, and esteem needs are deficiency needs, which arise due to deprivation. Why the other options are wrong (a) Higher needs In Maslow's model these are esteem and especially self-actualization, at the top of the pyramid. Physiological and safety needs sit at the base: the lower, prepotent needs that must be met before higher ones activate. (c) Greatest potency needs Not a Maslow term. A clever trap, since physiological needs ARE the most prepotent (most urgent and dominant when unmet), but Maslow's actual classification is 'lower' (basic) needs. (d) Transformational needs Not part of Maslow's hierarchy at all: a fabricated-sounding label that may appeal because self-actualization involves personal transformation. No level carries this name, least of all the base. Q73 Which ONE of the following is not a major construct of existential theory? a Coming to terms with anxiety b Confronting the universal fears of death c Uncovering our unconscious fears and desires d Understanding our ultimate isolation ✓ Answer: (c) Uncovering our unconscious fears and desires Freudian psychoanalysis, not existential theory (May, Frankl, Yalom) The concept Why (c) Uncovering unconscious fears and desires is a psychoanalytic aim, not an existential one, so it is the construct that does not belong. Background In Systems & Theories, existential psychology is a close cousin of humanism; both belong to the broad 'third force' reaction against Sigmund Freud and behaviourism. Where Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers stressed positive growth, existential thinkers like Rollo May , Viktor Frankl and later Irvin Yalom focused on the harder 'givens' of existence, drawing on philosophers such as Kierkegaard, Heidegger and Sartre. The givens Irvin Yalom names four ultimate concerns: death (confronting our mortality), freedom (and the responsibility it imposes), isolation (being ultimately alone) and meaninglessness. Therapy centres on coming to terms with the anxiety these produce, so a person lives authentically rather than fleeing into avoidance; death, isolation and anxiety, three of the options, map directly onto these. The odd one out Excavating buried, unconscious fears and desires is the project of Freudian psychoanalysis (the first force), which assumes hidden material from early life drives present behaviour and that cure comes from making the unconscious conscious. Existential therapy works with conscious, present awareness of existence: it asks how you will live with given truths, not what repressed wish lurks beneath. Exam tip Existential theory deals with death, freedom, isolation and meaning; uncovering the unconscious belongs to psychoanalysis. Panwar key Uncovering unconscious desires is a part of psychoanalytic theory and not existential theory. Why the other options are not the answer (a) Coming to terms with anxiety True: often called existential angst, anxiety is the natural response to confronting freedom, death and isolation. Anxiety also features in psychoanalysis and other therapies, but here it is squarely existential. (b) Confronting the universal fears of death True: one of Irvin Yalom's four ultimate existential concerns, arguably the defining one. It may seem morbid, but death awareness is the heart of existential theory. (d) Understanding our ultimate isolation True: another of Yalom's existential givens. However connected we are, each person ultimately faces existence alone; bleak, but a core existential concern. Q74 ______ is associated with the Gestalt school of psychology. a John Watson b William James c Ivan Pavlov d Max Wertheimer ✓ Answer: (d) Max Wertheimer Max Wertheimer, with Koffka and Kohler, phi phenomenon (1912) The concept Why (d) Max Wertheimer is the founder most directly associated with the Gestalt school of psychology. Background In Systems & Theories, Gestalt psychology arose in early-twentieth-century Germany against structuralism (Wilhelm Wundt, Edward Titchener), which broke consciousness into elementary sensations, and against the atomism of associationism. The German word Gestalt means 'form', 'shape' or 'whole': perception organises sensory elements into wholes that are more than the sum of their parts ('the whole is other than the sum of its parts'). The phi phenomenon Wertheimer launched the movement in 1912 with the phi phenomenon , the illusion of apparent motion when two stationary lights flash in sequence (the basis of cinema and neon signs). It proved the mind actively constructs experience rather than passively recording isolated sensations, directly refuting the structuralist program. Key figures His collaborators Kurt Koffka and Wolfgang Kohler (famous for insight learning in chimpanzees) made up the three founders; their work later influenced cognitive psychology and, through Fritz Perls , Gestalt therapy. Seeing a melody as a unified tune rather than separate notes is a classic Gestalt illustration. Exam tip Max Wertheimer, with Koffka and Kohler, founded Gestalt psychology: phi phenomenon and whole-over-parts. Contrast John Watson (behaviourism), William James (American functionalism) and Ivan Pavlov (classical conditioning). Panwar key Max Wertheimer was one of the founders of Gestalt Psychology alongside Kurt Koffka and Wolfgang Kohler. Why the other options are wrong (a) John Watson Founded behaviourism in 1913 ('Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It'), studying only observable stimulus-response behaviour. It emerged almost alongside Gestalt but is the opposite: it rejects the study of perception and inner organisation. (b) William James Led American functionalism and wrote The Principles of Psychology , studying how mental processes help organisms adapt. Functionalism concerns the purpose of mind, not the German Gestalt focus on perceptual wholes. (c) Ivan Pavlov Known for classical conditioning and reflexology (the salivating-dog experiments). His behavioural/physiological tradition of learned reflexes is the antithesis of Gestalt's holistic perception. Q75 Humanistic and Phenomenological approaches have been criticised for: a Focusing too much on Cognitive Processes involved in forming perceptions of the self b Missing the wider social and cultural contexts that influence experiences and its identities c Neglecting to include personal experiences and perceptions that influence how we form identity d Focusing too much on past experience and how they tend to shape identity ✓ Answer: (b) Missing the wider social and cultural contexts that influence experiences and its identities Sociological and cross-cultural critics of humanism The concept Why (b) Humanistic and phenomenological approaches concentrate so heavily on the individual's inner world that they can overlook the social and cultural forces that shape it. The approach In Systems & Theories, the phenomenological method, inherited from philosophers like Husserl and central to humanistic psychology (the third force), studies experience from the person's own first-person point of view, treating subjective perception as the proper object of study. Carl Rogers built person-centred therapy around the self-concept and personal frame of reference; Abraham Maslow traced motivation to needs within the person. Strength and weakness This inward focus was a deliberate corrective to behaviourism's neglect of inner life and psychoanalysis's deterministic drives, and is the school's defining strength. It is also the root of the standard criticism from sociological and cross-cultural critics: privileging the self neglects the social, cultural, economic and political structures that shape how identity forms. Example Someone raised in poverty, under caste oppression or within a particular cultural script is moulded by forces the purely individual lens can miss; even self-actualization may reflect Western, individualistic assumptions. Critics also note that heavy reliance on subjective experience makes the approach hard to test with rigorous scientific methods. Exam tip The recognised weakness of humanistic and phenomenological psychology is neglect of wider social and cultural context, precisely because they centre the individual's inner experience. Panwar key Humanistic and phenomenological approaches focus more on the internal aspects of the individuals rather than the wider social and cultural aspects. Why the other options are wrong (a) Focusing too much on Cognitive Processes involved in forming perceptions of the self The self-concept does involve perception, but these approaches stress holistic, felt, subjective experience, not information-processing cognition (the cognitive school's territory), so this is not the criticism they attract. (c) Neglecting to include personal experiences and perceptions that influence how we form identity The exact opposite of the truth, set to catch careless reading: phenomenological and humanistic psychology are precisely the schools that prioritise personal experience and subjective perception. (d) Focusing too much on past experience and how they tend to shape identity That criticism fits the psychodynamic approach, which roots present behaviour in early childhood. Humanism stresses the present, future potential and the actualizing tendency, so this misassigns a psychoanalytic weakness. Q76 In order from lowest to highest, what are Maslow's classes of needs? a Social-esteem-physiological-safety-selfactualization b Physiological-Safety-social-self-actualization-esteem c Physiological-safety-social-esteem-self actualization d Self-actualization-esteem-safety-social-physiological ✓ Answer: (c) Physiological-safety-social-esteem-self actualization Abraham Maslow, hierarchy of needs (1943) The concept Why (c) It is the exact lowest-to-highest order of Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs ; only this option preserves the genuine ascent without swapping any level. Background In Systems & Theories, Maslow, a founder of humanistic psychology (the third force) with Carl Rogers, proposed in his 1943 paper A Theory of Human Motivation that motivation is arranged in tiers people climb from the bottom up, a humanistic alternative to behaviourist and Freudian accounts. The five levels Build it level by level: physiological (food, water, sleep, warmth), safety (security, stability), social (love, belonging, acceptance; also called belongingness needs), esteem (respect, achievement, self-worth), and at the summit self-actualization (realising one's full potential). The first four are deficiency needs arising from a lack; the top is a growth need driven by the desire to develop. Prepotency Under prepotency , a lower-level deficit need must be reasonably satisfied before the next level becomes a strong motivator: someone struggling for safety is not driven mainly by esteem, and someone fighting for basic survival rarely pursues growth projects first. Knowing the order cold is the whole test here. Exam tip The ascending sequence is physiological, safety, social, esteem, self-actualization: deficiency needs below, the single growth need on top. Panwar key Maslow (1943) initially stated that individuals must satisfy lower level deficit needs before progressing on to meet higher level growth needs. Maslow gave the basic needs (Physiological, Safety, Social needs) and then the Higher order needs (Self-esteem and Self-actualization). Maslow said that once these basic needs are achieved then higher order needs are achieved. Why the other options are wrong (a) Social-esteem-physiological-safety-selfactualization Scrambles the base, placing physiological and safety ABOVE social instead of at the foundation. In Maslow's prepotency rule, survival needs always come first. (b) Physiological-Safety-social-self-actualization-esteem A near-miss that swaps the top two: esteem (the fourth level) must precede self-actualization (the fifth and highest), so reversing them breaks the hierarchy. (d) Self-actualization-esteem-safety-social-physiological The whole hierarchy inverted, highest need first, catching anyone who misreads 'lowest to highest' as 'highest to lowest'. Reading direction matters: self-actualization is the top, not the start. Q77 Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers were the proponents of ______ approach a Cognitive approach b Behavioural approach c Humanistic approach d Existential approach ✓ Answer: (c) Humanistic approach Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers, humanistic third force (1950s) The concept Why (c) Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers are the two defining proponents of the humanistic approach. Background In Systems & Theories, by the mid-twentieth century psychoanalysis (the first force) and behaviourism (the second force) dominated, both seen as deterministic and pessimistic. Maslow and Rogers founded humanistic psychology in the 1950s as the third force , an explicit alternative restoring the whole person, free will and the positive potential of human nature to the centre of the field. Maslow's pillar The hierarchy of needs , a model of motivation culminating in self-actualization , the realisation of one's full potential; he also described the qualities of self-actualized people and their peak experiences . Rogers' pillar Person-centred (client-centred) therapy and the theories of the self-concept, the ideal self, the actualizing tendency and unconditional positive regard , the warm, non-judgmental acceptance that lets a person grow. Both stress the whole individual over isolated behaviours or symptoms, conscious experience, free will and a growth-oriented view of human nature; treating clients as capable of self-direction, not objects to be shaped, is a concrete marker of humanism. Exam tip Maslow and Rogers are the proponents of the humanistic approach, the third force focused on the whole person and self-actualization. Contrast cognitive (information processing), behavioural (conditioning and reinforcement) and existential (a near relative: meaning, freedom, confronting death). Panwar key Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers were humanistic psychologists and the proponents of the humanistic approach to psychology, which looks at the whole individual & focuses on concepts such as free will, self-efficacy, and self-actualization. Why the other options are wrong (a) Cognitive approach Studies mental processes such as memory, attention, perception and thinking, linked to figures like Ulric Neisser and George Miller . Its subject is information processing, not the whole-person growth model Maslow and Rogers built. (b) Behavioural approach John B. Watson and B. F. Skinner: observable conditioning and reinforcement, rejecting the study of inner experience. It is the very second force humanism reacted against, the opposite of Maslow and Rogers's emphasis on inner experience and free will. (d) Existential approach Rollo May and Viktor Frankl : the closest distractor, sharing the third-force, whole-person spirit. But its specific focus is meaning, freedom, responsibility and death; Maslow and Rogers are specifically the humanists. Q78 The striving for fulfilment of one's potential is called a Self-concept b Self-efficacy c Self-Actualization d The ideal Self ✓ Answer: (c) Self-Actualization Abraham Maslow, self-actualization (top of the hierarchy of needs) The concept Why (c) Self-actualization is precisely the term for striving to fulfil one's full potential. Background In Systems & Theories, it is the centerpiece of humanistic psychology (the third force, founded by Abraham Maslow and Rogers as an answer to behaviourism and psychoanalysis) and sits at the very top of Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs as the highest growth need . What it is Maslow defined it as the drive to become everything one is capable of becoming, realising one's talents, creativity and deepest capacities once the lower deficiency needs are reasonably met. A self-actualized individual is autonomous, accepting of self and others, problem-centred and prone to peak experiences of profound fulfilment. Related terms Carl Rogers' fully functioning person lives openly and authentically in line with their true self, propelled by the actualizing tendency. Distinguish self-concept (one's overall self-image), self-efficacy (a Bandura term from social-cognitive theory: belief in succeeding at specific tasks) and the ideal self (Rogers: the person one wishes to be); only self-actualization names the active striving toward full potential itself. Exam tip Realising one's full potential is self-actualization, the peak of Maslow's hierarchy. Panwar key According to Maslow's theory of hierarchy of needs, an individual strives for fulfilling one's full potential. He termed this process as striving for self-actualization and a person who has achieved this is called a self-actualized individual. Why the other options are wrong (a) Self-concept The overall organised set of beliefs and perceptions one holds about oneself (a key Rogers construct). A humanistic 'self' term, but a static self-image, not the active striving to fulfil potential. (b) Self-efficacy Albert Bandura's social-cognitive term: belief in one's ability to succeed at a specific task or situation. It sounds achievement-oriented, but it is task-specific confidence, not the broad drive to realise one's whole potential.
