It tells you how well a set of items hang together as a measure of a single underlying construct. Worked intuition for the formula: if the items are perfectly redundant (each measures the same thing), the sum of item variances is small relative to the total test variance (because the items covary heavily and that covariance inflates the total), the bracket approaches 1, and alpha approaches 1. If the items are unrelated, the total variance is close to just the sum of the item variances, the bracket approaches 0, and alpha collapses. So alpha rises with (a) more items, k, and (b) higher average inter-item correlation. Conventional benchmarks to memorise: alpha at or above 0.70 is acceptable for research, at or above 0.80 is good, at or above 0.90 is excellent and is the level demanded for high-stakes individual clinical or selection decisions where a single person's score carries consequences. High-yield Alpha cut-offs are near-certain MCQs: 0.70 acceptable, 0.80 good, 0.90 excellent / high-stakes minimum. Alpha is the generalised internal-consistency coefficient: KR-20 is just Cronbach's alpha applied to dichotomous (right/wrong) items, so anything true of alpha is true of KR-20 for binary data. Exam trap A very high alpha (above about 0.95) is not automatically a good thing : it usually signals item redundancy (several items asking nearly the same question in slightly different words), which wastes test length and narrows construct coverage. Second, alpha does NOT prove unidimensionality : a scale measuring two correlated sub-traits can still post a high alpha simply by having many items, so "a high alpha shows the scale measures one thing" is a false statement the paper loves to plant. Alpha presupposes unidimensionality; it does not demonstrate it. To test dimensionality you need factor analysis, not alpha. Kuder-Richardson formulas: KR-20 and KR-21 When items are dichotomously scored (right/wrong, 1/0, true/false, pass/fail), Cronbach's alpha reduces to the Kuder-Richardson 20 (KR-20) . KR-20 uses each item's proportion of examinees passing (p) and failing (q = 1 minus p), summing the product p × q across all items in place of the item variances (for a binary item, the variance is p × q). KR-21 is a simplified hand-calculation shortcut that assumes every item has the same difficulty , so it needs only the test mean and total-score variance rather than item-by-item statistics. Because real items always differ in difficulty, that equal-difficulty assumption is optimistic in the wrong direction, and so KR-21 is always a lower-bound (more conservative, smaller) estimate than KR-20 on the same data. Exam trap KR-20 and KR-21 are only for dichotomously scored items . For polytomous items (5-point Likert agreement, partial-credit marking) you must use Cronbach's alpha, of which KR-20 is the special binary case. A question that pairs "KR-20" with a "5-point Likert scale" is testing exactly this error. Also keep the direction straight: KR-21 (assumes equal difficulty) is the smaller, more conservative of the two; do not state it as the upper bound. Correction for attenuation Because no real measure is perfectly reliable, the observed correlation between two variables is always weaker than the true correlation between the underlying constructs: random measurement error blurs each variable and so attenuates (shrinks) their correlation. The correction for attenuation formula estimates what the correlation would have been if both measures were perfectly reliable: r true = r xy / square root of (r xx × r yy ) , where r xy is the observed correlation and r xx , r yy are the reliabilities of the two measures. You are dividing the observed correlation by the geometric mean of the two reliabilities, mathematically stripping out the blurring effect of unreliability. Worked example: two scales correlate at r xy = 0.40, with reliabilities r xx = 0.64 and r yy = 0.81. The disattenuated correlation is 0.40 / sqrt(0.64 × 0.81) = 0.40 / sqrt(0.5184) = 0.40 / 0.72 = 0.56. The true constructs are more strongly related (0.56) than the noisy measures suggested (0.40). If you wish to correct for the unreliability of only one variable (say only the criterion), you put just that one reliability under the root: r = r xy / sqrt(r yy ). High-yield The correction for attenuation always increases the correlation (you divide by a number less than 1). It answers "what would the correlation be if both tests were perfectly reliable?". This is why unreliability is said to set a ceiling on observable validity: a predictor cannot correlate with a criterion more strongly than the square root of the product of their reliabilities allows. C. Item analysis parameters Item analysis is the quality control of test construction. After a draft test is trialled, you examine each item with two questions: "is it pitched at the right difficulty?" and "does it actually separate the able from the less able?". Three statistics answer these, and the examiner builds entire questions around their cut-off numbers and their counter-intuitive directions. Item difficulty index (p-value) The item difficulty index is simply the proportion of examinees who answered the item correctly, denoted p . Its name is a trap built into the statistic itself: a higher p means an easier item (more people got it right), so it is really a "facility" or "easiness" index despite being called difficulty. The range runs from 0 (nobody passed, impossibly hard) to 1 (everybody passed, trivially easy). Items at the extremes carry almost no information: an item everyone passes or everyone fails cannot tell two examinees apart. The most informative items sit around p = 0.50 , because an item passed by exactly half the group maximally discriminates between high and low scorers and contributes the most variance. For a multiple-choice item with guessing, the optimal p is nudged upward from 0.50 to the midpoint between perfect (1.0) and the chance level: for a 4-option MCQ where chance is 0.25, the ideal p is roughly (1.0 plus 0.25) / 2 = 0.625, because some passes are lucky guesses that should be discounted. Item discrimination index (d) Definition Item discrimination index: d = P(upper 27%) minus P(lower 27%), that is, the proportion of the top-scoring 27% of examinees who got the item right minus the proportion of the bottom-scoring 27% who got it right. It measures how sharply an item distinguishes high overall performers from low overall performers, and it ranges from minus 1 to plus 1. The 27% figure is Kelley's classic split : dividing at the upper and lower 27% maximises the expected difference between the two extreme groups for a normal distribution while still keeping enough cases in each group for a stable estimate (a tighter split, say the top 10%, gives a cleaner contrast but fewer, noisier cases; 27% is the optimum trade-off). Interpretation cut-offs to memorise: d at or above 0.40 is excellent; 0.30 to 0.39 is good; 0.20 to 0.29 is marginal (revise); below 0.20 is poor (drop or rewrite). A negative d is the red flag of item analysis: it means the weaker students passed the item more often than the stronger students, which almost always signals a miskeyed answer, an ambiguous stem, or a distractor that is accidentally more defensible than the keyed response. Worked example: if 80% of the top group and 30% of the bottom group answer an item correctly, d = 0.80 minus 0.30 = 0.50, an excellent discriminator; if 45% of the top group but 60% of the bottom group pass it, d = 0.45 minus 0.60 = minus 0.15, a faulty item to be pulled. Point-biserial correlation The point-biserial correlation (r pb ) is the correlation between performance on a single dichotomous item (right/wrong, coded 1/0) and the total test score (continuous). It is the standard index of item-total consistency : a high positive point-biserial means the examinees who got this item right also tended to score high on the test as a whole, so the item is pulling in the same direction as the rest of the test and earns its place. It is conceptually a smoother, correlation-based cousin of the d index: both ask "do good students do better on this item?", but where d uses only the extreme 27% groups, the point-biserial uses every examinee's full total score, so it is statistically more efficient. Like d, a near-zero point-biserial means the item is not discriminating, and a negative point-biserial flags a miskeyed or flawed item. Memory aid " p for pass, d for distinguish. " The p-value tells you how many passed (high p = easy); d tells you whether the item distinguishes strong from weak (high d = good discriminator). The target item is moderate-p (around 0.50) and high-d (above 0.30). And remember the counter-intuitive direction once more: a big p is an easy item. Exam trap High p means easy , not hard: the most common error on this topic. A negative discrimination (negative d or negative point-biserial) does not mean "a hard item"; it means a defective item, usually miskeyed. Do not confuse the point-biserial (a true dichotomy, the actual right/wrong outcome, correlated with a continuous total) with the biserial coefficient (used when the dichotomy is artificial , a continuum forced into two groups): item analysis uses the point -biserial because right/wrong is a genuine two-category split. D. Item Response Theory (IRT): modern psychometrics Classical Test Theory has a crippling limitation that IRT was built to escape: its statistics are sample-dependent . An item's CTT difficulty (p) looks "easy" in a bright sample and "hard" in a weak one; an item's discrimination shifts with the spread of the group; and a person's total score depends entirely on which particular items they happened to be given. None of these numbers are properties of the item or person alone; they are tangled together. Item Response Theory cuts the tangle by modelling the probability of a correct response as an explicit mathematical function of a single underlying latent trait, theta (the person's ability or standing on the construct), with item parameters that are, ideally, invariant across samples. This invariance is the whole reason IRT exists. Definition Latent trait (theta): the unobservable underlying ability or attribute (general intelligence, depression severity, mathematical skill) that IRT estimates for each person. Crucially, theta is placed on the same scale as item difficulty, so a person and an item can be compared directly: a person with theta = 1.5 has a better-than-even chance on any item whose difficulty b is below 1.5. The IRT models build up by progressively adding parameters, and each model plots an item characteristic curve (ICC) , an S-shaped (logistic) curve showing the probability of a correct response (vertical axis) against theta (horizontal axis). As ability rises, the probability of success rises along the S. Model Parameters What it models 1PL / Rasch b only (item difficulty) Items differ only in difficulty; discrimination is assumed equal across all items, so all ICCs are parallel and differ only in left-right position. The b parameter is the theta value at which a person has exactly a 50% chance of a correct response (the curve's inflection point). 2PL b and a Adds the discrimination parameter a , the steepness of the ICC at its inflection. A steeper curve (higher a) means the item sharply separates people whose ability is near its difficulty; a shallow curve discriminates weakly. 3PL b, a, and c Adds the pseudo-guessing parameter c , the lower asymptote : the probability that a very-low-ability examinee still gets the item right purely by guessing (about 0.25 for a 4-option MCQ). The left tail of the curve now flattens out at c instead of dropping to zero. Worked reading of an ICC: suppose an item has b = 0.0, a = 1.5, c = 0.20. The curve starts at probability 0.20 on the far left (a near-zero-ability guesser), rises steeply (because a = 1.5 is fairly high) through its midpoint at theta = 0.0 (where the probability is halfway between c and 1), and approaches 1.0 on the far right. Change b to plus 2.0 and the whole curve slides rightward (a harder item, needing more ability for the same success probability); raise a and the curve becomes more vertical (a more discriminating item); raise c and the entire left tail floats up (more guessing gets through). Exam trap Know exactly which parameter each model adds, in order: 1PL = difficulty b; 2PL adds discrimination a; 3PL adds guessing c. The Rasch model is mathematically the 1PL but philosophically distinct: Rasch insists the data must fit the model (discrimination is fixed equal by assumption, and misfitting items are discarded), whereas the 1PL pragmatically estimates one common discrimination value from the data. Also keep the scales straight: the b parameter lives on the same scale as theta (so a "difficult" item has a high b), while a is a slope and c is a probability floor. Swapping a (discrimination) for b (difficulty) is the standard distractor. Item and Test Information Functions In IRT the single global reliability coefficient of CTT is replaced by information , a quantity that can vary along the trait scale. The Item Information Function (IIF) shows how much measurement precision a given item supplies at each level of theta. An item delivers its most information for examinees whose ability is near its own difficulty b (an item of medium difficulty is wasted on very able or very unable people, who are far from the point where the item discriminates), and a high-discrimination (high-a) item produces a tall, narrow information peak, while a low-a item gives a short, broad one. The Test Information Function (TIF) is simply the sum of all the item information functions, showing where along the trait continuum the whole test measures most precisely. The decisive consequence is that the standard error of measurement in IRT equals the inverse square root of information and is therefore conditional on theta : a test can be highly precise for average examinees yet imprecise at the extremes. This is precisely the engine of computer-adaptive testing , which after each response selects the next item that supplies maximum information at the examinee's current estimated theta, narrowing the error band with the fewest possible items. Differential Item Functioning (DIF) Differential Item Functioning (DIF) occurs when examinees of equal underlying ability (matched on theta) but drawn from different groups (gender, language, culture, region) have different probabilities of answering a particular item correctly. DIF is the modern, rigorous operationalisation of item bias: because the two groups are equated on the trait itself, any residual group difference on the item must come from something construct-irrelevant in the item (a culturally loaded word, a context familiar to one group only, a translation artefact). It is detected with methods such as the Mantel-Haenszel statistic (which compares performance group-by-group within ability strata) or by directly comparing the item characteristic curves estimated separately in each group: if the ICCs do not overlap, the item functions differently for the two groups. DIF should not be confused with a mere difference in average scores between groups (that could be a true ability difference); DIF is a difference that survives matching on ability. High-yield The four headline advantages of IRT over CTT, a classic "which is NOT an advantage" item: (1) item parameters are sample-invariant (do not drift with the group); (2) person ability and item difficulty sit on one common scale and can be compared directly; (3) precision is expressed as information that varies across the trait rather than a single fixed reliability; (4) it enables computer-adaptive testing and rigorous bias detection through DIF. Memory aid Parameters add alphabetically downward through the curve: b moves it sideways (difficulty), a tilts it (the a ngle / discrimination), c lifts its floor (the c hance of guessing). "1, 2, 3 PL = 1 adds difficulty, 2 adds discrimination, 3 adds the chance of a correct guess." E. Construct validation and matrix analysis Reliability asks "is the measure consistent, free of random error?"; validity asks the deeper, more important question "does it measure what it claims to measure?". The two are separable: you can be perfectly reliable yet completely invalid. A bathroom scale read to two decimal places is exquisitely reliable, but it is an invalid measure of intelligence. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity; in fact reliability sets a mathematical ceiling on validity (the attenuation logic above). This subsection covers the quantitative tools the paper tests: Lawshe's content-validity ratio, the standard error of estimate in criterion prediction, the Campbell-Fiske multitrait-multimethod matrix, and the nomological network that frames them all. Lawshe's Content Validity Ratio (CVR) Content validity is the degree to which a test's items adequately sample the entire domain of the construct (a depression scale that asked only about sleep would have poor content validity, however reliable). Lawshe (1975) turned expert judgement of this into a number with the Content Validity Ratio: CVR = (n e minus N/2) / (N/2), where n e is the number of expert panellists who rate a given item as "essential" and N is the total number of panellists. The logic is built around the halfway point: if exactly half the panel call an item essential (n e = N/2), the numerator is zero and CVR = 0; if every expert calls it essential (n e = N), CVR = (N minus N/2)/(N/2) = plus 1; if none do, CVR = minus 1. Worked example: with N = 10 experts of whom n e = 9 call an item essential, CVR = (9 minus 5)/5 = 4/5 = 0.80. Items whose CVR falls below a critical value (which depends on panel size; the more experts, the lower the threshold needed for statistical significance) are dropped from the test. Averaging the CVRs of the surviving, retained items gives the overall Content Validity Index (CVI) for the test. Standard error of estimate When you use one test to predict a criterion (an aptitude test predicting later job performance, an entrance score predicting degree marks), the standard error of estimate (SE est ) is the standard deviation of the prediction errors, the residuals: it indexes how far, on average, the actual criterion scores fall above or below the values the regression line predicts. SE est = SD y × square root of (1 minus r 2 ) , where r is the validity coefficient (the correlation between predictor and criterion) and SD y is the standard deviation of the criterion. The higher the validity, the smaller the prediction error: at r = 1 the line passes through every point and SE est = 0; at r = 0 the predictor is useless and SE est equals the full SD y . Worked example: SD y = 20 and validity r = 0.60 give SE est = 20 × sqrt(1 minus 0.36) = 20 × sqrt(0.64) = 20 × 0.80 = 16. Notice the structural parallel to the SEM: SEM uses reliability under the root (the spread of an observed score around a true score), whereas SE est uses validity-squared (the spread of an actual criterion score around its predicted value). Same algebraic shape, two different jobs. The Multitrait-Multimethod (MTMM) matrix Campbell and Fiske (1959) gave the definitive procedure for establishing construct validity , splitting it into two complementary halves. Convergent validity is the requirement that a measure correlate with other measures of the same trait (two anxiety scales should agree). Discriminant validity is the equally important requirement that it not correlate too strongly with measures of different traits (an anxiety scale should not correlate as highly with a depression scale as two anxiety scales do, otherwise it is not measuring anything distinct). To test both at once, you measure several traits by several methods (for example, anxiety, depression and hostility, each assessed by self-report, by clinician rating, and by peer report) and arrange all the resulting correlations in the MTMM matrix. Four kinds of correlation appear in it, and naming each correctly is the single most-tested point in this whole subsection: Cell type Same / different trait Same / different method What it should show Monotrait-monomethod Same trait Same method The reliability diagonal : same trait measured by the same method = the highest values in the whole matrix (these are reliability coefficients). Monotrait-heteromethod Same trait Different method Convergent validity: the same trait measured by different methods should still correlate highly. These are the "validity diagonals" and should be large and significant. Heterotrait-monomethod Different trait Same method Method bias / a discriminant check: different traits that merely share a method. Should be LOW; if they are high, the shared method is artificially inflating the correlation (common-method variance). Heterotrait-heteromethod Different trait Different method Should be the LOWEST values of all: these cells share neither trait nor method, so there is nothing to make them correlate. They form the floor of the matrix. Worked reading of the matrix: to claim a trait is validly measured, you check (in order) that its convergent value is high; that this convergent value exceeds the heterotrait-heteromethod cells in the same row and column (the trait survives a method change better than unrelated things do, establishing discriminant validity); and that it also exceeds the heterotrait-monomethod cells (the trait correlation beats the pure method correlation, so trait variance dominates method variance). If a heterotrait-monomethod cell is as high as your convergent cell, your "measure" is really just measuring the method, not the trait. High-yield Campbell and Fiske's decision rules: (1) convergent (monotrait-heteromethod) values should be substantial and significantly greater than zero; (2) each convergent value should exceed the heterotrait-heteromethod values in its row and column (discriminant validity holds); (3) it should also exceed the heterotrait-monomethod values, or else method variance is swamping trait variance. The reliability diagonal (monotrait-monomethod) is always the highest set of all. Memory aid " Mono " = same, " hetero " = different; read trait first, method second. Monotrait-heteromethod = convergent (the same trait survives a change of method = good, want it HIGH). Heterotrait-monomethod = method bias (different traits look alike only because the method is shared = bad, want it LOW). Convergent wants high; discriminant wants low. Nomological networks Cronbach and Paul Meehl (1955) framed the whole enterprise with the nomological network : the wider theoretical web of lawful relationships ("nomological" from the Greek nomos , law) that links a construct to other constructs and to observable behaviours. Construct validity, in their account, is established by showing that the measure behaves exactly as the surrounding theory predicts it should. A valid depression measure should correlate positively with hopelessness and rumination, correlate negatively with life satisfaction, rise after a bereavement, and fall with effective treatment; each confirmed prediction is a strand of the network supporting validity, and each disconfirmed prediction either weakens the measure or forces revision of the theory. The MTMM matrix, convergent and discriminant evidence, and criterion prediction all sit inside this larger nomological framework as specific kinds of network-confirming evidence; it is the overarching concept, and a favourite "which is the broadest framework for construct validity" answer. Exam trap Keep the validity types distinct. Content validity = expert judgement that items sample the domain (Lawshe's CVR). Criterion validity = correlation with an external standard, either concurrent (now) or predictive (later), indexed by the validity coefficient and SE est . Construct validity = the overarching question, evidenced through convergent and discriminant data (MTMM) within the nomological network. The paper will offer "face validity" as a distractor: face validity is merely whether the test looks valid to a lay test-taker and is the weakest, most superficial form, not the same as content validity (which uses qualified experts and a quantified ratio). F. Variable control architecture in experimental design An experiment's entire job is to attribute changes in the dependent variable (DV) to the independent variable (IV) and to nothing else , which means systematically controlling the extraneous variables that could otherwise offer a rival explanation. An uncontrolled extraneous variable that actually covaries with the IV becomes a confound and destroys internal validity. Before any control technique can be applied, the variables must be operationalised : an operational definition specifies a construct by the concrete operations used to manipulate or measure it (for example "anxiety = the score on the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory", or "frustration = a blocked goal in a fixed-time puzzle"). Operationalisation is indispensable for replicability, but it has a recognised limit: any single operational definition captures only one facet of a rich construct (the STAI does not exhaust "anxiety"), so a confident construct claim needs multiple operationalisations converging on the same result. With variables defined, the control techniques you must be able to name and rank are: Elimination: physically remove the extraneous variable altogether (run every trial in a sound-proof room so that ambient noise simply cannot vary). It is the cleanest control when feasible, but most nuisance variables (a participant's mood, intelligence, prior experience) cannot literally be removed. Constancy (holding constant): when a variable cannot be eliminated, fix it at one single level for every participant (test everyone at 10 a.m., use the same room, the same instructions, the same experimenter). The variable still exists but is prevented from varying , so it cannot covary with the IV. The cost is reduced external validity: results proven only at 10 a.m. may not generalise to other times. Matching: equate the groups on a known nuisance variable by pairing participants with similar values and splitting each pair across conditions (for every treatment participant with IQ 110, place a control participant of IQ 110). Matching controls that specific, named variable precisely, but it controls only the variables you thought to match on and remains blind to unknown ones. Randomisation (random assignment): the single most powerful control technique. Allocating participants to conditions purely by chance distributes all extraneous variables, both the ones you know about and the ones you have never imagined, evenly across the groups on average. It is the only technique that controls variables you have not even thought of, which is exactly why random assignment is the defining feature of a "true" experiment and the gold standard for internal validity. (Note the distinction from random sampling , which concerns external validity / generalisation; random assignment concerns internal validity / causal inference.) Counterbalancing: used specifically in within-subjects (repeated-measures) designs, where every participant experiences every condition and so the order of conditions could confound the treatment through practice, fatigue or carryover. Counterbalancing systematically varies that order across participants (half do A then B, half do B then A) so that order effects spread evenly across conditions and cancel rather than masquerading as a treatment effect. Latin Square designs Complete counterbalancing means running every possible order of conditions, but the number of orders is k-factorial, which explodes quickly: 3 conditions give 6 orders, 4 give 24, 5 give 120, soon demanding impractically many participants. A Latin Square provides efficient partial counterbalancing. It is a k × k grid (k = the number of conditions) in which each condition appears exactly once in every row and exactly once in every column . Reading each row as one participant's sequence, this guarantees that across the design every condition occupies every ordinal position (first, second, third, ...) equally often, which balances simple, position-linked order effects (progressive practice and fatigue) using only k sequences instead of k-factorial. Worked example for k = 3 conditions A, B, C, one valid Latin square is the rows (A B C), (B C A), (C A B): column 1 holds A, B, C once each, column 2 holds B, C, A once each, and so on, so each condition is run first once, second once, and third once. High-yield The defining property of a Latin square is " each condition once per row and once per column ". It controls position / order (practice and fatigue) effects efficiently with k sequences. Counterbalancing in general, including the Latin square, belongs to within-subjects designs; randomisation is the corresponding tool for between-subjects designs. Exam trap Randomisation controls unknown extraneous variables; matching controls only the specific variable matched. This is the classic discriminator, and the paper plants it almost every year: if a question stresses that the technique handles variables "the experimenter has not anticipated", the answer is randomisation, never matching. A second trap: a Latin square balances position (order) effects but does not control differential carryover (asymmetric sequence effects, where the after-effect of condition A on a later B differs from that of B on a later A). For differential carryover you need full counterbalancing or a washout interval, not a Latin square. Do not say a Latin square "fully counterbalances": it only partially counterbalances. G. Causal pathway modelling: mediators vs moderators This pair is one of the most reliably tested distinctions in the entire research-methods syllabus, precisely because students confuse them so consistently. The two words sound alike and both describe "a third variable", yet they answer completely different questions and are tested completely differently. Get the core contrast first, then the machinery for each. Definition A mediator explains the mechanism : it is the intervening variable through which X transmits its effect to Y, so the causal chain is X causes M, and M causes Y. It answers how or why X affects Y. A moderator changes the strength or direction of the X-to-Y relationship depending on the moderator's own level; it sits to the side of the X-to-Y arrow rather than on the chain. It answers when , for whom , or under what conditions X affects Y. Worked illustration to fix the distinction. Suppose stress (X) predicts illness (Y). A mediator account: stress raises cortisol (M), and cortisol suppresses immunity, producing illness; cortisol is the mechanism on the chain, stress to cortisol to illness. A moderator account: the stress-to-illness link is strong for people with poor social support and weak for those with good support; social support (Z) does not lie on the causal chain, it dials the strength of the stress-to-illness arrow up or down. The same study can contain both: cortisol mediates how stress harms health, while social support moderates for whom it does so. Mediation: Baron and Kenny's causal steps and the Sobel test Baron and Kenny (1986) gave the classic four-step procedure for establishing mediation, using paths conventionally labelled c, a, b and c-prime: Step 1: X significantly predicts Y (path c , the total effect , is significant: there is an effect to be explained). Step 2: X significantly predicts the mediator M (path a : X actually moves the proposed mechanism). Step 3: M significantly predicts Y while controlling for X (path b : the mechanism affects the outcome over and above X). Step 4: when M is entered into the model, the X-to-Y effect shrinks . If it drops all the way to non-significance, that is full mediation (M accounts for the entire effect); if it weakens but remains significant (the reduced path c-prime ), that is partial mediation (M accounts for some of the effect, with a direct route remaining). The indirect effect , the amount of X's influence on Y that travels through M, is the product of the two constituent paths, a × b . The total effect decomposes as c = c-prime + (a × b): direct path plus indirect path. The Sobel test evaluates whether that indirect effect a × b is statistically significant by dividing it by its pooled standard error (a formula combining the standard errors of a and b) to yield a z statistic; a z beyond plus or minus 1.96 means significant mediation at the 5% level. Worked sketch: if a = 0.50 and b = 0.40, the indirect effect is 0.50 × 0.40 = 0.20, and the Sobel test asks whether 0.20 is large relative to its standard error. Because the sampling distribution of the product a × b is skewed (non-normal) in small samples, modern practice prefers bootstrapped confidence intervals for the indirect effect (the Preacher and Hayes approach: if the bootstrap CI excludes zero, mediation is supported) over the assumption-laden Sobel test, but you must still know the Sobel logic, because it is what the exam names. Moderation: interaction terms A moderator is tested in an entirely different way: by entering the product interaction term X × Z into a regression alongside the main effects of X and of Z. The regression is Y = b 0 + b 1 X + b 2 Z + b 3 (X × Z). If the coefficient on that product term, b 3 , is statistically significant, then Z moderates the X-to-Y relationship: the slope of Y on X is no longer constant but changes across levels of Z (the X effect is steeper at high Z than at low Z, say). To reduce the multicollinearity that arises because X and Z each correlate strongly with their own product, the predictors are usually mean-centred (each value minus its mean) before the product is computed, which also makes the lower-order coefficients interpretable at the average level of the other variable. When the moderator is categorical (sex, treatment group), the equivalent strategy is multi-group analysis: fit the model separately in each group, or use multi-group structural equation modelling, and test whether the X-to-Y path differs across groups. High-yield The two are tested by two different statistics, and the paper rewards knowing which goes with which: mediation is established through the indirect effect a × b (Baron and Kenny's steps, the Sobel test, or a bootstrap CI); moderation is established through the product interaction term X × Z in a regression. A mediator reduces the X-to-Y effect when added (full = to non-significance, partial = it merely weakens); a moderator produces a significant interaction . Memory aid Mediator = Mechanism, the Middle man (the how/why), sitting ON the chain X to M to Y. Moderator = Modifies the strength of the arrow (the when/for whom), sitting OFF to the side. Mediation uses a × b and the Sobel test; moderation uses the X × Z interaction term. Two M-words, two questions, two tests. Exam trap Do not say a moderator "explains why" X affects Y: that is a mediator's job (mechanism). A moderator never explains the effect; it only specifies the conditions under which the effect is stronger, weaker, or reversed. Conversely, do not test a mediator with an interaction term or a moderator with the Sobel test: matching the wrong analysis to the concept is the favourite trap here. And remember that a single variable can serve as both in a "moderated mediation" model, so the labels describe a variable's role in a given path, not a fixed property of the variable. H. Design typologies: factorial, quasi-experimental, single-subject Once you can control extraneous variables (Section F) and model causal pathways (Section G), the next question is how to arrange conditions into a design. The examiner's standard move here is a one-line scenario ("a researcher compares two intact classrooms before and after a new curriculum") and four design names as options; you win the mark by matching the structural signature of the scenario to the correct design. This subsection teaches the three families that dominate the paper: fully randomised factorial designs, quasi-experiments (treatment without randomisation), and single-subject designs (one participant as their own control). True factorial designs and higher-order interactions A factorial design manipulates two or more independent variables (called factors ) simultaneously, crossing every level of each factor with every level of the others, so it yields both main effects (the separate effect of each factor averaged over the others) and interaction effects (the effect of one factor depends on the level of another). The naming convention reads off the design directly: a 2 × 3 design crosses one two-level factor with one three-level factor, producing 2 × 3 = six cells (treatment combinations); a 2 × 2 × 4 design has three factors and 16 cells. The number of numbers tells you how many factors there are; the numbers themselves tell you the levels. Definition A main effect is the effect of one factor on the dependent variable, averaged across all levels of the other factor(s). An interaction effect exists when the effect of one factor is not constant but changes across the levels of another factor. A 2 × 3 design tests two main effects (one per factor) and one two-way interaction. The great efficiency of the factorial design is precisely its ability to detect interactions, which a series of separate one-variable studies could never reveal. Worked example: suppose factor A is a drug (placebo vs active) and factor B is therapy (none vs CBT). If the drug lowers depression by 5 points with no therapy but by 12 points when combined with CBT, the effect of the drug depends on the level of therapy : that is an A × B interaction, and no two single-factor experiments run in isolation could have found it. A higher-order interaction (a three-way A × B × C interaction) means a two-way interaction itself changes across the levels of a third factor; these are real but hard to interpret and demand large samples for adequate power, because the variance is sliced into ever smaller cells. High-yield The unique payoff of a factorial design is the interaction effect . When an interaction is significant, you must interpret it before the main effects, because a main effect can be misleading in the presence of an interaction (a "qualified" main effect). On an interaction graph, non-parallel lines = interaction present; parallel lines = no interaction ; crossing (disordinal) lines signal the strongest interactions, where the direction of an effect reverses across levels of the other factor. Quasi-experimental designs A quasi-experiment tests a treatment but lacks random assignment to conditions, often because randomising is unethical or impossible (you cannot randomly assign children to two existing schools, or randomly allocate a flood). This missing ingredient is decisive: without randomisation the groups may differ systematically before the treatment, so the design is exposed to selection-based confounds and its internal validity is weaker than a true experiment's. The three named designs each manage that weakness differently: Nonequivalent control group design: a treatment group and an intact (non-randomised) comparison group are both pre-tested and post-tested. The pre-test is the saving feature: it lets you check how comparable the groups were to start with. The signature threat is selection and the selection-by-maturation interaction , because the groups may have differed at baseline and may also change at different rates. Interrupted time-series design: a single group is measured repeatedly at many points before and after the intervention (the "interruption"). A genuine treatment effect shows as a change in the level (a jump) or the slope (a change in trend) of the series at exactly the intervention point, against the backdrop of the pre-existing trend. The chief threat is history : some other event coinciding with the intervention could produce the same discontinuity. Regression-discontinuity design: participants are assigned to treatment by a strict cut-off on a continuous assignment variable (for example, everyone scoring below 40 on a screening test receives remedial tutoring; everyone at or above 40 does not). A treatment effect appears as a discontinuity (a vertical jump) in the regression line of outcome on the assignment variable at the cut-off . Because assignment is governed by a fully known rule, the design has stronger causal warrant than other quasi-designs and, in the narrow band just either side of the cut-off, approaches the inferential strength of a true randomised experiment. How it is tested: the paper typically describes the assignment mechanism and asks you to name the design. The diagnostic cue is the assignment rule, not the outcome. A cut-off score that decides who gets treated is always regression-discontinuity; many measurements across time on one group is interrupted time-series; two intact pre-tested groups is the nonequivalent control group design. Single-subject (single-case) designs Single-subject designs study one participant (or a few) intensively across time, using each participant as their own control by comparing behaviour across phases rather than across groups. They are central to applied behaviour analysis and to clinical case research, where group designs are often impractical. The logic is that a behaviour that changes only when (and each time) the treatment is applied is hard to explain by anything other than the treatment. AB design: a baseline phase (A) followed by a treatment phase (B). It is the simplest but weakest design, because any change at B could be coincidental (a history or maturation event happening to fall at the same time), so it cannot establish a causal effect on its own. ABA (reversal/withdrawal): baseline, treatment, then withdrawal of treatment back to baseline. If behaviour improves under B and reverts when the treatment is removed, the treatment is implicated, because the behaviour tracks the treatment's presence and absence. Its ethical problem is that it ends on baseline (the participant is left without the helpful treatment). ABAB: adds a second treatment phase, so it both demonstrates the effect twice (much stronger causal evidence, two replications within one case) and ends on treatment (ethically preferable). This is the workhorse reversal design. Multiple-baseline design: used when reversal is impossible or unethical. Some effects cannot be reversed (you cannot un-teach a learned reading skill), and withdrawing a helpful treatment is often undesirable. Here treatment is introduced in a staggered sequence across several baselines: across subjects , across behaviours , or across settings . Each baseline should change only when its own treatment begins, and the staggering means a single external (history) event cannot explain why each baseline shifted at its own different time. Exam trap The reason to choose a multiple-baseline over an ABAB is precisely to demonstrate experimental control without therapeutic withdrawal : it controls the history threat by staggering the introduction of treatment, not by reversing it, so you never take away a working treatment and you never rely on the behaviour being reversible. ABAB requires the behaviour to be reversible; multiple-baseline does not. A scenario that says "the treatment teaches an irreversible skill" is steering you to multiple-baseline. I. Taxonomy of validity threats Campbell and Stanley's classic taxonomy of threats divides into internal validity (did the treatment truly cause the observed effect, free of confounds?) and external validity (does the effect generalise beyond this particular study, sample, and setting?). This is the single most scenario-tested topic in the methodology syllabus: the examiner gives a vignette and asks which specific threat it illustrates, so you must learn each threat by its signature , the structural feature that distinguishes it from its near neighbours. Internal-validity threats are about confounds inside the study; external-validity threats are about whether the finding travels outside it. Internal validity threats Threat Signature History An external event (not the treatment) occurs between pre- and post-test and affects the outcome. The cue is "something happened in the world" during the study. Maturation Internal changes within participants over time (growing older, more tired, more practised, spontaneously recovering) cause the change, not the treatment. (Localised maturation = a specific developmental trajectory present in one group only.) Testing Taking the pre-test itself changes performance on the post-test (practice on the items, sensitisation to the content). The cue is that the act of measuring caused the change. Instrumentation The measuring instrument changes over time: a tool drifts out of calibration, raters fatigue or grow lenient ("instrumentation decay"), or the scoring standard shifts. The participants are stable; the ruler moved. Statistical regression (regression to the mean) Groups selected for extreme scores drift back toward the mean on retesting purely as a statistical artefact, mimicking a treatment effect. The cue is selection on an extreme score. Selection Pre-existing differences between groups (arising from non-random assignment) rather than the treatment cause the difference. The cue is intact, self-selected, or non-randomised groups. Selection-maturation interaction The non-equivalent groups also mature at different rates, a combined confound common in quasi-experiments. Attrition (experimental mortality) Participants drop out non-randomly, so the groups that finish differ from the groups that started. Differential attrition (different dropout rates or reasons across groups) is the dangerous form. Compensatory equalisation Administrators or staff, feeling the control group is being deprived, give it extra resources, shrinking the real treatment difference. Worked discrimination: imagine a remedial programme is offered to the lowest-scoring 10% of a class, and on retest their scores rise. The naive reading is "the programme worked", but two threats compete. Statistical regression predicts that an extreme-low group will rise toward the mean on any retest with no treatment at all, and selection notes the group was chosen precisely for being extreme. A defensible design needs an equally extreme untreated comparison group to separate the real treatment effect from regression to the mean. Recognising that this specific scenario (selection on extremes plus retest gains) screams regression to the mean is a recurrent paper item. External validity threats Selection × treatment interaction: the treatment works only for the particular (often unrepresentative) sample studied, so it does not generalise to other populations (a therapy validated only on university volunteers may not transfer to an elderly clinical sample). Setting × treatment interaction: the effect holds only in the specific setting (a tightly controlled lab, one specialist clinic) and fails to transfer to ordinary settings (ecological generalisation fails). Reactive arrangements / Hawthorne effect: participants change their behaviour simply because they know they are being studied, not because of the treatment. (Named for the Hawthorne Works productivity studies, where output rose under almost any change in conditions, including reverting to the original conditions.) Demand characteristics: participants pick up cues about the hypothesis and consciously or unconsciously behave to confirm (or deliberately sabotage) it. Experimenter expectancy / Rosenthal effect: the experimenter's expectations unintentionally bias how they treat participants or record data, producing a self-fulfilling result. The double-blind procedure (neither participant nor experimenter knows the condition) is the standard control. Memory aid Internal-validity threats are about confounds inside the study (was it really the treatment?); external-validity threats are about generalising outside it (does it travel?). For the reactive trio: Hawthorne = being watched changes you; demand characteristics = the participant guesses the hypothesis; Rosenthal/expectancy = the experimenter's bias leaks out. All three are fixed by blinding. Exam trap Do not confuse testing (the pre-test changes the participant, an internal-validity confound) with the selection × treatment external-validity threat (the pre-test sensitises participants so the result only generalises to pre-tested populations, sometimes called "reactive testing"). Likewise, maturation is change inside the person, whereas history is change in the world; both occur over the same passage of time, and the only discriminator is whether the cause was internal or external. J. Inferential statistics: the hypothesis-gating parameters Before any specific test, inferential statistics rests on a small set of "gating" parameters that decide what counts as evidence: the theorem that licenses the use of normal-based tests, the two kinds of decision error, the threshold (alpha) at which we reject the null, and the probability (power) of detecting a real effect. These ideas are abstract but among the most heavily and repeatedly tested in the whole paper, often as direct definitional MCQs. Central Limit Theorem Definition The Central Limit Theorem (CLT): regardless of the shape of the parent population, the sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution as sample size increases, with the approximation generally adequate at N ≥ 30 . Its standard deviation (the standard error of the mean) equals the population standard deviation divided by the square root of N. The CLT is the large-sample licence to use z and t: parametric tests assume the sampling distribution of the mean is normal, not that the raw data are normal, and the CLT guarantees that normality once N is reasonably large even when the population is skewed. Worked example: a population of reaction times is heavily right-skewed with standard deviation 200 ms. If you draw samples of N = 64, the standard error of the mean is 200 / square root of 64 = 200 / 8 = 25 ms, and the distribution of those sample means is approximately normal despite the skewed parent. This is why a t-test on means of 64 skewed scores is defensible while the same test on the 64 individual scores might not be. Note the standard error shrinks with the square root of N: quadrupling the sample halves the standard error. Type I and Type II errors Null is actually TRUE Null is actually FALSE Reject null Type I error (alpha) : false positive Correct (power, 1 minus beta) Retain null Correct Type II error (beta) : false negative A Type I error (alpha) is rejecting a true null hypothesis: claiming an effect that is not real (a false positive). Alpha is set by the researcher in advance, conventionally at 0.05, meaning a 5% willingness to cry wolf. A Type II error (beta) is failing to reject a false null: missing a real effect (a false negative). The two errors trade off against each other along the decision threshold: pushing the threshold to make false positives rarer inevitably makes false negatives commoner, holding everything else constant. Memory aid Picture the boy who cried wolf. Crying "wolf" when there is none is the Type I (alpha) false alarm. Staying silent when the wolf is really there is the Type II (beta) miss. Alpha is the error you set ; beta is the error you estimate . "Type 1 = 1 false alarm, the positive you should not have made." Statistical power Power = 1 minus beta: the probability of correctly detecting an effect that truly exists (correctly rejecting a false null). The convention is power ≥ 0.80, so beta ≤ 0.20, accepting a 20% miss rate. Four things raise power: Larger sample size (N): the single most controllable lever; a bigger N shrinks the standard error, narrowing the sampling distributions so true and null distributions overlap less. Larger effect size (gamma): bigger true effects are easier to detect (this is a property of nature, not under your control, but it is estimated in advance for sample-size planning). A larger (more lenient) alpha: raising alpha from 0.01 to 0.05 increases power by moving the rejection threshold, but at the cost of more Type I errors. This is the fundamental alpha-power trade-off. Lower error variance / one-tailed tests: reducing measurement noise (better instruments, tighter procedures) or using a directional test concentrates the test's sensitivity where the effect is expected. Worked intuition: two studies test the same true effect of d = 0.5. The first uses N = 20 per group and achieves power around 0.34 (it will miss the real effect about two-thirds of the time, an underpowered study). The second uses N = 64 per group and achieves power around 0.80. Same true effect, same alpha, but the larger sample buys the detection probability. This is exactly why a non-significant result from a tiny study is uninformative: it may reflect low power, not absence of effect. High-yield Power = 1 minus beta. The cleanest way to raise power without inflating Type I error is to increase N . Lowering alpha (say to 0.01) reduces Type I error but reduces power too (raises beta). Alpha and beta trade off; only sample size and effect size buy you out of the trade-off. Exam trap "Increasing power requires increasing alpha" is a half-truth distractor: raising alpha does raise power, but at the cost of more false positives, so it is not the recommended route. The recommended route is increasing N , which raises power while leaving alpha untouched. Also: power is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null, not the probability the null is false. K. Effect size formulations A p-value tells you only whether an effect exists (whether it is distinguishable from chance); an effect size tells you how big the effect is, on a scale independent of sample size. This matters because a large enough sample renders even a trivially small effect "statistically significant", so effect sizes (and confidence intervals around them) are now mandatory reporting in every major journal and a favourite paper topic. The two families are standardised mean differences (the d family) and proportion-of-variance-explained indices (the eta and omega family). Cohen's d: the standardised mean difference, d = (mean 1 minus mean 2 ) / SD pooled , using the pooled standard deviation of the two groups in the denominator. It expresses the gap between two means in standard-deviation units. Benchmarks: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. ( Hedges' g is the small-sample-corrected version, applying a downward correction factor because d is slightly biased upward in small samples.) Eta-squared (eta 2 ): for ANOVA, the proportion of total variance explained by a factor = SS effect / SS total . Benchmarks: 0.01 small, 0.06 medium, 0.14 large. Partial eta-squared (partial eta 2 ): SS effect / (SS effect + SS error ): it removes other factors' variance from the denominator, so it asks what proportion of the variance not already explained by the other factors this factor explains. In multi-factor designs the partial values are larger than ordinary eta-squared and (a common trap) can sum to more than 1. Omega-squared (omega 2 ): a less biased, more conservative estimate of variance explained, preferred for small samples because eta-squared overestimates the population effect. Omega-squared adjusts for the number of groups and the error variance, pulling the estimate down toward the true population value. Worked example (Cohen's d): a treatment group has mean = 80 and a control group has mean = 74, and the pooled standard deviation is 12. Then d = (80 minus 74) / 12 = 6 / 12 = 0.5, a medium effect by Cohen's benchmarks: the groups differ by half a standard deviation. Notice this number does not change if you double the sample size, whereas the p-value would shrink: that independence from N is the whole point of an effect size. Worked example (eta-squared): an ANOVA reports SS between (the effect) = 40 and SS total = 200. Then eta-squared = 40 / 200 = 0.20, meaning the factor explains 20% of the total variance, a large effect. If the within (error) sum of squares were 60, the partial eta-squared would be 40 / (40 + 60) = 40 / 100 = 0.40, visibly larger than the ordinary eta-squared precisely because the denominator has been trimmed. Exam trap Eta-squared overestimates the population effect (it is positively biased, especially with small samples); omega-squared corrects this and is smaller. Do not report partial eta-squared as if it were ordinary eta-squared: partial values do not sum to the total variance explained and are inflated in factorial designs. And remember d is a mean-difference metric while eta-squared is a variance-explained metric: a question that pairs "Cohen's d" with "proportion of variance" is testing this category error. L. Parametric assumption testing: the diagnostic toolkit Every parametric test rests on assumptions about the data (normality, equal variances, independence, and for some designs sphericity or homogeneous regression slopes). This section is the examiner's goldmine because the questions are mechanical and specific: "which diagnostic test, which numeric threshold, and what do you switch to when the assumption fails?" Learn each diagnostic with its sample-size rule and its remedy. Normality Shapiro-Wilk test: the preferred normality test for small samples (N < 50) ; it is the most powerful normality test for small N. A significant result means the data depart from normality. Kolmogorov-Smirnov test: used for larger samples (N ≥ 50) ; it compares the cumulative sample distribution to a reference normal (with the Lilliefors correction when the mean and variance are estimated from the sample rather than known). Skewness and kurtosis: as a rough rule, values within roughly plus or minus 1 (some texts say plus or minus 2) indicate acceptable normality. Skewness is asymmetry (a long tail to one side); kurtosis is peakedness and tail-heaviness (positive kurtosis = a sharp peak with heavy tails). Exam trap The N split is highly testable: Shapiro-Wilk for N less than 50; Kolmogorov-Smirnov for N of 50 or more. Also note that with very large N, normality tests become hypersensitive and flag trivial, harmless departures as significant, so inspect skew/kurtosis and Q-Q plots too; do not reject normality on the p-value alone. Remember the assumption is about the residuals / sampling distribution, which the Central Limit Theorem protects at large N anyway. Homogeneity of variance Levene's test: the robust default; it tests equality of variances by running an ANOVA on the absolute deviations from each group's mean (or, in the more robust variant, the median, the "center alignment", which makes it resistant to non-normality). A significant Levene means the variances differ. Bartlett's test: more powerful than Levene if the data are genuinely normal, but very sensitive to departures from normality (it is a chi-square based check). Use Bartlett only when normality is well established; otherwise prefer Levene. Sphericity (repeated measures) Sphericity is an assumption specific to repeated-measures ANOVA: that the variances of the differences between all possible pairs of conditions are equal. It is tested with Mauchly's test . If Mauchly's test is significant, sphericity is violated, the F-test becomes too liberal (inflated Type I error), and you correct the degrees of freedom by multiplying them by an epsilon estimate (a number between 0 and 1 that shrinks the degrees of freedom, raising the critical F): Greenhouse-Geisser correction: the more conservative correction, used when the estimated epsilon is below 0.75 (a more severe violation). Huynh-Feldt correction: the less conservative correction, used when epsilon is above 0.75 (a milder violation), because Greenhouse-Geisser would over-correct and cost power. High-yield Sphericity applies ONLY to repeated-measures (within-subjects) designs. Mauchly's test detects violation; if violated, correct df with Greenhouse-Geisser (epsilon below 0.75) or Huynh-Feldt (epsilon above 0.75). Both shrink the degrees of freedom, which raises the critical F and restores a valid Type I error rate. There is no sphericity assumption in a purely between-subjects ANOVA, so a question applying Mauchly's test to independent groups is wrong by construction. Homogeneity of regression slopes (for ANCOVA) ANCOVA adjusts the dependent variable for a covariate (statistically equating groups on a nuisance variable), and it assumes the covariate-to-outcome relationship (the regression slope) is the same in every group : this is homogeneity of regression slopes . It is tested by checking the covariate × group interaction; if that interaction is significant, the slopes differ, the single adjusted comparison ANCOVA computes is misleading, and you should not use ANCOVA. Worked logic: if a covariate (baseline anxiety) predicts the outcome steeply in the treated group but flatly in the control group, no single "adjusted mean difference" is honest, because the group gap itself depends on the covariate value. Multicollinearity In multiple regression, multicollinearity (predictors highly correlated with each other) destabilises coefficient estimates, inflating their standard errors so that individually important predictors can appear non-significant. It is diagnosed with the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF): VIF > 5 signals serious redundancy (some texts use > 10 as the severe cut-off). VIF is the reciprocal of tolerance: VIF = 1 / Tolerance , where tolerance = 1 minus the R 2 of a predictor regressed on all the other predictors. Worked example: if one predictor is regressed on the others and yields R 2 = 0.90, then tolerance = 1 minus 0.90 = 0.10 and VIF = 1 / 0.10 = 10, a severe multicollinearity flag; that predictor is 90% explained by the others and adds little unique information. The remedy is to drop or combine the redundant predictors. M. Hypothesis-testing executions Now the engine room: the actual inferential tests, organised by how many groups, how many dependent variables, and whether the groups are related. The exam tests both the correct choice of test for a described situation and the internal logic (especially the F-ratio partition and the MANOVA statistics), so we teach the family tree with worked numbers. The t-test family One-sample t-test: compares one sample mean to a known or hypothesised population value (is this class's mean IQ different from the population norm of 100?). Independent-samples t-test: compares the means of two separate, unrelated groups (treatment vs control). Paired-samples (dependent) t-test: compares two related measurements (pre vs post on the same people, or matched pairs); it works on the difference scores, which removes stable between-person variation and so is more powerful when measurements are correlated. Welch's t-test: the correction used when the two groups have unequal variances (heterogeneity, flagged by Levene). It does not pool the variances and it adjusts the degrees of freedom downward (the Welch-Satterthwaite df), so it stays valid when the standard t-test's equal-variance assumption fails. Many statisticians now recommend Welch's as the routine default for two-group comparisons. Exam trap When Levene's test is significant (variances unequal), you do not abandon the t-test; you switch to Welch's t-test (the "equal variances not assumed" row in SPSS output). Switching to a non-parametric test (Mann-Whitney) is required when normality fails, not merely when variances are unequal. Conflating "unequal variances" with "use a non-parametric test" is the classic error. ANOVA and its variants Analysis of Variance compares means across three or more groups using a single F-ratio, thereby avoiding the inflated family-wise Type I error you would incur by running many separate t-tests. Its logic is variance partitioning: Definition SS Total = SS Between + SS Within . Total variability splits into between-groups variability (differences among the group means, the "signal", reflecting treatment plus error) and within-groups variability (variability of scores inside each group, the "noise", pure error). F = (SS Between /df between ) / (SS Within /df within ) = mean square between over mean square within. A large F means the signal exceeds the noise. Worked F-ratio: three groups of five participants each (total N = 15, so k = 3 groups). Suppose SS Between = 60 and SS Within = 36. The degrees of freedom are df between = k minus 1 = 2 and df within = N minus k = 15 minus 3 = 12. Then the mean squares are MS between = 60 / 2 = 30 and MS within = 36 / 12 = 3. The F-ratio is F = 30 / 3 = 10. You compare this 10 to the critical F at df = (2, 12); the larger the F, the stronger the evidence that the group means differ. (If F were near 1, signal and noise would be comparable, consistent with the null.) Factorial ANOVA: two or more factors, yielding main effects and interactions (see Section H). Repeated-measures ANOVA: the same participants measured under all conditions; more powerful (it removes stable between-subject variance from the error term) but assumes sphericity (Section L). ANCOVA: ANOVA with a covariate statistically removed first, increasing power by shrinking error variance; assumes homogeneity of regression slopes (Section L). MANOVA: ANOVA with two or more dependent variables analysed jointly via centroid (mean vector) comparisons, controlling Type I error across the outcomes and able to detect effects on the combination of DVs that no single univariate test would catch. MANOVA significance is read from four multivariate test statistics: Wilks' Lambda (the most commonly reported; a smaller Lambda means a bigger effect, because it is the proportion of unexplained variance), Pillai's Trace (the most robust to assumption violations and unequal group sizes, so it is preferred when the data are imperfect), Hotelling's Trace , and Roy's Largest Root. For a two-group comparison all four give identical results. Memory aid Wilks' Lambda is "leftover" variance: smaller is better (less unexplained = bigger effect). Pillai's Trace is the robust one : use it when assumptions are shaky or group sizes unequal. Hotelling's Trace is essentially the two-group case extended. Post-hoc correction protocols A significant omnibus ANOVA tells you some means differ but not which ; post-hoc tests make the pairwise comparisons while controlling the family-wise error rate that would otherwise balloon (with k groups there are k(k minus 1)/2 pairwise comparisons, and each carries its own chance of a Type I error): Tukey's HSD (Honestly Significant Difference): the standard for all pairwise comparisons; well balanced between power and Type I control when group sizes are equal. Bonferroni correction: divides alpha by the number of comparisons, alpha new = alpha / k. Simple and very conservative (it over-corrects with many comparisons, costing power). Worked example: with alpha = 0.05 and 10 comparisons, each is tested at 0.05 / 10 = 0.005. Scheffé's test: the most conservative of all; needed for complex contrasts (combinations of several means, not just pairs). Use it when comparisons are decided after seeing the data or involve groupings of means. Dunnett's test: the specialist test for comparing several treatment groups each against a single control ; more powerful than Tukey for that specific job because it makes fewer comparisons. High-yield Match the post-hoc to the question: Tukey HSD = all pairwise; Bonferroni = a few planned comparisons (alpha/k); Scheffé = complex contrasts (most conservative); Dunnett = many treatments vs one control. Bonferroni's formula alpha/k is a near-certain MCQ. N. Non-parametric and categorical equivalents When parametric assumptions fail and cannot be repaired (especially when normality is violated, or when the data are inherently ordinal or nominal), you switch to non-parametric tests , which work on ranks or frequencies rather than raw interval scores and so make no distributional assumption about the population shape. Knowing the parametric-to-non-parametric mapping cold is one of the most reliably tested facts in the section: Parametric test Non-parametric equivalent Use Independent t-test Mann-Whitney U Two independent groups, ordinal/non-normal data. Paired t-test Wilcoxon signed-rank Two related/matched measurements. One-way ANOVA Kruskal-Wallis H Three or more independent groups. Repeated-measures ANOVA Friedman's test (two-way ANOVA by ranks) Three or more related measurements. The shared logic: each test replaces the raw scores with their ranks, then asks whether the ranks are distributed differently across conditions than chance would allow. Because ranks discard the exact spacing between scores, non-parametric tests are slightly less powerful than their parametric cousins when the parametric assumptions actually hold , which is why you reserve them for when the assumptions fail rather than using them by default. Chi-square tests for categorical data Chi-square test of independence: tests whether two categorical variables are associated (laid out in a contingency table) by comparing observed and expected cell frequencies, where the expected count of a cell = (row total × column total) / grand total. Chi-square goodness-of-fit: tests whether one categorical variable's observed frequencies match a hypothesised distribution (does a die land on each face equally often?). Worked chi-square decision: a 2 × 2 table of treatment (drug vs placebo) by outcome (recovered vs not). Suppose a cell has observed count O = 30 and, from the row and column totals, an expected count E = 24. That cell contributes (O minus E) 2 / E = (30 minus 24) 2 / 24 = 36 / 24 = 1.5 to the chi-square statistic. You sum this contribution across all four cells to get the total chi-square, then compare it to the critical value at df = (rows minus 1) × (columns minus 1) = 1 × 1 = 1, which is 3.84 at alpha = 0.05. If the summed chi-square exceeds 3.84, the variables are associated (you reject independence). The key assumption: expected cell frequencies should be at least 5 (in most cells). When this fails, you must correct or switch: Yates' correction for continuity: applied to 2 × 2 tables to reduce chi-square's tendency to overestimate significance when counts are small (it subtracts 0.5 from each absolute observed-minus-expected difference before squaring). Fisher's exact test: the proper test for small samples / small expected frequencies in a 2 × 2 table; it computes the exact probability of the observed table directly rather than approximating with the chi-square distribution. McNemar's test: for paired nominal data (the same subjects measured twice, pre vs post), testing whether the proportions changed; it focuses only on the discordant cells (the people who switched category), ignoring those who stayed the same. Exam trap When expected frequencies fall below 5 in a 2 × 2 table, use Fisher's exact test (not ordinary chi-square). For paired nominal data (the same people before and after), use McNemar's , not the independence chi-square: McNemar is the nominal cousin of the paired t-test, whereas the chi-square of independence assumes independent observations and would be invalid on repeated measures of the same people. O. Correlation and regression Correlation quantifies the strength and direction of a relationship between variables; regression uses one or more variables to predict another. The exam mines this area heavily for two things: choosing the right coefficient for the data types in front of you (continuous, ordinal, true or artificial dichotomy), and the precise interpretation distinctions (partial vs semi-partial, stepwise vs hierarchical, log-odds vs odds ratio). Bivariate correlation coefficients Pearson's r: for two continuous, linearly related, normally distributed variables; the parametric coefficient. It ranges from minus 1 (perfect negative) through 0 (no linear relationship) to plus 1 (perfect positive), and its square (r 2 ) is the proportion of shared variance. Spearman's rho: the rank-order correlation; non-parametric, for ordinal data or non-linear but monotonic relationships (it is simply Pearson's r computed on the ranks of the scores). Kendall's tau: another rank correlation, based on the number of concordant versus discordant pairs; it is preferred over Spearman for small samples or data with many tied ranks , and it gives a more conservative (smaller in absolute value) coefficient. Special-distribution coefficients The exam loves the "true vs artificial dichotomy" distinction, where a true dichotomy is genuinely two categories (alive/dead) and an artificial dichotomy is a continuous variable forced into two (pass/fail carved from a continuous exam score): Coefficient Variable 1 Variable 2 Point-biserial True dichotomy (genuinely two categories, e.g. alive/dead) Continuous interval Biserial Artificial dichotomy (a continuous variable forced into two, e.g. pass/fail from a score) Continuous interval Phi (phi) True dichotomy True dichotomy Tetrachoric Artificial dichotomy Artificial dichotomy Memory aid " Bi serial has arti fic ial dichotomies hidden in it (both words bend a continuum); point -biserial is for a true two-category split. Phi = two TRUE dichotomies; Tetrachoric = two ARTIFICIAL dichotomies. True-true = phi; fake-fake = tetrachoric. Partial vs semi-partial correlation Partial correlation removes the variance of a third (control) variable from both primary variables, then correlates the residuals: it asks "what is the X-Y relationship with Z held constant for both?". Semi-partial (part) correlation removes the control variable's variance from only one of the two variables. In regression, the semi-partial squared is the unique variance a predictor adds to R 2 . Worked illustration: studying the link between exercise (X) and mood (Y) while controlling for sleep (Z), partial correlation cleans sleep out of both exercise and mood; semi-partial cleans sleep out of exercise only, leaving mood untouched, and so answers "how much does exercise uniquely add once we know sleep?". High-yield Partial = remove the covariate from BOTH variables; semi-partial = remove it from only ONE. Because partial cleans both variables, it is usually the larger of the two in absolute value. This one-word difference ("both" vs "one") is the entire exam point. Regression models Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression: fits a line minimising the sum of squared residuals (the vertical distances of points from the line); the standard linear model. Stepwise regression: predictors enter or leave automatically according to a statistical criterion (the data decide the order of entry). It is atheoretical and capitalises on chance (it can select predictors that fit this sample's noise), so it is widely criticised and should not be used to test theory. Hierarchical regression: the researcher enters predictors in theory-driven blocks in a predetermined order, examining the change in R 2 at each step (the increment a block adds over the earlier blocks). This is the preferred, theory-led approach. Adjusted R 2 : R 2 penalised for the number of predictors and the sample size, because raw R 2 always rises (never falls) when predictors are added even if they are useless. Always report adjusted R 2 in multiple regression. Logistic regression When the outcome is dichotomous (diagnosed vs not, relapsed vs not), OLS is inappropriate because it can predict impossible probabilities below 0 or above 1; instead you use logistic regression , which models the log-odds (the logit) of the outcome as a linear function of the predictors, mapping the unbounded linear predictor onto the 0-to-1 probability range through the logistic curve. Key quantities: Odds Ratio (OR) = e beta : exponentiating a coefficient converts log-odds back to an odds ratio. OR > 1 means the predictor raises the odds of the outcome; OR < 1 lowers them; OR = 1 means no effect. Worked example: a coefficient beta = 0.69 gives OR = e 0.69 = about 2.0, so a one-unit rise in that predictor doubles the odds of the outcome. Wald statistic: tests whether an individual predictor's coefficient differs significantly from zero (the logistic analogue of the t-test on an OLS regression coefficient). Hosmer-Lemeshow test: the goodness-of-fit test for logistic regression; it groups cases by predicted probability and compares observed and predicted frequencies across those groups. Here a non-significant result is the good outcome (it means the model's predictions match the data). Exam trap For the Hosmer-Lemeshow test you WANT a non-significant p-value (good fit). A significant Hosmer-Lemeshow means the model does NOT fit the data; this inverted interpretation is a favourite trick. Also remember OR = e beta , not beta itself: the raw coefficient is in log-odds units, so a coefficient of 0 corresponds to an odds ratio of 1 (no effect), not 0. P. Factor analytic modelling Factor analysis reduces many observed (measured) variables to a few underlying dimensions (factors), on the assumption that the observed correlations among items arise because the items share these latent causes. It is the statistical backbone of test construction (deriving the subscales of a personality inventory) and of construct validation, so the paper tests it through three decisions: the extraction method, the number of factors to keep, and the rotation type. PCA vs Principal Axis Factoring Definition Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a data reduction technique: it analyses total variance (common, unique, and error variance together) to produce components that summarise the variables as efficiently as possible. Principal Axis Factoring (PAF) is true factor analysis : it analyses only the shared (common) variance to uncover the latent constructs presumed to cause the correlations. Use PCA when the goal is pure dimension reduction or computing composite scores; use PAF (or maximum-likelihood factoring) when the goal is to model latent constructs, which is the usual clinical aim. The mechanical difference sits on the diagonal of the correlation matrix being analysed: PCA places 1.0 on the diagonal (all of each variable's variance), whereas PAF places the communalities there (the shared variance only). That single change is why PCA can look like it explains more variance: it is counting the unique and error variance that PAF deliberately excludes. Factor extraction criteria (how many factors to keep) Kaiser criterion: retain factors with eigenvalues greater than 1.0 (an eigenvalue is the amount of variance a factor explains in units of single variables; an eigenvalue below 1 means the factor explains less than a single original variable, so it is not worth retaining). Simple, but it tends to over-extract factors. Scree plot: plot the eigenvalues in descending order and find the "elbow" where the curve flattens; keep the factors above the bend (Raymond Cattell's scree test). Subjective but widely used. Horn's parallel analysis: the most accurate modern method: generate eigenvalues from many sets of random data of the same size as yours, and retain only those real factors whose eigenvalues exceed the corresponding eigenvalues from the random data. It corrects the over-extraction of the Kaiser rule. Exam trap The Kaiser criterion (eigenvalue > 1) tends to OVER-extract factors , and the scree test is subjective; Horn's parallel analysis is the recommended, most accurate criterion .
