Frederic Kuder, 1939 Interest in broad activity areas for career guidance K. Ethics and test-user competence Testing is not just technique; it carries duties to the person tested. The core principles map onto professional codes (APA and the RCI code in India). Competence: use only tests you are trained and qualified to administer, score, and interpret. Test publishers classify tests by user qualification level for this reason. Informed consent: explain the purpose, procedure, and use of results before testing. Confidentiality: protect records and release scores only to authorized parties. Test security: do not expose test items publicly, or scores lose meaning. Right to results and feedback: the person is entitled to a clear explanation in language they understand. Fair use and bias: use appropriate norms; be alert to cultural, linguistic, and disability bias that can make a score invalid for a particular person. Rule: A test result is a hypothesis, not a verdict. It must be integrated with history, interview, and observation before any clinical decision. Never diagnose from a single test score. Reliability is consistency (test-retest, parallel-forms, split-half with Spearman-Brown, internal consistency via Cronbach's alpha and KR-20, inter-rater via Cohen's kappa) and its individual-level cousin is the SEM. Validity is accuracy (face, content, criterion as concurrent/predictive, and the master concept construct validity with convergent/discriminant evidence and the Campbell-Fiske MTMM matrix). CTT gives sample-dependent item difficulty and discrimination; IRT and the Rasch model give sample-invariant parameters and power adaptive testing. Norms turn raw scores into z, T, IQ, stanine, sten, and percentile ranks. Learn the author-tool pairs: Terman (Stanford-Binet), Wechsler (WAIS/WISC/WPPSI), Raven (Matrices), Das-Naglieri (CAS/PASS), and the Indian set Bhatia, Malin (MISIC), Kamat (BKT), Bharat Raj (DST, VSMS adaptation), Seguin. On personality, MMPI-2 with its L/F/K validity scales, Cattell's 16PF (stens), Eysenck's EPQ, Costa-McCrae's NEO-PI-R; projectives from Rorschach (Exner system) and Murray-Morgan's TAT to Bellak's CAT and the drawing tests. Neuropsychology: Halstead-Reitan, Luria-Nebraska, and the Indian NIMHANS, PGI, and AIIMS batteries plus Bender-Gestalt. Clinical scales split into self-report (BDI, BAI, GHQ) and clinician-rated (HAM-D, HAM-A, PANSS, Y-BOCS); MMSE and MoCA screen cognition; VSMS gives a social quotient. Ethics rests on competence, consent, confidentiality, security, and fair use. 11 Research Methodology & Statistics From scratch: Research is a systematic, self-correcting way of answering a question so that the answer does not depend on who is asking. In clinical psychology we want to know things like "does cognitive behavioural therapy reduce depression more than a waitlist?" To answer that credibly we must define our terms precisely, design a fair comparison, sample people properly, measure carefully, and then use statistics to decide whether what we saw is real or just chance. This section builds that whole machine, piece by piece. 1. The research process & variables A variable is anything that can take different values. The independent variable (IV) is what the researcher manipulates or groups by (the presumed cause); the dependent variable (DV) is what is measured (the presumed effect). Therapy type is the IV; depression score is the DV. Extraneous variable , any variable other than the IV that could affect the DV. If it is not controlled it becomes a confounding variable : it varies systematically with the IV, so you cannot tell whether the IV or the confound caused the effect. If everyone in the therapy group is also younger, age confounds the result. Moderator , a variable that changes the strength or direction of the IV–DV relationship (an interaction; "for whom / when" the effect holds). Therapy works better for mild than severe cases: severity moderates. Mediator , a variable that explains how the IV affects the DV; it sits in the causal chain IV → mediator → DV. Therapy reduces depression by first changing negative thoughts. Key. Moderator = when/for whom (interaction). Mediator = how/why (mechanism, in the middle). An operational definition states a variable in terms of the exact operations used to measure it, making it observable and repeatable. "Depression = score on the Beck Depression Inventory." Hypotheses The null hypothesis (H0) states there is no effect or difference (any observed difference is chance). The alternative hypothesis (H1) states there is an effect. A non-directional / two-tailed H1 predicts a difference in either direction (μ1 ≠ μ2). A directional / one-tailed H1 predicts the direction (μ1 > μ2). We never "prove" H1; we reject or fail to reject H0 . 2. Research designs True (experimental) design , the researcher manipulates the IV and uses random assignment to conditions. Only this design supports strong causal claims. Quasi-experimental design , an IV is compared across pre-existing groups with no random assignment. Comparing two intact hospital wards. Weaker causal inference (selection confounds). Correlational design , no manipulation; two measured variables are related. Establishes association, not causation. Descriptive / survey design , describes a population's characteristics without testing relationships. Case study , intensive study of one individual/unit; rich detail, poor generalisability. Longitudinal , same people followed over time (tracks change, but attrition and cost). Cross-sectional , different age/cohort groups measured once (fast, but cohort effects confound age). Between vs within subjects Between-subjects : different participants in each condition (no carry-over, but individual differences add noise). Within-subjects (repeated measures) : same participants in all conditions (controls individual differences, more power, but risks order/carry-over effects ). Key. Control of confounds: randomization (random assignment spreads unknown confounds evenly across groups), counterbalancing (varying the order of conditions to cancel order effects in within-subjects designs), and matching (pairing participants on a key variable so groups are equated on it). 3. Sampling Probability sampling , every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection, so results generalise and sampling error can be estimated. Simple random , every member equally likely (lottery). Systematic , every k-th member from a list after a random start. Stratified , divide the population into strata (e.g. sex) and sample randomly within each; ensures representation. Cluster , divide into naturally occurring clusters (e.g. hospitals), randomly select whole clusters. Multistage , sampling in nested stages (states → districts → clinics → patients). Non-probability sampling , selection chances unknown; cheaper but biased. Convenience , whoever is available. Purposive , deliberately chosen for a characteristic (expert judgement). Quota , fill preset counts per subgroup, non-randomly (the non-random cousin of stratified). Snowball , participants refer others (for hidden populations). Trap: Stratified vs cluster: in stratified you sample from every stratum and want them internally homogeneous; in cluster you sample only some clusters, each meant to mirror the whole. Quota = non-probability version of stratified. 4. Measurement, scales The scale of a variable decides which statistics are legitimate. Scale Property Example Central tendency Stats allowed Nominal Categories only, no order Diagnosis, sex Mode Frequencies, chi-square Ordinal Ordered, unequal/unknown intervals Rank, Likert (strict view) Median Non-parametric, Spearman's rho Interval Equal intervals, no true zero IQ, temperature °C Mean Parametric (t, ANOVA, Pearson) Ratio Equal intervals + true zero Reaction time, weight Mean (geometric too) All, including ratios Key. Mnemonic NOIR (Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio). A true zero means "none of the quantity", 0 kg = no weight (ratio), but 0 °C is not no temperature (interval). 5. Descriptive statistics Central tendency: the mean (arithmetic average) suits symmetric interval/ratio data but is pulled by outliers; the median (middle value) is robust and preferred for skewed data or ordinal scales; the mode (most frequent value) is the only option for nominal data. Dispersion: the range (max − min) is crude; the variance is the mean of squared deviations from the mean; the standard deviation (SD) is the square root of variance, back in the original units and the most used spread measure. The normal distribution The normal distribution is a symmetric, bell-shaped curve where mean = median = mode. Under the empirical rule , about 68% of scores fall within ±1 SD, 95% within ±2 SD (±1.96 exactly), and 99.7% within ±3 SD of the mean. Many parametric tests assume it. Skewness measures asymmetry: positive (right) skew has a long right tail (mean > median), negative (left) skew a long left tail (mean < median). Kurtosis measures tailedness/peakedness: leptokurtic = tall, heavy tails; platykurtic = flat, thin tails; mesokurtic = normal. Trap: In a positively skewed distribution the order is Mode < Median < Mean (the mean chases the tail). Report the median for skewed income-type data. 6. Reliability & validity of measurement Reliability = consistency of measurement (test–retest, internal consistency via Cronbach's alpha , inter-rater); validity = whether it measures what it claims (content, criterion, construct). A test can be reliable but not valid (consistently wrong), but not valid without being reliable. (See the Assessment section for full detail.) 7. Inferential statistics, the logic We study a sample but want to speak about a population . The sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic (e.g. the mean) over all possible samples; its spread is the standard error (SE) = SD ÷ √n. Larger samples shrink the SE, giving more precise estimates. A confidence interval (CI) gives a range that would capture the true parameter in, say, 95% of repeated samples. Significance testing: assume H0 is true, compute how surprising the data are under it. The p-value is the probability of results at least as extreme as observed if H0 were true . If p < alpha (α) (the pre-set threshold, usually .05), we reject H0 and call the result "statistically significant." H0 is really TRUE H0 is really FALSE Reject H0 Type I error (α) , false positive Correct ( power , 1−β) Fail to reject H0 Correct (1−α) Type II error (β) , false negative Key. Type I error = rejecting a true null = seeing an effect that isn't there (false positive), probability α. Type II error = failing to reject a false null = missing a real effect (false negative), probability β. Statistical power = 1 − β = the probability of detecting a real effect; it rises with larger n, larger effect, and higher α. Effect size (e.g. Cohen's d = mean difference ÷ pooled SD; d ≈ 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large) reports the magnitude of an effect, independent of sample size, unlike the p-value. Trap: "Convict an innocent person" = Type I; "let a guilty person go free" = Type II. A tiny p-value does NOT mean a big effect: with huge n, trivial effects become "significant", always read the effect size. 8. The statistical tests Parametric tests assume interval/ratio data, normality, and (often) homogeneity of variance. t-test compares means: one-sample (sample vs known value), independent-samples (two separate groups), paired/dependent (same group twice or matched pairs). ANOVA (analysis of variance) compares means of three or more groups using the F ratio (between-group variance ÷ within-group variance). One-way = one IV; factorial = two+ IVs (tests interactions); repeated-measures = within-subjects. ANCOVA (analysis of covariance) = ANOVA that statistically removes the effect of a continuous covariate (e.g. adjusting post-scores for pre-scores). Pearson's r , linear correlation between two interval/ratio variables (−1 to +1). Regression predicts a DV from one (simple) or more (multiple) predictors, giving a line Y = a + bX. Non-parametric tests are used for nominal/ordinal data, small samples, or violated assumptions. Chi-square (χ²) , association between categorical variables (goodness-of-fit or independence). Mann-Whitney U , two independent groups (non-parametric independent t). Wilcoxon signed-rank , two related/paired conditions (non-parametric paired t). Kruskal-Wallis , three+ independent groups (non-parametric one-way ANOVA). Friedman , three+ related conditions (non-parametric repeated-measures ANOVA). Spearman's rho , correlation of ranked/ordinal data. 9. High-yield: Type I vs Type II error (with the false-positive/false-negative labels), moderator vs mediator, scale-of-measurement → permitted statistic, mean vs median under skew, and matching each parametric test to its non-parametric twin. Memorise the decision table and the NOIR mnemonic cold. Recap: Define variables and operationalise them; set H0 (no effect) vs H1 (directional = one-tailed). Choose a design (true experiment with randomization is the causal gold standard) and a sampling method (probability generalises; non-probability is convenient but biased). The measurement scale (NOIR) fixes your central-tendency and test options. Describe data with mean/median/mode + SD and read skew/kurtosis. Infer via the sampling distribution, standard error, and CIs; reject H0 when p < α, guarding against Type I (false positive) and Type II (false negative) errors, and always report power and effect size (Cohen's d). Finally, pick the test from the DATA/DESIGN → TEST table, swapping in the non-parametric equivalent when parametric assumptions fail. 10. Qualitative Research Methods The statistics you have met so far belong to the quantitative tradition: it measures variables as numbers, tests hypotheses, and prizes large samples that let findings generalise. Qualitative research asks a different kind of question. Instead of "how much" or "how many", it asks "what is this experience like" and "how do people make meaning". It works with words, images and observations rather than numbers, uses small purposive samples, and builds understanding from the ground up. From scratch: Quantitative research is usually deductive (start with a theory, deduce a hypothesis, test it) and aims for objectivity and generalisation. Qualitative research is usually inductive (start with data, build a theory upward) and aims for depth, context and the participant's own point of view. Neither is "better"; they answer different questions. The main qualitative designs Grounded theory (Barney Glaser & Anselm Strauss, 1967): builds a theory grounded in the data itself through constant comparison and coding (open → axial → selective), collecting data until theoretical saturation (no new categories emerge). Phenomenology (rooted in Edmund Husserl): describes the lived experience of a phenomenon from the first-person view; the researcher brackets (sets aside) prior assumptions. Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA; Jonathan Smith, 1996) is a common clinical variant. Case study : an intensive, holistic study of a single unit (person, family, institution, event) using many sources; strong on depth, weak on generalisation. Ethnography : immersion in a culture or group over time, often by participant observation , to describe it from the insider (emic) view. Narrative analysis : studies the stories people tell to understand how they construct identity and meaning over time. Ways to gather and analyse qualitative data Interviews : structured, semi-structured (fixed core questions plus probes, the clinical workhorse), or unstructured. Focus groups : a moderated group discussion (usually 6 to 10 people) that harvests interaction and shared meaning, not just individual answers. Thematic analysis : identifies, analyses and reports patterns (themes) across a data set; flexible and widely used (Braun & Clarke). Content analysis : systematically codes text into categories; can be quantitative (counting code frequencies) or qualitative. Key. Trustworthiness is the qualitative answer to reliability and validity. Its four criteria: credibility (are the findings believable, checked via member checking and triangulation), transferability (do they apply to other contexts, aided by thick description), dependability (are they consistent over time), and confirmability (do they reflect the participants, not the researcher's bias). Mixed-methods designs deliberately combine both traditions. Common types: explanatory sequential (quantitative first, then qualitative to explain it) , exploratory sequential (qualitative first to build an instrument, then quantitative) , and convergent parallel (both at once, then compare) . Triangulation across methods strengthens confidence in a finding. Trap: Do not equate "qualitative" with "no analysis" or "just anecdote". Rigorous qualitative work has explicit sampling, coding and audit trails. Also, a large sample is not a goal in qualitative work; saturation, not size, decides when to stop. 11. Correlation in Depth A correlation coefficient summarises the strength and direction of a relationship between two variables in a single number between −1 and +1. Zero means no linear relationship; the sign gives direction; the absolute value gives strength. Coefficient Use it when Both variables are Pearson product-moment (r) Linear relation, normal data Continuous (interval/ratio) Spearman's rank (rho) Monotonic relation, ranked or non-normal data Ordinal (or ranked) Point-biserial One true dichotomy vs one continuous One dichotomous, one continuous Phi coefficient 2×2 table of two true dichotomies Both dichotomous Key. The coefficient of determination is r squared: it is the proportion of variance in one variable explained by the other. If r = 0.60, then r squared = 0.36, so 36 percent of the variance is shared. This is why a "moderate" r of 0.5 explains only a quarter of the variance. Trap: Correlation is not causation. A correlation can arise from A causing B, B causing A, a third (confounding) variable causing both, or coincidence. Correlation also detects only linear (Pearson) or monotonic (Spearman) trends; a strong curved relationship can still give r near zero. 12. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) in Depth From scratch: A t-test compares two means. If you have three groups and run three separate t-tests, each at alpha = 0.05, the chance of at least one false positive across the set (the familywise error rate ) climbs well above 5 percent. ANOVA compares all the means in one test at a controlled alpha, which is why it is preferred over multiple t-tests. ANOVA works by partitioning the total variance into between-groups variance (differences among the group means, the "signal") and within-groups variance (variability inside each group, the "noise"). The F-ratio is their quotient (between / within). A large F means the group differences are large relative to random noise, pointing to a real effect. The family of ANOVA designs One-way ANOVA : one independent variable (factor) with three or more levels. Two-way ANOVA : two factors at once. It yields two main effects (the effect of each factor alone) and an interaction (does the effect of one factor depend on the level of the other). Repeated-measures ANOVA : the same participants measured under every condition (the within-subjects analogue), which controls individual differences. ANCOVA (analysis of covariance): ANOVA that statistically removes the effect of a continuous nuisance variable (a covariate) before comparing means. MANOVA (multivariate ANOVA): two or more dependent variables tested together. Key. A significant ANOVA tells you the means differ somewhere , not where . Post-hoc tests locate the specific pairs: Tukey's HSD (honestly significant difference, balanced designs), Scheffe (conservative, flexible for complex comparisons), and Bonferroni (divides alpha by the number of comparisons to hold familywise error). 13. Non-parametric Tests in Depth From scratch: Parametric tests assume the data are roughly normal, measured on an interval/ratio scale, with reasonably equal variances. When those assumptions fail (small samples, skewed data, ordinal or ranked scores, outliers), you switch to a non-parametric test, which usually works on ranks rather than raw values. Non-parametric tests are more robust but have slightly less power when the parametric assumptions actually hold. The simplest way to learn them is as the twin of a parametric test. Non-parametric test Parametric twin Situation Mann-Whitney U Independent-samples t-test Two independent groups Wilcoxon signed-rank Paired-samples t-test Two related/matched conditions Kruskal-Wallis H One-way ANOVA Three or more independent groups Friedman Repeated-measures ANOVA Three or more related conditions Sign test Paired-samples t-test (weaker) Direction of paired change only Chi-square – Frequencies/counts of categories Chi-square comes in two forms: goodness-of-fit (does one categorical variable's observed distribution match an expected one) and test of independence (are two categorical variables associated, using a contingency table). It compares observed with expected frequencies. Trap: The assumption that forces the switch is usually about the data (measurement level, normality), not the sample size alone. A large sample of ordinal data (for example, Likert ranks) still calls for a rank-based test such as Mann-Whitney, not a t-test. 14. Regression and Multivariate Methods Correlation asks whether two variables move together; regression goes further and lets you predict one variable from another. Simple linear regression fits a straight line, the regression line , of the form Y = a + bX, where a is the intercept and b is the slope (how much Y changes per unit of X). The line is placed to minimise the squared distances of the points from it (the least squares criterion). Multiple regression : predicts one outcome from several predictors at once (Y = a + b1X1 + b2X2 + ...), and reports how much variance the whole set explains (R squared). Factor analysis : a data-reduction method that finds a small number of underlying factors (latent dimensions) behind many correlated items; central to test construction (for example, identifying the factors behind an intelligence or personality scale). RML tilt: Expect one-liners that pair a purpose with a method: prediction → regression; data reduction / test construction → factor analysis; theory built from data → grounded theory. Know that r squared and R squared both mean "variance explained". 15. Effect Size, Power, Confidence Intervals and Meta-analysis A p-value tells you whether an effect is likely real; it does not tell you how big it is. Effect size answers the size question. Common measures: Cohen's d (a standardised mean difference, roughly 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large) and eta squared for ANOVA. Because a huge sample can make a trivial difference "significant", effect size is essential for judging practical importance. Statistical power is the probability of detecting an effect that is truly there (1 − beta). It rises with larger sample size, larger effect size and larger alpha. Convention targets power of at least 0.80. Sample-size (power) analysis uses effect size, alpha and desired power to work out how many participants a study needs before it begins. Confidence intervals give a range that would contain the true population value in a stated percentage (usually 95 percent) of repeated studies; a narrow interval means a more precise estimate. Meta-analysis statistically combines effect sizes from many studies into a single pooled estimate, giving greater power and a view of the overall evidence. 16. Research Ethics Who → what: Nuremberg Code (1947): the first international code, born from Nazi medical trials, establishing voluntary consent as essential. Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 1964): ethical principles for medical research on humans. Belmont Report (USA, 1979): named the three core principles, respect for persons , beneficence and justice . Every study with human participants must protect them. The core safeguards: Informed consent : participants freely agree after being told the purpose, procedures, risks and their right to withdraw at any time. Institutional ethics committee / Institutional Review Board (IRB) : an independent body that reviews and approves the protocol before data collection begins. Debriefing : after the study, telling participants its true purpose and correcting any misunderstanding. Deception : withholding or misstating information; permitted only when unavoidable, minimally harmful, approved by the committee, and followed by debriefing. Confidentiality and anonymity : protecting participants' data and identity. Plagiarism : presenting another's words or ideas as your own; a serious breach of research integrity, avoided by proper citation. Key. In India, the two codes to name are the APA Ethics Code (American Psychological Association, the standard psychology reference) and the ICMR (Indian Council of Medical Research) National Ethical Guidelines for biomedical and health research on human participants. Recap: Qualitative work seeks meaning and depth (grounded theory, phenomenology, thematic analysis) judged by trustworthiness. Correlation (Pearson, Spearman, point-biserial, phi) gives relationship and r squared is variance shared, never causation. ANOVA beats multiple t-tests by controlling familywise error, yields an F-ratio, and uses post-hoc tests to locate differences. Every parametric test has a rank-based non-parametric twin for when assumptions fail. Regression predicts; factor analysis reduces. Effect size, power and confidence intervals qualify the p-value; meta-analysis pools across studies. Ethics rests on consent, committee review and the Nuremberg, Helsinki and Belmont lineage. 17. Factorial and Repeated-Measures Designs Unpacked From scratch: A "design" is just the recipe for who gets what, in what order, and how many times you measure them. Two decisions define almost every experiment: (1) does each participant see only one condition (between-subjects) or every condition (within-subjects), and (2) how many independent variables (IVs, also called factors) are you manipulating at once. Get these two axes clear and the whole zoo of design names becomes readable. Between-subjects vs within-subjects, weighed properly In a between-subjects (independent-groups) design, separate people form each condition, so no one is compared to themselves. Its strength is that there are no carry-over effects: seeing condition A cannot contaminate condition B because no one sees both. Its cost is that individual differences (some people are just faster, smarter, calmer) fall into the error term, so you need larger samples to detect an effect. In a within-subjects (repeated-measures) design, the same people pass through every condition. Because each person is their own control, individual differences are removed from the error term, making the design far more powerful (it detects smaller effects with fewer people). The price is order effects : practice, fatigue, and carry-over. Rule: Repeated-measures buys statistical power by using each participant as their own baseline, but it owes a debt called order effects. You repay that debt with counterbalancing. Counterbalancing and the Latin square Counterbalancing means varying the order in which conditions are presented so that order effects cancel out across the sample rather than piling onto one condition. Complete counterbalancing uses every possible order; with 3 conditions that is 3! = 6 orders, but with 5 conditions it is 120, which is impractical. A Latin square is the economical fix: a square arrangement in which each condition appears exactly once in each position (first, second, third...). Example: with conditions A, B, C, one Latin square is ABC / BCA / CAB. Each of A, B, C sits in position 1 once, position 2 once, position 3 once, so no condition is systematically advantaged. Matched-pairs design A matched-pairs design is a compromise. You cannot use the same person twice (maybe the task can only be done once), so you pair participants who are similar on a nuisance variable (say IQ or age), then randomly assign one of each pair to each condition. It approximates the error-reduction of within-subjects without the order effects, but matching is only as good as the variable you match on, and you can never match on everything. Factorial designs: main effects and interactions A factorial design manipulates two or more IVs simultaneously so you can study not just each one but how they combine. The notation counts levels: a 2x2 has two factors each with two levels (four cells total); a 2x3 has one two-level and one three-level factor (six cells). The pay-off is the interaction . A main effect is the effect of one factor averaged across the levels of the other. An interaction exists when the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other. Example: Factor A = caffeine (yes/no), Factor B = sleep (rested/deprived). If caffeine helps performance a lot when deprived but does nothing when rested, that is an interaction: the caffeine effect changes depending on sleep. On a graph, non-parallel lines signal an interaction; parallel lines signal none. Trap: A significant interaction outranks the main effects. If A and B interact, reporting "the main effect of caffeine was significant" is misleading, because caffeine's effect is not one number, it flips with sleep. Always interpret interactions first, then qualify the main effects. Quasi-experimental and single-subject designs A quasi-experiment looks like an experiment but lacks true random assignment, usually because the grouping variable is pre-existing (gender, diagnosis, school attended). You can compare groups, but you cannot claim the groups were equivalent to begin with, so causal claims are weaker. Single-subject (single-case) designs study one participant intensively across time. In an ABAB (reversal) design , A is baseline, B is treatment; you introduce, withdraw, and reintroduce treatment. If behaviour tracks the on/off pattern, the treatment is likely causal. A multiple-baseline design staggers the start of treatment across several behaviours, people, or settings; when each one changes only after treatment reaches it, coincidence becomes an implausible explanation. Multiple-baseline is preferred when a behaviour cannot ethically or practically be reversed (you cannot un-teach reading). RML tilt: Expect an item that gives a scenario ("researcher withdrew and reintroduced the reward") and asks for the design name (ABAB reversal), or shows crossing lines on a graph and asks what they indicate (an interaction). 18. Threats to Validity (Campbell and Stanley) Who → what: Donald Campbell and Julian Stanley (1963) gave psychology its master checklist of ways an experiment can fool you, splitting them into threats to internal validity (did the IV really cause the change?) and external validity (does the finding generalise beyond this study?). Internal validity: eight classic threats Internal validity is the degree to which you can attribute the outcome to your IV rather than to something else. The classic threats: History: an outside event happens between pre- and post-test (a news story, a policy change) and affects the outcome. Maturation: participants simply change over time (grow older, tired, hungrier, more skilled) independent of treatment. Testing: taking the pre-test itself changes performance on the post-test (practice, sensitisation). Instrumentation: the measuring tool drifts, a rater gets stricter, or a scale is recalibrated between measurements. Statistical regression to the mean (Francis Galton): extreme scorers selected at pre-test tend to drift back toward average on retest simply because extremes contain measurement error. Example: pick the 20 most depressed people, retest a week later, and their average will improve even with no treatment, because part of their extreme score was random bad-day noise. Selection: the groups differed before the study began (common when assignment is not random). Attrition (mortality): participants drop out non-randomly, so the surviving sample is no longer comparable. Selection interactions: selection can combine with maturation or history so groups change at different rates. Rule: Random assignment to conditions is the single strongest defence against most internal-validity threats, because it makes the groups probabilistically equivalent on everything, measured and unmeasured, before treatment. External, construct, and statistical-conclusion validity External validity asks whether results generalise across populations, settings, and times. Its main enemies are non-representative samples (over-reliance on undergraduates), artificial lab settings, and interaction of testing with treatment. Construct validity asks whether the operations actually capture the abstract concept: does your button-press "aggression" task really measure aggression, or just reaction speed? Statistical-conclusion validity asks whether the statistical inferences are sound: was power adequate, were assumptions met, was the effect size honestly reported, were there fishing/multiple-comparison problems? Trap: Internal and external validity often trade off. Tightly controlled lab studies maximise internal validity but can sacrifice external validity (real-world generalisation), and vice versa for field studies. There is rarely a design that maximises both at once. 19. Sampling Methods in Full From scratch: A population is everyone you want conclusions about; a sample is the subset you actually study. The whole game of inferential statistics rests on the sample being a fair miniature of the population. How you draw it decides whether that assumption is credible. Probability sampling (every unit has a known, non-zero chance) Simple random sampling: every member has an equal chance; like drawing names from a hat or using a random-number generator. Gold standard for representativeness, but needs a complete list (sampling frame). Systematic sampling: pick every k-th unit from a list after a random start (k = population size / sample size). Easy, but dangerous if the list has a hidden periodic pattern that lines up with k. Stratified sampling: divide the population into meaningful strata (say age bands or gender) and sample within each, often proportionally. This guarantees each subgroup is represented and typically reduces sampling error relative to simple random. Cluster sampling: divide the population into naturally occurring clusters (schools, city blocks), randomly select whole clusters, and study everyone in the chosen clusters. Cheaper when the population is geographically spread, but usually less precise than stratified. Multistage sampling: combine the above in stages: randomly select states, then districts within states, then schools within districts, then students. Used for large national surveys. Rule: Stratified sampling divides then samples within every group (all strata contribute). Cluster sampling divides then samples whole groups (only chosen clusters contribute). This one distinction is the most-tested sampling point. Non-probability sampling (chance of selection is unknown) Convenience sampling: whoever is easy to reach (the psychology class down the hall). Fast, cheap, but prone to bias. Purposive (judgmental) sampling: the researcher deliberately picks cases that fit a purpose (expert informants, typical cases). Quota sampling: the non-probability cousin of stratified sampling; you fill fixed quotas for subgroups but select within each quota non-randomly. Snowball sampling: existing participants recruit others from their network; essential for hidden or hard-to-reach populations (people who use illicit drugs, undocumented workers). Sampling error and sample-size logic Sampling error is the natural discrepancy between a sample statistic and the true population value, arising purely because you measured a subset. It is not a mistake; it shrinks as sample size grows. Note it differs from sampling bias , which is a systematic tilt from a bad method and does not shrink with size. Larger samples give more precise estimates (narrower confidence intervals) and more power, but with diminishing returns, because precision improves with the square root of n, not n itself. Quadrupling the sample only halves the standard error. RML tilt: A stem describing "divided the city into wards, randomly chose five wards, surveyed everyone in them" is cluster sampling; "recruited through friends of friends" is snowball; "every 10th patient file" is systematic. 20. Describing a Distribution: Shape, Spread, and Position Choosing a measure of central tendency The mean (arithmetic average) uses every value and is preferred for symmetric, interval/ratio data, but it is dragged toward outliers. The median (middle value) ignores the size of extremes and is the honest choice for skewed data (income, reaction times) or ordinal data. The mode (most frequent value) is the only option for nominal data (most common blood type) and can flag bimodality. Rule: For a skewed distribution, report the median. The mean gets pulled toward the long tail, so in a positively skewed income distribution mean > median, and reporting the mean alone flatters the "typical" person. Measures of dispersion The range (max minus min) is crude and outlier-driven. The interquartile range (IQR) is the spread of the middle 50% (third quartile minus first quartile) and is robust to outliers, pairing naturally with the median. The variance is the average of squared deviations from the mean (why square? so positive and negative deviations do not cancel, and so larger deviations count more). The standard deviation (SD) is the square root of variance, returning to the original units, which is why it is the everyday measure of spread. From scratch: Deviation means "distance from the mean". Add up those distances raw and they cancel to zero. Square them first, average, and you get variance; take the square root and you are back in the original units as the SD. So SD is, loosely, the typical distance of a score from the mean. Skewness and kurtosis Skewness measures asymmetry. Positive (right) skew has a long right tail (mean pulled above median); negative (left) skew has a long left tail (mean pulled below median). Kurtosis measures tail-heaviness and peakedness: leptokurtic distributions are tall and heavy-tailed, platykurtic are flat and thin-tailed, and the normal curve is mesokurtic . The normal curve, z-scores, and percentiles The normal distribution is symmetric, bell-shaped, and defined fully by its mean and SD, with mean = median = mode at the centre. Its key property is the empirical (68-95-99.7) rule : about 68% of scores fall within 1 SD of the mean, about 95% within 2 SD, and about 99.7% within 3 SD. A z-score restates any raw score as "how many SDs above or below the mean": z = (score minus mean) divided by SD. This standardisation lets you compare scores from different scales. A percentile is the percentage of the distribution falling at or below a score; the 84th percentile corresponds roughly to z = +1 in a normal curve. Example: a test with mean 50, SD 10. A raw score of 70 has z = (70 minus 50)/10 = +2, so it beats about 97.7% of scores (it sits at roughly the 98th percentile). 21. From Sample to Population: The Sampling Distribution From scratch: Imagine drawing thousands of samples of the same size from a population, computing the mean of each, and plotting those means. That plot is the sampling distribution of the mean . It is not the distribution of individual scores; it is the distribution of a statistic . Understanding this imaginary distribution is the hinge on which all inferential testing turns. The central limit theorem and the standard error The central limit theorem (CLT) states that as sample size increases, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal shape regardless of the shape of the parent population , and it centres on the true population mean. This is why we can use normal-based tests even on non-normal raw data, provided n is reasonably large (a common rule of thumb is n of at least 30). The spread of this sampling distribution is the standard error of the mean (SE) , equal to the SD divided by the square root of n. The SE is how much sample means typically bounce around the true mean; it shrinks as n grows, which is precisely why bigger samples give more trustworthy estimates. Trap: Do not confuse SD with SE. SD describes variability among individual scores; SE describes variability among sample means. SE is always the smaller of the two and gets smaller with larger samples, whereas SD does not systematically shrink with n. 22. The Logic of Hypothesis Testing, Sharpened Null and alternative, tails, and alpha The null hypothesis (H0) states there is no effect or no difference; the alternative hypothesis (H1) states there is one. We never "prove" H1; we either reject or fail to reject H0, always keeping the possibility of error. A two-tailed test asks "is there a difference in either direction?"; a one-tailed test asks a directional question ("is the treatment group higher?") and concentrates all the rejection region in one tail, giving more power in that direction but none in the other. Alpha is the significance level you set in advance (conventionally 0.05), the risk of a false alarm you are willing to tolerate. p-value, the two errors, power, and effect size The p-value is the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as observed if the null were true . If p is less than alpha, you reject H0. A Type I error is rejecting a true null (a false positive; its probability is alpha). A Type II error is failing to reject a false null (a false negative; its probability is beta). Statistical power is 1 minus beta: the probability of correctly detecting a real effect. Power rises with larger samples, larger true effects, higher alpha, and lower variability. Trap: The p-value is not the probability that the null is true, and it is not the probability your finding was due to chance. It is a conditional probability computed assuming the null is true. Statistical significance also does not equal practical importance, which is why effect size matters. Effect size and confidence intervals Effect size quantifies how big an effect is, independent of sample size. Cohen's d expresses a mean difference in SD units (roughly 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large). Eta-squared is used in ANOVA and gives the proportion of variance in the outcome explained by the factor. A confidence interval (CI) gives a range of plausible values for the true parameter; a 95% CI means that if we repeated the study endlessly, about 95% of such intervals would capture the true value. A 95% CI for a difference that excludes zero corresponds to a significant result at alpha 0.05. 23. Parametric Tests: What Each One Is For From scratch: "Parametric" tests assume the data come from a distribution with estimable parameters (usually normal), assume interval/ratio measurement, and (for group comparisons) assume roughly equal variances (homogeneity of variance). Meet the assumptions and they are the most powerful tools available. z-test and the three t-tests A z-test compares a sample mean to a population mean when the population SD is known (rare in practice). The t-tests handle the common case where the population SD is unknown and estimated from the sample: One-sample t: compares one sample mean to a known or hypothesised value. Independent-samples t: compares the means of two separate groups (between-subjects). Paired-samples (dependent) t: compares two related measurements (before/after on the same people, or matched pairs). The ANOVA family and post-hoc tests When you compare three or more means, running many t-tests inflates the Type I error rate, so we use analysis of variance (ANOVA) , which yields an F-ratio (between-groups variance divided by within-groups variance). A significant F says "at least one group differs" but not which. One-way ANOVA has one factor; two-way ANOVA has two factors and can reveal an interaction; repeated-measures ANOVA is the within-subjects version; ANCOVA adds a covariate to statistically remove a nuisance variable's influence; MANOVA handles multiple dependent variables at once. To locate which groups differ after a significant F, use post-hoc tests : Tukey's HSD (all pairwise comparisons, good balance), Scheffe (most conservative, flexible for complex comparisons), and Bonferroni (divides alpha by the number of comparisons, simple and strict). Trap: Never run multiple t-tests instead of an ANOVA to compare 4 groups. With 4 groups there are 6 pairwise tests, and at alpha 0.05 each, the chance of at least one false positive climbs well above 5%. ANOVA controls this family-wise error. 24. Non-parametric Tests and Their Parametric Partners From scratch: When data are ordinal, badly skewed, or assumptions fail, non-parametric tests step in. They typically work on ranks rather than raw values, so outliers matter less. The trade-off is slightly lower power when parametric assumptions are actually met. Parametric test Non-parametric partner Use for Independent-samples t Mann-Whitney U Two independent groups Paired-samples t Wilcoxon signed-rank Two related measures One-way ANOVA Kruskal-Wallis H Three or more independent groups Repeated-measures ANOVA Friedman test Three or more related measures (binary before/after) Sign test Direction of change only Chi-square: two distinct uses Chi-square works on frequencies (counts) of categorical data. The goodness-of-fit version tests whether one categorical variable's observed frequencies match expected frequencies (are births evenly spread across weekdays?). The test of independence uses a contingency table to ask whether two categorical variables are associated (is smoking status related to diagnosis?). Both compare observed to expected counts; the larger the gap, the larger chi-square. RML tilt: A stem giving a 2x2 table of counts and asking which test applies is almost always chi-square test of independence. If the data are ranks of two independent groups, it is Mann-Whitney U. 25. Correlation and Regression, Deepened Choosing the right correlation coefficient Pearson r: two continuous, linear, normally distributed variables. Ranges from minus 1 to plus 1. Spearman rho: the rank-based version, for ordinal data or monotonic-but-nonlinear relationships; robust to outliers. Point-biserial: one continuous and one genuinely dichotomous variable (male/female vs a test score). If the two groups are cut from a continuous score (pass/fail), use biserial instead. Phi coefficient: two dichotomous variables (a 2x2 association). Trap: Correlation is not causation, and r only detects linear relationships. A strong curved (U-shaped) relationship can produce r near zero. Always look at the scatterplot. Partial correlation, regression, and r-squared Partial correlation measures the relationship between two variables while statistically holding a third constant, revealing whether an association survives once a confound is removed. Simple regression predicts an outcome from one predictor via a best-fit line (least squares minimises the summed squared vertical distances of points from the line). Multiple regression uses several predictors at once and reports each predictor's unique contribution while controlling the others. The coefficient of determination (r-squared) is the proportion of variance in the outcome explained by the predictor(s). Example: if r = 0.6, then r-squared = 0.36, so 36% of the variance in the outcome is accounted for, and 64% remains unexplained. Factor analysis and reliability as statistics Factor analysis reduces many observed variables to a few underlying latent factors by exploiting their intercorrelations. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) discovers structure with no prior model, letting the data suggest how many factors exist. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) tests a pre-specified model, asking whether the hypothesised factor structure fits the data. Reliability coefficients are themselves statistics: Cronbach's alpha summarises internal consistency (how well a set of items hang together, alpha above about 0.7 is acceptable), and a test-retest reliability coefficient is just a correlation between two administrations. 26. Qualitative Methods, Trustworthiness, and Mixed Designs Who → what: Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss founded grounded theory ; Virginia Braun and Victoria Clarke codified thematic analysis ; Egon Guba and Yvonna Lincoln gave qualitative work its quality criteria ( trustworthiness ). The main qualitative traditions Grounded theory (Glaser and Strauss): builds theory from the data through iterative coding (open, axial, selective) and constant comparison, sampling until theoretical saturation (no new categories emerge). Phenomenology: studies the lived, subjective experience of a phenomenon, aiming to capture its essence (rooted in Husserl). Ethnography: immerses the researcher in a culture or group over time, relying on participant observation and field notes. Case study: an in-depth examination of a single bounded unit (a person, clinic, event) using multiple data sources. Narrative research: analyses the stories people tell to understand how they make meaning of their lives. Analysing qualitative data Thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke) is a flexible six-phase method: familiarisation, generating initial codes, searching for themes, reviewing themes, defining and naming themes, and writing up. Content analysis systematically codes and often counts the occurrence of categories in text, so it can straddle qualitative and quantitative aims. The distinction to hold: thematic analysis seeks patterns of meaning; content analysis often quantifies manifest content. Trustworthiness (Lincoln and Guba) Because qualitative work cannot use reliability and validity in the quantitative sense, Lincoln and Guba proposed four parallel criteria: Credibility (parallels internal validity): are the findings believable? Achieved through triangulation, member checking, prolonged engagement. Transferability (parallels external validity): can findings apply elsewhere? Supported by rich, thick description so readers judge fit. Dependability (parallels reliability): would the process be consistent if repeated? Supported by an audit trail. Confirmability (parallels objectivity): are findings grounded in data, not researcher bias? Supported by reflexivity and audit. Mixed methods Mixed-methods research combines qualitative and quantitative approaches in one study to exploit the strengths of each: numbers for breadth and generalisation, words for depth and meaning. Common structures include explanatory sequential (quantitative first, then qualitative to explain it) and exploratory sequential (qualitative first to generate items, then quantitative to test them). RML tilt: Match-the-founder items are common: grounded theory to Glaser and Strauss, thematic analysis to Braun and Clarke, trustworthiness criteria to Lincoln and Guba. 27. Research Ethics and APA Reporting Core ethical safeguards Informed consent requires that participants agree voluntarily after being told the study's nature, risks, and their right to withdraw at any time without penalty. Deception is permitted only when necessary and when no less-deceptive alternative exists, and it must be followed by debriefing , a full explanation afterward that reveals any deception and restores the participant's understanding and wellbeing. An Institutional Review Board (IRB) or ethics committee reviews and approves the protocol before data collection to protect participants. Additional pillars are confidentiality/anonymity, protection from harm, and honest handling of data. Plagiarism (presenting others' work or ideas as your own) and data fabrication are the gravest integrity violations. APA style and report structure The standard empirical report follows a fixed skeleton: Title page, Abstract, Introduction (the literature review and hypotheses, which does not carry the heading "Introduction"), Method (participants, materials, procedure, in enough detail to replicate), Results (the statistics, tables, and figures with no interpretation), Discussion (interpretation, limitations, implications), and References . APA in-text citation is author-date (Sharma, 2021), and the reference list is alphabetical by author surname. Rule: Results states what you found (the numbers); Discussion states what it means . Putting interpretation in Results, or new statistics in Discussion, is a classic marking penalty and a favourite exam distinction. Big picture: your design (between vs within, factorial, quasi, single-subject) decides what causal claims are defensible and which validity threats loom. Your sampling decides who the conclusions cover. Descriptive stats summarise the sample; the sampling distribution and CLT bridge to the population; hypothesis testing quantifies your risk of being wrong (Type I vs Type II), tempered by effect size and confidence intervals . Pick the test by matching measurement level, number of groups, and independence to the decision table, choosing non-parametric partners when assumptions fail. For non-numeric questions, qualitative traditions plus Lincoln and Guba's trustworthiness apply, and everything runs on an ethical, APA-reported spine. 12 Indian Psychology (past & present) RML tilt: The RML CET-166 tests Indian psychology as a past AND present subject. Expect one cluster on the history of the discipline in India (firsts, founders, institutions) and another on classical Eastern frameworks (gunas, koshas, Yoga, Buddhist psychology). This is a recurring leak, so over-learn both halves. From scratch: "Indian psychology" means two overlapping things. (1) The history of the modern academic discipline as it grew in India from 1915 onward. (2) The indigenous psychological knowledge embedded in Samkhya, Yoga, Vedanta, Ayurveda and Buddhism, which long predates Western scientific psychology. Keep the two senses separate in your head and you will not mix up an exam item. 1. History of psychology in India Modern experimental psychology reached India through the University of Calcutta . The first psychology laboratory in India was set up at Calcutta in 1915 , and the first Department of Psychology in India was founded there in 1916 by Narendra Nath Sen Gupta . Sen Gupta had trained at Harvard under Hugo Münsterberg (a student of Wilhelm Wundt), so the German experimental tradition entered India through him. He is rightly called the founder of academic psychology in India. Who → what: Narendra Nath Sen Gupta → first Department of Psychology (Calcutta, 1916); trained under Hugo Münsterberg at Harvard. The towering early figure in Indian psychoanalysis was Girindrasekhar Bose , the first Indian psychoanalyst and the first Indian to earn a doctorate in psychology (Calcutta). In 1922 he founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Society , one of the earliest such societies outside the West. Bose corresponded with Sigmund Freud for many years, and though the two respected each other they disagreed on theory. Bose proposed his theory of opposite wishes : every wish coexists with its opposite in the mind, and repression is really the management of these paired opposing wishes rather than simple burial of a single drive. Bose argued the wish "to be a man" and the wish "to be a woman" can both be present, which he linked to Indian ideas of identification. Who → what: Girindrasekhar Bose → first Indian psychoanalyst; founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Society (1922); corresponded with Sigmund Freud ; "opposite wish" theory. Other builders of the discipline: Gunamudian David Boaz , a pioneer of psychology in South India, associated with the University of Madras , who helped establish applied and psychological-testing work. Durganand Sinha , the leading voice of the indigenization of psychology , author of Psychology in the Indian Context . He argued that psychology in India had been a borrowed, imitative Western import and needed to be rooted in Indian social reality. Jadunath Sinha , scholar of classical Indian Psychology , author of a major multi-volume study of cognition, emotion and will (conation) as treated in Indian philosophical systems. H. P. Maiti , an early experimental and applied psychologist in the Calcutta tradition. Institutionally, psychology gained a foothold when a dedicated psychology section of the Indian Science Congress was recognised, giving the field a scientific platform. Applied and clinical psychology then grew rapidly around mental-health institutions. The National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS) in Bangalore became the flagship for clinical training, and in 1992 the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) was established by an Act of Parliament to regulate and standardise the training of clinical psychologists and other rehabilitation professionals. Firsts in Indian psychology (compact list) First psychology laboratory: University of Calcutta, 1915. First Department of Psychology: University of Calcutta, 1916, founded by Narendra Nath Sen Gupta . First Indian psychoanalyst: Girindrasekhar Bose . First psychoanalytical society: Indian Psychoanalytical Society , 1922 (Bose). Regulatory body for clinical psychology: Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) , 1992. Trap: Do not confuse the laboratory (1915) with the department (1916) , and do not credit the department to Wilhelm Wundt or Hugo Münsterberg, Münsterberg was Sen Gupta's teacher , not the Indian founder. Also, RCI was founded in 1992 , not with NIMHANS. 2. Classical / Indian frameworks Samkhya , one of the oldest Indian schools, splits reality into two ultimate principles: purusha (pure consciousness, the witnessing self) and prakriti (primordial matter/nature, the source of mind and body). All experience arises when purusha appears entangled with prakriti ; liberation is discriminating one from the other. Prakriti is made of three gunas (qualities/strands) whose changing proportions shape personality and mental states: Guna Quality Psychological expression Sattva Purity, clarity, balance Calm, wisdom, self-control, contentment Rajas Activity, passion, restlessness Ambition, agitation, craving, drive Tamas Inertia, dullness, darkness Lethargy, confusion, ignorance, depression The Vedantic model of the self layers the person into five sheaths, the pancha kosha , from grossest to subtlest: Kosha (sheath) Made of Level Annamaya kosha Food/matter Physical body Pranamaya kosha Vital energy (prana) Breath / life-force Manomaya kosha Mind, sense-processing Emotional-mental body Vijnanamaya kosha Intellect, discernment Wisdom / knowing body Anandamaya kosha Bliss Innermost / causal body The inner instrument of mind is the antahkarana , classically divided into four functions: manas (the sensory-processing, doubting mind), buddhi (intellect, discrimination and decision), ahamkara (the ego, the "I-maker") and chitta (the storehouse of memory and impressions). Consciousness itself moves through four states, the avasthas : jagrat (waking), swapna (dreaming), sushupti (deep dreamless sleep) and turiya (the "fourth", pure witnessing consciousness beyond the other three). Key. Learn the four-part maps as sets: antahkarana = manas / buddhi / ahamkara / chitta ; avasthas = jagrat / swapna / sushupti / turiya . Single-word matching items live here. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras define yoga as "chitta vritti nirodha" , the stilling of the modifications of the mind. The path is ashtanga yoga , the eight limbs: yama (ethical restraints), niyama (observances), asana (posture), pranayama (breath control), pratyahara (withdrawal of the senses), dharana (concentration), dhyana (meditation) and samadhi (absorption). The last three combined form samyama . The Bhagavad Gita offers an applied psychology of action and motivation. Its central teaching is nishkama karma , performing one's duty without attachment to the fruits of action, which reduces anxiety and stabilises the mind. The Gita also applies the three gunas to classify personality, food, work and even faith, giving a full trait-like typology. Buddhist psychology centres on the Four Noble Truths : there is suffering ( dukkha ), it has a cause (craving, tanha ), it can cease ( nirodha ), and there is a path to its cessation (the Eightfold Path). Two ideas are heavily tested: anatta (no-self, there is no fixed, permanent self, only changing processes) and mindfulness / vipassana (non-judgemental moment-to-moment awareness), the direct ancestor of modern mindfulness-based clinical interventions. 3. Indigenous concepts & therapies The self in Indian thought is relational and interdependent, not the bounded, autonomous individual of Western psychology. Identity is embedded in family, community, duty ( dharma ) and the cosmos, which is why collectivist and role-based framings recur in Indian personality research. Ayurveda adds a mind-body model built on the tridosha , vata (air/movement), pitta (fire/metabolism) and kapha (earth-water/structure), alongside the mental gunas ( sattva, rajas, tamas ) as determinants of temperament and disorder. Interventions include yoga and meditation as psychological treatments (now evidence-based for anxiety, depression and stress), plus indigenous and faith-based healing practices that many Indian clients use in parallel with clinical care. 4. The present & new developments The modern field is defined by the indigenization movement that Durganand Sinha led: building a psychology fitted to Indian culture rather than importing Western tools wholesale. Classical Indian frameworks map neatly onto positive psychology , sattva , well-being, mindfulness, meaning and self-regulation are shared ground, and the Gita's nishkama karma anticipates ideas of flow and non-attachment. Clinically, the RCI licensing framework now governs training: an RCI-recognised M.Phil or the newer RCI MA in Clinical Psychology, plus registration, is required to practise. The living institutional map includes NIMHANS (Bangalore), the Central Institute of Psychiatry (CIP), Ranchi , the Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences (IHBAS) , Delhi, and RML Hospital , Delhi, the very centres whose entrance you are preparing for. Trap: "Indigenization" is Durganand Sinha , not Jadunath Sinha (classical Indian Psychology scholar), different people, similar surname. And anatta means no-self , not non-violence (that is ahimsa ). Recap: Calcutta gave India its first psychology lab (1915) and first department (1916) under Narendra Nath Sen Gupta (pupil of Hugo Münsterberg ); Girindrasekhar Bose was the first Indian psychoanalyst, founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Society (1922) , corresponded with Freud , and proposed the opposite-wish theory; Durganand Sinha drove indigenization , and the RCI (1992) regulates clinical training. Classically: Samkhya's purusha/prakriti and the three gunas ; the five koshas ; the four-fold antahkarana and four avasthas (ending in turiya ); Patanjali's ashtanga yoga ; the Gita's nishkama karma ; and Buddhist Four Noble Truths , anatta and mindfulness/vipassana , now flowing into positive psychology and RCI-governed practice at NIMHANS, CIP, IHBAS and RML . 5. The Six Darshanas (Orthodox Schools of Indian Philosophy) The word darshana means "a way of seeing" or a vision of reality. The six orthodox (astika) schools accept the authority of the Vedas. They are conventionally grouped in three pairs: Nyaya and Vaisheshika, Samkhya and Yoga, Mimamsa and Vedanta. Each carries an implicit psychology, a theory of the mind (manas), the self (atman or purusha), and how valid knowledge (pramana) is obtained. From scratch: "Orthodox" here is a technical label meaning Veda-accepting (astika); it does not mean religious or conservative. The heterodox (nastika) schools that reject Vedic authority are Buddhism, Jainism, and the materialist Charvaka. RML questions often ask which schools are astika versus nastika. Darshana Founder / key text Core psychological contribution Nyaya Gautama (Akshapada); Nyaya Sutras Logic and epistemology; four valid means of knowledge (perception, inference, comparison, testimony) Vaisheshika Kanada; Vaisheshika Sutras Atomism; categories of reality; manas (mind) as an internal sense organ Samkhya Kapila Dualism of purusha (consciousness) and prakriti (matter); the three gunas; theory of evolution of the mind Yoga Patanjali; Yoga Sutras Practical psychology of mind-control; states and stilling of consciousness Mimamsa Jaimini; Mimamsa Sutras Hermeneutics of ritual action (dharma); theory of meaning and duty Vedanta Badarayana; Brahma Sutras (later Shankara) Nature of the self (atman), ultimate reality (Brahman), and consciousness Nyaya and Vaisheshika: logic, atoms, and the mind Nyaya is the school of logic and epistemology. Its lasting psychological contribution is the theory of pramanas (valid means of knowledge): pratyaksha (perception), anumana (inference), upamana (comparison or analogy), and shabda (verbal testimony from a reliable source). This is effectively an early theory of cognition and how the mind acquires reliable beliefs. Vaisheshika , closely allied, is an atomistic metaphysics: all physical reality reduces to indivisible atoms (paramanu). For psychology, its key claim is that manas (mind) is itself a subtle, atomic internal organ that connects the self (atman) to the senses; because the mind is atomic and can attend to only one thing at a time, attention is serial. Samkhya: purusha and prakriti (the most weighted) Samkhya , attributed to the sage Kapila , is one of the oldest and most influential systems, and it supplies the metaphysics that Yoga later builds on. It is strictly dualist but not a mind-body dualism (René Descartes) in the Western sense. The two ultimate realities are: Purusha : pure consciousness, the witness (sakshi), inactive, plural, and eternal. It is the "seer." Prakriti : primordial matter or nature, unconscious, active, the source of everything mental and physical. It is the "seen." Crucially, in Samkhya the mind (including buddhi/intellect, ahamkara/ego, and manas) belongs to prakriti , not to purusha. The mind is material and unconscious; it only appears conscious because purusha's light is reflected in it. Prakriti evolves through the interplay of the three gunas (sattva, rajas, tamas). Bondage and suffering arise from the false identification of purusha with prakriti; liberation (kaivalya) is the discriminative knowledge (viveka) that they are separate. Trap: Samkhya is atheistic (nirishvara): it explains creation through prakriti's evolution and needs no God. Yoga (seshvara Samkhya) adds Ishvara. Do not attribute a creator God to Samkhya. Vedanta: Advaita and the four states of consciousness (also heavily weighted) Vedanta ("end of the Vedas") centres on the Upanishads and the nature of the self. The most examined branch is Advaita Vedanta (non-dualism), systematised by Shankara (Adi Shankaracharya, c. 8th century CE). Its central teaching is that atman (individual self) and Brahman (ultimate reality) are one and the same; the perceived plurality of the world is maya (appearance superimposed by ignorance, avidya). Liberation (moksha) is realising this identity. Advaita's key psychological model is the four states of consciousness (from the Mandukya Upanishad): Jagrat : waking state, awareness of the external world. Svapna : dreaming state, awareness of internal mental images. Sushupti : deep dreamless sleep, undifferentiated consciousness with no objects. Turiya : literally "the fourth," pure consciousness underlying and witnessing the other three; the true self. RML tilt: The four avasthas overlap with the "avasthas" mentioned in the base section. Here anchor them to Mandukya Upanishad and Advaita, and remember turiya = the witnessing fourth state, not a phase of sleep. 6. Yoga Psychology in Depth (Patanjali) Patanjali compiled the Yoga Sutras (c. 2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE), the foundational text of Raja Yoga. Yoga shares Samkhya's metaphysics but is theistic and, above all, practical: it is a systematic psychology of stilling the mind. Key. Patanjali defines yoga in the second sutra: "Yogah chitta-vritti-nirodhah" = yoga is the restraint (nirodha) of the modifications (vrittis) of the mind-stuff (chitta). When the mind's fluctuations cease, the seer rests in its own true nature. Chitta and the chitta-vrittis Chitta is the total mind-field (comprising buddhi, ahamkara, and manas). Its activities are the vrittis , five kinds of mental modification: pramana (valid cognition), viparyaya (error), vikalpa (imagination or verbal delusion), nidra (sleep), and smriti (memory). Yoga aims to still all vrittis. The five kleshas (afflictions) The kleshas are the root causes of suffering, the mental afflictions that drive the vrittis: Avidya : ignorance (the root of the other four). Asmita : egoism, false identification of the seer with the instrument of seeing. Raga : attachment to pleasure. Dvesha : aversion to pain. Abhinivesha : clinging to life, fear of death. Ashtanga: the eight limbs The path to stilling the mind has eight limbs (ashtanga yoga): # Limb Meaning 1 Yama Ethical restraints (non-violence, truth, non-stealing, continence, non-possession) 2 Niyama Observances (purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, surrender to God) 3 Asana Steady, comfortable posture 4 Pranayama Regulation of breath and vital energy 5 Pratyahara Withdrawal of the senses from their objects 6 Dharana Concentration, fixing attention on one point 7 Dhyana Meditation, sustained unbroken flow of attention 8 Samadhi Absorption, union with the object of meditation From scratch: The last three (dharana, dhyana, samadhi) together are called samyama and form the "inner" limbs of mental discipline, while the first five are preparatory or "outer" limbs. Types of samadhi Samadhi is graded. Samprajnata samadhi (with cognition) still has an object of awareness; it passes through subtler stages. Asamprajnata samadhi (without cognition) has no object and no seed. The highest is nirbija samadhi ("seedless"), in which even the latent impressions (samskaras) are dissolved and kaivalya (liberation) is attained. 7. Buddhist Psychology in Depth Buddhism is a nastika (Veda-rejecting) system founded by Siddhartha Gautama , the Buddha. It is intensely psychological: it analyses suffering, the mind, and the self without positing a permanent soul. The Four Noble Truths Dukkha : life involves suffering or unsatisfactoriness. Samudaya : suffering has a cause, namely craving (tanha) and attachment. Nirodha : suffering can cease (nirvana). Magga : there is a path to its cessation, the Noble Eightfold Path. The Noble Eightfold Path The path has eight factors, grouped into wisdom (prajna), ethical conduct (sila), and mental discipline (samadhi): right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. The three marks of existence Anicca : impermanence; all conditioned things are in flux. Dukkha : unsatisfactoriness inherent in clinging to the impermanent. Anatta : no-self; there is no permanent, unchanging soul. Trap: Anatta (no-self) is the sharpest contrast with the Hindu darshanas, which affirm an eternal atman or purusha. A common exam item pairs "Buddhism → anatta (no permanent self)" against "Vedanta/Samkhya → eternal self." The five skandhas (aggregates) What we call "self" is, in Buddhism, only a bundle of five ever-changing skandhas : rupa (form or body), vedana (feeling or sensation tone), samjna (perception), samskara (mental formations or volitions), and vijnana (consciousness). No aggregate is the self, and no self stands behind them. Abhidhamma, dependent origination, and mindfulness The Abhidhamma is the third "basket" of Buddhist scripture, a systematic analysis of mind and mental factors (a kind of early phenomenological psychology). Dependent origination (paticca-samuppada) is the doctrine that all phenomena arise in dependence on conditions, classically the twelve-linked chain from ignorance (avidya) through to suffering; nothing exists independently. Sati (mindfulness) is present-moment, non-judgemental awareness, cultivated through vipassana (insight meditation) to see the three marks directly. This lineage is the acknowledged root of modern mindfulness-based interventions (MBSR, MBCT). RML tilt: Expect a question linking vipassana/sati to contemporary mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (Zindel Segal, Mark Williams and John Teasdale). Know that Jon Kabat-Zinn's MBSR secularised the Buddhist sati tradition. 8. Bhagavad Gita Psychology The Bhagavad Gita (Krishna's counsel to Arjuna) offers a practical psychology of action and motivation. It presents three complementary yogas (paths to liberation): karma yoga (the path of selfless action), bhakti yoga (the path of devotion), and jnana yoga (the path of knowledge). Key. The central motivational teaching is nishkama karma : acting without attachment to the fruits of action ("you have a right to action alone, never to its fruits"). This decouples effort from outcome-anxiety, a theme that resonates with intrinsic motivation and non-attached engagement. The ideal person is the sthitaprajna , the one of steady, established wisdom: unshaken by pleasure or pain, free from craving and aversion, with senses under control (compared to a tortoise withdrawing its limbs). The sthitaprajna is the Gita's model of emotional equanimity and self-regulation. 9. Sri Aurobindo, Integral Psychology, and Ayurveda Sri Aurobindo's integral psychology Sri Aurobindo developed integral psychology , mapping consciousness as a graded hierarchy rather than a single layer. Below ordinary awareness lies the subconscient and inconscient ; ordinary mind sits in the middle; above it rise the higher mind, illumined mind, intuitive mind, overmind, and finally the supermind (supramental consciousness). The self also has an inner being (behind the surface) and a central psychic being (the evolving soul). His practice, Integral Yoga , aims not to escape the world but to bring the supramental consciousness down into life. His work is a cornerstone of the modern Indian psychology movement. Ayurveda's tridosha and the mind Ayurveda , the classical Indian medical system, models the body through three doshas (biological energies): vata (air/movement), pitta (fire/metabolism), and kapha (earth-water/structure). For the mind ( manas ), Ayurveda uses the three gunas (sattva, rajas, tamas) as the mental equivalent of the doshas, giving a constitutional temperament theory (prakriti as personality type) that predates and parallels later trait models. 10. Contemporary Indian Psychology and Psychologists Beyond the classical firsts, a distinct movement toward indigenous, culturally grounded psychology emerged from the 1970s onward, reacting against the wholesale import of Western frameworks. Who → what: Durganand Sinha → the leading voice of indigenization ; argued Indian psychology must fit Indian social reality, not simply replicate American paradigms. Jai B.P. Sinha → the nurturant-task (NT) leadership model, an Indian leadership style blending personal care (nurturance) with task orientation, suited to the Indian work context. Girishwar Misra → edited major surveys of Indian psychology and advanced culture-and-cognition and indigenous well-being research. Anand C. Paranjpe → bridged Indian thought and Western self-psychology; comparative work on the self and identity across traditions. K. Ramakrishna Rao → systematised "Indian psychology" as a field, drawing on consciousness studies and yoga; a founder of the contemporary movement. A parallel Indian positive-psychology and well-being movement reframes classical constructs (sukha, ananda, equanimity, the sthitaprajna ideal) as models of flourishing, and studies indigenous coping, spirituality, and resilience. Applied and clinical research is concentrated at the premier institutions: NIMHANS (National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences, Bengaluru), CIP Ranchi (Central Institute of Psychiatry), and IHBAS (Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences, Delhi), which anchor clinical psychology training, mental-health research, and culturally adapted therapy in India. Recap: Six darshanas (astika) vs Buddhism/Jainism/Charvaka (nastika). Samkhya = purusha/prakriti dualism, atheistic, three gunas. Vedanta (Advaita, Shankara) = atman is Brahman, four states with turiya as witness. Yoga (Patanjali) = chitta-vritti-nirodha, five kleshas, eight limbs, seedless samadhi. Buddhism = Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path, anicca/dukkha/anatta, five skandhas, dependent origination, vipassana. Gita = three yogas, nishkama karma, sthitaprajna. Aurobindo = integral psychology up to supermind. Contemporary = Durganand Sinha, Jai Sinha, Misra, Paranjpe, Rao, and NIMHANS/CIP/IHBAS. 11. The Triguna Theory of Personality Indian thought does not treat personality as a fixed set of traits you are born with and stuck with. It treats it as a balance of forces that can shift with diet, company, effort and stage of life. The oldest and most exam-relevant of these force models is the theory of the three gunas (Sanskrit guna = "strand, quality, constituent"). Everything in nature ( prakriti ) is woven from three strands, and the mind is no exception. From scratch: Think of the three gunas as three dials that are always present in every person at once. What changes from person to person, and from hour to hour in the same person, is the mix . Nobody is purely one guna. Personality is your habitual set-point of the three. The three strands Sattva ( sattva = purity, harmony, clarity): calm, wakeful, truthful, disciplined, compassionate, discriminating. The sattvic mind is luminous and steady. This is the guna a yogic or spiritual life tries to increase. Rajas ( rajas = passion, activity, restlessness): energetic, ambitious, driven, attached to results, prone to craving, anger and agitation. Rajas is the engine of action but also of turbulence. Tamas ( tamas = inertia, darkness, dullness): heavy, lethargic, confused, sleepy, procrastinating, ignorant. Tamas is needed for rest and sleep, but in excess it produces stagnation, delusion and depression-like states. Each guna colours cognition, emotion, food preference, work style and even the kind of faith a person holds. The Bhagavad Gita (chapters 14, 17 and 18) systematically classifies knowledge, action, doer, intellect, resolve, happiness and even charity into sattvic, rajasic and tamasic types. This is one of the world's earliest fully worked-out personality typologies, and RML has asked "which guna corresponds to X" style items. Guna Mental state Typical behaviour Modern rough analogue Sattva Clarity, peace Balanced, altruistic, self-controlled Well-being, high conscientiousness + low neuroticism Rajas Craving, agitation Ambitious, competitive, easily angered High drive + high neuroticism / Type-A Tamas Dullness, delusion Inert, avoidant, exploitative Low activation, apathy, some dark-triad features The Vedic Personality Inventory (VPI) Contemporary Indian and Western psychologists have tried to measure the gunas so the model can be tested empirically. The best-known instrument is the Vedic Personality Inventory (VPI) developed by David Wolf (1998, 1999) .
