It is a self-report scale with items loading onto three subscales, one for each guna, and it has shown that sattva correlates positively with mental health and life satisfaction, while tamas correlates with poorer adjustment and higher symptoms. Other guna scales exist (for example the Gita Inventory of Personality and various Indian-authored triguna scales), but the VPI is the one most likely to be named in an exam. RML tilt: Learn the pairing "Wolf → Vedic Personality Inventory → measures the three gunas." Also remember the direction: sattva up = good adjustment; tamas up = poor adjustment. Gunas are dimensions of prakriti , not of purusha , which stays untouched by them. 12. Purusharthas, Ashramas, and Karma as a Psychology of Motivation Western motivation theory asks "what energises and directs behaviour?" Indian thought answered this long ago with a structured account of legitimate human goals, a developmental sequence for pursuing them, and a moral law that keeps the whole system going across lifetimes. Together these form an indigenous theory of motivation and lifespan development. The four purusharthas (aims of life) Purushartha means "that which is sought by a person," the sanctioned goals of human life. There are four, and they are meant to be pursued in balance, not one at the expense of the others. Dharma (duty, righteousness, ethical order): living in accordance with one's role and moral law. It is placed first because it regulates the pursuit of the other three. Artha (wealth, security, resources, worldly success): the material and economic base of life. Kama (pleasure, desire, aesthetic and sensual enjoyment, love): legitimate enjoyment, not condemned but to be kept within dharma. Moksha (liberation, release from the cycle of birth and death): the ultimate goal, freedom of the self. Example: A householder earning a living (artha) and raising a family (kama) does so within ethical limits (dharma), while never losing sight of eventual liberation (moksha). Compare this with Maslow's hierarchy: artha and kama map loosely onto lower needs, dharma onto esteem and self-actualisation, and moksha onto self-transcendence, which Maslow added late in life. The four ashramas (stages of life) Ashrama means a stage or station of life. The classical scheme divides the ideal lifespan into four stages, giving each its own developmental task, a striking parallel to Erikson's psychosocial stages. Brahmacharya (student stage): celibate discipline, learning, skill acquisition under a teacher. Grihastha (householder stage): marriage, work, raising a family, pursuing artha and kama within dharma. Vanaprastha (forest-dweller / retirement stage): gradual withdrawal from worldly duties, handing over responsibility, turning inward. Sannyasa (renunciate stage): full renunciation, single-minded pursuit of moksha. Rule: Purusharthas = what to pursue (the goals). Ashramas = when to pursue it (the stages). The householder stage is the one where artha and kama are legitimately maximised; moksha dominates the later stages. Karma and rebirth as motivation Karma literally means "action," but as a doctrine it is the moral law that every intentional action leaves an imprint ( samskara ) that shapes future experience, in this life or a later one, through the cycle of rebirth ( samsara ). Psychologically this functions as a powerful internal locus of control (Julian Rotter, 1966) and a delay-of-gratification framework: because consequences are guaranteed even if not immediate, the doctrine motivates ethical restraint and long-horizon effort. It reframes suffering as intelligible rather than random, which can aid coping, though critics note it can also breed fatalism if misread. The Gita 's answer to this risk is nishkama karma , action performed as duty without attachment to its fruits, which keeps the person active while dissolving anxiety about outcomes. Trap: Karma is not "fate." Fate implies you are passive; karma insists the future is being authored by present action. It is closer to a lawful cause-effect view of moral behaviour than to predestination. Classical texts further sort karma into three kinds, which is worth knowing because it turns the doctrine into a clean theory of how past learning constrains present choice: sanchita karma (the whole accumulated store of past actions not yet ripened), prarabdha karma (the portion already "activated" and playing out as the circumstances of this life), and agami / kriyamana karma (fresh action being generated now, which feeds the store). Psychologically this is a layered model of learning history: prarabdha is the given you cannot change (like temperament and early conditioning), while agami is the space of present freedom. The therapeutic reading is that a person is never wholly determined; there is always a live margin of new, wilful action through which the pattern can be redirected. 13. The Self in Indian Psychology: Atman, Ahamkara, and the Inner Instrument Where does the sense of "I" come from, and is it the real self? Indian psychology draws a sharp line between the true self and the mistaken self, and it maps the inner apparatus that produces ordinary experience. This is arguably the most philosophically distinctive Indian contribution and a favourite exam area. Atman versus ahamkara (self versus ego) Atman is the true Self: pure consciousness, unchanging, the witness behind all experience. Ahamkara ( aham = "I" + kara = "maker," literally "the I-maker") is the ego, the manufactured sense of a separate self that says "I am the doer, this is mine." In Vedanta, suffering arises precisely from confusing the two: mistaking the changing ego and body for the changeless Atman. Liberation is the correct discrimination between them ( viveka ). The antahkarana (the inner instrument) Antahkarana means "inner instrument," the fourfold inner apparatus through which consciousness knows and acts. Learn the four parts and their division of labour: Component Meaning Function Manas Mind (lower) Sensory-processing mind: receives impressions, doubts, wavers, coordinates the senses. The "monkey mind." Buddhi Intellect Discriminating faculty: decides, judges, discerns true from false. The highest, most sattvic instrument. Chitta Memory / mind-stuff Storehouse of impressions ( samskaras ), the substrate on which experiences are recorded. Ahamkara Ego The I-sense that appropriates experience as "mine." From scratch: A simple worked example. You hear a sound at night. Manas registers the raw sensation and wavers ("what was that?"). Buddhi discriminates ("it is the wind, not a thief"). Chitta stores the memory of the fright. Ahamkara claims it: " I was afraid." The pure Atman merely witnesses all four operating. The panchakosha: five sheaths of the self The Taittiriya Upanishad gives a layered model of the person as five concentric koshas (sheaths or coverings) wrapped around the Atman, from grossest to subtlest. This is an early holistic, multi-level model of the human being and maps neatly onto a biopsychosocial-spiritual view. Annamaya kosha ( anna = food): the physical body, sustained by food. The gross, outermost sheath. Pranamaya kosha ( prana = vital energy / breath): the energy or life-force body governing physiological vitality. Manomaya kosha ( manas = mind): the mental-emotional sheath of thoughts, feelings and sensory processing. Vijnanamaya kosha ( vijnana = knowing): the sheath of intellect, discrimination and wisdom (buddhi). Anandamaya kosha ( ananda = bliss): the innermost blissful sheath, closest to the Atman. RML tilt: Order the koshas grossest to subtlest: Anna → Prana → Mano → Vijnana → Ananda ("A Person May Value Ananda"). Modern integrative and yoga-based therapies (for example the panchakosha model used at some Indian centres) assess a client across all five layers rather than only the psychological one. 14. Sattvavajaya and Prajnaparadha: Ayurveda's Cognitive Therapy Ayurveda is usually remembered only for the three body humours ( vata, pitta, kapha ). But it also contains a genuine mental-health framework that reads like an ancient forerunner of cognitive therapy, and this is under-taught, so it is worth knowing well. Manas and the mental gunas Ayurveda treats manas (mind) as having its own qualities. Alongside the physical doshas it names rajas and tamas as the two mental doshas (manasika doshas) , the disturbers of mental health, with sattva as the balanced ideal. Mental disorder is imbalance of these mental gunas, not only of the bodily humours. Prajnaparadha (crimes against wisdom) Prajnaparadha ( prajna = wisdom + aparadha = offence, literally "the failure or crime of wisdom") is Ayurveda's concept for acting against one's better judgement: knowing what is good yet doing the opposite, because intellect, restraint and memory have faltered. It is held to be a root cause of both physical and mental illness. Psychologically it is remarkably close to the idea of maladaptive choices driven by faulty cognition, an ancient statement that distorted thinking makes us ill. Sattvavajaya (mind control therapy) Sattvavajaya ( sattva = mind/purity + avajaya = conquest, literally "conquest of the mind") is Ayurveda's psychotherapy: the restraint of the mind from unwholesome objects and the cultivation of sattva. Charaka describes it as controlling the mind, redirecting it away from harmful desires, and strengthening knowledge, self-control and memory. Because it works by correcting the client's thinking and self-regulation , many contemporary Indian authors explicitly describe sattvavajaya as an indigenous cognitive-behavioural therapy. Who → what: Charaka (Charaka Samhita) → classical descriptions of sattvavajaya, prajnaparadha and the mental doshas rajas/tamas. Learn these three terms together as the "Ayurvedic mind" cluster. The three lines of treatment Ayurveda's mental-health management is classically organised into three approaches, and sattvavajaya is the psychological one of the three: daivavyapashraya (spiritual or faith-based measures such as mantra, ritual and religious observance), yuktivyapashraya (rational, physical measures such as diet, herbs and cleansing therapies aimed at the doshas), and sattvavajaya (non-pharmacological control of the mind). The presence of a distinct psychological line of treatment, separate from the bodily and the spiritual, shows that classical Indian medicine already recognised mind-directed therapy as a category in its own right. In addition, Ayurveda offers a temperament typology: it describes seven sattvic , six rajasic and three tamasic mental constitution types (the manasa prakriti ), an early classification of personality by dominant mental guna. 15. Indigenous and Asian Therapies: Yoga, Meditation, Morita and Naikan RML likes to test whether you can place Indian practices alongside other Asian indigenous therapies and against modern Western therapy. Treat this as a comparison table in your head. Yoga and meditation as therapy Beyond philosophy, yoga (postures, breath regulation or pranayama , and meditation) and meditative practices are used therapeutically in India for anxiety, depression, stress, hypertension and psychosomatic conditions. Their mechanism is understood as increasing sattva and reducing chitta-vritti (mental fluctuations), producing calmer autonomic arousal. This is the lineage that fed into modern mindfulness-based interventions : Buddhist sati (mindful awareness) was secularised by Jon Kabat-Zinn into MBSR (Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction) and later into MBCT (Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy) for relapse prevention in depression. Morita and Naikan (Japanese therapies) Two Japanese therapies rooted in Zen Buddhist thought are the standard comparison points, and they are frequently confused, so pin them down: Morita therapy (Shoma Morita, 1919): originally for shinkeishitsu (anxiety-based, obsessive, perfectionistic neurosis). Core idea: stop fighting your symptoms; accept feelings as they are and act on purpose anyway ("arugamama," acceptance of things as they are). Classic version uses phases of bed rest followed by graded light then heavy work. The lesson is character-building through purposeful action, not symptom elimination. Naikan therapy (Ishin Yoshimoto, mid-20th century, from Jodo Shinshu Buddhism): structured, guided self-reflection . The client meditates on three questions about significant people (usually starting with the mother): What did this person do for me? What did I do for them? What troubles and difficulties did I cause them? The aim is gratitude, realistic self-appraisal and repair of relationships. Therapy Origin Core mechanism Goal Yoga / meditation India (Hindu / Buddhist) Reduce mental fluctuation, raise sattva, regulate arousal Calm, insight, self-mastery Morita Japan (Zen) Accept feelings, commit to purposeful action Function despite symptoms; character Naikan Japan (Jodo Shinshu) Structured reflection on three questions Gratitude, self-honesty, mended relationships Trap: Do not swap Morita and Naikan. Morita = action and acceptance of symptoms; Naikan = reflection and gratitude. Memory hook: Naikan starts with "Nai/in" = looking inward at what others did for you. 16. The Growth and Indigenization of Psychology in India The contemporary section already names the leading psychologists. This part goes into the debate that shapes the discipline and adds a few concepts likely to be tested as short items. The indigenization debate Psychology in India began as an imported discipline (the first laboratory was set up at Calcutta University in 1915 under N. N. Sengupta, and much early work simply replicated Western studies). By the 1970s, Indian psychologists argued this borrowed psychology did not fit Indian realities. This launched the indigenization movement , usually described in three phases: Indigenization from without : importing Western concepts and testing them on Indian samples (early, imitative phase). Indigenization from within : building concepts, theories and methods out of Indian culture, texts and lived experience (the guna model, purusharthas, and so on). An integrated / cross-cultural psychology : combining both so that Indian psychology contributes to a genuinely universal discipline rather than a merely local one. Who → what: Durganand Sinha → pioneer of the critique of imported psychology; classic work on deprivation and the culture-rooted growth of Indian psychology. J. B. P. Sinha → the Nurturant-Task (NT) leadership model: an effective Indian leader is both caring/nurturant toward subordinates and firmly task-oriented, contingent on the subordinate's maturity. Girishwar Misra → edited major surveys of Indian psychology; champion of culture-sensitive, indigenous methods. Anand C. Paranjpe → bridged Indian thought and Western self/identity theory (self and identity across the two traditions). K. Ramakrishna Rao and Kiran Kumar Salagame → systematised "Indian psychology" as consciousness studies and well-being. Institutions and the present The discipline's growth in India has been carried by key institutions: the Indian Council of Social Science Research (ICSSR) and surveys of psychological research, NCERT and UGC shaping curricula (including moves to include Indian psychology in syllabi), and clinical and neuroscientific work led by NIMHANS (Bengaluru) and the ICMR . Applied strands now include health psychology, organisational behaviour rooted in Indian values, yoga-and-meditation research, and positive psychology drawing on classical concepts of well-being ( sukha ) and flourishing. RML tilt: High-probability pairings to memorise: Sengupta → first Indian psychology lab (Calcutta, 1915); Durganand Sinha → indigenization critique + deprivation; J. B. P. Sinha → Nurturant-Task leadership; Wolf → Vedic Personality Inventory; Paranjpe → self and identity. Know the three phases of indigenization by name. Recap: Personality in Indian psychology is the balance of three gunas (sattva, rajas, tamas), measurable via Wolf's Vedic Personality Inventory. Motivation and development are framed by the four purusharthas (dharma, artha, kama, moksha), the four ashramas, and the karma-rebirth law softened by nishkama karma. The self is analysed as true Atman versus the manufactured ahamkara, worked through the fourfold antahkarana (manas, buddhi, chitta, ahamkara) and the five koshas from food-body to bliss. Ayurveda adds an indigenous cognitive therapy: prajnaparadha (crimes against wisdom) as cause, sattvavajaya (mind conquest) as cure, with rajas and tamas as the mental doshas. Indigenous therapy sits beside Japan's Morita (accept feelings, act) and Naikan (reflect and give thanks), and beside modern MBSR/MBCT descended from Buddhist mindfulness. Finally, Indian psychology moved from imported replication to the three-phase indigenization movement led by Durganand Sinha, J. B. P. Sinha, Misra, Paranjpe, Rao and Salagame, supported by ICSSR, UGC/NCERT, NIMHANS and ICMR. 13 Social Work: the strand the psychology paper still asks you This section exists because of a hard fact from your own RML 2020 run: of the nine questions you lost, four were social work , not psychology. Question 4 (Joel Fischer's casework review), question 18 (the first school of social work in India), question 32 (what case management does and does not achieve) and question 82 (the common properties of a group) are all social work content. Three of those four were in reach with ten minutes of reading. None of them were hard. They were simply from a discipline nobody told you was on the paper. From scratch: why a psychology entrance asks social work at all. In India, mental health service delivery was built as a three-professional team : the psychiatrist (medical), the clinical psychologist (assessment and psychotherapy) and the psychiatric social worker (family, environment, rehabilitation, welfare linkage). All three are regulated together, the first by the National Medical Commission and the latter two by the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) . Because the professions were built as one team, entrance papers for clinical psychology in India routinely carry a slice of social work: its methods, its founders, its Indian institutional history. RML is one of the papers that does this. It is not a mistake in the paper. It is the syllabus. Key: Social work is a separate profession with its own founders, its own methods and its own Indian timeline. It is not "applied social psychology" and it is not counselling. Learning it as a distinct discipline, with its own names attached to its own dates, is what makes these questions free marks instead of coin flips. What social work is, and how it split from charity Social work is the organised, method-driven profession of helping people cope with problems in their social functioning : the fit between a person and the environment they live in. That last phrase is the whole definition. A clinical psychologist asks what is happening inside the person. A social worker asks what is happening between the person and their family, workplace, neighbourhood, welfare entitlements and law. The two overlap heavily in mental health, which is exactly why the entrance paper mixes them. The profession grew out of nineteenth-century charity, and its founding argument was that charity should stop being sentiment and start being method . Two rival movements did this in parallel, and RML-type papers like to contrast them: Movement Founded Core idea Descendant method Charity Organisation Society (COS) London 1869; Buffalo, USA 1877 Investigate each applicant individually, keep a record, coordinate relief so it is not duplicated. Sent "friendly visitors" into homes. Social case work Settlement house movement Toynbee Hall, London 1884 (Samuel Barnett); Hull House, Chicago 1889 ( Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr) Do not investigate the poor, live among them . Change the neighbourhood and the law, not the individual. Social group work and community organisation Who → what: Jane Addams → Hull House, Chicago, 1889, and the Nobel Peace Prize 1931, the settlement/reform tradition. Samuel Barnett → Toynbee Hall, London, 1884, the first settlement house. Mary Ellen Richmond → the Charity Organisation Society tradition and the birth of case work as a method. Trap: Toynbee Hall (1884, London) is the first settlement house; Hull House (1889, Chicago) is the famous American one. Papers swap the two and swap the founders. Barnett is London, Addams is Chicago. Method 1: Social case work, and the Fischer question Social case work is social work with the individual and the family as the unit of attention. Its founding text is Mary Ellen Richmond's Social Diagnosis (1917) , which imported the medical logic of study → diagnosis → treatment into helping work, and her What Is Social Case Work? (1922) , which named the method. Richmond's definition is the one to be able to recognise: case work is the set of processes that develop personality through conscious, individual by individual adjustments between people and their social environment. After Richmond the method split into two schools, and this split is examinable: Key: the two schools of case work. The Diagnostic school (Freudian, Smith College and New York School of Social Work; Gordon Hamilton , later Florence Hollis ) treats the worker as the expert who diagnoses and treats an intrapsychic problem; Hollis's version is called psychosocial case work , remembered by the phrase "the person-in-situation configuration". The Functional school (Rankian, University of Pennsylvania; Jessie Taft and Virginia Robinson ) rejects diagnosis, puts the client's own will at the centre, and uses the agency function and above all time (a defined beginning, middle and end) as the therapeutic instrument. Who → what: Mary Ellen Richmond → Social Diagnosis (1917), What Is Social Case Work? (1922), founder of case work. Gordon Hamilton → diagnostic school, Theory and Practice of Social Case Work . Florence Hollis → psychosocial case work, person-in-situation. Jessie Taft and Virginia Robinson → functional school, will and time, out of Otto Rank . Helen Harris Perlman → the problem-solving model (1957), the compromise between the two schools, remembered as the four Ps: Person, Problem, Place, Process (she later added a fifth and sixth P, Professional and Provisions). Felix Biestek → The Casework Relationship (1957) and the seven principles . Key: Biestek's seven principles of the casework relationship. Individualisation, purposeful expression of feelings, controlled emotional involvement, acceptance, non-judgemental attitude, client self-determination, confidentiality. If a question asks for "a principle of case work" and one option is something like "worker direction" or "moral evaluation", that option is the answer to an EXCEPT stem. From scratch: the Fischer question, which is the one that cost you a mark. By the 1960s case work had been the profession's flagship method for fifty years, but nobody had audited whether it worked. Joel Fischer did. His paper Is Casework Effective? A Review , published in the journal Social Work in 1973 , pulled together the controlled evaluation studies of professional casework and reported that the evidence did not show casework to be effective; in a number of the studies the treated clients did no better, and in some they did slightly worse, than untreated controls. The finding detonated inside the profession and is credited with pushing social work toward empirical practice , measurable outcomes and, eventually, evidence-based practice. So the correct association is: Fischer 1973 → casework effectiveness questioned → the empirical practice movement. Trap: The Fischer stem is almost always written so that the "nice" option is wrong. Fischer did not establish that casework works, did not develop a casework model, and is not a founder of casework. He is the man who asked whether it worked and answered "the evidence does not say so". If the options offer Richmond, Perlman, Hollis and Fischer against a stem about effectiveness or evaluation , it is Fischer. Method 2: Social group work, and what a group actually is Social group work is social work practised through the group: the worker uses the group experience itself as the instrument of change, so members grow through what happens between them rather than through what the worker does to them. It came out of the settlement houses, the YMCA/YWCA and the recreation movement, and was made a formal method largely by Grace Longwell Coyle ( Social Process in Organized Groups , 1930), with Gisela Konopka writing the standard mid-century text on group work in the treatment setting. Who → what: Grace Longwell Coyle → the founder of social group work as a method (1930s). Gisela Konopka → group work as a treatment method, group work with the emotionally disturbed. William Schwartz → the mediating/interactionist model. Robert Vinter → the remedial model. Charles Garvin and Paul Glasser → later systematisation. Compare with Kurt Lewin (group dynamics, T-groups, National Training Laboratories, 1946), who is psychology's side of the same coin. Key: the three classical models of group work. Social goals model (the settlement inheritance: build citizenship and social conscience, the group serves the community). Remedial model (Vinter: the group is a means of treating individual members, the worker is a change agent). Reciprocal/mediating model (Schwartz: the worker mediates between the individual and the group, both are the client). From scratch: the common properties of a group, which is question 82. Ask what makes a collection of people an actual group rather than a queue at a bus stop, and every textbook, sociological or social work, returns broadly the same list. A group has: (1) two or more people ; (2) interaction , they act on one another; (3) shared or common goals ; (4) a sense of "we-feeling" , belonging or common identity; (5) interdependence , what one does affects the others; (6) norms , shared rules of conduct; (7) roles and usually some structure or status differentiation ; and (8) some stability over time . What is not on that list is anything technical or theoretical: a group does not require an analytic base , a therapist, a formal theory, a written constitution, a fixed size or a professional worker. Groups exist without any of those. Trap: this is an EXCEPT question and you must pick the odd one out, not the weakest one. On a stem like "all of the following are common properties of a group EXCEPT", the four options will typically be three ordinary properties (interaction, common goal, we-feeling, norms) and one that sounds impressively technical. The technical-sounding one, analytic base , is the answer. Under time pressure the pull is to choose whichever property feels least important; that is the wrong instinct. On an EXCEPT stem your job is to find the option that is false , not the option that is weakest . Read every option, tick the three that are genuinely true, and take what is left. Key: stages of group development. Bruce Tuckman (1965) : forming, storming, norming, performing, plus adjourning added in 1977 with Mary Ann Jensen. The social work version is the Boston model of James Garland, Hubert Jones and Ralph Kolodny (1965) : pre-affiliation, power and control, intimacy, differentiation, separation. Know both, and know which is which: Tuckman is the psychology/management sequence, Garland-Jones-Kolodny is the social group work sequence. Method 3: Community organisation, and the rest of the method set Community organisation is social work with a community as the unit: identifying needs, building local capacity and matching resources to those needs. Murray G. Ross wrote the classic definition (a community identifies its needs, orders them, develops the confidence and will to work at them, and takes action, thereby extending cooperative attitudes). Jack Rothman (1968) gave the three models that get asked most: Rothman's model What it assumes Worker's role Locality development The community lacks skills and cohesion; consensus is possible Enabler, catalyst, teacher Social planning The problem is technical and substantive; needs expert data Fact-gatherer, analyst, programme implementer Social action The community is an oppressed group facing a power structure; conflict is expected Activist, advocate, negotiator, agitator Key: the methods of social work, primary and secondary. Primary (direct) methods: social case work, social group work, community organisation. Secondary (auxiliary, indirect) methods: social welfare administration, social action, social work research. Six in total. A stem asking for "the primary methods" wants the first three; a stem asking which is not a primary method is usually pointing at social work research or social welfare administration. Who → what: Murray G. Ross → the classic definition of community organisation. Jack Rothman → the three models (locality development, social planning, social action). Saul Alinsky → radical community organising, Rules for Radicals . Paulo Freire → Pedagogy of the Oppressed , conscientisation, the theory behind social action practice. Case management: what it does, and the thing it does not do Case management is the coordinating method that took over from classical casework in mental health, disability and long-term care after deinstitutionalisation. A person with a severe, long-running condition needs many services at once (medication, housing, income support, vocational training, family work) delivered by many agencies that do not talk to each other. The case manager is the single accountable point that assembles and holds that package together. Key: the core functions of case management. Assessment of need, planning (a written, individualised service plan), linkage/brokerage to services, coordination across providers, monitoring and review, advocacy for entitlements, and evaluation . The named models are the brokerage model (thin, link and refer), the clinical/therapeutic model (the manager also provides treatment), intensive case management , the strengths model (Charles Rapp and Ronna Chamberlain, University of Kansas: build on what the person and the environment already have) and Assertive Community Treatment (ACT) , developed by Leonard Stein and Mary Ann Test in Madison, Wisconsin, where a multidisciplinary team delivers services directly in the community with a low caseload and no time limit. From scratch: the outcomes question, which is question 32. What case management is evidenced to achieve is a narrow and specific list: it reduces hospitalisation and readmission , it improves continuity of care and engagement with services, it improves access to and coordination of services , it improves social functioning, housing stability and quality of life , it increases client and family satisfaction , and it can reduce total service costs by substituting community care for inpatient beds. What it does not do is cure anything. Case management is a service-delivery and coordination technology, not a treatment for the underlying disorder. It changes where and how care reaches a person; it does not change the natural history of schizophrenia. Trap: On "all of the following are outcomes of case management EXCEPT", the answer is the option that promises a clinical cure , remission , symptom elimination or "recovery from the illness". Every other option will be a coordination, access, continuity, satisfaction or cost outcome. Same discipline as question 82: find the false option, not the weak one. Social work in India: the dates and the institutions From scratch: the founding of social work education in India, which is question 18. Indian social work education begins in Bombay in 1936 with the Sir Dorabji Tata Graduate School of Social Work , the first school of social work in India and in Asia . It was founded by the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust and its first director was the American Protestant missionary Clifford Manshardt , who had been running the Nagpada Neighbourhood House, a settlement in Bombay; the settlement-house lineage runs straight into it. In 1944 the school was renamed the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS) , and it was granted deemed-university status in 1964. So a single chain to memorise: 1936 Sir Dorabji Tata Graduate School of Social Work → 1944 renamed TISS → 1964 deemed university , founder-director Clifford Manshardt , city Bombay/Mumbai . Trap: The distractors on this question are always the other plausible institutions and the other plausible years. It is not Delhi School of Social Work (founded 1946, later University of Delhi), not TISS-under-that-name (that name only exists from 1944), not NIMHANS (Bangalore, and a mental health institute, not a school of social work), and not 1947 or 1950. First school, first year: Bombay, 1936 . Year Milestone in Indian social work 1936 Sir Dorabji Tata Graduate School of Social Work , Bombay: first school of social work in India and Asia (director Clifford Manshardt) 1944 Renamed Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS) 1946 Delhi School of Social Work founded (YWCA; later part of University of Delhi) 1946 Bhore Committee report: recommends integrating mental health into general health services, the origin of Indian community mental health 1948 First psychiatric social work post in India, at the Child Guidance Clinic, Bombay 1960s Psychiatric social work training established at NIMHANS , Bangalore (M.Phil. in Psychiatric Social Work) and at the Ranchi institutes 1982 National Mental Health Programme (NMHP) ; the District Mental Health Programme (DMHP) follows from the 1985 Bellary model 1992 Rehabilitation Council of India Act : RCI regulates and registers both clinical psychologists and psychiatric social workers 2016 Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act , replacing the PWD Act 1995; 21 conditions including mental illness 2017 Mental Healthcare Act : rights-based, advance directive, nominated representative, decriminalises attempted suicide, and formally names the mental health professional categories Psychiatric social work: where the two professions touch Psychiatric social work is the specialisation you will actually work beside. Its unit of attention is the patient's environment: it takes the social history and family assessment, does psychoeducation with the family, works on expressed emotion (George Brown and colleagues) and family burden, arranges welfare entitlements and disability certification , runs vocational rehabilitation and aftercare, and does the community follow-up that stops relapse. In an Indian mental health team the division of labour that the paper expects you to know is: the psychiatrist diagnoses and prescribes; the clinical psychologist does psychological assessment and psychotherapy; the psychiatric social worker does the family, the environment, the entitlements and the rehabilitation. RML tilt: RML is a Delhi government teaching hospital with a service orientation, so it asks social work the way a hospital asks it: who does what on the team, what case management delivers, what the methods are called, and when Indian social work education began. Learn the names, the dates and the method labels . There is no reasoning to do on these questions; either you have the fact or you do not, which is exactly why they are the cheapest marks in the paper to recover. Honest note on frequency. Across the six live RML papers on this site (2020 to 2025, 570 questions), the social work strand is concentrated in 2020 . The 2021 to 2025 papers carry essentially none of it. So do not weight this section like the five carrying domains in the PYQ map ; it is a one evening read that insures you against a repeat, not a study block. But it is worth that evening: when it does appear it is four marks of pure recall, and on your own 2020 attempt it was the single largest cluster in your misses. Your four, in one table Q What it asked The answer Where it is taught above 4 Who questioned the effectiveness of social case work Joel Fischer , Is Casework Effective? A Review (1973) Method 1, casework 18 First school of social work in India Sir Dorabji Tata Graduate School of Social Work , Bombay, 1936 Social work in India 32 Outcomes of case management, EXCEPT Not cure : case management coordinates, it does not treat the disorder Case management 82 Common properties of a group, EXCEPT Not an analytic base : groups need interaction, goals, norms, we-feeling Method 2, group work Trap, and this one is worth more than the content: two of your four (Q32 and Q82) were EXCEPT stems, and on both you picked the weakest true option instead of the false one. That is a technique loss, not a knowledge loss, and it also cost you Q24 elsewhere in the paper. Fixed procedure for every EXCEPT, NOT and LEAST stem: circle the word, then mark each option T or F individually, then take the single F. Never rank options by importance on an EXCEPT. Recap: Social work is a separate profession organised around social functioning, born when nineteenth-century charity split into the investigating Charity Organisation Society (London 1869) and the live-among-them settlement movement (Toynbee Hall 1884, Samuel Barnett; Hull House 1889, Jane Addams). Its three primary methods are social case work, social group work and community organisation; its three secondary methods are social welfare administration, social action and social work research. Case work was founded by Mary Ellen Richmond ( Social Diagnosis 1917, What Is Social Case Work? 1922), split into the diagnostic school (Gordon Hamilton, Florence Hollis, person-in-situation) and the functional school (Jessie Taft, Virginia Robinson, will and time), was reconciled by Helen Harris Perlman's problem-solving model and its four Ps, given its seven relationship principles by Felix Biestek, and was then put on trial by Joel Fischer in 1973, whose negative review pushed the profession toward empirical practice. Group work was founded by Grace Longwell Coyle and runs on three models (social goals, remedial after Robert Vinter, reciprocal after William Schwartz); a group needs interaction, common goals, we-feeling, norms, roles and interdependence, and needs no analytic base. Community organisation follows Murray Ross and Jack Rothman's three models: locality development, social planning, social action. Case management assesses, plans, links, coordinates, monitors and advocates, reducing hospitalisation and improving continuity and quality of life, but it never cures. In India the chain is 1936 Sir Dorabji Tata Graduate School of Social Work in Bombay under Clifford Manshardt, renamed TISS in 1944, with Delhi School of Social Work in 1946, RCI regulation from 1992 and the Mental Healthcare Act in 2017. How to attack it from here Read the five carrying domains first, in this order: General & basic psychology (2), Assessment & tests (10), Research + Statistics (11), Abnormal (7), Biopsychology (3). The six-year PYQ map shows these are 65% of the paper. That is where the marks actually live. Make the founder pairs and acronyms reflexive from Counselling & Psychotherapy (9): who developed which therapy, and what every acronym stands for. This is RML's single most repeated question type. Over-prepare Indian Psychology (12), both ends: the modern history of the discipline in India and the classical frameworks. This is the recurring leak. Go ICD-deep on Abnormal (7): know the ICD-11 side and the older signs and eponyms, not DSM alone. Thin pass on Section A (1): a couple of timed reasoning sets plus the mental-health Acts and institutes. It is about 20 marks, do not over-invest. Then sit the six real PYQ mocks untimed ( 2020 , 2021 , 2022 , 2023 , 2024 , 2025 ), the same 570 questions the PYQ map is built from, and any weak spot they expose maps straight back to the section above. Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS prep · /notes/rml-study-material/ · RML CET-166 MA Clinical Psychology, the full subject syllabus built from scratch, tuned to how the RML clinical paper behaves · companion to the RML Task brief and the RML 2024 PYQ mock · built for Sihan 2026-07-02.

title: SGT University · MA Clinical Psychology Entrance · Study Material from Scratch
text: SGT University · MA Clinical Psychology Entrance · Study Material from Scratch Shree Guru Gobind Singh Tricentenary University, Gurugram · MA Clinical Psychology (RCI) · the whole general-psychology core taught from zero, packaged as one deep readable book. Built for Sihan, 2026-07-04. RML is in the bag, so this is the SGT drop. Here is the honest starting point: SGT does not publish a syllabus PDF the way RML's CET-166 does. The official line is that the entrance "syllabus will be as prescribed by SGT University as per the guidelines of the UGC," which in plain terms means a general psychology aptitude test drawn from the standard PG-psychology core, followed by a personal interview. So this book is not built off a leaked topic list; it is built off the seven areas a UGC-guideline general-psych test actually pulls from, the same base you have been grinding all cycle, just gathered into one place you can read top to bottom. Every theorist is given by full name, every test names its author, every therapy names who developed it, because that is exactly what a general-awareness paper rewards. Read it end to end and you have covered the subject core for SGT, and for every other general-psych entrance on your list. Entrance SGT MA Clinical Psychology (RCI) Two stages written test → interview No published syllabus UGC-guideline general psych 14 chapters · from scratch Exam ~11 Jul 2026, Gurugram campus Tracker SGT pattern & dates How to use this. This is a teaching text, not a cheatsheet: each chapter builds a topic from the ground up, then flags the exact traps a general-psych paper fishes for. The green Key boxes are the must-knows, the red Trap boxes are the confusions the paper exploits, the teal Who → what boxes are the theorist / founder / test pairings, and the amber Why boxes explain the mechanism so it sticks. The book now runs to fourteen content chapters: the seven core subject areas plus full stand-alone chapters on learning, memory and cognition, motivation and emotion, social psychology, personality, and intelligence, since a general-psychology paper samples every one of these. Read Section 1 first to set your priorities, then work the chapters. Because SGT has no negative-marking guidance published, treat every question as answerable and never leave a blank. Contents: 1 · How the SGT paper behaves 2 · Biopsychology & physiological 3 · Developmental 4 · Abnormal & clinical 5 · Assessment & testing 6 · Psychotherapy & counselling 7 · Statistics & research methodology 8 · General awareness & history 9 · Learning & conditioning 10 · Memory, attention & cognition 11 · Motivation & emotion 12 · Social psychology 13 · Personality 14 · Intelligence 15 · The attack plan & the interview 1 How the SGT paper behaves, and how to prep it Before any content, get the shape of the thing right, because half of prepping an entrance is knowing what you are walking into. SGT University runs its own offline entrance for the MA Clinical Psychology (RCI) programme at its Gurugram campus, in two stages: a written test followed by a personal interview . Unlike RML's CET-166, there is no standalone syllabus document, no published breakdown of number of questions, marks per question, duration, or negative marking. SGT's own pages say only that the syllabus follows UGC guidelines. That is not a gap in your prep; it is the design. A UGC-guideline general-psychology aptitude test means the paper samples broadly and shallowly across the whole PG-psychology base rather than drilling deep into one niche. Key. No published SGT syllabus is not a reason to panic; it is a reason to prep breadth over depth. The paper rewards the person who can recognise a term, a theorist, or a test from any corner of psychology, not the person who has memorised one topic to the bone. The seven areas the written test draws on Mapping the "UGC-guideline general psychology" wording onto how these general aptitude papers actually behave, the written test pulls from seven areas. This book has one section per area, in this order: # Area What it samples 2 Biopsychology / physiological Neuron, action potential, neurotransmitters, brain structures, endocrine, sensation & perception 3 Developmental Jean Piaget, Erik Erikson, Lev Vygotsky, attachment, moral & lifespan development 4 Abnormal / clinical DSM-5-TR & ICD-11, the major disorders, etiology, case vignettes 5 Assessment / testing Reliability & validity, intelligence & personality tests, projectives, Indian adaptations 6 Psychotherapy & counselling Psychoanalytic, behavioural, CBT, humanistic; who developed which therapy 7 Statistics & research methodology Descriptive & inferential stats, designs, sampling, ethics 8 General awareness / aptitude History & schools of psychology, learning, memory, social psychology, key theorists Why this order. Biopsychology and developmental are the highest-density "recognise the fact" areas in any general paper, so they lead. Assessment and therapy are where the "who made this" questions cluster, so full names are non-negotiable there. General awareness is last because it is the catch-all that ties the schools and theorists together once you have met them in the earlier sections. Trap. Do not confuse SGT's general aptitude test with a deep clinical M.Phil paper. A general-psych entrance will ask "who proposed the hierarchy of needs" (Abraham Maslow, 1943) far more often than it asks a fine-grained ICD-11 sub-code. Prep the recognisable landmarks of every area, not the deep cuts of one. How to spend the days you have Breadth pass first. Read all fourteen chapters once, front to back, so no area is a blank. That alone clears most of a general aptitude paper. Second pass on the founder boxes. The teal Who → what boxes are the single most exam-efficient thing here; a general paper is dense with "match the theorist / test / therapy to its author." Use your existing mocks as the drill. Everything on the site (the PYQ mocks, the common-section work, the bio and diagnostic sets) is the same base SGT samples. Sitting any of them is valid SGT practice. Prep the interview in parallel (Section 9): the second stage is a real gate, and it is the cheapest marks to secure because it rewards clarity about why you want clinical psychology, not more recall. 2 Biopsychology & Physiological Psychology Biopsychology (also called physiological psychology, biological psychology, or behavioural neuroscience) asks one question: how does the physical machinery of the body, above all the nervous system, produce behaviour, thought, emotion, and experience? To answer an entrance paper on this topic you must be able to build the brain from its smallest working part upward. We therefore start with the single cell, the neuron, and end with whole-brain imaging. Nothing here needs prior biology; every term is defined as it appears. 2.1 The Neuron: The Unit of the Nervous System The nervous system is built from billions of specialised cells called neurons (nerve cells) that receive, integrate, and transmit information as electrical and chemical signals. A neuron is not like an ordinary body cell; it is shaped for communication, with parts that collect signals at one end and pass them on at the other. Parts of a neuron Soma (cell body): the metabolic centre. It holds the nucleus and keeps the cell alive. Incoming signals are summed here. Dendrites: short, branching fibres that spread out from the soma like the branches of a tree (the word means "little tree"). They are the receiving surface; they collect signals from other neurons. Axon: a single long fibre that carries the outgoing signal away from the soma toward other cells. One neuron has many dendrites but usually just one axon (which may branch at its end). Myelin sheath: a fatty white insulating layer wrapped in segments around many axons. It speeds up signal conduction and stops the signal leaking. Myelin is why "white matter" is white. Nodes of Ranvier: the small unmyelinated gaps between segments of myelin. The signal jumps from node to node (see saltatory conduction). Terminal buttons (axon terminals, end feet): the swollen tips at the end of the axon branches. They store and release chemical messengers onto the next cell. Why. The neuron's shape is a receive-integrate-transmit pipeline: dendrites in, soma decides, axon out, terminals hand off. Every fact about signalling maps onto this direction of flow, so memorise the direction, not just the parts. Glial cells (neuroglia): the support staff Neurons are outnumbered by glial cells ("glia" means glue), which support, feed, insulate, and protect neurons. They do not fire signals themselves but are essential. Astrocytes: star-shaped cells that hold neurons in place, supply nutrients, mop up excess chemicals, and help form the blood-brain barrier. Oligodendrocytes: make the myelin sheath in the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord). One oligodendrocyte myelinates several axons. Schwann cells: make the myelin sheath in the peripheral nervous system (nerves outside the brain and cord). One Schwann cell myelinates one segment of one axon, and Schwann cells help peripheral nerves regenerate. Microglia: the immune cells of the nervous system; they clean up dead cells and fight infection. Trap. Papers love to swap myelin-makers: oligodendrocytes myelinate the CNS, Schwann cells myelinate the PNS. If a question mentions the brain or spinal cord, the answer is oligodendrocyte; if it mentions a peripheral nerve, the answer is Schwann. The neuron doctrine: Golgi versus Cajal In the late 1800s scientists argued whether the nervous system was one continuous web (the "reticular theory") or a set of separate cells. Camillo Golgi , an Italian physician, invented a silver-staining method (the "black reaction") that made single neurons visible, yet he believed the network was continuous. The Spaniard Santiago Ramon y Cajal used Golgi's own stain to show that neurons are separate, individual cells that merely communicate across tiny gaps. Cajal's view, the neuron doctrine , won. Who → what. Camillo Golgi → the silver stain that revealed neurons (but he backed the continuous-network theory). Santiago Ramon y Cajal → the neuron doctrine (neurons are discrete cells). They shared the 1906 Nobel Prize despite disagreeing. 2.2 Resting and Action Potentials: How a Neuron Fires The resting potential A neuron at rest is electrically charged, like a tiny battery. The inside of the axon is about −70 millivolts (mV) relative to the outside; this is the resting membrane potential . It exists because charged particles (ions) are unevenly spread across the membrane: sodium (Na+) is concentrated outside, potassium (K+) inside, and the inside carries a net negative charge. Key. Resting potential = about −70 mV, inside negative. The neuron is "polarised" and ready to fire. This imbalance is maintained by the sodium-potassium pump , a protein in the membrane that constantly pushes 3 sodium ions out for every 2 potassium ions it pulls in, using energy. Because it moves more positive charge out than in, it helps keep the inside negative. The action potential (the nerve impulse) When enough incoming signals push the membrane past a threshold (about −55 mV), the neuron fires an action potential , a rapid electrical spike that travels down the axon. It has clear phases: Depolarisation: sodium channels open, Na+ rushes in, and the inside shoots up toward +30 to +40 mV (briefly positive). Repolarisation: sodium channels close, potassium channels open, K+ flows out, and the charge drops back toward negative. Hyperpolarisation (undershoot): the charge briefly overshoots below −70 mV before the pump restores the resting state. Key. The all-or-none law : a neuron either fires a full action potential or none at all. The strength of a stimulus is coded by how often the neuron fires (frequency), not by making a bigger spike. Every spike is the same size. Refractory periods Absolute refractory period: immediately after firing, the neuron cannot fire again no matter how strong the stimulus (sodium channels are inactivated). Relative refractory period: shortly after, the neuron can fire again but only with a stronger-than-usual stimulus. Why. The refractory period forces the impulse to travel in one direction (down the axon, not backward) and sets an upper limit on firing rate. Saltatory conduction In myelinated axons the impulse does not crawl smoothly; it jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next (Latin saltare , to leap). This saltatory conduction is much faster and more energy-efficient than conduction along an unmyelinated fibre. Trap. When myelin is destroyed (as in multiple sclerosis), conduction slows and fails; saltatory conduction cannot occur without intact myelin and nodes. Do not confuse the nodes (bare gaps) with the myelin (insulation): the impulse jumps to the nodes because the myelinated stretches are skipped. 2.3 Synaptic Transmission: How Neurons Talk to Each Other Neurons do not touch. Between the terminal button of one neuron and the dendrite of the next lies a microscopic gap, the synapse (synaptic cleft). The signal crosses this gap chemically. The action potential reaches the terminal button of the presynaptic (sending) neuron. Calcium enters and causes tiny sacs called synaptic vesicles to move to the membrane. By exocytosis the vesicles fuse with the membrane and dump their neurotransmitter (chemical messenger) into the cleft. The neurotransmitter drifts across and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic (receiving) neuron, like a key in a lock. This opens channels and changes the postsynaptic cell's charge. The signal is then cleared by reuptake (the presynaptic neuron sucks the transmitter back in for reuse) or by enzymes that break it down. Excitation and inhibition EPSP (excitatory postsynaptic potential): the transmitter makes the postsynaptic cell more likely to fire (depolarises it toward threshold). IPSP (inhibitory postsynaptic potential): the transmitter makes it less likely to fire (hyperpolarises it away from threshold). Why. A neuron is a voting machine: it constantly adds up EPSPs and IPSPs arriving on its dendrites and soma (this is "summation"). Only if excitation outweighs inhibition past threshold does it fire. Behaviour is the net result of this balance across billions of cells. The discovery of neurotransmission Who → what. Otto Loewi → first proof of chemical neurotransmission. In a famous 1921 frog-heart experiment (reportedly designed in a dream) he stimulated the vagus nerve of one heart, collected its fluid, applied it to a second heart, and slowed that heart too. He named the substance "Vagusstoff" ("vagus substance"), later identified as acetylcholine , the first known neurotransmitter. Charles Sherrington → coined the term "synapse" and described reflex integration. 2.4 Major Neurotransmitters Different chemical messengers do different jobs, and many disorders and drugs work by changing one of them. Learn the function and the clinical link for each; entrance papers almost always test the link. Neurotransmitter Main function Disorder / drug link Acetylcholine (ACh) Muscle movement, learning, memory, arousal Loss of ACh neurons in Alzheimer’s disease; blocked at the junction in myasthenia gravis Dopamine Reward, motivation, voluntary movement, pleasure Too much (overactivity) linked to schizophrenia; too little (loss of cells) causes Parkinson’s disease Serotonin Mood, sleep, appetite, impulse control Low levels linked to depression and anxiety; SSRIs raise it Norepinephrine (noradrenaline) Alertness, arousal, fight-or-flight Involved in mood disorders and stress; targeted by some antidepressants GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) The main inhibitory transmitter; calms neural activity Low activity linked to anxiety and seizures; boosted by benzodiazepines and alcohol Glutamate The main excitatory transmitter; learning and memory Excess causes excitotoxicity (cell death from over-firing), implicated in stroke and seizures Endorphins Natural painkillers; pleasure and "runner’s high" Mimicked by opiate drugs (morphine, heroin), which bind endorphin receptors Key. Memorise the four highest-yield pairings: dopamine → schizophrenia (too much) and Parkinson’s (too little); serotonin → depression; GABA → anxiety (the calming brake); acetylcholine → Alzheimer’s and memory. Trap. GABA is inhibitory (the brain’s brake) and glutamate is excitatory (the accelerator). Papers reverse these constantly. Also note dopamine is the classic "two-disease" transmitter: excess → schizophrenia, deficit → Parkinson’s, which is why anti-schizophrenia drugs can cause Parkinson-like side effects. 2.5 Organisation of the Nervous System The whole nervous system splits into two great divisions: Central nervous system (CNS): the brain and the spinal cord. This is the control centre and integrator. Peripheral nervous system (PNS): all the nerves outside the CNS that connect it to the body and outside world. The PNS divides again: Somatic nervous system: carries sensory information in and controls voluntary skeletal muscles (moving your arm). Autonomic nervous system (ANS): controls involuntary functions of glands and internal organs (heartbeat, digestion). It has two opposing branches. Situation Sympathetic branch Parasympathetic branch Role "Fight or flight" (Walter Cannon, 1915) (arouses, spends energy) "Rest and digest" (calms, conserves energy) Heart rate Speeds up Slows down Pupils Dilate (widen) Constrict (narrow) Digestion Inhibited Stimulated Trap. Sympathetic and parasympathetic are opposites, but both belong to the autonomic system. A common wrong answer treats the sympathetic system as "voluntary"; it is involuntary. Voluntary muscle control is the somatic system. The spinal cord and the reflex arc The spinal cord relays messages between brain and body, but it can also act on its own in a reflex arc , a fast, automatic response that bypasses the brain. When you touch a hot stove: a sensory (afferent) neuron carries the pain signal to the spinal cord, an interneuron passes it across, and a motor (efferent) neuron orders the muscle to pull back, all before the brain even registers the pain. Why. Routing simple protective reflexes through the spinal cord alone saves the time it would take to consult the brain; the brain is informed a fraction of a second later. This is why you yank your hand away before you feel the burn. 2.6 The Brain The brain is traditionally divided into hindbrain, midbrain, and forebrain, roughly from bottom-and-back (older, survival functions) to top-and-front (newer, higher functions). Hindbrain Medulla (medulla oblongata): controls vital automatic functions, heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure. Damage is fatal. Pons: a bridge relaying signals between higher and lower brain; involved in sleep, arousal, and facial movement. Cerebellum ("little brain"): coordinates balance, posture, and smooth, well-timed voluntary movement; also involved in some learning. Damage causes clumsy, jerky movement. Midbrain A relay hub for vision and hearing reflexes and for movement. It contains parts of the reticular formation, a network running through the brainstem that controls arousal, alertness, and the sleep-wake cycle. Forebrain and the limbic system The forebrain contains the most advanced structures. Beneath the cortex sits the limbic system , the emotional and motivational core: Amygdala: the fear and emotion centre; tags experiences as threatening; central to aggression and emotional learning. Hippocampus: forms new long-term memories and supports spatial navigation. Damage causes an inability to form new memories. Hypothalamus: the body’s regulator; controls hunger, thirst, temperature, sex drive, and it commands the pituitary gland (the link between brain and hormones). Remember the "four Fs": feeding, fighting, fleeing, and sexual behaviour. Thalamus: the great relay station ; nearly all sensory information (except smell) passes through the thalamus on its way to the cortex. Trap. Do not confuse hippocampus (memory formation) with hypothalamus (drives and hormones), or thalamus (sensory relay) with hypothalamus (regulation and pituitary control). Amygdala = emotion/fear; hippocampus = memory. These four are the most-tested structures in the whole section. The cerebral cortex: four lobes The wrinkled outer layer of the forebrain, the cerebral cortex , is where perception, thought, and language happen. Each hemisphere has four lobes: Lobe Location Main function Frontal Front Planning, decision-making, personality, voluntary movement (motor cortex), speech production Parietal Top-back Touch, temperature, pain, body position (somatosensory cortex) Temporal Sides (near temples) Hearing, language comprehension, memory Occipital Back Vision (visual cortex) Language areas and hemispheric specialisation Who → what. Paul Broca → Broca’s area (in the left frontal lobe), for speech production ; damage causes Broca’s aphasia (halting, effortful speech, comprehension intact). Carl Wernicke → Wernicke’s area (in the left temporal lobe), for language comprehension ; damage causes Wernicke’s aphasia (fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension). Roger Sperry → split-brain research on hemispheric specialisation (Nobel Prize 1981). The two hemispheres are somewhat specialised (lateralisation): for most people the left hemisphere handles language, logic, and analysis, while the right hemisphere handles spatial ability, faces, and holistic processing. They are joined by the corpus callosum , a thick band of fibres. Roger Sperry studied "split-brain" patients whose corpus callosum was cut to treat epilepsy; his experiments showed the two halves could then work independently, revealing what each side does on its own. Trap. Broca = b roken, halting speech (production); Wernicke = w ordy, fluent nonsense (comprehension). Both areas are in the left hemisphere for most people. Also: each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body (contralateral control). 2.7 The Endocrine System Alongside the fast electrical nervous system runs a slower chemical one: the endocrine system , a set of glands that release hormones directly into the bloodstream to act on distant organs. Pituitary gland: the "master gland", sitting under the hypothalamus. It releases hormones that control the other endocrine glands (and it is itself controlled by the hypothalamus). Adrenal glands: release adrenaline (epinephrine) for fight-or-flight (Walter Cannon) and cortisol for stress. Thyroid gland: releases thyroxine, which sets the body’s metabolic rate. Pineal gland: releases melatonin, which regulates sleep and the day-night (circadian) cycle. The HPA axis and key hormones The stress response runs on the HPA axis : the H ypothalamus signals the P ituitary, which signals the A drenal glands to release cortisol. This is the body’s slow, sustained stress system. Cortisol: the main stress hormone; mobilises energy but harms health if chronically high. Adrenaline (epinephrine): the fast surge that races the heart in an emergency. Oxytocin: the "bonding" hormone; released in childbirth, breastfeeding, and social attachment. Thyroxine: controls metabolism and energy use. Melatonin: promotes sleep and tracks the light-dark cycle. Why. Nervous versus endocrine is a speed-versus-duration trade-off. The nervous system sends fast electrochemical signals down fixed wires for immediate, brief effects; the endocrine system sends slower hormones through the blood for widespread, longer-lasting effects. The hypothalamus is the bridge that lets the brain command the hormones. Trap. The pituitary is the "master gland", but it takes orders from the hypothalamus (a brain structure, not a gland in the usual sense). So the true top of the chain is the hypothalamus, which is why the same structure keeps appearing in both the brain and endocrine sections. 2.8 Sensation and Perception: The Basics Sensation is the raw detection of a stimulus by a sense organ; perception is the brain’s interpretation of that sensation into a meaningful experience. Sense organs first perform transduction : converting physical energy (light, sound, pressure) into the neural signals the brain can read. Thresholds and psychophysics Absolute threshold: the smallest amount of a stimulus a person can detect 50% of the time (e.g. a candle flame seen far away on a dark night). Difference threshold (just noticeable difference, JND): the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected. Who → what. Ernst Weber → Weber’s law: the JND is a constant proportion of the original stimulus, not a fixed amount (adding one candle to ten is noticeable; adding one to a hundred is not). Gustav Fechner → founded psychophysics and extended Weber’s work into a law relating physical stimulus strength to perceived sensation. The visual pathway Light enters the eye and lands on the retina , which holds two kinds of receptor cells: Rods: many, at the edges; work in dim light; see in black and white; give night vision. Cones: concentrated in the centre (fovea); work in bright light; give colour and sharp detail. Signals leave the eye by the optic nerve and travel to the visual cortex in the occipital lobe. Two classic theories explain colour vision: Who → what. Thomas Young and Hermann von Helmholtz → the trichromatic (three-colour) theory: the retina has three cone types tuned to red, green, and blue, and all colours arise from their combined activity. Ewald Hering → the opponent-process theory: colour is coded by opposing pairs (red-green, blue-yellow, black-white); one member of a pair is excited while the other is inhibited. Trap. The two colour theories are not rivals; both are correct at different stages. Trichromatic (Young-Helmholtz) operates at the cones (retina) ; opponent-process (Hering) operates later , in the retinal ganglion cells and brain. Opponent-process best explains afterimages (stare at green, look away, see red). Auditory basics Sound waves enter the ear, vibrate the eardrum, pass through three tiny bones, and reach the fluid-filled cochlea in the inner ear. Hair cells in the cochlea transduce the vibrations into neural signals sent along the auditory nerve to the temporal lobe. Pitch corresponds to the frequency of the wave and loudness to its amplitude (measured in decibels). 2.9 Research Methods in Biopsychology To study a brain we cannot open, biopsychologists use recording, imaging, and damage-based methods, plus genetics to separate nature from nurture. Recording and imaging techniques Method What it does Shows structure or function? EEG (electroencephalogram) Records electrical brain waves from scalp electrodes; excellent timing Function (activity over time) ERP (event-related potential) Averages EEG responses time-locked to a specific stimulus to isolate the brain’s reaction to it Function (precise timing) CT (computed tomography) X-ray scan giving a still picture of brain anatomy Structure PET (positron emission tomography) Tracks a radioactive tracer to show which areas use most glucose/blood Function (metabolic activity) fMRI (functional MRI) Tracks blood-oxygen flow to map active regions; good spatial detail Both, but prized for function Lesion studies Observe behaviour after a brain area is damaged or removed to infer its function Function (by loss) Trap. Sort methods by their strength: EEG and ERP have superb temporal resolution (when) but poor spatial detail (where); fMRI and PET have good spatial resolution (where) but slower timing. CT gives structure only; fMRI and PET show function. Lesion evidence shows what a region is needed for, not everything it does. Behaviour genetics Behaviour genetics studies how much of a trait comes from genes versus environment. Twin studies: compare identical (monozygotic, 100% shared genes) with fraternal (dizygotic, ~50% shared) twins. If identical twins are far more alike on a trait, genes matter more. Adoption studies: compare adopted children with both their biological and their adoptive parents to separate genetic from environmental influence. Heritability: the proportion of the variation in a trait across a population that is due to genetic differences. It ranges from 0 to 1. Trap. Heritability is about variation within a population , not about a single individual. A heritability of 0.5 does not mean "half of your intelligence comes from genes"; it means half of the differences among people in that group trace to genetic differences. This distinction is a favourite trick question. Recap. Neuron = dendrites (in) → soma (integrate) → axon/myelin (out) → terminals; oligodendrocytes myelinate the CNS, Schwann cells the PNS; Cajal’s neuron doctrine beat Golgi’s network (they shared the 1906 Nobel). Resting potential −70 mV kept by the sodium-potassium pump; the action potential is all-or-none (depolarise, repolarise), jumps node to node (saltatory). Otto Loewi proved chemical transmission (acetylcholine, "Vagusstoff"). Key transmitter links: dopamine → schizophrenia (excess) and Parkinson’s (deficit), serotonin → depression, GABA (inhibitory) → anxiety, glutamate (excitatory) → excitotoxicity, ACh → Alzheimer’s. CNS vs PNS; somatic (voluntary) vs autonomic (sympathetic fight-or-flight vs parasympathetic rest-and-digest); the spinal reflex arc bypasses the brain. Brain: medulla (vital signs), cerebellum (coordination); limbic amygdala (fear), hippocampus (memory), hypothalamus (drives + pituitary), thalamus (sensory relay); four lobes (frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital); Broca (speech production) vs Wernicke (comprehension), both left; Roger Sperry’s split-brain work. Pituitary is master gland under the hypothalamus; HPA axis releases cortisol. Weber-Fechner thresholds; rods (dim, night) vs cones (colour, detail); Young-Helmholtz trichromatic (cones) plus Hering opponent-process (later, explains afterimages). EEG/ERP = timing, fMRI/PET = location, CT = structure; twin and adoption studies define heritability as population-level variation, not an individual’s fixed fraction. 2.10 Sleep, consciousness and biological rhythms Consciousness is the awareness a person has of their own thoughts, feelings and surroundings at any given moment. It is not a single fixed state but a continuum that shifts across the day and night, from alert wakefulness through drowsiness into the various stages of sleep. Sleep is not simply the switching off of the brain. It is an active, organised, rhythmic process that the body drives on a roughly 24-hour schedule, and studying it reveals how deeply behaviour is governed by biology. Biological rhythms and the circadian clock A biological rhythm is any cyclical change in a bodily process that repeats over a regular period. The most important for behaviour is the circadian rhythm , from the Latin circa (about) and dies (a day), meaning a cycle that lasts about 24 hours. The sleep-wake cycle, body temperature, and the release of many hormones all follow a circadian pattern. Rhythms shorter than a day are called ultradian (for example the stages of a single sleep cycle repeating through the night), and rhythms longer than a day are called infradian (for example the roughly monthly menstrual cycle). The internal clock that keeps the circadian rhythm running is a tiny cluster of cells in the hypothalamus called the suprachiasmatic nucleus , usually shortened to the SCN. It sits just above the point where the optic nerves cross, which is why it can receive information about light directly from the eyes. Even with no external cues the SCN keeps ticking on a cycle close to, but not exactly, 24 hours. External cues that reset the clock to the true day are called zeitgebers , a German word meaning time-givers . Light is the most powerful zeitgeber. Who → what. The SCN was identified as the master circadian pacemaker through animal lesion studies in the 1970s: destroying it abolished the regular sleep-wake and hormonal rhythms, showing that this one small structure sets the body's daily timing. When light falls on the retina, signals travel to the SCN, which then instructs the pineal gland , a small structure deep in the brain, to adjust its output of the hormone melatonin . Melatonin promotes sleepiness. In darkness the pineal gland releases more melatonin, and in bright light it releases less. This is the chemical bridge between the light of the outside world and the felt urge to sleep. Key. Light → eye → suprachiasmatic nucleus (the clock) → pineal gland → melatonin (the sleep signal). Darkness raises melatonin; light lowers it. The sleep cycle: NREM and REM Sleep is measured chiefly with the electroencephalograph , or EEG, a device that records the electrical activity of the brain through electrodes on the scalp. As a person falls asleep and moves through the night, the EEG traces out characteristic patterns of brain waves that let researchers divide sleep into distinct stages. Sleep falls into two broad kinds: NREM (non-rapid-eye-movement) sleep and REM (rapid-eye-movement) sleep. Under the modern scheme, NREM sleep is divided into three stages, N1 to N3, followed by a period of REM. One full pass through these stages takes roughly 90 minutes, and the cycle repeats four to six times a night (an ultradian rhythm). As the night goes on, the deep NREM stages shorten and the REM periods lengthen. Stage N1 (light sleep): the brief transition from wakefulness into sleep. Brain waves slow from alpha toward theta. The person is easily woken and may experience sudden jerks. Stage N2: a deeper light sleep marked on the EEG by short bursts of activity called sleep spindles and single large waves called K-complexes . Most of a night is spent here. Stage N3 (slow-wave or deep sleep): the deepest sleep, dominated by large slow delta waves. It is hardest to wake someone from this stage, and it is thought to be the most physically restorative. Sleepwalking and night terrors, when they occur, arise here. REM sleep: after the deep stages the brain returns to a fast, active pattern resembling waking. The eyes dart rapidly beneath closed lids, and the body's voluntary muscles are effectively paralysed. Most vivid dreaming happens here. EEG wave patterns Each state of consciousness has a signature brain-wave pattern, described by its frequency (how many cycles per second, measured in hertz) and amplitude (how tall the waves are). As a rough rule, the more alert and active the brain, the faster and smaller the waves; the deeper the rest, the slower and larger the waves. Wave Frequency Typical state Beta Fast (about 13 to 30 Hz) Alert, awake, actively thinking or concentrating Alpha Moderate (about 8 to 12 Hz) Awake but relaxed, calm, eyes often closed; drowsy onset Theta Slow (about 4 to 7 Hz) Light sleep, stages N1 and N2 Delta Very slow (below about 4 Hz), high amplitude Deep slow-wave sleep, stage N3 Trap. Do not confuse fast small beta waves (busy waking mind) with slow tall delta waves (deepest sleep). A common exam catch is that REM sleep shows a fast, waking-like EEG even though the person is deeply asleep and hard to wake; this mismatch is why REM is called paradoxical sleep . REM, paradoxical sleep and dreaming REM sleep is called paradoxical sleep because the brain looks awake on the EEG while the body is at its most still, the large muscles being temporarily paralysed (a state called atonia that stops us acting out dreams). Rapid eye movements, irregular breathing and heart rate, and vivid narrative dreams all belong to REM. People woken from REM report dreaming far more often and in more detail than those woken from NREM. Newborns spend a very large proportion of sleep in REM, which has led to the idea that REM supports brain development and the consolidation of memory. Theories of why we sleep There is no single agreed answer to why sleep evolved, but two broad families of theory dominate. Restorative theory: sleep serves to repair and restore the body and brain. During sleep, especially deep NREM, the body releases growth hormone, repairs tissue, clears metabolic waste, and the brain consolidates memories. On this view we sleep because sleep does necessary maintenance. Evolutionary or adaptive theory: sleep evolved to keep an animal safe and to conserve energy during the hours when it cannot forage or defend itself effectively. On this view sleep is an adaptation that reduced risk and saved calories, and different species sleep in patterns suited to their ecological niche. Common sleep disorders in brief Insomnia: persistent difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or getting restful sleep, despite adequate opportunity, causing daytime distress or impairment. Narcolepsy: a neurological disorder marked by overwhelming daytime sleepiness and sudden uncontrollable sleep attacks, sometimes with sudden loss of muscle tone (cataplexy) triggered by emotion, reflecting intrusions of REM-like states into wakefulness. Sleep apnoea: repeated pauses in breathing during sleep, often because the airway collapses, which briefly wakes the person again and again and leaves them unrefreshed and sleepy by day. 2.11 Behavioural genetics and evolution Behavioural genetics is the field that studies how much of the variation in behaviour and psychological traits across people can be traced to inherited biological factors versus the environment. It is the modern, evidence-based way of examining the old nature-versus-nurture question. Genes, chromosomes and DNA Inside the nucleus of almost every cell in the body are chromosomes , thread-like structures made of a molecule called DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid). Humans normally have 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs, one of each pair inherited from each parent. DNA carries the coded instructions for building and running the body, and a gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a particular product or trait. Genes are the basic units of heredity passed from parents to offspring. Key. DNA is the molecule; a gene is a stretch of DNA that codes for something; chromosomes are the long packaged strands of DNA. Genes sit on chromosomes; chromosomes are made of DNA. Genotype versus phenotype The genotype is the full set of genes an individual carries, the inherited genetic blueprint. The phenotype is the set of observable characteristics that actually appear, such as eye colour, height, or a behavioural tendency. The phenotype results from the genotype interacting with the environment. Two people can share a genotype for a trait yet differ in phenotype because of different experiences, nutrition, or circumstances. Dominant and recessive Genes often come in alternative versions called alleles . An allele is dominant if a single copy is enough to express its effect in the phenotype, and recessive if its effect appears only when two copies are present (one from each parent). This is why a recessive trait can skip generations, hidden in carriers who possess one copy but do not show it. Heritability Heritability is a statistic, expressed from 0 to 1 (or as a percentage), that estimates how much of the variation in a trait within a population is due to genetic differences among its members. It is one of the most misunderstood ideas in psychology. Trap. Heritability is about variation across a group, not about a single person. A heritability of 0.5 for a trait does NOT mean half of one individual's trait is caused by genes. It means about half of the differences between people in that population are associated with genetic differences.
