Its three forms are the one-sample (one mean vs a fixed value), the independent-samples (two unrelated groups), and the paired-samples (two measurements on the same or matched subjects). Who → what. William Gosset (Student) → the t distribution and t-test, developed while doing quality control at the Guinness brewery; he published under the pen name "Student" because his employer forbade staff from publishing. Analysis of variance (Ronald Fisher) ANOVA extends the logic of the t-test to three or more groups in one test, avoiding the inflated Type I error you would get from running many t-tests. It works by partitioning total variability into between-groups variance (differences among group means) and within-groups variance (noise inside each group); the F ratio is between-groups over within-groups. A large F says the group means differ by more than chance noise predicts. A significant ANOVA says "at least one group differs" but not which, so a post-hoc test (Tukey's HSD, Bonferroni, Scheffe) then pinpoints the specific pairs. Who → what. Ronald Fisher → analysis of variance (ANOVA), the F distribution, the null-hypothesis testing framework, and the principle of randomization in experimental design. Chi-square The chi-square test works on frequencies / counts of categorical data. Goodness of fit checks whether one variable's observed frequencies match an expected pattern (are diagnoses evenly distributed across seasons?). The test of independence checks whether two categorical variables are associated (is treatment response related to gender?). Both compare observed counts to the counts expected if H0 were true. Parametric vs non-parametric Parametric tests (z, t, ANOVA, Pearson's r) assume the data are interval/ratio, roughly normally distributed, and (for group comparisons) have similar variances (homogeneity of variance) and independent observations. When those assumptions fail – ordinal data, small samples, heavy skew, outliers – we switch to non-parametric tests, which work on ranks or counts and assume much less. Parametric test Non-parametric equivalent Design Independent-samples t-test Mann-Whitney U Two independent groups Paired-samples t-test Wilcoxon signed-rank Two related measures One-way ANOVA Kruskal-Wallis Three or more independent groups Pearson's r Spearman's rho Association of two variables Key. Parametric tests are more powerful when their assumptions hold; non-parametric tests are the safe fallback when data are ordinal, badly skewed, or small. Match the test to the scale of measurement and the design (independent vs related groups) first. 7.7 Research methodology: the scientific method and designs The scientific method and steps of research Identify the problem and review existing literature. Formulate a clear, testable hypothesis and define concepts operationally (state exactly how each variable will be measured). Choose a research design and sampling method. Collect data using reliable, valid instruments. Analyse the data with appropriate statistics. Interpret results, draw conclusions, and relate them back to the hypothesis and theory. Report and disseminate; replication and peer review test the finding's durability. Why. An operational definition (for example, "depression = score above 13 on the Beck Depression Inventory") is what makes a study repeatable and testable. Without it, two researchers studying "depression" might measure completely different things. Research designs True experiment : the researcher manipulates the IV and uses random assignment to conditions. This is the only design that supports strong causal claims, because randomization equalizes confounders across groups on average. Quasi-experiment (Donald Campbell and Julian Stanley, 1963): has an IV manipulation or group comparison but lacks random assignment (comparing existing intact groups such as two schools). Causal inference is weaker because groups may differ at the start. Correlational : measures variables as they naturally occur and assesses association without manipulation. Good for prediction and for variables that cannot ethically be manipulated, but cannot establish cause. Case study : intensive, in-depth study of a single person, group, or event. Rich and hypothesis-generating (Sigmund Freud's cases, patient H.M.), but not generalizable and open to observer bias. Survey : self-report from a sample via questionnaire or interview; efficient for attitudes and prevalence, but vulnerable to response biases (social desirability, acquiescence). Observational : watching and recording behaviour, either naturalistic (in the field, no interference) or controlled (in a set-up like a lab playroom); high realism but limited control. Longitudinal : the same people followed over time (tracks true within-person change and development, but slow and prone to participant drop-out / attrition). Cross-sectional : different age or cohort groups compared at one time point (fast and cheap, but age differences can be confounded with cohort / generation effects). Internal vs external validity Internal validity is the degree to which we can be sure the IV, and not something else, caused the change in the DV. External validity is the degree to which the findings generalize beyond the study to other people, settings, and times. The two often trade off: tight laboratory control boosts internal validity but the artificial setting can hurt external validity. Common threats to internal validity include history (an outside event during the study), maturation (natural change over time), testing (practice effects from being measured before), instrumentation (the measuring tool drifting), regression to the mean (extreme scorers drifting toward average on retest), selection (pre-existing group differences), and attrition / mortality (non-random drop-out). Threats to external validity include unrepresentative samples (over-reliance on WEIRD or undergraduate samples) and artificial settings. Control techniques Randomization (random assignment): allocating participants to conditions by chance so that confounders are spread evenly across groups; the single most powerful control. Blinding : keeping participants ( single-blind ), or both participants and the researchers who interact with them ( double-blind ), unaware of condition, to block placebo and experimenter-expectancy effects. Counterbalancing : in within-subjects designs, varying the order of conditions across participants so that practice and fatigue (order effects) do not systematically favour one condition. Standardization : giving every participant the same instructions, environment, and procedure to hold extraneous variables constant. 7.8 Sampling How we pick the sample decides whether it fairly represents the population. Methods split into two families. Probability sampling (every member has a known, non-zero chance of selection; supports generalization and error estimation): Simple random sampling : every individual has an equal chance (names from a hat, random number generator). The gold standard for representativeness. Systematic sampling : pick every k-th person from a list after a random start. Easy, but risky if the list has a hidden periodic pattern. Stratified sampling : divide the population into meaningful subgroups (strata) such as age or gender, then sample randomly within each, guaranteeing each stratum is represented in proportion. Cluster sampling : divide the population into naturally occurring clusters (schools, clinics), randomly select whole clusters, and study everyone (or a sample) inside. Cheaper for geographically spread populations, but less precise. Non-probability sampling (selection chances unknown; convenient but hard to generalize from): Convenience sampling : whoever is easiest to reach (psychology undergraduates). Fast but biased. Purposive (judgmental) sampling : the researcher hand-picks cases fitting a criterion (experts, a specific diagnosis). Snowball sampling : existing participants recruit others they know; used for hidden or hard-to-reach populations (people who use illicit drugs). Quota sampling : fill preset quotas for subgroups (50 men, 50 women) but choose within each non-randomly. Trap. Do not confuse the two errors. Sampling error is the ordinary, random gap between a sample statistic and the true parameter simply because a sample is not the whole population; it shrinks as sample size grows. Sampling bias is a systematic tilt from a flawed selection method (a convenience sample, or non-response); it does NOT shrink with a larger sample – a bigger biased sample is just a bigger biased sample. Only better sampling design, not more people, fixes bias. 7.9 Reliability, validity, qualitative methods, and ethics Reliability and validity of research and measures Reliability is consistency: does the measure give the same result under the same conditions? Its forms are test-retest (stable across time), inter-rater (different observers agree), internal consistency (items hang together, indexed by Cronbach's alpha), and parallel-forms (two versions agree). Validity is accuracy: does the measure actually assess what it claims? Its forms include content validity (items cover the whole construct), criterion validity (correlates with an external benchmark, split into concurrent and predictive ), and construct validity (fits the theoretical network, with convergent and discriminant evidence). Key. A measure can be reliable without being valid, but not valid without being reliable. A miscalibrated scale that always reads 5 kg heavy is perfectly reliable (consistent) yet invalid (wrong). Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. Qualitative methods in brief Where quantitative research counts and measures, qualitative research seeks meaning in words and experience. Thematic analysis (Virginia Braun and Victoria Clarke, 2006) codes textual data and groups the codes into recurring themes. Grounded theory (Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss, 1967) builds a theory upward from the data through iterative coding, letting categories emerge rather than testing a pre-set hypothesis. Phenomenology aims to describe the essence of participants' lived experience of a phenomenon from their own point of view. These methods prize depth, context, and the participant's voice over generalizable numbers. Research ethics Informed consent : participants agree to take part after being told the study's purpose, procedures, risks, and their right to withdraw at any time without penalty. Special provisions cover minors and those unable to consent. Confidentiality and anonymity : personal data are protected, and identities are kept private or removed from records. Protection from harm : physical and psychological risk is minimized and justified by the study's value. Debriefing : after participation (especially if deception was used and justified), participants are fully informed of the true purpose and any deception is explained. Institutional review : an Institutional Review Board (IRB) or ethics committee must approve the study before data collection, weighing risks against benefits. Professional guidelines : the American Psychological Association (APA) Ethics Code (and in India the Rehabilitation Council of India norms) set standards for integrity, avoiding harm, and honest reporting of results. Trap. Deception is permitted only when a study cannot be done otherwise, the risk is low, and it is followed by a full debrief; it never overrides the duty to protect participants. Consent obtained by hiding real risks is not informed consent. And confidentiality has limits: a clinician-researcher who learns of imminent danger to self or others may have a duty to breach it. Recap. Statistics turns variable behaviour into defensible conclusions. Describe data with the right centre (mean for symmetric, median for skewed, mode for categories) and spread (SD, IQR). The normal curve plus z-scores let us locate and compare scores (68–95–99.7). Correlation (Karl Pearson's r for continuous, Charles Spearman's rho for ranks) measures association but never proves causation. Inference rests on sampling distributions and the standard error; we test a null hypothesis against an alpha, read a p-value and confidence interval, and weigh Type I against Type II error, always reporting effect size (Jacob Cohen's d) and power alongside significance. Pick the test by scale and design: William Gosset's t-tests for one or two means, Ronald Fisher's ANOVA for three or more, chi-square for frequencies, and non-parametric equivalents when assumptions fail. Sound methodology (true experiments with randomization, blinding, and counterbalancing), representative probability sampling, reliable and valid measures, and firm ethics (informed consent, confidentiality, debriefing, IRB approval) are what make the numbers trustworthy in the first place. 7.10 Comparing groups and modelling relationships Once a psychologist has collected data and summarised it, the central task is usually to ask a comparative or predictive question. Do two groups differ? Does one variable predict another? The family of procedures below answers such questions. Each one produces a test statistic (a single number computed from the data) which is then converted into a probability so the researcher can decide whether an observed difference is likely to be real or merely the product of sampling noise. The t-tests A t-test compares means when the sample is small and the population standard deviation is unknown. The test was devised by William Sealy Gosset , a chemist and statistician working at the Guinness brewery in Dublin, who published under the pen name "Student" in 1908 because his employer forbade staff from publishing. For this reason the distribution he derived is still called Student's t-distribution . There are three common forms. One-sample t-test. Compares the mean of one sample against a known or hypothesised population value. A clinic's mean depression score is compared against the published national average of 10. Independent-samples t-test. Compares the means of two separate, unrelated groups. Mean anxiety scores of a therapy group versus a waitlist group. Paired-samples (dependent) t-test. Compares two scores from the same people (or matched pairs), such as before and after an intervention. Each client's stress score at week 1 versus the same client's score at week 8. Who → what. William Sealy Gosset ("Student") → the t-test and t-distribution, born of quality control at a brewery, for making inferences from small samples. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) When there are more than two groups, running many t-tests inflates the chance of a false positive. Analysis of variance , developed by Sir Ronald Aylmer Fisher in the 1920s while working on agricultural experiments at Rothamsted, solves this by comparing all group means in a single test. ANOVA works by partitioning the total variability in the data into between-groups variance (differences among the group means) and within-groups variance (random variability inside each group). Their ratio is the F-ratio , named by later authors in Fisher's honour. A large F means the group means differ more than would be expected from chance alone. One-way ANOVA. One independent variable (factor) with three or more levels. Comparing three drug doses on reaction time. Factorial ANOVA. Two or more factors examined at once (for example a 2×2 design). It yields a main effect for each factor plus one or more interaction effects . Repeated-measures ANOVA. The same participants are measured under every condition or at several time points, the many-condition extension of the paired t-test. It removes stable individual differences, increasing sensitivity. Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). An ANOVA that first statistically removes the influence of a continuous nuisance variable, the covariate . Comparing therapies for depression while adjusting for each client's baseline severity. MANOVA. Multivariate analysis of variance handles two or more dependent variables simultaneously in one analysis. Key. An interaction effect means the effect of one factor depends on the level of another . A drug may help young patients but not older ones. The effect of "drug" changes across the levels of "age", so drug and age interact. When an interaction is present, main effects must be interpreted cautiously. Post-hoc tests A significant ANOVA tells the researcher that at least one group differs, but not which ones. Post-hoc ("after this") tests then compare pairs of groups while controlling the overall false-positive rate. The most widely taught is Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) , devised by John Wilder Tukey . Others include the Bonferroni correction (which divides the alpha level by the number of comparisons) and the Scheffe test. Linear regression Where correlation only measures the strength of a relationship, regression uses one or more variables to predict another. In simple linear regression a single predictor (independent variable) forecasts an outcome (dependent variable) through the equation of a straight line, conventionally written Y = a + bX, where a is the intercept (the predicted value of Y when X is zero) and b is the slope (how much Y changes for each one-unit rise in X). Multiple linear regression extends this with several predictors, each with its own slope, so the model becomes Y = a + b1X1 + b2X2 + and so on. The coefficient of determination, R-squared , states the proportion of variance in the outcome explained by the predictors: an R-squared of 0.40 means the model accounts for 40 per cent of the variability in Y. Trap. Correlation and regression are related but not identical. Correlation is symmetric and unitless: it merely describes how strongly two variables move together, with no direction of prediction. Regression is directional: it names one variable the predictor and one the outcome and produces an equation to estimate actual values. Reporting a regression slope as if it proved causation is a further, separate error. The chi-square test All the tests above need at least one continuous, roughly normal variable. When the data are frequencies of categories (counts, not measurements) the appropriate procedure is the chi-square (χ-squared) test , developed by Karl Pearson . It compares the counts actually observed against the counts expected under a hypothesis. There are two common uses. Goodness-of-fit. Tests whether one categorical variable follows an expected distribution. Are the four blood types present in the sample in the proportions the population predicts? Test of independence. Tests whether two categorical variables are associated. Is diagnosis (depression / anxiety / neither) independent of gender? Non-parametric tests Parametric tests assume the data are measured on an interval or ratio scale and are drawn from a roughly normal population. When these assumptions fail (small samples, ordinal data such as ranks, or badly skewed distributions), non-parametric alternatives are used. They work on ranks rather than raw scores and therefore make fewer assumptions about the shape of the distribution. Question Parametric test Non-parametric counterpart Two independent groups Independent-samples t-test Mann-Whitney U test Two related scores (before / after) Paired-samples t-test Wilcoxon signed-rank test Three or more independent groups One-way ANOVA Kruskal-Wallis test Three or more related conditions Repeated-measures ANOVA Friedman test Association between two variables Pearson's r Spearman's rank-order correlation (rho) Spearman's rank-order correlation , developed by the psychologist Charles Edward Spearman (also famous for the "g" factor of general intelligence), is simply Pearson's correlation computed on ranks; it captures any consistent monotonic relationship, even a curved one, and resists outliers. Trap. Non-parametric does not mean "no assumptions" or "always safer". These tests have less statistical power than their parametric cousins when the parametric assumptions actually hold, so defaulting to them needlessly can hide a real effect. Choose them because the assumptions are violated, not out of caution alone. 7.11 Decision errors, power and effect size Every significance test is a decision made under uncertainty, and any decision can be wrong. This subsection sets out the logic of that decision and the tools that describe how good it is. The two hypotheses Inference begins with two rival statements. The null hypothesis (H-nought) states that there is no effect, no difference, or no relationship in the population. The alternative hypothesis (H-one) states that there is one. The test never proves the null; it only decides whether there is enough evidence to reject it. If the evidence is weak, the researcher fails to reject the null, which is not the same as proving it true. The two error types Reality Test rejects H-nought Test keeps H-nought No true effect exists Type I error (alpha): false alarm Correct decision A true effect exists Correct decision (power) Type II error (beta): miss A Type I error is rejecting a true null: declaring an effect that is not really there. Its probability is alpha , conventionally set at 0.05. A Type II error is failing to reject a false null: missing an effect that is genuinely present. Its probability is beta . Trap. Students routinely swap the two. A memory aid: a Type I error is like convicting an I nnocent person (a false positive); a Type II error is letting a guilty one go free (a false negative). Lowering alpha to avoid false positives tends to raise beta, so the two errors trade off against each other. Statistical power Power is the probability of correctly detecting a real effect, defined as 1 minus beta. A study with power of 0.80 has an 80 per cent chance of finding an effect that truly exists. Power rises with a larger sample size, a bigger true effect, a larger alpha, and lower measurement error. Under-powered studies are a major cause of failed replications because they miss real effects and, when they do reach significance, tend to over-estimate the effect's size. Effect size A p-value tells you whether an effect is likely to be real, but not how large or important it is. With a huge sample, a trivial difference can be "statistically significant". Effect size measures the magnitude of an effect independently of sample size. Cohen's d. Devised by Jacob Cohen , it expresses the difference between two means in standard-deviation units. Rough conventions: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. Pearson's r. As an effect size it indexes the strength of a relationship, from 0 to 1 in absolute value. Eta-squared (η-squared). Used with ANOVA, it gives the proportion of variance in the outcome explained by a factor, similar in spirit to R-squared. Confidence intervals A confidence interval is a range of plausible values for a population parameter, computed from the sample. A 95 per cent confidence interval means that if the study were repeated endlessly, about 95 per cent of such intervals would contain the true value. A narrow interval signals a precise estimate; a wide one signals uncertainty. If a 95 per cent interval for a difference excludes zero, the result is significant at the 0.05 level, so intervals and tests carry consistent information while the interval also shows magnitude and precision. The meaning of a p-value Key. A p-value is the probability of obtaining data at least as extreme as those observed if the null hypothesis were true . It is NOT the probability that the null is true, NOT the probability the result happened "by chance", and NOT a measure of effect size. A small p (for example less than 0.05) means the data would be surprising under the null, so the null is rejected. One-tailed versus two-tailed, degrees of freedom, and assumptions A two-tailed test checks for a difference in either direction and is the default. A one-tailed test checks only one direction and is justified only when a directional prediction is made in advance; it has more power in that direction but is blind to an effect the other way. Degrees of freedom are the number of values in a calculation that are free to vary; for a one-sample t-test with n cases the degrees of freedom are n minus 1. They determine the exact shape of the reference distribution. Parametric tests rest on assumptions that should be checked: normality of the outcome (or of residuals), homogeneity of variance (roughly equal spread across groups, also called homoscedasticity), independence of observations, and an interval or ratio level of measurement . When these are seriously violated, the non-parametric tests of 7.10 are the safer choice. 7.12 Designs and validity threats The finest statistics cannot rescue a poorly designed study. Design determines what conclusions the numbers can bear, above all whether a cause can be claimed. Three broad design families True experimental designs. The researcher manipulates the independent variable and uses random assignment of participants to conditions. Only this combination licenses strong causal claims, because randomisation balances out unknown differences between groups. Quasi-experimental designs. There is manipulation or a comparison but no random assignment , often because groups are pre-existing (for example two schools). Causal inference is weaker because the groups may differ at the outset. Non-experimental designs. No manipulation at all; the researcher observes and measures (for example correlational and survey studies). These describe relationships but cannot establish cause. Further design distinctions Factorial designs. Two or more independent variables crossed together, allowing main effects and interactions to be studied at once, as in 7.10. Single-subject designs. One participant (or very few) is studied intensively across baseline and treatment phases, common in behaviour therapy. The classic form is the A-B-A-B reversal design , where A is baseline and B is treatment. Longitudinal designs. The same people are followed over time; they reveal genuine change but are slow and suffer participant drop-out (attrition). Cross-sectional designs. Different age or cohort groups are measured once at the same time; they are quick but confound age with cohort (generational) effects. Sequential designs. A hybrid that follows several cohorts longitudinally, separating true developmental change from cohort effects. Confounding and control A confounding variable is an extraneous factor that varies alongside the independent variable and offers a rival explanation for the result. If a new therapy is given only in the morning and the comparison therapy only in the evening, time of day confounds the comparison. Researchers reduce confounds through control : random assignment, holding conditions constant, counterbalancing the order of conditions, and using control or placebo groups. The four types of validity Validity here refers to the soundness of the inferences drawn from a study, a framework crystallised by Donald Thomas Campbell and Julian Stanley in their influential 1963 monograph on experimental design. Internal validity. The degree to which the study can claim that the independent variable, and nothing else, caused the change in the dependent variable. Threatened by confounds. External validity. The degree to which findings generalise to other people, settings, and times. Construct validity. Whether the operations used truly capture the intended theoretical concept (for example whether a questionnaire really measures "anxiety"). Statistical-conclusion validity. Whether the statistical inferences about the relationship are correct, threatened by low power, violated assumptions, or unreliable measures. Campbell and Stanley threats to internal validity Threat What it means History An outside event occurs during the study and affects the outcome. A news crisis raises everyone's anxiety mid-study. Maturation Participants naturally change over time (grow older, more tired, recover) regardless of treatment. Testing Taking a test the first time changes performance on a later administration (practice effect). Instrumentation The measuring tool or the raters change over the course of the study. Regression to the mean (Francis Galton, 1886) Extreme scorers tend to score nearer the average on retesting simply through statistical chance, mimicking a treatment effect. Selection Groups differ systematically before the study begins because they were not randomly assigned. Attrition (mortality) Participants drop out unevenly across groups, distorting the comparison. Who → what. Donald Thomas Campbell & Julian Stanley → the systematic catalogue of threats to internal and external validity, the backbone of experimental design teaching ever since. Trap. Regression to the mean (Francis Galton) is one of the most common causes of false "treatment works" claims. If you select the most distressed clients (the extreme scorers) and re-test them, their average will drift toward the mean even with no treatment at all. Without a control group, this natural drift is easily mistaken for a real effect. Recap. Choose the analysis to match the question and the data: t-tests (Gosset) for one or two means, ANOVA (Fisher) for several with interactions revealed in factorial designs, regression for prediction and R-squared, chi-square for category counts, and rank-based non-parametric tests when parametric assumptions fail. Every test can err: a Type I error is a false alarm (alpha), a Type II error is a miss (beta), power is 1 minus beta, and effect size plus confidence intervals describe magnitude that a p-value alone cannot. Finally, only a true experiment with random assignment supports strong causal claims; Campbell and Stanley's threats (history, maturation, testing, regression to the mean, selection, attrition) are the rival explanations that good design and adequate validity are built to rule out. 7.13 The complete map: statistics, designs & the people behind them This roster gathers, in one place, every statistical test, research design, and measurement technique that an aptitude paper is likely to name, each pinned to the person who invented it and boiled down to one exam line. Read it as a safety net: if a question drops a surname or a formula, you should be able to place it here in seconds. Grouped into four families (descriptive & correlation, inferential tests, design & validity, measurement & scaling), numbered continuously. Key. If a paper names a statistic, a design, or a scale, this table should let you attach the correct person and a one-line meaning at once. Anchor the tent-pole names first: Gauss (normal curve), Galton (correlation, regression to the mean), Karl Pearson (r, chi-square), Spearman (rho, factor analysis), Gosset (t-test), Fisher (ANOVA, randomised design), Cronbach (alpha), and the four scaling founders (Likert, Thurstone, Guttman, Osgood). The rest cluster naturally around these. 8 General Awareness: History, Schools & Core Psychology This section is the backbone of the SGT University MA Clinical Psychology paper. The examiners lean heavily on "general psychology" one-liners: who founded which school, which theorist is tied to which experiment, and which term names which effect. If you can attach a name to an idea and an idea to a date , you will clear most of these questions in seconds. We build every topic from zero, then flag the traps that catch tired candidates. Key. The examiner is testing associations: founder → school , experiment → theorist , effect → discoverer . Learn psychology as a set of linked pairs and the general-awareness block becomes free marks. 8.1 History & Schools of Psychology Psychology as a formal science is usually dated to 1879 , when Wilhelm Wundt opened the first psychology laboratory at the University of Leipzig, Germany. Before that, questions about the mind belonged to philosophy and physiology. Wundt made the mind a subject for controlled experiment, which is why he is called the "father of experimental psychology". After Wundt, psychology split into competing schools of thought , each with a founder and one core idea. The table below is the single most examined item in this whole section. School Founder(s) Core idea / method Structuralism Wilhelm Wundt; Edward Titchener Break conscious experience into its basic elements (sensations, feelings) using introspection . First lab, 1879. Functionalism William James Study what the mind is for – how mental processes help us adapt. His book "The Principles of Psychology" (1890) launched it. Gestalt Max Wertheimer, Wolfgang Kohler, Kurt Koffka Perception is organised into wholes: "the whole is other than the sum of its parts". Studied insight and perceptual grouping. Behaviourism John B. Watson; B.F. Skinner Study only observable behaviour, not the mind. Learning through conditioning. Watson's 1913 manifesto; Skinner's operant work. Psychoanalysis Sigmund Freud Behaviour driven by the unconscious , early childhood, and conflict between id, ego and superego. Humanistic ("third force") Abraham Maslow; Carl Rogers Focus on growth, free will, self-actualization and the whole person. A reaction against both behaviourism and psychoanalysis. Cognitive Ulric Neisser; George Miller The mind as an information processor . Neisser's "Cognitive Psychology" (1967) named the field; the "cognitive revolution" of the 1950s–60s. Evolutionary (rooted in Charles Darwin) Behaviour and mental traits shaped by natural selection for survival and reproduction. Positive psychology Martin Seligman Scientific study of strengths, wellbeing and flourishing, not just disorder. Founded around 1998. Who → what. Wundt → first lab (1879) + structuralism. James → functionalism. Wertheimer → Gestalt. Watson → behaviourism. Freud → psychoanalysis. Maslow/Rogers → humanistic. Neisser → cognitive. Seligman → positive psychology. Trap. Wilhelm Wundt is the founder of the lab, but the word "structuralism" and the word "introspection" as a formal method are most tightly associated with his student Edward Titchener . If a question asks who named structuralism, the answer is Titchener, not Wundt. Trap. The Gestalt slogan is "the whole is other than the sum of its parts" (Kurt Koffka's careful wording), often loosely quoted as "greater than". Either phrasing points to Gestalt, never to structuralism, which does the opposite by breaking wholes into elements. Why. These schools are not just history. Modern clinical practice inherits directly from them: behaviourism → behaviour therapy; cognitive → cognitive therapy; psychoanalysis → psychodynamic therapy; humanistic → person-centred therapy. Knowing the parent school helps you place any therapy question. 8.2 Learning: Classical Conditioning Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour due to experience. The oldest experimental model is classical conditioning , discovered by the Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov while studying dog digestion. A neutral stimulus that is repeatedly paired with a biologically important one comes to trigger the same response. Unconditioned stimulus (US): food, which naturally causes salivation. Unconditioned response (UR): salivation to food (unlearned). Conditioned stimulus (CS): the bell, after pairing with food. Conditioned response (CR): salivation to the bell alone (learned). Four processes are examined constantly: Acquisition: the CS and US are paired and the CR is built up. Extinction: the CS is presented without the US, and the CR fades. Spontaneous recovery: after a rest, an extinguished CR briefly reappears. Generalization: stimuli similar to the CS also trigger the CR (a bell of a slightly different pitch). Discrimination: the organism learns to respond only to the exact CS, not to similar ones. John B. Watson extended classical conditioning to humans in the famous "Little Albert" experiment (1920). He paired a white rat (neutral) with a loud, frightening noise (US) until the infant Albert became afraid of the rat (CR), and the fear generalized to other furry objects. This showed emotions themselves can be conditioned. Trap. Ivan Pavlov → dogs, salivation, classical conditioning (involuntary reflex). B. F. Skinner → rats/pigeons, levers, operant conditioning (voluntary behaviour + consequences). Do not swap them. John B. Watson used classical conditioning on Little Albert. 8.3 Learning: Operant Conditioning Operant conditioning explains how consequences shape voluntary behaviour. Its groundwork was laid by Edward Thorndike , whose law of effect states that behaviours followed by satisfying consequences are strengthened, and those followed by unpleasant ones are weakened (from his puzzle-box experiments with cats). B.F. Skinner formalised this using the "Skinner box", coining the terms reinforcement and punishment. Consequence Add a stimulus (positive) Remove a stimulus (negative) Reinforcement (behaviour increases) Positive reinforcement: give a reward praise, food pellet Negative reinforcement: remove something unpleasant seatbelt beep stops Punishment (behaviour decreases) Positive punishment: add something unpleasant a scolding Negative punishment: take away something pleasant lose phone privileges Trap. "Negative" does not mean bad, and "positive" does not mean good. Positive = add a stimulus; negative = remove a stimulus. Negative reinforcement increases behaviour (it is still reinforcement); only punishment decreases behaviour. Schedules of reinforcement (Charles Ferster and B. F. Skinner, 1957) govern how often a response is rewarded: Fixed ratio: reward after a set number of responses pay per 10 items made . Variable ratio: reward after an unpredictable number of responses; produces the highest, most persistent responding slot machines, gambling . Fixed interval: reward for the first response after a set time a weekly paycheck . Variable interval: reward for the first response after an unpredictable time checking for a text reply . Key. Variable-ratio schedules give the highest and most extinction-resistant response rate. This is the classic MCQ answer for "which schedule is hardest to extinguish". 8.4 Learning: Observational Learning Not all learning needs direct reinforcement. Albert Bandura showed we learn by watching others, in his Bobo doll experiment: children who watched an adult act aggressively toward an inflatable Bobo doll later imitated that aggression. This is the basis of his social learning theory (later "social cognitive theory"), which adds thinking and expectation to behaviourism. Bandura identified four steps for observational learning: attention (notice the model), retention (remember it), reproduction (be able to perform it), and motivation (a reason to do it, often via vicarious reinforcement – seeing the model rewarded). Who → what. Ivan Pavlov → classical conditioning. Edward Thorndike → law of effect (puzzle box). B. F. Skinner → operant conditioning + schedules. Bandura → observational learning + Bobo doll. 8.5 Memory Memory is examined through its models and its failures. The dominant framework is the multi-store model of Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin (1968), which proposes three stores information flows through. Sensory memory: very brief, large capacity; holds raw sensory input for under a second (iconic for vision, echoic for sound). Short-term memory (STM): holds about 7 ± 2 items (George Miller's "magical number seven") for ~15–30 seconds; kept alive by rehearsal. Long-term memory (LTM): effectively unlimited capacity and duration. Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch (1974) replaced the passive STM idea with working memory , an active system with a central executive directing two slave systems: the phonological loop (verbal/acoustic material) and the visuospatial sketchpad (visual/spatial material); Baddeley later added the episodic buffer . Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart (1972) proposed the levels of processing theory: memory strength depends on depth of processing, not on stores. Shallow processing (how a word looks) gives weak memory; deep semantic processing (what a word means) gives strong memory. For types of LTM, Endel Tulving distinguished: Episodic memory: personal events, tied to time and place your last birthday . Semantic memory: general facts and meanings the capital of France . Procedural memory: skills and how-to knowledge riding a bicycle ; part of implicit (non-declarative) memory. Forgetting was first measured by Hermann Ebbinghaus , whose forgetting curve showed memory drops sharply soon after learning, then levels off. Explanations include decay (traces fade with time), interference (proactive: old learning blocks new; retroactive: new learning blocks old), and retrieval failure (cues missing). Trap. STM capacity (7±2) is George Miller ; the multi-store model is Richard Atkinson & Richard Shiffrin ; working memory is Alan Baddeley & Graham Hitch ; levels of processing is Fergus Craik & Robert Lockhart ; episodic/semantic memory is Endel Tulving ; the forgetting curve is Ebbinghaus . These five pairs are a favourite matching question. 8.6 Motivation & Emotion Motivation is what energizes and directs behaviour. Key theories: Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs ( Abraham Maslow ): needs are arranged in a pyramid – physiological, safety, love/belonging, esteem, and self-actualization at the top. Lower needs must be reasonably met before higher ones drive behaviour. Drive-reduction theory ( Clark Hull ): a physiological need creates a drive (tension); behaviour aims to reduce the drive and restore homeostasis . Henry Murray's needs: a list of psychological needs (achievement, affiliation, power, autonomy). Murray also created the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) to measure them. Intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation: intrinsic = doing something for its own satisfaction; extrinsic = doing it for an external reward or to avoid punishment. Emotion theories are a guaranteed table question. They differ on the order of the physical arousal, the felt emotion, and the thinking. Theory Theorist(s) Core claim (order of events) James-Lange William James & Carl Lange Stimulus → bodily arousal first → we then feel the emotion. "We are afraid because we tremble." Cannon-Bard Walter Cannon & Philip Bard Arousal and emotion happen at the same time and independently. Two-factor Stanley Schachter & Jerome Singer Emotion = physiological arousal + a cognitive label for that arousal. Cognitive appraisal Richard Lazarus A cognitive appraisal of the situation must come first; thought precedes emotion. Basic emotions Paul Ekman A small set of universal, cross-cultural emotions with distinct facial expressions (happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust). Trap. James-Lange = "body first, then emotion". Cannon-Bard = "both at once". Schachter-Singer = "arousal + label". Do not confuse Schachter-Singer's two factors with Lazarus's appraisal; the two-factor theory needs bodily arousal plus a label, while Lazarus makes thought alone the trigger. 8.7 Intelligence & Cognition (capstone) Assessment is covered in its own section, so here we only need the concepts. Intelligence is broadly the capacity to learn, reason, and adapt to the environment. Charles Spearman proposed a general factor, "g" , underlying all mental abilities, plus specific factors ("s"). The g debate pits this single-factor view against multiple-intelligence views (Howard Gardner's multiple intelligences, Robert Sternberg's triarchic theory). The nature–nurture debate asks how much intelligence is inherited versus shaped by environment; the modern answer is that both interact. Thinking and problem-solving use mental shortcuts called heuristics . Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed these shortcuts produce systematic biases : Availability heuristic: judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind. Representativeness heuristic: judging by how well something matches a stereotype, ignoring base rates. Anchoring: relying too heavily on the first piece of information. Confirmation bias (Peter Wason, 1960): seeking evidence that supports what we already believe. Key. Heuristics and biases → Kahneman & Tversky . Kahneman's "System 1" (fast, automatic) versus "System 2" (slow, effortful) thinking is a common one-liner. 8.8 Social Psychology Core Social psychology studies how people influence one another. It contributes several of the most famous experiments in the discipline, each welded to one name. Attitudes & persuasion: an attitude has cognitive, affective and behavioural components. Persuasion is analysed via the elaboration likelihood model (central route = arguments; peripheral route = cues like attractiveness). Cognitive dissonance ( Leon Festinger ): the discomfort of holding two conflicting beliefs, or acting against a belief, drives us to change an attitude to restore consistency. Conformity ( Solomon Asch ): in the line-judgment study, people gave obviously wrong answers to match a unanimous group – normative social influence. Obedience ( Stanley Milgram ): participants delivered what they believed were dangerous shocks because an authority figure told them to; showed obedience to authority. Bystander effect ( John Darley & Bibb Latane ): the more bystanders present, the less likely any one person helps, due to diffusion of responsibility . Attribution theory ( Fritz Heider ): we explain behaviour by internal (dispositional) or external (situational) causes. The fundamental attribution error (Lee Ross, 1977) is overusing internal causes for others' behaviour while excusing our own as situational. Prejudice: a negative attitude toward a group; linked to stereotyping and discrimination. Groupthink ( Irving Janis ): the drive for group harmony overrides realistic appraisal of alternatives, leading to poor decisions. Trap. Solomon Asch = conformity (lines, peer group). Stanley Milgram = obedience (shocks, authority). Do not swap them: conformity is yielding to peers, obedience is following an authority's command. Who → what. Festinger → cognitive dissonance. Asch → conformity. Milgram → obedience. Darley & Latane → bystander effect. Heider → attribution. Janis → groupthink. 8.9 Indian Psychology & Context SGT is an Indian university, so a few Indian-context items appear. Modern scientific psychology in India began with the first laboratory and department at Calcutta University (1916). The figure most examined is Durganand Sinha , a pioneer who charted the growth of psychology in India, pushed for indigenization (psychology rooted in Indian realities rather than borrowed wholesale from the West), and wrote on the psychology of poverty and rural life. Papers also test survey-level familiarity with concepts drawn from Indian thought : The three gunas (from Samkhya philosophy and the Bhagavad Gita): sattva (purity, balance, clarity), rajas (activity, passion, restlessness), and tamas (inertia, dullness, darkness). Personality and mental states are seen as a mix of these qualities. Yoga psychology: Patanjali's Yoga Sutras describe the mind (chitta) and its modifications (vrittis), and a path of mental discipline and self-regulation toward samadhi ; a forerunner of ideas about attention and consciousness. The self in Indian philosophy: the distinction between the empirical self (ego, ahamkara) and the deeper true self (atman), and the goal of self-realization – a more spiritual, holistic view of the person than Western trait models. Finally, the regulation of the profession. The Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) , a statutory body under the Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment, regulates the training and practice of clinical psychologists in India. It maintains the Central Rehabilitation Register, and a clinical psychologist must hold an RCI-recognised qualification (such as the M.Phil in Clinical Psychology, now transitioning to RCI-approved MA/PsyD routes) and register with the RCI to practise legally. Key. For the Indian block, lock in three answers: Durganand Sinha → indigenization / growth of Indian psychology; three gunas → sattva, rajas, tamas; RCI → the statutory body that licenses clinical psychologists in India. Recap. Psychology became a science with Wilhelm Wundt's 1879 lab, then split into schools – structuralism, functionalism, Gestalt, behaviourism, psychoanalysis, humanistic, cognitive – each pinned to a founder. Learning runs from Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning through B. F. Skinner's operant conditioning (positive/negative reinforcement and punishment, variable-ratio being hardest to extinguish) to Albert Bandura's observational learning. Memory is the Atkinson-Shiffrin stores, Baddeley-Hitch working memory, Craik-Lockhart levels of processing, Endel Tulving's episodic/semantic/procedural, and Hermann Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve. Motivation spans Abraham Maslow's hierarchy, Clark Hull's drive reduction and Murray's needs; emotion is the James-Lange / Cannon-Bard / Schachter-Singer / Lazarus / Ekman table. Cognition adds the g debate and Kahneman-Tversky heuristics. Social psychology is a set of name-experiment pairs: Festinger dissonance, Asch conformity, Milgram obedience, Darley-Latane bystander, Heider attribution. For India, remember Durganand Sinha , the three gunas , and the RCI . Learn every idea as a name-attached pair and this section becomes your strongest scoring block. 8.10 The complete map: every school of psychology and its founders This is the safety-net roster. Five families, thirty-five rows: the early schools (structuralism, functionalism, Gestalt), the behaviourist line (Watson to Skinner, Tolman, Hull), depth psychology and its humanistic reply (Freud, Jung, Adler, the neo-Freudians, Maslow, Rogers), the cognitive and modern movements (the cognitive revolution, evolutionary, positive psychology), and the founding firsts (1879 lab, 1896 clinic, 1915 Calcutta department). If you can name the school, the person, and the one-line idea for each, no history-of-psychology item on the aptitude paper should surprise you. 9 Learning & Conditioning Almost everything a person does, from fearing a dentist's drill to typing without looking at the keys, was learned. Psychology treats learning not as a vague idea but as a precise process that can be measured in the laboratory. This chapter builds the topic from the ground up: what learning is (and is not), the two great forms of conditioning that dominate the exam, the observational and cognitive kinds of learning that go beyond simple stimulus and response, and the clinical applications that flow from all of them. The material is dense with names, so each theorist, test, and study is given in full at first mention; the test loves to ask you to match a person to an idea, and the surest way to lose marks is to confuse two similar-sounding mechanisms. 9.1 What learning is (and is not) Learning is defined as a relatively permanent change in behaviour or in behavioural potential that results from experience. Each clause of that definition matters. Relatively permanent excludes brief changes caused by fatigue, illness, hunger, or drugs, which fade once the state passes. Change in behaviour or behavioural potential allows for learning that has occurred but is not yet shown (a person may have learned a route without walking it). Results from experience is the decisive clause: it distinguishes learning from changes that are wired into the body by biology. Two such biological changes must be told apart from learning. Maturation is a change in behaviour due to physical growth and the unfolding of the genetic programme, not experience: an infant walks when the nervous system and muscles are ready, whether or not anyone teaches it. A reflex is an automatic, unlearned response to a stimulus, such as the knee-jerk or the eye-blink to a puff of air; reflexes are present from birth and do not require practice. Learning, by contrast, always traces back to what the organism has experienced. Trap. A change caused by fatigue, drugs, or maturation is not learning, even though behaviour changes. The exam sets traps by describing a behaviour change and asking whether it counts as learning; check whether the cause was experience . 9.2 Classical conditioning: Ivan Pavlov Classical conditioning (also called Pavlovian or respondent conditioning) is learning in which a neutral stimulus, by being paired with a stimulus that already produces a response, comes to produce that response by itself. It was discovered by the Russian physiologist Ivan Petrovich Pavlov while he studied salivation in dogs. Pavlov noticed that the dogs salivated not only when food touched the mouth but also at the sight of the attendant who fed them, and he set out to study this systematically. Who → what. Ivan Petrovich Pavlov → classical (respondent) conditioning; the salivating-dog experiments; the terms unconditioned and conditioned stimulus and response. The four core terms follow directly from his procedure. The unconditioned stimulus (UCS) is a stimulus that naturally and automatically triggers a response without any learning; for Pavlov this was the food (meat powder). The unconditioned response (UCR) is the natural, automatic reaction to the UCS; here, salivation to food. The conditioned stimulus (CS) is an originally neutral stimulus (a bell or metronome) that, after being paired repeatedly with the UCS, comes to trigger a response. The conditioned response (CR) is the learned reaction to the CS; salivation to the bell alone. Note that the CR and UCR are often the same behaviour (salivation) but are named by what triggers them. Why. Conditioning works because the CS comes to signal or predict the UCS. The dog salivates to the bell because the bell has become a reliable forecaster of food; learning is essentially the picking up of predictive relationships between events. Acquisition, extinction, and recovery Acquisition is the initial stage in which the CS and UCS are paired and the CR is established and strengthened. It works best when the CS appears just before the UCS (forward pairing) rather than at the same time or afterward. Extinction is the weakening and eventual disappearance of the CR when the CS is presented repeatedly without the UCS; the bell keeps ringing but no food comes, and salivation to the bell fades. Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of a weakened CR after a rest period, showing that extinction does not erase the original learning but suppresses it. Generalization, discrimination, higher-order conditioning Stimulus generalization is the tendency for stimuli similar to the CS to also trigger the CR: a dog conditioned to a bell of one pitch will salivate somewhat to bells of nearby pitches. Stimulus discrimination is the learned ability to respond to the CS but not to other, similar stimuli, achieved when only the true CS is paired with the UCS. Higher-order conditioning (second-order conditioning) occurs when an established CS is used to condition a new neutral stimulus: once a bell reliably produces salivation, pairing a light with the bell can make the light produce salivation too, even though the light was never paired directly with food. Trap. Do not confuse generalization with discrimination. Generalization is responding to similar stimuli (widening); discrimination is responding only to the exact CS (narrowing). They are opposite processes. 9.3 Watson, Little Albert, and Garcia's taste aversion John Broadus Watson , the American founder of the school of behaviourism , argued that psychology should study only observable behaviour and that emotions could be conditioned. With his assistant Rosalie Rayner, Watson conducted the famous Little Albert experiment in 1920. An eleven-month-old infant, "Albert," was shown a white rat (originally neutral, the CS), and each time he reached for it a loud clanging noise (UCS) was made behind him, producing fear and crying (UCR). After several pairings Albert cried and withdrew at the sight of the rat alone (CR), and this fear generalized to other furry white objects such as a rabbit and a fur coat. The study showed that an emotional reaction, a phobia, could be classically conditioned. Who → what. John Broadus Watson (with Rosalie Rayner) → behaviourism; the Little Albert study proving fear can be conditioned in humans. John Garcia demonstrated a striking exception to the rule that any CS can be paired with any UCS. In his studies of taste aversion , rats that consumed a flavoured solution and later felt nauseated (even hours afterward) developed a strong avoidance of that taste after a single pairing. Crucially, the aversion attached readily to tastes but not to sights or sounds. This is now called the Garcia effect , and it illustrates biological preparedness (Martin Seligman, 1970): organisms are evolutionarily prepared to associate certain stimuli (taste with illness) far more easily than arbitrary ones, because such associations aided survival. Who → what. John Garcia → conditioned taste aversion (the Garcia effect) and biological preparedness; learning with a long CS–UCS delay and in a single trial. Why. Taste aversion breaks two "rules" of ordinary conditioning: it forms after one trial and across a delay of hours. This is adaptive; an animal that got sick after eating something must avoid that food to survive, so evolution biased the learning system toward taste–illness links. 9.4 Operant conditioning: Thorndike and Skinner Operant conditioning (also called instrumental conditioning) is learning in which the consequences of a behaviour determine how likely that behaviour is to be repeated. Where classical conditioning concerns involuntary, reflexive responses elicited by stimuli, operant conditioning concerns voluntary behaviours emitted by the organism and shaped by their outcomes. The groundwork was laid by Edward Lee Thorndike , who studied how cats escaped from a puzzle box he built. A hungry cat placed inside had to operate a latch to get out and reach food. Over successive trials the cat escaped faster, and Thorndike concluded that behaviours followed by satisfying consequences are "stamped in." He named this the law of effect : responses that produce a satisfying outcome become more likely, and responses that produce discomfort become less likely, in a given situation. He described the improvement as gradual trial-and-error learning , not sudden insight. Who → what. Edward Lee Thorndike → the puzzle box, trial-and-error learning, and the law of effect (satisfying consequences strengthen a response). Burrhus Frederic Skinner extended this into a full experimental system. He invented the operant chamber , universally known as the Skinner box , in which an animal such as a rat or pigeon presses a lever or pecks a key to receive food, with responses recorded automatically. Skinner replaced Thorndike's mentalistic word "satisfying" with the observable concept of reinforcement : any consequence that increases the frequency of the behaviour it follows. Who → what. Burrhus Frederic Skinner → the operant chamber (Skinner box), the language of reinforcement and punishment, and schedules of reinforcement. Reinforcement and punishment Two dimensions define the four consequences. "Positive" means a stimulus is added ; "negative" means a stimulus is removed . "Reinforcement" always increases behaviour; "punishment" always decreases it. Combining them gives four cases. Positive reinforcement: adding a pleasant stimulus to increase behaviour. A rat gets a food pellet for pressing the lever, so it presses more. Negative reinforcement: removing an unpleasant stimulus to increase behaviour. A rat presses the lever to switch off a loud noise, so it presses more. Positive punishment: adding an unpleasant stimulus to decrease behaviour. A child touches a hot stove, feels pain, and stops touching it. Negative punishment: removing a pleasant stimulus to decrease behaviour. A teenager loses phone privileges for coming home late, so lateness drops. Trap. Negative reinforcement is NOT punishment. Both involve something unpleasant, but negative reinforcement increases a behaviour by removing the unpleasant thing, whereas punishment decreases behaviour. This is one of the most heavily tested confusions on the paper. Reinforcers themselves come in two kinds. A primary reinforcer satisfies a biological need and is reinforcing on its own, such as food, water, or warmth. A secondary reinforcer (also called a conditioned reinforcer) gains its power by being associated with a primary reinforcer; money, praise, and tokens are secondary reinforcers because they can be exchanged for or have been paired with primary rewards. Schedules of reinforcement A schedule of reinforcement is the rule determining which responses get reinforced. Under continuous reinforcement every correct response is reinforced; this produces fast learning but also fast extinction once reinforcement stops. Under partial (intermittent) reinforcement only some responses are reinforced, which produces slower learning but far greater resistance to extinction. There are four classic partial schedules, defined by whether reinforcement depends on the number of responses (ratio) or the passage of time (interval), and on whether the requirement is fixed or variable . Schedule Rule Response pattern Example Fixed-ratio (FR) Reinforce after a set number of responses High rate; brief pause after each reinforcer Pay per 10 items assembled Variable-ratio (VR) Reinforce after an unpredictable number of responses Very high, steady rate; most resistant to extinction Slot machine, gambling Fixed-interval (FI) Reinforce first response after a set time Scalloped; responding speeds up as the time nears Checking mail near delivery time Variable-interval (VI) Reinforce first response after an unpredictable time Slow, steady, consistent rate Checking for a text that may arrive any time Key. Variable-ratio schedules produce the highest response rate and the greatest resistance to extinction, which is exactly why gambling is so persistent. Ratio schedules generally yield higher rates than interval schedules. Partial reinforcement also explains a robust finding: the partial-reinforcement extinction effect , which states that behaviours learned under partial reinforcement resist extinction longer than those learned under continuous reinforcement. When reinforcement has always been intermittent, its absence is harder to detect, so the behaviour persists. Building complex behaviour New behaviours are rarely produced whole, so they are built up. Shaping is the reinforcement of successive approximations , that is, steps that come progressively closer to the target behaviour; to teach a rat to press a lever, one first reinforces facing the lever, then approaching it, then touching it, then pressing. Chaining links a sequence of separate behaviours into one continuous performance, with each step serving as the cue for the next. A related tool is the Premack principle , named after David Premack , which states that a more probable (preferred) behaviour can reinforce a less probable one: "eat your vegetables and then you may have dessert" uses the preferred dessert to reinforce the less-preferred vegetables. Who → what. David Premack → the Premack principle (a high-frequency, preferred activity can reinforce a low-frequency one). Escape and avoidance Two forms of negative-reinforcement learning are distinguished by timing. Escape learning is learning a response that terminates an aversive stimulus already present, such as opening an umbrella once the rain has started. Avoidance learning is learning a response that prevents an aversive stimulus from occurring at all, cued by a warning signal, such as taking an umbrella when clouds gather. Avoidance is important clinically because it maintains phobias: the person who flees before anxiety peaks never learns that the feared outcome would not have happened. 9.5 Observational learning: Albert Bandura Observational learning (also called social learning or modeling) is learning by watching the behaviour of others, called models , and its consequences, without direct reinforcement of one's own behaviour. Its leading figure is Albert Bandura , whose Bobo doll experiment demonstrated it. Children watched an adult behave aggressively toward an inflatable "Bobo" doll, hitting and kicking it; when later left alone with the doll, these children imitated the aggression far more than children who had not seen the model, and they even copied novel actions they had never performed before. Who → what. Albert Bandura → observational (social) learning, the Bobo doll experiment, and the concept of vicarious reinforcement. Bandura identified four processes required for observational learning to occur. In order they are: attention (the observer must notice the model's behaviour), retention (the behaviour must be remembered, usually stored as a mental representation), reproduction (the observer must be physically able to reproduce the action), and motivation (the observer must have a reason to perform it). Motivation is often supplied by vicarious reinforcement , which is the increase in a behaviour after seeing a model rewarded for it (and the corresponding vicarious punishment when the model is penalized). In the Bobo studies, children who saw the aggressive model rewarded imitated more than those who saw the model punished. Key. Bandura's four processes in order: A ttention → R etention → R eproduction → M otivation. Learning can occur through observation alone, without the observer ever being directly reinforced. 9.6 Cognitive learning: Tolman, Kohler, Seligman Strict behaviourism treated the mind as a "black box," but several findings forced the recognition that internal mental processes matter in learning. Edward Chace Tolman studied rats in mazes and found evidence of latent learning , learning that occurs without reinforcement and remains hidden until there is a reason to show it. Rats allowed to wander a maze with no reward later learned the rewarded route far faster than rats with no prior exposure, proving they had learned the layout all along. Tolman argued they had formed a cognitive map , an internal mental representation of the spatial environment. Who → what. Edward Chace Tolman → latent learning and cognitive maps; evidence that learning can occur without reinforcement and be stored mentally. Wolfgang Kohler , a founder of Gestalt psychology, studied problem solving in chimpanzees and described insight learning : the sudden grasp of a solution, experienced as an "aha" moment, rather than gradual trial and error. His chimpanzee Sultan , faced with a banana out of reach, suddenly fitted two sticks together to rake it in, or stacked boxes to climb to a hanging fruit, having apparently solved the problem mentally before acting. Insight contrasts sharply with Edward Thorndike's trial-and-error curve. Who → what. Wolfgang Kohler → insight learning; the chimpanzee Sultan solving problems suddenly by mental restructuring, not trial and error. Martin Seligman described learned helplessness , a state in which an organism exposed to unavoidable, uncontrollable aversive events stops trying to escape even when escape later becomes possible. Dogs given inescapable shocks failed to jump a low barrier to safety in a later situation where escape was easy, having "learned" that their actions did not matter. Seligman linked this to human depression, seeing a parallel between the passive giving-up of the animals and the hopelessness of a depressed person. Who → what. Martin Seligman → learned helplessness (giving up after uncontrollable aversive events) and its link to depression. 9.7 Classical versus operant conditioning Because the two forms of conditioning are constantly contrasted on the exam, the differences are worth setting side by side. Feature Classical conditioning Operant conditioning Chief figures Pavlov, John B. Watson Thorndike, B. F. Skinner Type of behaviour Involuntary, reflexive, elicited Voluntary, emitted Basis of learning Association of two stimuli (CS with UCS) Association of behaviour with its consequence Role of the organism Passive; response is drawn out Active; organism operates on the environment Order of events Stimulus comes before the response Consequence comes after the response Example Salivating to a bell Pressing a lever for food Trap. Classical conditioning shapes involuntary responses (salivation, fear, reflexes); operant conditioning shapes voluntary behaviour (lever-pressing, studying). If a question describes an automatic bodily reaction, think classical; if it describes a chosen action followed by a reward or penalty, think operant. 9.8 Applications The principles above underlie a family of practical techniques. Behaviour modification is the systematic use of operant principles (reinforcement, extinction, shaping) to change maladaptive behaviour and build adaptive behaviour, widely used with children, in classrooms, and in institutions. A prominent example is the token economy , in which desired behaviours earn tokens (secondary reinforcers) that can later be exchanged for privileges or goods; token economies have been used in psychiatric wards and special-education settings to encourage self-care and cooperation. Biofeedback applies conditioning to normally involuntary bodily processes. Instruments give the person moment-to-moment information about a physiological function such as muscle tension, heart rate, or skin temperature, and by using that feedback as a reinforcing signal the person gradually learns some voluntary control, which helps with tension headaches, hypertension, and anxiety. Key. A token economy is an application of operant conditioning: tokens are secondary (conditioned) reinforcers. Biofeedback teaches control over involuntary functions by turning a bodily signal into feedback the person can respond to. Recap. Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour due to experience, distinct from maturation and reflex. Classical conditioning (Ivan Pavlov; UCS, UCR, CS, CR; acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization, discrimination, higher-order conditioning; Watson's Little Albert; John Garcia's prepared taste aversion) links stimuli and governs involuntary responses. Operant conditioning (Thorndike's law of effect; B. F. Skinner's chamber; the four consequences; primary and secondary reinforcers; the four reinforcement schedules with variable-ratio strongest; shaping, chaining, Premack; escape versus avoidance) links behaviour to its consequences and governs voluntary action. Albert Bandura's observational learning adds modeling, four processes, and vicarious reinforcement; Edward Tolman (latent learning, cognitive maps), Wolfgang Kohler (insight, Sultan), and Martin Seligman (learned helplessness) add the cognitive dimension. Applications include behaviour modification, token economies, and biofeedback. Remember the two headline traps: negative reinforcement is not punishment, and classical is involuntary while operant is voluntary. 9.9 The complete map: every theory of learning and its theorist This is the safety-net roster: the full set of learning theories an aptitude paper can name, each pinned to its theorist and a one-line core idea. If a name shows up in a question stem, it should be recognisable from this table. Read it as three families: behavioural and associative, cognitive, and social and applied. Key. Match the theorist to the mechanism, not just the label. Ivan Pavlov, Edward Thorndike, Skinner and Guthrie all study association, but the unit differs: reflex pairing, stimulus and response bond, response and consequence, and stimulus and movement contiguity. Aptitude items reward that precision. learning is the strengthening of stimulus and response bonds. 3 Operant conditioning and reinforcement schedules Burrhus Frederic Skinner Behaviour is shaped by its consequences; schedules of reinforcement control response rate and persistence. 4 Contiguity and one-trial learning Edwin Guthrie A stimulus and a movement occurring together become linked in full on a single pairing;
