Three main schools Theravada or Hinayana Buddhism Mahayana Buddhism Vajrayana Buddhism Theravada ("way of the elders") Mahayana ("great vehicle") Vajrayana ("diamond / thunderbolt vehicle") Ideal Arhat : one who reaches nirvana through his own effort Bodhisattva : one who puts off final nirvana to help all beings, out of compassion ( karuna ) Bodhisattva ideal, plus the aim of enlightenment in this very life Method Ethics, study and meditation: samatha (calm) and vipassana (insight) Compassion plus wisdom; the teaching of emptiness ( shunyata , Nagarjuna); devotion to many Buddhas and bodhisattvas Tantric methods: mantras, mandalas, mudras and visualisation, under a guru (lama) Texts Pali Canon (the Tripitaka below) Sanskrit sutras, e.g. Lotus Sutra, Heart Sutra Tantras, plus Mahayana texts Where today Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, Laos China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam (includes Zen and Pure Land) Tibet, Bhutan, Mongolia (the Dalai Lama's tradition) Trap: "Hinayana" ("lesser vehicle") was a Mahayana put-down; the school calls itself Theravada. Vajrayana grew out of Mahayana, so it shares the bodhisattva ideal. Zen is Mahayana , not Theravada. Psychology link: vipassana-style mindfulness (along with Zen) fed into modern programmes such as Jon Kabat-Zinn's MBSR (1979), and the Abhidhamma is often called Buddhist psychology because it classifies mental states. Four Noble Truths Dukkha (suffering) Tanha (desire) Suffering can be overcome The Eightfold Path is the solution to suffering The Noble Eightfold Path Right Understanding Right Thought Right Speech Right Action Right Livelihood Right Effort Right Mindfulness Right Concentration Tripitaka Vinaya Pitaka (Discipline Basket) Sutta Pitaka (Discourse Basket) Abhidhamma Pitaka (Higher Teaching Basket) The Three Jewels (Three Refuges) Buddha (the enlightened one) Dharma (teachings) Sangha (community) Hinduism Dualist philosophy (Advaita philosophy is monist). Believes in the soul . Self in the Samkhya Philosophy Jiva or living being is made up of: Prakriti: concerned with the material world Purusha: represents Atman — metaphysical or cosmic energy Advaita Philosophy "Advaita" refers to the identity of the self ( atman ) and the whole ( brahman ). Considers moksha achievable by removing avidya (ignorance). Purushartha — the four goals Dharma: values Artha: prosperity Kama: love Moksha: liberation Tridoshas Dosha Elements Body parts associated Vata Space and air Small and large intestines Pitta Fire and water Liver, spleen, gall bladder, stomach, pancreas Kapha Earth and water Sinuses, nostrils, throat, bronchi, lungs Triguna Sattva: intelligent, fortitude, gentle, truthful, benevolent, virtuous Rajas: energy, harsh, angry, excessive activity, strong emotions, inclining towards violence and aggression Tamas: mass, heavy, obstructing, ignorance or lack of knowledge (confused), inactivity, sleep (more), generally dejected always, indecent How doshas and gunas shape temperament Both are Indian "type" theories, a little like Hippocrates' four humours, but they work at two different levels: Tridosha (Vata, Pitta, Kapha) Triguna (Sattva, Rajas, Tamas) Source Ayurveda ( Charaka Samhita , Sushruta Samhita ) Samkhya philosophy; Bhagavad Gita ch. 14 and 17 Level Body: physical constitution Mind: mental constitution How it sets temperament Everyone has all three. The mix that dominates from conception is one's prakriti (constitution), which shapes build, health and temperament. All three are present in every mind. Whichever dominates colours a person's thinking, feeling and behaviour, and the balance can shift with diet, habits and practice. Vata-dominant: lively, quick, creative; under stress anxious, restless, scattered. Pitta-dominant: sharp, focused, ambitious; under stress irritable, angry, critical. Kapha-dominant: calm, steady, loyal; under stress slow, lethargic, possessive. Example: after failing an exam, a sattvic response is to calmly review the mistakes and plan; a rajasic response is anger, blaming others and frantic activity; a tamasic response is sleeping, giving up and feeling hopeless. Trap: doshas = body (Ayurveda); gunas = mind (Samkhya). The link between them: the Charaka Samhita calls rajas and tamas the two doshas of the mind , while sattva is the clear, balanced quality. Sattva is the ideal, but the Gita (14.5) says all three gunas bind the self. Avasthatraya (the three states) and Turiya (the fourth) Avasthatraya literally means "the three states" ( avastha = state, traya = three). The Mandukya Upanishad describes these three and then a fourth, turiya (literally "the fourth"), which is not one more state but the pure consciousness present through all three. State What happens Name of the self in it (Mandukya) Jagrat (Jagratavastha): waking Consciousness faces outward; we experience the physical world through the senses Vaishvanara (Vishva) Swapna (Swapnavastha): dreaming Consciousness faces inward; the mind builds its own world out of stored impressions Taijasa Sushupti : deep, dreamless sleep (the notes call it Prajnavastha ) No dreams, no desires, no awareness of objects; a unified, blissful rest Prajna Turiya (Turiyavastha): "the fourth" Pure witness-consciousness ( sakshi ), identical with Atman; it underlies the other three and is not touched by them Atman itself Heads up: the PDF page says "Avasthatraya (the four states of consciousness)". Strictly, avasthatraya is three states: jagrat, swapna, sushupti. Turiya is the fourth that lies beyond them. "Prajna" is the name of the self in deep sleep, so the standard name of the state itself is sushupti . The Mandukya also maps the sounds A, U, M onto waking, dream and deep sleep, and the silence after AUM onto turiya. Panchkoshas Annamaya Kosha: food body Pranamaya Kosha: breathing body Manomaya Kosha: mental body Vijnanamaya Kosha: intelligence Anandamaya Kosha: bliss body Bhagavad Gita The Gita upholds the necessity of Karma . According to the Bhagavad Gita, the spiritual journey towards self-realization and attainment of peace involves movement across several stages: Abhyasa (exercise) Gyana (knowledge) Dhyana (meditation) Tyaga (renunciation) Shanti (peace) Jainism Atheistic , dualist philosophy. Believes in the soul . Teachers called tirthankars (24 in number). Gained prominence under Lord Mahavira . Focus areas Ahimsa Moksha Self-discipline or asceticism Indriya (Senses) In Jain thought (Umasvati's Tattvartha Sutra , ch. 2), every sense has two sides, a physical one and a psychic one, and both are needed for actual perception. Type Meaning Its two parts Dravyendriya (physical sense) The material sense organ Nirvritti : the formed organ itself (e.g. the eye). Upakarana : its supporting, protective parts (e.g. eyelids, eyelashes) Bhavendriya (psychic sense) The soul's own power to know through that organ Labdhi (Labdi; power): the capacity to sense, which appears as knowledge-obscuring karma thins out. Upayoga (manifestation): actually using that capacity, i.e. attending and perceiving The five senses, each having both a dravya and a bhava side: Chakshu (eyes, sight), Shrotra (ears, hearing), Ghrana (nose, smell), Jihva or Rasana (tongue, taste), Sparsha (skin, touch). Example: your eyes are healthy (dravyendriya intact) and you have the power of sight (labdhi), but while lost in thought you fail to see a friend waving at you: upayoga, the act of attending, was missing. Heads up: the PDF lists the five senses under "Dravyendriya or Gyanendriya". In the Jain scheme the five senses are not a subtype of dravyendriya; each of the five has both a physical (dravya) and a psychic (bhava) side, and dravyendriya's own two parts are nirvritti and upakarana. "Jnanendriya" (organ of knowledge, as opposed to karmendriya, organ of action) is a Samkhya and Vedanta term, not the Jain name for dravyendriya. Jains also rank living beings by number of senses, from one-sensed beings such as plants (touch only) to five-sensed beings such as humans. Characteristics of jiva or self Jiva has bio-energies called prana . Jiva is endowed with consciousness called chaitanya . Jiva is the enjoyer of the fruits of his own actions. Psychic exertion distinguishes the living from the non-living. Jiva is actively engaged in its karmic journey, experiencing the result of its actions and striving towards liberation. Key: In Jainism, the highest form of pure knowledge a soul can attain is called Kevala Jnana . Types of self Unsullied self: contains metaphysical energy Sullied self: empirical self Sufism Dualist philosophy. Believes in the soul . No rebirth. Layers of Sufism (outer to inner) Shariat (outward religion or law) — exoteric layer Tariquat (the path) — esoteric layer Haqeeqat (the inner truth) Maarifat (Divine knowledge) Path in Sufism Tawbah (repentance) Wara (fear of the Lord) Zuhd (renunciation or detachment) Faqr (poverty) Sabr (patience) Tawakkul (trust, surrender) Rida (satisfaction) Levels of the self or nafs Nafs Al Ammara — the commanding self / the tyrannical self; two sublevels: the animal self and the satanic self Nafs Al Lawwama — the blaming self / the regretful self Nafs Al Mulhamah — the inspired self Nafs Al Muttma'ina — the secure self / the serene self Nafs Al Radiyah — the content self / the pleased self Nafs Al Mardiyyah — the gratified self / pleasing self Nafs Al Kamilah — the complete self / the pure self The seven levels describe the ego ( nafs ) being purified step by step, from a self ruled by desire to a self wholly surrendered to God. Several names come from the Qur'an; the seven-step ladder is a later Sufi teaching model (in English, see Robert Frager, Heart, Self and Soul , 1999). Level What the person is like 1. Ammara (commanding) Ruled by desire, anger, greed and pride; obeys whatever the ego commands and does not see its own faults (Qur'an 12:53). Its two sublevels: the animal self chases pleasure without caring about right or wrong; the lower satanic self sets itself up against God. 2. Lawwama (blaming) Conscience wakes up (Qur'an 75:2): still slips, but now feels regret, blames itself and repents; swings between good and bad. 3. Mulhamah (inspired) Begins to enjoy prayer and good deeds and to receive inner inspiration (Qur'an 91:8); can still fall back, e.g. into spiritual pride. 4. Mutma'inna (secure / serene) Inner peace (Qur'an 89:27): trusts God, and the ego's desires have largely quietened. 5. Radiyah (content / pleased) Accepts whatever happens, good or bad, as God's will, with patience and gratitude: pleased with God (Qur'an 89:28). 6. Mardiyyah (pleasing) Pleasing to God (Qur'an 89:28): humble, loving, living in service of others. 7. Kamilah (complete / pure) The ego is fully purified; the "perfected human" ( insan al-kamil ) of Sufi thought. Trap: the order runs from the commanding self (lowest) to the complete/pure self (highest), and lawwama (2) comes before mulhamah (3). Radiyah = pleased with God; Mardiyyah = pleasing to God. A handy psychology parallel: impulse-driven (id-like) behaviour, then guilt and conscience, then self-transcendence. Who → what (philosophies): Buddhism → monist, no soul (anatta); Hinduism → dualist, believes in soul (Advaita is monist); Jainism → dualist, believes in soul; Sufism → dualist, believes in soul, no rebirth.

title: Research & Statistics
text: Research & Statistics — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Research & Statistics Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Type I vs Type II error Parametric vs non-parametric Reliability & validity t-test / ANOVA / factor analysis Research designs What this covers. Core research methodology and statistics for the exam: key terms, the research process, variables and designs, descriptive and inferential statistics (central tendency, dispersion, t-tests, ANOVA family), factor analysis and regression, reliability and validity (with threats), standard scores, and research ethics. Original diagrams. 14 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 9 to 13) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Terms to Know · 2 · What is Research (Steps & Types) · 3 · Variables · 4 · Research Designs · 5 · Descriptive Statistics · 6 · Inferential Statistics: t-test & ANOVA · 7 · Factor Analysis & PCA · 8 · Regression & Correlation · 9 · Reliability · 10 · Validity & Threats · 11 · Standard Scores · 12 · Research Ethics 1 · Terms to Know Research and statistics terms to know. Colour-coded cards defining core research and statistics terms, arranged around a central Type I and Type II error table. Psycho Didi notes · p. 9 Type I and Type II errors. A decision table that crosses the conclusion drawn with the true state of nature and marks the two correct conclusions (one labelled power), the Type I error and the Type II error. Psycho Didi notes · p. 9 Random assignment: giving every participant an equal chance of being in an experimental or control group. Internal validity: extent to which an experiment investigates what it is supposed to. External validity: generalisability. Demand characteristics: factors that influence a participant's behaviour based on what they think the purpose of the experiment is. Observer expectancy effect: experimenter communicates expectations unintentionally (Pygmalion / Rosenthal effect). Descriptive statistics: the branch of statistics which deals with descriptions of obtained data. Inferential statistics: deals with drawing conclusions about a large group of individuals on the basis of observations of a few participants. Parameter: a measurable characteristic of a population. Confidence interval: the mean of your estimate plus and minus the variation in that estimate. Null hypothesis: the claim that the effect being studied does not exist. Alternate hypothesis: statement that suggests there is a relationship between the variables being studied. Significance level: the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true, i.e., the probability of making a Type I error. Effect size: a quantitative measure of the magnitude of the experimental effect. The larger the effect size, the stronger the relationship between the two variables. Skewness: a lopsided and asymmetrical curve because of extreme data. Kurtosis: the term used to identify the degree of steepness or shallowness of a distribution. Post hoc test: "like a post mortem." Requires two conditions: a directional hypothesis and a significant F ratio. Trap: Type I error = null hypothesis is true but we reject it (alternate is false but we accept it) → "false alarm." Type II error = null hypothesis is false but we accept it (alternate is true but we reject it) → "miss." The significance level is the probability of making a Type I error. Key: Test power is the probability that the test will reject the null hypothesis when the alternate hypothesis is true, i.e., it will not make a Type II error. The decision table (conclusion vs true state of nature) The small red and green table in the diagram crosses what you conclude from your data (rows) with what is actually true in the population (columns). You never know the true state; the table lists the four possible outcomes. The framework of Type I and Type II errors comes from Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson (papers of 1928 and 1933). Your conclusion H 0 is actually true H a is actually true (H 0 false) Support H 0 / reject H a Correct conclusion (probability 1 − α) Type II error (probability β), a "miss" Support H a / reject H 0 Type I error (probability α), a "false alarm" Correct conclusion = power (probability 1 − β) Example: H 0 = "the new therapy has no effect." If the therapy really does nothing but your study finds a significant improvement, that is a Type I error. If the therapy really works but your study finds no significant difference (say, because the sample was too small), that is a Type II error. Correctly detecting a therapy that works is power. Trap: Power = 1 − β, not 1 − α (1 − α is the chance of correctly keeping a true H 0 ). Making α stricter (.05 to .01) cuts Type I errors but raises Type II errors, so power falls. Power rises with a larger sample, a larger effect size, a more lenient α and a one-tailed test. Jacob Cohen (1988) suggested .80 as the usual minimum power. Feature Parametric test Non-parametric test Assumptions Generalizable; normal probability curve; uses mean; homogeneity of variance; probability sample; large sample size Assumption-free test Test power Higher Low test power Data type Interval / ratio Nominal data only Example t-test, ANOVA Chi square 2 · What is Research (Steps & Types) Research is a systematic, controlled, empirical, critical investigation. Steps Steps of research. The eight steps of research, from identifying a research problem to reporting findings. Psycho Didi notes · p. 10 Identify a research problem Review of literature Formulate a hypothesis Research design Collect data Analyse data Interpret data Report findings 3 · Variables Variables. The definition of a variable and its types: independent, dependent, extraneous (controlled and confounding), stimulus, organismic and behavioural. Psycho Didi notes · p. 10 A variable in research is a characteristic, number, or quantity that can be measured or counted and can take on different values. Type Description Independent variable (IV) Manipulated. Dependent variable (DV) Not manipulated; changes with change in IV. Extraneous variables Any variable other than the IV that could affect the DV. Two kinds (as in the diagram): controlled and confounding . Controlled (extraneous) variables Extraneous variables the researcher has dealt with: removed, held constant for everyone, matched across groups, or spread evenly by random assignment. Confounding variables Uncontrolled extraneous variables that affect results. Stimulus variable e.g. light (always IV). Organismic variable e.g. age. Behavioural / response variable e.g. response rate (always DV). Example: testing whether music (IV) improves memory scores (DV). Room noise is an extraneous variable; testing everyone in the same quiet room makes it a controlled variable. If the music group is tested in the morning and the no-music group in the evening, time of day becomes a confounding variable: you cannot tell whether the music or the time caused the difference. Trap: "Extraneous" is the umbrella term. A confounding variable is an extraneous variable that was not controlled and changes along with the IV, so it threatens internal validity. 4 · Research Designs Research: steps, variables and types of research. A flowchart branching from types of research into experiment, observation, correlation and special designs, alongside boxes on research steps, the definition of research and variables. Psycho Didi notes · p. 10 How the flowchart reads: "Types of research" branches into four designs: experiment , observation , correlation and special designs . "Special designs" then branches into three: longitudinal , cross-sectional and cohort-sequential . The first three differ in how much control the researcher has; the special designs are about time and age and are used mostly in developmental research. Design What the researcher does Can it show cause and effect? Experiment Manipulates the IV and controls extraneous variables. Yes (most control) Observation Watches and records behaviour without manipulating anything. No (describes) Correlation Measures two variables as they naturally occur and checks how they go together. No (association and direction only) Special designs Plan when and whom to measure so that change with age can be studied. Mainly describe change over time Special design How it works Example Main weakness Longitudinal The same group (cohort) is measured again and again over years. Lewis Terman's study of gifted children, begun in 1921. Slow and costly; drop-outs (attrition); practice effects from repeated testing. Cross-sectional Different age groups are measured once, at the same time. Comparing memory in 20-, 40- and 60-year-olds this year. Cohort effects: differences may come from the era each group grew up in, not from age itself. Cohort-sequential Several age groups are each followed over time (cross-sectional + longitudinal). Proposed by K. Warner Schaie (1965). Schaie's Seattle Longitudinal Study of adult intelligence (from 1956). Separates age effects from cohort effects, but complex and expensive. Experiment Experiment (lab): complete control on secondary (error) variance, e.g. lab experiment. Field experiment: secondary variance just greater than lab experiment; happens in a real setting; difficult to control extraneous variables. Quasi experiment: secondary variance greatest; no random assignment; non-equivalent groups, e.g. ex post facto studies. Correlation Not causation established; only helps us understand association. Gives us the direction of the relationship. Can't control extraneous variables. Generalization is possible. Types: positive, negative, zero. Trap: Correlation is not causation. It shows association and direction but cannot control extraneous variables. Observation Can be naturalistic or controlled . Can be participant or non-participant . Tools used: survey, interviews, questionnaires, observation. Usually used to check attitude towards something. In the diagram, "Observation" is used broadly for non-experimental, descriptive research : the researcher records behaviour or opinions as they are, without manipulating any variable. The four kinds of observation: Kind Meaning Example Naturalistic Behaviour watched in its real setting, without interfering. Recording how children share toys in a school playground. Controlled (laboratory) Behaviour watched in a set-up, standardised setting. Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation, run in a lab playroom. Participant The observer joins the group being studied. A researcher living in a village to study its customs. Non-participant The observer stays outside the group. Watching a classroom through a one-way mirror. Survey vs observation: standard textbooks (e.g. Baron; Ciccarelli & White) treat the survey method as its own descriptive method: a large group is asked questions through questionnaires or interviews about their attitudes, opinions or behaviour. That is why attitude measurement sits in this box. Observation records what people do; a survey records what people say. Survey traps: the sample must be representative, and answers can be distorted by social desirability (people giving the "nice" answer). Special Designs Longitudinal design Involves taking a single group and studying it for a long period; the group is called a cohort . Founder note: Lewis Terman — eugenics (Francis Galton, 1883). Prospective study: looking at the future. Retrospective study: looking at the past. Cross-sectional design Various age groups are compared at the same time. Cohort-sequential (cross-sequential) Cross-sectional + longitudinal; also known as cross-sequential. Who → what: Lewis Terman — associated with eugenics and long-term longitudinal cohort study. 5 · Descriptive Statistics Statistics: descriptive and inferential. A flowchart splitting descriptive statistics into central tendency and variance, and inferential statistics into t-test and ANOVA tables with degrees of freedom and non-parametric equivalents. Psycho Didi notes · p. 11 Measures of Central Tendency Measure Definition Scale Mean Average; sensitive to extreme data; parametric. Interval / ratio Median Mid point. Ordinal Mode Most frequent data point. Nominal Key: Empirical relationship: Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean . Frequency is measured by: Ogive curve, Histogram, Bar graph. Variance / Dispersion How the scores are spread around the mean. Range = highest score − lowest score (scores, not frequencies: marks from 12 to 47 give a range of 35). Standard deviation: spread of scores around the mean. Variance: standard deviation squared. Average deviation: mean of absolute deviations. Quartile deviation (for median values): QD = (Q3 − Q1) / 2. Formulas: Standard deviation σ = √[ Σ(x i − μ)² / N ]. Average (mean) deviation AD = Σ|x i − μ| / N. Here x i = each score, μ = the mean, N = number of scores, Σ = "add them all up", and | | means ignore the minus sign. Worked example: scores 2, 4, 6. Mean = 4. Deviations from the mean: −2, 0, +2. SD: squares are 4, 0, 4; sum = 8; 8 / 3 = 2.67 (this is the variance); √2.67 = 1.63. AD: absolute deviations 2, 0, 2; sum = 4; 4 / 3 = 1.33. Heads up: the diagram writes the average deviation as Σ(x i − μ) / N, without the absolute-value bars. Raw deviations from the mean always add up to 0, so the bars are essential: AD = Σ|x i − μ| / N. Also, σ with N in the denominator is the population SD; the sample SD (s) divides by n − 1. 6 · Inferential Statistics: t-test & ANOVA t-test Type Description Degrees of freedom Non-parametric equivalent Single sample To verify whether the sample belongs to the population. N − 1 Wilcoxon signed rank test, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test Paired sample Studying a sample 2 times (pre-test and post-test). N − 1 Wilcoxon signed rank test Matched samples Meant to be a repeated-measures test, but due to participant attrition, their characteristics are matched with new participants. N − 1 Wilcoxon signed rank test Independent samples Between-groups test. N − 2 Mann-Whitney U test ANOVA ANOVA is used to compare two or more factors, i.e., the effect of two independent variables on a single dependent variable. Type Description Degrees of freedom Non-parametric equivalent One way Compares levels of a single independent variable over the dependent variable. Main: K − 1; Error: N − K; Total: N − 1 Kruskal Wallis H test Repeated measures Single group of participants measured at multiple levels. Main (conditions): K − 1; Subjects: n − 1; Error: (K − 1)(n − 1); Total: N − 1 (n = participants, N = n × K scores) Friedman's ANOVA Two way Effect of two independent variables. Main: K − 1 for each factor (K1 − 1 and K2 − 1); Interaction: (K1 − 1) × (K2 − 1); Error: N − K (K = number of cells, K1 × K2); Total: N − 1 No simple rank test for a full factorial design. Friedman's test is called a "two-way ANOVA by ranks" only because its two ways are subjects and conditions, so it is really the repeated-measures equivalent. MANOVA Assessing multiple dependent variables simultaneously. Main: K − 1; Interaction (two-factor designs): (K1 − 1) × (K2 − 1); Error: N − K; Total: N − 1 — ANCOVA Adjusts for the influence of a covariate in testing. Main: K − 1; Interaction (two-factor designs): (K1 − 1) × (K2 − 1); Error: N − K − 1 (one extra df lost for the covariate); Total: N − 1 — Reading the degrees-of-freedom columns Main = df of an IV's effect (between groups or between conditions) = K − 1, where K = number of groups or levels. Interaction = df of the A × B effect = (K1 − 1)(K2 − 1). It exists only when there are two or more IVs, which is why it is blank for one-way and repeated-measures ANOVA. Error = within-groups (residual) df, the denominator of the F ratio. One-way: N − K. Total = N − 1, where N = total number of scores. The parts (main + interaction + error, plus subjects or covariate where present) always add up to the total. Design Set-up df worked out Reported as One way 3 groups of 10 (N = 30) Main 2; Error 27; Total 29 F(2, 27) Repeated measures 10 people, each tested in 3 conditions (N = 30 scores) Conditions 2; Subjects 9; Error 2 × 9 = 18; Total 29 F(2, 18) Two way 2 × 3 design, 10 per cell (N = 60, 6 cells) A 1; B 2; A × B 2; Error 60 − 6 = 54; Total 59 F(1, 54) for A; F(2, 54) for B and for A × B MANOVA (one-way) 3 groups of 10, 2 DVs Main 2; Error 27; Total 29 (same as one-way ANOVA) Wilks' lambda, converted to an approximate F ANCOVA 3 groups of 10, 1 covariate Main 2; Covariate 1; Error 30 − 3 − 1 = 26; Total 29 F(2, 26) Why repeated measures has no "interaction" column entry: each person is measured in every condition, so the total variability (N − 1) splits into between-subjects (n − 1) and within-subjects; the within-subjects part splits into conditions (K − 1) and error (K − 1)(n − 1). That error term is technically the subjects × conditions interaction , which is why some books call it "interaction", but it is the error term (the F denominator), so in this table it belongs in the Error column, as the diagram shows. Trap: in the diagram's repeated-measures row, the N inside (K − 1)(N − 1) means the number of participants , while the N under Total means the number of scores . With 10 people and 3 conditions, error df = (3 − 1)(10 − 1) = 18, but total df = 30 − 1 = 29, not 10 − 1. This page writes participants as n to keep the two apart. 7 · Factor Analysis & PCA Factor analysis, PCA and regression. An overview of factor analysis, its confirmatory and exploratory types, PCA with a scree plot, factor rotation, regression and research ethics. Psycho Didi notes · p. 12 Who → what: Factor analysis was given by Charles Spearman while creating his theory of intelligence. It uses a correlational design. Types Type Purpose Details / Methods Exploratory For creating a new theory. Unique variance: one factor is enough to explain variance; method = principal component method (unrotated factors given). Common variance: gives factors that explain variance together but not individually; methods = principal axis method, maximum likelihood estimation, generalized least squares. Confirmatory For verifying another theory. Changes cannot be made. The arrow in the diagram runs from "Method: principal component method" (under Exploratory, unique variance) to the PCA box. It means the PCA box describes that same method: PCA is the most common way to extract factors in an exploratory analysis (it is the default extraction in SPSS), and the PCA box explains how to decide how many to keep. Unique vs common variance: the variance of each item has a part it shares with the other items ( common variance ) and a part special to that item, including measurement error ( unique variance ). PCA (Karl Pearson, 1901; developed by Harold Hotelling, 1933) analyses the total variance, common plus unique, and condenses many variables into a few components. The common-factor methods (principal axis, maximum likelihood, generalized least squares) analyse only the shared variance, looking for hidden factors that make the items correlate. That is the logic of the diagram's split: the method that keeps unique variance in (PCA) versus the methods that use common variance only. Trap: strictly, PCA is a data-reduction technique rather than "true" factor analysis, even though it is run from the factor analysis menu. Every extraction method first gives an unrotated solution; rotation (below) comes afterwards. PCA (Principal Component Analysis) Scree plot. A scree plot of eigenvalues against component number for 18 components, with arrows pointing to the 5th and 8th factors. Psycho Didi notes · p. 12 Uses Cattell's scree plot (for a large number of factors) and the Kaiser–Guttman criterion (for a small number of factors, < 20). Eigenvalues indicate how much variance we expect each factor to explain; an eigenvalue of 1 is the minimum expectation from each factor. In a scree plot: x-axis = order of factors; y-axis = unreduced eigenvalues. Identity matrix: all the factors have 0 correlation with each other except with themselves. Reading the scree plot A scree plot (Raymond Cattell, 1966) graphs each factor's eigenvalue (y-axis) against its order (x-axis). The first factors explain a lot of variance, so the line drops steeply; later factors explain little, so it flattens out. "Scree" is the loose rubble at the foot of a cliff: the flat tail is the rubble you discard. Rule: find the elbow , where the steep slope turns into the flat tail, and keep the factors before it. In the example plot (18 components), the eigenvalues fall from about 5.5 for the 1st to about 1.1 for the 5th, drop below 1 from the 6th onwards, and the line is almost flat from about the 8th. So the two arrows mark two possible cut-offs: the 5th factor is the last one with an eigenvalue above 1 (the Kaiser–Guttman rule would keep 5), and the 8th factor is where the curve levels off into scree (the elbow). Trap: the Kaiser–Guttman rule (Louis Guttman, 1954; Henry Kaiser, 1960) keeps every factor with an eigenvalue greater than 1; the scree test keeps the factors above the elbow. The two rules can give different numbers, as in this plot, so researchers also check whether the factors make theoretical sense. Spotting the elbow is a judgement call, which is the scree test's main weakness. Factor Rotation Allows us to decide if a second round of FA is required. Rotation Result Angle Types Oblique rotation Gives correlated factors; makes factors suitable for further FA. Non-90° angles oblimin, geomin, promax Orthogonal rotation Gives uncorrelated factors. 90° equimax, quartimax, varimax 8 · Regression & Correlation Regression and partial correlation. Boxes giving the simple and multiple regression equations and the definition of partial correlation. Psycho Didi notes · p. 12 Simple (bivariate) regression: Y = a + bx + E. Multiple regression: Y = a + b1x1 + b2x2 + b3x3 + E, where b = partial slope. The regression coefficient is indicated by β . R = geometric mean of partial correlation (range 0–1). Variance = R × R × 100%. Partial correlation Studying a single correlation in a multiple correlation matrix by removing the impact of other correlations. 9 · Reliability Reliability and validity. A reliability diagram linking test-retest, parallel forms, inter-rater, split half and internal consistency (with its three methods), above a validity wheel and a list of threats to validity. Psycho Didi notes · p. 13 Reliability checks if our test is consistent. It can be external and internal. Method Description Notes / Formula Test–retest Give the test to the same group after some time gap, and correlate the two tests (2 administrations). Source of error: practice effect, time sampling error, carryover effects. Parallel / equivalent forms Correlate the new test with a previous version of the test or a similar test. Can be done with or without a time gap. Split half Comparing the first half of the score with the 2nd half; odd-even method may be used. Formula: r = 2r / (1 + r), i.e. full-test r = 2 × (half-test r) / (1 + half-test r). This is the Spearman–Brown formula with K = 2: each half is only half as long as the real test, so the raw correlation between halves underestimates reliability. Example: halves correlate .60, so full-test reliability = 1.20 / 1.60 = .75. Works for any item format. Internal consistency Correlating performance on each item with overall performance across participants. Methods (as in the diagram): Cronbach's alpha, Kuder–Richardson, Spearman–Brown correction. Kuder–Richardson method Internal consistency for dichotomous items. Similar to Cronbach's alpha but can only be used for dichotomous items. Inter-rater Agreement of raters with regards to performance of participants. Cohen's kappa is used (r should be > .8). Key — Spearman–Brown correction: used to correct for the effect of the length of the test. Formula: Kr / (1 + (K − 1)r), where K = test length; r = correlation. Key — Cronbach's alpha: average of all possible split halves; applicable to dichotomous and polytomous items. The three internal consistency methods In the diagram, Cronbach's alpha, Spearman–Brown and Kuder–Richardson all branch off internal consistency as its methods: each estimates reliability from a single administration by checking whether the items of one test hang together. Method Who / when Item type What it does Cronbach's alpha Lee Cronbach, 1951 Any: dichotomous or polytomous (e.g. Likert) Average of all possible split halves; the most commonly reported reliability coefficient. Kuder–Richardson (KR-20, KR-21) G. Frederic Kuder and M. W. Richardson, 1937 Dichotomous only (right/wrong, yes/no) Same idea as alpha: KR-20 is what alpha becomes when items are scored 0/1. KR-21 is a shortcut that assumes all items are equally difficult. Spearman–Brown correction Charles Spearman and William Brown, 1910 Any Not a separate coefficient: it adjusts a reliability for test length, most often stepping a split-half correlation up to full length (K = 2), or predicting reliability if a test is lengthened or shortened. Trap: "similar to Cronbach's alpha but only for dichotomous items" describes Kuder–Richardson , not split half; split half works with any item format. Most testing textbooks also count split half itself as an internal consistency method, since it needs only one administration. 10 · Validity & Threats Types of validity. A four-part validity wheel (face, content, criterion and construct) with definitions and the concurrent, predictive, convergent and divergent sub-types. Psycho Didi notes · p. 13 Validity (the centre of the wheel) refers to the accuracy of the test : whether it measures what it claims to measure. A test can be reliable (consistent) without being valid, but it cannot be valid without being reliable. Example: a bathroom scale that always reads 2 kg too heavy is reliable but not valid. The four quarters of the wheel are four kinds of evidence for that accuracy. Validity Meaning Face validity What a judge or expert thinks about the test; how much a test appears to be accurate (MMPI (Starke Hathaway and J. Charnley McKinley, 1943) has poor face validity). Content validity Items are relevant and representative of the target construct. Construct validity Used to validate a theory. Comparing a new test with another test that correlates to the same construct. The extent to which the test measures the theoretical trait (construct) it claims to, such as anxiety or intelligence (Lee Cronbach and Paul Meehl, 1955). Criterion validity The extent to which the test fulfills the criteria made by another source. Trap: "refers to the accuracy of the test" defines validity as a whole (the centre of the wheel), not construct validity alone. The confusion has a source: the modern unified view (Samuel Messick, 1989) treats all validity evidence as ultimately evidence for construct validity. For an MCQ asking for the general definition, answer "validity". Sub-types Concurrent validity (criterion): the extent that a measure simultaneously relates to another measure that it is supposed to relate to, e.g. comparing a new personality questionnaire with the 16PF (Raymond Cattell). Predictive validity (criterion): the extent that a measure predicts another measure, e.g. predicting a real exam through mocks. Convergent validity (construct): the extent that different measures of the same construct converge or strongly correlate with one another. Divergent validity (construct): the extent that measures of different constructs diverge or minimally correlate with one another. Threats to Validity Threats to validity. Two lists of internal and external threats to validity. Psycho Didi notes · p. 13 Internal threats External threats Confounding variables; selection bias; test-taker history; maturation; repeated testing; mortality; diffusion; compensatory rivalry; experimenter bias Generalizability; aptitude-treatment interaction; situations; pre-test effect; post-test effect; Rosenthal effect 11 · Standard Scores Standard scores. A card showing when Z and T scores are used, with the mean and SD of sten and stanine scores. Psycho Didi notes · p. 9 Score Use Mean SD Z score Normal data (always preferred) 0 1 T score Clinical setting (non-normal) 50 10 Sten Standard ten 5.5 2 Stanine Standard nine 5 2 12 · Research Ethics Research ethics. A list of research ethics principles: risk-benefit ratio, informed consent, privacy, confidentiality, minimizing deception and debriefing. Psycho Didi notes · p. 12 Research ethics involve a subjective evaluation of the risk-benefit ratio. Informed consent: a person's explicitly expressed willingness to participate in a research project based on a clear understanding of the nature of the research. Privacy: the rights of individuals to decide how information about them is to be communicated to others. Confidentiality: information obtained from a research participant will be kept secret and private. Minimizing deception. Debriefing: explaining to participants the need for deception, addressing misconceptions, and removing harmful effects resulting from deception.

title: Biological Basis of Behaviour
text: Biological Basis of Behaviour — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Biological Basis of Behaviour Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes 4 lobes · limbic system · basal ganglia 7 neurotransmitters 12 cranial nerves Endocrine glands & hormones Sympathetic vs Parasympathetic What this covers. Development and organization of the nervous system; the forebrain and its four lobes; the limbic system and basal ganglia; diencephalon, midbrain and hindbrain; meninges and ventricles; important Broadmann's areas; techniques to study the brain; dysfunctions of the brain by region; neurotransmitters, hormones and the endocrine glands; glial cells; the peripheral nervous system (cranial and spinal nerves); and the autonomic nervous system. Original diagrams. 16 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 15 to 24) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Development & Organization of the Nervous System · 2 · The Forebrain & the Four Lobes · 3 · The Limbic System · 4 · The Basal Ganglia · 5 · Diencephalon: Thalamus, Hypothalamus, Epithalamus · 6 · Midbrain (Mesencephalon) · 7 · Hindbrain: Cerebellum, Pons, Medulla, ARAS · 8 · Meninges & Ventricles · 9 · Important Broadmann's Areas · 10 · Techniques to Study the Brain · 11 · Dysfunctions of the Brain · 12 · Neurotransmitters · 13 · Hormones & the Endocrine Glands · 14 · Glial Cells · 15 · Peripheral Nervous System & Cranial Nerves · 16 · The Autonomic Nervous System 1 · Development & Organization of the Nervous System Development of the brain. A flowchart that splits the nervous system into its divisions and traces each neural tube subdivision to the brain structures, ventricles and functions that develop from it. Psycho Didi notes · p. 15 The Nervous System is divided into the Central Nervous System (CNS) and the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) . Central Nervous System (CNS) — the Brain and the Spinal Cord . Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) — includes the Autonomic Nervous System (with its Sympathetic and Parasympathetic divisions) and the Somatic Nervous System (with its Afferent and Efferent nervous systems). Enteric Nervous System — controls the smooth muscle and glandular tissue in the digestive system. Development from the neural tube The brain develops from the neural tube , forming the following divisions: Primary vesicle Sub-division Becomes Its hollow becomes Forebrain (Prosencephalon) Telencephalon Cerebral hemispheres / four lobes; limbic structures (hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus); most of the basal ganglia Lateral ventricles (V1, V2) Diencephalon Thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus Third ventricle Midbrain Mesencephalon Midbrain Cerebral aqueduct Hindbrain (Rhombencephalon) Metencephalon Pons and cerebellum Fourth ventricle Myelencephalon Medulla The neural tube picture. The coloured drawing in the diagram shows the early embryonic brain at the three-vesicle stage : the prosencephalon (forebrain, blue) at the front, the mesencephalon (midbrain, magenta) in the middle and the rhombencephalon (hindbrain, green) behind it, running on into the spinal cord (yellow). The neural tube itself forms when the neural plate (from the embryo's outer layer, the ectoderm) folds up and closes, by about the end of the fourth week of pregnancy. Around the fifth week the forebrain splits into telencephalon and diencephalon and the hindbrain into metencephalon and myelencephalon, giving the five secondary vesicles in the table. The midbrain does not split. Exam trap. Count the vesicles: 3 primary (pros-, mes-, rhomb-encephalon) and 5 secondary (tel-, di-, mes-, met-, myel-encephalon). The mesencephalon is the only one that keeps its name. If the tube fails to close, the result is a neural tube defect : anencephaly at the head end, spina bifida at the tail end. Ventricles in the diagram. The neural tube is hollow, and each part's hollow becomes a fluid-filled space (last column of the table): the telencephalon's becomes the two lateral ventricles , the diencephalon's the third ventricle , the mesencephalon's the narrow cerebral aqueduct , and the hindbrain's the fourth ventricle . Below the brain the same channel continues as the central canal of the spinal cord. The diagram draws the 4th ventricle from the myelencephalon only; strictly it is the cavity of the whole hindbrain, lying between the cerebellum behind and the pons and upper medulla in front. Limbic system branch. The diagram also branches the limbic system off the telencephalon, listing under it the basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, substantia nigra, nucleus accumbens, subthalamic nuclei), the amygdala, the hippocampus and the cingulate gyrus. The amygdala, hippocampus, cingulate gyrus and the striatum (caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens) do develop from the telencephalon. Two exceptions: the substantia nigra is a midbrain structure and the subthalamic nucleus belongs to the diencephalon. Heads up: the diagram files the basal ganglia inside the limbic system. Standard texts treat the basal ganglia as a motor system and the limbic system as the emotion and memory system. The nucleus accumbens is where they meet: it links emotion and reward to action. Don't confuse. Afferent nerves carry sensory information toward the CNS; Efferent nerves carry motor commands away from the CNS. Similarly, the Sympathetic system drives "fight or flight" (Walter Cannon, 1915) while the Parasympathetic system drives "rest and digest." 2 · The Forebrain & the Four Lobes The forebrain contains the neocortex , which contains the primary and association cortexes . Key. In the cerebral cortex, grey matter is outside and white matter is inside . Lobe Functions Frontal Lobe Executive functioning; association; motor cortex; Broca's area (left hemisphere); metacognition Parietal Lobe Sensation; haptic memory; proprioception; the " where " pathway Occipital Lobe Awareness of visual stimuli Temporal Lobe Auditory cortex; Wernicke's area (left hemisphere); part of the hippocampus; stores declarative memories; olfactory bulb 3 · The Limbic System The limbic system. A table giving the function and dysfunction of each limbic system and basal ganglia structure, with a small brain illustration beside each name. Psycho Didi notes · p. 16 Key structures of the limbic system, their functions, and dysfunctions: Name Function Dysfunction Amygdala Fear and rage; emotional and flashbulb memory (Roger Brown and James Kulik, 1977); sense fear and aggression in others; recognize learning, memory consolidation of emotional memories Kluver-Bucy syndrome; Hyperorality; Hypersexuality Hippocampus Encoding new memory; shaped like a seahorse; located in temporal lobe Anterograde amnesia; PTSD Septum Pleasure; inhibits aggression Sham rage / Septal rage Thalamus Relay (contralateral); contains LGN, MGN, VLN, Pulvinar Extreme pain in opposite side of the body Hypothalamus Homeostasis; controls endocrine glands; eating (Lateral, Anterior, Ventromedial); sleep (Suprachiasmatic nucleus) Aphagia; Adipsia Cingulate gyrus Pain information transmission; recollecting pleasant memories; regulate aggression Aggressive behaviour; shyness Who → what. James Papez (1937) — the Papez circuit , a loop of structures he proposed as the brain's emotion circuit (paper: "A proposed mechanism of emotion"): hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies (hypothalamus) → anterior nucleus of the thalamus → cingulate gyrus → parahippocampal gyrus → back to the hippocampus . The "PAPEZ (1937)" label beside the limbic system title in the diagram refers to this. Paul MacLean (1952) later widened the idea, added the amygdala and septum, and coined the term "limbic system" (from Paul Broca's "limbic lobe", 1878). Exam trap. The amygdala is not part of Papez's original circuit ; MacLean added it. And although Papez proposed the circuit for emotion, it is now linked mainly to memory : damage to its parts (hippocampus, fornix, mammillary bodies, as in Korsakoff syndrome) causes amnesia. Amygdala (detail) Fear and rage center Encodes emotional memories Sense fear in others Hippocampus (detail) Encode declarative memories Role in PTSD Damaged by long exposure to glucocorticoids Cingulate gyrus (detail) Transmission Important in decision making Pain Social interaction Sex Largest part 4 · The Basal Ganglia The Basal Ganglia handle motor coordination and inhibition; they prevent unnecessary motor movements and activity in the white matter of the frontal lobe. Dysfunction: tremors, involuntary muscle movements, abnormal increase in tone, difficulty initiating movements, and abnormal posture. Components of the basal ganglia: caudate , putamen , globus pallidus , substantia nigra , nucleus accumbens , and subthalamic nuclei . Structure Function Dysfunction Caudate Planning; learning; memory; romantic interaction Overactivity Putamen Speech articulation; addiction; motor learning Overactivity Nucleus Accumbens Motivation and action; drug self administration Depression, addiction, anxiety, difficulty experiencing positive emotions Subthalamic Nucleus Regulate voluntary movement Hemiballismus: sudden, large, flailing movements on one side of the body Globus Pallidus Proprioceptive movement Parkinson's disease, dystonia, and gait abnormalities Substantia Nigra Motor movement; reward functioning Motor control issues, most notably seen in Parkinson's disease 5 · Diencephalon: Thalamus, Hypothalamus, Epithalamus Thalamus The largest part of the diencephalon . Nuclei include: Medial Geniculate nucleus Lateral Geniculate Nucleus Ventrolateral preoptic nucleus Pulvinar Hypothalamus Controls homeostasis and the endocrine glands (see the Limbic System section for detail). Epithalamus Penial (pineal) gland 3rd ventricle 6 · Midbrain (Mesencephalon) Tectum — Posterior (roof) Superior colliculi (vision) and inferior colliculi (audition) Orientation Tegmentum — Anterior (floor) Substantia nigra : black substance, reward learning Red nucleus : limb movements Periaqueductal gray : fear, pain response The Cerebral Aqueduct runs through the midbrain. 7 · Hindbrain: Cerebellum, Pons, Medulla, ARAS Cerebellum Classical conditioning (Ivan Pavlov) Motor coordination and proprioception Involuntary and voluntary movement Walking, gait, posture Pons Consciousness General arousal Sleep and wakefulness ARAS (Ascending Reticular Activating System) General arousal Consciousness 4As : alertness, attentiveness, arousal, awakeness Damage = unconsciousness Activates higher cortex Medulla Breathing Maintaining organ systems Heart circulation Respiratory control Houses the 4th ventricle 8 · Meninges & Ventricles Meninges of the Brain Meninges of the brain. A box listing the three meninges, dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater, with what the arachnoid and pia mater contain. Psycho Didi notes · p. 15 Dura mater Arachnoid mater — contains the subarachnoid space that holds CSF Pia mater — contains blood vessels Ventricles Ventricles. A cross diagram placing ventricles V1 and V2 on an intraventricular formation axis and V3 and V4 on a cerebral aqueduct axis with the choroid plexus at V4, beside a labelled drawing of the ventricular system. Psycho Didi notes · p. 17 Lateral Ventricles (V1, V2 — the two lateral ventricles) Third ventricle (V3) Fourth ventricle (V4) Connected via the cerebral aqueduct and intraventricular (interventricular) foramen Choroid plexus — produces CSF Reading the cross diagram. The cross is a memory aid for which passage joins which ventricles. The horizontal arm joins V1 and V2 (the two lateral ventricles, one in each hemisphere) and is labelled "intraventricular formation"; the correct term is the interventricular foramen , which the labelled drawing beside it calls the foramen of Monro . The vertical arm joins V3 (in the diencephalon) to V4 (between the cerebellum and the pons and medulla) through the cerebral aqueduct (aqueduct of Sylvius), which runs through the midbrain. "Choroid plexus" is written under V4. Step CSF flows from Through Into 1 Each lateral ventricle (V1, V2) Interventricular foramen (foramen of Monro), one on each side Third ventricle (V3) 2 Third ventricle Cerebral aqueduct (through the midbrain) Fourth ventricle (V4) 3 Fourth ventricle Median aperture (foramen of Magendie) and two lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka) Subarachnoid space around the brain and spinal cord (some also runs down the central canal) 4 Subarachnoid space Arachnoid granulations (villi) Venous blood (dural venous sinuses) Heads up: the cross makes it look as if V1 and V2 open into each other. They do not: each lateral ventricle opens separately into the third ventricle through its own interventricular foramen. Also, choroid plexus is found in all four ventricles (most of it in the lateral ventricles), not only in V4. Classic question: a blocked cerebral aqueduct (aqueductal stenosis) swells the lateral and third ventricles but not the fourth, because the fluid is trapped above the block (obstructive hydrocephalus). 9 · Important Broadmann's Areas Other important brain areas. The page header with the ventricles diagram, the visual system flow from V1 and V2 to V3, V4, V5 and V3A toward the temporal and parietal lobes, and the heading of the Broadman's areas table. Psycho Didi notes · p. 17 Important Broadman's areas: areas 1 to 5. A table giving the name, function and lesion effect of areas 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, with a brain image marking each area. Psycho Didi notes · p. 17 Important Broadman's areas: areas 6 to 45. A table giving the name, function and lesion causes for areas 6, 9, 10, 17, 22 and 37, Wernicke's area (22, 39, 40) and Broca's area (44, 45), with brain images marking most areas. Psycho Didi notes · p. 18 Alongside the Broadmann's areas, the note maps the visual system stream: areas V1, V2, V3, V3A, V4, V5 , running from the occipital lobe toward the temporal and parietal lobes. In the diagram, V3 (dynamic form) and V4 (recognition) sit under the temporal lobe , and V5 (motion) and V3A (shape) sit under the parietal lobe . A two-way arrow joins the temporal and parietal lobes at the top. The idea that each visual area handles one feature (form, colour, motion) is Semir Zeki 's functional specialization theory. The split toward two lobes is the two visual streams idea: Leslie Ungerleider and Mortimer Mishkin (1982) described a ventral "what" stream (occipital to inferior temporal lobe: recognising objects) and a dorsal "where" stream (occipital to posterior parietal lobe: location and motion); Melvyn Goodale and David Milner (1992) later recast the dorsal stream as "how" (vision for guiding action). Area Label in diagram Standard textbook job Damage V1 (area 17) Start point Primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe; first cortical stop, codes edges and orientation; feeds both streams Cortical blindness V2 (area 18) Relay Next to V1; passes signals on to the specialised areas V3 , V3A Dynamic form; shape Form, especially shapes in motion (Zeki) V4 Recognition Colour (and form); ventral "what" stream toward the temporal lobe. Whole-object recognition happens further along, in the inferior temporal cortex Achromatopsia (cerebral colour blindness) V5 , also called MT ( middle temporal area) Motion Motion ; dorsal "where/how" stream toward the parietal lobe. In humans it sits where the occipital and temporal lobes meet Akinetopsia (motion blindness), e.g. patient L.M. (Zihl and colleagues, 1983) Exam trap. Exams key V4 = colour and V5/MT = motion . MT stands for middle temporal (not medial temporal), and despite the "temporal" in its name V5/MT belongs to the dorsal (parietal) stream , not the temporal "what" stream. The diagram agrees with the standard view on these two: V4 on the temporal side, V5 on the parietal side. How the diagram is wired. V1 and V2 are each drawn as two boxes to show that separate channels leave from different parts of them. Following the arrows: V1 → V2 : the main route; both halves of V1 feed V2. V1 → V5 and V1 → V3A directly: a shortcut that skips V2, so motion signals reach V5 fast. V2 → V3 and V2 → V4 (temporal side), and V2 → parietal lobe (the other half of V2 sends a line straight up to the parietal lobe). V4 ↔ V5 : a two-way arrow, so the colour/form side and the motion side exchange information. Temporal lobe ↔ parietal lobe : the two streams also talk to each other at the top. The point of the wiring is that vision is processed in parallel : different features travel along different routes at the same time and are combined later. Area no. Name Function Lesion's effect 1, 2, 3 Primary somatosensory cortex Localization of touch, temperature, vibration, pain; sensory perception; orofacial movement Agraphesthesia, astereognosia, loss of vibration, proprioception and fine touch, potentially hemineglect if the non-dominant hemisphere is affected 4 Primary motor cortex Contralateral finger/hand/wrist or orofacial movements, learned motor sequences, breathing control, and voluntary blinking Paralysis of the contralateral side of the body 5 Somatosensory association cortex Stereopsis, line bisection judgments, processing chaotic patterns, using spatial imagery in deductive reasoning, motor execution, bimanual manipulation, working memory, language processing, visuomotor attention, pain perception, tactile localization, saccadic eye movement Ideomotor apraxia: loss of ability to produce purposeful, skilled movements. Astereognosis: tactile agnosia 6 Premotor and Supplementary Motor Cortex Motor sequencing/planning, laughter/smiling, interlimb coordination, movement learning and initiation, motor imagery, speech motor programming, language processing and switching, speech perception, object naming, lip-reading, word retrieval, lexical decision on words and pseudo-words, syntactical processing, working memory, mnemonic rehearsal, episodic long-term memory, topographic memory, visuospatial and visuomotor attention, attention to human voices Affect sensory guidance of movement and control of proximal and trunk muscles. Kinetic apraxia 9 Dorsolateral / anterior prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) Integrating sensory and mnemonic information, regulation of intellectual function and action, the act of deception and lying Dysexecution syndrome: problems with affect, social judgement, executive memory, abstract thinking, and intentionality 10 Anterior prefrontal cortex Reasoning, task flexibility, problem solving, planning, execution, working memory, processing emotional stimuli, inferential reasoning, decision making, calculation of numerical processes Similar to what would be seen in Area 9, since the two areas are associated 17 Primary visual cortex (V1) Contains a well-defined map of the spatial information required for vision Cortical blindness 22 Auditory association cortex (back part = Wernicke's area; the primary auditory cortex is 41 and 42) Involves complex language and auditory processing Difficulty finding words, semantic paraphasias, prosopagnosia, disturbances in drawing 37 Fusiform Gyrus Processing of color information, face and body recognition, word and number recognition Difficulties in visual recognition 22, 39, 40 Wernicke's area Helps people understand spoken and written language Language disorders 44, 45 Broca's area Production of speech Broca's aphasia: a deficit in the ability to speak and produce the proper words/sounds Where each area sits The brain pictures in the source mark each area in green. Korbinian Brodmann (1909) divided the cortex into 52 numbered areas by the look of their cell layers under the microscope (cytoarchitecture). The heading's "Broadmann" is a misspelling of Brodmann . Area Lobe Location 3, 1, 2 Parietal Postcentral gyrus: the strip just behind the central sulcus 4 Frontal Precentral gyrus: the strip just in front of the central sulcus 5 Parietal Superior parietal lobule, just behind the postcentral gyrus 6 Frontal In front of area 4: premotor cortex on the outer (lateral) surface, supplementary motor area on the inner (medial) surface 9 Frontal Upper front of the frontal lobe (superior and middle frontal gyri); part of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex 10 Frontal Frontal pole: the very front tip of the brain 17 Occipital Banks of the calcarine sulcus on the inner (medial) surface of the occipital lobe; areas 18 and 19 surround it as visual association cortex 22 Temporal Superior temporal gyrus; its back part is Wernicke's area. Strictly this is auditory association cortex: the primary auditory cortex proper is areas 41 and 42 on Heschl's gyrus (transverse temporal gyri) 37 Temporal and occipital Underside of the brain where the occipital and temporal lobes meet; includes the fusiform gyrus 39, 40 Parietal Angular gyrus (39) and supramarginal gyrus (40), together the inferior parietal lobule, next to the back of area 22 44, 45 Frontal Inferior frontal gyrus: pars opercularis (44) and pars triangularis (45), usually in the left hemisphere Exam trap. The central sulcus is the border: area 4 (motor) lies in front of it in the frontal lobe, areas 3, 1, 2 (touch) lie behind it in the parietal lobe. They are written 3, 1, 2 because that is their front-to-back order. And if asked for the primary auditory cortex, answer 41 and 42 , not 22. 10 · Techniques to Study the Brain Techniques to study the brain. A mind map branching from the title to history, ablation, neurosurgery, gene knockout, stereotaxic surgery, optogenetic stimulation, lesion types and imaging techniques, each with short notes and icons. Psycho Didi notes · p. 19 History Trephination : creating a hole in the skull or nail to relieve pressure or treat a health condition. Autopsy : a medical examination of a body after death. Ablation : complete removal of a part of the brain (mostly for treatment). Gene knockout : use of genetic engineering to inactivate or remove one or more specific genes from an organism. Imaging techniques Computed Axial Tomography (CAT) : introduced in the early 1970s (Godfrey Hounsfield, first patient scan 1971); 360-degree X-ray; 3D/2D structural image. EEG : electrical activity. EMG (electromyography): records the electrical activity of muscles , i.e. muscle tension ; used in sleep studies (muscle tone drops in REM sleep) and in biofeedback. MEG (magnetoencephalography): records the tiny magnetic fields produced by the electrical activity of neurons; millisecond timing like EEG, with better localization than EEG. EOG : sleep studies, eye movement. PET : introduced in 1973; functional image of the brain (2D); fluorodeoxyglucose (a radioactive tracer : active neurons take up more of it) injected in carotid artery. MRI : uses a strong magnetic field plus radio-wave pulses ; hydrogen nuclei (mostly in water) line up in the field and give off radio signals that are turned into an image; 3D image of structure; high spatial resolution. No radioactivity and no X-rays. fMRI : traces BOLD (Blood Oxygen Level Dependent) signal; gives structural as well as functional image. BOLD contrast: checks difference between active and inactive areas. Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) : non-invasive; uses magnetic pulses to stimulate the brain and treat conditions like depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder. Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) : 2D structural, 3D functional image; location of seizures can be checked. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) : optical imaging technique; light measures blood flow changes; good temporal resolution. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) : better spatial resolution than MRI. Heads up: the diagram above swaps two labels and garbles a third. It prints EMG as "magnetic activity" and MEG as "muscle tension"; the correct pairs are EMG = electrical activity of muscles (muscle tension) and MEG = magnetic fields from neural activity . Break the names up to remember: electro- myo -graphy (myo = muscle), magneto -encephalo-graphy (encephalo = brain). It also says MRI traces a "radioactive field of hydrogen": MRI uses a magnetic field and radio waves and involves no radioactivity . The techniques that use a radioactive tracer are PET (and SPECT). Surgical & stimulation techniques Stereotaxic surgery : uses an atlas and an instrument; useful for lesion and surgery; invasive. Optogenetic stimulation : a genetic technique that enables scientists to activate or inhibit the activity of specific neuron populations using light. Neurosurgery : done for treatment. Lesions (controlled destruction) Aspiration lesion : for suction action; only for shallow areas and cerebral cortex. Knife cut lesion : severing, tissue sectioning (for biopsy). Reversible lesion : functional lesion; cryogenic (put freezing agents); uses a cryoprobe (cryogenic blockade). Chemical lesion : excitotoxic lesions performed through stereotaxis — kainic acid (glutamate neuron), ibotenic acid, 6-hydroxy-dopamine (monoamine). Radiofrequency lesion : a high-frequency current is passed through the tip of an electrode placed by stereotaxic surgery, and the heat destroys the tissue around the tip. Used for small, deep (subcortical) lesions; the size depends on the current's strength and duration and on the electrode tip. It destroys everything near the tip, including axons just passing through, which excitotoxic chemical lesions spare. Applies to all lesions. The diagram's note "bilateral lesions show better effect than unilateral" sits beside the Lesions heading, so it is a general point about lesion studies, not about radiofrequency lesions only. Destroying a structure on both sides gives a much clearer effect on behaviour; after a unilateral (one-sided) lesion the intact twin structure in the other hemisphere can partly compensate, so the effect may be mild or hard to detect (Pinel, Biopsychology). 11 · Dysfunctions of the Brain Dysfunctions of the brain. A mind map of the deficits linked to each brain region, from lateralization and split brain to the hindbrain, lobes, midbrain and limbic system, with a Words to Know box of deficit terms. Psycho Didi notes · p. 20 Lateralization and Localization Specific parts of the brain control specific functions. Who → what. Franz Gall and Johann Casper — studies of localization. Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga — the Split Brain Experiment : severing the corpus callosum leads to the binding problem . Karl Lashley — controlled lesioning; concept of equipotentiality : each area of the brain has an equal role in each function. Lateralization = functional dominance of one hemisphere over the other. Broca's area : expressive aphasia. (Left inferior frontal gyrus, areas 44 and 45: frontal lobe .) Wernicke's area : fluent aphasia. (Left posterior superior temporal gyrus, back of area 22: temporal lobe .) The diagram lists these two under lateralization because language is the textbook example of hemispheric dominance: speech is controlled by the left hemisphere in about 95% of right-handers and roughly 70% of left-handers. Paul Broca (1861) described a patient, Leborgne (nicknamed "Tan"), who understood speech but could say almost nothing. Carl Wernicke (1874) described patients who spoke fluently but made little sense and understood poorly. Don't confuse. Broca's aphasia = non-fluent , effortful, telegraphic speech with agrammatism; comprehension fairly good; the patient knows and is frustrated. Wernicke's aphasia = fluent but empty speech (word salad, made-up words, wrong words); comprehension poor; the patient is often unaware. Broca's area is in the frontal lobe, not the temporal lobe. Damage to the arcuate fasciculus that links the two areas gives conduction aphasia (cannot repeat what is heard). Lobes Occipital Cortical blindness — people confabulate because they can't see. Anton syndrome : lack of insight Scotoma Nystagmus Agnosia Colour agnosia Frontal Recent memory impairments Reduced concentration Behaviour disorder Reduction in new information learning Lack of inhibition Flat affect Contralateral plegia Paresis Dysfunctional executive functioning Decreased fluency of speech Apathy Parietal Tactile agnosia Loss of haptic memory Hemineglect / Contralateral / Unilateral (in extreme cases, person forgets half of his/her body) Anosognia : not aware of deficit (hemineglect) Apraxia : unable to remember motor sequence Decreased proprioception Balint's syndrome : simultagnosia, ocular apraxia, optic ataxia Visual ataxia Temporal Decreased auditory processing Amnesia Korsakoff syndrome : due to thiamine deficiency (irreversible) Association agnosia (inferior temporal pathway) Prosopagnosia (damage to fusiform gyrus – right) Wernicke's area : fluent aphasia (Wernicke's area is in the temporal lobe; Broca's area, which gives expressive aphasia, is in the frontal lobe: see Lateralization and Localization above) Hindbrain Cerebellum Tremors Nystagmus (involuntary eye movement) Balint's syndrome (listed here by the source, but see the note below) Can't adjust to sharpen movement accuracy skills (the standard term is dysmetria : over- or under-shooting a target, as seen in the finger-to-nose test) Tone silent: improper tone estimation Detection: finger rhythm tapping with metronome Heads up: in the diagram, "Balint's syndrome" and "can't adjust to sharpen movement accuracy skills" are two separate cerebellum bullets; the second is not a definition of the first. Also, Balint's syndrome is not a cerebellar disorder. Balint's syndrome (Rezső Bálint, 1909) comes from damage to both parietal (parieto-occipital) regions and has three parts: simultanagnosia (cannot see more than one object at a time), ocular apraxia (cannot shift gaze at will) and optic ataxia (misreaching for things seen). That is why the source also lists it under Parietal. The optic ataxia can look like cerebellar clumsiness, but the cerebellar signs proper are ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor (worse as the hand nears the target, unlike the resting tremor of Parkinson's), nystagmus and low muscle tone. ARAS / Pons / Medulla ARAS : unconsciousness; altered consciousness (delirium) Pons : coma Medulla : death Midbrain and Limbic System Basal Ganglia Parkinson's Chorea (resembles dancing) Hypokinetic Tics, Tourette's (1 vocal tic, 2 motor tics) Caudate and putamen damage: chorea and hyperkinesia Limbic System Lateral Hypothalamus : aphagia (lack hunger) Ventromedial hypothalamus : Hyperphagia (very hungry) Amygdala : Kluver-Bucy syndrome; Hypersexuality; Hyperorality Thalamus Altered states of consciousness Loss of perception Thalamus syndrome : pain in opposite side of the body Hypothalamus Anterior Hypothalamus : issues with parasympathetic nervous system; asexual behaviour; issues with temperature regulation Posterior Hypothalamus : problems with sympathetic nervous system; Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) Corpus Callosum Split brain syndrome Words to Know Term Meaning Agnosia Not knowing Ageusia Can't taste Anosmia Can't smell Aphasia Language loss Apraxia Loss of motor memory Ataxia Loss of motor coordination Paralysis Complete loss of function Paresis Reduction in muscle strength Adipsia Lack of thirst Aphagia Lack of hunger Paraphegia Loss of function below stomach Agrammatism Not being able to use grammar 12 · Neurotransmitters Neurotransmitters. A table of six neurotransmitters giving their synthesis site or receptors, functions, agonists, antagonists, disorders and a historical note. Psycho Didi notes · p. 23 Name Synthesis / Receptors Functions Agonist Antagonist Disorders Misc. Acetylcholine Cholinergic pathways. Receptors: neuromuscular junction Stimulating muscles; communication between sensory and motor neurons; attention, arousal, sleep, memory Muscarine; Nicotine (low); Sarin Nicotine (high); Scopolamine; Bungarotoxin; Curare; Botulinum toxin; Hemicholinium Alzheimer's dementia Otto Loewi, 1921: discovered the role of acetylcholine as an endogenous neurotransmitter Norepinephrine Locus coeruleus (pons) Fight or flight (Walter Cannon); sympathetic activation; learning, memory, sleep, emotion Stimulants Clonidine (Catapres); Prazosin (Minipress); Terazosin Excess: anxiety. Low: depression — Dopamine Substantia Nigra (Tegmentum) (D2 receptors) Pleasure; motor movement Heroine; Alcohol; Opium; Nicotine; Amphetamine Chlorpromazine Excess: positive symptoms of schizophrenia. Low: Parkinson's — Serotonin Raphe Nuclei (pons) Controls aggression; mood stability; memory, learning, sleep; present in enteric nervous system SSRIs; MAOIs Ondansetron; Granisetron; Dolasetron; Palonosetron Low: depression — GABA Throughout CNS (enzyme: glutamate-decarboxylase) Inhibitory functions Benzodiazepines; Barbiturates Bicuculline; Picrotoxin Low: anxiety, tics, Tourette's — Glutamate NMDA; AMPA; Kainate LTP, memory Ibotenic, Kainic acid Memantine; Riluzole Excess: excitotoxicity, Huntington's. Low: Alzheimer's — Who → what. Otto Loewi (1921) discovered the role of acetylcholine as an endogenous neurotransmitter. Serotonin trap. MAOIs (monoamine oxidase inhibitors) are serotonin agonists , not antagonists, as the diagram shows. They block the enzyme monoamine oxidase, which breaks down serotonin (and noradrenaline and dopamine), so more serotonin stays in the synapse. SSRIs raise serotonin too, by blocking its reuptake. Both are indirect agonists, which is why both are antidepressants (and why combining them risks serotonin syndrome). The "-setrons" (ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, palonosetron) are the true antagonists here: they block 5-HT3 receptors and are used to stop nausea and vomiting, e.g. during chemotherapy. In both drug names, "inhibitor" refers to blocking an enzyme or a reuptake pump, not the serotonin receptor. 13 · Hormones & the Endocrine Glands Site → Hormone → Function Hormones: site, hormone and function. A table listing each hormone-producing site with its hormones and their functions, each site shown with a small organ icon. Psycho Didi notes · p. 21 Site Hormone Function Hypothalamus Releasing Hormone Promote release from pituitary Anterior Pituitary TSH; LH; FSH; ACTH; Prolactin; Growth Hormone (GH) Thyroid; ovulation; ovum maturation; steroid; milk production; body growth Posterior Pituitary Vasopressin; Oxytocin Increases BP, reduces urine volume; cervical contraction, milk production, sexual experience Penial (pineal) gland Melatonin Regulate sleep, circadian rhythm, etc. Testis Testosterone Development and maintenance of male sex characteristics Ovaries Oestrogen; Progesterone Reproductive and sexual development of women; supports menstruation and maintaining a pregnancy Pancreas Insulin; Glucagon Moving glucose from the blood into cells; breaks glycogen Kidney Renin Regulate blood pressure and sodium and potassium levels Adrenal Medulla Epinephrine; Norepinephrine Helps the body respond to stressful situations; increases alertness, arousal and attention Adrenal Cortex Aldosterone; Cortisol Reduces salt in urine; increases blood sugar Fat cells Leptin Fat set point Types of Hormones Types of hormones. Hormones grouped by structure into steroid and peptide types and by function into homeostatic, gonadal and glucocorticoid hormones, with examples of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 21 Based on structure: Steroid : synthesized from fat — e.g. testosterone, cortisol Peptide hormone : synthesized by DNA like protein — e.g. insulin, endorphin, growth hormone Based on function: Homeostatic hormones — Aldosterone, renin, ADH Gonadal hormones Glucocorticoids — immunosuppression (dementia, PTSD) Endocrine Glands: Gland → Hormone → Disease → Function Endocrine glands. A table of six endocrine glands giving each gland's hormones, related diseases and functions, with an organ illustration beside each gland. Psycho Didi notes · p. 22 Gland Hormone Disease Function Adrenal Cortex Aldosterone; Glucocorticoids Low: Addison's; High: Cushing's disease Regulates sodium and water balance in the body; mediates the body's response to stress Adrenal Medulla Epinephrine; Norepinephrine (catecholamines) Anxiety, depression, headaches, sleeping problems; low blood sugar (hypoglycemia); changes in blood pressure, heart rate Flight or Fight Thyroid Tetraiodothyronine T4; Triiodothyronine T3; Thyroxine PCOD; Hyperthyroidism; Hypothyroidism; Cretinism; Grave's disease; Goitre Metabolism, heart rate, and body temperature Pancreas Insulin (Beta cells); Glucagon (Alpha cells) Diabetes mellitus; glucagonoma Distributes glucose; turns glycogen to glucose Hypothalamus Releasing hormones Hypothalamic obesity; Diabetes insipidus; Cushing's disease; Prolactinoma; Hypothalamic hypothyroidism; Non-24-hour sleep-wake syndrome; Hypopituitarism; Oxytocin deficiency Controlling body temperature, hunger, and sleep Pituitary Anterior: TSH, LH, FSH, ACTH, Prolactin, Growth Hormone (GH). Posterior: vasopressin, oxytocin Acromegaly; Cushing's Syndrome; Diabetes Insipidus; Empty Sella Syndrome; Hypopituitarism Produces and releases hormones that control many bodily functions, including growth, metabolism, reproduction, and more 14 · Glial Cells Glial cells. A panel listing the CNS glial cells (astrocytes, ependymal cells, oligodendrocytes, microglia) and the PNS glial cells (satellite and Schwann cells) with what each one does. Psycho Didi notes · p. 24 CNS glial cells Astrocytes : maintain the structure of the cell; control concentration of neurotransmitters; maintain blood brain barrier Ependymal cells : produce CSF Oligodendrocytes : myelinate neurons of the CNS Microglia : brain's immune cell; soldiers of the nervous system PNS glial cells Satellite cells : similar function to astrocytes, but in the PNS Schwann cells : myelinate neurons of the PNS Don't confuse. Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS neurons; Schwann cells myelinate PNS neurons. Stress axes HPA axis and SAM pathway. Two arrow chains showing the HPA axis from CRF to insulin resistance and the SAM pathway from the hypothalamus to epinephrine and norepinephrine. Psycho Didi notes · p. 24 HPA Axis CRF → Anterior Pituitary ACTH → Adrenal cortex Cortisol → metabolism increase; insulin resistance SAM pathway Hypothalamus → SNS → Adrenal Medulla → Epinephrine and Norepinephrine 15 · Peripheral Nervous System & Cranial Nerves Peripheral nervous system. A page map covering glial cells, the 12 cranial nerves, spinal nerve counts, key PNS facts, the HPA axis and SAM pathway, and the sympathetic versus parasympathetic nervous systems. Psycho Didi notes · p. 24 The Peripheral Nervous System is anything apart from the brain and spinal cord. Who → what. Charles Sherrington — if the spinal cord detaches from the brain, it will still function. Bell-Magendie Law — all dorsal connections are sensory and ventral connections are motor. PNS nerves can reform after damage.
