Cranial Nerves (12) # Nerve Function 1 Olfactory Smell 2 Optic Vision 3 Oculomotor Eye movement 4 Trochlear Eye movement 5 Trigeminal Masticatory movement 6 Abducens Eye movement 7 Facial Facial movement 8 Auditory vestibular Hearing 9 Glossopharyngeal Tongue and pharynx 10 Vagus Heart 11 Accessory Neck muscles 12 Hypoglossal Tongue Spinal Nerves Region Number Cervical 8 Thoracic 12 Lumbar 5 Sacral 5 Coccygeal 1 16 · The Autonomic Nervous System Feature Sympathetic NS Parasympathetic NS Nerves Thoracic and Lumbar nerves (thoracolumbar outflow) Cranial and Sacral nerves (craniosacral outflow: cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and sacral S2 to S4) System "Flight or Fight" system "Rest and Digest" system Overall Spends energy for action Conserves energy: brain activity decreases; metabolic activity decreases Pupils Pupils dilate Pupils constrict Saliva Inhibits saliva (dry mouth) Stimulates flow of saliva Tear glands Tear ducts inhibited Stimulates tears Heart Increased heart rate Slows heartbeat Blood vessels Constrict blood vessels (skin and gut), sending blood to the muscles Little or no effect on most vessels Lungs Increased respiration; bronchi dilate (widen) Constricts bronchi Digestion Inhibits digestion Stimulates digestion Liver Stimulates glucose release Slight glycogen synthesis (glucose is stored) Adrenal medulla Stimulates release of adrenaline and noradrenaline No effect Sweat glands / GSR (Galvanic Skin Response) More sweating, so GSR increases (decreased skin resistance) GSR decreases (skin resistance increases). Sweat glands are driven by the sympathetic system, so this is mainly the sympathetic drive switching off Bladder Relaxes the bladder wall and tightens the sphincter, so urine is held (the source writes "constricts bladder") Contracts bladder, so it empties Sexual response Orgasm and ejaculation Arousal (erection) Transmitter at the organ Mostly noradrenaline (acetylcholine at sweat glands) Acetylcholine Heads up: the diagram gives the two systems as two separate lists, not matched pairs, so do not read across them line by line. In particular, "metabolic activity decreases" and "brain activity decreases" are general parasympathetic effects; they are not the opposite of "inhibits digestion" (that opposite is stimulates digestion ). The table above lines each organ up with the standard textbook effect on each side. Easy-to-misread pair: the source's "constricts bladder" (sympathetic) and "contracts bladder" (parasympathetic). Standard texts say the sympathetic system relaxes the bladder and holds urine, and the parasympathetic system contracts it to empty it. Don't confuse. Sympathetic = Thoracic and Lumbar nerves, "fight or flight (Walter Cannon)," pupils dilate, heart rate up, digestion inhibited, GSR increases. Parasympathetic = Cranial and Sacral nerves, "rest and digest," slows heartbeat, stimulates saliva, GSR decreases. Mechanism. In sympathetic arousal, galvanic skin response increases because sweat gland activity rises, which decreases skin resistance . Under parasympathetic dominance, GSR decreases as skin resistance increases.

title: Psychopathology
text: Psychopathology — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Psychopathology Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Biggest chapter (PDF pp. 25–55) DSM-5-TR (2022) & ICD-11 (2022) based Full disorder coverage, every duration cutoff MSE + all diagnostic groups + named syndromes Psychopharmacology appendix What this covers. The complete psychopathology core: the 4 D's of abnormality and the history of clinical psychology; the six approaches to treatment; case history and the full Mental Status Examination (MSE); the DSM and ICD classification systems and how they differ; then every major diagnostic group in DSM-5 order — neurodevelopmental, anxiety, OCD-related, depressive (mood), bipolar/mania, schizophrenia spectrum, trauma/stressor-related, dissociative, somatic, feeding/eating, sleep-wake, sexual/gender/paraphilic, personality, substance-related, and neurocognitive disorders — plus named eponymous syndromes, culture-specific syndromes, and a psychopharmacology reference. Original diagrams. 55 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 26 to 55) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Foundations & Approaches · 2 · Case History & MSE · 3 · DSM & ICD Classification · 4 · Neurodevelopmental Disorders · 5 · Anxiety Disorders · 6 · OCD & Related Disorders · 7 · Depressive (Mood) Disorders · 8 · Bipolar & Related Disorders · 9 · Schizophrenia Spectrum & Psychotic Disorders · 10 · Trauma & Stressor-Related Disorders · 11 · Dissociative Disorders · 12 · Somatic Symptom & Related Disorders · 13 · Feeding & Eating Disorders · 14 · Sleep-Wake Disorders · 15 · Sexual Dysfunctions, Gender Dysphoria & Paraphilias · 16 · Personality Disorders · 17 · Substance-Related & Addictive Disorders · 18 · Neurocognitive Disorders · 19 · Named / Eponymous Syndromes · 20 · Culture-Specific Syndromes · 21 · Psychopharmacology Reference 1 · Foundations & Approaches to Psychopathology Different Terms Introduction to psychopathology. Boxes listing the 4 D's of abnormality, early history of humane treatment, and definitions of abnormal, psychopathology and clinical psychology. Psycho Didi notes · p. 26 Abnormal: outlining atypicality. Abnormality depends on the intensity and frequency of behaviour. Psychopathology: part of abnormality — the medical angle of the abnormal (involves neuroimaging, aetiology, diagnosis, prognosis). Clinical Psychology: application of psychological principles in the treatment of mental disorders. The 4 D's of Abnormality: Deviance (social and statistical), Distress (causing unhappiness), Dysfunction (unable to show adaptive behaviour), Danger (to oneself and others). History of Clinical Psychology History of clinical psychology. A box noting the founding of the APA, Lightner Witmer's role, and the 1952 start of the DSM and ICD-6. Psycho Didi notes · p. 26 Historically the mentally ill were tied, chained and kept in inhumane conditions. 1826 — Philippe Pinel introduced moral therapy . 1802–1887 — Dorothea Dix advocated for humane treatment. APA founded 1892 ; first president G. Stanley Hall . Lightner Witmer — founder of clinical psychology; opened the first clinic. DSM introduced in 1952 ; ICD-6 in 1952 . Current diagnosis is more spectrum-oriented. Named figures. Pinel (moral therapy), Dorothea Dix (humane treatment advocacy), G. Stanley Hall (first APA president), Lightner Witmer (founder of clinical psychology, first clinic). The Six Approaches (with pros & cons) Approaches to psychopathology. A chart linking each approach's view of abnormality to its therapies and to its pros and cons. Psycho Didi notes · p. 26 Approach View of abnormality Methods Pros Cons Biological Organic problems, biochemical imbalances Drugs, ECT, surgery Effective for those who don't respond to other treatments Side effects; neglects non-biological problems Humanistic Failure to strive towards one's potential / being out of touch with feelings Client-centred, Gestalt, Existential Recognizes positive human goals, values and needs Unsupportive; limited research Behavioural Reinforcement history, environment Desensitization, aversion, operant conditioning (B. F. Skinner), token economy, modelling, social skills training Research supports effectiveness Not long-lasting; neglects cognitive processes Psychodynamic Internal / unconscious conflicts Free association, catharsis, analysis of resistance / transference / dreams First major alternative to biological treatment; abnormal function rooted in same processes as normal function Depends on therapist's subjective interpretation Cognitive Irrational / dysfunctional thoughts REBT, CBT Considerable research support Dysfunctional thinking may not cause abnormal functioning Sociocultural Dysfunctional society — — — 2 · Case History & Mental Status Examination Case History Case history and mental status examination. A one-page overview of case history taking, from personal information and history of present illness to past, family, personal and treatment history and physical examination. Psycho Didi notes · p. 27 Four assessment techniques are used: Observation, Conversation, Exploration, Testing . Personal information: name, father's/husband's name; sociodemographic profile (age, sex, education, occupation, socio-economic status, marital status, religion, residence, mother tongue, address); source of referral; type of admission; identification marks. Informant reliability — the 5 C's (SIMS): Contact (between patient and informant), Closeness of relationship, Continuity of the account, Consistency of the verbatim, Corroborativeness between sources. History of Present Illness — the factors The history of present illness opens with three parts, in this order: the patient's report of his illness in his own words; the informant's report (a relative or friend, whose reliability is judged by the 5 C's above); and the chief complaints , the main problems that brought the patient, each written with its duration and in the order they appeared, ideally in the patient's or informant's own words (e.g. "not sleeping, 2 months; hearing voices, 3 weeks"). The illness is then explored through the factors below and its onset, course and progress. Factor Definition Predisposing Factors operating from early life that determine vulnerability to develop a disorder Precipitating Events that occur shortly before the onset of a disorder Perpetuating Factors due to which the disorder is maintained or aggravated Limiting Factors which limit the illness from extensive progress Modifying Factors which modify the natural or expected course of the illness Mode of onset: abrupt, acute, insidious. Course of illness: continuous, episodic, fluctuating. Progress of illness: improving, deteriorating, static. Compliance: the extent to which the patient's behaviour (taking medications, following diets, other lifestyle changes) coincides with medical recommendations. Also covered: treatment history, past history (medical & psychiatric), family history (genogram, consanguinity), personal history (birth & early development, childhood disorders, home atmosphere, scholastic/extracurricular, occupational, menstrual, sexual & marital, forensic), premorbid personality (individualized styles of dealing with the environment characteristic of a person prior to onset), and physical examination (by physician). What each of these sections records, as checklists: Section What is recorded Treatment history Treatment obtained in the present episode. If help was sought, note: when the first contact was; voluntary or involuntary treatment; who saw the patient and for how long ; nature and modality of treatment (e.g. medicines, ECT, psychotherapy); medication (names and doses); length of treatment; reason for discontinuing treatment or for poor compliance (e.g. side effects, cost, no relief, no insight); any day treatment or hospitalization . Past history Past medical history (illnesses such as epilepsy, head injury or thyroid disease, which can themselves cause psychiatric symptoms); past psychiatric history (earlier episodes and how they were treated); clinical course indicators (the notes list this without detail: it means the pattern of the earlier episodes, how each began, how long it lasted and whether recovery was full, which tells you whether the illness is episodic or continuous). Family history Parents and siblings (age, health, personality, any mental illness); consanguinity (marriage between blood relatives, which raises genetic loading); relationships amongst family members (closeness, conflict); a genogram (a family-tree diagram, usually of three generations, marking who had mental illness, suicide or substance use). Personal history Birth and early development (milestones); presence of childhood disorders; home atmosphere in childhood and adolescence; scholastic and extracurricular activities; vocational/occupational history; menstrual history; sexual and marital history; forensic history (arrests, legal cases); general pattern of living (the patient's usual daily routine: work, sleep, food, habits such as tobacco or alcohol, leisure and social life). Physical examination (done by a physician) General survey (build, nourishment, pulse, blood pressure); cardiovascular system ; respiratory system ; abdomen ; central nervous system ; results of investigations , if any are available (e.g. blood tests, thyroid tests, EEG, brain scans); physical findings or diagnosis . Mental Status Examination (MSE) General appearance and behaviour. A panel of MSE parameters covering general appearance, dress, posture, eye contact, estimate of age, body build, facial expression and touch with surroundings, with the disorders each finding suggests. Psycho Didi notes · p. 28 Attitude towards the examiner. Definitions of frank, defensive, cooperative, seductive, hostile, guarded, attentive and evasive attitudes, with the disorders linked to each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 28 Rapport and motor behaviour. Six strategies and three types of rapport, followed by a grid of motor behaviour signs with their definitions and associated disorders. Psycho Didi notes · p. 29 Speech. A panel of speech parameters such as intensity, pitch, quality, reaction time, speed, ease, productivity, deviation and manner of relating, with example disorders. Psycho Didi notes · p. 30 Cognitive functions. Definitions of orientation, attention, abstract ability, intelligence, concentration and memory, with the conditions in which each is disturbed. Psycho Didi notes · p. 31 Mood and affect. Definitions of mood and affect and the dimensions of affect: quality, mobility, intensity, reactivity, communicability, appropriateness and diurnal variation. Psycho Didi notes · p. 31 Thought. A panel describing disturbances of thought under stream, form, possession and content, with definitions and linked conditions. Psycho Didi notes · p. 32 Perception. Sensory distortions (changes in intensity, quality and spatial form) and sensory deception (hallucinations in each sense). Psycho Didi notes · p. 33 Other psychotic phenomena. Definitions of somatic passivity and the made phenomena: made act, made affect and made impulse. Psycho Didi notes · p. 33 Judgement. A definition of judgement and its three types: social, personal and test judgement. Psycho Didi notes · p. 33 Insight. Intellectual versus true emotional insight and the six grades of the insight rating scale. Psycho Didi notes · p. 33 The part of clinical assessment describing the sum total of the examiner's observations and impressions of a psychiatric patient at the time of interview. General Appearance & Behaviour General appearance and behaviour is the evaluation of the patient's manner of presentation at the time of the interview: the external attributes (grooming, dress, posture, eye contact, face, build) the examiner can note before asking a single question. Parameter Finding & associations Eye contact Assesses rapport, truthfulness, insight, concentration. Partial (fleeting); Absent — complete loss (Paranoid Schizophrenia, Acute delusional disorder). Depression → lowered eyes; Anxiety → shifting gaze. Dress Gives an impression of the patient's cultural background and economic position. Appropriate (normal); Shabby (Dementia, Substance abuse); Inappropriate , e.g. rain hood on a dry day (Mania, Histrionic PD). Facial expression Depression → corners of mouth turned down, vertical furrows on brow. Anxiety → horizontal forehead creases, widened palpebral fissures, dilated pupils. May be fixed/wooden (parkinsonian drug side effects) or reflect thyrotoxicosis. Posture Depression → hunched shoulders, gaze downward. Anxiety → edge of chair, gripping sides. Agitated depression → tremulous, picking at fingernails. Mania → restlessness. Catatonia → odd postures. Estimate of age Younger than stated → Histrionic PD; Older than stated → Depression or Chronic Schizophrenia. General appearance Kempt (normal, OCPD); Overtly made up (mania/hypomania, histrionic/narcissistic PD, some schizophrenia); Unkempt/untidy (organic psychosis, dementia, substance abuse, severe depression, schizophrenia); Sickly ; Perplexed . Sickly = looks ill, or complete neglect of health (substance abuse, severe and long-standing dementia). Perplexed = a confusional state in which the patient looks puzzled and is unable to decide on a task or a solution. Touch with surroundings The patient's perception of himself in relation to his surroundings. Present (oriented; normal); Partial (some aspect of the surroundings, or their significance, is lost); Absent (cannot orient himself and behaves in a way inappropriate to the situation), seen in dementia and in substance abuse (intoxicated state). Body-build typologies. Ernst Kretschmer: Pyknics (stocky/rounded), Leptosomes (long/linear), Athletics (broad-shouldered/muscular). William Sheldon's somatotypes: Endomorph (round, fat abdomen), Mesomorph (cubical head, muscular), Ectomorph (thin, receding chin, spindly limbs). Attitude towards the examiner Frank and Cooperative / Attentive (normal). Defensive & Guarded (Paranoid Schizophrenia, Delusional disorder). Evasive (Organic psychoses, Substance abuse). Hostile (Paranoid Schizophrenia, Antisocial PD). Seductive . Attitude is defined as a "mental and neural state of readiness" (Gordon Allport's 1935 definition): here, how the patient is set to respond to the examiner. Attitude What it looks like Seen in Frank Talks openly about all his problems and deficiencies without guilt or embarrassment Normal Cooperative Helps the examiner conduct the interview smoothly (answers questions, follows requests) Normal Attentive Pays attention to the interviewer Normal Defensive Turns the examiner's attention away from his own deficiencies, or from anything that might make him feel guilty or embarrassed Paranoid schizophrenia, delusional disorder Guarded Restricts information, weighing what to reveal according to his own ideas of what matters Paranoid schizophrenia, delusional disorder Evasive Tries to escape a line of questioning and shifts topics Organic psychoses, substance abuse Hostile Covert aggression that creates strong negative feelings or anger in the examiner, or open anger shown towards the examiner Paranoid schizophrenia, antisocial PD Seductive Flirtatious, charming or sexually provocative behaviour aimed at winning the examiner over Histrionic PD ("inappropriately sexually seductive or provocative behaviour" is a DSM-5-TR criterion), mania Heads up: the diagram's Seductive box repeats the Attentive wording ("pays attention to the interviewer, a normal response"). Seductive is not a normal response; it is the flirtatious or provocative attitude described in the table. Rapport A bidirectional empathetic relationship. Easily established — normal persons, Mania; Established with difficulty — Schizophrenia, Dementia, Depression; Not possible — Paranoid Schizophrenia, Dementia, Depression. Six strategies for building rapport (from Ekkehard and Sieglinde Othmer's The Clinical Interview Using DSM ): Put the patient and yourself at ease : greet, introduce yourself, give a comfortable setting. Find the patient's pain and express compassion : notice what hurts him and acknowledge it ("that must have been very hard"). Evaluate the patient's insight and become an ally : see how far he accepts he is ill, and side with his goals. Show expertise : show that you know this kind of problem. Establish authority as a physician or therapist, so he trusts your advice. Balance the roles of empathic listener, expert and authority, shifting between them as the interview needs. Motor Behaviour (selected signs) Motor behaviour denotes both the quantitative aspects of a person's motor behaviour and level of activity (how much he moves: retardation vs hyperactivity) and its qualitative aspects (what kind of movement: e.g. mannerisms, stereotypies, tics). Sign Description / association Retardation Slowness of initiation/execution — Depression Hyperactivity Increased motor activity, often with over-talkativeness Mannerisms Unusual repeated goal-directed action (e.g. odd hand movements when shaking hands) Stereotypy Repetitive, non-goal-directed action carried out uniformly Grimace Non-goal-directed facial expression; e.g. Schnauzkrampf (snout spasm) — Schizophrenia Tics Sudden involuntary twitchings — Gilles de la Tourette syndrome (SIMS) Waxy flexibility Person maintains the body position into which they are placed Negativism Verbal/non-verbal opposition to suggestion — catatonic schizophrenia Echolalia Repeating another's words — catatonic schizophrenia Echopraxia Repetition by imitation of another's movements Ambivalence Co-existence of two opposing impulses toward the same thing — Schizophrenia, borderline state, OCD Automatic obedience Undue compliance with instructions — catatonia Waxy flexibility, odd posturing, rigidity, self-injury Catatonia; self-injurious behaviour → Borderline PD Also noted: preoccupied, restless, awkward (apraxia, MR), destructive (catatonic/manic excitement), silly smiling (Mania, Hebephrenia), aggressive, perseveration, dyskinesia, dystonia, chorea, athetosis, hallucinatory behaviour, gestures, touching the examiner. These other signs, defined: Sign Definition Seen in Restless Purposeless movement of the limbs: fiddling, stretching, shifting, cannot sit still, standing up and sitting down again Anxiety, agitated depression, mania. Also akathisia , an antipsychotic side effect felt as an inner urge to keep moving Preoccupied Excessively focused on one task or thought, neglecting or avoiding everything else Depression, paranoid schizophrenia Awkward Clumsy movements; little skill in handling the objects and events around him Apraxia, mental retardation (intellectual disability) Destructive Breaking, throwing or disrupting items nearby Catatonic excitement, manic excitement Rigidity Holds a rigid posture against all attempts to move him Catatonia (the notes also list mania and depression, where catatonic features can occur) Aggressive Hurting others either as an end in itself ( hostile aggression , e.g. hitting someone in rage) or as a means to some other goal ( instrumental aggression , e.g. hitting someone to snatch his phone) Delirium, frontal lobe syndrome, mania, paranoid schizophrenia Perseveration (motor) Senseless repetition of a goal-directed action that has already served its purpose, e.g. keeps drawing the circle he was asked to draw after being asked to draw a square Organic brain disorders (especially frontal lobe damage), dementia Dystonia Uncontrolled muscle spasms causing involuntary twisting movements or fixed postures of the eyelids, face, jaw, neck, hands and other parts Acute dystonia is an early antipsychotic side effect (e.g. stiff twisted neck, eyes rolling up) Dyskinesia Difficulty in performing voluntary movements; in practice the term is used for abnormal involuntary movements Tardive dyskinesia : lip-smacking, chewing and tongue movements after long-term antipsychotic use Chorea Random, involuntary, quick, jerky, purposeless movements Huntington's disease Athetosis Slow, twisting, writhing involuntary movements, especially of the hands, that produce strange postures Basal ganglia disorders Odd posturing Voluntary assumption of an inappropriate or bizarre posture, held for at least a minute (the notes' cut-off); the position may be taken up by the patient or imposed by the examiner Catatonia Hallucinatory behaviour Behaviour suggesting active hallucinations: postures of listening, looking intently at one point, talking or laughing in response to imaginary voices Psychoses (e.g. schizophrenia), delirium Gestures Conveying information by movements of the hands, arms or body Excessive in mania, hypomania Touching the examiner Touching the examiner in a way different from a formal greeting The notes give: touching the examiner's feet (depression); kicking or caressing (histrionic patient) Trap: perseveration vs stereotypy vs mannerism. A mannerism is an odd way of doing a normal goal-directed act (odd hand movement while shaking hands). A stereotypy is never goal-directed (rocking the same way for hours). Perseveration is a goal-directed act that keeps going after its goal is over, and points to organic brain disease. Also: in Indian culture touching an elder's feet is a normal greeting, so judge "touching the examiner" against the patient's culture. Speech Intensity: excessively loud (Mania, Hypomania), abnormally soft (vocal cord palsy, Depression, Paranoid Schizophrenia). Pitch: monotonous (parietal lobe damage, chronic schizophrenia, depression). Reaction time: increased (hypothyroidism, depression, schizophrenia), decreased (Mania). Speed: very slow (depression, dementia, hypothyroidism); rapid with prolixity/flight of ideas (mania, hypomania, hyperthyroidism). Pressure of speech — increased, accelerated, hard to interrupt (Mania, Schizophrenia, cognitive disorders). Ease: hesitant (head injury, anxiety), mutism (stupor, dementia), slurring (cerebellar damage), stuttering/stammering (severe anxiety, schizophrenia), whispering (pseudobulbar palsy), muttering (schizophrenia, dementia). Deviations: rhyming/punning (mania), talking past the point ( Ganser's syndrome , schizophrenia), clang association (schizophrenia, mania), stereotypy (catatonic schizophrenia), perseveration. Quality (how the sound seems to the listener's ears): soft , spoken politely, in low volume and slowly (OCPD, anxious avoidant PD); hoarse , spoken forcefully in a husky tone (mania, after shouting for long periods; also some normal individuals). Relevance: whether the answer is relevant to the question asked (relevant / irrelevant). Goal direction: whether speech reaches its goal and answers what the examiner asked. Coherence: how understandable the speech is (coherent / incoherent); incoherent speech is seen in schizophrenia, catatonic excitement and organic psychoses. Prosody: the use of pitch, loudness, tempo and rhythm to convey the structure and meaning of an utterance (e.g. "you're going?" as a question vs "you're going." as a statement). Flat, monotonous prosody fits the pitch findings above. Productivity (overall amount of speech: adequate / less / more): increased, overabundant in hypomania and mania; decreased, scant in negative schizophrenia, depression and catatonia. Speaking only when questioned (under ease of speech): no spontaneous speech, words used very economically, only answering what is asked. Perseveration (in speech): pathological repetition of the same response to different stimuli , e.g. asked his name, then his age, then where he lives, he answers "Ramesh" each time (cognitive disorders, schizophrenia and other mental disorders). Manner of relating is the way the patient speaks with and interacts with the examiner: Manner Seen in (as given in the notes) Excessively formal OCPD, antisocial PD, hypomania Tensed up Anxious trait/state, avoidant PD Inappropriately familiar (over-friendly, crosses the doctor-patient boundary) Histrionic PD, antisocial PD, hypomania Disinterested Schizophrenia, schizoid PD, severe depressive disorder Cognitive Functions Orientation (time, place, person), attention, concentration, memory (immediate / recent / remote), abstract ability, intelligence (comprehension, general information, vocabulary, calculation). Function Definition and how it is tested Disturbed in Orientation A state of awareness of oneself and one's surroundings in terms of time, place and person ("What is today's date? Where are you? Who is this?") Delirium (classic), dementia; the notes also list schizophrenia and severe depression Attention Directing the mind to a stimulus. Disturbance shows as easy distractibility, or difficulty in finishing tasks or concentrating on work Delirium (core feature), mania (distractibility), anxiety Concentration The ability to maintain attention on specific stimuli over an extended period; tested by serial 7s (100 minus 7, minus 7...) or naming the months backwards Depression, anxiety, delirium Memory Encoding, storage and retrieval of what was learned earlier. Immediate (repeat digits at once), recent (what he ate today, events of the past few days), remote (events of years ago, e.g. year of marriage) Dementia, Korsakoff's, head injury Abstract ability The ability to deal with concepts; tested by proverb meanings and similarities ("how are an apple and a banana alike?") Schizophrenia, dementia, past head injury Intelligence The ability to think logically, act rationally and deal effectively with the environment (David Wechsler's definition). Components: comprehension , general information , vocabulary , calculation Comprehension: inattentive states, dementia. General information: mental retardation (ID), dementia. Vocabulary: ID, autism, dementia Trap: orientation. Disorientation is the hallmark of organic states (delirium, dementia). In schizophrenia the sensorium is usually clear and the patient is oriented; the notes' listing of schizophrenia and severe depression applies only to some cases. In an MCQ, disorientation means think organic. Also, in dementia recent memory is lost before remote memory (Ribot's law: the newest memories go first). Thinking style Definition & association Concrete thinking Thinking bound to actual things/events & immediate experience — Schizophrenia, young children Functional thinking Abstraction relating only to functional aspects — Schizophrenia, MR Over-abstraction Excessive manifestation of a concept beyond relevance — Schizophrenia, philosophical preoccupations Mood & Affect Mood = persistent, sustained emotion colouring perception of the world. Affect = present emotional responsiveness inferred from expression. Quality: dysphoric, anxious, irritable, depressed, elevated, euphoric, elated, exalted, ecstatic, euthymic. Intensity: shallow (lack of depth), blunted (greatly diminished, uniform voice), flat (no affect displayed). Appropriateness: Paramimia — lack of unity between modes of emotional expression; Parathymia — expression opposite to what is expected (e.g. laughing at tragic news). Diurnal variation: worse in morning (endogenous depression, headache), worse in evening (anxiety, delirium/ sundowning ), worse at night (uremia). How quality is assessed: on two criteria. Subjective evaluation: the patient's own answer to "How do you feel?". Objective evaluation: what the interviewer observes (face, tears, voice). Record both, since they can differ (e.g. says "I'm fine" while tearful). Mobility: how easily and how far the affect shifts during the interview. Reduced (fixed or constricted, stuck in one emotion, e.g. depression) or increased ( labile , rapid shifts with little cause, e.g. mania, organic brain disease). Reactivity: the extent to which affect changes in response to environmental stimuli (e.g. brightens when his child visits). Lost in melancholic depression (DSM-5-TR: lack of reactivity to usually pleasurable stimuli); kept in atypical depression, where mood reactivity is the defining feature. Communicability: the ability of the patient's expressed affect to communicate his emotional response to another person, so the examiner can "feel with" him. Poor in schizophrenia: H. C. Rümke called the examiner's sense of no emotional contact the "praecox feeling" . Heads up: in the Mood & Affect diagram the Mobility box repeats the Intensity definitions (shallow, blunted, flat). Those belong to intensity; mobility is about how readily affect shifts, as above. Thought Aspect Key terms Stream Acceleration, pressured speech, flight of ideas (rapid, chance connections still understandable), prolixity (ordered flight, returns to task), retardation/bradyphrenia, poverty of speech (laconic), circumstantiality (reaches point via trivia), tangentiality (oblique, never reaches point), thought blocking (sudden arrest → blank) Form Negative type (loses ability to form concept) vs positive type (false concept by blending incongruous elements): loosening of associations, derailment, neologism, over-inclusion Possession Obsession , rumination , compulsion , thought alienation — insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting, thought echo Content Worry, phobias, impulse, somatic symptoms, religious preoccupations (OCD), magical thinking, depressive cognition (worthlessness/helplessness/hopelessness), suicidal/homicidal ideas, inflated self-esteem, delusion (a false firm belief) Form and possession terms, defined. Disturbance of form is a disorder in the logical connections between ideas; disturbance of possession is a loss of control, or of the sense of ownership, of one's thinking. Term Definition Loosening of associations Failure to communicate verbally adequately: unrelated, unconnected ideas shift from one subject to another. One of Eugen Bleuler's "4 A's" of schizophrenia Derailment The person's ideas slip off one track onto another that is completely unrelated or only obliquely related (Nancy Andreasen's term, used almost as a synonym for loosening) Neologism New words constructed by the patient, or ordinary words used in a special, private way Over-inclusion Widening of the boundaries of concepts, so things not closely connected are grouped together (described in schizophrenia by Norman Cameron) Obsession A persistent, recurrent idea, thought or impulse that cannot be eliminated from consciousness by logic or reason Rumination A train of thought, usually unproductive and prolonged, on one topic, experienced repeatedly but felt to be less intrusive than an obsession; it is linked to abnormal emotion (e.g. a depressed patient brooding over his failures) Compulsion Obsessional motor or mental acts : repeated behaviours (washing, checking) or mental acts (counting, praying) the person feels driven to perform, usually to reduce the anxiety of an obsession Thought alienation The patient experiences his thoughts as under the control of an outside agency , or feels others are participating in his thinking: insertion (thoughts put into his mind), withdrawal (thoughts taken out), broadcasting (thoughts known to others). These are Schneiderian first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia Trap: the notes list thought echo with thought alienation, and ICD-10's schizophrenia criterion (a) groups "thought echo, thought insertion or withdrawal, and thought broadcasting" together. Strictly, thought echo (hearing one's own thoughts spoken aloud) is an auditory hallucination, not alienation. Also: an obsession is resisted and felt as senseless; rumination is not resisted and fits the mood. Content terms, defined (elicited by listening to the content of the patient's speech): Term Definition and where seen Worry A subjective sense of tension or uneasiness Phobia Fear restricted to a specific object, situation or idea Impulse A sudden, spontaneous inclination or incitement to some usually unpremeditated action Somatic symptoms Bodily complaints, varied in anatomical location, usually not associated with any underlying physical pathology Antisocial urges Sudden, episodic urges or behaviours marked by aggressiveness, impulsiveness and rage, disregarding social rules and norms Philosophical ideas Preoccupation with philosophical issues; seen in normal individuals, mild depression, OCD and schizotypal PD Death wishes A passive wish to be dead ("I wish I would not wake up") without intent or plan; differs from suicidal ideas , which are active thoughts of killing oneself Preoccupation with precipitating factor Keeps returning to the event that triggered the illness (e.g. a job loss); seen in reactive depression Excessive daydreaming The notes link it to schizotypal PD. ICD-10 also lists "excessive preoccupation with fantasy and introspection" as a criterion of schizoid PD, so remember both Perception Perception is the conscious awareness of elements in the environment through the mental processing of sensory stimuli. Disturbances fall into two groups. Sensory distortion : a real object is perceived, but changed in intensity , quality or spatial form (e.g. a normal voice sounds painfully loud, or everything looks yellow). Sensory deception : a new perception arises that does not match the real stimulus, i.e. hallucinations (and illusions). Sensory distortion — intensity: hyperaesthesia, hyperacusis, hypoacusis. Quality: Xanthopsia (yellow), Chloropsia (green), Erythropsia (red/pink). Spatial form: Micropsia (smaller), Macropsia/megalopsia (larger), Porropsia (retreat into distance without size change). Sensory deception — Hallucination: perception without an adequate external stimulus (auditory, visual, olfactory, gustatory, tactile). Delusion vs Hallucination. A delusion is a false firm belief (a disorder of thought content ). A hallucination is a perception without an adequate external stimulus (a disorder of perception ). An illusion is a misperception of a real stimulus. Don't conflate them. Other psychotic phenomena. Somatic passivity — belief that outside influences play on the body. Made phenomenon — made act (actions under external control), made affect (feelings not one's own), made impulse (impulse admitted as one's own action but not one's own drive). Judgement & Insight Judgement: social, personal, test. Insight — degree of awareness/understanding of being ill (intellectual vs true emotional insight), rated on a 6-point scale: Insight — 6-point scale: Grade 1 complete denial → Grade 2 slight awareness but denying → Grade 3 attributed to external/physical factors → Grade 4 due to something unknown in self → Grade 5 intellectual insight → Grade 6 true emotional insight. Judgement is a complex mental process by which a person forms an opinion, makes a decision, or plans an action or response, after first analysing the issue and comparing the choices with acceptable social behaviour. Type What is assessed Example Social judgement The person's interaction with other members of society and with the interviewer A manic patient who hugs strangers or spends all his savings shows poor social judgement Personal judgement The person's own expectations, plans and attitudes (e.g. for the future) "What will you do after discharge?" A realistic plan shows intact personal judgement Test judgement The course of action the person would take in a socially difficult or disastrous situation, asked as a hypothetical question "What would you do if you found a stamped, addressed envelope on the road?" or "...if you smelled smoke in a crowded cinema?" Intellectual insight (grade 5) is the ability to comprehend the cause of the problem: the patient admits he is ill and that his symptoms come from his own irrational feelings, but does not apply this knowledge to change. True emotional insight (grade 6) is present when the patient's awareness of his own motives and deep feelings leads to a change in his personality or behaviour patterns. Trap: the difference between grades 5 and 6 is action. "I know my drinking is ruining my family" but still drinks = intellectual insight. Knowing it and acting on it (joins treatment, stops) = true emotional insight. 3 · Classification — DSM & ICD The DSM The DSM. "Eliminated" in ICD-11 What actually happened 1. Acute stress disorder ICD-10's acute stress reaction is no longer counted as a mental disorder; it moved to the chapter "Factors influencing health status or contact with health services" (code QE84), as a normal response to an extreme event 2. Gender incongruence ICD-10's gender identity disorders left the mental disorders chapter. The condition is renamed gender incongruence and placed in a new chapter, "Conditions related to sexual health", so it is no longer a mental disorder 3. Personality disorder categories The separate types (paranoid, schizoid, dissocial and so on) were dropped. ICD-11 has one personality disorder diagnosis rated by severity (mild, moderate, severe), with optional trait domains (negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, anankastia) and a borderline pattern specifier: a dimensional approach instead of categories Trap: these are three separate changes; gender incongruence was never "a personality disorder". Also, "eliminated" means removed from the mental disorders chapter: acute stress reaction and gender incongruence still exist in ICD-11, in other chapters. A flowchart of ADHD symptoms, differential diagnosis and treatment. Psycho Didi notes · p. 36 Earlier diagnosable only up to age 7, now up to age 12 ; stays into adulthood if untreated; many comorbidities. Inattention: distractible, loses interest, keeps shifting tasks, doesn't attend to detail, loses things. Hyperactivity: impulsive, can't wait, aggressive, can't wait for turn, squirms, talks excessively. Any 6 symptoms must be met; duration ≥ 6 months. Treatment: Ritalin, amphetamine, dextroamphetamine; behavioural modification, applied behavioural analysis, shaping, chaining, token economy, response cost; Modafinil; Clonidine, venlafaxine, bupropion, SNRI. DDx: oppositional defiant, conduct disorder, aggression, depression, substance use, ASPD; problems with frontal lobe & cerebellum; difficulty copying, rapid alternating movements, right-left discrimination. Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD / Pervasive Developmental Disorder) Autism spectrum disorder. A flowchart of ASD symptoms, differential diagnosis and treatment. Psycho Didi notes · p. 36 Chromosomes 2, 7, 4, 15, 19 involved. Impairment in social interaction (eye contact, social smile, attachment, expression, making friends, routine). Impairment in communication and language (delayed milestones, articulation difficulty, echolalia, verbigeration, saying "me" instead of "you"). Restrictive, repetitive, stereotyped behaviour, flapping, echopraxia; impaired theory of mind; high pain tolerance; biting/scratching/headbanging; isles of precocity (high skill in something). Psycho Didi notes · p. 36 Losing fine motor skills; head circumference decreases from 5–48 months; stereotyped movement; problems with walk/talk/eat/breathe; 75% seizures ; progressive; mostly in girls; microencephaly. A subtype of pervasive developmental disorder. Normal early development followed by partial/complete loss of speech, locomotion & hand-use skills with deceleration in head growth. Treatment symptomatic. Heller's Syndrome (Childhood Disintegrative Disorder, CDD) Heller's syndrome. The symptoms of Heller's syndrome. The symptoms of Asperger's syndrome. Psycho Didi notes · p. 37 Mild ASD; problems with social interaction; experience emotion but can't express; restrictive, repetitive, stereotyped behaviour. Tourette's: ≥ 2 motor and 1 vocal tic; knee-jerking responses; longer than 1 year. Vocal: barks, clicks, coughs, grunts. Coprolalia — swearing (bad-word) tics. Psycho Didi notes · p. 37 Language disorder: problems in spoken/written/sign language; expressive & receptive; vocabulary & grammar; speaks slower & less; academic issues; can co-exist with ADHD. Speech sound (phonological) disorder: substituting/omitting sounds (e.g. "ghaspetti" for "spaghetti"); diagnosed only in first language; 2–3% of preschool children; can coexist with other neurodevelopmental disorders (e.g. language disorder, ADHD, intellectual disability), so finding one should prompt a check for the others. General anxiety features, the features of neurosis, trait versus state anxiety, and motor, autonomic, cognitive, affective and other symptoms. Psycho Didi notes · p. 38 Anxiety disorders according to DSM 5. Notes on each DSM-5 anxiety disorder, from generalized anxiety disorder and phobias to selective mutism and unspecified anxiety disorder. Psycho Didi notes · p. 38 Neurosis — subjective distress; ego-dystonic; insight present; personality & behaviour preserved; absence of organicity; reaction to stress & adjustment; somatoform. Anxiety symptoms. Motor (tremors, restlessness, muscle twitch, fearful face); autonomic/visceral (palpitation, tachycardia, sweating, flushes, hyperventilation, chest constriction, mouth dryness, reduced micturition, mydriasis); cognitive (poor concentration, distractibility, hyperarousal, vigilance); affective (apprehension, fearfulness, inability to relax, irritability, feelings of doom); other (noise sensitivity, insomnia, increased startle response). Trait anxiety ("I often feel anxious") vs state anxiety ("I feel anxious now") — those with trait anxiety also have state anxiety. General features of anxiety (the notes' quick list): feelings of nervousness, sweating, tachycardia, restlessness, tremors, mydriasis (dilated pupils), and also diarrhoea , cold clammy skin (sweaty skin that feels cold because blood is diverted away from it) and hyperreflexia (brisk tendon reflexes). Most of these are signs of autonomic arousal, the body's "fight or flight" state. Trap: hyperthyroidism produces almost the same picture (tachycardia, tremor, sweating, diarrhoea, brisk reflexes), so a physical cause must be ruled out before diagnosing an anxiety disorder; this is why DSM-5-TR has "anxiety disorder due to another medical condition". Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) Most diagnosed anxiety disorder; free-floating anxiety; for 6 months or more ; constant low arousal of the sympathetic nervous system. DDx: OCD, PTSD, mood disorder, physical causes, realistic anxiety. Treatment: benzodiazepine, SSRI, barbiturates (old), CBT, relaxation, psychodynamic therapy. Social Anxiety Disorder Severe irrational fear of evaluation; dysfunction at work and relationships; ≥ 6 months ; sometimes only due to evaluation of performance. Specific Phobia Defence mechanism: displacement . Irrational, disproportional fear of certain animals, natural environment, situations, blood/injection, others. Fear out of proportion; insight present; inability to control fear; avoidance of the object. Agoraphobia Fear of being in a place where they can't get up and leave; fear of crowded/enclosed places. Treatment: clomipramine, venlafaxine, buspirone. Panic Disorder Feelings of impending doom; hippocampus and amygdala involved; periodic, discrete bouts of panic/terror in the absence of any real threat; feels like a heart attack; should be present for more than a month . Separation Anxiety Disorder Fear that something will happen to the attachment figure if away; can happen in adults; may have vomiting; ≥ 6 months in adults, ≥ 4 weeks in children . Selective Mutism Children remain silent except before close people; normal intelligence; family history of SAD; may develop SAD in adulthood; duration > 1 month ; treatment: social skills training. Other anxiety disorders Substance-induced anxiety disorder (from exposure/withdrawal to a medication); anxiety disorder due to another medical condition ; other specified anxiety disorder (clinician specifies reason for non-fulfilment); unspecified anxiety disorder (clinician does not specify). 6 · Obsessive-Compulsive & Related Disorders OCD related disorders according to DSM 5. Psycho Didi notes · p. 39 Young-adulthood onset; most common in males; family history. Obsessions: ego-dystonic, irrational, absurd, distressing, recognised as one's own idea. Compulsions: to neutralize the obsession; not realistic; irrational; insight present; subjective; may diminish the anxiety associated with the obsession. Major patterns: contamination, pathological doubt, intrusive thought, symmetry (tics). Aetiology. Dysfunction in fronto-striatal brain circuitry ( caudate ). Psycho Didi notes · p. 40 Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) Duration ≥ 2 weeks. Mnemonic SIGECAPS: S leep disturbance (REM latency, early-morning awakening); low I nterest; G uilt; E nergy deficit; reduced C oncentration; reduced A ppetite; P sychomotor agitation/retardation; S uicidal ideation. Specifiers/features: with psychotic features (schizoaffective); atypical features (hypersomnia, overeating); melancholic features (in old age); catatonic features. Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia) Symptoms persist for 2 years ; no suicidal ideation; no hospitalization; symptoms never absent for longer than 2 months. MDD vs Persistent Depressive Disorder. MDD = ≥ 2 weeks, may include suicidal ideation and hospitalization. Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) = ≥ 2 years, no suicidal ideation, no hospitalization, symptoms never absent > 2 months. Double depression = MDD superimposed on dysthymia (a poor-prognosis feature). Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (DMDD) For children and adolescents; a precursor to bipolar ; sudden anger, throwing fits, tantrums; persistent negative moods; sadness translated into complete outbursts. DDx: oppositional defiant disorder. Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) Mood shifts or other dysphoria in the week or two before the menstrual period. Prognosis, subtypes & aetiology Good prognosis Poor prognosis Acute onset; typical clinical features; severe depression; well-adjusted premorbid personality; good treatment response Comorbidity with personality disorder/alcohol abuse; double depression; chronic stress; unfavourable early environment; hypochondriacal features; poor drug compliance Endogenous Exogenous Absence of any precipitating life event Due to a precipitating life event; less likelihood of psychosis; more somatic complaints; less likelihood of suicide Physical signs. Veraguth's fold — triangular fold in the nasal corner of the upper eyelid. Omega sign on the forehead. Aaron Beck's cognitive triad — negative view of self, world, future. Also: learned helplessness (Martin Seligman). Aetiology: unipolar depression concordance rate 46%; abnormality in monoamine, acetylcholine and GABA neurotransmitters; hormonal disturbances; neuroanatomical — reduced dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and increased HPA axis. Treatment: pharmacotherapy takes 3–4 weeks; maintained for 6 months (prophylactic). Tricyclic antidepressants (block reuptake of serotonin & norepinephrine, the "-pramines"; anticholinergic side effects — constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, dry mouth). SSRIs / NaSSA / SNRI (side effects: nausea, anxiety, diarrhoea). MAOIs. Antipsychotics. Therapies: CBT, mindfulness, IPT, ECT, TMS, vagus nerve stimulation, deep brain stimulation, sleep deprivation therapy, phototherapy (1500–10,000 lux). More TCA side effects (beyond the anticholinergic ones): delirium (especially in the elderly, from the anticholinergic load); postural changes , i.e. decreased BP / hypotension on standing up (postural or orthostatic hypotension, which causes dizziness and falls); and arrhythmia , because TCAs slow conduction in the heart. This cardiac effect is why a TCA overdose can be fatal. More SSRI/SNRI side effects: sexual side effects, i.e. reduced libido and anorgasmia (delayed or absent orgasm), a common reason patients stop the drug; and sedation (most marked with the NaSSA mirtazapine, which also increases appetite and weight). 8 · Bipolar & Related Disorders (Mania) Mood Disorders: Mania. A one-page summary of mania with boxes for aetiology and prevalence, mania versus hypomania, treatment, the DIG FAST criteria and specifiers, plus a flowchart branching into Bipolar I, Bipolar II and cyclothymic disorder. Psycho Didi notes · p. 41 Manic episode criteria — mnemonic DIG FAST: D istractibility; I mpulsivity; G randiosity; F light of ideas; A ctivity (goal-directed) increase; S leep deficit; T alkativeness. Bipolar I Requires a manic episode . Major depressive episodes common but not required for diagnosis. Bipolar II A hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode ; there has never been a full manic episode. Bipolar I vs Bipolar II — and Mania vs Hypomania. Mania (Bipolar I): lasts 1 week , accompanied by less intense depression, may have psychotic features, requires hospitalization. Hypomania (Bipolar II): lasts 4 days , accompanied by major depressive episodes, may not require hospitalization, never a full manic episode. Bipolar I needs a manic episode; Bipolar II needs hypomania + ≥ 1 MDE and no full mania. Cyclothymic Disorder Periods with hypomanic symptoms (not meeting full criteria) and depressive symptoms (not meeting full criteria) for at least 2 years , during which symptoms have not been absent for more than 2 months. Specifiers Mood-congruent psychotic features; mood-incongruent psychotic features; catatonia; peripartum onset; seasonal pattern; hypomania; mixed episodes (cycle in 7 days); anxious distress; rapid cycling; melancholic features; atypical features. Aetiology & prevalence. Bipolar disorder is the most genetically influenced disorder (74% if both parents affected). Neurotransmitters: increased dopamine activity. Genetic factors: chromosomes 18q, 22q, 21q. Mania more common in men; depression more common in women; onset 30 years and above; more in divorced/single persons. Treatment: Lithium (side effects: postural tremors [treated with beta-blockers], memory disturbance, intracranial tension, peripheral neuropathy, hypothyroidism, polyuria, diabetes; lithium toxicity — tremors, renal impairment, ataxia, delirium, increased reflexes, convulsions, vomiting, kidney issues), Valproate (acute mania), Lamotrigine (depressive), Carbamazepine, Oxcarbazepine, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, antidepressants; ECT; therapy. Treatment continued for 2 years. The diagram's second side-effect list (acne, psoriasis, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea) sits under the other drugs, but these are classic lithium side effects: lithium can cause or worsen acne and psoriasis, and nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea are common early in lithium treatment (GI upset also occurs with valproate). Key side effects of the other mood stabilizers: valproate , weight gain, hair loss, tremor, liver toxicity, pancreatitis and neural tube defects if taken in pregnancy; carbamazepine , skin rash (including Stevens-Johnson syndrome), low white cell count (agranulocytosis) and low sodium; lamotrigine , a serious rash (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), which is why the dose is raised slowly. 9 · Schizophrenia Spectrum & Other Psychotic Disorders Schizophrenia and Other Psychotic Disorders. A grid of boxes covering positive and negative symptoms, history, types, epidemiology, prognosis, speech and catatonia, etiology, the duration rules for other psychotic disorders, and treatment. Psycho Didi notes · p. 49 History. Emil Kraepelin gave the term dementia praecox (1896); his classification: simple dementia, paranoia, catatonia, hebephrenia. Eugen Bleuler coined the term schizophrenia and gave the 4 A's : Ambivalence, Autism, Association (disturbance), Affect disturbance . Karl Kahlbaum — catatonia. Symptoms Negative symptoms: affective flattening, avolition, apathy, anhedonia, asociality, alogia. Negative symptom Meaning What you see Affective flattening Reduced or absent expression of affect Unchanging face, poor eye contact, monotonous voice, few gestures Avolition Decreased interest in, or desire for, goal-directed activities Sits idle all day, neglects bathing, does not look for work Apathy Lack of interest, enthusiasm or concern Indifferent to family events or his own future Anhedonia Lack of interest, enjoyment or pleasure from life's experiences Hobbies, food and company no longer give pleasure Asociality Lack of motivation to engage in social interaction, or a preference for solitary activities Withdraws from friends, stays in his room Alogia Speaking less: fewer words, or speaking only in response to others (poverty of speech) Answers "yes", "no", "don't know" and adds nothing Trap: negative symptoms are a loss of normal functions (positive symptoms are additions, like hallucinations). They were rated by Nancy Andreasen's Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms (SANS), respond poorly to typical antipsychotics, and predict poorer outcome. DSM-5-TR names two as most prominent: diminished emotional expression and avolition . Rule out look-alikes: depression and antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism can also make a person flat and slow. Schneider's First-Rank Symptoms (positive). Audible thoughts (1st person); voices heard arguing (3rd person); voices commenting on one's actions; thought withdrawal; thought diffusion/broadcasting; made feeling; made impulse; made actions; somatic passivity. Also: hallucinations; delusions (erotomania, grandeur, guilt, jealousy, passivity, persecution, poverty, reference, somatic, thought control). Speech disturbances: poverty of speech, echolalia, verbigeration (continual repetition of stereotyped phrases), perseveration. Catatonia (Karl Kahlbaum): agitation, catalepsy (holding a posture for a long time against gravity; not cataplexy , the sudden loss of muscle tone with strong emotion in narcolepsy), echolalia/echopraxia, exaggerated compliance, grimace, mannerism, mutism, stereotypy, posturing, waxy flexibility. Types (subtypes) Paranoid; Catatonic; Disorganized/Hebephrenic; Undifferentiated; Residual; Simple ( worst prognosis ). Also pfropfschizophrenie — schizophrenia and mental retardation coexisting. Type 1 Type 2 Ventricles Normal ventricles Dilated ventricles Damage No organic damage; no comorbidity — Medication response Good prognosis Low response to medication Duration & the psychotic-disorder family Disorder Duration Symptoms to be met Schizophrenia 6+ months All Schizophreniform disorder 1–6 months All Schizoaffective disorder 2 weeks Schizophrenia + mood disorder Delusional disorder 1 month Delusion Brief psychotic disorder 1 day and 1 night All Schizophreniform vs Schizophrenia (the classic duration trap). Schizophreniform = 1–6 months ; Schizophrenia = 6+ months — same full symptom set, only the duration cutoff differs. Brief psychotic disorder is even shorter (1 day–1 month), and schizoaffective requires both schizophrenia and a mood disorder. Etiology, epidemiology & prognosis Positive symptoms — excess dopamine in the mesolimbic tract (VTA → limbic region). Negative symptoms — dopamine dysregulation in the mesocortical pathway (VTA → prefrontal lobe). Genetic loci: 1q, 5q, 6p, 6q, 8p, 10p, 13q, 15q, 22q. Biochemical: dopamine, serotonin, glutamate, GABA. Epidemiology: 1% lifetime; 0.15–0.25% per 1000; good prognosis in females; bad prognosis with low SES. Good prognosis Poor prognosis Abrupt/sudden onset; late onset; catatonic; in females; positive symptoms present; history of mood disorders Insidious onset; early onset; simple/disorganized schizophrenia; in males; negative symptoms present; history of schizophrenia Treatment. Typical antipsychotics (dopamine receptor antagonists; side effect: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome, NMS) — Chlorpromazine (1950), Haloperidol, Phenothiazines, Thioxanthene, Butyrophenones. Atypical antipsychotics (target 5-HT receptors, partially block D2) — Clozapine (treatment-resistant schizophrenia), Olanzapine, Quetiapine; do not cause tardive dyskinesia. 10 · Trauma & Stressor-Related Disorders Trauma and Stress Related Disorders. An illustrated page summarising PTSD, complex PTSD, prolonged grief disorder, acute stress disorder, adjustment disorder, reactive attachment disorder and disinhibited social engagement disorder. Psycho Didi notes · p. 43 Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) Occurs after rape, floods, abduction, plane crash, soldiers of war; symptoms don't develop immediately. Was classified under anxiety disorders until DSM-IV-TR. Symptoms: avoidance of situations/places/memories; intrusive flashbacks, re-experiencing, nightmares; arousal (hypervigilance, exaggerated startle); depersonalization & derealization. Diagnosed if symptoms appear within 6 months after trauma; symptoms present for more than a month. Brain regions: hippocampus, amygdala. Acute Stress Disorder All PTSD symptoms for less than 1 month ; also experience dissociation; 9/14 symptoms of PTSD must be present. Acute Stress Disorder vs PTSD. ASD = PTSD symptoms lasting < 1 month (with prominent dissociation). PTSD = symptoms > 1 month, appearing within 6 months of trauma. Note ICD-11 eliminated acute stress disorder as a diagnosis. Complex PTSD (ICD-11) Prolonged or repeated exposure to trauma from which escape is difficult or impossible (e.g. torture, prolonged domestic violence, repeated childhood sexual or physical abuse). ICD-11 needs all the core PTSD symptoms (re-experiencing in the present, avoidance, a persistent sense of current threat such as hypervigilance) plus all three "disturbances in self-organization" (DSO) : (1) emotional dysregulation (severe problems in managing emotions), (2) negative self-concept (feeling diminished, defeated or worthless, with shame or guilt), (3) interpersonal disturbances (difficulty sustaining relationships and feeling close to others). Clinical features: re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal, impaired self-perception, difficulty maintaining relationships. Treatment: prevention/disaster management, practical help, SSRIs, benzodiazepines, EMDR (Francine Shapiro). Heads up: the trauma diagram lists "disturbances in self-organization" as one of three problems and says 2 of 3 are needed. In ICD-11, DSO is the umbrella name for the three problems (emotional dysregulation, negative self-concept, interpersonal disturbances), and all three are required, on top of PTSD. Complex PTSD exists only in ICD-11; DSM-5-TR has no such diagnosis. Prolonged Grief Disorder (DSM-5-TR & ICD-11) Intense, persistent grief; difficulty accepting loss; intrusive thoughts/memories; avoidance; emotional numbness; identity disturbance (feeling like we have died with the other person); unable to function for more than 6 months . Treatment: grief counselling, group therapy, SSRIs. Adjustment Disorder Not being able to adjust to a new situation; psychological and physical symptoms (depression, anxiety) for a span of 3–6 months . Specifiers: anxiety, depression, behaviour, conduct. Reactive Attachment Disorder Unable to form reciprocal relationships; faced rejection in childhood; periods of irritable sadness; issues develop before age 5 ; persistent if symptoms last longer than a year . DDx: ASD, depression. Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder Outcome of abuse, insufficient caregiving, neglect, frequent change; shyness; don't check in with regular caregiver; may become excessively familiar with strangers. 11 · Dissociative Disorders Dissociative & Somatic Disorders. A two-column page with dissociative disorders on the left (clinical features, types of gain, amnesia, fugue, depersonalization/derealization, DID and ICD-10 types) and somatic symptom, conversion, illness anxiety and factitious disorders on the right. Psycho Didi notes · p. 44 A group of normally integrated mental processes become separated from the rest. Clinical features: disturbance in integrated consciousness; sudden onset, temporary course; precipitatory stress; secondary gain; no physical abnormality; affects memory, identity, perception; produced unconsciously by the psyche. Types of gain. Primary — internal psychological motivation to reduce guilt. Secondary — external psychological motivation for assurance/social support. Tertiary — parent's/close person's benefit. Dissociative Amnesia (Psychogenic Amnesia) Types: circumscribed (personal event-specific), selective (forgetting some things), generalized (forgetting everything), continuous (from a stressful event till present), systematized (everything about an event). Dissociative Fugue Wandering/running off; losing old identity and picking up a new one; termination is abrupt. Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder Depersonalization — cutting off/detachment from oneself. Derealization — experience of what is real and not real may be lost. Occurs without overlap with other disorders. Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID) At least 2 distinct identities; personality states called alter egos . Other dissociative presentations (ICD-10) Dissociative trance or possession disorder; dissociative stupor; dissociative disorder of movement and sensation ( la belle indifférence ) — physical symptoms due to psychological causes. This is ICD-10's name for conversion: ICD keeps conversion under dissociative disorders, while DSM-5-TR files it as conversion disorder in the somatic group below. 12 · Somatic Symptom & Related Disorders Somatic symptom and related disorders are disorders of physical symptoms due to psychological causes : the person has real bodily complaints (pain, weakness, fits) or intense worry about illness, and psychological factors (stress, conflict, anxiety) start or keep them going. The DSM-5-TR group: somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder, conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder), psychological factors affecting other medical conditions, and factitious disorder. Traps. (1) DSM-5 dropped the old rule that symptoms must be "medically unexplained": in somatic symptom disorder the symptoms may or may not have a medical cause; what defines it is the excessive thoughts, feelings and behaviour about them. (2) Conversion sits here in DSM-5-TR but under dissociative disorders in ICD-10 and ICD-11. (3) ICD-11 calls the somatic symptom picture bodily distress disorder and moves hypochondriasis to obsessive-compulsive and related disorders. Somatic Symptom (Somatoform) Disorder Chronic pain without any physical cause; conviction persists despite negative test results; duration 6+ months ; onset may be due to stress. The count of 4 pain, 2 GI, 1 sexual and 1 pseudo-neurological symptom is the old DSM-IV rule for somatization disorder ; DSM-5-TR dropped it and needs only one or more distressing symptoms plus excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviour about them, usually lasting 6+ months. Treatment: psychotherapy. Illness Anxiety Disorder (Hypochondriasis) Over-concern with normal body function; terribly worried about having a serious illness; symptoms don't remain constant; unconsciously start mimicking symptoms (not psychotic); addicted to internet searches. Subtypes: care-seeking , care-avoidant . Duration 6+ months. Conversion Disorder (Hysteria / Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder) Body function is lost due to a psychological issue; primary and secondary gain; psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES) ; disturbance of consciousness; la belle indifférence ; duration 6+ months . Factitious Disorder Person wants to stay sick for attention; maintains the sick role; simulates symptoms. Types (DSM-5-TR): imposed on self (its chronic, severe form is Munchausen syndrome ); imposed on another (formerly Munchausen syndrome by proxy ), e.g. a parent keeping a child sick. Pseudologia fantastica — telling stories, pathological lying. Person pretends to have non-measurable diseases; "professionals as patients". 13 · Feeding & Eating Disorders Feeding & Eating Disorders. An illustrated page with the features, types, severity levels and treatment of anorexia, bulimia, binge eating disorder, rumination disorder, pica and avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder. Psycho Didi notes · p. 51 Anorexia Nervosa Restricted food intake to markedly reduced body weight; obsessing about obesity/weight gain; distorted self-perception of being overweight. Characteristic symptoms: disturbance of body image; fear of fatness & excessive emphasis on thinness; restriction of energy intake (significantly less weight than normal); amenorrhea (compulsory until DSM-IV), hypothermia, edema, bradycardia, reduced sexual activity; cuts food into small pieces and rearranges it; cooks for other people. Types: restricting type, purging type. Treatment: hospitalization, reinforcement for healthy eating, CBT, SSRIs. Bulimia Nervosa Normal body weight; binge eating followed by purging; gobbles food in large quantities; no distorted view of being overweight ; morbid fear of weight gain; normal sexual functioning; not secretive. Duration 3+ months. Severity (episodes/week): Mild 1–3; Moderate 4–7; Severe 8–13; Extreme 14 or more. Anorexia vs Bulimia. Anorexia → markedly reduced body weight and a distorted body image . Bulimia → normal body weight , binge-purge cycles, and no distorted view of being overweight; not secretive. Binge Eating Disorder Heavy episodes of eating; episodes often occur in private; craving for calorie-dense food with high speed of consumption; duration 3+ months ; severity measured like bulimia. Rumination Disorder Repeated regurgitation of food — chewed, swallowed, brought back to the mouth and chewed again; may lead to nutritional deficiency; may happen in infants and intellectually disabled children (usually males); malnutrition and vulnerability to disease; may increase gastro-oesophageal reflux; duration 1+ months . Pica Consuming non-nutritive, non-food substances; duration 1+ months ; regular dietary habits are disturbed (the craving for non-food items such as mud, chalk, paper or hair displaces normal meals); not eating normal food; nutritional deficiency; behaviour often recognized only when bowel-obstruction surgery becomes necessary; may be found in children with ID and ASD; usually low socioeconomic status. Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (Food Fad Disorder) Child becomes addicted to one kind of food and refuses anything else; may commence due to parent-child conflict. 3 categories: don't care about eating; restrict diet due to sensory issues; don't eat because of an unpleasant experience. DDx: anxiety. 14 · Sleep-Wake Disorders Why we sleep & sleep stages Sleep Disorders: Introduction and Stages. Theories of why we sleep, the features and brain waves of each sleep stage, a hypnogram of one sleep cycle, and notes on treatment and measurement. Psycho Didi notes · p. 50 Adaptive theory: organisms sleep for self-preservation. Restorative theory: to restore depleted chemical resources. Stage Features Waves Stage 1 Falling asleep Theta (the alpha of relaxed wakefulness fades out) Stage 2 Asleep; K-complexes / sleep spindles; dreams occur; maximum time spent here Theta, plus sleep spindles (12 to 14 Hz bursts) and K-complexes Stage 3 Transition to deep sleep Delta Stage 4 Deepest sleep Delta REM sleep Loss of muscle tone, paralysis, genital activity, fast brain waves, eye movement, dreams — The hypnogram (one sleep cycle). A hypnogram is a graph of sleep stage (vertical axis: W = wake, R = REM, N1, N2, N3) against time (horizontal axis). The diagram shows one cycle of about 90 minutes : the sleeper drops from wake through N1 and N2 into deep N3 within roughly the first half hour, stays in deep sleep, then climbs back up through N2 into the first REM period near the end of the cycle, sometimes with a brief awakening. A night has about 4 to 6 such cycles; early cycles hold most of the deep N3 sleep, and REM periods get longer towards morning. Trap: stages 3 + 4 = N3. The table above uses the older Rechtschaffen and Kales (1968) stages 1 to 4. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (2007) merged stages 3 and 4 into one stage, N3 (slow-wave or delta sleep), which is why the hypnogram shows only N1, N2, N3 and R. Parasomnias Parasomnia. A flowchart splitting parasomnias into REM and NREM types with examples of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 50 NREM: confusional arousal; sleepwalking (somnambulism); sleep/night terrors (usually during deep sleep). REM: REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams); recurrent isolated sleep paralysis (awake but unable to move); nightmare disorder. (Additional behaviours with or during sleep.) Dyssomnias Dyssomnia. A flowchart splitting dyssomnias into intrinsic and extrinsic types with examples of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 50 Intrinsic: obstructive sleep apnea (due to obesity); central sleep apnea (reduced oxygen to brain due to cardiovascular problems); psychophysiological insomnia; idiopathic insomnia; narcolepsy (excessive daytime sleepiness; cataplexy — sudden loss of muscle tone with intense emotions; hypnopompic & hypnagogic hallucinations). Extrinsic: circadian rhythm disorder (night shifts / pineal gland problem; suprachiasmatic nucleus disturbed); restless legs syndrome (leg sensations, impulse to move). Treatment: medication, melatonin. Measurement: polysomnography (EEG/EMG/EOG/ECG/GSR). 15 · Sexual Dysfunctions, Gender Dysphoria & Paraphilic Disorders Sexual Disorders. A diagram listing the sexual dysfunctions, defining gender dysphoria, and branching paraphilic disorders into anomalous activity and anomalous target preferences. Psycho Didi notes · p. 50 Sexual Dysfunctions Delayed ejaculation; erectile disorder; female orgasmic disorder; female sexual interest/arousal disorder; genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder; male hypoactive sexual desire disorder; premature ejaculation. Gender Dysphoria A marked incongruence between one's experienced/expressed gender and assigned gender; duration 6 months . Paraphilic Disorders Anomalous activity preferences — Courtship disorders (resemble distorted components of human courtship): Voyeuristic (spying on others in private), Exhibitionist (exposing the genitals), Frotteuristic (touching/rubbing against a non-consenting person). Algolagnic disorders (pain & suffering): Sexual masochism (arousal from undergoing humiliation/bondage/suffering), Sexual sadism (arousal from inflicting humiliation/bondage/suffering). Anomalous target preferences — directed at others: Paedophilic disorder (sexual focus on children). Directed elsewhere: Fetishistic disorder (nonliving objects or highly specific non-genital body-part focus); Transvestic disorder (sexually arousing cross-dressing); duration 6 months . 16 · Personality Disorders Personality Disorders. The page header with a box of general features of personality disorders (ego-syntonic, deviation from social norms, impairment, prevalence and course) next to the Cluster B label. Psycho Didi notes · p. 42 Features. A box listing five features of personality disorders: disharmonious attitude or behaviour, enduring pattern, clearly maladaptive, appearing during adolescence, and personal or social distress. Psycho Didi notes · p. 42 General features: ego-syntonic ; don't seek psychiatric help unless other symptoms co-occur; deviate from social norm — unhappy and impaired; abnormal behaviour and subjective experience causing significant impairment; disharmonious attitude; enduring, maladaptive pattern; appear during adolescence; personal/social distress. Prevalence: 10–20% of the general population, onset adolescence/early adulthood; symptoms fizzle out after 40. Cluster A — Odd & Eccentric Cluster A: Odd & Eccentric. A column of bullet lists for paranoid, schizoid and schizotypal personality disorders with their features, differential diagnosis and treatment. Psycho Didi notes · p. 42 Paranoid Personality Disorder Excessive suspiciousness; heightened self-importance; persistently bears grudges; conspiracy theories; suspicious of partner's fidelity. More common in men and in minority groups (Kaplan & Sadock also note immigrants and deaf people). Treatment: supportive psychotherapy, benzodiazepines, antipsychotics. DDx: delusional disorder. Schizoid Personality Disorder Emotional bluntness; lack of pleasure from activities; limited capacity to express feelings; indifference to praise/criticism; little interest in sexual experience; prefers solitary activities; preoccupation with fantasy and introspection; lack of close friends ; insensitivity to social norms ; 3/9 symptoms need to be present (as in the notes; for DSM-5-TR, 4 of 7 criteria); less likelihood of psychosis than schizotypal PD; more common in males . Treatment: psychotherapy, group therapy; benzodiazepines, SSRI, antipsychotics. Schizotypal Personality Disorder Ideas of reference; odd beliefs/magical thinking; eccentric behaviour; odd thinking; suspiciousness/paranoid ideas; inappropriate/constricted affect; poor rapport; obsessive rumination ; lack of close friends (a DSM-5-TR criterion for both schizoid and schizotypal PD); unusual perceptual experience; stereotypical thinking; quasi-psychotic episodes; belief in telepathy and thought broadcast; inner world like a child; may experience psychosis under severe stress; DSM-5-TR needs 5 of 9 criteria. ICD-10 puts it under schizophrenia (F21, schizotypal disorder, whose list of features includes "obsessive ruminations without inner resistance"). Treatment: antidepressants, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines; psychoanalysis, individual therapy. Schizoid vs schizotypal. Both lack close friends. Schizoid = detached and cold, prefers to be alone, but no odd beliefs and little risk of psychosis. Schizotypal = odd and eccentric: magical thinking, ideas of reference, unusual perceptions, brief psychotic episodes under stress; it is the PD closest to schizophrenia, which is why ICD-10 files it with schizophrenia. Cluster B — Dramatic & Emotional Cluster B: Dramatic & Emotional. A column of bullet lists for antisocial, histrionic, borderline and narcissistic personality disorders with their features, defence mechanisms and treatment. Psycho Didi notes · p. 42 Antisocial Personality Disorder Callous unconcern for others' feelings; disregard for social norms; can't maintain relationships; low frustration tolerance; can't experience guilt; proneness to blame others; history of conduct disorder; EEG abnormality; ADHD comorbidity; genetic predisposition; comes to psychiatry from legal authorities; 3/6 symptoms to be met . DSM-5 also includes impulse-control disorder. Treatment: carbamazepine, beta-blockers. Histrionic Personality Disorder Extreme attention-seeking; emotionalism seeps into all areas; self-dramatization; suggestibility; shallow and labile affect; continual attention-seeking; inappropriately seductive; over-concern with physical attractiveness; flamboyant. Defence mechanisms: acting out, dissociation. Treatment: antidepressants, psychotherapy. Borderline Personality Disorder Impulsive; labile; self-harm clearly visible to others; unstable relationships; fragile self-esteem; unclear preferences; devaluation or idealisation; fear of abandonment; chronic feelings of emptiness; accident proneness. Primary defence: splitting ; comorbidity with depression; also called emotionally unstable personality disorder . Treatment: Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT; Marsha Linehan, 1993) . Narcissistic Personality Disorder Sense of grandiosity; fantasy of unlimited success; attention/praise-seeking; lack of empathy; shaky self-esteem; thirst for admiration; unable to face criticism; tries to impress new people; believes they are special/talented; develops depression if faced with rejection. Cluster C — Anxious & Fearful Cluster C: Anxious & Fearful. A column of bullet lists for avoidant, dependent and obsessive-compulsive personality disorders with their features and treatment. Psycho Didi notes · p. 42 Avoidant Personality Disorder Feelings of inadequacy; belief that they are socially inept, inferior, unappealing; preoccupation with being rejected; unwillingness to involve socially; restricted lifestyle; 3/6 traits should be present; depression may develop. Treatment: beta-blockers, SSRI, CBT, social skills training. Dependent Personality Disorder Need for others to take care of them and make decisions; subordination of one's own needs; unwillingness to make demands; fear of being abandoned; can't make decisions without excessive reassurance; may develop passive-aggressive personality. Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder (OCPD) Excessive doubt; need to exert interpersonal control; preoccupation with details; excessive conscientiousness; adherence to social convention; others should submit to their ways; unwelcome thoughts. Psychodynamic view: fixation in the anal stage (Sigmund Freud, 1905). ICD calls it anankastic personality disorder. Treatment: psychotherapy. OCD vs OCPD. OCD (an anxiety-related disorder) involves ego- dystonic obsessions and compulsions with insight.
