OCPD (a personality disorder) is an ego- syntonic , pervasive pattern of perfectionism, control and orderliness — the person sees nothing wrong with it. ICD calls OCPD "anankastic." 17 · Substance-Related & Addictive Disorders Substance Related Disorders. An overview of clinical symptoms, etiology, other symptoms, dependence and harmful use, ending with the five classes of substances and examples of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 46 ICD-10: "mental and behavioural disorders due to psychoactive substance use" — more focus on consequence. Initial denial, then tolerance and withdrawal. Etiology. Brain areas: striatum, nucleus accumbens (addiction behaviour). Neurotransmitter systems: dopamine, opioid, catecholamines, GABA. Hereditary factors involved. Clinical syndromes (ICD) (1) Acute intoxication; (2) withdrawal state; (3) dependence syndrome ; (4) harmful use — causing harm to the individual but dependence criteria not met; damage to physical/mental health; issues in daily functioning. Dependence: behavioural, physical & psychological craving; difficulty controlling use; withdrawal symptoms; tolerance; neglect of alternative pleasures; persistence with substance use. Classes of substances CNS stimulants: cocaine, amphetamine, caffeine, nicotine. Depressants: alcohol, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, inhalants. Opioids: narcotics, heroin, morphine. Cannabis. Hallucinogen & phencyclidine. Slurred speech link. The classes diagram brackets alcohol, barbiturates and benzodiazepines with an arrow to slurred speech . All three are CNS depressants that boost the brain's main inhibitory transmitter, GABA, so intoxication with any of them looks alike: slurred speech, poor coordination, unsteady gait, drowsiness, poor attention and memory. Taken together their effects add up, which is why mixing alcohol with sleeping pills can stop breathing. Cocaine CNS Stimulants: Cocaine and Amphetamine. A table giving the effects, withdrawal symptoms and miscellaneous notes for cocaine and amphetamine. Psycho Didi notes · p. 46 Blocks D1, D2 dopamine receptors; increases dopamine & norepinephrine in the synapse; sympathomimetic; vasoconstriction; once used as an anaesthetic; crack = freebase of cocaine (high craving). Intoxication: euphoria, pupil dilation, tachycardia, sweating. Miscellaneous: nasal perforation, tongue turns black. Withdrawal: low energy/exhaustion, hunger, suicidal ideation. Acute intoxication (psychotic features, as placed in the notes' cocaine row): paranoid ideation , auditory hallucinations , visual illusions and tactile hallucinations , classically formication (Magnan's phenomenon / cocaine bugs) — sensation of insects crawling on/under the skin (tactile hallucination). Cocaine-induced psychotic disorder — similar to paranoid schizophrenia. Amphetamine Euphoria; potential for psychotic disorder; used for performance enhancement. Substances: methamphetamines, dextroamphetamines, methylphenidate. Acute intoxication: paranoid ideation, auditory hallucination, visual illusion (the notes place this list under cocaine; amphetamine produces the same picture, and DSM-5-TR groups the two as "stimulant intoxication"). Withdrawal: fatigue; vivid/unpleasant dreams; insomnia or hypersomnia; increased appetite; psychomotor agitation or retardation. Nicotine Substances: Nicotine to Inhalants. A table giving the effects, withdrawal symptoms and miscellaneous notes for nicotine, caffeine, opioids, hallucinogens and phencyclidine, cannabis, and inhalants. Psycho Didi notes · p. 47 Enhances attention, learning, reaction time, problem-solving. Most common in India as beedi; nicotine and carbon monoxide responsible for cardiovascular disorder. Withdrawal: craving, irritability, anxiety, difficulty concentrating, bradycardia, drowsiness, decreased REM sleep, increased appetite. Treatment: nicotine replacement therapy; Bupropion; Clonidine; Nortriptyline; Varenicline (new); behaviour therapy, CBT. Caffeine Effects: anxiety, jittery, restless, insomnia, flushed face. Withdrawal: headaches, fatigue, irritability, difficulty concentrating. Opioids Opiates (natural) — poppy; opioids (synthetic) — heroin (quick absorption). Effects: euphoria, warmth, high dependence potential, facial flushing, sedation. Overdose: respiratory depression, coma, pupil constriction, cyanosis. Withdrawal: muscle cramps, body aches, insomnia, anxiety, hypertension, tachycardia, nausea, vomiting, anorexia. Treatment: long-acting opioid — methadone, buprenorphine for 2–3 weeks, slowly tapered. Withdrawal duration: 6–8 hrs; peak 2nd–3rd day, reduces by 8–10 days. Hallucinogens & Phencyclidine LSD, psilocybin mushroom, MDMA (ecstasy), angel dust (PCP). Effects: depersonalization, derealization, synesthesia, hallucinations, illusions, autonomic hyperactivity, altered perception; may cause a "bad trip" (benzodiazepines given to reduce). No physical dependence; tolerance; withdrawal rarely seen; LSD associated with flashback phenomena . Treatment: psychotherapy. PCP (phencyclidine, angel dust) intoxication, per DSM-5-TR: problem behaviour (belligerence, assaultiveness, impulsiveness, unpredictability, agitation, impaired judgement) with vertical or horizontal nystagmus , raised blood pressure or heart rate, numbness or reduced response to pain, ataxia, dysarthria, muscle rigidity, seizures or coma, and hyperacusis. Heads up: the list "dizziness, nystagmus, slurred speech, unsteady gait ... rapid reach to lungs, brain and blood; overdose: brain lesions, cognitive deficits" belongs to inhalants in the notes' table (see Inhalants below), not to PCP. Nystagmus is common to both; the marks of PCP are violent, unpredictable behaviour and insensitivity to pain. Cannabis Bhang, charas, ganja, weed, hash. Effects: behavioural changes, impaired motor coordination, anxiety, slowed time, red eyes, increased appetite, dry mouth, rapid heartbeat, impaired judgement. Withdrawal: irritability, anger, aggression, nervousness, sleep difficulties, decreased appetite, restlessness, depressed mood. Treatment: rehabilitation, behaviour therapy, psychotherapy. Inhalants (Depressants) Gasoline, spray paint, thinner. Effects: behavioural changes, dizziness, nystagmus, slurred speech, unsteady gait ; like a depressant: lethargy, depressed reflexes, psychomotor retardation, tremors, generalized muscle weakness, blurred vision, stupor, euphoria. Because they are breathed in, the vapours make a rapid reach to the lungs, brain and bloodstream , so effects start within seconds. Overdose / heavy use: lesions in the brain and lasting cognitive deficits. Withdrawal: agitation/irritability, powerful headaches, nausea, excessive sweating, tremors and convulsions, abdominal cramping, intense cravings. Alcohol Alcohol. A table row for alcohol listing its effects, reverse tolerance, the withdrawal seizure timeline, Jellinek's and Cloninger's typologies, treatment and evaluation tools. Psycho Didi notes · p. 48 Jellinek's typology of alcoholism: (1) Alpha — psychological dependence, early stage, relieving emotional issues, can leave alcohol if desired; (2) Beta — physical consequences (liver cirrhosis) started, no psychological/physical dependence, no addiction; (3) Gamma — addiction with loss of control, tolerance, physical dependence; (4) Delta — maintenance drinking: cannot abstain even for a day or two, but keeps control over how much is drunk on any one occasion; (5) Epsilon — dipsomania, periodic/binge drinking, the type Jellinek said was least understood. Heads up: the diagram puts "loss of control" under Delta and calls Epsilon "most advance". Loss of control is the mark of Gamma ; the mark of Delta is the inability to abstain , with control over the amount kept. Epsilon (periodic, binge drinking) is not the most advanced type; Jellinek said it was the one least understood. Robert Cloninger's typology: Type 1 — later onset, more psychological dependence, guilt, no sense of control. Type 2 — starts early, socially disruptive, more physical dependence, sensation seeking, better sense of control. Effects of alcohol (from the notes): feelings of relaxation or drowsiness; a sense of euphoria or giddiness; changes in mood; lowered inhibitions; impulsive behaviour; slowed or slurred speech; nausea and vomiting; diarrhoea; head pain; changes in hearing, vision and perception; loss of coordination; trouble focusing or making decisions; loss of consciousness or gaps in memory ("blackouts", when the person cannot recall what happened while drinking). Trap: alcohol is a depressant , even though the early effects (euphoria, talkativeness, lowered inhibitions) look stimulating. That early "lift" comes from depression of the brain's inhibitory control, not from stimulation. Legal limit: 30 mg/dl. 10% discarded, 90% absorbed; peak absorption 30–90 minutes. Reverse tolerance: body degraded so much that even a lesser amount has effects. Withdrawal timeline (seizures): 6–8 hrs — coarse tremors; 12–24 hrs — alcoholic hallucinosis; 24–48 hrs — alcohol withdrawal seizures (tonic-clonic); 48–72 hrs — delirium tremens . Evaluation: CAGE questionnaire (John Ewing, 1984) — Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener; AUDIT; SADQ. Treatment: benzodiazepines, thiamine, carbamazepine, disulfiram, anti-craving agents; CBT, Alcoholics Anonymous, family/group therapy. 18 · Neurocognitive Disorders Neurocognitive Disorders. A mind map of neurocognitive disorders covering the 4 As, delirium, cortical, subcortical and pseudo dementia, and the features of Alzheimer's, TBI, vascular, Huntington's, Lewy body, Parkinson's, Korsakoff's, frontotemporal and mild neurocognitive disorder. Psycho Didi notes · p. 45 ICD-11: organic mental disorder. Episodic memory (Endel Tulving, 1972) is first to go; semantic memory is last to go. Defies Occam's razor: no single explanation. Marked by anxiety, sleep problems, psychosis. Cognitive impairment — the 4 A's: Aphasia, Agnosia, Amnesia, Apraxia. Plus disturbance of consciousness (delirium), visual hallucinations, transient delusions. Dementia (Major Neurocognitive Disorder) Amnesia, aphasia, apraxia, agnosia; personality changes (frontotemporal lobe); hallucinations, delusions, mood symptoms; progressive; reduced intellectual functioning; impaired memory & self-care; perseveration; disorientation in time/place/person. Type Examples & features Cortical dementia (fronto-, temporo-, parieto-) Hallucination, delusion; cognitive functioning more compromised. E.g. Alzheimer's, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (mad cow disease) Subcortical dementia Motor issues, depressive. E.g. Huntington's chorea, Parkinson's disease, progressive supranuclear palsy, Wilson's disease Alzheimer's Disease Most common dementia; 5% of people by age 65 (pre-senile); 2–30% by age 85 (senile) ; females outnumber males 3:1 ; linked with chromosomes 1, 14, 21 (autosomal). Marked by neurofibrillary tangles (barrier in the cholinergic pathway) and beta-amyloid plaques ; hippocampal degeneration. Symptoms: confusion with time/location, difficulty completing familiar tasks, misplacing items, memory loss, difficulty problem-solving, social withdrawal, poor judgement, unfounded emotions, difficulty with words, trouble with images; anterograde then retrograde amnesia. Delirium Metabolic encephalopathy; disturbance of consciousness; impaired attention; impaired time/place/person orientation; impaired immediate memory; perceptual disturbances (hallucinations); hypo/hyperactivity; disturbed sleep-wake cycle; autonomic disturbances. Sundowning — increased problems in the evening. Floccillation — patient picks at bedclothes. Occupational delirium. Acetylcholine and ARAS implicated. Predisposing factors: pre-existing dementia, extreme old age, history of delirium, drug dependence, cerebral lesions, surgery, severe psychological symptoms, psychotropic medicines. Treatment: treat underlying cause, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines. Delirium vs Dementia (and Pseudodementia). Delirium = acute, fluctuating disturbance of consciousness/attention with visual hallucinations; reversible. Dementia = chronic, progressive decline in cognition with clear consciousness. Pseudodementia (depressive) — complains about memory impairment, emphasizes disability/distress, says "don't know," recent-memory impairment, variable test performance, past history of mood episodes. Dementia due to Traumatic Brain Injury Loss of consciousness/delirium; male-predominant (bike accidents), elderly (falls); consciousness (4 A's) affected; diagnosable through scans; amnesia seen first; hemiparesis. Vascular Dementia Multi-infarction; small vascular strokes (heart issue); insufficient oxygen supplied to the brain. Huntington's 100% genetic — caused by the HTT gene (dominant) on chromosome 4 (short arm, 4p16.3); chorea; hyperkinesia; cognitive + motor deficit; glutamate excitotoxicity. Lewy Body Disease New in DSM-5. Lewy bodies = bits of alpha-synuclein protein (in cytoplasm) of brain cells, located in brainstem, substantia nigra, locus coeruleus. Cognitive symptoms start first, followed by motor symptoms; fluctuating attention; hallucinations ( can't prescribe antipsychotics ); late onset of Parkinson-like symptoms. Duration: chronic. Parkinson's Pill-rolling tremors, bradykinesia, rigidity, slow movements, stooped posture, postural instability, akinesia, freezing of gait, micrographia. Also in the notes' Parkinson's block: heavy instance of repeated head trauma (repeated head injury, as in boxers, raises the risk of parkinsonism); hyper- and hypokinesia (hypokinesia, too little and too slow movement, is the core sign; hyperkinesia, extra involuntary movements, typically appears as dyskinesia after years of levodopa treatment); procedural memory is affected (skills and habits depend on the basal ganglia, which Parkinson's damages through loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra), while memory for facts and events is relatively spared early on. Korsakoff's Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency caused by chronic alcoholism and lack of nutrition. Less severe — Wernicke's encephalopathy: global amnesia, confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; acute symptoms; sudden onset; reversible. Korsakoff's: irreversible, confabulation observed, chronic onset; found in older adults. Wernicke's vs Korsakoff's. Both from thiamine (B1) deficiency. Wernicke's encephalopathy = acute, sudden onset, reversible (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia). Korsakoff's = chronic, irreversible, with confabulation. Frontotemporal Dementia Accounts for 5% of all dementia; cortical dementia (hallucination and delusion); executive functions impacted. Behavioural variant — socially inappropriate, apathy, fixed mindset. Language variant — inappropriate words, grammar. Types: frontal variant; semantic dementia (temporal); progressive non-fluent aphasia. Mild Neurocognitive Disorder Doesn't meet criteria for major dementia but marked dysfunction; person scores below 1 standard deviation on tests; minor loss of cognitive functioning. 19 · Named / Eponymous Syndromes Miscellaneous Disorders. A grid of labelled boxes, each giving a short description of a named syndrome such as Capgras, Cotard's, Fregoli, Ganser, Kleine-Levin and Othello syndrome. Psycho Didi notes · p. 52 Delusional misidentification syndromes. Capgras syndrome — belief that a loved one or pet has been replaced by an identical imposter. Fregoli syndrome — belief that familiar people are in disguise or have changed their appearance. Syndrome of intermetamorphosis — delusion that people have swapped identities while maintaining the same appearance (total psychological + physical transformation, not just disguise). Syndrome of subjective doubles — delusion that others have swapped identities while keeping the same appearance. Reduplicative paramnesia — delusional belief that identical places and events exist. Other classic named syndromes. Cotard's syndrome (Dr Jules Cotard, 1882) — delusions that one is dead or does not exist; a nihilistic delusion ; treatment: ECT. Othello syndrome — delusional belief/overvalued idea that one's spouse/partner is unfaithful. De Clérambault's syndrome (erotomania) — the patient, often a single woman, believes an exalted person is in love with her. Charles-Bonnet syndrome — visual hallucinations without any other psychotic features or psychiatric disorder. Couvade syndrome — a spouse complains of obstetric symptoms during his partner's pregnancy and parturition. Diogenes syndrome — gross self-neglect, especially among elderly reclusive persons; often wealthy and intelligent; ~50% have no psychiatric illness (may have paranoid PD). Ganser syndrome — giving approximate answers to simple questions; a dissociative disorder; can understand but can't give pointed answers; happens in prisoners; clouding of consciousness, hallucinations, delusions. Kleine-Levin syndrome (KLS, "sleeping beauty disorder") — hypersomnolence, hypersexuality, hyperorality; early description by Alexandre Jacques François Brière de Boismont (1862) ; mostly adolescent males; spontaneous disappearance of symptoms. Blocq's disease (astasia-abasia) — inability to walk/stand in a normal manner; bizarre gait not suggestive of an organic lesion; a conversion symptom (dissociative motor disorder in ICD-10 / conversion disorder in DSM-5). Briquet's syndrome (St Louis hysteria) — multiple physical complaints in several systems with no physical cause; begins before age 30; chronic; frequent medical contact. Ekbom's syndrome — unpleasant sensations predominantly in the legs (rarely arms); occur only at rest; worse in the evening/night. Chronic fatigue (Myalgic encephalomyelitis) — fatigue, malaise, headache, pharyngitis, low-grade fever, cognitive complaints. Restless legs syndrome — uncomfortable leg sensation (like insects crawling under skin); urge to move/walk; difficulty initiating sleep; medication: Ropinirole. 20 · Culture-Specific (Culture-Bound) Syndromes Culture Specific Disorders. A table naming culture-bound syndromes from Ataque de Nervios to Ode-ori with the culture where each is seen and a short description. Psycho Didi notes · p. 53 Culture Specific Disorders (continued). The second part of the culture-bound syndrome table, adding more syndromes (many from regions of India) with their cultures and descriptions. Psycho Didi notes · p. 54 Disorder Culture Description Ataque de Nervios Hispanics Attacks of crying, trembling, uncontrollable shouting, physical/verbal aggression, intense heat in the chest moving to the head Amok, Mal de Pelea Malaysians, Laotians, Filipinos, Polynesians, Papua New Guineans, Puerto Ricans Dissociative disorder — outburst of violence, aggression or homicidal behaviour at people and objects Brain fag African Americans Problems with concentration/thinking among high-school and university students facing schooling challenges Bouffée Délirante Haitians Sudden outburst of aggression, agitation with confusion, psychomotor excitement; resembles brief psychotic disorder Colera Hispanics Anger and rage disturbing body balance → headache, screaming, stomach pain, loss of consciousness, fatigue Dhat East Indians, Chinese, Sri Lankans Extreme anxiety with sense of weakness, exhaustion and discharge of semen Koro Asians Desire to grasp the penis (in women, vulva/nipples) from fear it will retract into the body and cause death Falling Out African Americans Seizure-like symptoms from traumatic events such as robberies Ghost Sickness American Indians Weakness, dizziness, fainting, anxiety, hallucinations, confusion, loss of appetite from witches/evil forces Hwa-byung Asians Pain in the upper abdomen, fear of death, tiredness from imbalance between reality and anger Latah Asians Sudden fright → imitative behaviours beyond control (echopraxia/echolalia); follows commands, verbal repetition of obscenities Mal de ojo Hispanics Vomiting, fever, diarrhea and mental problems attributed to the "evil eye" Mal puesto, hex, root work, voodoo death African Americans, Hispanics Unnatural diseases/death from the power of people using evil spirits Ode-ori Nigerians Sensation of parasites crawling in the head, heat in the head, paranoid fears of attack by evil spirits Piblokto Arctic/subarctic Inuit Excitement, coma, convulsive seizures resembling abrupt dissociation; amnesia, withdrawal, irritability, irrational behaviour (breaking furniture, eating feces, obscenities) Susto, Miedo, Espanto, Pasmo Hispanics Tiredness and weakness from frightening/startling experiences Taijin kyofusho Asians Guilt about embarrassing others, timidity from feeling one's appearance/odor/expressions offend others Wacinko American Indians Anger, withdrawal, mutism, suicide as a reaction to disappointment and interpersonal problems Wind or Cold Illness Asians and Hispanics Fear of cold/wind; weakness and susceptibility to illness from belief that natural/supernatural elements are unbalanced Possession syndrome Rural India Possession by the soul/spirit of a dead relative or local deity; changed tone, even gender change if the possessing soul is of the opposite sex Dhat syndrome East India Nighttime discharges with severe anxiety, uneasiness, hypochondriasis; related to sexual ineptitude Koro Northeast India Fear of genital retraction and death; seen in both sexes Bhanmati sorcery South India Attributed to psychiatric illness — somatization, conversion, dysthymia, anxiety, schizophrenia, etc. Gilhari syndrome West Rajasthan Small blood-filled swelling that changes position (as if a squirrel/lizard moves in the body toward the neck, obstructing airways → death if not destroyed); medically explained as strong muscle contraction from severe tension/stress Jhinjhinia West Bengal Sudden sensation of tingling and numbness in the legs spreading upward through the body Suudu South India (Tamil culture) Extreme abdominal pain, dark-yellow urine, painful/burning micturition, headaches, fatigue, constipation, dry mouth Mass Hysteria India Short-lived epidemics of hysteria where hundreds to thousands behave in a way they normally would not Suchi-bai syndrome Bengal A condition like obsessional neurosis 21 · Psychopharmacology Reference Psychopharmacology. Drug lists grouped into typical and atypical antipsychotics, antidepressant classes, mood stabilizers, benzodiazepines, anti-epileptics, and drugs used for substance detoxification and abstinence. Psycho Didi notes · p. 55 Antipsychotics Typical (1st generation, D2 antagonism) Atypical (2nd generation, 5-HT2 + D2 antagonism) Effective for positive symptoms Effective for both positive and negative symptoms Phenothiazines: Chlorpromazine, Thioridazine, Triflupromazine, Fluphenazine, Perphenazine. Thioxanthenes: Thiothixene, Flupenthixol. Butyrophenones: Haloperidol, Droperidol, Penfluridol. Miscellaneous: Pimozide, Loxapine, Molindone. Clozapine (1st atypical antipsychotic), Olanzapine, Risperidone, Paliperidone, Iloperidone, Quetiapine, Ziprasidone, Aripiprazole, Sertindole, Zotepine, Lurasidone, Asenapine, Amisulpride. Antidepressants Class (mechanism) Agents TCAs & tetracyclics (block serotonin & norepinephrine transporters) Imipramine, Desipramine, Trimipramine, Amitriptyline, Nortriptyline, Protriptyline, Amoxapine, Doxepin, Maprotiline, Clomipramine SSRIs (block reuptake of 5-HT) Fluoxetine, Fluvoxamine, Citalopram, Escitalopram, Sertraline, Paroxetine, Vilazodone SNRIs (dual reuptake inhibitors) Venlafaxine, Desvenlafaxine, Duloxetine, Milnacipran, Levomilnacipran MAOIs (inhibit metabolism of monoamines) Tranylcypromine, Phenelzine, Isocarboxazid Atypical antidepressants Trazodone, Nefazodone, Mirtazapine, Bupropion, Tianeptine, Amineptine, Antipsychotics (some atypical antipsychotics, e.g. aripiprazole and quetiapine, are used as add-on treatment in depression that has not responded to an antidepressant alone) Heads up: "Antipsychotics" is the last item of the diagram's atypical antidepressants list. It has nothing to do with stopping smoking; nicotine abstinence uses replacement therapy, bupropion, clonidine, nortriptyline and varenicline (table below). Mood stabilizers, benzodiazepines & anti-epileptics Mood stabilizers: Lithium, Valproate, Carbamazepine, Oxcarbazepine, Lamotrigine. Benzodiazepines: Alprazolam, Chlordiazepoxide, Clorazepate, Diazepam, Halazepam, Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Prazepam, Quazepam, Clonazepam. Anti-epileptics: Carbamazepine, Lamotrigine, Levetiracetam, Sodium valproate, Pregabalin, Clobazam, Oxcarbazepine, Phenytoin. Substance detoxification, abstinence & overdose Detoxification = getting the person safely through withdrawal while the drug leaves the body (days to a few weeks). Abstinence (maintenance) = keeping him off the substance afterwards and preventing relapse (months to years). The diagram keeps these as two separate boxes: Substance Detoxification Abstinence (relapse prevention) and overdose Alcohol Benzodiazepines (particularly chlordiazepoxide ); Carbamazepine; antipsychotics for delirium tremens & alcoholic hallucinosis Deterrent agent: Disulfiram (blocks the breakdown of alcohol, so drinking causes flushing, nausea and palpitations). Anti-craving agents: Naltrexone, Acamprosate, Topiramate, Fluoxetine, Baclofen Opioids Methadone, Buprenorphine (long-acting opioids, tapered slowly); Clonidine (eases the sweating, restlessness and racing heart of withdrawal) Substitution: Methadone. Antagonist: Naltrexone. Overdose: Naloxone Nicotine (no separate detox box in the notes) Substitution: nicotine gums, lozenges, patches, inhalers & spray; Bupropion, Clonidine, Nortriptyline, Varenicline Naltrexone vs naloxone. Both block opioid receptors. Naltrexone is long-acting and taken to prevent relapse (opioids and alcohol). Naloxone is short-acting, given by injection or nasal spray, to reverse an opioid overdose in an emergency.

title: Psychological Testing
text: Psychological Testing — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Psychological Testing Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Neuropsychological batteries Intelligence & Indian tests Projective & objective personality tests MMPI · 16PF · NEO-PI · EPQ Test → author → what it measures What this covers. A complete tour of psychological tests for the clinical/NET syllabus: neuropsychology foundations and batteries (Halstead-Reitan, Luria-Nebraska, AIIMS, NIMHANS) plus individual neuro tests (WCST, Bender-Gestalt, Stroop, Tower tests, ROCF, CANTAB, MMSE, PGIBBD, WMS); intelligence tests (Stanford-Binet 5, Raven's, CFIT, Kaufman family, Leiter) and Indian adaptations (Bhatia's Battery, Binet-Kamat, Kulshreshtha, WAPIS, MISIC); and personality tests split into projective (Rorschach, TAT, Rosenzweig, Szondi, sentence-completion and drawing tests) and non-projective objective inventories (MMPI family, MCMI, MBTI, EPPS, Holland, MPQ, 16PF (Raymond Cattell), NEO-PI (Paul Costa and Robert McCrae), EPQ). Every test name, author, age range, subtest and cutoff is preserved. Original diagrams. 16 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 57 to 68) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Introduction to Neuropsychology · 2 · Neuropsychological Tests: goals, categories, approaches · 3 · Halstead-Reitan Battery · 4 · Other Neuropsychological Tests · 5 · Intelligence Tests · 6 · Indian Intelligence Tests · 7 · Personality Tests: overview · 8 · Projective Tests · 9 · Non-Projective Tests (Non Factor Analytic) · 10 · Non-Projective Tests (Factor Analytic) 1 · Introduction to Neuropsychology Intro to Neuropsychology. Mind map linking neuropsychology (the study of brain function and behaviour) to its history, neuroplasticity research findings and the two types of neuroplasticity. Psycho Didi notes · p. 57 Neuropsychology is the study of brain function and behaviour. Neuroplasticity Experience expectant — development according to expected growth pattern. Experience dependent — plasticity dependent on new learning, based on new experiences. History of the mind–brain question Mentalism (Aristotle) — a non-material psyche is responsible for behaviour. Dualism (René Descartes) — the body is like a machine (only controls reflex); the mind controls the machine. Materialism (Charles Darwin) — the mind is just our brain; neuroplasticity is based on evolution, the capacity to change. Research findings Florenz and Galls challenged localization: removed the cortex of 3 dogs. Young children can recover fast from brain damage (stem cells migrate). In adults, new neurons (2%) are formed in the hippocampus and striatum. Functioning improves with physiotherapy. 2 · Neuropsychological Tests: goals, categories, approaches Neuropsychological tests. Mind map of neuropsychological testing that branches into its introduction, goals, commonly named tests, categories assessed, sensitivity and specificity, and fixed versus flexible battery approaches. Psycho Didi notes · p. 57 Neuropsychological testing allows for an in-depth analysis of functional limitation associated with brain dysfunction, and is required for diagnosis by some diagnostic criteria for neurological disorders. Goals (Schaefer et al., 2023) Establish a baseline. Gauge an individual's cognitive strengths and weaknesses and aid in treatment planning. Assist in establishing diagnoses. Establish lateralization and possible etiology of brain lesions. Track progress in rehab. Determination of disability, return to work/school, driving ability or legal purposes. Categories assessed Abstract · Attention · Daily activities · Emotional Distress · Language · Memory · Motor skills · Orientation · Sensation · Perception · Visuospatial reasoning. Sensitivity and Specificity Key. Sensitivity = a test's ability to correctly identify people who have a disease. Specificity = a test's ability to correctly identify people who do not have a disease. Approaches to Neuropsychological tests Approach Description Example Fixed battery Uses the same battery of tests for every client; maintains a constant testing condition; comprehensive normative data; better psychometric properties; broader empirical base for interpretations. Halstead-Reitan Battery Flexible battery Only those measures directly related to the patient's presenting symptoms should be administered. The administered battery inherently changes with a patient's referral question. Uses a core battery of tests and techniques for clients with various syndromes; tests implemented vary based on the practitioner as well as context. Meyers Neuropsychological Battery Commonly named neuropsychological tests Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) Raven's Progressive Matrices Shipley Institute of Living Scale The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST; David Grant and Esta Berg, 1948) Proverbs The Wechsler Memory Scale (WMS) The Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure (ROCF) test The Benton Visual Retention Test (BVRT) Consonant trigrams Stroop test 3 · Halstead–Reitan Neuropsychological Test Battery Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Test Battery. Overview of the Halstead-Reitan battery with its introduction, extra information, five scales and other measures, illustrated with photos of the Booklet Category Test, Tactual Performance Test boards and a finger tapping device. Psycho Didi notes · p. 58 Founder note. The Halstead-Reitan battery arose from one of the first neuropsychology labs in America; it proposed the theory of "biological intelligence" . Introduction Created one of the first neuropsychology labs in America. First neuropsychological test to have a factor-analytic process. Was made to test head trauma. Created: 1935. Time taken: 6–8 hours. 1956: The Halstead-Reitan Test Battery begins to emerge as the premiere test battery in neuropsychology. Now it can detect tremors, cerebrovascular accidents, infections, degenerative diseases, learning disabilities, neurological disorders. Proposed theory of "biological intelligence". Extra information Total 7 scores. Removed: critical flicker fusion test, time sense test. For ages: 15+. Based on T-score value. 6-point score. Scales / Measures Category test — measures abstract reasoning and concept formation; requires the examinee to find the rule for categorizing pictures of geometric shapes. Tactual performance test (Seguin) — measures kinesthetic and sensorimotor ability; requires a blindfolded examinee to place blocks in the appropriate cutout on an upright board with the dominant hand, then non-dominant hand, then both hands; also tests for incidental memory of blocks (score: total time, memory, location). Seashore Rhythm Test — measures attention and auditory perception; requires the examinee to indicate whether paired musical rhythms are same or different. Speech sound perception test — measures attention and auditory-visual synthesis; requires the examinee to pick from four choices the written version of taped nonsense words. Finger tapping test — measures motor speed; requires the examinee to tap a telegraph-key-like lever as quickly as possible for 10 seconds. How the Category Test items are presented. In Halstead's original version each item is a picture of geometric figures projected on a screen. The examinee answers by pressing one of four keys numbered 1 to 4, and a bell (correct) or a buzzer (wrong) gives instant feedback. Nobody explains the rule: the person has to work it out from the feedback (for example, "the answer is the number of objects" or "the answer is the position of the odd one out"). The adult test has 208 items in 7 subtests ; each subtest runs on one rule, and the last subtest mixes earlier items to test memory for the rules. The photo on p.58 shows the Booklet Category Test (DeFilippis & McCampbell, 1979): the same items printed in a stand-up booklet, so no projector is needed. The examinee points to or says a number from 1 to 4 and the examiner says "right" or "wrong". The score is the number of errors . The Tactual Performance Test board. The TPT uses Halstead's modification of the Seguin-Goddard Formboard , a wooden board with cut-outs for geometric shapes (star, cross, triangle, square and so on). The form board goes back to Edouard Seguin , a 19th-century physician who used it to train children with intellectual disability; Henry Goddard later used it as a timed test. Halstead's change was the blindfold, so the shapes must be placed by touch and movement alone. The photo on p.58 shows two sizes: the standard adult board with 10 shapes and a smaller children's board with fewer (6) shapes . The "(1930)" under the photo dates that particular old board, not the invention of the test. Trap: the TPT memory and location scores are incidental memory. The examinee is not told in advance that they will have to draw the board, so these scores show what was learned without trying. Other measures Grip strength — requires the examinee to squeeze as hard as possible; separate trials with each hand. Trail making, parts A, B — requires the examinee to connect numbers (part A) or numbers and letters in alternating order (part B) with a pencil line under pressure of time. Tactile form recognition — requires the examinee to recognize simple shapes (e.g., triangle) placed in the palm of the hand. Sensory-Perceptual Exam — requires the examinee to respond to simple bilateral sensory tasks, e.g., detecting which finger has been touched. Aphasia Screening test — tasks include naming a pictured item (e.g., fork), repeating short phrases. Supplementary: WAIS-III, WRAT-3, MMPI-2, memory tests such as Wechsler Memory Scale-III or Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test. 4 · Other Neuropsychological Tests Other Neuropsychological Tests: Luria-Nebraska, Vineland, Bender-Gestalt, WCST. Mind map of the Luria-Nebraska battery, the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, the Bender-Gestalt Test and the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, with a clock-drawing sample, Bender-Gestalt design cards, Vineland-3 materials and WCST cards. Psycho Didi notes · p. 59 Luria-Nebraska Test Battery Founder note. Luria-Nebraska — started in 1978, standardized by Golden in 1980. The AIIMS and NIMHANS batteries are based on this. 269 items (0, 1, 2 scale); T scores are used. In some areas 2 scores are assigned to the same task: speed and accuracy. Can check any organic damage. Total 14 scales: motor, rhythm, tactile, visual, receptive speech, expressive speech, writing, reading, arithmetic, memory, intellectual scales, pathognomonic — left and right hemisphere. About the clock drawing in the diagram. The three clocks on p.59 are an example from a published paper, drawn by a patient with a neurological illness who was asked to draw a clock. The circles and tick marks are there, but the numbers are mostly missing or scattered and the hands are missing or unclear. Clock drawing is not a separate LNNB scale. It is best known as a quick stand-alone screen, the Clock Drawing Test , and it is also built into the MoCA and the Mini-Cog . The usual instruction is "draw a clock, put in all the numbers, and set the hands to ten past eleven". One drawing taps planning, visuospatial construction and executive control together. Trap: the MMSE has you copy two intersecting pentagons, not draw a clock; the MoCA has the clock (and a cube copy). Two classic error patterns: numbers crowded into the right half of the clock (left-sided neglect, usually from a right parietal lesion), and hands set to the 10 and the 11 because the word "ten" pulls the hand to the number 10 (a stimulus-bound, frontal error). The Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales (VABS) / Vineland Social Maturity Scale (VSMS) Founder note. Developed by American psychologist Edgar Arnold Doll (1935). Most widely used test to measure adaptive behaviour in existence; can be used from birth until death. For younger children, there is a semi-structured interview with parents. Domains: communication, daily living skills, socialization, motor skills, maladaptive behaviour (optional). Can check for Autism Spectrum Disorder, deficits in adaptation, genetic disorders, traumatic brain injury. Age 7–90: given only 3 subtests (not the motor skills subtest). Age 0–7: given all 4 subtests. The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) Founder note. Given by E.A. Berg (with David Grant) in 1948; Heaton published the standard version in 1981 with 128 response cards (two packs of 64). The 64-card WCST-64 is a later short form. Order: Colour → Form → Number. Can break rapport if the client is unable to answer correctly. Bilateral prefrontal dysfunction patients are excited to give the test even if they give wrong answers. Checks for perseveration. Scored using Milner's criteria. How the cards are laid out. Four key (stimulus) cards sit in a row in front of the examinee. In the picture on p.59 they are: one red circle, two green stars, three blue squares, four yellow crosses. The examinee takes the response cards one at a time and places each under the key card they think it matches. Every card can match on colour , form or number . Example: the response card with two red crosses matches card 1 by colour (red), card 4 by form (crosses) and card 2 by number (two), so which answer is "right" depends on the hidden rule. The examiner never states the rule and only says "right" or "wrong". After 10 correct sorts in a row the rule changes without warning (colour, then form, then number, then the cycle repeats) until six categories are completed or the cards run out. Main scores: categories completed, perseverative errors (still sorting by the old rule after it has changed) and failure to maintain set. Heads up: the picture above is a simplified internet illustration. The standard (Heaton) WCST key cards are one red triangle, two green stars, three yellow crosses and four blue circles, and the full test uses 128 response cards (two packs of 64). The 64-card version is a short form (WCST-64). The Bender-Gestalt Test (BGT) Founder note. Developed in 1938 by Lauretta Bender . Tests: hand-eye coordination, perseveration, prefrontal damage. Involves 13 designs for children less than 8 years and 12 designs for age 8 years and above. Memory recall process; global scoring system. Clients are given a lot of sheets, but asked to draw on only one. Visuospatial difficulties identified (lesions in right parietal lobe). What the designs look like. The original test has 9 cards : a sample card A and designs 1 to 8 , which Bender adapted from Max Wertheimer's 1923 Gestalt studies of perceptual grouping. Card A is a circle touching a tilted square (a diamond). Design 1 is a row of dots; 2 is rows of small circles arranged in slanting columns; 3 is dots forming widening arrowheads; 4 is an open square with a bell-shaped curve at its corner; 5 is an arc of dots with a slanting line of dots; 6 is two crossing wavy lines; 7 is two overlapping elongated hexagons; 8 is a long hexagon with a small diamond inside. The examinee copies each card onto a blank sheet. Scorers look for rotation of a design, distortion of shapes, perseveration (adding extra dots or loops) and failure to integrate parts that should touch or overlap; for children the usual system is the Koppitz Developmental Scoring System. Trap: the "13 designs below 8 years, 12 designs from 8 years" rule belongs to the Bender-Gestalt II (Brannigan & Decker, 2003), which has 16 cards in all. Bender's 1938 original has 9 cards (A plus 1 to 8). Seguin Form Board Test Other Neuropsychological Tests: Seguin, BVRT, Seashore, Stroop, ROCF, CANTAB, Tower tests. Mind map of the Seguin Form Board, Benton Visual Retention, Seashore, Stroop, Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure, CANTAB and Tower tests, with a form board photo, a Stroop colour-word chart, a sample complex figure drawing and a Tower of London diagram. Psycho Didi notes · p. 60 Founder note. Indian adaptation by J. Bharatraj ; norms by S. K. Goel . Part of the Halstead-Reitan test battery (1947). Client is asked to draw the board from memory. Earlier it was used to test eye-hand / visuomotor coordination. Earlier given as 10 blocks of Gesell figures. The Benton Visual Retention Test (BVRT) Founder note. Developed by Arthur Benton . Currently: 5th edition; includes 10 designs. Clients are required to see and copy 10 designs immediately out of memory. Time taken: 5 minutes. The Seashore Test Founder note. The tests were developed by Carl E. Seashore . Used in the Halstead-Reitan Battery. 3–5 errors considered normal. Measures musical ability and cerebral function. Seashore Rhythm Test — a subtest of the Seashore Measures of Musical Talent that measures generalized cerebral function; age-related problems occur. Stroop Test Test of selective attention, response conflict and inhibition; errors indicate dysfunction. Because of conceptual primacy, colour takes longer to recognize. No age bias. For checking smaller lesions, more items need to be added. Indicative of frontal functioning; biggest test is 4 block/trial. What the stimulus looks like. The chart on p.60 is the classic colour-word card from J. Ridley Stroop (1935): colour names printed in an ink of a different colour, for example the word "Red" printed in blue ink. The task is to name the ink colour as fast as possible (say "blue"), not to read the word. Most versions have three parts: read colour words printed in black, name the colour of patches (or rows of XXXX), then name the ink of the mismatched colour words. The third part is much slower and has more errors: this slowing is the Stroop effect (interference). Why it happens. Reading is so practised that it is automatic : the word gets read whether you want it or not, and it competes with the slower, less automatic job of naming a colour. Holding the word back needs inhibition, which is why the test is linked to frontal (executive) functioning. Trap: in the interference part the correct answer is always the ink colour . Reading the word aloud is the error. Tower Tests Tests for frontal, planning and executive dysfunction. A measure of means-end analysis (Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, 1972). Requires the client to reach the final goal in the least number of moves possible. Test Apparatus Least number of moves possible Tower of London Utilizes balls 5 Tower of Hanoi Utilizes rings 7 (3 discs; 2 n − 1 for n discs) Dependent on working backwards; one has to visualize; repeat-state avoidance. Checks for inhibition of conflicting responses and working memory. Prepotent: goal-subgoal conflict. What the Tower of London task looks like. Devised by Tim Shallice (1982). Three coloured balls sit on three pegs of different heights: the tallest peg holds three balls, the middle one two, the shortest one. The examinee sees a Begin arrangement and a Goal arrangement and must turn one into the other in the fewest moves, moving one ball at a time and only the top ball on a peg. The figure on p.60 is a "Count the Number of Steps" version from a research study: the person moves nothing, plans entirely in their head, and picks the minimum number of moves from the answers shown (3 or 4). Here the answer is 3 : red to the short peg, yellow to the middle peg, then blue on top of yellow. Trap: Tower of London = balls on pegs of unequal height (Shallice; his original problems need 2 to 5 moves). Tower of Hanoi = discs of different sizes on three equal pegs, and a bigger disc may never sit on a smaller one (a puzzle by the mathematician Edouard Lucas, 1883). The classic 3-disc Tower of Hanoi needs at least 7 moves (2 n minus 1); clinical versions use other start positions, so the count per problem varies. The Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure Test (ROCF) Founder note. Developed by Rey in 1941; standardized by Osterrieth in 1944. Measures visuospatial construction ability, visual memory, and executive functioning by the prefrontal lobe. 3 stages: copy, immediate recall, delayed recall. Uses one-for-one diagram. Checks for: fine motor coordination, visuospatial memory, planning and organization, attention and coordination. Age-related bias may be present. What the figure looks like. The Rey figure is a complex, meaningless line drawing: a large rectangle cut by two diagonals and a vertical and a horizontal midline, a triangle attached to its right side with a small diamond at the tip, a cross outside the top-left corner, a circle with three dots, five short parallel lines crossing a diagonal, a small square hanging below the bottom-left corner and other small details. The examinee first copies it with the model in view, then draws it from memory: immediate recall (often about 3 minutes later) and delayed recall (often about 30 minutes later). Osterrieth's scoring splits the figure into 18 units , each scored 0 to 2, so the maximum is 36 . The drawing on p.60 is a hand-drawn reproduction by a person, not the printed model. Trap: examiners also watch how the figure is copied. Good planners draw the big rectangle first and hang the details on it; people with executive (frontal) problems tend to build it piece by piece, so the copy comes out fragmented even when each piece is drawn well. Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB) Computerized test. Time taken: 40–45 mins. Checks for dementia; frontal, temporal, hippocampal dysfunction. Checks for organic as well as non-organic damage. Independent of language and not sensitive to gender. Subtests: psychomotor coordination and motor speed; reasoning and planning abilities; spatial memory; attention and vigilance. Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) Other Neuropsychological Tests: MMSE, PGIBBD, AIIMS, NIMHANS, WMS. Mind map of the Mini-Mental State Examination, the PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction, the AIIMS and NIMHANS neuropsychological batteries and the Wechsler Memory Scale. Psycho Didi notes · p. 61 Basic exam of cognitive screening; 11 items. A score of 23/30 and lesser is considered pathological. Domains: orientation, repetition, verbal recall, attention, calculation, language and visual construction. Made in 1975, standardized in 1995. Time taken: 5–10 mins. Used for people with neurocognitive disorder. Drawbacks: heavily verbal; the test has a "floor effect" (can't tell high deterioration). The Postgraduate Institute of Brain Dysfunction (PGIBBD) Founder note. Given by Prashad and Verma , 1990; 2007. Language: Hindi; available for all. For ages: 20–59 years. 19 domains. 5 subtests: PGI Memory scale: immediate, recent, very short term, long term, verbal, non-verbal. Bhatia short scale: Koh's block design, Alexander Pass Along. VAIS: 1. info, 2. digit span, 3. arithmetic, 4. verbal comprehension. Nahor Benson test: organic brain pathology. Bender Gestalt Test. The Wechsler Memory Scale (WMS) Given for the first time in 1945. 4th edition: 2009. Working memory deficits indicate frontal lobe damage; long-term memory deficits indicate temporal lobe damage. Checks for auditory, visual, visual working, immediate, and delayed memory. Does not check much of: verbal memory or verbal working memory and remote memory. Time taken: 80 minutes. Checks for neurocognitive disorders (Korsakoff). The AIIMS Neuropsychological Battery Founder note. Given by Surya Gupta , 2000 — a Hindi adaptation of the Luria-Nebraska test. Training only given by the author; very expensive. 160 items; ages 15–80 years. Used to assess cognitive function; has versions for younger individuals. Scales: motor, tactile, visual, receptive speech, expressive speech, reading, writing, arithmetic, memory, intellectual processes, left hemisphere, right hemisphere, pathognomonic. The NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery Founder note. Version used: 2004 by Dr. Rao . Inspired by Luria-Nebraska. The test is available but the manual is not. Developed on the principles of localization and lateralization. Checks for attention, visual search, mental search, psychomotor deficit, working memory (frontal lobe damage). Also checks for temporal (BVRT) and parietal lobe (BGT) damage. Includes 19 tests. Popular tests: tower test, Stroop task, complex figure, finger tapping, WCST. 5 · Intelligence Tests Intelligence Tests: history and timeline. Scroll tracing intelligence testing from anthropometry to psychometric testing, next to a timeline of milestones from 1890 to 2014. Psycho Didi notes · p. 62 History Anthropometry (Francis Galton) Chronometry — RT test (Fechner) Mental Test (Cattell) Psychometric testing (Binet) Dates and timeline Year Milestone 1890 Cattell — Mental test. 1905 1st psychometric test by Binet to identify children with special needs. 1912 Stern gave the term IQ. 1916 IQ formula; Stanford-Binet test. 1917 Army Alpha (Robert Yerkes, 1917) and Army Beta test. 1939 Wechsler Bellevue scale introduced deviation IQ. 2003 Stanford-Binet Test-5. 2004 The Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children (KABC II). 2008 WAIS. 2012 WPPSI. 2014 WISC. Stanford-Binet Test-5 Stanford-Binet Test-5. Tree diagram of the Stanford-Binet 5 showing its key facts, basal and ceiling age, and the five factor scores with the tasks under each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 62 Follows Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory; given in 2003. 10 subtests; deviation IQ used; uses factor analysis. Age: 2–85 years. Key: basal and ceiling. Basal = the level below which the examinee is assumed to pass everything: in the older age-scale Binets, the highest age level at which all items are passed. Ceiling = the level above which the examinee is assumed to fail everything: the lowest age level at which all items are failed . Testing starts near the expected level, goes down until the basal is found and up until the ceiling is reached, then stops. Example. A child passes every item at the 6-year level (basal age 6), passes some items at 7 and 8, and fails every item at 9 (ceiling 9). Testing stops at 9; mental age = the basal age plus credit (in months) for each item passed above it. The SB5 (Gale Roid, 2003) is a point scale, so it states the same idea as rules: the basal is the level where a set number of correct answers is reached, and the ceiling is the point where a set number of wrong answers shows the items are too hard. Its two routing subtests (Nonverbal Fluid Reasoning: Object Series/Matrices, and Verbal Knowledge: Vocabulary) decide where testing starts. Heads up: the SB5 diagram above defines the ceiling as the "lowest level where we get all answers correct". That is wrong: the ceiling is where the examinee gets all (or a set number of) answers wrong . Basal = all right; ceiling = all wrong. 5 factor scores Fluid reasoning — matrices, absurdities, inductive reasoning. Knowledge — procedural, general knowledge, missing details, vocabulary, difficult words. Quantitative reasoning — arithmetic problem, word problem, counting. Visuospatial reasoning — puzzles, direction problems. Working memory — words, sentences, short visual info. Raven's Progressive Matrices Intelligence Tests: CAS-II, Kaufman tests and culture fair tests. Panel covering the Cognitive Assessment System-II, the three Kaufman tests (KABC, KAIT, KBIT), culture fair tests (Draw A Person, Leiter), the Culture Fair Intelligence Test and Raven's Progressive Matrices, with sample KBIT pictures and a Raven's matrix item. Psycho Didi notes · p. 63 Coloured Progressive Matrices (36 cards). Advanced Progressive Matrices (48 cards). Standard Progressive Matrices (60 cards). Power and speed test; measures Fluid Intelligence. Mean = 100; SD = 15. What an item looks like. Each item is a pattern or grid of figures with one piece missing (marked "?"). The examinee picks, from the options shown with it, the piece that completes the pattern. No words are needed, only spotting the rule. In the sample on p.63 the shape stays the same along each row (squares, stars, hexagons) while the shading changes across the columns (plain, dotted, striped), so the missing cell must be a striped hexagon : option B. The test was published by John C. Raven in 1938 to measure Spearman's g , especially "eductive" ability (working out relations). Items get harder within each set, hence "progressive". Trap: SPM = 60 items in 5 sets (A to E) of 12; CPM = 36 items (sets A, Ab, B) with coloured backgrounds, for young children and for older or impaired adults; APM = 48 items, for above-average adults. Real Raven items offer 6 or 8 answer choices; the p.63 sample shows only 3. Culture Fair Intelligence Test (CFIT) Founder note. By Raymond Cattell . Group test; speed and power test; 3 forms; only non-verbal test. Different from other tests in reading, experience, language, speed/tempo, environmental experiences. Can be given in groups. The Kaufman Adolescent and Adult Intelligence Test (KAIT) Founder note. Kaufman tests by Alan Kaufman . Age: 11–85+. Based on Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory (fluid and crystallized intelligence) and some part of Jean Piaget's theory. Culture biased. Cognitive Assessment System-II (CAS-II) Based on PASS theory (Das, Naglieri). Only for adolescents; used for scholarship tests. Contains the Naglieri Nonverbal Aptitude test. Mean: 100, S.D.: 3. The Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children (KABC) Based on PASS theory. 4 global scales: Simultaneous, Successive, Mental Processing, Achievement. Culture biased. The Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test (KBIT) Age: 4–90 years; both verbal and nonverbal. Time taken: 20 minutes. Mean: 100, SD: 15. Item format. The six pictures on p.63 are a sample item from the KBIT-2 (Alan and Nadeen Kaufman, 2004) subtest Verbal Knowledge : the examiner says a word or asks a general-knowledge question, and the examinee simply points to the one of six pictures that fits (a word like "storm", for instance, would be answered by pointing to the windy, rainy scene). The KBIT-2 has three subtests: Verbal Knowledge and Riddles (the crystallized, verbal scale) and Matrices (the fluid, nonverbal scale: choose the picture or design that completes a pattern). Answers need only pointing or a single word, with no reading, writing or timed motor work, which keeps it to about 20 minutes. Trap: the KBIT is a brief screening test, not a full IQ battery like the KABC or the WISC, so it is not used on its own for detailed diagnosis. Culture Fair Tests Draw A Person Test (DAPT) 1926; performance test to measure observation and conceptual thinking. Leiter International Performance Scale Performance test; made for African groups; elimination of verbal instruction; no time limit. Tests: reasoning, visualisation, attention, memory. 6 · Indian Intelligence Tests Indian Intelligence Tests. Tree diagram grouping Indian intelligence tests into a performance test (Bhatia's Battery), tests based on Binet's test (Binet Kamat, Kulshreshtha) and tests based on Wechsler's test (WAPIS, MISIC), with a photo of the MISIC kit. Psycho Didi notes · p. 63 Three groups. The diagram sorts the Indian tests by the model they copy. Knowing the group tells you how each test works: Group Tests What that means Performance test Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests (C. M. Bhatia) Non-verbal tasks done with materials (blocks, pass-along pieces, drawing patterns) instead of language, so it suits examinees with little schooling. Tests based on Binet's test Binet Kamat Test (V. V. Kamat); Kulshreshtha Intelligence Test (S. K. Kulshreshtha) Age scales: items are grouped by age level, the result is a mental age, and IQ is a ratio IQ (mental age ÷ chronological age × 100). Tests based on Wechsler's test WAPIS (Prabha Ramalingaswami); MISIC (Arthur J. Malin) Point scales: items are grouped into subtests by type (information, block design, and so on) rather than by age, adapted from the WAIS and WISC. Trap: Bhatia's battery is the classic Indian performance test; Binet Kamat is heavily verbal . Both Binet-based Indian tests use ratio IQ, the Wechsler-based ones do not use age levels. Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence Given in 1940; normed for ages 11–16 years. Performance test. Includes: Koh's block design — speed and power. Alexander Pass along — speed and power. Pattern drawing — speed and power. Immediate memory: digit span — verbal and power. Picture construction. Different norms for rural and urban population. Can be only administered individually. Not completely culture fair. Binet Kamat Test Bombay Karnataka version of the Binet Simon Scale; based on the 1916 Simon Binet test. Used ratio IQ. Ages: 3–22 years, separate norms. Measures: language, reasoning, conceptual thinking, social intelligence, memory, visuomotor performance. Heavily verbal — can't check subnormal intelligence. Items are not appropriate to current times; easy to administer. Can't differentiate between severe and profound mental retardation (intellectual disability). Both groups score at or near the bottom of the test, so it cannot tell them apart; the likely reason is a floor effect, since the easiest items are pitched at the 3-year level. It can show that a person is severely impaired, but not which of the two levels applies. Kulshreshtha Intelligence Test 1960; Hindi adaptation of the Stanford-Binet (Lewis Terman, 1916) test. Ages: 2–22 years; each age level = 6 items. Verbal and performance tests; uses ratio IQ. Tests based on Wechsler's test Wechsler Adult Performance Intelligence Scale (WAPIS) Founder note. Made by Prabha Ramalingaswami (1974). 11 subtests (from WAIS): 6 verbal, 5 non-verbal. Picture completion and picture arrangement have been modified. Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC) Founder note. Arthur J. Malin of Nagpur reformed Wechsler's scales. Ages: 6–15 years; 2–2.5 years. 11 subtests: 6 verbal: i. information, ii. general comprehension, iii. arithmetic, iv. analogy and similarity, v. vocabulary, vi. digit span. 5 non-verbal: i. block design, ii. picture completion, iii. object assembly, iv. symbol coding, v. maze. 7 · Personality Tests: overview Personality Tests. Tree diagram of personality assessment showing an introduction timeline and four types (personality inventories, non projective tests, projective tests, observation), with the California Personality Inventory, Bell's Adjustment Inventory and observational tests in boxes below. Psycho Didi notes · p. 64 Projective tests began in 1800. 1st test: Word Association test — Francis Galton, Emil Kraepelin, Carl Jung . 1916: Carl Jung's first standardized word association test. 1917: 1st objective test — Woodworth's Personal Data Sheet. Types / categories of personality assessment The diagram gives four types : Type What it is Examples Personality inventories (self-report: forced choice) The person answers fixed questions about themselves by picking from given answers (yes / no, true / false); scoring is objective. Bell's Adjustment Inventory, California inventory (below); MMPI Non-projective tests Structured (objective) tests with clear items and standard scoring. This book splits them into non-factor-analytic and factor-analytic tests. MMPI, MCMI, MBTI, EPPS (section 9); 16 PF, NEO-PI, EPQ (section 10) Projective tests An ambiguous stimulus (inkblot, picture, unfinished sentence, a drawing to make) and a free response; the idea is that people "project" their unconscious needs and conflicts onto it. The term "projective methods" was introduced by Lawrence K. Frank (1939). Rorschach, TAT, Rosenzweig P-F, sentence completion, HTP (section 8) Observation Observational tests — rating scales and interview technique. Rating scales: judgement about personality in some categories. Interviews: structured and unstructured. Behaviour rating scales, clinical interview Trap: "forced choice" here just means the person must pick one of the fixed answers instead of replying freely. In the strict technical sense, a forced-choice format pairs two statements of similar social desirability and asks which is more like you (as in the EPPS), which gives ipsative scores. Bell's Adjustment Inventory and the California inventory below are both examples of the first type, personality inventories (self-report). The standard name of the second is the California Psychological Inventory (CPI) , by Harrison Gough : a true / false inventory built for normal (non-clinical) people, measuring everyday "folk concepts" such as dominance, sociability and responsibility. Bell's inventory (Hugh M. Bell, 1934) measures adjustment in four areas on the student form: home, health, social and emotional. Bell's Adjustment Inventory 1934; to diagnose adjustment problems. Home: satisfaction/dissatisfaction; health: shyness, introversion. Student form and occupation form; 140 Qs. Adapted in Indian languages. California Personality Inventory 1957, 1987; work-related inventory. Measures behaviour in the organizational setting. 8 · Projective Tests Projective Tests: association techniques and construction tests. Page splitting projective tests into association techniques and construction tests, covering the Word Association Test, Rorschach Inkblot Test, Blacky's Picture Test, Thematic Apperception Test and Rosenzweig Picture Frustration Study. Psycho Didi notes · p. 65 Association techniques Rorschach Inkblot Test Founder note. 1921, by Herman Rorschach ; he created it while playing klexography. Projective vs objective. The Rorschach is a projective association technique studying unconscious thoughts, unlike objective self-report inventories (MMPI, 16PF). Scoring is subjective and system-dependent (Exner etc.), not criterion-keyed. Administration: 10 cards, 7×10 inches, shown one at a time in sequence. Card Theme i Paranoia ii Violence, communication, dominance iii Sexual preference iv Father card v Hostility, castration complex, schizophrenia vi Intimate relationships vii Mother card viii Emotions / complex situations ix Uncertainty / ambiguity x Life situation / oral fixation Phases: Performance proper. Enquiry: ask what, why, where it was seen. Testing the limits: done to give participants with weird responses another chance. Studies unconscious thoughts. Average number of responses: 20–25; per card: 3–5. Scoring system: Levey, Beck S., Hertz, Klopfer, Exner (1974). Latest scoring system by Exner : 1993. Scoring based on: location, determinant, form quality, content, popular responses. Blacky's Picture Test Based on Sigmund Freud's psychosexual stages; for children ages 5 and older; 11 cartoon stimuli. In addition to requesting a story for each card, the examiner also presents multiple-choice questions based on stages of psychosexual development. Word Association Test Founder note. Also known as free association technique. First systematically described by Francis Galton (1879); introduced into the psychological laboratory by Wilhelm Wundt ; first applied to the study of abnormality by Emil Kraepelin ; adapted for use as a projective technique by Carl Jung . Construction tests Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) Founder note. Given by Henry Murray and Christiana Morgan (1935, 43); based on Murray's theory of personology. Can be both idiographic and nomothetic. 19 cards, for male, female, boys, girls; total cards that can be given: 20. Blank card: Card no. 16. Bellack's scoring system is used. Analysis: Hero · Needs of the hero · Thema · Outcome. Needs of the hero: Needs motivated by desire for power, property, prestige, knowledge, creativity: achievement, acquisition, aggression, construction, counteraction, dominance, exposition, recognition, understanding. Needs motivated by affection, admiration, sympathy, love, dependence: affiliation, deference, nurturance, sex, succorance. Needs motivated by desire for freedom, change, excitement, play: autonomy, change/travel adventure, excitation/dissipation, play. Miscellaneous needs: abasement, blame avoidance, cognizance, harm avoidance, passivity, rejection, retention, sentience. Presses: Press of deprivation: acquisition, retention. Press descriptive of an empty, alien, or rejecting environment: lack of things/opportunities/friends, human support; loss; rejection; uncongenial environment. Press of coercion and restraint: dominance; imposed task, duty or training. Press descriptive of a hostile aggressive environment: aggression. Press of danger, injury, death: affliction, death of hero, physical danger, physical injury. Press of friendliness, sympathy, respect, dependent, love: affiliation, deference, nurturance, sex, succorance. Miscellaneous press: birth of offspring, claustrum, cognizance, example, exposition, luck. 3 levels of interpretation: descriptive level, interpretive level, diagnostic level. What to ask: current situation; thoughts and feelings of the character; preceding events; outcome. Focus on: content of the story, feeling or tone, subject's behaviour apart from the responses. How these fit the TAT. Murray's standard instruction asks the examinee to tell a dramatic story for each picture: what led up to the scene ( preceding events ), what is happening now ( current situation ), what the characters are thinking and feeling , and how it ends ( outcome ). If a story leaves one of these out, the examiner asks for it. While interpreting, the clinician looks at three things: the content of the story (who the hero is, the hero's needs, the press from the environment, the outcome), its feeling or tone (hopeful, gloomy, hostile and so on), and the examinee's behaviour apart from the responses (long pauses, rejecting a card, side comments). Trap: both lists belong to the TAT , as the p.65 diagram shows. A Rorschach response is a percept ("this looks like a bat"), not a story, so "content of the story" cannot apply to it. In the Rosenzweig P-F Study the examinee does not tell a story at all: they write, in the empty speech balloon, the first reply the frustrated person would make. Rosenzweig Picture Frustration Study Consists of 24 cartoon pictures each portraying two persons in a frustrating situation. Responses are scored as to whether, and to what degree, they indicate that the subject exhibits aggression towards the source of the frustration; assumes blame or guilt as the cause of frustration; or justifies, minimizes or denies the frustration. The score is based on a total of nine factors derived from combinations of three types of reaction and three directions of aggression. Three types of reaction: obstacle dominance, ego defense, need persistence. Three directions of aggression: extraggression (blames others), intraggression (blames self), imaggression (blames no one, glosses over it). Rosenzweig's older names: extrapunitive, intropunitive, impunitive. Choice or ordering tests: Szondi Projective Tests: choice or ordering, completion and expressive tests. Page linking projective tests to choice or ordering tests (Szondi), completion tests (Sentence Completion, Sack's Sentence Completion) and expressive tests (House Tree Person, Draw A Man, Kinetic Family Drawing). Psycho Didi notes · p. 66 Founder note. Developed by Leopold Szondi in 1935. Intended to reveal a person's innermost suppressed traits, the parts of yourself you have pushed down into your subconscious. Number of photos: 48. The test involves looking at a series of 48 photos of people with distinct expressions on their faces. The patient picks the friendliest faces and the unfriendliest, the idea being that a person identifies with like people and that their choices from the pictures would represent traits of themselves. Completion tests Sentence Completion Test Semi-projective. 1940: first given by Rohde and Hidreth . Sack's Sentence Completion Test Founder note. By Joseph M. Sacks . Developed to explore specific clusters of attitudes or significant areas of an individual's life. Number of items: 60. 4 subscales: family, sex, relationships, self concepts — each measured on 15 different attitudes such as fears, guilt, and goals. A rating sheet with the four appropriate stems rearranged under the 15 attitude headings allows a clinician to rate the examinee's responses on a continuum that ranges from no significant disturbance to severely disturbed. Expressive tests House Tree Person Test (HTP) Asks for the drawing of a house, a tree, and a person, in order to evaluate them together and globally. Person: who is the person; how old he is; what does he do best; what does he like least. Tree: what kind of tree it is; how old it is; what season it is; has someone tried to cut it down; who waters it; does it have enough light to grow. Usually administered on children. Draw A Man Test Founder note. Goodenough , 1926. Scoring: Chen-Sea (2000). Patients are given a blank piece of paper (8.5×11) entitled "Draw an Entire Man" and a pencil, and are asked to draw an entire man from memory. Kinetic Family Drawing Founder note. Burns and Kaufman , 1970. Helps assess a child's self-concept and family dynamics. The child is asked to draw a picture of their family, including themselves, "doing something". 9 · Non-Projective Tests (Non Factor Analytic) Non-Projective Tests (Non Factor Analytic): MMPI family, MCMI, MBTI. Boxed fact cards for the MMPI, MMPI-2, MMPI-II-RF, MMPI-A, MMPI-3, the Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory and the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator. Psycho Didi notes · p. 67 Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) Founder note. Given by Starke Hathaway & J. C. McKinley (University of Minnesota, published 1943); for adults. 1989 is the year of the revision, the MMPI-2 (below), and "ages 18 and above" also belongs to the MMPI-2. 566 items (550 different statements, 16 of them printed twice). The p.67 MMPI card says 567, but 567 is the MMPI-2 count. 1943: 1st test of validity scales. 1989: Revision. MMPI-A published in 1992. Uses the criterion keyed method (criterion validity). T scores. Time taken: 40–45 minutes. Validity Scales CNS — cannot say. L — Lie scale. F — Infrequency scale, faking bad (1st half). K — Defensiveness / Evasiveness. Fb — Faking bad (last half). VRIN — Variable Response Inconsistency. TRIN — True Response Inconsistency. F-K — Honesty of test. S — Superlative self presentation. Fp — Faking psychopathology in a clinical setting. Fs — Overreporting somatic symptoms. Why it matters. People scoring high on the K scale show high adjustment, insight, higher socioeconomic status, education. People scoring low on the K scale: masochistic tendencies. Clinical Scales Hs — Hypochondriasis D — Depression Hy — Hysteria Pd — Psychopathic deviate Mf — Masculinity Femininity Pa — Paranoia Pt — Psychasthenia Sc — Schizophrenia Ma — Hypomania Si — Social Introversion Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory 2 (MMPI-2) Founder note. Still published under Hathaway & McKinley's names (1989); the restandardization was done by Butcher, Dahlstrom, Graham, Tellegen & Kaemmer with new, more representative US norms. Ages 18 and above; 567 items . Validity scales and clinical scales: same as MMPI. It kept the original L, F and K validity scales and the 10 clinical scales, and added new validity scales: VRIN, TRIN and Fb came with the MMPI-2, and Fp and S were added in later updates. Fs (listed with the MMPI validity scales above) is an MMPI-2-RF scale. Version Author / Year Age Items Scales MMPI Hathaway & McKinley (1943) Adults 566 Validity + Clinical MMPI-2 Hathaway & McKinley (1989 restandardization by Butcher et al.) 18+ 567 Validity + Clinical (same as MMPI, plus new validity scales) + the Other Scales below MMPI-2-RF (restructured form) 2008 18+ 338 50 (an alternative to MMPI-II, not a total replacement) MMPI-A Adolescents 14–18 478 Validity and clinical same as MMPI-2; additionally F1 & F2 scales and other subscales MMPI-3 Yossef Ben-Porath & Auke Tellegen (2020) — 335 52 Other Scales 28 Harris-Lingoes subscales. Content scales: Butcher, Graham, Williams & Ben-Porath (1990). Content component scales (Ben-Porath & Sherwood, 1993). Personality Psychopathology Five scales (PSY-5; Harkness et al., 2002). Restructured clinical scales (Tellegen et al., 2003). These supplementary scales are scored on the MMPI-2 , which is why the p.67 diagram puts the "Other Scales" box under the MMPI-2 card. The Harris-Lingoes subscales are older (built for the original MMPI in 1955) and were carried over; the content, content component, PSY-5 and restructured clinical scales were all developed for the MMPI-2. Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory (MCMI) Founder note. Given by Theodore Millon . 4th edition based on DSM-5. 5th grade reading level; made for age 18+. 195 true or false questions. Time taken: 25–30 mins. Scales 15 personality pattern scales. 10 clinical syndrome scales. 5 validity scales: 3 modifying indices, 2 random response indicators. 45 Grossman personality facet scales. Clinical scales — severe SS — thought disorder CC — major depression PP — delusional disorder A — generalized anxiety H — somatic symptom N — Bipolar D — Persistent depression B — Alcohol use T — Drug Use R — PTS Validity Scales X — disclosure Y — desirability Z — debasement V — invalidity W — inconsistency Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) Founder note. By Isabel Myers and Katherine Briggs ; made by the theoretical method (Carl Jung). Highly used by organizations. Interest inventory: Ipsative (every single option has the same value). Types: extroversion vs introversion; sensing vs intuiting; thinking vs feeling; judging vs perceiving. Criticism: little scientific evidence; weak validity; incomprehensive and vague. Allport, Vernon & Lindzey — Study of Values Scale Non-Projective Tests (Non Factor Analytic): Study of Values, EPPS, Holland, MPQ. Boxed fact cards for the Allport, Vernon and Lindzey Study of Values scale, the Edwards Personal Preference Schedule, Holland's Interest Inventory with a RIASEC hexagon, and the Multiphasic Personality Questionnaire. Psycho Didi notes · p. 68 Ipsative; given in 1931. Based on six value orientations: theoretical, economic, aesthetic, social, political, religious. 240 points; interest inventory. Edwards Personal Preference Schedule (EPPS) Founder note. By Allen L. Edwards ; derived from Murray's theory. Interest inventory: ipsative. Validity scales: social desirability, consistency. 225 items; used in vocational training. Based on Murray's needs: Achievement, Deference, Order, Exhibition, Autonomy, Affiliation, Intraception, Succourance, Dominance, Abasement, Nurturance, Change, Endurance, Heterosexuality, Aggression. Holland's Interest Inventory Based on Holland's Theory of Vocational Types or the RIASEC model. Vocational Types: Realistic (R), Investigative (I), Artistic (A), Social (S), Enterprising (E), Conventional (C). The theory is John L. Holland's (first set out in 1959): people and work environments can both be described by six types, and people are most satisfied in an environment that matches their type ( congruence ). His best-known test is the Self-Directed Search (SDS). The p.68 hexagon shows what each type likes: Type Likes (from the hexagon) Typical jobs Realistic (R) Building, machines, things, plants, animals, outdoors, hands-on work Mechanic, electrician, farmer, engineer Investigative (I) Observing, analyzing, problem solving, ideas, science, math Scientist, researcher, doctor Artistic (A) Creating, music, drama, design, media, self-expression Musician, writer, actor, designer Social (S) Teaching, helping, guiding, serving people, communicating Teacher, counsellor, nurse, psychologist Enterprising (E) Leading, business, persuading, decisions, action, risk-taking Manager, salesperson, lawyer, entrepreneur Conventional (C) Data, routines, procedures, standards, detail Accountant, clerk, bank teller Trap: the order around the hexagon is fixed (R, I, A, S, E, C). Neighbouring types are the most alike (R and I), and opposite types are the least alike: R vs S, I vs E, A vs C. A person is described by a three-letter Holland code made of their top three types, for example SIA. Multiphasic Personality Questionnaire (MPQ) Founder note. Developed by Murthy (1964); the Indian version of MMPI-2. Age: 18 and above. 100 statements, forced choice type. 2 validity scales: K scale, Repressor Sensitiser. 7 clinical scales: Anxiety, Manic, Psychopathic deviation, Depression, Paranoid, Schizophrenia, Hysteria. 10 · Non-Projective Tests (Factor Analytic) Non-Projective Tests (Factor Analytic): 16 PF, EPQ, NEO-PI. Fact cards for Cattell's 16 PF (traits, 16 source traits, types of data), the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire and the NEO-PI. Psycho Didi notes · p. 68 16 PF Founder note. By Raymond Cattell ; made using factor analysis. Type of traits: temperamental, ability, dynamic (bipolar). Surface traits are a combination of source traits. Oblique design used for factor analysis. Gave the specification equation R = f(S,P). Identified 11 second-order factors. Used multiple abstract variance analysis to measure heritability of traits. 16 source traits Warmth · Reasoning · Emotional stability · Dominance · Liveliness · Rule conscious · Social boldness · Sensitivity · Vigilance · Abstractness · Privateness · Apprehension · Open to change · Self reliance · Perfection · Tension. Types of data Key. Objective measurement: the participant should not know what is being measured. L data — D, J, K, P factors are a part of L data. Q data T data Global 5 scale — created out of second-order factors. Response style scales: acquiescence; impression management (narcissists will show a lot of social desirability); infrequency. NEO-PI Founder note. By Paul Costa and Robert McCrae ; based on the five factor model / big five model. Year: 1978. No lie scale, no validity scales. Number of items: 240; orthogonal rotation used. Three versions: NEO-PI (1985), NEO-PI-R (1992), NEO-PI-3 (2005). Domains measured by NEO-PI: Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism, Openness, Conscientiousness. Each domain has 6 facets. The psychoticism scale of EPI correlates negatively with agreeableness and conscientiousness scales. Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ) Founder note. By Hans Eysenck . Theory: Type → Trait → Habit → S-R (smallest). Focuses on nature (biological disposition) only. 108 items; current version: EPQ-R (1985). Can measure 22 personality disorders.
