Three dimensions (PEN): Psychoticism – Impulse control (gave this dimension after working at Maudsley hospital). Extroversion – Introversion. Neuroticism – Emotional Stability. 4th dimension: Lie scale. Reliability vs validity check. Note the distinct validity-scale families across objective tests: MMPI (Starke Hathaway and J. Charnley McKinley, 1943) uses criterion-keyed validity scales (L, F, K, VRIN, TRIN…); MCMI uses X/Y/Z/V/W; EPPS uses social desirability + consistency; MPQ uses K + Repressor-Sensitiser; the 16PF uses response-style scales (acquiescence, impression management, infrequency); NEO-PI has no validity/lie scales, whereas the EPQ (Hans Eysenck and Sybil Eysenck, 1975) adds a Lie scale as its 4th dimension. Don't confuse a validity scale (detects faking) with a clinical/content scale (measures the trait).

title: Psychological Interventions
text: Psychological Interventions — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Psychological Interventions Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Psychodynamic → Sigmund Freud Behaviour therapy: 3 wings CBT waves 1–3 Humanistic & existential Stress, coping & counselling What this covers. The full sweep of psychological interventions: psychodynamic psychotherapy (Freud, defence mechanisms, transference) and transactional analysis (Eric Berne); behaviour therapy across its classical-conditioning, operant and modelling wings; the three waves of cognitive-behaviour therapy (Beck's CT and Ellis's REBT, then DBT, MBCT, MBSR (Jon Kabat-Zinn, 1979) and ACT with other third-wave therapies); EMDR (Francine Shapiro); gestalt therapy (Fritz Perls) and its many techniques; humanistic and existential therapy (Carl Rogers, Karl Jaspers, Sartre, Viktor Frankl, Irvin Yalom); stress and coping models; and the principles of counselling and guidance. Original diagrams. 25 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 70 to 80) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Psychodynamic Psychotherapy · 2 · Transactional Analysis · 3 · Behaviour Therapy · 4 · Cognitive-Behaviour Therapy (Waves 1–3) · 5 · EMDR · 6 · Gestalt Therapy · 7 · Humanistic & Existential Therapy · 8 · Stress and Coping · 9 · Counselling and Guidance 1 · Psychodynamic Psychotherapy Psychodynamic psychotherapy: Freud. Infographic page on Freud with his photo, early life, career, important therapy processes, defence mechanisms, dreams and dream work, and an illustration of a client on a couch with a therapist. Psycho Didi notes · p. 70 Psychodynamic psychotherapy → Sigmund Freud. Worked with Joseph Breuer (the case of Anna 'O' ); influenced by Jean-Martin Charcot (hypnosis) and Breuer (catharsis). Freud — early life & career Was his mother's favourite child; observed his own life; was attracted to his mother and scared of his father. Started teaching at the University of Vienna in 1873. Died in Britain from jaw cancer. Career milestones: cocaine exploration; influence of Jean-Martin Charcot (hypnosis) and Josef Breuer (catharsis); movement from resistance to suggestion → concentration technique → free association; publication of Studies on Hysteria . Defence mechanisms Defence Core idea Repression Keeping unpleasant memories or thoughts buried in the unconscious. Primal : innately part of the Id. Proper : unacceptable derivatives of original id impulses. Denial Refusing to recognise an unpleasant reality. Rationalization Creating a socially acceptable excuse to justify unacceptable behaviour. Reaction formation Not acknowledging unacceptable impulses and over-emphasising their opposite. Projection Transferring one's unacceptable qualities or impulses to others. Important processes Process Meaning Resistance Reluctance to discuss certain topics; conscious defence mechanisms. Transference The patient projects feelings meant for others onto the therapist. Counter-transference The therapist develops emotional reactions towards the patient. Working through Discussing emotionally charged material over many therapy sessions. Trap — transference vs counter-transference. Transference = patient → therapist (patient projects feelings for others onto the therapist). Counter-transference = therapist → patient (therapist develops emotional reactions towards the patient). Dreams Manifest content: the clearly identifiable stories, characters, events and actions. Latent content: the unconscious thoughts, desires, fears and conflicts. Dream work Mechanism Function Condensation Condensing multiple thoughts into a single dream element or symbol. Displacement Shifting emotional significance from one object to another. Symbolization Representing an action or idea through symbols. Secondary revision Rationalizing latent content. 2 · Transactional Analysis Transactional analysis: Eric Berne. Introduction and four types of analysis beside three circles showing the Parent ego (nurturing and critical), Adult ego and Child ego (free and adapted). Psycho Didi notes · p. 71 Transactional Analysis → Eric Berne. Transactional Analysis is a psychotherapeutic method characterised by a creative combination of cognitive and psychodynamically oriented psychotherapy, enriched by aspects of communication therapy and gestalt therapy (Fritz Perls) processes. Types of analysis Structural analysis: individual personality analysis. Transactional analysis: dialogue analysis. Game analysis: saying something and meaning something else (analysis of ulterior transactions). Script analysis: compulsive, rigid transactions that people act out compulsively. Ego states Parent ego — Nurturing parent and Critical parent. Adult ego. Child ego — Free child and Adapted child. Transactions Transactions. Three Parent-Adult-Child diagrams with arrows showing complementary, crossed and ulterior transactions between two people. Psycho Didi notes · p. 71 Complementary transactions. Crossed transactions. Ulterior transactions: e.g. saying "You love my brother so much!" while really meaning "You don't love me." A transaction is Eric Berne's unit of social exchange: one person sends a message (the stimulus) from one of their ego states to an ego state of the other person, and the other replies (the response). In the diagrams each arrow is one message, drawn from the sender's ego state to the ego state it is aimed at. Berne gave one "rule of communication" for each type. Type What the arrows show Example Berne's rule Complementary (parallel) The reply comes from the same ego state the message was aimed at, and goes back to the ego state that sent it, so the two arrows run parallel. The diagram shows the simplest case: Adult to Adult, answered Adult to Adult. "What time is the exam?" (A to A). "Ten o'clock." (A to A). As long as transactions stay complementary, communication can go on indefinitely. Crossed The reply comes from a different ego state from the one addressed, or goes to a different ego state from the one that sent it, so the arrows cross. In the diagram an Adult-to-Adult question gets a Parent-to-Child reply. "Have you seen my keys?" (A to A). "You're always losing things, you're so careless!" (P to C). When a transaction is crossed, communication breaks down until one or both people shift ego states. Ulterior Two messages travel at once. The social level is the overt message, the actual words (by convention a solid arrow, usually Adult to Adult). The psychological level is the hidden message (by convention a dashed arrow, usually from or to the Parent or Child). The words "You love my brother so much!" sound like a plain observation; the hidden message (the dashed arrow) is "You don't love me", a hurt Child asking for reassurance. The outcome is decided at the psychological level, not the social level. Traps. Complementary does not mean Adult-only or pleasant: a Parent-to-Child scolding answered Child-to-Parent ("Go to bed!" / "Okay, sorry") is still complementary, because the arrows are parallel. Ulterior transactions are the raw material of games (Berne, Games People Play , 1964), which is why game analysis is called the analysis of ulterior transactions. In the ulterior diagram above the ego states are drawn unusually (the hidden message sits on the Adult line); go by the convention that the dashed arrow carries the hidden message. 3 · Behaviour Therapy Behaviour therapy: introduction, applications and features. Introduction and assumptions of behaviour therapy, its applications and fields of use, and its key features, with a small illustration of three people. Psycho Didi notes · p. 72 Behaviour therapy is the application of experimentally derived principles of learning to the treatment of psychological disorders. Assumptions An empirical approach. Most behaviour is learned and therefore can be unlearned. Maladaptive behaviours are learned in the same manner as adaptive ones. The historical account of the development of a problem behaviour is less relevant than the present factors. It rejects the assumptions of traditional trait theory. Features Focus on present factors. Functional assessment and behavioural analysis. Recognition of individual–environment interaction. Active client participation. Two core features: extinction and counter-conditioning . Goal is to reduce maladaptive behaviours. Applications Used in treating anxiety, depression, PTSD, substance abuse, eating and sexual disorders, and hypertension. Applied across diverse fields: developmental disability, mental illness, education and special education, community psychology, clinical psychology, rehabilitation, business, self-management, and sports-psychology interventions. Techniques based on classical conditioning Techniques based on classical conditioning. Notes on systematic desensitization with its steps, aversion therapy, and flooding and implosion, with small illustrations. Psycho Didi notes · p. 72 Systematic desensitization Systematic desensitization → Joseph Wolpe (1958). Based on reciprocal inhibition : the process in which maladaptive responses learned due to prior conditioning with aversive events are eliminated by developing antagonistic responses. Steps: Jacobson's Progressive Muscle Relaxation (JPMR). Development of an anxiety hierarchy and exposure in vitro . Desensitization (Subjective Unit of Distress < 25). Flooding Involves therapist-controlled, prolonged exposure to anxiety-provoking conditioned stimuli (CS), simultaneously blocking the individual's chance of escape and avoidance. Implosion Implosion → Thomas Stampfl (1966). A variant of flooding, but it takes place at the imaginary level. Trap — systematic desensitization vs flooding. Systematic desensitization (Wolpe) is graded : it climbs an anxiety hierarchy with relaxation, keeping distress low (reciprocal inhibition). Flooding is maximal : prolonged full-intensity exposure with escape/avoidance blocked, no gradual hierarchy. Implosion (Stampfl) = flooding done in imagination. Aversion therapy An avoidance-learning method in which the individual is required to perform a response to avoid punishment. Example: alcohol + disulfiram causes vomiting, so the person learns to avoid alcohol. Used for treating OCD, paraphilia and substance-use disorders. Techniques based on operant conditioning (1st wave) Techniques based on operant conditioning (1st wave). Differential reinforcement and its four types, token economy, response cost, time out, shaping and chaining. Psycho Didi notes · p. 72 Differential reinforcement Refers to the implementation of two clearly different degrees of reinforcement for two behaviours, one of which is to be replaced by the other. Type Purpose DRO — of other behaviour (or zero-rate behaviour) Reinforcing the non-occurrence of the target behaviour. DRL — of low-rate behaviour Designed to decrease a behaviour to an acceptable level. DRI — of incompatible behaviour Reinforcing responses that are topographically incompatible with the possibility of the target behaviour. DRA — of alternate behaviour The reinforced behaviour need not be topographically incompatible; it may be any desirable alternate behaviour. Other operant techniques Technique Core idea Token economy (Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin, 1968) A reinforcement system based on the delivery of tokens. Tokens earned for specific target behaviour can be spent on different things within a defined therapeutic environment, or saved for future purchases. Response cost Withdrawal of acquired positive reinforcers following undesirable or problematic behaviour. Time out Temporarily separating a person from an environment where an unacceptable behaviour has occurred. Example: a player getting a red card in a football match. Shaping Reinforcing behaviours that are successively closer approximations of the desired or targeted behaviour. Chaining Teaching a behaviour using behaviour chains — sequences of individual behaviours that, when linked together, form a terminal behaviour. Techniques based on modelling Techniques based on modelling. Introduction, functions and variants of modelling, with a nesting doll illustration. Psycho Didi notes · p. 72 Modelling → Albert Bandura (S-O-R theory). Process of learning: attention → retention → motor reproduction → motivation. Functions: teaching through demonstration, promoting behaviour, motivating behaviour, anxiety reduction, and discouraging behaviours. Variants: Overt : live modelling, symbolic modelling (film, video), participant modelling, self-modelling. The model is actually seen. Covert : imaginal modelling (the client only imagines the model). 4 · Cognitive-Behaviour Therapy (Waves 1–3) Key — the three waves. 1st wave = behaviour therapy (operant/classical conditioning). 2nd wave = cognitive therapy — Beck's CT and Ellis's REBT. 3rd wave = acceptance/mindfulness-based therapies (DBT, MBCT, MBSR (Jon Kabat-Zinn), ACT, and others). Beck's Cognitive Therapy (2nd wave) Beck’s cognitive therapy (2nd wave). Introduction to Beck’s cognitive therapy, a cognitive triad triangle of self, world and future around negative feelings, and a list of twelve cognitive distortions. Psycho Didi notes · p. 73 Cognitive therapy → Aaron Beck. Based on the concept that our thoughts, feelings, physical sensations and actions are interconnected, and that negative thoughts and feelings can trap us in a vicious cycle. Cognitive triad Self — "I am a failure." World — "Everybody is unfair." Future — "I will never succeed." Aaron Beck's negative cognitive triad is his model of the thinking in depression: a negative view of the self (worthless, a failure), of the world (other people and experiences are unfair, demands are too great) and of the future (things will never get better). In the diagram these three corners surround "Negative feelings" at the centre: the three negative views feed the low mood, and the low mood makes the negative views seem more true, which is the vicious cycle the introduction describes. Therapy breaks the cycle by catching the distortions below and testing them against evidence. Traps. The triad belongs to Beck, not Ellis. Its "future" corner is hopelessness, the part most closely tied to suicide risk. Do not mix it up with Seligman's explanatory-style dimensions (permanent, global, internal), which are about how a person explains the causes of events, not about views of self, world and future. Cognitive distortions Distortion Meaning All or nothing Dichotomous, extremes of language such as "always". Mental filter Only paying attention to certain evidence, skewing it as meaning more than it does. Mind reading Assuming you know what someone else is thinking or feeling. Overgeneralizing Seeing a pattern based on a single event, or being overly broad in your conclusions. Disqualifying the positive A type of mental filter discounting the good things that have happened or that you have done. Fortune telling Assuming you know what will happen in the future. Magnification Blowing things out of proportion. Emotional reasoning "Because I'm thinking or feeling it, it must be true." Labelling Assigning labels to ourselves or others, putting people in a box so they can't and won't change. Minimization Inappropriately shrinking something to make it seem less important; rationalization, justification, blaming. Shoulds and musts Unrealistic expectations. Personalization Taking responsibility for something that is not yours to own. Self-instruction training Self instruction training. Steps of Meichenbaum’s self instruction training, with an illustration of a hand pointing at an open book. Psycho Didi notes · p. 73 Self-instruction training → Donald Meichenbaum. Modelling: demonstrating assertive behaviour. Practice: role playing. Self-instruction: overt, then covert. Practice in real life. Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy (REBT) Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy. Notes on Ellis’s REBT with an A-B-C-D-E flow diagram, the three major irrational clusters and REBT techniques. Psycho Didi notes · p. 73 REBT → Albert Ellis (a directive therapy). Ellis coined the term musterbation to indicate that irrational beliefs are usually expressed as musts, shoulds, ought-tos, have-tos and got-tos. The ABCDE model Ellis's core idea is that events do not upset us directly; our beliefs about events do. The diagram runs A → B → C, then D challenges B and leads to E. Letter Stands for Example: failing an exam A Adversity or Activating event: what happened. You fail the exam. B Belief about A, here an irrational one (a rigid "must"). "I must never fail. Failing proves I am worthless." C Consequences : the emotional and behavioural result of B. Depression, shame, avoiding your books. D Disputation : the therapist and client actively challenge B (is it logical, is there evidence, does it help?). "Where is it written that I must never fail? Does one failure make a whole person worthless?" E New effective rational belief (effective new philosophy) that replaces B. "I strongly prefer to pass. Failing is disappointing, not a catastrophe, and I can prepare better." The feeling shifts from depression to healthy concern, and studying resumes. Traps. In REBT it is B, not A, that causes C: the same exam result upsets two students differently because their beliefs differ. Textbooks write A as "Activating event"; this diagram writes "Adversity"; both are accepted. D is the therapy step itself, which is why REBT counts as active and directive. Three major irrational clusters: "I must do well and win approval for my performances." "Others must treat me kindly and considerately." "Conditions under which I live must be arranged so that I get practically everything I want comfortably, quickly and easily." Techniques: Socratic questioning, confrontation, role playing, and shame-attacking exercises (homework outside of therapy). Trap — Beck vs Albert Ellis. Beck (Cognitive Therapy) targets cognitive distortions and the cognitive triad (self–world–future) through collaborative empiricism and Socratic guided discovery. Ellis (REBT) targets irrational beliefs ("musterbation": musts/shoulds) and is more directive/confrontational, using the ABC framework and shame-attacking exercises. Third-wave therapies (3rd wave) Cognitive-behaviour therapy: 3rd wave. Four boxes on MBCT, ACT with its six-process triangle, MBSR, and DBT with its four skill modules, plus a list of other third-wave therapies. Psycho Didi notes · p. 74 Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT) DBT → Marsha M. Linehan. Emerged as a treatment for chronically parasuicidal women with Borderline Personality Disorder. Three main principles: Everything is interconnected or interrelated. Reality is not static. The truth (which is always evolving) can be found by integrating or synthesizing differing (and possibly opposite) views. Four core skill modules: core mindfulness skills, interpersonal effectiveness skills, emotion regulation skills, and distress tolerance skills. Steps / stages: Identifying safety and life-threatening behaviours. Addressing therapy-interfering behaviours. Enhancing quality of life. Adaptation and growth. Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT) MBCT → Zindel Segal, Mark Williams & John Teasdale. Features: thought-process focused; promotes a new way of being with painful affect and challenging circumstances; distinguishing thoughts as thoughts (vs statements of fact); noticing and allowing thoughts and feelings without fixing, changing or avoiding; behavioural interventions focused on developing present-moment awareness; and the therapist also embodies the approach. Structure: 8 consecutive weekly sessions of about 2 hours each — Phase 1 (teaching), Phase 2 (application). Used for: anxiety disorders, bipolar disorder, depression associated with medical illness, low mood, unhappiness, depression-relapse prevention, and treatment-resistant depression. Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) Structure: 8 consecutive weekly sessions, 5 hours per week — Phase 1 (teaching), Phase 2 (application). Features: focuses on cultivating mindfulness, contemplation, listening and speaking; a briefer integrative practice. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) ACT → Steven Hayes. The ACT acronym: A: Accept your thoughts and feelings, and be present. C: Choose a valued direction. T: Take action. Six core processes (grouped as Open up / Be present / Do what matters): Contact with the present moment (be here now). Defusion (watch your thinking). Acceptance (open up). Self as context (pure awareness). Values (know what matters). Committed action (doing what it takes). The triangle in the diagram sorts the six processes into three pillars, two per pillar: Pillar Processes What it means in practice Be present Contact with the present moment; Self as context Paying attention to here and now, and noticing thoughts from the stance of an observing self ("I am the one noticing this thought"). Open up Defusion; Acceptance Stepping back from thoughts so they lose their grip ("I am having the thought that I'm a failure"), and making room for painful feelings instead of fighting them. Do what matters Values; Committed action Knowing what you care about and taking concrete steps towards it, even while discomfort is present. At the centre the diagram writes "Therapeutic process". In Steven Hayes's six-sided hexaflex model the centre is psychological flexibility , the overall goal of ACT that all six processes build. The simpler three-pillar "triflex" (Be present, Open up, Do what matters) is the version popularised by Russ Harris in ACT Made Simple (2009). Trap. ACT does not try to change or dispute the content of thoughts (that is Beck and Ellis, 2nd wave). It changes your relationship to thoughts (defusion, acceptance) and then points behaviour at values. The goal is psychological flexibility, not symptom removal. Other third-wave therapies Functional Analytic Psychotherapy (FAP). Metacognitive Therapy (MCT). Compassion Focused Therapy (CFT). 5 · Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR). Key facts about EMDR and its five-step procedure, with an illustration of a person hugging her knees beside two shadow figures. Psycho Didi notes · p. 75 EMDR → Francine Shapiro (1987). Considered a behaviour therapy by some authors. Used in PTSD. Not falsifiable. Book: Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing: Basic Principles, Protocols . Procedure History taking. Desensitization: focus on emotion and bodily sensation. Bilateral stimulation: eye movement, tactile, auditory stimulation. Reprocessing: the trauma that occurred in the past. Installation: of positive beliefs. 6 · Gestalt Therapy Gestalt therapy. One box covering the introduction to gestalt therapy, the integration sequence, boundaries, contact and its levels, types of awareness, and contact disturbances. Psycho Didi notes · p. 75 Gestalt therapy → Fritz Perls and Laura Perls (1940s). Influenced by the existential school, phenomenology and field theory. Focuses on re-owning disowned parts of the self. Self: internal and external (one dominates or is dominated). Real change comes when we try to be our true self rather than being someone else. Increasing awareness enables informed choices and leads to a more meaningful life. Insight comes through the help of therapy. A directional, confrontational therapy Emphasizes that one must understand the field-theory diagram in order to understand oneself. Clients should take responsibility for their life problems. Movement from environmental support to self-support. A confrontational therapy style — Perls intentionally frustrated clients (skilful frustration) . Focuses on restoring awareness. Types of awareness (Polster & Polster, 1973) Sensation and action. Feeling. Wants. Values and assessment. Focus on current experience: the here and now; the what and how. Contact and levels Contact: interacting meaningfully with others. Fusion: fusing with others. Level of contact Description Phony layer People complimenting when they want something from you. Phobic layer Avoidance of pain, grief. Impasse layer Unable to change and unable to solve. Implosive layer Becoming aware of self but keeping feelings inside. Explosive layer Taking action and expression. When contact is not genuine and authentic (Polster & Polster) Disturbance Meaning Introjection Swallowing whole, or accepting others' views without questioning. Retroflection Doing to ourselves what we would like to do to other people. Projection Assigning aspects of ourselves onto others. Deflection Avoidance. Confluence The boundary between oneself and others becomes muted. Integration sequence Discovery: self-realization prompting newfound awareness. Accommodation: skills to navigate challenging situations. Assimilation: learning to influence the environment. Boundaries Boundaries are rigid and must be challenged and crossed; language must be used as a method to challenge boundaries. Types of boundaries: body boundaries, value boundaries, familiarity boundaries, expressive boundaries. Gestalt therapy techniques Gestalt therapy techniques. Ten gestalt therapy techniques, each with a short description and an illustration. Psycho Didi notes · p. 76 Technique Description The Internal Dialogue Exercise (top dog vs underdog) The topdog is the voice of what the person should do; the underdog is the rebellious part that resists the topdog's demands. The client converses as both. The Empty-Chair Technique (by Joseph Moreno) A role-playing technique in which all the parts are played by the client, so introjects can surface and the client can experience the conflict more fully. Future Projection Technique An anticipated event is brought into the present moment and acted out. Making the Rounds Asking a person in a group to go up to others and either speak to or do something with each person — to confront, to risk, to disclose the self, to experiment with new behaviour, and to grow and change. The Reversal Exercise Clients take the plunge into the very thing fraught with anxiety and make contact with submerged, denied parts of themselves. The Rehearsal Exercise Rehearsing aloud in a group so that others can experience the internal thinking process. The Exaggeration Exercise Repeating and exaggerating a movement or gesture to help clients become more aware of their emotions. Staying With the Feeling At key moments when clients wish to flee an unpleasant feeling, the therapist urges them to stay with and go deeper into the feeling or behaviour they wish to avoid. Dream Work The Gestalt approach does not interpret and analyze dreams; instead, it brings dreams back to life and relives them as though happening now. "I" statements Clients are encouraged to use the phrase "I" to take responsibility for their own feelings and actions. 7 · Humanistic & Existential Therapy Humanistic and existential therapy. Notes on Carl Rogers, Karl Jaspers, Jean Paul Sartre, Viktor Frankl with the meaning triangle, and Irvin Yalom, with photos of the theorists. Psycho Didi notes · p. 77 Carl Rogers — Client-Centred Therapy Client-centred therapy → Carl Rogers. Rogers believed that people can consciously and rationally change their thoughts and behaviour from undesirable to desirable. Conditions of therapy: A congruent therapist. Unconditional positive regard for the client. Accurate empathy. After therapy, the person gets closer to becoming a congruent and fully functioning person. Karl Jaspers — Boundary Situations Boundary situations are conditions of human life that are difficult to overcome. They are basic facts about human life, such as death, suffering, guilt and struggle. They are unchanging and unalterable, although the way they appear to humans may change; they are experienced at the limit of one's existence. Significance of boundary situations: Reveal being as such. Reveal the potential for self-realization. Remove the cover of a private world view. Expose people to the reality of opposites, contradictions and death. Jean-Paul Sartre — Existential Psychoanalysis Believed there is no inherent meaning to life; any meaning you find is your own. People are "condemned to be free". In existential psychoanalysis , the therapist's role is to confront excuses for misery. Viktor Frankl — Logotherapy Logotherapy → Viktor Frankl. Emphasis on existential and spiritual questions. Meaning is found through the "meaning triangle" of Attitude , Experience and Creativity . Books: Man's Search for Meaning ; Recollections: An Autobiography . Techniques for transcending problems: Attitude modulation: changing negative to positive. Dereflection: redirecting focus from our issue to other, greater issues. Paradoxical intention: cracking jokes about difficult situations. Socratic dialogue (by Guttman): guided questioning — the approach questions beliefs, the guidance busts misunderstanding, and the outcome is reduced self-absorption. Irvin Yalom Focus: death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness. Themes: Death and existence — live authentically. Freedom and responsibility. Existential isolation. Meaning and purpose. Authenticity and self-awareness. 8 · Stress and Coping Stress and coping: stress and the Social Readjustment Rating Scale. Definition of stress, types of stressors and stress, and notes on Holmes and Rahe’s Social Readjustment Rating Scale. Psycho Didi notes · p. 78 Stress and coping illustration. Illustration of a woman with leaves and flowers growing from her head. Psycho Didi notes · p. 78 Stress is a state brought on by any situation that threatens, or appears to threaten, a person's sense of well-being, thus challenging the person's ability to cope. Types of stressors and stress Acute: a short-term stressor that has a definite endpoint. Chronic: a long-term stressor that often lacks a definite endpoint. Eustress: an optimal amount of stress required to motivate you. Distress: stress that occurs when we are unable to meet the demands of our environment with our limited resources. Personality & stress Personality and stress. Type A, B, C and D personalities with their traits and the illness each is prone to. Psycho Didi notes · p. 78 Type A / Type B personality → Meyer Friedman & Raymond Rosenman (cardiologists, late 1950s). Type Traits Prone to Type A Self-driven, competitive, achievers, risk-takers, show hostility. Coronary heart disease. Type B Charismatic, easy-going, not easily stressed, lacking a sense of urgency. — Type C Introverts, lone workers, sticklers for details, perfectionists, unassertive. Cancer. Type D Negative affectivity (worry, gloominess) and social inhibition; distressed. Poorer heart outcomes after a cardiac event (Denollet); also depression and anxiety. Why the Type A idea came up: in the late 1950s the cardiologists Meyer Friedman and Ray Rosenman noticed that many of their heart patients seemed to share the same personality traits: hurried, impatient, intensely competitive and easily angered. (The often-told story is that an upholsterer repairing their waiting-room chairs pointed out that only the front edges were worn, as if the patients sat on the edge of their seats.) They called this the Type A behaviour pattern and its relaxed opposite Type B , then tested the idea in the Western Collaborative Group Study, which followed about 3,000 healthy men and found Type A men developed coronary heart disease at roughly twice the rate of Type B men. Traps. Friedman and Rosenman described only Type A and Type B. Type C (cancer-prone) is linked to Lydia Temoshok and Type D (distressed) to Johan Denollet. Later research found that the hostility (cynical anger) component, rather than the whole Type A pattern, is the part most strongly linked to heart disease. The Social Readjustment Rating Scale Social Readjustment Rating Scale → Thomas Holmes & Richard Rahe (1967). They compiled a list of 43 events likely to change a person's life and therefore cause stress. Based on participant ratings, each event was assigned a point value from 1 to 100; these units were called life change units . Types of stressors (Thomas Holmes & Rahe): catastrophic/cataclysmic events, and daily hassles. Physiological responses to stress Physiological responses to stress. Two flowcharts for the HPA axis and the SAM pathway, with notes on allostasis and cortisol. Psycho Didi notes · p. 78 HPA axis: CRF → anterior pituitary → ACTH → adrenal cortex → cortisol → metabolism increase and insulin resistance. SAM pathway: hypothalamus → SNS → adrenal medulla → epinephrine and norepinephrine. Allostasis is a process of adaptation to acute stress by releasing stress hormones in the event of a challenge, with the goal of restoring homeostasis; it occurs because the HPA axis is activated during stress. Constant cortisol release causes immunosuppression. Cognitive appraisal / mediation theory Cognitive appraisal / mediation theory. Lazarus’s primary and secondary appraisal of a stressor. Psycho Didi notes · p. 78 Cognitive appraisal (mediation) theory → Richard Lazarus. Primary appraisal: we examine the stressor and assess how severe it is — identifying it as a threat (a future danger), a challenge (a current situation to be confronted and overcome), or a harm or loss . Secondary appraisal: we evaluate our own resources and ability to cope with the threat, challenge or loss. General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) General Adaptation Syndrome. The three GAS stages listed above a graph of resistance to stress over time across the alarm, resistance and exhaustion stages. Psycho Didi notes · p. 78 General Adaptation Syndrome → Hans Selye. Stage 1: alarm. Stage 2: resistance. Stage 3: exhaustion. Hans Selye, who first described GAS in 1936 from experiments on rats, proposed that the body reacts to any stressor, whatever its kind, with the same three-stage pattern. The graph plots the body's resistance to stress against time: Stage What the curve does What is happening 1. Alarm Resistance first dips below the normal level , then starts to climb. The initial shock lowers resistance briefly; then the body mobilises (sympathetic arousal, adrenaline, the fight-or-flight response). 2. Resistance Resistance rises above normal and stays high. The body adapts to the continuing stressor (sustained cortisol), and the person seems to be coping, but resources are steadily being used up. 3. Exhaustion Resistance falls steeply , below normal. If the stressor goes on, reserves run out; the person becomes vulnerable to illness (Selye's "diseases of adaptation"), and in extreme cases death. Example: exam season. The first day you see the timetable you feel panic (alarm); for weeks you study late, running on adrenaline and feeling fine (resistance); if the pressure continues without a break, you fall ill right after the exams (exhaustion). Traps. Resistance to stress is highest in the resistance stage , not in the alarm stage, and the alarm stage begins with a drop. GAS is nonspecific : the same response for any stressor. GAS is Selye's; the appraisal model (primary and secondary appraisal) is Lazarus's. Response to stress & coping Response to stress. Tree diagram splitting response to stress into defending and coping, coping into adaptive and maladaptive, and adaptive coping into problem focused and emotion focused. Psycho Didi notes · p. 79 The diagram is a tree, not a set of separate pairs. Each level splits the one above it: Response to stress splits into: Defending: protecting yourself from the anxiety rather than dealing with the stressor, through unconscious defence mechanisms (Freud) such as denial or projection. Coping: splits into: Adaptive coping , which splits into: Problem-focused coping: for things in your control . Emotion-focused coping: for things out of your control . Maladaptive coping: labelled "defence mechanisms" in the diagram. Responses such as denial (and, more broadly, habits like substance use or withdrawal) ease distress for a while but leave the problem in place. The problem-focused / emotion-focused split is from Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman (1984) , who defined coping as constantly changing cognitive and behavioural efforts to manage specific external and/or internal demands that are appraised as taxing or exceeding the person's resources. Which kind a person uses depends largely on their secondary appraisal : can I change this or not? Problem-focused coping Emotion-focused coping Aim Change the stressor or the situation itself. Manage the emotional distress the stressor causes. Works best when The situation is controllable (you can do something about it). The situation is uncontrollable (it has to be accepted or endured). Examples Making a study timetable for a hard exam, gathering information, talking to the professor, solving the problem step by step. Venting to a friend, relaxation or meditation, positive reappraisal ("this is a chance to grow"), distancing; e.g. coping with a bereavement or a terminal diagnosis. Traps. Problem-focused vs emotion-focused is about control (can the situation be changed?), not about whether the cause is external or internal: external/internal is the "source" dimension of Seligman's explanatory styles below. Neither type is always better; what matters is the fit with the situation, and most people use both in the same episode. Note that the page shows defence mechanisms twice (as "defending" and as maladaptive coping); because Lazarus and Folkman's definition stresses deliberate effort, many textbooks keep unconscious defences separate from coping. Explanatory styles Explanatory styles. Optimistic and pessimistic styles compared for a negative event and a positive event by duration, scope and source, with an illustration of a woman with flowers in her hair. Psycho Didi notes · p. 79 Explanatory styles → Martin Seligman. The characteristic manner in which we explain events; explanatory styles make a difference in how we appraise and respond to stressors. Seligman's three dimensions are duration (permanence: will the cause last?), scope (pervasiveness: does it affect everything or just this?) and source (personalization: is it me or something outside me?). The page gives two cases, because the pattern flips depending on whether the event is bad or good. Case 1: a negative (bad) event , e.g. failing an exam. Dimension Optimistic style Pessimistic style Duration Temporary Permanent Scope Specific Global Source External Internal Optimist: "That paper was unusually hard (external), I was unwell that week (temporary), and it is only this one subject (specific)." Pessimist: "I'm stupid (internal), I'll always fail (permanent), I mess up everything (global)." Case 2: a positive (good) event , e.g. getting selected in an interview. Dimension Optimistic style Pessimistic style Duration Permanent Temporary Scope Global Specific Source Internal External Optimist: "I'm well prepared and capable (internal), it will keep working for me (permanent), and it shows I'm good at things (global)." Pessimist: "I got lucky (external), it was a one-off (temporary), it was just this one panel (specific)." Trap. Do not memorise "optimist = temporary, specific, external" as a fixed rule: that is true only for bad events. For good events the optimist takes the credit (permanent, global, internal). The pessimistic style for bad events (internal, stable, global) is the attributional style that the reformulated learned helplessness theory (Abramson, Seligman & Teasdale, 1978) links to depression. Interventions Interventions for stress. Stress interventions split into a physiological level and a psychological level, with two small illustrations. Psycho Didi notes · p. 79 Physiological level: Simple breathing exercises — pranayam, box breathing. Guided imagery: a method of treating stress and anxiety in which one replaces disturbing memories with positive mental energy. Biofeedback: a self-regulation technique through which patients learn to voluntarily control what were once thought to be involuntary body processes. Progressive Muscle Relaxation — introduced by Edmund Jacobson (1920) , also called JPMR; types of relaxation: top-down and bottom-up. Psychological level: Mindfulness meditation: slows racing thoughts, living in the present, letting go of negativity to calm body and mind — attitude, attention and intention. Stress inoculation (by Donald Meichenbaum, 1985 ): stages of education/conceptualization → rehearsal/skill acquisition → implementation/skill application and follow-through. Social support: an effective, active, problem-focused network of friends; ask for help. 9 · Counselling and Guidance Counselling and guidance. One page covering the dimensions, need, goals, process, stages, steps and important steps of counselling, plus the relationship, termination, influencing factors and qualities of counsellor and client, with an illustration of a woman. Psycho Didi notes · p. 80 Dimensions A good counselling relationship, therapeutic intervention, and psychological process. Essential features Theorist Essential features for counselling Carl Rogers Unconditional positive regard, empathy, congruence. Carkhuff Respect, confrontation, immediacy, concreteness, self-disclosure. Need & goals Need: when stress-related symptoms are out of proportion, loneliness, job issues, career problems. Goals: Healthy development of personality. Providing support. Emotional release. Awareness. Value clarification and change. Process & steps Process: pre-counselling (see if the client is suitable) → identify the need for counselling → prepare for counselling → conduct counselling → follow-up. Steps of counselling: Identify → Prepare → Conduct → Termination → Follow-up. Important steps: background information → identifying core issues → case formulation → goal setting → intervention implementation → evaluation → closure. Length and intensity of counselling depend on the severity of the problem, motivation of the client, type of problems, and age of the client. Stages of counselling: Beginning → Middle → Ending Developing a relationship / beginning: establish a safe environment, help people express, active listening, paraphrasing, focus on feelings. Middle: transform the problem into a goal, explore approaches to the goal, help the person choose a way towards the goal, make a contract to fulfil the plan, summarize and get verification, get feedback and confirmation. Analysing fears: abandonment, rejection, not being enough. It is important that clients gain recognition for their skills and experience; being confronted from a caring position; re-experiencing past events in the present. Analysis of transference and countertransference — the reaction to the counsellor–client relationship. Termination of a relationship The client no longer requires help. The counsellor cannot provide any more benefit to the client. Premature termination: termination before it is due. Referral: when the client needs to be referred to another professional. Follow-up. Factors affecting counselling Structure: the psychological and physical atmosphere. Initiative: whether the client himself wants to change or not (difficult if the client is reluctant). Settings. Qualities of counsellor and client Qualities of a counsellor: self-aware, honest, congruent, good communication skills, knowledgeable. Trap — YAVIS vs HOUND clients. YAVIS = Young, Attractive, Verbal, Intelligent, Successful → tend to get better help. HOUND = Homely, Old, Unattractive, Nonverbal, Dumb → less likely to be helped. Working in a relationship Leading: redirecting the conversation towards change. Accurate empathy — components: empathic rapport, communication attunement. Types: primary ; advanced (making implicit explicit, identifying themes, connecting islands). Self-disclosure: the counsellor's problems, facts about the counsellor's role, and reaction to the client. Analysis of transference and countertransference.

title: Health Psychology, Ethics & Laws
text: Health Psychology, Ethics & Laws — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Health Psychology, Ethics & Laws Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Health-behaviour models (HBM, TPB, TTM) Levels of prevention APA Ethics Code (Principles A–E) Mental Healthcare Act 2017 RCI & RPWD Acts What this covers. Two linked areas. First, Health Psychology : epidemiology basics, the levels of prevention (primordial, primary, secondary, tertiary), and the major health-behaviour and illness models (Health Belief Model, Theory of Planned Behaviour, Transtheoretical Model, biopsychosocial model (George Engel, 1977)). Second, Psychology in Practice — Ethics & Laws : the APA General Principles and Ethical Standards, and the history of Indian mental-health legislation from the colonial Lunacy Acts through the RCI Act, the disability acts, and the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 and its 2022 amendment. Original diagrams. 8 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 82 to 85) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: Health Psychology · Ethics & Laws Health Psychology Epidemiology and disease measures Epidemiology. Definition of epidemiology with morbidity, incidence, prevalence and mortality, under an illustration of two researchers with a magnifying glass. Psycho Didi notes · p. 82 Epidemiology is the study of the frequency, distribution and causes of infectious and non-infectious disease in a population. Its core measures are: Term Meaning Morbidity The number of cases of a disease that exist at some given point in time. Incidence The number of new cases at some given point of time. Prevalence The total number of existing cases at some given point of time. Mortality The number of deaths due to particular causes. Don't confuse. Incidence counts only new cases; prevalence counts all existing cases (new + old). Morbidity is about illness; mortality is about death. Levels of prevention Types of prevention. Diagram branching from types of prevention to primordial, primary, secondary and tertiary prevention, each with examples and an icon. Psycho Didi notes · p. 82 Level Focus Primordial prevention Inhibit the emergence of risk factors in the form of environmental, economic, social, and behavioral conditions and cultural patterns of living, etc. Primary prevention Awareness programs, psychoeducation, vaccination, wearing a helmet. Secondary prevention Early detection and treatment; reversal of problems/damage. Tertiary prevention Only management, since reversal is not possible; stopping further progression of problems. Key. Order by when they act: Primordial (before risk factors even appear) → Primary (before disease) → Secondary (early disease, still reversible) → Tertiary (established disease, manage and limit progression). Health-behaviour models Biopsychosocial model of health. Venn diagram of biological, psychological and social or environmental factors that overlap around mental health. Psycho Didi notes · p. 82 Health belief model, TTM and theory of planned behaviour. Notes on the six constructs of the health belief model, the six stages of the transtheoretical model, and the three components of the theory of planned behaviour. Psycho Didi notes · p. 82 The Health Belief Model (HBM) Given by Rosenstock . It explains health behaviour through six constructs : Perceived susceptibility — a person's subjective perception of the risk of acquiring an illness or disease. Perceived severity — a person's feelings on the seriousness of contracting an illness or disease. Perceived benefits — a person's perception of the effectiveness of various actions available to reduce the threat of illness or disease. Perceived barriers — a person's feelings on the obstacles to performing a recommended health action. Cue to action — the stimulus needed to trigger the decision-making process to accept a recommended health action. Self-efficacy (Albert Bandura, 1977) — the level of a person's confidence in his or her ability to successfully perform a behaviour. Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) Given by Icek Ajzen ; earlier called the Theory of Reasoned Action . According to this theory, a health behaviour is the direct result of a behavioural intention . Behavioural intentions are themselves made up of three components: Attitudes toward the specific action — beliefs about the outcomes of the behaviour (e.g. "if I change my diet, I will lose weight, improve my health, and be more attractive") and evaluations of those outcomes (e.g. "being healthy and looking good are desirable"). Subjective norms regarding the action — normative beliefs (e.g. "my family and friends think I should change my diet") and motivation to comply (e.g. "I want to do what they want me to do"). Perceived behavioural control — e.g. "I will be able to change my diet". Transtheoretical Model of behaviour change (TTM) Given by James Prochaska . It posits that health behaviour change involves progress through six stages of change : Precontemplation Contemplation Preparation Action Maintenance Termination Biopsychosocial model of health Health and illness are understood as the product of interacting biological, psychological, and social factors, rather than biology alone. Proposed by the psychiatrist George Engel (1977) as a challenge to the older biomedical model , which explains illness only through bodily causes (germs, genes, damaged tissue). Engel argued that the same disease runs a different course in different people because their thoughts, emotions and social situation also shape it. The Psycho Didi diagram draws the model as three overlapping circles with mental health in the middle: Circle Factors listed in the diagram Biological Physical health, disabilities, genetic predisposition, neurochemistry, immune response. Psychological Beliefs, behaviour, personality, self-esteem, coping skills, emotions, social skills. Social and environmental Peer relationships, family circumstances, cultural traditions, social support, education, poverty. Where the circles overlap (factors that belong to two domains at once): Biological + social: drug effects (a substance acts on the brain, but whether and how a person uses it depends on peers, culture and availability). Biological + psychological: temperament (an inborn, partly genetic style that shows up as personality and emotional reactions). Social + psychological: family relationships and life events. All three: mental health sits at the centre, where all the circles meet. The two side notes on the diagram make the practical point: your mental health can be affected by many different factors, and what works for one person might not work for someone else. Example: two people with the same depression diagnosis may need different help; one mainly needs medication for a strong family history, the other mainly needs support after losing a job. Don't confuse. The biopsychosocial model is Engel's . It explains health and illness as a whole, whereas HBM (Rosenstock), TPB (Ajzen) and TTM (Prochaska) explain why a person does or does not carry out a particular health behaviour. Its opposite in MCQs is the biomedical model (illness = biology only). Model → author. Health Belief Model → Rosenstock Theory of Planned Behaviour (formerly Theory of Reasoned Action) → Ajzen Transtheoretical Model (TTM) → James Prochaska Don't confuse. HBM's self-efficacy vs TPB's perceived behavioural control — both are about confidence to perform the behaviour but belong to different models. TPB's older name is the Theory of Reasoned Action (which lacked perceived behavioural control). Ethics & Laws APA Ethical Principles and Code of Conduct APA code of conduct: introduction. Banner title and introduction describing the parts of the APA Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct. Psycho Didi notes · p. 84 APA preamble and five general principles. The preamble and goal of the APA ethics code, followed by general principles A to E. Psycho Didi notes · p. 84 APA ten ethical standards. The ten sections of the APA ethical standards with a one-line summary of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 84 The American Psychological Association's (APA) Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct consists of an Introduction, a Preamble, five General Principles (A–E) , and specific Ethical Standards . The Ethics Code applies only to psychologists' activities that are part of their scientific, educational, or professional roles as psychologists. Preamble and goal In the Preamble, psychologists are committed to increasing scientific and professional knowledge of behavior, respect and protect civil and human rights, and strive to help the public in developing informed judgments and choices concerning human behavior. Goal of the Ethics Code: the welfare and protection of the individuals and groups with whom psychologists work, and the education of members, students, and the public regarding the ethical standards of the discipline. General Principles (A–E) Key. The General Principles are aspirational in nature; they cannot form the basis for sanctions. The Ethical Standards (below) are the enforceable rules. Principle Content A: Beneficence and Non-maleficence Psychologists strive to benefit those with whom they work and take care to do no harm. B: Fidelity and Responsibility Psychologists establish relationships of trust; they are aware of their professional and scientific responsibilities to society and to the specific communities in which they work. C: Integrity Psychologists seek to promote accuracy, honesty, and truthfulness in the science, teaching, and practice of psychology; they strive to keep their promises and to avoid unwise or unclear commitments. D: Justice Psychologists recognize that fairness and justice entitle all persons to access to and benefit from the contributions of psychology, and to equal quality in the processes, procedures, and services conducted by psychologists. E: Respect for People's Rights and Dignity Psychologists respect the dignity and worth of all people, and the rights of individuals to privacy, confidentiality, and self-determination. Ethical Standards (Sections 1–10) Section Standard 1. Resolving Ethical Issues Address ethical conflicts, report serious violations, and avoid retaliation against whistleblowers. 2. Competence Work within areas of expertise, seek ongoing training, and refer cases beyond one's competence. 3. Human Relations Avoid discrimination, exploitation, and conflicts of interest; obtain informed consent and minimize harm. 4. Privacy and Confidentiality Maintain confidentiality, inform clients of its limits, and securely handle records. 5. Advertising and Public Statements Ensure honesty in self-promotion, avoid misleading claims, and do not use client testimonials. 6. Record Keeping and Fees Keep accurate records, maintain transparency in billing, and handle financial matters ethically. 7. Education and Training Provide fair, accurate instruction and ensure students meet competency standards. 8. Research and Publication Obtain informed consent, protect participants, avoid plagiarism, and credit contributions properly. 9. Assessment Use valid tests, ensure fairness in administration and interpretation, and explain results clearly. 10. Therapy Obtain informed consent, clarify roles in multi-client settings, avoid dual relationships, and ethically terminate treatment. Why it matters. Informed consent and confidentiality recur across multiple standards (Human Relations, Privacy & Confidentiality, Research, Assessment, Therapy). They are not single rules but threads that run through the whole code. Mental Health Laws in India Mental health laws in India. Road timeline of Indian mental health laws from the colonial Lunacy Acts to the Mental Healthcare (Amendment) Bill 2022, with notes on each law. Psycho Didi notes · p. 85 Colonial laws 1851 — The Lunatic Removal Act 1858 — The Lunacy (Supreme Courts) Act 1858 — The Lunacy (District Courts) Act of 1858 The Mental Health Act, 1987 Implemented in 1993 . It is organized into 10 chapters (98 sections): Chapter Subject I Preliminary (title, definitions) II Mental Health Authorities (Central and State) III Psychiatric hospitals and nursing homes: establishment, licences, maintenance IV Admission and Detention V Inspection, discharge, leaves VI Property of Mentally Ill VII Maintenance of mentally ill VIII Protection of human rights IX Penalty and Procedure X Miscellaneous Characteristics (these sit inside the 1987 Act block on the Psycho Didi page, and they match the 1987 Act's own sections): A person admitted under special circumstances (on a relative's or friend's application, without his own consent) can't be held for more than 90 days except under the Act's other provisions (Section 19). Appeal to Magistrate for discharge: the patient, a relative or a friend can apply to a Magistrate for discharge (Sections 19 and 43). Magistrates also issued the reception orders for involuntary admission. Monthly checks: Visitors appointed for each psychiatric hospital must inspect it every month (Sections 37 and 38). Licensing and supervision: nobody may run a psychiatric hospital or nursing home without a licence (Section 6), under the Central and State Mental Health Authorities. Hospitals run by the Central or State Government were exempt (Section 6(2)), which is the "government hospitals don't need a licence" disadvantage below. Government support: the government may set up and maintain psychiatric hospitals (Section 5) and bears the cost of maintaining some detained patients (Section 78). Legal aid at State expense for a mentally ill person who cannot afford a lawyer (Section 91). Advantages: better than the Lunacy Act; OPD for outpatient cases; prohibition on research without consent; separate spaces for children and adults. Disadvantages: treatment like criminals; isolation from society; exclusion of dementia and mental retardation; government men don't need a license; suicide considered an offence; excessive focus on hospitalization; no provision for rehabilitation. Other key statutes and milestones 1982 — NMHP (National Mental Health Programme) launched: treatment of disorder within the community using PHC (Primary Health Centres), providing training. 1985 — Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act. 1992 — RCI Act (Rehabilitation Council of India Act). 1995 — Persons with Disabilities Act: mental illness was considered a disability for the first time. 2013 — New Mental Health Bill: no solitary confinement; community living; confidentiality; right to contact family; legal aid. 2016 — Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act (RPWD). 1995 Persons with Disabilities Act — recognized disabilities Physical: cerebral palsy, leprosy, dwarfism, muscular dystrophy, acid attack Visual impairment Hearing impairment Speech and language Intellectual disability (ID): autism, specific learning disabilities 2016 Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act (RPWD) — added disabilities and benefits Additional recognized conditions: Neurological: multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease Blood diseases: thalassemia, sickle cell anaemia Mental illness (vague) Multiple disabilities Benefits: 5% reservation in education; 4% reservation in jobs; punishment for violation; special courts. Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 Heads up: which Act is which. The list "90 days, appeal to Magistrate, monthly checks, licensing, government support, legal aid" belongs to the 1987 Act (see above), not to the 2017 Act. The 2017 Act works differently: involuntary ("supported") admission is up to 30 days (Section 89), and longer supported admission is up to 90 days in the first instance, extendable to 120 days and then 180 days at a time (Section 90). Admissions are reviewed by the Mental Health Review Board , not a Magistrate, and establishments must be registered with the Mental Health Authority. Legal aid is the one feature in both: the 2017 Act makes it a right (Section 27). Advantages: Decriminalizes suicide. Everybody has the right to mental health care. Central and State Mental Health Authority to advise government. Client's role in admission, treatment and discharge. Prohibits ECT (in specified circumstances). Establish hospitals nearby. Insurance. Financial punishment (₹50k–₹500k) and jail. No sterilization. Disadvantages: Not made by mental health professionals. Does not talk about awareness and prevention. Western-standard based. Expenditure allocation not clear. Key. The advance directive is a signature feature of the 2017 Act: a person can state in advance how they wish to be treated (or not treated) for mental illness and nominate a representative. Mental Healthcare (Amendment) Bill, 2022 Decriminalizes suicide. Strengthens community mental health. Ensures patient rights and care quality. Mandates insurance for mental illnesses. Reduces stigma through awareness. Don't confuse the three big acts. Mental Health Act 1987 (implemented 1993, 10 chapters, hospitalization-heavy, suicide an offence, 90-day cap, Magistrate decides discharge) → Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (decriminalizes suicide, advance directive, right to care, Mental Health Review Boards) → Mental Healthcare (Amendment) Bill 2022 (reinforces decriminalized suicide, community care, mandatory insurance). Watch the years. Lunatic Removal Act 1851 ; Lunacy Acts 1858 ; NMHP 1982 ; NDPS Act 1985 ; MHA 1987 (implemented 1993); RCI Act 1992 ; Persons with Disabilities Act 1995 ; New Mental Health Bill 2013 ; RPWD Act 2016 ; Mental Healthcare Act 2017 ; Amendment Bill 2022 .

title: Cognitive Psychology
text: Cognitive Psychology — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Cognitive Psychology Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Sensation & perception Attention & SDT Learning & conditioning Memory models & forgetting Intelligence & creativity Thinking · problem solving · language What this covers. The whole cognitive block: how a stimulus becomes a perception (Gestalt organization, constancies, motion and depth cues, colour and sound theories, top-down vs bottom-up perception), theories of attention and signal detection, classical and operant conditioning (B. F. Skinner) plus cognitive/social learning, the multi-store, working-memory and levels-of-processing (Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart, 1972) models, forgetting and memory distortion, the major theories of intelligence and creativity, thinking and concept formation, problem-solving heuristics and cognitive biases, and theories of language development. Original diagrams. 107 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 87 to 107) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Sensation & Perception · 2 · Colour & Sound Perception · 3 · Attention · 4 · Classical & Operant Conditioning · 5 · Cognitive & Social Learning · 6 · Memory Models · 7 · Forgetting & Memory Distortion · 8 · Intelligence · 9 · Creativity · 10 · Thinking & Concepts · 11 · Problem Solving, Reasoning & Decision-Making · 12 · Language Development 1 · Sensation & Perception Process and types of perception. Flow from stimulation to transduction, sensation, attention and perception, with arrows splitting perception into top-down and bottom-up types. Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 The perceptual sequence runs stimulation → transduction → sensation → attention → perception . Perception can be driven two ways: Top-down — expectation driven (knowledge and context shape what we perceive). Bottom-up — stimulus / data driven (the raw sensory input drives perception). Top-down vs bottom-up. Top-down = expectation/knowledge driven (constructivist, e.g. Gregory). Bottom-up = stimulus/data driven (direct/ecological, e.g. Gibson). Endogenous attention is top-down; exogenous attention is bottom-up. Gestalt psychology Gestalt psychology. Notes on the phi phenomenon, the six laws of organization and Pragnanz, with an overlapping rings drawing for Pragnanz. Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 Core dictum: the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. Key ideas include the Phi phenomenon and the law of Prägnanz — every stimulus pattern is seen so that the resulting structure is as simple as possible. Prägnanz in practice (the ring drawing). Prägnanz, also called the law of good figure or law of simplicity , is the master law of the Gestalt psychologists (Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Köhler): of all the ways a pattern could be organised, we see the simplest, most regular and most stable one. The page shows interlocking rings drawn two ways. In the black version (the Olympic logo) we see five complete circles lying over each other, not a puzzle of curved pieces and odd-shaped gaps. In the blue version the overlapping bits are only dashed, yet we still see five whole rings, because "five circles" is the simplest reading and the mind fills the gaps. Prägnanz vs closure. Closure is one specific law (filling small gaps to see a whole). Prägnanz is the general principle that sits above all the laws: proximity, similarity, closure, continuity and common fate are all ways of reaching the simplest organisation. If an MCQ asks for the "fundamental" or "overall" Gestalt law, the answer is Prägnanz. Max Wertheimer — founder of Gestalt perception; described the Phi phenomenon , a type of stroboscopic motion , best seen at a time interval of 30 to 200 milliseconds . Laws of Perceptual Organization Law Principle Proximity Objects physically close together are grouped together. Continuity Stimuli falling along the same plane tend to be grouped together. Closure We fill in small gaps so objects are still perceived as whole. Similarity Stimuli resembling one another tend to be grouped together. Common region Stimuli in a common area or ground are grouped together. Common fate Objects moving in a similar direction are grouped together. Perceptual Constancy Perceptual constancy. Definitions of colour or brightness constancy, size constancy and shape constancy. Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 Colour / brightness constancy — perceiving colour or brightness as constant despite changes in lighting. Size constancy — perceiving an object as the same size regardless of its distance from the observer. Shape constancy — perceiving an object as maintaining its shape despite changes in orientation. Apparent (Illusory) Motion Apparent motion and the autokinetic effect. Definition of apparent motion and the autokinetic effect found by Muzafer Sherif (1935). Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 Induced motion. Definition of induced motion with a photo of the moon behind drifting clouds as the example. Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 Phi phenomenon, motion parallax and stroboscopic effect. Three panels on the phi and beta phenomena with critical flicker fusion, motion parallax with a train passenger drawing, and the stroboscopic effect with a multi-exposure dancer photo. Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 Perception of motion when there actually is none. Autokinetic effect — a stationary point of light appears to move in a dark room. Found by Muzafer Sherif (1935) . Induced motion — motion of one object causes a nearby stationary object to appear to move (e.g. clouds moving past the moon make the moon appear to race through the clouds). Phi phenomenon — an optical illusion in which stationary objects shown in rapid succession, past the threshold at which they can be perceived separately, appear to move. Temporal threshold: 30–200 ms . Beta phenomenon — similar to the phi phenomenon but usually circular motion. Critical Flicker Fusion Frequency — the frequency at which a flickering light appears steady; the threshold where separate/discontinuous images seem to fuse. Motion parallax — as we move, nearby objects appear to glide rapidly past us in the direction opposite to our own movement , while more distant objects move more slowly; very distant objects such as the moon seem to stand still or even travel along with us (the moon "follows" the car). In the page's drawing the passenger keeps his eyes on the house (the fixation point) while he travels to the left: things nearer than the house, like the grass, sweep backwards against his direction of travel, while things beyond the house drift slowly forwards, the same way he is going. Strictly, motion parallax is a real difference in how fast images move across the retina, and it is used as a monocular depth cue (see Depth & Distance Cues below), not an illusion of motion. Stroboscopic effect — a rapid succession of still images or lights creates the illusion of motion. Worked example: a cinema film is a series of still frames shown at 24 frames per second; a flip-book, or a neon sign whose bulbs light one after another, works the same way. Each picture is still, but shown quickly enough in sequence the brain sees one smooth movement. The dancer photo on the page is a stroboscopic (multi-flash) photograph: a strobe light flashed many times while the dancer moved, so one picture holds a row of frozen positions. Flash those positions one after another fast enough and you would see a single continuous movement. Under a strobe light or on film, a spinning wheel can look frozen or even turn backwards (the wagon-wheel effect ), another stroboscopic illusion. Phi vs stroboscopic. The phi phenomenon (Max Wertheimer, 1912) is one particular kind of stroboscopic motion: two stationary lights flashed one after the other at the right interval (about 30 to 200 ms) look like one light jumping across. "Stroboscopic motion" is the wider term for any apparent motion produced by a series of still images. Depth & Distance Cues Depth perception and the visual cliff. Visual cliff apparatus drawing next to notes on binocular cues (convergence, retinal, vertical and horizontal disparity, horopter) and monocular cues. Psycho Didi notes · p. 88 Monocular cues Cue Description Accommodation Change in the lens shape as the eye focuses. Interposition (overlap / partial occlusion) A closer object cuts off the view of part or all of a more distant one. Relative size The closer of two same-size objects casts a larger image on the retina. Texture gradient Closer objects have a coarser, more distinct texture; far objects appear more densely packed / smooth. Aerial / atmospheric perspective Closer objects appear sharper than more distant, hazy objects. Relative height / elevation Objects closest to the horizon appear farthest; the lowest objects in the field of vision seem closest. Linear perspective Parallel lines (e.g. edges of sidewalks) seem to converge in the distance. Relative brightness The closer of two identical objects reflects more light to your eyes. Relative clarity Hazy, blurry objects are judged farther away than sharp, clear ones, because light from far objects passes through more air. Example: on a misty day distant hills look farther away than they really are. This is essentially the same cue as aerial perspective; some books (e.g. Myers) use this name. Motion parallax When you move, near objects shift across your view quickly and in the opposite direction to your movement, far objects shift slowly. Example: riding in a bus, the roadside poles race backwards past the window, distant trees crawl, and the moon seems to keep pace with you. The brain reads "fast-moving" as near and "slow-moving" as far. It needs only one eye, so it is a monocular cue (often called a motion-produced cue). Motion parallax: depth cue, not illusion. These notes also list motion parallax under apparent motion, but in standard textbooks it is a monocular depth cue : the movement on the retina is real, and its speed tells you distance. If an MCQ asks which depth cue depends on the observer's own movement, the answer is motion parallax. Binocular cues Binocular convergence — depth cue based on the inward movement of the eyes as they focus on nearby objects. Retinal disparity — the slight difference in the images seen by each eye, used by the brain to perceive depth. Vertical disparity — due to the image falling on a different place in the retina. Horizontal disparity — due to the difference in angles at which the eyes are placed. Horopter — the imaginary line at which an object placed there produces no disparity. Eleanor Gibson & Richard Walk — the Visual Cliff depth-perception experiment on 3–6 month-old babies; concluded that depth perception is innate . The visual cliff apparatus (Gibson & Walk, 1960): a table-high platform covered by one sheet of thick, strong glass, with a raised centre board running down the middle where the baby is placed. On the shallow side a red-and-white checkered pattern sits directly under the glass, so it looks like solid floor. On the deep side the same checkered pattern is laid on the floor a few feet below and seen through clear glass, so it looks like a sudden drop (the "cliff"). Touch tells the baby the glass is solid on both sides; only vision says "drop". The mother calls the baby first from the shallow side, then from the deep side. In the original study, of the 27 babies who moved off the centre board, all crawled onto the shallow side at least once, but only 3 crept onto the deep side; many cried or crawled away from the mother when she called from the deep side. Heads up on ages and "innate". Gibson and Walk's 1960 study tested crawling infants, about 6 to 14 months old (a baby must crawl to be tested), not 3 to 6 months as written above. Because these babies already had months of visual experience, the study shows depth perception is present by crawling age; it does not by itself prove it is inborn. Joseph Campos and colleagues (1970) later placed 2-month-olds (too young to crawl) over the deep side and found their heart rate slowed (interest, not fear); fear of the drop appears around the time infants start crawling. Perceptual Set Perceptual set. Bruner and Goodman (1947) coin study notes, with a coin and a same-size cardboard disc showing that the coin loomed larger. Psycho Didi notes · p. 88 Refers to the influence of values on perception. Jerome Bruner & Goodman (1947) — coins were perceived as larger than same-size cardboard discs, and more so by poor children than rich children. Because coin size correlates with value, valuable coins "loomed larger" in perception even when the cardboard was the same size. Top-Down Theories of Perception Top-down theories of perception. Three columns on Gregory's processing theory, template matching theory and prototype theory. Psycho Didi notes · p. 88 Constructivist theory (Processing theory) — proponent Richard Gregory (1970) . Perception is a hypothesis based on prior knowledge; we actively construct our perception of reality from the environment and stored information. Higher-order thinking is involved. Template Matching theory — a template is an internal construct that, when matched by sensory stimuli, leads to recognition of an object. "Lock and key" idea of pattern recognition; the object must match the template exactly . Prototype theory (Eleanor Rosch, 1975) — an alternative to template matching. A prototype for each object is stored in memory; a pattern is checked against the prototype and recognised if resemblance is found. Not as rigid as templates. Shortcoming: does not account for exceptions. Bottom-Up Theories of Perception Bottom-up theories of perception. Notes on Gibson's direct perception, feature detection theory, Biederman's geon theory and Selfridge's pandemonium model with its four demons. Psycho Didi notes · p. 88 J. J. Gibson — Direct (Ecological) Perception : the information in the stimulus itself is the important element; learning and cognition are unnecessary because there is enough information in the environment to make an interpretation. Constraints — a barrier in the environment that helps perception. Affordance — a mediator in the environment that helps perception. Light feedback — from the reflection of light we decide whether to move forward or backward. Feature Detection theory — object recognition is high-order processing preceded by a step in which complex incoming stimuli are identified according to simpler features. Irving Biederman (1987) — Geon theory (aka recognition by components ): the human information-processing system has a limited number of simple geometric shapes ( geons , "geometric ions") that combine to form meaningful objects. Identifying an object from its geons = the principle of componential recovery ; each geon's unique set of Non-Accidental Properties gives geons the property of discriminability . Oliver Selfridge — Pandemonium Model ("pandemonium" = a very noisy, chaotic place). Four kinds of demons: image demons (sensation) → feature demons (feature separation) → cognitive demons (compare with memory) → decision demons (perception). 2 · Theories of Colour & Sound Perception Vision — photoreceptor cells Vision. Labelled human eye anatomy diagram with notes on rods and cones, properties of colour, opponent process and trichromatic theories, dark vs light adaptation and the visual pathway. Psycho Didi notes · p. 89 Parts of the eye (labels on the diagram) Light enters through the cornea , passes the pupil and the lens , crosses the vitreous body and lands on the retina , where rods and cones turn it into nerve signals that leave through the optic nerve . Part What it is / does Sclera The tough white outer coat of the eyeball; protects it and keeps its shape. Conjunctiva Thin clear membrane covering the white of the eye and lining the eyelids (inflamed in "conjunctivitis"). Cornea Clear dome at the very front; light is bent (focused) here first, and it does most of the eye's focusing. Iris Coloured ring of muscle (gives eye colour); widens or narrows the pupil. Pupil The hole in the centre of the iris; dilates in dim light, constricts in bright light. Lens Clear, flexible structure behind the pupil; changes shape to fine-tune focus (rounder for near objects). This change is accommodation , itself a monocular depth cue. Ciliary body and muscle Ring of muscle holding the lens; by contracting or relaxing it changes the lens shape. Vitreous body Clear jelly filling the large chamber behind the lens; keeps the eyeball round. Retina Light-sensitive inner lining at the back of the eye containing rods and cones; the image falls on it upside down and reversed. Macula Small central area of the retina; its centre, the fovea , is packed with cones and has no rods, so it gives the sharpest, colour vision. Optic nerve Bundle of ganglion-cell axons carrying signals to the brain. Where it leaves the eye (optic disc) there are no rods or cones, creating the blind spot . Retinal blood vessels Supply the retina with blood. Fovea vs blind spot. The fovea (in the macula) is the point of sharpest vision, all cones.
