The blind spot (optic disc) is where the optic nerve exits and has no receptors at all. Rods are densest in the periphery, which is why a dim star is easier to see out of the corner of your eye. Rods Cones Vision Achromatic, night vision (scotopic) Chromatic vision (photopic) Number ~120 million ~6–8 million Photopigment Rhodopsin (from vitamin A) Photopsin Activated Only in low-light / scotopic vision Bright light; types L, M, S cones Visual pathway: Photoreceptors → Horizontal cells → Bipolar cells → Amacrine cells → Ganglion cells → Optic nerve → Optic chiasm → Optic tract → Lateral geniculate nucleus → Primary visual cortex. Properties of colour Visible spectrum of light: 380 to 760 nm . Hue — the actual colour seen. Saturation — concentration of colour. Brightness — intensity of light. Young–Helmholtz — Trichromatic theory of colour : the retina has three types of colour receptor, each especially sensitive to red, green or blue ; stimulating combinations produces all other colours. Ewald Hering — Opponent-Process theory : three sets of opponent retinal processes enable colour vision — red–green, yellow–blue, white–black . If one colour of a pair is perceived, the other cannot be. Explains afterimages . Dark vs Light adaptation Light adaptation Dark adaptation Transition Rod → cone dominance Cone → rod dominance Mechanism Photopigment bleaching; pupil constriction Chemical changes in photoreceptors; pupil dilation Photosensitivity Low High Time Takes less time Takes more time (rods must be regenerated) Audition Audition. Labelled ear anatomy diagram with notes on properties of sound, the auditory pathway, place theory, frequency theory and the volley principle. Psycho Didi notes · p. 89 Properties of sound Audible frequency: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz . Amplitude — height of the sound wave; determines loudness. Frequency — waves per second; determines pitch. Timbre — quality of sound. Hermann von Helmholtz — Place theory : we hear different pitches because different sound waves trigger activity at different places along the cochlea's basilar membrane. Best explains high pitches . Rinne & Rutherford (1880) — Frequency theory : the brain reads pitch by monitoring the frequency of neural impulses travelling up the auditory nerve. Does not explain sound sensing above 1000 Hz. Best explains low pitches . Key — Volley principle (Ernest Wever and Charles Bray, 1930). Supports frequency theory: neurons fire in alternating rapid succession so that, combined, they achieve a frequency above 1000 waves per second. Auditory pathway: Pinna → Auditory canal → Tympanic membrane → Hammer (Malleus) → Anvil (Incus) → Stirrup (Stapes) → Cochlea → Auditory nerve → Cochlear nerve → Superior olivary complex → Lateral lemniscus → Inferior colliculus → Medial geniculate body → Auditory cortex. Parts of the ear (labels on the diagram) Region Parts Job Outer ear Ear pinna, auditory canal Collects sound and funnels it to the eardrum. Boundary Tympanic membrane (eardrum) Vibrates when sound waves hit it. Middle ear (air-filled) The three ossicles : malleus (hammer, attached to the eardrum) → incus (anvil) → stapes (stirrup, pressing on the oval window of the cochlea); plus the Eustachian tube The ossicles pass the eardrum's vibration to the much smaller oval window, which boosts the pressure enough to move the cochlear fluid. The Eustachian tube links the middle ear to the throat and equalises air pressure (why your ears "pop" in a plane). Inner ear (fluid-filled) Cochlea (snail-shaped), with the basilar membrane and hair cells (organ of Corti); the looped semicircular canals beside it belong to the vestibular (balance) system Hair cells are the auditory receptors: they turn fluid waves into nerve impulses (transduction). Nerve Cochlear nerve Carries signals from the hair cells; it joins the vestibular nerve to form cranial nerve VIII (vestibulocochlear) and goes to the brainstem. Common traps. The stapes is the smallest bone in the body. "Auditory nerve" and "cochlear nerve" in the pathway above are the same nerve, not two steps. Damage to the outer or middle ear (eardrum, ossicles) gives conductive hearing loss; damage to hair cells or the cochlear nerve gives sensorineural (nerve) deafness. Other senses Proprioception. Proprioception branching into kinesthetic and vestibular senses, each with a stick-figure illustration. Psycho Didi notes · p. 89 Kinesthetic / Proprioception — sense of body position and movements. Vestibular — sense of head positioning (parietal lobe); semi-circular canals and cerebellum involved. How the page groups them. The diagram puts proprioception at the top as the umbrella "sense of where the body is", with two branches: kinesthetic (receptors in muscles, tendons and joints telling you the position and movement of your limbs, e.g. touching your nose with your eyes closed) and vestibular (the inner-ear sense of balance and head position: the semicircular canals detect head rotation, the otolith organs detect tilt and straight-line acceleration, e.g. knowing you are tilting in a lift or on a swing). This wide use follows Charles Sherrington, who coined "proprioception" (1906) and counted the inner-ear balance organs among the proprioceptors. Terminology trap. Many textbooks (e.g. Ciccarelli, Baron) use "proprioception" and "kinesthesis" almost as synonyms and list the vestibular sense separately. So "kinesthetic = body/limb position and movement" and "vestibular = balance and head orientation" is what to remember; whether proprioception includes the vestibular sense depends on the book. Motion sickness is a conflict between vestibular and visual signals. 3 · Theories of Attention Attention is the concentration of mental activity that lets you take in a limited portion of the vast stream of information available from both your sensory world and your memory. Sequence: sensation → attention → perception . Types of attention (source) Introduction to attention. Definition of attention, the sensation to attention to perception sequence, and exogenous (bottom-up) vs endogenous (top-down) attention. Psycho Didi notes · p. 90 Hierarchical model of attention. Sohlberg and Mateer pyramid of attention levels from focused at the base through sustained, selective and alternating to divided at the top, with definitions and the determinants of vigilance. Psycho Didi notes · p. 90 Exogenous — controlled by the stimulus; bottom-up. Endogenous — the brain internally decides what is important; top-down. Sohlberg & Mateer (1987, 1989) — Hierarchical model of attention : focused → sustained → selective → alternating → divided. Focused attention — ability to focus attention on a stimulus. Sustained attention (vigilance) — ability to attend to a stimulus/activity over a long period. Determinants: sensory factor, temporal certainty, spatial certainty, clarity of stimuli. Selective attention — ability to attend to a specific stimulus in the presence of distracting stimuli. Alternating attention — ability to shift focus between two or more stimuli. Divided attention (multitasking) — ability to attend to different stimuli at the same time. Why a pyramid, not a list. Sohlberg and Mateer drew the five types as levels : focused attention is the base and divided attention the top, and each level needs the ones below it to be working. You cannot divide attention between two tasks if you cannot first select one stimulus, sustain it, and switch between them. The model is a clinical one, built for rehabilitating people with brain injury: their Attention Process Training (APT) trains the lowest impaired level first and then moves up. Level (bottom to top) Everyday example 1. Focused Turning towards your name being called, or responding to a touch. 2. Sustained Listening to a one-hour lecture without drifting; a radar operator watching for blips (vigilance). 3. Selective Reading in a noisy canteen while ignoring the chatter. 4. Alternating Switching between reading a recipe and stirring the pot. 5. Divided Driving while holding a conversation. Order trap. Exams ask for the sequence: focused → sustained → selective → alternating → divided . Divided is the highest (most demanding) level, focused the most basic. Alternating = switching back and forth; divided = both at the same moment. Signal Detection Theory (SDT) Signal detection theory. SDT notes with a two by two table of hit, correct rejection, false alarm and miss for liberal and conservative responders. Psycho Didi notes · p. 90 Wesley W. Peterson & Theodore G. Birdsall — Signal Detection Theory : detection of a signal depends on sensitivity and response bias . Sensitivity (d′) = number of hits − number of false alarms. Signal present Signal absent Responds "yes" Hit (correct) False alarm (incorrect) Responds "no" Miss (incorrect) Correct rejection (correct) For a liberal participant the receiver-operating (ROC) curve peaks towards the right; for a conservative participant it peaks towards the left. The page's second table: sorting outcomes by responder type. Response bias is where a person sets the criterion for saying "yes, I detected it". Liberal responder (low criterion: says "yes" readily) Conservative responder (high criterion: says "yes" only when sure) Correct outcome they make more of Hit Correct rejection Error they make more of False alarm Miss Example: a radiologist scanning X-rays for a tumour. A liberal radiologist calls anything doubtful "tumour": she catches almost every real tumour (hits) but also flags many healthy patients (false alarms). A conservative one calls "tumour" only when certain: few false alarms and many correct rejections, but she misses some real tumours. Their sensitivity can be identical; only the bias differs. Traps. (1) Both responders can make all four outcomes; bias only shifts the balance between them. (2) Changing the criterion trades hits against false alarms but does not change sensitivity (d′); d′ changes only if the signal becomes easier or the observer more skilled. (3) "Hits minus false alarms" above is shorthand: formally d′ = z(hit rate) − z(false-alarm rate). Theories of Selective Attention Theories of selective attention. Notes on Cherry, Broadbent's filter model and Treisman's attenuation model, with flow diagrams of the selection filter and the attenuator. Psycho Didi notes · p. 90 Late selection model. Deutsch and Deutsch notes with a flow diagram where messages pass physical analysis and semantic analysis before the attended message reaches awareness and response. Psycho Didi notes · p. 91 Multimode attention theory and perceptual load. Notes on Johnston and Heinz's three-stage multimode theory and Lavie and Tsal's perceptual load theory. Psycho Didi notes · p. 91 Feature integration theory. Treisman and Gelade notes with a diagram of colour and orientation feature maps feeding a map of locations, plus example displays of a colour singleton search and a conjunction search. Psycho Didi notes · p. 91 Spotlight theory of attention. Spotlight theory notes with a circular blurred-text illustration marking the focus, fringe and margin. Psycho Didi notes · p. 91 Shortcomings of selective attention. Definitions of inattentional blindness and change blindness. Psycho Didi notes · p. 91 Heads up: the diagram above dates Treisman's attenuation model to 1980; the standard date is 1960/1964 (Anne Treisman's attenuation theory). 1980 is the date of a different theory, Feature Integration Theory (Treisman & Gelade, 1980). Selective attention is tested with a shadowing / dichotic listening task. Colin Cherry (1953) — early selection model : no overlap in dichotic listening; we do not understand a stimulus before we perceive it. Donald Broadbent (1958) — Filter model (a bottleneck model): we filter information right after we notice it, at the sensory level. Tracing Broadbent's diagram. (1) Two messages (stimulus 1 and stimulus 2, e.g. one in each ear) enter a sensory register (sensory buffer) together, where they are held briefly and only their physical features (ear, pitch, loudness, voice) are available. (2) A selection filter picks one channel on the basis of those physical features and blocks the other completely . (3) Only the selected message passes on to short-term memory and is analysed for meaning. The unattended message is lost before its meaning is ever processed, which is why it is called an early selection model. It fits Colin Cherry's shadowing findings: people noticed a change of voice in the unattended ear but not its content or language. Why Broadbent needed revising. If the filter blocks the other channel completely, nothing meaningful should get through. But Neville Moray (1959) found people often noticed their own name in the unattended ear, and Gray and Wedderburn (1960) found people reported "Dear Aunt Jane" when the words were split between the two ears. Meaning was leaking through, which led to Treisman's attenuation model. Anne Treisman (1960, 1964) — Attenuation model : explains the cocktail-party phenomenon . Instead of blocking stimuli out, the filter merely weakens the strength of stimuli other than the target. Tracing Treisman's diagram. (1) Input from both ears enters the sensory buffer . (2) An attenuator analyses physical features and turns the unattended channel down (like a volume knob), not off; the attended channel passes at full strength. (3) Only after the attenuator is meaning extracted: both the strong attended message and the weak unattended one go through a "dictionary" of words, each with its own threshold. Important or primed words (your own name, "fire", a word that fits the story you are shadowing) have low thresholds , so even the weakened signal can trigger them and reach short-term memory . Treisman (1960) showed this when a story being shadowed switched ears: people briefly followed the meaning into the "wrong" ear. Broadbent vs Treisman. Both put the filter early (before meaning). Broadbent's filter is all-or-none (blocks); Treisman's attenuates (weakens). Hearing your name at a party is explained by Treisman's low-threshold words, not by Broadbent. Deutsch & Deutsch (1963) — Late Selection model : stimuli are filtered out only after being analysed for both their physical properties and their meaning. Tracing the late selection diagram. All incoming messages, attended or not, go through (1) physical analysis and then (2) semantic analysis (their meaning is fully worked out). Only at the last stage, (3) awareness and response , is one message (the most important or relevant) selected for conscious report and action; the rest are understood but quickly forgotten. So the bottleneck is at response , not at perception. Criticism: analysing everything for meaning would be very wasteful, and people detect far fewer targets in the unattended ear than in the attended one. Nilli Lavie's perceptual load theory (below) reconciles the two camps: under low load, selection is late; under high load, it is early. Early vs late in one line. Broadbent: filter before meaning, blocks. Treisman: filter before meaning, weakens. Deutsch & Deutsch: everything gets meaning, selection only at response. Johnston & Heinz (1978) — Multimode attention theory : attention is a flexible system that selects a stimulus at three stages — (1) sensory representations created, (2) semantic representations created, (3) both sensory and semantic representations enter consciousness. More processing requires more mental effort. Lavie & Tsal (1994) — Perceptual Load theory : perception is a limited-capacity process that proceeds automatically until that capacity is filled. Anne Treisman & Garry Gelade (1980) — Feature Integration Theory (FIT) : explains how an individual combines pieces of observable information about an object to form a complete perception. Two kinds of visual search: feature search (fast, pre-attentive, primitive features) and conjunction search (slower, effortful; targets defined by a conjunction of features). Tracing the FIT diagram. FIT has two stages. (1) Pre-attentive stage: the scene is broken into separate feature maps , registered automatically and in parallel: colour maps (one for blue, red, green) and orientation maps (vertical, tilted, horizontal lines). At this stage features are "free-floating"; nothing yet says which colour goes with which line. (2) Focused-attention stage: attention is directed to one spot on the map of locations , like a spotlight. Everything found at that location (say, blue + vertical) is bound together into a temporary object representation ("object file": its properties at time t and place x). (3) This object file is compared with the recognition network , the stored descriptions of objects with their names, and the object is identified. The two search displays on the page. (a) Feature (colour singleton) search (b) Conjunction search Display One blue T among orange Ts and green Xs. Only orange Ts and green Xs; the target is defined by a combination, e.g. a green T, which shares its colour with the Xs and its shape with the Ts. Why The target is the only item on the "blue" map, so it pops out without attention. No single feature map singles out the target; attention must visit items one by one to bind colour and shape. Effect of adding distractors Search time stays flat (parallel search). Search time rises steadily with every extra item (serial search). Illusory conjunctions. FIT predicts that if attention is overloaded or the display is flashed too briefly, features can be wrongly combined (e.g. reporting a red X when a red O and a blue X were shown). Treisman and Schmidt (1982) found exactly this, which is key evidence for FIT. Eriksen & St James (1986); Michael Posner et al. — Spotlight theory of attention : people can attend to only one region of space at a time. Inspired by William James , attention has a focus (central area extracting high-resolution information where attention is directed), a fringe (extracts information more crudely, extending over a specified area), and a margin (the cut-off between them). Reading the spotlight illustration. The page shows a circle of German text. Only the word at the very centre ("noch") is sharp: that is the focus , where attention gives full detail. The words around it are blurred but still recognisable as words: that is the fringe , where information is taken in only crudely. The edge of the circle is the margin , the boundary beyond which nothing is processed. Like a torch beam in a dark room, attention lights up one region of space at a time and can be moved around without moving the eyes (covert attention). Michael Posner (1980) showed this with a cueing task: people respond faster to a target that appears where a cue had pointed than elsewhere. Spotlight vs zoom lens. In the spotlight model the beam has a fixed size. Eriksen and St James (1986) are best known for the zoom-lens version: the beam can be widened or narrowed, and the wider it is, the less detail it gives (a trade-off between area and resolution). Shortcomings of selective attention Inattentional blindness (Arien Mack and Irvin Rock, 1998) — people fail to see things that are actually there. Change blindness — inability to detect changes in objects or scenes being viewed. 4 · Classical & Operant Conditioning Key — definition. Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour as a result of experience. Two basic kinds of learning Introduction to learning. Psycho Didi notes · p. 92 Non-associative learning (short term) — learning about a single stimulus: Habituation — a decreased behavioural response to an innocuous stimulus. Sensitization — an increase in a behavioural response to an intense stimulus. Associative learning (long term) — learning relationships among events: classical conditioning and instrumental (operant) conditioning . Classical Conditioning Strength of conditioning. Psycho Didi notes · p. 93 Ivan Pavlov (1897) — first researched classical conditioning: a previously neutral stimulus becomes associated with another stimulus through repeated pairing. Based on three broad principles: Contiguity — nearness in space and time. Contingency — prediction power. Blocking — a CS blocks conditioning with another neutral stimulus. Principles of conditioning Principle Meaning Example (Pavlov's dog) Acquisition CS & US repeatedly paired so CS acquires US properties. Dog learns to salivate to the bell. Extinction CS presented without US; CR fades and disappears. Dog stops salivating to the bell. Spontaneous recovery After extinction & rest, CS again produces a faint CR. Dog salivates again on hearing the bell. Generalization CR shown to stimuli similar to the CS. Dog salivates to other bell-like noises. Discrimination CR shown only to the CS, not to similar stimuli. Dog salivates only to the specific bell. The three stages of conditioning (Pavlov's dog, as in the page's panels) Stage What is presented What happens Before conditioning (a) Food alone. (b) Bell alone. (a) Food (UCS) → salivation (UCR), an inborn reflex. (b) Bell = neutral stimulus → no salivation (at most the dog pricks up its ears). During conditioning Bell, then food, paired again and again. The dog salivates, but this is still the UCR , triggered by the food. After conditioning Bell alone, no food. Bell is now the CS → salivation, now called the CR . UCR vs CR. The response is the same behaviour (salivation); what changes its name is the trigger. Salivation to food = UCR; salivation to the bell = CR. The CR is usually weaker than the UCR. The neutral stimulus becomes the CS only after learning. Second-order (higher-order) conditioning — once a CS elicits a CR, that CS can briefly be used as a US to condition a response to a new stimulus. Phase Training Result (test) First-order Bell + food → salivation Bell alone → salivation Second-order (no food at all) Light + bell → salivation Light alone → salivation The light was never paired with food; it gained its power only from the bell. Everyday example: a child gets a painful injection from a doctor in a white coat (first-order: white coat → fear). Later the clinic's smell is repeatedly present along with the white coat, and the smell alone starts producing anxiety (second-order). Why second-order learning is weak. Each light + bell trial is also a bell-without-food trial, so the bell itself is slowly being extinguished . Second-order responses are therefore weaker and short-lived, and third-order conditioning is very hard to get. Strength / timing of conditioning Type Timing (CS vs US) Note Delayed Bell rings and, while still ringing, food is presented. Conditioning occurs the fastest . Trace CS, then a short break, then the US. — Simultaneous CS and US presented at the same time. — Backward US presented first, followed by the CS. E.g. taste aversions in pregnancy / chemotherapy. The timing arrows as a timeline (read left to right; each column is a moment in a trial): Type Moment 1 Moment 2 Moment 3 Moment 4 Overlap? Delayed CS CS CS + US US Yes: CS starts first and is still on when the US begins. Trace CS CS (gap: nothing) US No: CS ends before the US starts; the dog must hold a memory "trace" of the CS across the gap. Simultaneous CS + US CS + US Complete: both start and stop together. Backward US US CS CS No: the CS comes after the US. Order of effectiveness. Delayed (forward) is strongest, then trace (weaker as the gap grows), then simultaneous; backward is weakest and often produces little or no conditioning, because the CS predicts nothing. The key is whether the CS predicts the US. Note: chemotherapy and food taste aversions are usually explained as forward pairing with a long delay (the food is eaten before the nausea), not true backward conditioning. Contiguity and Contingency Robert Rescorla — conditioning involves cognitive components. The CS must be a reliable predictor of the US (contingency); mere temporal contiguity is not enough. Positive contingency — CS predicts the presence of the UCS → excitatory conditioning . Zero contingency — no pattern, so no learning takes place. Negative contingency — CS predicts the absence of the UCS → inhibitory conditioning . Classical conditioning & biological preparedness Animals and humans are biologically prepared to make certain connections more easily (e.g. learned taste aversions can be learnt in a single trial). John Garcia & Robert Koelling (1966) — rats more readily learned certain associations: food more likely to become CS for nausea ; noise more likely to become CS for shock . The "bright, noisy, tasty water" experiment. Rats drank water that was sweet (flavoured) and, at the same time, every lick set off a click and a flash of light. So each drink gave a taste cue and an audio-visual cue together. Then one group was made nauseous (by radiation or a toxin) and another group got pain (electric shock through the floor). Later each cue was tested alone: Cue Paired with nausea Paired with pain (shock) Sweet taste Acquires aversion (rats avoid the sweet water) Does not "Click" (+ light) Does not Learns defence (rats avoid the noisy water) Within each group, the taste and the click were always paired with the consequence together, equally often, so pure contiguity predicts equal learning for both cues. Instead, taste linked only with illness, and sound/light only with external pain. Evolution has "prepared" rats to blame sickness on what they ate and pain on what they saw or heard. This challenged the behaviourist idea of equipotentiality (any CS can be linked with any US equally well) and supports Martin Seligman's concept of preparedness (1970). Two Garcia facts examiners love. (1) Taste aversion can form in one trial . (2) It works even with a delay of hours between the taste and the sickness, breaking the usual rule that the CS and US must be close in time. Key — classical conditioning at a glance. Totally based on reflexes ; response is elicited by the stimulus (also called respondent conditioning ); passive learning; reflexes can be conditioned or unconditioned; magnitude of response matters; it is an S–S type of conditioning. The amygdala (lateral nucleus) organizes emotional responses provoked by aversive stimuli. Operant Conditioning Operant conditioning introduction. Psycho Didi notes · p. 94 Learning and maintaining fear. Two-stage account of fear: classical conditioning or escape learning first, then instrumental avoidance learning. Psycho Didi notes · p. 94 Edward Thorndike — learning theory leading to operant conditioning (B. F. Skinner); used a cat in a puzzle box ( trial-and-error learning ). His theory is called associationism / connectionism . Three laws: law of readiness , law of practice/exercise , and the law of effect (behaviour followed by pleasant consequences is repeated; behaviour followed by unpleasant consequences is stopped). Thorndike's puzzle box (1898, Animal Intelligence ). A hungry cat was shut inside a wooden slatted cage with food (fish) placed outside , in view. The way out was a simple mechanism: in the page's drawing, pulling a string (loop) that opens the trap door ; other boxes used a lever or latch. At first the cat scratched, bit and clawed at random; by accident it pulled the string, the door opened and it reached the food. Over repeated trials the useless actions dropped out and the time to escape fell gradually , not suddenly. Thorndike took this smooth learning curve as evidence of trial-and-error learning strengthened by its consequences (the law of effect), not of insight. B. F. Skinner (1937) — coined the term operant conditioning . The Skinner box delivers food via a lever/disk; the food is a reinforcer and giving it is reinforcement . Operant/instrumental conditioning = learning the relationship between responses and outcomes (an S–R association). Parts of the Skinner box (operant chamber) on the page. Part Use Response lever (a key or disk for pigeons) The operant response the animal learns to make. Food dispenser (pellet tray) Delivers the reinforcer: positive reinforcement. Lights Signals, e.g. "pressing pays only when the light is on": used to teach discrimination (the light is a discriminative stimulus). Loudspeaker Sounds/tones used as signals or warning stimuli in the same way. Electrified grid (floor) Delivers mild shock: used for punishment (shock follows a press) or negative reinforcement (pressing turns the shock off, i.e. escape and avoidance learning). Puzzle box vs Skinner box. Thorndike's puzzle box used discrete trials (the cat escapes, the trial ends, the cat is put back) and measured time to escape . Skinner's box is a free-operant setup: the animal stays inside and can respond at any time, and the measure is rate of responding , drawn automatically on a cumulative recorder. Principles of operant conditioning Acquisition — the rat learns to press the bar for food. Extinction — the rat unlearns the bar–food connection and stops pressing. Spontaneous recovery — after extinction and rest, the rat presses the bar again. Generalization — the rat presses other objects that look like the bar. Discrimination — the rat learns to press only a particular bar. Reinforcement & Punishment Positive (add) Negative (remove) Reinforcement (increases behaviour) Deliver a pleasant stimulus after the response (add pleasant). Remove an unpleasant/aversive stimulus after the response (remove unpleasant). Punishment (reduces behaviour) Deliver an unpleasant/aversive stimulus after the response (add unpleasant). Remove a pleasant stimulus after the response (remove pleasant). Negative reinforcement ≠ punishment. Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant to increase a behaviour; punishment reduces a behaviour. Don't confuse "negative" (remove) with "punishment" (weaken). Shaping and Chaining Shaping — reinforces the steps used to reach the desired behaviour. Chaining — animals are taught to perform a number of responses successively to get a reward. Reinforcement schedules Two basic types: Continuous (rewarded every time; better for learning new behaviour) and Partial (better once behaviour is learnt; more resistant to extinction ). Schedule Reinforcement provided... Fixed ratio After a fixed number of responses. Variable ratio After a number of responses that varies unpredictably. Fixed interval After a fixed amount of time since the last reinforcement. Variable interval After an amount of time that varies unpredictably since the last reinforcement. Comparing the four schedules. The page's graph ranks them by the steepness of their lines: variable ratio steepest, then fixed ratio, then variable interval, with fixed interval lowest . Strictly, the y-axis in such graphs is the cumulative number of responses (as drawn by Skinner's cumulative recorder), so a steeper line means a faster rate of responding. Schedule Response pattern Resistance to extinction Everyday example Variable ratio Highest, steady rate; no pauses Highest Slot machines, lottery tickets Fixed ratio High rate, with a short pause after each reward Lower than the variable schedules Piece-rate pay (paid per 10 shirts sewn) Variable interval Moderate, steady rate High Checking messages; surprise quizzes Fixed interval Lowest; "scalloped": slow just after a reward, speeding up as the time for the next one nears Lower than the variable schedules Monthly salary; cramming just before a scheduled exam Rules of thumb. Ratio schedules (reward depends on number of responses) give faster responding than interval schedules (reward depends on time ). Variable schedules give steadier responding and more resistance to extinction than fixed ones, because the learner can never tell when the next reward is due. Continuous reinforcement is fastest for learning but extinguishes fastest. Learning and maintaining fear (two-factor) Stage 1 — classical conditioning / escape learning: through repeated pairing of the warning light (CS) and shock (UCS), the animal learns the light predicts the shock and shows a conditioned fear response (CR) to the light alone. Stage 2 — instrumental conditioning / avoidance learning: successful reduction of the aversive stimulus reinforces and strengthens the avoidance behaviour. It gives temporary relief, but the long-run consequences of avoidance are detrimental. What the page adds to stage 1: instrumental escape learning. Stage 1 is not only classical. While the shock is actually on, the animal also learns an escape response: jumping to the safe side ends the shock, and the ending of the shock negatively reinforces the jump. So stage 1 = light → fear (classical) plus shock → jump to escape (instrumental). In stage 2 the animal starts jumping as soon as the light comes on, before any shock: this is avoidance , reinforced by the drop in fear. This is O. Hobart Mowrer's two-factor theory (1947): fear is acquired by classical conditioning and kept going by operant avoidance. Escape vs avoidance. Escape ends an aversive stimulus that is already present (jump while shocked). Avoidance prevents it from arriving (jump at the warning light). Because the avoider never stays to learn that the light is no longer followed by shock, the fear never extinguishes. That is why phobias persist, and why treatment uses exposure with response prevention . 5 · Cognitive & Social Learning Learned Helplessness Learned helplessness. Maier and Seligman two-stage experiment notes with a drawing of the shuttle box, its warning light, electrified grid floor and barrier. Psycho Didi notes · p. 94 Cognitive approach to learning. Notes on Woodworth's S-O-R approach and Kohler's insight learning with chimpanzees. Psycho Didi notes · p. 94 Martin Seligman — cognitive approach to learning: control over the outcome of behaviour is as important for learning as contiguity and contingency. Experiment — Maier & Seligman (1976): Stage 1: some dogs learn that whether they receive a shock depends on their own behaviour; other dogs learn they have no control over the shock. Stage 2: both groups placed in a shuttle box; a tone signals an imminent shock, and the dog must jump the barrier to avoid it. Found: control dogs learn the response rapidly; yoked dogs do not. They had learned that shocks were uncontrollable, and this non-control made avoidance learning impossible → learned helplessness . The shuttle box (as drawn on the page). A box with two compartments, each with a metal grid floor , separated by a low barrier the dog can easily jump. A warning signal comes first: in the drawing a light dims (the notes' text says a tone; either can be used). A few seconds later the grid floor on the dog's side is electrified , while the other side stays safe . If the dog jumps the barrier during the warning it avoids the shock completely; if it jumps after the shock starts it escapes it. Dogs given controllable shock in stage 1 (or no shock) quickly learn to jump. Dogs given inescapable (yoked) shock mostly lie down and whine, taking the shock even though escape is one easy jump away. Dates and yoking. The original dog studies were by Overmier & Seligman (1967) and Seligman & Maier (1967); Maier & Seligman (1976) is their major review. "Yoked" means the helpless dog received exactly the same shocks as its partner, but its own responses had no effect; so the only difference between the groups is control , not the amount of shock. Seligman linked this to depression . Robert Woodworth — S–O–R approach : to predict the response we must know not only the stimulus but also the organism stimulated; human motivations and conscious decisions play an important part in behaviour. Wolfgang Köhler (1925) — Insight learning , studied on chimpanzees: insight occurs when one suddenly realises how to solve a problem. Learning happens in a sudden way due to insight, not gradual strengthening of the S–R connection. Social Learning Theory Social learning theory. Bandura notes with the attention, retention, motor reproduction and motivation sequence and three Bobo doll conditions: reinforced, not reinforced and punished model. Psycho Didi notes · p. 94 Albert Bandura — Social Learning Theory (aka observational learning ): learning is achieved by mentally rehearsing and then imitating the observed actions of models. An S–O–R theory. Process of learning (sequence): attention → retention → motor reproduction → motivation. Bobo doll experiment — conditions: model hits doll and is reinforced (vicarious reinforcement), model hits doll and is not reinforced , model hits doll and is punished (vicarious punishment). Key. Learning occurs in all three conditions irrespective of reinforcement; however, reproduction of behaviour was dependent on reinforcement. Tolman's Purposive Behaviourism Tolman's purposive behaviourism. Tolman and Honzik latent learning notes with a graph of maze errors over 17 daily trials for rewarded, never-rewarded and delayed-reward rat groups. Psycho Didi notes · p. 95 Edward Tolman — Purposive behaviourism (aka latent learning, expectancy, place learning, sign-stimulus theory). Experiment: Tolman & Honzik (1930) . Group A — reinforced on each trial; Group B — never reinforced; Group C — not reinforced on days 1 to 10, then reinforced (food in the goal box) from day 11 onwards . Found: Group C had actually learnt the maze without reinforcement ( latent learning ) but showed it once reinforcement appeared. The rats developed a cognitive map — a mental representation of the maze. Reading the graph (one trial per day for 17 days; y-axis = average errors, i.e. wrong turns into blind alleys). The rewarded group's errors fall steadily from day 1. The no-reward group improves only slightly (getting out of the maze was a small reward in itself). The delayed-reward group runs level with the no-reward group for 10 days; then, right after it first finds food on day 11, its errors drop sharply , catching up with the rewarded group almost at once and then making even slightly fewer errors over days 11 to 17. So the learning had already happened during the unrewarded days; the food only gave the rats a reason to show it. Learning vs performance. Tolman's point is that reinforcement affects performance , not learning itself. A drop that sudden cannot be explained by gradual S–R strengthening from just one or two rewards. Group C was rewarded on every day from 11 on, not "only on day 11". Components of learning: the significate (desired outcome/goal), the sign (stimulus prompting action), and means–end relations (the learner's internal thought process). Field Theory Field theory. Lewin's field theory notes with a life space diagram (person, driving and restraining vectors, barrier, goal) and the four types of conflict. Psycho Didi notes · p. 95 Kurt Lewin (1930) — Field Theory , based on Gestalt psychology, an S–O–R approach: a person's psychological state affects their social field and vice versa. "Field" = the totality of a person's experiences, needs and topography; field forces (intrinsic or extrinsic) drive behaviour. Reading the life space diagram. Lewin summed up his theory as B = f(P, E) : behaviour is a function of the person and their psychological environment. The life space (outer boundary) is everything that matters to the person at that moment, as they see it. Inside it: Person : the circle on the left. Goal marked + : it has positive valence (attraction). A feared object would have negative valence (−). Driving force (vector): an arrow pushing the person towards the goal. A vector has direction and strength. Restraining force (vector): an arrow pointing back, holding the person away from the goal. Barrier : the hatched wall between person and goal, an obstacle that blocks movement. Example: a student's goal is a seat in an M.Phil Clinical Psychology course (+ valence). Driving forces: interest in clinical work, family support. Restraining forces: fear of failure, the cost of another year. Barrier: the entrance exam and its limited seats. Behaviour (studying, applying) depends on the balance of these forces; Lewin's later force-field analysis says change happens by strengthening driving forces or weakening restraining ones. Types of conflict Conflict Description Vacillation / equilibrium Approach–approach Two goals, both valued. Low vacillation, low equilibrium. Avoidance–avoidance Two goals, both undesirable; running away is more likely. More vacillation and equilibrium. Approach–avoidance One goal has both positive and negative vectors. Highest vacillation; equilibrium stage very long. Double approach–avoidance Multiple goals each with positive and negative vectors. Conflict resolved more easily when equilibrium is less. 6 · Theories of Memory Introduction to memory. Definition of memory as the capacity to register, store and recover information, with a brain and clock icon. Psycho Didi notes · p. 96 Key — definition. Memory is our capacity to register, store and recover information over time — the persistence of learning over time. It is a complex mental system involving multiple stages of information processing. Early models Models of memory: early models. Primary memory (William James) and secondary memory (Waugh and Norman, 1965) with what each holds. Psycho Didi notes · p. 96 In the mid-1960s researchers proposed two structures of memory: Primary memory — proposed by William James ; holds temporary information currently in use. Secondary memory — proposed by Waugh & Norman (1965) ; holds information permanently or for a very long time. Sperling & iconic memory George Sperling and iconic memory. Iconic memory notes with the Sperling (1960) letter grid figure comparing whole report and partial report. Psycho Didi notes · p. 96 George Sperling — iconic memory : a type of visual memory lasting only a fraction of a second. Sensory memory capacity is much larger than believed. In Sperling's test, partial report was more successful than whole report; partial report showed about 9 of 12 letters were briefly available in iconic memory, roughly twice what whole report suggests. Sperling's experiment (1960), step by step (the page's figure): Whole report Partial report Display A grid of 12 letters (3 rows of 4) flashed for a very brief time (15 to 500 ms; usually 50 ms), then a blank screen. Task Report as many of the 12 letters as you can. Right after the display goes off, a tone (high, middle or low) tells you which one row to report. Result About 4 to 5 of 12 letters (33 to 40 percent). About 3 to 4 of the 4 letters in the cued row (75 to 100 percent). Why partial report proves a bigger store. The person does not know which row will be cued until the letters are gone. If they can report 3 of 4 from any row cued, then about 75 percent of all 12 letters (about 9) must have been available at that instant. Whole report underestimates this because the image fades while the person is still naming the first few letters. When the tone was delayed, the advantage shrank, and by about 1 second (1000 ms) it had gone: the icon lasts well under a second. Numbers to remember. Iconic memory: large capacity, about 250 ms to 1 s . Echoic memory (auditory sensory memory) lasts longer, about 2 to 4 s. Exams often ask "partial report technique" = Sperling; "whole report underestimates sensory memory". Multi-Store Model Multi-store model. Atkinson and Shiffrin flow diagram from sensory memory through selective attention and encoding to STM and LTM, with maintenance and elaborative rehearsal and retrieval loops. Psycho Didi notes · p. 96 Richard Atkinson & Richard Shiffrin (1968) — Multi-Store (modal) Model : information passes from one storage system to the next in a fixed order — Sensory memory → STM → LTM . Store Duration Capacity Notes Sensory memory 1–4 sec Limited, but more than STM Subtypes: iconic (visual), echoic (auditory), haptic (touch). Short-term memory (STM) 18–30 sec 7 ± 2 Temporary storage; gate to LTM; prone to forgetting. Long-term memory (LTM) Very long / permanent Unlimited Reached via elaborative rehearsal ; accessed by retrieval. Flow: Sensory memory → (selective attention → encoding) → STM → (maintenance rehearsal keeps it in STM; elaborative rehearsal moves it) → LTM. The arrows in the diagram. Maintenance rehearsal is drawn as a small loop on STM itself : repeating information over and over (like saying a phone number until you dial it) keeps it alive in STM but does little to move it into LTM. Stop repeating and it is lost in about 18 to 30 seconds. Elaborative rehearsal is the arrow from STM down to LTM : linking the new item to meaning and to what you already know (e.g. connecting a new term to an example) transfers it to LTM. Retrieval is the arrow from LTM back up to STM : to use a stored memory you must bring it back into STM (working consciousness). So the flow is two-way: STM is both the gate into LTM and the place where LTM contents are used. Heads up on "prone to forgetting". The diagram prints "prone to forgetting" under LTM; the text table above attaches it to STM. Standard answer: forgetting can happen at every stage, but in different ways. Sensory memory: the trace decays within a second or so. STM: information is lost quickly by displacement and decay unless rehearsed, so STM is the store described as "fragile". LTM: storage is relatively permanent; forgetting there is mainly retrieval failure and interference , not loss. George Miller (1956) — the magic number 7 ± 2 : the average number of items held in short-term memory. Emphasized recoding / chunking of information. Working Memory Model The working memory model. Baddeley and Hitch diagram with the central executive above the episodic buffer, fed by the visuo-spatial sketchpad and the phonological loop with its articulatory subsystem. Psycho Didi notes · p. 97 Alan Baddeley & Graham Hitch (1974) — Working Memory Model : temporarily holds and manipulates information during cognitive tasks. Memory span is determined by the speed with which we rehearse information. Component Role Central executive (master subsystem) The attention controller : decides what to attend to, switches attention between tasks, and coordinates the two slave systems. It has no storage of its own. Visuo-spatial sketchpad (slave subsystem) Handles visual and spatial information (1–2 sec). It has two parts: a visual part (shape and colour: "what it looks like") and a spatial part (location and movement: "where it is"), which also helps plan motor movement . Robert Logie (1995) named these the visual cache and the inner scribe. Phonological loop (slave subsystem) Holds verbal/acoustic information (1–4 sec); the articulatory subsystem performs subvocal rehearsal. Episodic buffer (added by Baddeley, 2000) Takes information from everywhere (both slave systems and LTM) and integrates it into single multi-sensory "episodes"; it is the link with LTM, so it helps determine what goes into LTM . Limited capacity (Baddeley later put it at about four chunks). The arrows in the diagram. Both slave systems (sketchpad and phonological loop) send their contents up into the episodic buffer , which combines them, e.g. the sound of a word with the picture it names. The buffer and the central executive are joined by a two-way arrow : the executive directs what the buffer holds and draws on the integrated result. Example: following spoken directions while looking at a map uses the loop (the words), the sketchpad (the map), the buffer (one combined route) and the executive (switching between listening and looking). Who does what. Integration and the link to LTM belong to the episodic buffer (as the diagram shows); control of attention belongs to the central executive . Do not swap them in an MCQ. The diagram's "20–30 sec" beside the buffer is not a standard figure: Baddeley described the buffer's limit in chunks, not seconds. STM vs Working memory. STM (Atkinson–Shiffrin) is a passive store (~7±2 items, 18–30 sec). Working memory (Baddeley–Hitch) is an active system that holds and manipulates information via a central executive plus slave subsystems. Psycho Didi notes · p. 98 Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885) — systematically tested his own memory of lists of nonsense syllables . Found a huge drop in retention soon after learning that eventually levelled off (the method of savings ); emphasized overlearning / revision . Retrieval types Types of retrieval. Psycho Didi notes · p. 98 Retrieval Note Recall Without a cue — the hardest . Cued recall Easier than free recall. Recognition Easiest. Relearning The most sensitive measure of learning. Neural basis Long-term potentiation. LTP notes with a drawing comparing a normal and a potentiated synapse, showing the presynaptic terminal, synaptic cleft, receptors and dendritic spine. Psycho Didi notes · p. 98 Long-term depression. Definition of LTD as the long-term weakening and pruning of unused synaptic connections. Psycho Didi notes · p. 98 Long-Term Potentiation (LTP; Timothy Bliss and Terje Lømo, 1973) — persistent strengthening of a synaptic connection lasting minutes to hours; based on the Hebbian principle ("neurons that fire together, wire together"). NMDA glutamate receptors are necessary for memory formation; AMPA receptors — dendrites double their contact surface by splitting in two; terminal buttons release more neurotransmitter after potentiation; nitric oxide acts as a catalyst. In the lab, a high-frequency electric charge is applied to the pre-synaptic neuron. Reading the LTP drawing (normal vs potentiated synapse). Left, a normal synapse: the presynaptic terminal releases a few vesicles of neurotransmitter (glutamate) across the synaptic cleft (only about 20 nm wide) onto receptors on a dendritic spine , letting in a little Na + and Ca 2+ . Right, after high-frequency stimulation, the same synapse is "potentiated": (1) the presynaptic terminal releases more neurotransmitter ; (2) extra receptors (AMPA receptors) are inserted into the spine's membrane; (3) so more Na + and Ca 2+ flow in and the postsynaptic response to the same input is bigger. That bigger response is the "stronger synapse". Sequence to remember: strong, repeated input → glutamate → AMPA receptors depolarise the spine → this removes the magnesium (Mg 2+ ) block from NMDA receptors → Ca 2+ floods in → enzymes add more AMPA receptors (postsynaptic change), and a retrograde messenger such as nitric oxide travels back to make the terminal release more transmitter (presynaptic change). With lasting LTP the spine can also grow or split, adding contacts. Trap: the NMDA receptor is the "coincidence detector": it opens only when glutamate is bound and the postsynaptic cell is already depolarised, which is Hebb's rule in molecular form. Bliss and Lømo first showed LTP in the rabbit hippocampus . In a brain slice it lasts hours; in a living animal it can last days or weeks. Long-Term Depression (LTD) — long-term weakening of a synaptic connection; prunes unused synapses, trimming unimportant connections and leaving only the salient connections strengthened by LTP. Theories of forgetting Decay theory of forgetting. Decay theory in two points beside an illustration of a brain breaking into fragments. Psycho Didi notes · p. 98 The serial position curve. Serial position notes with a U-shaped recall curve labelling the primacy effect, the recency effect and the interference at the low middle. Psycho Didi notes · p. 98 Interference theory of forgetting. Bergstrom's interference theory with definitions of proactive and retroactive interference and two factors for forgetting. Psycho Didi notes · p. 99 Decay theory — forgetting is an automatic process; the engram for the information disappears. Interference theory — supported by the serial-position curve. Serial Position Curve Represents the probability of recall of a word given its serial position in a list. Primacy effect — superior recall of words at/near the beginning of a list (into LTM). Nothing came before them, so they suffer no proactive interference ; they are exposed only to retroactive interference from the later words. They also get the most rehearsal. Recency effect — superior recall of words at/near the end of a list (still in STM). Nothing comes after them, so they suffer no retroactive interference ; they are exposed only to proactive interference from the earlier words. Middle of the list : the low point of the curve. These words get both proactive interference (from words before) and retroactive interference (from words after), and little rehearsal, so they are recalled worst. How to read the curve's labels. The diagram writes "retroactive interference" at the primacy end, "proactive interference" at the recency end, and "retroactive & proactive" at the dip. Each label names the only kind of interference that part of the list is exposed to , not the cause of the effect. That matches the standard account: proactive interference (earlier learning) hurts recall of later items; retroactive interference (later learning) hurts recall of earlier items. How each end is wiped out. Recency disappears if recall is delayed by about 30 seconds of a distracting task (e.g. counting backwards), because the last items drop out of STM; primacy is unaffected (Murray Glanzer and Anita Cunitz, 1966). Primacy shrinks if words are presented faster, because there is less time to rehearse them into LTM. This double dissociation is classic evidence for separate STM and LTM stores. John Bergström (1892) — Interference theory of forgetting . Proactive vs retroactive interference. Proactive — old information learned before disrupts recall of the new item (forward-acting). Retroactive — new information disrupts retrieval of previously learned information (backward-acting). Factors: learning new information unlearns previous; response competition between similar materials. Motivated forgetting Motivated forgetting. Freud's account of motivated forgetting through unconscious repression of traumatic memories. Psycho Didi notes · p. 99 Sigmund Freud — motivated forgetting via repression : we unconsciously prevent traumatic events from entering awareness to avoid anxiety or blows to self-concept. The repressed material is not lost, but hidden from consciousness. Encoding specificity Encoding specificity. Tulving's encoding specificity with state dependent and context dependent memory. Psycho Didi notes · p. 99 Endel Tulving — encoding specificity . Two related types: State-dependent memory — information is better retrieved in similar emotional and physical states to those at encoding. Context-dependent memory (Duncan Godden and Alan Baddeley, 1975) — information is easier to retrieve in the place/environment where it was originally learnt. The Zeigarnik effect Zeigarnik effect. Definition of the Zeigarnik effect, credited to Bluma Zeigarnik. Psycho Didi notes · p. 98 Bluma Zeigarnik — the Zeigarnik effect : unfinished, incomplete and unpleasant tasks are not forgotten as easily as completed ones. The Seven Sins of Memory The seven sins of memory. Schacter's (2001) list of memory sins with sub-points on blocking, suggestibility, the five biases and misattribution, beside a devil cartoon. Psycho Didi notes · p. 99 Daniel Schacter (2001) — the Seven Sins of Memory . Transience Absent-mindedness Blocking — blocked by sensory information; e.g. the tip-of-the-tongue (Roger Brown and David McNeill, 1966) phenomenon. Suggestibility / misinformation — occurs due to a reality-monitoring error. Bias — five types: consistency, change, hindsight, egocentric, stereotypical. Misattribution — occurs due to a source-monitoring error. Persistence (Also noted as memory failings: encoding failure .) Seven, not eight. The page lists encoding failure among the sins, which makes eight items. Schacter's list has exactly the seven above. Encoding failure (the information never got into memory, e.g. not being able to draw the details of a coin you see every day) is a separate cause of forgetting; within Schacter's scheme it is closest to absent-mindedness. Schacter splits the seven into sins of omission (forgetting: the first three) and sins of commission (distortion or unwanted memory: the last four). Sin Meaning Example Transience Memory fades with time. Forgetting most of a lecture's details a month later (the Ebbinghaus curve). Absent-mindedness Lapse of attention when encoding or when you need to remember. Forgetting where you put your keys; forgetting to take a tablet. Blocking The memory is stored but temporarily cannot be retrieved, often because a similar wrong item keeps coming to mind. Tip-of-the-tongue: you know the name, can give its first letter, but cannot say it. The page's example: "if you hadn't said XYZ, I would be able to remember", i.e. the wrong word someone else said is blocking the right one. Misattribution Right memory, wrong source. Believing you read a fact in a textbook when a friend told you; unknowingly "inventing" a tune you had actually heard before (cryptomnesia). Suggestibility Memories altered by leading questions or others' suggestions. Loftus's "smashed" vs "hit" study below. Bias Present beliefs and knowledge reshape memories of the past. Hindsight: "I always knew she would win." Consistency: remembering your past opinions as closer to your present ones than they were. Persistence Unwanted memories you cannot forget. Intrusive flashbacks in PTSD; replaying an embarrassing moment. Blocking vs transience. In blocking the memory is still there (it often pops up later); in transience it has actually faded. Misattribution is a source-monitoring error (where did I learn this?); suggestibility is memory being changed by outside information. Distorted / manufactured memories The lost in the mall study. Group 1 was asked how fast the cars were going when they " smashed " into each other (implying a severe accident); Group 2 heard " hit " (milder). Those who heard "smash" remembered higher speeds and were more likely to (falsely) report broken glass — there was none in the film. Psycho Didi notes · p. 99 Helpful for consolidation: Categorical clustering — organizing a list into a set of categories. Interactive images — creating images that link the isolated words in a list. Keyword system — an interactive image linking the sound and meaning of a foreign word with a familiar word. 8 · Theories of Intelligence Introduction to intelligence. Wechsler's 1944 definition of intelligence and the first two theories, Binet's unifactor and Spearman's two-factor theory. Psycho Didi notes · p. 100 Key — definition. Wechsler (1944): intelligence is the aggregate or global capacity of the individual to act purposefully, think rationally, and deal effectively with his environment. The first theory of intelligence was Alfred Binet's unifactor theory ; the second was Charles Spearman's two-factor theory . Spearman's Two-Factor Theory Charles Spearman and the tetrad equation. Spearman's split of intelligence into a general g factor and specific s factors, with notes on tetrad difference and the tetrad equation. Psycho Didi notes · p. 100 Charles Spearman (1904) — Two-factor theory ; laid the groundwork of factor analysis . Intelligence has a general 'g' factor (an overriding intelligence, almost exclusively inherited) and specific 's' factors (competence in specific abilities such as mathematics, language, music). Spearman used the method of tetrad difference : the tetrad difference should be zero but was not, due to a common g factor. Tetrad equation: r 12 × r 34 = r 23 × r 14 . Psycho Didi notes · p. 100 Raymond Cattell — general intelligence = fluid (Gf) + crystallized (Gc) intelligence (aka the investment theory ); used factor analysis and second-order factors. Fluid intelligence (Gf) Crystallized intelligence (Gc) Nature Basic capacity for learning and problem solving, independent of education/experience. Result of the interaction of fluid intelligence and culture; learned knowledge and skills. Development Grows rapidly in adolescence to the 20s, then declines (does not disappear). Keeps increasing until death; created by the investment of fluid intelligence into the environment. Environment Cannot be affected by environment. Strong environmental influence. John Horn — expanded the Gf–Gc model with additional abilities: visual processing ( Gv ), short-term acquisition & retrieval ( SAR / Gsm ), long-term storage & retrieval ( TSR / Glr ), processing speed ( Gs ), auditory processing ( Ga ), reaction/decision speed ( Gt ), quantitative ability ( Gq ), and broad reading–writing ( Grw ). Jensen's two sets of abilities, Level 1 (memory, simple associative learning) and Level 2 (abstract reasoning), and his method of study. Level 1 abilities — memory functions and simple associative learning; equally distributed among the races. Vernon's Hierarchical Theory Vernon's hierarchical theory of intelligence. Four-level tree from general ability g through the v:ed and k:m major groups and six minor group factors down to specific abilities s. Psycho Didi notes · p. 101 Philip Vernon — hierarchical theory. Level 1: general ability (g). Level 2 (major group): verbal-educational (v:ed) and spatial-mechanical (k:m). Level 3 (minor group): creative abilities, verbal fluency, numerical factors, spatial factors, psychomotor factors, mechanical-information factors. Level 4: specific abilities (s). Which minor factors sit under which major factor (Philip Vernon, 1950): Major group factor (Level 2) Minor group factors under it (Level 3) v:ed (verbal-educational) Creative abilities, verbal fluency, numerical factors k:m (spatial-mechanical, also called practical-mechanical) Spatial factors, psychomotor factors, mechanical-information factors Each minor factor then splits into many specific (s) abilities at Level 4. Read from the top, the tree goes from the broadest ability (g) to the narrowest (s). Traps. Numerical ability sits under v:ed (it is school-taught), not k:m. Psycho Didi notes · p. 102 Robert Sternberg — Triarchic theory ; no factor analysis, rejected g ; disagrees with Charles Spearman, agrees with Howard Gardner. Intelligence Involves Analytical / Componential The page's tree shows four kinds of components: metacomponents (plan, monitor and evaluate a task), performance components (carry out the plan), knowledge-acquisition components and retention components . Only the knowledge-acquisition components branch into the three selective processes: selective encoding (picking out the relevant information), selective comparison (relating it to what you already know) and selective combination (putting the pieces together). Sternberg's best-known (1985) version lists three kinds: metacomponents, performance and knowledge-acquisition components. Creative / Experiential Having insights, synthesizing, adapting to unique situations; selective encoding & selective combination (in Sternberg's account of insight, the same selective processes are applied to novel problems). Practical / Contextual Everyday tasks and relating to the world (aka "wisdom"); three acts — environmental adaptation, shaping, selection. The three acts of practical intelligence , with a workplace example: Adaptation : changing yourself to fit the environment (learning the unwritten rules of a new job). Shaping : changing the environment to fit you (persuading the team to adopt a better system). Selection : choosing a new environment when neither works (moving to a different job). Components: potential abilities, environmental context, internal motivation. PASS = Planning, Attention, Simultaneous and Successive processing. Intelligence is seen as four cognitive processes rather than one g or a list of abilities: Process What it does Example task Luria's functional unit (brain area) Attention (attention-arousal) Keeps the brain alert and focused on the relevant stimulus while resisting distraction. Spotting every "7" in a page of numbers. First unit : brain stem (reticular activating system) and related areas Simultaneous processing Integrates separate pieces into one whole that is grasped all at once. Solving a pattern-completion (matrices) item; understanding a map. Second unit : occipital, parietal and temporal lobes (receive, process and store information) Successive processing Handles information in a fixed serial order, one item after another. Repeating a list of words or digits in order; following the sequence of sounds in a word. Planning Sets goals, chooses strategies, monitors and corrects one's own performance (executive control). Input enters, the three functional units work together (two-way arrows), and output (behaviour) leaves from the planning unit. All of them rest on a base of knowledge : what a person already knows (conceptual, perceptual, memory) shapes how each process works. Psycho Didi notes · p. 103 Heads up: the flow above shows "Incubation" twice; the fourth box should read Illumination . The correct order is orientation (only in some five-step versions) → preparation → incubation → illumination → verification. Graham Wallas (1926) — the first theory of creativity (stage model of the creative process, in his book The Art of Thought ). Wallas's own model has four stages; these notes add orientation at the start, giving five steps. Orientation (only in the five-step version): becoming aware of and defining the problem. Preparation : conscious hard work, gathering information and trying solutions. Incubation — unconscious: you stop working on the problem and the mind keeps working on it in the background. Illumination — maximum creative thinking (insight): the "aha" moment when the idea suddenly appears. Verification — evaluation and revision: testing and refining the idea. Example: a researcher reads everything on a problem for weeks (preparation), gives up and goes on holiday (incubation), suddenly sees the answer while walking on the beach (illumination), then returns to test it (verification). What exams key. The standard answer is Wallas's four stages: preparation → incubation → illumination → verification . Wallas also described intimation (the feeling that a solution is about to arrive) just before illumination, which is why some books count five stages. Thinking involves the mental manipulation and processing of information — generating and/or evaluating ideas, arguments, beliefs and statements. Its two major components are mental images and concepts . Concepts Thinking. Tree splitting thinking into mental images and concepts, with concepts branching into simple, complex (conjunctive, disjunctive), natural and artificial types. Psycho Didi notes · p. 104 Natural concept — a mental representation of an object/event drawn from personal experience, used to categorize other objects/events. Artificial concept — a concept defined by a specific set of characteristics. Simple concept — has a single common feature. Complex concept : Conjunctive — simultaneous presence of two or more common characteristics. Disjunctive — presence of one common characteristic or another. Learning concepts (concept formation) Learning concepts: hypothesis-testing model. Bruner, Goodnow and Austin strategies split into scanning (simultaneous, successive) and focusing (conservative focusing, focus gambling). Psycho Didi notes · p. 104 Jerome Bruner, Goodnow & Austin (1956) — the hypothesis-testing model of concept formation. Strategies participants may use: Strategy Description Simultaneous scanning Start with all possible hypotheses and eliminate the untenable ones. Successive scanning Begin with a single hypothesis, keep it if successful; if not, change it based on all previous experience. Conservative focusing Formulate a hypothesis, pick a positive instance as focus, then reformulate changing only one feature at a time, noting each outcome. Focus gambling Change more than one feature at a time, gambling to determine the concept more quickly. Two families of strategy (as the page groups them): Family Strategies How it works Scanning Simultaneous scanning, successive scanning You work with hypotheses (guesses about the whole concept) and test them: all at once (simultaneous) or one at a time (successive). Focusing Conservative focusing, focus gambling You start from one positive instance (an example that fits the concept, the "focus") and change its features to see which ones matter: one at a time (conservative) or several at once (gambling). Example: in Bruner, Goodnow and Austin's card task, each card varies in shape, colour, number of figures and number of borders, and the hidden concept is, say, "red circles". Told that a card with two red circles and one border is an example, a conservative focuser next picks a card that differs only in colour (two green circles, one border). If it is not an example, colour matters; and so on, one feature at a time. Which is best? Simultaneous scanning is the most demanding on memory (you must hold every possible hypothesis). Conservative focusing is the safest and most efficient. Focus gambling can reach the answer faster but risks having to start over. Successive scanning is the easiest on memory but slow. Trial and error — try a number of different solutions until the correct one is reached. Algorithm — sequences of operations that, in theory, guarantee a solution. Heuristics — general rules of thumb that help achieve a solution while decreasing effort by letting us examine fewer cues. The page splits heuristics into formal and informal . Formal heuristics (deliberate strategies for solving problems and choosing between options): Heuristic Description Satisficing (Herbert Simon, 1956) Consider options one by one and select the first that is satisfactory / good enough to meet a minimum level of acceptability. Elimination by aspects Eliminate alternatives by focusing on aspects of each, one at a time. Selection by aspects Select from alternatives by focusing on aspects of each, one at a time. Lexicographic heuristic Choose the option best on a single criterion, ignoring other factors. Analogy Use an old solution to solve a new problem. Means–end analysis Compare current position with the goal and take steps to reduce the difference. Example: Tower of Hanoi . Repeated state avoidance A formal heuristic: avoiding repetition leads to solution in the minimum number of steps. Hill climbing A formal heuristic: at each step, take the move that seems to bring you closest to the goal, like always walking uphill to reach a summit. Risk: you can get stuck on a "local peak", because the method never takes a step that moves you temporarily away from the goal. (The page's wording, "combine two or more steps into a single step", is not the standard definition.) Formal vs informal: which list is which. On the page, the list above (satisficing to hill climbing) sits under formal , and the list in the next section (availability to framing) sits under informal , marked as obstacles to problem solving. An earlier version of these notes called the list above "informal"; that was wrong, and contradicted its own "formal heuristic" rows. Note that the formal/informal split is this source's own grouping. Standard textbooks (e.g. Sternberg, Galotti) instead separate problem-solving heuristics (means-end analysis, hill climbing, analogy), decision-making strategies (satisficing; elimination by aspects, Amos Tversky, 1972; lexicographic) and judgment heuristics (availability, representativeness, anchoring: Tversky and Kahneman, 1974). Judgment & decision-making heuristics Heuristics listed under informal. The right-hand heuristic list from availability to framing, including the halo and horn effects under anchoring. Psycho Didi notes · p. 105 Heuristic Description Availability Judge frequency/likelihood by the ease with which relevant instances come to mind. Representativeness Judge frequency/likelihood by how much the event resembles the typical case. Anchoring & adjustment Judge by starting from an anchor and adjusting up or down. Simulation Judge by the ease with which you can imagine or mentally simulate an event. Peak–end Judge past experiences almost entirely on their peak and their end. Base rate Decide based on probability (base rates). Contagion Decide based on the idea that things once in contact continue to influence each other. Scarcity Place more value on objects that are scarce. Framing Decide based on how information is presented rather than the information itself. Halo effect (Edward Thorndike, 1920) — being influenced by a person's initial impression or external features (favourable). Horn effect — allowing an unfavourable first impression to influence overall judgment. Why the page puts halo and horn under anchoring. On the page these two effects are sub-points of the anchoring and adjustment heuristic. The logic: the first impression works as an anchor , and later judgments are adjusted from it, but not enough. Example: an interview candidate who is well dressed and confident (anchor) is then rated as more competent and honest too (halo); one who arrives late and untidy is rated lower on everything else (horn), even on qualities the first impression says nothing about. Classification trap. In standard textbooks the halo effect (Edward Thorndike, 1920, from officers rating their soldiers) is treated as a separate bias in person perception and rating, not as a "type" of the anchoring heuristic; the anchor link is this source's way of explaining it. Anchoring proper (Tversky and Kahneman, 1974) is usually shown with number estimates: after a rigged wheel of fortune stopped at 10 or at 65, people estimated the percentage of African countries in the United Nations at about 25 and 45 respectively. All the heuristics in the table above are the page's informal heuristics: fast judgment shortcuts that usually work but often lead to biases, which is why the page marks them as obstacles to problem solving. Obstacles to problem solving Obstacles to problem solving. Mind map of five obstacles: fixed mindset, mental set, functional fixedness, fallacies (gambler's, hot hand, sunk cost, conjunction) and cognitive biases. Psycho Didi notes · p. 106 Fallacies — a failure in reasoning that renders an argument invalid. Fixed mindset — belief that you have a fixed amount of intelligence/skill and no effort can improve performance. Mental set — tendency to keep trying a previously used solution even when an easier method exists; represents overactive top-down processing. Functional fixedness (Karl Duncker, 1945) — the uses we assign to an object tend to remain fixed/stable. The mind map's five branches. The page shows five separate obstacles: (1) fixed mindset, (2) mental set, (3) functional fixedness, (4) fallacies and (5) cognitive biases . Fallacies and biases are two different branches: Branch What it is Items under it on the page Fallacies Errors in reasoning that make an argument or conclusion invalid (especially about chance and probability). Gambler's fallacy, hot-hand fallacy, sunk-cost fallacy, conjunction fallacy Cognitive biases Systematic tendencies in how we notice, remember and judge information, which can lead to cognitive distortions. Confirmation bias (with the Barnum effect), hindsight bias, overconfidence, illusory correlation The table in the Cognitive biases section below lists all eight together; the first four rows are the biases branch and the last four the fallacies branch. Classic examples. Mental set: Abraham Luchins's (1942) water-jar problems, where people keep using a long formula after a simpler one becomes possible. Functional fixedness: Duncker's candle problem (fix a candle to the wall with a box of tacks; the answer is to use the box as a shelf). In wider literature the four fallacies are often called judgment biases too (gambler's and conjunction fallacies are explained by the representativeness heuristic), so an MCQ may label them either way. Metacognition in problem solving Metacognition in problem solving. Tree splitting metacognition into knowledge (declarative, conditional, procedural) and regulation (planning, checking outcomes, monitoring). Psycho Didi notes · p. 106 Metacognition (John Flavell, 1976) — cognition about cognitive phenomena; thinking about thinking. Components: Metacognitive knowledge — declarative knowledge, procedural knowledge, conditional knowledge. Metacognitive regulation — planning (prior to a problem), monitoring (during learning), and checking outcomes. Cognitive biases Cognitive biases. Definitions of confirmation bias with the Barnum effect, hindsight bias, overconfidence and illusory correlation. Psycho Didi notes · p. 106 All cognitive biases can lead to cognitive distortions. Bias / fallacy Description Confirmation bias (Peter Wason, 1960) Attending to information that confirms one's beliefs while ignoring the rest. (Related: Barnum effect — accepting vague, general personality descriptions as uniquely applicable to oneself, e.g. astrology.) Hindsight bias (Baruch Fischhoff, 1975) Believing, in retrospect, that we easily saw all the signs leading to an outcome. Illusory correlation (Loren Chapman, 1967) Seeing events/attributes as going together even when they do not. Overconfidence Over-evaluating one's skills, knowledge or judgement. Fallacies (a separate branch on the page's mind map) Gambler's fallacy Belief that if an event occurred more than normal in the past, it is less likely in the future. Hot-hand fallacy Belief that a person with past successes has a greater chance of success in future attempts. Sunk-cost fallacy (Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer, 1985) Continuing to invest in something simply because one already has, hoping to recover the investment. Conjunction fallacy (Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, 1983) Giving a higher estimate for a subset of events than for the larger set containing it. 12 · Theories of Language Development Key. Sensitive period of language development: 0 years to 5–7 years . When does language develop? When does language develop?. Milestone list from cooing at 2 to 4 months to pragmatics at 4 to 5 years, with holophrase errors and errors of growth. Psycho Didi notes · p. 107 Age Milestone 2–4 months Pre-vocal learning; cooing . 6 months Babbling ; phonemes — meaningless units of speech. 1 year Learns morphemes — the smallest unit of speech that carries meaning (content morphemes; function morphemes = tense / singular–plural). Uses a holophrase — one word conveying a full sentence. 2 years Learns syntax — the rules of grammar. 3 years Telegraphic speech (Roger Brown and Colin Fraser, 1963) — 2–3 word phrases; makes errors of growth from overuse of syntax. 4–5 years Learns pragmatics (not necessary for language development). Holophrase errors: over-extension (child calls every dog "Timmy") and under-extension (mummy is only my mummy). Errors of growth: overregularization and over-generalisation . Components of language Components of language and order of learning. The five components of language defined, beside the serial order in which they are learnt from phonemes to pragmatics. Psycho Didi notes · p. 107 Phonology — sound system of a language. Morphology — units of meaning involved in word formation. Syntax — rules for combining words into phrases/sentences. Semantics — meaning of words and sentences. Pragmatics — appropriate use of language in different contexts. Serial order of learning: Phonemes → Morphemes → Semantics (Holophrase) → Syntax → Pragmatics. Sapir–Whorf Hypothesis The Sapir Whorf hypothesis. The linguistic relativity hypothesis (1956) that the language people speak shapes how they think. Psycho Didi notes · p. 107 Sapir–Whorf Hypothesis (1956) — linguistic relativity : speakers of different languages have differing cognitive systems that influence how they think about the world; we cannot think about things not experienced in our culture.
