Behaviorist approach Behaviorist approach. Skinner's six elementary verbal operants laid out as a grid of definitions, plus the secondary autoclitic operant. Psycho Didi notes · p. 107 B. F. Skinner — identified six elementary verbal operants plus one secondary operant. Verbal operant Description Mand A demand. Tact Speaker names things/actions in the environment; the "naming explosion". Echoic Repeating what has been heard. Intraverbal Speaker responds to another speaker's verbal behaviour. Textual Reading without any implication that the reader understands what is read. Transcription Writing/spelling words that are spoken to the individual (Skinner also called this "taking dictation"). Autoclitic (secondary) Softens or modifies the effect of subsequent statements (e.g. "I don't mean to criticize, but..."). Vygotsky's theory of language Vygotsky's theory of language. Vygotsky's primitive, naive, external (egocentric) and ingrowth stages of language with short descriptions. Psycho Didi notes · p. 107 Lev Vygotsky — stages of language development. Primitive stage — infant experimenting with sound production; cooing / "ga-ga". Naive stage — baby speaks words without grasping their purpose and meaning. External (egocentric) stage — child uses objects to signify meaning and words; rhyming is used in this phase. Ingrowth stage — inner speech shortens (called predication ). Nativist theory — Chomsky Nativist theories: Noam Chomsky. Chomsky's language acquisition device, modularity, deep vs surface structure, transformational grammar and ambiguous sentences. Psycho Didi notes · p. 107 Noam Chomsky — nativist theory: children have an innate Language Acquisition Device (LAD) . Language is modular — a set of specific linguistic abilities that do not follow the principles of other cognitive processes. Deep structure — the underlying syntactic structure linking phrase structures through transformation rules. Surface structure — the phrase structures resulting from applying transformational rules. Transformational grammar — two sentences may have very different surface structures but similar deep structures. Ambiguous sentences — two sentences may have identical surface structures but very different deep structures. Bruner — LASS Jerome Bruner. Bruner's language acquisition support system of parents, teachers and elders. Psycho Didi notes · p. 107 Jerome Bruner — Language Acquisition Support System (LASS) : parents, teachers and elders act as a support system that helps in the acquisition of language.

title: Personality & Motivation
text: Personality & Motivation — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Personality & Motivation Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Sigmund Freud · Carl Jung · Karen Horney · Alfred Adler · Erich Fromm Humanistic & Existential Murray's Personology Motivation: drive, arousal, need theories nAch · ERG · Self-Determination What this covers. The major approaches to personality — psychoanalytic/psychodynamic (Freud), the neo-Freudians and analytical psychology (Jung, Horney, Adler, Fromm), humanistic (Carl Rogers), existential and transpersonal approaches (Heidegger, Rollo May, Wilber), and Murray & Morgan's personology — followed by the theories of motivation (instinct, arousal, drive-reduction, and the need theories of Abraham Maslow, Alderfer, David McClelland, Edward Deci & Richard Ryan, and Zuckerman). Original diagrams. 18 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 109 to 115) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Psychoanalytic & Psychodynamic (Freud) · 2 · Neo-Freudian & Analytical Psychology · 3 · Humanistic Approach (Rogers) · 4 · Existential & Transpersonal Approaches · 5 · Personology (Murray & Morgan) · 6 · Theories of Motivation & Emotion 1 · Psychoanalytic & Psychodynamic (Freud) Approaches to personality: psychodynamic (Freud). Freud's topographical model drawn as an iceberg, beside notes on life and death instincts, the id, ego and superego, three types of anxiety and the defence mechanisms. Psycho Didi notes · p. 109 Theory → Theorist. Psychosexual / psychodynamic personality theory → Sigmund Freud . Freud — the psychodynamic model Sigmund Freud used a topographical model of the mind and held that behaviour springs from innate instincts and unconscious conflict. The iceberg: topographical model (three levels of awareness) Freud set out the topographical model in The Interpretation of Dreams (1900). It divides the mind by how aware we are of its contents, drawn as an iceberg: Level Where on the iceberg What it holds Example Conscious The tip above the water Whatever you are aware of right now. Reading this sentence. Preconscious The band at the waterline Not in awareness now, but easily recalled when you turn attention to it. Your phone number or what you ate yesterday. Unconscious The huge mass under the water Wishes, impulses and memories kept out of awareness (often by repression); they show up indirectly in dreams, slips of the tongue and symptoms. A forgotten childhood conflict driving adult anxiety. The drawing also places the structural model (id, ego, superego; The Ego and the Id , 1923) on the same iceberg: the id lies wholly below the water (entirely unconscious), while the ego and superego stretch across all three levels, so each has conscious, preconscious and unconscious parts. Trap. Topographical model (1900) = levels of awareness (conscious, preconscious, unconscious). Structural model (1923) = id, ego, superego. Examiners swap the two names. Also, "ego = conscious" is wrong: much of the ego works unconsciously (for example, defence mechanisms are unconscious ego operations). Only the id is purely unconscious. Life and death instincts — both are innate: Life instinct (eros) — libidinal energy that pushes us to function; survival-related instincts. Death instinct (thanatos) — instincts to hurt; destructive energy. The Id, Ego and Superego Structure Principle Develops in Id Pleasure principle — seeks immediate gratification Oral phase Ego Reality principle Anal phase Superego Morality principle Phallic stage The superego consists of two parts: Ego ideal — rewards ideal behaviour. Conscience — punishes with guilt. Three types of anxiety (Freud) Anxiety Nature Description Realistic anxiety Realistic fear The fear of an actual item. Moral anxiety Social fear Fear of punishment; represented by shame and guilt. Neurotic anxiety Nervous fear The fear of being overwhelmed; feeling that you are about to lose it; fear of the id taking over. Defence mechanisms Repression — keeping unpleasant memories or thoughts buried in the unconscious. Primal: innately part of the id. Proper: unacceptable derivatives of original id impulses. Denial — refusing to recognize an unpleasant reality. Rationalization — creating a socially acceptable excuse to justify unacceptable behaviour. Reaction formation — not acknowledging unacceptable impulses and over-emphasizing their opposite. Projection — transferring one's unacceptable qualities or impulses to others. Displacement — diverting one's impulses to a more acceptable target. Sublimation — channelling socially unacceptable impulses into acceptable activities. Regression — reverting to immature ways of responding. Identification — enhancing self-esteem by imagining or forming alliances with others. Intellectualization — ignoring troubling emotional aspects by focusing on abstract ideas or thoughts. Suppression — actively choosing to ignore something to do what is better and more important at the moment. Key. Id = pleasure principle (oral); Ego = reality principle (anal); Superego = morality principle (phallic), made of the ego ideal (rewards) and conscience (guilt). Repression is the "primal" defence; suppression is conscious, repression is unconscious. 2 · Neo-Freudian & Analytical Psychology Jung — Analytical Psychology Jung: analytical psychology. A comparison of Freud and Jung on the role of libido, the forces that influence personality and the unconscious. Psycho Didi notes · p. 109 Jung's structure of the psyche, energy principles and archetypes. A circle split into ego, personal unconscious and collective unconscious with arrows to their features, plus Jung's energy principles, psychological types and major archetypes. Psycho Didi notes · p. 110 Theory → Theorist. Analytical psychology → Carl Jung . Point of difference Sigmund Freud Jung Role of libido Sexual energy Broad psychic energy Forces that influence personality Present in the past only Present in the past as well as the future The unconscious Personal unconscious Personal and collective unconscious Structures of the psyche: Ego — is in control of itself; the conscious mind. Its main role is to be the centre of consciousness: it is made of our conscious perceptions, thoughts, feelings and memories, acts as the "gatekeeper" that decides what is allowed into awareness, and gives us a sense of identity and continuity. Personal unconscious — accessible once in a while; personal memories that have lost their intensity. Contains complexes : emotionally charged clusters of thoughts, feelings and memories organized around one theme (for example a mother complex or a power complex ). Jung found them through his word association test , where a delayed or disturbed reaction to a stimulus word signals that the word has touched a complex. A strong complex can take over the personality for a time. Each complex is built around an archetypal core from the collective unconscious, which is why the original notes link the two. Collective unconscious — shared memories (patterns of behaviour), motifs, primordial patterns, inherited by all humans. Its contents are the archetypes . Trap. Personal unconscious → complexes (from your own life). Collective unconscious → archetypes (inherited, shared by all humans). Also, Jung's ego is the centre of consciousness only, while the Self is the archetype of wholeness and the centre of the whole psyche (conscious plus unconscious). Do not mix up ego and Self. Energy principles: The principle of opposites — every wish or feeling has its opposite. The principle of equivalence — there is a constant amount of energy in our psyche. The principle of entropy — redistribution of energy within our psyche. Four functions: thinking, feeling, sensing, intuiting. Psychological types — attitudes: introversion / extraversion. Rational / irrational is not an attitude; it is how Jung grouped the four functions. In Psychological Types (1921) Jung described two attitudes (the direction psychic energy flows) and four functions (ways of taking in and handling experience). The functions fall into two pairs: Function Group What it does Thinking Rational (judging) Judges by logic: tells you what a thing is. Feeling Rational (judging) Judges by value: tells you whether a thing is good or bad, agreeable or not. It is evaluation, not emotion. Sensing Irrational (perceiving) Perceives through the senses: tells you that something exists, here and now. Intuiting Irrational (perceiving) Perceives via hunches and the unconscious: tells you where a thing came from and where it is going (possibilities). The two attitudes are introversion (energy flows inward, to the inner world) and extraversion (energy flows outward, to people and things). Combining 2 attitudes with 4 functions gives Jung's eight psychological types , for example the introverted thinking type or the extraverted feeling type . The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (Katharine Cook Briggs and Isabel Briggs Myers) is built on this scheme. Trap. Attitudes = introversion and extraversion only. Rational (judging) = thinking and feeling. Irrational (perceiving) = sensing and intuition. "Irrational" does not mean illogical or abnormal; it means the function simply perceives without judging. Archetypes and the anima/animus: Anima — the female archetype in the male psyche. Animus — the male archetype in the female psyche. Syzygy — anima and animus (Carl Jung) together. Self — finding a balance between the different aspects of ourselves. Persona — a mask, a facade to meet society's demands; a compromise between your needs and society's demands. Shadow — deepest, darkest instincts; comparable to the id. Other major archetypes: Joker , Wise Old Man , Hero , Witch , Villain . Horney Horney: neurotic needs. Notes on Karen Horney with a diagram of the three neurotic orientations, towards, against and away from people, and the needs under each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 110 Karen Horney gave the concept of womb envy . When children are born they have basic anxiety ; if they are met with love and care this anxiety subsides and a healthy personality develops. In the neurotic personality there is a huge difference between the ideal and the real self, because of a rigid ideal self. Neurotic needs — three orientations: Orientation Normal Neurotic Needs Towards people Friendly Compliant Seeks acceptance and help all the time; need for affection and approval; need for a partner who will control their life. Against people Competitive Aggressive Need for power, prestige, personal achievement; need to exploit other people; need to compete all the time. Away from people Autonomous Detached Need to move away from people; independence; self-reliance; perfection; narrow limits. Adler — Individual Psychology Adler: individual psychology. Key ideas of Adler with the types of inferiority, his birth order traits, three types of problems and four styles of life. Psycho Didi notes · p. 111 Theory → Theorist. Individual psychology → Alfred Adler . Adler's approach is future-oriented , non-deterministic and idiographic . Fictional finalism — dreams that may not come true and are fictional, but motivate the child to do well in life. Masculine protest — when female children feel male children within the family are being treated better, they behave more like boys as a protest. Organ inferiority — experienced by each child when they are young. Types of inferiority: Type Description Primary inferiority The "original and normal feeling" of inferiority maintained by an infant. This feeling is productive, as it provides motivation for the child to develop. Secondary inferiority The inferiority feeling in the adult that results when the child develops an exaggerated feeling of inferiority. These feelings in the adult are what are harmful, and they comprise the inferiority complex . Adler's interpretation of birth order: Position Typical characteristics First born Perfectionist, achiever, leader, bossy, responsible, motivated, conscientious, controlling, cautious, reliable. Middle born Adaptable, independent, go-between, people pleaser, can be rebellious, feels left out, peacemaker, social. Last born Social, charming, outgoing, uncomplicated, manipulative, seeks attention, self-centred, fun, confident. The only child Conscientious, responsible, perfectionist, centre of attention, mature for their age, seek approval, sensitive, leader. Three types of problems: problems of occupation; problems of love; problems involving our behaviour towards others. Four styles of life: the dominant type; the getting type; the avoiding type; the socially useful type. Erich Fromm Erich Fromm: needs and character types. Fromm's needs listed beside a branching diagram of five character types with a short description of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 111 Erich Fromm was a Neo-Freudian . He identified two fundamental needs: freedom and belonging . Character orientations: Type Description Productive Nurturing, loving, meaningful; a good spouse and friend; the only healthy approach. Exploitative Deceives; manipulative; disregard for others' well-being. Marketing Relationship is considered a transactional exchange; shallow; opportunistic. Receptive Compliant; dependent. Hoarding Possession. Needs: Relatedness — connection. Transcendence — meaning. Rootedness — belonging to a safe space; if too much, causes inflexibility. Don't confuse — Freud vs Carl Jung vs Alfred Adler. Freud: libido = sexual energy, personality shaped by the past , only a personal unconscious. Jung: libido = broad psychic energy, past and future , personal and collective unconscious (archetypes). Adler: future-oriented, striving from inferiority, birth order and social interest, non-deterministic and idiographic. Karen Horney = womb envy + three interpersonal orientations; Erich Fromm = freedom vs belonging + five character types. 3 · Humanistic Approach (Rogers) Theory → Theorist. Person-centred / self theory → Carl Rogers . Humanists hold that humans want to reach their highest potential. Actualization is the process of becoming a fully functioning individual. Rogers Humanistic: Rogers. Notes on Rogers with a table of conditional versus unconditional positive regard, circles showing congruence and incongruence of self concept and experience, and a star of the fully functioning person's traits. Psycho Didi notes · p. 112 Phenomenology argues that the only reality of which we can be sure is our own subjective world of experience — our inner perception of reality. The phenomenal field is the accumulation of a person's experiences. Research technique — Q-sort (mixed method): Qualitative: ideal self, through preference arrangement. Quantitative: factor analysis. The Fully Functioning Person: open to experience; existential living; trusts feelings; creativity and spontaneity; a fulfilled life; freedom of choice; a continual need to grow. Congruence vs incongruence — the degree of overlap between the self-concept and experience : congruence = they match; incongruence = a gap between them. Conditional vs unconditional positive regard: Conditional Unconditional Having conditions that need to be met in order to receive love. Love without any condition. An effort to manipulate the actions of individuals. No effort to manipulate or control an individual. Child develops conditions of worth . Congruent personality; child develops the organismic valuing process ; does not need therapy. Key. Unconditional positive regard → organismic valuing process → congruent, healthy personality. Conditional regard → conditions of worth → incongruence. 4 · Existential & Transpersonal Approaches Existential approach Existential: Heidegger and Rollo May. Heidegger's existential anxiety and four modes of Dasein, and Rollo May's types of anxiety and four stages of development shown as a cycle of arrows. Psycho Didi notes · p. 112 Proponents: Rollo May , Viktor Frankl , Martin Heidegger . Meaning in life is what keeps you grounded. Dasein = "to be in the world". Heidegger Martin Heidegger's modes of being-in-the-world: Mode Meaning Umwelt One's relationship with the natural world or environment. Mitwelt Our relationship with other people and the meanings given to those relationships. Eigenwelt One's relationship with oneself and how we interpret things based on self. Uberwelt Spirituality. Existential anxiety — the fear that we won't be alive. It can motivate us to achieve our best potential (proportionate), or demotivate us so that we wish to give up, thinking nothing really matters (neurotic). Rollo May Types of anxiety: Normal ; Neurotic (disproportionate to the situation). Four stages of development: Innocence — physical and psychological dependence. Rebellion — people define themselves in opposition to or defiance of another. Ordinary — the normal adult ego; a healthy, mature personality. Creative — transcending our usual limited viewpoint and catching a glimpse of ultimate reality. Transpersonal psychology Transpersonal psychology. Notes on the origins, methods and altered states of transpersonal psychology, Ken Wilber's stages, and a diagram of the pre-personal, personal and transpersonal groups. Psycho Didi notes · p. 113 Founded by Abraham Maslow and Stanislav Grof ; it also has roots in earlier work by psychologists such as William James and Carl Jung . Methods: psychedelic; transpersonal therapy; dreamwork; mindfulness. Altered state of consciousness: connectedness beyond ego boundaries; altruism, creativity, intuitive wisdom; a journey into self-exploration. Groups: Pre-personal (when you don't understand self fully); Personal (concerns of the ego); Transpersonal (concerns beyond the ego). These three groups are the broad realms of Ken Wilber's model of development. Pre-personal (pre-egoic) covers infancy and early childhood, before a stable, separate sense of self has formed. Personal (egoic) is the ordinary adult self that thinks rationally and has a clear identity. Transpersonal (trans-egoic) lies beyond the ego: states in which the sense of self widens past the individual. The stages below sit inside these groups: vision logic is the highest personal stage, and psychic, subtle, causal and the final (nondual) stage are transpersonal . So pre-personal is a group, not one of the stages. Trap: Wilber's pre/trans fallacy. Because both pre-personal and transpersonal states are "non-rational", people confuse them: either treating a mystical (trans) state as a regression to infancy (Wilber's criticism of Freud), or glorifying an infantile (pre) state as spiritual. Pre-rational is not the same as trans-rational. Ken Wilber's transpersonal stages of development: Vision logic — integration of mind and body. Psychic — empathetic understanding. Subtle — across archetypal forms. Causal — non-dual awareness. Final — freely transverse between all stages. 5 · Personology (Murray & Morgan) Personology: Henry Murray and Christiana Morgan. Murray and Morgan's principles, needs, divisions of id, ego and superego, press, thema and complexes. Psycho Didi notes · p. 113 Theory → Theorist. Personology → Henry Murray & Christiana Morgan (the notes spell her name "Christina"; she is Christiana Morgan, who also co-created the Thematic Apperception Test with Murray). Principles Personality is rooted in the brain. The process of tension reduction is satisfying, but a tension-free state is a source of distress. An individual's personality develops over time. Personality is not fixed or static. Each person is unique. Structures: Id — innate impulses that society considers unacceptable; Ego : the central organizer of behaviour; Superego — internalization of cultural values. Henry Murray ( Explorations in Personality , 1938) kept Freud's three divisions but changed their weight. The id holds all innate impulses: the unacceptable ones listed above, but also, unlike Freud's id, socially acceptable ones such as empathy. The ego is much stronger than Freud's: it is the central organizer of behaviour , which consciously decides and plans what to do and actively promotes the satisfaction of needs, rather than only refereeing between id and superego. The superego is the culture's values, learned mainly from parents, which tell the ego which needs may be expressed, when and how. Trap. In a Freud vs Murray question, the answer is that Murray's ego is an active planner and organizer of behaviour, not a weak mediator. Needs Category Description Primary Survival-related. Secondary Emotional or psychological. Proactive Spontaneous; achievement-related. Reactive Response to object; harm-avoidance. Types of needs: materialistic, affiliation, information, power, achievement, sensual. Press, thema and complexes Press — the influence of environment and past events on the current activation of a need. Thema — need × press + how they affect personality = unity thema. Subsidation: one need will activate another, and the second need will fulfil the first need. Complexes: Complex Description Claustral (womb) The desire to reinstate the conditions experienced in the mother's womb. Oral Same as Freud's. Anal Same as Freud's. Urethral Characterized by excessive ambition and a distorted, enlarged sense of self-esteem. Genital Castration complex. 6 · Theories of Motivation & Emotion Instinct theory Instinct theory. Notes on instinct theory and Freud's object relations theory, including the four characteristics of an instinct. Psycho Didi notes · p. 114 Behaviour is motivated by instincts that are inborn and that are activated by environmental stimuli. Sigmund Freud's object relations theory — basic instincts from eros motivate us; explains motivation in terms of primary needs. Homeostatic approach — disturbance of homeostasis creates drive. Instincts have four basic characteristics (S-A-I-O): Source — source of deficit (internal). Aim — what we want to do. Impetus — the drive that propels us to act. Object — that through which the instinct achieves its aim. Heads up: the notes (and diagram) label this "Freud's object relations theory". Object relations theory is usually credited to later analysts such as Melanie Klein, Ronald Fairbairn and Donald Winnicott. What is listed here is Freud's own instinct (drive) theory : the four characteristics, source, aim, impetus (pressure) and object, come from his paper "Instincts and Their Vicissitudes" (1915). Arousal theory Theories of motivation: arousal theory. Notes on arousal theory and the Yerkes-Dodson law beside an inverted U graph of performance quality against arousal level for difficult and easy tasks. Psycho Didi notes · p. 114 Behaviour is motivated by the need to achieve optimum levels of arousal. Yerkes-Dodson law — arousal increases performance up to a point, after which additional arousal impedes performance. The law comes from Robert Yerkes and John Dodson (1908). The graph plots performance against arousal as an inverted U : Low arousal (left end): boredom or apathy, so performance is poor. Moderate arousal (the peak): the optimal level, where performance is best. High arousal (right end): high anxiety, so performance falls again. The two curves show that the best level depends on the task. Difficult tasks (blue curve) peak at a lower level of arousal; easy or well-practised tasks (red curve) peak at a higher level. Example: solving a tricky exam paper goes best when you are only mildly keyed up, while a simple, well-learned task like a sprint can benefit from being highly pumped up. Trap. Higher arousal helps easy tasks and hurts difficult ones sooner. Do not reverse this. Also, arousal theory is the answer when a question asks why people seek stimulation (for example thrill seeking or curiosity), which drive-reduction theory cannot explain. Alderfer's ERG theory Alderfer's ERG theory. Notes on ERG theory above a pyramid that lines up Maslow's five levels with Alderfer's growth, relatedness and existence needs. Psycho Didi notes · p. 114 One does not necessarily start from the lowest level. Moving from a lower level to an upper level of the hierarchy is called satisfaction-progression . Moving from a higher level to a lower level is called frustration regression . Heads up: the original notes write "succession progression"; the standard term is satisfaction-progression (a satisfied need lets you move up to the next one). Clayton Alderfer (1969) squeezed Maslow's five levels into three groups of needs, E-R-G : Letter Need Meaning Maslow's levels it covers E Existence Material and physical needs for staying alive and safe. Physiological + safety R Relatedness Needs for meaningful relationships with family, friends and co-workers. Belonging/love + the external part of esteem (recognition and respect from others) G Growth Needs to develop yourself and use your abilities fully. The internal part of esteem (self-esteem) + self-actualization How ERG differs from Maslow: there are 3 needs, not 5; more than one need can be active at the same time ; there is no fixed order; and if a higher need is frustrated a person can slide back and put more effort into a lower one ( frustration-regression ). Example: an employee blocked from promotion (growth) may start demanding more pay or spending more time socialising at work. Trap. Esteem is split in ERG: esteem from others goes under Relatedness, self-esteem goes under Growth. And frustration-regression belongs to Alderfer, not Maslow (Maslow's model moves only upward). Maslow's need hierarchy Maslow's need hierarchy. Notes on Maslow's theory above an eight level pyramid with deficiency needs at the base and growth needs at the top. Psycho Didi notes · p. 114 Theory → Theorist. Hierarchy of needs → Abraham Maslow . Lower needs come from deficiencies; higher needs come from satisfaction. Measured with the Personal Orientation Inventory (Everett Shostrom, 1964), a test of self-actualization. Progression is only upward, but not automatic. Jonah complex — fear of your own best potential. Abraham Maslow proposed the hierarchy in 1943 ("A Theory of Human Motivation") with five levels. In his later writings (up to about 1970) he added cognitive, aesthetic and transcendence needs, giving the eight-level pyramid in the diagram. Read from the bottom up: # Level What it means Example Type 1 Physiological Bodily survival needs. Food, water, sleep, warmth. Deficiency needs (D-needs): felt when lacking; once met, they stop motivating. 2 Safety Security and stability. A safe home, a steady job, health. 3 Belonging and love Affection and acceptance. Friends, family, a partner, a group. 4 Esteem Respect from others and self-respect. Recognition, status, confidence. 5 Cognitive To know and understand. Curiosity, learning, exploring. Growth needs (being or B-needs): they grow stronger as they are fed. 6 Aesthetic Beauty, order, symmetry. Enjoying art, music, nature. 7 Self-actualization Becoming everything one is capable of becoming. Fulfilling your potential; peak experiences. 8 Transcendence Going beyond the self. Helping others reach their potential; spiritual or mystical experience. Trap. Check whether a question means the original five levels (1943) or the expanded eight . In the five-level version, self-actualization is the top and only growth need; in the eight-level version, transcendence is the top. Esteem is always a deficiency need, not a growth need. Self-determination theory Self determination theory. The three basic needs of self determination theory and the three causality orientations with the needs and motivation linked to each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 114 Three basic needs: Autonomy — the need to control the course of our lives. Competence — the need to be effective in dealing with the environment. Relatedness — the need to have close, affectionate relationships with others. Causality orientations: Orientation Needs satisfied Motivation Autonomous Autonomy, competence, relatedness Intrinsic motivation Controlled Competence, relatedness Extrinsic motivation Impersonal None Amotivation Drive-reduction theory (Clark Hull) Drive reduction theory. A cycle from bodily need to drive, motivated behaviour and homeostasis, labelled with the terms of Hull's equation, next to the equation and a key to each term. Psycho Didi notes · p. 115 Theory → Theorist. Drive-reduction theory → Clark Hull . A homeostatic approach. A bodily need (e.g. hydration) creates a drive ; the organism is motivated to satisfy the drive through goal-directed behaviour, restoring homeostasis (drive reduced, need satisfied). Equation: SER = V × D × J × K × SHR − SIR − IR − SOR − SLR Term Meaning SER Excitatory / reaction potential V Stimulus-intensity dynamism: how strong the stimulus is (the notes and diagram gloss V as "need") D Drive J Delay K Size of incentive SHR Habit strength SIR Conditioned inhibition IR Fatigue (reactive inhibition) SOR Random error (behavioural oscillation) SLR Reaction threshold: the minimum reaction potential needed before a response occurs (the notes put it as minimum reinforcement required for learning to occur) Reading the cycle in the diagram (Clark Hull, Principles of Behavior , 1943, and his later revisions). Each stage carries the term of the equation that acts there: Stage in the cycle Term What happens (thirst example) Bodily need V The body is short of water. The diagram puts V here; strictly, V is how intense the stimulus is (for example a strongly felt dry mouth). Drive D The need produces drive, an unpleasant state of tension (thirst). More hours without water means more D. Organism motivated to satisfy the drive J , K How motivated you are also depends on the incentive (K: a cold drink pulls harder than a sip of warm water) and on how long you must wait for it (J: delay). Goal-directed behaviour SHR You do what has worked before, such as walking to the water cooler. Habit strength (SHR) grows each time that response was reinforced. Drive reduced, need satisfied Drinking reduces the drive. Hull held that this drive reduction is the reinforcement that strengthens the habit. Homeostasis The body is back in balance until the next need arises, and the cycle repeats. The terms after the minus signs pull reaction potential down: tiredness from repeating a response (IR), learned inhibition (SIR), random moment-to-moment variation (SOR), and the threshold the result must exceed for any response to appear (SLR). Note that D and SHR are multiplied : if either is zero, there is no response, however strong the other is. Heads up: the diagram and the notes call V "need". In Hull's system V is stimulus-intensity dynamism (stimulus strength); the need itself shows up as drive (D). Likewise SLR is the reaction threshold . Trap: drive-reduction theory cannot explain behaviour that raises tension, such as curiosity or thrill seeking; arousal theory was offered to cover those cases. McClelland's theory of needs McClelland's theory of needs. Three overlapping circles for power, achievement and affiliation, next to lists of the qualities of high and low achievers. Psycho Didi notes · p. 115 Theory → Theorist. Need for achievement / acquired-needs theory → David McClelland . All three needs are learned : Power (nPow) , Achievement (nAch) , Affiliation (nAff) . Qualities of the high achiever (high nAch) Qualities of the low achiever (low nAch) High motivation to achieve success Low motivation to achieve success Low motivation to avoid failure High motivation to avoid failure Focuses on the pride of success Focuses on shame and worry that may result from failure Ascribes success to stable and internal factors Ascribes success to unstable and external factors Ascribes failure to unstable and external factors Ascribes failure to stable and internal factors within one's control Internal locus of control (Julian Rotter, 1966) for success External locus of control for success High perceived competence; believes achievement is within own control Low perceived competence; believes achievement is outside own control Seeks out challenges and able competitors and tasks Usually adopts outcome goals; avoids challenge, seeks out very difficult or very easy tasks and competitors Performs well in evaluative conditions; likes feedback Performs badly in evaluative situations; dislikes feedback Zuckerman's sensation-seeking theory Zuckerman's sensation seeking theory. A branching diagram of the four types of sensation seeking above a drawing of hikers climbing a hill. Psycho Didi notes · p. 115 Theory → Theorist. Sensation-seeking theory → Marvin Zuckerman . Four types: Thrill and adventure seeking Experience seeking Disinhibition Boredom susceptibility Key. Need theories to keep straight: Abraham Maslow (hierarchy, deficiency vs growth needs), Alderfer (ERG — satisfaction-progression vs frustration regression), David McClelland (learned nAch/nPow/nAff), Edward Deci & Richard Ryan (self-determination — autonomy, competence, relatedness). Clark Hull's drive-reduction is the homeostatic model; Yerkes-Dodson governs the optimum-arousal model. Don't confuse — the need theorists. Abraham Maslow = a fixed upward hierarchy driven by deficiency then growth; Alderfer's ERG = flexible, allows frustration regression; David McClelland = three learned needs measured by projective tests, no hierarchy. And in McClelland's model, high-nAch people take internal credit for success while low-nAch people show an external locus for success and an internal one for failure.

title: Developmental Psychology
text: Developmental Psychology — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Developmental Psychology Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Prenatal stages & teratogens Jean Piaget · Erik Erikson · Lawrence Kohlberg · Sigmund Freud Attachment: Mary Ainsworth · John Bowlby · Harry Harlow Jerome Bruner · James Marcia · Urie Bronfenbrenner · Elkind Lifespan & reflexes What this covers. The full arc of human development: prenatal screening and prenatal stages, teratogens and genetic/chromosomal disorders, the lifespan phases and infant reflexes, then the major stage theories: Freud's psychosexual stages, Erikson's eight psychosocial stages, Piaget's cognitive and moral stages, Kohlberg's moral levels, plus Bruner , Marcia , Elkind and Bronfenbrenner , and finally theories of attachment ( Ainsworth , Bowlby , Harlow ). Original diagrams. 18 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 117 to 120) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Prenatal screening & development · 2 · Genetic, chromosomal & congenital disorders · 3 · Lifespan development & reflexes · 4 · Freud's psychosexual stages · 5 · Erikson's psychosocial stages · 6 · Piaget's cognitive stages · 7 · Piaget's moral development · 8 · Kohlberg's moral development · 9 · Bruner, Marcia, Elkind & Bronfenbrenner · 10 · Theories of attachment 1 · Prenatal screening & development Ways to sample for abnormalities Ways to sample for abnormalities. A box listing prenatal screening methods with when each is done and what it checks for. Psycho Didi notes · p. 117 Method Timing What it checks / does Amniocentesis 14th week Checks for genetic abnormalities; done through amniotic fluid Fetoscopy 5 weeks Checks for haemophilia, sickle cell anaemia, limb defects Ultrasound — Tells about the size, shape, and placement of the foetus Maternal Blood Analysis 2nd month Can check for neural tube defect Chorionic villus sampling 8th week Chorionic biopsy is performed; detects all genetic problems Prenatal development stages Stages. A box listing the germinal, embryonic and foetal stages of prenatal development with small foetus drawings. Psycho Didi notes · p. 117 Stage Period Germinal stage Ovulation and implantation Embryonic stage Up to 8 weeks Foetal stage 8+ weeks Teratogens Drugs / Alcohol Alcohol: heart defects Cocaine: vascular disruption Valproate: ear problems Vitamin A deficiency: Spina bifida Infections Rubella: microcephaly Toxoplasma: hydrocephalus Varicella: limb defects Conditions Diabetes: neural tube defects Key. Match the screening method to its window: Fetoscopy (5 wk) → CVS (8 wk) → Amniocentesis (14 wk); Maternal Blood Analysis in the 2nd month checks for neural tube defect. 2 · Genetic, chromosomal & congenital disorders Prenatal deformities. A flowchart that branches prenatal deformities into teratogenic, genetic (recessive, dominant and X linked), genetic mutation and congenital causes, with example disorders and their features under each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 117 The overall map: four kinds of prenatal deformity The flowchart above starts from prenatal deformities (problems that arise before birth) and splits them into four branches by cause. The notes cover the first branch in Section 1 and the other three below: Branch Cause Examples on the page Teratogenic Something harmful in the womb environment (a teratogen ): drugs, alcohol, infections, maternal conditions. The genes are normal. Alcohol, cocaine, valproate, vitamin A deficiency; rubella, toxoplasma, varicella; maternal diabetes (see Section 1, Teratogens ) Genetic A faulty single gene passed on from parents, sorted by inheritance pattern: recessive, dominant, X-linked. Tay Sachs, PKU, Huntington's, Fragile X, haemophilia Genetic mutations An error in a whole chromosome : the wrong number of chromosomes (numerical) or a broken, missing or extra piece (structural). Usually a new error in the egg or sperm, not inherited. Down's (trisomy 21), Turner's (XO), Klinefelter's (XXY); Cri du Chat, Prader Willi Congenital Present from birth because of problems during pregnancy or delivery. Cerebral palsy, Fetal Alcohol Syndrome Heads up. The page's "genetic mutations" branch is what textbooks call chromosomal abnormalities . And Fetal Alcohol Syndrome sits under "congenital" on the page, but its cause, alcohol, is a teratogen ; if an MCQ asks for the cause type, answer teratogen. Genetic disorders Inheritance patterns include Recessive , Dominant , and X-linked . Autosomal recessive: the faulty gene sits on a non-sex chromosome and a child is affected only with two copies, one from each parent. Parents with one copy are healthy carriers ; two carrier parents have a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child each pregnancy. Autosomal dominant: one copy is enough. An affected parent has a 1 in 2 chance of passing it to each child. X-linked: the gene is on the X chromosome. Boys (XY) have only one X, so one faulty copy affects them; girls (XX) are usually carriers or milder. So these disorders are far more common in males, passed on through carrier mothers. Disorder Inheritance Key features Tay Sachs Autosomal recessive CNS degeneration; usually die at 3-4 y/o Cystic Fibrosis Autosomal recessive Lungs secrete mucus PKU (Phenylketonuria) Autosomal recessive Intellectual disability; phenylalanine hydroxylase is absent; damage to CNS when exposed to proteins Sickle Cell Anaemia Autosomal recessive Sickle-shaped RBC; pain; swelling; short life span Huntington's disease Autosomal dominant Neurocognitive; death after 10-20 years of symptoms; excitotoxicity; mental deterioration Marfan syndrome Autosomal dominant Tall, elongated arms and limbs; heart defects; eye abnormalities; skeletal deformity; death in young adulthood Fragile X syndrome X-linked Mutation in FMR1 gene (Fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein is not made); developmental delays; learning disability, intellectual disability, Autism Spectrum Disorder; elongated face Haemophilia X-linked recessive Blood fails to clot; excessive internal bleeding Diabetes insipidus Mixed: see note below. The X-linked form is nephrogenic DI; the inherited central form is usually autosomal dominant Insufficient production of vasopressin (central DI) or kidneys that do not respond to vasopressin (nephrogenic DI); excessive thirst Duchenne muscular dystrophy X-linked recessive Muscular dystrophy; death from weakness of heart muscle; loss of ability to walk Heads up on diabetes insipidus. The page lists it under X-linked, which fits only one form. Nephrogenic DI (the kidneys ignore vasopressin) is most often X-linked, but it also has autosomal forms. The "insufficient production of vasopressin" feature describes central DI, whose inherited form is usually autosomal dominant. Most DI is not inherited at all (head injury, tumours, surgery, drugs such as lithium). If an MCQ lists DI among X-linked disorders, it means nephrogenic DI. Don't confuse. Huntington's is dominant , even though symptoms usually begin in mid-life, often after the person has already had children. Down's syndrome is not in this table because it is a chromosomal (numerical) error, not single-gene inheritance. Genetic mutations (chromosomal) Numerical Disorder Features Trisomy 21 (Down's syndrome) Intellectual disability; weak muscle tone; intellectual disability Turner's syndrome (XO) In females; heart defects; abnormal secondary sexual characteristics; webbed neck Klinefelter's syndrome (47, XXY) In males; too tall; osteoporosis; sterility Triple X syndrome (47, XXX) — Structural Disorder Features Cri Du Chat (5p) Microcephaly; intellectual disability; autism/ADHD symptoms; low birth weight; respiratory impairment Pallister Killian Presence of extra material on chromosome 12; intellectual disability; mosaicism; poor muscle tone; seizures; cataracts; stiff joint Prader Willi (15a) Intellectual disability; reduced social functioning; rigid behavioural preferences Congenital Cerebral Palsy Due to head trauma to mother and other problems during development Motor deficits / epilepsy / intellectual disability Classification (based on body parts affected): mono, hemi, di, quadri Types: spastic, ataxic, mixed, athetoid Fetal Alcohol Syndrome Cause: having alcohol during pregnancy Structural: microcephaly, irregular facial features, decreased muscle tone Neurological: intellectual disability, epilepsy, poor eye-hand coordination Functional: low IQ, developmental disability, learning disorders, language development delays 3 · Lifespan development & reflexes Lifespan development phases Lifespan development. A silhouette row from crawling baby to elderly adult above a list of lifespan phases and their age ranges. Psycho Didi notes · p. 118 Phase Age range Prenatal Conception to birth Infancy and toddlerhood Birth to 2 years Early childhood 2-6 years Middle childhood 6-12 years Adolescence 12-20 years Emerging adulthood (Jeffrey Arnett, 2000) 20-25 years Young adulthood 25-45 years Middle adulthood 45-60 years Later adulthood 60 years to death Infant reflexes Reflexes. A list of infant reflexes with a short description of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 118 Reflex Description Moro reflex Fight-or-flight reaction, sympathetic nervous system response; "monkey hanging from a tree" Rooting reflex Autonomic response to locate food and breast Palmar Grasp Reflex Autonomic flexion of the fingers to grab when the palm is stimulated Asymmetric Tonic Neck Reflex Assists with movement through birth canal at delivery; important for cross-pattern movement Spinal Galant Reflex Important during the birthing process; helps to facilitate movement of the hips during descending the birthing canal Babinski reflex Toes spread out when sole of the foot is touched Plantar / stepping reflex — 4 · Freud's psychosexual stages of development Freud's psychosexual stages of development. A list of the five psychosexual stages with the age, erogenous zone and fixation types for each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 118 Theory → theorist. Psychosexual stages of development were proposed by Sigmund Freud . Stage Age Erogenous zone Key features Oral stage 0-2 years Mouth Types of oral fixation — oral incorporative: dependent, naïve, collecting and hoarding objects; oral biting: sarcastic, mean Anal stage 2-3 years Anus Ego develops. Fixations — anal retentive: rigid, strict, excessive organization, excessive cleanliness, OCD type, hoarding, miserly, stingy; anal expulsive: spendthrift, disorganized, messy Phallic stage 3-7 years Genitals Superego develops; Oedipus complex Latency stage 7-11 years None No fixation; sexual energy is sublimated towards activities like sports, studies, same-gender friendships Genital stage 11 and above Genitals Healthy adult development occurs here; interest in opposite sex develops Trap. Don't confuse anal retentive (rigid, overly clean, hoarding, OCD-type) with anal expulsive (messy, disorganized, spendthrift) — they are opposite fixations of the same anal stage. 5 · Erikson's psychosocial development theory Erikson's psychosocial development theory. Key features of Erikson's theory, how it differs from Freud, and the maladjustment linked to each pole of every crisis. Psycho Didi notes · p. 119 Erikson's eight stages. A table of Erikson's eight stages with the age, the crisis and the basic strength for each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 119 Theory → theorist. The eight psychosocial stages were given by Erik Erikson , rooted in ego psychology and the epigenetic principle of development. Stage Age Crisis (ways of coping) Basic strength Oral-sensory 0-1 Trust vs Mistrust Hope Muscular-anal 1-3 Autonomy vs Shame and Doubt Will Locomotor-genital 3-5 Initiative vs Guilt Purpose Latency 6-11 Industry vs Inferiority Competence Adolescence 12-18 Identity vs Role confusion Fidelity Young adulthood 18-35 Intimacy vs Isolation Love Adulthood 35-55 Generativity vs Stagnation Care Old age 55+ Integrity vs Despair Wisdom Differences from Freud 8 stages of personality Greater emphasis on ego Impact on personality of cultural and historical forces Maladjustment (per pole of each crisis) Pole Maladjustment Trust Sensory maladjustment Mistrust Withdrawal Autonomy Shameless wilfulness Shame Compulsion Initiative Ruthlessness Guilt Inhibition Industry Narrow virtuosity Inferiority Inertia Identity Fanaticism Role confusion Repudiation Intimacy Promiscuity Isolation Exclusivity Generativity Overextension Stagnation Rejectivity Integrity Presumption Despair Disdain Why it matters. Erik Erikson's development is discontinuous (stages) and governed by the epigenetic principle : each stage builds on the resolution of the one before it, with a specific basic strength (virtue) as the payoff. Trap. Erikson stages are easily confused. Note the age boundaries: Latency (6-11) = Industry vs Inferiority maps onto Sigmund Freud's latency, but Erik Erikson adds three adult stages (Intimacy, Generativity, Integrity) that Freud's genital stage collapses into one. 6 · Piaget's stages of cognitive development Piaget's stages of cognitive development. Notes on the four Piagetian stages with pictures of the three mountains task and a liquid conservation task. Psycho Didi notes · p. 119 Theory → theorist. The four stages of cognitive development were given by Jean Piaget . Stage Age Key learning / task Sensorimotor stage Birth to 2 years Child learns object permanence ; tested with the A-not-B task Preoperational stage 2-7 years Learns symbolic thought , animism ; egocentrism tested with the Three Mountains task Concrete operational stage 7-11 years Learns conservation , reversibility , mathematical operations; conservation task Formal operational stage 11 and above Learns hypothetico-deductive reasoning and abstract reasoning; pendulum task The three mountains task (egocentrism) Devised by Jean Piaget and Bärbel Inhelder (1956) . A child sits at a table with a model of three mountains of different sizes and markings (one has snow on top, one a house, one a red cross). A doll is placed on another side of the table, as in the picture. The child is shown pictures of the model from different sides and asked to pick the one showing what the doll sees. Preoperational children (roughly under 7) tend to pick the picture of their own view. Piaget called this egocentrism : being unable to take another person's point of view. Trap. Egocentrism here is a thinking limit , not selfishness. Later studies (for example Martin Hughes' "policeman doll" task, 1975) found that much younger children can take another's viewpoint when the task makes sense to them, so Piaget probably underestimated preschoolers. The conservation task (liquid) Conservation (Jean Piaget) is understanding that an amount stays the same when only its appearance changes. In the classic task, shown in the three pictures: the child sees two identical short glasses with the same amount of water and agrees they are equal. Then the water from one is poured into a taller, narrower glass while the child watches, and the child is asked whether the two glasses now hold the same amount or one has more. Preoperational child (about 2 to 7): says the tall glass has more, because it looks higher. He fixes on one feature ( centration ) and cannot mentally reverse the pouring. Concrete operational child (about 7 to 11): says they are the same, and can explain why: "you just poured it" (identity), "pour it back and it's the same" ( reversibility ), "it's taller but thinner" (compensation). Children do not master every type of conservation at once (number and liquid come before weight and volume); this unevenness is horizontal décalage , described below. Sensorimotor: sequence of events Motor reflexes Primary circular reactions — e.g. putting everything in the mouth Secondary circular reactions — manipulation of objects Synthesis of secondary circular reactions Tertiary circular reactions — object permanence achieved here; goal-directed behaviour; mental representations; concept formation Imitation involves: Deferred imitation: repeating action after some time has passed Inferred imitation: imitating only correct behaviour and not the incorrect one Horizontal décalage When a child is able to perform conservation of mass (or any other thing) but unable to do the conservation task for length or density (or anything else). Trap: assimilation vs accommodation. In Jean Piaget's framework, assimilation fits new information into an existing schema, while accommodation changes the schema to fit new information. Do not swap them. Trap: Piaget vs Lev Vygotsky. Piaget saw cognitive development as an individual, stage-based process driven from within the child. Vygotsky emphasized the social and cultural context (learning through interaction, scaffolding, the Zone of Proximal Development) driving development. Piaget = discovery within stages; Vygotsky = socially mediated learning. 7 · Piaget's theory of moral development Piaget's theory of moral development. Notes on heteronomous and autonomous morality with the age range and main idea of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 120 Stage Age Also known as / features Heteronomous Morality 5-9 years Moral realism — morality imposed from the outside Autonomous Morality 9-10 years Moral relativism — morality based on your own rules; children recognize there is no absolute right or wrong and that morality depends on intentions, not consequences 8 · Kohlberg's theory of moral development Kohlberg's theory of moral development. Notes on Kohlberg's study and his three levels of morality with the substages under each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 120 Theory → theorist. The three levels of morality were given by Lawrence Kohlberg . He presented children, adolescents and young adults with stories that included moral dilemmas, such as the story of Heinz , in his longitudinal study. He studied a group of boys in the age group 10-16 for over 20 years. Level Substages Pre-conventional morality Punishment avoidance; instrumental or reward Conventional morality Good boy/girl, social acceptance, good interpersonal relationship; social order / avoiding censure (Law and Order orientation) Post-conventional morality Social contract and individual rights; universal ethical principles Trap. Keep Piaget's moral stages (Heteronomous / Autonomous, ages 5-10) distinct from Lawrence Kohlberg's three levels (Pre-conventional / Conventional / Post-conventional). Kohlberg used the Heinz dilemma ; Piaget did not. 9 · Bruner, Marcia, Elkind & Bronfenbrenner Jerome Bruner's theory of cognitive development — modes of representation Jerome Bruner's modes of representation. A list of Bruner's enactive, iconic and symbolic modes of representation with what each involves. Psycho Didi notes · p. 118 Mode Description Enactive Mode Learning through actions and motor responses Iconic Mode Learning through mental images and visual representations Symbolic Mode Learning through abstract symbols like language and numbers James Marcia's theory of identity development James Marcia's theory of identity development. A table rating the four identity statuses as low or high on exploration and commitment. Psycho Didi notes · p. 118 Identity status is defined by two dimensions: Exploration and Commitment . Identity status Exploration Commitment Identity diffusion Low Low Identity foreclosure Low High Identity moratorium High Low Identity achievement High High Elkind's adolescent egocentrism Elkind's adolescent egocentrism. A list of the three types of adolescent egocentrism with the typical thought behind each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 118 There are three types of adolescent egocentrism: The imaginary audience — "everyone is looking at me" The mythological fable — "that won't ever happen to me" The personal fable — "nobody knows what it's like to be me" Ecological systems theory Ecological systems theory. Nested coloured circles with arrows pointing to Bronfenbrenner's micro, meso, exo, macro and chrono systems and a definition of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 118 Theory → theorist. Ecological systems theory was given by Urie Bronfenbrenner (1979) . System Description Microsystem Concerns relations between the developing person and the immediate environment Mesosystem Connections among immediate settings Exosystem Social settings that affect but do not contain the developing person Macrosystem The values, laws, customs, and resources of the culture that affect activities and interactions at all inner layers Chronosystem Not a specific context; refers to the dynamic, ever-changing nature of the person's environment 10 · Theories of attachment Mary Ainsworth's attachment styles Theories of attachment: Mary Ainsworth's attachment styles. A table of how infants with each attachment style react when the mother leaves and when she returns. Psycho Didi notes · p. 120 Theory → theorist. Attachment styles (measured via the Strange Situation) were given by Mary Ainsworth . Style Mother leaves Mother returns Secure Upset Happy Anxious / avoidant Indifferent Indifferent Ambivalent / resistant Cries; upset Angry Disorganized Dazed and scared Dazed and scared Trap. On reunion, secure babies are comforted (happy), avoidant babies stay indifferent, ambivalent/resistant babies are angry (seek but resist contact), and disorganized babies look dazed and scared. Watch the reunion column, not just the separation. Contact Comfort Theory Contact Comfort Theory. Notes on the Harlows' monkey study comparing a wire feeding mother with a cloth mother. Psycho Didi notes · p. 120 Theory → theorist. Contact Comfort Theory was given by Harry Harlow and Margaret Harlow . They raised monkeys with two artificial mothers — one a bare wire cylinder with a wooden head and an attached feeding bottle; the other a cylinder with no bottle but covered with foam rubber and wrapped with terry cloth. The infants much preferred contact with the comfortable cloth mother, even while feeding from the nourishing mother. John Bowlby's ecological theory of attachment (1969) John Bowlby's ecological theory of attachment. A list of Bowlby's four phases of attachment with the age range and main features of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 120 Theory → theorist. The four phases of attachment were given by John Bowlby (1969) . Phase Age Features Pre-attachment phase Birth to 6 weeks Recognize their own mother's smell, voice and face Attachment-in-the-making phase 6 weeks to 6-8 months Infants respond differently to a familiar caregiver than to a stranger, but they still do not protest when separated from mother Clear-cut attachment phase (monotropy) 6-8 months to 18 months-2 years Clear-cut attachment with 1 primary attachment figure Formation of a reciprocal relationship 18 months to 2 years and on Rapid growth in representation and language permits toddlers to understand some of the factors that influence the parent's coming and going and to predict her return; children negotiate with the caregiver, using requests and persuasion to alter her goals Key. Bowlby's term monotropy = the child's clear-cut, single primary attachment figure, emerging in the clear-cut attachment phase (6-8 months onward).

title: Social Psychology
text: Social Psychology — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Social Psychology Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Attribution & biases Cognitive dissonance (Leon Festinger, 1957) Persuasion & social influence Conformity · Compliance · Obedience Helping · Proxemics What this covers. The core of social psychology as it appears in MPhil Clinical and UGC NET JRF papers: a timeline of landmark thinkers and studies, attribution theory and its many biases, Harold Kelley's covariation model, cognitive dissonance (Leon Festinger, 1957) and attitude change, the Elaboration Likelihood Model (Richard Petty and John Cacioppo, 1986), the three types of social influence (compliance, conformity, obedience) with their techniques and classic experiments, social norms, prosocial helping (the decision stage model), and proxemics (personal space zones). Original diagrams. 16 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 122 to 123) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Timeline of Social Psychology · 2 · Attribution & Attributional Biases · 3 · Kelley's Covariation Model · 4 · Cognitive Dissonance · 5 · Attitude Change (Elaboration Likelihood Model) · 6 · Social Influence: Compliance, Conformity, Obedience · 7 · Social Norms · 8 · Prosocial Behaviour & Helping · 9 · Proxemics (Personal Space) 1 · Timeline of Social Psychology Timeline of social psychology. A winding road timeline marking key social psychology figures and studies from 1917 to 1994. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Key figures and landmark studies that shaped the field, in chronological order. Year Figure Contribution 1917 John Dewey The need for social psychology 1935 Muzafer Sherif Conformity studies 1940s — Field theory (Kurt Lewin) 1950s Solomon Asch Conformity study 1954 Gordon Allport Nature of prejudice 1959 Erving Goffman Presentation of self 1961 Serge Moscovici Social representation 1963 Stanley Milgram Obedience study 1965 William Glasser Choice theory 1968 Robert Zajonc Mere exposure effect 1971 Philip Zimbardo Stanford Prison experiment 1971 Elliot Aronson Jigsaw classroom 1972 Spence and Helmreich Attitude towards women 1977 Brown and Kulik Flashbulb memories 1994 Ignacio Martín-Baró Liberation psychology 2 · Attribution & Attributional Biases Attribution. Notes defining attribution and its two categories, dispositional and situational. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Attribution refers to the way in which people assign responsibility for certain outcomes. Typically attribution falls into two categories: Dispositional (individual) — assumes that the cause of a behaviour or outcome is internal. Situational — assigns the cause to the environment or external conditions. Watch the biases. Several attributional biases are easily confused. The fundamental attribution error (Lee Ross, 1977) is about judging others , while the actor–observer bias and self-serving bias concern how we explain our own actions. Learn the direction (internal vs external) each one pulls. Types of attributional bias Flexible attribution. A list of attributional biases, each with a one-line definition. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Flexible attribution — a general label for the shifting, motivated way people assign causes. Fundamental attribution error — when judging the behaviour of others, people are more likely to overestimate the role of dispositional attributes and to underestimate the role of the situation. Self-serving bias — seeing the cause of actions as internal when the outcomes are positive and external when the results are negative. Actor–observer bias — we tend to attribute our own actions to the situation. Optimism bias — we like to believe that bad things happen to other people, but not to ourselves. Just-world belief ( M. J. Lerner ) — a belief that the world is essentially fair and just (leads to victim blaming). Self-fulfilling prophecy — because person A expects person B to achieve or fail, person B is likely to do just that. Positive: Rosenthal / Pygmalion effect Negative: Golem effect 3 · Kelley's Covariation Model Kelley's Covariation Model (1967). A table showing the levels of consensus, consistency and distinctiveness that lead to an internal or an external attribution. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Covariation model → Harold Kelley (1967). Explains whether we make an internal or external attribution based on three kinds of information: consensus, consistency, and distinctiveness. Information Internal attribution External attribution Consensus Low High Consistency High High Distinctiveness Low High 4 · Cognitive Dissonance Cognitive dissonance. Notes on Festinger's cognitive dissonance, the minimum justification effect, the types of dissonance and the ways to reduce it. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Cognitive dissonance → Leon Festinger. Cognitive dissonance refers to the tension that results from holding conflicting beliefs, attitudes, opinions, or values, or when our actions do not coincide with these cognitions. Key — minimum justification effect. Dissonance is experienced when external rewards are not adequate to justify behaviour. Therefore: Large reward = small attitude change Small reward = large attitude change Types of cognitive dissonance Free choice — when you liked both options. Forced choice — when you dislike both options. Methods of reducing dissonance Changing one's attitude Changing one's behaviour Trivialization 5 · Attitude Change (Elaboration Likelihood Model) Elaboration Likelihood Model. A table comparing the central and peripheral routes by audience, processing effort and how long the attitude change lasts. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 Elaboration Likelihood Model → Richard Petty and John Cacioppo (1986). Route Audience Processing Duration of change Central route Motivated; analytical High effort Long-lasting Peripheral route Unmotivated; non-analytical Low effort Temporary 6 · Social Influence: Compliance, Conformity, Obedience Social influence. A short list of the three main types of social influence and what each behaviour change is based on. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 There are three main types of social influence: Compliance — behaviour change based on a request. Conformity — behaviour change based on social pressure. Obedience — behaviour change based on instruction from an authority. Don't confuse the three. Compliance follows a request , conformity follows social pressure (peers/group), and obedience follows an authority's instruction . The source of the influence is the key distinction. Compliance — Principles of Persuasion Compliance. Cialdini's principles of persuasion with the compliance techniques listed under each principle. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 Principles of persuasion → Robert Cialdini. Principle Techniques Friendship / liking Ingratiation (flattery and praise to get others to like you) Commitment / consistency Foot-in-the-door; Lowball technique Scarcity Deadline technique; Playing hard to get Reciprocity Door-in-the-face; That's-not-all Social validation — Authority — Obedience Obedience: teacher-learner experiment. An illustration of Milgram's set-up with the learner, the teacher participant and the experimenter, followed by the factors that affect obedience and a drawing of people talking. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 Teacher–learner experiment → Stanley Milgram (1963). The set-up (Stanley Milgram, Yale, published 1963). Volunteers were told the study was about the effect of punishment on learning. A rigged draw always made the real volunteer the "teacher". The diagram labels the three roles: Role Who it really was What they did Learner A fake test subject: an actor working for Milgram (a confederate) Sat strapped in the next room, made planned mistakes on a word-pair memory task and pretended to receive shocks (protests, screams, then silence). No real shock was ever given. Teacher The real participant Read the word pairs and pressed switches on a shock generator (15 to 450 volts, rising in 15-volt steps) after every wrong answer, believing the shocks were real. Experimenter The authority figure in a lab coat Stood beside the teacher and urged him to continue with set prods such as "Please continue" and "The experiment requires that you continue". Result: in the 1963 study, 26 of 40 men ( 65% ) went all the way to the maximum 450 volts, far more than psychiatrists had predicted. Later variations showed obedience dropped when the learner was closer (same room, or the teacher had to hold the learner's hand on the shock plate) and when the experimenter gave orders by telephone instead of standing there. These are the "distance" factors listed below. Trap. The participant was the teacher , not the learner, and the study measured obedience to authority , not learning (the learning story was the cover). Milgram's study is also the classic example used in ethics questions on deception and stress to participants. Factors impacting the level of obedience: Distance between experimenter and subject Distance between teacher and learner Expertise of the experimenter Signs of authority of the experimenter Conformity Conformity. A tree splitting conformity into normative and informative social influence, with the motive, type and duration of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 The autokinetic effect experiment (1935). A cartoon of Sherif's study in which people give different reports about whether a single point of light in the dark moved. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 Line judgement task (1951). A cartoon of Asch's study showing a row of stooges, one innocent participant and the card of comparison lines A, B and C. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 Stanford Prison experiment (1971). A photo from Zimbardo's study with notes that it examined role conformity and deindividuation. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 Line judgement task (1951) → Solomon Asch. The set-up (Solomon Asch, 1951). A group of about 7 to 9 people sat round a table. All except one were stooges (confederates of Asch); the one innocent participant sat near the end, so he answered after hearing most of the others. On each trial the group saw a standard line and three comparison lines labelled A, B and C , and each person said aloud which comparison line matched the standard. The answer was obvious (people tested alone almost never erred). On the planned "critical" trials, the stooges all gave the same wrong answer. Result: participants went along with the wrong majority on roughly one third of critical trials, and about three quarters conformed at least once. Conformity fell sharply when just one other person broke from the group (a dissenter), and when participants wrote their answers privately. Stanford Prison experiment (1971) → Philip Zimbardo and colleagues — studied role conformity and the effects of deindividuation. The autokinetic effect experiment (1935) → Muzafer Sherif. The set-up (Muzafer Sherif, 1935). In a completely dark room, people looked at a single, stationary point of light. With nothing else visible to anchor it, the light seems to drift: this illusion is the autokinetic effect . Asked how far it moved, people tested alone gave very different answers (in the cartoon: "it moved left", "no it didn't", "it did, a bit"). When they then judged it together in small groups, their estimates gradually converged on a shared group answer , a group norm, and people kept to that norm when tested alone again later. Type Motive Nature Duration Normative For social approval Public conformity Short term Informative For rational reasons Private conformity Long term Don't confuse Sherif and Asch. Sherif : an ambiguous task (there is no right answer, since the light never moves), so people use others as information: informative influence, private acceptance, a norm that lasts. Asch : an unambiguous task (the right line is obvious), so people conform to avoid standing out: normative influence, public conformity that drops when answers are private. 7 · Social Norms Norms. A tree dividing norms into descriptive and injunctive, with injunctive norms split into prescriptive and proscriptive. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 Descriptive norms — simply tell what to do (what is actually done). Injunctive norms — tell what ought to be done. Prescriptive — what to do. Proscriptive — what not to do. 8 · Prosocial Behaviour & Helping Decision stage model of helping. A flowchart of the five steps a bystander goes through before helping, with the reason help fails at each step. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Decision stage model of helping → John Darley and Bibb Latané (1970). Steps involved in helping behaviour, and why a bystander may fail at each step: Step Not helped due to 1. Noticing the event Distraction 2. Interpret the event as an emergency Pluralistic ignorance; ambiguity; relationship between attacker and victim 3. Assume responsibility Diffusion of responsibility 4. Know the appropriate form of assistance Lack of knowledge; lack of competence 5. Implement the decision Audience inhibition; costs exceed rewards 9 · Proxemics (Personal Space) Theory of Proxemics. Concentric circles showing Edward Hall's four personal space zones with their distances and typical uses. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Theory of Proxemics → Edward Hall (1966). Zone Distance Used for Intimate space 6–18 inches Hugging, whispering or touching Personal space 1.5 to 4 feet Family members or close friends Social space 4 to 12 feet Acquaintances Public space 12 to 25 feet Public speaking situations
