title: Effects, Phenomena, Theories & Originators
text: Effects, Phenomena, Theories & Originators One consolidated lookup for every named effect, phenomenon, illusion, theory, complex and the people behind them. The five old sweeps overlapped heavily (an "effect" carries an originator; a theory carries a theorist), so each item now lives in exactly one entry: the definition, who coined it, the classic study, and the confusable lookalike, together. Drill it both directions: cover the "Who" column and name the person; cover the description and name the term. High-yield NIMHANS / MET ask this two ways. (1) Name the "____ effect / theory / complex" and ask who proposed it (answer = a person). (2) Describe a scene/finding with no name and ask you to name it (answer = the effect/theory). Almost every trap is a same-family lookalike (halo↔horn, Pygmalion↔Golem, placebo↔nocebo, James-Lange↔Cannon-Bard, McCall's T↔Student's t). Always learn each item with its twin. In this reference Named effects (grouped) Phenomena, illusions, biases & clinical signs Theories & models (by domain) Named complexes & syndromes Who originated what — theorists Psychometrics, statistics & standard scores 1. Named effects Every named "____ effect," its originator, and the one-line hook. Grouped by domain so the good-twin / bad-twin pairs sit together. 1.1 Memory & learning effects Effect Who What it is Zeigarnik effect Bluma Zeigarnik Interrupted / unfinished tasks are remembered better than completed ones. Von Restorff (isolation) effect Hedwig von Restorff The odd-one-out item in a list stands out and is recalled best. Serial position effect Ebbinghaus (named by Murdock) First + last items in a list recalled best (= primacy + recency together). Primacy effect — First items recalled well (rehearsed into long-term store). Recency effect — Last items recalled well (still in short-term store). A delay/distractor kills recency, not primacy. Spacing (distributed practice) effect Ebbinghaus Spread-out study beats cramming for long-term retention. Testing effect — Retrieving (self-testing) cements memory better than re-reading. Generation effect Slamecka & Graf Info you generate yourself is remembered better than info you just read. Self-reference effect Rogers, Kuiper & Kirker Material related to yourself is encoded and recalled better. Misinformation effect Elizabeth Loftus Post-event misleading info distorts the original memory (eyewitness work). Picture superiority effect Allan Paivio (dual-coding) Pictures are remembered better than words. Encoding-specificity / context effect Tulving & Thomson Recall is best when retrieval cues match the encoding context (state/context-dependent memory). Levels-of-processing effect Craik & Robert Lockhart Deeper (semantic) processing → better memory than shallow (visual/acoustic). Trap Remove the delay/distractor and it's the recency end that vanishes (STM decays); primacy survives. Zeigarnik = unfinished remembered; von Restorff = distinctive remembered — don't merge them. 1.2 Attention & perception effects Effect Who What it is Stroop effect J. Ridley Stroop Slower to name ink colour when the word spells a different colour (automatic reading interferes). Cocktail-party effect Colin Cherry Selective attention to one voice in a crowd, yet you still catch your own name. McGurk effect McGurk & MacDonald What you see the mouth do changes what you hear (audio-visual speech fusion). Ventriloquist effect — Sound is mislocated toward a plausible visual source. Troxler effect (fading) Ignaz Troxler Fixate steadily and unchanging peripheral stimuli fade from awareness. Motion aftereffect (waterfall illusion) — After staring at motion, a static scene appears to drift the opposite way. Bouba/kiki effect Wolfgang Köhler (later Ramachandran) People map "bouba" to round shapes, "kiki" to spiky ones (sound symbolism). Tetris effect — Heavy repeated activity intrudes into imagery/dreams. Trap The phi phenomenon and autokinetic phenomenon are labelled "phenomena," not "effects" — they live in §2.1. Same content, the label decides where the examiner files it. 1.3 Social & expectancy effects Effect Who What it is Halo effect Edward Thorndike One good trait (e.g. looks) bleeds into an overall positive judgement. Horn(s) effect — The negative mirror of halo: one bad trait darkens the whole impression. Pygmalion (Rosenthal) effect Rosenthal & Jacobson High teacher/leader expectations → the person actually performs better (self-fulfilling prophecy). Golem effect — Low expectations → worse performance (the dark twin of Pygmalion). Hawthorne effect Elton Mayo (Western Electric studies) People change behaviour because they know they're being observed. John Henry effect Saretsky A control group tries extra hard because it knows it's the comparison (a research artefact). Mere-exposure effect Robert Zajonc Repeated exposure alone increases liking (also a persuasion lever: familiarity breeds liking). Bystander effect Latané & John Darley More onlookers → less likely any one helps (diffusion of responsibility). After Kitty Genovese. 5-step decision model: notice → interpret → take responsibility → know how → act. (Theory form in §3.6.) Ringelmann effect Max Ringelmann Per-person effort drops as group size grows (precursor to social loafing). Pratfall effect Elliot Aronson A competent person becomes more likeable after a small blunder. Spotlight effect Thomas Gilovich Overestimating how much others notice you. False-consensus effect Lee Ross Overestimating how many people share your views/choices. Lake Wobegon / above-average effect — Most people rate themselves above average (illusory superiority). Cheerleader effect — Faces look more attractive in a group than alone. Overjustification effect Lepper, Greene & Richard Nisbett Paying for an already-enjoyed activity kills the intrinsic motivation. Boomerang effect Hovland tradition (akin to Brehm) Persuasion backfires, shifting the attitude the opposite way (cousin of reactance, §3.6). Trap Same-study, different name: Pygmalion = Robert Rosenthal & Lenore Jacobson (high expectation lifts), Golem = low expectation drops, Hawthorne = Mayo (being watched changes behaviour). Examiners swap these three constantly. 1.4 Judgment & decision effects Effect Who What it is Barnum / Forer effect Bertram Forer Accepting vague, general descriptions as uniquely true of you (horoscopes, cold reading). Dunning–Kruger effect Dunning & Kruger Low-skill people overestimate their own competence. Anchoring effect Tversky & Daniel Kahneman First number seen drags later estimates toward it. (Bias form: §2.6.) Framing effect Tversky & Kahneman Same facts, different wording (gain vs loss) flips the choice. Endowment effect Richard Thaler You value a thing more just because you own it. IKEA effect Norton, Mochon & Ariely You over-value things you partly built yourself. Decoy (asymmetric dominance) effect Huber et al. A third inferior option nudges choice between the other two. Bandwagon effect — Adopting a belief because many others hold it. Actor–observer effect Jones & Richard Nisbett Your own acts blamed on the situation, others' on their character. Availability in judgment Tversky & Kahneman Easily recalled examples seem more frequent than they are (availability heuristic — §2.6). Pollyanna effect Matlin & Stang Positive items are processed and recalled more readily than negative. High-yield Anchoring, framing and availability are written up both as effects (here) and as cognitive biases/heuristics (§2.6). If the stem says "bias/heuristic," it's §2.6; if it says "effect," it's here. Same content, two labels — scan both. 1.5 Persuasion, media & population effects Effect Who What it is Sleeper effect Carl Hovland (Yale) A message from a low-credibility source persuades more over time once you forget the source. Werther effect David Phillips Spike in copycat suicides after a publicised one. Papageno effect Niederkrotenthaler Responsible media coverage of coping can reduce suicide (the protective opposite of Werther). Mozart effect Rauscher et al. A brief, small spatial-reasoning bump after Mozart (popularly overstated). Flynn effect James Flynn Population IQ scores have risen generation on generation (forces test re-norming). Matthew effect Robert Merton "Rich get richer": early advantage compounds (reading, science credit). Kuleshov effect Lev Kuleshov Viewers read emotion into a neutral face based on the adjacent shot (film editing). 1.6 Biological & clinical effects Effect Who What it is Placebo effect — Improvement from an inert treatment driven by expectation. Nocebo effect — Negative symptoms from an inert treatment (the dark twin of placebo). Garcia effect (taste aversion) John Garcia One-trial conditioned aversion to a taste; biological preparedness; defies classic CC timing rules. Coolidge effect Frank Beach (named it) Renewed sexual interest when a novel partner is introduced. Westermarck effect Edvard Westermarck Reverse sexual imprinting: people raised together in early childhood feel no attraction (incest avoidance). Kindling effect Goddard (seizure model) Repeated sub-threshold stimulation lowers the threshold for episodes (mood/seizure recurrence). Tolerance / sensitisation — Same drug dose gives less effect (tolerance) or more (sensitisation) with repetition. Trap Six "good twin / bad twin" pairs: placebo↔nocebo, Werther↔Papageno, Pygmalion↔Golem, halo↔horn, primacy↔recency, tolerance↔sensitisation . Learn only one of each and the distractor will be the other. 2. Phenomena, illusions, biases & clinical signs Named things the mind/brain does : illusions, attention failures, memory glitches, group phenomena, biases and neuropsych signs. The stem usually describes the experience and wants the name (or who described it). 2.1 Perceptual illusions Illusion Who What you see Müller-Lyer Franz Müller-Lyer Two equal lines look unequal depending on arrow-head direction (inward vs outward fins). Ponzo Mario Ponzo Two equal lines on converging "railway" lines look unequal (depth misread). Ebbinghaus (Titchener) circles Ebbinghaus A circle ringed by big circles looks smaller than the same circle ringed by small ones. Zöllner Johann Zöllner Parallel lines look slanted because of crossing hatch marks. Kanizsa triangle Gaetano Kanizsa You "see" a white triangle edge that isn't drawn (illusory/subjective contours). Necker cube Louis Necker A wire cube flips between two 3-D orientations (bistable perception). Rubin's vase Edgar Rubin Faces-or-vase: figure–ground reversal. Ames room Adelbert Ames A distorted room makes equal-size people look giant vs tiny. Moon illusion — The moon looks larger near the horizon than overhead. Hermann grid — Ghostly grey blobs appear at the white intersections of a black grid. Café wall Gregory & Heard Straight mortar lines look wedge-shaped between offset tiles. Phi phenomenon Max Wertheimer Lights flashing in sequence look like one moving light (the founding Gestalt demo of apparent motion). Autokinetic phenomenon used by Muzafer Sherif A still point of light in the dark seems to drift; Sherif used it to study norm formation. Trap Three "size of equal lines" illusions: Müller-Lyer = arrow fins; Ponzo = converging rails; Ebbinghaus = circle surrounded by other circles. Examiners mix these three. 2.2 Gestalt grouping principles From Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka & Wolfgang Köhler. "The whole is other than the sum of its parts." Master law = Prägnanz (we see the simplest, most stable form). The Gestalt theory of perception itself is in §3.11. Principle What groups together Proximity Things close together are seen as a group. Similarity Things that look alike are grouped. Continuity (good continuation) We follow smooth, continuous lines over abrupt changes. Closure We fill gaps to see a complete figure. Figure–ground We split a scene into an object and its background. Common fate Things moving together are grouped. Prägnanz (good form) The overarching law: perceive the simplest, most regular organisation. 2.3 Attention & perception phenomena Phenomenon Who What it is Inattentional blindness Mack & Rock; Simons & Chabris (gorilla) You miss an obvious unexpected object while attending elsewhere. Change blindness Simons & Levin You fail to notice a large change across a visual interruption. Attentional blink Raymond, Shapiro & Arnell Brief inability to detect a 2nd target ~200–500 ms after the 1st. Cocktail-party phenomenon Colin Cherry Tracking one voice in noise, yet still catching your own name (effect form: §1.2). Weber's law / JND Ernst Weber The just-noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the stimulus. Fechner's law Gustav Fechner Sensation grows with the log of stimulus intensity (founded psychophysics). Sensory adaptation — Constant stimulation → declining response (you stop feeling your clothes). Pareidolia — Seeing meaningful patterns (faces) in random stimuli (clouds, toast). Synaesthesia — One sense automatically triggers another (hearing colours, tasting words). Blindsight Lawrence Weiskrantz Responding to visual stimuli without conscious sight (V1 damage). Perceptual constancy — Objects seen as stable in size/shape/colour despite changing retinal image. 2.4 Memory phenomena Phenomenon Who What it is Tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) Brown & McNeill Knowing a word is there but not retrieving it (you often get its first letter/length). Flashbulb memory Brown & Kulik Vivid, confident memory of where you were during a shocking event (often inaccurate). Déjà vu / jamais vu — Novel scene feels familiar / familiar scene feels alien. Reminiscence bump — Older adults recall disproportionately many memories from ages ~10–30. Childhood (infantile) amnesia — Few/no episodic memories before ~age 3–4. Proactive interference — Old learning blocks new (old password keeps coming up). Retroactive interference — New learning blocks old (new password erases the old one). Forgetting curve Hermann Ebbinghaus Retention drops sharply then levels off; relearning is faster (savings). Misattribution / source-monitoring error Daniel Schacter Right memory, wrong source (cryptomnesia: feeling you invented something you read). 2.5 Group & social phenomena Phenomenon Who What it is Social facilitation Norman Triplett; Robert Zajonc Presence of others boosts easy tasks, harms hard ones. Social loafing Bibb Latané; Ringelmann roots Individuals slack in groups when effort isn't identifiable. Diffusion of responsibility Darley & Latané The mechanism behind the bystander effect: "someone else will." Group polarisation Serge Moscovici; Stoner (risky shift) Group discussion pushes members to a more extreme version of their leaning. Groupthink Irving Janis Cohesive group suppresses dissent for consensus → bad decisions (illusion of unanimity, self-censorship; e.g. Bay of Pigs). Deindividuation Leon Festinger; Philip Zimbardo Loss of self-awareness/restraint in a crowd or anonymity. Conformity Solomon Asch Going along with a group's wrong judgement (line task); normative conformity. Obedience Stanley Milgram Following authority's orders against your own conscience (shock study). Bystander apathy Latané & John Darley The umbrella phenomenon: less help as the crowd grows (effect form: §1.3). Risky shift Stoner Groups make riskier decisions than individuals (early name for polarisation). 2.6 Cognitive biases & heuristics Heuristics = mental shortcuts (largely Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman). Biases = the systematic errors they cause. Bias / heuristic Who What it is Availability heuristic Tversky & Kahneman Judge frequency by how easily examples come to mind. Representativeness heuristic Tversky & Kahneman Judge by resemblance to a prototype (ignores base rates → conjunction fallacy). Anchoring & adjustment Tversky & Kahneman Cling to an initial value when estimating (effect form: §1.4). Confirmation bias Peter Wason Seeking/weighting evidence that fits your belief. Hindsight bias Baruch Fischhoff "I knew it all along" after the outcome is known. Fundamental attribution error coined by Lee Ross Over-attributing others' behaviour to character, under-weighting situation. Self-serving bias — Credit success to self, blame failure on circumstance. Sunk-cost fallacy — Continuing because of past investment that can't be recovered. Gambler's fallacy — Believing past random outcomes change future odds. Loss aversion / framing Kahneman & Tversky (prospect theory) Losses hurt more than equivalent gains feel good. Trap Tells: "judged by ease of recall" = availability; "judged by stereotype/prototype" = representativeness; "blamed the person not the situation" = FAE (Ross). Don't swap the two heuristics. 2.7 Neuropsych & clinical phenomena/signs Phenomenon / sign Who What it is Phantom limb Mitchell; Ramachandran Sensation/pain in an amputated limb (cortical remapping). Capgras delusion Joseph Capgras Belief that a loved one has been replaced by an identical impostor. Fregoli delusion — Belief that different people are one person in disguise. Cotard delusion Jules Cotard Belief that one is dead, doesn't exist, or is rotting (nihilistic delusion). Folie à deux Lasègue & Falret A shared delusion transmitted between two close people. Anosognosia Joseph Babinski Unawareness/denial of one's own deficit (e.g. paralysis after stroke). Confabulation — Filling memory gaps with fabricated events without intent to lie (Korsakoff). Hemispatial neglect — Ignoring one side of space after (usually right) parietal damage. Sundowning — Worsening confusion/agitation in the late afternoon/evening (dementia). Pseudobulbar affect — Uncontrollable laughing/crying out of proportion to feeling. La belle indifférence — Surprising lack of concern about a disabling symptom (conversion disorder). Trap Delusional misidentification trio: Capgras = loved one is an impostor; Fregoli = strangers are one disguised person; Cotard = "I am dead." A classic NIMHANS distractor set. (More eponymous syndromes in §4.) 3. Theories & models Every named theory/model, its author and the one-line claim, grouped so rival theories (each other's distractors) sit side by side. Learn the contrast , not the theory alone. 3.1 Learning theories Theory Author Core claim Classical conditioning Ivan Pavlov Neutral stimulus paired with a reflex-evoking one comes to evoke the reflex. Connectionism / Law of Effect Edward Thorndike Responses followed by satisfaction are stamped in (trial-and-error, puzzle box). Operant conditioning B. F. Skinner Behaviour is shaped by its consequences (reinforcement/punishment). Contiguity theory Edwin Guthrie One-trial learning by sheer stimulus–response pairing in time. Insight learning Wolfgang Köhler Sudden restructuring of a problem ("aha"), shown in chimps (Sultan). Latent learning / cognitive maps Edward Tolman Learning happens without reinforcement and shows up later (maze rats). Social / observational learning Albert Bandura We learn by watching and modelling others (Bobo doll). Rescorla–Wagner model Rescorla & Wagner Conditioning depends on surprise / prediction error, not mere pairing. Premack principle David Premack A high-frequency activity can reinforce a low-frequency one ("grandma's rule"). Conditions / hierarchy of learning Robert Gagné Eight learning types from signal learning up to problem-solving; later five learned capabilities + nine instructional events. Meaningful learning / advance organizers David Ausubel New material is anchored to existing knowledge; pre-teach an advance organizer first. Reception, not discovery. Discovery learning Jerome Bruner Learn by exploring and figuring it out yourself; spiral curriculum; enactive → iconic → symbolic representation. Two-factor (avoidance) theory O. H. Mowrer Avoidance = classical conditioning of fear + operant reinforcement from escaping it. Explains why phobias persist. 3.2 Motivation theories Theory Author Core claim Hierarchy of needs Abraham Maslow Needs climb from physiological → safety → love → esteem → self-actualisation. ERG theory Clayton Alderfer Existence, Relatedness, Growth (Maslow condensed; allows regression). Two-factor (motivation-hygiene) Frederick Herzberg Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivators create satisfaction. Drive-reduction Clark Hull Behaviour reduces physiological drives to restore homeostasis. Arousal theory / Yerkes–Dodson law Yerkes & Dodson Performance peaks at moderate arousal (inverted-U); optimum is lower for hard tasks. Self-determination theory Deci & Ryan Intrinsic motivation needs autonomy, competence, relatedness. Expectancy theory Victor Vroom Effort = expectancy × instrumentality × valence. Goal-setting theory Edwin Locke Specific, hard, accepted goals drive higher performance. Need for achievement (nAch) David McClelland; Atkinson Achievement/affiliation/power needs; measured via TAT. Atkinson: hope-of-success vs fear-of-failure tug-of-war. Flow Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi Total absorption when challenge matches skill. Opponent-process theory Richard Solomon Every emotional state triggers an opposing after-reaction (addiction, thrill). Theory X / Theory Y Douglas McGregor Managers assume workers dislike work and need control (X) or seek responsibility and self-direction (Y). Incentive theory (behaviourist tradition) Behaviour is pulled by external rewards/goals, not just pushed by internal drives. Attribution theory of motivation Bernard Weiner How you explain success/failure (locus × stability × controllability) shapes future emotion & expectancy. 3.3 Emotion theories (the order of events is the trap) Theory Author Sequence James–Lange James & Lange Stimulus → bodily arousal → emotion ("we're afraid because we tremble"). Emotion = reading your own physiology. Cannon–Bard Cannon & Bard Stimulus → arousal and emotion simultaneously (thalamic); body feedback not needed. Schachter–Singer two-factor Schachter & Singer Arousal + cognitive label → emotion (same racing heart becomes fear or excitement by context). Cognitive appraisal Richard Lazarus Appraisal of the event comes first; cognition precedes emotion. Affective primacy Robert Zajonc Emotion can occur before and without cognition ("preferences need no inferences"; mere-exposure is his evidence). Facial-feedback hypothesis Tomkins; Paul Ekman Facial expressions feed back to intensify/trigger the felt emotion. Basic emotions Paul Ekman Six universal, cross-cultural facial emotions. Wheel of emotions Robert Plutchik Eight primary emotions in opposing pairs, combining into others. Trap The classic swap: James-Lange = body first ; Cannon-Bard = both at once ; Schachter-Singer = arousal + label ; Lazarus = appraisal first ; Robert Zajonc = feeling before thinking . Lazarus vs Zajonc is the famous "primacy of cognition vs affect" debate. 3.4 Personality theories Theory Author Core idea Psychoanalytic Sigmund Freud Id/ego/superego; psychosexual stages; unconscious conflict & defences. Analytical psychology Carl Jung Collective unconscious, archetypes, introversion/extraversion. Individual psychology Alfred Adler Inferiority/superiority, striving for superiority, style of life, birth order. Trait (idiographic) Gordon Allport Cardinal/central/secondary traits; functional autonomy. 16PF / factor trait Raymond Cattell 16 source traits via factor analysis; fluid vs crystallised intelligence. PEN model Hans Eysenck Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism (biological arousal basis). Big Five / Five-Factor (OCEAN) Costa & Robert McCrae Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism. Need-press / personology Henry Murray Needs interact with environmental "press"; gave the TAT. Personal construct theory George Kelly "Man as scientist"; we build bipolar constructs to predict events. Social-cognitive Albert Bandura Reciprocal determinism; self-efficacy. Locus of control / social learning Julian Rotter Behaviour = expectancy × reinforcement value; internal vs external control. Person–situation / CAPS Walter Mischel Behaviour is situation-specific; cognitive-affective system; delay of gratification (marshmallow test). Self theory (humanistic) Carl Rogers Self-concept, congruence, unconditional positive regard, fully-functioning person. Interpersonal theory Harry Stack Sullivan Personality forms in relationships; the self-system (good/bad/not-me). Somatotype theory William Sheldon Endomorph/mesomorph/ectomorph body types map to temperament (Ernst Kretschmer was the precursor). Neurotic needs / basic anxiety Karen Horney Childhood basic anxiety drives 10 neurotic needs, grouped into moving toward / against / away from people. Critiqued Freud's penis envy with "womb envy". Humanistic psychoanalysis Erich Fromm Personality shaped by the need to escape isolation/freedom; character orientations (productive vs non-productive). Psychodynamic–learning (frustration-aggression) Dollard & Miller Recast Freud in learning terms; habit hierarchy; the frustration–aggression hypothesis. 3.5 Developmental theories Theory Author Core idea Cognitive development Jean Piaget 4 stages: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete & formal operational. Sociocultural Lev Vygotsky Learning is social; ZPD & scaffolding; language drives thought. Psychosocial development Erik Erikson 8 lifespan stages, each a crisis (trust vs mistrust … integrity vs despair). Psychosexual development Sigmund Freud Oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital stages. Moral development Lawrence Kohlberg Pre-conventional → conventional → post-conventional reasoning. Ethic of care Carol Gilligan Critiqued Kohlberg; women reason via care/relationships, not just justice. Ecological systems Urie Bronfenbrenner Micro/meso/exo/macro/chrono systems; later PPCT model. Attachment theory John Bowlby Innate bonding system; secure base; internal working models; maternal deprivation. Strange Situation / styles Mary Ainsworth Secure, anxious-ambivalent, avoidant (Main later: disorganised). Identity statuses James Marcia Diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, achievement (crisis × commitment). Temperament types Thomas & Chess Easy, difficult, slow-to-warm-up; goodness-of-fit. Maturation theory Arnold Gesell Development unfolds on a biological timetable (norms). Trap Jean Piaget = development drives learning, individual discovery, fixed stages. Lev Vygotsky = learning drives development, social/cultural, ZPD. Erikson's stages (psychosocial, 8 across the lifespan) ≠ Freud's (psychosexual, 5 to puberty). 3.6 Social-psychology theories Theory Author Core idea Cognitive dissonance Leon Festinger Tension from clashing cognitions drives attitude change (usually change the attitude, not the act). Social comparison Leon Festinger We evaluate ourselves by comparing to others when no objective yardstick exists. Attribution theory Fritz Heider We explain behaviour as internal (dispositional) or external (situational); people as naive scientists. Covariation model Harold Kelley Attribution uses consensus, consistency, distinctiveness. Correspondent inference Jones & Davis We infer disposition from freely chosen, unexpected, low-social-desirability acts (non-common effects). Balance theory Fritz Heider We seek consistency among our liking/relationships (P-O-X triangles). Social identity theory Tajfel & Turner Group membership shapes self-concept; in-group favouritism (minimal group paradigm). Realistic conflict theory Muzafer Sherif Competition over scarce resources breeds intergroup hostility; superordinate goals dissolve it (Robbers Cave). Elaboration Likelihood Model Petty & John Cacioppo Persuasion via central (thoughtful, lasting) vs peripheral (cues, weak) route. Yale attitude-change approach Carl Hovland Persuasion mapped by source × message × audience (also gave the sleeper effect, §1.5). Self-perception theory Daryl Bem We infer our own attitudes by observing our behaviour (rival to dissonance). Psychological reactance Jack Brehm (1966) Threatened freedom → wanting the forbidden thing more (engine of reverse psychology). Prof-flagged. Social exchange theory Thibaut & Kelley Relationships weighed by rewards minus costs (comparison level). Equity theory J. S. Adams We want a fair ratio of inputs to outcomes vs others. Bystander effect / diffusion of responsibility Latané & John Darley More witnesses → less help; 5-step decision model (notice → interpret → take responsibility → know how → act). Effect form: §1.3. Social impact theory Bibb Latané Influence of a group = strength × immediacy × number of sources. Frustration–aggression hypothesis John Dollard et al. (rev. Leonard Berkowitz) Frustration breeds aggression; Berkowitz added that aggressive cues are needed. Authoritarian personality (F-scale) Adorno et al. A rigid type that submits to authority and is hostile to out-groups; proposed to explain susceptibility to fascism. Mnemonic Compliance techniques cluster with reactance: foot-in-the-door (Jonathan Freedman & Scott Fraser, small→big), door-in-the-face and low-ball (Robert Cialdini et al.), and Cialdini's 6 principles of influence (reciprocity, commitment/consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity — scarcity works because of reactance). Trap Scenario tell: "told he can't have X, so he wants it more / does it anyway" = reactance (Brehm) . "Tried, failed repeatedly, gave up even when he could win" = learned helplessness (Seligman, §3.10) . Don't swap them. 3.7 Intelligence theories Theory Author Core idea Two-factor (g + s) Charles Spearman A general factor g plus task-specific factors; factor analysis. Primary mental abilities Louis Thurstone 7 independent abilities, no single g . Fluid vs crystallised (Gf-Gc) Raymond Cattell & Horn (→ CHC) Fluid = reasoning power (peaks young); crystallised = accumulated knowledge (holds with age). Structure of intellect J. P. Guilford 180 abilities (operations × content × products); divergent thinking. Multiple intelligences Howard Gardner 8+ independent intelligences (linguistic, musical, bodily-kinesthetic…). Triarchic theory Robert Sternberg Analytical, creative, practical intelligence (also the love triangle). Hierarchical model Philip Vernon g at top → verbal-educational & spatial-mechanical → specifics. Emotional intelligence Peter Salovey & John Mayer (popularised by Daniel Goleman) Perceiving, using, understanding, managing emotion. PASS theory Das, Naglieri & Kirby Intelligence = Planning, Attention, Simultaneous & Successive processing (built on Luria). Three-stratum theory (CHC) John Carroll g at top, 8 broad abilities below, ~70 narrow ones; merged with Cattell-Horn into the CHC model behind modern IQ tests. 3.8 Memory & cognition models Model Author Core idea Multi-store model Atkinson & Richard Shiffrin Sensory → short-term → long-term, linked by attention & rehearsal. Working memory model Baddeley & Hitch Central executive + phonological loop + visuospatial sketchpad (+ episodic buffer). Levels of processing Craik & Robert Lockhart Memory depends on depth of encoding, not a fixed store (effect form: §1.1). Episodic vs semantic memory Endel Tulving Memory for events vs general knowledge (later: procedural; encoding specificity). Dual-coding theory Allan Paivio Verbal + visual codes; images are remembered better (picture superiority, §1.1). Spreading activation Collins & Elizabeth Loftus Semantic network where activating one concept primes related ones. Reconstructive memory / schema theory Frederic Bartlett Memory isn't a recording; we rebuild it to fit our schemas ("War of the Ghosts"). Basis of eyewitness error. 3.9 Language-development theories Theory Author Core idea Behaviourist (learning) B. F. Skinner Language is learned via imitation + reinforcement. Nativist / LAD / Universal Grammar Noam Chomsky Innate language-acquisition device; grammar is hard-wired (rebutted Skinner). Critical period hypothesis Eric Lenneberg Language must be acquired within an early window. Interactionist / LASS Jerome Bruner Social interaction (language acquisition support system) scaffolds language. Linguistic relativity (Sapir–Whorf) Sapir & Benjamin Lee Whorf Language shapes/constrains thought. Cognitive Jean Piaget Language follows cognitive development (thought before language). Trap The famous clash: B. F. Skinner (learned via reinforcement) vs Noam Chomsky (innate LAD/UG). Chomsky's review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior launched the cognitive revolution. 3.10 Stress & abnormal-psychology models Model Author Core idea General Adaptation Syndrome Hans Selye Alarm → resistance → exhaustion response to chronic stress. Transactional model of stress Lazarus & Susan Folkman Stress = primary + secondary appraisal; problem- vs emotion-focused coping. Diathesis–stress model — Disorder arises when a predisposition (diathesis) meets enough stress. Biopsychosocial model George Engel Illness from interacting biological, psychological & social factors. Learned helplessness Seligman & Maier Uncontrollable aversive events → giving up; model of depression. (Later: learned optimism, Martin Seligman.) Cognitive triad Aaron Beck Depression = negative views of self, world & future; schemas. ABC model Albert Ellis Activating event → Belief → Consequence; irrational beliefs drive distress (REBT). Hopelessness theory Abramson, Metalsky & Alloy Reformulated helplessness: a depressive attributional style. 3.11 Perception theories Theory Author Core idea Gestalt Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Köhler The whole is organised by grouping laws (Prägnanz). Principles in §2.2. Direct / ecological perception James Gibson Bottom-up: the optic array provides enough info directly (affordances). Constructivist perception Richard Gregory Top-down: perception is hypothesis-testing from prior knowledge. Feature-integration theory Anne Treisman Features detected in parallel; attention binds them into objects. Signal detection theory Green & Swets Detection = sensitivity (d′) + response criterion (bias), not a fixed threshold. 3.12 Career & counselling theories Theory Author Core idea RIASEC / vocational types John Holland Match person type to work environment (Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising, Conventional). Life-span, life-space Donald Super Career develops across life stages; self-concept implemented in work. Developmental career choice Eli Ginzberg Occupational choice as a developmental process (fantasy → tentative → realistic). Social learning / happenstance John Krumboltz Career shaped by learning experiences and planned chance. Needs theory of career Anne Roe Early parent-child climate shapes person-oriented vs non-person-oriented careers. Circumscription & compromise Linda Gottfredson Children narrow options by gender, then prestige, then interests; compromise when reality bites. 4. Named complexes & syndromes The eponym family NIMHANS loves. Same "name → who → what" format. The three at the top of the trap box were specifically flagged by Sihan's professor. Trap Prof-flagged, lock these cold. Icarus complex = Henry Murray. McCall's T score = William McCall (mean 50, SD 10; §6 — recognise it from the definition ; the trap is Student's t, a test statistic by Gosset). Psychological reactance = Jack Brehm (§3.6 — recognise it from a scenario ). Two question shapes: "who coined this named complex" AND "here's a phenomenon described in words, name it." Complex / syndrome Who What it is Icarus complex Henry Murray Soaring ambition + craving for attention/admiration ending in a fall; fascination with fire, ascent, falling, narcissism. (Same Murray who gave the TAT, needs/press, personology — §5.) Jonah complex Abraham Maslow Fear of your own greatness; running from self-actualisation (opposite flavour to Icarus). Inferiority / superiority complex Alfred Adler Core of Adlerian theory; overcompensation for felt inferiority. Oedipus / Electra complex Sigmund Freud (Oedipus); Carl Jung coined Electra Phallic-stage attachment to the opposite-sex parent. Cinderella complex Colette Dowling Unconscious wish to be taken care of / fear of independence. Peter Pan syndrome Dan Kiley Adult who refuses to grow up. (Kiley also: Wendy syndrome , the over-mothering partner.) Diogenes syndrome Clark et al. Senile self-neglect, squalor, hoarding, social withdrawal. Othello syndrome John Todd Delusional / morbid jealousy of a partner. Munchausen syndrome Richard Asher Feigning illness for the sick role (factitious disorder). Couvade syndrome — Father develops pregnancy symptoms ("sympathetic pregnancy"). Stockholm syndrome Nils Bejerot (named it) Captive bonds with the captor. Trap Complex ownership: inferiority/superiority = Alfred Adler ; womb envy = Karen Horney ; Electra = Carl Jung (named it), Oedipus = Sigmund Freud; Jonah = Abraham Maslow ; Icarus = Murray . Don't default everything to Freud. 5. Who originated what — theorists The reverse drill: name → what they own . For a person you'll meet here, the named effect, theory or complex they coined is defined in §§1–4; this section bundles each theorist so one concept pulls the whole name up. The distractor is always a same-field contemporary. 5.1 Psychoanalytic & neo-Freudian Theorist What they own Sigmund Freud Psychoanalysis; id/ego/superego; psychosexual stages; defence mechanisms; the unconscious; dream interpretation; Oedipus complex; free association & transference. Carl Jung Analytical psychology; collective unconscious; archetypes; introversion/extraversion; coined the Electra complex; word-association. Alfred Adler Individual psychology; inferiority/superiority complex; striving for superiority; style of life; birth order; social interest. Karen Horney Basic anxiety; moving toward/against/away from people; womb envy (reply to penis envy); neurotic needs. Erik Erikson 8 psychosocial stages; identity crisis; ego psychology. Erich Fromm Escape from Freedom; character orientations; humanistic psychoanalysis. Harry Stack Sullivan Interpersonal theory; the self-system; good-me / bad-me / not-me. Melanie Klein Object relations; play therapy; paranoid-schizoid & depressive positions. Anna Freud Child psychoanalysis; systematised the defence mechanisms. D. W. Winnicott Good-enough mother; transitional object; holding environment; true/false self. Heinz Kohut Self psychology; narcissism; empathic mirroring. 5.2 Humanistic, existential & trait theorists Theorist What they own Abraham Maslow Hierarchy of needs; self-actualisation; peak experiences; Jonah complex. Carl Rogers Person-centred therapy; self-concept; congruence; unconditional positive regard; fully-functioning person; real vs ideal self. Gordon Allport Cardinal/central/secondary traits; functional autonomy (a motive outliving its original cause); idiographic approach; contact hypothesis. Raymond Cattell 16PF; source vs surface traits; fluid vs crystallised intelligence; factor analysis of personality. Hans Eysenck PEN model; biological/arousal basis of personality (introverts over-aroused, extraverts under-aroused). Costa & Robert McCrae Big Five / NEO-PI (OCEAN). Henry Murray Personology; needs & press; the TAT (with Morgan); Icarus complex; nAch roots. George Kelly Personal construct theory; Rep grid; "man as scientist." Julian Rotter Locus of control (internal/external); social learning; expectancy × reinforcement value. Walter Mischel Person–situation debate; CAPS; the marshmallow test (delay of gratification). Rollo May / Viktor Frankl Existential psychology; May (anxiety/the daimonic); Frankl (logotherapy, meaning, paradoxical intention). William Sheldon Somatotypes (endo/meso/ectomorph). Ernst Kretschmer Body-build → temperament types (pyknic/asthenic/athletic); precursor to Sheldon. 5.3 Behaviourist & learning theorists Theorist What they own Ivan Pavlov Classical conditioning; the salivating dogs. John B. Watson Founded behaviourism; Little Albert; "give me a dozen healthy infants…". B. F. Skinner Operant conditioning; reinforcement schedules; Skinner box; verbal behaviour; radical behaviourism. Edward Thorndike Law of Effect; connectionism; puzzle box; the halo effect. Edward Tolman Latent learning; cognitive maps; purposive behaviourism. Wolfgang Köhler Insight learning (chimps); Gestalt; the bouba/kiki demo. Albert Bandura Social learning; Bobo doll; self-efficacy; reciprocal determinism. Edwin Guthrie Contiguity theory (one-trial learning). Clark Hull Drive-reduction theory; mathematico-deductive behaviourism. Joseph Wolpe Systematic desensitisation; reciprocal inhibition. Mnemonic The animal-study set: dogs = Ivan Pavlov ; cats/puzzle box = Edward Thorndike ; chimps/insight = Wolfgang Köhler ; monkeys/contact comfort = Harry Harlow ; rats/cognitive maps = Edward Tolman ; Bobo doll = Albert Bandura ; Little Albert = John B. Watson . 5.4 Cognitive & developmental theorists Theorist What they own Jean Piaget Cognitive-development stages; schemas; assimilation/accommodation; object permanence; conservation. Lev Vygotsky Sociocultural theory; ZPD; scaffolding; private speech. Jerome Bruner Discovery learning; spiral curriculum; enactive/iconic/symbolic; LASS. Lawrence Kohlberg Stages of moral development. Urie Bronfenbrenner Ecological systems; PPCT model. John Bowlby Attachment theory; maternal deprivation; internal working models. Mary Ainsworth Strange Situation; secure/anxious/avoidant attachment. Harry Harlow Rhesus monkeys; contact comfort over food (wire vs cloth mother). Noam Chomsky Universal grammar; LAD; rebutted B. F. Skinner; cognitive revolution. Ulric Neisser "Cognitive Psychology" (named the field); ecological memory. Endel Tulving Episodic vs semantic memory; encoding specificity. Baddeley & Hitch Working-memory model. Elizabeth Loftus Misinformation effect; eyewitness memory; false memories. 5.5 Social psychologists Theorist What they own Leon Festinger Cognitive dissonance; social comparison; deindividuation roots. Kurt Lewin Father of social psych; field theory; B = f(P,E); action research; group dynamics. Solomon Asch Conformity (line task); impression formation (central traits). Stanley Milgram Obedience to authority; small-world / six degrees. Philip Zimbardo Stanford prison experiment; deindividuation; the Lucifer effect. Muzafer Sherif Realistic conflict; Robbers Cave; autokinetic norm formation. Fritz Heider Attribution theory; balance theory. Harold Kelley Covariation model (consensus, consistency, distinctiveness); social exchange (with John Thibaut). Jones & Davis Correspondent inference theory. Lee Ross Coined the fundamental attribution error; false-consensus effect. Bernard Weiner Attribution theory of motivation (locus × stability × controllability). Tajfel & Turner Social identity theory; minimal group paradigm. Irving Janis Groupthink. Latané & John Darley Bystander effect; diffusion of responsibility; Bibb Latané's social impact theory. Carl Hovland Yale attitude-change approach; the sleeper effect. Petty & John Cacioppo Elaboration Likelihood Model. Daryl Bem Self-perception theory. Robert Cialdini Six principles of influence; door-in-the-face & low-ball. Jack Brehm Psychological reactance. Adorno et al. Authoritarian personality (F-scale). Norman Triplett First social-psych experiment → social facilitation. 5.6 Intelligence & testing Theorist What they own Alfred Binet First practical intelligence test (with Simon); mental age. Lewis Terman Stanford-Binet; longitudinal study of gifted children ("Termites"); popularised the ratio IQ. David Wechsler WAIS/WISC; deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15). Charles Spearman Two-factor theory; g ; factor analysis (stats role in §6). Louis Thurstone Primary mental abilities; attitude scaling (equal-appearing intervals). J. P. Guilford Structure of intellect; divergent thinking. Howard Gardner Multiple intelligences. Robert Sternberg Triarchic theory; love triangle. Salovey & Mayer Emotional intelligence (Daniel Goleman popularised). Hermann Rorschach The inkblot test. William Stern Ratio IQ (MA/CA × 100). Trap CBT-family ownership (therapy founders in §5.7): cognitive triad & cognitive therapy = Beck ; REBT & ABC = Albert Ellis ; DBT = Marsha Linehan ; ACT = Hayes . Beck and Ellis are the constant distractor pair. 5.7 Therapy founders Founder Therapy Sigmund Freud Psychoanalysis (free association, transference). Aaron Beck Cognitive therapy / CBT; cognitive triad. Albert Ellis REBT; ABC model; irrational beliefs. Carl Rogers Person-centred / client-centred therapy. Fritz Perls Gestalt therapy; empty chair; here-and-now. Joseph Wolpe Systematic desensitisation; behaviour therapy. Viktor Frankl Logotherapy (meaning); paradoxical intention. William Glasser Reality therapy; choice theory. Marsha Linehan Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT). Steven Hayes Acceptance & commitment therapy (ACT). Eric Berne Transactional analysis (Parent-Adult-Child). Salvador Minuchin Structural family therapy. Jacob Moreno Psychodrama; group psychotherapy; the term "group therapy." Irvin Yalom Existential & group therapy; 11 therapeutic factors. Francine Shapiro EMDR. 6. Psychometrics, statistics & standard scores The "who gave what" layer NIMHANS bolts onto the clinical material: measurement terms, statistical tests, and the standard-score family. Two of the three prof-flagged curveballs (McCall's T, Student's t) live here. 6.1 Psychometrics & measurement terms Term Originator What it is T score (mean 50, SD 10) William McCall A standard score rescaled to mean 50, SD 10, killing negatives and decimals. MMPI reports it. This is the McCall's T the prof asked. Factor analysis, g , two-factor theory Charles Spearman Invented factor analysis; argued intelligence is one general factor (g) plus specific factors. Spearman–Brown prophecy formula; rank correlation (rho) Spearman Predicts how reliability rises with test length; rho correlates two sets of ranks. Coefficient (Cronbach's) alpha Lee Cronbach Standard index of internal consistency (items hang together). Above ~0.7 acceptable. Construct validity (the paper) Cronbach & Paul Meehl A test is valid if it behaves the way the underlying construct theoretically should. KR-20 / KR-21 Kuder & Richardson Internal-consistency formulas for right/wrong (dichotomous) items; special case of alpha. Kappa (inter-rater); Cohen's d (effect size) Jacob Cohen Kappa = chance-corrected rater agreement; d = mean difference in SD units (0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large); statistical power. Product-moment correlation (r); chi-square Karl Pearson r = strength/direction of a linear relationship (−1 to +1); standard deviation term. Correlation concept; regression to the mean Francis Galton First conceived correlation; regression to the mean; eugenics; first mental tests. Likert (summative agree–disagree) scale Rensis Likert Strongly-agree-to-strongly-disagree; sum item scores. Treated as interval-ish. Equal-appearing intervals; law of comparative judgment; PMA Louis Thurstone Attitude scales with judged equal intervals; argued for several primary mental abilities, not one g. Guttman scalogram (cumulative scaling) Louis Guttman Agreeing with a strong item implies agreeing with all weaker ones; score pins your exact pattern. Semantic differential Charles Osgood Rate a concept between bipolar adjective pairs; dimensions = evaluation, potency, activity. Multitrait–multimethod matrix; convergent/discriminant validity Campbell & Fiske A grid checking a test correlates with same-trait measures (convergent) but not different ones (discriminant). Item Response Theory / Rasch model Georg Rasch (IRT also Lord & Novick) Models a correct answer from person ability and item difficulty on one scale (basis of adaptive testing). Critical incident technique John Flanagan Collect real examples of effective/ineffective behaviour to define what a job requires. Ratio IQ (MA/CA × 100) William Stern (popularised by Lewis Terman) Old IQ = mental age ÷ chronological age × 100; breaks down in adulthood, replaced by deviation IQ. Deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15) David Wechsler Modern IQ: standing relative to your age group on a normal curve. 6.2 Statistical tests & who gave them High-yield Student's t = William Sealy Gosset. "Student" is a pseudonym , not a person. Gosset worked at the Guinness brewery in Dublin and published the t-test in 1908 under the pen name because Guinness barred staff from publishing. "Who was Student / who gave the t-test" → Gosset. The t-test compares means when the sample is small and the population SD is unknown . Test Who gave it What it's for Student's t-test / t-distribution W. S. Gosset ("Student", 1908) Compare means, small n, σ unknown. Flavours: one-sample (df = n−1), independent two-sample (df = n₁+n₂−2), paired (before/after, same people). ANOVA / F-test Ronald Fisher (the F named for Fisher by Snedecor) Compare 3+ group means at once. F = between-group var ÷ within-group var. Also: null hypothesis, p < .05, experimental design. Chi-square (χ²) Karl Pearson Association / goodness-of-fit for categorical data. Pearson r Karl Pearson Linear correlation, interval data. Spearman rho (ρ) Charles Spearman Rank correlation (ordinal / non-normal). Mann–Whitney U Mann & Whitney Nonparametric twin of the independent t (two unrelated groups). Wilcoxon signed-rank Frank Wilcoxon Nonparametric twin of the paired t. Kruskal–Wallis H Kruskal & Wallis Nonparametric twin of one-way ANOVA. Friedman test Milton Friedman Nonparametric repeated-measures ANOVA. McNemar test Quinn McNemar Paired nominal data (before/after yes-no). Trap "Student" is Gosset , not a real student, and McCall's T (a standard score) ≠ Student's t (a test statistic) — the shared letter is the bait. 2 groups → t-test; 3+ groups → ANOVA (don't run repeated t-tests). Parametric → nonparametric: independent t → Mann–Whitney , paired t → Wilcoxon , one-way ANOVA → Kruskal–Wallis . F-test/ANOVA = Fisher ; chi-square = Pearson . Definition t vs z: use z when the population SD is known and/or n is large; use t when SD is estimated from a small sample. As df → ∞ the t-distribution becomes the normal (z) curve. t is shorter and fatter-tailed than z. 6.3 The standard-score family (so McCall's T sits in context) Score Mean SD Note z-score 0 1 The base; everything else is a rescaled z. T score (McCall) 50 10 No negatives, no decimals needed; MMPI uses T. Stanine 5 ~2 1–9 scale ("standard nine"). Sten 5.5 2 1–10 ("standard ten"); used in 16PF. Deviation IQ 100 15 Wechsler (Stanford-Binet SD 16). Wechsler scaled (subtest) 10 3 Each subtest; sum → index/IQ. SD 3 is a common distractor. Wechsler index 100 15 VCI, PRI/WMI, PSI etc. NCE (normal-curve equiv.) 50 21.06 Looks like a percentile but is equal-interval; matches percentile at 1, 50, 99. Percentile rank — — Not equal-interval; bunches near the mean. Don't average percentiles. Definition Conversion you can be asked: T = 50 + 10z. So z = +1 → T = 60; z = −2 → T = 30. MMPI clinical-range cut is usually T ≥ 65 . Linear T = rescaled z (keeps the shape); normalised T = forced to a normal curve via percentile→z first. Both still mean 50, SD 10.

title: Lookalikes — telling two close terms apart on the options
text: Lookalikes — telling two close terms apart on the options For when plain definitions aren't enough and the trap is a near-identical distractor. Each block is one confusable pair: what's the same (why both look right), what differs (line by line), and the one tell — the single thing in the stem that splits them. Read the tell, not the whole block, on exam day. Built 2026-05-25. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes How to use it. The examiner picks two real, correct-sounding terms and bets you can't split them. Don't re-derive both definitions. Find the tell word in the stem (added vs removed? up vs down? before vs after? thought vs act?) and the option falls out. These are the pairs that actually bleed marks on MET/NIMHANS. Jump to: 1. Learning & conditioning 2. Developmental 3. Sensation & perception 4. Memory & cognition 5. Stats & research 6. Abnormal / clinical 7. Defense mechanisms 8. Therapy 9. Social 10. Intelligence 1. Learning & conditioning Classical conditioning vs Operant conditioning Same: both are associative learning; both show acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation and discrimination. Classical (Ivan Pavlov) Operant (B. F. Skinner) Behaviour Involuntary, reflexive (salivation, fear) Voluntary, emitted (lever press) Association Stimulus → stimulus (CS–US) Behaviour → consequence (response–reinforcer) Learner Passive, responds to a cue Active, operates on the environment Reinforcer timing Comes before/with the response Comes after the response The tell: Is the behaviour automatic and triggered by a cue that comes first (classical), or voluntary and shaped by what happens after (operant)? Any "reward / consequence / punishment" in the stem → operant. Negative reinforcement vs Punishment Same: both are operant procedures and both usually involve an aversive/unpleasant stimulus, so they read alike. Negative reinforcement Punishment Effect on behaviour Increases it Decreases it What happens Removes an aversive stimulus (take painkiller → pain gone) Adds aversive (positive) or removes pleasant (negative) "Negative" means Subtraction, not "bad" — The tell: Did the behaviour go up or down ? Up = reinforcement (negative = the bad thing was taken away ). Down = punishment. "Negative" is about removal, never about being unpleasant. Positive punishment vs Negative punishment Same: both decrease a behaviour. Positive punishment Negative punishment Operation Add something aversive (scolding, spanking) Remove something pleasant (take phone, time-out, fine) Other name — Response cost / omission The tell: Positive = something was added ; negative = something was taken away . Both still reduce the behaviour, so judge by add vs subtract, not by good vs bad. Primary reinforcer vs Secondary reinforcer Same: both strengthen behaviour when they follow it. Primary Secondary (conditioned) Why it reinforces Innately satisfies a biological need (food, water, sex, warmth) Learned value through association Learning needed? No Yes (money, tokens, praise, grades) The tell: Does it satisfy a body need directly (primary) or only because you learned it stands for something else (secondary)? Money is the classic secondary reinforcer. Shaping vs Chaining Same: both build complex operant behaviour using reinforcement. Shaping Chaining What's reinforced Successive approximations to one target behaviour Linking a sequence of already-learned behaviours Picture it Refining one act closer and closer Step 1 → step 2 → step 3 as a chain The tell: One behaviour polished step-by-step (shaping) vs several separate behaviours joined in order (chaining). Stimulus generalisation vs Stimulus discrimination Same: both describe how a conditioned response transfers (or doesn't) across stimuli. Generalisation Discrimination Response to similar cues Yes — spreads to stimuli like the CS No — only the exact CS triggers it Little Albert (John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner, 1920) Feared all furry white things Would fear only the rat The tell: Response spreads to lookalikes (generalisation) vs narrows to one exact cue (discrimination). 2. Developmental Assimilation vs Accommodation (Jean Piaget) Same: the twin processes of adaptation ; both are how a schema deals with new information. Assimilation Accommodation Schema Stays the same — new info forced into it Changes / a new one is created to fit reality Example Calls a whale a "fish" Learns a whale is a mammal, makes a new category The tell: Did the existing schema stay put (assimilation) or did it have to change (accommodation)? If the child updated their mental category, it's accommodation. Piaget vs Lev Vygotsky Same: both constructivists; both say the child actively builds knowledge rather than passively absorbing it. Piaget Vygotsky Engine of development The individual child exploring; cognition leads language Social/cultural interaction; language leads cognition Signature terms Stages, schema, assimilation/accommodation, egocentrism ZPD, scaffolding, More Knowledgeable Other, private speech The tell: Is the driver the child alone (Piaget) or a guiding social other / ZPD (Vygotsky)? Any "scaffolding" or "zone of proximal development" → Vygotsky. 3. Sensation & perception Sensation vs Perception Same: both are stages of taking in stimulus information. Sensation Perception What it is Raw detection by sense organs + transduction Brain's organisation & interpretation of it Direction Bottom-up (data in) Top-down (meaning added) The tell: Detecting the raw signal at the receptor (sensation) vs making sense of / recognising it (perception). Interpretation, meaning, recognition → perception. Absolute threshold vs Difference threshold (JND) Same: both are psychophysics thresholds (Weber/Fechner). Absolute threshold Difference threshold (JND) Detects Minimum intensity to detect a stimulus 50% of the time Smallest detectable change between two stimuli Law — Weber's law: JND is a constant proportion The tell: Detecting that one stimulus is present (absolute) vs detecting a difference between two (difference / JND). "Just noticeable difference" → difference threshold. 4. Memory & cognition Proactive interference vs Retroactive interference Same: both are forgetting caused by interference between old and new learning. Proactive Retroactive Direction Old blocks new (forward) New blocks old (backward) What you forget The new material The old material Example Old password keeps coming up New password wipes the old one The tell: Which is forgotten? Forget the new → proactive (" pro = prior learning interferes forward"). Forget the old → retroactive. Recall vs Recognition Same: both are measures of retrieval from long-term memory. Recall Recognition Task Produce the info with little/no cue (essay, free recall) Identify the correct item among options (MCQ) Difficulty Harder Easier — the answer is in front of you The tell: Generate it from scratch (recall) vs pick it out of choices (recognition). A multiple-choice exam tests recognition. Anterograde amnesia vs Retrograde amnesia Same: both are memory loss, usually after brain injury, defined relative to the moment of injury. Anterograde Retrograde Lost memories Can't form new memories after the event Lost old memories from before the event Time direction Forward from injury Backward from injury The tell: " Antero = after" — no new memories form. Retrograde = the past is gone. (H.M. (studied by William Scoville and Brenda Milner, 1957) = classic anterograde.) Explicit (declarative) vs Implicit (non-declarative) memory Same: both are long-term memory systems. Explicit / declarative Implicit / non-declarative Awareness Conscious — you can state it Unconscious — shows in performance Contents Facts (semantic) + events (episodic) Skills (procedural), priming, conditioning The tell: Can you consciously declare it (explicit) or does it just show up as a skill/habit (implicit)? Riding a bike = implicit/procedural. 5. Stats & research methods Type I error vs Type II error Same: both are wrong decisions in null-hypothesis testing. Type I (α) Type II (β) Mistake Reject a true null = false positive Fail to reject a false null = false negative In words Claim an effect that isn't there Miss a real effect The tell: False alarm = Type I (α). Miss = Type II (β). "Type I = I see something that isn't there." Reliability vs Validity Same: both are desirable psychometric properties of a test or measure. Reliability Validity Question it answers Is it consistent / repeatable? Does it measure what it's supposed to? Relationship Can be reliable but not valid (consistently wrong) Validity requires reliability, not vice versa The tell: Consistency = reliability; accuracy/measures-the-right-thing = validity. Same spot every time = reliable; the bullseye = valid. Independent variable vs Dependent variable Same: both are the variables defined in an experiment. Independent (IV) Dependent (DV) Role Manipulated — the presumed cause Measured — the outcome (depends on the IV) The tell: What the experimenter changes = IV; what they measure as the result = DV. 6. Abnormal / clinical Delusion vs Hallucination Same: both are psychotic symptoms; both appear in schizophrenia. Delusion Hallucination Disturbance of Thought content — a false, fixed belief Perception — a false sensory experience Example "The FBI is tracking me" Hearing voices with no one there The tell: A wrong belief (delusion) vs a wrong perception (hallucination). If there's a sensory experience, it's a hallucination. Illusion vs Hallucination Same: both are perceptual disturbances. Illusion Hallucination External stimulus? Yes — a real stimulus is misperceived No — perception with no stimulus at all Example A shadow looks like an intruder Seeing a person who isn't there The tell: Is there a real object being misread (illusion) or nothing there to begin with (hallucination)? Obsession vs Compulsion Same: both are core to OCD; both are distressing and unwanted. Obsession Compulsion Type Intrusive thought , image or urge (mental) Repetitive act or ritual (behaviour) Function Causes the anxiety Done to relieve the anxiety The tell: The thought that intrudes (obsession) vs the act done to neutralise it (compulsion). Hand-washing = compulsion; the fear of germs = obsession. Affect vs Mood Same: both describe emotional state in a mental status exam. Affect Mood Timescale Momentary, observable expression Sustained, pervasive feeling Analogy The weather The climate The tell: Short-term, outwardly observed = affect; sustained, subjectively reported = mood. Delirium vs Dementia Same: both cause cognitive impairment and confusion, often in older patients. Delirium Dementia Onset Acute, fluctuating (hours–days) Gradual, progressive (months–years) Consciousness Clouded, attention impaired Clear early; memory leads Reversible? Usually yes Usually no The tell: Sudden onset + fluctuating + altered consciousness = delirium. Slow, progressive, alert = dementia. Neurosis vs Psychosis Same: both are older umbrella categories of mental disorder. Neurosis Psychosis Reality contact Intact — insight present Lost — no insight Examples Anxiety, phobia, OCD Schizophrenia, delusional disorder The tell: Is reality testing intact with insight (neurosis) or broken (psychosis)? Delusions/hallucinations → psychosis. Positive vs Negative symptoms (schizophrenia) Same: both are symptom clusters of schizophrenia. Positive Negative Nature Added to normal experience Loss / absence of normal function Examples Hallucinations, delusions, disorganised speech Flat affect, alogia, avolition, anhedonia The tell: Excess / something added = positive; deficit / something missing = negative. 7. Defense mechanisms Repression vs Suppression Same: both push distressing material out of awareness. Repression Suppression Awareness Unconscious, involuntary Conscious, deliberate The tell: Done unknowingly (repression) vs on purpose (suppression). "Decided not to think about it" = suppression. Displacement vs Sublimation Same: both redirect an unacceptable impulse onto a new target. Displacement Sublimation New target A safer but still similar target A socially valued, productive outlet Example Yell at the kids instead of the boss Channel aggression into sport or surgery The tell: Just a safer target (displacement) vs a constructive, socially-approved channel (sublimation). Sublimation is the mature one. Projection vs Reaction formation Same: both defend against one's own unacceptable feelings. Projection Reaction formation Strategy Attribute your impulse to someone else Act the opposite of your impulse Example "He hates me" (when you hate him) Hating someone → being overly nice to them The tell: Pin the feeling on someone else (projection) vs flip to the opposite behaviour (reaction formation). 8. Therapy Transference vs Countertransference Same: both are displaced feelings inside the psychodynamic therapeutic relationship. Transference Countertransference Whose feelings The client's , redirected onto the therapist The therapist's , redirected onto the client The tell: Client → therapist = transference. Therapist → client = countertransference. 9. Social Conformity vs Compliance vs Obedience Same: all three are behaviour change due to social influence. Conformity Compliance Obedience Source of pressure Implicit group norm A direct request An order from authority Study Solomon Asch (lines) Foot-in-the-door (Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser, 1966) Stanley Milgram (shocks) The tell: Group norm with no one asking (conformity) vs someone requests (compliance) vs an authority commands (obedience). Stereotype vs Prejudice vs Discrimination Same: all three are components of intergroup bias and constantly swapped in options. Stereotype Prejudice Discrimination Component (ABC) Cognition — a belief Affect — a negative attitude Behaviour — an action The tell: Thought = stereotype, feeling = prejudice, action = discrimination. Map it to A ffect / B ehaviour / C ognition. 10. Intelligence Fluid intelligence vs Crystallised intelligence (Raymond Cattell) Same: both are Cattell's components of general intelligence (Gf–Gc). Fluid (Gf) Crystallised (Gc) What it is Reasoning with novel problems, independent of knowledge Accumulated knowledge, vocabulary, learned skills With age Declines earlier Holds up / keeps rising The tell: On-the-spot novel reasoning (fluid) vs stored, learned knowledge (crystallised). If age makes it better , it's crystallised. That's the lookalikes set. If a pair you keep missing isn't here, send it and I'll add a block. Related sweeps: Phenomena , Effects , Theories , Theorists . Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS prep · /notes/differentiators/ · built 2026-05-25

title: The Textbook — Everything in One Page
text: The Textbook — Everything in One Page Your single self-contained source. Built 2026-05-22, the night before MET. This is the one page. Read it top to bottom and you have read everything. Every list, definition, table, trap box and concept you have ever been given is inlined here, organised by your 8 exam sections, with a ★C common-section concept pack right at the top (the high-yield general psych that section hammers, the foundations and the confusable pairs that quietly cost marks), plus a §9 rapid-recall sweep (the easily-forgotten names/durations and the general-psych foundations) at the end, so it reads like your own textbook. There are no links out to other pages, nothing to chase, all the content lives right here. Study from this page only tonight. Sections are folded so it isn't a wall of text: tap any one to open it, or hit Expand all to read straight through. Jump to ★ Your mock misses, fixed ★C. Common-section concept pack 1. Biopsychology / Neuro 2. Developmental 3. Abnormal 4. Assessment / Tests 5. Psychotherapy / Learning / Ethics 6. Research / Biostats 7. Language 8. Social / Memory / Acts / Founders 9. Rapid Recall (easily forgotten + general psych) Exam-day rules Expand all Collapse all Tap a section to open it. Everything is still here, just folded away. ★ Your mock misses, fixed here Every question you got wrong, guessed, or flagged on the real NIMHANS 2024 PYQ mock (91.25/100) maps to a block below. If you only have an hour, read these rows, then read the red trap boxes. What tripped you The fix Section WAIS scaled score of 10 = ? Exactly average, 50th percentile (subtest mean 10, SD 3) Biostats WAIS-IV core subtest NOT in WISC-V Letter-Number Sequencing (the keyed answer; strictly WAIS-IV supplemental and WISC-V secondary, core only in the WISC-IV; WISC-V's primary working-memory pair is Digit Span + Picture Span) Assessment IQ test = which kind of test? Ability test (maximum performance). Not power, not speed.
