Common-Section Concept Pack high-yield general psych · the foundations · the bits that quietly cost marks This is the section that is bleeding your marks. The subject blocks above are your strong ground; the common section is general psychology, and it punishes shaky foundations and confusable pairs more than raw facts. So this pack is built differently: every block ends in the exact distinction the examiner uses to separate the two options that look identical. Read it for the contrasts, not the trivia. If you can run the cover-and-test set at the very end (C.11) clean, the common section stops costing you. C.1 The schools of psychology (the "isms"), in order Almost every general paper has one "who founded / what method / which school" item. Learn them as a story: each school is a reaction to the one before it. School Core claim Method Key names Structuralism Break consciousness into its basic elements (sensations, feelings) Introspection Wilhelm Wundt (first lab, 1879), Edward Titchener Functionalism Why does the mind do what it does; its purpose and adaptation Observation, applied focus William James, Dewey, Angell Gestalt The whole is different from the sum of its parts; perception is organised Phenomenology Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Köhler Psychoanalysis Behaviour is driven by the unconscious and early conflict Free association, dream analysis, case study Sigmund Freud, later Jung, Alfred Adler Behaviourism Study only observable behaviour; the mind is a black box Controlled experiment, conditioning John B. Watson, Ivan Pavlov, Skinner, Edward Thorndike Humanistic People are growth-oriented and free; the "third force" Phenomenology, client report Maslow, Carl Rogers Cognitive Mind as an information processor; mental processes are real and studiable Experiment, modelling, reaction time Ulric Neisser (coined it, 1967), Miller, Donald Broadbent Biological Behaviour reduces to brain, neurochemistry, genes Lesion, imaging, twin studies Sperry, Hebb Evolutionary Behaviour was selected because it aided survival/reproduction Cross-species, adaptationist reasoning Buss, Tooby & Cosmides Positive Study strengths, well-being and flourishing, not just pathology Empirical, intervention trials Seligman, Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi TRAP: Wilhelm Wundt = structuralism + introspection (the first lab). James = functionalism . Ulric Neisser = cognitive . John B. Watson named behaviourism but Wundt is "father of experimental psychology"; Kurt Lewin is "father of social psychology"; Wundt is NOT a functionalist. Gestalt is a perception school, not a therapy (do not confuse it with Perls' Gestalt therapy ). C.2 Sensation vs perception, and psychophysics Sensation = the raw signal a receptor sends up (bottom-up). Perception = the brain organising and interpreting it (adds top-down expectation, context, schema). Same retinal image, two perceptions = perception > sensation. Absolute threshold: the smallest intensity detectable 50% of the time. Difference threshold = JND (just noticeable difference): the smallest change you can detect 50% of the time. Sensory adaptation: constant unchanging stimulus, receptors stop responding (you stop feeling your watch). Law What it says The hook Weber's law The JND is a constant proportion of the original stimulus, not a fixed amount Add 1 candle to 1, you notice; add 1 to 100, you do not Fechner's law Sensation grows with the logarithm of stimulus intensity Built psychophysics on Weber's finding Stevens' power law Sensation is a power function of intensity (fits more senses than Fechner) The modern refinement Signal Detection Theory (David Green and John Swets, 1966): detection is not just sensitivity, it is a decision. Four outcomes: Hit (signal there, said yes), Miss (signal there, said no), False alarm (no signal, said yes), Correct rejection (no signal, said no). d′ = true sensitivity; the criterion (β) = how willing you are to say "yes". A tired or motivated observer shifts criterion, not sensitivity. TRAP: Weber = constant ratio (JND). Fechner = log . Do not say Weber gives a fixed amount. SDT separates sensitivity (d′) from response bias (criterion); a question about "willingness to report" is about the criterion, not d′. C.3 Gestalt organisation, constancies, depth cues Gestalt grouping laws: figure-ground (Edgar Rubin, 1915), proximity (near things group), similarity (alike things group), closure (fill the gap), continuity / good continuation (smooth lines), common fate (things moving together group), Prägnanz (we see the simplest possible form). The umbrella principle is Prägnanz, "the law of good figure". Perceptual constancies: size, shape, colour, brightness stay stable even as the retinal image changes. A door is still rectangular when open (shape constancy). Depth cues: binocular = retinal disparity + convergence (need both eyes, work near). Monocular = relative size, interposition/overlap, linear perspective, texture gradient, aerial perspective, motion parallax, light & shadow (work with one eye, mostly for distance). TRAP: Retinal disparity and convergence are the only two binocular cues; everything else is monocular. Motion parallax is monocular even though it sounds complex. C.4 Learning: the distinctions that quietly cost marks Classical (Ivan Pavlov) Operant (B. F. Skinner) What is learned An association between two stimuli An association between behaviour and its consequence Behaviour is Reflexive, involuntary (elicited) Voluntary (emitted) Order Stimulus comes before the response Consequence comes after the response Example Dog salivates to a bell Rat presses a lever for food Classical terms: UCS → UCR (unlearned); the NS becomes the CS when paired, producing the CR . Acquisition (learning), extinction (CS alone, CR fades), spontaneous recovery (the CR returns after a rest), generalisation (similar stimuli also trigger it), discrimination (only the exact CS does). Little Albert (John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner, 1920) = generalised fear; Garcia effect = one-trial taste aversion (biological preparedness). The four operant contingencies (the classic trap): "Positive" = add a stimulus, "Negative" = remove one. "Reinforcement" = behaviour increases , "Punishment" = behaviour decreases . Increases behaviour (reinforcement) Decreases behaviour (punishment) Add stimulus (positive) Positive reinforcement (give a treat) Positive punishment (give a scolding) Remove stimulus (negative) Negative reinforcement (stop the alarm by buckling up) Negative punishment / omission (take away the phone) TRAP (this is the one people miss): Negative reinforcement is NOT punishment. It removes something unpleasant to increase a behaviour. Taking aspirin to end a headache is negatively reinforced. Punishment always decreases behaviour. Reinforcement schedule Pattern Response feature Fixed ratio (FR) Reward after a set number of responses High rate, short post-reward pause Variable ratio (VR) Reward after an unpredictable number Highest, steadiest rate; most resistant to extinction (gambling) Fixed interval (FI) Reward for the first response after a set time Scalloped (work speeds up near the deadline) Variable interval (VI) Reward after an unpredictable time Slow, steady (checking for a text) Other learning terms: Shaping = reinforcing successive approximations. Primary reinforcer = innately satisfying (food, water); secondary = learned value (money, tokens). Premack principle = a high-frequency behaviour reinforces a low-frequency one ("eat your veggies, then dessert"). Continuous reinforcement learns fastest; partial reinforcement resists extinction best (the partial-reinforcement effect). TRAP: "Most resistant to extinction" = variable ratio . "Fastest acquisition" = continuous . Do not swap those two questions. C.5 Motivation Theory Core idea Instinct Behaviour is innate and species-typical (early, now largely rejected as a full account) Drive-reduction (Clark Hull) A need creates a drive (tension); behaviour reduces it to restore homeostasis Arousal / optimal level We seek an optimum level of arousal, not zero (explains curiosity); see Yerkes-Dodson Incentive External rewards pull behaviour (drives push, incentives pull) Abraham Maslow's hierarchy Physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualisation; lower needs first Self-determination (Edward Deci & Richard Ryan) Three innate needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness David McClelland Acquired needs: achievement (nAch), affiliation, power Yerkes-Dodson law: performance is an inverted-U of arousal. The optimum is lower for difficult/complex tasks and higher for simple/well-learned ones. TRAP: Intrinsic motivation = the activity itself is the reward; extrinsic = an outside reward. The overjustification effect: paying someone for something they already enjoy can reduce the intrinsic motivation. Drives push (internal need), incentives pull (external goal). C.6 Emotion: the theories side by side Every emotion question turns on the order of three events: the stimulus, the bodily arousal, and the felt emotion. Learn the sequence each theory claims. Theory The sequence it claims James-Lange Stimulus → bodily arousal → emotion. "We are afraid because we tremble." Emotion follows the body. Cannon-Bard Stimulus → arousal AND emotion at the same time (thalamus routes to both). Body and feeling are simultaneous, not causal. Schachter-Singer two-factor Stimulus → arousal → cognitive label of that arousal → emotion. Same arousal, different label, different emotion (the adrenaline study). Lazarus appraisal Stimulus → cognitive appraisal comes first → arousal + emotion. Thinking precedes feeling. Facial feedback The face itself feeds emotion: holding a smile can lift mood. TRAP: James-Lange = body first , then emotion. Cannon-Bard = simultaneous . Schachter-Singer adds a cognitive label to arousal. Lazarus puts appraisal first . A stem about "interpreting your racing heart as either fear or excitement" is Schachter-Singer. C.7 Memory Multi-store (Atkinson-Shiffrin): sensory register (iconic ~0.5 s, echoic ~2–4 s) → short-term (~7±2 items, ~15–30 s, lost by displacement/decay) → long-term (effectively unlimited). Rehearsal moves STM → LTM. Working memory (Alan Baddeley): the central executive directs three slaves: the phonological loop (verbal), the visuospatial sketchpad (visual/spatial), and the episodic buffer (binds + links to LTM). This replaced the passive STM "box". LTM types: Explicit/declarative (conscious) splits into episodic (events, what/where/when) and semantic (facts). Implicit/non-declarative includes procedural (skills), priming, and conditioning. Levels of processing (Fergus Craik & Robert Lockhart): deeper, semantic processing yields better recall than shallow (visual/phonemic) processing. Serial position: first items recalled well ( primacy , rehearsed into LTM) and last items recalled well ( recency , still in STM). A delay before recall wipes recency but not primacy. Forgetting: decay (trace fades), interference , cue-dependent (encoding-specificity, state- and context-dependent recall), motivated forgetting (repression). Ebbinghaus = the forgetting curve (steep then levels off). Memory is reconstructive: Frederic Bartlett's schemas ("War of the Ghosts"), Elizabeth Loftus's misinformation effect (leading questions reshape eyewitness memory). TRAP: Proactive interference = old learning blocks new ("pro" = forward, old pushes ahead). Retroactive = new learning blocks old ("retro" = backward). Recall (produce it) is harder than recognition (pick it out). Episodic = tied to a time and place; semantic = a free-floating fact. C.8 Intelligence and IQ scoring Theory Claim Spearman A general factor g underlies all abilities, plus task-specific s Thurstone 7 independent primary mental abilities, no single g Cattell-Horn Fluid (reasoning on novel problems, declines with age) vs crystallised (accumulated knowledge, holds/rises) Howard Gardner 8 multiple intelligences (linguistic, logical-math, spatial, musical, bodily, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalist) Robert Sternberg Triarchic: analytical, creative, practical Peter Salovey & John Mayer / Goleman Emotional intelligence (the model / the popularisation) Scoring foundations: Ratio IQ = (mental age / chronological age) × 100 (old Stanford-Binet). Deviation IQ (Wechsler) = mean 100, SD 15 ; it compares you to your age peers. A WAIS subtest scaled score has mean 10, SD 3 , so a 10 is exactly average (50th percentile). The Flynn effect = average IQ scores rose across the 20th century, so norms need re-standardising. TRAP: Full-scale IQ mean 100 SD 15; scaled subtest mean 10 SD 3. A scaled score of 10 = average, NOT low. Fluid intelligence (Raymond Cattell and John Horn) falls with age; crystallised does not. C.9 Statistics & research the common section quietly tests Central tendency: mean (pulled toward the tail by skew/outliers), median (robust, best for skewed income-type data), mode (the only one usable for nominal data). In a positive (right) skew the order is mode < median < mean; in a negative skew it reverses. The mean is dragged toward the longer tail. Normal curve: symmetrical, mean = median = mode. 68 / 95 / 99.7 of cases fall within 1 / 2 / 3 SD. A z-score = how many SDs a value sits from the mean. Correlation: r ranges −1 to +1 ; the sign is direction, the absolute value is strength. r = 0 means no linear relationship. r² (coefficient of determination) = proportion of variance shared. Correlation does not equal causation (third-variable, directionality problems). Reliability (consistency) vs validity (accuracy). Reliability types: test-retest, inter-rater, internal consistency (Cronbach's α, split-half). Validity types: content, construct, criterion (concurrent + predictive). A test can be reliable but not valid (a consistent bathroom scale that reads 5 kg heavy). It cannot be valid without being reliable. Levels of measurement (NOIR; Stanley Smith Stevens, 1946): Nominal (categories), Ordinal (ranked), Interval (equal gaps, no true zero, e.g. Celsius/IQ), Ratio (true zero, e.g. weight, reaction time). Variables: the independent variable is manipulated; the dependent variable is measured. A confound varies with the IV and offers a rival explanation. Random assignment (to groups) controls confounds; random sampling gives generalisability. They are not the same thing. TRAP: Reliable ≠ valid: consistency is not accuracy. In a positively skewed distribution the mean is the highest of the three averages (pulled right). Random assignment ≠ random sampling . Interval has no true zero; ratio does. C.10 Developmental spine (compact) Piaget stage Age Hallmark Sensorimotor 0–2 Object permanence develops Preoperational 2–7 Symbols, egocentrism, no conservation Concrete operational 7–11 Conservation, reversibility, logic on concrete things Formal operational 11+ Abstract and hypothetical reasoning Erik Erikson (8 crises): trust v mistrust → autonomy v shame → initiative v guilt → industry v inferiority → identity v role confusion (adolescence) → intimacy v isolation → generativity v stagnation → integrity v despair. Lawrence Kohlberg: Preconventional (punishment/reward) → Conventional (social approval/law-and-order) → Postconventional (social contract/universal ethics). Attachment (Ainsworth Strange Situation): secure; insecure-avoidant; insecure-resistant/ambivalent; (Main & Solomon) disorganised. Harry Harlow's monkeys = contact comfort over food; John Bowlby = the attachment behavioural system + monotropy. TRAP: Jean Piaget's assimilation = fit new info into an existing schema; accommodation = change the schema to fit new info. Object permanence = sensorimotor ; conservation = concrete operational . Lev Vygotsky stresses the social/ZPD, Piaget the individual constructor. C.11 Cover-and-test: the confusable pairs that quietly cost marks This is the highest-yield drill in the pack. Cover the right column. If you can give the distinction for every row without peeking, the common section is no longer your weak point. Confusable pair The one-line distinction Sensation vs perception Sensation = raw detection (bottom-up); perception = interpretation (adds top-down) Negative reinforcement vs punishment Neg. reinforcement increases behaviour by removing something bad; punishment decreases behaviour Positive vs negative (in conditioning) Positive = add a stimulus; negative = remove one. Nothing to do with good/bad Classical vs operant Classical = involuntary, stimulus before response; operant = voluntary, consequence after response Proactive vs retroactive interference Proactive = old blocks new; retroactive = new blocks old Recall vs recognition Recall = produce it from scratch (harder); recognition = identify the right one (easier) Assimilation vs accommodation Assimilate = bend the world to the schema; accommodate = bend the schema to the world Reliability vs validity Reliability = consistent; validity = measures what it claims. Reliable need not be valid Random sampling vs random assignment Sampling = who gets in the study (generalisability); assignment = which group they go to (controls confounds) Independent vs dependent variable IV = manipulated cause; DV = measured effect Mean vs median in skew The mean chases the tail; the median resists it. Use median for skewed data Fluid vs crystallised intelligence Fluid = reason on the novel (falls with age); crystallised = stored knowledge (holds) Ratio vs deviation IQ Ratio = MA/CA×100 (old); deviation = SD-based comparison to age peers (mean 100, SD 15) James-Lange vs Cannon-Bard James-Lange = body first then emotion; Cannon-Bard = both at once Intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation Intrinsic = the act rewards itself; extrinsic = an outside reward. Beware the overjustification effect Drive vs incentive Drives push from an internal need; incentives pull from an external goal Episodic vs semantic memory (Endel Tulving, 1972) Episodic = tied to a time/place; semantic = a free-standing fact Weber vs Fechner Weber = JND is a constant ratio; Fechner = sensation grows with the log of intensity Binocular vs monocular depth cues Binocular = disparity + convergence (two eyes); everything else, incl. motion parallax, is monocular Conformity vs obedience Conformity (Solomon Asch) = matching peers; obedience (Stanley Milgram) = following an authority's order g vs s (Spearman) g = the general factor across all tasks; s = ability specific to one task Primacy vs recency Primacy = early items (into LTM via rehearsal); recency = last items (still in STM, wiped by delay) If you run C.11 clean, you have closed the gap. These pairs are exactly the "looks like two right answers" items that the common section uses to separate the 70s from the 90s. 1. Biopsychology & Neuropsychology MET 15 Q · NIMHANS 15 Q 1.1 The neuron and glia Dendrites receive input (spines multiply surface area). Soma integrates input. Axon hillock = trigger zone, decides if threshold is reached. Axon conducts the AP. Axon terminals release neurotransmitter. Neuron types: Sensory (afferent, periphery → CNS, pseudounipolar); Motor (efferent, CNS → muscle/gland, multipolar); Interneurons (local CNS processing, most common). Glial cell Location Function Oligodendrocyte CNS Myelinates many axons (one cell, many segments) Schwann cell PNS Myelinates one axon segment per cell Astrocyte CNS Blood-brain barrier, K+ buffering, NT recycling Microglia CNS Immune defence, phagocytosis Ependymal cell Ventricles Produces and circulates CSF Satellite cell PNS ganglia Supports cell bodies in PNS TRAP: CNS myelination = oligodendrocyte. PNS myelination = Schwann cell. 1.2 The action potential (the single most testable neurophysiology topic) An AP is a ~1 ms electrical pulse travelling down the axon. The whole story is " Na+ in, K+ out ": Na+ rushing in depolarises; K+ leaving repolarises. Resting membrane potential ~ −70 mV. Set by K+ leak channels (membrane ~50× more permeable to K+), NOT by the Na/K pump. Threshold ~ −55 mV. Na/K pump: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP. Electrogenic. Maintains the gradient but does not set RMP. Phase 1 Depolarisation: voltage-gated Na+ channels open → Na+ in → spike to ~ +30 mV. Phase 2 Repolarisation: Na+ channels inactivate, voltage-gated K+ channels open (slower) → K+ out. Phase 3 Hyperpolarisation: K+ channels stay open briefly → undershoot below −70 mV. Phase 4 Return: K+ channels close, Na/K pump restores ions. Ion concentrations: "K is in, Na is out, Cl is out, Ca is way out." Equilibrium potentials: K+ −90 mV, Na+ +60 mV, Cl− −65 mV, Ca²⁺ +120 mV. All-or-none law: once threshold is reached the AP fires at constant amplitude; stimulus intensity is coded by frequency , not amplitude. Refractory periods: Absolute = Na+ channels inactivated, no stimulus however strong can fire another AP (ensures one-way propagation). Relative = membrane hyperpolarised (K+ still open), a stronger stimulus can fire one. TRAP: Inactivated ≠ closed. The Na+ channel has 3 states: closed (resting), open (during AP), inactivated (after, "ball and chain" blocks the pore). Resets only after repolarisation. Propagation: continuous (unmyelinated C fibres, 0.5–2 m/s) vs saltatory (myelinated, AP jumps between Nodes of Ranvier, up to 120 m/s in A-alpha). Conduction velocity rises with myelination > axon diameter > temperature. Demyelination (MS, Guillain-Barré) slows/blocks conduction. Synaptic transmission: AP arrives → voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open, Ca²⁺ enters → vesicles fuse (SNARE proteins, synaptotagmin = Ca²⁺ sensor) → NT released → binds postsynaptic receptors → EPSP (Na+/Ca²⁺ in, depolarising) or IPSP (Cl− in or K+ out, hyperpolarising) → cleared by reuptake, enzymatic breakdown, or diffusion. Summation (spatial + temporal) at the axon hillock decides if a new AP fires. TRAP: Ca²⁺ is the trigger ion for NT release at the terminal. Without Ca²⁺ entry, no transmitter is released. 1.3 Neurotransmitters (the 7 families) NT Class / made from Cleared by Clinical link Acetylcholine (ACh) Choline + acetyl-CoA Acetylcholinesterase Low in Alzheimer's; myasthenia gravis (anti-AChR); NMJ Dopamine Catecholamine (Tyrosine → DOPA → DA) Reuptake, MAO, COMT ↑ mesolimbic = +ve schizophrenia. Low nigrostriatal = Parkinson's. Reward/addiction. Norepinephrine Catecholamine (DA + β-hydroxylase) Reuptake, MAO Arousal, sympathetic. Locus coeruleus. Low in depression. Serotonin (5-HT) Indolamine (Tryptophan) Reuptake (SERT), MAO Mood, sleep, appetite. Low → depression, OCD. Raphe nuclei. Glutamate Amino acid (Glutamine) Astrocyte reuptake Main excitatory NT. NMDA/AMPA/kainate. LTP, learning. Excess = excitotoxicity. GABA Amino acid (from Glutamate via GAD) Reuptake Main inhibitory NT. GABA-A ionotropic = target of benzos, alcohol, barbiturates. Endorphins Peptide (POMC) Peptidases Pain modulation, runner's high. μ, κ, δ receptors. TRAP: Hippocampal LTP depends on the NMDA receptor (coincidence detector — needs glutamate AND postsynaptic depolarisation to displace the Mg²⁺ block; Ca²⁺ entry triggers LTP). AMPA carries the fast EPSP. Hebb: "neurons that fire together wire together." 1.3a Neurotransmitters — the deep note, one per transmitter The table above is the cheat-sheet. This is the full read: for each transmitter — what it is, where it's made, its receptors, what it does in brain and body, what too much or too little looks like, and the drugs that hit it. If a question asks "which NT" or "which drug," the answer is in one of these boxes. The two-minute frame: Glutamate is the gas (excitatory), GABA is the brake (inhibitory) — together they run ~90% of fast CNS signalling. The monoamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin, plus histamine) are the slow, mood/arousal modulators that nearly every psych drug targets. ACh straddles muscle, the parasympathetic body, and memory. Everything else (peptides, glycine, gases) fills in the edges. ① Glutamate — the main excitatory transmitter Aspect Detail What it is An amino-acid neurotransmitter. The principal excitatory NT of the CNS — most fast excitation in the brain is glutamate. Where it's made From glutamine via the glutamate–glutamine cycle (astrocytes recycle released glutamate back to glutamine); also from α-ketoglutarate (Krebs cycle). Made in the presynaptic terminal. Receptors Ionotropic: NMDA (Ca²⁺-permeable, Mg²⁺-blocked coincidence detector → LTP), AMPA (fast Na⁺ EPSP), kainate. Metabotropic: mGluR1–8 (G-protein, slow modulation). Brain & body Fast excitation, learning and memory (LTP) , cortical processing, sensory transmission. Building block of GABA and of protein. Too much Excitotoxicity — Ca²⁺ overload kills neurons: stroke, traumatic brain injury, ALS, neurodegeneration. Also seizures. Too little / blocked NMDA hypofunction → psychosis (a leading schizophrenia model); cognitive and memory impairment. Drugs that hit it NMDA antagonists: ketamine and PCP (dissociatives, model psychosis; ketamine is also a rapid antidepressant), memantine (Alzheimer's), dextromethorphan. Glutamate-lowering: riluzole (ALS), lamotrigine (reduces release). TRAP: Ketamine/PCP cause psychotic-like states by blocking NMDA, not by raising dopamine — this is the glutamate (NMDA-hypofunction) model of schizophrenia. ② GABA — the main inhibitory transmitter Aspect Detail What it is γ-aminobutyric acid, an amino-acid NT. The principal inhibitory NT of the CNS — the brain's brake. Where it's made From glutamate by the enzyme GAD (glutamic acid decarboxylase), which needs vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate) as a cofactor. Receptors GABA-A (ionotropic, opens Cl⁻ channel → hyperpolarisation; has the benzodiazepine, barbiturate, alcohol and neurosteroid sites). GABA-B (metabotropic, ↑K⁺ efflux / ↓Ca²⁺; target of baclofen). Brain & body Dampens excitability, anxiolysis, sedation/sleep, regulates muscle tone, prevents runaway firing. Too much / enhanced Sedation, ataxia, respiratory depression — especially when alcohol + benzodiazepines are combined. Too little Anxiety, seizures (epilepsy), spasticity. B6 deficiency lowers GABA → seizures. Drugs that hit it Benzodiazepines (↑ frequency of Cl⁻ channel opening), barbiturates (↑ duration ), alcohol, z-drugs (zolpidem); baclofen (GABA-B, spasticity); tiagabine (reuptake block), vigabatrin (GABA-transaminase block), valproate. TRAP: Benzos increase how often the chloride channel opens; barbiturates increase how long it stays open. Barbiturates can open it without GABA at high dose → far more lethal in overdose. ③ Dopamine — reward, movement, psychosis Aspect Detail What it is A catecholamine (monoamine), made from the amino acid tyrosine. Where it's made Tyrosine → L-DOPA (by tyrosine hydroxylase , the rate-limiting step) → dopamine (by DOPA decarboxylase). Cell bodies in the substantia nigra (pars compacta) , VTA , and hypothalamus (arcuate). Four pathways Nigrostriatal (movement — lost in Parkinson's), mesolimbic (reward; excess → positive symptoms), mesocortical (cognition; low → negative symptoms), tuberoinfundibular (inhibits prolactin). Receptors D1-like (D1, D5 — Gs, excitatory) and D2-like (D2, D3, D4 — Gi, inhibitory). Antipsychotics work mainly by blocking D2. Cleared by Reuptake (DAT), then MAO and COMT. Too much Mesolimbic excess → positive symptoms of schizophrenia (delusions, hallucinations); reward/addiction; mania. Too little Nigrostriatal loss → Parkinson's (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia); D2 blockade → hyperprolactinaemia (galactorrhoea) and extrapyramidal side-effects; low mesocortical DA → negative/cognitive symptoms. Drugs that hit it Raise it: L-DOPA + carbidopa, agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, bromocriptine), stimulants (amphetamine, cocaine, methylphenidate block DAT/release DA), MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline), COMT inhibitors (entacapone). Block it: antipsychotics — typicals (haloperidol) and atypicals. TRAP: The same drug class trades one problem for another. Block dopamine to treat psychosis → you risk Parkinsonism + raised prolactin. Boost dopamine to treat Parkinson's → you risk psychosis. It is one transmitter pulling four levers. ④ Serotonin (5-HT) — mood, sleep, appetite, impulse Aspect Detail What it is An indolamine (monoamine), made from the amino acid tryptophan. Where it's made Tryptophan → 5-HTP (by tryptophan hydroxylase , rate-limiting) → 5-HT. CNS source = the raphe nuclei of the brainstem. ~90% of body serotonin is in the gut (enterochromaffin cells); also stored in platelets. Receptors Seven families (5-HT1–7), almost all GPCRs. 5-HT3 is the only ionotropic one (cation channel → nausea/vomiting). 5-HT1A (anxiety/depression autoreceptor), 5-HT2A (psychedelics; atypical-antipsychotic target). Cleared by Reuptake via SERT , then MAO → 5-HIAA (the urinary metabolite). Brain & body Mood, sleep, appetite/satiety, impulse control, temperature; in the body: gut motility, vasoconstriction, platelet aggregation. Too much Serotonin syndrome (agitation, hyperthermia, clonus, autonomic instability — often SSRI + MAOI or + tramadol); carcinoid syndrome. Too little Depression, anxiety, OCD, increased aggression/impulsivity. Drugs that hit it SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline), SNRIs (venlafaxine), TCAs, MAOIs; buspirone (5-HT1A partial agonist); triptans (5-HT1B/1D, migraine); ondansetron (5-HT3 block, antiemetic); LSD/psilocybin (5-HT2A agonists); atypical antipsychotics (5-HT2A antagonism). TRAP: 5-HT3 is the odd one out — it's the only ligand-gated ion channel in the serotonin family, and blocking it (ondansetron) stops vomiting. Every other 5-HT receptor is a G-protein receptor. ⑤ Acetylcholine (ACh) — muscle, parasympathetic, memory Aspect Detail What it is An ester; the first neurotransmitter ever discovered (Otto Loewi's "Vagusstoff"). Where it's made Choline + acetyl-CoA via choline acetyltransferase (ChAT). Found at the neuromuscular junction , all autonomic ganglia, all parasympathetic postganglionic neurons (+ sympathetic to sweat glands), and the basal forebrain (nucleus basalis of Meynert) for memory. Receptors Nicotinic (ionotropic, ligand-gated Na⁺/K⁺ — NMJ, ganglia, CNS) and Muscarinic (M1–M5, GPCR — parasympathetic targets and CNS). Cleared by Acetylcholinesterase → choline + acetate (choline is recycled). Brain & body Muscle contraction (NMJ), "rest and digest" parasympathetic tone, arousal, attention, and learning/memory . Too much Cholinergic crisis (SLUDGE / DUMBELS — salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhoea, miosis…) from organophosphate pesticides and nerve agents that block acetylcholinesterase. Too little Alzheimer's (degeneration of basal-forebrain cholinergic neurons → memory loss); myasthenia gravis (autoantibodies vs nicotinic AChR → fatigable weakness). Drugs that hit it AChE inhibitors: donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine (Alzheimer's); pyridostigmine/neostigmine (myasthenia); physostigmine. Anticholinergics: atropine, scopolamine, benztropine. Neuromuscular blockers: curare, succinylcholine. TRAP: "Dry as a bone, red as a beet, mad as a hatter" = anticholinergic (muscarinic-block) toxicity. The opposite — wet everywhere (SLUDGE) — is cholinergic excess. Atropine treats the wet one. ⑥ Norepinephrine (noradrenaline) — arousal & fight-or-flight Aspect Detail What it is A catecholamine (monoamine), one step beyond dopamine. Where it's made Dopamine + dopamine β-hydroxylase → norepinephrine. CNS source = the locus coeruleus (pons). Also released by sympathetic postganglionic neurons and the adrenal medulla. Receptors Adrenergic α1, α2, β1, β2, β3 (all GPCR). α2 is the presynaptic autoreceptor that shuts off its own release. Cleared by Reuptake (NET), then MAO and COMT. Brain & body Arousal, vigilance, attention, mood; sympathetic fight-or-flight (Walter Cannon, 1915) — ↑heart rate, ↑BP, bronchodilation, pupil dilation. Too much Anxiety, hypertension, PTSD hyperarousal/nightmares ; pheochromocytoma. Too little Depression, fatigue, poor concentration (a target in ADHD). Drugs that hit it SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine), atomoxetine (NRI, ADHD), TCAs, stimulants. α2 agonists clonidine/guanfacine lower central NE (ADHD, anxiety, BP). β-blocker propranolol (performance anxiety, akathisia). α1-blocker prazosin (PTSD nightmares). Note — epinephrine (adrenaline): made from norepinephrine by the enzyme PNMT in the adrenal medulla. It is mostly a circulating hormone (the main adrenal output) and only a minor CNS transmitter. ⑦ Histamine — wakefulness, allergy, gastric acid Aspect Detail What it is A monoamine, made from the amino acid histidine (by histidine decarboxylase). Where it's made CNS: the tuberomammillary nucleus of the hypothalamus. Periphery: mast cells, basophils, and enterochromaffin-like cells of the stomach. Receptors H1 (allergy + wakefulness), H2 (gastric acid), H3 (presynaptic CNS autoreceptor), H4 (immune). Brain & body Promotes wakefulness/arousal , regulates appetite; drives allergy/inflammation and gastric acid secretion in the body. Clinical / drugs H1 blockers: diphenhydramine (sedating — crosses the blood-brain barrier), loratadine (non-sedating). H2 blockers: famotidine, ranitidine (acid/ulcers). H1-blocking side-effects (sedation, weight gain) explain a lot of antipsychotic and antidepressant tolerability. ⑧ Glycine — the spinal-cord brake Aspect Detail What it is The simplest amino acid; the major inhibitory NT of the spinal cord and brainstem . Where it's made From the amino acid serine. Receptors Glycine receptor (ionotropic, opens Cl⁻ → inhibition); also an obligatory co-agonist at the NMDA receptor (glutamate alone is not enough). Brain & body Inhibits motor neurons; provides reciprocal inhibition so opposing muscles relax. Clinical Strychnine blocks glycine receptors → convulsions/rigidity. Tetanus toxin blocks glycine release → spastic paralysis (lockjaw). ⑨ Endorphins & endogenous opioids — the body's painkillers Aspect Detail What they are Neuropeptides: β-endorphin (cleaved from POMC), enkephalins , and dynorphins . Receptors Opioid receptors μ (mu), δ (delta), κ (kappa) — all inhibitory (Gi) GPCRs. μ drives most analgesia and euphoria. Brain & body Pain modulation (down the PAG/descending pathway), reward, "runner's high," mood; in the body, constipation and (via μ) respiratory depression. Drugs that hit it Agonists: morphine, heroin, fentanyl (μ). Antagonist: naloxone/naltrexone (reverses overdose, blocks reward). Partial agonist: buprenorphine. ⑩ The rest — neuropeptides & unconventional transmitters Transmitter Made from / where Does what / clinical hook Substance P Peptide; sensory (pain) neurons Carries pain signals via the NK1 receptor; NK1 blockers (aprepitant) treat nausea. Oxytocin Peptide; paraventricular/supraoptic hypothalamus → posterior pituitary Bonding, trust, labour contractions, milk let-down. Vasopressin (ADH) Same hypothalamic source → posterior pituitary Water retention, blood pressure; also social/aggression behaviour. Nitric oxide (NO) Gasotransmitter; from arginine, made on demand Retrograde messenger (postsynaptic → presynaptic); vasodilation (penile erection — sildenafil works here). Endocannabinoids (anandamide, 2-AG) Lipids; made on demand from membrane Retrograde messengers at CB1 (CNS — appetite, mood; the THC target) and CB2 (immune). Two "backwards" transmitters: nitric oxide and the endocannabinoids are retrograde — they're released by the post synaptic cell and act back on the pre synaptic terminal to turn its output down. Opposite direction to every classical NT above. 1.4 Nervous system organisation Nervous System ├── CNS (brain + spinal cord) └── PNS ├── Somatic NS (voluntary, skeletal muscle) └── Autonomic NS ├── Sympathetic ("fight/flight") — thoracolumbar T1–L2, NE ├── Parasympathetic ("rest/digest") — craniosacral (CN III,VII,IX,X + S2–S4), ACh └── Enteric ("gut brain") ANS contrasts: Sympathetic ↑ heart rate, dilates pupil, ↓ GI; pre/post-ganglionic NT = ACh/NE (sweat glands are the ACh exception). It works as a loop: cortex → striatum → pallidum → thalamus → back to cortex. Structure Function Lesion / disorder Striatum = caudate + putamen Main input zone, receives signals from the cortex Degenerates in Huntington's (chorea) Caudate Cognition, goal-directed action, part of OCD circuitry Overactive caudate loops in OCD and Tourette's Putamen Habit learning and motor execution Loss of movement automaticity Globus pallidus (GPi / GPe) Output zone; GPi is the main inhibitory output to the thalamus Pallidotomy / deep-brain-stimulation target in Parkinson's Subthalamic nucleus Brake within the indirect pathway Lesion = hemiballismus (wild flinging of one side) Substantia nigra (pars compacta) Supplies dopamine to the striatum Degenerates in Parkinson's (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia) Direct vs indirect pathway: the direct pathway (dopamine on D1, the "go" route) facilitates movement; the indirect pathway (dopamine on D2, the "no-go" route) suppresses it. Huntington's and hemiballismus are hyperkinetic (too much movement, loss in the caudate/putamen and subthalamic nucleus). The red nucleus is midbrain, NOT basal ganglia. 1.6 Cranial nerves I–XII # Name Type Function I Olfactory S Smell. Only CN that does NOT relay through thalamus. II Optic S Vision. Optic disc = blind spot. Pathway: retina → optic nerve → chiasm (nasal fibres cross) → optic tract → LGN → V1. Theories: trichromatic (Young-Helmholtz, retinal) + opponent-process (Ewald Hering, post-retinal). Dorsal stream "where/how" (parietal); ventral stream "what" (temporal). Audition: outer → middle (malleus, incus, stapes) → cochlea → hair cells on basilar membrane → CN VIII → cochlear nuclei → MGN → Heschl's gyrus. Place theory (Békésy): base = high frequencies, apex = low; best for high. Frequency theory (Ernest Rutherford, 1886): firing rate = frequency, works <500 Hz. Volley principle (Ernest Wever and Charles Bray, 1930) bridges mid-range. Somatosensation: dorsal column-medial lemniscus (touch, vibration, proprioception, decussates at medulla) vs spinothalamic (pain, temp, decussates at spinal level of entry). Taste: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami. CN VII / IX / X. Insula = primary gustatory cortex. Smell: olfactory epithelium → bulb → piriform cortex (no thalamus relay), closest to limbic system. 1.8 Motor systems Pyramidal (corticospinal): M1 (Brodmann 4) → internal capsule → peduncle → pons → medullary pyramids. Extrapyramidal: rubrospinal (flexor bias), vestibulospinal (postural extensor), reticulospinal (locomotion), tectospinal (head/neck orienting). N3 dominates the first half; REM dominates the second half and lengthens through the night. Stage EEG / signature Notes NREM 1 (~5%) Theta (4–8 Hz) Light, hypnic jerks, hypnagogic images NREM 2 (~45–55%) Sleep spindles + K-complexes Most of the night; spindles gate sensory input NREM 3 (~15–20%) Delta (0.5–4 Hz, high amplitude) Deep/slow-wave. Growth hormone. Parasomnias (sleepwalking, night terrors, enuresis) come OUT of N3 REM (~20–25%) Mixed, low-voltage (looks awake) Paradoxical : brain active, body in atonia . Vivid dreams, eye bursts, autonomic instability, thermoregulation fails. NOT delta-dominant. Neural control: sleep pressure from adenosine (caffeine blocks adenosine receptors); VLPO = GABAergic "sleep switch"; wake driven by the ARAS (histamine, orexin, NE, 5-HT, ACh). SCN = master circadian clock, entrained by light via the retinohypothalamic tract → pineal → melatonin in darkness. REM-ON = cholinergic (PPT/LDT); REM-OFF = aminergic (NE, 5-HT). Memory: declarative consolidated in NREM (delta replay); procedural in REM + spindles; emotional in REM. Disorders: Narcolepsy = orexin/hypocretin deficiency; cataplexy is pathognomonic. RBD = loss of atonia in REM, older men, α-synucleinopathy warning (Parkinson/Lewy body). RLS = urge to move legs at rest (dopamine/iron). Kleine-Levin = the 3 H's (hypersomnia + hyperphagia + hypersexuality), young males. Insomnia DSM-5: 3 nights/wk × 3 months. 1.12 Emotion, arousal, learning & LTP Theories of emotion: James-Lange (body first, "we feel sad because we cry"); Cannon-Bard (body + emotion simultaneously, thalamic); Schachter-Singer (two-factor: arousal + cognitive label); Lazarus (appraisal precedes emotion). Yerkes-Dodson law: inverted-U of arousal vs performance. Optimum is lower for complex tasks, higher for simple/well-learned tasks. Memory substrates: hippocampus (declarative consolidation), amygdala (emotional/fear), striatum (procedural/habit), cerebellum (motor conditioning). LTP strengthens synapses (NMDA receptor critical, Ca²⁺ entry, AMPA insertion); LTD weakens them. Papez circuit: hippocampus → fornix → mammillary → anterior thalamus → cingulate → entorhinal → hippocampus. 1.13 Mania first-line drugs & psychopharmacology First-line for acute mania: Lithium · Valproate (Divalproex) · atypical antipsychotics (Olanzapine, Risperidone, Quetiapine, Aripiprazole). Developmental Psychology MET 15 Q · NIMHANS 10 Q 2.1 Foundational principles Cephalocaudal (head → toe) · Proximodistal (centre → periphery). Critical period = rigid biological window, lost if missed (Lorenz imprinting). Sensitive period = optimal but flexible (language acquisition). Continuity vs discontinuity; nature vs nurture (interactionist consensus); active vs passive child (bidirectionality). Prenatal stages: Germinal (0–2 wk), Embryonic (2–8 wk, most vulnerable to teratogens, organogenesis) , Fetal (8 wk–birth, growth). Teratogens: alcohol (FAS, most common preventable ID), tobacco, thalidomide (limbs), rubella (1st trimester), lead/mercury, Zika (microcephaly). 2.2 Piaget — cognitive development Stage Age Achievements / limits Sensorimotor 0–2 Object permanence (~8 mo), goal-directed action, A-not-B error Preoperational 2–7 Symbolic thought, language, pretend play; egocentrism, animism, centration, no conservation Concrete Operational 7–11 Conservation, reversibility, classification, seriation, decentration Formal Operational 11+ Abstract, hypothetico-deductive logic; adolescent egocentrism (imaginary audience, personal fable) Key concepts: Schema; Assimilation (fit new info into schema); Accommodation (modify schema); Equilibration (the engine of change). Sensorimotor 6 substages: reflexes → primary CR (on body) → secondary CR (on objects) → coordination (8–12 mo, object permanence) → tertiary CR (experimentation) → mental representation (deferred imitation). TRAP: Object permanence (sensorimotor, ~8 mo) ≠ Conservation (concrete operational, ~7 yr). And Piagetian "egocentrism" = a cognitive limit, NOT narcissism. 2.3 Vygotsky — sociocultural ZPD = gap between what a child can do alone vs with help from a more knowledgeable other (MKO). Scaffolding = temporary tailored support, withdrawn as competence grows. Private speech → inner speech, guides cognition. Language is the master tool, internalised from social interaction. TRAP: "Scaffolding" is Jerome Bruner's term, applied to Vygotsky's ZPD. Vygotsky's own terms are ZPD and MKO. One line: Jean Piaget = child as lone scientist (development → learning). Lev Vygotsky = child as apprentice (learning → development, mediated by culture). 2.4 Bronfenbrenner — ecological / bioecological systems System What it is Examples Microsystem Direct, face-to-face settings; bidirectional Family, school, peers, daycare Mesosystem Interactions between microsystems (a system of microsystems, not a setting) Parent-teacher meeting, home-school link Exosystem Settings the child is not in but which still affect them Parent's workplace, school board, mass media Macrosystem Cultural blueprint Ideology, customs, laws, religion, SES Chronosystem Time dimension. Added later (originally 4 systems) Divorce, pandemic, sociohistorical era PPCT (1994 Bioecological refinement): P rocess = proximal processes, the engine (regular reciprocal interactions over time). P erson = Demand (visible: age/gender), Resource (skills, intelligence), Force (temperament, motivation). C ontext = the 5 systems. T ime = micro/meso/macro time. TRAPS: Exosystem ≠ no influence (acts via the microsystem, e.g. dad loses job). Mesosystem is NOT a setting, it's the link between two. Mass media = exosystem, not macrosystem. Chronosystem was added later (originally 4 systems). If the stem mentions: nested environments, cultural context, parent's workplace, indirect influence → answer is Urie Bronfenbrenner . Psychological Assessment & Tests MET 15 Q · NIMHANS 10 Q The whole map: a psychological test is a measuring instrument that must be (a) consistent = reliability and (b) accurate = validity . Everything else is a way to estimate one of those, interpret scores against norms, or an example of a real test. 4.1 Item analysis Difficulty index p = proportion who got the item right (0–1). Sweet spot 0.50 for free-response, ~0.625 for a 4-option MCQ (halfway between guessing 0.25 and ceiling). p > 0.80 too easy, < 0.20 too hard. Discrimination index D = p(top 27%) − p(bottom 27%), range −1 to +1. D > 0.40 good. Negative D = mis-keyed/ambiguous item, discard immediately. 4.2 Reliability (consistency) Classical test theory: Observed = True + Error. Reliability = proportion of variance that is true. Test-retest (across time; standard window 2–4 wks). Parallel forms (across forms). Split-half + Spearman-Brown correction (r_full = 2·r_half / (1 + r_half)); Cronbach α (≥0.7 acceptable, ≥0.8 good) = mean of all possible split-halves; KR-20 for dichotomous (0/1) items. Inter-rater: Cohen κ (categorical, Landis & Koch: 0.61–0.80 substantial, 0.81+ almost perfect), ICC (continuous). SEM = SD·√(1 − r_xx). Higher reliability → smaller SEM → tighter confidence band around a score. TRAP: Cronbach α is NOT a measure of unidimensionality — a test can have high α and still measure two constructs. And κ is NOT internal consistency. 4.3 Validity (accuracy) Content: covers the domain (expert panels, Lawshe's CVR). Face validity = looks valid to a layperson, the weakest form. Criterion: Concurrent (criterion now) vs Predictive = Postponed (criterion later). Construct: convergent (correlates with similar) + discriminant (not with unrelated) + nomological network. Campbell & Fiske's multitrait-multimethod matrix (MTMM, 1959). Validity ceiling: max validity = √(reliability). Unreliable tests cannot be strongly valid. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. 4.4 Test classification Type Means Maximum performance (ability/aptitude/achievement, e.g. IQ) Do your best . There is a right answer Typical performance (personality, interest, attitude) What you usually do. No right answer Power test Hard items, generous time — measures ceiling of ability Speed test Easy items, tight time — measures how fast The exact trap you missed: an IQ test is an ability test (maximum performance), not a power or speed test. Achievement = what you learned (past, WIAT). Aptitude = what you can learn (future, DAT/SAT). Intelligence = general capacity. Norm-referenced (vs peers) vs criterion-referenced (vs absolute standard). Formative (during) vs summative (end). 4.5 Standard scores & norms Standard score = M + (SD × z). "paradoxical intention" appears in BOTH Frankl and strategic family therapy — context decides Family / systemic — match the tool to the school: School Signature components Structural (Salvador Minuchin) Family map · boundaries (clear / rigid-disengaged / diffuse-enmeshed) · joining · enactment · restructuring Strategic (Jay Haley, Watzlawick) Directives · paradoxical intervention · ordeal therapy · "symptom serves a function" Bowenian Differentiation of self · triangles · genogram · emotional cutoff Satir / experiential Communication stances (placater, blamer, computer, distractor, leveller) · family sculpting Milan Circular questioning · hypothesising · neutrality · reflecting team Narrative (White, Epston) Externalising the problem · re-authoring · unique outcomes SFBT (de Shazer, Berg) Miracle question · scaling questions · exception-seeking 5.7 Learning & conditioning Family Terms Classical (Pavlovian) Extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization, discrimination Operant shaping tools Shaping, chaining, fading, prompting Operant schedules FR, VR, FI, VI Cognitive / social Latent (Edward Tolman), insight (Wolfgang Köhler), observational (Albert Bandura) Non-associative Habituation, sensitization Shaping = reinforce successive approximations of a new behaviour. Chaining = link existing behaviours (each is the S D for the next; backward chaining preferred clinically). Fading = remove the prompt (extinction removes the reinforcer ). Prompting hierarchy: physical → modelling → gestural → verbal → visual. Extinction: watch for the extinction burst ; extinction suppresses, doesn't erase. Spontaneous recovery proves the memory is intact. Generalization is the default; discrimination is trained by differential reinforcement. Schedules: VR = highest, steadiest rate, most resistant to extinction (gambling). VI = steady moderate (checking phone). FR = post-reinforcement pause then burst (piece-work). FI = scallop (studying before a weekly quiz). Resistance: VR > VI > FR > FI > continuous. Latent learning (Tolman, cognitive map — learning without reinforcement, shown later). Insight learning (Köhler's Sultan, sudden "aha"). Observational learning (Bandura Bobo doll; 4 processes ARRM: Attention → Retention → Reproduction → Motivation; vicarious reinforcement). Habituation vs sensitization (Eric Kandel, Aplysia, non-associative). Escape vs avoidance (your mock guess): Escape = behaviour terminates an aversive stimulus that is already present (turn off a loud alarm). Avoidance = behaviour prevents the aversive stimulus from starting (leave before the alarm). Both are negative reinforcement. 5.8 Ethics in practice Principle (Beauchamp & Childress) One line / in practice Autonomy Respect the client's right to decide — informed consent, right to refuse Beneficence Act for the client's good — choose the treatment most likely to help Non-maleficence "First, do no harm" — withhold harmful/unproven methods, stay within competence Justice Fairness — no discrimination, equitable access Informed consent = disclosure + capacity + voluntariness. Assent = a minor's agreement alongside a parent's consent. Paternalism = overriding a competent person's choice (violates autonomy). Confidentiality = your duty; privacy = the client's right; privileged communication = legal protection in court. Other terms: Fidelity (loyalty), Veracity (truth-telling), Competence, Dual/multiple relationship (boundary violation), Negligence (below standard of care). Confidentiality is NOT absolute — it breaks for risk of serious harm to self/others, suspected child/elder abuse (mandatory reporting), or court order. Tarasoff duty to warn/protect: a credible threat against an identifiable person obliges the therapist to act — non-maleficence/beneficence to a third party overrides confidentiality. The classic swap: beneficence = do good vs non-maleficence = avoid harm . 6. Language & Communication Skills MET 15 Q · NIMHANS 5 Q · highest fast-marks ratio 7.1 Subject-verb agreement The verb agrees with the subject in number, not the nearest noun. Each, every, either, neither, one, anyone, everyone, nobody → singular ("Each of the participants was given…"). Either/or, neither/nor → verb agrees with the nearer subject ("Neither the patient nor the family members were informed"). "A number of" = plural; "the number of" = singular. None defaults singular in formal writing. "Data are" — data is technically plural (datum singular); treat as plural in exam contexts. Singular-looking: news, mathematics, physics, politics, statistics. Plural-only: scissors, trousers, glasses. 7.2 Voice & conditionals Active → passive: object becomes subject; verb → "be" + past participle. "The committee will announce the results" → "The results will be announced by the committee." Conditional If-clause Main clause Zero (general truths) present present First (real future) present will + base Second (hypothetical) past would + base Third (counterfactual past) past perfect ("Had she taken") would have + past participle Mixed past perfect would + base " Had she taken the medication, she would have recovered sooner" = third conditional (inversion is formal). 7.3 Punctuation & prepositions Restrictive vs non-restrictive clauses: non-restrictive (extra info, removable) → commas + "who"; restrictive (defines which) → no commas, "that". "The patient, who was anxious, refused" (one patient) vs "The patient who was anxious refused" (picks out one of several). Semicolon joins two independent clauses; colon introduces a list/explanation. It's = it is; its = possessive. Prepositions: insist on , depend on, comply with, consist of, refer to, suffer from, object to, accuse of, married to (not with), prefer X to Y, superior/inferior to (not than), discuss (no preposition). "Between you and me ." 7.4 Modifiers, parallelism & common corrections Dangling modifier: "Walking down the street, the building looked tall" (the building isn't walking). Parallelism: "reading, writing, and swimming" (not "to swim"). Like (before a noun) vs as (before a clause). Who (subject) vs whom (object). Less (uncountable) vs fewer (countable). Between (two) vs among (3+). "The reason is that " (not "because"). Predicate adjective follows a linking verb ("The data were inconclusive "). 7.5 Vocabulary, one-word substitutions & idioms Word Meaning / pairing Gregarious Sociable (antonym: reclusive) Ephemeral Lasting briefly (synonym: transient) Ambivalent Mixed feelings (NOT indifferent = no feeling) Garrulous / loquacious / verbose Talkative / wordy Laconic / taciturn / reticent Few words / reserved Sagacious / cogent / pragmatic Wise / convincing / practical Frugal / abstemious Sparing with money / with food & drink Capricious / whimsical / vacillate Unpredictable / playful / waver Egregious / belligerent / obstinate Outstandingly bad / hostile / stubborn Definition Word Fluent in many languages Polyglot Fear of confined / open spaces Claustrophobia / Agoraphobia Hates / loves humanity Misanthrope / Philanthropist Walker in sleep Somnambulist Cure-all medicine Panacea Speech without preparation Extempore Never drinks alcohol Teetotaller Idioms: bury the hatchet (make peace), hit the nail on the head (be right), beat around the bush (avoid the point), bite the bullet (endure), a blessing in disguise, cut corners, burn the midnight oil. Social psych first since that is where the named-experiment questions cluster. Theorist What they actually did · the trap Social psychology Solomon Asch Conformity. Line-judgement task: pick which of 3 lines matches a standard. Confederates deliberately gave a wrong answer; about 75% of real subjects conformed at least once, ~33% on average. Conformity is normative (fit in / avoid disapproval), not informational. Trap: Asch = group peer pressure; Stanley Milgram = authority . Conformity dropped sharply with one dissenting ally. Milgram Obedience. "Teacher" told by experimenter to shock a "learner" for wrong answers, up to 450V. 65% went to the maximum shock. Showed ordinary people obey a legitimate authority. Trap: obedience = following an authority's order ; conformity (Asch) = matching peers . Philip Zimbardo Stanford Prison Experiment. Students randomly assigned guard/prisoner roles; "guards" turned abusive fast, study stopped after 6 days. Power of the situation/assigned role over personality (deindividuation). Trap: situational, not dispositional. Muzafer Sherif Robbers Cave / realistic conflict theory. Two boys' camp groups; competition bred hostility, and superordinate goals (shared tasks neither group could solve alone) reduced it. Contact alone was not enough. Henri Tajfel Social identity theory + minimal group paradigm. Even arbitrary grouping (e.g. coin toss) produced in-group favouritism . Identity comes from group membership; basis of prejudice. Leon Festinger Cognitive dissonance + social comparison theory. Festinger & J. Merrill Carlsmith: people paid $1 to lie about a boring task changed their attitude more than those paid $20 (less external justification → more internal change). Trap: the smaller reward causes the bigger attitude shift. Latane & John Darley Bystander effect / diffusion of responsibility (Kitty Genovese). More bystanders → less likely any one helps. Steps: notice → interpret as emergency → assume responsibility → help. Kurt Lewin "Father of social psychology." Field theory (B = f(P,E): behaviour is a function of person and environment); leadership styles; unfreeze–change–refreeze model of change. Fritz Heider Attribution theory + balance theory. We explain behaviour by internal (dispositional) vs external (situational) causes. Related: fundamental attribution error = over-blaming the person, under-weighting the situation. Harold Kelley Covariation model of attribution: we judge cause using consensus, consistency, distinctiveness . Bem Self-perception theory: we infer our own attitudes by observing our own behaviour (the reverse of dissonance). Learning Ivan Pavlov Classical conditioning. Neutral stimulus (bell) paired with food (UCS) becomes a conditioned stimulus producing salivation (CR). Terms: acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation, discrimination. John B. Watson Behaviourism founder. Little Albert: conditioned a baby to fear a white rat (paired with a loud noise); fear generalised to furry things. Edward Thorndike Law of effect (cat puzzle box): responses followed by satisfaction are stamped in. Precursor to operant conditioning. B. F. Skinner Operant conditioning. Behaviour shaped by consequences. Reinforcement schedules: variable-ratio gives the highest, most extinction-resistant response rate. Positive/negative reinforcement both increase behaviour; punishment decreases it. Albert Bandura Social learning / Bobo doll: children imitated aggression they observed , no direct reward needed. Also self-efficacy and reciprocal determinism. Edward Tolman Latent learning + cognitive maps (purposive behaviourism). Tolman & Honzik maze: the group given a reward only from day 11 suddenly matched the always-rewarded group, proving they'd learned the maze all along without reinforcement. Behaviour is goal-directed ; animals build a mental "map." Trap: learning ≠ performance. Julian Rotter Social learning theory + locus of control. Behaviour potential = expectancy × reinforcement value . Internal LOC ("I control my outcomes") vs external LOC ("luck/fate/others do"); measured by his I–E Scale . Cognitive bridge between behaviourism and personality. Memory Ebbinghaus Forgetting curve using nonsense syllables; most forgetting happens fast then levels off. Also the spacing effect. Miller "Magic number 7 ± 2" : short-term memory holds about 5–9 chunks. Alan Baddeley Working memory model (4 parts): central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, episodic buffer. Replaced the single STM box. Endel Tulving Long-term memory split: episodic (events) vs semantic (facts) vs procedural (skills). Elizabeth Loftus Misinformation effect: leading questions distort eyewitness memory ("smashed" vs "hit" changed speed estimates). Memory is reconstructive. Frederic Bartlett Reconstructive memory + schemas ("War of the Ghosts"): recall is rebuilt to fit existing schemas, not replayed. Development Jean Piaget 4 cognitive stages: sensorimotor (object permanence), preoperational (egocentrism, no conservation), concrete operational (conservation), formal operational (abstract). Assimilation vs accommodation. Lev Vygotsky Sociocultural: learning is social. Zone of proximal development = gap between what a child can do alone vs with help; scaffolding . Erik Erikson 8 psychosocial stages , each a crisis (e.g. trust vs mistrust, identity vs role confusion in adolescence). Spans the whole lifespan. Lawrence Kohlberg Moral development: 3 levels (pre-conventional, conventional, post-conventional), 6 stages. Trap: Carol Gilligan criticised it as male-biased and added the ethic of care . Bowlby / Ainsworth Attachment. Ainsworth's Strange Situation → secure, anxious-ambivalent, avoidant (+ disorganised). Harry Harlow's monkeys: contact comfort beats food.
