Beck / Ellis Aaron Beck = cognitive triad + CBT; Albert Ellis = REBT , the ABC model. Both target distorted thinking. Selye / Lazarus Hans Selye = General Adaptation Syndrome (alarm, resistance, exhaustion); Lazarus = cognitive appraisal of stress (primary/secondary). 9.2 Durations & numbers Item Lock this Major depressive episode at least 2 weeks Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) at least 2 years (1 year in children) Manic episode at least 1 week (or any length if hospitalised) Hypomanic episode at least 4 days Generalised anxiety disorder at least 6 months PTSD symptoms longer than 1 month Acute stress disorder 3 days to 1 month Schizophrenia 6 months total, at least 1 month active phase Schizophreniform 1 to 6 months Brief psychotic disorder 1 day to 1 month Insomnia disorder 3 nights per week for at least 3 months Iconic memory (visual sensory) about 0.25 to 1 second (George Sperling) Echoic memory (auditory sensory) about 2 to 4 seconds Short-term memory 15 to 30 seconds, capacity 7 plus or minus 2 (Miller) IQ standard deviation Wechsler 15, Stanford-Binet 16 (SB-5 uses 15) 9.3 Components & "how many" Model The parts DBT (4 skill modules) mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness ACT hexaflex (6) acceptance, defusion, present moment, self-as-context, values, committed action Carl Rogers' core conditions (3) congruence/genuineness, unconditional positive regard, empathy Aaron Beck's cognitive triad (3) negative view of self, world, future Ellis ABC Activating event, Belief, Consequence Big Five (OCEAN) Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism Baddeley working memory (4) central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, episodic buffer Kubler-Ross (5) denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance Yalom therapeutic factors 11 (e.g. universality, instillation of hope, catharsis, group cohesiveness) Piaget stages (4) sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational Lawrence Kohlberg 3 levels (pre-conventional, conventional, post-conventional), 6 stages 9.4 General psychology nuggets Area Lock this Perception: psychophysics Weber's law (JND is a constant proportion of the stimulus); Fechner's law (sensation grows with the log of intensity) Perception: signal detection hit / miss / false alarm / correct rejection; d-prime = sensitivity, beta = response criterion Perception: feature integration (Treisman) preattentive feature detection, then attention binds features into objects Gestalt laws proximity, similarity, closure, continuity, common fate, figure-ground Attention models Broadbent early-selection filter; Treisman attenuation; Deutsch-Norman late selection; Stroop = automatic reading interferes Memory model Atkinson-Shiffrin: sensory then short-term then long-term; serial position = primacy + recency Emotion theories James-Lange (arousal then emotion), Cannon-Bard (simultaneous), Schachter-Singer two-factor (arousal + label), Lazarus (appraisal first) Arousal Yerkes-Dodson: performance is best at moderate arousal (inverted U) Reinforcement schedules variable ratio gives the highest steady rate and is most resistant to extinction 9.5 Landmark experiments Study Showed Stanley Milgram Obedience to authority (65 percent went to the maximum shock) Solomon Asch Conformity to a wrong majority Philip Zimbardo (Stanford Prison) Power of assigned roles / situation Darley & Bibb Latane Bystander effect, diffusion of responsibility (Kitty Genovese) Festinger & Carlsmith Cognitive dissonance (the 1 dollar group changed attitude more than the 20 dollar group) Muzafer Sherif (Robbers Cave) Realistic conflict; superordinate goals reduce it Henri Tajfel (minimal group) Social identity, in-group favouritism from arbitrary grouping Albert Bandura (Bobo doll) Observational learning / modelling of aggression Martin Seligman Learned helplessness TRAP: James-Lange = body first ("I tremble, therefore I am afraid"). Cannon-Bard = body and feeling at once. Schachter-Singer = body plus a cognitive label. Mixing these up is a classic exam trap. 9.6 Schools / perspectives of psychology Perspective Core idea · key name Structuralism Break consciousness into elements via introspection · Wundt, Edward Titchener Functionalism What is the purpose of behaviour (adaptation) · William James Behaviourism Only observable behaviour; stimulus–response · John B. Watson, Skinner, Ivan Pavlov Gestalt "The whole is more than the sum of parts" · Max Wertheimer, Koffka, Köhler Psychoanalytic Unconscious drives, early childhood · Sigmund Freud Humanistic ("3rd force") Free will, self-actualisation, growth · Rogers, Abraham Maslow Cognitive Mind as information processor; memory, thinking · Ulric Neisser Biological / Evolutionary Behaviour from brain, genes, neurochemistry / shaped by natural selection Trigger: "lab + introspection" → Wundt/structuralism. "purpose/adaptation" → James/functionalism. "whole > parts" → Gestalt. "free will/self-actualisation" → humanistic. 9.7 Motivation & drive Theory Says Abraham Maslow's hierarchy Physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualisation . Lower needs first Drive-reduction (Clark Hull) Need → drive → behaviour to restore homeostasis Arousal / Yerkes-Dodson Seek optimal arousal; moderate arousal = best performance (inverted-U); hard tasks need lower arousal Incentive theory Pulled by external rewards (vs pushed by internal drives) Intrinsic vs extrinsic For its own sake vs for a reward. Overjustification effect : paying for an enjoyed task kills intrinsic motivation Self-determination (Edward Deci & Richard Ryan) Three needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness David McClelland Need for achievement, affiliation, power 9.8 States of consciousness (sleep one-glance) Item Recall Sleep stages NREM 1→2→3 (deep / slow-wave / delta), then REM (dreaming, paralysis, EEG looks awake) Cycle length ~90 min; REM lengthens toward morning Circadian rhythm ~24 hr clock; suprachiasmatic nucleus + melatonin (pineal) Sleep spindles / K-complexes Hallmark of Stage 2 NREM Delta waves Stage 3 deep sleep; sleepwalking / night terrors arise here 9.9 Personality — theories & types Approach One thing to remember Big Five (OCEAN) Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism — the dominant trait model Hans Eysenck Three dimensions: Extraversion, Neuroticism, Psychoticism (PEN); biologically based Raymond Cattell 16 PF ; source vs surface traits; factor analysis Gordon Allport Cardinal, central, secondary traits Sigmund Freud (structural) Id (pleasure) – Ego (reality) – Superego (morality) Albert Bandura Reciprocal determinism : person ↔ behaviour ↔ environment; self-efficacy Carl Rogers Self-concept; congruence between real and ideal self; conditions of worth Locus of control (Julian Rotter) Internal ("I control outcomes") vs external ("luck/fate does") 9.10 Intelligence — theories Theorist Model Spearman Two-factor: general g + specific s ; factor analysis Thurstone 7 primary mental abilities (no single g) Cattell-Horn Fluid (novel reasoning, declines with age) vs crystallised (knowledge, stable/rises) Howard Gardner Multiple intelligences (linguistic, logical, musical, spatial, bodily, inter/intra-personal, naturalist) Robert Sternberg Triarchic : analytical, creative, practical Goleman / Salovey-Mayer Emotional intelligence (perceive, use, understand, manage emotion) Cross-link: IQ scoring, deviation IQ, WAIS/WISC subtests live in §4 Assessment ; "scaled score 10 = 50th percentile" is your mock miss. 9.11 Freudian defense mechanisms Defense Quick example Repression Push a threatening thought out of awareness (the master defense) Denial Refuse to accept reality ("I'm not sick") Projection Attribute your own impulse to someone else ("you hate me") Displacement Redirect a feeling to a safer target (yell at the dog, not the boss) Sublimation Channel an impulse into a useful act (aggression → surgery/sport) — the "mature" one Reaction formation Act the opposite of the true feeling (hate disguised as overcare) Rationalisation Logical-sounding excuse for the real motive ("I didn't want it anyway") Regression Revert to an earlier developmental stage under stress Intellectualisation / Undoing Use abstract thinking to avoid the feeling / ritually cancel an act 9.12 Heuristics & cognitive biases Bias / heuristic What it is Availability heuristic (Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, 1973) Judge likelihood by how easily examples come to mind (plane crashes feel common) Representativeness Judge by resemblance to a prototype; ignores base rates Anchoring Over-rely on the first number/info given Confirmation bias (Peter Wason, 1960) Seek info that confirms what you already believe Framing effect (Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, 1981) Same info, different wording → different choice (90% survive vs 10% die) Hindsight bias (Baruch Fischhoff, 1975) "I knew it all along" after the outcome is known Functional fixedness / Mental set Can't see a novel use for an object / stuck on a strategy that worked before 9.13 Learning — fast contrasts Pair Difference Classical vs operant Ivan Pavlov: involuntary, stimulus pairing. B. F. Skinner: voluntary, consequences shape behaviour Positive vs negative Positive = add a stimulus; Negative = remove one. Reinforcement ↑ behaviour, punishment ↓ it Escape vs avoidance Escape ends an aversive stimulus already on; avoidance prevents its onset (your mock miss) Shaping / spontaneous recovery Reward successive approximations / an extinguished response briefly returns after a pause Conditioning detail (escape/avoidance, alliance, object relations) is in §5 ; emotion-theory and psychophysics rows are in 9.4 above. 9.14 Biostatistics rapid recall NIMHANS's biggest gap Cue Lock this Choosing the test — 2 groups, parametric independent t-test (paired data → paired t-test) 3+ groups, parametric ANOVA (one-way); repeated measures if same subjects 2 groups, non-parametric Mann-Whitney U (paired → Wilcoxon signed-rank) 3+ groups, non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis Two categorical variables Chi-square (Fisher's exact if cells small) Strength of a linear relationship Pearson r (parametric) / Spearman rho (ranks) Odds ratio / relative risk = 1 no association ; >1 = risk, <1 = protective (your mock miss) NNT = 1 / ARR ; ARR = control event rate − treatment event rate Type I error (alpha) false positive — reject a true null Type II error (beta) false negative — keep a false null; power = 1 − beta p-value P(data this extreme if null true). NOT the probability the null is true Sensitivity vs specificity Sensitivity = true-positive rate ( SnNout , rules out); specificity = true-negative rate ( SpPin , rules in) PPV / NPV depend on prevalence ; sensitivity/specificity do not Skew Positive (right) skew: mean > median > mode ; tail points to the higher numbers Parametric assumptions normal distribution, homogeneity of variance, interval/ratio data r and r² r ranges −1 to +1; r² = proportion of variance explained ; correlation ≠ causation TRAP: "Data is plural" (one datum, many data). And p < 0.05 only means statistically significant, not clinically important or "null is false." 9.15 Assessment — reliability, validity & score conversions Item Lock this Reliability types test-retest (stability), inter-rater (between scorers), internal consistency ( Cronbach's alpha / split-half), parallel forms Validity types content, criterion ( concurrent + predictive ), construct ( convergent + discriminant ), face Reliability vs validity Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity; a test can be reliable but not valid, never valid without being reliable z-score mean 0 , SD 1 T-score mean 50 , SD 10 Deviation IQ (Wechsler) mean 100 , SD 15 (Stanford-Binet old = 16) Wechsler scaled subtest score mean 10 , SD 3 — so scaled score 10 = 50th percentile (your mock miss) Sten / Stanine sten mean 5.5 (SD 2); stanine mean 5 (SD 2) Normal curve 68 / 95 / 99.7 within 1 / 2 / 3 SD; percentile = % scoring at or below you 9.16 Abnormal — disorder → hallmark & first-line Disorder Hallmark · first-line Major depression 2+ weeks low mood/anhedonia · SSRI (+ CBT) Bipolar I (mania) 1+ week elevated mood · lithium / valproate (mood stabiliser); antidepressant alone can trigger mania Schizophrenia positive + negative symptoms, 6 months · antipsychotic; clozapine for treatment-resistant OCD obsessions + compulsions · SSRI (high dose) + ERP (exposure & response prevention) Panic disorder recurrent unexpected attacks · SSRI + CBT Specific phobia marked fear of object/situation · exposure therapy (systematic desensitisation) PTSD symptoms >1 month after trauma · trauma-focused CBT / EMDR; SSRI GAD 6 months excessive worry · CBT; SSRI/SNRI (buspirone) Borderline PD instability of mood/relationships/self, fear of abandonment · DBT ADHD inattention/hyperactivity · stimulants (methylphenidate) Trigger: "compulsions/rituals" → OCD & ERP. "fear of abandonment + DBT" → BPD. "treatment-resistant schizophrenia" → clozapine. 9.17 Neuro one-glance — cranial nerves, localisation, aphasia Item Recall 12 cranial nerves (order) O lfactory, O ptic, O culomotor, T rochlear, T rigeminal, A bducens, F acial, V estibulocochlear, G lossopharyngeal, V agus, A ccessory, H ypoglossal Sensory / motor / both " Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most " (S/M/B per nerve) Broca's aphasia non-fluent, effortful, comprehension intact · frontal (Broca's area) Wernicke's aphasia fluent but meaningless, poor comprehension · temporal (Wernicke's area) Conduction aphasia can't repeat · arcuate fasciculus Frontal lobe executive function, planning, personality (Phineas Gage) Hippocampus forming new long-term memories (H.M. → anterograde amnesia) Amygdala fear, emotional salience Cerebellum balance, coordination, motor learning Hypothalamus homeostasis, 4 F's, drives the pituitary 9.17a Motor control — who does what classic NIMHANS swap-trap Structure Job Lock the trap Premotor cortex plans externally / sensory-cued movement (see it, reach for it); preps posture before M1 fires premotor = external / cue-driven SMA (supplementary motor area) plans internally generated, self-initiated movement; sequencing from memory + bimanual coordination SMA = internal / from within (premotor vs SMA = external vs internal) Basal ganglia initiate / select / gate movement; set vigour , scale force & amplitude "scales force / amplitude" → basal ganglia · resting tremor (Parkinson's) · chorea = Huntington's Cerebellum timing, coordination, balance, error correction; compares intended vs actual and smooths on the fly "timing / smoothing / coordination" → cerebellum · intention tremor, ataxia, dysmetria Two traps: resting tremor = basal ganglia, intention tremor = cerebellum. "Force/amplitude" = basal ganglia, "timing/smoothing" = cerebellum. Full version on the biopsych cheatsheet §8 . 9.18 The Acts, founders & "X is to Y" Pairing Lock this Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (India) — decriminalised suicide, right to treatment, advance directive RPwD Act (Rights of Persons with Disabilities) 2016 — 21 disabilities, replaced the 1995 Act RCI Act (Rehabilitation Council of India) 1992 — regulates training of psychologists/therapists POCSO 2012 — Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Wilhelm Wundt : ___ first psychology lab (1879) Binet : ___ first practical intelligence test (mental age) Aaron Beck : ___ cognitive therapy / cognitive triad Carl Rogers : ___ client-centred therapy Joseph Wolpe : ___ systematic desensitisation Beck vs Albert Ellis cognitive triad / collaborative empiricism vs REBT / ABC, more confrontational 9.19 Language — grammar traps & one-word substitutions Trap The fix Subject-verb agreement "Each / every / neither / one of" takes a singular verb; "a number of" = plural, "the number of" = singular Either/neither ... or/nor verb agrees with the nearer subject Fewer vs less fewer = countable, less = uncountable Between vs among between = two, among = three or more Lie vs lay lie (recline, no object) vs lay (put down, takes an object) One-word: fear of enclosed spaces claustrophobia (open/public spaces = agoraphobia) One-word: study of populations demography One-word: one who knows many languages polyglot One-word: incapable of being corrected incorrigible One-word: bitter attack in speech/writing diatribe (vs panegyric/eulogy = praise) Highest fast-marks section — grammar and vocab are pure recall, no reasoning. Deeper drills in §7 . Exam-day rules Longest option is often correct on these papers, but only as a tiebreaker, never over knowledge. "NOT" / "EXCEPT" questions — circle the NOT, you're hunting the odd one out. This is where tired people lose marks. Negative marking −0.25: answer if you can eliminate 2 options; skip a pure blind guess. Don't change a first instinct unless you find a concrete reason to. That's the whole syllabus on one page. Read it through once tonight, then on a second pass just the tables and the red trap boxes. Everything you flagged in the mocks is inlined here. You already scored 91.25 — tonight is about locking what you know , not learning new things. Stop early, sleep, trust yourself tomorrow. Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS prep · /notes/textbook/ · the one self-contained source · built 2026-05-22

title: Mock Debriefs & Weak-Spot Fixes
text: Mock Debriefs & Weak-Spot Fixes Every concept you got wrong, guessed, or flagged across all the mocks (MET Mock 1, the NIMHANS PYQ-based mock, the diagnostic-baseline drills, and the MPhil/PEP sets) consolidated into one corrective read, organised by topic, not by which mock it came from. Where a miss recurred across mocks it is marked as a persistent weak spot. This is where you fix what tripped you. Nothing is cut: every corrected answer, distractor analysis, mnemonic, and exam trap from the originals lives here, merged so each concept appears once. In this book The recurring weak spots (read first) Exam-day execution rules Biopsychology & neuroanatomy Neurochemistry, endocrine & pharmacology Famous cases & amnesias Assessment, IQ history & tests Research methods & biostatistics Psychotherapy: who founded what Abnormal psychology & classification Social psychology & the self Developmental psychology Cognitive: memory, learning, psychophysics, creativity Language & verbal reasoning MPhil layer: ethics, law, culture, MSE The recurring weak spots (read first) Across every mock the same clusters bled marks. These are your real syllabus, ranked by how often and how badly they recurred. Each links to its full fix below. Weak spot Where it recurred The fix in one line Pituitary / hypothalamus / endocrine axis NIMHANS mock (3 of 6 biopsych wrongs), diagnostic baseline FLAT PiG anterior pituitary; melatonin is pineal; cortisol is adrenal cortex , not medulla; hypothalamus integrates endocrine + autonomic Neuroanatomy: tracts, lobes, basal ganglia MET Mock 1 (6 biopsych wrongs) Corticospinal crosses at medullary pyramids; right parietal → left neglect; red nucleus is NOT basal ganglia Therapy school attribution MET Mock 1 (4 wrongs), NIMHANS (3 wrongs) Match technique → school → founder by trigger word; empty chair = Fritz Perls, musterbation = Albert Ellis, therapeutic community = Maxwell Jones Standard scores & WAIS structure Both mocks, diagnostic Subtest scaled M=10 SD=3; index M=100 SD=15; +1 SD = 84th pct; VCI + PRI = 3 core subtests each Reliability statistic ↔ concept NIMHANS, MET, diagnostic (Cohen's kappa missed twice) Kappa = inter-rater categorical; alpha/KR-20 = internal consistency; ICC = inter-rater continuous Sampling: stratified vs cluster vs non-probability MET Mock 1 + NIMHANS (quota/cluster swapped) Stratified = sample within strata; cluster = whole clusters; "can't compute sampling error" = non-probability (quota) ICD vs DSM durations NIMHANS (schizophrenia), MET (dysthymia, PTSD clusters) NIMHANS leans ICD: schizophrenia ≥1 month (ICD) vs ≥6 months (DSM); read which classification the stem names Named social-psych concepts NIMHANS (Genovese, Type D, anomie all wrong) Pure trivia: learn the named effect + its discoverer + its two-factor mechanism Sleep architecture (REM vs delta) Diagnostic (twice), MET Mock 1 (elimination) REM = atonia + wake-like EEG (paradoxical); delta/N3 = slow wave + normal tone; parasomnias (sleepwalking) are N3 "NOT / EXCEPT" negation-blindness Every mock — careless misses Underline the negation before reading options; this is your most expensive avoidable error High-yield Your self-notes are the syllabus. Every "wtf is X" / "never read this" / "don't know shit about this" you wrote on a question is a topic you had not opened. The same notes recurred across mocks, which means a gap left unfixed reappears. The NIMHANS mock sat at 71.25 vs an 80 cutoff (gap 8.75 = roughly 9 wrongs to convert); 6 of those wrongs were in biopsych alone, so fixing that one section clears the line. On MET Mock 1 your attempted-accuracy was 92% (49 right, 4 wrong) but you skipped 47 — there the gap was coverage, not accuracy. PYQ analysis of 300 NIMHANS questions (2023–25) shows Therapy + Abnormal + Biopsych together = ~49% of marks; that is where to spend time. Trap Your guessing is luck-loaded. On the NIMHANS mock you guessed ~17 times and got 14 right; that regresses toward ~50% on the real paper, so plan against a score nearer 68 than 71. A guess is only worth it on MET-style scoring (+4/−1) once you have eliminated 2+ options. Exam-day execution rules Underline NOT / EXCEPT / LEAST / ALL in the stem before reading options. Half your "knew it but got it wrong" misses are negation-blindness (the ACTH/melatonin pituitary question, the Bandura "not required" question). ~20% of NIMHANS PYQs are NOT-stems. On a NOT-question, pick the outlier , not the most familiar item. On antonym / odd-one-out items, find the outlier first. If 3 of 4 options agree in meaning, the 4th is almost always the answer (gregarious: 3 synonyms + reclusive). Read the relationship in the stem — synonym? antonym? part-whole? cause-effect? — before scanning options. Eliminate extreme-word options on RC main-idea questions: "every, always, never, all, none, only, must" are usually too strong. Pick the most general statement the passage actually supports. Hedging language ("can," "may," "in some cases," "a range of") → tone is "supportive but qualified," not absolute. If the stem names ICD, give ICD durations; if DSM, give DSM. If unspecified on NIMHANS, default to ICD (Indian exam). MET often leans DSM. Don't guess on biostats unless the RR/OR/HR/NNT table is firm. You were guessing 4–5 of 10 biostats questions — a coin flip on ~20% of NIMHANS marks. Pacing: 100 Qs / 90 min ≈ 54 sec/Q. Over 90 sec → mark and skip, return later. Don't change a first instinct unless you find a concrete reason. Last 5 minutes: never leave a blank where there is no negative marking; with −0.25, only answer if you eliminated 2 options. Length of options is not a reliable tell on the real paper — don't lean on it. NIMHANS uses heavy case-vignette stems; practise extracting the diagnostic core fast. Biopsychology & neuroanatomy This was the single biggest leak: 6 wrong on each of the two full mocks. You are not weak on biopsych in general — you are weak on where structures are , which side does what , and endocrine/neurology trivia . Lock the locations and the lesions follow. Motor & sensory tract decussations The corticospinal tract decussates at the pyramids of the medulla. You missed this twice (picked "pons" once, "spinal cord at level of entry" once). ~85–90% of fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla to form the lateral corticospinal tract ; the remaining ~10–15% stay ipsilateral as the anterior corticospinal tract and cross only at the spinal segmental level (that is the trap behind the "level of entry" distractor — only the minor anterior pathway crosses there). Tract Function Decussation site Corticospinal (lateral, ~85%) Voluntary motor Pyramids of medulla Corticospinal (anterior, ~15%) Voluntary motor Spinal cord, segmental level Spinothalamic (anterolateral) Pain, temperature, crude touch Spinal cord, 1–2 levels above entry Dorsal column / medial lemniscus Fine touch, proprioception, vibration Medulla (caudal, internal arcuate fibres) Optic nerve (nasal fibres) Vision Optic chiasm (→ bitemporal hemianopia if sectioned) Trochlear (CN IV) Superior oblique Decussates before exit; only CN to do so + only one exiting dorsally Mnemonic Motor crosses in the medulla ; sensory pain/temp crosses in the cord ; touch/proprioception crosses in the medulla . So a hemisection ( Brown-Séquard syndrome ) gives ipsilateral motor + ipsilateral fine-touch loss + contralateral pain/temperature loss starting 1–2 segments below the lesion. UMN lesion = spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski up; LMN = flaccid, atrophy, fasciculations, areflexia. Lobe-by-lobe lesion signs You picked "prosopagnosia" for a right parietal lesion; the answer is left hemispatial neglect . Right inferior parietal (supramarginal/angular) lesions cause the patient to ignore the left side of space (eats only the right of the plate, draws only the right half of a clock). Prosopagnosia is right/bilateral fusiform (temporo-occipital), not parietal. Lobe / region Side Classic lesion sign Frontal (Broca, BA 44/45) L Broca's aphasia (non-fluent, comprehension intact) Frontal (orbitofrontal) any Phineas Gage: disinhibition, poor judgment, personality change Frontal (DLPFC) any Executive dysfunction, perseveration (WCST) Temporal (Wernicke, BA 22) L Wernicke's aphasia (fluent nonsense, poor comprehension) Temporal (medial) bilateral Anterograde amnesia (H.M., hippocampus) Temporal (fusiform) R or bilateral Prosopagnosia Parietal (inferior) R Left hemispatial neglect Parietal (Gerstmann) L Acalculia + agraphia + finger agnosia + L–R disorientation Occipital any Cortical blindness, Anton's syndrome (denial of blindness) The aphasia table (NIMHANS rotates these every paper) Broca's lesion = posterior inferior frontal gyrus (BA 44/45), dominant hemisphere → expressive aphasia: telegraphic, agrammatic, effortful speech, but comprehension relatively intact and the patient is aware their output is broken (hence frustration/depression). Type Fluency Comprehension Repetition Lesion Broca (expressive) Non-fluent Intact Impaired L inferior frontal (44/45) Wernicke (receptive) Fluent (nonsense) Impaired Impaired L superior temporal (22) Conduction Fluent Intact Impaired Arcuate fasciculus Global Non-fluent Impaired Impaired Large L MCA (Broca + Wernicke) Transcortical motor Non-fluent Intact Intact Above Broca, watershed Transcortical sensory Fluent Impaired Intact Below Wernicke, watershed Transcortical mixed Non-fluent Impaired Intact Both watersheds Anomic Fluent Intact Intact Angular gyrus / diffuse Mnemonic "Transcortical = repetition spared" because the perisylvian loop (Broca ↔ arcuate ↔ Wernicke) is intact, just disconnected from the rest of cortex. The "A" deficits (you asked "what's ataxia") Term Deficit Apraxia Can't sequence learned, purposeful movements despite intact motor/sensory function (can't mime brushing hair) Ataxia Loss of coordination and balance (cerebellar) — unsteady gait, dysmetria. A motor-control problem, not planning Agnosia Can't recognise objects/faces/sounds despite intact senses (e.g. prosopagnosia) Aphasia Language deficit (see table above) Alexia / Agraphia Acquired inability to read / write Anomia Word-finding / can't name objects Basal ganglia inventory You picked "subthalamic nucleus" as the NOT-a-basal-ganglion answer; the correct outlier is the red nucleus (midbrain tegmentum, origin of the rubrospinal tract; lesion = rubral tremor + ataxia). Subthalamic nucleus IS basal ganglia (lesion = hemiballismus, contralateral wild flinging). Striatum = caudate + putamen (input nucleus). Lentiform nucleus = putamen + globus pallidus. Globus pallidus (internal + external); output via GPi. Subthalamic nucleus (STN) — drives the indirect pathway. Substantia nigra = pars compacta (dopamine to striatum, lost in Parkinson's) + pars reticulata (output, like GPi). Lesion patterns: Parkinson's = SNc dopamine loss → rest tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability. Huntington's = caudate atrophy (medium spiny neurons) → chorea + cognitive decline. STN lesion = hemiballismus. Wilson's disease = copper in putamen → movement + psychiatric signs. Cranial nerves (reliable +1 every paper) # Name Type Function MCQ hook I Olfactory S Smell Only nerve bypassing thalamus; lost early in Parkinson's/Alzheimer's II Optic S Vision CNS tract; chiasm lesion = bitemporal hemianopia III Oculomotor M Most extraocular muscles + levator palpebrae + pupil constriction Lesion = ptosis + "down & out" eye + dilated pupil IV Trochlear M Superior oblique Smallest CN; only one decussating AND exiting dorsally; vertical diplopia down stairs V Trigeminal B Face sensation + mastication Trigeminal neuralgia; corneal reflex afferent VI Abducens M Lateral rectus Long course = first affected in raised ICP VII Facial B Facial expression + taste ant. ⅔ + lacrimal/salivary Bell's palsy (LMN, whole half-face); UMN spares forehead VIII Vestibulocochlear S Hearing + balance Acoustic neuroma = CN VIII schwannoma at CP angle IX Glossopharyngeal B Post. ⅓ taste + pharyngeal sensation + parotid Gag reflex afferent X Vagus B Parasympathetic thorax/abdomen, palate, larynx Gag reflex efferent; vagal stimulation = ↓ HR XI Spinal accessory M SCM + trapezius Shoulder shrug + head turn XII Hypoglossal M Tongue movement Tongue deviates toward the lesion on protrusion Mnemonic Names: "On Old Olympus' Towering Tops, A Finn And German Viewed Some Hops." Type (S/M/B): "Some Say Marry Money, But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter More." Pure motor: III, IV, VI, XI, XII. Pure sensory: I, II, VIII. Mixed: V, VII, IX, X. Parasympathetic carriers: III (pupil), VII (lacrimation/salivation), IX (parotid), X (thoraco-abdominal). Vision quick reference Cones are most concentrated at the fovea centralis (you picked "peripheral retina"). Fovea = almost pure cones, sharpest acuity + colour; rods dominate the periphery; the optic disc has neither (= blind spot). Rods: ~120 million, peripheral, low light, no colour, rhodopsin. Cones: ~6 million, foveal, bright light, colour (S/M/L = blue/green/red). Trichromatic theory (Young-Helmholtz) = receptor level. Opponent-process (Ewald Hering) = ganglion-cell level (red-green, blue-yellow, black-white). Lateral inhibition (horizontal/amacrine cells) → edge enhancement (Mach bands). Pathway: retina → optic nerve → chiasm → optic tract → LGN (thalamus) → V1 (BA 17, calcarine sulcus). Dorsal stream (where/how, parietal) vs ventral stream (what, temporal → fusiform face area). Sleep architecture (recurring miss — confused twice) The persistent error: confusing REM and Stage 3 NREM (delta) . The discriminator is muscle atonia , which happens in REM, not delta.
